summary: Adler and Van Doren's reading method: four levels of reading, with analytical reading in three stages, applied to different kinds of books and ending in syntopical reading.

unitSummaries.Chapter 1: Reading is an active skill: reading for information differs from reading for understanding, and learning from a book means working like a learner who has only the page to teach.
unitSummaries.Chapter 2: There are four cumulative levels of reading: elementary, inspectional, analytical and syntopical, each containing the one before.
unitSummaries.Chapter 3: Elementary reading is learning to read words, it comes in stages, and it differs from the higher levels that serious readers still need.
unitSummaries.Chapter 4: Inspectional reading sizes up a book fast: skim it systematically, then read it through once without stopping, at a speed that suits the book.
unitSummaries.Chapter 5: A demanding reader asks four questions of every book and makes it their own by marking it, taking notes and forming habits.
unitSummaries.Chapter 6: Before reading closely, classify the book: what the title promises, whether it teaches knowing or doing, and what kind of theory it offers.
unitSummaries.Chapter 7: State the book's unity in a few sentences, outline its parts, and work out what problems the author set out to solve.
unitSummaries.Chapter 8: Find the words that carry the author's meaning, tell words from terms, and work out the meanings the author gives them.
unitSummaries.Chapter 9: Find the key sentences, restate them as propositions, follow how propositions form arguments, and decide which problems the author solved.
unitSummaries.Chapter 10: Criticize only after understanding: be teachable, notice rhetoric, suspend judgment, avoid contentiousness and settle disagreement by reasons.
unitSummaries.Chapter 11: Judge a book on its merits: say where the author is uninformed, misinformed, illogical or incomplete before agreeing or disagreeing.
unitSummaries.Chapter 12: Other sources, such as reference books, commentaries and the author's context, can help you understand a book once you have read it yourself.
unitSummaries.Chapter 13: Practical books say what to do and how: judge them by their ends and means, and by whether you agree with their goals.
unitSummaries.Chapter 14: Imaginative literature works on feeling and experience, so read it for the experience it gives, and judge it by its beauty and truth.
unitSummaries.Chapter 15: Read stories, plays and poems with the right questions: grasp the whole, then the parts, and criticize only after you have shared the experience.
unitSummaries.Chapter 16: Read history by asking what actually happened, why, and how the story is told, and compare accounts of the same events.
unitSummaries.Chapter 17: Read science and mathematics by finding the problems, assumptions and proofs, and by seeing how theory ties to evidence.
unitSummaries.Chapter 18: Read philosophy by finding the questions posed and the reasons given, and by judging how far its answers rest on thought rather than special experiment.
unitSummaries.Chapter 19: Read social science, which mixes theory and fact, by noticing its sources, its models and the problems it tries to answer.
unitSummaries.Chapter 20: Syntopical reading compares many books on one subject, building your own analysis from several authors rather than following one.
unitSummaries.Chapter 21: Reading well makes the mind grow, and the habit of reading is a lifelong way of keeping the mind alive.
unitSummaries.Reading the book as a whole: Choose the level of reading a situation calls for, run the steps in order, and know what a finished analytical reading looks like.

concepts.title: Reading at the right speed
concepts.question: What reading speed does the preface recommend, at a time when speed-reading courses had become a national fad?

paragraphs: The preface to the 1972 edition explains why the 1940 book was rewritten. One change since then was a fad for speed-reading courses, which promised adults faster reading and better comprehension at the same time.

The authors answer with variable-speed reading. What a skilled reader needs is the ability to read different things at different, appropriate speeds, not to read everything at top speed. Pascal warned that reading too fast or too slowly leaves us understanding nothing.
The aim is to read better every time. Sometimes that means going faster, and sometimes it means going slower.
card.example: A reader has a weekend newspaper, a mortgage offer and a sonnet. She skims the newspaper, slows right down on the clauses about fees, and reads the sonnet slowly, twice. Each speed fits what the material asks of her. One fast pace for all three would lose the fee details and the sense of the poem.
card.rule: Match your reading speed to the material, aiming to read better rather than faster.
card.limits: Speed is not the enemy: crawling through easy material also loses the sense, as Pascal warned. The rule says speeds must vary; it does not by itself tell you which speed suits which text.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.title: Instruction that stops too soon
concepts.question: Where does reading instruction usually stop, and does a reader's skill have to stop there too?

paragraphs: The preface names something else that had not changed since 1940: reading instruction rarely goes past the elementary level. Most of the money, effort and ingenuity goes into the first six grades, and little formal training follows to carry students to higher, distinct levels of skill.

Adler quotes James Mursell, writing in 1939. Reading improves steadily up to about the fifth or sixth grade, and then the curves flatten out. The cause is not a natural limit: with special tuition, older children and adults can improve enormously.
So a reader who stalls at that level has stopped being taught, not stopped being able to learn. The higher levels of reading are skills that can still be trained.
card.example: An accountant reads emails, reports and novels every day, yet finds a book on the philosophy of law impossible, and decides she has reached her limit. On the preface's account, her schooling stopped training her reading at the elementary level. Deliberate practice in the higher skills could still move her a long way.
card.rule: Treat reading as a skill you can keep training beyond what school taught, not as a capacity fixed in childhood.
card.limits: The claim is about the average reader, not readers who need special remedial help. And improvement is not automatic: Mursell says readers can and need to improve, but without further training most do not.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.title: What the stalled reader cannot do
concepts.question: What kinds of reading defeat a reader whose skill stopped at the elementary level?

paragraphs: Mursell's second paragraph, quoted in the preface, describes the average high-school graduate. He has read a great deal, and will read more in college, yet he is likely to be a poor reader. He can follow and enjoy a simple piece of fiction.

Give him a closely written exposition, an economically stated argument, or a passage that calls for critical thought, and he is lost. Tests showed students were very poor at naming the central thought of a passage, or the levels of emphasis and subordination in an argument.

Emphasis and subordination means which points are main and which serve them. Seeing this is what separates higher reading from following the words. In Mursell's phrase, such a student stays a sixth-grade reader well into college.
card.example: Two students read a newspaper editorial on a new tax. One can retell every point in order. The other says the central claim is that the tax will hurt small shops, and that the rent figures and a shopkeeper's story both support it. Only the second has grasped the central thought and what is subordinate to it.
card.rule: Test your reading of an argument by stating its central thought and which points are subordinate to it.
card.limits: How much someone reads proves little either way. The test fits exposition and argument; a simple story read for enjoyment does not demand it, which is how fiction can hide the gap.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.title: Four levels as the plan of the book
concepts.question: What change controls the organization of the rewritten book, and what does each of its four parts do?

paragraphs: The preface calls one change the basic and controlling one in the new edition: the distinction of four levels of reading, elementary, inspectional, analytical and syntopical. Part One introduces them.

Part Two sets out the rules of analytical reading. It is the only part that closely follows the 1940 book, and even it was largely recast. Part Three, the largest addition, shows how to approach different kinds of reading matter, from practical books, poetry, history and science to philosophy, reference books, journalism and advertising.
Part Four, on syntopical reading, is wholly new. Further additions include new rules of reading and a fuller, better-ordered analysis of the art.
card.example: A reader wants help with a history of the French Revolution. The plan of the book sends her first to the rules of analytical reading in Part Two, then to Part Three's advice on reading history.
card.rule: Use the four levels as the map of the book: each part trains a level or applies one to a kind of reading.
card.limits: The parts are a map, not separate skills: Part Three applies the analytical rules rather than replacing them. The preface names the levels but does not yet explain how they differ.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.title: Reading related books together
concepts.question: What real problem of reading did the joking title How to Read Two Books point to?

paragraphs: A year after the 1940 book appeared, a parody came out called How to Read Two Books, and I. A. Richards wrote a serious treatise, How to Read a Page. Adler says the rewritten book fully treats the problems both titles suggest, the joking one as well as the serious one.

The joke points to a real problem: how to read a number of related books in relation to one another. The aim is to grasp clearly what they say about a common subject, both where they complement each other and where they conflict.
This is the work of syntopical reading, the fourth level, treated in the wholly new Part Four.
card.example: A parent reads three books on teenage sleep. One at a time, each seems convincing. Read in relation to one another, they show that two agree school starts too early, while the third blames screens and disputes the others' evidence. Only reading them together shows where they agree and where they clash.
card.rule: When several books treat one subject, read them in relation to one another to see where they agree and where they conflict.
card.limits: Comparing books does not replace reading each one well, since a higher level includes the lower ones. And books do not share a subject just because their titles share a word.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.title: Readers in an age of broadcasting
concepts.question: According to the authors, have radio and television made reading unnecessary for understanding the world?

paragraphs: Chapter 1 opens by saying the book is for readers: people who still get a large share of their information about, and understanding of, the world from the written word. Even before radio and television some learning came from speech and observation, but curious people knew that was never enough, and they read.

Some feel reading is less necessary now. The authors grant that broadcasting does some jobs very well: television conveys news events with great impact, and radio informs us while we drive, a great saving of time.
But they question whether the new media have much improved our understanding of the world in which we live. A source can deliver plenty of information without adding to understanding.
card.example: A commuter hears hourly radio bulletins on an election and knows every poll figure. Asked why one region swung, she has no idea. The bulletins served her need for information; understanding the swing needs a different kind of source, and more work from her.
card.rule: Judge a source by whether it improves your understanding, not only by how much information it delivers.
card.limits: This is no case against broadcasting: the authors credit radio and television with real strengths. Their doubt concerns understanding, and they raise it as a question rather than a proven finding.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.title: When facts get in the way
concepts.question: How much do facts help understanding, and when can more of them get in the way?

paragraphs: Perhaps we know more about the world than people used to. Insofar as knowledge is needed for understanding, that is good. But the authors say knowledge is less of a prerequisite to understanding than is commonly supposed.

We do not have to know everything about something in order to understand it. Too many facts are often as much of an obstacle to understanding as too few. In that sense, modern people are flooded with facts to the detriment of understanding.
So piling up facts is not the same as coming to understand. Understanding asks what the facts mean, and more of them does not answer that by itself.
card.example: A new manager is handed forty spreadsheets on staff turnover. After reading them all she knows hundreds of numbers but cannot say why people leave. A colleague who reads three key reports and asks what they show grasps the pattern sooner.
card.rule: Gather the facts you need to understand something, and stop treating more facts as more understanding.
card.limits: Facts are not the enemy: some knowledge is needed, and too few facts block understanding too. The warning is against equating a pile of facts with understanding, not against learning facts.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.title: Packaged opinions
concepts.question: When a ready-made view is delivered to you, how can you tell whether you made up your own mind?

paragraphs: The authors say the modern media are designed to make thinking seem unnecessary, though this is only an appearance. Packaging intellectual positions and views is one of the busiest enterprises of some of the best minds of the day.

Viewers, listeners and magazine readers are given a whole set of aids, from clever rhetoric to carefully selected data and statistics, so they can make up their own minds with minimum effort. The packaging often works so well that they do not make up their minds at all.
Instead, the person inserts a packaged opinion like a cassette into a player, then presses a button and plays it back when it seems fitting. He performs acceptably without having had to think.
card.example: At dinner, Ana states a firm view on rent controls, with two statistics. Asked how the statistics support the view, she cannot say: she is repeating a podcast almost word for word. She holds an opinion, but she did not form it.
card.rule: Before holding a view, work through its reasons yourself rather than adopting a ready-made package.
card.limits: Agreeing with a source is not the fault, nor is learning from a well-made case. The fault is taking the conclusion without the thinking; a view you have worked through can match the package exactly.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.title: Rules for every kind of print
concepts.question: Do the book's rules of reading apply only to books, or to other printed matter as well?

paragraphs: The book's main concern is skill in reading books. But the authors say the rules that build this skill, if followed and practised, can also be applied to printed material in general.
That includes newspapers, magazines, pamphlets, articles, tracts and even advertisements. The habits that open a difficult book also help with a leaflet or a sales pitch.
The preface promises the same range: Part Three gives advice not only on books of every kind but also on reference books, current journalism and advertising.
card.example: A flyer through the door claims a supplement will triple your immunity. Read actively, it raises the questions a book does: what exactly is claimed, what is offered as support, and is it true? The rules that serve a treatise serve the flyer too, though the flyer needs far less time.
card.rule: Bring the rules of active reading to any printed matter, not only to books.
card.limits: Applying the rules does not mean giving every text the same time or effort; an advertisement needs far less than a treatise. The book's main aim remains reading books well.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.title: The more active, the better
concepts.question: Can reading be completely passive, and what makes one reader better than another?

paragraphs: All reading is an activity, so all reading is active to some degree. Completely passive reading is impossible: we cannot read with our eyes immobilized and our minds asleep.
So the contrast between active and passive reading is a scale, not a switch. Reading can be more or less active, and the more active the better.
One reader is better than another in proportion as he can bring a greater range of activity to reading and puts in more effort. He is better if he demands more of himself and of the text before him.
card.example: Two colleagues read the same quarterly report. One moves her eyes down the pages while thinking about lunch. The other asks what the report claims, notices where the numbers do not add up, and questions a vague phrase. Both read it; the second read it more actively, and so better.
card.rule: Make your reading as active as you can, demanding more of yourself and of the text.
card.limits: Activity means the work of the mind on the text, not hours spent or pages covered. And how much activity is called for depends on the goal: reading purely for entertainment demands the least.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.title: The reader as catcher
concepts.question: What does the baseball catcher show about the reader's part in communication?

paragraphs: Many people think writing and speaking are active while reading and listening are passive: the writer works and the reader receives. The mistake is to think that receiving communication is like receiving a blow, a legacy or a court's judgment.

The authors say the reader is more like the catcher in baseball. Catching is as much an activity as pitching or hitting. The pitcher or batter starts the ball moving; the catcher's activity stops it. Both are active, in different ways.
If anything is passive, it is the ball. In reading, the passive object is the written work, shared by the writing that begins the process and the reading that ends it.
card.example: A manager reads a staff email proposing a new rota. Receiving it like a legacy, she lets it land and files it. Reading as a catcher, she moves toward it: what does the writer want, what problem does the rota solve, what is unclear? The email is the same; her activity is not.
card.rule: Read as a catcher plays: actively receiving what the writer sends.
card.limits: The analogy fits the activity of receiving, not everything about reading. A ball is either caught or dropped, while a piece of writing can be received in part, more or less completely.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.title: Catching every pitch
concepts.question: What does it take for communication between a writer and a reader to succeed?

paragraphs: The analogy goes further. The art of catching is the skill of catching every kind of pitch: fast balls, curves, changeups and knuckleballs. So the art of reading is the skill of catching every sort of communication as well as possible.

Pitcher and catcher succeed only as far as they cooperate, and so do writer and reader. The writer is not trying to avoid being caught, though it can seem so. Communication succeeds whenever what the writer wanted received reaches the reader's possession.

Writers vary as pitchers do. Some have excellent control: they know exactly what they want to convey and convey it precisely. Other things being equal, they are easier to catch than a wild writer without control.
card.example: A tax guide written with control states each rule, gives an example and flags the exceptions. A colleague's rambling email circles its request three times. Both writers want to be understood; the guide is easier to catch, and the email asks more of its reader.
card.rule: Cooperate with the writer to receive what he meant to send, whatever kind of writing it is.
card.limits: A controlled writer is easier to catch, other things being equal, but the catching is still the reader's work. A wild writer makes the catch harder; the reader still aims to receive what was meant.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.title: Catching in degrees
concepts.question: Where does the catcher analogy break down, and what decides how much of a piece of writing a reader catches?

paragraphs: The analogy breaks down in one respect. A ball is a simple unit: it is either completely caught or not caught. A piece of writing is a complex object.
So writing can be received more or less completely, anywhere from very little of what the writer intended to the whole of it.
How much the reader catches usually depends on how much activity he puts into the reading, and on the skill with which he performs the different mental acts involved.
card.example: Three people read the same article on a new vaccine. One catches only that a vaccine exists. Another also catches how it was tested. A third catches the method, the results and the stated doubts about long-term data. None dropped the article; they caught different amounts of it.
card.rule: Expect to catch a text in degrees, and raise the degree with more activity and more skill.
card.limits: Effort raises the catch only with skill in the right acts. And the authors say usually: other things are not always equal, and a writer without control can limit what even a good reader catches.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.title: More active and more skilful
concepts.question: Given the same text, what two things make one person read it better than another?

paragraphs: What does active reading involve? The book returns to this question many times. For now the authors say that, given the same thing to read, one person reads it better than another first by reading it more actively, and second by performing each of the acts involved more skilfully.
The two are related. Reading, like writing, is a complex activity. It consists of a large number of separate acts, all of which must be performed in a good reading.
The person who can perform more of these acts is better able to read. So improving means both working harder at reading and learning to do each act well.
card.example: Two cooks follow the same recipe. One is keen but has never learned to fold or temper; the other knows each technique but is half asleep. Neither makes the dish well. Reading likewise needs both effort and skill in its many separate acts.
card.rule: To read better, read more actively and perform each act of reading more skilfully.
card.limits: Neither half works alone: effort without skill in the separate acts gains little, and skills left unused do nothing. This chapter does not yet list the acts; later parts of the book set them out.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
concepts.title: A first measure of success
concepts.question: How do the authors first measure success in reading, and why do they call that measure too simple?

paragraphs: Suppose you have a mind, and a book you want to read. The book is language written by someone to communicate something to you. Your success in reading it is the extent to which you receive everything the writer intended to communicate.
The authors call this too simple. There are two possible relations between your mind and the book, not just one, and each gives a different experience of reading.
Either you understand perfectly everything the author has to say, or you do not. Which of these is true decides what kind of gain a reading can bring you.
card.example: A nurse reads a hospital's new hand-hygiene policy. If she can state every step and its purpose as the policy's authors meant them, she has received what they intended, and by this first measure her reading succeeded.
card.rule: Measure a reading by how much of what the writer intended you actually received.
card.limits: The measure says nothing about the kind of gain. Receiving everything from a book you already fully understood brings information at most, so the measure needs the two relations to be useful.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
concepts.title: When a book is easy throughout
concepts.question: If you understand a book perfectly from start to finish, what can you have gained from reading it?

paragraphs: Take the first relation. As you go through the pages, you understand perfectly everything the author has to say. You may have gained information, but you cannot have increased your understanding.

If the book is completely intelligible to you from start to finish, you and the author are like two minds in the same mold. The symbols on the page only express the understanding you shared before you met.
Ease is therefore a signal. A book that gives you no trouble anywhere is adding to your store of information, not raising your understanding.
card.example: A keen gardener reads a magazine piece on pruning roses. Every step makes sense at once, and she notes two new dates for her calendar. She has gained information. Her understanding of how roses grow is where it was, because the article held nothing beyond it.
card.rule: When a book is easy throughout, count what it gave you as information, not as growth in understanding.
card.limits: Ease is a signal, not proof: a reader who is not alert and honest can feel he understands when he does not. And the authors admit that facts and insights are not always easy to tell apart.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
concepts.title: Knowing that you do not understand
concepts.question: What must a reader notice before a book can raise his understanding, and what helps him notice it?

paragraphs: Now take the second relation: you do not understand the book perfectly. Suppose too, which is not always true, that you understand enough to know that you do not understand it all.
Then you know the book has more to say than you understand, and so it holds something that can increase your understanding.

The signal is puzzlement. Reading something beyond you brings a shock of puzzlement and perplexity at being in over your depth, if you are both alert and honest. A reader who is neither may not feel it, and so may miss what the book could teach.
card.example: Halfway through an article on inflation, Lin realises she cannot say why raising interest rates should lower prices. Rather than reading on as if it made sense, she marks the passage. That moment of admitted puzzlement tells her the article can teach her something.
card.rule: Notice and admit where a book goes beyond you, since that is where it can raise your understanding.
card.limits: Puzzlement shows where understanding could grow; it does not grow it. Noticing a gap is only the start, and a book can also puzzle you for poor reasons, such as a wild writer's lack of control.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
concepts.title: Two ways out that fail
concepts.question: When part of a book is over your head, which two common responses fail to do the job of reading?

paragraphs: What do you do once you know a book is beyond you? You can take it to someone who you think reads better, and have him explain the parts that trouble you. That someone may be a living person or another book, such as a commentary or a textbook.
Or you can decide that what is over your head is not worth bothering about, and that you understand enough.
In either case, the authors say, you are not doing the job of reading that the book requires. That job is done in only one way: by working on the book yourself.
card.example: A reader stuck on a chapter of a book about game theory could look up a summary video, or skip the chapter and call the rest enough. Both leave the chapter unread in the authors' sense. The remaining option is to go back to the chapter and work at it until it yields.
card.rule: When a book is over your head, neither hand the hard parts to someone else nor dismiss them; work on them yourself.
card.limits: The authors allow one kind of situation in which outside help with a difficult book is appropriate, taken up in the chapter on reading philosophy. The warning targets help used in place of your own effort.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
concepts.title: The art of reading defined
concepts.question: What do the authors mean by the art of reading, in the sense this book is about?

paragraphs: The job of reading is done in one way. Without outside help of any sort, you go to work on the book. With nothing but the power of your own mind, you operate on the symbols before you until you gradually lift yourself from understanding less to understanding more.

So the authors define the art of reading as the process by which a mind, with nothing to work on but the symbols of the text and no help from outside, raises itself by its own operations. The skilled operations that make this happen are the acts that make up the art.
It feels like pulling yourself up by your bootstraps: a major exertion. The books thought harder, and so only for better readers, are the ones most likely to deserve and demand it.
card.example: Maya cannot follow the second chapter of a book on probability. Instead of searching online, she rereads it, works the author's example with her own numbers, and finds where she went wrong. By the end she understands something she did not before, using only the book and her own mind.
card.rule: Work on a hard book with your own mind until you understand more than when you began.
card.limits: This is the reading a challenging book deserves, not every text: easy reading needs no such exertion. And the no-help condition has one exception that the authors discuss later.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
concepts.title: Two senses of reading
concepts.question: In what two senses do the authors use the word reading, and what kind of text belongs to each?

paragraphs: The authors use reading in two senses. In the first, we read newspapers, magazines or anything else that, given our skill and talents, is at once thoroughly intelligible to us. Such reading may add to our store of information but cannot improve our understanding.

In the second sense, a person tries to read something he does not at first completely understand. The text is initially better or higher than the reader, and the writer has something that can increase his understanding.

Learning in this second sense means understanding more, not remembering more information of the kind you already have. The line between what can be read in the first way and what must be read in the second is often hazy.
card.example: A reader who knows facts of American history and sees them in a certain light can add more such facts with ease: reading in the first sense. A history that throws a new, more revealing light on all the facts he knows calls for the second sense, and can raise his understanding if he manages it.
card.rule: Read in the second sense whenever a text is better than you: work to understand more, not only to collect more facts.
card.limits: The senses do not sort books into two piles: which applies depends on the reader's skill as well as the text, and the line is often hazy. Facts can sometimes lead to understanding too.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
concepts.title: Learning from your betters
concepts.question: Under what two conditions can reading for understanding take place?

paragraphs: Reading for understanding takes place under two conditions. First, there is an initial inequality in understanding. The writer must be superior to the reader in understanding, and his book must convey in readable form the insights he has and his readers lack.
Second, the reader must be able to overcome this inequality to some degree: seldom fully, perhaps, but always moving toward equality with the writer.

In short, we can learn only from our betters. We must know who they are and how to learn from them. Everyone who can read has some of this ability, and all of us can learn to read better and gain more by working on more rewarding books.
card.example: A first-year nursing student reads a textbook on the heart by a leading cardiologist. The writer understands far more than she does: the first condition. Working chapter by chapter, she grasps more each week, never all of it, but closer each time: the second.
card.rule: Choose writers who understand more than you, and work to close part of the gap.
card.limits: Inequality alone is not enough: if you can close none of the gap, the book cannot teach you yet. And full equality is seldom reached; the aim is to approach it.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
concepts.title: Information takes care of itself
concepts.question: What happens to reading for information once you learn to read for understanding?

paragraphs: The authors admit that facts, which lead to more information, and insights, which lead to more understanding, are not always easy to tell apart. Sometimes a mere recital of facts can itself lead to greater understanding.

Their point is that this book is about the art of reading for the sake of increased understanding. Fortunately, they say, if you learn to do that, reading for information will usually take care of itself.
card.example: A reader who has trained on a hard economics book finds that the business pages, which once took effort, now yield their facts quickly. Practising the harder kind of reading made the easier kind easier, with no separate training.
card.rule: Train yourself to read for understanding; reading for information will usually follow.
card.limits: The authors say usually, not always. And the line between facts and insights is not sharp: well-chosen facts can themselves bring understanding, so information is not worthless.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
concepts.title: Reading for entertainment
concepts.question: Where does reading for entertainment fit among the goals of reading, and how much does the book say about it?

paragraphs: Besides information and understanding there is a third goal, entertainment. The book says little about it: it is the least demanding kind of reading, needs the least effort, and has no rules. Anyone who can read at all can read for entertainment.

Any book that can be read for understanding or information can probably be read for entertainment too, just as a book that can raise understanding can be read only for its information. The proposition does not reverse: not every book that can be read for entertainment can be read for understanding.
The authors do not urge you to avoid reading good books for entertainment. Their subject is the art of reading good books when understanding is the aim.
card.example: A historical novel can entertain on a beach, inform about the period, and, read with effort, deepen understanding of the people in it. A light thriller can entertain, but there may be nothing in it to understand more deeply.
card.rule: Decide your goal for each book, and save the rules and effort for reading to understand.
card.limits: Entertainment is a fair use of a good book; the authors do not forbid it. But it brings no rules and little growth, so it cannot stand in for reading to understand a book that could raise you.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
concepts.title: Informed versus enlightened
concepts.question: What is the difference between being informed and being enlightened by what you read?

paragraphs: Getting more information is learning, and so is coming to understand what you did not understand before, but they differ. To be informed is to know that something is the case. To be enlightened is to know, in addition, why it is the case, how it connects with other facts, and in what respects it is the same and different.

The distinction is like that between remembering something and being able to explain it. If you remember what an author says, you have learned something. But if you used only your memory, you have gained information, not enlightenment.
Enlightenment comes only when, besides knowing what an author says, you know what he means and why he says it. Being informed is a prerequisite; the point is not to stop there.
card.example: Two students read that a central bank raised interest rates. One can repeat the fact and the date. The other can explain why the bank did it, how it connects to the inflation figures, and how this rise differs from last year's. The first is informed; the second is enlightened.
card.rule: After learning what an author says, go on to learn what he means and why he says it.
card.limits: Enlightenment does not replace memory: you must still remember what the author said, since being informed comes first. And knowing why an author says something is not the same as agreeing with him.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
concepts.title: Widely read is not well-read
concepts.question: Is a widely read person the same as a well-read one, according to the authors?

paragraphs: Montaigne speaks of an abecedarian ignorance that comes before knowledge, and a doctoral ignorance that comes after it. The first belongs to those who cannot read at all, because they do not know their ABCs. The second belongs to those who have misread many books.

Alexander Pope called such people bookful blockheads, ignorantly read. There have always been literate ignoramuses who have read too widely and not well. The authors say the Greeks' name for this mix of learning and folly fits the bookish but poorly read of every age: sophomores.
The error to avoid is assuming that being widely read and being well-read are the same thing.
card.example: Max has skimmed two hundred business books and quotes them freely, but cannot explain the argument of any one. Nell has read twelve, each worked through until she could say what it meant and why. Max is widely read; Nell is well-read.
card.rule: Judge your reading by how well you understood what you read, not by how much you have read.
card.limits: Wide reading is not the fault; reading many books badly is. A reader can be both widely and well read.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
concepts.title: Instruction and discovery
concepts.question: What is the difference between learning by instruction and learning by discovery, and why must discovery exist?

paragraphs: Educators have long distinguished learning by instruction from learning by discovery. Instruction occurs when one person teaches another through speech or writing.

But we can also gain knowledge without being taught. If we could not, and every teacher had to be taught what he teaches, there would be no beginning to knowledge. So there must be discovery: learning by research, investigation or reflection, without being taught.

Discovery stands to instruction as learning without a teacher stands to learning with one. In both, the learning goes on in the learner. It is a mistake to think discovery active and instruction passive: there is no inactive learning, just as there is no inactive reading.
card.example: A naturalist who watches a pond for a season and works out the life cycle of a dragonfly learns by discovery. A student who reads the naturalist's account learns by instruction. Both must think; the second has the naturalist's help.
card.rule: Notice whether you are learning from a teacher's words or directly from the world, and stay active either way.
card.limits: The distinction concerns whether a teacher helps, not how hard the learner works: instruction is no more passive than discovery.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
concepts.title: Instruction as aided discovery
concepts.question: Why do the authors call instruction aided discovery, and who does the learning when a teacher helps?

paragraphs: A better way to put the distinction, the authors say, is to call instruction aided discovery. Teaching is a very special art. It shares an exceptionally important feature with only two other arts: agriculture and medicine.

A doctor may do many things for a patient, but in the end the patient must get well. A farmer does much for plants or animals, but they must grow. Likewise a teacher may help a student in many ways, but the student must do the learning: knowledge must grow in his own mind.
So being taught, by a person or by a book, is discovery with help. The help is real, but it does not do the learning for you.
card.example: A coding course gives a learner lectures, exercises and a mentor. Still, on the night recursion finally makes sense, it does so in her head, after she has traced the calls herself. The course aided the discovery; it could not make it for her.
card.rule: Treat every lesson or book as aid to a discovery you must make yourself.
card.limits: Aid matters: farmers and doctors make real differences, and so do good teachers and books. The point is that help supports the learning rather than replacing it, not that help is useless.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
concepts.title: Reading discourse, reading the world
concepts.question: What separates aided from unaided discovery, and why do the authors call reading and listening one art?

paragraphs: The difference between aided and unaided discovery lies mainly in the materials the learner works on. When being instructed, the learner acts on something communicated to him: he performs operations on discourse, written or spoken, by acts of reading or listening.

Minor differences aside, reading and listening are the same art: the art of being taught. When the learner works without any teacher, the operations of learning are performed on nature or the world rather than on discourse. Their rules make up the art of unaided discovery.
Using the word loosely, unaided discovery is the art of reading nature or the world, and instruction is the art of reading books or, to include listening, of learning from discourse.
card.example: A birdwatcher who identifies a new song by watching which bird sings it is reading the world. The same birdwatcher learning songs from a field guide or an expert's talk is learning from discourse. The subject is the same; the materials differ, and so does the art.
card.rule: Ask what you are working on, discourse or the world, to know which art of learning you are using.
card.limits: Treating reading and listening as one art sets aside minor differences between them, which matter elsewhere. And reading the world is a loose use of the word, not a literal one.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
concepts.title: Thinking and imagining while reading
concepts.question: Does reading call for thinking, observation, memory and imagination as much as discovery does?

paragraphs: If thinking means using our minds to gain knowledge or understanding, and instruction and discovery are the only ways to gain it, then thinking must happen in both. We must think while reading and listening, just as in research, though the kinds of thinking differ.

Many tie thinking to research because they suppose reading and listening take little effort. That may hold for reading for information or entertainment, but not for the effort to understand, which no one who has tried it would call thoughtless.

Learning also uses the senses and imagination: observing, remembering, and imagining what cannot be observed. Many assume a poet needs imagination to write a poem but a reader does not need it to read one. In fact reading uses all the skills of unaided discovery: keen observation, ready memory, range of imagination and a trained intellect.
card.example: Reading a novel set in a city she has never seen, Ama pictures its streets, notices a detail the narrator repeats, recalls it when it returns forty pages later, and asks why the author placed it there. Observation, memory, imagination and analysis all go into one reading.
card.rule: Bring thinking, observation, memory and imagination to reading, as you would to discovery.
card.limits: The kinds of thinking in reading and in research differ, as the two ways of learning do. And reading for information or entertainment probably needs less thinking; the claim is strongest for reading to understand.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.title: The book as an absent teacher
concepts.question: Why do the authors put reading ahead of listening, and what must you do when you question a book?

paragraphs: Reading and listening are both ways of being instructed, and many of the book's rules apply to both. Yet the authors put reading first. Listening is learning from a teacher who is present, a living teacher; reading is learning from one who is absent.

Ask a living teacher a question and he will probably answer. If puzzled, you can spare yourself the thinking by asking what he means. Ask a book a question and you must answer it yourself. In this a book is like nature: it answers only as far as you do the thinking and analysis.

Students in school often read hard books with a teacher's help. But outside school, and for any book not assigned, our continuing education depends mainly on books read alone. So we must know how to make books teach us well, which is the primary goal of this book.
card.example: Ola takes an evening class in statistics and asks the tutor whenever a step confuses her. After the course she reads a statistics book on her own. Now every question she puts to it, she must answer herself, by rereading, comparing passages and working examples. The book is an absent teacher.
card.rule: When you question a book, answer it yourself by your own thinking and analysis.
card.limits: A living teacher is no shortcut to understanding: only a question of fact is settled by his answer, and an explanation must still be understood by you. What he gives is a lift that a book's words alone do not.

concepts.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading

concepts.title: Goal sets the way, effort sets the gain
concepts.question: What decides the way you read a book, and what decides how much you gain from reading it?

paragraphs: The chapter opens by gathering three points from the one before. First, your goal shapes how you read. A reader after entertainment, one after information and one after understanding should not handle the same pages in the same way.

Second, how well you read depends on the effort and skill you bring. The authors' rule is that more effort is better, above all with books that start out beyond you, because only such books can lift you from understanding less to understanding more.

Third, most reading happens with no teacher at hand. Like discovery without help, reading is learning from a teacher who is not there to answer your questions, so you succeed only if you know how to do the work yourself.
card.example: Maya has three things to read: a thriller for a train ride, a council notice about bin collection days, and a hard book on the history of science. She reads the thriller for pleasure, scans the notice for the two facts she needs, and saves her real effort for the history of science, the only one that can raise her understanding.
card.rule: Name your goal before you start, and give the most effort to the books that are at first beyond you.
card.limits: Extra effort pays only where the book can teach you something you do not yet grasp. Heavy effort spent on a notice whose facts you follow at once is wasted, because there is no gap in understanding to close.

concepts.title: Four levels, each holding the last
concepts.question: Why do the authors call the four ways of reading levels rather than kinds?

paragraphs: The authors name four levels of reading: elementary, inspectional, analytical and syntopical. They insist that you must grasp how these differ before any real improvement in your reading can happen.

They chose the word level on purpose. Kinds are separate from one another, as apples are from pears. Levels are cumulative: each higher one contains the ones below it and then goes further. The first level is not lost in the second, nor the second in the third.

So the fourth level, syntopical reading, includes all three others. A reader at a high level is still recognising words, still surveying the book and still reading closely, while doing something more on top.
card.example: Think of a building. You cannot have a fourth floor without the first three, and standing on the fourth floor does not remove the floors beneath you. A reader relating five books on climate policy still has to read each sentence, see what each book is about and follow each argument.
card.rule: Treat each level of reading as resting on the ones below it, so that a higher level adds to the lower skills instead of replacing them.
card.limits: Cumulative does not mean every reading must climb all four levels. You pick the level your goal needs; the point is only that whatever level you reach still uses the skills of the levels beneath it.

concepts.title: Elementary reading: what does the sentence say?
concepts.question: What problem does a reader solve at the first level, and when do skilled adults meet it again?

paragraphs: The first level is elementary reading, which could also be called rudimentary, basic or initial reading. Mastering it takes a person from not reading at all to the start of literacy, and it is usually learned in elementary school.

Here the task is to recognise the words on the page. A child reading a sentence about a cat on a hat is not asking whether cats sit on hats. The one question is what the sentence says, taken in its plainest sense.
Skilled readers never fully leave this level. Reading a language you know poorly sends you back to it: first you identify the actual words, and only then can you work out what they mean.

Many adults still have mechanical trouble at this level in their own language, some of it traced to how they were first taught. Fixing it usually speeds reading up, which is why most speed reading courses aim here.
card.example: A tourist in Lisbon reads a sign: Proibido estacionar. Before she can wonder whether the rule covers her hire car, she has to make out the words themselves and learn that they forbid parking. That is elementary reading, done by an adult.
card.rule: When the words themselves are the obstacle, settle what each sentence says before asking what it means or whether it is true.
card.limits: Knowing what a sentence says is only the first step. A reader who stops there has recognised the words but has not asked what the book is about, what it argues or whether it is right.

concepts.title: Inspectional reading: the most in a set time
concepts.question: What can a time-limited, systematic skim of a book tell you, and how does it differ from browsing?

paragraphs: The second level is inspectional reading, and its mark is time. The reader has a set, usually short, period, such as fifteen minutes for a whole book. The aim is to get the most out of the book in that time, which is by definition too little to get everything.

Another name for it is skimming or pre-reading, but not casual flipping through pages. Inspectional reading is skimming done systematically: you examine the surface of the book on purpose and learn all that the surface can teach, which is often a good deal.

The typical question here is what the book is about. Related surface questions ask what its structure is and what its parts are. By the end you should also be able to say what kind of book it is: a novel, a history, a scientific treatise and so on.
card.example: With fifteen minutes before a seminar, Sam inspects a book on city planning. The contents show that Part One describes failing city centres and Part Two proposes remedies, and the preface shows the author argues rather than reports. Sam can now say it is an argument in two parts about repairing city centres.
card.rule: Given a short, fixed time, skim a book systematically to learn what it is about, how it is built and what kind of book it is.
card.limits: An inspectional reading teaches only what the surface can show. It cannot get everything out of the book, and random flipping through pages does not count as inspection at all.

concepts.title: Do not plow in at page one
concepts.question: What goes wrong when you start a book at page one and read straight through without surveying it first?

paragraphs: The authors note that most people, even many quite good readers, do not know the value of inspectional reading. They open a book at page one and plow steadily through it, often without even reading the table of contents.

Such readers give themselves two jobs at once. They must pick up a surface knowledge of the book, what it covers and how it is laid out, while also trying to understand it. Doing both together makes each harder: the difficulty compounds.
Inspecting first separates the jobs. A short survey supplies the map, so the careful reading that follows can spend its attention on understanding.
card.example: Two students get the same economics textbook. Ana first reads the contents and the chapter summaries and learns that chapters 1 to 4 build a model which chapters 5 to 9 apply. Ben starts at page one. When chapter 5 turns to trade, Ana expects it; Ben must work out where he is while also following the argument.
card.rule: Survey a book's surface before reading it closely, so that you are not learning its layout and its meaning at the same time.
card.limits: A survey prepares a careful reading; it does not replace one. And a short text you already know well has no hidden layout to discover, so surveying it first gains little.

concepts.title: Analytical reading: chewing and digesting
concepts.question: What makes analytical reading the best reading you can do, and what does the reader actively do at this level?

paragraphs: The third level is analytical reading. It is more complex and more systematic than the first two, and how heavy its demands are depends on how difficult the text is. The authors call it thorough, complete or good reading: the best reading you can do.

Set it beside inspection. Inspectional reading is the best and most complete reading possible in a limited time; analytical reading is the best and most complete reading possible given unlimited time.

It is intensely active. The reader asks many questions of the book, in an organised way, and works at it until the book becomes the reader's own. The authors borrow Francis Bacon's remark that some books are to be tasted, others swallowed and a few chewed and digested. Analytical reading is the chewing and digesting.
card.example: A nurse studying a hard book on medical ethics reads a chapter, then stops to ask what it claims, how it uses its key terms and what reasons it gives, writing her answers in the margin. She keeps returning to the book until she could explain its case to a colleague in her own words.
card.rule: When a book deserves your best reading, take the time to question it in an orderly way until you have made it your own.
card.limits: Unlimited time is not the point in itself: long hours over a book without organised questions are not analytical reading. And most books deserve only tasting or swallowing, not chewing and digesting.

concepts.title: Analytical reading is for understanding
concepts.question: When does a reader need analytical reading, and when can it be left aside?

paragraphs: The authors tie analytical reading back to the goals from the start of the chapter. If you read only for information or entertainment, analytical reading is hardly ever needed. It exists above all for the sake of understanding.
The link also runs the other way. Moving your mind, with a book's help, from understanding less to understanding more is almost impossible without at least some skill in analytical reading.
So your goal tells you whether this level is worth its cost. Reading to find a fact or to pass an evening calls for less; reading to grasp an idea you do not yet grasp calls for the full work.
card.example: Leo reads the weather report to decide about an umbrella, a comic novel on holiday, and an essay on why prices rise when money is printed, which he finds hard. Only the essay calls for analytical reading: it is the one where he aims to understand more than he did before.
card.rule: Choose analytical reading when your goal is to understand something you do not yet grasp, and keep it for those books.
card.limits: Hardly ever needed is not the same as never. A book picked up for information can turn out to hold ideas you want to understand, and then the goal, and the reading, change.

concepts.title: Syntopical reading: many books, one subject
concepts.question: What does a syntopical reader do with many books on one subject that goes beyond comparing them?

paragraphs: The fourth and highest level is syntopical reading, which could also be called comparative reading. The reader reads many books, not one, and places them in relation to one another and to a subject they all revolve around.

Comparing texts is not enough. With the books' help, the syntopical reader builds an analysis of the subject that may not be in any one of them. That makes it the most active and effortful reading of all.

It is demanding even when the books are easy, because the hard work lies in relating them and building the analysis. The authors admit the art is not easy and its rules are not widely known, but they rate it probably the most rewarding of all reading.
card.example: A city councillor reads six books on remote work, by economists, a planner, managers and a psychologist. Rather than ranking them, she sets out the questions they all touch, where they agree and where they clash, and drafts her own analysis of what remote work means for the city centre, an analysis none of the six gives.
card.rule: When reading several books on one subject, relate them to each other and to the subject until you can build your own analysis of it.
card.limits: Syntopical reading rests on the lower levels: a reader who cannot grasp each book cannot relate them. And setting summaries side by side without an analysis of the subject is comparison, not syntopical reading.

concepts.title: Why reading became a public worry
concepts.question: What three historical trends, according to the authors, came together to make elementary reading a matter of public concern?

paragraphs: The chapter opens in the early 1970s, when officials, best sellers and researchers were all busy with how children learn to read. The authors trace this ferment to three trends that met at the same time.

First, the long American effort to educate every citizen, which at the very least means making everyone literate. Teaching a small number of eager children of literate parents is very different from teaching every child, however unmotivated or deprived.

Second, the methods of teaching beginners kept changing. Third, Americans have criticized their schools for more than a century, and reading instruction has drawn the harshest criticism of any subject.
card.example: Picture a school that once taught only children whose parents read to them every night. When it opens its doors to every child in the district, the same lessons that worked before start to fail for many newcomers, critics write about the failures, and new methods are tried in response.
card.rule: The concern about reading came from three trends together: schooling for everyone, shifting teaching methods, and a long habit of criticizing the schools.
card.limits: These trends explain the attention paid to the first level of reading. They say nothing about the higher levels, which the authors think were neglected partly because the first level absorbed so much effort.

concepts.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading

concepts.title: Synthetic and analytic methods
concepts.question: How do synthetic and analytic methods of teaching beginners differ, and did any one method prove best for every child?

paragraphs: For most of the nineteenth century American children learned by the ABC method: name the letters, then combine them into syllables, meaningful or not, until the set was mastered. The phonic method varied this by recognizing a word through its sounds instead of its letter names. Both are synthetic: they build words up from parts.

The sight method, from Germany and promoted by Horace Mann after about 1840, went the other way. Pupils first recognized whole words, later whole sentences, and only afterwards the words and letters inside them. This analytic approach was most popular in the 1920s and 1930s, along with a shift from reading aloud to silent reading.
Later the pendulum swung back toward phonics, and many newer programs have appeared since, from linguistic approaches to programmed instruction.
card.example: Teaching the word cat. ABC method: say the letter names, then join them. Phonic method: say the sounds of the three letters and blend them. Sight method: show the whole word, perhaps beside a picture, until the child knows it on sight, and point out its letters later.
card.rule: Synthetic methods build words from letters or sounds; analytic methods start from whole words or sentences and break them down.
card.limits: Neither family proved best for everyone: each method succeeded with some pupils and failed with others, and the authors think it too early to say whether any new method is a cure for all reading problems.

concepts.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading

concepts.title: Four stages toward mature reading
concepts.question: What are the four stages a child passes through on the way to mature elementary reading ability?

paragraphs: One useful finding of reading research is that children pass through at least four fairly distinct stages on the way to what educators call mature reading ability. Knowing them helps you see where a learner stands and what comes next.

Stage one is reading readiness, from birth to about six or seven. Stage two is reading very simple materials, starting with a few sight words. Stage three brings rapid vocabulary growth and skill in working out unfamiliar words from context. Stage four refines these skills and lets the reader carry ideas from one text to another.
The stages come in order, each building on the one before. The fourth should be reached in the early teens, and the reader should go on building on it for life.
card.rule: Place a learner by asking which of the four stages, readiness, simple materials, vocabulary and context, or refinement, they have mastered.
card.limits: The stages describe the usual path, not a fixed timetable: many normal children are not typical, and many learners never reach the fourth stage at all. Reaching it does not end a reader's growth.

concepts.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading

concepts.title: Reading readiness and its timing
concepts.question: What kinds of readiness should be in place before reading lessons begin, and what happens when lessons start too early?

paragraphs: Reading readiness is the first stage, starting at birth and usually lasting to about six or seven. It has four sides: physical (good sight and hearing), intellectual (taking in and remembering a whole word and its letters), language (speaking clearly and putting several sentences in the right order) and personal (working with others, keeping attention, following directions).

The authors stress timing. Starting too early usually defeats itself: a child taught before he is ready gets frustrated, and his dislike of the experience can last into later schooling and even into adult life.
Starting somewhat late is far less serious, even though anxious parents may fear that their child is backward or not keeping up with his peers.
card.example: Leo, five, sees and hears well and talks in full sentences, but cannot sit with a group for more than a minute or follow a two-step instruction. His personal readiness is missing, so formal reading lessons should wait.
card.rule: Check all four kinds of readiness before starting reading lessons, and when in doubt wait rather than rush.
card.limits: Waiting is the safer error, not a reason for endless delay: readiness normally arrives by six or seven, and a ready child should begin. Readiness belongs to the child, so a peer group's pace is no guide.

concepts.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading

concepts.title: Stage two and the discovery of meaning
concepts.question: What does a child learn in the second stage of reading, and what remarkable feat happens during it?

paragraphs: In the second stage children learn to read very simple materials. In the United States they usually begin with a few sight words and master perhaps three hundred to four hundred words by the end of the first year. Basic skills are introduced too, such as using context or meaning clues and noticing the beginning sounds of words.
By the end of the stage, pupils are expected to read simple books on their own and with enthusiasm.

Something almost magical happens along the way. Marks on a page that meant nothing to a child come, perhaps within two or three weeks, to say something. The authors suggest this discovery of meaning in symbols may be the most astounding intellectual feat a person ever performs, and most people perform it before they are seven.
card.rule: Judge the second stage by whether the child reads simple books independently and with enthusiasm, using sight words, context and beginning sounds.
card.limits: Second-stage skill is enough for simple books only: rapid vocabulary growth and unlocking harder words come later. And knowing that a child discovers meaning in symbols is not the same as knowing how it happens.

concepts.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading

concepts.title: Stage three: vocabulary and context
concepts.question: How does a third-stage reader deal with unfamiliar words, and what new purposes for reading does this stage open up?

paragraphs: The third stage brings rapid vocabulary growth and growing skill in unlocking the meaning of unfamiliar words through context clues: the sentence and passage around a word suggest what it must mean.

Children also learn to read for different purposes and in different subjects, such as science, social studies and language arts. They discover that reading is not only something done at school but something they can do on their own, for fun, to satisfy curiosity, or to widen their horizons.
card.example: A child meets the sentence: The drought lasted so long that the river bed cracked and the crops withered. Without a dictionary she reasons from the cracked earth and dying crops that a drought must be a long spell without rain.
card.rule: When a word is unfamiliar, use the surrounding sentence and passage to work out what it must mean.
card.limits: Context gives clues, not proof: a passage may fit several meanings or give too little to go on, and then the guess needs checking. Unlocking words is also not the same as comparing ideas across texts, which belongs to the next stage.

concepts.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading

concepts.title: Stage four: assimilating what you read
concepts.question: What new ability marks the fourth stage of learning to read, and when should a reader reach it?

paragraphs: The fourth stage refines and strengthens the skills already gained. Above all, the reader begins to assimilate reading experiences: to carry concepts over from one piece of writing to another, and to compare the views of different writers on the same subject.
This is the mature stage of elementary reading, and young people should reach it in their early teens. Ideally they keep building on it for the rest of their lives.
card.example: A thirteen-year-old reads a news story about a new dam, then a textbook chapter on rivers. She uses the textbook's idea of a watershed to make sense of the news story, and notices that the reporter and the textbook disagree about whether dams harm fish.
card.rule: Read each new text in the light of others: carry ideas across and compare what different writers say on the same subject.
card.limits: Comparing writers at this stage is still elementary reading, the end of the first level rather than the higher reading the book teaches. Many readers never get this far, and those who do need to keep building rather than stop.

concepts.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading

concepts.title: The neglected higher levels
concepts.question: What seldom-noticed cause of poor reading do the authors point to, and what remedy do they say it calls for?

paragraphs: Many young people never reach the fourth stage, and the reasons are many. The authors add one cause that is seldom noticed: so much attention has gone to reading readiness and to methods for teaching the rudiments that the higher levels of reading have been slighted.

They find this understandable, given how urgent and widespread the first-level problems are. Still, they insist that the overall reading deficiencies cannot be cured unless efforts are made on all levels of reading, not only the first.
card.example: A district spends its whole reading budget on first-grade lessons. Early test scores rise, but its high school graduates still cannot follow the argument of an editorial. In the authors' terms, it has worked on one level and neglected the others.
card.rule: Work on reading at every level, not only the elementary one, if you want to cure poor reading.
card.limits: This is not an argument against early instruction: the first level must come first and its problems are real. Solving it is necessary but not enough.

concepts.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading

concepts.title: The stages belong to the first level
concepts.question: How do the four stages of learning to read relate to the four levels of reading?

paragraphs: The book describes four levels of reading: elementary, inspectional, analytical and syntopical. The four stages of learning to read are not these levels. All four stages lie inside the first level: they are stages of elementary reading.

The stages roughly follow elementary schooling. Readiness matches pre-school and kindergarten. Word mastery matches first grade and gives first grade literacy. Vocabulary growth and use of context is typically reached by the end of fourth grade, giving fourth grade, or functional, literacy. The fourth stage comes as the pupil leaves elementary or junior high school, and is sometimes called eighth, ninth or tenth grade literacy.
These grades describe the typical child, and many quite normal children are not typical in this sense.
card.rule: Treat the four stages as steps inside elementary reading, roughly matching the years of elementary schooling, not as the four levels of reading.
card.limits: The grade match describes the typical child, not every normal child. And finishing all four stages completes only the first level; three higher levels still lie beyond.

concepts.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading

concepts.title: Two senses of a mature reader
concepts.question: In what sense is a fourth-stage reader mature, and why is that not yet mature in the sense the authors intend?

paragraphs: At the end of the fourth stage a pupil is called a mature reader: he can read almost anything, though in a fairly unsophisticated way.
The authors use mature in a stronger sense. Such a pupil has mastered the first level and can read on his own, but he does not yet know how to read beyond the elementary level.

So the word has two uses. Mature in the elementary sense means reading almost anything independently; mature in the authors' sense means knowing how to read beyond the elementary level, which the rest of the book sets out to teach.
card.rule: Ask in which sense a reader is mature: able to read almost anything on their own, or able to read beyond the elementary level.
card.limits: Mature elementary reading is a real achievement and the base for everything else; the distinction does not belittle it. It marks only that reading on your own is not yet reading well.

concepts.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading

concepts.title: From aided to unaided reading
concepts.question: Why must all four elementary stages be mastered before a reader can move on to the higher levels and learn alone?

paragraphs: The four stages are usually passed with the help of living teachers. Children differ, and some need more help than others, but a teacher is usually there to answer questions and smooth over difficulties during the elementary school years.
Only when all four stages are mastered is a child prepared for the higher levels of reading. Only then can he read independently and learn on his own.
The authors tie this to the difference between aided and unaided discovery: elementary reading is learned with a teacher's help, while reading beyond it means learning on your own.
card.rule: Master the elementary stages first, with help where needed, so that you can read and learn on your own.
card.limits: Mastering the stages makes independent reading possible, not automatic. And the path there varies: some children need far more help than others.

concepts.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading

concepts.section: Higher Levels of Reading and Higher Education
concepts.title: Remedial reading is not higher reading
concepts.question: Why do the authors say that most reading courses in colleges do not teach the higher levels of reading?

paragraphs: High schools traditionally gave little reading instruction and colleges none. As high school enrollments grew, educators found they could not assume entering students read effectively, and offered remedial reading, sometimes to 75% or more of them. Colleges later followed: of about 40,000 freshmen entering the City University of New York in 1971, more than 20,000 needed remedial training in reading.

Remedial instruction is not instruction in the higher levels. It only brings students up to the maturity in reading they should have reached by the end of elementary school. The courses in speed, effective or competent reading that many colleges have added are, on the whole and with exceptions, remedial in the same way.

The authors' standard is higher: a good liberal arts high school should turn out competent analytical readers, and a good college competent syntopical readers, able to read any kind of material written for general readers.
card.rule: Ask whether a reading course aims beyond the first level or only repairs it; only the first kind teaches higher reading.
card.limits: Remedial courses are needed and useful for students who lack elementary skill; the point is that they are not higher reading. And the authors allow exceptions among speed and effective reading courses.

concepts.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading

concepts.section: Reading and the Democratic Ideal of Education
concepts.title: Beyond a nation of functional literates
concepts.question: How do the authors reconcile teaching everyone the basics first with their call for a nation of truly competent readers?

paragraphs: The authors do not want to sound like carping critics. With so many new students arriving, and many unable to read well at the elementary level, the first task must be to teach them to read in the lowest, largest-common-denominator sense.
They would not want it otherwise. They hold that educational opportunity limited only by each person's desire, ability and need is the most valuable service a society can give its members.

But finishing that task will not finish the whole task. A nation of functional literates is not enough: the authors call for a nation of truly competent readers, which they say the coming world will need.
card.rule: Teach everyone the basics first, but do not stop at functional literacy: aim for truly competent reading.
card.limits: The call for competence does not mean limiting education to the few or neglecting basic literacy; the authors back opportunity for all. Competence here means skill at the higher levels, which basic literacy alone does not give.

concepts.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
concepts.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
concepts.title: Inspectional reading: what it builds on and its two steps
concepts.question: What must you already be able to do before reading inspectionally, and what are its two steps?

paragraphs: The levels of reading are cumulative: each higher level contains the ones below it. Inspectional reading, the second level, contains elementary reading. So you cannot inspect a book well unless you can read its text fairly steadily, without stopping often to look up words or tripping over the grammar, and can make some sense of most of its sentences and paragraphs.

Inspectional reading has two steps. The first is systematic skimming, also called pre-reading: a quick, ordered look at a book to learn what it is and whether it deserves more time. The second is superficial reading: reading the book through once without stopping at the parts you do not understand.
