The two steps are really aspects of one skill. The authors advise beginners to treat them as separate activities, done one after the other. Experienced readers learn to do both at the same time.
card.example: Asked to size up a long report on city housing, a new reader first skims it (contents, summary, a few pages) and then reads it straight through, passing over the tables he cannot follow. A policy analyst with years of practice does both in a single pass.
card.rule: Treat inspectional reading as two steps, skimming and then a straight-through first reading, and keep them separate until you are practised enough to combine them.
card.limits: Both steps assume you can already read the text steadily. If you stop on every line for a word or the grammar, the trouble lies at the elementary level, and inspection cannot fix it. Doing both steps at once is a skill for practised readers, not a shortcut for beginners.

concepts.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
concepts.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
concepts.title: When to skim, and what a skim must yield
concepts.question: When should you skim a book, and what should a skim tell you even if you never read the book again?

paragraphs: Skimming fits a common situation. You have a book in hand and do not know whether it deserves a careful reading, though you suspect it holds information or insight worth digging out. And you have only a limited time to find out. Skimming, or pre-reading, is the first step of inspectional reading.

Its main aim is a decision: does this book need a more careful reading? The authors compare skimming to threshing, the farm process that separates the chaff from the kernels worth eating. Some books turn out to be worth no more than the skim.

Even when you decide not to go on, a skim should leave you knowing at least two things: the author's main contention and what kind of book it is. That is why the time spent is not wasted, whichever way the decision goes.
card.example: A manager is handed a book on remote work and has half an hour before a meeting. She skims it and finds it is a practical guide whose main claim is that teams need written routines. She decides it does not need a careful reading, but she can now say what it argues and what kind of book it is.
card.rule: Skim a book when you are unsure it deserves careful reading and time is short, and come away knowing its main contention, its kind and whether to read on.
card.limits: A skim decides how much more time a book deserves; it cannot tell you whether the author is right or what each argument says. Treating the skim as a full reading of a book that deserves more is the slip to avoid.

concepts.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
concepts.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
concepts.title: Step 1: the title page and preface
concepts.question: What should the title page and preface tell you, and what should you do with that before going further?

paragraphs: The first skimming step is to look at the title page and, if the book has one, the preface, reading each quickly. Pay special attention to subtitles and other signs of the book's scope or aim, or of the author's particular angle on the subject.

By the end of this step you should have a good idea of the book's subject. The authors suggest pausing for a moment to place the book in a category in your mind: which pigeonhole, already holding other books, does this one belong in?
card.example: A book titled Salt Roads carries the subtitle How One Mineral Shaped Trade in Medieval Europe. The title alone is vague; the subtitle fixes the scope (one mineral, one continent, one period) and the angle (trade history). You might shelve it in your mind with other histories of commerce.
card.rule: Read the title page and preface quickly for the book's subject, scope, aim and angle, then place it in a mental category alongside similar books.
card.limits: Titles and prefaces can mislead or say little, so treat what they suggest as a first guess to test against the contents, the index and the pages you sample. The category you choose here is provisional, not a final classification.

concepts.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
concepts.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
concepts.title: Step 2: the table of contents as a road map
concepts.question: What can a table of contents show about a book, and why do the authors want you to read it carefully?

paragraphs: The second skimming step is to study the table of contents for a general sense of the book's structure. The authors liken it to a road map you study before a trip. They find it astonishing how many readers never glance at it unless they want to look something up, wasting the care authors put into it.

Older books often had very full contents pages. Milton wrote more or less lengthy headings, which he called Arguments, for each book of Paradise Lost, and Gibbon gave his history of the fall of Rome an extensive analytical table of contents for each chapter. Such summaries are now rare.

Modern chapter titles are often vaguer, partly because publishers feel a mysterious contents page tempts buyers more than a frank one. Even so, the authors say, read the table of contents carefully before going on to the rest of the book.
card.example: A book on sleep lists its chapters as The Body Clock, Dreams, Sleep Across a Lifetime, Disorders and Better Nights. Before reading a page, you can see that it moves from explanation to practical advice, and where to look for the part that interests you.
card.rule: Read the table of contents carefully, like a map before a trip, to get a general sense of how the book is built.
card.limits: A contents page shows how a book is divided, not what it argues or whether it is right. Vague or teasing chapter titles reveal little, so the structure you infer is a sketch to check against the index and sampled pages.

concepts.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
concepts.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
concepts.title: Step 3: checking the index for crucial terms
concepts.question: How can a quick look at the index point you to the terms and passages on which a book hinges?

paragraphs: The third skimming step is to check the index, if the book has one; most expository books do. Make a quick estimate of the range of topics covered and of the kinds of books and authors referred to.

When you see terms that seem crucial, look up at least some of the passages cited. You judge which terms matter from the general sense of the book you got from the title page, preface and contents. The passages may hold the crux, the point on which the book hinges, or the new departure that is the key to the author's approach.
card.example: Skimming a book on city planning, you notice the index names several urban historians, lists zoning and traffic, and has a long run of pages under walkability. The contents already showed that the book argues for denser neighbourhoods, so you read two of the walkability passages and find the author's central test for a good street.
card.rule: Scan the index for the range of topics and sources, then look up a few passages under the terms your skim so far suggests are crucial.
card.limits: The step needs an index; most expository books have one, and a book without one skips it. An index shows where words appear, not how they are argued, so a few cited passages give clues to the crux rather than a reading of it.

concepts.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
concepts.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
concepts.title: Step 4: the blurb, and the first decision point
concepts.question: How much can a publisher's blurb tell you, and what decision should the first four skimming steps let you make?

paragraphs: The fourth step, for a new book with a dust jacket, is to read the publisher's blurb. Some people think blurbs are nothing but puffery, but that is often untrue, especially for expository books. Authors often write their own blurbs, with help from the publisher's publicity staff, and try to summarize their main points as accurately as they can.
If a blurb is nothing but a puff for the book, you can usually tell at a glance.

After these four steps you may already know enough: either that you want to read the book carefully, or that you do not want or need to read it at all. Either way, you can put it aside for now. If you are still unsure, you go on to skim the book properly.
card.example: The jacket of a book on urban birds says it shows how three common species have changed their songs to be heard over traffic, and argues that cities are a new frontier of evolution. That is a statement of the main contention, not praise, and it tells you what to look for in the last chapter.
card.rule: Read the blurb as a possible summary of the main points, then use the first four steps to decide: read carefully, drop the book, or skim on.
card.limits: A blurb is written to sell, so its claims are something to check, not proof of what the book achieves. The step is for a new book with a dust jacket; without a blurb, it is skipped.

concepts.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
concepts.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
concepts.title: Steps 5 and 6: pivotal chapters, sampled pages and the last pages
concepts.question: When the first four steps leave you unsure, where in the body of the book should you look, and why there?

paragraphs: If the first four steps have not settled the matter, you are ready to skim the book properly. Step five: from your still vague sense of the contents, look at the chapters that seem pivotal to the argument. If they have summary statements in their opening or closing pages, as they often do, read those carefully.

Step six: turn the pages, dipping in here and there, reading a paragraph or two, sometimes several pages in sequence, but never more than that. Keep looking for signs of the main contention, listening for the basic pulse of the book.

Above all, read the last two or three pages. Few authors can resist summing up there what they think is new and important in their work. You want that summing-up, even though the author's own judgment of what matters may be wrong.
card.example: Skimming a book on the history of vaccines, you see from the contents that chapters 4 and 9 seem to carry the argument. You read the opening and closing pages of each, dip into a page in five other chapters, and read the last three pages, where the author claims that public trust, more than science, has been the real bottleneck.
card.rule: When the first four steps leave you unsure, read the summaries of the pivotal chapters, sample pages across the book, and make sure to read the last few pages.
card.limits: Sampling means a few pages at most at any point; settling into whole chapters turns the skim into a full reading. The last pages give the author's own view of what matters, which may itself be mistaken.

concepts.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
concepts.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
concepts.title: Skimming as quick, active detective work
concepts.question: How long should a systematic skim take, and what keeps it from turning into idle flipping?

paragraphs: A full systematic skim takes a few minutes, an hour at most. At the end you should know whether the book holds matter you still want to dig out, and you should be able to place it more accurately than before in your mental card catalogue, for reference if the need ever arises.

Skimming is a very active kind of reading. You cannot do it without being alert, with all your faculties awake. It guards against a common experience: daydreaming through several pages and waking to find you have no idea what you covered. Following a system keeps you on a general thread.
The authors suggest thinking of yourself as a detective, looking for clues to the book's general theme or idea and alert to anything that makes it clearer.
card.example: A student has forty minutes in a library with a book on the history of maps. At each step she asks what the book's main claim seems to be, notes that the index has many entries under empire and propaganda, and finds the last pages arguing that maps are tools of power. She leaves knowing the claim and where to file the book in her mind.
card.rule: Skim within an hour, actively, like a detective following a thread of clues to the book's main idea.
card.limits: The time limit fits skimming, not careful reading; a book that earns an analytical reading needs far longer. Alertness keeps a skim from drifting, but even a sharp skim gives a sketch of a book, not an understanding of it.

concepts.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
concepts.title: Superficial reading: read it through without stopping
concepts.question: On a first reading of a difficult book, what should you do when you reach something you do not understand?

paragraphs: The second step of inspectional reading is superficial reading. The authors choose the word on purpose, though it usually sounds negative. Their rule: when tackling a difficult book for the first time, read it through without ever stopping to look up or ponder the things you do not understand right away.

Pay attention to what you can understand. Go on past the point where you have trouble, and you will soon reach things you do understand; concentrate on those. Do not let paragraphs, footnotes, comments or references that escape you hold you up.
If you let one stumbling block stall you, you are lost. In most cases you will not puzzle the thing out by sticking at it.
card.example: A student starts a hard book on the philosophy of mind. A paragraph on page 12 makes no sense to her, and a footnote cites three writers she has never heard of. Instead of stopping, she reads on. By chapter 4 the idea returns in plainer terms, and by the end she has the book's main lines.
card.rule: On a first reading of a difficult book, keep going past what you do not understand and concentrate on what you do.
card.limits: The rule is for a first reading. It does not ban close study, since what you pass over is meant for a later reading. It also assumes you can follow much of the text; if almost nothing makes sense, the trouble is at the elementary level.

concepts.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
concepts.title: Do not expect too much from a first reading
concepts.question: When a difficult book defeats you, where does the mistake usually lie, and what is a partial first reading worth?

paragraphs: Many readers start a difficult book with high hopes, struggle, and conclude it was a mistake to try it at all. The authors disagree: the mistake was expecting too much from the first going-over. Approached the right way, no book written for the general reader, however difficult, need be a cause for despair.

What you understand on a full first reading, even if it is half the book or less, helps when you go back later to the places you passed over. A second reading has a much better chance of making sense of them, but it requires that you have read the book through at least once.
Even if you never go back, understanding half of a really tough book is much better than understanding none of it, which is what happens if you let the first hard passage stop you.
card.example: A reader tackles a classic of political theory and follows perhaps four chapters in ten. Instead of giving up, he finishes it. Months later he rereads it, and the chapters that defeated him now connect to the ones he understood.
card.rule: Expect only partial understanding from a first reading of a hard book, finish it anyway, and use what you grasp as the base for a second reading.
card.limits: The authors' promise covers books written for the general reader. A work written for specialists may demand knowledge that no first reading can supply. And half-understanding is a starting point, not a finished reading.

concepts.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
concepts.title: Reference aids used too early, and the Shakespeare lesson
concepts.question: Why can dictionaries, footnotes and commentaries hurt a first reading, and when should you use them?

paragraphs: Most of us were taught to attend to what we did not understand: to go to a dictionary for an unfamiliar word, to an encyclopedia or other reference work for an allusion, and to footnotes and scholarly commentaries for help. The authors say that when these things are done too early, they impede reading instead of helping it.

Their example is Shakespeare in school. Generations of high school students went through Julius Caesar or Hamlet scene by scene, looking up every strange word in a glossary and studying every footnote. By the end they had forgotten the beginning and lost sight of the whole, so they never really read the play.
The students should have read the play at one sitting and discussed what they got from that quick reading. Only then would they have understood enough of it to study it closely and learn more.
card.example: Reading a novel set in eighteenth-century Japan, Kenji meets an unfamiliar word for a garment on page 3 and a footnote on court ranks. He reads on. By the end he has the story whole, and on a second reading he uses the glossary and notes, which now answer questions he really has.
card.rule: Keep dictionaries, footnotes and commentaries for after a first reading of the whole work; used first, they break it into pieces.
card.limits: The advice is about timing, not a ban on aids. Close study with glossaries, footnotes and commentaries is the step the authors want once you have read the whole.

concepts.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
concepts.title: Missing the forest for the trees
concepts.question: What happens when you insist on mastering every page of an expository book before moving on?

paragraphs: The rule holds with equal force for expository works, and the best proof is what happens when you ignore it. The authors' example is Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations, chosen because it is more than a textbook or a work for specialists: it is written for the general reader.

If you insist on understanding everything on every page before going on, you will not get far. In mastering the fine points you will miss the big ones Smith makes so clearly: the wages, rents, profits and interest that enter the cost of things, the market's role in setting prices, the evils of monopoly, the case for free trade.
You will miss the forest for the trees, and you will not be reading well on any level.
card.example: A reader of a long history of the internet stalls for a week on a chapter about network protocols. Meanwhile she has not reached the author's larger points: who paid for the network, why it was left open, and how that shaped what came after.
card.rule: On a first reading of an expository book, keep moving so that you catch the big points, and leave the fine points for later.
card.limits: The rule is about the first reading. Fine points matter, and a careful reading must deal with them; the trouble lies only in demanding them before you have the big points.

concepts.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
concepts.title: Inspection is fast, whatever the book
concepts.question: How fast should inspectional reading go, and how does it differ from what speed reading courses mostly teach?

paragraphs: In Chapter 2 the authors defined inspectional reading as the art of getting the most out of a book in a limited time, and nothing in this chapter changes that. Both of its steps, skimming and superficial reading, are taken rapidly. A competent inspectional reader carries them out quickly, however long or difficult the book.

That raises the question of speed reading. The authors regard most speed reading courses as basically remedial: they teach mainly, if not only, reading at the elementary level, taking in the words faster, rather than any of the higher levels.
card.example: Two books land on a reviewer's desk: a 150-page essay and a 900-page history of China. She gives each an inspection in under an hour. The history may take weeks to read analytically, if it earns that, but sizing it up does not.
card.rule: Carry out both inspectional steps quickly, whatever the book's length or difficulty, to get the most from it in the time you have.
card.limits: Speed belongs to the inspectional level; it says nothing about how fast a book should be read analytically. Faster word reading, which speed courses teach, is an elementary skill, not a substitute for knowing what to look for.

concepts.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
concepts.title: Many speeds, each in its place
concepts.question: Should you try to read everything faster, and if not, what should decide how fast you read?

paragraphs: The authors are wholly in favour of most people learning to read faster. Much of what we must read is not worth much time, and reading it slowly is a waste. But many people also read some things too fast and ought to slow down.
So a good speed course should teach you many speeds, not one speed faster than you manage now, and let you vary your rate with the nature and complexity of the material.

Many books are hardly worth even skimming; some should be read quickly; and a few deserve a rate, usually quite slow, that allows complete comprehension. The ideal is to be able to read at different speeds and to know when each is appropriate.
card.example: In one morning a lawyer skims a trade newsletter in two minutes, reads a news report on a court ruling at a brisk pace, and then spends an hour on the ruling's three key paragraphs, word by word.
card.rule: Match your reading speed to the nature and complexity of the material: fast where it deserves little time, slow where it deserves much.
card.limits: Having several speeds helps only if you judge well which one a text deserves; speed by itself does not tell you what to look for. Reading fast is not a virtue in itself, nor is reading slowly.

concepts.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
concepts.title: Speed is not the main obstacle
concepts.question: If you could read twice as fast, would difficult books become easier, and what actually stands in the way?

paragraphs: Reading a book slowly when it deserves only a fast reading wastes time, and speed reading skills can fix that. But the authors call this only one reading problem.

The obstacles to understanding a difficult book are not ordinarily, and perhaps never primarily, physical or psychological. They arise because the reader does not know what to do when approaching a difficult and rewarding book: he does not know the rules of reading or how to marshal his mind for the task.
However fast he reads, he is no better off if he does not know what he is looking for and does not know when he has found it.
card.example: Two students read a dense chapter on game theory. One reads at 600 words a minute and can repeat its examples but not its argument. The other reads at half that speed, asks what problem the chapter solves, and finds the answer in its third section.
card.rule: Before trying to read a hard book faster, learn what to look for in it and how to tell when you have found it.
card.limits: Speed skills do solve a real problem: wasting time on material that deserves only a fast reading. The claim is about difficult, rewarding books; with easy material, reading faster may be all that is needed.

concepts.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
concepts.title: Fast by reading less, and varied speed within a book
concepts.question: Why is inspectional reading fast, and should every part of a book get the same speed, even in careful reading?

paragraphs: Inspectional reading is done quickly, but not only because you read faster, though you do. You also read less of the book, and you read it in a different way, with different goals in mind: to find out what the book is and whether it deserves more time.

Analytical reading is usually much slower. Even so, you should not read all of a book at the same speed when reading it analytically. Every book, however difficult, contains interstitial material, the connecting stretches between its main points, which can and should be read quickly.
And every good book also contains difficult matter that should be read very slowly.
card.example: In a careful reading of a book on the causes of the First World War, a student moves quickly through chapters retelling diplomatic visits and slows to a crawl on the two pages where the author weighs whether the alliance system made war inevitable.
card.rule: Speed up through the connecting material and slow down for the hard core of a book, even in a careful reading.
card.limits: Telling connecting material from the hard core takes judgment, and a passage that looks like filler may turn out to matter. The advice is to vary speed within a book, not to skip parts of a book you are reading analytically.

concepts.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
concepts.title: Sub-vocalizing, fixations and regressions
concepts.question: What eye habits slow most untrained readers down, and how often do they occur?

paragraphs: Speed reading courses rightly stress a finding known for half a century or more: most people go on sub-vocalizing, silently sounding out the words, for years after they first learn to read.

Films of eye movements show more. The eyes of young or untrained readers fixate, that is, stop on the line, as many as five or six times per line. The eye is blind while it moves and sees only when it stops, so such readers take in single words, or two- or three-word phrases, in jumps across the line.
Worse, the eyes of incompetent readers regress as often as once every two or three lines: they go back to phrases or sentences already read.
card.example: Filmed reading a newspaper column, a ten-year-old's eyes stop six times on each line, taking in a word or two each time, and every few lines jump back to a phrase already read. Each stop and each jump back costs time.
card.rule: Check whether you sound out the words, stop many times per line, or keep jumping back, since these habits slow your reading.
card.limits: These are elementary-level habits of the eye. Correcting them speeds up taking in the words; by itself it does nothing for understanding what the words mean or argue.

concepts.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
concepts.title: Let the mind, not the eyes, set the pace
concepts.question: Why do fixations and regressions waste time, and what becomes possible once they are corrected?

paragraphs: Fixations and regressions are wasteful because the mind, unlike the eye, does not need to read a word or a short phrase at a time. The mind can grasp a sentence, or even a paragraph, at a glance, if the eyes give it the information it needs.
So the primary task of speed reading, recognized as such by all the courses, is to correct the fixations and regressions that slow readers down. The authors say this can be done quite easily.
Once it is done, you can read as fast as your mind will let you, not as slowly as your eyes make you.
card.example: After practice, a reader who used to stop five times per line takes in a line in one or two sweeps. On a light news story her speed triples; on a dense legal paragraph she still slows down, because now her mind, not her eyes, sets the pace.
card.rule: Train your eyes to feed your mind larger units, so that your reading pace is set by your mind rather than by your eyes.
card.limits: Removing the eye's limit lets the mind set the pace, but the mind's pace still depends on the material. A hard passage still needs slow reading after the eyes are trained.

concepts.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
concepts.title: Using your hand as a pacer
concepts.question: How can you break the habit of eye fixations using nothing but your own hand?

paragraphs: There are devices for breaking eye fixations, some of them complicated and expensive. Usually nothing more is needed than your own hand, which you can train yourself to follow as it moves faster and faster across and down the page.

Put your thumb and first two fingers together. Sweep this pointer across a line of type a little faster than is comfortable for your eyes, and force yourself to keep up with your hand. You will soon be able to read the words as you follow it.
Keep practising and keep increasing the speed of your hand, and before you know it, the authors say, you will have doubled or trebled your reading speed.
card.example: Each evening Sam reads a light novel for ten minutes with his fingers sweeping each line a touch faster than feels easy. At first he loses words; by the second week he follows the hand comfortably, so he nudges it faster again.
card.rule: Sweep a three-finger pointer across each line a little faster than is comfortable, make your eyes keep up, and raise its speed as you practise.
card.limits: The pointer trains the eyes; by itself it speeds up taking in the words and nothing more. Pushing it at top speed through material that deserves slow reading works against reading each thing at the speed it deserves.

concepts.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
concepts.title: Concentration is not comprehension
concepts.question: Does a pacer that raises your speed and concentration also raise your comprehension, and what does comprehension really involve?

paragraphs: What have you gained by reading much faster? Time, certainly; but what about comprehension? Every speed course the authors know claims to raise comprehension along with speed, and there is probably some basis for the claim. A hand or other timer improves concentration: while you follow it, it is harder to doze, daydream or let your mind wander.

Concentration is another name for what the authors call activity in reading: the good reader reads actively, with concentration. But concentration alone does little for comprehension properly understood.

Comprehension is much more than answering simple factual questions about a text. That limited kind is only the elementary ability to answer the question of what a text says. The further questions whose answers show higher comprehension are seldom asked, or taught, in speed courses.
card.example: After a speed course, Lee reads an essay on free will in ten minutes and scores ten out of ten on a quiz asking who, when and which examples. Asked what the author means by freedom, and whether her argument works, he has no answer.
card.rule: Use pacing to concentrate, but judge your comprehension by questions that go beyond what the text says.
card.limits: Concentration is still needed, since it is part of active reading; it is not enough on its own. Answering factual questions is the elementary layer of comprehension, so a high score on them does not show that a book has been understood.

concepts.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
concepts.title: One short document, many speeds: the Declaration
concepts.question: How can one short document deserve both a fast reading and a reading that takes years?

paragraphs: Take the Declaration of Independence, less than three pages in print. How fast should you read it? Its second paragraph ends by promising to submit facts to a candid world. The two pages of facts that follow, some of them dubious, can be read quickly: a general idea of the kind of facts cited is enough, unless you are a scholar of the period.

The last paragraph, ending with the signers' pledge of their lives, fortunes and sacred honour, can also be read quickly. It is a rhetorical flourish, and the authors give rhetoric of that kind a quick reading.

But the first two paragraphs need far more. The authors doubt anyone can read them much faster than 20 words a minute. Words such as inalienable, rights, liberty, happiness, consent and just powers are worth dwelling on. Read for full comprehension, those paragraphs might take days, weeks or even years.
card.rule: Within one text, read the supporting lists and rhetorical flourishes quickly, and slow right down for the passages and words that carry the ideas.
card.limits: What deserves speed depends on your purpose: a scholar of the period has reason to read the list of facts closely. And full comprehension of the key paragraphs is the work of analytical reading, which no single pass completes.

concepts.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
concepts.title: The formula for reading speed
concepts.question: What single formula should govern how fast you read any book?

paragraphs: In summary, there is no single right speed for reading. The ideal is the ability to read at various speeds and to know when each is appropriate. Great speed is a dubious achievement: it is of value only when what you have to read is not really worth reading.
The authors offer a better formula: read every book no more slowly than it deserves, and no more quickly than you can read it with satisfaction and comprehension.
In any case, speed, fast or slow, is only a fraction of most people's problem with reading.
card.example: A reader gets through a light travel memoir in an evening, slowing only for a chapter she enjoys. The next week she takes a month over a short book on ethics, because faster than that she cannot follow its arguments. Both speeds obey the same formula.
card.rule: Read each book no more slowly than it deserves and no more quickly than you can read it with satisfaction and comprehension.
card.limits: The formula needs a judgment of what a book deserves, and a skim or first reading helps you make it. It sets limits on speed but says nothing about what to do while reading, which is most of the problem.

concepts.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
concepts.title: Skim every book, and race through hard ones first
concepts.question: Should you skim a book you already plan to read carefully, and how should you take a hard book the first time?

paragraphs: Skimming a book is always a good idea. It is necessary when you do not know, as is often the case, whether the book in hand is worth reading carefully. And it is generally worth skimming even a book you intend to read carefully, to get some idea of its form and structure.
Finally, do not try to understand every word or page of a difficult book the first time through. The authors call this the most important rule of all, the essence of inspectional reading.
Do not be afraid to be, or to seem, superficial. Race through even the hardest book. You will then be prepared to read it well the second time.
card.example: Asked to master a dense book on evolution for a seminar, Tara first skims it in half an hour to see its parts. She then races through it in two evenings, passing over the hardest chapters. Only then does she begin a slow reading, already knowing where the argument goes.
card.rule: Skim every book first, even one you mean to study, and race through a hard book once before reading it closely.
card.limits: Racing through is preparation, not the reading itself: a book that deserves understanding still needs a careful second reading. Seeming superficial is acceptable on the first pass only because a better reading is meant to follow.

concepts.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
concepts.title: How inspection prepares for analytical reading
concepts.question: How do the two steps of inspectional reading prepare you for the stages of analytical reading?

paragraphs: Inspectional reading also serves the next level, analytical reading, described in the second part of the book. Its two steps can both be thought of as anticipations of steps the reader takes when reading analytically.
Systematic skimming prepares you to answer the questions of the first stage of analytical reading. In other words, skimming anticipates grasping the book's structure.
Superficial reading serves the reader at the second stage of analytical reading. It is the first necessary step in interpreting the book's contents.
card.example: Hugo skims a book on urban design and notes that it has three parts: problems, principles and case studies. He then reads it straight through. Weeks later, reading it analytically, he starts his outline from those three parts and his interpretation from the passages he understood on the first pass.
card.rule: Use your skim as a first sketch of the book's structure and your straight-through reading as the first step toward interpreting its contents.
card.limits: Anticipation is not completion: a skim gives a sketch of the structure, not a finished outline, and a first reading only begins the interpretation. Analytical reading still has its own stages to carry out.

concepts.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
concepts.title: Reading to profit means reading awake
concepts.question: What decides whether you stay mentally awake through a good book, and what do readers who drift usually lack?

paragraphs: The authors open with a joke: falling asleep over a book is easy. Pick a comfortable spot, poor light and a book you do not care about. Staying awake is not the reverse of that recipe. Readers by candlelight stayed alert in bad conditions because it mattered to them whether they read the book in hand.

So wakefulness depends mostly on your goal. If you read to profit, to grow in mind or spirit, you must stay awake, which means reading as actively as you can and making an effort you expect to be repaid. Letting your mind drift through time set aside for understanding defeats your own purpose.

Many people know the difference between reading for understanding and reading for entertainment, and still fail at their reading plans. According to the authors, what they lack is know-how: they do not know how to make their mind do the work that earns the profit.
card.example: Ana sets aside Sunday morning for a history of the printing press. After an hour she has turned forty pages and remembers almost none of them. Her light and chair were fine; her mind had nothing to do. The authors would say she needs a way to keep her mind working on the book, not a better armchair.
card.rule: When you read for understanding, stay awake by giving your mind active work to do on the book.
card.limits: The demand is for reading meant to profit you. Reading purely to relax does not call for this effort. And open eyes are not enough: the authors count a wandering mind during planned reading time as the same as falling asleep.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

concepts.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
concepts.title: The one prescription: ask questions
concepts.question: What single habit turns passive reading into active reading, and what does a reader who skips it end up with?

paragraphs: Active reading takes effort, but effort needs a direction. The authors reduce active reading to one prescription: ask questions while you read, questions that you yourself must try to answer in the course of reading.

Not any questions will do. Above the elementary level, the art of reading is the habit of asking the right questions in the right order. Reading a book is an effort to question it and to answer those questions as well as you can.
This separates the demanding reader from the undemanding one. The undemanding reader asks the book nothing, so the book answers nothing. Answers come to the reader who asks.
card.example: Reading a report on remote work, Raj stops after each section and asks what it claims and on what evidence, then tries to answer. His colleague reads the same report straight through. Next day Raj can explain the report's case; his colleague remembers only that it was about remote work.
card.rule: Ask the book questions as you read, and work at answering them yourself while you read.
card.limits: Asking is half the job: questions left unanswered earn little. And stray questions are not yet the art; the authors mean particular questions asked in a particular order, which the next idea sets out.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

concepts.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
concepts.title: The four questions to ask of any book
concepts.question: What four questions should a demanding reader ask of a book, and in what order?

paragraphs: The authors name four questions. First, what is the book about as a whole: its leading theme, and how the author develops it in order through subordinate themes. Second, what is being said in detail, and how: the main ideas, assertions and arguments that make up the author's particular message.
Third, is the book true, in whole or in part? Fourth, what of it: why does what it says matter, to the author and to you, and what follows from it?

The order matters. The first two questions are about understanding the book; the last two are about judging it and weighing its significance. Later in the book these four questions become the rules of analytical reading.
card.example: Applied to a book on sleep science: (1) It is about why we sleep, developed through parts on the brain, the body and habits. (2) It argues that most adults are short of sleep, using studies of memory and health. (3) Is that argument sound, wholly or partly? (4) If it is, what should change in my own evenings?
card.rule: Ask four questions in order: what is it about as a whole, what is said in detail and how, is it true, and what of it.
card.limits: As stated, the four questions fit expository works such as nonfiction. Fiction and poetry need adapted versions, which the authors take up in later chapters.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

concepts.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
concepts.title: Judge truth after understanding, then do judge
concepts.question: When may you ask whether a book is true, and why is knowing the author's mind not enough?

paragraphs: The third question, is it true, cannot be answered until the first two are. You have to know what is being said before you can decide whether it is true. A verdict on a book you have not understood is a verdict on something you imagined.

The authors push the other way too. Once you understand a book, and you are reading seriously, you are obliged to make up your own mind. Knowing what the author thinks is not the end of reading; you must decide what you think.
The verdict need not be all or nothing. The question asks whether the book is true in whole or in part, so a reader may accept some claims and reject others.
card.example: Mia reads a book claiming that standing desks improve health. Halfway through she is tempted to dismiss it, but first she works out what the author claims and from which studies. Having understood, she decides the evidence on back pain is strong but the claim about longer life is not shown. That is a judgment in part.
card.rule: Find out what the book says before asking whether it is true, and once you understand it, reach your own verdict.
card.limits: The order puts understanding first; it does not excuse you from judging. A reader who understands a book but declines to make up his mind has stopped short of what serious reading asks.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

concepts.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
concepts.title: What of it? Asking about significance
concepts.question: Once you understand and have judged a book, what question remains, and how does it differ for information and enlightenment?

paragraphs: The fourth question asks about significance. If a book has given you information, ask why the author thinks it is important to know these things, and whether it is important to you to know them.

If the book has done more than inform you, if it has enlightened you, the question reaches further: what else follows, what is implied or suggested beyond what the author says? Understanding gained opens onto further understanding to seek.
This question comes last for a reason. You need the first three answered before you can weigh a book's significance, even if only in your own scheme of things.
card.example: A book on bees reports that colonies have collapsed in many regions. Asking what of it, a reader notes the author's reason, that many crops depend on pollinators, and her own, that she grows fruit. Because the book also explained why colonies fail, she goes on to ask what that implies for the pesticide her town sprays.
card.rule: After judging a book, ask why what it says matters to the author and to you, and what further follows from it.
card.limits: Asked too early, the question builds on sand. A reader who leaps to applications before understanding and judging the book may draw consequences from a misreading or from a claim that is false.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

concepts.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
concepts.title: The four questions at every level
concepts.question: How well does each level of reading answer the four questions, and what kinds of text deserve them?

paragraphs: The four questions apply to anything worth reading: a book, an article, even an advertisement. They are not reserved for great books.

Levels answer them unevenly. Inspectional reading gives more accurate answers to the first two questions than to the last two, though it helps with all four. An analytical reading is not finished until you can answer the last two: some idea of the book's truth, wholly or in part, and of its significance, if only to you.
In syntopical reading, where you read several books on one subject, the last question, what of it, is probably the most important of the four.
card.example: A ten-minute look at a book on negotiation tells Sara it is a practical guide in three parts: preparing, bargaining and closing. That answers the first two questions roughly. Whether its tactics work, and whether they suit her job, stay guesses until she reads it analytically.
card.rule: Ask the four questions of anything worth reading, and do not count an analytical reading done until you can say whether it is true and what of it.
card.limits: Answers to the questions of truth and significance that come from an inspectional reading are provisional. Treat them as hunches to test in a closer reading, not as verdicts.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

concepts.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
concepts.title: Habit, art, and the skill to stretch
concepts.question: Why do willing readers still tire over good books, and what marks a reader who is both demanding and skilled?

paragraphs: Knowing the four questions is not enough. You must remember to ask them as you read; that habit marks a demanding reader. You must also know how to answer them precisely and accurately; that trained ability is the art of reading.

People fall asleep over good books not because they refuse the effort but because they do not know how to make it. Good books are over your head; they would not be good for you otherwise. A book above your level wears you out unless you can reach up to it.

What tires you is not the stretching but stretching unsuccessfully, for lack of skill. To keep reading actively you need both the will and the skill to lift yourself to what at first seems beyond you.
card.example: Two runners take on a steep hill. One has plenty of determination but no idea of pacing and stops halfway, frustrated. The other paces and breathes with practised technique and reaches the top tired but satisfied. The authors see readers of hard books split the same way: will gets you to the hill, skill gets you up it.
card.rule: Bring both the will and the skill: remember to ask the questions, and learn to answer them precisely.
card.limits: Skill does not make a good book effortless; it turns tiring frustration into productive effort. And will alone, without technique, ends in the frustration the authors describe.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

concepts.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
concepts.title: Write between the lines to own a book
concepts.question: When does a book truly become yours, and why do the authors want a pencil in your hand?

paragraphs: Asking questions is not enough; you must try to answer them. In theory you could do that in your head, but it is much easier with a pencil in hand. The pencil becomes the sign of your alertness while you read.
There is an old saying that you must read between the lines. The authors add: write between the lines too. Unless you do, you are unlikely to read in the most efficient way.

Buying a book gives you a property right in it, as buying a coat does. But purchase is only the prelude. Full ownership comes when you make the book part of yourself, and the best way to do that is by writing in it.
card.example: Two colleagues buy the same management book. One keeps it spotless on a shelf. The other fills its margins with questions, objections and short summaries. Both own the book legally; according to the authors, only the second has begun to own it in the fuller sense.
card.rule: Read with a pencil and write your answers and reactions in the book, so that it becomes part of you.
card.limits: The marks matter because they record your thinking. Idle highlighting that answers nothing is not what the authors mean; writing counts when it holds your questions, answers and reactions.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

concepts.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
concepts.title: Three reasons to mark a book
concepts.question: Why do the authors call marking a book indispensable to reading it?

paragraphs: The authors give three reasons. First, marking keeps you awake: not merely conscious, but wide awake.

Second, active reading is thinking, and thinking tends to express itself in words, spoken or written. Someone who says he knows what he thinks but cannot express it usually does not know what he thinks. Writing tests whether a thought is really there.
Third, writing your reactions down helps you remember the thoughts of the author.
card.example: After a chapter on inflation, Leo feels he understood it. He tries to write one margin note stating the chapter's main point and cannot get past half a sentence. By the authors' second reason, he has found out that he does not yet know what he thinks, while there is still time to reread.
card.rule: Mark as you read to stay wide awake, to put your thinking into words, and to fix the author's thoughts in memory.
card.limits: The reasons assume the marks hold your own thinking. Copying the author's words, or marking out of habit, keeps the hand busy without testing a thought in words.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

concepts.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
concepts.title: Reading as a conversation with the author
concepts.question: In what sense is reading a conversation, and when do the authors say you may argue with the author?

paragraphs: The authors describe reading a book as a conversation between you and the author, who presumably knows more about the subject than you do.
Understanding runs both ways. The learner has to question himself and question the teacher. He even has to be willing to argue with the teacher, once he understands what the teacher is saying.
Marking a book records that conversation: it expresses where you differ from the author and where you agree. The authors call it the highest respect you can pay him.
card.example: Beside a claim that cities should scrap minimum parking rules, Lou writes: why? Two pages later, having followed the argument, he writes: agreed for downtown, but what about suburbs with no buses? His margin now holds a question, an agreement and a disagreement, each made at the right time.
card.rule: Treat reading as a conversation: question yourself and the author, and argue once you understand.
card.limits: Arguing is earned by understanding. Objections written before you grasp the author's point are talking past him, not conversing with him.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

concepts.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
concepts.title: Marks that pick out what matters
concepts.question: Which marks pick out important passages, and how sparingly should the strongest one be used?

paragraphs: The authors list devices for marking a book. Several pick out what matters. Underlining marks major points and important or forceful statements. Circling key words or phrases does much the same job as underlining.
Vertical lines in the margin stress a statement already underlined, or point to a passage too long to underline.

A star, asterisk or similar mark in the margin is for the ten or dozen most important statements or passages in the whole book, used sparingly. Folding the corner of those pages, or slipping paper between them, lets you later open the book at them and refresh your memory.
card.example: In a 300-page history, Ivy underlines the author's main claims, circles the terms coup and junta, draws a margin line beside a two-page account of the decisive meeting, and stars eleven passages in the whole book. A year later, the slips at her starred pages let her review the book's core in twenty minutes.
card.rule: Underline or circle key points and terms, use margin lines for emphasis or long passages, and save stars for the dozen most important passages.
card.limits: The strongest mark works only if it is rare. A star on every page no longer picks out the dozen passages that matter, so the slips and folded corners lead nowhere useful.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

concepts.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
concepts.title: Marks that connect and comment
concepts.question: Which marks trace an argument's steps and link scattered passages, and what goes in the margins in words?

paragraphs: Numbers in the margin show a sequence of points the author makes in developing an argument: 1, 2, 3 beside each step.

Page numbers in the margin show where else in the book the author makes the same point, a related one, or a contradictory one. They tie together ideas that belong together though many pages apart. Many readers write Cf before them, meaning compare or refer to.

Writing in the margin, or at the top or bottom of the page, records the questions a passage raises (and perhaps answers), reduces a complicated discussion to a simple statement, and tracks the sequence of major points through the book.
card.example: On page 88 of an economics book, Tara numbers the author's four steps toward the claim that rent control cuts housing supply. Beside step 3 she writes Cf 41, where the author said something that seems to cut the other way. At the foot of the page she writes: price caps shrink supply, but does that square with page 41?
card.rule: Number the steps of an argument, cross-reference related pages, and write your questions and summaries in the margins.
card.limits: These marks map the author's argument only if they follow it. Numbering points the author does not link, or citing pages that are not really related, draws a false map of the book.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

concepts.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
concepts.title: Endpapers: a personal index and an outline
concepts.question: What belongs on a book's back and front endpapers, and why is the front outline a measure of understanding?

paragraphs: The blank endpapers give room for notes on the whole book. At the back, make a personal index of the author's points in the order of their appearance.

To habitual markers the front endpapers matter most. Some people save them for a fancy bookplate, but that shows only financial ownership. After finishing the book and the back index, turn to the front and outline the book as an integrated structure, with a basic outline and an order of parts, not page by page or point by point.
That outline measures your understanding of the work. Unlike a bookplate, it expresses your intellectual ownership of the book.
card.example: After finishing a history of medicine, Sam lists on the back endpapers thirty points with page numbers, in order. On the front he writes: Part 1, medicine before germs; Part 2, the germ revolution; Part 3, the age of antibiotics, noting how each part leads to the next. The back is his index; the front is his grasp of the whole.
card.rule: Index the author's points in order at the back, and after finishing, outline the book's integrated structure at the front.
card.limits: A front outline that lists points one after another is the back index again. It measures understanding only when it shows how the parts fit into a whole.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

concepts.title: Structural notes in inspectional reading
concepts.question: What notes fit an inspectional reading, what questions do they answer, and where in the book should they go?

paragraphs: The kind of notes you make depends on the level at which you are reading. Inspectional reading is limited in time, so there may be little room for notes, yet it answers important questions, and it is worth recording the answers while they are fresh.

Inspectional reading answers three questions: what kind of book is it, what is it about as a whole, and what is the structural order by which the author develops that subject? The best place for notes on these answers is the contents page, or perhaps the title page.

These notes concern the book's structure, not its substance, at least not in detail. The authors call them structural notes. They are especially worth making if days or months may pass before an analytical reading.
card.example: Jon inspects a book on climate science before a trip. On the contents page he writes: theoretical, science for general readers; about how the climate system works and is changing; three parts, physics, evidence, projections. Two months later he opens it for an analytical reading and starts from his own map.
card.rule: During an inspectional reading, note on the contents or title page what kind of book it is, what it is about, and how it is ordered.
card.limits: Structural notes stop at structure. Judgments of whether the book's statements are accurate or true belong to a later, careful reading, not to these notes.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

concepts.title: Conceptual notes in analytical reading
concepts.question: What do conceptual notes record, at which levels are they made, and how do they differ from structural notes?

paragraphs: An inspectional reading may give you some insight into the author's ideas, but often it will not, and judging the truth or accuracy of statements should wait for a more careful reading. During an analytical reading you must answer questions about the book's truth and significance.

So notes made at the analytical level are conceptual. Structural notes, made in inspectional reading, record only a book's kind, subject and plan. Conceptual notes concern the author's concepts, and also your own, as your reading has deepened or broadened them.
In syntopical reading, when you read several books on one subject, notes again tend to be conceptual.
card.example: Reading a book on free will analytically, Rosa writes beside chapter 4: by free the author means not forced from outside; I had meant uncaused, so his argument is narrower than I thought. The note records his concept and the change in hers.
card.rule: In analytical reading, make conceptual notes on the author's ideas and on how your own ideas have changed.
card.limits: Conceptual notes are not for a first inspection. Recording verdicts on truth during a quick look skips the careful reading those verdicts need.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

concepts.title: Dialectical notes on a whole discussion
concepts.question: What notes can an expert syntopical reader make beyond conceptual ones, and why do they often need separate sheets?

paragraphs: Beyond conceptual notes there is a further step that a truly expert reader can take when reading several books syntopically: notes on the shape of the discussion itself, the discussion all the authors are engaged in, even if they do not know it. The authors call these dialectical notes.

Because they concern several books rather than one, dialectical notes often have to go on a separate sheet or sheets of paper. They imply a structure of concepts: an ordered set of statements and questions about a single subject. The authors return to them in Chapter 20.
card.example: After five books on whether zoos should exist, Noor writes on a separate sheet: Question 1, do animals have a right to liberty? A and C say yes, B and E say no, D does not address it. Question 2, can conservation justify captivity? B, D and E agree it can. Her sheet maps a debate no single author set out.
card.rule: When reading several books on one subject, map the questions and the authors' positions on separate sheets.
card.limits: Dialectical notes need several books and an expert reader; one book has no cross-author discussion to map. They also rest on conceptual notes: you must grasp each author's ideas before placing them in the debate.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

concepts.title: Skill is a habit formed by doing
concepts.question: What does it mean to possess a skill such as reading, and how is that different from knowing its rules?

paragraphs: Any art or skill belongs to those who have formed the habit of operating according to its rules. That is what separates the skilled craftsman from someone who lacks the skill.

The only way to form a habit of operating is by operating: you learn to do by doing. Practice changes your facility and readiness. What you did badly at first, you come to do with almost automatic ease, as if you were born to it. That is what it means to call habit second nature.

Knowing the rules is not the same as having the habit. Yet you need the rules: you cannot follow rules you do not know, and you cannot acquire a skill without following rules. The art as taught is a set of rules; the art as possessed is the habit those rules produce.
card.example: Two people have read the same guide to touch typing. One can recite where each finger belongs but still hunts for the keys. The other has drilled every day for a month and types without looking. Both know the rules; only the second has the skill.
card.rule: Learn the rules, then practise them until operating by them becomes habit; only the habit counts as the skill.
card.limits: Practice without the rules does not build the skill, because you cannot follow rules you do not know. And rules you can recite but have not practised give knowledge about the art, not the art itself.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

concepts.title: Original artists still follow rules
concepts.question: Does highly original work show that skilled artists ignore rules, and which rules do they follow?

paragraphs: Some people point to a highly original painter or sculptor and say he follows no rules, since he is doing something never done before. The authors think this misses which rules the artist follows.

There are no final, unbreakable rules for making a painting or a sculpture. But there are rules for preparing canvas, mixing and applying paint, moulding clay and welding steel. The artist must have followed those, or he could not have made the work.

However original the result, and however little it obeys the traditional rules of art, the artist had to be skilled to produce it. That skill, the craft, is the art the authors mean, and it consists in operating by rules.
card.example: A sculptor makes a piece unlike anything seen before: twisted steel that seems to float. Critics call it lawless. Yet to make it she had to cut, bend and weld steel so the joints would hold, following the rules of welding exactly. Her originality lies in what she made, not in skipping the craft.
card.rule: Behind any original work, look for the craft rules the maker had to follow; originality rests on skill, not on its absence.
card.limits: The claim covers the rules of craft, not rules of style or taste. An artist can break traditional conventions about what art should look like; what he cannot skip are the rules for handling his materials.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

concepts.section: From Many Rules to One Habit
concepts.title: Learn the acts separately, then fuse them
concepts.question: Why must the separate acts of a complex skill be learned one at a time before they can run together?

paragraphs: The authors compare reading to skiing. Done by an expert, both are graceful; done by a beginner, both are awkward, frustrating and slow. An adult on skis must almost learn to walk again, and the instructor's list of commands seems endless.

The expert skier does not think about the separate acts; he looks ahead, anticipates bumps and enjoys the run. You must learn to forget the separate acts to perform them well. But to forget them as separate acts, you must first learn them as separate acts.

Reading is the same. You cannot fuse many acts into one smooth performance until you are good at each. Each act needs your full attention while you do it. After practising the parts separately, you do each with more ease and less attention, and gradually put them together into a smoothly running whole.
card.example: Learning analytical reading, Omar spends a few weeks only classifying books and stating their unity, then a few weeks finding key terms and arguments. At first each step takes all his attention. Months later he classifies, outlines and spots arguments in one flowing reading without thinking about any single step.
card.rule: Practise each act of reading separately with full attention, then let the practised acts combine into one performance.
card.limits: Separate practice is a stage, not the goal; the expert forgets the separate acts. And trying to fuse acts you have not yet mastered one by one is what the authors say cannot be done.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

concepts.section: From Many Rules to One Habit
concepts.title: Many rules, one habit
concepts.question: What does the long list of reading rules really indicate, and where does the reader's attention go once the habit forms?

paragraphs: A newcomer to any complex skill faces an array of rules. Someone who has acquired one complex skill knows not to fear them, nor to worry about how all the separate acts will work together. Recalling your patience in learning another skill makes you more tolerant of a long list of reading rules.

The number of rules shows how complex the one habit is, not that there are many distinct habits. As each part becomes automatic, the parts coalesce. When the subordinate acts run more or less on their own, you have the habit of the whole performance.

Then attention can move. The beginner attends to himself and his skill in the separate acts. Once the acts have lost their separateness, the reader attends to the goal his technique lets him reach, such as a book he once thought too hard for him.
card.example: A typist once thought about every key; now she thinks only about the sentence she is writing. A practised reader likewise stops asking himself which rule comes next and thinks about what the author means.
card.rule: Treat the many rules as parts of one habit, be patient while they fuse, and let your attention move from technique to the book.
card.limits: The fusing comes only after separate practice; a beginner cannot jump straight to attending only to the goal. A long list of rules is no reason for despair, but it is no reason to skip any of them either.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader

concepts.title: Why the rules speak of whole books
concepts.question: Why are the rules of analytical reading stated for whole books, and what do they mean for an article or a short story?

paragraphs: The rules of analytical reading are stated for whole books, yet the authors say they apply to anything you read. They choose whole books because reading a long, difficult book poses the hardest problems a reader can face.

Skill carries downward within a kind of writing. Reading a short story is almost always easier than reading a novel, and an article almost always easier than a book on the same subject. If you can read a history or a scientific treatise, you can read an article or an abstract in the same field.
So when the rules mention books, take them to cover shorter and easier pieces of the same kinds as well. Now and then a rule fits a short piece less fully; then you adapt it rather than drop it.
card.example: Maya has learned to read long economics books analytically. Handed a ten-page economics article, she brings the same rules: what kind of piece is it, what is it about, what does it argue? Where a rule asks about the parts of a whole book, she applies it to the article's sections.
card.rule: Bring the rules learned on whole books to shorter pieces of the same kind, adapting a rule where it fits less fully.
card.limits: The authors pair each long form with shorter pieces of the same kind, so skill with novels is offered as help with short stories, not with lab reports. A rule built for a long book may also need trimming to fit a single page.

concepts.title: Rule 1: know the kind, early
concepts.question: What does the first rule of analytical reading ask of you, and how early should you meet it?

paragraphs: The first rule of analytical reading is about classification. You must know what kind of book you are reading, and you should know it as early in the process as possible, preferably before you begin to read.
The rule has two parts. Knowing the kind is a must. Knowing it early is a should: the sooner you know the kind, the sooner it can guide what you look for.
Hence the chapter's title, pigeonholing: you place the book in a category, as a clerk sorts letters into pigeonholes, before you start working on it.
card.example: Before starting a book titled The Craft of Sail Repair, Tom reads the title, the contents and the preface, and decides it is a book that teaches a skill rather than a story. He makes the call in a few minutes, before chapter one, so it can shape his reading from the first page.
card.rule: Decide what kind of book you have as early as you can, preferably before you begin to read it.
card.limits: An early classification is a working judgment, not a final verdict. Some books cannot be placed from the outside, and you may have to read some way into the text before you can say what kind they are.

concepts.title: Fiction or expository
concepts.question: What makes a book expository rather than fiction, and how broadly do the authors take the word knowledge?

paragraphs: The first split in classifying is between fiction, such as novels, plays, epics and lyric poems, and expository works. Most readers can tell one from the other at a glance.

An expository book is one that mainly conveys knowledge, and the authors take knowledge broadly. A book made up mostly of opinions, theories, hypotheses or speculations counts, provided it claims that they are true in some sense.
So the test is not whether the claims are proven, or whether you accept them. It is whether the book offers them as true, rather than telling a story.
card.example: A book argues that cities should ban cars from their centres, with reasons and forecasts. Many readers will reject its view, and its forecasts are speculation. Still, it offers them as true, so it is expository, not fiction.
card.rule: Call a book expository when it mainly offers claims as true in some sense, and fiction when it mainly tells a story.
card.limits: Placing a book as expository is only a first step: it does not yet tell you how the book instructs. And the line between fiction and exposition is not always sharp.

concepts.title: When fiction and exposition blur
concepts.question: Why can a novel be hard to tell from a social study, and which signs should not settle the question?

paragraphs: Telling fiction from exposition looks easy, yet it is not always so. Some contemporary novels carry so much social science, and some sociology so much fiction, that the two are hard to keep apart.

The authors' examples include novels that read like studies of town life, farm life, drug abuse or a period of history. All were in fact novels and sold as fiction. Novels can carry physics and chemistry too, as some science fiction does.
Readability is no guide either. A popular book explaining relativity is not fiction, yet it can read as easily as a novel, and more easily than some demanding novelists.
card.example: A novel follows one family through a factory town's decline, packed with wage figures and union history. It could pass for a sociological study, but it is built as a story about invented people, so it is fiction.
card.rule: When a book could pass for fiction or for a study, decide by whether it tells a story or offers claims as true, not by readability or a list's label.
card.limits: A list category, a publisher's label or a lively style can point the right way; none of them settles the question. Some books really are partly both, and then you can only say which side dominates.

concepts.title: In what way does it instruct?
concepts.question: Once you know a book is expository, what more must you find out about the way it instructs?

paragraphs: Most people know an expository book when they see one. The harder task is to see that there are various kinds of expository book. It is not enough to know that a book instructs; you need to know in what particular way it instructs.
A history and a philosophical work give different kinds of enlightenment. A book on physics and one on morals deal with different problems, and their writers use different methods to solve them.
That is why the authors say Rule 1, though it applies to all books, applies particularly to expository works: there the kinds are many, and their differences shape how you should read.
card.example: Two books both have happiness in the title. One traces what thinkers through the centuries said about it; the other argues what a happy life consists in. Both instruct, but one reports past views and the other reasons toward a conclusion, so you would bring different questions to each.
card.rule: For an expository book, go on to name the particular way it instructs: the kind of problem it takes up and the kind of method it uses.
card.limits: At this stage you need only the broad kind, such as history, philosophy or physics; finer distinctions come later. Naming the kind also tells you nothing yet about whether the book succeeds.

concepts.title: Front matter as signal flags
concepts.question: Where do you look to classify a book before reading it, and whose fault is it if the signs are missed?

paragraphs: How do you meet Rule 1 before you begin to read? By inspecting the book: read the title, the subtitle and the table of contents, at least glance at the preface or introduction and at the index, and read the publisher's blurb if there is one.
The authors call these the signal flags the author waves to let you know which way the wind is blowing. They are there to help you place the book.
If you miss them, the fault is yours, not the author's. The signals work only for a reader who will stop, look and listen.
card.example: A book's subtitle reads A Practical Guide for New Managers, its contents run from hiring to running meetings, and its blurb promises tools for the first year. A few minutes with these flags tells you it teaches how to do something, before you read a page.
card.rule: To classify a book before reading it, read its title, subtitle, contents, preface, index and blurb as signals of its kind.
card.limits: Signals help only a reader who stops to read them. Some books give weak or confusing signals, and then you have to classify from the text itself.

concepts.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
concepts.title: Ask: what sort of book is this?
concepts.question: Why do the authors open any discussion of a book by asking what sort of book it is?

paragraphs: Many readers pay no attention to the signals. The authors found this with students again and again: asked in the most general terms what sort of book they had read, the students often could give no answer.

Yet the authors call this question a good, almost indispensable way to begin discussing a book. One reason readers ignore titles and prefaces is that they do not think classifying a book is important.
A reader who cannot answer the question, and never asks it of himself, will be unable to answer many other questions about the book. His confusion grows rather than clears.
card.example: Asked what kind of book he is reading, Leo says a really interesting one. That is a verdict, not a kind. Asked again, he says a book explaining how the London Underground was engineered, and now he knows what to look for as he reads.
card.rule: Begin reading or discussing any book by stating, in the most general terms, what sort of book it is.
card.limits: Asking is not answering: a label such as a good read or a classic names a verdict, not a kind. A general answer is enough to start with, and it may need revising as you read.

concepts.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
concepts.title: Read the title, word for word
concepts.question: What goes wrong when readers think they already know a title, and how does Darwin's book show it?

paragraphs: Many people think they know a book's title without ever having read it carefully. The authors asked about twenty-five well-read people for the title of Darwin's 1859 book, and more than half said The Origin of the Species.
The extra word is not harmless. Those readers assumed the book was about the human species. It has little or nothing to do with that subject, which Darwin took up in a later book, The Descent of Man.

The Origin of Species is about what its title says: how a vast number of species of plants and animals arose from far fewer, mainly through natural selection. Reading each word of the title, and asking what it means, would have told them so.
card.example: A book is titled Why Nations Fail. Read word for word, it promises an explanation (why) of a general pattern (nations, plural) of failure, not the story of one country and not a guide to success. Each word narrows what you should expect.
card.rule: Read the exact title word by word, and ask what each word tells you about the book.
card.limits: A title is a compressed promise, not a summary. Reading it carefully narrows your expectations, but a word may be used in an unusual sense, so test what the title suggests against the contents and preface.

concepts.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
concepts.title: Draw inferences from the title
concepts.question: What can a title tell you about where a book begins and ends, and how did Gibbon's readers miss it?
