paragraphs: Reading a title carefully means drawing inferences from it, not only getting its words right. Gibbon's famous history is called The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, and almost everyone knows that title.

Yet the same well-read people could not say why its first chapter describes the extent and military force of the Empire in the Age of the Antonines. They were puzzled to find no account of the Roman Republic.

Without noticing, they had turned decline and fall into rise and fall. A book about a decline should begin at the high point; read with care, the title would have told them that the Age of the Antonines was that high point.
card.example: A book is titled The Last Days of the Silk Road Caravans. The word last tells you to expect it to open with the caravans still running, perhaps at their height, and to follow them to their end, rather than to start with how the routes were founded.
card.rule: Before reading, work out what the title implies about the book's scope, its starting point and its end.
card.limits: A title's implications can be pushed too far: decline implies a high point to start from, but not how long the decline lasted or what caused it. Infer the frame, and leave the details to the book.

concepts.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
concepts.title: Prefaces and chapter headings
concepts.question: What do authors put in prefaces and chapter headings to help you classify, and how should you use it?

paragraphs: Authors think it important for readers to know what kind of book they are being given. That is why they make the kind plain in the preface, and usually try to make the title, or at least the subtitle, descriptive.

Einstein and Infeld, in the preface to The Evolution of Physics, say they expect the reader to know that a scientific book, even a popular one, must not be read in the same way as a novel. They also give an analytical table of contents to show the details of their treatment in advance.
In any book, the chapter headings listed at the front amplify the meaning of the main title. A reader who ignores all this has only himself to blame if he cannot say what kind of book it is.
card.example: A book has the plain title Sleep. Its contents run: what sleep is; the brain at night; sleep across species; what happens when we go without. The headings expand the one-word title into an explanatory, scientific book rather than a self-help guide.
card.rule: Read the preface and the chapter headings for what the author says about the book's kind and about how it should be read.
card.limits: A preface shows what the author intends, and an author can describe a book better than the book carries it out. Treat the preface as strong evidence of kind, then confirm it against the contents and the text.

concepts.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
concepts.title: Bring categories with you
concepts.question: Why can even the clearest title fail to help you classify a book, and what must you already have in mind?

paragraphs: Reading titles is important, but it is not enough. The clearest titles and the most explicit front matter will not help you classify a book unless you already have the broad lines of classification in your mind.

Take Euclid's Elements of Geometry and William James' Principles of Psychology. You will not see how they are books of the same sort unless you know that geometry and psychology are both sciences, and that elements and principles mean much the same in these two titles.

Nor can you tell the two apart unless you know there are different kinds of science. Likewise, to see how Aristotle's Politics and Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations are alike and different, you must know what a practical problem is, and what kinds there are.
card.example: Two titles: Principles of Optics and Principles of Ethics. A reader with no categories sees two textbooks. A reader who carries categories asks whether each is a science, of what kind, and whether either is about what we should do. The titles alone answer none of this.
card.rule: Carry a set of categories into every book, so that its title and front matter have somewhere to place it.
card.limits: Categories help only if they are sound; a crude scheme places books crudely. And a shared title word, such as principles, does not mean the same thing in every book: in Euclid's and James' titles it happens to match, not in general.

concepts.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
concepts.title: Group books, then name the kind
concepts.question: When titles do not show that books belong together, how can you group them, and why is grouping not enough?

paragraphs: Titles sometimes make grouping easy: anyone can see that Euclid's Elements, Descartes' Geometry and Hilbert's Foundations of Geometry are three mathematical books.

Often they do not. From their titles alone it is hard to tell that Augustine's The City of God, Hobbes' Leviathan and Rousseau's Social Contract are political treatises. A careful look through their chapter headings would reveal the problems the three have in common.
Even then, grouping books as the same kind is not enough. To follow Rule 1 you must know what that kind is, and the title and front matter will not tell you unless you have categories to apply.
card.example: Three books are titled The Hive, Common Ground and The Long Table. Their chapter headings all deal with who should hold authority, how laws are made and what citizens owe one another. The headings group them; naming the group, political treatises, is a further step.
card.rule: When titles hide what books share, look through their chapter headings for common problems, and then name the kind they share.
card.limits: Shared problems in the headings suggest a group; they do not yet fix its kind. A group with no name, books that are somehow alike, does not meet Rule 1.

concepts.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
concepts.title: A rough scheme, without principles
concepts.question: What rough scheme of classification do the authors start from, and what does it still lack?

paragraphs: The authors' rough scheme has one main split, between works of fiction and expository works. Among expository works it further separates history from philosophy, and both of these from science and mathematics.
The categories are fairly clear, and most people could place most books in them if they thought about it. But not all books in all categories.

The trouble is that the scheme has no principles of classification, nothing that says why the lines fall where they do. So the authors add one basic distinction that applies across all expository works: between theoretical and practical books.
card.example: A reader sorts her shelf: a novel about a whaling voyage goes to fiction, a life of Lincoln to history, a geometry text to mathematics, a study of volcanoes to science, an essay on the nature of time to philosophy. Most of her books find a slot within a minute.
card.rule: Use fiction, history, philosophy, science and mathematics as a first sorting, and add the theoretical and practical distinction to handle what the first sorting cannot.
card.limits: The scheme is rough: it lists categories without saying why they are the right ones. It gives you slots, but no way of settling the hard cases.

concepts.title: Knowledge or action
concepts.question: What do theoretical and practical really mean, once the hardheaded man's rough view of them is polished?

paragraphs: Everyone uses the words theoretical and practical, but not everyone knows what they mean. To the hardheaded practical man, theoretical means visionary or even mystical, and practical means something that works and pays off at once.
There is an element of truth in this. The practical has to do with what works in some way, at once or in the long run. The theoretical concerns something to be seen or understood.

Polish that rough truth and you reach the distinction the authors use: knowledge and action are the two ends a writer may have in mind. A theoretical book aims at knowledge; a practical book aims at action.
card.example: One book on bridges explains why arches carry loads as they do. Another sets out how to design and build a footbridge over a stream. Both are about bridges; the first aims at your understanding, the second at what you will do.
card.rule: Classify an expository book by its end: theoretical if it aims at knowledge, practical if it aims at action.
card.limits: Practical does not mean quick to pay off, and theoretical does not mean dreamy or useless. A practical book may aim at action only in the long run, and a theoretical one may prove useful without aiming to be.

concepts.title: Practical books convey knowledge too
concepts.question: If expository books convey knowledge, how can some of them aim at action instead?

paragraphs: A puzzle: expository books convey knowledge, so how does action come into it? The answer is that intelligent action depends on knowledge. Knowledge can be used to control nature and invent useful machines, and also to direct human conduct and regulate skilled work in many fields.
The authors compare the distinction to the one between pure and applied science.

Some books and teachers limit themselves to the knowledge itself. They do not deny its usefulness; they leave its application to others. Those others care about the problems of human life that knowledge can help solve, and teach knowledge with an emphasis on its application.
card.example: Two chemistry teachers cover the same reactions. One explains why they happen and stops there, without claiming the knowledge is useless. The other teaches the same reactions as tools for making fertiliser safely. Both convey knowledge; only the second does so with a view to applying it.
card.rule: Treat a book as practical when it conveys knowledge with a view to applying it, and as theoretical when it stops at the knowledge itself.
card.limits: A theoretical writer is not hostile to use and need not think knowledge is good only for its own sake; he limits his task. A theoretical book's silence about applications is not a claim that there are none.

concepts.title: Knowing that, knowing how
concepts.question: What must happen to knowledge to make it practical, and how does knowing that differ from knowing how?

paragraphs: To make knowledge practical, we must convert it into rules of operation. We must pass from knowing what is the case to knowing what to do about it, if we want to get somewhere.

The authors sum this up as the difference between knowing that and knowing how. Theoretical books teach you that something is the case. Practical books teach you how to do something you want to do, or think you should do.
The test, then, is what the book leaves you with: a truth to understand, or a rule to follow.
card.example: Book A shows that sound loses strength with distance from its source. Book B tells you how to place speakers in a hall so that everyone hears clearly. B rests on truths of A's kind, but turns them into rules of operation.
card.rule: Ask whether a book teaches that something is so or how to do something: the first is theoretical, the second practical.
card.limits: A practical book contains many statements that something is the case, and a theoretical one may mention what follows for practice. Classify by what the book as a whole is for, not by single sentences.

concepts.title: What counts as practical
concepts.question: Which books fall in the practical class, and why do treatises on ethics and politics belong there alongside manuals?

paragraphs: Any book that tells you either what you should do or how to do it is practical. The authors say their own book is practical, not theoretical, and that any guidebook is practical.

So the practical class includes every exposition of an art to be learned, every manual of practice in a field such as engineering, medicine or cooking, and every treatise conveniently called moral, such as books on economic, ethical or political problems.
The authors call this last group normative, and promise to explain later why it is a very special category of practical books.
card.example: Three books: a manual on wiring a house, a guide to writing persuasive essays, and a treatise arguing how a just state should tax its citizens. The first two tell you how to do something; the third tells you what should be done. All three are practical.
card.rule: Count as practical any book that tells you what you should do or how to do it, from cookery manuals to treatises on ethics and politics.
card.limits: A field's name is a hint, not a verdict: a book in economics or politics that only reports or measures is not practical. Telling you what to do also differs from telling you what others did.

concepts.title: Disagreeing does not make a book impractical
concepts.question: If you think a book's advice is wrong or would not work, does that make it a theoretical book?

paragraphs: The hardheaded man might deny that a book on ethics or economics is practical, on the ground that it is not true or would not work. The authors call this beside the point, though a book on economics that is not true is a bad book.

Any ethical work teaches us how to live, tells us what we should and should not do, and often states the rewards and penalties. So whether or not we agree with its conclusions, it is practical. The same holds for most works on economics.

Kant's Critique of Practical Reason grounds right conduct in duty, an emphasis many modern readers find repellent and call impractical. What they mean is that Kant is wrong. That does not make his book any less practical.
card.example: A reader dislikes a diet book's plan and is sure it would fail. She may be right, and then it is a bad diet book. But it still tells people what to eat and how, so it remains a practical book, and she should read it as one.
card.rule: Classify a book by what it aims to do, not by whether you agree with it or think its advice would work.
card.limits: The class says nothing about quality: a practical book can be wrong, and then it is a bad practical book. Judging whether its advice is sound is a separate, later task.

concepts.title: Reporting behaviour is theoretical
concepts.question: When is a book about society or economics theoretical rather than practical?

paragraphs: Some modern sociological studies only report how people actually behave, without judging it. The authors say these are neither ethical nor practical books; they are theoretical works, works of science.

The same holds in economics. Reportorial, mathematical or statistical studies of economic behaviour are theoretical. Other works on economics usually teach how to organise economic life, say what should and should not be done, and warn of the penalties for not doing it.
So the line runs between describing what people do and prescribing what they should do, whatever the field.
card.example: Two books on gambling. One surveys how often people in different age groups gamble and how much they lose. The other argues that governments should limit gambling advertising. The first describes, so it is theoretical; the second prescribes, so it is practical.
card.rule: Classify a book on human behaviour as theoretical if it only reports or measures what people do, and practical if it judges what they should do.
card.limits: A report can be framed to push a view, and a statistical study may end with recommendations. Look at what the book as a whole sets out to do, not at whether it contains numbers.

concepts.title: Practical books also persuade
concepts.question: Why does every practical book contain some oratory, and what should you expect from its author?

paragraphs: Besides manuals and moral treatises, there is one more kind of practical writing: the oration, such as a political speech or a moral exhortation. It tries to tell you what you should do or how you should feel about something.

Anyone who writes practically not only tries to advise you but also tries to persuade you to follow the advice. So there is an element of oratory or exhortation in every moral treatise, and also in books that teach an art.
The authors admit this of their own book: besides teaching you to read better, they try to persuade you to make the effort.
card.example: A guide to saving money explains how to set up a budget, and also tells stories of people who retired early and urges you to start today. The how-to is the advice; the stories and the urging are the persuasion that comes with it.
card.rule: In a practical book, expect persuasion along with the advice, and notice where the author is urging rather than explaining.
card.limits: Persuasion in a practical book is normal, not a sign of dishonesty. But being persuaded to follow advice is not the same as being shown that the advice is sound.

concepts.title: Oratory is not the whole of the practical
concepts.question: If every practical book persuades, what separates a practical treatise from mere oratory or propaganda?

paragraphs: Every practical book is somewhat oratorical and hortatory, but it does not follow that oratory and exhortation cover the whole of the practical.

There is a difference between a political harangue and a treatise on politics, and between economic propaganda and an analysis of economic problems. The Communist Manifesto is a piece of oratory, but Marx's Capital is much more than that.
So when you meet persuasion, ask whether the work is mainly urging you, or analysing a practical problem and then advising.
card.example: Two pamphlets on rent control. One is a page of slogans calling tenants to march on the town hall. The other sets out how rents have moved, weighs three policies and recommends one. Both aim at action; the first is a harangue, the second a short treatise.
card.rule: When a practical work persuades, ask whether it is mainly oratory or an analysis of a practical problem that also advises.
card.limits: The line is a matter of degree: a treatise has some oratory, and a speech may contain some analysis. One author can write both, as Marx did, so judge each work on its own.

concepts.title: Practical titles
concepts.question: Which words and field names in a title signal a practical book, and how far can you trust them?

paragraphs: Sometimes a title shows at once that a book is practical. If it contains phrases such as the art of or how to, you can spot it immediately.
If the title names a field you know to be practical, such as ethics or politics, engineering or business, and in many cases economics, law or medicine, you can classify the book fairly readily.
Note the hedge: economics, law and medicine signal a practical book in many cases, not in all.
card.example: Titles on a shelf: The Art of Bookbinding, How to Lead a Team, Business Ethics for Managers, Engineering Small Dams. Each signals a practical book before you open it: two by their phrases, two by the fields they name.
card.rule: Scan titles for phrases like the art of or how to, and for names of practical fields, as quick signs that a book is practical.
card.limits: Field names are signs, not proof: some books in economics are theoretical, and some titles promise to teach how to do what is mainly a matter of understanding. Confirm the sign with the front matter or the text.

concepts.title: Validity or purpose: Locke's two titles
concepts.question: How can the wording of a title or a stated aim show whether a book asks a theoretical or a practical question?

paragraphs: Titles can tell you more. Locke wrote An Essay Concerning Human Understanding and A Treatise Concerning the Origin, Extent, and End of Civil Government. From the titles alone, the first looks theoretical, since any analysis of understanding would be, and the second practical, since problems of government are practical.

Inspection takes you further. In his introduction to the first book, Locke states his aim: to inquire into the origin, certainty and extent of human knowledge. The phrasing echoes the second title, with one key difference.

In one case Locke asks about certainty, the validity of knowledge; in the other, about the end of government, the purpose it serves. Questions about validity are theoretical; questions about the end or purpose of something are practical.
card.example: Two reports on school tests. One asks how reliable and accurate the tests are as measures of learning. The other asks what the tests are for and whether they serve it. The first asks about validity, so it is theoretical; the second asks about an end, so it is practical.
card.rule: In a title or stated aim, read questions about validity or certainty as theoretical, and questions about the end or purpose of something as practical.
card.limits: A word such as end can be used loosely, and a stated aim may not match what the book goes on to do. Check the aim against the rest of the front matter and the text.

concepts.title: When the front matter fails, read in
concepts.question: What should you do when a book's title and front matter do not show whether it is theoretical or practical?

paragraphs: Inspectional reading does not ordinarily stop at the front matter and the index. You should also read passages that look like summaries, and the beginning and end of the book and of its major parts.
This becomes necessary when a book cannot be classified from its title and front matter. Then you depend on signs in the body of the text.
By attending to the words, and keeping the basic categories in mind, you should be able to classify a book without reading very far.
card.example: A book called Threshold has no subtitle and a contents page of one-word chapters. You read its opening pages, the summary at the end of Part One and its last chapter. They keep saying what a designer should do at each stage of a project, so you place it as practical within twenty minutes.
card.rule: When front matter cannot settle the kind, read summary passages and the opening and closing of the book and its parts, watching the words with your categories in mind.
card.limits: Reading in is for classifying, not judging, and should take minutes, not days. A few samples can mislead if the book changes character between parts, so sample more than one place.

concepts.title: Should and ought, or is
concepts.question: Which words and statements reveal a practical book, and what does a theoretical book keep saying instead?

paragraphs: A practical book soon betrays its character by the frequent use of words such as should and ought, good and bad, ends and means.

Its characteristic statement says that something should be done or made, that this is the right way of doing or making something, or that one thing is better than another as an end to seek or a means to choose.

A theoretical book keeps saying is, not should or ought. It tries to show that something is true, that these are the facts, not that things would be better otherwise and here is the way to make them better.
card.example: Book A: crop yields fall when soil loses nitrogen, and legumes restore it. Book B: farmers should plant legumes every third year, the best means of keeping soil healthy. A keeps saying is; B keeps saying should and best, so B is practical.
card.rule: Listen to a book's characteristic statements: frequent should, ought, good, bad, ends and means mark it as practical; a steady is marks it as theoretical.
card.limits: Single words prove little: a theoretical book may say a result ought to be checked, and a practical one states many facts. Weigh the characteristic statements across passages, not one word in one sentence.

concepts.title: Be suspicious of the signs
concepts.question: Why must you mistrust the signs of practical and theoretical books, and which cases trip readers up?

paragraphs: Telling theoretical from practical is not as simple as telling coffee from milk. The signs are only a start, and the better you understand the distinction, the better you will be able to use them.

You also have to learn to mistrust them. Economics is mainly a practical matter, yet some books on economics are purely theoretical. Understanding is mainly a theoretical matter, yet some books, most of them terrible in the authors' view, claim to teach you how to think.
Some authors do not know the difference between theory and practice, just as some novelists do not know the difference between fiction and sociology.
card.example: A book titled How to Think About the Economy turns out to be a survey of how economists build models, with no advice at all. Its title has a practical phrase and a mostly practical field, yet the book is theoretical. Only a reader who checked past the title would catch it.
card.rule: Treat each sign as evidence to confirm, not a verdict, and check a classification against more than one sign before relying on it.
card.limits: Suspicion should not become paralysis: most books give honest signs, and the aim is a sound working classification, not certainty. Where an author confuses theory and practice, note the confusion rather than forcing a clean label.

concepts.title: Books of two sorts
concepts.question: What should you do with a book that is partly theoretical and partly practical?

paragraphs: Some books are partly of one sort and partly of another. The authors give Spinoza's Ethics as an example.

Even so, the authors say it remains to your advantage as a reader to detect the way an author approaches his problem. In practice, that means asking at each point whether he is trying to show you what is so or to tell you what to do.
A mixed book does not cancel the distinction. It means you apply it with more care, and the label for the whole may need a qualifier, such as mainly theoretical with a practical ending.
card.example: A book on nutrition spends eight chapters on how digestion works and two on what to eat. A careful reader calls it mainly theoretical with a practical ending, and reads each part for what it offers: understanding first, then advice to weigh.
card.rule: When a book mixes the two sorts, still work out how the author approaches his problem, and label the whole with the mix it shows.
card.limits: Do not force a mixed book into one box, and do not give up on classifying it either. A qualified label, such as mainly practical, is an honest result, not a failure.

concepts.title: History: narration, time and place
concepts.question: What marks a theoretical book as history, and what does the word chronotopic remind you of?

paragraphs: The traditional subdivision of theoretical books is history, science and philosophy. Everyone knows the differences roughly; trouble comes when you try to make them precise, so rough approximations will do for now.

For history, the title usually does the trick. If the word history is missing, the front matter is likely to show that the book is about something that happened in the past, perhaps long ago, perhaps only yesterday.

The essence of history is narration: knowledge of particular events or things that existed in the past and changed over time. History is chronotopic, from the Greek chronos, time, and topos, place: it always deals with things at a particular date and place.
card.example: A book follows the building of one railway across a desert between 1880 and 1895, year by year and town by town. It narrates particular events, tied to dates and places, as they changed over time. It is history, though the word never appears in its title.
card.rule: Classify a theoretical book as history when it narrates particular past events or things, tied to definite times and places, as they changed.
card.limits: Past does not mean distant: a history can cover events of last year. And dates alone do not make a history; a book can mention dates while seeking general laws or arguing a point.

concepts.title: Science seeks laws
concepts.question: How does a scientific book's aim differ from a history's, when both deal with facts?

paragraphs: Science is not concerned with the past as such. It treats matters that can happen at any time or place.

The scientist seeks laws or generalisations. He wants to find out how things happen for the most part, or in every case, not, as the historian does, how some particular things happened at a given time and place in the past.
So a history and a science can share a subject yet differ in aim: one narrates particulars, the other seeks what holds generally.
card.example: Two books on volcanoes. One tells the story of the eruption that buried Pompeii in 79 AD. The other explains why volcanoes erupt when pressure builds in magma chambers, wherever and whenever that happens. The first is history; the second is science.
card.rule: Classify a theoretical book as science when it seeks laws or generalisations about what happens at any time or place, for the most part or in every case.
card.limits: A scientific book uses particular cases as evidence, and a history may note patterns. Ask what the book is finally after: the story of particular events, or the general law the cases support.

concepts.title: Why science titles reveal less
concepts.question: Why is a scientific book harder to classify from its title than a history, and what blurs the words science and philosophy?

paragraphs: The title of a scientific work is usually less revealing than that of a history. The word science sometimes appears, but more often the title names a subject, such as psychology, geology or physics.

Then you must know whether that subject belongs to the scientist, as geology clearly does, or to the philosopher, as metaphysics clearly does. The trouble comes with unclear cases, such as physics and psychology, which scientists and philosophers have both claimed at various times.

Even the words have shifted. Aristotle called his Physics a scientific treatise, though today we would call it philosophical; Newton titled his great work Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy, though for us it is a masterpiece of science.
card.example: A book titled Mind could be a laboratory study of memory or a reflection on what a mind is. The subject name does not tell you which, since psychology has been claimed by both scientists and philosophers. You need a further test.
card.rule: Do not classify a book as science or philosophy from its subject name alone; ask whose subject it is, and expect older titles to use the words differently.
card.limits: Some subject names are reliable, such as geology for science and metaphysics for philosophy. The caution applies most to disputed fields and to books written before the words science and philosophy took their present senses.

concepts.title: Special or common experience
concepts.question: What test tells a scientific book from a philosophical one, and what kind of experience does each appeal to?

paragraphs: Philosophy is like science and unlike history in seeking general truths rather than an account of particular events. But the philosopher does not ask the same questions as the scientist, nor use the same kind of method to answer them.

The authors offer a criterion they think always works, though you may have to read some of the book to apply it. If a theoretical book emphasises things outside your normal, routine, daily experience, it is scientific. If not, it is philosophical.

Galileo asks you to imagine or repeat experiments with inclined planes; Newton's Opticks refers to dark rooms, prisms and controlled rays; Darwin's facts came from years of fieldwork. A philosophical book appeals to nothing beyond the ordinary person's experience, and asks you to check its points against your own.
card.example: Book A asks you to recall how you decide between two choices and whether you could have chosen otherwise. Book B reports brain scans of volunteers making choices in a laboratory. A relies on experience everyone has, so it is philosophical; B relies on special observation, so it is scientific.
card.rule: To tell science from philosophy, note the experience a book relies on: special experience from laboratory, field or clinic means science; common experience means philosophy.
card.limits: The test applies only to books that are either science or philosophy, not to histories or practical books. And it may take some reading before you can see which experience a book depends on.

concepts.title: Note the experience a point requires
concepts.question: How do you apply the experience test to a book, like James's, that appeals to both kinds of experience?

paragraphs: William James took a middle course. His Principles of Psychology reports many examples of special experience that only a careful, trained observer can know, yet it often asks readers to judge from their own experience whether what is said is true.
So, in the authors' view, the book is both a scientific and a philosophical work, though primarily scientific.

The working method is to note, as you read, the sort of experience referred to as a condition of understanding what is said. The difference in method shows itself in scientific and philosophical books, and it is how you tell which you are reading.
card.example: A book on habits reports a sleep laboratory's findings in one chapter and, in the next, asks you to recall how a habit of your own formed. Noting which experience each point needs, you see the book draws on both, and you can judge which kind dominates.
card.rule: As you read, ask what experience you must have, or imagine, to understand each point, and classify the book by the kind that dominates.
card.limits: One appeal to common experience does not make a scientific book philosophical, nor one laboratory report the reverse. Weigh the pattern across the book; a book can be mainly one while drawing on both.

concepts.title: Armchair and laboratory
concepts.question: Is philosophy's armchair thinking inferior to science's experiments, and how does each prove its conclusions?

paragraphs: The distinction is popularly put this way: science is experimental or depends on elaborate observation, while philosophy is armchair thinking. The authors say the contrast should not be invidious, that is, it should not rank one method below the other.

Some problems, some of them very important, can be solved in an armchair by someone who knows how to think about them in the light of common human experience. Others no amount of the best armchair thinking can solve; they need investigation in a laboratory or the field, extending experience beyond the everyday.

Nor is the philosopher a pure thinker and the scientist only an observer. Both observe and think, but about different sorts of observation, and they prove their conclusions differently: the scientist by pointing to special experience, the philosopher by pointing to experience common to all.
card.example: Whether a promise made under threat binds you can be worked out by reflecting on what promising involves, from experience everyone has. Whether a new drug lowers blood pressure cannot; it needs a controlled trial. Neither method is the lesser; each fits its problem.
card.rule: Judge armchair and laboratory methods by whether they fit the problem, and expect each to prove its conclusions from its own kind of experience.
card.limits: Some problems need both: reflection to frame the question and investigation to settle the facts. A thinker who ignores relevant special findings, or an investigator who ignores common experience, can still go wrong.

concepts.title: Different kinds argue differently
concepts.question: Why does knowing whether a book is history, science or philosophy matter for following its arguments?

paragraphs: Classifying matters because, beyond the different experiences they depend on, scientists and philosophers do not think in exactly the same way. Their styles of arguing differ, and you must be able to find the terms and propositions that make up each sort of argument.
The same is true of history. Historical statements differ from scientific and philosophical ones; a historian argues differently and interprets facts differently.

The typical history is narrative in form, and a narrative is a narrative, whether fact or fiction. So the historian must write poetically, obeying the rules for telling a good story. Locke's Essay and Newton's Principia, whatever their excellences, are not good stories.
card.example: Reading a history of a shipwreck, you follow how one event led to the next. Reading a science of buoyancy, you look for the law and the evidence for it. Reading philosophy on courage, you test each claim against your own experience. Same reader, three ways of following.
card.rule: Classify a theoretical book so you know what kind of argument to look for: a narrative in history, laws and evidence in science, appeals to common experience in philosophy.
card.limits: Styles blend: a history may argue a thesis, and a scientific book may tell the story of a discovery. The kind tells you what to expect mainly, not everything you will meet.

concepts.title: Read each kind in its own way
concepts.question: Why must each kind of book be read in its own way, and what does the classroom comparison show?

paragraphs: Is classifying a book before reading it really so important? The authors answer with a comparison. Walk into a classroom and you can soon tell whether the class is history, science or philosophy, from how the teacher proceeds, the words used, the arguments, the problems set and the responses expected.
Knowing which it is matters if you want to listen intelligently. The methods of teaching different kinds of subject matter differ, as any teacher knows.

Just as the art of teaching differs between fields, so does the art of being taught: the student's activity must respond to the teacher's. Books relate to readers as teachers to students. So, as books differ in what they teach, we must learn to read each kind in an appropriate manner.
card.example: Ten minutes into a strange lecture you hear dates, names and why a war began: history. You stop expecting proofs and start following the story. A reader opening a book can make the same adjustment, if he has classified it first.
card.rule: Classify a book so you can adjust your reading to the way that kind of book teaches, as a student adjusts to a history, science or philosophy class.
card.limits: Classifying sets your expectations; it does not do the reading for you. A book that mixes kinds asks you to shift your manner as it shifts, not to hold one manner throughout.

concepts.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
concepts.title: Every book has a skeleton
concepts.question: What lies beneath the surface of a book, and why must an analytical reader look for it?

paragraphs: The authors picture a book as a body: a skeleton, covered with flesh, dressed in clothes. The surface you meet first is the prose, the examples and the stories. Underneath it is a firm structure that holds everything together.

You do not need to tear the book apart to reach that structure, but you do need to read with X-ray eyes. For the authors, grasping how a book is built is an essential part of understanding it, not an extra.
The chapter turns this demand into rules. They apply to any book, poetry as well as science, though they work out differently for each kind.
card.example: A cookbook's surface is recipes, photos and anecdotes. Its skeleton might be: basic techniques first, then dishes grouped by cooking method, then menus that combine them. A reader who sees that order understands why the stock recipe sits in chapter one and why later recipes keep referring back to it.
card.rule: Read every book looking for the structure that holds its surface together.
card.limits: X-ray reading looks through the surface, not past it: you still read the prose and examples to find the bones. A reader who guesses a skeleton without reading the flesh has not found the book's structure, only invented one.

concepts.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
concepts.title: Expect unity in any book worth reading
concepts.question: Which books have a unity and an organization of parts, and does that unity look the same in every kind?

paragraphs: The authors claim that every book worth reading, without exception, has a unity and an organization of parts. A book that lacked them would be a mess, and bad books are hard to read for exactly that reason.

The unity is not the same in every kind of book. A novel hangs together differently from a treatise on politics, and their parts are of different sorts, arranged in different ways. The rules stay the same; how you apply them depends on the kind.
Going in with this expectation changes how you read: you search for the plan instead of waiting to see whether one turns up.
card.example: A reader opens a history of jazz and a manual on bookkeeping. She expects each to have one main point and an ordered set of parts. In the history she looks for the thread running through the eras; in the manual she looks for the sequence of tasks that ends in balanced books.
card.rule: Approach any book worth reading expecting a unity and an ordered set of parts, then look for the form they take in that kind of book.
card.limits: The expectation is a starting stance, not a guarantee: a loose collection or a badly made book may not reward the search. And the form of unity you look for must suit the kind of book, or you will search for the wrong thing.

concepts.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
concepts.title: Rule 2: state the unity briefly
concepts.question: What does Rule 2 ask you to produce, and how long may it be?

paragraphs: Rule 2 of analytical reading: state the unity of the whole book in a single sentence, or at most a few sentences forming a short paragraph. In plain terms, say what the whole book is about as briefly as you can.
The statement covers the whole book, not one chapter or a favourite part. It is something you put into words, not a general impression you carry around.
Rule 2 comes after Rule 1, which asked you to classify the book. Having placed the book in its kind, you now say what this particular book is about.
card.example: After reading a book on urban trees, a reader writes: This book argues that city trees are public infrastructure, showing how they cool streets, absorb storm water and improve health, and proposing how cities should budget to plant and maintain them. One sentence covers the whole book.
card.rule: State what the whole book is about in one sentence or a short paragraph.
card.limits: Brevity is the aim, but not at any price. A sentence so short that it would fit a dozen other books, or one that leaves out a major part, does not state this book's unity.

concepts.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
concepts.title: What it is about versus what kind it is
concepts.question: What is the difference between saying what kind of book it is and saying what it is about?

paragraphs: The word about has two senses. In one, a book is about a type of subject matter, treated in a certain way. Knowing that tells you what kind of book it is, which was the work of Rule 1.

In the other, everyday sense, we ask what a person is about: what he is up to. Asking what an author is up to, what he is trying to do, leads you to the book's theme or main point. Rule 2 asks for this second sense.
A statement of kind could fit many books. A statement of theme should fit this one.
card.example: Kind: a practical book on personal finance. Theme: it argues that most people should stop picking shares and instead buy low-cost index funds automatically, and shows how to set that up and stay with it through market falls.
card.rule: When stating the unity, say what the author is up to in this book, not only what kind of book it is.
card.limits: Kind and theme are not rivals: Rule 1 still comes first. A theme statement made without knowing the kind can misread the author's aim, for instance treating a practical book as if it only described how things are.

concepts.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
concepts.title: A good book's unity runs through it
concepts.question: In what sense is a book a work of art, and how does its quality relate to its unity?

paragraphs: The authors call a book a work of art, using art in a broad sense: not only fine art, but anything made with skill. An author is a maker of books, and the book is something he has made for the reader's benefit.
Like music, paintings, novels and plays, a book has a more nearly perfect, more pervasive unity in proportion as it is good. The authors say this holds just as much for books that convey knowledge.
Pervasive means the unity reaches every part. In a well-made book each chapter is there because of the whole, and contributes to it.
card.example: In a strong biography of a scientist, even the chapter on her childhood bears on the main theme, say, how stubbornness drove her discoveries. In a weaker one, the childhood chapter is a pile of anecdotes that could be cut without anything else needing to change.
card.rule: Expect the unity of a good book to run through all its parts, and take that as a sign of how well it is made.
card.limits: Pervasive unity is a mark of a good book, not something a quick skim can confirm or rule out; a unity you have not found yet may still be there. And a book with patchy unity can still contain worthwhile parts.

concepts.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
concepts.title: Too many words means a multiplicity
concepts.question: How can you tell whether you have seen a book's unity or only a list of its contents?

paragraphs: Granting vaguely that a book has unity is not enough; the authors want you to grasp it definitely. The test is whether you can tell yourself or someone else what the unity is, in a few words.
If it takes too many words, you have seen not the unity but a multiplicity: the many things the book contains rather than the one thing it does.
A long statement usually reads like a list joined by and. A real unity statement shows how the items hang together under one main point.
card.example: Multiplicity: The book covers sleep stages, dreams, caffeine, shift work, naps, teenagers and insomnia. Unity: The book argues that sleep is the foundation of health, showing what it does for body and mind and how modern habits rob us of it.
card.rule: Say the unity in a few words; if you need many, look again for the one point that ties them together.
card.limits: Few words is not the same as vague words: a short statement that could fit any book on the topic has dropped the content rather than found the unity. Some rich books need a short paragraph, which the rule still allows.

concepts.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
concepts.title: Do not settle for feeling the unity
concepts.question: Why is a felt sense of a book's unity not enough, and what counts as knowing it?

paragraphs: Some readers say: I know what the book is about, but I cannot say it. The authors are blunt: such a reader probably does not even fool himself.
The only way to know you have grasped the unity is to be able to put it into words, for yourself or for someone else. A feeling you cannot express is not yet knowledge of the unity.
Saying it aloud or writing it down is therefore part of the reading, not a chore for afterwards.
card.example: Asked what a novel was about, Sam says he gets it but cannot explain. He tries to write one sentence and cannot finish it: he does not know what the brothers' quarrel has to do with the sale of the farm. Until he can finish the sentence, he has a feeling, not the unity.
card.rule: Test your grasp of the unity by saying or writing it; do not settle for a feeling you cannot express.
card.limits: Being able to produce a sentence is needed but not enough: a fluent statement can be borrowed from a blurb or be a lucky guess. And needing a moment to find the words is fine; the trouble is never finding them.

concepts.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
concepts.title: A story's unity is its plot
concepts.question: How do you state the unity of a story, and what happens to everything else in it?

paragraphs: A story can be crowded with adventures, episodes and complications, yet a good one has a single unity of action: a main thread of plot that ties everything together. The authors cite Aristotle, who held this to be the mark of every good story, novel or play.

Aristotle showed it by stating the plot of the Odyssey in a few sentences: a man long absent from home and harried by a god; his household ruined by suitors; his return, and his destruction of them. That, he said, is the essence of the plot; the rest is episode.
Once you know the plot this way, you can put the parts of the story into their proper places, each seen by its relation to the main thread.
card.example: A film: a cautious accountant is forced to drive a stranger across the country; obstacles pile up; she learns to take risks and in the end chooses a new life. The chase scenes, the diner fight and the flat tyre are episodes hung on that thread.
card.rule: For a story, state the main thread of plot in a few sentences and treat the rest as episode placed along it.
card.limits: Episode does not mean unimportant: episodes carry much of a story's life and quality. And a loose anthology of tales has no single thread to state.

concepts.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
concepts.title: Few plots, many stories
concepts.question: If many stories share the same plot, what makes one better than another?

paragraphs: The authors suggest practising the plot test on good novels, such as Tom Jones or Crime and Punishment. Reduced to its plot, Tom Jones gives a familiar formula: boy meets girl, boy loses girl, boy gets girl. That, they say, is the plot of every romance.
Seeing this shows what it means to say there are only a small number of plots in the world. Stated at the level of essence, many stories share one.
So the plot alone does not make a story good. The difference between good and bad stories with the same essential plot lies in what the author does with it: how he dresses the bare bones.
card.example: Two crime novels share a plot: a detective is hired, follows false leads, and unmasks an unexpected culprit. One is forgettable; the other lives through its characters, its city and the detective's doubts. Same bones, different flesh.
card.rule: State a story's plot to see its unity, then look to how the author dressed that plot to judge the story's quality.
card.limits: A shared formula does not make two stories the same book, and it says nothing about quality or freshness. A familiar plot is no mark against a novel; what counts is what the author made of it.

concepts.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
concepts.title: Let the title help
concepts.question: How can a book's title help you state its unity?

paragraphs: You do not always have to find the unity alone; the author often helps. Sometimes the title is all you need to read.

Eighteenth-century writers liked elaborate titles that told the reader what the whole book was about. The authors give Jeremy Collier's attack on the morals of Restoration drama: A Short View of the Immorality and Profaneness of the English Stage, together with the Sense of Antiquity upon this Argument.
From that title you can guess the book: many instances of immorality on the stage, backed by what ancient writers said against the theatre. A title read with care is a first statement of the unity.
card.example: A title: The Quiet Engine: How Rail Freight Built the Modern City. The main title names the subject; the subtitle states the claim. Before page one, a reader can draft: the book argues that freight railways shaped how cities grew.
card.rule: Read the title, and any subtitle, as the author's own first hint at the unity.
card.limits: Many titles are catchy rather than descriptive, and even a descriptive one is only a start: it may promise more or less than the book delivers, so the draft must be checked against the whole book.

concepts.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
concepts.title: Exposition states its plan early
concepts.question: Where can you expect an expository author to state the plan, and why does fiction differ?

paragraphs: Sometimes the author states the unity of his plan in the preface. Here expository books differ sharply from fiction: a scientific or philosophical writer has no reason to keep you in suspense.
Indeed, the less suspense he keeps you in, the more likely you are to keep reading to the end. Like a newspaper article, an expository book may summarise itself in its first paragraph.
A novel works the other way. Not knowing where the story is going is part of its design, so its unity usually comes clear only as the whole unfolds.
card.example: A report on remote work opens: This study finds that hybrid schedules raised output in teams that set shared office days and lowered it where days were left to each person; we recommend fixed anchor days. The rest of the report supports that paragraph.
card.rule: In an expository book, look for the author's statement of the plan in the preface or the opening paragraph.
card.limits: The expectation fits exposition, not fiction, where looking for an early summary will usually fail. And an early statement of plan is a promise that the book may not fully keep.

concepts.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
concepts.title: Use the author's plan, but check it
concepts.question: How far should you trust the author's own statement of the plan, and whose job is finding the unity?

paragraphs: The authors advise: do not be too proud to accept the author's help, but do not rely completely on what he says in the preface either. The best-laid plans of authors often go awry.
Let the author's prospectus guide you. But the obligation to find the unity belongs finally to the reader, just as the obligation to have one belongs to the writer.
You can meet that obligation honestly only by reading the whole book. A preface tells you what the author meant to do; the book shows what he did.
card.example: A preface promises a balanced history of a trade dispute, giving both nations' cases. Reading through, Lena finds the later chapters argue for one side. Her statement of the unity follows the book she read: a history that turns into a case for one country's policy.
card.rule: Take the author's stated plan as a guide, then test it against the whole book before adopting it.
card.limits: Distrust is not the default either: a good author's own statement is often excellent and may need only small additions. The aim is to test it, not to reword it for the sake of independence.

concepts.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
concepts.title: Elaborate the opening summary of a history
concepts.question: How should you build on an author's opening summary once you have read the whole history?

paragraphs: Herodotus opens his history of the war between Greeks and Persians with a fine summary: he publishes his researches to preserve the memory of what men have done, to keep the great deeds of Greeks and Barbarians from losing their glory, and to record the grounds of their feud.

That is a good start, but the authors say not to stop there. After reading all nine parts, you will probably want to elaborate it: name the Persian kings Cyrus, Darius and Xerxes, the Greek hero Themistocles, and the major events, such as the crossing of the Hellespont and the battles of Thermopylae and Salamis.
The rest of Herodotus' fascinating detail can be left out. The unity of a history, like that of fiction, is a single thread of plot.
card.example: A history of a city's subway opens: this book tells how the subway was built and why it nearly failed. After reading, a reader adds the 1904 opening, the bankrupt private company, the 1940 city takeover and the mayor who forced it. Hundreds of other names stay out.
card.rule: After reading a history, enrich the author's opening summary with its main figures and turning points, and leave the rest of the detail out.
card.limits: Elaborating is not listing everything: once minor figures and side events creep in, the statement becomes a multiplicity. And the thread-of-plot form suits histories and stories; other kinds of book are unified in other ways.

concepts.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
concepts.title: Compress a long statement of plan
concepts.question: What should you do when the author's own statement of the plan runs to several pages?

paragraphs: Some authors state their plan at length. Adam Smith opens The Wealth of Nations with the plan of the work, but it takes several pages. The authors show that the unity can be put far more briefly.

Their version is a short paragraph: an inquiry into the source of national wealth in an economy built on the division of labour, relating wages, profits and rent to prices, discussing the uses of capital and the origin of money, comparing systems of political economy, and arguing for free trade.

They give a similar paragraph for Aristotle's Ethics: an inquiry into happiness and how it is gained or lost, stressing moral and intellectual virtue, while recognising other goods such as health, wealth, friends and a just society.
card.example: A strategy document spends six pages on a firm's plan. A reader compresses it: the firm will move from selling hardware to selling subscriptions, retraining its sales staff, cutting two product lines and pricing service tiers to keep current customers.
card.rule: When the author's plan is long, compress it into your own short paragraph that keeps every major element.
card.limits: Compressing is not dropping: a short version that leaves out a major part, such as Smith's case for free trade, is shorter but less accurate. Where the author's own statement is already brief and sound, there may be nothing to compress.

concepts.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
concepts.title: Add what a good statement leaves out
concepts.question: When an author's own statement of the unity is excellent, what might a reader still need to add?

paragraphs: Locke summed up his Essay Concerning Human Understanding as an inquiry into the origin, certainty and extent of human knowledge, together with the grounds and degrees of belief, opinion and assent. The authors call this excellent and do not quarrel with it.

They add only two subordinate qualifications, to do justice to the first and third parts of the essay: that there are no innate ideas, all knowledge coming from experience; and that language is discussed as a medium of thought, with its proper use and common abuses.
The pattern: keep a sound statement, and add what it leaves out so that every major part is covered.
card.example: A cookbook's introduction says it teaches weeknight cooking from a short list of pantry staples. A reader keeps that and adds: with a final section on batch cooking for the freezer, which the introduction never mentions.
card.rule: If the author's statement of the unity misses a major part, keep it and add subordinate qualifications that cover what it leaves out.
card.limits: Qualifications are for major parts, not for every topic: piling on additions turns the statement into a list. And you can tell what is missing only after reading the parts the statement skips.

concepts.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
concepts.title: A rich book may need a short paragraph
concepts.question: Can a statement of unity run longer than one sentence and still be a unity, and when?

paragraphs: The authors' statement of Darwin's Origin of Species is one long sentence: variation over countless generations producing new groups of plants and animals; domestic and natural variation; the struggle for existence and natural selection; species as varieties in transition rather than fixed; supported by fossils, embryology and anatomy.
They admit it may seem a big mouthful. But the book was an even bigger one for many nineteenth-century readers, partly because they did not trouble to find out what it was really about.
A rich book may need a short paragraph. What keeps the statement a unity is that every clause hangs on one main claim.
card.example: A unity statement for a dense book on vaccines: it explains how vaccines train the immune system, traces their history from smallpox on, weighs the evidence on safety, and argues that falling uptake threatens shared protection. Long, but every clause serves the main point.
card.rule: Let a rich book's unity run to a short paragraph if it must, as long as every clause serves one main point.
card.limits: The allowance stops at a short paragraph. Once clauses stop hanging on the main point and start adding topics, the statement has become a multiplicity, however tidy it looks.

concepts.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
concepts.title: Why most readers cannot say it
concepts.question: Why are most readers at a loss when asked to say briefly what a whole book is about?

paragraphs: The authors note how often authors, especially good ones, help the reader state the plan. Yet most readers are at a total loss when asked to say briefly what a whole book is about.
They give three reasons. Many people cannot speak concise sentences. Many neglect the rule while reading. And many pay as little attention to the author's introductory words as they do to the title.
Each cause points to a remedy: practise saying things briefly, keep the unity question in mind while reading, and read the opening pages and the title with care.
card.example: Tom skips a book's introduction to reach the first real chapter. Asked later what the book argued, he flounders. The introduction had stated the thesis in one paragraph, and he never read it.
card.rule: Read the author's introductory words and title with care, and keep the unity question in mind as you read.
card.limits: Reading the introduction helps but does not finish the job: what it says still has to be tested against the book. And some books offer no helpful introduction, so the reader must find the unity unaided.

concepts.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
concepts.title: Brief, accurate, comprehensive
concepts.question: Is there one correct statement of a book's unity, and how do you tell a better statement from a worse one?

paragraphs: The authors warn against treating their sample statements as final. A unity can be stated in various ways; there is no one right way to do it.
One statement is better than another in proportion as it is brief, accurate and comprehensive. Quite different statements may be equally good, or equally bad.
The authors themselves sometimes stated a unity quite differently from the author's own words, without apology, and they expect readers to differ from them in turn.
card.example: Two statements of a book on bees. A: It shows that colonies collapse from several stresses at once and argues for farming that reduces all of them. B: Bees are dying from pesticides, mites, poor diet and lost habitat together, and only broad changes in farming will save them. Different words; both brief, accurate and comprehensive.
card.rule: Judge a statement of unity by how brief, accurate and comprehensive it is, not by whether it matches a model answer.
card.limits: No one right way does not mean any way: a statement that is brief but inaccurate, or accurate but missing a major part, is worse. The three marks can pull against each other and have to be balanced.

concepts.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
concepts.title: Different readers, same book
concepts.question: If readers state a book's unity differently, what stops the statements from being matters of taste?

paragraphs: A book is something different to each reader, the authors grant, so it would not be surprising if readers stated its unity differently.
But that does not mean anything goes. Though readers differ, the book is the same, and there can be an objective check on the accuracy and fidelity of what anyone says about it.
Differences of wording and emphasis are fine. A statement the text contradicts, or one that leaves out what the text puts at the centre, fails the check.
card.example: Three readers state the unity of a book on minimum wages. Two word it differently but agree it argues for raising the wage gradually, using evidence from many regions. The third says it argues for abolishing minimum wages. The book itself shows the third is wrong.
card.rule: Word the unity your own way, then check it against the text, which is the same for every reader.
card.limits: The check tests fidelity to the text, not which wording is nicest. Where a book is itself unclear, the text may support more than one reading, and the check narrows the options rather than settling them.

concepts.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
concepts.title: Rule 3: set forth the parts and their order
concepts.question: What does Rule 3 ask you to set out, and why is knowing a book's unity not enough?

paragraphs: Rule 3: set forth the major parts of the book, and show how they are organized into a whole, by being ordered to one another and to the unity of the whole.
The reason is that nothing people make is absolutely simple. A book is a complex unity, and you have not grasped a complex unity if all you know is how it is one. You must also know how it is many.
Not a many made of separate things, but an organized many. If the parts were not related to one another, there would be no whole at all, only a collection.
card.example: A book on starting a bakery has four parts: the business case, the kitchen, the menu and suppliers, and opening day. Rule 3 asks for more than that list: the business case sets the budget, the budget limits the kitchen, and the kitchen shapes the menu.
card.rule: Name the major parts of the book and show how each is ordered to the others and to the whole.
card.limits: A bare list of chapter topics does not meet the rule; the relations are the point. And a true collection, such as an anthology of unrelated pieces, has parts but no single order to show.

concepts.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
concepts.title: A house, not a heap of bricks
concepts.question: How is a well-made book like a house rather than a heap of bricks or a row of houses?

paragraphs: A heap of bricks differs from the house they can make, and a single house differs from a collection of houses. A book, say the authors, is like a single house: a mansion of many rooms, on different levels, of different sizes, shapes and uses.

Each room is partly independent, with its own structure and decoration. But the rooms are joined by doors, arches, corridors and stairways, what architects call a traffic pattern. Because they connect, each room's partial function adds to the usefulness of the whole house.

So with a book's major parts: each has some independence and may have its own inner structure and style, yet each must be related functionally to the others, or it adds nothing to the intelligibility of the whole.
card.example: A guide to raising a puppy has parts on feeding, training, health and travel. Each can be read alone, like a room. But the training part uses feeding times for rewards, and the travel part depends on the health part's vaccination schedule. Those links are the corridors.
card.rule: Treat each major part as a room: see what it does on its own, and find the corridors that connect it to the rest.
card.limits: The analogy fits well-made books; a poorly made one may have rooms with no doors between them. And a part's partial independence lets you read it alone, but its full sense depends on its connections.

concepts.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
concepts.title: The best books are the most readable
concepts.question: Why do the authors say the best books are also the most readable, even though they are more complex?

paragraphs: As houses are more or less livable, books are more or less readable. The most readable book, say the authors, is an architectural achievement by its author, and the best books are those with the most intelligible structure.
Great books are usually more complex than poorer ones. But their greater complexity is also a greater simplicity, because their parts are better organized and more unified.
That is one reason the best books are also the most readable, while lesser works are, in fact, more bothersome to read.
card.example: A long, demanding history of the Roman Republic proves easier to follow than a short, chatty one, because each chapter of the long book builds on the last toward one question. The short book jumps between topics with no plan.
card.rule: Expect a well-structured book, however complex, to be easier to follow than a loosely made one, and credit its structure for that.
card.limits: Readable here means intelligible in structure, not light or quick: a great book can still be hard going sentence by sentence. And a smooth, easy style does not show a book is well built.

concepts.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
concepts.title: Find the plan even in lesser books
concepts.question: What should you do when a book is poorly organized and its plan is hard to see?

paragraphs: Lesser books are more bothersome to read. Yet to read them as well as they can be read, the authors say, you must still try to find some plan in them.

Such books would have been better if their authors had seen the plan more clearly. But if a book hangs together at all, if it is a complex unity to any degree and not a mere collection, there must be a plan, and you must find it.
More of the work falls on the reader here: you may have to reconstruct an order the author only half achieved.
card.example: A rambling memoir by a retired engineer jumps between decades. Patiently, a reader sees that most chapters circle one question: whether his biggest project was worth what it cost his family. Arranged around that question, the memoir becomes readable.
card.rule: Even in a poorly made book, look for the plan, since any book that hangs together has one.
card.limits: A true collection has no single plan to find, and the reader must not invent an order the book does not support. Some books reward only a rough plan.

concepts.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
concepts.title: Why unity and parts are two rules
concepts.question: If Rules 2 and 3 describe one structure, why do the authors give them as two rules?

paragraphs: Rules 2 and 3 are closely related. A well-stated unity points to the major parts; you cannot grasp a whole without somehow seeing its parts. And unless you grasp how the parts are organized, you cannot know the whole fully.
Why two rules, then? Mainly for convenience: a complex, unified structure is easier to grasp in two steps than in one. Rule 2 turns your attention to the unity, Rule 3 to the complexity.
There is a second reason. The major parts may come into view the moment you grasp the unity, but each part usually has an inner structure of its own, which takes further work to see.
card.example: Planning a wedding: first you say what the day is for, a small family celebration in the garden. Then you work out the parts: ceremony, meal, music. Each part turns out to have parts of its own; the meal needs a caterer, seating and toasts.
card.rule: Work on the structure in two steps, first the unity and then the complexity, keeping each in view of the other.
card.limits: The two steps are a convenience, not two separate readings: each corrects the other as you go. A unity worked out with no attention to the parts has not been checked.

concepts.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
concepts.title: Outline the parts as smaller wholes
concepts.question: Why is listing a book's major parts not enough, and what does outlining add?

paragraphs: Rule 3 involves more than an enumeration of the parts. It means outlining them: treating each part as if it were a subordinate whole, with a unity and a complexity of its own.
So each major part gets the same two questions the whole book got. What is this part about, said briefly? What are its own parts, and how are they ordered?
The process repeats downward. A part's sections have parts of their own, down to the smallest units worth identifying.
card.example: A book on the immune system has a part on vaccines. As a subordinate whole, its unity might be: vaccines train the body with harmless copies of germs. Its own parts: how the training works, how vaccines are made and tested, and why boosters are needed.
card.rule: Outline each major part as a smaller whole: state its unity, then find its own parts and their order.
card.limits: The descent stops somewhere: below the smallest units worth identifying, further division adds bulk, not understanding. And a part's unity must still be tied to the whole book's unity, not stated as if the part stood alone.

concepts.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
concepts.title: The outlining formula
concepts.question: What is the authors' formula for outlining a book, step by step?

paragraphs: Rule 2 gave you: the whole book is about so-and-so. Rule 3 can then follow a formula. First: the author carried out this plan in, say, five major parts; the first is about this, the second about that, and so on.

Second: the first major part is divided into, say, three sections, which consider X, Y and Z. Third: in the first section of the first part, the author makes, say, four points, A, B, C and D. And so on.
The formula moves from the whole to its parts, from parts to sections, from sections to points, saying at each level how many there are and what each one does.
card.example: Whole: a guide to starting a vegetable garden. Parts: planning, soil, planting, care. Planning has three sections: choosing the site, picking crops, drawing a plan. In picking crops the author makes four points: suit the climate, start easy, grow what you eat, stagger harvests.
card.rule: Outline by stating the whole, then its major parts, then each part's sections, then each section's points.
card.limits: The formula is a guide, not a form to fill in: the counts come from the book, and not every part divides neatly. Forcing a book into fixed numbers distorts it.

concepts.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
concepts.title: A rough approximation is enough
concepts.question: Do good readers really outline every book in full detail, and what does the rule actually require?

paragraphs: The formula can look like a lifetime's work for one book. But it is only a formula. Good readers do this kind of thing habitually, and so easily and naturally.
They may not write it all out, or even put it into words while reading. But if asked to give an account of the book's structure, they could produce something that approximates the formula.

A good rule describes the ideal performance, and a person can be skilled in an art without being the ideal artist. The authors say you should be satisfied with a very rough approximation to what the rule requires.
card.example: Asked about a history of the printing press she read last month, Ines has no notes. But she can say it has three parts, the invention, its spread through Europe, and its effects on religion and science, and roughly what each covers. That approximates the formula.
card.rule: Aim to be able to give an approximate account of the structure when asked, without necessarily writing out the full outline.
card.limits: Approximation is not permission to skip the work: you must still be able to give an account of the structure on demand. If you cannot say what the parts are, the approximation is too rough.

concepts.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
concepts.title: Vary how closely you outline
concepts.question: How closely should you outline a given book, and what decides it?

paragraphs: Even skilled readers do not give every book the same effort. The authors say the best readers make a fairly close approximation to Rule 3 for relatively few books; for most, a rough notion of the structure satisfies them.
How close you go depends on the character of the book and your purpose in reading it.
Yet the rule itself stays the same. Whether you follow it closely or only roughly, you must know how to follow it.
card.example: Pat outlines a dense textbook for an exam section by section and point by point. For a popular book on birds read on holiday, a three-part sketch in her head is enough. Same rule; different closeness.
card.rule: Decide how closely to outline by the book's character and your purpose, while knowing how to follow the rule fully.
card.limits: Rough is a choice, not an excuse: you can choose a rough outline well only if you could make a close one. A rough sketch that cannot say what the main parts are has dropped below what the rule allows.

concepts.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
concepts.title: Outline the book, not the subject
concepts.question: Why can no outline of a book be perfect, and what must an outline leave out?

paragraphs: The limits on outlining are not only of time and effort. You are finite, but so is a book, and like everything people make it is defective. No book deserves a perfect outline, because no book is perfect. It goes only so far, and so must you.
The rule does not ask you to put into the book what the author did not put there. Your outline is of the book itself, not of the subject matter the book is about.
An outline of a subject might go on indefinitely; an outline of a book stops where the book's own treatment stops.
card.example: A short book on the French Revolution says little about the countryside. A reader who adds a section on peasant revolts, from what she knows elsewhere, is outlining the Revolution, not the book. Her outline of the book should show that part as thin, because it is.
card.rule: Outline what the book contains, stopping where the author's treatment stops, and add nothing from the subject that the author left out.
card.limits: Noticing a gap is fine; filling it as if the author had is not. You may record what the book leaves out as your own observation, kept apart from the outline of what is there.

concepts.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
concepts.title: Commentaries: the rule near perfection
concepts.question: Can an outline be longer than the book, and where can you see the rule followed near perfection?

paragraphs: A unity fits in a paragraph, but a careful outline of a large book, down to the smallest units worth identifying, would take many pages. In theory, the outline could be longer than the original.

Some great medieval commentaries on Aristotle are longer than the works they comment on, as are some modern ones on Kant's Critique of Pure Reason. They hold more than an outline, since they interpret sentence by sentence. A variorum Shakespeare may be ten times as long as the play.

To see the rule followed nearly to perfection, look at such a commentary. Aquinas opens each section with an outline of Aristotle's points and always says how that part fits the whole, especially the parts before and after.
