card.example: A study guide to a dense philosophy book opens each chapter with a short map: this chapter answers the objection raised in chapter 2 and prepares the definition used in chapter 5. That is Aquinas's habit in miniature.
card.rule: When outlining a part, say how it fits the whole, especially the parts that come before and after it.
card.limits: A commentary's length shows how far the rule can go, not how far a reader usually should. And commentaries add interpretation; only part of their work is the outline that maps the structure.

concepts.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
concepts.title: Dividing a familiar document
concepts.question: What does outlining a well-known document, such as the U.S. Constitution, teach about dividing a work into parts?

paragraphs: The authors illustrate Rule 3 with the U.S. Constitution, a practical and well-organized document. Its major parts are fairly clearly marked, though finding the main divisions takes some thought.

They suggest eight: the Preamble; Articles I, II and III on the legislative, executive and judicial departments; Article IV on the states and the federal government; Articles V to VII on amendment, supremacy and ratification; the Bill of Rights; and the later amendments. Then they outline Article I by its sections.

This is only one way. The first three Articles could form one division, or the amendments could be grouped by the problems they deal with. Making your own division, and the parts of the parts, reveals much you never saw.
card.example: A reader outlines her firm's staff handbook. She first follows the headings, then notices that leave, sick pay and parental leave sit in three separate sections. Grouped as time away from work, they form one major part she had never seen as a whole.
card.rule: Divide a familiar work into its main parts yourself, then the parts of the parts, and expect more than one reasonable division.
card.limits: Several divisions can be reasonable, but not every one: a division must follow the work's real joints. Grouping parts that do not belong together is not a fresh view, only a mistake.

concepts.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
concepts.title: Your outline need not follow the chapters
concepts.question: Should your outline follow the book's chapter divisions, and why make your own?

paragraphs: The authors outline Aristotle's Ethics in six main parts: happiness as the end of life; voluntary action and habits; the virtues and vices; states neither virtuous nor vicious; friendship; and pleasure, completing the account of happiness.

These parts do not match the ten books of the Ethics. The first part fills Book I; the second runs through Book II and half of Book III; pleasure comes at the end of Book VII and again at the start of Book X.

So you need not follow the apparent structure of the chapters. It may be better than your outline, or worse; either way, make your own. The author made his to write a good book; you make yours to read it well. Only a perfect writer and a perfect reader would arrive at the same one.
card.example: A cookbook's chapters run Monday to Sunday. Outlining it, a reader finds three real parts: quick dinners, slow weekend cooking, and the leftovers that link them. Her outline cuts across the days and shows a plan the chapter titles hide.
card.rule: Make your own outline of the book's real parts, even where they cut across the chapter divisions.
card.limits: Your outline is not automatically better than the author's divisions; they may be the sounder guide. Cutting across chapters is justified by the book's logic, not by a wish to be different.

concepts.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
concepts.title: Use headings as guides, not crutches
concepts.question: How should you use an author's chapter headings and section divisions when outlining?

paragraphs: Making your own outline does not mean ignoring the author's chapter headings and sections. The authors did not ignore them when outlining the Constitution, though they did not follow them slavishly either.
Headings are meant to help you, as titles and prefaces are. Use them as guides for your own activity, not as something to rely on passively.
Few authors carry out their plan perfectly, but there is often more plan in a good book than meets the eye. The surface can deceive; you must look beneath it to find the real structure.
card.example: A report's headings are Background, Findings and Discussion. Starting from them, a reader sees that Discussion holds two separate arguments, one about cost and one about safety, each drawing on different findings. Her outline keeps the headings but splits Discussion in two.
card.rule: Start from the author's headings, then look beneath them for the structure they point to, adjusting where the book's real parts differ.
card.limits: Looking beneath the surface is not distrusting it by habit: often the headings are the real structure. Nor can they be skipped for your own scheme; they are part of the evidence.

concepts.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
concepts.title: The outline backs up the unity
concepts.question: Why can't you trust a statement of unity made without outlining the parts?

paragraphs: Rule 2 cannot be followed well without Rule 3. From a cursory glance you might produce an adequate statement of a book's unity in two or three sentences. But you would not know it was adequate.
Someone who had read the book better might know, and give you high marks. For you, though, it would be a good guess, a lucky hit.

The authors compare a two-year-old who says two plus two is four: the statement is true, but the child does not know what it means. Outlining the parts, and showing how they exemplify and develop the main theme, is what supports your statement of the unity.
card.example: From the cover and contents, Raj guesses that a book argues for banning cars from city centres. He is right. Only after outlining it does he see why: the parts on air, safety and shops all build toward the ban. Now he can defend his statement, not only repeat it.
card.rule: Back up your statement of the unity by outlining the parts and showing how each develops the main theme.
card.limits: A guess can be right; the trouble is that you cannot tell. Outlining does not make a correct guess more true, but it turns it into knowledge you can show and defend.

concepts.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
concepts.title: Reading and writing are reciprocal
concepts.question: How are the rules for reading a book's structure related to the rules for writing one?

paragraphs: The two structural rules look like rules of writing too, and they are. Writing and reading are reciprocal, as are teaching and being taught.

If authors and teachers did not organize what they communicate, unifying it and ordering its parts, there would be no point in telling readers or listeners to search for the unity and uncover the structure.
But the rules are not followed in the same way. The reader tries to uncover the skeleton the book conceals; the author starts with the skeleton and tries to cover it up.
card.example: A speechwriter starts from an outline: one message, three supporting points, a call to action. She then writes stories and phrases that clothe the outline. A careful listener works backwards from the stories to recover the message and the three points.
card.rule: Look in a book for the unity and order its author built, working from the finished surface back to the plan.
card.limits: Reciprocal does not mean identical: the reader does not need the author's notes, and the author's private plan may differ from what reached the page. The reader recovers the structure in the book, not the drafting process.

concepts.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
concepts.title: Why books are not bare outlines
concepts.question: Why isn't an expository book a bare outline, and what does the covering of the skeleton add?

paragraphs: A good writer covers the skeleton artistically. He does not bury a puny skeleton under a mass of fat, nor leave the flesh so thin that the bones show through. If the flesh is thick enough and not flabby, the joints can still be detected, and the motion of the parts shows how they articulate.

Why not write expository books as bare outlines? Partly because most readers cannot read outlines. And a self-respecting reader, ready to do his own job, would find such a book repellent: he would expect the author to do his.
But more than that: the flesh is as much a part of the book as the skeleton. Spelling out the outline adds an essential dimension, a kind of life the work would not otherwise have.
card.example: Two guides to negotiating a salary: a one-page list of seven steps, and a short book that walks through each step with cases, mistakes and sample scripts. The list has the bones; the book gives them life, and its joints are still easy to find.
card.rule: Read through the flesh to find the joints, but treat the flesh as part of the book, not as padding to discard.
card.limits: Not all flesh is healthy: some books bury a thin skeleton under fat, so that length hides a lack of substance. Telling living flesh from padding is part of seeing how well a book is made.

concepts.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
concepts.title: Unity, clarity and coherence
concepts.question: How do the old writing virtues of unity, clarity and coherence map onto the reader's two structural rules?

paragraphs: An old maxim says a piece of writing should have unity, clarity and coherence. The authors call it a basic maxim of good writing, and the two rules of this chapter answer to writing that follows it.
If the writing has unity, the reader must find it. If it has clarity and coherence, the reader must appreciate them by finding the distinction and the order of the parts.
What is clear is clear by the distinctness of its outlines. What is coherent hangs together in an orderly arrangement of parts.
card.example: A grant report has unity (one aim: show the project worked), clarity (each section handles one question, without overlap) and coherence (results follow methods, conclusions follow results). A reader finds the aim, sees where each section begins and ends, and follows why each comes where it does.
card.rule: Find the unity; then see clarity in where each part begins and ends, and coherence in why the parts come in their order.
card.limits: The maxim describes good writing, and many books fall short of it. Where parts blur together or come in no order, failing to find clarity and coherence may reflect the book rather than the reader.

concepts.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
concepts.title: Telling well-made books from badly made ones
concepts.question: When you cannot find a book's unity or parts, how do you decide whether the fault is yours or the book's?

paragraphs: The two rules can be used to tell well-made books from badly made ones. If, once you have enough skill, no amount of effort lets you grasp a book's unity or see its parts and their relations, the book is very likely a bad one, whatever its reputation.
Do not make this judgment too quickly; perhaps the fault is yours. But do not refuse ever to make it, always assuming the fault is yours.

In fact, say the authors, whatever your own failings, the fault usually lies in the book: most books, the great majority, are badly made, in the sense that their authors did not write them by these rules.
card.example: Ana, a practised reader, works hard at a celebrated business book: two careful readings, notes, an attempt at an outline. She still cannot say what ties chapters 4 to 9 to the rest. She concludes, with care, that the book is loosely made, despite its fame.
card.rule: If, after skilled and honest effort, you cannot find a book's unity and the order of its parts, judge it probably badly made, whatever its reputation.
card.limits: The judgment needs real skill and effort first: a beginner's failure after one skim says more about the reading than the book. And badly made does not mean worthless; a loosely built book can still contain good material.

concepts.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
concepts.title: Using the rules on part of a book
concepts.question: Can the unity and outline rules be used on part of a book, and does that work for novels too?

paragraphs: The two rules can also be used on any substantial part of an expository book. If the part is itself a relatively independent, complex unity, you must find its unity and complexity to read it well.
Here books of knowledge differ from novels, plays and poems. The parts of an expository book can be much more autonomous than the parts of a story.

Someone who says of a novel that he has read enough to get the idea cannot be right: if the novel is any good, the idea is in the whole. But you can get the idea of Aristotle's Ethics or Darwin's Origin by reading some parts carefully, though you could not then follow Rule 3 for the whole book.
card.example: A manager needs only the chapter on hiring from a long management book. She states that chapter's unity and outlines its sections, and reads it well. A friend reads half of a mystery and says she gets the idea; the solution, and with it the idea, is in the half she skipped.
card.rule: Apply the unity and outline rules to any substantial, fairly independent part of an expository book, but read a story whole before claiming its idea.
card.limits: Reading a part well is not reading the book: one part cannot give the outline of the whole. And parts vary in independence; a chapter that leans on earlier definitions may not stand alone.

concepts.title: Rule 4: find the author's problems
concepts.question: What does Rule 4 ask you to find, and what is a book's problem?

paragraphs: Rule 4: find out what the author's problems were. The author of a book starts with a question or a set of questions, and the book, on the face of it, contains the answer or answers.
The author may or may not tell you the questions. Whether he does or not, and especially if he does not, it is your task as a reader to formulate them as precisely as you can.

The authors say the rule needs little explanation: in another form it repeats what you did with Rules 2 and 3. But the repetition is useful, because it throws the whole and its parts into a new light.
card.example: A book on the decline of local newspapers seems a heap of facts until a reader asks what question it answers: why did local papers fail when national ones survived, and what has replaced them? Each chapter now reads as part of an answer.
card.rule: State, as precisely as you can, the question or questions the book sets out to answer.
card.limits: The rule asks for the problems the book addresses, not guesses about the author's private life or motives. And a question stated in the preface is a lead to check against the book, not the final word.

concepts.title: Main and subordinate questions, in order
concepts.question: Once you have found the author's questions, how should you arrange them?

paragraphs: You should be able to state the main question the book tries to answer, and the subordinate questions if the main one is complex and has many parts.
Beyond grasping all the questions, put them in an intelligible order. Which are primary and which secondary? Which must be answered first if others are to be answered later?
Ordered this way, the questions retrace the work of Rules 2 and 3: the main question sits where the unity does, and the subordinate questions line up with the major parts.
card.example: Main question of a book on a city's housing crisis: why are homes unaffordable here? Subordinate questions: how far have prices risen? What drove the rise? What has been tried? What would work? The first two must be answered before the last two make sense.
card.rule: State the main question and its subordinate questions, then order them so that those that must be answered first come first.
card.limits: Not every book has a neat ladder of questions; some pursue several questions side by side. Forcing a strict order the book does not follow distorts it.

concepts.title: Why the problem holds the structure together
concepts.question: What goes wrong when a reader skips finding the author's problems, and how does Rule 4 help the other rules?

paragraphs: Rule 4 duplicates, in a sense, the work of stating the unity and finding the parts. But it can help you do that work, so it is useful alongside the other two. Being less familiar, it may help even more with a difficult book.
Yet most readers, however skilled otherwise, often fail to follow it. Their idea of the book's main point may then be badly deficient, and their outline chaotic.
They miss the unity because they do not see why the book has the unity it has, and their grasp of its skeleton lacks the end the skeleton serves.
card.example: A reader outlines a hard book on ethics as eight chapter topics that will not cohere. Then she asks what question the author is trying to answer: can we act well without knowing what the good is? The chapters line up as steps toward an answer.
card.rule: When the unity or the outline will not come together, ask what problem the book is solving, and let the answer organize the parts.
card.limits: Rule 4 helps the other rules but does not replace them: a question stated without checking it against the parts can be as much a guess as an unchecked unity statement. Use the three together.

concepts.title: The problem, not the author's psyche
concepts.question: How does finding an author's problems differ from trying to read the author's mind?

paragraphs: The authors warn against what critics call the intentional fallacy: thinking you can discover what was in an author's mind from the book he wrote. It applies particularly to literary works; trying to psychoanalyze Shakespeare from the evidence of Hamlet is, they say, a grave error.
Even so, with a poetical work it is often extremely helpful to try to say what the author was trying to do. With expository works the rule has obvious merit.
The difference: Rule 4 asks what problem the work addresses, as the work shows it. It does not ask about the author's private feelings, wishes or psychology.
card.example: Reading a novel about a widower, Jamal writes: the author must have been grieving his own wife. That is a guess about the author's mind. A better note: the novel asks how a man rebuilds a life when the person he lived for is gone, as its plot and closing chapters show.
card.rule: State the problem the work itself addresses, and do not try to read the author's private mind from it.
card.limits: The line is not always sharp: an author's stated aims, in a preface for instance, can be evidence of the problem. The fallacy lies in treating guesses about inner life as findings about the book.

concepts.title: Theoretical and practical questions
concepts.question: What kinds of questions do authors set out to answer, and how can knowing them help you find a book's problem?

paragraphs: If you know the kinds of questions anyone can ask about anything, you will become adept at detecting an author's problems. Theoretical questions include: does it exist? What kind of thing is it? What caused it, or under what conditions can it exist? What purpose does it serve? What follows from it? What are its traits, its relations to other things, its behaviour?

Practical questions include: what ends should be sought? What means should be chosen to a given end? What must one do to reach an objective, and in what order? Under these conditions, what is the right or the better thing to do?

The list is far from exhaustive, but it covers the questions most often asked in pursuit of theoretical or practical knowledge. Run a book against it to draft the main question and its subordinate questions, then put them in order.
card.example: A book on sleep asks: does sleep debt exist, what causes it, what follows from it? Those are theoretical questions. A book on fixing your sleep asks: what should you aim for, which habits serve that aim, and in what order should you change them? Those are practical.
card.rule: Check a book against the common theoretical and practical questions to find which ones it is trying to answer.
card.limits: The list is a prompt, not a complete catalogue: a book may ask a question the list does not name, or mix theoretical and practical questions.

concepts.section: The First Stage of Analytical Reading
concepts.title: The first stage: four rules, one aim
concepts.question: What do the first four rules of analytical reading achieve together, and which basic question do they answer?

paragraphs: The first four rules form a group with a single aim: together they give the reader knowledge of a book's structure. Applying them to a book, or to anything long and difficult, completes the first stage of analytical reading.

The four rules: classify the book by kind and subject matter; state what the whole book is about with the utmost brevity; enumerate its major parts in order and relation, outlining them as you outlined the whole; define the problem or problems the author is trying to solve.

Together they answer the first basic question about a book: what is it about as a whole? That means finding its leading theme, and how the author develops it in order through its essential subordinate themes.
card.example: First stage on a book about antibiotics. Rule 1: a theoretical work of medical science for general readers. Rule 2: it explains how bacteria evolve resistance to antibiotics and how that resistance spreads. Rule 3: four parts, how the drugs work, how resistance arises, how it spreads, what it means for medicine. Rule 4: why are our drugs failing, and how does resistance travel?
card.rule: Apply the four structural rules together to answer what the book is about as a whole.
card.limits: The first stage gives the structure, not the interpretation or the verdict: knowing the shape of a book is not yet knowing exactly what it says, still less whether it is true.

concepts.section: The First Stage of Analytical Reading
concepts.title: Stages, not separate readings
concepts.question: Must you finish the first stage before starting the later stages of analytical reading, and how does inspection fit in?

paragraphs: Do not take stage in a chronological sense, except perhaps when you are first learning analytical reading. You need not read a book through to apply the first four rules and then read it again and again for the others. The practised reader does all the stages at once.
Still, knowing a book's structure is a real stage toward reading it analytically. And although these are rules of analytical reading, inspecting a book well before you read it helps you apply them.
Your answer to what the book is about as a whole will also grow more accurate as you go on to apply the later rules and answer the other questions.
card.example: Mei skims a book on habits for twenty minutes, noting its parts. As she reads closely she works out its terms and claims while refining her outline. By the end her statement of the unity is sharper than her first draft, though she never made separate passes.
card.rule: Inspect first, then apply the structural rules alongside the later ones as you read, revising your statement of the whole as you go.
card.limits: All at once is the practised reader's way; a beginner may need separate passes at first. And all at once does not mean skipping the structural work; it means doing it alongside the rest.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Coming to terms: the first step of interpretation
concepts.question: Why must a reader come to terms with an author before trying to interpret what the book says?

paragraphs: Analytical reading moves in stages. The first stage ends when you know what kind of book you hold, what it is about as a whole and how its parts are arranged. The second stage interprets what the book actually says, and its first step is called coming to terms.

The phrase comes from business, where coming to terms is the last step of a negotiation, right before signing. In reading it opens the second stage, because a term is the basic unit in which knowledge can pass from one mind to another.
If reader and author never share terms, no knowledge passes between them, however many words the reader takes in. The later steps of interpretation are built out of terms, so they wait on this one.
card.example: A reader has outlined a book on climate economics: five parts, one main question. Now she turns to what it says. Before weighing any claim, she settles what the author means by his key words, such as discount rate and cost. That settling is coming to terms.
card.rule: Once a book's structure is outlined, make coming to terms with its author your first step in interpreting what it says.
card.limits: Terms open interpretation but do not finish it: sharing an author's meanings does not yet tell you what he asserts as a whole, nor whether he is right. Those questions come in later steps.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: A term is not a word
concepts.question: Why does finding an author's important words not yet mean you have come to terms with him?

paragraphs: A term is not the same thing as a word. If it were, spotting a book's important words would be enough to come to terms with it. But a word, and above all an important word, can carry many meanings.

Suppose the author uses a word in one meaning and you read it in another. Words have passed between you, but terms have not. Where ambiguity of this kind is left unresolved, communication fails, or at best is incomplete.
So the question to ask of an important word is not only which word it is, but which of its meanings the author has in mind at this point.
card.example: A report says a new drug was effective. The author means it did better than a placebo in one trial; a reader takes it to mean it cures the disease. Both had the same word in front of them, yet they shared no meaning, and the reader comes away believing something the report never said.
card.rule: Count an important word as understood only when you also know which meaning the author gives it.
card.limits: Not every gap in meaning matters: ordinary words used in ordinary ways rarely mislead, and a small difference may not touch the point. The danger lies in unresolved ambiguity in the words that carry the author's argument.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Communication means something held in common
concepts.question: When has communication between a writer and a reader succeeded, and what is shared when it fails?

paragraphs: The word communication is related to the word common, as community is: a community is a group of people with something in common. To communicate is to try to share something with another, such as knowledge, a decision or a feeling.

Communication succeeds only when a common something results, such as a piece of knowledge that both parties now hold. When the communication of knowledge is ambiguous, the only things held in common are the words: one person wrote them and the other read them.
For success, both parties must use the same words with the same meanings. The authors call the result two minds with a single thought.
card.example: Two colleagues swap emails about a deadline at the end of the week. One means Friday at five; the other means Sunday night. The same phrase sat in both inboxes, but nothing else was held in common. Only when both take it as Friday at five has the deadline been communicated.
card.rule: Judge communication by whether a meaning, not only a set of words, has come to be held in common.
card.limits: A shared meaning is not agreement: two people can hold one thought in common and still differ on whether it is true. The demand for exactly shared meanings applies to the communication of knowledge, the kind this chapter is about.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: A term is a word used unambiguously
concepts.question: If almost every word has several meanings, how can any word serve as a term?

paragraphs: One might define a term as an unambiguous word, but strictly there are no such words. Nearly every word in the dictionary has several meanings.

The better definition is that a term is a word used unambiguously. A word with many meanings can still be used in one of them at a time. When writer and reader both use a word in one and only one meaning for a stretch of text, then for that stretch they have come to terms.
So being a term is a matter of how a word is used, not of the word itself.
card.example: Bank has several meanings. In a passage about rivers, writer and reader both take it as the land beside the water, so for that passage it works as a term. If the writer drifts into talk of loans without signalling the change, the word stops working as a term for the reader.
card.rule: Ask of each key word whether, in this passage, it is being used in one definite sense.
card.limits: One sense at a time does not mean one sense per book: an author may use a word in different senses in different places and still offer terms, provided each use is definite and the reader can follow the change.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Terms are made in communication, not found in dictionaries
concepts.question: Where do terms come from, if a dictionary cannot supply them?

paragraphs: You cannot look terms up in a dictionary, though it holds the materials for them. A dictionary lists the meanings a word can have; it cannot tell you which one a particular author is using on a particular page.
Terms occur only in the process of communication. They arise when a writer tries to avoid ambiguity and a reader helps by trying to follow the writer's use of words. Both sides do part of the work.
Success comes in degrees. Coming to terms is an ideal that writer and reader strive toward, and the authors describe terms as a skilled use of words for the sake of communicating knowledge.
card.example: A dictionary gives culture several senses: the arts, a people's way of life, a growth of bacteria in a dish. An anthropologist's book uses it for a people's shared way of life. The dictionary offered the candidates; only following the author's usage tells you which one is his term.
card.rule: Work out an author's meaning from how he uses a word, treating the dictionary as a list of candidates rather than the answer.
card.limits: A dictionary is still useful: it shows the range of senses a word can have and helps with words you have never met. What it cannot do is choose among those senses for you.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Terms are demanded of expository books, not poems
concepts.question: Does the demand for unambiguous terms apply to every kind of book, or only to some?

paragraphs: Everything said here about terms concerns expository books: works that convey knowledge, in the broad sense. The rule asks you to come to terms with an expository author.

Poetry and fiction are far less concerned with using words unambiguously. It can even be argued that the best poetry is the most richly ambiguous, and a good poet is sometimes ambiguous on purpose. This is one of the main differences between poetry and expository or scientific writing.
So ambiguity is a fault in a work that tries to convey knowledge, but it may be a strength in a poem.
card.example: A poem calls the sea a grey cloth folding the light. Several readings live in that line at once, and the poem is richer for them. A geology textbook that let shore mean three different things on one page would only confuse its reader.
card.rule: Before demanding definite terms, ask whether the work is expository, where ambiguity is a fault, or imaginative, where it may be intended.
card.limits: The line is not always sharp: an expository author may use a vivid image, and a novel may contain stretches of argument. Judge by what a passage is trying to do, not only by the shelf the book sits on.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Rule 5: find the important words and come to terms
concepts.question: What does the fifth rule of reading ask you to do, and what are its two parts?

paragraphs: The fifth rule of analytical reading, and the first of the second stage, is: find the important words and through them come to terms with the author. Roughly put, spot the words that matter and work out how the author is using them.
The rule has two parts. The first is to locate the important words, the ones that make a difference. The second is to determine, with precision, what these words mean as the author uses them.
The parts depend on each other but are distinct. A list of key words with no meanings attached is only half the job, and you cannot fix meanings precisely for words you have not first picked out.
card.example: Reading an essay on attention, you underline attention, distraction and focus, the words the argument turns on. That is the first part. Then you work out that by attention the author means effort a person directs, not interest that is caught. That is the second part, and only then have you come to terms.
card.rule: Pick out the words that make a difference, then fix precisely what each means as the author uses it.
card.limits: The rule is stated for expository works. It does not ask you to define every word: precision is needed for the important words, and most words on a page need no special work.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Two steps: from the words to the thought
concepts.question: Why does each rule of interpretation take two steps, one about words and one about thought?

paragraphs: The fifth rule is like the other rules of the interpreting stage in one respect: each takes two steps. One deals with the language as such; the other goes beyond the language to the thought behind it. The authors call these the grammatical and the logical aspects.

The grammatical step deals with words. The logical step deals with their meanings, that is, with terms. Both are needed: language used without thought communicates nothing, and knowledge cannot be communicated without language.

If language were a perfect medium, with every word an ideal term, the two steps would merge. The reader would see straight through the words into the writer's mind, and interpretation would be unnecessary. Language is not like that, so the steps stay separate.
card.example: In a sentence on markets, the grammatical step notices that the word efficient is doing the work. The logical step asks what thought it expresses: efficient in using resources, or efficient in reflecting information in prices? Only the second step reaches the term.
card.rule: For each key word, take the step from the word on the page to the thought it carries for the author.
card.limits: The steps are separate in analysis, not always in time: a skilled reader often takes them together. And the logical step cannot skip the grammatical one, since the thought reaches you only through the words.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Meeting the author halfway
concepts.question: Whose job is it to get past the barrier that language puts between a writer and a reader?

paragraphs: Because language is an imperfect medium for knowledge, it also acts as an obstacle to communication. The rules of interpretive reading exist to overcome that obstacle.

A good writer does his best to reach you through the barrier, but he cannot do the whole job alone. The reader must meet him halfway, working through from his own side. Teaching fails without a matching activity of being taught; in the same way, no author, however skilled, communicates without matching skill in his readers.

The authors picture two crews tunnelling through a mountain from opposite sides, each digging toward the other. They meet only if both make their calculations by the same principles of engineering: reader and writer must work by the same rules.
card.example: A dense essay on justice gives careful definitions in its first pages. A reader who skims past them and then calls the essay unclear has left the author digging alone. A reader who works through the definitions and tracks how they are used later meets him in the middle.
card.rule: Do your share of the work against the barrier of language instead of waiting for the author to reach you.
card.limits: Halfway is a picture, not a measure: some books ask more of a reader than others. And the reader's effort is aimed at the author's meaning; building a meaning of your own and crediting it to the author is not meeting him.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: One word, many terms
concepts.question: How can one word carry several terms, and how do you read each use in the author's sense?

paragraphs: The central point about words and terms has two sides: one word can be the vehicle for many terms, and one term can be expressed by many words.

Take the word reading. In this book it has meant reading to be entertained, reading for information and reading for understanding. Call the word X and the three meanings a, b and c. Then Xa, Xb and Xc are one word but three terms, provided writer and reader both know which sense is in use at each place.
If the authors write Xa and you read Xb, you are reading the same word, but not in the same way. Minds cannot meet in X itself, only in Xa, Xb or Xc. Meeting there is coming to terms.
card.example: In an article on work, labour sometimes means effort and sometimes the workforce as a group. Call them Xa and Xb. When the author writes that labour is scarce, he means Xb; read as Xa, the sentence would claim that people are making little effort, which he never said.
card.rule: For each use of a key word, ask which of its senses the author means there, and read it in that sense.
card.limits: Labelling senses works only when the author's uses are definite. Where he slides between senses without signalling, the letters cannot be assigned with confidence, and the honest finding is that the word is being used ambiguously.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Important words are words used in a special way
concepts.question: How can you tell which of an author's many words are important enough to work on?

paragraphs: Most of the words an author uses are not important. The important ones are those he uses in a special way. This is a matter of degree, but at one extreme are words used as anyone would use them in conversation, and these give a reader no trouble.

Ordinary words still shift meaning, but readers follow such shifts every day by context. The astronomer A. S. Eddington could write of pointer readings on dials, and elsewhere of reading nature, and trust you to follow, since both are ordinary senses.

Eddington could not use cause so lightly when he discussed the theory of causation. There the word carries a special sense, and how it is understood makes a difference that writer and reader must both attend to.
card.example: A cookbook writer makes a stock and, a page later, checks the stock of jars in her pantry. No reader stumbles: both are ordinary senses. But when she says a sauce must be emulsified, she means something exact about how fat and water combine, and a cook who reads it loosely may split the sauce.
card.rule: Pass lightly over words used as anyone would use them, and direct your effort to the words the author uses in a special way.
card.limits: Ordinary use is judged against your own time and place, so old or translated books need more care. And a familiar word can be used specially without warning, so looking ordinary is not proof of being ordinary.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Ordinary words in old books and translations
concepts.question: Why is it harder to tell ordinary words from special ones in an old book or a translation?

paragraphs: You know which words are used ordinarily today because you are alive today. Contemporary writers use most words as people now use them.

In a book written in the past, it is harder to tell which words the author used as most people of his time and place did. Some authors also use archaic words, or archaic senses of words, on purpose. Translation from another language complicates the matter further.
So in such books your sense of what is ordinary is a less reliable guide, and words that look familiar deserve a second look.
card.example: In older English, awful could mean full of awe or worthy of awe. A modern reader who takes an older writer's awful sight as an unpleasant one, treating the word as ordinary in today's sense, may read the passage the wrong way round without noticing.
card.rule: In old or translated books, ask whether a word was ordinary in the author's time and language, not only in yours.
card.limits: Most words in an old book still read much as they always have; the extra care is for words that matter or look slightly odd. And a translation can be only as definite as the translator's own grasp of the author's terms.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: A few key words, with one at the centre
concepts.question: On a typical page, how many words carry the author's meaning, and how do they relate to one another?

paragraphs: Take any page of an expository book and count the words you could read as you would in talk with friends: all the prepositions, conjunctions and articles, and nearly all the nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs. Most words can be read that way.
By the authors' own count, the opening of their chapter on terms used only a few important words: word, term, ambiguity, communication, and perhaps one or two more.

Among those few, term is the most important, and the others matter in relation to it. Key words are not a flat list: in that passage one word is central and the rest matter through how they bear on it.
card.example: A short essay on trust runs to hundreds of words. The ones doing the work are trust, reliance, betrayal and vulnerability. Trust is central; reliance, betrayal and vulnerability matter because of how they bear on it.
card.rule: On each page, pick out the handful of words that carry the meaning, and ask which one the others turn on.
card.limits: The number of key words varies: a dense technical passage may have many. And a single page may not show which word is central; that may become clear only across a chapter or the whole book.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Finding key words by trying to understand
concepts.question: How can you find the key words of a passage you do not yet understand?

paragraphs: You cannot locate the key words without trying to understand the passage they occur in. This sounds like a paradox: if you understand the passage, you already know which of its words matter most.

If you do not fully understand it, the likely reason is that you do not know how the author is using certain words. Those are the words to mark. Since words used in an ordinary way should give you no trouble, the words that do trouble you may well be the ones the author uses specially.
So the effort to understand and the search for key words go together.
card.example: A paragraph on evolution reads smoothly until it says that fitness rose while the animals grew weaker. The sentence stops you. Marking fitness, the word that will not fit its everyday sense, turns your confusion into a lead: the author must be using it in a special way.
card.rule: Try to understand each passage, and when you cannot, mark the words that stop you as likely key words.
card.limits: Trouble can have other causes: a long sentence, a missing step in the argument, or your own tiredness. A word that stops you is a candidate for special use, not proof of it.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: The words that trouble you
concepts.question: Which words are most important from your side as a reader, and are they always the author's key words?

paragraphs: From the reader's point of view, the most important words are those that give you trouble. It is likely that they are important for the author as well.

But they may not be. A word can trouble you because it is new to you, while the author uses it in its everyday sense. Such a word is still important for you, because until you understand it you cannot follow the passage.
The reader's list of important words and the author's overlap, but they are not the same list.
card.example: In a book on the brain, plasticity and the word sedulous both stop you. Plasticity turns out to be one of the author's key words, used in a special sense. Sedulous was only unfamiliar to you; a dictionary settles it, and it carries none of the argument.
card.rule: Treat the words that trouble you as important for you, and check whether each is also one of the author's key words.
card.limits: Settling a troubling word that matters little to the author is worth doing, but it will not bring you to terms with his main ideas. And words that cause you no trouble can still be key words.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Work where you have not yet come to terms
concepts.question: If one of an author's key words gives you no trouble, do you still have work to do on it?

paragraphs: Words that are important for the author may not bother you at all, precisely because you understand them. In that case you have already come to terms with him on those words.
Only where you fail to come to terms do you have work still to do. Effort belongs where understanding has not yet been reached, not spread evenly over every key word.
card.example: A reader of a book on statistics already knows what a median is, in exactly the author's sense. She notes it as a key word but spends no time on it, and turns her effort to confidence interval, which she cannot yet explain.
card.rule: Spend your effort on the key words you have not yet come to terms with, and pass over those you already share with the author.
card.limits: Feeling no trouble is good evidence only when your sense really matches the author's use. A familiar word that the author uses in a special way can feel easy while you misread it.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Words the author stresses
concepts.question: What positive signs does an author give that a word is one of his important words?

paragraphs: Finding key words because they are not ordinary for you is a negative method: you notice them because they bother you. There are also positive signs.

The first and plainest is explicit stress. An author may mark a word with quotation marks or italics. He may discuss its various senses and say how he will use it here and there. Or he may stress it by defining the thing that the word is used to name.
Each of these is the author doing part of your work, by showing where his key words are.
card.example: A book on happiness prints flourishing in italics on first use, spends a page on how others have used it, and then says: by flourishing I shall mean a life going well as a whole. Three signals point at one word. Whatever else you mark, mark that one.
card.rule: Look for the words an author marks in type, discusses in their senses, or uses to name things he defines.
card.limits: Type can stress a word for other reasons: italics for a foreign phrase or a title, quotation marks for irony or for quoting someone. Check that a marked word carries the argument, not only that it is marked.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Defined things and opening principles
concepts.question: In a book built from definitions and first principles, which words should you treat as basic?

paragraphs: No one can read Euclid without seeing that point, line, plane, angle and parallel are of first importance. These words name the geometrical entities that Euclid defines.

Other words, such as equals, whole and part, name nothing that is defined. You know they are important because they occur in the axioms. Euclid states his primary propositions at the very start, and the terms that make them up are basic.

So two signs point to key words: a word names something the author defines, or it appears in his opening principles. Such words may give you no difficulty, since Euclid seems to use them in their common sense, yet they are still basic.
card.example: A board game's rulebook opens by defining tile, turn and territory, then states its principles: each turn places one tile, and a territory scores when it is closed. Score and closed are not defined, but appearing in the opening principles marks them as basic too.
card.rule: Treat as key words those that name things the author defines and those that appear in his opening principles.
card.limits: Few books set out definitions and axioms as plainly as Euclid. Where they do not, these signs must be looked for, not expected at the start. And a basic word may be a common one, so being basic does not mean being hard.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Every field has a technical vocabulary
concepts.question: Why must readers of most books discover a technical vocabulary for themselves?

paragraphs: If all authors wrote as Euclid did, reading would be easier. Some thinkers have held that any subject could be set out in this geometrical manner, but the method of exposition and proof that works in mathematics does not fit every field of knowledge.

What is common to every kind of exposition is that each field of knowledge has its own technical vocabulary. Euclid makes his plain at the start, as do writers such as Galileo or Newton who write in the geometrical manner.
In books written differently, or in other fields, the technical vocabulary must be discovered by the reader.
card.example: A history of the Industrial Revolution never lists its terms. Yet enclosure, putting-out system and factory discipline do the work of a technical vocabulary. The reader finds them by noticing which words the argument keeps resting on.
card.rule: Expect every expository book to have a technical vocabulary, and find it yourself when the author does not set it out.
card.limits: A technical vocabulary need not be strange words: it may be ordinary words used in fixed senses. And not every field's vocabulary is well settled, so what counts as technical can vary from author to author.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Prior knowledge and the book's structure as guides
concepts.question: When an author does not point out his technical words, what can help you find them?

paragraphs: If the author has not pointed out his technical words, prior knowledge of the subject helps. A reader who knows some biology or economics before opening Darwin or Adam Smith already has leads toward their technical words.

The rules for analysing a book's structure help too. Knowing what kind of book it is, what it is about as a whole and what its major parts are helps you separate technical words from ordinary ones. The title, the chapter headings and the preface can be useful here.
From such clues you can tell, for example, that wealth is a technical word for Adam Smith, and species for Darwin.
card.example: A book is titled The Attention Economy, with chapters headed Scarcity, Capture and Markets for Focus. Before reading a page, a reader can expect attention, scarcity and capture to be used technically, and watch for how the author fixes their senses.
card.rule: Use what you already know of the subject, and of the book's kind, unity, parts, title, headings and preface, to pick out its technical words.
card.limits: Prior knowledge can mislead when an author uses a field's word in his own sense: what you know is a lead, not a definition. And titles and headings suggest candidates that the text itself must confirm.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: One technical word leads to another
concepts.question: Once you have found one technical word, how can it help you find the rest?

paragraphs: Technical words come in families. Once you know that wealth is a technical word for Adam Smith, others follow, and you can soon list his important words: labor, capital, land, wages, profits, rent, commodity, price, exchange, productive, unproductive, money and so on.

In Darwin, some you cannot miss are variety, genus, selection, survival, adaptation, hybrid, fittest and creation. One technical word leads to another, because each is tied to the others in the author's analysis.
So making a list is part of the method: write down each technical word you find and ask which others it calls for.
card.example: In a book on epidemics, a reader spots transmission as technical. Transmission calls for carrier, incubation and exposure, and exposure in turn leads to dose. Within a chapter the list has grown from one word to five, each found through the last.
card.rule: Keep a list of the technical words you find, and use each one to look for the others it is tied to.
card.limits: A list built by association can pull in words the author uses ordinarily, and can miss key words that stand apart from the family. A list locates terms; each word on it still needs its meaning fixed.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Common words made technical
concepts.question: Why are common words that an author turns into technical ones the most misleading kind?

paragraphs: Where a field has a well-established technical vocabulary, finding the important words is fairly easy: you spot them through acquaintance with the field, or because they are plainly not ordinary. But many fields have no settled technical vocabulary.

Philosophers are known for private vocabularies. Some words have a traditional standing in philosophy, though writers do not all use them alike. And philosophers often coin new words, or take a word from common speech and make it technical.
The second practice misleads most, because a reader who thinks he knows the word treats it as ordinary. Most good authors foresee this confusion and give an explicit warning when they do it.
card.example: A philosopher writes that only beings with interests have rights, and warns that by interests she means whatever can go better or worse for a being, not what it cares about. A reader who skips the warning and reads interests in its everyday sense will think she excludes every creature that cannot want things.
card.rule: When a familiar word seems to carry more weight than its everyday sense allows, look for the author's warning and read the word in his sense.
card.limits: Most familiar words in a philosophical book are still ordinary. And not every author warns: where no warning is given, the shifted use must be inferred from how the word behaves in context.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Words the author quarrels about
concepts.question: What does it tell you when an author argues with other writers about how a word should be used?

paragraphs: One clue to an important word is that the author quarrels with other writers about it.
When an author tells you how a word has been used by others, and why he chooses to use it otherwise, you can be sure the word makes a great difference to him.
So a dispute about a word is a strong positive sign, alongside typography, definitions and opening principles.
card.example: A book on poverty opens by noting that many economists define poverty as income below a fixed line, and argues that this misses people who cannot take part in ordinary life. The author then uses poverty in his broader sense throughout. The quarrel tells you poverty is his key word.
card.rule: When an author disputes how others use a word and explains his own choice, mark that word as one that matters greatly to him.
card.limits: A quarrel shows that the word matters to the author; it does not show that his usage is better or the rival usage wrong. Judging that comes later, once you understand both.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: The author's special vocabulary
concepts.question: What is an author's special vocabulary, and how is it wider than his technical words?

paragraphs: Technical vocabulary should not be taken too narrowly. The relatively small set of words that express an author's main ideas, his leading concepts, makes up his special vocabulary. These are the words that carry his analysis and his argument.

If he is saying something original, some of these words will be used in a very special way, while others may be used in the way that has become traditional in his field. Either way, they are the most important words for him.
They should be important for you too. But in addition, any other word whose meaning is not clear to you is important for you as a reader.
card.example: In a book on democracy, deliberation and legitimacy are used in the field's traditional senses, while the author's own phrase, quiet citizenship, is new. All three belong to her special vocabulary, since they carry her argument. A word like gerrymander, which you do not know, goes on your list too, though it is not one of her leading concepts.
card.rule: List the few words that carry the author's main ideas, traditional or new, and add any other word whose meaning is unclear to you.
card.limits: The special vocabulary is small; listing every technical-sounding word swamps it. And a word unclear to you is important for you without being one of the author's leading concepts, so keep the two kinds apart.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: The fault of inattention to words
concepts.question: What is the commonest reason readers fail to come to terms, and what habit prevents it?

paragraphs: The trouble with most readers is that they do not pay enough attention to words to locate their difficulties. They fail to tell the words they understand well enough from the words they do not.

All the aids for spotting important words are useless unless you make a deliberate effort to note the words you must work on. A reader who fails to ponder, or at least to mark, the words he does not understand is, in the authors' phrase, headed for disaster.

A book that can increase your understanding will contain words not fully clear to you. Reading them as if they were as plain as a newspaper's makes no headway. The outstanding fault of the non-active reader is inattention to words, and so a failure to come to terms.
card.example: Two students read a chapter on immunity. One reads it like a news story and finishes quickly. The other circles antigen, adaptive and tolerance, which she cannot yet explain. A week later only she can say what the chapter claimed, because she knew where her understanding stopped.
card.rule: As you read, deliberately mark the words you do not fully understand, so that you know where to work.
card.limits: Marking is a start, not the finish: circled words do nothing until you work out their meanings. And a text that teaches you nothing new may contain no such words, so finding none is not always a failure.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: One sense or several?
concepts.question: Once you have marked a troubling word, what is the first thing to settle about how the author uses it?

paragraphs: Spotting the important words only locates the places where you must work. The second part of the fifth rule begins once you have marked the words that trouble you.

There are two main possibilities. Either the author uses the word in a single sense throughout, or he uses it in two or more senses, shifting from place to place. In the first case the word stands for a single term; in the second, for several. Euclid is a good example of keeping key words to one meaning.
So the first question about a marked word is whether it carries one meaning or many in this book.
card.example: In a book on evolution, a reader marks selection and fitness and checks a dozen uses of each. Selection names the same process every time, so it is one term. Fitness sometimes means reproductive success and sometimes good health, so it stands for two terms, and she must watch which is in play.
card.rule: For each marked word, first find out whether the author uses it in one sense throughout or in several.
card.limits: One sense or several is a fact about this book, not about the word: a word that keeps one sense in one book may shift in another. And knowing a word has one sense is not yet knowing what that sense is.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Relating senses and tracking shifts
concepts.question: When an author uses a word in several senses, how do you follow him from one to another?

paragraphs: If a word has many meanings in a book, the procedure goes on. Try to see how the meanings are related to one another.
Then note the places where the word is used in one sense or another, and see whether the context gives any clue to the reason for the shift.
This last step lets you follow the word through its changes of meaning with the same flexibility the author shows.
card.example: In a book on government, state means a nation, the apparatus of government, and, now and then, a condition, as in the state of the roads. The first two are related, the apparatus being part of the nation. The reader notes that state means the apparatus wherever the author discusses officials and budgets, and the nation wherever he discusses wars and treaties.
card.rule: For a word with several senses, see how the senses are related, then mark where each is used and what in the context explains the shift.
card.limits: Some shifts have no reason worth finding, as when an everyday sense slips in by habit. And not every author shifts with care: where the context gives no clue, a shift may be a lapse rather than a design.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Finding meanings from the words you know
concepts.question: How do you find out what an author means by a word you do not understand?

paragraphs: The procedure so far leaves the main question open: how do you find out what the meanings are? The answer may seem unsatisfying at first. You discover the meaning of a word you do not understand by using the meanings of all the other words in the context that you do understand.

It can feel like going round in circles, but there is no other way. Most words around a difficult word are familiar, and they are its context. A comparison of our own, not the authors': this is the context skill a child uses on new words, now aimed at an author's special senses.
Patience and practice show that the method works: the reader already has, in the surrounding words, the materials needed for the job.
card.example: A history says the guild enforced a monopsony on wool: no weaver could sell to anyone but its members, so the guild set the price it paid. You may not know monopsony, but you know sell, anyone but, set and price. Together they fix it: a market with only one buyer.
card.rule: To find an unfamiliar meaning, work from the meanings of the surrounding words you already understand.
card.limits: Context can fix a meaning only when enough of it is understood; a passage dense with unknown words may call for easier reading first. And context shows the meaning a word has here, which may not be its meaning elsewhere.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Definitions work through words you know
concepts.question: How does a definition bring you to terms, and what must you already understand for it to work?

paragraphs: A definition shows the context method best. A definition is stated in words, and if you do not understand the words in it, you cannot understand the word that names the thing defined.

Euclid wants point used in only one way, so he first defines the thing: a point is that which has no part. He assumes you know the other words well enough. Whatever has parts is a complex whole; the opposite of complex is simple; to be simple is to lack parts. And is and that which tell you a point is an entity of some sort.
You acquire meanings by working with meanings you already possess. If every word in a definition had itself to be defined, nothing could ever be defined.
card.example: A guidebook defines a col as the lowest point on a ridge between two peaks. You know lowest, ridge, between and peak. From them you build the meaning of col without ever having stood on one.
card.rule: To grasp a definition, work from the words in it that you already understand, and build the defined word's meaning from them.
card.limits: A definition helps only if its own words are clear to you; one stated in other unfamiliar words passes the difficulty along. A chain of definitions has to rest, in the end, on words understood without one.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: A hard book is not all Greek
concepts.question: Why is it a mistake to give up on a hard book as if it were written in a language you do not know?

paragraphs: If every word in a book were strange to you, as in a book in a wholly foreign language, you could make no progress at all. That is what people mean when they say a book is all Greek to them.

Usually they have not tried to understand it, which would be fair only if it really were in Greek. Most words in a book in your own language are familiar. They surround the strange words, the technical ones, and form the context in which those must be interpreted. The reader has the materials for the job.
The authors do not claim the job is easy, only that it is possible. If it were not, no one could pass from understanding less to understanding more by working on a book alone.
card.example: A reader opens a book on quantum computing and meets qubit, superposition and decoherence on the first page. It feels like Greek. But the sentences around them are ordinary English: a qubit, unlike a bit, can be in two states at once. Those familiar words are her way in.
card.rule: Before calling a book unreadable, use the familiar words that surround its strange ones.
card.limits: A book can be beyond you for now if too few of its words, or too little of its background, are familiar; then an easier book on the subject is a sensible first step. The claim is that the job is possible, not that every book suits every reader today.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Fitting meanings like a jigsaw
concepts.question: How do the meanings of a book's difficult words fall into place as you read?

paragraphs: There is no rule of thumb for finding meanings. The process is something like putting a jigsaw puzzle together by trial and error.

A book comes to you with many words already in place. A word in place is a term: it is fixed by the meaning you and the author share. The remaining words must be put in place by trying them this way and that.

The more pieces you fit, the easier the rest become, if only because fewer remain. The better you see the picture that the placed words already show, the easier it is to make terms of the remaining ones. Each word put in place makes the next easier.
card.example: In a book on bird migration, you already share the author's meaning for flight, season and route. Zugunruhe puzzles you. It appears where caged birds grow restless each spring and autumn, at the times they would be travelling. With the pieces around it in place, it fits: migratory restlessness.
card.rule: Fit uncertain meanings in by trial, using the terms already in place, and let each fitted word help place the next.
card.limits: Trial and error is for words the author leaves you to place; where he defines a word plainly, that piece comes already fitted. And some fits will turn out wrong and need moving later.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: When the pieces will not fit
concepts.question: When the meanings in a book will not fit together, how do you tell your own mistake from the author's?

paragraphs: You will make errors. You may think you have found where a word belongs, then find that placing another word forces a whole series of readjustments. Errors get corrected because, while they remain, the picture cannot be completed.
With experience you learn to check yourself. You will know whether you have succeeded, and you will not blithely think you understand when you do not.

But the jigsaw comparison assumes that every piece fits, and no book is ideally good. The better the book, the better its terms are made and put together. With a bad book the rules mostly show how bad it is: if the author uses words ambiguously, you cannot find out what he means, only that he was not precise.
card.example: A reader takes reform, in a book on schools, to mean change of any kind. Then the author calls a sweeping change no reform at all. Her reading no longer fits, so she readjusts: by reform he means change that gives teachers more freedom. With that sense, the earlier passages fit too.
card.rule: When meanings will not fit, readjust your own readings first, and conclude the author was imprecise only when no reading makes his words fit.
card.limits: Telling your error from the author's takes judgment: blaming the author too soon stops you learning, while blaming yourself forever can hide a muddled book. Honest, repeated readjustment that still fails is the sign to look for.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Several senses are not the same as ambiguity
concepts.question: Is an author who uses an important word in several senses using it ambiguously?

paragraphs: It is usual for authors to use words in several senses, especially their most important words. That alone is not ambiguity.
To use a word ambiguously is to use it in several senses without distinguishing or relating them. An author who does that has not made terms that a reader can come to.

An author who distinguishes the several senses in which he uses a critical word, and so lets the reader make a matching discrimination, is offering terms. The authors admit they probably used important ambiguously themselves, not always making clear whether they meant important for the author or for the reader.
card.example: An economist writes: I use demand in two senses, the amount people want at a given price and the whole schedule of amounts at every price, and I will say which I mean. Two senses, both offered as terms. Another writer slides between the same two senses unannounced, and her readers cannot tell which claim she is making.
card.rule: Judge an author's use of a many-sensed word by whether he distinguishes and relates its senses, not by how many senses it has.
card.limits: Distinguishing can be done by context as well as by announcement: an author need not label every shift if the context makes it plain. And offered terms are not yet shared ones; the reader must still follow.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Using a word for several senses at once
concepts.question: Can one use of a word stand for several of its senses at once and still be a term?

paragraphs: A word with several distinct but related meanings can be used in a single sense or in a combination of senses.

Take reading again. In some places the authors use it for reading any kind of book; in others, for reading books that instruct rather than entertain; in others, for reading that enlightens rather than informs. Calling the three meanings a, b and c, the first use is Xabc, the second Xbc and the third Xc.
So when several meanings are related, a word can stand for all of them, for some, or for only one at a time. As long as each use is definite, the word so used is a term.
card.example: A guide to exercise uses training for all physical activity, then for planned workouts only, then for workouts aimed at a race. The word widens and narrows, but each use is definite in its passage, so each is a term.
card.rule: When a word covers several related senses, ask how much of its range each use takes in: all, some or one.
card.limits: A combined use is a term only if it is definite: a use that might take in all the senses or only one, with nothing to decide, is ambiguous. And combining works for related senses; unrelated ones, like a river bank and a savings bank, do not combine.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Many words, one term
concepts.question: When an author changes his word, has he changed his meaning?

paragraphs: Repeating one word over and over is awkward and dull, except in mathematical writing. So good authors often substitute words with the same or very similar meanings for their important words.

This is the opposite of one word standing for several terms: here one term is expressed by two or more words used as synonyms. Let X and Y be enlightenment and insight, and a the meaning both can carry, a gain in understanding. Then Xa and Ya are one term, though distinct as words.
When the authors speak of reading for insight and reading for enlightenment, they mean the same kind of reading. The words differ; there is one term to grasp.
card.example: A report on cities uses sprawl, low-density spread and scattered suburban growth on different pages. Checking the contexts, a reader finds all three describe the same pattern. She records one term with three names, not three ideas.
card.rule: When an author changes words, check whether the term has changed or only the word.
card.limits: Near-synonyms are not always synonyms for an author: he may switch words precisely to mark a new sense. Treat a change of word as a question to settle from context, not as an answer either way.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Phrases can be terms too
concepts.question: Can a whole phrase express one of an author's terms, and why might he prefer a phrase to a single word?

paragraphs: A phrase that works as a unit, one that could be the subject or predicate of a sentence, is like a single word: it can refer to something being talked about. So a term can be expressed by a phrase as well as by a word.
All the relations between words and terms hold for phrases too. Two phrases may express the same term, and one phrase may express several terms, depending on how its words are used.

In general a phrase is less likely to be ambiguous than a word. Each word in it sits in the context of the others, which restricts their meanings. So a writer who wants to be sure you get his meaning often puts a fairly elaborate phrase in place of a single word.
card.example: To be sure readers come to terms about reading, the authors replace the word with reading for enlightenment, and then with a longer phrase about passing from understanding less to understanding more by the work of your own mind on a book. One term, expressed by a word, a short phrase and a long one.
card.rule: Treat an author's unified phrases as possible terms, and use his longer phrases to pin down what his key words mean.
card.limits: Longer is not always clearer: a phrase built from vague words can be as ambiguous as a single word. And not every group of words is a unit; a phrase expresses a term only when it works as a whole.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Vocabulary and terminology in two columns
concepts.question: How can two lists, one of words and one of meanings, show how an author's words and terms are related?

paragraphs: One way to remember that one word can represent several terms is to distinguish an author's vocabulary from his terminology.
List the important words in one column and their important meanings in another. The links between the columns show the relation between the vocabulary and the terminology.

You will find two kinds of link. A single word may be linked to several terms, and a single term may be linked to several words. Supposing that every change of word is a change of term is as great an error as supposing that the same word always carries the same term.
card.example: Reading a book on learning, a reader makes two columns. Words: practice, rehearsal, drill, memory. Meanings: repeating a skill to improve it; storage of past experience; the power to recall on demand. Practice, rehearsal and drill all link to the first meaning; memory links to both the second and the third.
card.rule: Keep the author's important words and his important meanings in separate columns, and draw the links between them.
card.limits: The columns record your reading, so they can be wrong and need revising as you readjust. And a neat table can hide a muddled book: where you cannot link a word to any definite meaning, mark the gap instead of forcing a link.

concepts.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
concepts.title: Beyond the rule: further study and a small habit
concepts.question: What further questions about words does practising this rule raise, and why is the habit worth forming even without them?

paragraphs: The authors say they have only touched on the essentials. A full account of words and terms would take many chapters of grammatical and logical explanation.

As you practise, you will want to know about literal and metaphorical uses of words, abstract and concrete words, proper and common names, and definition: defining words versus defining things, and why some words are indefinable yet have definite meanings. You will also want to know about the emotive use of words, to stir feeling or move people to act rather than to convey knowledge.

Books on these subjects profit you more when you bring questions born of your own reading. But even if you go no further, finding the important words, following their shifting meanings and coming to terms will greatly increase your comprehension. Seldom does so small a change in habit have so large an effect.
card.example: A reader who practises coming to terms notices that a charity appeal calls its cause a battle and its donors soldiers. She begins to wonder about metaphor, and about words chosen to stir feeling rather than to inform. That question, born of her reading, is what makes a book on rhetoric worth opening.
card.rule: Make finding key words and their meanings a habit, and let the questions it raises guide any further study of language.
card.limits: Further study of grammar and logic helps only when tied to practice; studied in the abstract, it adds little to your reading. And the habit pays off without that study.

concepts.title: A proposition is a judgment, not an offer
concepts.question: When an author makes a proposition, what is he doing, and how does that differ from a trader's proposition?

paragraphs: In business a proposition is an offer: a buyer or seller declares how he intends to act. A proposition in an expository book is also a declaration, but of another kind. It expresses the author's judgment about something.

The author affirms what he thinks is true, or denies what he judges to be false. He asserts that this or that is the case. So a proposition is a declaration of knowledge, or of what the author takes to be knowledge, not a declaration of intentions.
