When you look for an author's propositions, then, you look for what he claims about his subject, not for what he plans to do in the book or hopes you will feel.
card.example: A book on oceans says: 'In this chapter I will explain why sea levels rise.' That states an intention. Two pages later: 'Most of the recent rise comes from seawater expanding as it warms.' That is a proposition: a judgment the author affirms as true.
card.rule: To find a proposition, ask what the author is affirming as true or denying as false.
card.limits: Statements of plans, questions and wishes are not propositions, even inside an expository book. And a declaration tells you only what the author thinks, not yet why he thinks it.

concepts.title: Checking the preface's promises
concepts.question: How can you tell whether an author has kept the promises he makes at the start of his book?

paragraphs: Authors often state their intentions at the start, in a preface or introduction. In an expository book the usual promise is to instruct you about something: to explain a cause, settle a question, show how something works.

A promise is not a delivery. Intentions describe what the author hopes to do; propositions are what he actually declares. To see whether he kept his word, set the promises beside the propositions you find in the body of the book.
If the preface promises an explanation and the chapters hold only descriptions, anecdotes and questions, the promise has not been met, however confident the preface sounded.
card.example: A preface says the book will show why some industrial cities recovered from decline and others did not. Reading on, you list what the author affirms: the recovering cities kept their universities, diversified early and drew in newcomers. Those propositions are the delivery you measure against the promise.
card.rule: Measure an author's stated intentions against the propositions he actually makes.
card.limits: A preface can understate as well as overstate, and some books deliver more than they promise. A book with no preface still has propositions; the promises are a useful yardstick, not a requirement.

concepts.title: Terms come before propositions
concepts.question: Why must a reader usually come to terms with an author before finding out what he proposes?

paragraphs: In business, people usually hear the proposition first and come to terms afterwards. Reading runs the other way. A term is a word used in one definite sense, and coming to terms means sharing the author's senses for his key words. You usually have to do that before you can tell what judgment he declares.
The reason is that a proposition is built out of terms. If you have not settled what learning or value means in this book, you cannot know what a sentence using those words affirms.
That is why Rule 5 of analytical reading deals with words and terms, and Rule 6 with sentences and propositions.
card.example: An economics book says that inflation is a monetary phenomenon. Until you know whether the author means by inflation a rise in prices or growth in the money supply, you cannot tell whether he is stating a discovery or restating his definition.
card.rule: Settle what the key words mean before deciding what a sentence asserts.
card.limits: The order is the usual one, not a fixed sequence. Only the key words need settling first; ordinary words can be read in their everyday sense. And sometimes a puzzling sentence is what shows you which words need work.

concepts.title: Opinions need reasons
concepts.question: Why is knowing an author's propositions not enough when you care about the subject rather than the author?

paragraphs: We usually trust an author to be honest in declaring what he thinks. But knowing his opinions only tells you about him. According to the authors, propositions without supporting reasons are nothing but expressions of personal opinion.

If your interest is the subject, you want to know why the author thinks you should accept his claims. That is the work of the seventh rule: finding his arguments, the reasons he offers for his propositions.
Reasons come in many kinds. Some arguments try to show that something is true; others defend no more than a probability. Every kind relates statements so that one is said because of another.
card.example: A nutrition writer says breakfast is the most important meal. That tells you her view. Learning that she rests it on trials of concentration in schoolchildren who did and did not eat breakfast tells you why she holds it, which is what you need before weighing the claim.
card.rule: For each important proposition, find the reasons the author gives for accepting it.
card.limits: If you read only to learn about the author as a person, his bare opinions may be what you want. And finding his reasons is not yet judging them; that comes after you understand.

concepts.title: Words that signal an argument
concepts.question: Which words in a passage tell you that an argument, rather than a list of claims, is being made?

paragraphs: An argument relates statements so that one is said because of another. The word because signals that a reason is being given. Other connecting words do the same work: if this, then that; since this, therefore that; it follows from this that.
These words mark the joints of reasoning. Spotting them shows you which statements are offered as grounds and which as the point being supported.
The authors point to their own earlier reasoning as an example: if we want to go on learning after school, then we must know how to learn from books, which are absent teachers.
card.example: A news analysis says: since the central bank has raised rates twice, borrowing has slowed, and it follows that house prices should cool. Since marks a reason; it follows that marks the conclusion drawn.
card.rule: Use connecting words such as because, since, therefore and if... then to locate the reasons and conclusions in a passage.
card.limits: Signal words are clues, not proof. Since can mark time (since Monday), and many arguments leave their connections unstated, so sometimes you must supply the link yourself.

concepts.title: What makes statements an argument
concepts.question: What makes a set of statements an argument, and how much text does an argument need?

paragraphs: An argument is a set or series of statements in which some provide the grounds or reasons for another, the conclusion. Because it needs more than one statement, an argument needs at least a collection of sentences, often a paragraph, to express it.

The grounds are called premises or principles. They are not always stated first; an author may give the conclusion and then the reasons. Wherever they appear, the premises are the source of the conclusion.
A string of claims on one topic is not yet an argument. What makes it one is the relation: some statements are offered as support for another.
card.example: Conclusion first: the library should stay open until midnight in exam weeks. Most students revise late at night, and the reading rooms are full by evening. The second and third statements are the premises, even though they come after the conclusion.
card.rule: To find an argument, sort its statements into the grounds offered and the conclusion they support.
card.limits: What counts is statements, not sentences: one compound sentence can hold premises and conclusion together. And a list of related facts with no claim of support is not an argument, however long.

concepts.title: Valid is not the same as true
concepts.question: If a conclusion follows from its premises, does that make the conclusion true?

paragraphs: If an argument is valid, its conclusion follows from its premises: granting them, you must grant it. Validity is about the link between grounds and conclusion.
That does not make the conclusion true. One or all of the premises may be false, and false premises can lead validly to a false conclusion.
So two different questions arise about any argument: does the conclusion follow, and are the premises true? Answering one does not answer the other.
card.example: All birds can fly; penguins are birds; so penguins can fly. The conclusion follows from the premises, so the argument is valid. But the first premise is false, and so is the conclusion.
card.rule: Ask separately whether a conclusion follows from the premises and whether the premises are true.
card.limits: Validity alone guarantees nothing about truth, and true premises do not rescue a conclusion that does not follow from them. While interpreting, you note the structure; judging the premises belongs to criticism.

concepts.title: From words to sentences to paragraphs
concepts.question: Why do the rules of interpretation move from words to sentences to groups of sentences?

paragraphs: The rules of interpretation have a grammatical side and a logical side. Logically they go from terms to propositions to arguments. Grammatically they go from words and phrases to sentences to groups of sentences such as paragraphs. Each step builds a more complex unit out of simpler ones.
It is true that a book consists of words, but saying so is not adequate. It also consists of groups of words taken as units, and of groups of sentences taken as units.
So the active reader attends to sentences and paragraphs as well as words. There is no other way to find the author's terms, propositions and arguments.
card.example: Reading a policy report, you can define subsidy and demand exactly and still miss the claim that subsidies raise prices, which lives in a sentence, and the case for that claim, which runs across a paragraph.
card.rule: Read in units of growing size: words for terms, sentences for propositions, groups of sentences for arguments.
card.limits: The match between grammatical and logical units is loose. A sentence can hold several propositions, and an argument can sit inside one sentence or run across many paragraphs, so the units guide attention without fixing it.

concepts.title: Where outlining and interpreting meet
concepts.question: Where do outlining a book's structure and interpreting its contents meet, and why does that meeting matter?

paragraphs: In the first stage of analytical reading you outline: you go from the book as a whole down to its major parts and their divisions. Interpretation runs the other way, up from terms to propositions to arguments.

The two movements meet. Keep dividing a part and you reach a point where you can only say: in this part, the following points are made. Each point is likely to be a proposition, and several together probably form an argument.
So outlining works down to propositions and arguments, and interpretation works up to them. When both are done, the authors say, you can claim to know the contents of a book.
card.example: Outlining a book on public health, you divide Part Two into chapters on vaccines and sanitation, then the vaccine chapter into three points. Interpreting its key sentences, you find three propositions and an argument linking them. If the two lists match, each process supports the other.
card.rule: Work down by outlining and up by interpreting until both arrive at the same propositions and arguments.
card.limits: The meeting point is a check, not a guarantee: a careless outline can match a misreading. And some parts of a book, such as reports of evidence or digressions, contain few propositions of their own.

concepts.title: Units of language, units of thought
concepts.question: What is the difference between a sentence and a proposition, or between a paragraph and an argument?

paragraphs: Sentences and paragraphs are grammatical units: units of language. Propositions and arguments are logical units: units of thought and knowledge.

The difference matters because language is not a perfect medium for thought. One word can have several meanings, and several words can have one meaning. The same looseness affects sentences and propositions.
So when you interpret, keep asking which you are handling: the sentence on the page, or the proposition it expresses. You mark sentences; you understand propositions.
card.example: 'The meeting is cancelled' and 'There will be no meeting' are two sentences in different words. They express one proposition. Rewrite either in French and you have a third sentence, still with the same proposition.
card.rule: Treat the sentence as the vehicle and the proposition as what it carries.
card.limits: The distinction is a tool for reading, not a licence to ignore wording. Exact wording can matter a great deal, as in contracts or poems, and you reach the proposition only through the sentence.

concepts.title: No one-to-one match
concepts.question: What do the authors call the greatest error in applying the rules of interpretation, and how do buttons and buttonholes illustrate it?

paragraphs: On a well-made coat there is a button for every buttonhole and a hole for every button: a one-to-one relation. Words and terms are not like that. One word can express several terms, and one term can be expressed by several words.

The same holds between sentences and propositions, and between paragraphs and arguments. According to the authors, the greatest error in applying these rules is to suppose a one-to-one relation between elements of language and elements of thought.
They add a caution even about coats: jacket sleeves carry buttons with no holes, and a worn coat may have a hole with no button.
card.example: A report repeats the sentence the policy works in three chapters. In one it means the policy cuts costs, in another that voters like it, in the third that it meets its legal target. Treating the three identical sentences as one claim is a one-to-one error.
card.rule: Never assume that one sentence equals one proposition, or one paragraph one argument.
card.limits: Often the match does hold: a simple sentence whose words are used unambiguously usually expresses one proposition. The warning is against assuming the match, not against ever finding it.

concepts.title: Questions, wishes and intentions
concepts.question: Which sentences in a book do not express propositions, and what can they still tell you?

paragraphs: Not every sentence in a book expresses a proposition. Some ask questions: they state problems rather than answers. Propositions are the answers to questions. That is why sentences expressing them are called declarative, and sentences that ask are called interrogative.
Other sentences express wishes or intentions. They may tell you about the author's purpose, but they do not convey the knowledge he is trying to expound.
Such sentences are still worth reading. A question tells you what problem the author is about to answer; an intention tells you what he hopes to do. The propositions are where he gives his answers.
card.example: An essay opens: 'Why do some languages die out while others spread? I want to suggest an answer that may surprise you.' The first sentence states the problem, the second the author's intention. The proposition comes later: languages spread along trade routes more than through conquest.
card.rule: Separate declarative sentences, which can carry propositions, from questions and statements of wishes or intentions, which cannot.
card.limits: Not every declarative sentence is a key proposition either: many are background or side remarks. The test sets aside sentences that cannot carry the author's knowledge; it does not tell you which of the rest matter most.

concepts.title: One sentence, two propositions
concepts.question: How can the very same sentence express two different propositions?

paragraphs: Words are ambiguous, so the same sentence can express different propositions when its words shift from one term to another.

The authors' example is the sentence 'Reading is learning.' If learning means acquiring information in one place and developing understanding in another, the sentence stays the same but the proposition changes, because the terms are different.
So when a key sentence recurs, check whether its words carry the same terms each time before treating it as one repeated claim.
card.example: A school brochure says 'Our students succeed' on the admissions page, where succeed means passing exams, and on the alumni page, where it means building careers. Same sentence, two propositions, and evidence for one says little about the other.
card.rule: When a sentence recurs, check whether its key words carry the same terms each time.
card.limits: Most repeated sentences in a careful book mean the same thing each time. The check is for key sentences whose words have more than one sense, not a reason to suspect every repetition.

concepts.title: Compound sentences hold several propositions
concepts.question: How many propositions can one grammatical sentence contain, and how do you find them?

paragraphs: A simple sentence with unambiguous words usually expresses one proposition. A compound sentence expresses two or more, even when its words are clear. It is really a collection of sentences joined by words such as and, if... then, or not only... but also.
The line between a long compound sentence and a short paragraph can be hard to draw. A compound sentence can even express several propositions related as an argument.

The authors take a sentence from Machiavelli's The Prince: a prince should inspire fear so that, if he does not win love, he avoids hatred, because he can bear being feared while not hated, which lasts as long as he leaves his citizens' property and women alone. The because marks the main break.
card.example: The authors find three propositions: (1) a prince ought to inspire fear in a certain way; (2) the reason is that he can endure being feared so long as he is not hated; (3) he can avoid hatred only by keeping his hands off his subjects' property and women.
card.rule: Break each long key sentence at its connecting words and list the separate propositions it contains.
card.limits: Not every and joins two claims: a sentence about salt and pepper sitting on the table makes one claim about a pair. Look at what is asserted, not only at the joining words.

concepts.title: Separate before you judge
concepts.question: Why must you separate the propositions in a complex sentence before agreeing or disagreeing with it?

paragraphs: To agree or disagree with an author, you must first understand what he is saying. If one sentence says three things, you may disagree with one of them and agree with the others.

With Machiavelli's sentence, the authors note, you might reject his advice that a prince rule by fear on any grounds, yet grant his shrewdness in saying the prince had better not add hatred to fear, and accept that leaving subjects' property and women alone is needed to avoid hatred.
Unless you see the distinct propositions, your verdict can only be on the whole sentence, which is too coarse to be fair.
card.rule: Split a complex sentence into its propositions so you can judge each one on its own.
card.limits: Separating is part of understanding; agreeing and disagreeing come later, in criticism. And propositions linked as premise and conclusion are not independent: if you reject a premise, the conclusion loses the support it gave.

concepts.title: Simple sentences can say several things
concepts.question: Can a grammatically simple sentence assert more than one thing, and how do lawyers handle this?

paragraphs: Lawyers examine sentences carefully to see exactly what a plaintiff alleges or a defendant denies. The sentence 'John Doe signed the lease on March 24' looks simple, but it says several things.

It asserts that John Doe signed, that what he signed was the lease, and that he signed it on March 24. Some of these may be true and others false: he may have signed, but not on that date, and the date may matter.
So even a grammatically simple sentence sometimes expresses two or more propositions. Its dates, places and qualifiers can each add a claim.
card.example: The sentence 'A 2019 trial showed the drug halved deaths' asserts that there was a trial in 2019, that it tested this drug, and that deaths fell by half. A critic might accept the trial and dispute the size of the effect.
card.rule: Ask of each key sentence, even a simple one, which separate claims its parts make.
card.limits: Splitting can go too far. Break a sentence only into claims that could be true or false separately and that matter to the author's point; listing every grammatical detail gives noise, not understanding.

concepts.title: One proposition, many sentences
concepts.question: How can you tell that two different sentences express one and the same proposition?

paragraphs: The mismatch runs the other way too: one proposition can be expressed by two or more different sentences.

The authors' example: 'Teaching and being taught are correlative functions' and 'Initiating and receiving communication are related processes.' If you have grasped their terms through the words they use as synonyms, you will see that the two sentences say the same thing.
To recognize such pairs, look past the words to the terms. Where the terms match and the relation asserted between them matches, the proposition is the same.
card.example: A biology text says in chapter 2 that organisms inherit traits from their parents, and in chapter 8 that offspring receive characteristics from those who produced them. Different words, same terms, same proposition: the reader should not count two discoveries.
card.rule: Look past different wording to the terms and the relation asserted; if both match, the proposition is the same.
card.limits: Similar wording can hide a real difference: changing one qualifier, such as all to most, makes a different proposition. Sameness is judged by what is asserted, not by how close the words feel.

concepts.title: Enough grammar to see through words
concepts.question: Why do the authors say some grammar is indispensable for reaching an author's terms, propositions and arguments?

paragraphs: The authors assume you know some grammar: not everything about syntax, but enough to attend to the order of words in a sentence and how they relate to one another.

You cannot deal with terms, propositions and arguments, the elements of thought, until you can get beneath the surface of language. While words, sentences and paragraphs stay opaque and unanalyzed, they are a barrier to communication rather than a medium of it.
Without this, the authors warn, you will read words but not receive knowledge.
card.example: 'The committee only approved the budget on Friday' and 'The committee approved only the budget on Friday' differ in where one word sits. The first stresses how late the approval came; the second says nothing else was approved. A reader blind to word order gets the words and misses the claim.
card.rule: Look at how the words of a key sentence are ordered and related before deciding what it asserts.
card.limits: The authors do not ask for formal analysis or technical vocabulary. You can attend to how words relate without naming the parts of speech; grammar serves understanding and is not the goal.

concepts.title: Rules 6 and 7 and where they apply
concepts.question: What do Rules 6 and 7 tell the reader to do, and to which kinds of book do they mainly apply?

paragraphs: Rule 5 was to find the important words and come to terms. Rule 6 is to mark the most important sentences in a book and discover the propositions they contain. Rule 7 is to locate or construct the basic arguments in the book by finding them in the connection of sentences.
Rule 7 says sentences rather than paragraphs on purpose; the authors explain later that arguments and paragraphs do not line up.

Like the rule about terms, these rules apply primarily to expository works, books that convey knowledge. For novels, plays and poems the rules about propositions and arguments are quite different, and the authors treat them later.
card.example: In a history of vaccines, you mark the sentences stating its main claims (Rule 6) and trace how they support one another (Rule 7). In a novel about a plague, the sentences tell a story, and these rules need reshaping before they fit.
card.rule: In an expository book, mark the key sentences for their propositions and trace how sentences connect into arguments.
card.limits: Applied unchanged to a novel, play or poem, these rules mislead: a character's speech is not the author's proposition, and a story does not argue the way a treatise does.

concepts.title: Every sentence understood, a few studied
concepts.question: If only a few sentences in a book are key, what should you do with all the rest?

paragraphs: A book contains relatively few key sentences, but that does not mean you can ignore the rest. You have to understand every sentence.
Most sentences, like most words, cause no difficulty. You read them relatively quickly, as the earlier discussion of reading speeds suggested.
The few key sentences get the slow, careful reading. Varying your pace this way gives each sentence the attention it needs, no less and no more.
card.example: In a twenty-page chapter on vaccine trials, most sentences report dates, numbers of volunteers and procedures, and you follow them at a steady pace. Three sentences state what the trials showed and why the results can be trusted; those you read slowly, perhaps twice.
card.rule: Understand every sentence, read the easy majority quickly, and save slow reading for the few that need it.
card.limits: Quick reading of ordinary sentences still means understanding them. If an easy-looking sentence turns out to carry a key claim, or you lose the thread, slow down; the pace follows the difficulty, not a fixed ratio.

concepts.title: The sentences that resist you
concepts.question: From your own point of view as a reader, which sentences in a book are the important ones?

paragraphs: From the reader's side, the important sentences are those that need an effort of interpretation because, at first sight, they are not perfectly intelligible. You understand them just well enough to know there is more to understand.

These are the sentences you read much more slowly and carefully than the rest. They may not be the ones most important to the author, but they are likely to be, because you will have the most trouble with the most important things he has to say.
So difficulty is a guide: the sentences that resist you are good candidates for the book's leading propositions.
card.example: Reading a book on evolution, you move easily through descriptions of finches and fossils. Then: selection acts on individuals, but its results show up in populations. You half understand it and sense there is more. That sentence is important for you, and probably for the author too.
card.rule: Treat the sentences you understand only partly as your key sentences, and give them your slowest reading.
card.limits: Difficulty is a clue, not a proof. A sentence can be hard because it is badly written or uses a rare word in passing, and a key sentence can seem easy if you have misread it. Check against the author's own emphasis.

concepts.title: The judgments the argument rests on
concepts.question: From the author's point of view, which sentences are the important ones, and how do you separate them from the rest?

paragraphs: From the author's side, the important sentences express the judgments on which his whole argument rests.

A book contains much more than its bare arguments. The author may explain how he came to his view, or why he thinks it has serious consequences. He may discuss the words he must use, comment on the work of others, and add all sorts of supporting and surrounding discussion.

The heart of his communication is his major affirmations and denials and the reasons he gives for them. To come to grips with the book, see those sentences as if they were raised from the page in high relief.
card.example: A book argues that cities should tax land rather than buildings. Chapters tell the idea's history, profile its champions and reply to critics. The sentences that matter most say that taxing buildings discourages construction and that a land tax cannot be passed on to tenants.
card.rule: Separate the author's main affirmations, denials and reasons from the discussion that surrounds them.
card.limits: Surrounding discussion is not worthless: it can explain a key sentence or show why it matters. Seeing the main sentences in high relief means letting them stand out, not ignoring everything else.

concepts.title: Signals and formats that mark key sentences
concepts.question: How do some authors and book formats point out the leading sentences, and what do careless readers do with such signals?

paragraphs: Some authors help. They tell you when a point is important, or use typographical devices to make leading sentences stand out. Yet the authors report meeting many readers who ignored even such clear signs and read on instead of stopping to examine the sentences.

Some formats give leading propositions a special place. Euclid states his definitions, postulates and axioms at the start and labels every proposition to be proved. Aquinas heads each section with a question, states objections to his answer, and marks where he argues his own point with the words 'I answer that.'
Even in such books, a reader who treats everything as equally important, at one speed, sees only a blur.
card.rule: Stop at the sentences an author or format marks as leading, and examine them before reading on.
card.limits: Signals help only if you use them, and most books lack Euclid's or Aquinas's format. Authors also emphasise sentences for other reasons, such as a striking phrase, so a marked sentence still needs your own judgment of its role.

concepts.title: Be perplexed and know it
concepts.question: Why do the authors say that being perplexed, and knowing it, is an essential part of reading?

paragraphs: Where a book's format does not point out the important sentences, the reader must find them himself. One way is to notice the difference between passages you understand readily and those you do not.
That is why it matters to be perplexed and know it. The authors say wonder is the beginning of wisdom, in learning from books as in learning from nature.
If you never ask yourself questions about the meaning of a passage, you cannot expect the book to give you any insight you do not already have.
card.example: Reading an essay on free will, you notice you have been nodding along for pages, then stop at a sentence you cannot restate. Instead of moving on, you ask what the author means by caused here and how it fits what came before. That question marks a sentence to work on.
card.rule: Notice where you are puzzled, and turn the puzzle into a question about the passage's meaning.
card.limits: Perplexity is a starting point, not a verdict. Some confusion comes from fatigue or haste, and some clears as you read on; the aim is to locate the real puzzles, not to halt at every unfamiliar phrase.

concepts.title: Key words lead to key sentences
concepts.question: How do the words you have marked help you find key sentences, and must the rules be followed in a fixed order?

paragraphs: Another clue to the important sentences is the words that compose them. If you have already marked the important words, they will lead you to the sentences that deserve attention. So the first step of interpretation prepares for the second.
The reverse also happens: you may mark certain words only after a sentence has puzzled you. The rules are stated in a fixed order, but you need not follow them in that order.

Terms make up propositions, and propositions contain terms. If you know the terms a sentence's words express, you have caught its proposition; if you understand the proposition, you have arrived at the terms as well.
card.example: A sentence puzzles you: the market is a discovery procedure. Working on it, you realise discovery is used in a special sense and mark it as a key word. That mark then leads you to three other sentences that use the word.
card.rule: Use your marked key words to find key sentences, and let puzzling sentences send you back to words you have not yet marked.
card.limits: A key word appears in many sentences, not all of them key, so it narrows the search without finishing it. And moving back and forth between the rules is no excuse for skipping the work on terms.

concepts.title: Sentences that form a sequence
concepts.question: How can spotting sentences that form a sequence, with a beginning and an end, lead you to the principal propositions?

paragraphs: A further clue: the principal propositions must belong to the book's main argument, so they must be either premises or conclusions. If you can detect sentences that seem to form a sequence, with a beginning and an end, you have probably found important ones.

Every argument takes time to state. You may speak a sentence in one breath, but an argument has pauses: you say one thing, then another, then another. It begins somewhere, goes somewhere, gets somewhere. It is a movement of thought.
The movement can run either way. It may start with the conclusion and then give the reasons, or start with evidence and reasons and arrive at the conclusion.
card.example: In an essay on bees: these pesticides impair bees' navigation. Bees that cannot navigate fail to return to the hive. Colonies that lose their foragers collapse. So these pesticides contribute to colony collapse. The four sentences form a sequence with a start and an end, which marks them as key.
card.rule: Look for sentences that form a sequence moving from a start to an end; they are likely the premises and conclusions of the main argument.
card.limits: Not every sequence is an argument: a story or a set of instructions also has a beginning and an end. Check that some sentences are offered as support for others, not only placed after them.

concepts.title: Slow down for puzzles, not curiosities
concepts.question: Over which sentences do readers wrongly slow down, and why is this a special obstacle with older books?

paragraphs: Many people believe they know how to read because they read at different speeds. But they pause and go slowly over the wrong sentences: the ones that interest them rather than the ones that puzzle them.

This is a great obstacle with any book that is not wholly contemporary. An old book contains facts that surprise us because they differ from what we know. That kind of novelty is not what you seek when reading for understanding.
Interest in the author, his language or his world is one thing; concern to understand his ideas is another. The rules of this chapter serve the second.
card.example: Reading an eighteenth-century treatise on trade, you linger over prices in shillings and odd spellings, and skim a sentence claiming that a nation grows rich by producing goods, not by hoarding gold. The curiosities got the slow reading; the idea needed it.
card.rule: Slow down where sentences puzzle you, not where they only interest or surprise you.
card.limits: Curiosity is not forbidden; interest in a period is a fine reason to read an old book. The point is not to mistake satisfying curiosity for understanding the author's ideas.

concepts.title: A proposition is what the sentence means
concepts.question: Once you have found a leading sentence, what does discovering its proposition require?

paragraphs: Locating the leading sentences is not the whole of Rule 6. You must also discover the proposition or propositions each one contains, which is another way of saying you must know what the sentence means.
You find terms by finding what a word means in a given use. You find propositions in a similar way, by interpreting all the words that make up the sentence, and especially its principal words.
So the work on terms feeds straight into the work on propositions: a sentence's meaning is built from the senses of its principal words.
card.example: A key sentence in a book on politics reads: liberty is the absence of interference. To find its proposition you settle liberty (political freedom, not free will) and interference (deliberate obstruction by other people). Only then can you say what is asserted.
card.rule: For each leading sentence, settle what its principal words mean and state what the sentence as a whole asserts.
card.limits: Knowing each word's sense is necessary but not sufficient: how the words are combined also shapes the claim. And a sentence may contain more than one proposition, so finding its meaning may mean finding several.

concepts.title: How modifiers shape the claim
concepts.question: How do modifying words and clauses change the proposition a sentence expresses?

paragraphs: To interpret a sentence you need to know the role adjectives and adverbs play, how verbs work with nouns, and how modifying words and clauses restrict or amplify the meaning of the words they modify.

Ideally you should be able to dissect a sentence by the rules of syntax, though not necessarily in a formal way. The authors grant that grammar is taught less than it was, but assume readers know this much, if a little rusty.
Restricting modifiers narrow a claim (most, in cities, under some conditions); amplifying ones widen or strengthen it (all, everywhere, greatly). Getting them right is getting the proposition right.
card.example: 'Moderate exercise in older adults slightly reduces the risk of falls.' Strip the modifiers and you get: exercise reduces falls. Moderate, in older adults and slightly each restrict the claim, so the author asserts much less than the bare version.
card.rule: Find each modifier in a key sentence and decide whether it narrows or widens the claim.
card.limits: Dissection serves meaning; you need not label every part. And it is not always clear what a modifier attaches to, so the surrounding sentences may be needed to decide.

concepts.title: Use the surrounding sentences
concepts.question: What larger context do you need to find a sentence's proposition, compared with finding a word's term?

paragraphs: The authors name only two differences between finding terms and finding propositions. The first is that for propositions you use a larger context. You bring all the surrounding sentences to bear on the sentence in question, just as you used the surrounding words to interpret a particular word.
In both cases you proceed from what you do understand to the gradual clearing up of what at first is relatively unintelligible.
A sentence obscure on its own often becomes clear from the sentence before, which sets up a question, or the one after, which gives an example or a consequence.
card.example: Alone, 'The second effect outweighed the first' tells you nothing. The paragraph before lists two effects of raising the minimum wage: some jobs lost, and higher pay for those who kept theirs. Now the proposition is clear: the gain in pay outweighed the job losses.
card.rule: When a key sentence is obscure, read the sentences around it and work from what you understand toward what you do not.
card.limits: Context can mislead if you borrow from the wrong place. An opponent's view reported next to the author's sentence is context of contrast, not part of what the author asserts.

concepts.title: Separate, number and relate
concepts.question: When is your interpretation of a complicated key sentence complete, and what exercise do the authors suggest for it?

paragraphs: The second difference between finding terms and finding propositions is that complicated sentences usually express more than one proposition. You have not finished interpreting an important sentence until you have separated out all its different, though perhaps related, propositions.

Skill in this comes with practice. The authors suggest taking complicated sentences from their own book, stating in your own words each thing being asserted, then numbering the assertions and relating them.
Numbering makes you count the claims; relating them shows which is a reason, which a condition and which the main point.
card.example: 'Because remote work weakens mentoring, which matters most for new hires, firms should bring juniors in three days a week.' (1) Remote work weakens mentoring. (2) Mentoring matters most for new hires. (3) Firms should bring juniors in three days a week. Together, 1 and 2 support 3.
card.rule: Split each complicated key sentence into all its propositions, state each in your own words, number them and show how they relate.
card.limits: Some long sentences hold only one proposition dressed in qualifiers; do not invent claims to fill a list. Numbering is a tool for understanding: the relations matter more than the count.

concepts.title: The own-words test
concepts.question: What is the best test of whether you have understood the proposition in a sentence?

paragraphs: State it in your own words. If, when asked what an author means by a sentence, all you can do is repeat his words with minor changes in their order, suspect that you do not know what he means.

Ideally you should be able to say the same thing in totally different words. The match can be closer or looser, but if you cannot get away from the author's words at all, only words have passed from him to you, not thought or knowledge.
In the authors' phrase, you then know his words, not his mind.
card.example: An economics text says money is a medium of exchange. A reader who replies that it is a medium for exchanging has shuffled words. One who says people accept money in trade, not because they want it for itself, but because they can pass it on for things they do want, has shown the thought.
card.rule: Test your grasp of a key sentence by restating it in entirely different words.
card.limits: Some technical terms have no everyday equivalent and must be kept; the test is whether the rest of the sentence can be rebuilt around them. And a fluent paraphrase can still be wrong, so check it against the author's meaning in context.

concepts.title: Translating within your own language
concepts.question: Why is restating an English sentence in other English words a better test of understanding than translating a French one?

paragraphs: Translating from a foreign language bears on the test. If you cannot state in English what a French sentence says, you know you do not understand it. But even if you can, your translation may stay at the verbal level: a faithful English replica can leave you unsure what the French writer meant.
Translating one English sentence into another is not a matter of words alone. The new sentence is not a verbal replica of the original; if accurate, it is faithful to the thought only.
That is why the authors call it the best self-test: it shows whether you have digested the proposition or only swallowed the words. Failing it uncovers a failure of understanding.
card.example: A student turns a German sentence about Kant word for word into fluent English and still cannot explain it. Asked to restate the English in other English words, he stalls. The second failure, not the first success, tells him where he stands.
card.rule: Prove you have the thought by producing a new sentence in your own language that keeps the thought and changes the words.
card.limits: Passing the test shows grasp of the thought, not that the thought is true. And a translation across languages is still a useful first check: failing it shows you lack even the words.

concepts.title: Recognizing and offering equivalents
concepts.question: Why must a reader be able to tell when two statements are equivalent, and what does failing to do so show?

paragraphs: An author may express the same proposition in different words in the course of his book. A reader who has not seen through the words to the proposition is likely to treat the equivalent sentences as statements of different propositions.

Imagine someone who did not know that 2 + 2 = 4 and 4 - 2 = 2 are different notations for one arithmetic relation: four as the double of two, or two as the half of four. You would conclude he did not understand the equation.
The same holds for anyone who cannot tell when equivalent statements are being made, or cannot offer an equivalent himself when he claims to understand.
card.example: A finance book says in one chapter that diversification reduces risk, and later that holding many unrelated assets makes it less likely that all your losses arrive at once. A reader who lists these as two separate findings has missed that the author said one thing twice.
card.rule: Show you understand a proposition by recognizing its restatements and by producing one of your own.
card.limits: Not every near-equivalent is equivalent: a later restatement can quietly add or drop a qualifier because the author is refining his claim. Check the terms and the relation before treating two sentences as one proposition.

concepts.title: Comparing authors through their words
concepts.question: When comparing several authors, how can differences or likenesses of wording mislead a reader?

paragraphs: These points bear on syntopical reading, the reading of several books on the same subject. Different authors often say the same thing in different words, or different things in almost the same words.

A reader who cannot see through the language to the terms and propositions will never be able to compare such works. Misled by verbal differences, he may read the authors as disagreeing; misled by verbal likeness, he may miss their real differences.
So before declaring that two authors agree or disagree, state each one's proposition in your own words and compare the propositions, not the sentences.
card.example: One economist writes that minimum wages destroy jobs; another, that wage floors reduce hiring of the least skilled. They sound different but may assert much the same. Meanwhile two writers who both say growth is good may mean output and wellbeing, and disagree deeply.
card.rule: Compare authors by their propositions, stated in your own words, not by their wording.
card.limits: Sometimes a difference of wording is the point: an author may choose a new word to mark a real change of view. Restating everyone in your own words must not erase distinctions the authors meant to draw.

concepts.title: The example test
concepts.question: Besides restating it in your own words, what second test shows whether you understand a proposition?

paragraphs: The other test is to point to some experience you have had that the proposition describes, or to which it is in any way relevant. Can you exemplify the general truth by referring to a particular instance of it?

To imagine a possible case is often as good as citing an actual one. If you cannot exemplify or illustrate the proposition at all, either imaginatively or from actual experience, suspect that you do not know what is being said.
Giving an example connects the general statement to the particular things it is about.
card.example: A psychology text says people value things more once they own them. You recall refusing to sell a battered bicycle for a price you would never have paid for it. That instance shows you have grasped the claim.
card.rule: Test a proposition you think you understand by giving an actual or imagined instance of it.
card.limits: An example shows you grasp the claim; it does not prove the claim true. And some propositions need special experience, such as work in a laboratory, before you can exemplify them.

concepts.title: Propositions refer to the world
concepts.question: Why must a proposition connect with actual or possible facts, and which propositions are hard to exemplify?

paragraphs: Not all propositions are equally open to the example test. To be sure you have grasped certain scientific propositions, you may need the special experience only a laboratory can give.
But the main point holds. Propositions do not exist in a vacuum; they refer to the world we live in.
Unless you can show some acquaintance with actual or possible facts to which a proposition refers or is relevant, you are playing with words, not dealing with thought and knowledge.
card.example: A chemistry text says a catalyst speeds a reaction without being used up. Even without a lab, a reader can point to a real case: a pinch of manganese dioxide makes hydrogen peroxide fizz into oxygen quickly, and the black powder is still there, unchanged, when the fizzing stops. Claims about particular reaction rates may need measuring in a lab.
card.rule: Tie each proposition to some actual or possible fact it is about, and notice when that needs special experience you lack.
card.limits: Lacking special experience does not prove you misunderstand; it may mean your grasp is partial until you can get it. Abstract fields have instances too, though they may be other abstract cases rather than everyday ones.

concepts.title: Restate, then exemplify
concepts.question: How do the two tests, restating and exemplifying, work together on a proposition, as in the authors' metaphysics example?

paragraphs: The authors give a basic proposition of metaphysics: nothing acts except what is actual. Many students repeated those words to them with an air of satisfied wisdom, as if perfect repetition were all that was owed.

The sham showed as soon as they were asked for other words. Seldom could they say, for instance, that if something does not exist, it cannot do anything, though that translation is apparent to anyone who understood.

Failing a translation, the authors would ask for an example. A student who said that grass is not made to grow by showers that might fall but have not, or that a bank balance does not rise because of a raise one has not received, had grasped the proposition.
card.rule: Apply both tests: restate the proposition in other words, then give an instance of it.
card.limits: Either test alone can be passed by luck, with a borrowed paraphrase or a memorised example. Passing both, in your own words and with your own instance, is stronger evidence of understanding, though still not proof that the proposition is true.

concepts.title: The vice of verbalism
concepts.question: What is verbalism, and why do the authors call it the besetting sin of readers who do not read analytically?

paragraphs: The authors define verbalism as the bad habit of using words without regard for the thoughts they should convey and without awareness of the experiences they should refer to. It is playing with words.
As the two tests show, verbalism besets those who fail to read analytically. They never get beyond the words; they hold what they read as a verbal memory they can recite emptily.

Some modern educators charge that the liberal arts encourage verbalism. The authors argue the opposite: readers untrained in grammar and logic show how lack of such discipline makes them slaves to words rather than masters of them.
card.example: Asked in an interview about his leadership style, a candidate says it is servant leadership with a growth mindset. Asked what he did last month that showed it, he repeats the phrase. That is verbalism: words that point to no thought and no experience.
card.rule: Guard against verbalism by checking that every key sentence you can recite, you can also restate and illustrate.
card.limits: Memorising exact wording is not in itself verbalism: a quotation, a formula or a legal phrase may need its exact words. It becomes verbalism when recitation takes the place of understanding.

concepts.title: Arguments do not follow paragraphs
concepts.question: Why does Rule 7 speak of sentences rather than paragraphs, and how do arguments relate to paragraphs?

paragraphs: The authors did not frame Rule 7 as finding the most important paragraphs, because writers have no settled conventions for building them. Montaigne, Locke and Proust write very long paragraphs; Machiavelli, Hobbes and Tolstoy relatively short ones; and modern writers, influenced by newspapers and magazines, cut theirs short for quick reading.

Beyond length, the argument is not uniquely tied to any unit of writing, as terms are tied to words and propositions to sentences. An argument may sit in one complicated sentence, in part of a paragraph, in exactly one paragraph, or run through several.
Many paragraphs express no argument at all: they detail evidence, report how it was gathered, or digress. These can be read rather quickly.
card.rule: Look for arguments wherever they run, in a sentence, part of a paragraph or across paragraphs, not paragraph by paragraph.
card.limits: Paragraphs are still useful clues: in some books, especially mathematical ones, a paragraph often is one argument. The warning is against assuming the match, not against using paragraph breaks at all.

concepts.title: Find or construct the argument
concepts.question: What should you do when a book does not state its important arguments in single paragraphs?

paragraphs: The authors restate Rule 7: find, if you can, the paragraphs that state a book's important arguments; if the arguments are not expressed that way, construct them, taking a sentence from this paragraph and one from that, until you have gathered the sequence of sentences stating the propositions that make up the argument.

Once you have found the leading sentences, this should be relatively easy. You can write the propositions out on paper, but usually better is to put numbers and other marks in the margin, showing where the sentences to be tied together occur.

Authors who write in a geometrical or mathematical style, such as Euclid, Galileo and Newton, come close to making one paragraph one argument. Most other writing puts two or more arguments in a paragraph, or runs one through several.
card.rule: Find an argument in a paragraph if it is there; otherwise build it by gathering its sentences, in order, from wherever they lie.
card.limits: Constructing must stay faithful: gather sentences the author offers as connected, and do not stitch together claims he never linked. Margin numbers record the author's argument, not one you would prefer him to have made.

concepts.title: Loose books and the author's summaries
concepts.question: How can an author's summaries help you find his arguments, and what makes loosely built books harder?

paragraphs: The more loosely a book is built, the more diffuse its paragraphs. You often have to search all the paragraphs of a chapter to find the sentences that make up one argument. Some books make you search in vain, and some do not even encourage the search.

A good book usually summarizes itself as its arguments develop. When the author sums up at the end of a chapter or section, look back over the preceding pages and find the materials he gathered into the summary. Darwin ends The Origin of Species with a chapter that recapitulates his whole argument.
The reader who has worked through the book deserves that help; one who has not cannot use it. If you inspected the book first, you already know whether summaries exist and where.
card.rule: Use the author's summaries as a map back to his arguments, and know from inspection where they are.
card.limits: A summary is not a substitute for the argument: reading only the summary gives you conclusions without the steps. Summaries can also simplify, so check each point against the pages it sums up.

concepts.title: Make every step explicit
concepts.question: Why should a reader make every step of an argument explicit, even the steps the author leaves out?

paragraphs: Another sign of a bad or loosely built book is the omission of steps in an argument. Sometimes steps can be left out without harm, because readers can supply the missing propositions from common knowledge.

But sometimes the omission misleads, and may even be meant to. A familiar trick of the orator or propagandist is to leave unsaid things that are highly relevant to the argument but might be challenged if made explicit.
We do not expect such devices from an honest author whose aim is to instruct. Still, the authors call it a sound maxim of careful reading to make every step in an argument explicit.
card.example: An article argues that crime in a town rose after a new bar opened, so the bar caused the rise. The unstated step is that nothing else relevant changed in that time. Stated openly, it invites the question of what else happened.
card.rule: Write out the unstated steps an argument needs, so each one can be seen and questioned.
card.limits: Supplying a step is interpretation, not invention: add only what the argument needs and the author would accept. Spelling out every trivial step can bury the argument; focus on steps that carry weight or could be disputed.

concepts.title: Single arguments in a nutshell
concepts.question: What must you be able to do with every argument in a book, and why focus on single arguments within longer chains?

paragraphs: Whatever kind of book it is, the reader's obligation is the same. If the book contains arguments, you must know what they are and be able to put them into a nutshell. Any good argument, the authors say, can be put into a nutshell.
There are arguments built upon arguments. In an elaborate analysis one thing may be proved in order to prove another, which in turn is used to make a further point.
But the units of reasoning are single arguments. If you can find these in any book, you are not likely to miss the larger sequences they form.
card.example: A book on climate policy argues (1) that recent warming is caused by human emissions, uses that to argue (2) that cutting emissions would slow it, and uses (2) to argue (3) for a carbon tax. Argument (2) in a nutshell: since human emissions drive warming, cutting them slows warming.
card.rule: Break long chains of reasoning into single arguments and state each one in a nutshell.
card.limits: A nutshell keeps the premises and the conclusion, not every supporting detail; if it drops a premise the argument needs, it misrepresents it. And a nutshell of the whole chain is no substitute for knowing each link.

concepts.title: No logician needed, but stay awake
concepts.question: Do you need training in logic to find a book's arguments, and where should you start once you spot part of one?

paragraphs: A reader may object: without knowing the structure of arguments as a logician does, how can I find them, let alone construct them? The authors answer that you need no logician's knowledge. Most books that instruct are written for the general reader, not for specialists in logic.

The human mind, they hold, is as naturally sensitive to arguments as the eye is to colours. But the eye will not see if it is not kept open, and the mind will not follow an argument if it is not awake. A mind that comes to terms and reaches the propositions will see the arguments too.
One practical help: every argument has some statements giving reasons for a conclusion. If you find the conclusion first, look for the reasons; if you find the reasons first, see where they lead.
card.rule: Keep your mind awake, and from whichever part of an argument you find first, work toward the other.
card.limits: Natural sensitivity is no licence for sleepy reading: the authors admit disappointing experiences and joke that some people may be argument-blind. Formal logic is not required, but attention is.

concepts.title: From facts or from general truths
concepts.question: How do arguments from particular facts differ from arguments from general statements, and how does science use both?

paragraphs: A second help: tell apart the argument that points to particular facts as evidence for a generalization from the argument that offers general statements to prove a further generalization. The first is usually called inductive, the second deductive, but the authors say the names matter less than the ability to tell them apart.

In science the distinction appears whenever proof by reasoning is contrasted with establishment by experiment. Galileo speaks of illustrating by experiment conclusions already reached by mathematical demonstration. Harvey wrote that the circulation of the blood had been shown by reason and experiment.
Sometimes a proposition can be supported both ways; sometimes only one method is available.
card.example: Inductive: in fifty towns that added bike lanes, cycling rose, so bike lanes increase cycling. Deductive: whatever lowers the cost of a kind of trip increases such trips; bike lanes lower the cost of cycling trips; so bike lanes increase cycling.
card.rule: For each argument, ask whether it rests on particular facts or on general statements, and in science whether on experiment, reasoning or both.
card.limits: Real arguments often mix the two: a general premise may itself rest on evidence. Telling them apart helps you see how a claim is supported; it does not rank one kind above the other.

concepts.title: Assumed, proved or self-evident
concepts.question: Why must every argument start from something unproved, and where can a line of argument start?

paragraphs: A third help: observe what the author says he must assume, what he says can be proved or otherwise shown, and what needs no proof because it is self-evident. He may honestly list his assumptions, or just as honestly leave you to find them.

Not everything can be proved, just as not everything can be defined. If every proposition had to be proved, no proof could begin. Axioms, assumptions or postulates are needed to prove other propositions, and once proved, those can serve as premises in further proofs.
So every line of argument starts somewhere: with assumptions agreed between writer and reader, which can be anything as long as both agree, or with self-evident propositions, which neither can deny.
card.example: A book on economic policy assumes that people generally prefer more income to less, proves from that a claim about how a tax change will alter work choices, and treats as self-evident that a total is greater than any of the regional figures that make it up.
card.rule: Sort an author's starting points into what he assumes, what he proves and what he takes as self-evident.
card.limits: An unstated assumption is not a dishonest one; finding it is part of your job. And calling something self-evident does not make it so: it must be undeniable, not only familiar.

concepts.title: Tautologies and self-evident truths
concepts.question: How does a self-evident proposition differ from a tautology true by definition, and can self-evident truths teach anything?

paragraphs: Self-evident propositions are now often called tautologies, sometimes with contempt, as if a truth were put in by defining your words and pulled out like a rabbit from a hat. The authors say that is not always so.

Compare 'a father of a father is a grandfather' with 'the whole is greater than its parts.' The first is a tautology: it thinly hides a decision to call a parent's parent a grandparent. The second expresses our understanding of how finite wholes and their parts are related, whatever words we use.

It is self-evident because its opposite is immediately seen to be false: you cannot think an uncut page is less than the half you hold after cutting it. Such truths are indemonstrable but undeniable, part of common-sense knowledge; Euclid called them common notions.

According to the authors they also instruct. Locke, they say, saw no difference between the grandparent kind, which teaches nothing, and the whole-and-part kind, which does; moderns who call all such propositions tautologies make the same mistake.
card.rule: Ask whether a proposition is true only because of how its words are defined, or because its opposite is seen at once to be false about things.
card.limits: The line can be hard to draw, and the authors' view is contested: many philosophers treat all such truths as matters of language. Know what the authors hold and why, and note that it is their position.

concepts.title: Find the author's solutions
concepts.question: After grasping terms, propositions and arguments, what final questions should you ask about the author's problems?

paragraphs: Rule 8 is to find out what the author's solutions are. It brings the rules about terms, propositions and arguments to a head, and ties the first stage of analytical reading, outlining the structure, to the second, interpreting the contents.

Under Rule 4 you named the main problems the author tried to solve. Now check your findings against them. Which problems did he succeed in solving? In solving them, did he raise new ones? Of the problems he failed to solve, old or new, which did he himself know he had failed on?
A good writer, like a good reader, should know whether a problem has been solved, though the authors note that admitting it is likely to cost the reader less pain.
With Rules 5 to 8 applied, you can feel reasonably sure you understand the book. Until now you have kept your mind open and your mouth shut, following the author. From here on you may argue with him.
card.rule: Sort the author's problems into solved, newly raised and unsolved, and among the unsolved note which ones he admits.
card.limits: Rule 8 still belongs to interpretation: you record what the author's arguments achieve on his own terms. Arguing with him about whether he is right comes in the next stage.

concepts.section: The Second Stage of Analytical Reading
concepts.title: The four rules of interpretation
concepts.question: What do Rules 5 to 8 accomplish together, and which basic question about a book do they answer?

paragraphs: Rules 5 to 8 make up the second stage of analytical reading: the rules for finding what a book says, or interpreting its contents. They supply the materials for the second basic question about anything you read: what is being said in detail, and how?

In summary: (5) come to terms with the author by interpreting his key words; (6) grasp his leading propositions by dealing with his most important sentences; (7) know his arguments by finding them in, or constructing them out of, sequences of sentences; (8) decide which of his problems he solved and which not, and of the latter, which he knew he had failed to solve.
When this is done, you know what the author says, and you are ready for the last two basic questions: is it true, and what of it?
card.rule: Use Rules 5 to 8 together to answer what is being said in detail, and how, before asking whether it is true.
card.limits: The rules are stated in order but used together; you will move back and forth between words, sentences and arguments. And finishing this stage means you understand the book, not that you accept it.

concepts.title: The reader has the last word
concepts.question: In the conversation between a book and its reader, who speaks last, and what does that turn require of the reader?

paragraphs: The authors treat reading a book as a conversation. It can look one-sided, since the author does all the talking. But once the author has had his say, it is the reader's turn, and the reader has the last word.

The conversation ought to be orderly: each side speaks in turn, without interruption. An undisciplined reader can spoil that order, and the author cannot stop him. He cannot ask the reader to wait until he has finished, or protest that his point has been missed.
So the reader has both an opportunity and an obligation. Nothing can stop him from replying, and because the other party cannot defend himself, he must reply well.
card.example: Ravi finishes a long essay arguing for a four-day working week. He does not close the tab and move on. He writes three lines: what the author claims, where he is convinced, and one point he will check. The author spoke first and finished; Ravi has now taken his turn.
card.rule: When the author has finished, take your turn and answer him, knowing he cannot answer back.
card.limits: The last word comes after the author has had his whole say. A reader who delivers a verdict on page one takes his turn too early and may be answering a point the author never made.

concepts.title: Intellectual etiquette, not social politeness
concepts.question: What separates a profitable conversation with a book from bickering, and why is that not a matter of social politeness?

paragraphs: Conversation is worth having only when it is carried on civilly. The authors do not mean social conventions, such as courteous phrases; those matter little. They mean an intellectual etiquette: a code of conduct for exchanging ideas.

Without that etiquette, conversation becomes bickering rather than profitable communication. The code matters when the subject is serious, a matter on which people can agree or disagree, because the profit of a good conversation is something learned.

What holds between people holds even more when a book has spoken and the reader answers. The authors take it for granted, for now, that a good book has done its part well; the question is how the reader can do his.
card.example: Two neighbours argue about a new bus lane. One is gentle in tone but never addresses the other's figures; the other is blunt but restates his neighbour's case before replying to it. By the authors' standard, the blunt one keeps the intellectual etiquette better, because his reply makes learning possible.
card.rule: Judge your reply to a book by whether it makes learning possible, not by whether it sounds polite.
card.limits: The authors frame the code for serious matters on which people can agree or disagree. In small talk where no claim is at issue there is little to learn, so the code has little to govern.

concepts.title: A considered judgment is owed
concepts.question: What does a reader owe an author who tried to teach him, even when the reader is not convinced?

paragraphs: The author of a book that conveys knowledge aims to instruct: to convince or persuade the reader of something. He has succeeded only if the reader can finally say that he has been taught, that something has been shown true or probable.

If the reader is not convinced, the author's effort still deserves respect. The reader owes him a considered judgment. If he cannot agree, he should at least have grounds for disagreeing, or for suspending judgment.

So active reading does not end with understanding; it is completed by criticism. The undemanding reader puts the book aside and forgets it. The authors count that as worse than faint praise, because it gives the book no critical consideration at all.
card.example: Omar reads a book on the history of money, finds the last third unconvincing, and shelves it. A month later he cannot say why he was unconvinced. By the card's standard he has not finished reading: he owed the author grounds for his doubt, not a silent shelf.
card.rule: After understanding a book, give it a considered judgment, with grounds for any disagreement or suspended judgment.
card.limits: The debt is to a book that tries to teach and that you have worked to understand. It is not a duty to agree, and a book you only leafed through to decide whether to read it has not yet earned a verdict.

concepts.title: Read to weigh and consider
concepts.question: What aim should a reader bring to a book: refuting it, believing it, finding talking points, or something else?

paragraphs: Some people hold that a good book is above the criticism of an ordinary reader: reader and author are not peers, and an author should be judged only by his equals. Francis Bacon's advice is often recalled in this spirit.

Bacon names three wrong aims. Reading to contradict looks only for faults to refute. Reading to believe takes everything for granted. Reading to find talk gathers material for conversation. Against all three he sets weighing and considering: examining what is said on its merits.
Sir Walter Scott is harsher still about those who read to doubt or to scorn. The authors grant that there is truth in these warnings.
card.example: Three people read the same report on remote work. Ana marks every weak sentence to attack it; Ben copies its conclusions into his notes as settled; Cal picks out striking statistics to quote at dinner. None of them weighs the report, which would mean asking what it claims, on what evidence, and how far the evidence goes.
card.rule: Read a book to weigh and consider it, not to refute it, swallow it, or harvest talking points.
card.limits: Weighing does not forbid ending in disagreement or agreement; the fault is starting with the verdict. Nor do these warnings put a good book beyond an ordinary reader's criticism.

concepts.title: No book is beyond fault
concepts.question: Is a great book beyond the criticism of an ordinary reader, and what attitude do the authors call false piety?

paragraphs: The authors grant some truth to warnings like Bacon's and Scott's, but they reject the halo of perfection often put around great books. Treating such books as beyond an ordinary reader's criticism produces what they call false piety.

Readers may be like children in that great authors can teach them, but that does not mean they must stay silent. Cervantes said no book is so bad that nothing good can be found in it. The authors are less sure of that, and more certain that no book is so good that no fault can be found in it.
card.example: A student reading a famous economist spots a gap in one argument and crosses out her note, feeling she must have misread him. If, after checking, she still sees the gap, crossing it out is false piety: the book's fame is no proof that it has no faults.
card.rule: Expect even a great book to have faults, and do not let its reputation silence your criticism once you understand it.
card.limits: Respect for a great book is right while you are still learning from it; the point is that it must not become a ban on judging after you understand. Expecting faults is not assuming that every difficulty is one.

concepts.title: Understanding makes you a peer
concepts.question: When does a reader earn the standing to criticize a book that is above him, and what does he owe the author then?

paragraphs: The authors accept one part of the warning. A book that can enlighten its readers is, in that sense, superior to them, and they should not criticize it until they understand it.
Understanding changes the relation. A reader who understands a book has raised himself almost to the author's level. The author has done what he could to make the reader his equal.
So the reader should now act as the author's peer: converse with him and talk back. If he holds back his critical powers at this point, he does the author an injustice.
card.example: A nurse works slowly through a dense book on hospital management until she can explain each chapter to a colleague. Her doubts about its staffing model are now not presumption. By the authors' reasoning, keeping them to herself would wrong an author who wrote to bring readers up to his level.
card.rule: Withhold criticism of a book that can teach you until you understand it, and then criticize it as the author's peer.
card.limits: Near-equality comes from understanding this book, not from general cleverness or confidence. A reader who has not yet understood is still the pupil, and his objections are premature however strongly he feels them.

concepts.title: Teachability is an active virtue
concepts.question: What is teachability, and why do the authors say the most teachable reader is also the most critical?

paragraphs: The authors call this attitude the virtue of teachability, and say it is almost always misunderstood. It is often confused with subservience: a person is wrongly thought teachable if he is passive and pliable, accepting whatever he is told.

In fact teachability is an extremely active virtue. No one is really teachable who does not freely use his own power of independent judgment. Someone who only absorbs and complies can perhaps be trained, but not taught.
So the most teachable reader is the most critical. He is the one who in the end responds to a book with the greatest effort to make up his own mind about the matters it discusses.
card.example: Two trainees attend a course on negotiation. One writes down every tip and follows them all to the letter. The other tests each tip against cases she knows, keeps most, and argues against one. The first has been trained; by the authors' account, the second has been taught.
card.rule: Show teachability by using your own judgment on what the author teaches, not by passively accepting it.
card.limits: Active judgment comes at the end, after the teacher has been heard and understood. A reader who argues from the first page is not more teachable, only premature; independence is not the same as resistance.

concepts.title: Hear first, and judge by method
concepts.question: Why does teachability require hearing the teacher out first, and why is hard effort not enough to judge a book well?

paragraphs: The authors say the teachable reader makes up his mind finally, and the word matters. Teachability requires that a teacher be fully heard, and more than that understood, before he is judged.

Sheer effort is not a good measure of teachability. Trying hard does not make a reader a good judge, any more than it makes him a good interpreter. He must know how to judge a book, just as he must know how to reach an understanding of it.

That is why the third stage of analytical reading has its own rules. Some are general maxims of intellectual etiquette, given in this chapter; others are more specific criteria for points of criticism, given in the next.
card.example: Lina spends ten hours writing a critique of a book on sleep science. She attacks it hard but never checks what the author meant by his central term. Her effort is real, but effort without a method of judging produces a critique of the wrong target.
card.rule: Hear and understand the author fully before judging, and judge by method, not by effort alone.
card.limits: Method does not replace effort; judging a hard book well still takes work. The point is that effort counts only when it is spent on the right tasks in the right order.

concepts.title: Rhetoric governs the third stage
concepts.question: Which of the three liberal arts governs criticism, and how does it relate to the arts behind the first two stages?

paragraphs: The authors find a reciprocity between the art of teaching and the art of being taught. The same principles of grammar and logic guide good writing and good reading: a considerate writer aims at being intelligible, a considerate reader at understanding.

Skill in the first two stages of analytical reading comes from mastery of grammar and logic. The third stage goes beyond understanding to critical judgment, and here the remaining art comes in: rhetoric, taken in its broadest sense.
The rules of the third stage are offered as a code of etiquette. The authors note that etiquette serves two purposes, not one: it makes the reader polite in talking back, and also effective.
card.example: A debate judge must first follow a speech's words and see how its reasons connect; that is grammar and logic at work. Only then does she ask how far the speech should move her, which is the rhetorical question.
card.rule: Use grammar and logic to understand a book, and rhetoric to govern your critical response to it.
card.limits: The arts divide the work by stage. Rhetoric here means skill in responding to attempts to convince or persuade, not fine speaking, and it has nothing to work on until grammar and logic have done theirs.

concepts.title: Convincing and persuading
concepts.question: Where does rhetoric come into communication, and how does convincing someone differ from persuading them?
