paragraphs: We usually link rhetoric with orators and propagandists. In its most general sense, the authors say, rhetoric is involved wherever people communicate. A speaker or writer wants not only to be understood but also, in some sense, to be agreed with.

When the purpose is serious, the aim is to convince or persuade. More precisely, one convinces about theoretical matters, what is true, and persuades about matters that in the end affect action or feeling.
So every serious book is, at least in part, an attempt to win the reader's assent, and a reader who takes it seriously must respond to that attempt.
card.example: A book on vaccines that explains how immunity works is trying to convince: it wants you to accept an account of how things are. A leaflet urging you to book your flu jab this week is trying to persuade: it wants you to act. Many works do both, the first preparing the second.
card.rule: Ask whether the author is trying to convince you that something is true or persuade you to act or feel, and respond to that aim.
card.limits: The distinction concerns the end in view, not the tone: a calm piece can persuade and a passionate one can aim only to convince. Many works mix the two, so sort the parts, not only the whole.

concepts.title: Responsive and responsible
concepts.question: What is the difference between a responsive reader and a responsible one, and why must a judgment be your own?

paragraphs: To receive a serious communication seriously, the authors say, you must be both responsive and responsible. You are responsive to the extent that you follow what has been said and note the intention that prompts it.

You are responsible when you go on to take a position. That position is yours, not the author's. To treat anyone but yourself as answerable for your judgment is, in the authors' words, to be a slave rather than a free man.
The authors add that this is where the liberal arts get their name: they are the arts of a free mind, one that judges for itself.
card.example: After reading an op-ed on rent caps, Jo can state its claim and sees that it was written to sway a council vote; she is responsive. She then decides she accepts the diagnosis but not the remedy, and can say why. That position is hers; she is now responsible as well.
card.rule: Follow what the author says and why, then take a position of your own and answer for it.
card.limits: Owning a judgment does not mean forming it without help or refusing an author's view. You may end where the author ends; what matters is that you hold the view for reasons you accept, not because he said so.

concepts.title: Rhetorical skill on both sides
concepts.question: What is rhetorical skill on the writer's side and on the reader's side, and what prepares the reader to use it?

paragraphs: For a speaker or writer, rhetorical skill is knowing how to convince or persuade. Since that is the final aim, the other parts of communication serve it. Writing clearly and intelligibly, through grammar and logic, has merit in itself, but it is also a means to this end.

On the reader's side the skill is reciprocal: knowing how to react to anyone who tries to convince or persuade us. Here too grammar and logic serve. By letting us understand what is being said, they prepare the way for a critical reaction.
card.example: A brochure for solar panels is clear and well ordered, and every clear sentence moves you toward buying. A reader with rhetorical skill first makes sure she understands each claim, then asks how far the claims should move her, rather than being carried along by the clarity.
card.rule: Meet an author's effort to convince or persuade with a deliberate reaction, built on first understanding what he says.
card.limits: A writer's clarity is no proof of a sound case; it serves his aim of convincing. Nor is a reader's reaction skilled because it resists: the skill lies in reacting rightly, which may mean being convinced.

concepts.title: Rule 9: understand before you judge
concepts.question: What must a reader be able to say before agreeing, disagreeing or suspending judgment, and what does saying it bring with it?

paragraphs: Rule 9 is the first general maxim of critical reading: do not begin to talk back until you have listened carefully and are sure you understand. The authors restate it: you must be able to say, with reasonable certainty, I understand, before you say I agree, I disagree, or I suspend judgment.
The condition is honest satisfaction that you have done the first two stages of analytical reading: you know what the book is about as a whole and what it says in detail.
Meeting that condition does two things. It earns you the right to turn critic, and it puts on you the duty to do so.
card.example: Before writing her review of a book on sleep, Mei checks herself: can she state its main question, its key terms and its leading argument? She can, with reasonable certainty. Only then does she write that she agrees with its account of sleep debt and disagrees with its advice on naps.
card.rule: Say I understand, with reasonable certainty, before you say I agree, I disagree, or I suspend judgment.
card.limits: The bar is reasonable certainty, not perfect certainty; waiting for complete understanding would put judgment off indefinitely. And the rule delays criticism; it does not excuse you from it.

concepts.title: Criticism comes last, even for experts
concepts.question: Can the stage of criticism be combined with the first two stages, as they can be combined with each other?

paragraphs: Rule 9 means that the third stage of analytical reading must always follow the other two in time.

The first two stages interpenetrate. Even a beginner can combine them somewhat, and an expert combines them almost completely: he breaks the whole book into its parts while building the whole from its terms, propositions and arguments. Some of their work can even be done during a good inspectional reading.
Criticism is different. The expert, no less than the beginner, must wait until he understands before he starts to criticize.
card.example: An experienced editor outlines a manuscript's structure and notes its key terms in a single pass. She does not, in that pass, decide whether its argument holds. She notes questions in the margin, and gives her verdict only once she can state what the whole manuscript says.
card.rule: Let outlining and interpreting run together if you can, but start criticizing only after both are done.
card.limits: What waits is the verdict: agreeing, disagreeing or suspending judgment. Questions, puzzles and points to check can still be noted as you read, since they serve understanding rather than replace it.

concepts.title: Agree, disagree, suspend: all are criticism
concepts.question: What critical positions can a reader take, and why is agreeing as much a critical judgment as disagreeing?

paragraphs: The authors say the three remarks in Rule 9, I agree, I disagree and I suspend judgment, exhaust the critical positions a reader can take.

A popular misconception identifies criticism with disagreement. Even constructive criticism, the authors note, is disagreement. But to agree is just as much an act of critical judgment as to disagree, and you can be just as wrong in agreeing as in disagreeing.
Each position needs understanding behind it. In the authors' words, to agree without understanding is inane, and to disagree without understanding is impudent.
card.example: One colleague praises a report on a new pricing plan as excellent but cannot say what it recommends for small customers. Another dismisses it and cannot say either. Both have made critical judgments, and both are empty: the praise is inane, the dismissal impudent.
card.rule: Treat agreeing as a critical judgment that needs the same understanding and care as disagreeing.
card.limits: The three positions are judgments on what the book says. A remark on its style or on how much you enjoyed it may be fair, but it takes none of the three positions on the author's claims.

concepts.title: Suspending judgment is a position
concepts.question: Why is suspending judgment a critical position rather than a way of avoiding one?

paragraphs: It may not be obvious at first, but suspending judgment is also an act of criticism. It takes the position that something has not been shown: you are saying you are not convinced or persuaded one way or the other.

Like agreeing and disagreeing, it needs understanding behind it. The authors say that doubt or detachment is no more intelligent than affirming or denying in a reader who does not know what he is suspending judgment about.
card.example: After reading a book claiming that a new teaching method raises test scores, Pat says he suspends judgment: the studies it cites are small, and none ran longer than a term. That is a position. Had he said he suspends judgment because he skipped the chapters on evidence, it would not be.
card.rule: When you suspend judgment, say what has not been shown, and do so only after you understand what was claimed.
card.limits: Suspending is a position, not a resting place for every hard question. If you have understood the book and its case is in fact made, holding back is no longer suspension but avoidance of the duty to judge.

concepts.title: The restating test
concepts.question: Why do the authors state Rule 9 explicitly, and how can you test whether a critic understands the position he attacks?

paragraphs: Rule 9 sounds like common sense, so why state it? The authors give two reasons: many people identify criticism with disagreement, and, like the golden rule, the maxim gets more lip service than intelligent obedience.

Authors suffer reviews by critics who skipped the first two stages, and lecturers get questions not based on what they said. Someone may even say, in one breath, that he does not know what you mean but thinks you are wrong.

The authors' remedy is a test: ask the critic to state your position for you. If he cannot repeat it satisfactorily in his own words, he does not understand, and his criticism is irrelevant. When someone understands you as well as you do, his agreement is a delight and his dissent a serious matter.
card.example: At a planning meeting, a resident objects to a proposed cycle lane. The planner asks her to describe what is proposed, and she describes a different route. Her objection, however heated, is aimed at a plan nobody made. A second resident describes the plan accurately and then objects; his objection deserves an answer.
card.rule: Test any criticism, your own included, by asking whether the critic can restate the position in his own words.
card.limits: Passing the test shows understanding, not correctness: a critic who restates you well may still be wrong. And repeating the author's exact words is not passing; the test asks for the critic's own words.

concepts.title: Hesitate before saying I understand
concepts.question: With a good book, how readily should you say I understand, and who decides whether you have earned the right to say it?

paragraphs: With a good book, the authors say, you ought to hesitate before you say I understand. The presumption is that you have a lot of work to do before you can say it honestly and with assurance.
No one else can make that call for you. You must judge yourself, and that makes the responsibility more severe: the main check on a premature I understand is your own honesty.

Reading with students for years, the authors found that many not only disagreed with what they did not understand but also agreed with positions they could not express in their own words. Their discussion, like their reading, was all words.
card.example: Tom reads a short, famous essay on liberty in an evening and feels he has it. Before saying so, he tries to write its main argument in five sentences of his own and finds he cannot explain one key step. By the card, his I understand should wait.
card.rule: With a good book, treat I understand as a claim to be earned and checked, not a feeling to be trusted.
card.limits: Hesitation is a check, not a ban; the bar remains reasonable certainty. With a simple or slight book, far less work may be needed before you can honestly say you understand.

concepts.title: Saying I don't understand
concepts.question: When does saying I don't understand count against the book rather than the reader, and how should it be said?

paragraphs: Saying I don't understand is also a critical judgment. But it reflects on the book rather than on you only after you have tried your hardest. If you have done everything that can be expected and still do not understand, the book may be unintelligible.

The presumption, though, is in favour of the book, especially a good one. With good books, failure to understand is usually the reader's fault, so the reader must stay with the first two stages a long time before moving to the third.
So watch your tone when you say it. It should concede that the fault may not be the author's.
card.example: Kim gives up on a famous philosophy book after twenty pages and tells her book group it is unreadable. Lee works through the same book twice, outlines it and looks up its key terms, then says: I lose the thread at chapter four; it may be my failure, but here is where. Only Lee's remark begins to count against the book.
card.rule: Say I don't understand about a good book only after your hardest effort, and say it in a way that allows the fault may be yours.
card.limits: The presumption favours a good book, not every book. After real effort a reader may fairly conclude that a book is unintelligible; the presumption places the burden on the reader, it does not settle the question.

concepts.title: Part of a book, part of a system
concepts.question: When should a reader be especially slow to claim understanding, and why can reading one book of an author's larger work mislead?

paragraphs: Two conditions call for special care with Rule 9. If you have read only part of a book, it is harder to be sure you understand, so you should be more hesitant to criticize.
Second, a book may depend for its full meaning on other books by the same author. Then too you should be slower to say I understand and slower to raise your critical lance.

The authors' examples: critics who judged Aristotle's Poetics without seeing that its principles rest partly on his works on psychology, logic and metaphysics; readers who judge Kant's first Critique without his second, Smith's Wealth of Nations without his Theory of the Moral Sentiments, or The Communist Manifesto without Marx's Capital.
card.example: A student assigned one chapter of a book on justice finds its defence of markets cold and calls the author heartless. In a later chapter, which she did not read, the author limits markets for the sake of the poor. Her verdict judged a part as if it were the whole.
card.rule: Be slower to judge when you have read only part of a book, or when it depends on the author's other works.
card.limits: Many books stand on their own; the caution grows with how much a book leans on what you have not read. A reader can still judge what a part says on its own terms, if she labels the judgment as partial.

concepts.title: Rule 10: disagree reasonably
concepts.question: When you disagree with an author, how should you disagree, and what is wrong with winning an argument you suspect you should lose?

paragraphs: Rule 10 is the second general maxim of critical reading: when you disagree, do so reasonably, not disputatiously or contentiously.

There is no point in winning an argument if you know or suspect you are wrong. In practice, the authors admit, it may get you ahead in the world for a short time, but honesty is the better policy in the slightly longer run.
Most people, they say, think winning the argument is what matters, not learning the truth. The authors take the opposite view.
card.example: In a meeting, Raj sees halfway through that a colleague's figures are right and his own are out of date. He could keep pressing a side issue and leave with the room on his side. Rule 10 says to concede: a win he suspects is wrong gains him nothing he should want.
card.rule: Disagree to find out what is true, and drop any argument you know or suspect you should lose.
card.limits: Rule 10 governs how you disagree, not whether you may. Firm, sustained disagreement on good grounds is reasonable; what the rule rules out is disagreement aimed at victory rather than truth.

concepts.title: Truth above friends
concepts.question: What do Plato and Aristotle teach about losing an argument, and what should rank above loyalty to the people and views you hold dear?

paragraphs: The authors learned Rule 10 first from Plato and Aristotle. In Plato's Symposium, Agathon tells Socrates he cannot refute him and will assume that what Socrates says is true. Socrates corrects him: say rather that you cannot refute the truth, for Socrates is easily refuted.

Aristotle echoes this in the Ethics. For the sake of truth, he says, we should be ready to give up even what touches us closely, especially as lovers of wisdom: friends and truth are both dear, but piety requires us to honour truth above our friends.
Both treat being beaten in argument as yielding to the truth, not to a person.
card.example: A researcher's mentor proposed a theory that his students have long defended. New data she gathered herself count against it. Following Aristotle, she publishes the data, because loyalty to her mentor ranks below the truth.
card.rule: When you cannot answer an argument, credit the truth rather than the arguer, and put truth above loyalty to persons.
card.limits: Being unable to refute an argument on the spot does not by itself prove it true. The point is to yield to the truth when you see it, not to treat every argument you cannot yet answer as settled.

concepts.title: Reading for a quarrel
concepts.question: What happens to a reader who treats a book as an opponent to beat, and why is victory over an author so easy?

paragraphs: Someone who treats conversation as a battle can win only by being an antagonist, by disagreeing successfully, whether he is right or wrong. A reader in this spirit reads a book only to find something to disagree with.
For the contentious, the authors say, a bone to pick a quarrel over can always be found, and it makes no difference whether the bone is really a chip on the reader's own shoulder.

In the privacy of his study, such a reader can seem to win easily, since the author is not there to defend himself. For the empty satisfaction of seeming to show the author up, he hardly needs to finish the book: a glance at the first few pages will do.
card.example: A blogger who dislikes a famous economist reviews his new book after reading only the introduction, seizing on a loose phrase about growth. The review is widely shared. By the card, the victory is empty: the author was absent, the phrase was a pretext, and nothing was learned.
card.rule: Notice when you are reading to find a quarrel, and read instead to find out what the book teaches.
card.limits: Finding real faults is not bone-picking; the authors want readers to show where an author is wrong. The difference lies in aim and order: faults found after understanding, not a pretext sought first.

concepts.title: You win by learning
concepts.question: What is the only real profit in a conversation with an author, and how should a reader feel when he ends up agreeing?

paragraphs: The only profit in conversation, with living or dead teachers, is what you can learn from them. You win only by gaining knowledge, not by knocking the other person down. Seen that way, contentiousness is futile.

The authors do not say a reader should not end by disagreeing and showing where the author is wrong. They say he should be as ready to agree as to disagree, and that one consideration alone should decide which: the facts, the truth about the case.

Honesty requires admitting a point when you see it. But a reader also should not feel beaten when he has to agree. If he does, he is disputatious by habit, and his problem is emotional rather than intellectual.
card.example: Dana starts a book arguing that homework does little for young children, expecting to rebut it. By the end its evidence has convinced her, and she feels oddly deflated, as if she had lost. By the card she gained: she learned something, and the deflation is a feeling to notice, not a reason to resist.
card.rule: Measure a reading by what you learned, and let the facts alone decide whether you agree or disagree.
card.limits: Readiness to agree is not a lean toward agreeing; the facts may lead to disagreement, and then you should disagree. The point is that neither outcome should count as a victory or a defeat in itself.

concepts.title: Disagree in hope, not hopelessly
concepts.question: Why should a reader treat a disagreement as something that can be resolved, and where do disagreements come from?

paragraphs: The third maxim is close to the second. Where Rule 10 warns against disagreeing contentiously, this one warns against disagreeing hopelessly. It recommends regarding disagreements as capable of being resolved.

The authors say all rational people can agree, not that they do. Even when they do not agree, they can. Disagreement is futile agitation unless it is undertaken in the hope that it may lead to resolving an issue.

Both facts come from human nature. Reason is the source of our power to agree. Our animal nature, with the imperfect reason it brings, causes most disagreements: we are creatures of passion and prejudice, and language is an imperfect medium, clouded by emotion, coloured by interest, and not fully transparent to thought.
card.example: Two neighbours have argued about a boundary hedge for years and assume they will not agree. A mediator gets each to say what the hedge is for: one wants privacy, the other light. Once the hope of settling returns, the dispute becomes a problem to solve rather than a feud to endure.
card.rule: Disagree in the hope of resolving the issue, on the assumption that rational people can come to agree.
card.limits: Can agree is not do agree: the maxim promises neither quick nor certain agreement. A long failure to agree does not show that agreement is impossible, only that its obstacles have not yet been removed.

concepts.title: Misunderstanding and ignorance: two cures
concepts.question: What two kinds of disagreement can be cured, and what should a disagreeing reader keep in mind about himself?

paragraphs: Disagreement that is only apparent, arising from misunderstanding, is certainly curable. Another kind comes from inequality of knowledge: the less informed wrongly disagree with the more informed about matters beyond their knowledge. This too can be corrected, since inequality of knowledge is curable by instruction.

There may be deeper disagreements lodged in reason itself, but they are hard to be sure of. The great majority can be resolved by removing misunderstanding or ignorance; both cures are usually possible, though often difficult.

So whoever disagrees should hope to agree in the end, and be as ready to have his own mind changed as to change another's. He may be the one who misunderstands or is ignorant. Disagreement is an occasion for being taught as well as for teaching.
card.example: A patient insists antibiotics will cure her cold; her pharmacist disagrees. If the patient means any medicine by antibiotics, the disagreement is apparent, and agreeing on the word cures it. If she means drugs that kill bacteria but does not know colds are viral, it comes from unequal knowledge, and a short explanation cures it.
card.rule: When you disagree, ask whether misunderstanding or ignorance, on either side, is the cause, and seek the matching cure.
card.limits: Some disagreements may survive both cures; the authors admit they cannot be sure about those. And the better-informed party is not fixed in advance: on a given point, the reader may be the one with something to teach.

concepts.title: Not just a matter of opinion
concepts.question: What goes wrong when people treat every disagreement as a clash of private opinions, and how do the authors say real issues are settled?

paragraphs: Many people treat disagreement as unrelated to teaching or being taught. Everything is a matter of opinion: I have mine, you have yours, and our right to them is as inviolable as private property. On that view, conversation cannot increase anyone's knowledge.

The authors compare such talk to a ping-pong game of opposed opinions in which no one keeps score, no one wins, and everyone is satisfied because no one loses: each ends holding the views he started with.

They hold instead that knowledge can be communicated and discussion can produce learning. Where knowledge is at stake, disagreements are either apparent, removed by coming to terms, or real, and real issues can be resolved in the long run by appeals to fact and reason. The maxim is to be patient for the long run.
card.example: At dinner, two guests disagree about whether a new drug works. One ends it: that is your opinion and this is mine. Both go home unchanged. Had they asked what trials exist and what they show, the question might not have been settled that night, but it could be settled in time, by evidence.
card.rule: Where knowledge is at stake, treat a disagreement as an issue that facts and reasons can settle in time, not as a standoff of opinions.
card.limits: The maxim covers matters of knowledge; by extension, a question of taste or preference may be no more than personal opinion. And patience for the long run means some real issues will not be settled within one conversation.

concepts.title: When you disagree with a book
concepts.question: When a reader disagrees with a book, what should he check first, and what must he then decide about the point at issue?

paragraphs: Applied to reading, the third maxim works in steps. When you find yourself disagreeing with a book, first make sure the disagreement is not owing to misunderstanding.

If you have observed Rule 9 and are satisfied there is no misunderstanding, the maxim then asks you to distinguish genuine knowledge from mere opinion, and to treat an issue of knowledge as one that can be resolved.

Pursuing it, you may be instructed by the author on points that change your mind. If not, your criticism may be justified, and, metaphorically at least, you may instruct the author: you can hope that, were he alive and present, his mind could be changed.

If an author gives no reasons for a proposition, it can be treated only as his personal opinion. A reader who does not separate reasoned knowledge from bare opinion is not reading to learn: he treats the book as a case history and judges the man, not the book.
card.example: A reader disagrees with a historian's claim that a famine was caused by policy, not drought. She rereads and confirms what he means. Then she checks: does he give evidence? He does, and so does she. It is an issue of knowledge, so she sets her evidence against his, expecting either to learn or to have something to teach.
card.rule: When you disagree with a book, rule out misunderstanding first, then treat a question of knowledge as one the evidence can settle between you and the author.
card.limits: The steps apply to reasoned claims; bare assertions tell you about the author, not the subject. And ruling out misunderstanding comes first, because a disagreement that rests on a misreading is not with the author at all.

concepts.title: Rule 11: give reasons for every judgment
concepts.question: What must a reader add to every judgment of agreement or disagreement, and how does that differ between agreeing and disagreeing?

paragraphs: A reader interested in the book rather than the man must apply the distinction between knowledge and opinion to himself as well as to the author. So he must do more than agree or disagree: he must give reasons.

When he agrees, it is enough that he actively shares the author's reasons for the point. When he disagrees, he must give his own grounds. Otherwise he treats a matter of knowledge as if it were opinion.
Hence Rule 11: respect the difference between knowledge and mere personal opinion by giving reasons for any critical judgment you make.
card.example: Reviewing a book on urban heat, Ana writes: I agree that trees cool streets, for the author's reason: the shade and evaporation data in chapter 2 persuade me. I disagree that green roofs matter as much, because the studies he cites measured roof surfaces, not street temperatures. Each verdict carries its reason.
card.rule: Give reasons for every critical judgment: share the author's reasons when you agree, and give your own when you disagree.
card.limits: Sharing the author's reasons means holding them actively, not noting that he gave some. And a reason for disagreeing must bear on the claim; disliking the author or the conclusion is a motive, not a ground.

concepts.title: Knowledge is defensible opinion
concepts.question: If most knowledge can be corrected, what still separates knowledge from mere opinion?

paragraphs: The authors do not claim there is much absolute knowledge. Self-evident propositions seem to them both indemonstrable and undeniable, but most knowledge lacks that certainty. We know subject to correction: the weight of the evidence supports a belief, but new evidence may some day overturn it.

That does not erase the line between knowledge and opinion. Knowledge, in their sense, consists of opinions that can be defended, opinions for which there is evidence of some kind. If we really know something, we must believe we can convince others of it.

Opinion, in the sense they have been using, is unsupported judgment, hence the words mere and personal. We can only opine when nothing but feeling or prejudice stands behind a statement. We can say we know when we have objective evidence that other reasonable people are likely to accept.
card.example: Two people say a local river is cleaner than it was ten years ago. One has a feeling it looks better. The other has a decade of water-quality readings. Either could turn out wrong, but only the second is knowledge in the authors' sense: a defensible opinion that others could be brought to accept.
card.rule: Call a judgment knowledge only when you can back it with evidence other reasonable people would accept, while holding it open to correction.
card.limits: Being correctable does not make knowledge mere opinion, and being supported does not make it certain. Self-evident propositions are the exception the authors allow: undeniable, though they cannot be demonstrated.

concepts.title: The three maxims together
concepts.question: What do the three general maxims of critical reading require together, and why do reasons hold the hope of resolution?

paragraphs: Together the three maxims state the conditions of critical reading and the manner in which a reader should talk back. The first, Rule 9, requires him to complete the task of understanding before rushing in. The second, Rule 10, urges him not to be disputatious or contentious.

The third, Rule 11, asks him to view disagreement about matters of knowledge as generally remediable, and goes further: he must give reasons for his disagreements, so that issues are not merely stated but defined. In that, the authors say, lies all hope for resolution.
These are general maxims of intellectual etiquette. The more specific criteria for points of criticism come in the next chapter.
card.example: A reader of a book on school funding outlines and interprets it until she can restate its case (Rule 9). She notices she wants to beat the author and checks that impulse (Rule 10). She disagrees on one point and says which evidence she reads differently, turning a vague no into a defined issue (Rule 11).
card.rule: Understand first, disagree without contentiousness, and give reasons that define the issue so it can be resolved.
card.limits: The maxims set conditions and manner; they do not say what counts as a point of criticism. Following them makes a judgment fair, not correct: a courteous, reasoned disagreement can still be mistaken.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.title: First say whether you understand
concepts.question: Before you agree or disagree with a book, what must you be able to say, and what do you do if you cannot?

paragraphs: The first thing a reader can say about a book is that he understands it or that he does not. Every further remark, agreeing, disagreeing or holding back, depends on the first being yes.

If the honest answer is no, the authors' advice is blunt: make no critical remark at all, and go back to work on the book. Criticism of a book you have not understood is criticism of something you made up.
So the third stage of analytical reading opens with a test of the first two. Only a reader who has outlined the book and interpreted it can say I understand and mean it.
card.example: Rana finishes a book on monetary policy and feels sure the author is wrong about interest rates. Asked to state the author's main argument in her own words, she cannot. Her verdict waits; she returns to the chapters where the argument is built.
card.rule: Say I understand before you say anything else about a book, and if you cannot, keep quiet and reread.
card.limits: The test is your honest ability to state what the book says, not a feeling of familiarity. Keeping quiet is a pause, not permanent silence. One exception, taken up next: a supported charge that the book itself is unintelligible.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.title: When I don't understand is a criticism
concepts.question: When can saying you do not understand a book count as a criticism of the book rather than of yourself?

paragraphs: There is one exception to keeping quiet. I don't understand can itself be a critical remark, but only if the reader can support it by showing that the fault lies in the book, not in himself.

To do that he must locate the sources of trouble. He might show that the book's structure is disorderly, that its parts do not hang together, that some of it is irrelevant, or that the author equivocates, using an important word in shifting senses.
To the extent that he can support the charge that the book is unintelligible, he has no further critical duties toward it. There is nothing more to agree or disagree with.
card.example: A reader of a report on remote work cannot follow its case. Checking, she finds that productivity means output per hour in chapter 2 and total output in chapter 5, and the conclusion leans on both senses at once. Her I don't understand now points to a place in the book.
card.rule: Turn I don't understand into a criticism only by pointing to where the book itself is disorderly, disconnected, irrelevant or equivocal.
card.limits: With a good book, failure to understand is usually the reader's. Your own confusion is not evidence; only defects you can show in the text are. A hard book is not an unintelligible one.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.title: Full agreement ends the work; disagreement needs argument
concepts.question: When is an analytical reading finished, and why does a reader who disagrees need to know the principles of argument?

paragraphs: Suppose you understand a good book and agree thoroughly with what it says. Then the work is over: the analytical reading is done, and you have been enlightened and convinced. Further steps are needed only when you disagree or suspend judgment, and the authors say disagreement is the more usual case.
Authors argue with their readers and expect them to argue back. So a good reader must know the principles of argument and be able to carry on controversy that is both intelligent and civil.
Following an author's arguments is not enough. Only by meeting them, testing them as an opponent would, does a reader reach agreement or disagreement worth the name.
card.rule: Treat thorough agreement after understanding as the end of the reading, and meet the arguments, not only follow them, wherever you disagree or hold back.
card.limits: Agreement ends the work only when it is thorough and comes after understanding. Agreeing with most of a book while doubting one step leaves that step open.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.title: Two senses of agreement
concepts.question: If understanding a book means your mind meets the author's, how can you still disagree with him?

paragraphs: Understanding is itself a kind of agreement: reader and writer agree about the use of language to express ideas, so the reader sees through the words to the author's thoughts. That raises a puzzle. If your mind and the author's have become one, what mind is left to judge with?

The puzzle comes from running together two senses of agreement. One is agreement about what the words mean. The other is agreement about whether what they say is so. People who confuse them conclude that all disagreement comes from misunderstanding.

But an author makes judgments about the world: theoretical claims about how things are, or practical claims about what should be done. Such claims can be right or wrong, justified only so far as they are true or probable in the light of evidence.
card.rule: Separate agreement about what the author means from agreement about whether he is right, and expect the second to stay open after the first is reached.
card.limits: The distinction does not make every disagreement real. If the shared understanding of the words is missing, a seeming disagreement about facts may still be a misunderstanding.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.title: Misread disagreement versus a real issue
concepts.question: When is a disagreement with an author a real issue, and when is it irrelevant because it rests on a misreading?

paragraphs: The authors' example: someone says all men are equal. If we take this to mean that all are born with equal intelligence and strength, we disagree, because the facts say otherwise. But if the speaker meant that all should have equal political rights, our disagreement was irrelevant. We were disputing a claim nobody made.
Correct the misunderstanding and two outcomes remain: we agree, or we disagree. If we now disagree, there is a real issue, because we understand the position and hold a contrary one.
So shared understanding of the words is the condition of any genuine dispute about facts or policy. You can make up your own mind about an author because of, not in spite of, having met his mind.
card.rule: Before counting a disagreement as real, check that you take the author's words in the sense he meant, and drop any objection that rests on a misreading.
card.limits: Correcting a misreading does not settle the issue in the author's favour. It only makes the issue real: the corrected claim may still be one you can show to be false.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.title: Reasons, not feelings: acknowledge your emotions
concepts.question: How can you tell whether you disagree with an author for reasons or because of strong feelings?

paragraphs: A reader who understands and then disagrees should do so because he thinks the author can be shown to be wrong on some point, not to voice a prejudice or vent an emotion.

The authors set out three ideal conditions for well-conducted controversy. The first starts from the fact that people are animals as well as rational beings: acknowledge the emotions you bring to a dispute, and those that arise as it goes on.
Unacknowledged emotion passes itself off as argument. You may be giving vent to feelings instead of stating reasons, and you may even believe you have reasons when all you have is strong feeling.
card.example: Halfway through a book defending zoos, Kim notices she is angry. She writes down that she grew up campaigning against them, then lists her objections. Two survive as reasons with evidence; one turns out to be only her anger in other words.
card.rule: Name the feelings you bring to a book, and check that each objection is a reason you could show, not a feeling dressed as one.
card.limits: The aim is not to have no feelings, which is impossible, but to keep them from standing in for reasons. A feeling can point you toward a real flaw; it cannot be the evidence for it.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.title: Make your assumptions explicit
concepts.question: Why must you know your own prejudgments before disagreeing, and how should you treat what an author asks you to assume?

paragraphs: The second condition: make your own assumptions explicit. Know what your prejudices are, in the literal sense of prejudgments, the things you took as settled before you began.
Otherwise you will not admit that the author may be equally entitled to different assumptions. Good controversy should not be a quarrel about assumptions.

If an author explicitly asks you to take something for granted, the fact that the opposite could also be taken for granted should not stop you from honouring the request. A reader whose unacknowledged prejudices lie on the other side cannot give the author's case a fair hearing.
card.rule: List your own prejudgments on the subject, and grant the author the assumptions he openly asks for, so the dispute is about his argument.
card.limits: Honouring a stated assumption is for following the case fairly. It is not a promise never to examine it; and an assumption the author hides rather than states is not a request you have agreed to.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.title: Try to take the author's point of view
concepts.question: Since every disputant takes a side, what can you do to keep your disagreement with a book civil rather than contentious?

paragraphs: The third condition: an attempt at impartiality is a good antidote to the blindness that partisanship almost always brings. Controversy without taking sides is impossible, so the aim is not to stop being a partisan.

To get more light and less heat, each side should at least try to take the other's point of view. If you could not read a book sympathetically, your disagreement with it is probably more contentious than civil.

The authors call the three conditions, acknowledging emotions, making assumptions explicit and attempting impartiality, the indispensable conditions of profitable conversation, and reading is a conversation between reader and author.
card.rule: Before disagreeing, read the book once from the author's side, as sympathetically as you can.
card.limits: Impartiality is attempted, not achieved: you remain on a side. And sympathy is a way of reading, not a verdict; a reader who sees the author's view fully may still disagree.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.title: Criticize the book; do not attack it
concepts.question: Since the ideal conditions of fair controversy are hard to meet, what lapses should you watch for, and what do the authors offer instead?

paragraphs: The three ideal conditions can only be approximated. The authors admit breaking their own rules: attacking a book instead of criticizing it, knocking down straw men, denouncing where they could not support a denial, and proclaiming their prejudices as if theirs were better than the author's.
A straw man is a weaker version of the author's position, set up so it can be knocked down. Denouncing is condemning a claim without the support that would show it false.

Believing that criticism can still be disciplined, the authors replace the ideal conditions with easier prescriptions: four specific ways a book can be adversely criticized. A reader who confines himself to these is less likely to indulge emotion or prejudice.
card.rule: Aim criticism at what the author actually wrote, with support for each denial, and keep to specific kinds of fault instead of general attack.
card.limits: Discipline lowers the risk of these lapses but does not remove it; even the authors slip. A sharp, even severe, criticism is not an attack if it is aimed at the real position and supported.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.title: The four adverse remarks
concepts.question: After saying I understand but I disagree, what four remarks can a reader make to the author?

paragraphs: Picture the reader talking back to the author. Having said I understand but I disagree, he can make four remarks: (1) you are uninformed; (2) you are misinformed; (3) you are illogical, your reasoning is not cogent; (4) your analysis is incomplete.
The authors think these may be exhaustive, and are sure they are the principal points a disagreeing reader can make. Each names a different kind of defect.
The defects are not mutually exclusive. Making one remark does not stop you making another; a book can earn several, or all four.
card.example: Reading a book arguing that cities should ban gas boilers, a reader notes: it ignores newer heat-pump costs (uninformed); it says gas is cheaper to run than the price data show (misinformed); it concludes a ban is needed from evidence that only shows heat pumps are possible (illogical); it never considers rural homes off the grid (incomplete).
card.rule: Turn I disagree into one or more of four remarks: uninformed, misinformed, illogical, or incomplete.
card.limits: The four are adverse remarks for a reader who already understands. They are not a tally of everything a reader dislikes: tone, style or an unwelcome conclusion fit none of them.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.title: Specify the respect and give reasons
concepts.question: What must a reader add to any of the adverse remarks to make it a fair criticism rather than a label?

paragraphs: None of the remarks may be made vaguely. The reader must be definite and precise about the respect in which the author is uninformed, misinformed or illogical.
The reason is that no book is uninformed or misinformed about everything, and none is totally illogical. A charge that names no place is a charge about nothing in particular.
Specifying is not enough either. The reader must also support the point: give reasons for saying what he says.
card.example: Weak: the author does not know the economics. Better: in chapter 5 he assumes rents fall when supply rises without citing the 2019 data on his own city, where rents rose; that bears on his main conclusion.
card.rule: For each adverse remark, name the exact point where the author goes wrong and give reasons that show it.
card.limits: Precision is about the respect, not about length or detail for its own sake. A precise charge that is not relevant to the author's conclusions is still not worth making.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.title: You are uninformed
concepts.question: What does it mean to call an author uninformed, and what must you show to support the charge?

paragraphs: To say an author is uninformed is to say he lacks some piece of knowledge relevant to the problem he is trying to solve. Unless the knowledge would have been relevant, there is no point in the remark.
To support it you must state the knowledge the author lacks yourself, and show how it is relevant: how it makes a difference to his conclusions.

The authors' examples: Darwin lacked the knowledge of genetics later supplied by Mendel and others, a major defect in The Origin of Species; Gibbon lacked facts later historical research found bearing on the fall of Rome. In science and history, such gaps are usually found by later research.
card.rule: Charge an author with being uninformed only when you can state the knowledge he lacks and show how it would change his conclusions.
card.limits: A gap that would not change the author's conclusions is not worth charging. And uninformed means lacking knowledge, not asserting falsehood; an author can lack something without saying anything false.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.title: Gaps found later, and knowledge lost
concepts.question: How are an author's gaps in knowledge usually discovered in science and history, and why can philosophy be different?

paragraphs: In science and history, an author's lack of information is usually revealed by later research. Better techniques of observation and long investigation make knowledge in these fields tend to grow, so later work exposes what earlier authors lacked.
In philosophy, the authors say, there is as likely to be loss as gain with time. Knowledge well established by earlier thinkers can be missing from later ones.

Their example: the ancients sharply distinguished what we can sense and imagine from what we can understand. Yet in the eighteenth century Hume showed no grasp of this distinction between images and ideas, though earlier philosophers had worked it out.
card.rule: To find what an author lacks, look to later research in science and history, and in philosophy look also to what earlier thinkers had already established.
card.limits: The pattern is a tendency, not a law. Later science can also forget, and later philosophy often gains; the point is that in philosophy you cannot assume a newer book knows more.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.title: You are misinformed
concepts.question: What does it mean to call an author misinformed, and how must you support that charge?

paragraphs: To say an author is misinformed is to say he asserts what is not the case. The error may come from a lack of knowledge, but it is more than a lack: it is an assertion contrary to fact. He claims knowledge he does not have.
Point it out only if it is relevant to his conclusions. To support the charge you must argue that a position contrary to the author's is true, or more probable.

The authors' examples: Spinoza seems to say democracy is a more primitive form of government than monarchy, against well-established political history, and the error bears on his argument. Aristotle was misinformed about the female's role in animal reproduction, and so reached unsupportable conclusions about procreation.
card.rule: Charge an author with being misinformed only where you can argue that a contrary position is true or more probable, and the error bears on his conclusions.
card.limits: Saying you doubt a claim is not showing it is false. And a relevant error must be one he asserts; a point he leaves out belongs to being uninformed, not misinformed.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.title: Weigh an error by what it supports
concepts.question: How do you decide whether a factual error in a book is worth pointing out?

paragraphs: Not every error matters. The authors say a factual mistake should be pointed out only if it is relevant to the author's conclusions, so the critic must see how much of the argument rests on it.

The authors contrast two cases. Aquinas wrongly supposed that the matter of the heavenly bodies differs in kind from earthly matter, since he thought they changed only in position. Modern astrophysics corrects this. But the error has limited relevance: it leaves his metaphysical account of all sensible things, as composed of matter and form, untouched.
Spinoza's error, that democracy is a more primitive form than monarchy, by contrast bears on his political argument, so it counts against his conclusions.
card.rule: Before pointing out an error, trace which of the author's conclusions depend on it, and weigh it by that.
card.limits: Limited relevance is not no relevance. An error that leaves the main conclusion standing may still bear on a lesser one, and is worth pointing out there.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.title: Gaps and errors: defects in the premises
concepts.question: How are being uninformed and being misinformed related, and what part of an author's case do both attack?

paragraphs: The first two remarks are related. Lack of information may cause false assertions, and whenever an author is misinformed in some respect he is also uninformed in that same respect.

Still, it matters whether the defect is only negative or positive as well. A lack of relevant knowledge makes it impossible to solve certain problems or support certain conclusions. Erroneous suppositions lead to wrong conclusions and untenable solutions.
Taken together, the two remarks charge the author with defects in his premises. He needs more knowledge than he has; his evidence and reasons are not good enough in quantity or quality.
card.rule: Classify a defect in an author's starting points as a gap (uninformed) or an error (misinformed), and expect a gap to leave conclusions unsupported but an error to make them wrong.
card.limits: The two charges both concern premises, not reasoning. If the premises are sound and the conclusion still fails to follow, the fault is of a different kind.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.title: You are illogical: the non sequitur
concepts.question: What does it mean to call an author illogical, and what does a conclusion that does not follow look like?

paragraphs: To say an author is illogical is to say he has committed a fallacy in reasoning. Fallacies are of two general sorts. One is the non sequitur: what is drawn as a conclusion does not follow from the reasons offered. The other is inconsistency.

The authors' example comes from Machiavelli's The Prince. Good laws are the foundations of states; there cannot be good laws where the state is not well armed; so, Machiavelli concludes, where states are well armed they have good laws.

That does not follow. Good laws may depend on an adequate armed force without armed force guaranteeing good laws. Compare: happiness may depend on health, but it does not follow that all who are healthy are happy.
card.rule: Test each main conclusion by asking whether it follows from the reasons given, and charge a non sequitur only where you can show that it does not.
card.limits: A conclusion that does not follow may still be true; the charge is that these reasons do not establish it. And the authors set aside whether Machiavelli's premise is true: illogic is a fault of inference, not of premises.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.title: You are illogical: inconsistency
concepts.question: How can an author be illogical even when each of his arguments looks valid on its own?

paragraphs: The second sort of fallacy is inconsistency: two things the author has tried to say are incompatible. Each may be argued well where it stands; the trouble appears only when they are put side by side.

The authors' example is Hobbes. In one place he argues that all bodies are nothing but quantities of matter in motion, with no qualities at all. Elsewhere he says man is nothing but a body, and that sensory qualities such as colours and tastes are nothing but motions of atoms in the brain.
But what is said of all bodies in motion must apply to any particular group of them, including the atoms of the brain. So the second claim admits qualities into a world the first said had none.
card.rule: Set the author's claims from different places side by side, and charge inconsistency where you can show that two of them cannot both be true.
card.limits: An apparent contradiction may be one word used in two senses; check the terms before charging. And finding an inconsistency shows that both claims cannot stand, not which one is false.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.title: Logic that matters, and fallacies that hide
concepts.question: Which lapses of reasoning are worth charging, and why are they hard to find in good books?

paragraphs: To charge an author with illogic, show the precise respect in which his argument lacks cogency. And care about the defect only to the extent that his major conclusions are affected. A book may safely lack cogency in irrelevant respects.

Illogic is hard to illustrate because few really good books make obvious slips in reasoning. When slips do occur, they are usually elaborately concealed, and it takes a very penetrating reader to discover them.
card.rule: Look closely for slips in reasoning, and press only those that touch the author's major conclusions.
card.limits: Concealed does not mean absent; nor does a flaw found make a book bad. An invalid step in a side argument leaves the main case standing, so the charge must say which conclusion falls.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.title: Bad reasoning from good grounds
concepts.question: When is the charge of illogic most important, and how does it differ from charges against the premises?

paragraphs: The third remark is related to the first two. An author may fail to draw conclusions that his evidence or principles imply, which makes his reasoning incomplete. But the main concern of the charge of illogic is the author who reasons poorly from good grounds.
Finding faulty reasoning from premises that are themselves untrue, or from inadequate evidence, is interesting but less important.

Someone who reaches a conclusion invalidly from sound premises is, in a sense, misinformed: he ends up asserting something unsupported. Still, the authors think it worth distinguishing an error that comes from bad reasoning from one that comes from other defects, especially insufficient knowledge.
card.rule: Before charging illogic, check that the premises are sound, so that the fault you name lies in the reasoning itself.
card.limits: Bad reasoning from bad premises is still bad reasoning and can be noted; it is only less important. And failing to draw an implied conclusion is a lack, not a fallacy.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.title: No fault found: you must agree
concepts.question: If you understand a book but cannot show the author uninformed, misinformed or illogical, what are you obliged to do?

paragraphs: The first three remarks deal with the soundness of the author's statements and reasoning. Suppose you have said you understand, and you cannot support any of them on a relevant matter.
Then, the authors say, you must agree with the author as far as he has gone. You have no freedom of will about this. It is not your sacred privilege to decide whether you will agree or disagree.

The reasoning behind this: if his premises are adequate and true, and his conclusions follow from them, nothing is left to disagree with. Agreement is not a favour you grant; it is what the arguments compel.
card.rule: If you can support none of the first three remarks on a relevant point, agree with the author as far as he has gone.
card.limits: The obligation covers what the author has argued, not what he left out; incompleteness is a separate matter. And it binds only a reader who truly understands; failing to find faults in a book you misread proves nothing.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.title: Disliking a conclusion is not disagreeing
concepts.question: What does it mean to say you find no fault in an author's premises or reasoning but still reject his conclusion?

paragraphs: Many readers say: I find nothing wrong with your premises and no errors in your reasoning, but I don't agree with your conclusions. The authors say this is not disagreement at all.
All it can mean is that you do not like the conclusions. You are expressing emotion or prejudice, not a judgment. If you have been convinced, you should admit it.
And if, unable to support any of the first three remarks, you still honestly feel unconvinced, perhaps you should not have said you understood in the first place.
card.rule: If you can fault neither the premises nor the reasoning, admit you are convinced, or go back and check whether you understood.
card.limits: Lingering doubt is not forbidden; it is a signal to look again at the premises and steps. What the authors rule out is treating that doubt as if it were a reasoned disagreement.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.title: Your analysis is incomplete
concepts.question: What does it mean to call an author's analysis incomplete, and what makes that charge more than a cheap remark?

paragraphs: The first three remarks concern the author's terms, propositions and arguments, the elements he works with. The fourth concerns the structure of the whole: how adequately he carries out the task he chose.

An analysis is incomplete if the author has not solved all the problems he started with, has not used his materials as well as he could, has not seen all their implications, or has failed to make distinctions relevant to his undertaking.
Anyone can call any book incomplete; all human works are finite. So the remark has a point only if the reader defines the inadequacy precisely, by his own knowledge or with the help of other books.
card.example: The authors' cases: Aristotle's Politics does not consider democracy based on universal suffrage, representative government or the federated state; Dewey's How We Think omits the thinking done in reading and learning by instruction.
card.rule: Charge incompleteness only by naming exactly which problem, implication or distinction the author's task required and he left out.
card.limits: The charge is measured against the task the author set himself. Leaving out what his problems did not require is choosing a scope, not failing to finish.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.title: Agree in part, suspend on the whole
concepts.question: If a book is sound as far as it goes but incomplete, should you disagree with it, and if not, what verdict fits?

paragraphs: The fourth remark is not, strictly, a basis for disagreement. It is adverse only in marking the limits of what the author achieved.

So a reader who finds no reason to call the author uninformed, misinformed or illogical must agree with the book in part. In the light of its incompleteness, he may still suspend judgment on the whole.
Suspended judgment is the fitting response to an author's failure to solve his problems perfectly: what he showed is accepted, and the verdict on the whole waits.
card.rule: When a sound book is incomplete, agree with what it shows and suspend judgment on the whole instead of disagreeing.
card.limits: Suspension applies to the whole, not to the parts you could not fault; those you must accept. And where one of the first three remarks does apply, you may disagree on that point.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.title: Comparing books: count the distinctions
concepts.question: How can you judge which of two books on the same subject is better, and what makes the deepest comparison?

paragraphs: The four criteria also let you compare related books in the same field. One is better than another as it speaks more truth and makes fewer errors. If you read for knowledge, the best book is the one that treats its subject most adequately.
One author may lack information another has; one may make false suppositions another avoids; one may reason less cogently from similar grounds.

But the profoundest comparison is by completeness, and its measure is the number of valid and significant distinctions each account contains. That is why grasping the author's terms pays off: the number of distinct terms goes with the number of distinctions.
card.rule: Compare books on the same subject by the four criteria, and above all by how many valid and significant distinctions each one makes.
card.limits: Only valid and significant distinctions count; hair-splitting or false distinctions do not make a book more complete. And the comparison assumes the books treat the same subject and problem.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.title: Completeness ties the three stages together
concepts.question: How does judging a book's completeness connect back to the first and second stages of analytical reading?

paragraphs: The fourth critical remark ties the three stages of analytical reading together. Each stage ends on the author's problems.

The last step of outlining is to know the problems the author is trying to solve. The last step of interpretation is to know which of them he solved and which he did not. The last step of criticism is the point about completeness.
Completeness touches outlining in asking how adequately the author stated his problems, and interpretation in measuring how satisfactorily he solved them.
card.example: A reader's notes on a book about inflation: Rule 4 listed three questions (causes, effects, cures). Rule 8 marked causes and effects solved, cures left open and admitted. Criticism then asks: were the three questions well framed, and is the open one a real gap in the task he set?
card.rule: Judge completeness by going back to the problems you listed in outlining and the solutions you marked in interpreting.
card.limits: The judgment is only as good as the earlier work. If the problems were never stated in outlining, or the solutions never checked in interpreting, a charge of incompleteness has nothing to be measured against.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
concepts.title: The rules of the third stage
concepts.question: What are the seven rules for criticizing a book, and how are they grouped?

paragraphs: The third stage has seven rules in two groups. General maxims of intellectual etiquette: (9) do not begin criticism until you have completed your outline and interpretation, that is, until you can say I understand; (10) do not disagree disputatiously or contentiously; (11) show you know the difference between knowledge and personal opinion by giving good reasons for any critical judgment.
Special criteria for points of criticism: show wherein the author is (12) uninformed, (13) misinformed, (14) illogical, and (15) wherein his analysis or account is incomplete.
Of the last four, the first three are criteria for disagreement. Failing all of them, you must agree at least in part, though you may suspend judgment on the whole in the light of the fourth.
card.rule: Criticize under the three maxims of etiquette, and base any verdict on the four criteria, disagreeing only on the first three.
card.limits: Following the maxims does not make a criticism correct, and meeting a criterion does not excuse breaking a maxim. A reader needs both: the right conduct and grounds that hold.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
concepts.title: Is it true? The highest test of a book
concepts.question: To what kinds of writing does the question of truth apply, and what standard do the authors set against novelty and sensation?

paragraphs: The last seven rules help answer the third and fourth basic questions: Is it true? and What of it? The question of truth can be asked of anything we read, in one sense of truth or another: mathematical, scientific, philosophical, historical, poetical.
No higher praise, the authors say, can be given a work than for the measure of truth it achieves. Criticizing it for failing in truth is to treat a serious work as seriously as it deserves.
They lament that many readers and reviewers now judge books by novelty, sensationalism, seductiveness, force or power to bewilder, instead of by their truth, clarity and power to enlighten.
card.rule: Ask of everything you read whether it is true, in the sense of truth that fits its kind, and judge it by truth, clarity and power to enlighten before novelty or force.
card.limits: Truth comes in different senses; a poem is not true the way a theorem is, so the test must fit the kind of work. The lament about reviewers is the authors' opinion of their time.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
concepts.title: What of it? Facts come interpreted
concepts.question: Once you judge that what you read is true, why must you still ask what significance its facts have?

paragraphs: Unless what you have read is true in some sense, the authors say, you need go no further. If it is, you must face the last question: What of it?

Even reading for information cannot be done intelligently without deciding what significance is, or should be, attached to the facts presented. Facts seldom reach us without some interpretation, stated or implied.

This is especially so with digests, which must select facts by some judgment of their significance, some principle of interpretation. And in reading for enlightenment, What of it? renews the inquiry at every stage of learning; it has no end.
card.rule: After judging a text true, ask what significance its facts carry, including the significance already built into how they were chosen.
card.limits: The question waits on the question of truth: a text judged false in some respect gives you nothing to build on in that respect. And significance is not settled once; further learning keeps raising it.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
concepts.title: Why reading has these stages
concepts.question: What features of human communication make each of the four basic questions about a book necessary?

paragraphs: The four basic questions sum up all the obligations of a reader. The first three, the authors say, correspond to something in the very nature of human discourse.

If communications were not complex, structural outlining would be unnecessary. If language were a perfect medium instead of a relatively opaque one, there would be no need for interpretation. If error and ignorance did not hem in truth and knowledge, we would not have to be critical.

The fourth question turns on the distinction between information and understanding. When what you read is mainly informational, you are challenged to go further and seek enlightenment; even when enlightened, you are called on to keep searching for significance.
card.rule: Treat each stage of reading as the answer to a feature of communication: complexity calls for outlining, opaque language for interpretation, error for criticism.
card.limits: These features are matters of degree, so the work each stage takes varies with the text. None of them ever vanishes entirely: no real text is perfectly simple, perfectly clear and free of error.

concepts.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
concepts.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
concepts.title: An ideal to approach, books read on their merits
concepts.question: If few readers ever meet the ideal the rules describe, what are the rules for, and which books deserve reading well?

paragraphs: The rules of analytical reading describe an ideal performance. Few people have read any book that way, and those who have probably read very few books so. The ideal is still the measure: you are a good reader to the degree you approach it.
Great writers have been great readers, often of fewer books than colleges now require, but read well. Having mastered them, they became peers of their authors.

You approach the ideal by applying the rules to a single book, not by skimming many. Many books are worth reading well; many more should only be inspected. To be well-read, use your skill with discrimination, reading each book according to its merits.
card.rule: Measure your reading against the ideal of the rules, and spend that full effort on the books that deserve it, inspecting the rest.
card.limits: Approaching the ideal is not reaching it; falling short is the normal case, not failure. And reading by merits needs inspection first: you cannot tell what a book deserves before looking at it.

concepts.title: Intrinsic and extrinsic reading
concepts.question: What separates reading a book in itself from reading it in the light of something outside it?

paragraphs: Intrinsic reading means working on a book by itself, apart from all other books, with only your own mind and the rules for reading that book. Every rule taught before this chapter is a rule of intrinsic reading: none of them sends you outside the book to find out what it means.

Extrinsic reading means reading a book in the light of other books and outside sources. Any aid that lies outside the book you are reading is an extrinsic aid, whether it is a dictionary, a commentary or your own experience of life.
The authors held back extrinsic aids until now on purpose, but they do not reject them. Outside help can be useful, and for some books it is needed for full understanding.
card.example: A reader works through a treatise on property rights, outlining it and listing its key terms from the text alone: that is intrinsic reading. Afterwards she checks a word in a dictionary and compares the treatise with an earlier book it answers: that is extrinsic reading.
card.rule: Before reaching for help, know whether you are working on the book itself or drawing on something outside it.
card.limits: The label says where help comes from, not how good it is: an aid can be extrinsic and still necessary. Calling something extrinsic is not a verdict against using it.

concepts.title: No book is read in isolation
concepts.question: Why can no book be read entirely on its own, even by a reader following only the rules of intrinsic reading?

paragraphs: In actual reading, intrinsic and extrinsic reading tend to fuse. When you outline, interpret or criticize a book, you cannot help bringing your experience to it. Nobody begins a reading life with analytical reading; you have read other books before this one.

So you measure a writer's statements and conclusions against what you already know from other books and from life, even if you do it less systematically than you should. The authors call it common sense that no book can be read in complete isolation, and so none should be.
The aim is not to stop this but to do it well: bring that knowledge to bear deliberately, and notice when a judgment rests on it.
card.example: Reading a novel about a struggling family farm, a reader who grew up in a farming village judges at once that the money worries ring true. That judgment draws on life outside the book, though she opened no other source.
card.rule: Bring your experience of life and of other books to a book deliberately, and notice when a judgment rests on it.
card.limits: Outside knowledge is a measure, not a replacement: if what you already believe overrides what the author says before you have understood it, you have stopped reading his book and started reading your own.

concepts.title: Do your best alone first
concepts.question: Why do the authors want you to work on a book by yourself before seeking outside help?

paragraphs: The main reason the authors delayed any talk of outside aids is that many readers lean on them too heavily. They wanted you to find out that most of this help is unnecessary.
Their principle: do all you can by yourself before going outside the book. Readers who act on it consistently find they need less and less outside help, because their own skill grows with use.
Reading with a dictionary in one hand, or running to a commentary at the first puzzle, is the habit they warn against. This does not ban dictionaries or commentaries; it decides when they come in.
card.example: A student meets a dense paragraph in an economics text. Instead of searching online for an explanation, she rereads it, finds its key terms and checks how the next page uses them. Afterwards only one sentence still puzzles her, and that is the one she looks up.
card.rule: Do everything you can with the book yourself before seeking outside help, and let the help answer only what remains.
card.limits: Working alone first is not working alone forever: some books stay unclear after your best effort, and then refusing help is stubbornness, not skill. The principle governs the order of help, not whether help is allowed.

concepts.title: The four aids and when to use them
concepts.question: What are the four kinds of outside aid, and at what point should a reader turn to them?

paragraphs: The authors sort extrinsic aids into four kinds and discuss them in this order: relevant experience, other books, commentaries and abstracts, and reference books such as dictionaries and encyclopedias.

No rule can say how and when to use each one in every case. But one common-sense maxim covers all four: seek outside help when a book, in whole or in part, is still unintelligible after you have done your best with the rules of intrinsic reading.
The maxim has two conditions. You must really have done your best, and something must still be unclear. Help sought before the first condition is met, or without the second, is help you did not need.
card.example: After a careful reading of a book on monetary policy, a reader follows the argument except in one chapter that leans on a term she cannot pin down from the text. That chapter, and that term, is where an aid belongs.
card.rule: Turn to outside aids for what remains unclear after a full effort with the book itself, and choose the kind of aid that fits the difficulty.
card.limits: The maxim governs seeking help to understand the book. It does not keep your experience out of your reading, which it enters anyway, and it sets no fixed schedule: when you have done your best is a judgment, not a page count.

concepts.title: Common and special experience
concepts.question: What makes an experience common rather than special, and must common experience be shared by everyone?

paragraphs: Common experience comes to men and women because they are alive. Special experience must be actively sought, and only those who take the trouble to get it have it. The clearest case of special experience is a laboratory experiment, but a laboratory is not required: an anthropologist who travels to study a remote people gains it too.

Common does not mean universal. Family life is common experience even though some people are orphans from birth, because most people share it in the ordinary course of life. Being taught is common for the same reason, though some never go to school.
So the test is not whether everyone has an experience, but whether it comes with ordinary living or only through deliberate effort.
card.example: Waiting in a queue, falling ill, losing a friend: common experience. Watching cells divide under a microscope, or recording sea-floor temperatures from a research ship: special experience, since few people gain these without going out of their way.
card.rule: Count an experience as common if most people meet it in ordinary life, and as special if it must be deliberately sought.
card.limits: Do not read common as shared by literally everyone. And an ordinary experience can still be studied specially, as when researchers observe family life systematically; the subject is common, the study is special.

concepts.title: Which experience fits which book
concepts.question: Which kind of experience should you bring to a novel, a philosophy book, a science book and a history?

paragraphs: The two kinds of experience help with different books. Common experience matters most for fiction and for philosophy. Whether a novel is true to life is judged almost wholly by common experience: does the story fit life as most people, ourselves included, live it?
