Philosophers do no work in laboratories or field research; they appeal to the common experience of mankind. To understand and test a philosopher's leading principles you need no special experience, only your common sense and daily observation of the world.

Special experience matters most for science: to judge a scientist's inductive arguments, you must follow the evidence he reports as their basis. History needs both. As a story with plot and characters it calls on common experience; as research in documents and interviews it rests on special experience.
card.example: A reader tests a philosopher's claim that habits shape character against her own life. Reading a study of sleep, she must instead follow the experiments the researchers report.
card.rule: Before judging a book, ask which kind of experience it rests on, and bring that kind to bear.
card.limits: These are main tendencies, not walls: a novel may describe surgery, and a philosophy book may cite an experiment. Common experience helps you understand a work; it does not tell you what the author means. Chapter 14 refines this for imaginative works.

concepts.title: The concrete example test
concepts.question: How can you tell whether you have really brought your experience to bear on a point you think you understand?

paragraphs: This is the test from Chapter 9, now applied to your own experience: try to give a concrete example of a point you feel you understand. The authors call it the surest test of whether you are using your experience well. If you can, your experience has met the author's words.

The example should be your own, not one the author already gave. Aristotle says again and again that virtue is a mean between the extremes of excess and defect, and he offers some cases. Can you supply others? If so, you have grasped his general point.
If you cannot supply one, the authors' advice is plain: go back and read the discussion again.
card.example: Courage as the mean between cowardice and rashness is Aristotle's own case. A reader adds generosity, between stinginess and throwing money at everyone, then frankness, between hiding everything and voicing every passing thought. New cases show she holds the principle, not only his illustrations.
card.rule: Test whether you have grasped a point by supplying a concrete example of your own, and reread if you cannot.
card.limits: An example close to the author's own proves little, since it may be memory in new clothes; but it need not be exotic either. What counts is that you found the case yourself and that it keeps the principle while the details change.

concepts.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
concepts.title: Great books need their neighbours
concepts.question: Why do many readers of great books soon feel lost, even when they read each book with care?

paragraphs: People often start a course of reading great books with enthusiasm and soon feel hopelessly inadequate. Part of the reason is that many do not know how to read even one book well. But the authors name a second reason.

Readers expect to understand the first great book they pick up without having read the others to which it is closely related. They try The Federalist Papers without first reading the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution, or all of these without Montesquieu, Rousseau and Locke.
Many great books answer, extend or quarrel with earlier ones. Read cold, such a book leaves you missing what it is responding to.
card.example: A reader starts a famous essay attacking an earlier theory of free trade. Its sharpest pages make little sense to her until she reads the shorter work it attacks; then each objection lands on something she recognises.
card.rule: When a book is part of a larger discussion, read the closely related books it depends on.
card.limits: This is not a reason to postpone every book until all its sources are read, which could go on without end. And feeling lost can also come from a weak reading of the book itself, which no amount of further reading fixes.

concepts.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
concepts.title: Read related books in order
concepts.question: In what order should related books be read, and why does the order matter for understanding the later ones?

paragraphs: Many great books are related, and they were written in an order that should not be ignored. A later writer has often been influenced by an earlier one, so reading the earlier writer first may help you understand the later one.
The authors call this a basic common-sense maxim of extrinsic reading: read related books in relation to one another, and in an order that makes the later ones more intelligible.

The reason is the one that governs reading any single book: context. You use the whole book to interpret its words and sentences. Related books give an even larger context in which to interpret the book in your hands.
card.example: A reader plans three books on liberty: an older treatise, a famous essay that builds on it, and a modern critique of both. Read in that order, each argument arrives after the one it builds on, so the later books' moves are recognisable.
card.rule: Read related books in an order that makes the later ones intelligible, usually the earlier influence before the later work.
card.limits: Order helps only where books are related by influence or response; unrelated books gain nothing from any sequence. And reading the influence first does not replace reading each book well.

concepts.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
concepts.title: Joining the great conversation
concepts.question: What is the conversation among the great books, and how can a reader join it?

paragraphs: It has often been observed that the great books are involved in a prolonged conversation. Their authors were great readers, and one way to understand them is to read the books they read.
As readers, those authors talked back to earlier authors, much as every reader carries on a conversation with the books he reads, though most of us do not answer by writing books.

To join the conversation, read the great books in relation to one another and in an order that respects chronology, since the conversation takes place in time. You may go from past to present or from present to past; the forward direction is more natural, but either respects the sequence.
card.example: A reader curious about debates on property reads a modern economist, then the nineteenth-century writer he keeps answering, then the seventeenth-century philosopher behind both. She travels from present to past, but still meets the voices in the order in which they spoke.
card.rule: To understand a great author, read the books he was answering, in an order that respects when they were written.
card.limits: Dates order the conversation but do not show who is talking to whom: two books close in time may never have met, and a book's real partner may be centuries older. Find out which authors a writer actually read.

concepts.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
concepts.title: Which books need their relatives most
concepts.question: For which kinds of books does reading related books matter most, and for which least?

paragraphs: The need to read books in relation to one another applies more to history and philosophy than to science and fiction.
It is most important in philosophy, because philosophers are great readers of one another. A philosopher's question often comes from an earlier philosopher, and his answer is often a reply.
It is probably least important for novels and plays. If they are really good, they can be read in isolation, although a literary critic will not want to confine himself to doing so.
card.example: A reader picks two books for the summer: a classic novel and a treatise in political philosophy. She reads the novel on its own, but before the treatise she reads the shorter, earlier work it argues against.
card.rule: Weigh how much related reading a book needs by its kind: most for philosophy, much for history, least for good novels and plays.
card.limits: The ranking describes how much a reader needs related books, not a ban: a good novel read alone can still gain from its relatives, as critics know, and a philosophy book may be grasped well enough alone for a first reading.

concepts.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
concepts.title: Commentators can be wrong
concepts.question: Why should commentaries be used sparingly, given that commentators can be wrong?

paragraphs: Commentaries and abstracts should be used wisely, which the authors say means sparingly. Their first reason: commentators are not always right about a book. Some commentaries are enormously useful, but this is true less often than one could wish.

Student handbooks and study guides are often particularly misleading. They claim to tell a student everything needed about an assigned book, yet they are sometimes badly wrong in their interpretations.
A commentary is one reader's account, and it can be mistaken. You can catch its mistakes only if you know the book yourself.
card.example: A study guide to a famous novel says its narrator is reliable throughout. A student who has read the novel remembers scenes where the narrator's account clashes with what others see, and so catches the guide's error.
card.rule: Use commentaries sparingly, and treat each as one reader's account that may be wrong.
card.limits: Sparingly is not never: some commentaries are enormously useful. The warning targets leaning on a commentary in place of the book, not consulting a good one to answer a real question.

concepts.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
concepts.title: A correct commentary is still partial
concepts.question: How can even a correct commentary narrow your understanding of a book?

paragraphs: The authors' second reason for using commentaries sparingly: even when a commentary is right, it may not be exhaustive. You may be able to find important meanings in a book that its commentator never found.
Reading a commentary, especially a very self-assured one, therefore tends to limit your understanding of the book, even if your understanding is correct as far as it goes.
The danger here is not error but narrowness. A commentary gives you a set of points, and points it does not raise tend to drop out of view.
card.example: A guide to a play explains its themes of ambition and guilt accurately. A reader who goes straight to the guide sees those themes and little else. Another reader, who met the play first, also noticed how its comic servants mirror their masters, a pattern the guide never mentions.
card.rule: Treat even a correct commentary as a partial account, and look in the book for meanings it does not mention.
card.limits: Partial is not useless: a correct commentary can still answer the question you bring to it. The narrowing is worst when the commentary comes first and sounds certain, and least when you already know the book well.

concepts.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
concepts.title: The book before the commentary
concepts.question: Should you read someone else's commentary or introduction to a book before reading the book, or after?

paragraphs: The authors' near-basic maxim for commentaries: do not read a commentary by someone else until after you have read the book. This applies particularly to scholarly and critical introductions.

It reverses a rule of intrinsic reading. You should read the author's own preface and introduction before his book, because they belong to it. Someone else's introduction is commentary, so it comes after.

Read first, such works are likely to distort your reading: you tend to see only the points the scholar or critic makes and miss others that may be equally important. Used properly, they come after your best effort, to answer questions that still puzzle you.
card.example: A new edition of a classic opens with a forty-page essay by a professor, followed by the author's short preface. The reader reads the author's preface, then the book, and only then the professor's essay, bringing three questions she could not settle alone.
card.rule: Read the book before anyone else's commentary on it, and bring the commentary your remaining questions.
card.limits: The rule concerns other people's commentary, not the author's own preface, which comes first. It sets an order, not a ban, and it presumes you will read the book; a handbook read instead of the book is a different and worse problem.

concepts.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
concepts.title: Meeting commentators as an equal
concepts.question: How does reading the book first change your position toward a commentator or a handbook?

paragraphs: Reading an introduction after the book brings a real pleasure. You have read and understood the book; so has the introduction's writer, perhaps many times, with his own understanding. You meet him on essentially equal terms. Read his introduction first, and you are at his mercy.

The same holds for handbooks. A handbook cannot hurt you if you have read the book and know where the handbook is wrong, if it is. But if you depend wholly on the handbook and never read the original, you may be in bad trouble.
Equal terms means you can answer back: accept what the commentator shows you, and object where he misreads.
card.example: Having read a famous history of a plague year, a reader opens a scholar's essay on it. The scholar clears up a chapter she found murky. She disagrees with his view of the ending, which she reads differently and can cite pages for.
card.rule: Read the book first, so you meet its commentators as an equal who can judge where they are right and where they are wrong.
card.limits: Equal terms does not mean equal knowledge: a scholar may know much more of the book's background, and a careful reader learns from that. The equality lies in having read the book, which lets you weigh what he says.

concepts.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
concepts.title: The habit of dependence
concepts.question: What happens to a reader who gets into the habit of leaning on commentaries and handbooks?

paragraphs: There is a further cost. If you get into the habit of depending on commentaries and handbooks, you will be totally lost when you cannot find one.
A commentary may help you understand one particular book. But the habit of depending on them makes you, in general, a worse reader.
The trade is a short-term gain for a long-term loss: each book handled through a commentary leaves your own skill where it was, and many books you will want to read have no commentary at all.
card.example: A student reads every assigned novel with a study guide and does well in class. After graduating she picks up a new novel with no guide available and cannot say what it is about, though she has read dozens of novels.
card.rule: Do not let commentaries become a habit; use each one so that your own reading still does the work.
card.limits: The warning is against dependence, not against a single well-timed use. A reader who has done her own work and consults a commentary for a leftover question is not building the habit the authors describe.

concepts.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
concepts.title: The two uses of abstracts
concepts.question: For what two purposes are abstracts and plot digests useful, and what can they not do?

paragraphs: The rule for commentaries applies also to abstracts and plot digests. The authors say they are useful in two connections, and in those two only.

First, they can jog your memory of a book you have already read. Ideally you made such an abstract yourself while reading the book analytically; if you did not, a published abstract or digest can be an important aid.

Second, in syntopical reading they can help you judge whether a work is likely to bear on your project. An abstract can never replace reading the book, but it can sometimes tell you whether you want or need to read it.
card.example: Preparing a report on remote work, a researcher reads abstracts of forty books to choose the eight she will read. A year later, before giving a talk, she rereads her own summary of one of those eight to bring its argument back to mind.
card.rule: Use an abstract to recall a book you have read or to decide whether to read one, and not in place of reading it.
card.limits: An abstract can mislead even in choosing: it may miss the part of a book that bears on your question. Treat its verdict on relevance as a first sort, and an abstract of an unread book as no knowledge of what the book says.

concepts.title: Reference books need knowledge
concepts.question: Why does using a reference book well require that you already know a good deal?

paragraphs: It is not always realized that a good deal of knowledge is needed before you can use a reference book well. A reference book is an antidote to ignorance only in a limited way: it cannot cure total ignorance, and it cannot do your thinking for you.

First, you must have some idea, however vague, of what you want to know. The authors picture your ignorance as a circle of darkness surrounded by light. You want to bring light into the dark circle, and you can do so only if light surrounds it.
Put another way, you must be able to ask a reference book an intelligible question. If you are wandering lost in a fog of ignorance, it will be no help to you.
card.example: One reader wants the year a treaty was signed and knows its name: a reference book answers her at once. Another senses that something about trade in the 1700s matters to his novel but cannot say what; no index can find a question he cannot yet ask.
card.rule: Before opening a reference book, frame what you want to know well enough to ask it a question.
card.limits: The question can start vague, and looking things up can sharpen it. What fails is total fog: when you cannot name even the area of your ignorance, a reference work has nothing to answer.

concepts.title: The right reference book, used rightly
concepts.question: What must you know about reference books themselves before any one of them can help you?

paragraphs: Second, you must know where to find what you want: what kind of question you are asking, and which kinds of reference books answer that kind. No reference book answers all questions; each is a specialist. So you need a fair overall knowledge of the major types before you can use any one type well.

Third, you must know how the particular work is organized. Knowing what you want and which kind of book to use does no good if you cannot work this one. There is an art of reading reference books, as of reading anything else.
So the rule of reading the preface first applies with special force here. Do not try to use a reference book before getting the editor's advice on how to use it.
card.example: A reader wants the origin of a word: that calls for a dictionary with word histories, not an atlas or a book of biographies. Opening it, she first reads the guide to its abbreviations, so the marks after each entry tell her something.
card.rule: Match your question to the right kind of reference book, then read its instructions before you use it.
card.limits: Knowing the types and the layout gets you to the right page; it does not guarantee that the page answers your question. You still have to judge whether what you find answers what you asked.

concepts.title: Only the agreed is in reference books
concepts.question: Which kinds of questions can a reference book answer, and which can it not?

paragraphs: Not every question is answered in reference books. You will not find there the answers to questions like those in Tolstoy's stories: what men live by, or how much land a man needs. Reference books hold only what people generally and conventionally agree on; unsupported opinions have no business there, though they sometimes creep in.

We agree that dates of birth and death can be known, that words and things can be defined, and that the history of almost anything can be sketched. We do not agree on moral questions or on questions about the future, so these are not found in reference books.

This is the fourth requirement: know that what you want is considered knowable by the work's compilers. All four show that reference books are useless to people who know nothing; they are not guides to the perplexed.
card.example: A reader can look up when a famine began, how many died and what the word famine means. Whether the government of the day was to blame, or whether famines will return this century, she will not find settled there.
card.rule: Ask a reference book only what people generally agree can be known, not moral questions or questions about the future.
card.limits: What counts as knowable shifts over time, and finding an opinion in a reference book does not make it agreed, since some opinions creep in. A reference book can tell you that people disagree without settling who is right.

concepts.title: The dictionary as a teaching book
concepts.question: What kind of book is a dictionary, and how should knowing that change the way you use it?

paragraphs: The first rule of reading any book, knowing what kind of book it is, applies to the dictionary. From the start, the authors say, the educational motive dominated dictionary-making. The first dictionaries were glossaries of Homeric words, made to help Romans read the Iliad, the Odyssey and other Greek works that used that old vocabulary.

Some dictionary makers also aimed to keep the language pure and orderly. The Oxford English Dictionary, begun in 1857, broke with this by recording every type of usage historically rather than dictating it. But however it is made, a dictionary is primarily an educational instrument.

Use it that way. Treat it as a spelling book or a pronunciation guide and you will use it poorly. See that it holds a wealth of history crystallized in the growth of language, and you will attend not only to the many meanings under a word but to their order and relation.
card.example: A reader looks up nice and finds senses running from foolish, through precise, to pleasant. Reading them in order, she sees the word's meaning drift over centuries, which explains why an old poem calling someone nice is not paying a compliment.
card.rule: Use a dictionary as an educational instrument: read the order and relation of a word's meanings, not only its spelling.
card.limits: Not every dictionary orders senses by history; some put the most common sense first. Read the front matter to learn which order a given dictionary uses before you draw conclusions from it.

concepts.title: Which words to look up, and when
concepts.question: Which words deserve a trip to the dictionary, and when during your reading should you make it?

paragraphs: For a reader, the dictionary's primary use is to help with books that would otherwise be too hard because of their vocabulary: technical words, archaic words, literary allusions, or familiar words used in obsolete senses.

But vocabulary is only one of the problems in reading a book well. On a first reading of a difficult book, sitting with the book in one hand and the dictionary in the other is a mistake: look up too many words at the start and you lose track of the book's unity and order.

The dictionary serves best when you meet a technical word or one wholly new to you. Even then, during a first reading of a good book, the authors would not look it up unless it seems important to the author's general meaning.
card.example: On a first reading of a classic on economics, a reader meets entrepot in a passing list of ports and reads on. Later she meets a word the author uses in each chapter's main claim and cannot pin down from the context; that one she looks up.
card.rule: On a first reading, look up only the new or technical words that seem important to the author's general meaning, and save the rest.
card.limits: This governs the first reading of a difficult book. On a later, closer reading, or when one word blocks the main argument, looking words up is exactly what the dictionary is for.

concepts.title: A book about words, not things
concepts.question: Why can a dictionary not settle an argument about justice or freedom?

paragraphs: Several negative rules follow. Do not try to settle an argument about communism, justice or freedom by quoting the dictionary. Lexicographers deserve respect as authorities on how words are used, but they are not the final founts of wisdom.
Another: do not swallow the dictionary. Do not try to grow word-rich quick by memorizing lists of fancy words whose meanings are unconnected with any experience of yours.
Both rules come from one fact: the dictionary is a book about words, not about things. It can tell you how the word justice is used; it cannot tell you what justice requires.
card.example: Two friends argue whether a new tax is fair. One reads out a dictionary definition of fair. The definition records how people use the word; it does not show whether this tax treats people as they deserve, which is what the friends disagree about.
card.rule: Use a dictionary for questions about words, and do not ask it to settle questions about things.
card.limits: A dictionary can settle a dispute that really is about usage, such as whether a word has a certain sense or how it is spelled. The rule applies when the disagreement is about the thing the word names.

concepts.title: Four questions to ask about a word
concepts.question: What four kinds of question can you ask a dictionary about a word?

paragraphs: From the fact that a dictionary is about words, the authors derive its uses from four ways of looking at words. First, words are physical things, written marks and spoken sounds, so there are standard ways to spell and pronounce them, though variations occur and uniformity matters less than some teachers suggest.

Second, words are parts of speech, each playing a grammatical role in a phrase or sentence; in English the same word often shifts from one part of speech to another. Third, words are signs with many meanings, related as synonyms or antonyms, and named as proper or common, concrete or abstract.

Fourth, words are conventional, man-made signs, so each has a history: its roots, prefixes and suffixes, its changes in spelling and sound, and which senses are archaic, current, idiomatic, colloquial or slang. A good dictionary answers all four kinds of question, and its explanatory notes and list of abbreviations show you how.
card.example: Looking up run, a reader checks its pronunciation (a physical thing), notes it can be a verb or a noun (a part of speech), picks the sense of managing a business from dozens (a sign), and sees from its etymology that it comes from Old English (a convention).
card.rule: Know which of the four questions you are asking a dictionary about a word, and read its notes and abbreviations so you can find the answer.
card.limits: The four questions concern the word, not your author's use of it: the dictionary shows the senses a word can bear, but which one a writer intends still has to come from his context.

concepts.title: Facts in relation
concepts.question: What should you look for in an encyclopedia beyond isolated facts, and how can you find it?

paragraphs: Many people use an encyclopedia only to look up dates, places and simple facts, as many use a dictionary only for spelling. That under-uses it: like dictionaries, encyclopedias are educational tools as well as informational ones. Reading one straight through, though, is as vain as reading a dictionary through.

An encyclopedia's subject is the world, and the world is not arranged alphabetically; the real question is how knowledge is ordered. Medieval encyclopedias followed the seven liberal arts, as universities did. Modern ones divide knowledge into specialties roughly like university departments, but the alphabetical arrangement masks this structure.

A good user looks for that underlying structure, because understanding, as opposed to information, comes from seeing facts in relation to other facts. Follow the editors' directions, which often send you to the index first: its breakdowns under each main entry gather discussions of one subject scattered through the volumes.
card.example: A reader wants to understand the printing press. The article on printing gives dates and inventors. The index also sends her to articles on the Reformation, literacy and paper-making, and the relations among them show her why printing mattered.
card.rule: Use an encyclopedia to see facts in relation to other facts, starting from its directions and index rather than a single article.
card.limits: Some look-ups really are for one fact, and then one entry is enough. And the index lists its topics alphabetically too, so it shows the structure of knowledge only in part: a help, not a full map.

concepts.title: Settling disputes of fact
concepts.question: Which arguments can an encyclopedia settle, and why consult more than one on a subject?

paragraphs: Encyclopedias, like dictionaries, are valuable aids to reading good books, but it is wise not to enslave yourself to one. And, as with dictionaries, they are not for settling arguments that rest on differences of opinion.

They should, however, be used to end disputes about matters of fact as quickly and permanently as possible. Facts should not be argued about in the first place, and an encyclopedia, being full of facts, makes that vain effort unnecessary.

One difference from dictionaries: dictionaries usually agree in their accounts of words, but encyclopedias often disagree in their accounts of facts. So if you really care about a subject and depend on encyclopedic treatments of it, read more than one, preferably written at different times.
card.example: Two colleagues argue over the height of a famous mountain; an encyclopedia ends it in a minute. They then argue whether climbers should be allowed on it at all; no encyclopedia settles that. Writing a report on its glaciers, one reads three encyclopedias from different decades and finds their figures differ.
card.rule: Use encyclopedias to end disputes of fact, not of opinion, and compare several, written at different times, on a subject you care about.
card.limits: An encyclopedia ends a dispute of fact only where its facts are sound; when sources disagree, the dispute moves to their evidence. And a question that looks factual may hide a disagreement of judgment underneath.

concepts.title: Four points about facts
concepts.question: What must you understand about facts in order to ask an encyclopedia the right questions?

paragraphs: As a dictionary is about words, an encyclopedia is about facts, and the authors make four points about facts. First, facts are propositions: statements combining words, such as the date of Lincoln's birth. For understanding you must also know a fact's significance, how it bears on the truth you are seeking.

Second, facts are propositions taken as true: what is generally agreed, not opinion. An encyclopedia that slips in its editors' unsupported opinions is dishonest; it may report opinions only if it labels them, as in some hold this, others that. So it cannot properly settle moral questions, only report disagreements about them.

Third, facts reflect reality: single pieces of information or relatively unquestioned generalizations. Theories and speculations are not facts until generally agreed. Fourth, facts are to some extent conventional: what one age or culture takes as fact may be revised by more careful observation, especially in science.
card.example: An entry says gold's atomic number is 79. The four questions: what does this statement tell me for my purpose? Is it agreed, not one chemist's view? Is it a generalization about matter rather than a speculation? Could later science revise it, even if that seems unlikely?
card.rule: Ask four things of any fact you look up: what it signifies for your question, whether it is agreed, whether it reflects reality rather than theory, and whether it may change.
card.limits: The four points describe what an encyclopedia should contain, not a guarantee that it does: opinions creep in, and facts get revised. An entry's confident tone does not tell you which points it meets.

concepts.title: What an encyclopedia cannot give
concepts.question: Why is an encyclopedia an unsatisfying tool for pursuing understanding?

paragraphs: The art of using an encyclopedia is the art of asking proper questions about facts; the authors suggest the questions, and the encyclopedia supplies the answers. But an encyclopedia is not the best place to pursue understanding.
It can give insight into the order and arrangement of knowledge, an important but limited subject. Many things understanding requires are not there, and two omissions stand out.

First, it contains no arguments, except to report the course of arguments now widely accepted or of historical interest, so a major element of expository writing is missing. Second, it contains no poetry or imaginative literature, though it may hold facts about poets. Since understanding needs both reason and imagination, an encyclopedia must leave you unsatisfied.
card.example: A reader looks up justice and learns which thinkers wrote on it and when. To follow one of them reasoning toward a conclusion, or to feel the weight of injustice in a story, she has to go to the books themselves.
card.rule: Use an encyclopedia for facts and the arrangement of knowledge, and go to arguments and imaginative works themselves for understanding.
card.limits: An encyclopedia can still point you to the arguments and poems you need, and it reports arguments that are widely accepted. What it cannot give is the experience of following them yourself.

concepts.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
concepts.title: General rules, particular books
concepts.question: Why do the rules of analytical reading need adapting to each kind of book, and what stays the same across every kind?

paragraphs: General rules have a cost. The more general a rule, the fewer rules you need and the easier each one is to understand, but the further it sits from the details of the actual case in which you try to follow it.

The rules of analytical reading were stated generally so that they would fit any expository book. Yet nobody reads a book in general: you read a particular history, a mathematics text or a political tract. So the authors ask for flexibility, and expect you to learn by practice how the rules work on each sort of book.

Two points frame the rest of the book. The fifteen rules do not apply unchanged to fiction and poetry, which do not proceed by terms, propositions and arguments; a parallel set of rules comes in the next chapter. What carries across every kind is the four questions, so Part Three dwells on which questions matter most for each kind and what answers to expect.
card.example: A reader who has used the rules on a science book picks up a cookbook. Hunting for an argument in every recipe would be mechanical. Asking what the book is about and what it wants the cook to do, then adjusting the rules to that, is the flexible use the authors have in mind.
card.rule: Carry the four questions into every book, and adapt the rules to the particular kind of book in front of you.
card.limits: Adapting is not discarding. A practical or historical book is still expository, so its structure, terms and arguments still need finding; only imaginative literature calls for a different set of rules.

concepts.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
concepts.title: Only action solves a practical problem
concepts.question: Why can no practical book, however good, solve the practical problem it is about?

paragraphs: A theoretical book can solve its own problems: once you understand its explanation, the question it asked is answered. A practical problem is different. It concerns something to be done, so it is solved only when it is done.

When your problem is how to earn a living, a book on how to make friends and influence people may suggest things to do, but it cannot solve the problem; only earning a living does. The authors apply this to their own book: if your interest in it is practical, the problem of learning to read is solved only when you actually read, this book and many others.
Action happens in the world, not on the page. A practical book can help by pointing out what to do, but the solving is left to the reader.
card.example: Someone reads three books on public speaking and feels ready. The problem of speaking well is not solved until they stand up and speak; the books have only prepared the ground.
card.rule: Treat a practical book as help toward a problem that only your own action can solve.
card.limits: A practical book can be read with a purely theoretical interest, for instance to understand how an art works. Then understanding is the goal, and no action is owed.

concepts.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
concepts.title: The reader supplies the particulars
concepts.question: What must a reader add to a practical book's rules before they can guide an actual action?

paragraphs: Every action happens in a particular situation, here and now, under particular circumstances. You cannot act in general. So the judgment that comes immediately before acting has to be highly particular. It can be put into words, but it seldom is.

An author cannot foresee the concrete situations of all his readers. However hard he tries, he cannot give them concrete practical advice; only someone in exactly the same situation could. What a practical book can give is rules general enough to cover many situations of the same sort.
That leaves work for the reader. To use the rules, you add two things the book cannot contain: your knowledge of your own situation, and your judgment of how the rule applies to that case.
card.example: A parenting book advises consistent bedtimes. One parent works night shifts; another has twins with different sleep needs. Each must bring knowledge of the household and judge what consistent means there; the book cannot do that for them.
card.rule: Bring your knowledge of the particular case and your judgment of how each general rule fits it.
card.limits: Fitting a rule to your case is not the same as rewriting it to suit your wishes. A reader who bends every rule until it costs nothing has stopped learning from the book.

concepts.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
concepts.title: The theory behind the rules
concepts.question: Besides rules, what else can a practical book contain, and what kind of knowledge is it?

paragraphs: Any book that gives rules, prescriptions, maxims or general directions is easy to recognize as practical. But a practical book may also try to state the principles beneath its rules, the reasons that make them intelligible.

Such principles are usually scientific: items of theoretical knowledge. Taken together they are the theory of the thing, as in the theory of bridge building or of contract bridge, meaning the principles that make the rules of good procedure what they are.

This book does it too: here and there it explains its reading rules with brief accounts of grammar, rhetoric and logic. So a practical book can contain theoretical knowledge without ceasing to be practical; the theory is there to make the rules understandable.
card.example: A baking manual says to rest bread dough before shaping. A side panel explains that gluten relaxes during the rest, so the dough stretches without tearing. The instruction is a rule; the account of gluten is a principle, a piece of the theory behind the rule.
card.rule: In a practical book, separate the rules from the principles that explain them, and treat the principles as the theory of the practice.
card.limits: A principle explains a rule but does not by itself say what to do. Knowing the theory of bridge building does not tell you how to build this bridge on this river.

concepts.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
concepts.title: Books of rules and books of principles
concepts.question: What are the two kinds of practical book, and how do you tell which kind you are holding?

paragraphs: Practical books fall into two main groups. Some, like a cookbook, a driver's manual or this book on reading, are mainly presentations of rules; whatever else they discuss is there for the sake of the rules. The authors note that there are few great books of this sort.
The other kind is mainly about the principles that generate rules. Most of the great books in economics, politics and morals belong here.
The line is not sharp. Rules and principles can appear in the same book, so the question is one of relative emphasis: which does the book mainly offer, and which serves the other?
card.example: A guide to running a small shop lists steps for pricing, stock and staff, with short explanations: a book of rules. A treatise on what makes a market fair, with few direct instructions, is a book of practical principles, even though both talk about prices.
card.rule: Decide whether a practical book mainly gives rules or mainly gives the principles behind rules, judging by where its emphasis falls.
card.limits: The sorting is by emphasis, not a strict boundary. A rule-book with some explanation is still a rule-book, and finding a rule or two in a book of principles does not move it to the other pile.

concepts.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
concepts.title: When principles look like theory
concepts.question: How can you tell that a book of practical principles is practical when it reads like a theoretical book?

paragraphs: A book of rules is recognizable as practical at once. A book of practical principles can look theoretical at first, and in a sense it is: it deals with the theory of a particular kind of practice. Its propositions say that something is the case, and its arguments try to show that it is so.
What gives it away is the nature of its problems. It is about a field of human behaviour in which people can do better or worse: how to govern, how to live, how to run an economy.
So the test is not the grammar of its sentences but the field it addresses. If the subject is conduct that can be done well or badly, the book is practical, however abstract it sounds.
card.example: A work of political philosophy discusses at length what a well-ordered state is, in calm declarative sentences, with hardly an instruction. It concerns how people govern themselves, where they can do better or worse, so it is a book of practical principles.
card.rule: Classify a book as practical when its problems concern a field of human behaviour where people can do better or worse, even if it reads like theory.
card.limits: A human subject is not enough. A book that only describes or measures what people do, without bearing on how to do it better, stays theoretical.

concepts.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
concepts.title: Spotting a rule in any wording
concepts.question: How do you recognize a rule in a practical book, whether it is worded as a command or as a statement?

paragraphs: In a book that is mainly rules, the main propositions to look for are the rules. A rule is most directly put as an imperative, a command: take a stitch in time to save nine.
The same rule can be put as a statement: a stitch in time saves nine. Both forms say that being prompt is worth while, the command a little more emphatically, though not necessarily more memorably.

So the mark of a rule is not its grammar. A sentence is a rule when it recommends something as worth doing to gain some end. Good reading involves coming to terms is a rule in statement form; the word good gives it away, since it implies that such reading is worth doing.
card.example: A fitness book says: The wise runner warms up before every run. It looks like a description of runners, but the word wise recommends warming up as worth doing, for the sake of running well and safely. As a command: warm up before you run.
card.rule: Count a sentence as a rule when it recommends something as worth doing for some end, whether it is worded as a command or as a statement.
card.limits: Not every statement in a practical book is a disguised rule. A sentence that says what is so without recommending anything, such as a definition or a piece of history, is a principle or background, not a rule.

concepts.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
concepts.title: Two ways to argue for a rule
concepts.question: What two sorts of argument support the rules in a practical book, and what is each one good for?

paragraphs: In a rule-book, the arguments try to show you that the rules are sound. The authors name two sorts. One appeals to principles: it explains why the rule works. The other illustrates: it shows the rule working in concrete cases.

Look for both. According to the authors, the appeal to principles is usually the less persuasive of the two, but it has one advantage: it explains the reason for a rule better than examples of its use can.
Examples convince by showing; principles convince by explaining. A careful reader notes which sort of support each rule has, and which it lacks.
card.example: A guide to job interviews advises asking questions at the end. It tells how one candidate won a job with a single sharp question, an illustration, and explains that questions signal interest and show how you think, an appeal to principle.
card.rule: Find both the appeal to principles and the illustration by cases among the arguments for a book's rules.
card.limits: Neither sort settles a rule alone. An example shows the rule working once, and a principle shows why it should work, not that it will work in your case.

concepts.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
concepts.title: Reading between the lines for rules
concepts.question: When a practical book states principles rather than rules, what must the reader do to read it as practical?

paragraphs: In a book of practical principles, the main propositions and arguments look like those of a theoretical book: they say that something is the case and try to show that it is so. Read only that way, the book is read as theory.

Because its final problems are problems of action, an intelligent reader reads between the lines or in the margins. He looks for the rules the author may not state but that can be derived from the principles, and goes further: he works out how those rules should be applied in practice.

According to the authors, failing to read a practical book as practical is reading it poorly: you do not really understand it, and cannot criticize it properly. Rules get their intelligibility from principles; principles get their significance from the rules and actions they lead to.
card.example: A book on the ethics of friendship argues that true friends wish each other well for the friend's own sake. Read as practical, it yields a rule, do not keep a friend only for what you gain, and a question: what would that mean for a friendship you have now?
card.rule: In a book of practical principles, derive the rules its principles imply and work out how they would apply in practice.
card.limits: Derived rules are your inference, not the author's statement. Check that a rule really follows from the principles, and mark it as yours when you report what the book says.

concepts.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
concepts.title: Two tests of practical truth
concepts.question: When is a rule of conduct practically true, and how does that differ from the truth of a theoretical claim?

paragraphs: Understanding either kind of practical book also points to the final standard for judging it. For a theoretical book, agreement or disagreement turns on the truth of what is said, its fit with how things are. Practical truth is different.

According to the authors, a rule of conduct is practically true on two conditions. It must work: following it gets you where it promises. And its working must lead to the right end, an end you rightly desire.
So a rule can pass the first test and fail the second. If you think careful reading is not worth doing, the rules of this book have little practical truth for you, however sound they are as means.
card.example: A guide offers rules for winning every argument at work, and the rules do work. A reader who thinks winning arguments harms a team counts them practically false for her: they work, but toward an end she does not rightly desire.
card.rule: Count a rule practically true only if it works and its working leads to an end rightly desired.
card.limits: The second test is not a matter of whim. The end must be one you rightly desire, so judging it means asking whether the end deserves to be sought, not only whether you happen to want it.

concepts.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
concepts.title: Everything turns on the ends
concepts.question: In judging a practical book, why does everything turn on its ends rather than its means?

paragraphs: In judging a theoretical book, the reader compares his own basic principles or assumptions with the author's. In judging a practical book, according to the authors, everything turns on the ends or goals.

If you do not share Marx's fervour about economic justice, his economic doctrine and the reforms it suggests will likely seem practically false or irrelevant. If, like Edmund Burke, you think preserving the existing order matters most, a book like The Communist Manifesto will seem badly wrong.
So your main judgment is about ends, not means. We have no practical interest in even the soundest means to ends we disapprove of or do not care about.
card.example: Two readers finish a book on paying off debt as fast as possible. One wants to be debt-free quickly and judges the book by whether its steps work. The other thinks some debt is fine; for her the book is practically irrelevant, however sound its method.
card.rule: Make your main judgment of a practical book about its ends: decide whether you share the goal before weighing the means.
card.limits: Rejecting the end is no excuse for misreading the book: understand its means and its case for the end first. And once you do share the end, the means need judging too.

concepts.title: Two questions: ends and means
concepts.question: What two questions should you put to any practical book, and why are they harder for a book of principles?

paragraphs: The discussion of practical truth yields two major questions to ask of any practical book. First: what are the author's objectives? Second: what means for achieving them is he proposing?
Answering both is necessary for understanding a practical book and for criticizing it. You cannot judge the ends until you know what they are, nor weigh the means until you can say what they are.
According to the authors, the questions may be harder to answer for a book of principles than for a book of rules, because there the ends and means are likely to be less obvious.
card.example: A cookbook's objective and means sit on every page: this dish, made this way. A treatise on the good life may never say do this; the reader has to work out that its objective is a life of a certain kind, and that its means are the habits it describes at length.
card.rule: Ask of every practical book what the author's objectives are and what means he proposes for reaching them.
card.limits: The two questions find the author's ends and means; they do not yet judge them. Answering them is understanding, and whether to accept the ends comes after.

concepts.title: Why practical authors persuade
concepts.question: Why must the author of a practical book also be something of an orator, and is that a fault?

paragraphs: Every practical book carries some oratory or propaganda. The authors say they have never read a work of political philosophy, however abstract, that did not try to persuade the reader about the best form of government. Moral treatises urge a view of the good life, and this book has tried throughout to persuade you to read in a certain way.

The reason lies in how practical books are judged. Since your final judgment turns on whether you accept the author's goal, he has to win you to his ends. To do that he must appeal to your heart as well as your mind, playing on your emotions and seeking to direct your will.

According to the authors, there is nothing wrong in this. Practical thinking and action are not affairs of the mind alone; nobody acts without being moved somehow from below the neck. A practical writer who forgets this will be ineffective, and a reader who forgets it is likely to be sold a bill of goods.
card.example: A book on saving for retirement shows tables of compound interest, then describes an old age spent in comfort with grandchildren. The tables address the mind; the picture of old age addresses the heart, so that the reader will want the end the tables serve.
card.rule: Expect a practical author to appeal to your feelings as well as your reason, since he must win you to his ends.
card.limits: That oratory is natural in practical writing does not make every appeal deserve your assent. An appeal that moves you toward an end the arguments do not support still needs weighing.

concepts.title: Recognizing propaganda
concepts.question: What is the best protection against propaganda in a practical book, and what lets a reader apply it?

paragraphs: According to the authors, the best protection against propaganda of any sort is to recognize it for what it is. Only hidden, undetected oratory is really insidious.

An appeal that reaches the heart without passing through the mind tends to bounce back and put the mind out of business. Propaganda taken in that way works like a drug you do not know you are swallowing: afterwards you do not know why you feel or think as you do.

The reader who knows a practical book's basic terms, propositions and arguments can detect its oratory. With the argument laid out, he can spot the passages that make an emotive use of words, the ones that move him without adding to the case.
card.example: An article on a new housing law states its argument in three steps, then calls opponents heartless speculators. A reader who has outlined the three steps sees that the label adds feeling and no premise, and can notice its pull instead of being steered by it.
card.rule: Protect yourself from propaganda by recognizing it: know the book's terms, propositions and arguments well enough to spot where words work on your emotions.
card.limits: Recognizing an appeal is not rejecting it. Emotive language can accompany a sound argument; spotting it tells you what to weigh, not that the case is false.

concepts.title: Sales resistance, not deafness
concepts.question: How much resistance should a reader offer to a practical book's appeals?

paragraphs: Aware that he is subject to persuasion, the intelligent reader can do something about it: he can weigh the appeals. In the authors' phrase, he has sales resistance.

But according to the authors it need not be one hundred percent. Sales resistance is good when it keeps you from buying hastily and thoughtlessly. A reader who thinks he should be totally deaf to all appeals might as well not read practical books.
Practical books exist to move readers to act. A reader whom nothing can move has made them useless to himself, much as one whom everything moves has made himself their tool.
card.example: Reading a book on volunteering, a reader meets a moving story about a lonely neighbour. She neither lets it decide for her nor throws it out. She asks whether it fits the book's argument that small, regular visits help, and lets it count once it does.
card.rule: Weigh a practical book's appeals with enough resistance to avoid hasty acceptance, but without making yourself deaf to every appeal.
card.limits: Weighing is not meeting every appeal halfway. An appeal on behalf of an end you have good reason to reject deserves little weight; the right resistance depends on the case, not on a fixed middle setting.

concepts.title: The author's life and times
concepts.question: Why does knowing an author's character, life and times matter more for a practical book than for a theoretical one?

paragraphs: Because of the nature of practical problems, and because practical writing always carries some oratory, the authors say the personality of the author matters more in practical books than in theoretical ones.

You need know nothing about the author of a mathematical treatise: his reasoning is good or not, whatever kind of man he is. But to understand and judge a moral treatise, a political tract or an economic discussion, you should know something of the writer's character, life and times.

Their examples: in reading Aristotle's Politics it is highly relevant that Greek society rested on slavery. The Prince is lit up by the Italian politics of Machiavelli's day and his relation to the Medici. Hobbes wrote Leviathan having lived through the English civil wars, deeply distressed by violence and disorder.
card.example: A book argues for strict limits on public protest. Learning that its author wrote it soon after riots wrecked his city does not settle whether he is right, but it explains why order weighs so heavily with him, and helps you see which of his ends you share.
card.rule: For a moral, political or economic book, learn something of the author's character, life and times to understand and judge his recommendations.
card.limits: Background explains a view but does not refute it; dismissing a recommendation because of who made it, or when, skips the argument. And for a proof in mathematics, the author's life is beside the point.

concepts.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
concepts.title: What he wants you to do, and how
concepts.question: How do the first two questions change when you read a practical book, and which rules become dominant?

paragraphs: The first question, what is the book about as a whole, hardly changes. A practical book is expository, so you still outline its structure. But one part of the task, Rule 4's demand that you find the author's problems, becomes the dominant one.

To know an author's problems is to know his objectives, and in a practical book knowing what he wants to do comes down to knowing what he wants you to do. Adapted, Rule 4 reads: find out what the author wants you to do.

The second question, what is being said and how, also hardly changes: you still find terms, propositions and arguments. But its last part, Rule 8's demand that you say which problems the author solved and which not, now looms largest. Adapted, it reads: find out how he proposes that you do this.
card.example: Reading a guide to public speaking, you still outline its parts and find its key terms. But your main notes answer two lines: it wants me to speak to groups calmly and with a clear point; it proposes that I prepare three points, rehearse aloud and speak from notes, not a script.
card.rule: In a practical book, outline and interpret as usual, but make it your main task to state what the author wants you to do and how he proposes you do it.
card.limits: The adapted rules sharpen the old ones; they do not replace them. A reader who jumps to listing instructions without outlining the book or coming to terms will often misstate the author's aim or his means.

concepts.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
concepts.title: Judging truth in a practical book
concepts.question: How does the third question, whether a book is true, change when the book you are judging is practical?

paragraphs: For a theoretical book, the third question is answered by comparing the author's account of what is or happens in the world with your own knowledge of it. If it fits your experience of how things are, you must grant it some truth.

For a practical book there is still some comparison with reality. But the main consideration, according to the authors, is whether the author's objectives, his ends together with the means he proposes, accord with your own conception of what it is right to seek and of the best way of seeking it.
So the third question asks two things of you: is his end right to seek, and is his way the best way to it?
card.example: A book on running a small farm proposes intensive methods that raise yields. You check them against what you know of soil and weather: they would work. Then you ask whether high yields at that cost to the land are what a farm should seek, and whether a gentler method would reach a better end.
card.rule: To ask whether a practical book is true, ask whether its ends are right to seek and its means the best way to reach them.
card.limits: Your conception of what is right can itself be mistaken. The third question measures the book against your considered view of the right end, so that view needs thinking through, not a passing preference.

concepts.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
concepts.title: Agreement means action
concepts.question: Why does agreeing with a practical book commit you to act, when agreeing with a theoretical book does not?

paragraphs: The fourth question, what of it, changes most. After a theoretical book, if your view of its subject has changed, you must adjust your general view of things; if no adjustment is called for, you have learned little. But the adjustments need not be dramatic, and they do not necessarily imply any action.

Agreement with a practical book does imply action. If you are convinced or persuaded that the author's ends are worthy, and further convinced or persuaded that his means are likely to reach them, it is hard to see how you can refuse to act as he wishes.
So for a practical book, the honest answer to what of it is a change in what you do, not only in what you think.
card.example: A reader finishes a book arguing that daily walks protect health in old age. She agrees the end is worth having and that walking would serve it. On the authors' account, her agreement commits her: the natural next step is a first walk, not another chapter.
card.rule: If you accept both a practical book's ends and its means, act as it recommends.
card.limits: The commitment follows only when you accept both the end and the means. Admiring the goal while doubting the method, or the reverse, does not carry it.

concepts.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
concepts.title: What inaction reveals
concepts.question: If a reader says he agrees with a practical book's ends and means but does not act, what does that reveal?

paragraphs: The authors admit that agreement does not always lead to action. But they want you to see what it means when it does not: despite his apparent agreement with the ends and acceptance of the means, the reader does not really agree or accept. If he did both, he could not reasonably fail to act.

They apply this to their own book. If after Part Two you agreed that reading analytically is worth while, and accepted the rules as serving that aim, you must have begun to read that way. If you did not, it was not only laziness or tiredness: you did not really mean one of the two.
Inaction thus works as a test of agreement. It sends you back to ask which you did not really accept, the end or the means.
card.example: A manager says she agrees that weekly one-to-one meetings matter and that a fixed slot would protect them. Months pass with no slots booked. On the authors' account, the honest question is not why she is busy but whether she really accepts the end, or the fixed slot.
card.rule: When you have not acted on a practical book you say you agree with, ask whether you really accept its end, its means, or neither.
card.limits: The test assumes the action is open to you and meant for you. Where you cannot act, or the end is aimed at a group you honestly do not belong to, inaction does not show disagreement.

concepts.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
concepts.title: Ends for everyone, ends for some
concepts.question: When can a reader who accepts a practical book's end and means fairly decline to act?

paragraphs: The authors raise one apparent exception. A reader agrees that chocolate mousse is good and that an article's recipe would make it, yet never makes one, because, in their dated example, he is a man who never goes into the kitchen.

This marks a distinction. Some ends are universal, meant for all human beings, as with this book's claim that everyone should read better; then the implication to act applies to every reader. Other ends are selective, meant for a certain class. The reader must decide whether he belongs to it: if he does, he is more or less obligated to act; if not, he may not be.

May not, say the authors, because the reader may be fooling himself about his motives. The mousse reader is probably saying someone else should make it. Often we concede the end and the means but leave the action to others. This is a psychological problem more than a reading one, but it affects how well we read practical books.
card.example: A book on running a marathon has a selective end: it is for people who want to run one, and a reader with no such wish may fairly decline. A book urging everyone to wash their hands before meals has a universal end; a reader who agrees and still does not do it is probably excusing himself.
card.rule: Decide whether a practical book's end is meant for everyone or for a class, ask honestly whether you belong to that class, and act if you do.
card.limits: The exception covers only real non-membership. Deciding you are outside the class because the action is inconvenient is the self-deception the authors warn against.

concepts.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
concepts.title: Easy to enjoy, hard to say why
concepts.question: Why can a reader enjoy a novel yet be unable to say what in it caused the enjoyment?

paragraphs: The authors point to a paradox. Reading imaginative literature well is harder than reading expository books, yet the skill seems far more common. Part of the answer may be self-deception: asked what they liked about a novel, readers often go tongue-tied. They know they enjoyed it but cannot say what in the book pleased them.

Some conclude that a person can read fiction well without being a good critic. The authors call this at best a half-truth. Criticism depends on how fully you have grasped a work, so a reader who cannot say what he liked has probably not gone below the surface.

The rest of the paradox lies in the aim. Imaginative literature mainly pleases rather than teaches. Being pleased is easier than being taught, but knowing why you are pleased is harder: beauty is harder to analyse than truth.
card.example: Two friends both loved a film. One can say only that it was great. The other notices that the silent last scene answers a question the first scene raised, and that this is what moved her. Both enjoyed it; the second has looked below the surface.
card.rule: Test your reading of a story by trying to say what in it caused your pleasure, not only that it pleased you.
card.limits: Failing to explain your pleasure straight away does not prove a poor reading; beauty is hard to analyse, and the words may come with reflection. And a fluent account can describe your mood rather than the work.

concepts.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
concepts.title: An experience, not knowledge
concepts.question: Is this work trying to tell me something about experience, or to give me an experience to have?

paragraphs: Expository books try to convey knowledge about experiences the reader has had or could have. Imaginative works try to communicate an experience itself, one the reader can have or share only by reading. When they succeed, they give the reader something to enjoy.

The two aims call on different powers. We experience things through our senses and imagination; we know things through judgment and reasoning, which are intellectual. The authors stress that this is a matter of emphasis: we cannot think without imagination, and sense experience is never wholly cut off from reflection.

Fiction appeals mainly to the imagination, which is one reason it is called imaginative literature, while science and philosophy appeal mainly to the intellect. The authors build their advice on this difference: it explains why a novel cannot be read like an argument.
card.example: A field guide explains how wolves hunt and why packs form. A novel told by a young wolf lets you live through one hard winter hunt. The guide adds to what you know about such experiences; the novel gives you an experience to have.
card.rule: Before reading, ask whether the work offers knowledge about experience or an experience itself, and read it for what it offers.
card.limits: The split is one of emphasis, not a wall: reasoning uses imagination, and stories set readers thinking. Some books mix the two aims, so ask what a given part is trying to do.

concepts.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
concepts.title: Let the story act on you
concepts.question: Did I let the story move me, or did I hold it at arm's length, watching for flaws?

paragraphs: From the aim of fiction comes what the authors call probably the most important negative rule: do not resist the effect that a work of imaginative literature has on you.

All reading should be active, but the activity differs. A reader of expository work should be like a bird of prey, alert and ready to pounce on a vague term or a gap in reasoning. With a story, the right activity is what the authors call passive action or, better, active passion.

You act in such a way that you let the story act on you. You allow it to move you and to do whatever work it wants, and you make yourself open to it. A reader who stays on guard for flaws blocks the experience the work exists to give.
card.example: Reading a thriller, Sam stops every few pages to list implausible details and grade the prose. He finishes unmoved and cannot say what the book was like. On a second try he lets the suspense build, and only afterwards thinks about how it was done.
card.rule: While reading a story, stay open to its effect and let it move you, instead of guarding against it.
card.limits: Openness is not drifting: active passion still takes full attention. Nor is it a final verdict; judging comes after you have had the experience, and a work that manipulates can be criticized then.

concepts.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
concepts.title: Escape to a deeper reality
concepts.question: If imaginative literature takes us away from the everyday world, where do the authors think it should take us?

paragraphs: Expository writing, the philosophy, science and mathematics, has shaped the real world we live in. But the authors add that we could not live in this world if we could not, from time to time, get away from it.

They do not mean that fiction is essentially escapist; in the ordinary sense they find that idea contemptible. If we escape reality, it should be to a deeper, greater reality: our inner life and our own unique vision of the world. Discovering it satisfies a part of us we do not ordinarily touch.
This sets the goal of the rules for reading a great literary work: a profound experience. The rules should clear away whatever stops us from feeling as deeply as we possibly can.
card.example: Two readers finish a novel about a lighthouse keeper. One calls it a pleasant break from work and forgets it. The other finds she sees her own solitude differently for days. Both got away from the world for a while; the second reached what the authors call a deeper reality.
card.rule: Use the rules for reading fiction to clear away what blocks deep feeling, aiming at the profound experience a great work can give.
card.limits: The authors speak of great works; much fiction aims lower, and reading it for rest is not wrong. Deep feeling is the aim, not a test: forcing emotion you do not have is another way of not reading.

concepts.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
concepts.title: Meaning between the lines
concepts.question: Am I attending to what a poem or story implies between its lines, as well as to what its words say?

paragraphs: Because their aims differ, the two kinds of writing use language differently. The imaginative writer makes the most of the latent ambiguities of words, to gain the richness and force of their multiple meanings. Metaphors are the units he builds with, as the logical writer builds with words sharpened to a single meaning.
Dante said The Divine Comedy must be read as having several distinct though related meanings. The authors say this generally holds for poetry and fiction.

Expository writing aims at unambiguous explicitness: nothing left between the lines. Imaginative writing relies as much on what is implied as on what is said; its metaphors put almost more content between the lines than in the words. The whole poem or story says something none of its words says.
card.example: A story ends with a widow setting out two cups from habit, then putting one back in the cupboard. No sentence says she has begun to accept her husband's death, yet the scene says it. A report on grief would state the point outright.
card.rule: In a poem or story, read for what the words imply and what the whole says, not only for what each sentence states.
card.limits: Implication is not licence for any meaning you like: the related meanings must be supported by the work. And in an expository book, meaning left between the lines is a fault, not a richness.

concepts.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
concepts.title: No terms, propositions or arguments
concepts.question: Am I trying to pull terms, propositions and an argument out of a poem or story, as if it were expository?

paragraphs: From the difference in language comes another negative rule: do not look for terms, propositions and arguments in imaginative literature. These are logical devices, not poetic ones.

The poet Mark Van Doren remarked that in poetry and drama, statement is one of the obscurer mediums. What a lyric states cannot be found in any one of its sentences. The whole, all its words acting on one another, says something that will not fit inside propositions.

The authors add that imaginative literature does contain elements analogous to terms, propositions and arguments, which they take up later. The rule forbids reading a novel as a philosophical argument; it does not forbid reading it closely.
card.example: A student sums up a war novel as three claims: war is futile, leaders are cynical, comradeship redeems. Then she marks the sentences that state them. She has turned the novel into an essay and lost what it does: the long march, the friend's death, the silence at the end.
card.rule: Read a story or poem for what the whole work does, not for terms, propositions and arguments to extract.
card.limits: The ban is on hunting for logical devices, not on close reading or reflection: fiction has analogues of terms and arguments. And the rule covers imaginative works only; it is no excuse for vague terms in an essay that happens to be well written.

concepts.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
concepts.title: Learning through created experience
concepts.question: How can a story teach me anything, if it does not set out the knowledge an expository book offers?

paragraphs: We can learn from poems, stories and especially plays, but not in the way science and philosophy teach. We learn from the experiences of daily life, and we can also learn from the vicarious, artistically created experiences that fiction produces in our imagination. In this sense stories teach as well as please.

Expository works do not give us new experiences; they comment on experiences we have or can get. So the authors say expository books teach primarily, while imaginative books teach only derivatively, by creating experiences from which we can learn.

The work falls differently on the reader. To learn from fiction, we must do our own thinking about the experience. To learn from scientists and philosophers, we must first try to understand the thinking they have done.
card.example: After a novel about a man who lies to protect his son, a reader finds herself asking when loyalty excuses deceit. The novel argued no position. The question and her answer are her own thinking about an experience the book gave her.
card.rule: To learn from a story, think for yourself about the experience it gave you, as you would about something you lived through.
card.limits: Thinking about the experience is not hunting for the author's lesson; the conclusions are the reader's own. And a lesson drawn from one invented case can be as hasty as one drawn from a single real event.

concepts.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
concepts.title: A likely story, not a verified one
concepts.question: Am I faulting a story for factual errors it never offered as knowledge, rather than asking whether it is a likely story?

paragraphs: The last negative rule: do not criticize fiction by the standards of truth and consistency that apply to communicating knowledge. The truth of a good story is its verisimilitude, its intrinsic probability or plausibility. It must be a likely story, but it need not describe life or society in a way research could verify.

The authors cite Aristotle: the standard of correctness is not the same in poetry as in politics, physics or psychology. Errors of anatomy, geography or history should be criticized when a book offers itself as a treatise on those subjects. Misstatements of fact do not mar a story if the teller surrounds them with plausibility.

From a history we want the truth in some sense, and may complain if we do not get it. From a novel we want a story true only in the sense that it could have happened in the world of characters and events the novelist has created.
card.example: A detective novel puts a river on the wrong side of a real city. In a geography textbook that error would be a real failure. In the novel it does no harm if the chase along the river still feels inevitable and the story's world holds together.
card.rule: Judge a story's truth by whether it could have happened in the world the author has made, not by whether its facts check out.
card.limits: Plausibility is itself a standard: events that break the logic of the story's own world fail it. And when a work offers itself as fact, as a history does, factual errors count against it.

concepts.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
concepts.title: A unique world, not a theory to test
concepts.question: Am I judging a play or story by whether its events match my own life, as I would test a philosophical theory?

paragraphs: Once we understand a philosophical book, we test it against the common experience that inspired it, its only excuse for being. We ask: Is this true? Have we felt this? Have we always thought this without realizing it? Is the theory, however complicated, simpler than the muddled opinions we held before?
If we can answer mostly yes, a community of understanding binds us to the author. We must admit that this is our common sense of the matter: we have tested the theory and found it correct.

Not so with poetry. We cannot test Othello against our experience unless we too are Moors married to Venetian ladies we suspect of treachery. Even then, Othello is not every Moor, and most such couples never meet an Iago. The character and the play are unique.
