card.example: A reader dismisses a novel about a woman who leaves her family to sail alone round the world, because nobody she knows would do that. She is testing it like a theory of human nature. The novel offers one unique life, not a claim about how people generally act.
card.rule: Test an expository book against common experience, but do not accept or reject a story because its particular events match or miss your own life.
card.limits: The story must still be likely in its own world. And a story can still touch your life: you learn from it by thinking about its experience. Plausibility draws on common experience; what fails is making your own particular life the test.

concepts.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
concepts.title: Lyric, novel or play
concepts.question: Do I know whether I am reading a lyric, a novel or a play, and how that should change the way I receive it?

paragraphs: The negative rules need constructive ones, which the authors develop by analogy with the three groups of rules for expository books: structural, interpretive and critical. The first structural rule becomes: classify a work of imaginative literature according to its kind.

A lyric tells its story mainly through a single emotional experience. Novels and plays have far more complicated plots: many characters, their actions and reactions upon one another, and the emotions they suffer along the way.

A play differs from a novel because it narrates entirely through actions and speeches. The playwright can never speak in his own person, as the novelist can and often does. Such differences call for differences in the reader's receptivity, so recognise at once what kind you are reading.
card.example: In a novel, the narrator may tell you that a quiet clerk is secretly furious. In a play no one can tell you; you must infer his fury from what he says and does, perhaps from one slammed door. Knowing you hold a play tells you where to look.
card.rule: Recognise at once whether a work is a lyric, a novel or a play, and adjust how you receive it to that kind.
card.limits: The kinds are not sealed: the authors note some interesting exceptions to the rule that plays narrate only through action and speech. Classify to set your expectations, then let the work correct them.

concepts.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
concepts.title: Unity as a brief narration
concepts.question: Can I state the unity of this story in a sentence or two, as a brief narration rather than a thesis?

paragraphs: The second structural rule: grasp the unity of the whole work, and test yourself by stating it in a sentence or two. An expository book's unity lies in the main problem it tries to solve, so it can be stated as that question or as the propositions that answer it.

A story's author also faces a problem, but it is to convey a concrete experience. So the unity of a story is always in its plot. You have not grasped the whole until you can summarise the plot in a brief narration, not a proposition or an argument.

Even a lyric has a plot in this sense. Yet the plot is not the experience the work re-creates in you, only its framework or occasion. It stands for the unity, which properly lies in the experience, as a logical summary stands for an expository book's argument.
card.example: Thesis: the novel shows that pride destroys families. Narration: a proud farmer will not forgive his son's marriage, loses the farm he meant to leave him, and dies alone; the son comes back too late. The second states the story's unity; the first is a proposition about it.
card.rule: State a story's unity as a brief narration of its plot, remembering that the plot is the framework of the experience, not the experience itself.
card.limits: A plot summary is not the work: knowing it does not give you the experience, so it cannot replace reading. And a short lyric's plot may be only a movement of feeling, not a chain of events.

concepts.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
concepts.title: Parts arranged in time
concepts.question: Can I say where this story really begins, what crises lead to its climax, and what follows the climax within the story?

paragraphs: The third structural rule: discover how the whole is built from its parts. In an expository book the parts are partial solutions to parts of the problem. In fiction the parts are the steps the author takes to develop the plot: the details of characterization and incident.
The arrangement differs too. In science and philosophy the parts must be ordered logically. In a story they must fit a temporal scheme, a progress from a beginning through the middle to an end.

So know where the narrative begins, which is not necessarily on the first page, what it goes through and where it comes out. Know the crises that lead to the climax, where and how the climax occurs, and the aftermath: what happens within the narrative after the climax.
card.example: A film opens on a man in a hospital bed, then goes back ten years. Its narrative begins with the earliest scene the flashback shows, not the opening shot. Crises: a lost job, a quarrel, a reckless drive. Climax: the crash. Aftermath: his slow recovery in the bed we first saw.
card.rule: Trace how a story's parts build its plot in time: its real beginning, its crises, its climax and its aftermath.
card.limits: The aftermath stops where the narrative stops; guessing what happens after the story is over is not part of its structure. And a story told out of order still has a temporal scheme; the first page may sit in the middle of it.

concepts.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
concepts.title: Get to know the characters
concepts.question: Am I familiar enough with the characters and events to say I have lived through the story?

paragraphs: The interpretive rules for expository books tell you to find terms, propositions and arguments. With fiction you should not do that, but you must do something analogous to it.

The elements of fiction are its episodes and incidents, its characters, and their thoughts, speeches, feelings and actions. Each is an element in the world the author creates, and by manipulating them he tells his story. They are like the terms in logical discourse.

As you come to terms with an expository writer, here you must become acquainted with the details of incident and characterization. You have not grasped a story until you are familiar with its characters and have lived through its events.
card.example: In a long family saga, Ines kept mixing up two cousins and could not say why one resented the other. She slowed down, noticed what each said and did, and felt the old slight between them. The later quarrels then made sense: she had come to know the story's elements.
card.rule: Get to know a story's characters and incidents as closely as you would an author's key terms, until you have lived through its events.
card.limits: Acquaintance is not a catalogue: listing names and facts without living through the events is the expository habit in disguise. And the analogy with terms is loose; characters change and surprise in ways a defined term should not.

concepts.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
concepts.title: At home in the imagined world
concepts.question: Do I know the story's world well enough to feel like one of its inhabitants rather than an onlooker moving pieces?

paragraphs: In expository books terms connect in propositions. The elements of fiction are connected by the total scene or background against which they stand out. The imaginative writer creates a world in which his characters live, move and have their being.

So the analogue of finding propositions is to become at home in this imaginary world. Know it as if you were an observer on the scene. Become a member of its population, willing to befriend its characters, sharing in its happenings by sympathetic insight, as you would in the actions and sufferings of a friend.

Then the elements stop being isolated pawns moved mechanically on a chessboard. You find the connections that make them members of a living society. The setting is a static connection among the elements, as a proposition is.
card.example: In a novel set in a fishing village, a reader who knows the tides, the debts owed to the boat owner and who drinks with whom sees why a refused loan is a catastrophe. A reader who skipped the village scenes sees only a man saying no.
card.rule: Make yourself at home in the story's world, as an observer and a member of its society, so its characters connect into a living whole.
card.limits: Being at home is not being uncritical: sympathy while reading does not prevent judging the work afterwards. And a short lyric may offer little world to live in beyond the speaker's situation.

concepts.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
concepts.title: A finger on the pulse of the plot
concepts.question: Am I following the unfolding of the plot closely, the way I would follow an argument in an expository book?

paragraphs: If an expository book has any motion, it is the movement of the argument from reasons to the conclusions they support, and the reader must follow it. Fiction has an analogous last interpretive step.

Once you know the characters and have joined their world, consenting to its laws, breathing its air, tasting its food and travelling its roads, you must follow them through their adventures. The setting is the static connection of fiction's elements, like a proposition; the unravelling of the plot is the dynamic connection, like an argument.
Aristotle said that plot is the soul of a story, its life. To read a story well, you must keep your finger on the pulse of the narrative and be sensitive to its very beat.
card.example: Reading a mystery, Dev notices the pace slow in a calm chapter where a minor character mentions the weather. He senses something gathering and reads closely; the chapter holds the clue. A reader racing ahead to the solution skims past it.
card.rule: Follow the characters through the plot as it unfolds, sensitive to its pace and turns, as you would follow the steps of an argument.
card.limits: Following the plot is not racing to the end: the pulse includes slow passages that prepare what comes. And in a short lyric the motion may be a turn of feeling rather than adventures.

concepts.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
concepts.title: Hold the analogy loosely
concepts.question: Am I using the expository rules as a loose guide to fiction, or forcing a story through them point by point?

paragraphs: The authors warn against examining their analogy between the rules for expository books and for fiction too closely. An analogy of this sort is like a metaphor: press it too hard and it falls apart.
The three interpretive steps, getting to know the characters, entering their world and following the plot, trace how a reader becomes progressively aware of the writer's artistic achievement.
Far from spoiling your enjoyment, the steps should enrich it, by letting you know intimately the sources of your delight. You will know not only what you like but also why you like it.
card.example: A reader insists each character must stand for one fixed idea, as a term has one meaning, and is annoyed when a heroine is both generous and cruel. He has pressed the analogy too hard: characters are like terms in their role, not in having a single meaning.
card.rule: Use the expository rules as a loose guide to fiction, letting them deepen your enjoyment rather than forcing the story to fit them point by point.
card.limits: Loose is not idle: the steps still have to be carried out. And the caution concerns the analogy, not the difference between expository and imaginative books, which the authors keep firmly.

concepts.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
concepts.title: The rules reach the lyric
concepts.question: How do the rules for reading stories help with a short lyric poem that tells no story?

paragraphs: The structural and interpretive rules apply mainly to novels and plays. They apply to lyric poems to the extent that a lyric has a narrative line. But they do not cease to apply to lyrics that tell no story, though the connection is much less close.

A lyric represents a concrete experience, as a long story does, and tries to re-create that experience in the reader. Even the shortest lyric has a beginning, middle and end, because any experience, however brief and fleeting, has a temporal sequence.
And though the cast of a short lyric may be very small, there is always at least one character: the speaker of the poem.
card.example: A four-line poem: the speaker sees an old coat on its hook, reaches to touch it, and stops. No story is told, yet the poem moves from seeing to reaching to stopping, and it has one character, the speaker, whose hesitation is the experience.
card.rule: Read even a short lyric for its movement from beginning to end and for its speaker, the one character it always has.
card.limits: The fit is looser for lyrics: there may be no chain of events to summarise, only a shift in feeling. And the speaker is a character within the poem, who need not be the poet in person.

concepts.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
concepts.title: Appreciate before you criticize
concepts.question: Have I actually had the experience the author tried to give me, before saying whether I like the work?

paragraphs: The critical rules come last. For expository books the maxim was: do not agree or disagree until you can say you understand. For imaginative writing it becomes: do not criticize until you fully appreciate what the author has tried to make you experience.

By appreciation the authors mean having the experience the author tried to produce in you by working on your emotions and imagination. Before you express likes and dislikes, be sure you have made an honest effort to appreciate the work.

You cannot appreciate a novel by reading it passively, any more than you can understand a philosophical book that way; you must read it passionately. Appreciation, like understanding, takes active reading: all the acts of analytical reading set out for fiction.
card.example: Halfway through a slow novel, Marta calls it boring and stops. A friend later shows her that its slowness builds toward a sudden, shattering ending. Marta judged before she had the experience the book was built to give; her verdict was about a book she had not yet read.
card.rule: Before saying whether you like a work, make an honest, active effort to have the experience its author tried to give you.
card.limits: Appreciating first does not mean you must end up liking the work; a full reading can end in dislike. And you may put a book down unread, but then you have no critical verdict on it to give.

concepts.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
concepts.title: Grant the author his world
concepts.question: Am I objecting to the world the author chose to create, rather than to what the author made of it?

paragraphs: A corollary follows from the maxim of appreciation. The good reader of a story does not question the world the author creates, the world that is re-created in the reader himself.
Henry James, in The Art of Fiction, said we must grant the artist his subject, his idea, his donné, the starting point he is given or chooses; our criticism applies only to what he makes of it.

So we accept that a writer sets his story in, say, Paris, and do not object that it would have been better set in Minneapolis. But we have a right to criticize what he does with his Parisians and with the city itself.
card.example: A novel is set on a ship drifting for centuries between stars. One reviewer says it should have been set on Earth, where readers could relate. Another notes that the ship's isolation is never made to matter to the characters. The second criticizes what the author made; the first refuses the donné.
card.rule: Grant the author the world, subject and starting situation he chose, and criticize only what he makes of them.
card.limits: Granting the donné is not granting everything: what the author does inside his world, including whether it holds together, is open to criticism. Nor must you enjoy the chosen subject; preferring other kinds of story is taste, not criticism.

concepts.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
concepts.title: Like or dislike, not agree or disagree
concepts.question: Am I judging this story as a claim to agree with, or by whether I like it and find it beautiful?

paragraphs: We do not agree or disagree with fiction; we either like it or we do not. Our critical judgment of expository books concerns their truth. In criticizing belles-lettres, as the word itself suggests, we consider chiefly their beauty.
The authors tie beauty to pleasure: the beauty of any work of art is related to the pleasure it gives us when we know it well.

So the critical reply to a story differs in kind from the reply to an argument. Agreement and disagreement answer claims to truth. Liking and disliking, and finally a judgment of beauty, answer an experience.
card.example: After a novel narrated by a cheerful swindler, Paul says he disagrees with it, since swindling is wrong. But the novel asserted nothing about swindling. The fair questions are whether he liked it and whether, once he knew it well, it gave him the pleasure that goes with beauty.
card.rule: Judge a story by whether you like it and by its beauty, not by agreeing or disagreeing with it as if it made claims.
card.limits: Liking is where judgment starts, not where it ends; the next step is to say why. And because beauty is tied to pleasure in a work known well, a reaction to a work you barely know is weak evidence about it.

concepts.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
concepts.title: From taste to a standard
concepts.question: Can I point to what in the book caused my liking or dislike, and so say what is good or bad in it?

paragraphs: After a full, active reading you are competent to judge. Your first judgment will be one of taste: you like or dislike the book, and you say why. Those reasons have some critical relevance, but at first they are more likely to be about you, your preferences and prejudices, than about the book.

To complete the criticism, objectify your reactions by pointing to the things in the book that caused them. Pass from saying what you like or dislike and why, to saying what is good or bad about the book and why.

The better you discern the causes of your pleasure, the nearer you come to the artistic virtues of the work itself. You gradually develop a standard of criticism, and may find many others of similar taste. The authors think good taste in literature is acquired by anyone who learns to read.
card.example: First reaction: I disliked the novel; I hate sad endings. That is about the reader. Objectified: the ending fails because the hero's sudden death is prepared by nothing earlier; it feels imposed rather than earned. Now the judgment points to the book.
card.rule: Move from what you like and why to what is good or bad in the book and why, by pointing to what in it caused your reactions.
card.limits: Objectifying does not erase taste: careful readers may still weigh the same virtues differently. And a standard built from your own pleasures must keep meeting new works, or it hardens into prejudice.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: The first three questions, for imaginative works
concepts.question: How do the first three reading questions translate when the book in your hands is a story, a play or a poem?

paragraphs: The questions you ask of any book still apply to imaginative literature, but the answers take a different shape. The first, what the work is about as a whole, is answered by describing the unity of its plot. Plot is taken broadly: a lyric poem has an action or movement too, and that counts as its plot.

The second, what is said in detail and how, is answered when you can tell what part each character plays and retell the key incidents in your own words. The third, whether the work is true, becomes a question of poetical truth: is it a likely story, does it satisfy your heart and your mind, do you find it beautiful?
For each of these judgments the authors add one more demand: be able to say why. A verdict with no reasons behind it is a reaction, not yet a reading.
card.example: After a short story about a fisherman's last voyage, a reader writes the plot in two sentences; then who the fisherman, his son and the harbour master are and what each does; then: a likely story, because every choice the old man makes follows from his pride.
card.rule: Answer the first three questions of a story, play or poem with the unity of its plot, its characters and key incidents in your own words, and a reasoned verdict on its poetical truth.
card.limits: A verdict counts only with its reasons: I loved it, or it felt false, is a reaction until you can say why. And this frame says nothing yet about the fourth question, which works quite differently for imaginative literature.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: What of it? for a story
concepts.question: What, if anything, must you do after reading a novel, play or poem well?

paragraphs: For an expository book, the fourth question, What of it?, asks for action once you agree. Agree with a practical book's ends and means, and you should act on it; be convinced by a theoretical book, and you should adjust your views to its conclusions. That second kind of action is mental.

For imaginative literature the authors read the question quite differently. Strictly speaking, nothing is required of you after reading a story, play or poem well. Answer the first three questions, about plot, about characters and incidents, and about poetical truth, and your duties as a reader are done.
In that sense the fourth question is irrelevant to stories and poems. The work is not asking you to do or to believe anything; it is asking to be read well.
card.rule: Count your reading of a story, play or poem complete once you have answered the first three questions, without demanding a practical upshot.
card.limits: Strictly speaking is the key phrase: stories do move readers to act, and that is not wrong. The point is that such action is not part of what reading the work well requires.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: Stories that move readers to act
concepts.question: Why do some stories lead readers to act, and why do the authors still call that effect inessential to them?

paragraphs: Strictly, a story asks nothing of you. Yet imaginative works have often moved readers to act. A story can carry a political, economic or moral point better than an essay making the same point: the authors cite Orwell's Animal Farm and 1984 against totalitarianism, and Solzhenitsyn's The First Circle on the petty cruelty of Soviet bureaucracy.

That power is why such books have been banned and censored so often. The authors quote E. B. White: a despot fears an eloquent writer preaching freedom less than a drunken poet whose joke may take hold.
Even so, these practical consequences are not of the essence. Imaginative writing can lead to action, but it does not have to, and leading to action is not what makes it good imaginative writing.
card.rule: Recognise a story's power to move readers to act, but do not take that effect as the measure of the story.
card.limits: This does not make a story's practical effect unimportant to you as a citizen or a person; it is only beside the point when the question is whether you have read the story well.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: Fine art: an end in itself
concepts.question: In what sense is a story or poem a work of fine art, and what does that say about its purpose?

paragraphs: The authors place imaginative writing in the realm of fine art. Fine here does not mean refined, or finished. It comes from the Latin finis, end: a work of fine art is an end in itself.
Such a work does not move toward some result beyond itself. Emerson said of beauty that it is its own excuse for being, and the authors apply the remark to stories and poems.

This is why the fourth question loses its grip on imaginative literature. A book written to produce a further result can be asked what follows from it; a work that is its own end is complete when it is experienced.
card.example: A kitchen knife is good if it cuts well: its value lies in what it does next. A song heard in full needs nothing further to justify it. The authors put stories and poems on the song's side of that line.
card.rule: Treat a story or poem as an end in itself, and judge it as the thing it is rather than by what it leads to.
card.limits: End in itself describes what the work is, not how it may be used: a teacher can still use a novel to open a discussion, but that use is the teacher's purpose, not the work's.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: Trace the urge to act
concepts.question: When a story makes you want to go out and do something, what exactly are you responding to?

paragraphs: Because a story is an end in itself, the authors advise caution in asking What of it? of one. If a book leaves you feeling impelled to act, ask whether it contains some implied statement that produced the feeling.

Poetry, properly speaking, is not the realm of statement. Still, many stories and poems have statements in them, more or less deeply buried, and the authors say it is quite right to notice them and react to them.
But when you do, you are reacting to something other than the story or poem itself. The work subsists in its own right, and to read it well, all you have to do is experience it.
card.example: After a novel about a lonely widower, Sam resolves to visit his grandfather every week. Tracing the urge, he finds a claim the novel never states outright: the old are abandoned by the young. He can act on that claim, but his reading of the novel was complete once he had experienced it.
card.rule: When a story moves you to act, trace the urge to the implied statement behind it, and treat your response as a response to that statement rather than to the work.
card.limits: Tracing the statement is not dismissing it, or your feelings: the authors call reacting to it quite right. And not every strong feeling a story stirs is an urge to act; grief or delight can be the experience itself.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: Read quickly, with total immersion
concepts.question: Why do the authors want a story read quickly and with total immersion, and what does each half of that advice secure?

paragraphs: The authors' first advice for a story: read it quickly and with total immersion. Ideally read it at one sitting. Busy people with long novels rarely can, but the ideal can be approached by compressing the reading into as short a time as is feasible.
Spread a story out too long and you forget what happened; the unity of the plot escapes you, and you are lost. Speed serves the first question, what the story is about as a whole.

Immersion serves the details. Reading intensely, letting the story work on you, is what lets you see the characters and incidents the second question asks about. Quick but not intense misses the details; intense but slow misses the unity.
card.example: Two readers take on the same 400-page novel. One reads twenty pages a night for three weeks and by the end cannot recall why the brothers quarrelled in chapter two. The other reads it over one long weekend and can trace the quarrel straight through to the ending.
card.rule: Read a story as fast as is feasible and as intensely as you can, so that you hold both its unity and its details.
card.limits: Quickly does not mean skimming: speed bought by dropping attention loses the details. And the one-sitting ideal bends to long novels and busy lives; the aim is to compress the reading, not to finish 800 pages in a night.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: The trouble with savouring
concepts.question: Why might drawing out a novel you love be a sign that you are not really reading it?

paragraphs: Some readers, when they love a novel, want to savour it: to pause over it and draw out the reading for as long as they can. The authors are wary of this.

Such readers, they suggest, are probably not so much reading the book as satisfying their more or less unconscious feelings about its events and characters. The lingering serves the reader's feelings rather than the grasp of the story.
The cost is the one that quick reading guards against: the longer the reading stretches, the more the plot's unity slips away, however much each page is enjoyed.
card.rule: When you catch yourself stretching out a novel you love, ask whether you are reading it or feeding your feelings about its people, and keep the reading compressed.
card.limits: The warning concerns how you read a story through. It says nothing against rereading a loved book later, or returning to a favourite scene once you have grasped the whole.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: Live in the story's world
concepts.question: What does total immersion in a story ask of you, and what must you hold back until you have lived in its world?

paragraphs: Total immersion means letting the story work on you. Let the characters into your mind and heart, and suspend your disbelief about the events, if disbelief is what you feel.

Do not disapprove of something a character does before you understand why he does it, and perhaps not even then. Try as hard as you can to live in his world rather than yours; there, what he does may be quite understandable.
The same goes for the story's world as a whole: do not judge it until you are sure you have lived in it as fully as you are able.
card.example: In a novel set in a feudal village, a daughter accepts a marriage her father arranged. A reader who condemns her at once judges her by his own world. A reader who lives in hers first sees the debts, the customs and the danger of refusing, and only then asks whether the story makes her choice credible.
card.rule: Live in the story's world before you judge it: let the characters in, set aside disbelief, and understand why a character acts before you disapprove.
card.limits: Immersion postpones judgment; it does not cancel it. Once you have lived in the world you still owe a reasoned verdict on the work, and understanding why a character acts is not the same as approving of it.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: A crowd of characters
concepts.question: How should you handle a big novel whose crowd of characters seems impossible to keep straight?

paragraphs: A story's terms are its characters and incidents, and you need to get to know them and sort them out. But many readers start a big novel such as War and Peace, are swamped by a crowd of characters with strange-sounding names, and give up, sure they will never learn who is who.

The authors point out that the same thing happens when you move to a new town, start at a new school or job, or arrive at a party. You do not give up there: after a while individuals stand out from the crowd, and you remember the person you talked with for an hour, not everyone you met.

A novel works the same way. You need not remember every character; many are background figures who are there to set off the main ones. By the end you know who matters, and those names stay with you, perhaps for years.
card.rule: Read on through a crowded novel, expecting the important characters to emerge as they would at a party, and let the background figures stay in the background.
card.limits: Letting names go is for background figures, not for the main characters. If by the end you cannot say who mattered and what each did, the crowd has not sorted itself, and the second question is still open.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: Clear only looking back
concepts.question: Why should you not worry if a story is unclear at the start, and when does its order of events become clear?

paragraphs: Amid many incidents you soon learn what is important, and authors help. They do not want you to miss what is essential to the unfolding of the plot, so they flag it in various ways.

Even so, do not be anxious if all is not clear from the beginning; it should not be clear then. A story is like life: we do not understand events with full clarity as they happen, but looking back, we do. The reader who looks back after finishing understands how the events relate and why the actions came in that order.
All of this comes to one point: you must finish a story before you can say you have read it well.
card.rule: Tolerate confusion early in a story, notice the author's signals, and finish it, because the relations among its events come clear only looking back.
card.limits: Early confusion is expected, but it is no licence for inattention: the signals an author plants are there to be noticed as you go. Tolerating what is unclear is not the same as ignoring the text.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: The story stops on its last page
concepts.question: Why do the authors call it pointless to wonder what happens to characters before a story begins or after it ends?

paragraphs: A story is like life in that its sense comes looking back. But on its last page it stops being like life. Life goes on; the story does not.

Its characters have no life outside the book. Your picture of what happened to them before the first page or after the last is no better than the next reader's, and the authors call all such speculation meaningless. Preludes to Hamlet have been written; the authors call them ridiculous.
We are satisfied with Shakespeare's and Tolstoy's creations partly because they are limited in time. The limits are part of the shape of the work; we need no more.
card.rule: Take a story's first and last pages as its limits, and spend your effort on what lies between them rather than on imagined befores and afters.
card.limits: This rules out speculating about events the book does not contain. It does not rule out reading what the book itself implies, such as a past the characters recall within the story.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: Why we need fiction
concepts.question: Why is fiction a human necessity, and how can it make us like a book more than it deserves?

paragraphs: Most books people read are stories of one kind or another. People who cannot read listen to stories, and we even make them up for ourselves. The authors explain the need this way: fiction satisfies unconscious as well as conscious needs. Expository writing touches only the conscious mind; fiction reaches the unconscious too.

That reach can mislead judgment. We like or dislike certain kinds of people without always knowing why, and when such people are rewarded or punished in a novel, we may feel more strongly about the book than it merits artistically.

The authors' examples: we are pleased when a sympathetic character inherits money, without admitting we would like to; we enjoy identifying with characters who love more freely than we do; and unconscious sadism and masochism find outlets in conquerors and victims. In each case we say only that we like that kind of book.
card.rule: When you like or dislike a story strongly, ask whether it is answering a hidden wish of yours rather than earning the feeling as art.
card.limits: This is no case against enjoying such stories, or against fiction reaching the unconscious; that reach is part of why fiction matters. It is a check on how much weight your liking should carry in a judgment.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: Poetic justice
concepts.question: What deep need do stories meet by rewarding and punishing their characters, and how does a bad story fail it?

paragraphs: Beneath much of our reading lies a suspicion that life is unjust. Why do good people suffer and bad ones prosper? We do not know, and cannot know, and the fact troubles everyone.

In stories, whether novels, narrative poems or plays, this disorder is put right, and that is deeply satisfying. People usually get what they deserve: the author, who is like a god to his characters, rewards or punishes them according to their true merit. We call this poetic justice.

So one of the most irritating things about a bad story is that its people are punished or rewarded with no rhyme or reason. The great storyteller makes no mistakes here: he convinces us that justice has been done.
card.rule: Ask of a story whether its rewards and punishments follow from what its characters truly are and do, and whether it convinces you that justice has been done.
card.limits: Poetic justice is not a happy ending or a sermon: in tragedy good people suffer terribly, and the story can still satisfy. Nor is the test whether the story matches how life in fact treats people.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: Justice in tragedy: understanding
concepts.question: How can a tragedy, where terrible things happen to good people, still satisfy our need for justice and understanding?

paragraphs: The authors say poetic justice holds even in high tragedy. There terrible things happen to good men, but the hero, even if he does not wholly deserve his fate, at least comes to understand it.

We have a deep desire to share that understanding: if we only knew why, we could bear whatever the world has in store for us. The authors note that a story by Sherwood Anderson is called I Want to Know Why, a title that would fit many stories.
The tragic hero does learn why, often only after his life is ruined. The reader shares his insight without sharing his suffering.
card.rule: In a tragedy, look for what the hero comes to understand about his fate, and take that understanding, rather than a reward, as the justice the story offers.
card.limits: Understanding does not undo the hero's ruin, and it is not a reward in disguise. A sad story in which the sufferer grasps nothing gives suffering without the insight the authors find in tragedy.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: Private needs and universal ones
concepts.question: When you criticize fiction, how do you tell a book that meets your private needs from one that meets almost everyone's?

paragraphs: In criticizing fiction, the authors ask you to separate two kinds of books. Some satisfy your own particular unconscious needs: these are the books that make you say you like them without really knowing why.

Others satisfy the deep unconscious needs of almost everybody: a belief in justice and understanding, and relief from anxiety. These, the authors hold, are the great stories, which live on for generations and centuries and will go on satisfying people as long as people are what they are.
We cannot be sure the real world is good. But the world of a great story is somehow good, and we want to live there as often and as long as we can.
card.rule: Before praising a story as great, ask whether its pull on you is private or the kind of need nearly everyone shares, and rest the claim on the second.
card.limits: The line is hard to draw from inside one reader's head, and a book you love for private reasons may also be great. The distinction guards a judgment of greatness, not your right to enjoy what you like.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: Honoured but unread: the epics
concepts.question: Why are the great epic poems at once so honoured and so little read, and what makes a finished one so rare?

paragraphs: The great epics are Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, Virgil's Aeneid, Dante's Divine Comedy and Milton's Paradise Lost. The authors call them perhaps the most honoured and probably the least read books in the great tradition of the Western world.

Judging by how few have been completed successfully in 2,500 years, a long epic poem seems the hardest thing a writer can attempt. Not for lack of trying: hundreds have been begun, and some, like Wordsworth's Prelude and Byron's Don Juan, grew very long without ever really being finished.
So the authors give honour to the poet who completes an epic, and greater honour to one who reaches the quality of the five. But they add that these poems are certainly not easy to read.
card.rule: Approach the great epics knowing they are rare achievements and hard reading, so that their difficulty neither surprises nor defeats you.
card.limits: Rarity explains the honour, not the reading: knowing how hard an epic is to write does not make it easier to read. Why the epics are hard, and what they repay, is a separate question.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: What the epics demand and repay
concepts.question: What makes the great epics hard to read, and what do the authors say a reader gains by making the effort?

paragraphs: The difficulty of the epics is not mainly that they are in verse: except for Paradise Lost, all five can be had in prose translation. It lies rather in their elevation, in how they approach their subject matter. They make enormous demands on the reader's attention, involvement and imagination.

Most of us do not know what we lose by not making that effort. The authors hold that the rewards of a good, analytical reading of these epics are at least as great as those of any other books, certainly any other fiction. But the rewards go only to readers who do a good job.
There is a further satisfaction. Homer, Virgil, Dante and Milton are the authors every good poet has read. With the Bible, the authors say, they form the backbone of any serious reading program.
card.rule: Give an epic the attention, involvement and imagination its elevation demands, and read it analytically, because its rewards come only to readers who do a good job.
card.limits: A prose translation removes the verse, not the difficulty; the elevation remains. And a half-hearted reading does not earn half the reward: the authors say readers who do less than a good job do not gain it.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: A play is a story with no description
concepts.question: In what ways is reading a play like reading a story, and where must the reader of a play do extra work?

paragraphs: A play is fiction, a story, and so far as that is true it should be read like a story: grasp the unity of its plot, sort out its characters and incidents, and judge it only after you have lived in its world.

One difference shows on the page. A novel abounds in description; a play has almost none. So perhaps, the authors suggest, the reader must be more active in creating the background, the world in which the characters live and move.
Apart from that, the authors say, the problems of reading a play and a story are essentially similar.
card.example: A novel opens with a page on a rain-soaked port, the inn, the smell of tar. A play opens with a line: A tavern. Night. Two sailors. The reader of the play has to build the port, the weather and the mood from that line and from what the characters say.
card.rule: Read a play as a story, and supply for yourself the setting and atmosphere a novel would have described for you.
card.limits: Supplying the background is not inventing a different play: what you imagine must fit the words and actions given. The authors add one larger difference, taken up in the next idea: a play on the page is incomplete.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: A play on the page is incomplete
concepts.question: Why is a play read in a book not the complete work, and what must its reader supply?

paragraphs: There is one important difference between a play and a story. When you read a play you are not reading a complete work. The complete play, the work its author meant you to take in, exists only when it is acted on a stage.
The authors compare it to music, which must be heard. Read in a book, a play lacks a physical dimension: voices, movement, the actors' bodies in a space. The reader must supply that dimension.
The only way to supply it, they say, is to pretend to see the play acted.
card.rule: Read a play as you would a musical score: supply its missing physical dimension by imagining it performed.
card.limits: The words are complete; what is missing is how they are seen and heard. Imagining a performance fills that gap, but it cannot change the lines, which are there before you.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: Direct the play in your head
concepts.question: How can you supply a play's missing performance, and why do the authors call a reading without it partial?

paragraphs: Once you have worked out what a play is about, as a whole and in detail, and answered the other questions you ask of any story, try directing it. Imagine half a dozen good actors in front of you, waiting for your instructions.

Tell them how to say this line and how to play that scene. Explain why these few words matter, and how that action is the climax of the work. The authors promise you will have fun and learn a great deal about the play.

They hold that this is always worth doing, however explicit the playwright was about what we should see. Until you have pretended to put a play on the stage, you have probably given it only a partial reading.
card.rule: After answering the usual questions, direct the play in your head: decide how each key line is said and each scene played, and why.
card.limits: Directing comes after understanding, not instead of it: staging a play you have not grasped as a whole only stages your confusion. And it settles how things look and sound, not what is said.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: Decide what the text leaves open
concepts.question: When a playwright leaves a key fact about the action unstated, what must the reader do, and why does it matter so much?

paragraphs: The authors' example comes from Hamlet. Polonius tells the king and queen that Hamlet is mad for love of Ophelia, and proposes that he and the king hide behind an arras to overhear Hamlet with her. Moments later Hamlet enters, reading.

Later, talking reasonably with Ophelia, Hamlet suddenly asks whether she is honest. Did he overhear the plan to spy on him? If he did, his talk with Polonius and with Ophelia means one thing; if not, another. Shakespeare left no stage direction.
The reader, like a director, must decide, and the decision will be central to understanding the play. Many of Shakespeare's plays call for this kind of activity.
card.rule: Where the text leaves open what a character saw, heard or knew, make a reasoned decision about it, and read the scenes in the light of that decision.
card.limits: Deciding is not guessing at random: the choice should be the one the words best support. And it is worth seeing how the scenes change if the other choice is made.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: When the playwright speaks directly
concepts.question: How can a playwright speak to the reader directly, and what do the authors advise when one has done so?

paragraphs: As a rule a playwright, unlike a novelist, cannot address the reader directly; Fielding in Tom Jones is the authors' example of a novelist who does. But there are interesting exceptions, nearly twenty-five centuries apart.

Aristophanes wrote the only surviving examples of Old Comedy. In each play, at least once, the leading actor would step out of character, perhaps move toward the audience, and deliver a political speech unrelated to the action, thought to express the author's own feelings.

Shaw hoped his plays would be read as well as acted. He published them all, with long prefaces explaining their meaning and very full stage directions. To read a Shaw play without its preface, the authors say, is to turn your back on an important aid.
card.rule: When a playwright has spoken to readers directly, in a preface or an aside to the audience, use it as an aid to understanding the play.
card.limits: Direct address is the exception: most plays come with no preface. And a preface explains a play without replacing the reading and the mental staging it still needs.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: Read hard verse aloud, then the notes
concepts.question: What should you do when a passage of Shakespeare's verse is hard to follow, and when should you turn to the notes?

paragraphs: Read a play through, as nearly as possible at one sitting, to get a feel for the whole. With Shakespeare there is a further problem: the plays are mostly in verse, and in places the verse is more or less opaque, because the language has changed since 1600.

The authors' advice is to read a puzzling passage out loud. Read slowly, as if an audience were listening, and with expression, trying to make the words mean something to you as you say them. This device, they say, will clear up many difficulties.
Only after it has failed should you turn to the glossary or the notes.
card.rule: Read the play through for the whole, and when the verse turns opaque, read the passage aloud, slowly and with expression, before you consult the notes.
card.limits: Reading aloud clears many difficulties, not all: a word whose meaning has changed may still need the glossary. The rule sets the order of the tools; it does not forbid the notes.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: Few plays, but very great ones
concepts.question: Why do the authors think most plays are not worth reading, and which plays do they make exceptions for?

paragraphs: Most plays, the authors say, are not worth reading. The reason is the one already met: they are incomplete. They were meant to be acted, not read.

There are many great expository works and many great novels, stories and lyric poems, but only a few great plays. Those few are very great indeed: the tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, the plays of Shakespeare, Molière's comedies, and the works of a very few moderns.
These contain some of the deepest and richest insights ever expressed in words, which is why they repay the extra work a reader must do to supply their performance.
card.rule: Choose the plays you read with care, and give the few great ones the full effort that their incompleteness on the page demands.
card.limits: A play not worth reading may still be worth seeing: it was made for the stage. The authors' judgment concerns reading, not the theatre.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: Why Greek tragedy is hard
concepts.question: What makes Greek tragedy especially hard for a beginning reader, and why do the authors think it worth the struggle?

paragraphs: Among the great plays, Greek tragedy is probably the toughest for beginners. First, tragedies were presented three at a time, often on a common theme, but except for Aeschylus's Oresteia only single plays survive from each group.
Second, it is almost impossible to stage the plays mentally, since we know almost nothing about how Greek directors staged them.

Third, the plays often rest on stories their audiences knew well but that we know only through the plays. Knowing Oedipus as well as we know George Washington and the cherry tree, and watching Sophocles comment on it, differs greatly from meeting his play as the primary story.

Yet the authors say the plays are powerful enough to triumph over these obstacles. They tell us much about life as we still live it, and they form a framework for many later plays, such as Racine's and O'Neill's.
card.rule: Read a Greek tragedy aware of what you lack, the companion plays, the staging and the familiar story behind it, and do not let those gaps stop you.
card.limits: Naming the obstacles explains the difficulty without removing it: the lost plays and the lost staging stay lost, and the reader must work around them rather than wait for them.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: Tragedy is the lack of time
concepts.question: What do the authors call the essence of tragedy, and what question should you ask as you read a Greek tragedy?

paragraphs: The authors' first advice for Greek tragedy: remember that the essence of tragedy is time, or rather the lack of it. There is no problem in any Greek tragedy that could not have been solved with enough time, but there is never enough.
Decisions and choices must be made in a moment, with no time to think and weigh the consequences. And since tragic heroes are fallible, perhaps especially fallible, the decisions are wrong.
It is easy for us, reading at leisure, to see what should have been done. But would we have been able to see it in time? That, the authors say, is the question to ask in reading any Greek tragedy.
card.rule: In reading a tragedy, find where the lack of time forces a hasty decision, and ask whether you would have seen the right course in time.
card.limits: The question does not excuse every tragic choice; the hero is still fallible. Nor is hindsight useless: seeing what should have been done helps you grasp the tragedy, provided you remember the hero had no such leisure.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: The chorus and the giants
concepts.question: How should you picture the speakers of a Greek tragedy as you read, and why?

paragraphs: One thing we do know about Greek staging: the tragic actors wore buskins, raised shoes that lifted them several inches off the ground, and masks. The chorus did not wear buskins, though they sometimes wore masks.

The difference in height between the protagonists and the chorus was highly significant. So, the authors advise, imagine the chorus's words spoken by people of your own stature, and the protagonists' words coming from giants, figures who did not only seem but actually were larger than life.
card.rule: Hear the chorus as people of your own size and the protagonists as giants, so that the scale of the tragedy stays in view.
card.limits: This rests on one known fact about staging, not a full reconstruction: it fixes the scale of the speakers, while most of how the plays were staged remains unknown.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: What counts as lyric poetry
concepts.question: What do the authors take lyric poetry to be, and why do they reject definitions that are too broad or too narrow?

paragraphs: The simplest definition of poetry, the authors say, is that it is what poets write. Some would call it instead a spontaneous overflowing of the personality, which might take the form of words, action, sound or feeling. There is a kernel of truth here, but in that sense anyone can make poetry at any time: too broad for the authors' purpose.
Other definitions are too narrow: that poetry must praise, or rouse to action, or rhyme, or use a special poetic diction. Each has a kernel of truth, but each leaves out much that is poetry.

For the authors, poetry consists of words arranged in a more or less orderly and disciplined way. Between the broad and narrow definitions lies a central core that reasonable people would accept, and nine times in ten, or more, you would agree with them that one thing is a poem and another is not.
card.rule: Take a lyric poem as words arranged in an orderly, disciplined way, and do not let an over-broad or over-narrow definition decide for you what counts.
card.limits: The authors deliberately do not state the central core precisely, so the working definition settles most cases, not every borderline one. And it says what a poem is, not whether a poem is good.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: Read the poem through without stopping
concepts.question: What is the first rule for reading a lyric poem, and why does stalling on the opening lines defeat so many readers?

paragraphs: Many people believe they cannot read lyric poetry, especially modern poetry, which they think too obscure to be worth the work. The authors reply that poetry does not demand as much work as you may think if you go about it the right way, and that it is often worth whatever effort you spend.

Their first rule: read the poem through without stopping, whether you think you understand it or not. Readers faced with Eliot or Dylan Thomas plunge in, are brought up short by the first line, puzzle over the words and syntax, and soon give up, sure that modern poetry is beyond them.

But any good lyric has a unity, and you cannot grasp it unless you read all of it, all at once. The essence of a poem is almost never in its first line, or even its first stanza; it is found only in the whole.
card.rule: Read a lyric straight through without stopping, understood or not, to catch the unity that only the whole poem holds.
card.limits: Reading straight through is a first step, not the whole job: a good poem can be worked at and reread for a lifetime. The rule forbids stalling at the start, not close work afterwards.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: Read the poem again, aloud
concepts.question: Why do the authors call reading a poem aloud essential, and what does speaking the words do that silent reading does not?

paragraphs: The second rule for lyrics: read the poem through again, out loud. For poetic drama like Shakespeare's, reading aloud was helpful; for a lyric, the authors call it essential.

Speaking the words forces you to understand them better. You cannot glide over a misunderstood phrase so easily when you have to say it, and your ear is offended by a misplaced emphasis your eyes might miss. The rhythm, and the rhymes if there are any, help by making you put the emphasis where it belongs.

Reading aloud also opens you to the poem, so that it can work on you as it should. The authors think readers who believe they cannot read poems would have little difficulty if they followed these first two rules.
card.rule: After the first read-through, read the poem aloud, letting rhythm and rhyme set the emphasis and letting your ear catch what your eye glided over.
card.limits: The voice helps only if you attend to what it reveals; reciting on autopilot glides over phrases as easily as silent reading. And reading aloud here serves understanding; it is not a performance to be judged.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: Rhetorical questions and key words
concepts.question: Once you grasp a poem's unity, what questions should you ask it, and how do you find its key words?

paragraphs: Once you have grasped a poem in its unity, even vaguely, you can begin to ask it questions; as with expository works, that is the secret of understanding. But the questions differ. Those you ask of an expository book are grammatical and logical; those you ask of a lyric are usually rhetorical, though they may also be syntactical.

You do not come to terms with a poem, but you must discover its key words, and you find them by rhetorical rather than grammatical discernment. Why do certain words leap out of the poem at you? Does the rhythm mark them, or the rhyme? Are they repeated?
Ask too whether several stanzas seem to be about the same ideas, and if so, whether those ideas form a sequence. Anything of this kind you discover will help your understanding.
card.rule: After grasping the whole, find a poem's key words by asking what makes them stand out, rhythm, rhyme or repetition, and trace whether its stanzas form a sequence of ideas.
card.limits: A poem's key words are not terms to be defined and agreed on, as in an expository book; you note what they do in the poem. And these questions follow the read-through and the reading aloud; they do not replace them.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: Find the conflict, named or implied
concepts.question: What should you look for at the heart of most good lyrics, and how can you find it when the poem does not name it?

paragraphs: Most good lyrics contain some kind of conflict. Sometimes two antagonists, people, images or ideas, are named and the conflict between them is described; then it is easy to find. Often, though, the conflict is only implied.

A great many lyrics, perhaps most of the great ones, are about the conflict between love and time, between life and death, between the beauty of passing things and the triumph of eternity, even when those words do not appear in the poem.

Shakespeare's sonnets show both cases. Sonnets 64 and 116 name time outright as love's enemy. Sonnet 138, in which the speaker believes his love's oaths though he knows she lies, is about love and time too, though the word time appears nowhere in it.
card.rule: Look in a lyric for the conflict between two things, people, images or ideas, and when none is named, ask whether an implied one, such as love against time, lies beneath it.
card.limits: Love against time is a frequent conflict, not a master key: forcing it onto every poem misreads the ones about something else. An implied conflict must be found in the poem's words, not imposed on them.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: The title as a clue
concepts.question: How can a poem's title reveal a conflict that the poem itself does not name?

paragraphs: It is harder, the authors say, to see that Archibald MacLeish's You, Andrew Marvell is about the same subject as Marvell's poem. MacLeish asks us to imagine someone lying face down in the noonday sun, yet feeling the chill of dusk as the shadow of night sweeps across the world, over Persia, Baghdad, Crete and Spain, until it comes on swiftly and secretly.

The poem does not use the word time and mentions no lover. But its title reminds us of Marvell's lyric, with its theme of world enough and time. Poem and title together invoke the same conflict, between love, or life, and time.
So the title is part of the evidence. When a poem's words leave its subject implicit, ask what the title adds.
card.rule: Read a poem's title as part of the poem, and ask whether it points to a theme or conflict the lines do not name.
card.limits: A title is evidence, not a verdict: it must fit what the poem says, and some titles are only labels. An allusion in a title helps only if you know what it points to, as MacLeish's depends on knowing Marvell.

concepts.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
concepts.title: The poem before its context
concepts.question: How much do you need to know about a poet's life and times to read a poem, and what matters more?

paragraphs: Readers of lyrics often feel they must know more about the poets and their times than they need to. We put much faith in commentaries, criticism and biographies, perhaps because we doubt our own ability to read. Almost anyone can read any poem, the authors say, if he will go to work on it.

Whatever you learn about a poet's life or times is valid and may help. But a vast knowledge of a poem's context is no guarantee that the poem itself will be understood. To be understood, it must be read, over and over.

Reading a great lyric is a lifetime job: not that it goes on without a break, but that a great poem deserves many return visits. And during vacations from a poem, we may learn more about it than we realise.
card.rule: Put the poem itself first: read it over and over across the years, and use biography and commentary as help, never as a substitute.
card.limits: This is no ban on background: the authors call what you learn about the poet valid and possibly helpful, and some allusions need it. The point is that context cannot do the reading for you.

concepts.title: What the authors mean by history
concepts.question: What kind of writing do the authors mean by history, and what makes even a pile of documents count as one?

paragraphs: The word history can mean the past itself or a written record of it. Since facts cannot be read, the authors mean the written record. Many writings get called histories: collections of documents, interview transcripts, diaries, letters, almost anything from a period a reader is curious about.
The authors narrow this to narrative accounts, told in a more or less formal way, of a past period, event or series of events. They take this to be the ordinary meaning of the word and keep to it.

They also widen it. In their view, which not every historian shares, the essence of history is narration: the word itself ends in story. Even a collection of documents tells a story implicitly, whether or not it is put in a meaningful order; otherwise no one would call it a history of its time.
card.example: An archive prints two hundred letters from a 1920s mining strike, in date order, with no commentary. On the authors' view it is still a history of the strike: these letters, about this strike, already tell a story, even though the editor never states one.
card.rule: Read any history, even a bare collection of documents, as a story about the past, and look for the story it tells, stated or implied.
card.limits: Not every historian accepts that history is essentially narration, and the authors say so. A diary or a bundle of letters may be called a history, but it was written with another intention, so read it first for what it is.

concepts.title: The juror and the historian
concepts.question: Why is it harder to know what happened in history than to decide what happened in a court case?

paragraphs: Anyone who has sat on a jury knows how hard it is to rebuild even one recent event from the memories of people who saw it. A court has living witnesses, strict rules of evidence and cross-examination, and witnesses may not guess, estimate or suppose. Even so, a juror is seldom absolutely sure what happened.
The law expects this. It does not demand certainty; it asks only whether a doubt is reasonable, meaning strong enough to trouble the juror's conscience.

The historian works without the court's protections. Most events are long past and the witnesses dead. Their testimony followed no rules: they guessed, estimated and assumed, cannot be watched for signs of lying, were never cross-examined, and may not have known what they were talking about.
So the authors conclude that a historical fact, for all the solid feel of the word, is one of the most elusive things in the world.
card.example: A juror hears three witnesses describe a car crash from last month and still has some doubt. A historian has two letters, by men long dead, describing a riot two centuries ago. If the juror cannot be certain, the historian has far less ground for certainty.
card.rule: Hold historical facts with the doubt the evidence warrants, remembering that historical witnesses lack the safeguards a court provides.
card.limits: Elusive does not mean unknowable. Some facts, such as well-recorded dates, are about as certain as anything can be, and a doubt that refuses to accept them is not a reasonable one.

concepts.title: Dates are not understanding
concepts.question: If we know the exact dates of an event, how much do we understand about it?

paragraphs: Some historical facts are close to certain. The authors cite the American Civil War: it began with the firing on Fort Sumter on April 12, 1861, and ended with Lee's surrender to Grant at Appomattox on April 9, 1865. Everyone agrees on those dates.

Yet knowing the dates teaches little. Even when the war began and ended is disputed: some date it from Lincoln's election, some from years earlier; fighting went on in remote places after the surrender; and some say it is not over yet.
A date also answers none of the questions that matter most. Why was the fort fired on? Could war still have been avoided afterwards? Questions of cause are where understanding a history begins.
card.example: A student memorises that a strike began on 3 March and ended on 20 May. She can pass a quiz on dates but cannot say why the workers walked out or why they went back, which is what a history of the strike is mainly about.
card.rule: Treat a well-established date as the start of reading a history, and go on to ask why the event happened.
card.limits: Dates still matter: they fix the order of events, and any account of causes needs that order. The point is that a date is a frame, not understanding, and an agreed date may not mark where an event really began or ended.

concepts.title: What makes a fact significant
concepts.question: Why do the authors doubt that a firmly dated event is, by that alone, a significant historical fact?

paragraphs: The authors press the Sumter example further. Suppose war had been avoided after the attack. Would anyone now care that a fort was fired on one spring day more than a century ago?

Many forts have doubtless been attacked without anyone knowing or caring today. Had the Sumter attack led nowhere, it would probably have joined them. Its weight as a historical fact comes from what followed it, and from our caring about that.
So significance is not stamped on an event by its date or its certainty. It depends on the event's place in a larger story, which is one reason a history is more than a list of verified facts.
card.example: A border clash in one year is known today only to a few specialists, while a similar clash in another year opened a long war and fills textbooks. The two facts may be equally certain; their significance is very different.
card.rule: Ask of any historical fact why it matters, and look for the larger story that gives it weight.
card.limits: This does not make significance a matter of taste: it rests on what the event led to. By the same reasoning, later events can change how much an earlier event is seen to matter, so a judgment of significance may need revising.

concepts.title: History sits closer to fiction
concepts.question: If history must be grouped with fiction or with science, where do the authors place it, and what does that placement not mean?

paragraphs: If history has to be filed with either fiction or science, the authors say it more often goes with fiction. If it may sit between the two, it is usually admitted to lie closer to fiction.

This does not mean the historian makes up facts. The authors add that even a novelist does not invent from nothing: a fictional world must not be wholly unlike ours, its maker learned through ordinary senses, and its characters use our words.
In this sense history shares fiction's form: it tells a story, with people, actions and a shape. So a reader brings a story reader's expectations to it as well as a fact checker's.
card.example: A reader opens a history of a polar expedition expecting a report and is puzzled that the author builds suspense and dwells on the leader's character. Read as a story bound to the facts, those choices make sense, and she can still ask whether the facts support them.
card.rule: Read a history as a story bound by the facts: expect narrative shape and judgment, without assuming the facts are invented.
card.limits: Closer to fiction does not license reading history as fiction. A good historian holds himself bound to accuracy, and a reader may hold a history to the facts in a way no one holds a novel.

concepts.title: Every historian supplies something
concepts.question: What must every historian supply that the record of events does not provide by itself?

paragraphs: A good historian does not make up the past; he holds himself bound by some standard of accuracy. Even so, the authors insist, every historian must make up something.

Either he finds a general pattern in events, or imposes one on them, or he supposes he knows why the people in his story did what they did. The record holds events; the pattern or the motives are what the historian brings to it.
This is no fault. Without a pattern or motives, events are a disconnected list. But it means part of every history is the historian's own contribution, and a reader needs to see which part that is.
card.example: Records show a minister resigned two days after a scandal broke. One historian writes that he resigned in shame; another, that rivals forced him out. The dates are the same in both books; the motive is what each historian supplied.
card.rule: In any history, separate what the record shows from what the historian has supplied: a pattern in events or the motives behind actions.
card.limits: Supplied does not mean groundless. A pattern or a motive can be well argued from evidence. The aim is to see the historian's contribution and weigh it, not to throw it out.

concepts.title: Pattern or causes: which way he works
concepts.question: How can a reader tell whether a historian fits events to a theory or assigns causes event by event?

paragraphs: Historians supply what the record lacks in one of two ways. Some hold a general theory or philosophy, for instance that Providence rules human affairs, and make the history fit it.

Others reject any pattern imposed from outside or above and claim only to report what happened. But such a historian is likely to be forced to assign causes to events and motives to actions, one by one.

The authors call it essential to recognise which way the historian you are reading works, because it tells you where his contribution lies: in the overall design, or in the explanations spread through the story.
card.example: One history of an empire's fall presents each defeat as a step in a destined decline. Another treats each defeat on its own: a general's vanity here, a drought there. The first wears its theory openly; in the second, the supplied parts are the many local causes.
card.rule: Recognise whether your historian fits events to a general theory or assigns causes and motives event by event, and look for his contribution accordingly.
card.limits: Many histories mix the two, with a loose overall view and many local explanations. A historian who says he only reports facts may also hold a theory he never states, so the label he gives himself is not the last word.

concepts.title: The view that history has no pattern
concepts.question: What is the third position on history, and what does a historian who holds it believe about causes?

paragraphs: There is one way to avoid both finding a pattern and assigning motives: assume that people do not act for a purpose, or that their purposes, if they exist, cannot be discovered. Then history has no pattern at all.

Tolstoy, a novelist rather than a historian, held this view. He thought the causes of every human action so many, so complex and so deeply hidden in unconscious motives that it is impossible to know why anything happened. Many historians, especially modern ones, have held the same view.
The authors call this a theory of history too. A reader who meets it should recognise it as one more way a historian's outlook shapes the account.
card.example: A historian of a stock-market crash declines to name its causes, saying that millions of hidden decisions make it impossible to know why prices fell when they did. He is not being neutral or lazy; he is taking the no-pattern position.
card.rule: When a historian holds that why events happened cannot be known, recognise the no-pattern theory at work and read the account in its light.
card.limits: Not every refusal to explain is this theory. A historian may leave one cause open for lack of evidence while explaining much else; the no-pattern view holds that the causes of human action cannot be known at all.

concepts.title: The first rule: read more than one account
concepts.question: Why do the authors make reading more than one account the first rule of reading history?

paragraphs: Theories of history differ, and a historian's theory affects his account of events. It follows, the authors say, that to understand an event or period you must read more than one account of it. They call this the first rule of reading history.

The rule matters most when the event has practical significance for you. Their example is the American Civil War: Americans still live in a world it helped to make, yet cannot understand it through the eyes of only one man, one side or one faction of historians.

The rule follows from the earlier ideas. Every historian supplies something, and different historians supply different things, so a single account mixes the record with one historian's contribution, with no way to tell the two apart.
card.example: A reader wants to understand the partition of a country decades ago. One history, by a writer from one side, blames the other side's leaders. Before accepting it, she reads a history from the other side and one by a scholar from neither.
card.rule: If you want to understand an event or period, read more than one account of it, especially when it bears on your own life.
card.limits: Sometimes only one account exists, or there is no time for more; then the authors say you must admit how little you can learn of what really happened. Several accounts copied from one source also add less than their number suggests.

concepts.title: Every history has a point of view
concepts.question: Can a history be written from no point of view, and how should a reader respond to the one it has?

paragraphs: The authors recall a new Civil War history offered as an impartial, objective history from the point of view of the South. The author seemed serious, and the authors allow that perhaps such a thing is possible.
Their wider point is that every narrative history has to be written from some point of view. Deciding which events to tell, whose actions to follow and what to explain means standing somewhere.

So the aim is not a history with no viewpoint, which may not exist, but to look at the event from more than one viewpoint. Seeing it through the eyes of only one man, one side or one faction is the slip to avoid.
card.example: Two histories of a long strike: one follows the owners' meetings, the other the strikers' homes. Neither need be false, and neither is viewpoint-free. A reader of both sees the strike from two places and can judge better than with either alone.
card.rule: Identify the point of view each history is written from, and seek out others before judging the event.
card.limits: A point of view is not the same as distortion: a history can stand somewhere and still be accurate. Treating every viewpoint as bias leads to dismissing all histories instead of comparing them.

concepts.title: One account and the lay reader
concepts.question: With only one history of an event, what must a lay reader admit, and what else can reading it offer?
