paragraphs: Often we cannot read more than one history of an event. Then, the authors say, we must admit we have little chance of learning what really happened. But that is not the only reason to read history.

The professional historian, writing a history himself, must cross-examine his sources by checking each against the others, leaving no stone unturned. The irresponsible amateur reads history only for amusement.

The lay reader stands between them: more serious than the amateur, but not bound to the professional's exhaustive checking. What such a reader can gain from even a single account is the subject of the ideas that follow.
card.example: Thucydides wrote the only major contemporary history of the Peloponnesian War, so in a sense there is nothing to check it against. A lay reader cannot learn from it exactly what happened, yet the authors think it well worth reading.
card.rule: When you can read only one account, admit its limits as a record of what happened, and read it for what else a good history offers.
card.limits: The lighter duty excuses the lay reader from exhaustive source checking, not from care. Where other accounts are at hand, the first rule of reading more than one still applies.

concepts.title: Histories that shaped what came after
concepts.question: Why read a history whose events no longer touch our lives, such as Thucydides on the Peloponnesian War?

paragraphs: The Peloponnesian War was fought twenty-five centuries ago in what is now a small country. Its fighters, the things they fought for, its victories and its cities are long gone. Almost all that remains of it is Thucydides' account.

Yet that account still matters, because it influenced later history. Leaders in later ages read Thucydides, compared their own position with that of Athens or Sparta, and used his story as an excuse, a justification and even a pattern of conduct.

So, the authors say, the world was changed, perhaps only a little, by one man's view of a small part of it. We read Thucydides less because he described perfectly what happened before him than because he partly shaped what happened after, and to know what is happening now.
card.example: A statesman facing a rising rival power describes the moment as a new Athens and Sparta. The old book now shapes how a modern crisis is understood, and a reader who knows it can follow the comparison, and question it.
card.rule: Read an influential history for how it has shaped what came after, not only for whether it records the past exactly.
card.limits: Influence is not accuracy. A history can shape later events while describing its own period imperfectly, so learning how influential it is does not settle whether its account is true.

concepts.title: Good history is universal too
concepts.question: In what sense is a good history universal, though it is tied to particular events?

paragraphs: Aristotle wrote that poetry is more philosophical than history, meaning more general: a good poem is true in all times and places. History is tied to events in a way poetry is not, so it is less universal. But, the authors say, any good history is also universal.

Thucydides said he wrote so that people of the future would not repeat the mistakes he had seen and suffered from. He described kinds of human mistakes that mean something to people other than Greeks, and very similar errors have been made again and again since.

So a reader who goes to history only to discover what really happened misses the main thing a good historian has to teach. Read well, the authors add, Thucydides may even lead you to give up trying to find out exactly what happened.
card.example: A history of a failed expedition shows its leaders ignoring warnings from local guides to keep to a schedule set far away. The ships and men are long gone, but the mistake, distant planners overruling people on the spot, is recognisable in many organisations today.
card.rule: Read a good history for the human actions and mistakes that hold beyond its own time and place, not only for what happened there.
card.limits: Universal is not the same as identical. History stays tied to its events, so a lesson drawn from one age needs checking against how the present differs before it is applied.

concepts.title: The story of what led up to now
concepts.question: What do the authors mean by calling history the story of what led up to now, and what does that let a reader learn?

paragraphs: For the authors, history is the story of what led up to now. What interests us is the present, and the future, which the present partly determines. So even a historian who lived more than two thousand years ago can teach us something about the present and the future.

They sum up two suggestions for reading history. First, if you can, read more than one history of an event or period that interests you. Second, read a history not only to learn what happened at a particular time and place, but to learn how people act in all times and places, especially now.
The two serve different aims. The first brings you nearer to what happened; the second lets even a single account teach you about people and the present.
card.example: A reader studies a history of a nineteenth-century banking panic. She compares two accounts to judge what happened, and also notes how depositors behaved when rumours spread, which helps her follow news of a bank run this year.
card.rule: Read history as the story of what led up to now: compare accounts for what happened, and read each for how people act today.
card.limits: Reading toward the present can tempt a reader to notice only what echoes today's concerns. The second suggestion asks how people act in all times and places, not only where the past resembles now.

concepts.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
concepts.title: Read history as an expository work
concepts.question: Since history is closer to fiction, why do the authors still say it should be read as an expository work?

paragraphs: Most histories are closer to fiction than to science, yet the authors say they can be read as expository works, and therefore should be. A history tells a story, but it also puts forward claims about what happened and why, which can be understood and judged.
So the reader asks a history the same four questions asked of any expository book: what is it about as a whole, what is being said in detail and how, is it true, and what of it.

Because of the special nature of history, the authors say, the questions must be asked a little differently, and the answers will be of slightly different kinds. The ideas that follow take the questions in turn.
card.example: A reader of a history of a famine asks: what period and place does it cover, how is the story told and what does the author treat as basic, is the account believable and well sourced, and what does it suggest for famine relief today.
card.rule: Ask a history the four questions of any expository book, adapting each to a story of past events.
card.limits: The questions carry over, but not unchanged. Asking them of a history exactly as of a scientific treatise, looking for general laws and proofs, misses what is special about history.

concepts.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
concepts.title: What it is about, and what it is not
concepts.question: What must a reader find out about a history's subject before understanding or criticising it?

paragraphs: Every history has a particular and limited subject, yet readers often do not trouble to find out what it is. Above all, they fail to note the limits the author sets himself.

A history of the Civil War is not a history of the world in the nineteenth century, and probably not of the American West in the 1860s. It could, though perhaps it should not, leave out the state of American education in that decade or the movement of the frontier.

So read to learn precisely what the history is about and what it is not about. You need the first to read it well. You need the second before you criticise it, because an author cannot be blamed for not doing what he did not try to do.
card.example: A history of a city's water supply from 1850 to 1900 says little about the city's politics. A reviewer complains that it ignores the mayor's corruption. If the subject is the water supply, the complaint misses; if corruption shaped the water supply, it may still hit.
card.rule: Find exactly what a history covers and what it leaves out, and judge it by what it set out to do.
card.limits: Stated limits do not shelter every omission. The authors suggest a Civil War history perhaps should not ignore some matters, so a reader may still ask whether a left-out subject bears on the chosen one.

concepts.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
concepts.title: How the story is told
concepts.question: How has the historian chosen to tell the story, and which aspect of it does he treat as most fundamental?

paragraphs: A history's general outline is set by time, since the story happened in time, so a reader need not search for it. But there is more than one way to tell a story, and the reader must find out how this historian has chosen to tell his.

Does he divide the book into chapters by years, decades or generations? Or by headings of his own choosing, with the economic history of the period in one chapter and its wars, religious movements and literature in others?

Then ask which of these aspects matters most to him. If you can say which part of the story seems most fundamental to the historian, you understand him better. You may disagree with his judgment of what is basic and still learn from him.
card.example: One history of a century gives a chapter to each decade. Another opens with three chapters on trade and only then turns to politics and the arts, explaining both by trade. The second historian has shown that he treats the economy as fundamental.
card.rule: Find how the historian divides his story and which aspect he treats as most basic, before judging his account.
card.limits: Order and space hint at what an author thinks basic but do not prove it; an early chapter may only be background. Check the hint against how the other parts are explained.

concepts.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
concepts.title: Do people act that way?
concepts.question: What does it mean to judge that a history lacks verisimilitude, and when may a reader make that judgment?

paragraphs: Criticism of history, the authors say, takes two forms. The first is to judge, but only after understanding what is said, that a historian's work lacks verisimilitude: people do not act that way.

Even when the historian documents his statements and the sources are relevant, we may feel he has misunderstood them or judged them wrongly, perhaps through some failure in his grasp of human nature or human affairs.

The authors' example: many readers now distrust older historians who say little about economic matters. Thinking that people act out of self-interest, we may grow suspicious when a history ascribes too much nobility to its hero.
card.example: A history of a merchant family portrays every head of the family acting only for the good of the city, never for profit. A reader who has understood the account may fairly say it lacks verisimilitude: merchants who never weighed their own interest seem unlike real people.
card.rule: Once you understand a history, ask whether its people act as people do, and say so if they do not.
card.limits: This judgment rests on your own grasp of human nature, which may be weaker than the historian's. It never replaces understanding first, and a portrait that seems unlikely can still be true.

concepts.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
concepts.title: Sources, and the storyteller and scientist
concepts.question: What is the second way to criticise a history, and why do the authors rank it below the first?

paragraphs: The second form of criticism suits a reader with special knowledge of the subject: we judge that the historian has misused his sources. We may find he has not read a book we have read, or that he is misinformed about the facts. Then he cannot have written a good history; we expect a historian to be informed.
The authors rank the first criticism, lack of verisimilitude, as the more important. A good historian must combine the talents of the storyteller and the scientist.
He must know what is likely to have happened as well as what some witnesses or writers said did happen. Sources tell him what was said; his grasp of human affairs tells him what is likely.
card.example: A historian of a famous trial reports a witness's claim that the accused confessed in a crowded tavern. The record is quoted accurately, but a historian with a storyteller's sense of the likely would ask whether anyone confesses before a crowd, and weigh the claim accordingly.
card.rule: Check whether a historian is informed and uses his sources well, but weigh more heavily whether he knows what is likely to have happened.
card.limits: Ranking does not make sources unimportant: a misinformed historian cannot write a good history. And a sense of the likely can mislead when events really were unusual, so it too must answer to the evidence.

concepts.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
concepts.title: What of it? History and action
concepts.question: How do the authors answer the question What of it for history, and why does it matter that history be read well?

paragraphs: On the last question, What of it?, the authors suggest that perhaps no kind of literature affects human action more than history. Satires and pictures of ideal societies have little effect: we seldom act on authors who only describe the gap between the real and the ideal.

History tells what people of the past actually did, and that often leads us to try to better our lot. It suggests the possible: what has been done might be done again, or perhaps avoided. Statesmen, the authors note, have in general been more learned in history than in other disciplines.
So the main answer to What of it? lies in practical, political action. That is why history must be read well: leaders have often acted with some knowledge of history, but not enough.
card.example: A city council debating a congestion charge reads how three other cities fared with one. The histories show what has been tried and what followed, suggesting what might work there and what to avoid.
card.rule: After reading a history, ask what it shows could be done again or avoided, and read well enough to act on it.
card.limits: History suggests the possible, not the certain: that something was done once does not mean it can be done now, under other conditions.

concepts.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
concepts.title: Biography: the story of a real person
concepts.question: Why do the authors say biography has a mixed character, and what must a reader ask of any biography?

paragraphs: A biography is a story about a real person. The authors call this a mixed inheritance, and it gives biography a mixed character: part story, part history.

Ordinarily a biography is a narrative account of a life, the history of a man or woman, so it poses many of the same problems as a history. Some biographers would object to this description, the authors grant.

So the reader asks the questions asked of any book, and two more: what is the author's purpose, and what are his criteria of truth? The answers sort biographies into kinds, which the next ideas take up.
card.example: Two lives of the same explorer: one written to celebrate him at a centenary, one written to test every claim in his journals. Asking each author's purpose and standard of truth tells a reader how far to trust each.
card.rule: Read a biography as both story and history, and ask the author's purpose and criteria of truth.
card.limits: The two questions start the judgment of a biography but do not finish it. A biographer may state one purpose and serve another, so the answers must be checked against the book itself.

concepts.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
concepts.title: The definitive biography
concepts.question: What makes a biography definitive, and how should a reader treat one?

paragraphs: A definitive biography is meant to be the final, exhaustive, scholarly work on the life of someone important enough to deserve one. The author goes through all the sources, reads all the letters and examines a great deal of the history of the time.
Definitive biographies cannot be written about living persons, and they seldom appear until several non-definitive biographies, often somewhat inadequate, have come first.

A definitive biography is a slice of history: the history of a person and his times, seen through his eyes. It should be read as history. Gathering materials is a different talent from shaping them, so such books are not always easy reading, though Boswell's Life of Johnson shows a scholarly book need not be dull.
card.example: A scholar spends twenty years on the papers of a reformer dead for a century, after three earlier lives of her had appeared. The result is heavy going in places, but a reader can treat it as the history of the reformer and her times.
card.rule: Read a definitive biography as history, the life and times of its subject, and expect thoroughness rather than ease.
card.limits: Definitive names an aim, not a guarantee. Boswell's Life of Johnson is certainly definitive, yet other biographies of Johnson have appeared since; new sources can still change the picture.

concepts.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
concepts.title: The authorized biography
concepts.question: How should a reader read an authorized biography, and what can and cannot be learned from it?

paragraphs: An authorized biography is usually commissioned by the heirs or friends of an important person and written so that his errors and triumphs appear in the best possible light. It can be very good, because the author is given access to all the material by those who control it.
But it cannot be trusted as a definitive biography can. The reader should understand that it may be biased: it shows how the subject's friends and associates want him to be known.

It still teaches. It shows what interested persons want the public to know, and much about the time it was written in: its customs, manners and acceptable attitudes. It does not give the real private life. Most biographies of living persons are of this kind.
card.example: A foundation commissions a life of its founder and opens every archive to the writer. The book is rich in detail, but his business failures appear as brave risks. A reader learns much about what the foundation wants remembered and the values of its day, but should look elsewhere for the whole man.
card.rule: Read an authorized biography as the picture its sponsors want known: use it for what it shows of them and its time, not as the private truth.
card.limits: Authorized does not mean false. Such books can be very good, with access other writers lack. The caution is against trusting them as definitive, not against reading them.

concepts.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
concepts.title: Ordinary and didactic biographies
concepts.question: What should a reader expect from an ordinary biography, and from a didactic one like Plutarch's Lives?

paragraphs: Biographies that are neither definitive nor authorized the authors call ordinary. From them we expect accuracy and, above all, the feeling of viewing the life of a real person in another time and place. They are not trustworthy as definitive biographies are, but are often very good reading, like Izaak Walton's lives of his poet friends.

Some biographies are didactic: they have a moral purpose. Plutarch told the lives of great Greeks and Romans to help his contemporaries be great and avoid the errors of the great. Though often our only account of its subjects, his Lives is read more for its view of life than for biographical information.
Plutarch's book also shaped later history: as Plutarch shows Alexander modelling himself on Homer's Achilles, later conquerors modelled themselves on Plutarch's Alexander.
card.example: A modern book of short lives of reformers, written to inspire young readers to public service, is didactic. A reader learns most by asking what view of a good life it teaches, not by treating each sketch as a complete record.
card.rule: From an ordinary biography expect accuracy and a real life; read a didactic one chiefly for the view of life it teaches.
card.limits: Reading a didactic life for its lessons does not make its facts irrelevant; where it is the only source, they still need the care owed any single account. A moral purpose can also bend a story to fit its lesson.

concepts.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
concepts.title: No autobiography is wholly true, or wholly false
concepts.question: Why do the authors doubt that any autobiography is wholly true, and why is none wholly false?

paragraphs: Autobiographies raise problems of their own. It is doubtful whether anyone has written a true autobiography. If it is hard to know another person's life, it is harder still to know your own, and every autobiography is about a life not yet complete.

When no one can contradict you, the temptation to tell less than the truth, or more, which may be the commoner fault, is almost irresistible. Everyone has secrets he cannot bear to tell, and illusions about himself he can hardly see as illusions.
Yet no autobiography is wholly untrue. As no one can be a perfect liar, every autobiography tells us something about its author, if only that there are things he wants to conceal.
card.example: A retired general's memoir blames every defeat on others and claims every victory as his own plan. Its version of the war needs checking, but the pattern itself tells the reader something true about the man: what he could not bear to admit.
card.rule: Read an autobiography expecting both concealment and embellishment, and read even these for what they reveal about the author.
card.limits: Doubt is not dismissal: an author often knows facts of his life no one else could, and much of what he says may be true. The point is to weigh his account, not to discard it.

concepts.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
concepts.title: The author in every book
concepts.question: In what sense is much of any book autobiographical, and how much attention should a reader give to the author's character?

paragraphs: It is often said that Rousseau's Confessions, or a book of about that time, was the first real autobiography. The authors think this overlooks Augustine's Confessions and Montaigne's Essays, and makes a more serious error: much of what anyone writes on any subject is autobiographical.

There is much of Plato in the Republic, of Milton in Paradise Lost, of Goethe in Faust, though we may not be able to point to it exactly. Words are found and written by a living person; even if Plato and Aristotle had agreed completely, they could not have written the same books.

So a reader interested in people will read any book partly to discover its author's character, within reasonable limits. This should never be the main concern, and overdone it becomes a fallacy. Do not hunt a writer's secrets so hard that you miss what he says plainly.
card.example: A reader of a treatise on government notices the author's distrust of crowds and wonders what in his life produced it. The curiosity is fair, but she first makes sure she can state the treatise's argument; the author's character comes second.
card.rule: Read any book partly for the person behind it, but first and mainly for what it plainly says.
card.limits: Some books show their authors far less than others, and guesses about an author's character drawn from his book are hard to check, so they should stay tentative.

concepts.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
concepts.title: Rules for reading lives
concepts.question: What summary advice do the authors give for reading biographies and autobiographies, and how do they answer What of it for them?

paragraphs: Biographies and autobiographies are special kinds of history, often more poetical than expository. If you wish to know the truth about a person's life, read as many biographies of him as you can find, including his own account if he wrote one.
The authors' summary: read biography as history and as the cause of history; take all autobiographies with a grain of salt; and never argue with a book until you fully understand what it is saying.

As to What of it?, biography, like history, can lead to practical, moral action. A biography can inspire: it is the story of a life, usually a more or less successful one, and we too have lives to lead.
card.example: A nurse reads three biographies of a pioneering doctor and the doctor's own memoir. She weighs the memoir with caution, compares the lives, and comes away with a truer picture and a resolve to change how her own ward handles complaints.
card.rule: To know a life, read several accounts including the subject's own, discount the self-portrait, and ask what the life suggests for your own.
card.limits: Inspiration is not imitation: a life lived under other conditions cannot be copied step by step. And a grain of salt is not a reason to set the self-portrait aside; it is still evidence.

concepts.section: How to Read About Current Events
concepts.title: The four questions for the news
concepts.question: Why must the four questions be asked even of newspapers and magazines, where full analytical reading is unnecessary?

paragraphs: The authors qualify an earlier claim. Analytical reading is not always necessary; much of what we read does not call for that effort. But the four questions must always be asked of anything we read, including newspapers, magazines and books about current events.
History did not stop long ago. People keep writing about what is happening now, and as human beings and citizens we have an obligation to try to understand the world around us.

The difficulty is knowing what is actually happening now, and whether the news we get is true. It is the problem history poses: we cannot be sure we have the facts about the present any more than about the past, yet we must try.
card.example: A commuter reads a ten-minute article on a new housing law. She does not outline it, but she asks what it is about, what it claims and on what grounds, whether that seems true, and what it means for her rent.
card.rule: Ask the four questions of every piece of current-events reading, even when you relax the full rules of analytical reading.
card.limits: Asking the four questions does not mean a slow, full analysis of every news item; the rules can be relaxed while the questions stay. And recency does not make news more certain than history.

concepts.section: How to Read About Current Events
concepts.title: The reporter's mind is a filter
concepts.question: Why do the authors say the most important thing to know about a news report is who wrote it?

paragraphs: No one can be everywhere at once, overhear every conversation or look into every heart, so for current events we depend on reporters, people supposed to know what is happening in a small area. What we can know depends on them.

Ideally a reporter is a clear glass through which reality shines. But the human mind is not a clear glass. It reflects poorly, and when reality passes through it, it filters, separating out what it takes to be untrue. That is proper, since a reporter should not report what he thinks false, but he may be mistaken.

So the most important thing to know about any report of current events is who wrote it: less the reporter as a person than the kind of mind, the kind of filter, he has. The authors offer five questions to find out.
card.example: Two reporters cover the same protest. One, who has long covered the police, leads with the arrests; the other, who covers housing, leads with the rents that sparked it. Neither invents anything, but each mind filtered the same afternoon differently.
card.rule: Before trusting a report of current events, find out what kind of mind wrote it, since every report has passed through that filter.
card.limits: Knowing the filter does not mean every report is distorted; filtering out what one believes false is proper. And a reader cannot always learn about the writer, so sometimes the report itself must reveal its filter.

concepts.section: How to Read About Current Events
concepts.title: What he wants to prove, and to whom
concepts.question: What does a reader learn by asking what a current-events author wants to prove and whom he wants to convince?

paragraphs: The authors' five questions for current-events writing begin: What does the author want to prove? Whom does he want to convince? It is mostly safe to assume that every current-events book wants to prove something, and the thesis is often easy to find: the blurb or the preface usually states it.

Next ask whom the author is trying to convince. Is the book for those in the know, and are you one of them? Is it for a small group who can do something, and quickly, about the situation described? Or is it for everyone?
If you are not in the audience the book is written for, the authors say, you may not want to read it.
card.example: A book on a pending trade deal has a jacket blurb saying the deal will ruin small farms and a preface addressed to members of parliament. A general reader now knows the thesis to test, and that the book is pitched at people who can vote on the deal.
card.rule: Find what a current-events author wants to prove, usually from the blurb or preface, and whom he is writing for, before you read on.
card.limits: Not being the intended reader is a reason you may skip a book, not a rule that you must; an outsider can still learn from it, provided she knows it was not written for her.

concepts.section: How to Read About Current Events
concepts.title: Assumptions and special language
concepts.question: Why must a reader of current events find the author's assumptions and special language, and look at his own as well?

paragraphs: The third question asks what special knowledge the author assumes. Opinion or prejudice, the authors say, might be better words. Many authors write only for readers who agree with them; if you disagree sharply with a reporter's assumptions, you may only be irritated by his book.

Such assumptions are hard to find. Basil Willey wrote that it is almost impossible to become aware of one's own habitual assumptions, doctrines felt as facts; they are easier to see in another age. About our own time we lack that distance, so we must see through the filter of our own mind as well as the author's.

The fourth question asks what special language the author uses. Certain words provoke responses in us that they might not provoke in readers a century later; the authors' example is Communism. We should control these responses, or at least know when they occur.
card.example: An article on a new tax calls it a burden on job creators. A reader who shares the author's view nods along; one who does not bristles. Both should notice the assumption that taxes mainly hurt jobs, and the charged phrase, before judging the facts.
card.rule: Identify the assumptions an author expects you to share and the charged words he uses, and watch for your own assumptions and reactions too.
card.limits: Spotting an assumption does not show it is false, and a charged word may still be accurate. The aim is to see them for what they are, not to reject everything that rests on them.

concepts.section: How to Read About Current Events
concepts.title: Does he know? Let the reader beware
concepts.question: Beyond the reporter's bias, what else must a reader of current events consider, and what warning sums up the authors' advice?

paragraphs: The fifth question, probably the hardest, asks whether the reporter knows what he is talking about. Is he privy to the perhaps secret thoughts and decisions of the people he writes about? Does he know all he should to give a fair and balanced account?

Bias is not the only danger. With the best will in the world, a reporter may be uninformed about secret actions or treaties, since the management of news reaches reporters too. He may know this, or not; if not, his reader is in special peril.

The five questions are variations on those asked of any expository book; knowing an author's special language, for instance, is coming to terms. The authors sum up with a warning: Caveat lector, let the reader beware. A contemporary author, or his sources, may have an interest in your understanding things a certain way; know it and allow for it.
card.example: A well-meaning correspondent reports that talks between two governments have collapsed, relying on briefings from officials. Unknown to him, a secret channel is still open. His honesty is not in doubt; his information is incomplete, and the officials who briefed him had their reasons.
card.rule: Ask whether a reporter is in a position to know, not only whether he is biased, and read contemporary writing warily, allowing for the interests of the author and his sources.
card.limits: Wariness is not cynicism: the authors say an author may have such an interest, not that he must. And they say readers need not be wary in this way with Aristotle, Dante or Shakespeare.

concepts.title: What digests are good for
concepts.question: What job do news digests do well, and when is a digest not enough?

paragraphs: The distinction between reading for information and reading for understanding has a further consequence: sometimes we must read for information about understanding, to find out how others have interpreted the facts.

Most newspapers, magazines and even advertising we read for information, and there is far more of it than anyone can read. News magazines and digests meet that need. Their writers are first of all readers, skilled at reading for information far beyond the average, who cut the core of solid information out of pages of less substantial material.

For the average article, mainly informational, a condensation is usually adequate, sometimes better than the original. But the very best articles, like the best books, cannot be condensed without loss. A digest of Montaigne would serve well only if it sent us to the original.
card.example: A busy reader relies on a weekly digest of trade news, which serves her well. When it summarises a celebrated essay on the ethics of work, she treats the summary as a pointer and reads the essay itself.
card.rule: Use digests for mainly informational writing, and treat a summary of first-rate writing only as a reason to read the original.
card.limits: Even for informational material, a digest has passed through its editors' reading, and the more it condenses, the more that matters. A digest saves reading time, not the work of reading.

concepts.title: The more condensed, the harder to read
concepts.question: Why do the authors call reading digests sometimes the most demanding reading of all?

paragraphs: A digest saves us the extent of reading, not the work of it. We still have to read the digest, and the task is the one its editors performed on the originals. Their service profits us only if we read their digest as well as they read the sources.

That takes reading for understanding as well as for information. The more condensed a digest, the more selection has occurred. Cutting 1,000 pages to 900 matters little; cutting them to ten, or to one, makes the question of what was left out critical.

So the greater the condensation, the more we need to know the character of the condensor; the warning to let the reader beware applies with more force. Since we cannot consult the original, we must infer what was left out from the condensation itself, reading between the lines.
card.example: A one-paragraph news brief says a study found a drug ineffective. The study ran to forty pages, with exceptions for some patients. A careful reader asks who wrote the brief, what a forty-page study likely contained, and what qualifications such briefs tend to drop.
card.rule: The more a text has been condensed, the more you should ask who condensed it and infer what was left out.
card.limits: Inferring what was left out is guesswork without the original; when the original is at hand, checking it beats inference. And light condensation calls for little of this effort.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
concepts.title: Classics written for you
concepts.question: Why do the authors think a lay reader can read the great scientific classics when most modern science is closed to them?

paragraphs: Until about the end of the nineteenth century, the major scientific books, by writers such as Galileo, Newton and Darwin, were written for a lay audience. Educated people were expected to read science along with history and philosophy, and no field was fenced off from them.

Today science is mostly written by experts for experts. That speeds research, because specialists reach the frontier of a problem quickly, but a serious paper usually assumes so much training that an outsider cannot read it at all. The authors see philosophy, economics and even history drifting the same way.

So the authors limit their advice to two kinds of reading: the great classics and modern popularizations. They urge you to try at least some classics. None, they say, is impossibly difficult, not even Newton's Principia, if you are willing to make the effort.
card.example: A reader curious about evolution finds a current journal article on gene regulation unreadable. Darwin, writing for the educated public of his day, set out the founding problem of the same field in ordinary prose, and his book is within her reach.
card.rule: Turn to the great scientific classics, which were written for lay readers, and attempt them rather than assuming they are beyond you.
card.limits: The advice does not reach modern specialist monographs, which assume training a lay reader lacks; the authors say they cannot help with those. And within reach means with effort, not without it.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
concepts.title: State the scientist's problem
concepts.question: Which rule of analytical reading do the authors single out as most helpful for a scientific classic, and why does it fit science?

paragraphs: The most helpful advice the authors give for scientific classics is a rule you already know from analytical reading: state, as precisely as you can, the problem the author tried to solve. The rule holds for every expository book, but they call it particularly relevant to science and mathematics.

A scientific classic is built to answer a question about nature, and its experiments, measurements and proofs serve that question. Once you can say what the question was, each detail has a place, even details you cannot yet follow.
A statement of the problem is a question, not a topic. Light names a subject; why white light spreads into colours through a prism names a problem.
card.example: Harvey's book on the circulation of the blood. A useful statement of its problem: where does the blood go once the heart pumps it out, and how does it get back? With that question in mind, each dissection and measurement he reports has a job to do.
card.rule: Before anything else in a scientific or mathematical book, state in a sentence or two the problem the author was trying to solve.
card.limits: Stating the problem starts the reading but does not finish it: you still need the terms, propositions and evidence. And a vague statement, such as he studied blood, names a subject rather than a problem.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
concepts.title: Read for the problems and their background
concepts.question: If not to master the subject, what is a lay reader of a scientific classic reading it for?

paragraphs: As a lay reader you do not read the classics to become knowledgeable in their subjects in a contemporary sense; much in them has since been corrected, and a modern textbook teaches the current state of a subject better. You read them to understand the history and philosophy of science: how science came to be and what kind of activity it is.

The authors call this the layman's responsibility toward science, and say how to meet it: become aware of the problems the great scientists were trying to solve, and also of the background of those problems, meaning what was known, assumed or puzzling when the author wrote.

Scientists now take this seriously too. The history of science, once looked down on, has become a respected field, and research into Newton's work and personality has grown into what has been called the Newton industry.
card.example: Reading Copernicus, a lay reader gains little by checking his planetary tables against modern data. She gains much by asking what difficulties the earth-centred system posed for astronomers of his day and why a sun-centred arrangement seemed to answer them.
card.rule: Read a scientific classic to learn what problems its author faced and against what background, not to master the subject as it stands today.
card.limits: This purpose suits a lay reader. A student facing an examination in the subject, or anyone who needs current results, is better served by a modern textbook or the current literature.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
concepts.title: Tracing the strands of science
concepts.question: What do you gain by tracing how a science's facts, assumptions, principles and proofs connect?

paragraphs: To follow the strands of scientific development is to trace how facts, assumptions, principles and proofs depend on one another: which facts a principle rests on, which assumptions a proof needs, which earlier results a new one builds on.

The authors give three reasons this is worth doing. It shows human reason at work where it has probably had most success. It dispels some of the apparent unintelligibility of science. And, most important, it belongs to education, whose central aim since Socrates has been to free the mind through the discipline of wonder.
The result is that science stops looking like a list of facts handed down by authorities and starts looking like a chain of reasons that you can follow and check.
card.example: A reader knows that blood circulates. Tracing the strand, she finds Harvey's measured fact (the heart pushes out more blood in an hour than the whole body holds), his assumption that the body cannot make and use up blood that fast, and his conclusion that the same blood must return. The result now feels reasoned, not handed down.
card.rule: Trace how a science's facts, assumptions, principles and proofs are linked, so that its results become intelligible.
card.limits: Tracing strands is slow and serves understanding, not quick use: if you need a result to act on today, a reliable modern statement of it serves better. Collecting results without their links is not tracing at all.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
concepts.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
concepts.title: What a scientific book reports
concepts.question: What makes a book scientific in the authors' sense, and what kind of problem does every such book try to solve?

paragraphs: By a scientific book the authors mean a report of findings or conclusions in some field of research, whether the research was done by experiment in a laboratory or by observing nature as it is found, outside the laboratory.

The scientific problem, they say, is always of one kind: to describe the phenomena as accurately as possible, and to trace the interconnections between different kinds of phenomena. A scientific author is doing two jobs at once, careful description and showing how one kind of event bears on another.
This gives the rule of stating the problem a shape for science: ask which phenomena the author is describing, and which connections between kinds of phenomena he is trying to establish.
card.example: A naturalist records for years the dates on which birds in a valley lay their eggs, and also logs spring temperatures. Recording the laying dates accurately is the first job. Showing that warmer springs go with earlier laying traces a connection between two kinds of phenomena.
card.rule: Read a scientific book as a report of research, and ask which phenomena it describes and which connections between kinds of phenomena it traces.
card.limits: A book that reports no research, or that argues about what people ought to do, is not scientific in this sense, even if it borrows scientific words. Using the vocabulary of science does not make a book a report of findings.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
concepts.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
concepts.title: Assumed versus established
concepts.question: How do the authors suggest you detect and allow for the bias in a great scientific work?

paragraphs: The great works of science contain no oratory or propaganda: they do not try to move you by emotion or by appeals to your interests. They may still have a bias, in the sense of initial presuppositions, things the author takes for granted before his argument begins.

You detect that bias, and take account of it, by separating what the author assumes from what he establishes through argument. In effect you keep two lists as you read: the starting points he asks you to grant, and the conclusions he works to prove from evidence and reasoning.

The two lists tell you where to aim your questions. An established conclusion can be checked against the evidence and reasoning offered for it; an assumption must be weighed on its own, since the book does not argue for it.
card.example: A physiologist's book takes for granted that living bodies obey the same physical laws as non-living matter, then shows by measurements that working muscles give off heat. The first claim goes on the assumed list; the second, with its measurements, on the established list.
card.rule: Separate what a scientific author assumes from what he establishes by argument, and so detect and allow for his initial bias.
card.limits: Bias in this sense is not a fault to remove; every science starts from some presuppositions. Finding an assumption does not show the book is wrong, only where its conclusions rest on something unproved.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
concepts.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
concepts.title: Objectivity as confessed bias
concepts.question: According to the authors, what makes a scientific author objective, if not freedom from bias?

paragraphs: A common picture of the objective scientist is someone who comes to nature with no presuppositions at all. The authors reject that picture: scientific objectivity is not the absence of initial bias, but is reached by frank confession of it.

So the more objective a scientific author is, the more often he will say outright that he is asking you to take this or that for granted. Phrases such as we shall assume, let it be granted, or we take as given are signs of objectivity, not of weakness.
This helps the reader. An author who confesses his presuppositions has done much of the work of separating assumptions from conclusions for you.
card.example: Two reports on the same drug trial. One says: we assume patients took the pills as directed, since we could not check. The other never mentions the matter. The first is the more objective, though both may rest on the same assumption.
card.rule: Judge a scientific author's objectivity by how frankly he states what he asks you to take for granted, not by whether he seems to assume nothing.
card.limits: Confession makes an assumption visible; it does not make it true. A frankly stated assumption may still be one you reject, and confessing it does not excuse the reader from weighing it.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
concepts.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
concepts.title: Technical terms, general propositions
concepts.question: How do the leading terms and main propositions of a scientific book differ from those of a history?

paragraphs: The leading terms of a scientific work are usually carried by uncommon or technical words, such as momentum, valence or species. They are relatively easy to spot, and through them you can readily grasp the propositions they appear in.

The main propositions are always general. Science, in the authors' word, is not chronotopic, meaning tied to a particular time and place. A historian tells what happened then and there; a scientist tries to get away from locality in time and place and say how things generally are and behave.

So when you list a scientific book's main propositions, expect general statements. A particular observation, such as what one dish did on one Tuesday, is evidence for a proposition, not the proposition itself.
card.example: A chapter on gases uses the technical words pressure, volume and temperature. They lead you to its main proposition: at a fixed temperature, the pressure of a gas rises as its volume shrinks. The table of one afternoon's readings is evidence; the general statement is the proposition.
card.rule: Use a scientific book's technical words to find its leading terms, and expect its main propositions to be general statements, not tied to time or place.
card.limits: Technical words point to terms but do not define them; you still must learn the sense the author gives each. And a scientific book's particular reports are not its main propositions, though they matter as evidence.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
concepts.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
concepts.title: Follow the reported evidence
concepts.question: Why is following the reported evidence the first main difficulty in reading a scientific book?

paragraphs: The authors expect two main difficulties in a scientific book: the arguments and the mathematics. The first arises because science is primarily inductive. Its characteristic arguments establish a general proposition by appeal to observable evidence: a single case created by an experiment, or a large array of cases gathered by patient investigation.

Science also uses deductive arguments, in which a proposition is proved from other propositions already established; so far as proof goes, the authors say, science differs little from philosophy. It is the inductive argument that is characteristic of science.

To understand an inductive argument you must be able to follow the evidence the scientist reports as its basis: what was done or observed, and how it bears on the general claim. Accepting the conclusion without grasping that basis is not understanding the argument.
card.example: Pasteur concluded that the microbes that spoil broth come from the air, not from the broth itself. To follow the argument, a reader must grasp his evidence: broth in flasks with long, bent necks, which let air in but trapped dust, stayed clear, and spoiled once the neck was broken off.
card.rule: For each inductive argument in a scientific book, follow the experiment or observations the author reports as its basis before accepting its conclusion.
card.limits: Some arguments in science are deductive, proved from established propositions; there the task is to follow the reasoning rather than the evidence. And sometimes the book alone cannot make the evidence clear.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
concepts.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
concepts.title: Seeing the experiment yourself
concepts.question: What should you do when a scientific book alone cannot make its evidence clear to you?

paragraphs: Following the evidence is not always possible with nothing but the book in hand. A description of an experiment may take for granted that you have seen the apparatus or the specimen it describes.

Then, the authors say, the reader has one recourse: to get the necessary special experience at first hand. You may need to watch a laboratory demonstration, look at and handle apparatus like that in the book, or go to a museum to observe specimens or models.

There are classical experiments as well as classical books. Anyone who wants to understand the history of science should come to know its crucial experiments by direct experience. A classic becomes more intelligible once you have seen with your own eyes and done with your own hands what the scientist describes.
card.example: A reader cannot picture Galileo's account of balls rolling down a sloping board. At a science museum she times the balls on a working model herself, and his description of how the distance grows with each equal interval of time becomes clear.
card.rule: When the text fails to make a scientist's evidence clear, seek the experience it describes at first hand: a demonstration, apparatus, specimens, or the classical experiment itself.
card.limits: First-hand experience is for evidence the text cannot convey. Where the book makes its evidence clear, the text is enough, and the authors do not require you to repeat every step before you can start.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
concepts.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
concepts.title: Start with the illuminating parts
concepts.question: How can you take something worthwhile from a scientific classic such as Lavoisier's without reading all of it in detail?

paragraphs: Lavoisier's Elements of Chemistry, published in 1789, is no longer useful as a chemistry textbook; a student would be unwise to study it even for a high school examination. Yet its method was revolutionary, and its conception of a chemical element is still, on the whole, the one used today.
To receive those impressions you do not have to read the book through in detail. Some parts carry the main impression, and the Preface, with its emphasis on method in science, is one of them.

There Lavoisier says every physical science consists of facts, the ideas that represent them, and the words that express them, so a science cannot be improved without improving its language, nor the reverse. He improved chemistry by improving its nomenclature, as Newton had improved physics by ordering its language, developing the calculus on the way.
card.example: A reader with two evenings reads Lavoisier's Preface and the pages where he explains what he means by an element, passing quickly over the detailed accounts of his apparatus. She comes away knowing why his method mattered and what he meant by an element.
card.rule: Make a start on a scientific classic by reading its most illuminating parts, such as a preface on method, rather than waiting until you can follow every detail.
card.limits: Key parts give an impression of the book, not a full analytical reading of it. To judge a particular argument, you must read that argument's evidence and steps, not only the preface.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
concepts.title: The fear of mathematics
concepts.question: What explanations do the authors weigh for the common fear of mathematics, and what do they conclude about it?

paragraphs: Mathematics is the second main difficulty in scientific books. Many people are frightened of it and think they cannot read it at all. The authors admit no one is quite sure why.

Some psychologists speak of symbol blindness: an inability to set aside dependence on the concrete and follow the controlled shifting of symbols. The authors grant there may be something in this, but point out that words shift too, and because their shifts are more or less uncontrolled, words may be even harder to follow.

Others blame the teaching of mathematics, and the authors welcome research on teaching it better. Their own diagnosis is that we are not told early enough that mathematics is a language we can learn, nor how beautiful and satisfying it can be.
card.example: A reader who follows a lawyer's shifting use of the word reasonable across a long contract is tracking shifts that no rule controls. Following x through three lines of algebra, where each step obeys a stated rule, is in that respect the easier task.
card.rule: Do not take your fear of mathematics as proof that you cannot read it; its symbols shift by rule, which words do not.
card.limits: This does not make all mathematics easy: advanced work assumes much prior learning. The point is that the elementary barrier is lower than fear suggests, not that effort is unnecessary.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
concepts.title: Mathematics as a language
concepts.question: In what sense is mathematics a language, and what does that imply about learning to read it?

paragraphs: Part of the trouble, the authors say, is that we are not told early enough that mathematics is a language, which we can learn like any other, our own included. We learn our own language twice, first to speak it and then to read it. Mathematics, being almost wholly a written language, has to be learned only once.

Learning any new written language puts us back at the elementary level of reading, where the task is to recognize arbitrary symbols and memorize certain relations among them. Even good readers return to that level whenever they meet an unknown word or a puzzling sentence.

So mathematics has its own vocabulary, grammar and syntax, and the beginner must learn them, memorizing certain symbols and relations. The language differs, but the task is in principle no harder than learning to read English, French or German, and at the elementary level it may even be easier.
card.example: A reader meets a large Greek letter sigma with small numbers above and below it. Like a new word, it has to be learned: it means add up the terms as a counter runs from the lower number to the upper. Once that is memorized, the line reads like a sentence.
card.rule: Treat mathematics as a written language: learn its symbols and the rules for combining them as you would the vocabulary and grammar of a foreign language.
card.limits: Learning the vocabulary and syntax lets you read at the elementary level; it does not by itself give the understanding a proof or argument requires, which belongs to the higher levels of reading.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
concepts.title: A language without feelings
concepts.question: Why, according to the authors, can two people understand a mathematical statement alike more readily than ordinary talk?

paragraphs: Any language, the authors say, is a medium of communication among people on subjects they can mutually comprehend. The subjects of ordinary discourse are mainly emotional facts and relations, and these are not entirely comprehensible by any two different persons.

Two people can, however, comprehend a third thing outside them and emotionally separated from both, such as an electrical circuit, an isosceles triangle or a syllogism. Trouble begins mainly when we invest such things with emotional connotations.
Mathematics lets us avoid that. Properly used, its terms, propositions and equations carry no emotional connotations, which helps two readers understand a mathematical statement in the same way.
card.example: Two neighbours argue over a proposed tower: one hears progress, the other loss. They can agree at once that it is 90 metres high and how long its shadow will be at noon in midwinter. The measurement and the geometry carry no feelings; the quarrel lies in what each attaches to them.
card.rule: Read mathematical terms and equations without emotional connotations, as statements about a third thing that writer and reader can both comprehend.
card.limits: The point holds for mathematics properly used. A number placed in a heated argument, such as a tax rate or a casualty figure, can pick up strong feelings, and is then no longer read as pure mathematics.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
concepts.title: Constructions, theorems and their order
concepts.question: What two kinds of proposition does Euclid's Elements contain, and why do constructions come before the first theorem?

paragraphs: The authors suggest beginning mathematics with Euclid's Elements of Geometry, which they call one of the most lucid and beautiful works of any kind. Its propositions are of two kinds: problems of construction, which require that something be done, and theorems, which require that something be proved.
Euclid marks the difference at the end of each proposition. A construction ends with Q.E.F., Latin for what was required to be done; a theorem ends with Q.E.D., what was required to be proved.

The first three propositions of Book I are constructions, because the theorems need them. Proposition 5, that the base angles of an isosceles triangle (one with two equal sides) are equal, uses Proposition 3, cutting a shorter line from a longer. Proposition 3 uses Proposition 2, which uses Proposition 1.
card.example: Reading Book I, ask of each early construction what later proposition needs it. Working back from Proposition 5 through 3, 2 and 1 shows that the opening of the book is not a random collection of exercises but groundwork laid for the first theorems.
card.rule: In a mathematical work, tell constructions, which are to be done, from theorems, which are to be proved, and trace which earlier propositions each proof uses.
card.limits: The dependence is not always visible at once: the authors note it does not show in the first four propositions and appears only in the fifth. And dependence is not the only reason constructions come early.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
concepts.title: Assumed or proved possible
concepts.question: How does a construction proposition differ from a postulate, when both say a geometrical operation can be performed?

paragraphs: The authors give constructions a second purpose. Constructions resemble postulates: both assert that a geometrical operation can be performed. The difference is that in a postulate the possibility is assumed, while in a construction proposition it is proved, and the proof uses the postulates.

So a construction can show that a defined figure exists, given the postulates. Euclid defines the equilateral triangle in Definition 20, and one might wonder whether there is any such thing. Proposition 1 shows that if there are straight lines and circles, as the postulates grant, then there are equilateral triangles.
The authors set aside the thorny question of whether mathematical objects exist at all. What a construction gives is conditional: from the possibilities assumed, a new one follows.
card.example: A building manual takes for granted that standard bricks and mortar can be had and laid. It then shows, step by step, how to raise an arch from them. The bricks are assumed; the arch's possibility is demonstrated from them.
card.rule: When a mathematical work says an operation can be performed, ask whether that possibility is assumed as a postulate or proved as a construction from the postulates.
card.limits: A construction proves possibility only relative to the postulates; it does not settle whether mathematical objects exist in some further sense, a question the authors leave aside.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
concepts.title: What a proof proves
concepts.question: What exactly has been proved when a Euclidean theorem such as Proposition 5 is proved?

paragraphs: When Proposition 5 reaches its conclusion, through steps that refer to earlier propositions and the postulates, it has been proved. What has been shown is this: if something is true (we have an isosceles triangle), and if further things are valid (the definitions, postulates and earlier propositions), then something else is true (its base angles are equal).

The proposition asserts this if-then relationship. It does not assert that the hypothesis is true, nor that the conclusion is true except when the hypothesis is. Nor is the connection seen to be true until the proof is done. It is the truth of the connection that is proved, and nothing else.

The authors find this beautiful: a truly logical exposition of a truly limited problem. Ordinary discourse, even good philosophy, finds it hard to limit its problems so tightly or to use logic so plainly.
card.example: Proved: if a triangle has two equal sides, its base angles are equal. Not proved: that the roof truss in front of you has two equal sides. Measure the truss; only if its sides are equal does the theorem tell you anything about its angles.
card.rule: Read a proved proposition as asserting only that its conclusion follows from its hypothesis, given the definitions, postulates and earlier propositions.
card.limits: The theorem says nothing about whether any particular figure meets its hypothesis; that has to be found out separately. And until the proof is complete, even the connection is not yet established.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
concepts.title: Real premises need checking
concepts.question: Why must you examine a syllogism's assumptions in a way you need not with a Euclidean theorem?

paragraphs: Compare Proposition 5 with a simple syllogism: all animals are mortal; all men are animals; therefore all men are mortal. Treated as pure reasoning it is as satisfying as Euclid: granting that there are animals and men and that animals are mortal, the conclusion follows with the same certainty.

The trouble is that there really are animals and men. The syllogism assumes something about real things, something that may or may not be true, so we have to examine its assumptions in a way we do not in mathematics.

Euclid's proposition does not suffer from this. It does not matter to him whether there are isosceles triangles: if there are, and if they are defined in a given way, their base angles are equal, now and forever.
card.example: All of a bank's branches open at nine; the Elm Street office is one of its branches; so it opens at nine. The logic is as tight as Euclid's, but whether you find the door open depends on whether the first premise is true of the real branches this week.
card.rule: When an argument's premises are about real things, examine whether they are true, since valid form secures only the connection, not the conclusion.
card.limits: This does not make arguments about real things less logical; their form can be as sound as Euclid's. Checking premises is added work that the subject brings, not a sign of bad reasoning.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
concepts.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
concepts.title: Pencil or skip: it depends on your aim
concepts.question: How should your handling of the mathematics differ between a mathematics book and a scientific book that uses mathematics?

paragraphs: Mathematics is one of the main obstacles in scientific books. First, the authors say, you can probably read elementary mathematics better than you think. Spend several evenings with Euclid and much of your fear should go; then glance at other Greek mathematicians, Archimedes, Apollonius and Nicomachus. They are not very difficult, and you can skip.

Second, your intention decides how you read. If you are reading a mathematical book for itself, read it from beginning to end, pencil in hand; writing in the margins and on scratch paper is more necessary here than with any other kind of book.

If you are reading a scientific work that has mathematics in it, skipping is often the better part of valour. Usually you can understand something of the matter without going deeply into the mathematics.
card.example: Mia is reading an introduction to number theory to learn number theory, so she works each step on scrap paper. Leo is reading Newton's Principia to see what problem Newton solved and how, so he reads the statements and passes over most of the working.
card.rule: Read a mathematics book for itself from beginning to end with a pencil, but skip freely through the mathematics of a scientific work you are reading for its science.
card.limits: Skipping serves only while the mathematics is not your object. If a claim you care about rests on a particular calculation, or you mean to learn the mathematics, the working has to be followed.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
concepts.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
concepts.title: Reading the Principia selectively
concepts.question: How do the authors suggest a lay reader work through Newton's Principia without working every proof?

paragraphs: The Principia contains many propositions, both constructions and theorems, but you need not read all of them in detail, especially the first time through. Read the statement of each proposition and glance down its proof to get an idea of how it is done.

Read the statements of the lemmas (propositions proved to help prove others) and corollaries (results that follow at once from one already proved). And read the scholiums, which discuss how the propositions relate to one another and to the work as a whole. You then begin to see how Newton's system is built: what comes first and second, and how the parts fit.

Go through the whole work this way, avoiding the diagrams if they trouble you and only glancing at much of the interstitial matter, but be sure to find and read the passages where Newton makes his main points. One is the General Scholium closing Book III, which sums up the work and states the great problem of almost all later physics.
card.example: A reader spends a week on the Principia. She reads each statement, skims each proof for its method, reads the scholiums closely, and saves her slowest reading for the General Scholium. She ends able to outline how Newton's system is put together, though she has worked few proofs.
card.rule: In a mathematical scientific classic, read each proposition's statement, glance at its proof, read the lemmas, corollaries and scholiums, and be sure to find the main passages.
card.limits: This yields the structure of the system and its main points, not mastery of its proofs. Anyone who needs to check or use a particular result must work that proof in full.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
concepts.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
concepts.title: Repeat the simple experiments
concepts.question: How do the authors suggest reading a classic like Newton's Optics, whose pages look mathematical but mostly describe experiments?

paragraphs: Newton's Optics contains very little mathematics, though at first glance it seems to, because its pages are sprinkled with diagrams. The diagrams illustrate Newton's experiments: holes letting sunlight into a dark room, prisms set to intercept the beam, sheets of white paper placed to catch the colours.

Where the experiments are simple, you can repeat some of them yourself, and the authors say this is fun, for the colours are beautiful and the descriptions very clear. Besides the experiments, read the statements of the theorems or propositions and the discussions at the end of each of the three Books, where Newton sums up his discoveries and suggests their consequences.
The end of Book III is famous: there Newton makes statements about the scientific enterprise itself that are well worth reading.
card.example: A reader sets a glass prism in a sunny window and lets the spread of colours fall on a white card. She then puts a second prism in the path of one colour and sees that it does not split again. Newton's account of the same steps now reads as a record of something she has seen.
card.rule: When a scientific classic describes simple experiments, repeat some of them, and read its proposition statements and the author's summing-up discussions.
card.limits: Not every experiment can be repeated at home; some need apparatus or materials a reader lacks, and some would be unsafe. Then demonstrations, museums or the descriptions themselves must serve.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
concepts.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
concepts.title: When there is no mathematics
concepts.question: Why can a scientific classic without mathematics be harder to read, and what should you keep in mind when reading one?

paragraphs: Scientific writers use mathematics mainly for its preciseness, clarity and limitedness. So, oddly, even a reader terrified of mathematics may find its absence causes more trouble. Galileo's Two New Sciences, on the strength of materials and on motion, is hard for modern readers because it is presented not mainly as mathematics but as a dialogue.

The dialogue form suits the stage, and philosophy in a master's hands such as Plato's, but the authors think it not really appropriate to science. It is hard to discover what Galileo is saying, though when you do, you find he is stating revolutionary things.

Not all classics use or need mathematics: there are Hippocrates on medicine, Harvey on the circulation of the blood, Gilbert on magnets. They can be read without much difficulty if you keep in mind that your primary obligation is not to become competent in the subject but to understand the problem.
card.example: Hippocrates needs no mathematics, and his view of medicine can be found in the text: medicine is the art of keeping people well rather than of curing them once they are sick. With that in mind, his varied advice on diet, air and exercise falls into place.
card.rule: In a non-mathematical scientific classic, work to discover what is being claimed, keeping in mind that your obligation is to understand the problem, not to master the subject.
card.limits: The difficulty lies in the form, not in the lack of mathematics as such: a plainly argued treatise such as Harvey's can read easily. And understanding the problem does not excuse you from finding what the author actually claims.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
concepts.title: What popularizations leave out
concepts.question: Why should popularizations be easier for a reader who has tried the classics, and why does the lay reader need them?

paragraphs: Because science today is written by experts for experts, and no one can become expert in every field, the general reader must fall back on scientific popularizations: books and articles written for a wide audience, not only for specialists. Some are good and some bad; it matters both to know the difference and to read the good ones with understanding.

If you have read some classics, popularizations should give you little trouble. Though about science, they generally skirt the two main problems of an original scientific work: they contain relatively few descriptions of experiments, reporting results instead, and relatively little mathematics, unless they are popular books about mathematics itself.
Popular articles are usually easier than popular books, though not always. The authors praise Scientific American and the somewhat more technical weekly Science.
card.example: A magazine piece reports that a new vaccine sharply cut infections in a trial. It does not say how the trial was run or give the statistics. The reader is spared both main difficulties, but receives the result without the evidence for it.
card.rule: Expect a popularization to report results rather than describe experiments and to keep mathematics to a minimum, and read it knowing what it leaves out.
card.limits: Easier is not effortless, as the next ideas show. And a popular book about mathematics itself will contain mathematics, so the second simplification does not apply to it.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
concepts.title: At the mercy of the reporter
concepts.question: What risk do the authors see in learning science from even the best popular magazines?

paragraphs: Even excellent, carefully and responsibly edited publications such as Scientific American or Science pose a problem the authors raised about reading current events: you are at the mercy of reporters who filter the information for you.

If the reporters are good, you are fortunate. If they are not, you have almost no recourse, because the popular account is all you have; the original research is written for specialists, and you cannot check it yourself.

So the quality of what you learn depends on a filter you cannot inspect. Reading popular science well includes remembering that you are reading a report, shaped by someone's choices about what to keep and what to leave out.
card.example: A news story says a common food doubles the risk of a disease. The study itself, written for specialists, found a small rise in one group and called for more research. A reader with only the news story has no way to see what the filter removed.
card.rule: When you read popular science, remember that a reporter has filtered the findings for you, and weigh the account knowing you depend on that filter.
card.limits: The point is dependence, not distrust: the authors praise good popular journals, and a good reporter serves you well. Where an original source is within your reach, reading it removes the filter.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
concepts.title: Reading popular science actively
concepts.question: Why do the authors say active reading matters more for popular science than almost anywhere else, and what does it involve?

paragraphs: Scientific popularizations are never easy reading in the way a story is, or seems to be. Even a three-page article on DNA with no experiments, diagrams or formulas demands considerable effort; you cannot read it for understanding without keeping your mind awake. So active reading matters more here than almost anywhere else.

The familiar rules apply with particular force: identify the subject matter; discover how the whole relates to its parts; come to terms and find the propositions and arguments; and work at understanding before you criticize or assess the work's significance.

Short articles are usually mainly informational: you must follow the author's account, but often need go no further. Excellent popular books, such as Whitehead's Introduction to Mathematics or Barnett's The Universe and Dr. Einstein, require more; their writing is compact and needs constant attention.
card.example: A two-page piece on how vaccines train the immune system: name its subject, see how its sections serve the main point, mark its key terms, such as antigen and antibody, and state its main claim before asking whether it convinces you.
card.rule: Read popular science actively: identify its subject, relate its parts to the whole, find its terms, propositions and arguments, and understand before you judge.
card.limits: The depth varies: a short informational article may need only careful following of its account, while a popular book calls for fuller analysis. Active reading does not mean doubting every sentence; criticism comes after understanding.

concepts.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
concepts.title: Theory that bears on action
concepts.question: Why might a theoretical popular science book still call on its reader to act, or to stay informed?

paragraphs: Commoner's The Closing Circle, on the environmental crisis, is not a practical book in the sense of Chapter 13, yet its theoretical conclusions have important consequences.
