The environment is our own; if it is in crisis, we are involved, and the thing to do in a crisis is usually to act in a certain way, or stop acting in a certain way.

A careful reader will not miss such implications, even where an author does not spell them out, though Commoner does. Barnett's The Universe and Dr. Einstein, a theoretical history of research into the atom, also had practical consequences when it appeared, amid fear of atomic war.

Even without such urgency, the authors see a practical necessity to read theoretical works on the great achievements of the age, such as atomic physics, which promise much and threaten much. Whitehead's Introduction to Mathematics shows the attentive reader that the mathematician is an ordinary man, not a magician.
card.example: A popular book explains, in purely theoretical terms, how bacteria become resistant when antibiotics are overused. It gives no advice. A careful reader still draws the practical conclusion: if overuse breeds resistance and resistance threatens us, taking antibiotics only when needed is part of the response.
card.rule: When a theoretical popular book bears on your own situation, work out what its conclusions imply you should do or stop doing.
card.limits: Drawing implications is not finding rules in the book: the work stays theoretical, and the step to action is the reader's inference, which needs checking. Not every theoretical book implies an action; some matter for the understanding they give.

concepts.title: The child's kind of question
concepts.question: What kind of question do great philosophical books share with children, and how does it differ from most adult curiosity?

paragraphs: The authors open with the questions children ask: why are there people, what makes the cat tick. What sets the child apart is not how many questions he asks but their character. Adults stay curious, but their curiosity narrows: they want to know whether something is so, while the child wants to know why.

The authors suspect parents and schools: children are told there is no answer, or to stop asking, and learn that too much curiosity is impolite. By college most people ask only for information, the kind of question an encyclopedia can settle.

One remarkable thing about the great philosophical books, the authors say, is that they ask the same profound questions children ask. Reading them well starts with spotting that question beneath the technical surface.
card.example: A news story reports that a city banned cars from its centre. An information question asks whether traffic fell. A child's question asks why anyone should give up a convenience for a common good at all. Only the second is the kind a philosophy book pursues.
card.rule: In a philosophical book, look for the basic why-question a child might ask, not only for information about whether something is so.
card.limits: Not every why-question is philosophical: why the bus is late has a factual answer. The child's question matters here when no fact-finding could settle it. And keeping the child's questions does not mean thinking like a child.

concepts.title: Simple questions, wise replies
concepts.question: What do the authors mean by asking childishly simple questions while giving maturely wise replies?

paragraphs: The authors do not ask you to think as a child; children cannot understand existence, if anyone can. They ask you to see, wonder and ask as children do, while bringing adult understanding to the answers.

The complexities of adult life get in the way of the truth. The great philosophers cleared them away and saw simple distinctions, simple once stated and very hard to see before. The rare person who keeps a child's view of the world, and understands maturely what keeping it means, is the one likely to add something important.
For a reader this sets two tests. Is the question basic, stripped of the clutter that hides it? And is the answer worked out with care, rather than as naive as the question?
card.example: A manager asks what a weekly meeting is for. The question is childishly simple, yet it cuts through habit and office politics. A wise reply then weighs the purposes a meeting can serve and which of them this one meets, instead of cancelling it on impulse.
card.rule: Ask questions as plainly as a child, and answer them with mature, careful reasoning.
card.limits: Simplicity belongs to the question, not the answer: a childish answer to a simple question is not what the authors praise. And a distinction that looks simple once stated may have taken great effort to see.

concepts.title: Questions about being
concepts.question: What kinds of questions does a philosopher ask about being or existence, and why are they hard?

paragraphs: One family of basic questions concerns being, or existence. What is the difference between existing and not existing? What do all existing things have in common? Are there different modes of being: do some things exist only in or for the mind, and others outside it, whether known or not?

Others follow. Does everything exist physically, or can something exist apart from matter? Does everything change, or is something immutable? Does anything exist necessarily, or might everything that exists not have existed? Is the realm of the possible larger than the realm of the actual?

Such questions are easy to state and understand but enormously hard to answer, so hard that some philosophers, especially recent ones, hold that they cannot be answered satisfactorily. Knowing this family lets you see when a book is exploring being itself.
card.example: An essay asks whether a nation exists the way a mountain does, or only in the minds of its citizens. Under its political surface it asks about modes of being: whether some things exist only for the mind.
card.rule: When a book asks what it is for things to exist, and in what ways they can exist, recognise that it is asking questions about being.
card.limits: Ease of stating is no guide to ease of answering. And whether a particular thing exists, such as a newly reported animal, is a matter for investigation, not a question about being itself.

concepts.title: Questions about change
concepts.question: What does a philosopher ask about change, and how do those questions relate to questions about being?

paragraphs: A second family of questions turns from being to becoming. The things we say exist also change: they come to be and pass away, move from place to place, grow or shrink, and alter in quality, as an apple changes colour when it ripens.

What is involved in any change? Does something endure while some aspect of it alters? When you learn, you change in what you know yet stay the same person; otherwise you could not be said to have changed. Is that true of birth and death too, or only of motion, growth and alteration?

Further questions: how many kinds of change are there, do the same causes act in all of them, what is a cause of change, and are the causes of becoming the same as the causes of being? A philosopher of change also tries to relate becoming to being.
card.example: A biography says a soldier came home from war a different man. A philosopher asks: different in what respect? If nothing endured, whose change was it? His habits and moods altered, but something must have stayed for him to be the one who changed.
card.rule: When a book asks what endures and what alters in change, how many kinds of change there are and what causes them, recognise questions about becoming.
card.limits: Asking what caused a particular change, such as why this bridge rusted, is a question for investigation. The philosophical question asks what any change involves and what a cause of change is.

concepts.title: The wider speculative questions
concepts.question: Beyond being and change, which other theoretical questions do philosophers ask, and what makes a question speculative?

paragraphs: The authors only list the rest of the theoretical range: necessity and contingency; the material and the immaterial; the physical and the non-physical; freedom and indeterminacy; the powers of the human mind; the nature and extent of human knowledge; the freedom of the will.

All of these, like the questions about being and change, are speculative or theoretical in the sense the book gave those words earlier: they ask what is or what happens, not what should be done. Whether the will is free asks about the world, even though the answer bears on conduct.
Knowing the list helps you place a book quickly. If its leading question concerns what the mind can do or how far knowledge reaches, you are in theoretical philosophy, whatever its examples.
card.example: A popular book on decision-making spends many pages on whether our choices are fixed in advance by brain chemistry. Its leading question, whether the will is free, is theoretical: it asks what is the case about human choice, not how to choose well.
card.rule: Treat questions about necessity, the immaterial, freedom, the mind's powers and the reach of knowledge as theoretical, since they ask what is the case.
card.limits: A book can raise a theoretical question on the way to a practical one: a manual on habits may touch free will only to tell you how to change. Classify by the question the book mainly pursues, not by every topic it mentions.

concepts.title: Good and evil, right and wrong
concepts.question: What do philosophers ask about good and evil, and why do the authors treat good and evil and right and wrong as different pairs?

paragraphs: Philosophy is not limited to theoretical questions. Children care about the difference between good and bad, and adults keep wondering. Is there a universally valid distinction between good and evil? Are some things always good and others always bad, whatever the circumstances? Or, as Hamlet said, is nothing good or bad but thinking makes it so?

Good and evil are not the same as right and wrong; the two pairs seem to refer to different classes of things. Even if whatever is right is good, we probably do not feel that whatever is wrong is evil. Making that difference precise is itself a philosophical task.
When you read moral philosophy, notice which pair the author is using and whether he keeps them apart. The authors leave these questions open; they list them as the kind philosophy asks.
card.example: Arriving late to a friend's dinner without warning is wrong, a breach of what you owe, yet few would call it evil. A book that treats every wrong act as evil has merged two pairs the authors keep apart.
card.rule: In moral philosophy, ask whether the author treats good and evil as universal or relative, and check whether he keeps good and evil distinct from right and wrong.
card.limits: The authors raise these questions without answering them, so the chapter gives no verdict on whether good and evil are universal. And the pairs overlap: what is right may well be good, so distinct does not mean unrelated.

concepts.title: The order of goods
concepts.question: What questions about the many goods do philosophers ask, and why does the word good lead quickly into philosophy?

paragraphs: Good is an important philosophical word and an everyday one. Trying to say what it means, the authors warn, will draw you deep into philosophy before you know it.

There are many goods, as the authors prefer to put it. Can they be put in order? Are some more important than others? Do some depend on others? Are there circumstances in which goods conflict, so that choosing one means forgoing another?

These questions are practical in the book's sense: they bear on what to seek. When a book weighs health against wealth, or freedom against security, it is asking about the order of goods. Look for its ranking and the reasons it offers.
card.example: A city must choose between a hospital wing and a park on the same plot. Both are goods. The choice forces the questions whether one matters more, whether the park's value depends partly on health, and what is lost either way.
card.rule: When a book compares goods, look for how it ranks them, which it makes depend on others, and what it says to do when they conflict.
card.limits: Asking which phone gives more for the price compares means to one aim you already hold; the philosophical question asks how different goods stand to each other. And the authors pose these questions here; they do not rank the goods.

concepts.title: The wider practical questions
concepts.question: Which further questions belong to the practical side of philosophy, and what do they have in common?

paragraphs: Again the authors only list the rest of the practical range: duties and obligations; virtues and vices; happiness and the purpose or goal of life; justice and rights in human relations; the state and its relation to the individual; the good society, the just polity and the just economy; war and peace.

What these share with good and evil, right and wrong and the order of goods is that they concern what ought to be done or sought. Each asks about a goal or a standard of conduct, for a person or for a community.
The list helps you place a book. A treatise on what citizens owe the state, or on whether a war can be just, is asking a practical philosophical question, even if it is full of history.
card.example: A book on taxation spends chapters on rates and collection methods, but its central question is whether a just economy may take more from the rich. That leading question belongs to the practical side of philosophy, among the questions about the just economy.
card.rule: Treat questions about duties, virtues, happiness, justice, the state, the good society and war and peace as practical, since they ask what ought to be done or sought.
card.limits: A book can mention justice or war while asking only what happened or how something works, as a history of a battle does. The topic word is not enough; ask whether the book's question is about what ought to be.

concepts.title: Two divisions: theoretical and normative
concepts.question: How do the authors divide philosophy into two main parts, and how can you tell which part a book belongs to?

paragraphs: The two groups of questions mark the two main divisions of philosophy. Questions about being and becoming concern what is or happens in the world; they belong to theoretical, or speculative, philosophy.

Questions about good and evil, right and wrong, concern what ought to be done or sought. They belong to the division sometimes called practical and, the authors say, more accurately called normative. The word points to norms: standards of what ought to be.
To place a philosophical book, find its leading question and ask whether it is about what is or about what ought to be. That decides the division, and the finer sorting into branches depends on it.
card.example: A book asking whether time is real belongs to theoretical philosophy. A book asking how we ought to treat future generations belongs to normative philosophy, even though both are about time in some way.
card.rule: Place a philosophical book in theoretical philosophy if its question is about what is or happens, and in normative philosophy if it is about what ought to be done or sought.
card.limits: Many books touch both: a normative argument may rest on a theoretical claim about human nature. Place the book by its leading question, and expect theoretical premises inside normative works.

concepts.title: Normative philosophy versus how-to books
concepts.question: How does a work of normative philosophy differ from a cookbook or a driving manual?

paragraphs: Books that tell you how to make or do something, like a cookbook or a driver's manual, need not argue that you ought to cook well or drive well. They assume you want the result and tell you how to succeed.
Books of normative philosophy are concerned first with the goals everyone ought to seek, such as a good life or a good society. Because they cannot assume you accept those goals, they argue for them.

And they go no further than prescribing, in the most universal terms, the means that ought to be used. A how-to book gets down to particular steps; normative philosophy stops at principles that hold for all.
card.example: A fitness guide assumes you want to be fit and lays out a twelve-week plan. A work of normative philosophy asks whether health belongs to a good life and what place it should have among other goods; it would not tell you how many push-ups to do.
card.rule: Ask whether a book argues that you ought to seek its goal and stays at universal means, or assumes the goal and gives particular steps.
card.limits: The two can sit in one book: a treatise may argue for a goal and then add practical advice. And a how-to book is not worse for assuming its goal; it does a different job.

concepts.title: Metaphysics, nature and knowledge
concepts.question: How do you tell whether a work of theoretical philosophy is metaphysics, philosophy of nature or epistemology?

paragraphs: The questions also mark branches within each division. A theoretical work is metaphysical if it is mainly about being or existence. It belongs to the philosophy of nature if it is about becoming: the nature and kinds of change, their conditions and causes.

If its main concern is knowledge, what is involved in knowing anything, the causes, extent and limits of human knowledge, its certainties and uncertainties, it is epistemology, another name for theory of knowledge.
To classify, ask which of the three a book mainly pursues: being, change or knowledge. Many books touch all three; the main concern decides the branch.
card.example: A book asking whether we can be certain the world exists outside our minds is epistemology, since its question is about the limits of knowledge, even though it mentions existence. A book on what time and motion are is philosophy of nature.
card.rule: Classify a theoretical work by its main concern: being for metaphysics, change for philosophy of nature, knowledge for epistemology.
card.limits: The branches are not sealed off: a question about knowledge may lead into one about being. And philosophy of nature is not natural science; it asks what change is, not how fast a body falls.

concepts.title: Ethics and politics
concepts.question: How do you tell whether a work of normative philosophy is ethics or political philosophy?

paragraphs: Within normative philosophy the main distinction is between ethics and politics. Ethics covers the good life and what is right or wrong in the conduct of the individual.
Politics, or political philosophy, covers the good society and the conduct of the individual in relation to the community.
Both are normative: both ask what ought to be done or sought. The difference lies in what is in view: one person's life, or a community and the person's place in it.
card.example: An essay on whether a person should forgive a friend's betrayal is ethics. An essay on whether a state may punish citizens for breaking unfair laws is political philosophy, since it concerns the individual in relation to the community.
card.rule: Classify a normative work as ethics if it asks about the individual's good life and conduct, and as politics if it asks about the good society and the individual's relation to it.
card.limits: The line is not a wall: a citizen's duty to obey concerns one person, yet it is conduct toward the community, so it falls under politics. Many great works treat both together.

concepts.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
concepts.title: First-order and second-order questions
concepts.question: What separates a first-order philosophical question from a second-order one?

paragraphs: For brevity the authors call questions about what is and happens in the world, or about what people ought to do or seek, first-order questions. The theoretical and normative questions met so far are all first-order.
Second-order questions are about our first-order knowledge: about the content of our thinking when we try to answer first-order questions, and about the ways we express such thoughts in language.
The test is the target. A first-order question aims at the world or at conduct; a second-order question aims at our thought or talk about them.
card.example: Is it wrong to break a promise? is first-order. What do we mean when we call an act wrong? is second-order: it asks about our moral language, not directly about promises.
card.rule: Ask whether a philosophical question aims at the world or at conduct, which is first-order, or at our thought and language about them, which is second-order.
card.limits: The orders are linked: clarifying a word, a second-order task, can change how a first-order question is asked or answered. So a second-order study is not irrelevant to the large questions.

concepts.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
concepts.title: Why modern philosophy is hard to read
concepts.question: Why do the authors say modern philosophy is as hard for non-philosophers as science is for non-scientists?

paragraphs: The distinction explains what happened to philosophy in recent times, as the authors saw it. Most professional philosophers no longer believe philosophers can answer first-order questions. They attend to second-order questions, very often about the language in which thought is expressed.

Second-order questions are, almost by definition, of narrow appeal. And professional philosophers, like scientists, write for other experts. So philosophy, like contemporary science or mathematics, is no longer written for lay readers.

The result is that such philosophy is as hard for non-philosophers as science for non-scientists. The authors say they cannot advise you on reading modern philosophy while it keeps to second-order questions.
card.example: A reader picks up a recent journal article whose title uses a word she knows, truth, and finds it is about the logical form of sentences containing the word, written for specialists who know the debate. That is the kind of work the chapter's advice does not reach.
card.rule: Expect modern works confined to second-order questions and written for experts to be as hard as specialist science.
card.limits: This describes the profession as the authors saw it when writing, and it is a generalization: some modern philosophers write first-order books for lay readers. Judge each book by its questions and its audience, not by its date.

concepts.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
concepts.title: Criticism without abandonment
concepts.question: What do the authors welcome in modern philosophy's turn to second-order questions, and what do they regret?

paragraphs: The authors do not attack second-order work. Attending to our knowledge, thought and language is all to the good, they say, for it never hurts to be critical.

Their complaint is the wholesale giving up of first-order questions. Those are the questions most likely to interest lay readers, and abandoning them leaves the general reader with little written for him.
The balance this suggests for a reader: welcome careful criticism of words and thought, but do not let it replace the large questions about being, change and how to live.
card.example: A reading group spends a month on what the word freedom means and never returns to whether people are free. Clarifying the word was useful; letting the clarification replace the question is the loss the authors regret.
card.rule: Value critical attention to thought and language, but keep asking the first-order questions it serves.
card.limits: The complaint is about wholesale abandonment, not about any single second-order study; a book on the meaning of one word may be exactly what a first-order inquiry needs.

concepts.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
concepts.title: Classics written for the general reader
concepts.question: Which philosophical books do the authors say a lay reader can and should read, and why are they accessible?

paragraphs: Up to about 1930, or a little later, philosophical books were written for the general reader. Philosophers hoped their peers would read them, but they also wanted ordinary, intelligent men and women to read them.

Their reason: the questions they asked concerned everyone, so everyone should know what they thought. All the great classical works, from Plato onward, were written in this spirit, and they ask first-order questions.

The authors say these books are accessible; you can succeed in reading them if you wish to. It is no accident, they add, that the books asking first-order questions were the ones written mainly for lay readers. The rest of the chapter aims to help you read them.
card.example: A reader who wants to think about justice need not start with current journal debates. Plato's Republic asks what justice is and why anyone should be just, in a conversation written for anyone willing to follow it.
card.rule: Choose philosophical books that ask first-order questions and were written for lay readers, beginning with the classics from Plato onward.
card.limits: Accessible does not mean easy: the authors promise success to readers who wish it and work at it. And a classic may contain passages of other kinds; its accessibility lies in its main questions.

concepts.title: Nothing to do but think
concepts.question: How does a philosopher answer a first-order question, and how does that differ from scientific or historical research?

paragraphs: Suppose you are troubled by a first-order question, such as what all existing things have in common or what change is. If the question were scientific, you would design an experiment or observe a wide range of phenomena. If it were historical, you would do research of another kind, in documents.

But no experiment shows what existing things share precisely as existing. No special phenomena, and no documents, reveal what change is or why things change. All you can do is reflect on the question. There is, the authors say, nothing to do but think.
This is what makes a question philosophical in the authors' sense, and it tells the reader what to expect: arguments built by reflection, not reports of findings.
card.example: Whether a new drug lowers blood pressure is settled by a trial. Whether a person who has lost all memory is still the same person is not settled by any trial, though trials can show what such patients can do; it has to be thought through.
card.rule: Ask whether a question could be settled by experiment, observation or documents; if only reflection can answer it, treat it as philosophical and expect reasoning, not findings.
card.limits: Thinking is the method, but not thinking in a vacuum: philosophy draws on common experience, as the next idea shows. And a question that research can settle is not philosophical, even if a philosopher asked it.

concepts.title: Thinking grounded in common experience
concepts.question: If philosophy is only thinking, what keeps it from being idle speculation, and what tests its answers?

paragraphs: Thinking is not done in a vacuum. Good philosophy, the authors say, is not pure speculation, thinking divorced from experience. Ideas cannot be put together any old way, and there are stringent tests of philosophical answers.
Those tests rest on common experience alone: the experience you have because you are a human being, not because you are a philosopher. Everyone meets change, choice, learning and wanting every day.

So when you read a philosophical argument, check it against your own ordinary experience. A conclusion that conflicts with what everyone meets daily needs very strong reasons; one that fits it has passed a first test.
card.example: A philosopher argues that motion is impossible. Every reader has walked across a room. The argument may be clever, but common experience sets a firm test: either it shows how experience misleads us, or something in its reasoning has gone wrong.
card.rule: Test a philosophical answer against common experience, the everyday experience every human being has, not against special findings.
card.limits: Common experience is a test, not a proof: it can show that an answer fails to fit, but fitting does not make an answer true. And it does not reach matters that only special research can, such as the make-up of the stars.

concepts.title: What makes the great philosophers great
concepts.question: If everyone shares the experience philosophers think about, what distinguishes the great philosophers from the rest of us?

paragraphs: As far as the experience of change goes, the authors say, you are as well placed to think about it as the greatest philosophers. Everything around you changes, and you know it as well as anyone.

What distinguishes the great philosophers is that they thought about it extremely well. They formulated the most penetrating questions that could be asked, and they developed careful, lucid, worked-out answers.

Not by investigation, and not by having more experience than the rest of us, but by thinking more profoundly about the experience everyone has. For a reader this means you already have what you need to follow them; what to watch is how they framed the question and built the answer.
card.example: Everyone has broken a promise and felt that it mattered. A great moral philosopher starts from that same experience but asks what makes a promise binding at all, then builds an answer step by step. The reader's job is to trace that question and that construction.
card.rule: Follow how a great philosopher framed his question and worked out his answer from experience you share, rather than looking for special facts he knew.
card.limits: Being equally placed in experience does not make you equally placed in thought: the gap lies in how well they thought. And a philosopher who had less scientific information than you is not great for that reason, nor lesser.

concepts.title: Questions that belong to science
concepts.question: How can you tell when a philosopher has taken up a question that later science, not thought, could answer?

paragraphs: Not every question philosophers asked is truly philosophical. Some could be answered by scientific investigation, though the philosopher may not have known that when he wrote. A reader who misses this can be confused by them.

To the unaided eye, the heavenly bodies seemed to change only in place: they did not come to be or pass away, grow or alter. So the ancient philosophers concluded that the heavens must be made of a different kind of matter from earthly things.

They could hardly have guessed what the telescope would show. Galileo's discovery of Jupiter's moons led to Kepler's claim that heavenly and earthly matter are the same, and that prepared Newton's mechanics, with one set of laws for all bodies. The question had been one for science.
card.example: An old treatise argues about how many humours in the blood govern a person's temper. It sounds like a question about nature for reflection, but it can be settled by medical investigation, so it belongs to science.
card.rule: For each question a philosopher raises, ask whether scientific investigation could now answer it; if so, set it apart from his truly philosophical questions.
card.limits: The test uses hindsight: the philosopher often could not know a question was scientific. And a question is not scientific because it mentions nature; what change itself is remains a question for thought.

concepts.title: Setting aside outdated science
concepts.question: How should a reader treat the scientific errors in a classical philosopher's work?

paragraphs: On the whole, the authors say, the misinformation or lack of information about scientific matters in the classical philosophers is irrelevant, apart from the confusion it can cause.

The reason is that when we read a philosophical work, it is the philosophical questions we care about, not the scientific or historical ones. Those can be answered only by thinking. If we could build a telescope or microscope to examine the properties of existence we should, but no such instrument is possible.

So a reader judges a classical philosopher by his philosophy. Dated astronomy or biology in his pages tells you about his time; it does not decide whether his account of being, change or the good life holds.
card.example: A medieval treatise on the soul assumes the heart is the seat of thought. That error belongs to the science of its time. Its argument that understanding differs from sensing must be judged on its own reasoning, which the anatomical error may not touch.
card.rule: Judge a classical philosopher by his philosophical questions and arguments, setting aside his dated science as largely irrelevant.
card.limits: Irrelevant on the whole, not in every case: where an argument rests on a scientific error, as the view of heavenly matter did, the error matters to that argument. Check whether the philosophy depends on the dated science before setting it aside.

concepts.title: Research cannot settle norms
concepts.question: Why can't a survey or experiment answer a normative question such as how one ought to live?

paragraphs: Philosophers are not the only ones who mistake the kind of question they face. Suppose a scientist becomes troubled by what kind of life a person ought to lead. That is a question of normative philosophy, and the only way to answer it is by thinking about it.

The scientist may not realize this. He may ask a thousand people what kind of life they would like to lead and base his answer on theirs. The authors call that answer as irrelevant as Aristotle's speculations about the matter of the heavenly bodies.

The two errors mirror each other: the ancients tried to settle by thought what needed research; the scientist tries to settle by research what needs thought. A survey tells you what people want, not what they ought to seek.
card.example: A company asks its staff which work schedule they prefer and adopts the most popular one. That answers a question of fact about preferences. Whether that schedule is good for them, or fair to all, is a further question the vote cannot settle.
card.rule: Do not accept surveys or experiments as answers to normative questions; they report what is wanted or done, not what ought to be sought.
card.limits: Research can still inform a normative argument: facts about what people want, or what a policy leads to, can serve as premises. What research cannot supply by itself is the ought.

concepts.title: One method, five styles
concepts.question: What five styles of exposition have the great philosophers used, and why should a reader tell them apart?

paragraphs: There is only one philosophical method, but at least five styles of exposition in the Western tradition. A reader should be able to tell them apart and know the advantages and disadvantages of each.

The five are: the dialogue, as in Plato; the treatise or essay, as in Aristotle and Kant; the meeting of objections, perfected by Aquinas; the systematic, geometrical style of Descartes and Spinoza; and the aphoristic style of Nietzsche.

The style tells you how to read: whether to follow a conversation, a continuous line of argument, a set of formal articles, a chain of propositions, or a string of brief sayings. Style is how the thinking is presented, not another way of thinking.
card.example: Opening an unfamiliar philosophy book, a reader sees numbered propositions with proofs and corollaries. She can tell at once that it uses the geometrical style, and adjust: she will follow chains of demonstration rather than a story or a conversation.
card.rule: Identify which of the five styles a philosophical work uses, and read it in the way that style demands.
card.limits: A philosopher may use more than one style: Descartes wrote geometrical arguments and also traditional treatises. And verse alone does not make a sixth style; the authors treat Lucretius' poem as an essay in form.

concepts.title: The dialogue: discovery by conversation
concepts.question: What makes Plato's dialogues heuristic, and how should a reader read a dialogue that may end without a doctrine?

paragraphs: The first style in time is Plato's dialogue. It is conversational, even colloquial: several people discuss a subject with Socrates, and often, after some fumbling, Socrates leads with questions and comments that clarify it.

In a master's hands the style is heuristic: it leads the reader to discover things for himself, and the drama of Socrates' story makes it powerful. Others who tried it, such as Cicero and Berkeley, wrote flat, dull dialogues. That only Plato managed it may suggest the form is ill suited to philosophy.

Plato seems to have had no system or doctrine, unless it was to keep talking and asking. Yet he and Socrates raised most of the important questions later philosophers had to deal with. So read a dialogue for the questions it opens and what you discover by following them.
card.example: In a dialogue about courage, three definitions are proposed and each fails under questioning; the talk ends without agreement. A reader hunting for Plato's final answer finds none. A reader who follows the questioning comes away with sharper distinctions and a question he now understands.
card.rule: Read a philosophical dialogue heuristically, following the questioning to discover things for yourself, and look for the questions it raises rather than a finished doctrine.
card.limits: Heuristic does not mean anything goes: discoveries must be earned by following the argument. And because a dialogue works like a play, skipping parts of it loses the thread.

concepts.title: Philosophy, early science or a mixture
concepts.question: How do Aristotle's surviving works show that one author's books may be philosophy, science or a mixture, and why does that matter?

paragraphs: Aristotle studied under Plato for twenty years. His dialogues survive only in fragments; what survives are difficult treatises, which scholars suggest may have been lecture notes, his own or a student's. Either way, the Aristotelian treatise was a new style.

His works fall into groups: popular works, mostly dialogues, now fragments; documentary collections, chiefly 158 constitutions of Greek states, of which only that of Athens survives, recovered from a papyrus in 1890; and the major treatises.

The treatises differ. Some, like the Physics, Metaphysics, Ethics, Politics and Poetics, are purely philosophical. Some, like On the Soul, mix philosophical theory with early scientific investigation. Some, like the biological works, are mainly science.
card.example: A reader of On the Soul meets a passage on how the senses relate to the mind, then one on the sense organs of particular animals. The first asks a philosophical question; the second reports early natural history. Reading both the same way would muddle her judgment of each.
card.rule: Classify each work, and each part of a mixed work, as purely philosophical, a mixture with early science, or mainly scientific, before deciding how to read it.
card.limits: The author's name does not settle the kind: the same great philosopher wrote natural history. And within a mixed work the sorting has to be done passage by passage.

concepts.title: Following a treatise's order
concepts.question: How does a treatise in the manner of Aristotle or Kant present a philosophical view, and how should you follow it?

paragraphs: Kant, though more influenced by Plato in philosophy, adopted Aristotle's style of exposition. Unlike Aristotle's, his treatises are finished works of art. They state the main problem first, go through the subject in a thorough, business-like way, and treat special problems along the way or at the end.

The clarity of both lies in the order they impose on a subject: a philosophical beginning, middle and end. Aristotle in particular reports the views and objections of others, philosophers and ordinary people, which makes the treatise resemble the dialogue in one way.

But the drama is missing: a view is developed by straightforward exposition, not through a conflict of positions as in Plato. So read a treatise by finding its main problem, tracking its order, and noting where it reports and answers other views.
card.example: A treatise on justice opens by asking what justice is, surveys common opinions and earlier theories, develops its own account across chapters, and closes with special problems such as punishment. A reader who maps this order can find the main argument and see where each part fits.
card.rule: In a treatise, find the main problem stated first, follow the thorough treatment through its beginning, middle and end, and note where special problems are handled.
card.limits: Not every treatise is a finished work of art: Aristotle's, possibly lecture notes, state their principles with less clarity. And because the reasoning is continuous, a treatise cannot be read by skipping.

concepts.title: The article form of Aquinas
concepts.question: What are the parts of an article in Aquinas's Summa, and where do you find the author's own answer?

paragraphs: The style developed in the Middle Ages and perfected by Aquinas in the Summa Theologica joins question-raising, as in Plato, with objection-meeting, as in Aristotle. The Summa is divided into parts, treatises, questions and articles, and every article has the same form.

A question is posed. The opposite, wrong answer is given, with arguments in its support. These are countered first by an authoritative text, often from Scripture. Then Aquinas gives his own answer, introduced by the words I answer that. Finally he replies to each argument for the wrong answer.
To read an article, locate each part. The view presented first is not the author's; his position comes after I answer that, and the replies show how he deals with each objection.
card.example: An article asks whether lying is ever permitted. It first gives arguments that it is, such as lying to save a life. An authority is cited against them. Then I answer that introduces Aquinas's view, and each opening argument receives its own reply.
card.rule: In an article of Aquinas, find the question, the wrong answer and its arguments, the authority against them, the author's answer after I answer that, and his reply to each argument.
card.limits: The opening answer is not the author's view; quoting it as his is the common slip. And the authoritative text only counters the objections; the author's reasoning for his position comes in his own answer.

concepts.title: The value of meeting objections
concepts.question: What do the authors value most in Aquinas's style, and what does it teach a reader to look for in any philosophical work?

paragraphs: The neatness and order of the Thomistic style appeal to orderly minds, but that is not its most important feature. What matters most is Aquinas's explicit recognition of conflicts, his reporting of different views, and his attempt to meet all possible objections to his own solutions.

The idea that truth evolves out of opposition was common in the Middle Ages. Philosophers defended their views in public disputes, often before crowds of students. Books were few and the culture largely oral; a proposition was not accepted unless it could meet the test of open discussion.
The authors note the style is little used today, which seems to them a shame given its advantages. As a reader, value any work that states the strongest objections to its view and answers them.
card.example: Two essays defend the same policy. One ignores critics; the other states the three strongest objections and replies to each. The second gives you far more to judge, because you can see whether the author's view survives the opposition.
card.rule: Value and look for a work's explicit recognition of opposing views and its attempt to answer the strongest objections to its position.
card.limits: Stating objections is not the same as meeting them: replies can be weak, and objections can be set up as straw men. Judge whether the replies answer the objections at their strongest.

concepts.title: Philosophy in geometrical dress
concepts.question: What did Descartes and Spinoza try to do with philosophy's form, and how well do the authors think it worked?

paragraphs: In the seventeenth century Descartes and Spinoza, fascinated by the promised success of mathematics in organizing knowledge of nature, tried to organize philosophy itself in a way akin to mathematics.

Descartes, a great mathematician, tried to clothe philosophy in mathematical dress, giving it the certainty and formal structure Euclid had given geometry. He was not wholly unsuccessful, and his demand for clarity and distinctness was partly justified in the chaotic intellectual climate of his time. He also wrote more traditional treatises, including replies to objections.

Spinoza went farther: his Ethics is in strict mathematical form, with propositions, proofs, corollaries, lemmas and scholiums. But metaphysics and morals, the authors judge, are not very satisfactorily handled this way, which suits geometry better than philosophy.
card.example: Opening Spinoza's Ethics, a reader finds definitions and axioms, then Proposition 1 with its demonstration, then corollaries. She recognizes the geometrical style and reads each proposition by asking which earlier definitions and propositions its proof uses.
card.rule: Recognize the geometrical style by its propositions, proofs, corollaries and scholiums, and follow each proof back to the definitions and propositions it uses.
card.limits: The form promises mathematical certainty, but the authors doubt that metaphysics and morals fit it well; a proof-like layout does not make a philosophical conclusion as certain as a theorem.

concepts.title: Where you can skip, and where you cannot
concepts.question: In which philosophical styles can a reader skip, and why not in others?

paragraphs: A sign that the geometrical form suits philosophy poorly, the authors say, is that in Spinoza you can skip a great deal, in the same way that you can skip in Newton.
You cannot skip anything in Kant or Aristotle, because the line of reasoning is continuous. And you cannot skip anything in Plato, any more than you would skip part of a play or a poem.

So the style tells you how much you may skip. In a geometrical work, propositions can be passed over and returned to when a later proof needs them. In a treatise or a dialogue, skipping breaks the thread the whole depends on.
card.example: Reading Spinoza, a reader skips several propositions whose proofs she finds tedious, noting what each states, and returns only when a later proof cites one. Trying the same with a chapter of Kant leaves her unable to follow the next chapter, which builds on the one she skipped.
card.rule: Skip freely in geometrically arranged works, but read treatises and dialogues straight through, because their reasoning is continuous.
card.limits: Skipping in a geometrical work still means noting what each skipped proposition states, since later proofs may cite it. And skimming at the inspectional level, a first look at a book, is a different matter from skipping during analytical reading.

concepts.title: When form defeats communication
concepts.question: Why do the authors doubt that philosophy in mathematical form, or science in dialogue form, can communicate well?

paragraphs: There are probably no absolute rules of rhetoric, the authors grant. Still, they question whether a satisfactory philosophical work can be written in mathematical form, as Spinoza tried, or a satisfactory scientific work in dialogue form, as Galileo tried.
Both men, they say, failed to some extent to communicate what they wished to communicate, and the form they chose was probably a major reason for the failure.

For a reader, this means a work's form can stand between you and its meaning. When a book feels harder than its ideas should be, ask whether the form suits the subject, and work to recover the content from the form.
card.example: A reader of a moral treatise laid out as numbered propositions finds herself checking whether each proof is valid, and forgets to ask whether its definitions fit her experience of courage or kindness. The form has pulled her attention toward deduction and away from the common experience the subject rests on.
card.rule: Be alert when a work's form mismatches its subject, as with philosophy in mathematical dress or science in dialogue, and recover the content from the form.
card.limits: The authors call the form a likely reason, not a law: there are probably no absolute rules of rhetoric, and a master can sometimes make an unlikely form work, as Plato did with the dialogue.

concepts.title: Aphorisms: the hit-and-run style
concepts.question: What are the advantage and the disadvantage of the aphoristic style, and how should a reader handle it?

paragraphs: The fifth style, probably less important than the others, is the aphoristic style of Nietzsche, in works like Thus Spake Zarathustra, and of certain modern French philosophers. Its popularity may owe something to Western interest in the aphoristic wisdom books of the East, and perhaps to Pascal's Pensées, though Pascal died before he could write his book out in essay form.
Its great advantage is that it is heuristic: the reader feels more is being said than is said, because he does much of the thinking himself, making connections and constructing arguments.

That is also its great disadvantage; it is hardly exposition at all. The author is like a hit-and-run driver: he touches a subject, suggests an insight, and runs off without defending it. Poetic readers enjoy it; those who want to follow and criticize a line of thought find it irritating.
card.example: A book of sayings declares that what does not destroy us makes us stronger. A reader feels its force, then notices that she is the one supplying the argument and the exceptions; the author gave neither. Before agreeing, she marks which reasons were hers.
card.rule: In an aphoristic work, notice where you are building connections and arguments the author never gave, and do not credit him with a defence he did not make.
card.limits: The insight may still be true; the trouble is only that it is undefended. And Pascal's Pensées are aphoristic by accident, not design, so they are better read as an unfinished work than as a chosen style.

concepts.title: Weighing the five styles
concepts.question: How do the authors rate the five styles for writing and reading philosophy, and what do they regret about one of them?

paragraphs: Summing up, the authors know of no other important style in the Western tradition. Lucretius' On the Nature of Things is no exception: it was written in verse, but in style it is an essay, and we usually read it in prose translation. Every great philosopher used one or more of the five.

The treatise or essay is probably the most common form, past and present, ranging from formal, difficult works like Kant's to popular essays or letters. Dialogues are notoriously hard to write. The geometrical style is enormously difficult both to write and to read. The aphoristic style is highly unsatisfactory from a philosophical point of view.

The Thomistic style has been little used in recent times. Perhaps modern readers would not accept it, the authors say, but that seems a shame given its advantages. Knowing these judgments helps you set expectations before you start.
card.example: A reader planning a year of philosophy notes that most books ahead will be treatises, so she practises tracking a continuous argument. She expects Spinoza to be slow going, and reads the aphorists with an eye on what is left undefended.
card.rule: Before reading, use the style to set expectations: most works are treatises, dialogues and geometrical works are hard, aphorisms are philosophically unsatisfying, and the objection-meeting form is rare.
card.limits: These are the authors' judgments, not laws, and they describe styles in general; a particular dialogue or essay may be easier or harder than its style suggests.

concepts.title: First, find the questions
concepts.question: What is the most important thing to discover in reading any philosophical work, and what do you do if it is never stated?

paragraphs: The most important thing to discover in reading any philosophical work, the authors say, is the question or questions it tries to answer. Everything said so far about philosophy points here: philosophy is the asking and answering of basic questions.

The questions may be stated explicitly, or they may be implicit to some extent. Either way, you must work out what they are. Without them you cannot tell what the arguments are for, or whether the conclusions answer anything.

In practice, state each question in your own words, and check that the book's main conclusions can be read as answers to it. If a conclusion answers no question you have found, you have probably missed one.
card.example: An essay on the death penalty spends pages on deterrence statistics and the history of executions. A reader asks what all of it serves and finds the question implicit: may a state ever take a life as punishment? Now the statistics read as one consideration among others.
card.rule: Before anything else, state in your own words the questions a philosophical work tries to answer, whether the author states them or leaves them implicit.
card.limits: Finding the questions is the first step, not the last: the answers depend on principles you must also find. And a title or chapter heading may name a topic without stating the question.

concepts.title: Controlling principles
concepts.question: What is a philosopher's controlling principle, and how can you find one the author never states?

paragraphs: How an author answers his questions depends deeply on his controlling principles, the underlying assumptions or insights that shape his work. The great philosophers do not hide them dishonestly; it is the mark of a great philosopher to make them clearer than others can. Still, they may go unstated in the book you are reading, treated in another book or never stated at all.

The authors give Plato as an example: his controlling idea that conversation about philosophical subjects is perhaps the most important human activity. It is seldom stated outright, though Socrates may be saying it in the Apology, where he says the unexamined life is not worth living.

Plato shows it instead: in the Protagoras the audience disapproves when Protagoras will not keep talking with Socrates, and in the Republic Cephalus leaves for other business. Refusing the search for truth seems to betray our deepest nature. Look for such a principle in what an author repeatedly shows, not only in what he says.
card.example: An essayist rarely says that honesty matters most, but in essay after essay the admired figures tell hard truths and the despised ones evade them. The repeated pattern points to a controlling principle the author never states.
card.rule: Look for an author's controlling principles, stated or unstated, in what his work repeatedly shows as well as in what it says, and look in his other works too.
card.limits: The authors admit they are not sure they can tell you how to discover these principles; it can take years and many rereadings. Any example would be disputed, so a claimed principle is an interpretation to defend. One scene is not enough; the pattern must recur.

concepts.title: Principles stated elsewhere
concepts.question: Why might an author's controlling principles lie outside the book you are reading, and where should you look for them?

paragraphs: A philosopher may treat his controlling principles in another book, or never treat them explicitly but let them pervade all his works. So reading one book well can mean looking at others by the same author.
In reading any work of Aristotle, the authors say, remember that things said in his other works are relevant. The basic principles of logic, set out in the Organon, are assumed in the Physics.

Kant opposed his critical philosophy to dogmatism, the presumption that the intellect can reach the most important truths by pure thinking without knowing its own limits. The limitation of the mind is a controlling principle, stated in the Critique of Pure Reason, assumed and unstated in the Critique of Judgment, his work on esthetics, yet controlling there too.
card.example: A reader of an economist's later book finds terms used without definition and conclusions that seem to come from nowhere. Checking the author's earlier book, she finds the principles laid out there; the later book takes them for granted.
card.rule: When a philosophical book seems to rest on unstated principles, look for them in the author's other works, where they may be stated or assumed throughout.
card.limits: Looking elsewhere means the author's own works, not books about him. And a principle found in another work is a lead, still to be confirmed in the book in hand.

concepts.title: A controlling insight: the whole good
concepts.question: What controlling insight do the authors find in Aristotle's Ethics, and why does it take a careful reader to see it?

paragraphs: Aristotle's treatises, partly because they are not finished works of art, do not always state their controlling principles with satisfactory clarity. The Ethics is about many things: happiness, habit, virtue, pleasure and more.

Its controlling insight, the authors say, is found only by the very careful reader: happiness is the whole of the good, not the highest good, for then it would be only one good among others. So happiness does not consist in self-perfection or self-improvement, though these are the highest of the partial goods.

Happiness is the quality of a whole life, whole in time and in all the aspects from which a life can be viewed. The happy person puts it all together and keeps it there. This insight affects almost every other idea in the Ethics, though it is not stated nearly as explicitly as it might be.
card.example: Two readers of the Ethics ask whether a brilliant scholar who neglects health and friends is happy. One, taking happiness as the highest good, says yes: he pursues the best activity. The other, who has found the controlling insight, says no: his life lacks parts of the good.
card.rule: Test a candidate controlling insight by asking whether it changes how you read almost every other idea in the work.
card.limits: This is the authors' interpretation, and they admit philosophers would dispute such examples. A controlling insight must also be found in the text, not imposed from outside to make the book tidier.

concepts.title: No shortcut through books about philosophers
concepts.question: How long may finding an author's controlling principles take, and why do the authors advise against reading books about philosophers instead?

paragraphs: The authors say this is all they can tell you about finding controlling principles; they are not sure they can tell you how. Sometimes it takes years, and many readings and rereadings.
Still, it is the ideal goal of a good and thorough reading, and you must keep it in mind if you are to understand your author.

Despite the difficulty, they do not recommend the shortcut of reading books about the philosophers, their lives and opinions. The discovery you make on your own will be much more valuable than someone else's ideas.
card.example: A student frustrated by Kant buys a guide that names his controlling principle in a sentence. She can repeat the sentence but cannot show where it works in the text. A classmate who reread the Critique three times found the principle herself and can trace it through each chapter.
card.rule: Treat finding an author's controlling principles as a long-term goal of rereading, and make the discovery yourself rather than borrowing it from books about philosophers.
card.limits: The authors advise against this shortcut, not against all help: the author's other works, and other great philosophers on the same problems, are worth reading. And not finding the principle on a first reading is no failure.

concepts.title: Does the author keep to his principles?
concepts.question: Once you have found an author's controlling principles, what should you check next, and what if he is inconsistent?

paragraphs: Once you have found an author's controlling principles, decide whether he adheres to them throughout his work. Unfortunately, the authors say, philosophers, even the best of them, often do not.
Emerson called consistency the hobgoblin of little minds. The authors grant that the carefree remark is worth remembering, but they hold that inconsistency in a philosopher is a serious problem.

If a philosopher is inconsistent, you have to decide which he really means: his first principles as stated, or conclusions that do not in fact follow from them. Or you may decide that neither is valid.
card.example: A book's opening principle is that only what can be observed is real. Late in the book it argues for the reality of an unobservable cause. The reader must decide: does the author mean the principle, so the late argument fails; the conclusion, so the principle must give way; or neither?
card.rule: Check whether an author's conclusions follow from his stated principles, and if they do not, decide whether he means the principles, the conclusions, or neither.
card.limits: An apparent inconsistency may come from your own misreading: a term used in two senses, or a principle qualified in another work, can dissolve it. And deciding what he really means is an interpretation you must defend.

concepts.title: Explaining, not describing
concepts.question: How does a theoretical philosophical work's task differ from science's, and what does that mean for how you read its answers?

paragraphs: Reading philosophy has special aspects that come from the difference between philosophy and science. The authors here consider only theoretical works, such as metaphysical treatises or books in the philosophy of nature.

The philosophical problem, they say, is to explain the nature of things, not to describe it as science does. Philosophy asks about more than the connections of phenomena; it seeks to penetrate to the ultimate causes and conditions underlying them.

Such problems are satisfactorily explored only when the answers are supported by clear arguments and analysis. So in a theoretical philosophical work, look for the argument and analysis behind each answer, not for new observations.
card.example: A science book reports that ice melts at a fixed temperature under standard pressure and charts how the rate changes with heat. A philosophy of nature asks what it is for one thing to become another at all, and what must underlie any such change. Its answer stands or falls on its argument.
card.rule: In theoretical philosophy, look for explanations of ultimate causes and conditions supported by argument and analysis, not for descriptions of how phenomena are connected.
card.limits: The contrast applies to theoretical works; normative works ask what ought to be, not what underlies things. And an answer offered without argument or analysis has not met philosophy's standard, however deep it sounds.

concepts.title: Effort on terms and starting points
concepts.question: Where should a reader of theoretical philosophy put the major effort, and why do familiar words cause trouble?

paragraphs: Because philosophy explains through argument and analysis, the reader's major effort, the authors say, must go into the terms and the initial propositions: the starting points from which the argument proceeds.
Like the scientist, the philosopher has a technical vocabulary. But his words are usually taken from common speech and used in a very special sense.

This demands special care. A reader who does not overcome the tendency to read familiar words in their familiar way will probably make gibberish and nonsense of the book. So when an ordinary word bears heavy weight, stop and ask what the author means by it.
card.example: A treatise says that every substance has an essence. A reader who takes substance to mean stuff like flour or glue, and essence a scent extract, finds the sentence absurd. Read in the author's sense, roughly a thing existing in its own right and what makes it the kind of thing it is, the sentence makes a definite claim.
card.rule: Put your main effort into a philosopher's terms and initial propositions, and read his ordinary words in the special sense he gives them.
card.limits: Not every ordinary word is a term; most carry their usual sense. Look for the words that bear the argument's weight. And the special sense must come from the author's usage, not from your guess.

concepts.title: Abstract terms: understand, do not picture
concepts.question: Why are a philosopher's abstract terms no special difficulty, and what goes wrong when readers try to picture them?

paragraphs: The basic terms of philosophy are abstract, but so are those of science; no general knowledge can be expressed except in abstract terms. There is nothing especially difficult about abstractions; we use them every day. Yet the words abstract and concrete trouble many people.

Whenever you talk generally about anything, you are using abstractions. What you perceive through the senses is concrete and particular; what you think with the mind is abstract and general. To understand an abstract word is to have the idea it expresses: to understand some general aspect of things you experience concretely.

You cannot see, touch or even imagine that general aspect; if you could, there would be no difference between the senses and the mind. People who try to imagine what ideas refer to befuddle themselves and end up hopeless about all abstractions.
card.example: Asked what justice is, a reader tries to picture it and gets a blindfolded statue holding scales. The image tells him nothing about what makes an act fair or right. He makes progress only when he asks what all fair and right acts have in common, which he can think but not picture.
card.rule: Grasp an abstract term by understanding the general aspect it names in things you experience, and do not try to picture what it refers to.
card.limits: Images and examples can help you reach an idea, but they are not the idea; any picture shows a particular case. And abstract does not mean vague: a well-defined abstract term can be precise.

concepts.title: Granting assumptions to see what follows
concepts.question: How should a reader treat the assumptions a philosopher asks him to make, especially ones he does not share?

paragraphs: As inductive arguments are the main focus in reading science, so in philosophy you must pay closest attention to the philosopher's principles. They are of two kinds: things he asks you to assume with him, and matters he calls self-evident.
Assumptions cause no trouble, the authors say. Make them to see what follows, even if you hold contrary presuppositions. It is a good mental exercise to pretend to believe something you do not.
And the clearer you are about your own prejudgments, the less likely you are to misjudge those made by others. So before you resist an author's assumption, name your own on the same point.
card.example: A treatise assumes that every event has a cause. A reader who doubts it grants the assumption anyway, follows the argument to its conclusion, and only then asks whether the assumption holds. Along the way she notes her own leaning toward chance, so she can tell her objection from her bias.
card.rule: Grant a philosopher's assumptions to see what follows, even if you hold contrary ones, and get clear about your own prejudgments so you do not misjudge his.
card.limits: Granting an assumption for the sake of argument is not accepting it; you may challenge it once you have seen what follows. Self-evident principles, the other kind, are tested differently.

concepts.title: Testing self-evident principles
concepts.question: How do you test the propositions a philosopher calls self-evident, and why don't you need special research to do it?

paragraphs: The other kind of principle may cause trouble. Few philosophical books fail to state some propositions the author regards as self-evident. These are drawn directly from experience rather than proved by other propositions.

That experience, unlike the scientist's special experience, is the common experience of mankind. The philosopher does no laboratory or field work, so to understand and test his leading principles you need no outside aid from methodical investigation. He refers you to your own common sense and daily observation of the world.

So when an author calls something self-evident, check it against your own experience. If it fits what you meet daily, grant it as a starting point; if your experience gives clear counterexamples, the claim of self-evidence is in trouble.
card.example: A treatise calls it self-evident that a whole is greater than any of its parts. The reader checks her experience: a loaf is more than a slice, a team more than one player. She finds no counterexample and grants it. Another book calls it self-evident that people act only for pleasure; she recalls painful acts of duty and questions the claim.
card.rule: Test a philosopher's self-evident principles against your own common sense and daily observation, not against special research.
card.limits: Common experience can rebut a claimed self-evident principle but cannot prove one. And a principle that seems obvious to you may reflect your own prejudgment, so ask whether others' common experience agrees.

concepts.title: Read it as it was written
concepts.question: Why do the authors say the rules of analytical reading apply most directly to philosophical books?

paragraphs: The method by which you should read a philosophical book, the authors say, is very like the method by which it was written. A philosopher facing a problem can do nothing but think about it. A reader facing a philosophical book can do nothing but read it, which means thinking about it.

There are no other aids but the mind itself: no laboratory, no field trip, no archive. This essential loneliness of reader and book is exactly the situation the authors imagined when they began setting out the rules of analytical reading.
That is why they say those rules apply more directly to philosophical books than to any other kind. Coming to terms, finding propositions and arguments, and judging fairly carry the whole load here.
card.example: With a history book a reader can consult a museum or a map; with a science book she might watch a demonstration. With a book of metaphysics she has only the text and her own thinking, so every analytical rule, from outlining the whole to judging fairly, carries the full load.
card.rule: Read a philosophical book by thinking with it, using every rule of analytical reading, since no outside aid will do the work for you.
card.limits: No outside aids does not mean no other books: the authors still urge reading other philosophers on the same problem before judging. It means no special experience or research can stand in for your thinking.

concepts.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
concepts.title: Set the background aside, join the conversation
concepts.question: In judging a theoretical philosophical work, what can you set aside, and what should you read before making up your mind?

paragraphs: A good theoretical work in philosophy is as free from oratory and propaganda as a good scientific treatise. You need not be concerned with the author's personality, or investigate his social and economic background.

There is value, though, in reading other great philosophers who have dealt with the same problems. The philosophers have carried on a long conversation with each other through the history of thought. You had better listen in on it before you make up your mind about what any of them says.
So the context that matters is not the author's life but the debate he joined: who else asked his question, and how they answered it.
card.example: Before deciding whether one classic's account of free will is right, a reader reads two other great philosophers who answered the same question differently. Their disagreements show her which of the first author's steps are contested and where his argument must hold up.
card.rule: Judge a theoretical philosophical work without investigating the author's background, but read other great philosophers on the same problem before making up your mind.
card.limits: This applies to theoretical works; the book's advice on practical works asks for something of the author's life and times. And listening in prepares your own judgment; it does not replace it.

concepts.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
concepts.title: Why disagreement need not trouble you
concepts.question: Why do the authors say philosophers' disagreements should not trouble a reader?

paragraphs: The fact that philosophers disagree should not trouble you, the authors say, for two reasons.
First, persistent disagreement may point to a great unsolved problem, perhaps an insoluble one. It is good to know where the true mysteries are.

Second, the disagreements of others are relatively unimportant. Your responsibility is only to make up your own mind. In the presence of the long conversation the philosophers have carried on, you must judge what is true and what is false.
card.example: A reader finds that great philosophers have disagreed for two thousand years about whether the will is free. Rather than conclude that philosophy is futile, she takes the disagreement as a marker of a deep problem, studies the strongest positions, and forms her own reasoned view.
card.rule: Treat persistent disagreement among philosophers as a sign of a deep, perhaps unsolved problem, and still make up your own mind.
card.limits: Disagreement marks a mystery only when it persists among serious thinkers; a dispute that comes from misread terms is no mystery. And recognizing a mystery is no excuse for leaving your own judgment unformed.

concepts.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
concepts.title: Answer it yourself
concepts.question: What is the most distinctive mark of philosophical questions, and why can't you rely on experts to answer them?

paragraphs: It is the most distinctive mark of philosophical questions, the authors say, that everyone must answer them for himself. Taking the opinions of others is not solving them but evading them.
Your answers must be solidly grounded, with arguments to back them up. Above all, this means you cannot depend on the testimony of experts, as you may have to in science.
The reason, the authors say, is that the questions philosophers ask are more important than the questions asked by anyone else, except children. The chapter ends where it began.
card.example: A reader can reasonably accept a physicist's word that light bends near the sun, since she cannot make the measurements herself. Whether a life of comfort is a good life is different: no expert's say-so settles it for her; she must weigh the reasons and reach her own answer.
card.rule: Answer philosophical questions for yourself, with solid arguments, rather than adopting others' opinions or relying on expert testimony.
card.limits: Answering for yourself does not mean answering alone: reading other philosophers is part of grounding your answer. And in science, where special experience is needed, relying on experts can be reasonable.

concepts.title: Natural and dogmatic theology
concepts.question: How do natural and dogmatic theology differ, and which of them is a branch of philosophy?

paragraphs: There are two kinds of theology, the authors say. Natural theology is a branch of philosophy, the last chapter, as it were, of metaphysics.

Suppose you ask whether causation is an endless process, whether everything is caused. If you answer yes, you may find yourself in an infinite regress, and so posit an originating cause that is not itself caused. Aristotle called it an unmoved mover; you might call it God. Either way you reached the idea by the unaided, natural working of your mind.

Dogmatic theology differs from philosophy in that its first principles are articles of faith held by the members of some religion. A work of dogmatic theology depends on dogmas and on the authority of a church that proclaims them. To classify a theological book, ask where its first principles come from: reason or faith.
card.example: One book argues from the order of nature to a designer, appealing only to what any reader can observe and reason about. Another explains the doctrine of the Trinity as a church teaches it. The first is natural theology; the second is dogmatic theology.
card.rule: Classify a theological book by its first principles: natural theology if they are reached by unaided reason, dogmatic theology if they are articles of faith proclaimed by a church.
card.limits: Calling a work natural theology does not make its arguments sound; that still has to be judged. And, by extension, a book may mix arguments from reason with arguments from dogma, and then each part can be classified on its own.

concepts.title: Dogmas: like axioms, yet not assumptions
concepts.question: How should a reader outside a faith treat the dogmas of a theological book, and what must he remember about them?

paragraphs: If you are not of the faith, the authors say, you can still read a work of dogmatic theology well by treating its dogmas with the same respect you give the assumptions of a mathematician.
But keep in mind that an article of faith is not something the faithful assume. Faith, for those who have it, is the most certain form of knowledge, not a tentative opinion.

So a non-believing reader holds two things at once: he grants the dogmas as starting points, as he would a geometer's postulates, and he recognizes that for the author they are not hypotheses but certainties. Mistaking one for the other misreads the book.
card.example: A non-believing reader of a treatise on grace grants its doctrine of original sin as a starting point and follows the argument. When she summarizes the book, she does not write that the author supposes original sin for argument's sake, because for him it is certain truth.
card.rule: Grant a theological book's dogmas as you would a mathematician's assumptions, while remembering that for the faithful they are certain knowledge, not tentative assumptions.
card.limits: The comparison with mathematics concerns how the outsider reads, not what the dogmas are; they are not postulates for the believer. And granting them while reading does not commit you to them afterwards.

concepts.title: Two mistakes with dogmatic theology
concepts.question: What two mistakes do readers make with dogmatic theology, and how should a non-believer read such a book instead?

paragraphs: Many readers today find this hard, the authors say, and typically make one or both of two mistakes.

The first is to refuse to accept, even temporarily, the articles of faith that are the author's first principles; the reader keeps struggling with them and never really attends to the book. The second is to assume that because the first principles are dogmatic, the arguments, reasoning and conclusions built on them are dogmatic in the same way.

If principles are accepted and the reasoning on them is cogent, the conclusions must be accepted too, at least as far as the principles are. But defective reasoning leads to invalid conclusions from the most acceptable principles. So the non-believer accepts the principles while reading, then reads with all the care any good expository work deserves.
