card.example: A sceptic reading a medieval treatise grants its premise that God creates each soul, then checks each step. One argument follows validly; another slips from the soul's creation to its immortality without support. Her criticism lands on the reasoning, not the dogma.
card.rule: As a non-believing reader, accept a theological book's first principles while reading, then judge its reasoning with full care, since dogmatic premises do not make the arguments dogmatic.
card.limits: Accepting the principles is for the reading, not a verdict on them. And the authors limit this advice to non-believers; a faithful reader of a book essential to his faith faces different problems.

concepts.title: What makes a book canonical
concepts.question: What makes a book canonical for its readers, and what kind of institution stands behind such reading?

paragraphs: The authors use the term canonical for books an older tradition might call sacred or holy, words that no longer fit all of them. A prime example is the Bible read not as literature but as the revealed Word of God. Orthodox Marxists read Marx in much the same way, and a faithful Chinese Communist so read Mao's Little Red Book.

Consider any institution, a church, a party or a society, that is a teaching institution, has a body of doctrine to teach, and has a faithful and obedient membership. Its members read reverentially. They do not, even cannot, question the authorized reading of the books canonical for them.

The faithful are debarred by their faith from finding error, let alone nonsense, in the text. The authors' examples range from Jews, Christians and Muslims with their scriptures to orthodox Freudians with Freud and U.S. Army officers with the infantry manual.
card.example: A new employee notices that colleagues quote the founder's handbook to settle disputes, the firm trains all staff in it, and no one may say it is wrong. The three marks are present: teaching, doctrine and obedient members. For them the handbook is read canonically.
card.rule: Recognize a canonical reading by the institution behind it: one that teaches, has a body of doctrine, and has faithful members who may not question the authorized reading.
card.limits: Canonical describes a way of reading, not the book alone: the Bible read as literature is not read canonically. And a group lacking one of the three marks, such as a fan club with no doctrine, does not produce canonical reading.

concepts.title: One right reading, and its obligations
concepts.question: What obligations does a canonical book place on its faithful reader, and what does he gain in return?

paragraphs: The character of canonical reading is summed up in the word orthodox, from Greek roots meaning right opinion. These are books with one and only one right reading; any other is fraught with peril, from the loss of an A to the damnation of one's soul.

This carries an obligation. The faithful reader must make sense of the book and find it true, in one or another sense of true. If he cannot do this by himself, he must go to someone who can: a priest or rabbi, a superior in the party hierarchy, or a professor. And he must accept the resolution offered him.
He reads essentially without freedom. But in return, the authors say, he gains a kind of satisfaction that is possibly never obtained when reading other books.
card.example: A believer puzzled by an apparent contradiction between two passages of scripture does not conclude that the text is wrong. She looks for a sense of true in which both hold, and when she cannot find one, asks her teacher and accepts his reconciliation.
card.rule: Recognize that a canonical book has one right reading and obliges its faithful reader to make sense of it, find it true, and accept the authorized resolution when stuck.
card.limits: These obligations bind the faithful reader within the institution; they are not the rules for reading other books, where the reader is free to disagree. And the satisfaction comes at the price of that freedom.

concepts.title: When we all read canonically
concepts.question: In what ordinary situations do most of us read canonically, and why do the authors call Scripture the hardest reading of all?

paragraphs: Almost all of us, the authors say, have approached the situation in which we must read canonically. A fledgling lawyer intent on the bar exams must read certain texts in a certain way to get a perfect score. So with doctors and other professionals, and with students required, at the peril of failure, to read a text by the professor's interpretation. Not all professors punish disagreement, they add.
Noticing when you read this way matters, because it is reading without freedom: the aim is to match an authorized interpretation, not to judge the text.

The authors stop at the hardest case. Reading the Holy Book, if you have faith that it is the Word of God, is the most difficult problem in reading. More books have been written on reading Scripture than on all other aspects of the art together. In the European tradition, the Bible has been the most widely and most carefully read book.
card.example: A student preparing for an exam on a novel learns the instructor's interpretation and writes it back, setting aside her own doubts. Later, rereading the novel for herself, she notices the switch: now she may disagree, and her reading becomes a judgment rather than a performance.
card.rule: Notice when you are reading to match an authorized interpretation, as for an exam or a professional test, and know that this is canonical reading without freedom.
card.limits: Reading canonically for an exam is a temporary role, not a verdict; the authors note that not all professors punish disagreement. And they stop short of giving rules for reading Scripture, calling it the most difficult problem in the field.

concepts.title: Social science is everywhere you read
concepts.question: Where, besides textbooks, does a reader meet social science ideas, and how can you tell them apart from the plain facts?

paragraphs: The authors open by noting how far social science reaches into everyday reading. Apart from the brief who-what-when-where report, most journalism wraps its facts in interpretation, commentary and analysis, and that interpretation leans on social science concepts and terms.

The same vocabulary runs through the stream of books and articles on crime, poverty, education, welfare, war and government that the authors group as social criticism. It reaches fiction too: some novels, plays and films build artificial models of society to explore, for instance, what a new technology would do to the way people live.

Specialists in these fields are also called in to frame and help handle almost every social, economic or political problem, and social science courses now draw more students than literature, languages or the pure sciences.
card.example: A news story says unemployment in a town rose to 5 percent last month. That is a fact you could check. The next sentence says the rise reflects growing alienation among young workers. That is interpretation, and alienation is a social science concept the reporter has borrowed.
card.rule: When reading news, social criticism or social-problem fiction, separate the reported facts from the social science interpretation laid over them.
card.limits: Not every sentence carries a theory: a short report of who did what, when and where may hold little interpretation. And spotting a borrowed concept tells you a piece draws on social science, not that its interpretation is wrong.

concepts.title: The core and the fringe of social science
concepts.question: Which fields do the authors place at the core of social science, and which ones only partly inside it?

paragraphs: Social science is not one subject, so the authors build a working definition. At its core are anthropology, economics, politics and sociology, the fields almost every social scientist would include.

Around the core lies a fringe. Much of the writing in law, education and public administration counts, some of the writing in business and social service, and a large share of psychology. The authors admit the boundary is imprecise.

Why are schools of law, business and education usually kept out of university social science divisions? The common reason is purpose: those schools train people for professional work outside the university, while the core departments seek systematic knowledge of human society.

Newer interdisciplinary centres mix statistics, demography, polling, policy studies and more. Their reports may draw on a dozen specialties, and the authors warn that it takes real sophistication even to see the separate strands, let alone judge the findings.
card.example: A study of why juries in different regions convict at different rates comes from a law school, but it seeks systematic knowledge of how a social institution works, so by the purpose test it falls in the fringe. A handbook on courtroom technique from the same school trains for practice.
card.rule: To place a work, ask whether it belongs to a core field, or, if it comes from law, education or a similar field, whether it seeks systematic knowledge of society.
card.limits: The authors call their definition imprecise, so fringe cases call for judgment, not a lookup. The purpose test also says nothing about quality: a training manual can be excellent and a research study poor.

concepts.title: Psychology, behavioral science and history
concepts.question: How do the authors handle psychology, the behavioral sciences and history at the edges of social science?

paragraphs: Psychology divides social scientists. Strict ones leave it out, since it studies individual traits while social science proper studies cultural, institutional and environmental factors. Looser ones give physiological psychology to biology but count the rest, because an individual cannot be separated from his social surroundings.

Behavioral science first named a group of fields, from sociology to parts of biology and law, that stressed observable, measurable behavior able to yield verifiable findings. The term is now used almost as a synonym for social science, though purists object.

History supplies social science with data and examples. But history, as an account of particular events and persons, does not by itself yield systematic knowledge of patterns or laws of behavior, so the authors do not count it as a social science.
card.example: A study of reaction times in single subjects after a dose of caffeine leans toward biology. A study of how peer groups shape teenagers' choices treats the person inside a social setting, so the looser social scientists would count it.
card.rule: At the edges, ask whether the work studies people in their social setting and seeks general patterns, rather than isolated individuals or particular events.
card.limits: The edges are disputed: the authors report the strict and loose views of psychology without settling them, so classifying an edge case is a judgment. Measurable data alone also do not make a work a social science.

concepts.section: The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
concepts.title: Why social science feels easy
concepts.question: Why does much social science writing feel easy to read, and why is that feeling a poor guide to understanding?

paragraphs: A lot of social science seems like the easiest reading there is. Its data often come from experiences the reader already knows, as in poetry or philosophy, and its style is usually narrative, familiar from fiction and history.
Its subjects are ones the reader hears about almost daily, and much of the writing carries strong feeling and vivid metaphor. All of this makes the pages go down smoothly.

The authors call this ease deceptive. Smooth reading tells you the material is familiar, not that you have grasped the author's terms, propositions and arguments. The next ideas show how the same features make the reading hard.
card.example: An essay on loneliness in the suburbs describes cul-de-sacs, long commutes and empty weekends that you know well. You finish quickly and nod along. Asked what the author means by community, or what evidence links commuting to loneliness, you may find you cannot say.
card.rule: When a social science text reads smoothly, check whether you can state its terms and argument before deciding you understood it.
card.limits: Ease is not always a false signal: a clear writer on a familiar topic may really be easy to understand. The point is to test your grasp, not to distrust every readable book.

concepts.section: The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
concepts.title: Pin down familiar jargon
concepts.question: Can you say what a familiar social science word, such as society or social, means in the passage in front of you?

paragraphs: Social science jargon has entered daily talk: culture and subculture, in-group, alienation, status, consensus and many more. Because we use these words often, we assume we know what they mean.

The authors single out society as a chameleon word. Dozens of adjectives can go in front of it, the affluent society, the acquisitive society and so on, and through all of them it keeps only the broad sense of people living together rather than in isolation.

The adjective social is as slippery. In the stock phrase political, economic and social problems, most readers could say what political and economic problems are. Ask what the author, or you, meant by social problems, and the answer is often missing.
card.example: A report warns of the social costs of a new motorway. Pin it down: does social mean harm to neighbourhood ties, to health, or to people's sense of safety? Each reading calls for different evidence, and the report may never say which it means.
card.rule: When a familiar social science word carries weight in a passage, stop and say what it means there, and what it adds to the words beside it.
card.limits: Pin down the words that carry the argument, not every passing use. And an author may in fact define his term; then the job is to find his definition and hold him to it.

concepts.section: The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
concepts.title: We come to social science committed
concepts.question: Why do strong opinions on its subjects make social science feel easier to read than philosophy, and why is that misleading?

paragraphs: Philosophy also deals with the world as we commonly know it, but the authors note that readers are not usually committed on philosophical questions. Few people feel their loyalty is at stake in a question about the nature of change.
Social science is different. Its subjects, such as crime, race, taxes, schools and welfare, are matters on which readers already hold firmly developed attitudes and feelings.

The authors count those settled feelings among the things that make social science deceptively easy. A reader with a firm view feels at home in the subject before the author has said anything, and that feeling of being at home passes for understanding.
card.example: A reader who has argued about rent control for years picks up a study of it and races through, nodding or bristling. The pages felt easy because the subject was home ground. Asked to state the study's main argument, she finds she was following her own debate rather than the author's.
card.rule: Expect a social science subject you feel strongly about to seem easier to read than it is.
card.limits: The rule follows the feeling, not the field: some social topics leave a reader cold and some philosophical ones stir her. And strong views are to be set aside while understanding, not abandoned.

concepts.title: Check your opinions at the door
concepts.question: Why must a reader set aside commitments while working out what a social science book says, even when that feels disloyal?

paragraphs: The authors call it a paradox: the features that make social science seem easy also make it hard. Take commitment. Many readers feel it would be disloyal to their convictions to stand apart and question a book impersonally.

Yet analytical reading needs that stance, at least for the rules of outlining and interpreting. To answer the first two questions, what the book is about as a whole and what it says in detail, you must, as the authors put it, check your opinions at the door.
The reason is that you cannot understand a book if you refuse to hear what it is saying. A reader who argues with every page while outlining ends up outlining his own view.
card.example: A reader who opposes a carbon tax reads an economist's case for one. Before objecting, she writes his main claim and three supporting reasons as he would put them. Only when she thinks he would sign her summary does she list her objections.
card.rule: While outlining and interpreting a social science book, set your own views aside until you can state the author's case as he would.
card.limits: The setting aside serves the first two questions, understanding the book; it does not ask you to give up your convictions or never judge. You may not shed them fully, so the test is whether your summary is fair.

concepts.title: Stretched technical terms
concepts.question: What happens to a reader when a writer stretches a technical term like GNP beyond the sense it has in serious work?

paragraphs: The familiarity of social science terms is itself an obstacle to understanding. Many social scientists object strongly to the way popular writers pick up technical concepts and use them loosely.

The authors' example is Gross National Product, or GNP. In serious economic writing it has a fairly limited sense. Some social scientists complain that reporters and columnists make it do too much work, using it widely without really understanding what it means.
The result for you is direct: if the writer is confused about a key term, you, reading him, will be confused too. Checking how a writer uses a technical term is part of coming to terms with him.
card.example: A columnist writes that rising GNP proves families are happier. In its limited sense GNP measures the value of what a nation produces; it says nothing direct about happiness. The columnist has loaded the term with a meaning it does not carry, and a reader who follows him inherits the confusion.
card.rule: When a popular writer leans on a technical term, compare his use with the term's limited sense in serious work before accepting what he builds on it.
card.limits: Wider use is not always misuse: a term may be extended with care and explained. And you need some idea of the careful sense to notice stretching; without it, ask the writer's own meaning.

concepts.title: Stipulated usage and game structure
concepts.question: What does it mean for a hard scientist to stipulate his usage, and how should a reader treat those stipulations?

paragraphs: The authors contrast social science with the hard sciences, such as physics and chemistry. A hard scientist makes clear what he assumes and what he wants to prove, and his terms and propositions are easy to spot, so much of the work of coming to terms is done for you.
He does this by stipulating his usage: telling you which terms are essential to his argument and how he will use them, usually at the start, in definitions, postulates and axioms.

That is why such fields are said to have a game structure. Stipulating usage is like setting a game's rules. A poker player does not dispute that three of a kind beats two pairs; a reader does not dispute a scientist's stipulations, but accepts them and goes on.
Such books can still be hard: the mathematics may resist you, and judging their truth needs a firm grasp of the arguments and the evidence behind them.
card.example: A physics text opens: by work we mean force times the distance moved in the direction of the force. A reader who protests that holding a heavy bag still is hard work has missed the point. Within the book, work means what the definition says, and the argument goes on from there.
card.rule: When an author stipulates his essential terms at the outset, find those stipulations and read the rest of the book by them, as a player accepts a game's rules.
card.limits: Accepting a stipulation is a condition for reading the book, not a verdict that its conclusions describe the world. And the rule fits fields where usage is stipulated, which social science often is not.

concepts.title: Terms social scientists struggle with
concepts.question: Why do social scientists seldom stipulate their usage, and what does that leave the reader to do with key terms?

paragraphs: Until quite recently, the authors say, stipulating usage was much less common in social science than in the hard sciences. One reason is that the social sciences were typically not mathematical.

Another is that stipulation is harder there. Defining a circle or an isosceles triangle is one thing; defining an economic depression or mental health is quite another. Even when a social scientist tries, readers tend to question his usage.

So the author keeps struggling with his own terms throughout the work, and his struggle becomes the reader's problem. Coming to terms may be very hard, though the authors hold that some common understanding of the key terms is usually possible.
card.example: A book uses mental health to mean the absence of diagnosed illness in chapter 2 and coping well with daily life in chapter 6. A careful reader notes each use, marks the shift, and reads chapter 6's conclusions in the sense used there.
card.rule: With a social science book, track how each key term is used as the book goes on, and work toward a shared understanding of it rather than waiting for a fixed definition.
card.limits: Some social scientists do stipulate, and recent work stipulates more; there you read by the stipulation. Shared understanding is the aim, not perfect precision: demanding a definition as exact as a triangle's would stall the reading.

concepts.title: A shifting mixture of strands
concepts.question: What kinds of writing are mixed in a social science book, and why is the mixture harder to handle than history's?

paragraphs: The authors name the most important source of difficulty: social science is a mixed, not a pure, kind of expository writing. Much of it blends science, philosophy and history, often with some fiction thrown in.

History is a mixture too, of fiction and science, but it is always the same mixture, so readers have learned to handle it. Social science is not. The mix shifts from book to book, and the strands can change within a single book.
So the reader has to identify the strands as he goes: here a measured finding, there an argument about what people should value, there an account of past events, there an imagined case.
card.example: A book on inequality opens with the story of one family (close to fiction), surveys tax records since 1900 (history), fits a statistical model to wage data (science), and closes by arguing what a fair society owes its members (philosophy). Each part asks to be read in its own way.
card.rule: As you read a social science work, name which strand, science, philosophy, history or fiction, each part belongs to, and watch for the mixture changing.
card.limits: Not every work is equally mixed; a narrow statistical paper may be almost all science. And strands can overlap in one passage, so the labels guide reading rather than cut the text cleanly.

concepts.title: The analytical rules, step by step
concepts.question: Which steps of analytical reading are hard with social science, which are not, and which matters most?

paragraphs: The first rule of analytical reading asks what kind of book this is. For fiction, science and philosophy that is fairly easy, and a reader of history at least knows he is reading history. In social science the shifting strands make the question very hard, as hard as defining social science itself.
Yet the authors call this question not only the reader's first task but his most important one. A reader who can say which strands make up the book has gone a good way toward understanding it.

Outlining poses no special problem. Coming to terms can be very hard, because authors cannot easily stipulate usage, though some common understanding is usually possible. Propositions and arguments pose no special problem if the book is good. The question what of it calls for restraint.
card.example: Reading a report on youth unemployment, a reader first writes: mostly science (survey data), some history (past policies), a closing strand of philosophy (what society owes young people). With that in hand, outlining the report goes quickly; the hard work lies in pinning down terms like employable.
card.rule: With a social science work, spend your first and greatest effort on naming the strands that make it up, and expect the hardest later work to lie in coming to terms.
card.limits: The claim that outlining and arguments pose no special problem assumes a good book; a badly built one can make every step hard.

concepts.title: I cannot fault it, but I disagree
concepts.question: What does it show when you cannot fault a social science author's conclusions yet still disagree with them?

paragraphs: The last question of analytical reading, what of it, calls for considerable restraint with social science. Here the authors expect a familiar situation: the reader says, in effect, I cannot fault the author's conclusions, but I nevertheless disagree with them.

They explain it by prejudgment. The reader came to the book with views about the author's approach and his conclusions, and those views, rather than any defect he can point to, are doing the disagreeing.

Restraint means noticing this before acting on it. A disagreement you cannot tie to a flaw in the author's evidence or reasoning is a sign of your commitments at work, not yet a criticism of the book.
card.example: After a careful study of school choice, a reader finds the data sound, the terms clear and the reasoning valid, yet feels the conclusion is wrong. Before saying so, she asks what exactly is mistaken. Finding nothing, she recognises that her prior view of school choice is speaking, and holds back her verdict.
card.rule: When you disagree with a social science conclusion, name the flaw in the evidence or reasoning; if you cannot, treat the disagreement as your prejudgment and restrain it.
card.limits: A felt disagreement can be a clue to a flaw you have not yet found, so look again before setting it aside. Restraint asks you to hold the disagreement back until you can support it, not to pretend it is not there.

concepts.title: Read the literature, not one book
concepts.question: Why do the authors speak of social science literature rather than a social science book, and what should a reader do about it?

paragraphs: The authors deliberately say social science literature rather than social science book. In this field it is customary to read several works on a subject rather than one book for its own sake.

One reason is that social science is young and has few classic texts. Another is that the reader's eye is usually on a problem, such as law enforcement, race relations, education, taxation or local government, rather than on an author. On such subjects there is typically no single authoritative work.
A sign of this: social scientists must keep bringing out revised editions to keep up, and new works supersede older ones and quickly make them obsolete.

Something similar holds in philosophy, where you should read the thinkers your author read, and in history, where several accounts beat one. But there a major authoritative work is likelier to exist, so the need is most urgent in social science.
card.example: Someone wants to understand rising homelessness in her city. No one book settles it. She gathers an economist's study of housing costs, a sociologist's interviews, a recent government report and the newest edition of a standard text, and reads them with the problem in view.
card.rule: In social science, choose a problem and read several current works on it, rather than relying on one book as if it settled the subject.
card.limits: Several works does not mean any works: each must still be read well, and quantity cannot replace quality. A single good source may serve a narrow, factual question.

concepts.title: The bridge to syntopical reading
concepts.question: Why does reading several works on one problem call for new rules, and why does social science close Part Three?

paragraphs: The rules of analytical reading apply to each work you read on a subject, and to read any one of them well you must follow them. But those rules are not in themselves fit for reading several works on the same subject together. That calls for new rules, those of the fourth level, syntopical reading.

This explains the order of Part Three. Practical books came first, because agreeing with them obliges you to act. Fiction and poetry came next, with problems unlike those of expository books. Then came three kinds of theoretical writing: science and mathematics, philosophy, and social science.
Social science came last because it needs to be read syntopically. Its chapter therefore ends Part Three and opens Part Four.
card.example: A reader has read four studies of minimum wages analytically, each outlined, its terms and arguments found. She still cannot say how they bear on one another: do they use wage in the same sense, answer the same question, conflict, or talk past each other? Those questions need further rules.
card.rule: Read each work on a subject analytically, then treat relating them to one another as a further task that needs the rules of syntopical reading.
card.limits: Syntopical rules add to analytical reading rather than replace it, and a poorly read single work weakens any comparison. The need is most urgent in social science, but it arises in history and philosophy too.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Two requirements before you start
concepts.question: Before a syntopical project can begin, what two things must you know about the books, and which is harder?

paragraphs: Syntopical reading is the reading of two or more books on one subject. Its first requirement is knowing that more than one book is relevant to your question. That is usually easy: most questions worth asking have been treated by several writers.

The second requirement is knowing, in a general way, which books should be read. The authors say this is a great deal harder than the first. Knowing that a literature exists is not the same as knowing which part of it bears on your question.
card.example: A manager wants to understand what makes teams trust each other. She soon sees that psychologists, management writers and philosophers have all written on trust, so the first requirement is met. Deciding which of hundreds of titles address trust inside working teams is the hard part.
card.rule: Confirm that several books bear on your question, then work out, in a general way, which of them belong on your list.
card.limits: At the start you can know which books to read only roughly. The chapter goes on to show that this cannot be fully settled before the reading itself begins.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: What counts as the same subject
concepts.question: When two books share a word or a setting, how can you tell whether they treat the same subject?

paragraphs: Syntopical reading is defined as reading books on the same subject, but that phrase hides a problem. Two books can share a key word, a setting or a period and still be about different things.
The authors' first illustration: Gone With the Wind and War and Peace are both novels about a great war, and there the resemblance mostly stops. Sharing a war did not give them a shared subject.
The trouble is not limited to novels. Expository books that use the same key word, such as love, may turn out to be about quite different things. A shared label is a clue to check, not proof.
card.example: Two books have money in their titles. One is a memoir about a family quarrel over an inheritance; the other analyses why central banks set interest rates. A reader studying how money gets its value would find the second on her subject and the first only touching it.
card.rule: Treat a shared word, setting or period as a clue to check, and keep a book only if it addresses your actual question.
card.limits: A shared word is often how relevant books are first found, so it is useful as a lead. The authors also grant that for a single historical event the shared label can be a fair guide.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Backdrop is not subject
concepts.question: How do you tell the subject a book is really about from the context it happens to be set in?

paragraphs: A subject can run through a book as background without being what the book is about. In War and Peace and Stendhal's The Charterhouse of Parma, war is the setting, as it is for much of human life, but the authors fix our attention on the stories.

You can still learn something from the background. Tolstoy said he learned much of what he knew about battles from Stendhal's account of Waterloo. Yet a reader whose main aim is to study war would not go to novels for it.
The authors expect this gap in fiction, because a novelist does not communicate as an expository writer does. Their point is that the same gap appears in expository books too.
card.example: A cookbook set in a Tuscan farmhouse is full of details about rural Italian life, but its attention is on the recipes. A reader studying farm economics may pick up a few facts there, but would not build her study on it.
card.rule: Ask what the author fixes your attention on, and count a book as on your subject only if your subject is its concern rather than its backdrop.
card.limits: A backdrop can still teach incidental facts, as Stendhal taught Tolstoy about battles. The test decides what you study a subject from, not whether a book can hold anything useful about it.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: The range of reference of a word
concepts.question: When a word like love is used for almost everything, how do you decide whether there is one subject to study?

paragraphs: Suppose you collect expository works on love. A quick look shows an enormous range of reference: writers say stones love the earth's centre, iron filings love the magnet, animals love their masters, people love money, wine, a cause or mankind, and God is said to be love.

So you cannot take for granted that there is a single subject. When one person loves cheese, another football and a third mankind, is the word used in any common sense? Cheese is eaten, football is played, and neither act fits mankind.

The authors allow that there may be some deep reason, not visible on the surface, for the shared word. But until you have asked whether a common meaning unites the uses, you have not identified your subject.
card.example: A reader studying play finds the word used for children's games, a theatre play, the loose play in a steering wheel, and playing the stock market. Before comparing books she must ask whether these share a meaning; the steering wheel probably does not belong with children's games.
card.rule: Survey how widely your key word is used, and ask whether its uses share a common meaning before treating them as one subject.
card.limits: The question can be hard and may take much reading to answer. The authors do not conclude that the uses share nothing; a deep common meaning may lie beneath very different uses.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Narrowing the enquiry
concepts.question: If you narrow a sprawling subject to a manageable part, what problems should you still expect to find inside it?

paragraphs: Faced with the chaos of love's uses, you might limit the enquiry to human love, love between human beings. That rules out cheese, football and stones, and makes the project workable.

But even a small part of the literature on human love shows a wide range of conceptions. Some writers say love is wholly acquisitive desire, usually sexual. Others say love properly contains no acquisitive desire and consists in pure benevolence.

A third group holds that love is cognitive, not appetitive: an act of the intellect, in which knowing that a person is admirable comes before desiring him or her. Narrowing cut out the wildest uses, not the disagreement.
card.example: A reader narrows a study of leadership to leadership in small businesses. She still finds writers who say leadership is setting a vision, others who say it is serving the staff, and others who say it is making decisions. The field is workable, but the rival conceptions remain.
card.rule: Narrow a chaotic subject to a manageable part, then list the competing conceptions that remain within it.
card.limits: Narrowing makes a project workable; it does not settle what the subject is. Narrowing by the wrong line can also cut out works that bear on your question.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: A common meaning, then many forms
concepts.question: After finding a common meaning in rival conceptions, what further questions does the literature on a subject still raise?

paragraphs: Acquisitive desire wants a good for oneself; benevolence wants a good for another. They seem opposed, yet the authors note they share a common note of tendency, a desire in a very abstract sense. Looking for such shared notes is how a common meaning is found.
The authors think a common meaning in the conceptions of human love can be found. Even then, the problems do not end. Love shows itself in many relationships, and each raises its own questions.

Is courting love the same as married love, love at twenty the same as at seventy? Is a woman's love for her husband the same as for her children? Do love and friendship differ because the words differ? Can we love someone we have never met?
card.example: A reader studying trust finds trust in a friend, in a bank and in a vaccine. She finds a common note: relying on something you cannot fully check. New questions then open: is trust in an institution the same as trust in a person, and can trust survive one betrayal?
card.rule: Look for the common note that rival conceptions share, then expect the subject to break into further questions about its different forms.
card.limits: A common note found at a very abstract level may be too thin to guide a study, and finding one does not answer the many questions about how the thing varies across relationships.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: The paradox: subject after reading
concepts.question: Why must the subject of a syntopical reading, in a sense, be identified after the reading rather than before it?

paragraphs: Syntopical reading is defined as reading two or more books on the same subject, which suggests you name the subject first and then read. The authors point out a paradox: in a sense, identifying the subject must follow the reading, not precede it.

With love, you might have to read a dozen or a hundred works before you could decide what you were reading about. Only then would you know which conception unites the field, and which books belong to it.
So the subject you start with is a working guess. Expect to refine it as you read, and let the refined subject change what counts as relevant.
card.example: A journalist sets out to compare books on populism. After reading twenty, she sees that the books disagree less about populism than about what it is, and her real subject is how to define it. That discovery came from the reading; she could not have had it on day one.
card.rule: Treat your starting subject as a working guess, and let the reading settle what the subject really is.
card.limits: Some starting idea of the subject is still needed, or you cannot choose anything to read. For a single historical event the subject may be fairly clear at the start; the paradox bites hardest with broad ideas.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Half the list may not belong
concepts.question: After much reading, what may you have to conclude about many of the works on your original list?

paragraphs: The paradox has a sting in its tail. Once you have read enough to decide what your subject is, you may find that many of the works you read were not on it at all. The authors say half might turn out to be off the subject.
This is not a failure of the reader. A list made before the subject is clear has to be made by guesswork: by titles, catalogue headings and other people's advice.
The right response is to be willing to judge works irrelevant to this study, rather than stretching the subject to make them fit.
card.example: A reader studying fairness reads thirty books chosen by keyword. Having settled that her subject is fairness in distributing goods, she finds that twelve deal with fair play in sport or fair trials. She sets them aside instead of widening her subject to include them.
card.rule: Be ready to drop works from your study once the subject is clear, instead of stretching the subject to keep them.
card.limits: Dropping a work from this study is not a verdict on its worth. If your subject shifts again, works set aside may become relevant once more.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Inspection as the main tool
concepts.question: How do the lower levels of reading prepare for syntopical reading, and which of them becomes its main tool?

paragraphs: The levels of reading are cumulative: a higher level includes those below it. Earlier, the two steps of inspection prepared for analytical reading: skimming for classifying and outlining a book, superficial reading for coming to terms with it and following its arguments.
In a similar way, both inspectional and analytical reading prepare for syntopical reading. But the authors single out inspection: here it comes into its own as a major tool.
The reason is scale. Syntopical reading starts from a bibliography that may run to a hundred titles or more, and only a fast kind of reading can deal with that many books.
card.example: An engineer starting a review of battery research has eighty papers. Her analytical skills will matter for the few that prove central, but her first weeks go to inspecting: abstracts, figures and conclusions, to see what each paper is about.
card.rule: Bring your inspectional and analytical skills into syntopical reading, and lean on inspection as the main tool for handling a large list.
card.limits: Inspection's prominence does not make analytical skill unneeded: the relevant works must still be understood. Inspection handles breadth; it cannot by itself tell you what a book's argument is.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Why a short cut is needed
concepts.question: Why can't you read every book on a large bibliography analytically, and what follows from that?

paragraphs: Suppose your bibliography on love has a hundred or so titles. If you read every one analytically, you would end up with a clear idea of the subject and would know which books were off it. That would resolve the paradox the slow way.

But reading a hundred books analytically might well take ten years, and even full time many months. Since you cannot know which books matter until you read, and cannot read everything thoroughly, a short cut is needed.
The short cut is not to read badly. It is to use a different, faster kind of reading for the first pass, and to save analytical reading for later.
card.example: A doctoral student finds 150 papers on her topic. At two weeks per paper for a thorough reading, that is close to six years. She needs a first pass that tells her which twenty deserve the two weeks.
card.rule: Do not commit to reading every title on a large list analytically; use a faster first pass to decide where thorough reading will go.
card.limits: With a short list the cost argument weakens, and you may be able to read everything analytically. The short cut saves time on the survey; it does not replace thorough reading of the works that matter.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Inspect every book first
concepts.question: Once your bibliography is assembled, what must you do with every book on it before reading any one analytically?

paragraphs: The short cut is inspectional reading. The first thing to do with an assembled bibliography is to inspect all of the books on it. The authors are firm: do not read any of them analytically before inspecting all of them.

Inspection will not show you all the intricacies of the subject or every insight your authors offer. That is not its job. Its job is to survey the whole list before you commit deep effort to any part of it.
Starting with a deep reading of one promising book is the tempting mistake. You cannot yet know whether that book is central, marginal or off the subject.
card.example: A teacher building a unit on climate history has twelve books. Instead of reading the first one cover to cover, she spends an hour on each: title, contents, index, a few key pages. Only after all twelve does she choose which to read closely.
card.rule: Inspect every book on your list before reading any one of them analytically.
card.limits: The rule is about where a project starts; it does not forbid reading books analytically later. Inspection gives a survey, not the understanding that only a full reading supplies.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: What inspection does for you
concepts.question: What two things does inspecting the whole bibliography do for a syntopical reader?

paragraphs: Inspecting every book on your list performs two essential functions. First, it gives you a clear enough idea of your subject that your later analytical reading of some of the books is productive.
Second, it lets you cut your bibliography down to a more manageable size. Books that turn out to be off the subject, or to say nothing important about it, can be dropped.
The two functions feed each other. A clearer idea of the subject is what lets you judge which books to cut, and seeing what each book covers is what clarifies the subject.
card.example: A podcaster researching the history of coffee inspects thirty books. She learns her real interest is coffee as a trade, not as a drink, and with that clearer subject she cuts the list to nine: the cookbooks and café guides fall away.
card.rule: Inspect the whole list both to sharpen your idea of the subject and to cut the list to the books worth reading.
card.limits: Inspection gives a clear enough idea for productive reading, not a final one; the subject keeps sharpening during the syntopical reading itself. A cut made early can be revisited.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Not every book gets equal time
concepts.question: Why do even capable advanced students waste effort in research reading, according to the authors?

paragraphs: The authors think the advice to inspect first is among the most useful they can give graduate and research students. A certain number of such students can read actively and analytically, get at the meat of a book and fit it into a plan of their subject.
Their efforts are still enormously wasteful, because they do not know how to read some books faster than others. They spend the same time and effort on every book or article.
The result cuts both ways: the books that deserve a really good reading do not get it, and time is wasted on works that deserve less attention.
card.example: A research assistant gives each of forty articles a careful three-hour reading. The three that prove central get no more than the rest, though they needed a day each, while the ten marginal ones eat thirty hours.
card.rule: Match the time and effort you give each book to what it deserves for your subject, instead of reading everything at one rate.
card.limits: Varying speed needs a basis: you can give a book its due only once inspection has shown roughly what it holds. Uniform care makes sense only if every item really is equally important, which is rare.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Return for light, or not
concepts.question: During a quick inspection, what decision about each book can a skilful inspectional reader already make?

paragraphs: A skilful inspectional reader does more than file a book in a mental card catalogue and gain a surface knowledge of it. In the short time inspection takes, he also discovers whether the book says something important about his subject.

He may not yet know what that something is; finding out usually waits for another reading. But he has learned one of two things: either this is a book he must return to for light, or it contains no enlightenment on his subject and need not be read again.
The second verdict holds however enjoyable or informative the book is. The test is whether it throws light on your subject.
card.example: Inspecting a lively travel memoir for a study of how cities grow, a planner sees it is full of colourful facts but offers no account of why cities grow. She enjoys it, notes it as not to be reread for this study, and moves on.
card.rule: For each book you inspect, decide whether you must return to it for light on your subject or need not read it again.
card.limits: The verdict is about this subject only; a book with no light for one study may matter for another. A must-return verdict says a book is important, not yet what it says.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Inspect, then analyse: two passes
concepts.question: Can a skilful reader inspect all the books and read them analytically at the same time, according to the authors?

paragraphs: In analytical reading, a skilful reader does at once steps that a beginner must take separately. By analogy, you might think that inspecting the whole list could be done along with the analytical reading of its books.
The authors deny this: they do not believe any reader, however skilful, can do it. It is, they say, the mistake that many younger researchers make.

Trying to collapse the two steps into one, these researchers end up reading everything at the same rate. That rate may be too fast or too slow for a given work, but it is wrong for most of the books they read.
card.example: A researcher decides to save time by reading each book carefully as she finds it and judging its relevance as she goes. Ten books in, she has spent a week each on two marginal books and hurried past a central one she had not yet recognised as central.
card.rule: Finish inspecting the whole list before you begin analytical reading, however skilful you are.
card.limits: The warning is about merging the survey of a list with deep reading. Within a single analytical reading, the authors grant, a skilled reader can still take several steps at once.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: A different aim from analytical reading
concepts.question: Once inspection has found the relevant books, why do the authors say read them syntopically rather than analytically?

paragraphs: Once inspection has identified the relevant books, the authors say you proceed to read them syntopically, and they point out that they did not say analytically.
You do read each work with the skills learned from the rules of analytical reading. But analytical reading is an art for reading a single book, with understanding of that book as the aim.
Syntopical reading has a quite different aim. You read the books for the light they throw on a subject or problem that spans them, not to understand any one of them for its own sake.
card.example: A lawyer reads five court opinions on privacy. She uses her close-reading skills on each, but she is not trying to master any single opinion as a whole; she is building an answer to how courts weigh privacy against security.
card.rule: Use analytical skills on each relevant work, but keep your aim on the problem that spans the books rather than on understanding any one book.
card.limits: A different aim does not license misreading: you must still understand a passage before you use it. When a single book is your object, analytical reading's aim is the right one.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: The five steps at a glance
concepts.question: What are the five steps of syntopical reading, and why do the authors stop short of calling them rules?

paragraphs: With the relevant books identified, syntopical reading proper has five steps: find the relevant passages; bring the authors to terms; get the questions clear; define the issues; analyze the discussion.
The authors decline to call these rules, though they say they might. If any step is not taken, syntopical reading becomes much more difficult, perhaps impossible.

They present the steps roughly in the order in which they occur, but add that in a sense all of them have to take place for any of them to. Terms, questions and issues take shape together as the reading goes on.
card.example: A student comparing books on free will drafts a few neutral terms, then finds that framing her questions forces her to revise those terms, and defining the issues sends her back for new passages. She moves forward through the steps but keeps looping back.
card.rule: Carry out all five steps in roughly their order, expecting to return to earlier steps as later ones reveal more.
card.limits: The order is rough, not a strict sequence, so treating it as a rigid checklist misreads the authors. Skipping a step is not forbidden by a rule, but it makes the work much harder.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Step 1: find the relevant passages
concepts.question: In the first step of syntopical reading proper, what are you looking for in the books already judged relevant?

paragraphs: The first step is another inspection, this time of the whole works already identified as relevant. Its aim is to find the passages in those books that are most germane to your needs.
It is unlikely that the whole of any book is directly on your subject. Usually the relevant matter is a chapter here, a few pages there. Finding those passages is the work of this step.
Even if a whole book is on your subject, which very rarely happens, the authors say to read it quickly, remembering that you read it for the light it throws on your problem.
card.example: A historian studying public health in Victorian cities has six relevant books. In a biography of an engineer, only two chapters on the sewers bear on her question; in an economic history, one section on housing. She marks those passages and leaves the rest.
card.rule: Inspect each relevant book again to find the passages most germane to your problem, rather than reading the whole work.
card.limits: Finding passages is the start, not the whole job: you still have to understand them. A passage marked without regard to its surroundings can be misread.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Your problem comes first
concepts.question: In syntopical reading, whose needs come first, yours or the books', and how does that change the way you read?

paragraphs: If you read each relevant book thoroughly, you would be putting the individual books first and your problem second. In syntopical reading, the authors say, the order is reversed.
It is you and your concerns that are primarily to be served, not the books. You read each book for an ulterior purpose, for the light it may throw on your problem, not for its own sake.
That is why speed is right here. Keeping your purpose in view stops you from being drawn into each book's own line of thought and losing track of what you came for.
card.example: A teacher planning a unit on persuasion opens a classic on rhetoric. Its long sections on ancient law courts are fascinating, but her question is how persuasion works in advertising. She takes what bears on that and moves on, instead of following the book wherever it leads.
card.rule: Put your problem first, and read each book for the light it throws on that problem rather than for its own sake.
card.limits: Serving your problem does not mean bending what the books say to suit it; passages must still be read accurately. The priority belongs to syntopical reading, not to reading one book for understanding.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Keep the two searches apart at first
concepts.question: When can you look for relevant passages while still deciding which books are relevant, and when should you keep these apart?

paragraphs: Finding passages might seem possible during the first inspection, the one that judged whether each book was relevant at all. Often it is, the authors say, but it is unwise to assume it always is.

The first inspection also served to zero in on the subject, and an adequate grasp of the problem may come only after inspecting many books. Hunting for passages before you know the problem is perilous.
So tell early books from later ones. With the first books, keep the two steps rigorously separate. With books you reach after many others, your problem is clear and the two steps can coalesce.
card.example: Early in a study of loneliness, a researcher marks passages on solitude in her first three books, then realises her subject is social isolation in old age. Most marks must be redone. By the twentieth book she judges relevance and marks passages in one sitting.
card.rule: Keep identifying relevant books and finding relevant passages as separate steps at first, and merge them only once your problem is clear.
card.limits: A very skilful reader, or one already familiar with the subject, may merge the steps sooner, the authors allow. The danger lies in merging before the problem is clear, not in merging as such.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Help the author never intended
concepts.question: Can an author help with your problem even if the book was written for a quite different purpose?

paragraphs: Your task in step one is not to reach an overall understanding of the book before you. It is to find out how the book can be useful to you, in a connection that may be very far from the author's own purpose in writing it.
At this stage that distance does not matter. An author can help you solve your problem without having intended to.
So do not dismiss a passage because its author was after something else. Ask what it shows about your problem, whatever it was written to show.
card.example: A city planner studying how people find their way in unfamiliar places reads a medieval pilgrim's travel diary. The writer meant to record a religious journey, but his notes on landmarks and on getting lost bear directly on her question.
card.rule: Look for how each passage can serve your problem, even when that use lies far from the author's purpose.
card.limits: Using a passage for your purpose is not the same as claiming the author meant it so. When you report what an author held, state his own purpose fairly.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Master, not disciple
concepts.question: How does the reader's relation to the authors in syntopical reading differ from the relation in analytical reading?

paragraphs: Because the books serve you, the authors call syntopical reading the most active reading you can do. Analytical reading is active too, but in it you stand to the book as disciple to master.
In syntopical reading you must be the master of the situation. You set the problem, choose the passages, and decide how each author bears on the question.
Being master here means directing the inquiry, not looking down on the authors. You still need their help; you are the one who decides what it is help with.
card.example: A manager reads four books on negotiation. Reading one analytically, she would follow its author's framework. Reading syntopically, she sets her own question, when to walk away from a deal, and calls on each author only where he speaks to it.
card.rule: In syntopical reading, direct the inquiry yourself instead of following any one author's lead.
card.limits: Mastery of the situation is not mastery of the subject: you may know far less than your authors. In the analytical reading of a single great book, the disciple's stance remains the right one.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Step 2: bring the authors to terms
concepts.question: In syntopical reading, who sets the terms, and how does this reverse the rule of coming to terms with an author?

paragraphs: In analytical reading, the first rule of interpretation asks you to come to terms with the author: find his key words and discover how he uses them. You take on his vocabulary to understand him.

In syntopical reading you face many authors, who are unlikely to have used the same words or even the same terms. So it is you who must establish the terms and bring your authors to them, rather than the other way around.
In practice, that means stating what each author holds in your own set of terms, whatever words the author used.
card.example: Comparing books on happiness, a reader finds one author speaks of flourishing, another of contentment, a third of pleasure. She sets her own terms, say lasting well-being and passing pleasure, and states each author's view in them.
card.rule: Establish your own set of terms and state every author's views in them, instead of adopting each author's vocabulary in turn.
card.limits: Your terms must still fit what each author meant; forcing him into a term that distorts him fails this step. You need to understand his own usage before you can translate it.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Refuse any one author's vocabulary
concepts.question: Why must a syntopical reader refuse to adopt any single author's terminology, even a great author's?

paragraphs: The authors call bringing the authors to terms probably the most difficult step. It comes down to forcing an author to use your language rather than his, and all our normal reading habits oppose it.

When we read a book analytically we treat the author as our better, especially if the book is great, and tend to accept his terms and his organization of the subject. In syntopical reading that habit gets us lost.
Adopt one author's terminology and you may understand his book, but you will fail to understand the others, and little light will fall on your subject. So resolutely refuse it.
card.example: A student comparing economists on inequality adopts one famous author's vocabulary of capital and returns. His book becomes clear, but two writers who think in terms of opportunity and mobility now look confused or irrelevant, though they are neither.
card.rule: Resolutely refuse to adopt any one author's terminology as your framework, however great the author.
card.limits: Refusing an author's terminology as your framework does not mean ignoring it: you must learn it in order to translate him. The refusal concerns which vocabulary organises the whole study.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: When your term matches an author's
concepts.question: What should you do when one of your authors happens to use the very term you would choose?

paragraphs: Beyond refusing any one author's terminology, you must face the possibility that no author's terminology will be useful to you. Any coincidence between your terms and an author's should be treated as accidental.
Such a coincidence is often inconvenient. If you take over one of an author's terms, you may be tempted to take others of his terms too, and these may get in the way rather than help.
A borrowed word also brings its owner's meaning with it, which may not be the meaning you need.
card.example: Studying motivation, a reader likes one author's term intrinsic drive and adopts it. Soon she is also using his words reward circuit and set point, and finds herself describing every other author in his framework without having decided to.
card.rule: Treat any match between your terms and an author's as accidental, and watch that one borrowed term does not pull in the rest of his vocabulary.
card.limits: A shared word is not forbidden; sometimes an author's word really is the best one. The danger is unexamined borrowing, which carries his meaning and his neighbouring terms in with it.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Syntopical reading as translation
concepts.question: In what sense is syntopical reading an exercise in translation, and what must the reader's set of terms accomplish?

paragraphs: Syntopical reading, the authors say, is to a large extent an exercise in translation. Not from French to English, but from each author's terms into a common terminology that you impose on all of them.
This is needed because your authors, whatever natural language they shared, may not have been concerned with your problem, and so may not have created the ideal terminology for dealing with it.
As you go on, build a set of terms that does two things: first, helps you understand all of your authors, not only one or a few; second, helps you solve your problem.
card.example: A historian of medicine compares writers who speak of humours, miasma and germs. She builds terms such as cause located in the body and cause carried from outside. These let her state every writer's view, and they fit her question about how ideas of contagion changed.
card.rule: Build a common terminology that fits all of your authors and serves your problem, and translate each author into it.
card.limits: Translation can lose shades of meaning, and a term broad enough to fit everyone may be too broad to separate real differences. Test the set against both demands and refine it.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Step 3: get the questions clear
concepts.question: How does a syntopical reader turn many authors' different statements into propositions that can be compared?

paragraphs: In analytical reading, the second rule of interpretation asks you to find an author's key sentences and grasp his propositions. Propositions are made of terms, so once you have set the terms yourself, you must also establish a set of neutral propositions.
The best way, the authors say, is to frame a set of questions that shed light on your problem and to which each of your authors gives answers.
Each author's position then becomes his answer to your question, stated in your terms. That is what makes the positions comparable.
card.example: Comparing books on punishment, a reader frames the question: should punishment aim mainly at deterring future crime? One author's long chapter on prisons becomes the answer yes; another's essay on desert becomes no; a third's becomes yes, but only alongside reform.
card.rule: Establish neutral propositions by framing questions that bear on your problem and that each author can be read as answering.
card.limits: A question works only if it can be put to most authors fairly; one loaded with an author's assumptions makes his view the standard. Good questions usually take several drafts.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Questions the authors never asked
concepts.question: What two demands must your questions meet, and why may the authors never have seen them as questions?

paragraphs: Framing the questions is hard because they must meet two demands. They must be stated and ordered so that they help you solve the problem you started with. And they must be framed so that all or most of your authors can be interpreted as answering them.
The difficulty is that the questions you want answered may not have been seen as questions by the authors. Their view of the subject may have been quite different from yours.
So the answers often have to be found by interpretation, in passages written for another purpose, rather than read straight off the page.
card.example: A designer asks: should a city street favour walkers over drivers? Writers from the 1800s never posed that question; they wrote about carriages, trade and health. Yet their views on how streets should serve commerce and clean air can be read as answers to it.
card.rule: Frame questions that both advance your problem and can be answered by most of your authors, even if the authors never posed them.
card.limits: Some authors will not answer some questions at all, even by interpretation; the next idea covers that. A question far from every author's view may serve your problem yet draw no answers.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Silent or indeterminate
concepts.question: What should you record when an author gives no answer to one of your questions?

paragraphs: Sometimes you have to accept that an author gives no answer to one or more of your questions. The authors say that in that case you must record him as silent or indeterminate on the question.

The authors do not define the two words. A useful reading: silent means he says nothing that bears on the question; indeterminate means what he says does not settle which answer he would give. Either way, the record admits the gap instead of filling it.
A record of silence is information. It shows where an author's view of the subject stopped short of yours, and it keeps you from inventing a position for him.
card.example: In a table of answers on whether animals have rights, a reader marks one eighteenth-century philosopher as silent: he discusses cruelty to animals but never addresses rights. She leaves the cell marked silent instead of guessing yes or no.
card.rule: When an author gives no answer to a question, record him as silent or indeterminate rather than assigning him an answer.
card.limits: Before marking silence, check for an implicit answer, which the next idea covers. Silence on one question says nothing about an author's answers to the others.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Implicit answers, with restraint
concepts.question: When may you attribute an answer to an author who never stated one, and what limits that?

paragraphs: Even when an author does not discuss a question explicitly, you can sometimes find an implicit answer in his book. If he had considered the question, you may conclude, he would have answered it in such and such a way.
Restraint is necessary here. You cannot put thoughts into your authors' minds or words into their mouths.
But you also cannot depend entirely on their explicit statements about the problem. If you could depend on any one of them in that way, the authors note, you would probably have no problem to solve.
card.example: An author never discusses remote work, but argues at length that trust between colleagues grows only through daily face-to-face contact. A reader may fairly record him as implicitly doubting remote work, citing that argument; she may not credit him with views on video calls he never touched.
card.rule: Look for implicit answers where an author's stated views point plainly to one, and refuse to attribute answers his text does not support.
card.limits: The line between an implicit answer and an invented one is a judgment; where the text does not point plainly, record silence instead. Every implicit answer should rest on passages you can cite.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Putting the questions in order
concepts.question: In what order should a syntopical reader put the questions, according to the authors' general guidance?

paragraphs: The questions must be put in an order that helps the investigation. The order depends on the subject, but the authors suggest a general pattern.

First come questions about the existence or character of the phenomenon or idea. If an author says the phenomenon exists or has a certain character, further questions can be asked of his book: how the phenomenon is known, or how the idea shows itself.
A final set of questions may concern the consequences of the answers to the earlier ones.
card.example: Studying free will: first, does free will exist, and what is it? Next, for authors who say it exists: how do we know we have it, and how does it show itself in choices? Last: what follows for praise, blame and punishment?
card.rule: Order your questions from the existence or character of the thing, to how it is known or shows itself, to the consequences of those answers.
card.limits: The pattern is a general direction, not a fixed rule; the subject decides the order. Later questions may apply only to authors who answered the earlier ones in a certain way.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: No agreement, no shortcut
concepts.question: Why should a syntopical reader expect the authors to answer the questions differently?

paragraphs: You should not expect all your authors to answer your questions in the same way. If they did, the authors say, you would once again have no problem to solve: it would have been solved by consensus.
Disagreement among the authors is therefore not a failure of your questions. It is the normal state of subjects worth reading syntopically, and it sets up the next step, defining the issues.
When answers line up, check before you conclude: the agreement may be real, or your questions may be too vague to bring out the differences.
card.example: A reader frames the question: does homework improve learning? Some authors say yes, some no, some only for older pupils. Rather than worry that her question failed, she sees she has found exactly what the next step needs.
card.rule: Expect and record differing answers to your questions; they are the material from which issues are defined.
card.limits: Authors do agree on some questions, and the authors later say agreement usually accompanies disagreement. Expecting difference does not mean manufacturing it where authors really agree.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Step 4: define the issues
concepts.question: What turns a clear question and the authors' differing answers into an issue, and how are several answers handled?

paragraphs: If a question is clear, and you can be reasonably certain that authors answer it in different ways, perhaps pro and con, an issue has been defined. It is the issue between the authors who answer one way and those who answer in an opposing way.
When all the authors examined give only two answers, the issue is relatively simple. Often, though, more than two alternative answers are given.
In that case, order the opposing answers in relation to one another, and classify the authors according to the answers they adopt.
card.example: On whether punishment should aim mainly at deterrence, a reader finds three answers: yes; no, it should give offenders what they deserve; and only alongside reform. She arranges them with deterrence at one end, desert at the other, reform between, and lists the authors under each.
card.rule: Define an issue wherever a clear question gets opposing answers, and when there are several answers, order them and group the authors under each.
card.limits: An issue needs a clear question and real differences; disagreement over an unclear question is not yet an issue. Ordering many answers is a judgment the reader must be able to defend.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Is the issue truly joined?
concepts.question: When are two authors truly disagreeing, rather than answering different questions under the same words?

paragraphs: An issue is truly joined, the authors say, when two authors who understand a question in the same way answer it in contrary or contradictory ways.
This happens less often than one might wish. Differences in answers must often be put down to different conceptions of the question, as often as to different views of the subject.
So before recording two authors as opponents, check that they are answering the same question. If one means one thing by it and the other another, they may not be disagreeing at all.
card.example: Two writers answer whether markets are free. One says yes, meaning no government sets prices; the other says no, meaning poor buyers have no real choice. They understand the question differently, so the issue between them is not yet joined.
card.rule: Count two authors as truly opposed only when they understand the question in the same way and answer it in contrary or contradictory ways.
card.limits: Different conceptions of a question do not make the authors irrelevant to each other; they show the question needs reframing. An apparent agreement can also hide different conceptions.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Framing the issue so it is joined
