concepts.question: What should the syntopical reader do when the authors' questions do not line up well enough for a real disagreement?

paragraphs: Because issues are so often not truly joined, the authors give the syntopical reader a task: define the issues so as to ensure that they are joined as well as may be.

Sometimes this forces the reader to frame the question in a way that no author explicitly uses. The question is built so that each author's view, properly translated, becomes an answer to the same thing.

The chapter's closing summary repeats the point: an issue does not always exist explicitly between authors, and sometimes it has to be constructed by interpreting their views on matters that may not have been their main concern.
card.example: One writer argues that zoos educate the public; another, that wild animals suffer in captivity. They never address each other. A reader frames the question: do the benefits of keeping wild animals outweigh the harms to them? Now both can be placed as answers, and the issue is joined.
card.rule: Where authors talk past each other, frame the question yourself so that their views become opposing answers to one question.
card.limits: A constructed question must still fit each author's actual view; forcing a fit fabricates a debate. Some authors may go on answering different questions however the issue is framed.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Issues grouped into controversies
concepts.question: How should many related issues be grouped and arranged in a syntopical analysis?

paragraphs: A problem may involve many issues, but they are likely to fall into groups. Questions about the character of the idea under study, for example, may generate several connected issues.
The authors call a number of issues revolving around a closely connected set of questions the controversy about that aspect of the subject.

A controversy may be very complicated. It is the syntopical reader's task to sort it out and arrange it in an orderly and perspicuous fashion, clear and easy to follow, even if no author has managed to do that.
card.example: Studying privacy, a reader finds issues about what privacy is, whether it is a right, and whether it covers personal data. She groups the first two as a controversy about the nature of privacy and the data issues as a controversy about its scope, and lays out each with its sides.
card.rule: Group closely connected issues into controversies, and lay out each controversy in a clear order, even if no author has done so.
card.limits: Grouping is the reader's construction and must follow real connections between questions; a neat arrangement that splits linked issues misleads. Not every issue need belong to a larger controversy.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Step 5 and the four questions
concepts.question: How do the five syntopical steps line up with the four questions a reader asks in analytical reading?

paragraphs: The first four syntopical steps correspond to the first two groups of rules for analytical reading. Those rules let you answer, of a single book, What does it say? and How does it say it?
After the first four syntopical steps you can answer the same questions about the discussion of your problem: what the authors say on it and how their views are arranged.
In analytical reading two questions remained: Is it true? and What of it? The fifth step, analyzing the discussion, prepares you to ask similar questions about the discussion as a whole.
card.example: After mapping what eight economists say about minimum wages and how their positions divide, a reader can describe the discussion fully. Only now does she turn to asking how far the discussion reaches the truth and what follows from it.
card.rule: Use steps one to four to establish what the discussion says and how it is arranged, and only then take up whether it is true and what of it.
card.limits: The parallel is loose: in syntopical reading the truth is sought in the discussion as a whole, not in one author's propositions, as the next idea explains.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Truth in the conflict of answers
concepts.question: Where should a syntopical reader look for the truth about a perennial problem on which thoughtful people disagree?

paragraphs: Suppose your problem is one of the perennial ones, which thinkers have struggled with for centuries and on which good people have disagreed and can go on disagreeing.
Then your task is not only to answer the questions yourself. The truth about such a problem is not found so easily, and it would probably be presumptuous to expect it in any one set of answers.
Rather, the authors say, it is to be found, if at all, in the conflict of opposing answers, many of which may have persuasive evidence and convincing reasons behind them.
card.example: On whether people are selfish by nature, a reader finds strong evidence and arguments on several sides. Instead of crowning one answer, she studies how the answers conflict: what each side explains well and what it leaves out.
card.rule: On a perennial problem, look for the truth in the conflict of opposing, well-supported answers rather than in any single set of answers.
card.limits: This holds for perennial, disputed problems; a question with a settled answer does not need it. It does not say every answer is equally good, only that the truth is unlikely to sit in one.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Analyzing the ordered discussion
concepts.question: What must a syntopical reader do before claiming to have analyzed, and understood, the discussion of a problem?

paragraphs: The truth, insofar as it can be found, lies rather in the ordered discussion itself than in any set of propositions about it. So it is not enough to ask the questions and answer them.

You must ask the questions in a certain order and be able to defend that order. You must show how the questions are answered differently, and try to say why. And you must be able to point to the texts that support your classification of the answers.

Only when all this is done can you claim to have analyzed the discussion, and only then to have understood it. Each demand guards against a failure: an arbitrary order, an unexplained list of opinions, a classification no one can check.
card.example: A reader on free speech orders her questions from what speech is to when it may be limited, and can say why. She shows that authors split over harm partly because they define harm differently, and for each placement cites the passage that puts the author there.
card.rule: Order the questions defensibly, show and explain how the answers differ, and cite the texts behind each classification before claiming to understand the discussion.
card.limits: Explaining why authors differ is something to attempt, not always achieve; the authors say try to say why. A defended order is one good arrangement, not the only possible one.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Groundwork for a breakthrough
concepts.question: What can a thorough analysis of a discussion achieve beyond the reader's own understanding?

paragraphs: The authors think a thorough analysis may do more than give the reader understanding. It may provide the groundwork for further productive work on the problem by others.

It can clear away the deadwood and prepare the way for an original thinker to make a breakthrough. Without the analysis, that might not have been possible, because the dimensions of the problem might not have been visible.
In a footnote they hope their own published studies of ideas such as progress, freedom, happiness, justice and love will serve in this way.
card.example: A review that maps forty years of conflicting research on sleep and memory, showing which questions are settled and which split the field, lets a young scientist see where an experiment could decide between rival accounts.
card.rule: Aim for an analysis thorough enough that others can see the problem's dimensions and build on it.
card.limits: The analysis prepares the ground; it is not itself the breakthrough. It serves others only if it stays fair to every side, the demand the next section takes up.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Camps, not lone voices
concepts.question: Besides the basic oppositions, what else must an adequate analysis of a discussion report about the authors?

paragraphs: An adequate analysis of a discussion identifies and reports the major issues, the basic intellectual oppositions, in it.
That does not mean disagreement dominates every discussion. Agreement usually accompanies disagreement: on most issues, each opposing view is shared by several authors, often by many.
Seldom is a controversial position held by a solitary exponent. So the report should show who stands together on each side, not only where the sides clash.
card.example: A report on the debate over a four-day work week lists the major issues: productivity, wellbeing, cost. Under each it shows the camps, say twelve authors broadly in favour, seven against, three undecided, so readers see the alliances as well as the oppositions.
card.rule: Report the major issues of a discussion and, for each side, the authors who share it.
card.limits: Agreement within a camp does not mean its members agree on everything; allies on one issue may oppose each other on the next. A lone position can exist; it is only rare.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Presumption and counter-presumption
concepts.question: What do agreement and disagreement among authors each suggest about the truth of their opinions?

paragraphs: The agreement of people about the nature of things in a field of inquiry establishes some presumption that the opinions they commonly hold are true.
Their disagreement establishes a counter-presumption: that none of the opinions in conflict, whether shared or not, may be wholly true.
A presumption is a reasonable starting assumption, not a proof. Agreement tilts the scale toward truth; disagreement tilts it toward thinking that each side holds less than the whole truth.
card.example: Nearly all historians agree that a famine happened in a certain year; that gives the claim some presumption of truth. Historians disagree sharply about its causes, which suggests that no single account of the causes may be wholly right.
card.rule: Treat agreement as some presumption that a shared opinion is true, and disagreement as a counter-presumption that no conflicting opinion is wholly true.
card.limits: Neither is decisive: the authors note that even an opinion on which all seem to agree may be false. Presumptions guide where to look, not what to conclude.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Four possibilities about the truth
concepts.question: When opinions conflict, what possibilities about their truth should the syntopical reader keep open?

paragraphs: Among conflicting opinions, one may be wholly true and the rest false. But it is also possible that each expresses some portion of the whole truth.

Except for flat and isolated contradictions, which are rare in discussions of these problems, it is even possible that all the conflicting opinions are false, in the way that an opinion on which all seem to agree may be false.
And some opinion not yet expressed may be the truth, or nearer to it. The reader keeps all these possibilities open rather than assuming one.
card.example: On how best to teach reading, one camp favours phonics, another whole-language methods. One may be right, each may hold part of the truth, both may be wrong, or a method no one has proposed may work better.
card.rule: Keep open that one conflicting opinion is wholly true, that each holds part of the truth, that all are false, or that an unexpressed opinion is nearer the truth.
card.limits: The authors imply that where two opinions flatly contradict each other, both cannot be false, though such cases are rare here. Keeping options open is not refusing to weigh evidence.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Dialectical, not dogmatic
concepts.question: Why must a syntopical analysis avoid declaring which side of an issue is true?

paragraphs: The aim of syntopical reading is not final answers to its questions or a final solution of the problem. This holds especially for any report of the reading.

If the report asserted or tried to prove the truth or falsity of any view on the important issues, it would be dogmatic, not dialectical. It would cease to be syntopical and become one more voice in the discussion, losing its detached and objective character.

One more voice still carries weight, the authors grant. But a different kind of contribution can and should be made, one that is resolutely objective and detached throughout. They sum up its quality as dialectical objectivity.
card.example: A scholar writes an analysis of the debate over nuclear power. If her final chapter argues that nuclear power is the answer, her book becomes one more pro-nuclear voice. If it lays out every side fairly and stops there, it makes a different kind of contribution.
card.rule: In a syntopical analysis, report the issues without asserting or trying to prove any side, so the analysis stays dialectical rather than dogmatic.
card.limits: This governs the syntopical report, not the reader's whole thinking: the authors grant that one more voice has weight, so she may argue her own view elsewhere. Detachment means taking no side in the analysis, not having no views.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Look at all sides, take no sides
concepts.question: Of the two halves of the syntopical ideal, looking at all sides and taking no sides, which is harder, and why?

paragraphs: The syntopical reader tries to look at all sides and to take no sides. He will fail in this exacting ideal, the authors admit: absolute objectivity is not humanly possible.
He may succeed in taking no sides, presenting the issues without prejudice to any partisan view and treating opposing views impartially. But taking no sides is easier than looking at all sides.
In looking at all sides he will undoubtedly fail, because all possible sides of an issue cannot be exhaustively listed. Nevertheless, he must try.
card.example: An analyst reports the debate on rent control fairly between the two camps she found. Later she learns of a third position, held by planners who reject both camps' framing. She took no side, but she did not see all sides; she adds the third and keeps looking.
card.rule: Take no side in presenting the issues, and keep searching for sides you have not yet found, knowing the list can never be complete.
card.limits: Failing to find every side is expected and is no reason to stop trying. Impartiality between the sides you found is no proof that you have found them all.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: How bias slips in unstated
concepts.question: How can bias enter a syntopical report even when the writer never says which side is right?

paragraphs: Taking no sides is easier than looking at all sides, but it remains difficult. Perfect dialectical objectivity is not guaranteed by avoiding explicit judgments on the truth of conflicting opinions.

Partiality can intrude in subtle ways: by the manner in which arguments are summarized, by shades of emphasis and neglect, by the tone of a question or the colour of a passing remark, and by the order in which the different answers to key questions are presented.
The syntopical reader must resist these temptations and know his own mind.
card.example: A report on a vaccine debate never says who is right. But one side's case gets two pages and the other's a paragraph; one camp's view is introduced as what the evidence shows, the other's as what some claim; and the favoured side's critics are summarized at their weakest.
card.rule: Check your summaries, emphasis, tone and order of presentation for partiality, not only your explicit verdicts.
card.limits: Some difference in space is fair if one side's argument really is longer or more complex. The test is whether each side would accept its treatment as fair, not identical word counts.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Quote the authors' own words
concepts.question: What device helps a syntopical reader guard against distortion, and how does it fit with using neutral terms?

paragraphs: To avoid some of these dangers, the authors recommend one device, to be used as much as possible. Constantly refer back to the actual text of your authors, reading the relevant passages over and over.
When you present your results, quote each author's opinion or argument in his own language. Summaries are still given in your neutral terminology, not the author's; that requirement stands.
But the author's own words, carefully quoted so as not to wrench them out of context, must accompany the summary, so that your reader can judge for himself whether your interpretation is correct.
card.example: A report states one philosopher's view in its neutral terms: liberty is the absence of interference by others. Beside it, a short quotation from his chapter on liberty lets readers check that the summary is fair.
card.rule: Present each author's view in your neutral terms and accompany it with a carefully chosen quotation in the author's own words.
card.limits: A quotation misleads if it is wrenched from context; it must represent the passage fairly. Quoting does not replace the neutral summary; it lets readers check it.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Balance, and the writer as judge
concepts.question: Beyond quoting, what keeps a syntopical report objective, and who alone can know whether it succeeded?

paragraphs: Other departures from dialectical objectivity, the authors say, can be prevented only by the syntopical reader's firm intention to avoid them.
The ideal demands a deliberate effort to balance question against question, to forgo any comment that might be prejudicial, and to check any tendency toward overemphasis or underemphasis.
In the last analysis, a reader may judge how effective a written report is, but only its writer, the syntopical reader himself, can know whether he has satisfied these requirements.
card.example: Revising her report on school testing, an analyst notices she put three probing questions to one camp and one to the other, and she cuts a witty aside about the other camp's leading author. No editor flagged either; she caught them because she was looking.
card.rule: Deliberately balance your questions, cut prejudicial comments and correct lopsided emphasis, holding yourself responsible for objectivity.
card.limits: Self-judgment is fallible, which is why the quotations remain for others to check what they can. Balance is fair treatment, not mechanical equality of length.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
concepts.title: Building the list on progress
concepts.question: How did the authors build their bibliography on progress, and what does that show about finding relevant works?

paragraphs: The authors' study of the idea of progress took several years. The first task was to amass a bibliography of works to examine for relevant passages; it finally ran to more than 450 items.

It was built by a series of inspectional readings of several times that many books, articles and other pieces. Many items finally judged relevant were found more or less by accident, or with the help of educated guesses.
There were obvious places to start: many recent books have progress in their titles. But others do not, and most of the older books, though relevant, do not even use the term.
card.example: A reader studying the idea of resilience searches catalogues for the word and finds recent books. Older works on fortitude, endurance and recovery from disaster never use the word, yet treat the same subject; she finds them by following leads and making educated guesses.
card.rule: Build your bibliography by inspecting many more works than you will keep, and search beyond titles that contain your subject's word.
card.limits: A keyword search remains a fair starting point; the warning is against stopping there. Accident and guesswork cannot be planned away, so expect the list to grow as you read.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
concepts.title: Why fiction was mostly left out
concepts.question: Why did the authors mostly leave novels, plays and poems out of their syntopical study of progress?

paragraphs: A few fictional and poetical works were read, but the authors chose to concentrate on expository works. Including novels, plays and poems in a syntopical project is difficult, for several reasons.

First, the backbone of a story is its plot, not its positions on issues. Second, even talkative characters seldom take clear positions on an issue; they mostly talk about other matters, chiefly emotional relations.

Third, even when a character makes such a speech, as Settembrini does about progress in Thomas Mann's The Magic Mountain, we cannot be sure it is the author's view. The author may be ironic. Placing a fiction on an issue takes great effort for dubious results, so it is usually prudent to abstain.
card.example: A reader studying whether technology improves life finds a novel whose hero praises machines in a rousing speech. The novel ends with the hero ruined by his own invention. She cannot tell whether the speech is the author's view or the target of his irony, so she leaves the novel out of her table of positions.
card.rule: Concentrate a syntopical project on expository works, and generally abstain from placing fiction on one side of an issue.
card.limits: The authors did read a few fictional works, and call abstaining usually prudent, not required. With intensive interpretation a fiction can sometimes be placed, at great cost and with uncertain results.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
concepts.title: Non-meliorative advance
concepts.question: When authors use the same key word for incompatible ideas, how should a syntopical reader name their positions?

paragraphs: The word progress is used by authors in several ways. Most differences are only shades of meaning and can be handled in the analysis. But some authors use the word for a movement forward in history that is not an improvement.
Most authors use it for a historical change in the human condition that is for the better, and betterment is of the essence of the idea. So the same word could not serve both views.

The majority kept the word. The minority were referred to as authors who assert non-meliorative advance in history: advance without betterment. When discussing their views, the authors could not use the word progress, even though those writers had used it themselves.
card.example: In a study of growth, most economists mean rising wellbeing, but a few mean any rise in output, even if people end up worse off. The reader keeps growth for the majority sense and calls the minority view output expansion, so one word never stands for two ideas.
card.rule: When a key word is used for incompatible ideas, keep it for the majority sense and give the other view its own neutral name.
card.limits: Shades of meaning do not call for a new name; only incompatible conceptions do. Keeping the word for the majority is a practical choice, not a judgment that the majority is right.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
concepts.title: The primary question about progress
concepts.question: What first question did the authors find all writers on progress could be read as answering, and what answers did they find?

paragraphs: The first question to ask, the one to which authors can be read as giving various answers, turned out to be: does progress occur in history? That is, is the general course of historical change toward improvement in the human condition?
Basically, three answers are given: yes, no, and we cannot know.

But there are a number of ways of saying yes, several ways of saying no, and at least three ways of saying we cannot know. The primary question sorts the authors into camps, and each camp has its own internal variety.
card.example: A reader studying whether economic growth improves wellbeing frames the primary question: does growth make people's lives better overall? Writers answer yes, no, or that we cannot tell, and within the yes camp some point to health, others to freedom of choice.
card.rule: Find the primary question that every author can be read as answering, sort its main answers, and then the different ways each answer is given.
card.limits: Three answers is what the progress literature yielded, not a fixed pattern; another subject may give two or five. The camps are only a first sort; their internal differences matter too.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
concepts.title: General and special controversies
concepts.question: How did the authors separate the controversy all writers join from the one joined only by those who assert progress?

paragraphs: The many interrelated answers to the primary question, does progress occur, make up what the authors call the general controversy about progress. It is general because every author with anything significant to say on the subject takes sides on its issues.

There is also a special controversy, made up of issues joined only by progress authors, those who assert that progress occurs. These issues concern the nature or properties of the progress they all assert.

There are three: is progress necessary, or contingent on other occurrences? Will it continue indefinitely, or come to an end or plateau out? Is there progress in human nature itself, or only in human institutions and the external conditions of life?
card.example: In a study of whether cities improve their residents' lives, the general controversy covers everyone: yes, no, cannot know. A special controversy, among those who say yes, asks whether improvement is inevitable as cities grow, and whether it will continue without limit.
card.rule: Separate the general controversy that every author joins from special controversies joined only by authors who accept a basic answer.
card.limits: Authors who deny progress take no part in the special controversy, so their absence there is not neutrality. The three special issues are the progress study's result, not a template for every subject.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
concepts.title: Subordinate issues: in what respects?
concepts.question: What subordinate issues did the authors find among progress authors, and what special problem did one of them raise?

paragraphs: Finally there is a set of subordinate issues, again only among progress authors, about the respects in which progress occurs. The authors identified six areas: knowledge, technology, economics, politics, morals, and the fine arts.
Some authors say progress occurs in one or more of these areas while others deny it there, though never in all of them, since by definition they assert some kind of progress.
The fine arts raise a special problem: in the authors' opinion, no author genuinely asserts that aesthetic progress occurs, although a number of writers deny it.

This structure of general, special and subordinate issues is how the authors took steps four and five. Something like it, they say, must always be done by a syntopical reader, even one who writes no long book.
card.example: A study of whether medicine has improved might find subordinate issues by area: diagnosis, surgery, mental health care, end-of-life care. Writers who say medicine has improved may still deny improvement in one area, and the map shows which.
card.rule: Map the areas in which the phenomenon is said to occur, and record for each area which authors affirm it and which deny it.
card.limits: An area where no one genuinely affirms the phenomenon is not a joined issue in the usual way; report it as you find it. The six areas are the progress study's result, not a list for every subject.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
concepts.title: The fundamental problem
concepts.question: What is the fundamental problem of syntopical reading, and why may an expert adviser be only a partial help?

paragraphs: The authors admit they have not solved the paradox: unless you know what books to read, you cannot read syntopically, but unless you can read syntopically, you do not know what to read. As the fundamental problem: without knowing where to start you cannot begin, and finding the relevant books and passages may take longer than all the other steps combined.
In theory you could know the literature so well that you knew where every idea is discussed; then you would need no help. Or you could ask someone with that knowledge.

But such an adviser may hinder almost as much as help. If he has researched the subject, he will find it hard to tell you where to read without telling you how. If he has not, he may know little more than you, though it may seem otherwise to you both.
card.example: A student asks a professor where to read about civil disobedience. The professor, author of a book on it, lists passages and explains what each one really means. The student now reads them through his interpretation, before she has formed her own.
card.rule: Get help in finding where to read, but guard against advice that also tells you how to read the passages.
card.limits: Advisers remain useful for locating material; the risk lies in absorbing their interpretation. An adviser who has not studied the subject may also seem more knowledgeable than he is.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
concepts.title: An index that does not interpret
concepts.question: What is the Syntopicon, what makes it a good starting point, and what is its main defect?

paragraphs: What is needed is a reference book that tells you where to find relevant passages on many subjects without saying how they should be read, without prejudging their meaning or significance. The Syntopicon is an example.

Produced in the 1940s, it is a topical index to the set Great Books of the Western World. Under some 3,000 topics it lists references to pages where each is discussed, from long stretches to key paragraphs or parts of paragraphs.

Its major defect: it indexes one set of books, large as it is, and gives only rough hints about others. Still, it always offers a place to start, and the set's books are ones you would almost always want to read in such a project anyway.
card.example: A reader starting a study of courage looks up the topic in a topical index to a collection of classics. She gets page references to passages in Plato, Aristotle and others, with no commentary, then extends her search to modern psychology, which the index does not cover.
card.rule: Start from a topical index that points to passages without interpreting them, then extend your search beyond the set it covers.
card.limits: The index covers one set of books; treating it as the whole literature leaves out much relevant work. It saves preliminary labour, but you must still read and interpret the passages yourself.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
concepts.title: Reading in before reading through
concepts.question: How can a topical index help a beginner start on the great books, and lead the reader beyond the first topic?

paragraphs: The Syntopicon saves the mature scholar much preliminary labour, but the authors say it is much more useful to the beginner, in three ways: initiatively, suggestively and instructively.

Initiatively: the classics are a little overpowering, and reading programs that require whole books seldom achieve the desired result. The Syntopicon lets a person start with a subject he cares about and read relatively short passages from many authors on it. It helps us read in the great books before we have read through them.

Suggestively: starting from one interest, it may arouse interest in related subjects. And once started on an author, it is hard not to explore the context; before you know it, you have read a good part of the book.
card.example: A nurse curious about what makes a death good looks up the topic and reads short passages from a dozen classic authors. One passage leads her to read the surrounding chapter, then most of the book, and she starts on a second topic, grief.
card.rule: Begin on hard classics by reading short passages on a subject you care about, and follow the interests and contexts they open.
card.limits: Reading in is a way to start, not a substitute for reading through; the authors expect it to draw you into whole books. Short passages read out of context can be misread if never followed up.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
concepts.title: Three ways topics teach interpretation
concepts.question: In what three ways does reading passages by topic train a reader's skill in interpretation?

paragraphs: Syntopical reading with the Syntopicon also works instructively, in three distinct ways; the authors count this among the major benefits of this level of reading.

First, the topic gives direction in interpreting a passage but does not say what it means, since a passage may bear on a topic in many ways. The reader must discover precisely what relevance it has, a major skill in the art of reading.

Second, reading many passages on one topic from different works sharpens the interpretation of each: passages from one book clarify each other, contrasting passages accentuate each other, and one author's comments can illuminate another's.

Third, a passage is often cited under several topics. Interpreting it somewhat differently for each shows its amplitude of meaning and makes the mind alert to the many strains of meaning a rich passage contains.
card.example: A passage from a classic on friendship is cited under friendship, justice and happiness. Read for friendship, it is about loyalty; for justice, about what friends owe each other; for happiness, about friendship as part of a good life. The reader sees how much the passage holds.
card.rule: Work out exactly how each passage bears on its topic, read passages against one another, and reread a passage in the light of each topic it serves.
card.limits: Each reading for a different topic must still fit the text; multiple interpretation is no licence to make a passage mean anything. The topic directs interpretation but does not settle it.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
concepts.title: Small s and capital S
concepts.question: How do the authors distinguish syntopical reading in general from Syntopical reading with the Syntopicon?

paragraphs: Believing the Syntopicon useful to beginner and scholar alike, the authors adopted its name for this level of reading, and they ask forgiveness for what may seem a small self-indulgence.

They then point out a distinction. Syntopical reading with a capital S means reading the great books with the help of the Syntopicon. Syntopical reading with a small s is the general level of reading this chapter describes.
The capital-S kind can be part of any small-s project, and perhaps it would always be wise to start there. But small-s syntopical reading is a term of much wider application.
card.example: A team studying trust in online marketplaces might begin with classic passages on trust and promise-keeping found through the index. Most of their project, though, reads economics papers and platform studies that no great-books index covers: syntopical reading in the wide sense.
card.rule: Treat reading the great books with the Syntopicon as one possible first part of a syntopical project, not as the whole of syntopical reading.
card.limits: The authors offer starting with the index tentatively, as perhaps always wise. For subjects the great books barely touch, its contribution will be small.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.section: On the Principles That Underlie Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Three objections, three replies
concepts.question: What three objections are raised against syntopical reading, and how do the authors answer each?

paragraphs: Some say syntopical reading is impossible. First, imposing even a neutral terminology on an author is wrong: his terms are sacrosanct, and translating terms is dangerous. Second, authors far apart in time and style are separate universes, not one conversation. Third, how an author says something matters more than what he says.

To the first, the authors reply that denying an idea can be put in other terms is like denying translation between languages. A translator of the Koran called it impossible, then explained how he did it. Translation is difficult, but the difficult is not the impossible.

To the second: if Aristotle walked in with an interpreter, we could within ten minutes be discussing shared problems. So books can talk to one another through an interpreter, the syntopical reader, who must know both as well as he can.
To the third: told to follow Corridor B to the exit, you can test what was said whatever the tone. Human communication has a rational content beyond tone and gesture.
card.example: A reader comparing an ancient physician and a modern epidemiologist on contagion is told she distorts both by translating them into common terms. She replies that the translation is hard, quotes each so readers can check it, and notes that both make claims about causes that can be compared.
card.rule: Treat translation between authors' terminologies as difficult but possible, act as the interpreter between books, and attend to what each author says, not only how.
card.limits: The replies show syntopical reading is possible, not easy: care is needed, and you must know each book well. Tone matters, especially where emotional relations are the content; it is not all that matters.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: Two stages: survey, then read
concepts.question: What are the two main stages of syntopical reading, and how do the two preparatory steps affect each other?

paragraphs: The authors' summary divides syntopical reading into two main stages: surveying the field in preparation, and syntopical reading proper.

Preparation has two steps: create a tentative bibliography from library catalogues, advisers and the bibliographies in books; then inspect all the books on it to find which are germane and to get a clearer idea of the subject.

These two steps are not strictly separate in time. They affect each other, and the second, inspection, in particular modifies the first: what you learn while inspecting changes what belongs on the list.
card.example: A reader builds a list on civic trust from a library catalogue, a librarian's advice and the references in a good survey book. Inspecting the books, she learns that trust between neighbours matters to her question, adds three works on local associations, and drops five on trust in banks.
card.rule: Prepare by building a tentative bibliography and inspecting all of it, letting the inspection revise the list, before beginning syntopical reading proper.
card.limits: The stages are not sealed off: the subject keeps sharpening during syntopical reading proper, and new works may still join the list. The bibliography stays tentative.

concepts.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
concepts.title: What the summary adds
concepts.question: How does the authors' closing summary sharpen the five steps, especially on issues, ordering and objectivity?

paragraphs: The summary restates the steps with added precision. Terms and questions are neutral ones that all, or the great majority, of the authors can be interpreted as using or answering, whether or not they use the words or treat the questions explicitly.

Issues, major and minor, are defined by ranging authors' opposing answers on one side or another. An issue may not exist explicitly between authors; it may have to be constructed by interpreting views on matters that were not their main concern.
The discussion is analyzed by ordering questions and issues to throw maximum light on the subject: more general issues before less general ones, with the relations among issues shown.
Dialectical detachment should ideally be kept throughout. One way is to accompany each interpretation of an author's views with an actual quotation from his text.
card.example: A reader's report on immigration opens with the general issue, whether nations may restrict entry at all, then the narrower ones, such as how many and whom, noting that these arise only for those who answer yes. Each author's placement is paired with a quotation.
card.rule: Order issues from more general to less general, show how they relate, and pair each interpretation of an author with a quotation from his text.
card.limits: The summary condenses the chapter; it does not replace cautions such as restraint with implicit answers. All or the great majority of authors, not every one, must fit the terms and questions.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
concepts.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
concepts.title: Method needs materials
concepts.question: Besides the rules of reading, what else does a reader need in order to keep improving, and why will not any book do?

paragraphs: Having finished teaching the rules, the authors hand the work to you. If you accept their aim, reading as well as possible, and their means, the rules of inspectional, analytical and syntopical reading, then, as with any practical book, you are bound to act on them.

But the word means has a second sense. Besides the method there are the materials: the books you apply it to. A method with nothing fit to work on is as useless as fine materials with no method for working on them.

The rules fit any kind of book, fiction or nonfiction, practical or theoretical, yet many books do not call for the full analytical method. A book that only amuses, or only adds facts, leaves your skill where it was. The authors call a mind fuller of facts a change in quantity, not an improvement.
card.example: A carpenter who has learned fine joinery but only ever works with cardboard will not become a better carpenter, and good oak in untrained hands is wasted. Skill grows where good technique meets material that demands it. In reading, that means the rules applied to books that deserve them.
card.rule: Pair the rules of reading with books worth applying them to, since neither the method nor the materials improves you on its own.
card.limits: The pairing matters for improvement. When you want a book only for a fact or an evening's fun, the full method is more than it needs, and choosing it carefully matters little.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
concepts.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
concepts.title: Practise on books over your head
concepts.question: What kind of book must you practise on to improve as a reader, and should you fear that such books are truly beyond you?

paragraphs: A reader who wants to improve cannot read any book at all. Books well within your capacity let you use skills you already have, so they never make you reach. Only books over your head, books that seem beyond you, make you stretch your mind, and unless you stretch you do not learn.

Earlier the authors asked the good reader to make demands on himself. Here they add that the book must make demands too. The books you practise analytical reading on should seem to exceed your capacity.

You need not fear that they truly do. The authors hold that no book is wholly out of reach if you apply the rules, though the rules work no instant miracles. Some books will keep extending you however good you become, and those are the ones to seek out.
card.example: A manager reads business summaries he could have written himself; each one goes down easily and leaves his reading unchanged. He then takes on a dense classic of economics, struggles, outlines it, rereads hard chapters, and comes out a stronger reader.
card.rule: To grow as a reader, practise on books that seem beyond your present capacity, trusting the rules to bring them within reach.
card.limits: Over your head does not mean any hard book: one that is hard because it is muddled offers nothing to reach for. And the rules bring a hard book within grasp gradually, not at the first attempt.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
concepts.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
concepts.title: The hardest books may be poems
concepts.question: Which books stay hardest to read however skilled you become, and why might they not be science or philosophy?

paragraphs: Many readers assume that the books which never stop challenging them must lie in unfamiliar fields, which in practice means science and perhaps philosophy. The authors think this is far from the case.

Great scientific authors take pains to help you: they make their terms clear, point out their key propositions and set out their main arguments. Poetical works give none of these helps, so in the long run they are likely to be the most demanding books you can read.

Homer, the authors say, is in many ways harder to read than Newton, even though you may get more out of Homer on a first reading. The reason is that Homer deals with subjects that are harder to write well about.
card.example: A reader works through a classic of chemistry in a month, because its author defines each term and states each conclusion. A great play is easier to enjoy at first, yet years later she is still discovering what its scenes are doing.
card.rule: Include great imaginative works among the books you practise on, since without the helps scientific authors give, they may demand the most of you.
card.limits: The claim is about great works and the long run. A first reading of a poem may be easier and more rewarding than a scientific classic, and many novels make no lasting demand at all.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
concepts.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
concepts.title: Hard because rich, or hard because empty
concepts.question: When a book resists your efforts, how can you tell whether it is a good difficult book or a bad one?

paragraphs: A bad book is hard to read too. It resists analysis: whenever you think you have pinned it down, it slips away. The reason, the authors say, is that there is really nothing there to pin down, so the struggle brings no reward and is not worth the effort.

A good book also resists at first, but it rewards you for trying. As you work, terms come into focus and propositions and arguments emerge, and you end up understanding more than you did. The best books reward you most of all.
So difficulty alone does not mark a book worth your struggle. What matters is whether the struggle yields something you can grasp.
card.example: Two reports on the same policy each take Ana an evening. In the first, each hard paragraph turns out to state a claim she can restate and weigh. In the second, every sentence dissolves into slogans when she tries to restate it. The first was difficult; the second was empty.
card.rule: Persist with a book whose difficulty repays you in understanding, and stop struggling with one that slips away because there is nothing in it to grasp.
card.limits: At first the two can feel alike, since a good book also resists before it yields. Blame the book only after honestly applying the rules, or you will mistake your own unfinished work for the author's emptiness.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
concepts.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
concepts.title: Two rewards: skill and wisdom
concepts.question: What two rewards does a good difficult book give, and which do the authors count as more important?

paragraphs: A good book rewards the effort of reading it in two ways. The first is better reading skill, which grows each time you successfully tackle a good, difficult work.
The second, which the authors call much more important in the long run, is that the book teaches you about the world and about yourself. You learn more about life, not only more about reading.

The authors call this becoming wiser, which is not the same as becoming more knowledgeable. Books that offer nothing but information can make you more knowledgeable. Wisdom here means a deeper awareness of the great and enduring truths of human life.
card.example: After working through a great tragedy, a reader has sharpened her skill at following an action and its turns. She also sees her own stubbornness, and the price of pride, better than before. The first gain is skill; the second is wisdom.
card.rule: Read good difficult books for both rewards, better skill and deeper wisdom, and value the wisdom more.
card.limits: Wisdom is not a larger stock of facts, so a book can leave you better informed and no wiser. And the rewards come from good books read well; a book that only amuses gives neither.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
concepts.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
concepts.title: Questions no one can settle
concepts.question: Why do the authors think the greatest books are worth reading on questions that no one will ever finally answer?

paragraphs: Some human problems have no solution, and on some relationships no one can have the last word. In science and philosophy, no one has reached, or ever will reach, final understanding of nature and its laws, or of being and becoming.

The same is true of familiar, everyday matters: the relation between men and women, between parents and children, or between a person and God. These are questions you cannot think about too much, or too well.
No book will settle them for you. The greatest books help you think better about them, because they were written by people who thought better about them than others did.
card.example: A father wondering how much freedom to give his teenage son will find no formula that ends the question. A great novel about fathers and sons will not give him one either, but it can show him the question more deeply than he saw it before.
card.rule: Turn to the greatest books for help in thinking better about lasting human questions, not for final answers to them.
card.limits: Thinking better is not settling. A reader who expects a great book to close such a question will be disappointed, and one who wants a settled fact or technique needs a different kind of book.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
concepts.title: The pyramid: most books need only a skim
concepts.question: How do the authors sort the world's books into levels, and how should you read the great mass at the bottom?

paragraphs: Picture the several million books of the Western tradition as a pyramid. The broad base, more than 99 per cent, cannot make enough demands on you to improve your reading. They can be read only for amusement or information.
That amusement or information may be varied and interesting, but you should not expect to learn anything important from such books. You need not read them analytically at all: skimming will do.

Above the base sits a far smaller class of good books, perhaps one in a thousand or fewer, from which you can learn both how to read and how to live. At the very top is a tiny group, fewer than a hundred, that no reading can exhaust.
card.example: In a year a reader meets dozens of thrillers, topical books and guides. On the authors' scheme she skims nearly all of them for what she wants, keeps her analytical effort for the handful of good books, and saves rereading for the rare one that keeps giving.
card.rule: Skim the great mass of books for amusement or information, and save analytical reading for the small number that can teach you to read and to live.
card.limits: The percentages are the authors' rough estimates, not a count. And skimming the base is about improvement: a book there can still be worth reading for the fact or the pleasure you want from it.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
concepts.title: Good books: read analytically once
concepts.question: How should you treat the good books in the middle of the pyramid, and what are your notes in them for?

paragraphs: The second class, probably no more than a few thousand books, are the good books: carefully made by their authors and conveying significant insights about subjects of lasting human interest. They make severe demands, and from them you learn both how to read and how to live.

The authors say these books are worth reading analytically once. A skilful reader gets everything they can give in one good reading, then puts them on the shelf, knowing they will not have to be read again.

You may still return to check a point or refresh your memory of an idea or episode. Here notes made in the margin or elsewhere in the book are especially valuable: they take you to what you need without a second full reading.
card.example: A reader works carefully through a good history of medicine, marking its key arguments. Two years later, preparing a talk, she opens it, scans her margin notes and the passages they point to, and has what she needs in an hour.
card.rule: Give each good book one thorough analytical reading, and mark it so that later you can consult it rather than reread it.
card.limits: One reading is enough only if it is skilful and complete; a careless pass has not earned the right to shelve the book. And a book that keeps calling you back may belong to a higher class.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
concepts.title: Milked dry, or more there?
concepts.question: After your best reading of a book, how can you tell whether it has anything more to give you?

paragraphs: You know you are finished with a good book by your own mental reaction. As it stretches your mind, you come to realize, in a way the authors call more or less mysterious, that it will not change you any further. You have grasped it whole; in their phrase, you have milked it dry.

With a very few books the reaction differs. After reading as well as you can, you shelve the book with a sneaking suspicion that there is more in it than you got. You cannot say what. If you could, your duty as an analytical reader would send you straight back to find it.
Instead you find you cannot forget the book. You keep thinking about it and about your reaction to it, and in the end you return to it.
card.example: Months after careful readings, Dev rarely thinks of one excellent book on economics; it did its work. But a certain novel keeps surfacing in his thoughts, in arguments and on walks, though he could not name what he missed. The second book is calling him back.
card.rule: After your best reading, notice whether a book feels finished or keeps working on you, and return to the ones you cannot stop thinking about.
card.limits: The suspicion may be only a suspicion and can prove mistaken on return. And it differs from knowing what you missed: a known gap calls for going back at once, not for waiting to see whether the book lingers.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
concepts.title: The return visit: smaller, or grown with you
concepts.question: What happens when you return to a book after years, and what does the result tell you about the book and about you?

paragraphs: Return to a good book of the second class and it seems to hold less than you remembered. The book has not changed; you have. Your mind is fuller and your understanding greater, so the return is bound to disappoint.

Return to a book of the highest class and it seems to have grown with you. You see whole sets of new things in it. Your earlier understanding still stands, if you read well the first time, but now the book is true in further ways too.

A book cannot change once published. The explanation is that it was so far above you at first that it stays above you. A great book is accessible at different levels: it lifted you once and lifts you again, and can go on doing so all your life.
card.example: At twenty, Ana read a great play as a story of young love and its ruin. At forty, a parent herself, she finds it is also about the parents' feud and their failures. Her first reading was not wrong; the play holds both.
card.rule: On returning to a book, notice whether it seems smaller or larger than you remember, and keep returning to those that grow with you.
card.limits: A book that seems smaller is not thereby a bad book; you outgrew it partly because it taught you. And new insight adds to a sound first reading but cannot rescue a careless one.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
concepts.title: Your own short list of great books
concepts.question: Why is the set of inexhaustible books smaller for each reader than for readers in general, and what should you do about it?

paragraphs: The authors estimate that well under a hundred books can keep lifting readers in this way. For any one reader the number is smaller still, because people differ not only in the power of their minds but in taste: different things appeal to different people.

You may never feel about Newton as you do about Shakespeare. You might read Newton so well that you never need to return, or mathematical systems of the world may not appeal to you. For someone like Charles Darwin, to whom they did appeal, Newton might be among the few great books and Shakespeare not.

So the authors refuse to say that any particular book must be great for you. Their first appendix lists books that have had this value for many readers, but the task is yours: seek out the few that can have it for you, the books you will return to again and again.
card.example: Two friends admire the same famous list of classics. For one, a work of political philosophy opens up on every reading; for the other it was finished after one good reading, while a book of poems keeps growing. Each has found a different short list.
card.rule: Treat lists of great books as suggestions, and find through your own reading and returning the few that keep growing for you.
card.limits: Taste does not make a book great: a book you reread for comfort without seeing anything new is not one of them. And a book that is not great for you may still deserve one good reading.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
concepts.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
concepts.title: Ten books on a desert island
concepts.question: What can imagining a life marooned with only ten books teach you, and why do the authors think the test is not so unreal?

paragraphs: An old test asks you to suppose you will be marooned on a desert island for life, or for a long time, with time to prepare. Besides useful supplies, you may take ten books. Which would you choose?

Drawing up the list can show which books you would most like to read and reread, but the authors think that matters less than what you learn about yourself. Imagine life cut off from the usual sources of amusement, information and understanding: no radio, no television, no library, only you and ten books.

The situation sounds bizarre, but the authors think it is not so unreal. All of us are to some extent marooned. We face the same challenge we would face on the island: finding within ourselves the resources to live a good human life.
card.example: Asked to choose, Kai first picks ten gripping thrillers, then realizes he would finish them in a month and be left with nothing. Swapping in books he could return to for years, he learns what his mind actually depends on.
card.rule: Use the desert-island choice to test what you could rely on without outside stimulation, and build the inner resources a good life needs.
card.limits: The list itself is the minor product; arguing over the right ten books misses the point. And the exercise reveals your inner resources without supplying them: that takes reading of the kind the list points to.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
concepts.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
concepts.title: The mind can grow for life, or waste away
concepts.question: How does the mind differ from the body in its power to grow, and what danger comes with that difference?

paragraphs: The body has limits the mind does not. By about thirty, most people's bodies are as good as they will ever be, and many have begun to decline. The mind has no such ceiling: it can keep growing in skill and understanding until the brain itself loses its vigour in old age.
The authors suggest this may be the major difference between human beings and other animals, which seem not to grow mentally beyond a certain stage.

The advantage carries a peril. Like a muscle, the mind can atrophy if it is not used. The authors point to the many busy people who die soon after retiring: their work kept their minds active from outside, and with no inner resources, they stop thinking once its demands end.
card.example: A surveyor's job kept her mind busy with problems for forty years. Planning her retirement, she takes up a demanding history and a language course, so that when the job's demands stop, her mind's work will come from within.
card.rule: Keep exercising your mind by your own effort throughout life, rather than leaving its activity to outside demands such as a job.
card.limits: The growth does end, in senescence, when the brain itself fails. And the retirement deaths are the authors' interpretation, which they say they can find no other explanation for, rather than a proven cause.

concepts.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
concepts.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
concepts.title: Artificial props and a living mind
concepts.question: Why do the authors call television, radio and similar sources artificial props, and what do they offer in their place?

paragraphs: Television, radio and the other sources of amusement and information around us can make our minds feel active, because we must react to stimuli from outside. The authors call them artificial props, like the demands of a job.

Their power to keep us going is limited. They work like drugs: we grow used to them, need more and more, and in the end they have little or no effect. If we then lack inner resources, we stop growing intellectually, morally and spiritually, and when we stop growing, the authors say, we begin to die.
Against this they set reading well, which means reading actively. It is a good in itself and can help your career, but it also keeps the mind alive and growing, because the activity comes from you.
card.example: Every evening Joe scrolls news feeds for hours and feels mentally busy, yet he needs ever more to stay interested and keeps little. When he spends the same hour reading a demanding book and asking questions of it, the effort is his own, and it builds on itself.
card.rule: Rely on active reading, not on a stream of outside stimulation, to keep your mind working and growing.
card.limits: The fault is passive reaction, not the medium alone: by the same reasoning, a book read without effort props the mind no better. And the authors do not deny that broadcasts can inform or amuse.

concepts.title: Matching the level to the goal
concepts.question: Given what I want from this reading and how many works it involves, which level of reading does the situation call for?

paragraphs: Choosing a level starts with two questions. What do you want from this reading: pleasure, information or understanding? And is your object one work, or a subject that several works treat? The authors tie analytical reading to understanding and say it is hardly ever needed when the goal is information or entertainment.

Put the answers together. To learn in a short, set time what a work is, what it covers and whether it deserves more, read it inspectionally. To understand one work that is at first beyond you, read it analytically. To understand a subject that runs through many works, read them syntopically.
Elementary reading is less chosen than returned to. When the words or sentences themselves stop you, that trouble must be settled first, whatever level you were aiming at.
card.example: Nadia has a recipe for tonight, a hard essay on why cities sprawl, and a week to prepare a council brief on housing from six books. She takes in the recipe for its information and cooks. She reads the essay, which she does not yet understand, analytically. She reads the six books syntopically, building her own account of the housing question from them.
card.rule: Pick the level from your goal and your object: inspection to size up a work or take its surface in a set time, analytical reading to understand one work, syntopical reading to understand a subject across many.
card.limits: Goals can change mid-reading: a work picked up for information may turn out to deserve understanding. And reading several works for one fact, such as three reviews before buying a kettle, is gathering information, not syntopical reading.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole

concepts.title: Placing a difficulty at its level
concepts.question: When a reading goes badly, which level's question can I not answer, and what kind of work would fix it?

paragraphs: Each level has a question of its own. Elementary: what does the sentence say? Inspectional: what is the book about, what kind of book is it, and what are its parts? Analytical: what does it say in detail, is it true, and what of it? Syntopical: how do many works bear on one subject?

A difficulty belongs to the level whose question you cannot yet answer, and it yields to work at that level. Trouble making out sentences is elementary; outlining will not fix it. Feeling lost halfway through a book usually means its surface was never surveyed, the plowing-in the authors warn against.

Following every sentence yet missing the case points to analytical work on terms, propositions and arguments. And when two books seem to clash, check whether they use the same words for different things before deciding they disagree.
card.example: Three students say a book on economics is hard. Ali cannot untangle its long sentences: elementary trouble, met by slower work on the sentences. Bea is lost in chapter six because she never looked at the contents: she needs inspection. Cal follows each page but cannot say what the author argues: he needs analytical reading.
card.rule: Name the level whose question you cannot answer, and work on the difficulty at that level.
card.limits: Levels are cumulative, so one difficulty can hide another: a reader stuck on sentences may also lack the structure. And some trouble lies in the book, not the reader: a badly unified book resists every level's question.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole

concepts.title: When time is short
concepts.question: With little time for a work that deserves more, what reading gets the most from it, and how should I treat what it yields?

paragraphs: The authors define two levels by time. Inspectional reading is the best and most complete reading possible in a limited time; analytical reading is the best and most complete possible given unlimited time, that is, as much as the work demands. So when time is short, their own definitions point to a full inspection.

A full inspection, a skim and then a straight-through reading, gives answers you can use: what kind of work it is, what it is about, how it is built, and whether it deserves more. A few chapters studied closely, by contrast, give pieces of an analysis with no frame to hold them.

Treat what inspection suggests about truth and significance as provisional, a hunch for a later reading. If you mean to return, note the kind, subject and plan on the contents page while they are fresh.
card.example: Priya has forty minutes before a committee discusses a long consultant's report. Rather than study the first two sections closely, she skims the whole and reads it straight through. She arrives knowing its kind, its main recommendation and its four parts, marks her doubts about its figures as questions, and notes the plan on the cover for a later, careful reading.
card.rule: When time is short, give a work the fullest inspection the time allows, and hold its verdicts as provisional until a later analytical reading.
card.limits: Inspection is the best use of short time, not a substitute for analysis: a work you must understand still needs the later reading. And with a short text and time enough to finish it, analytical reading may fit at once.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole

concepts.title: Going further, one level at a time
concepts.question: At the end of each level, how do I decide whether a work deserves the next one, and when is stopping the right call?

paragraphs: The level is rarely fixed at the start. Each level ends with a decision about the next. A skim decides whether a straight-through reading is worth it; that reading shows whether the work deserves analytical reading; and an analytical reading can raise a question that other works treat, which may begin a syntopical project.

Stopping is a proper result at every rung. The authors say many books are worth reading well and many more should only be inspected; a good reader reads each according to its merits. A skim that ends the matter has done its job.
Two moves go wrong: committing to a full analytical reading of a work you never inspected, and dropping a work after one hard page before seeing it whole.
card.example: A journalist skims ten books on water policy in an afternoon. Seven end there: she knows what each argues. Two she reads straight through; one proves hard and central, so she reads it analytically. Its leading question, who should own rivers, then sends her to several of the others, read now for how they treat that question.
card.rule: Treat each level as a gate: finish it, then decide from what it showed whether the work earns the next level or has given you what you need.
card.limits: A stop is tied to your present purpose: a work set aside after a skim may deserve more when your needs change. And the gates assume the work is new to you; a book you already know well can be taken up at the level you need.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole

concepts.title: Four questions, three stages, fifteen rules
concepts.question: Which of the fifteen rules serve which of the four basic questions, and why do three stages answer four questions?

paragraphs: The whole method hangs on the four questions. Rules 1 to 4, the first stage, answer what the book is about as a whole: classify it, state its unity, outline its parts, define its problems. Rules 5 to 8, the second stage, answer what is said in detail and how: terms, propositions, arguments, and which problems were solved.

Rules 9 to 15, the third stage, serve the last two questions, is it true and what of it. Three maxims govern how to criticize: understand first, do not quarrel, give reasons. Four criteria supply the grounds: uninformed, misinformed, illogical, incomplete. Three stages answer four questions because the critical rules carry both truth and significance.

Read the rules as means and the questions as ends. When a rule seems pointless for a particular work, ask which question it serves: the question tells you what you still have to find, even when the rule itself must be adapted.
card.example: A reader checks her notes on a book about loneliness. Under question one: its kind, a one-sentence unity, an outline, the author's two questions. Under question two: five key terms, the main claims in her words, two arguments, one problem left open. Under questions three and four: where she thinks the author is misinformed, and how the book changes her view of isolation.
card.rule: Use each stage's rules to answer its question: Rules 1 to 4 for what the book is about, 5 to 8 for what it says and how, and 9 to 15 for whether it is true and what of it.
card.limits: The map fits expository books. Imaginative literature answers the same questions through a parallel set of rules, not the fifteen. And the numbering gives the logical order, not separate passes through the book.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole

concepts.title: Each step feeds the next
concepts.question: What does each step of analytical reading hand to the next, and where should I look when a later step goes wrong?

paragraphs: The steps are ordered because each uses what the one before produced. Knowing the kind of book tells you what sort of terms and arguments to expect. The statement of unity guides the outline, and the outline shows where the important sentences are likely to sit.

Within interpretation the chain is tight: terms make up propositions, and propositions are the premises and conclusions of arguments. The problems listed under Rule 4 are what Rule 8 checks off as solved or not, and what Rule 15 later measures for completeness.

So a fault early on travels forward. An outline built on the wrong unity scatters the search for key sentences; a misread term distorts every proposition that uses it. When a later step stalls, look back along the chain before blaming the book.
card.example: Reading a book on public health, Jonas cannot make its central argument hang together. Tracing back, he finds he took prevention to mean vaccination, while the author uses it for every measure taken before illness. With the term corrected, the propositions change, and the argument now follows.
card.rule: Treat each step's result as material for the next, and when a later step fails, check the earlier results it rests on.
card.limits: The chain shows dependence, not a one-way sequence: later steps also correct earlier ones, as interpretation sharpens the statement of unity. And sometimes the fault is the author's: a book with no real unity cannot be repaired by rechecking your outline.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole

concepts.title: From first look to last word
concepts.question: In what order should inspection, the analytical stages, notes and outside aids come when I read one book well?

paragraphs: For one book read well, the steps fall into a sequence. Skim first: it sketches the structure and decides whether to go on. Read straight through without stopping at hard places: this begins the interpretation. Then read analytically, outlining and interpreting together, with notes that move from the book's structure to its concepts.

Outside aids come after your own best effort, and only for what still resists you. Someone else's commentary comes after you have read the book; the author's own preface comes before. The authors warn that many readers lean on aids too much, and that doing all you can yourself leaves you needing less help.
Last comes the verdict: agree, disagree or suspend judgment, with reasons, and then what of it. Questions and doubts can be noted at any point; what waits is the verdict.
card.example: Asked to report on a book about ageing, Ruth skims it in twenty minutes and notes its parts on the contents page. She reads it through in two evenings, passing over a chapter on cell biology. Reading closely, she outlines and marks terms, then looks up two biological terms the book never explains. Only when she can restate the argument does she write her assessment.
card.rule: Inspect, read through, analyze, consult aids for what still resists you, and give your verdict last.
card.limits: The sequence is for a learner and a hard book; a practised reader runs much of it together. And your own experience is not an aid you can postpone: it enters outlining, interpretation and criticism from the start.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole

concepts.title: Classifying picks the rules
concepts.question: How does deciding what kind of book I hold change which rules I apply, and what stays the same?

paragraphs: Rule 1 works like a switch. Its first decision, a story or a work that conveys knowledge, selects the rule set. Expository books take the fifteen rules. Imaginative literature takes a parallel set: find the unity of the plot, know the characters and incidents, and appreciate what the author tried to make you experience before you criticize.

Within expository books the next decision, practical or theoretical, adapts the rules. For a practical book Rule 4 becomes find out what the author wants you to do, and Rule 8 becomes find out how he proposes you do it. Theoretical books divide further into history, science and philosophy, each read in its own way.

What does not switch is the four questions. Every kind of book is asked what it is about, what it says, whether it is true and what of it, though for a story the last question, strictly speaking, asks nothing of you.
card.example: Mia has a lyric poem, a first-aid manual and a history of the plague on her desk. For the poem she looks for its single emotional experience, not an argument. For the manual she asks what it wants her to do and how. For the history she notes its subject and its limits. The same four questions frame all three.
card.rule: Classify a work before applying the rules, and let its kind decide which rule set and which adaptations you use.
card.limits: Kinds mix: a novel can carry social science, and a philosophical book can end in advice, so the switch may need resetting as the work shifts. And a classification is a first guess to confirm, not a label that ends inquiry.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole

concepts.title: Where each kind puts the weight
concepts.question: For each kind of book, which of the four questions needs the most care, and what kind of answer should I expect?

paragraphs: The four questions stay, but each kind of book shifts their weight. For a practical book the authors say the first two questions change little, the third more, and the fourth most: is it true becomes whether its ends are right and its means good, and agreeing with it commits you to act.
