For a history, the first question needs special care: what exactly does it cover, and what does it leave out? Its what of it points, the authors say, toward practical and political action. For social science, the first question is the hardest and most important: which strands of science, history and philosophy make up the book.

For a scientific book, terms and propositions are usually easy to spot, but following its inductive arguments, part of grasping what is said in detail, needs the evidence the scientist reports. For a story, the fourth question strictly asks nothing: answering the first three discharges the reader's duty.
card.example: A reader plans her week: a manual on public speaking, a history of the 1918 flu, a report on youth crime, and a short story. She will press the manual on what it wants her to do and whether to do it, the history on its exact scope, the report on its mix of strands, and the story only through plot, characters and its truth as a story.
card.rule: Ask all four questions of every book, but spend the most care where its kind puts the weight.
card.limits: These are emphases, not exemptions: a practical book still needs outlining, and a history still has terms and arguments. And a book that mixes kinds carries the weights of each kind it mixes.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole

concepts.title: What a finished analytical reading holds
concepts.question: When can I say I have finished reading a book analytically, and what should I be able to produce at that point?

paragraphs: A finished analytical reading leaves you able to produce answers, not only memories. For the first question: the book's kind, its unity in a few sentences, an outline of its major parts, and the problems it set out to solve.

For the second: its key terms and the senses in which it uses them, its leading propositions in your own words, its main arguments, and which of its problems it solved. The test of understanding applies here: could you restate its position, in your own words, well enough to satisfy the author?

For the last two: a verdict, agree, disagree or suspend judgment, in whole or in part, backed by reasons and the criteria of criticism; and an answer to what of it, the difference the book makes to your views or actions. The authors say an analytical reading is not done until these last answers exist.
card.example: Kemal's record of a book on sleep fits on two pages: a theoretical work of science, a three-sentence unity, four parts, two problems. Then six terms, five propositions in his words, the main argument, one problem left open. Last, he agrees with its account of memory, judges its advice on naps uninformed about shift workers, and has rethought his own sleep.
card.rule: Count an analytical reading finished only when you can state the book's structure, restate its message in your own words, and give a reasoned verdict and its significance.
card.limits: Finished is measured against an ideal: few readings reach every answer, and a suspended verdict is a proper result, not a gap. And a finished reading is not final; rereading, other books or new experience may revise it.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole

concepts.title: What finished means at each level
concepts.question: What counts as done at the inspectional, analytical and syntopical levels, and what record shows that each is done?

paragraphs: Each level has its own finish line. An inspection is done when you can say what kind of work it is, what it is about and how it is ordered, and have decided whether it deserves more. Its record is structural notes, best kept on the contents or title page.

An analytical reading is done when all four questions have answers, the last two included. Its record is conceptual notes on the author's ideas and on how your own have changed. For a story, the finish comes after the first three questions.

A syntopical reading is done when you have analyzed the discussion: the questions ordered and defended, the authors' answers set out and explained, each placement backed by texts. Its record is dialectical notes on separate sheets. The aim is not final answers: the authors ask the syntopical reader to look at all sides and take none.
card.example: One reader, three finishes. Her inspection of a book on cities ends with a few lines on its contents page. Her analytical reading of the best book on the subject ends with margin notes on its concepts and her verdict. Her syntopical project ends with sheets mapping the issues and who holds what, with quotations, and no verdict of her own.
card.rule: Know the finish line of the level you chose, and keep the record that shows you reached it: structural, conceptual or dialectical notes.
card.limits: The finish lines are ideals to approach. Perfect objectivity is not humanly possible, the authors admit, and all sides of an issue cannot be listed. And a reading finished at one level can be the start of the next.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole

concepts.title: Reading How to Read a Book itself
concepts.question: What does an analytical reading of How to Read a Book itself look like, judging by the authors' own hints?

paragraphs: In an appendix, the authors turn the rules on their own book and give hints, not answers. Rule 1 is easy: it is a practical book. Its unity you must state more briefly than they did anywhere. Your outline might well comment on why elementary reading gets short treatment and analytical reading the most.

For Rule 4, they warn that their problem is not teaching people to read in general; nothing in the book would help a first-grade teacher much. It is reading in a certain way, with certain goals, which you must describe precisely. Terms, propositions and arguments they leave to you: listing them would mean writing the book over.

On Rule 8 they claim to have solved their main problem but not every reading problem, since many turn on individual differences. On Rule 15 they call their account incomplete: elementary reading could be treated much more, and syntopical reading more still. A finished reading of any book, theirs included, can find such gaps without rejecting it.
card.rule: Apply all the rules even to a book you admire: state its kind, unity, problems and solutions yourself, and name precisely where its account falls short.
card.limits: The authors' hints are not an answer key: the unity, terms and arguments must still be your own. And their admissions of incompleteness concern their stated task; faulting the book for not teaching children to decode words judges it by a task it never set.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors of How to Read a Book, the ideal reader reads every kind of material at the greatest speed they can manage.
questions.explain: The preface rejects a single top speed for everything. The card next shows what it proposes instead.
questions.rule: One speed for everything is not the goal.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: What does the preface propose as the answer to the speed-reading fad?
options: Slow, careful reading of every text, so nothing is missed
Speed-reading courses combined with training in recall
Variable-speed reading: different speeds for different material
Reading only those books that can be read quickly and easily, skipping the rest
optionExplain: Careful reading sounds safe, but the preface wants some things read faster too: sometimes slower, sometimes faster.
The preface doubts the courses' promises; it does not add to them.
Right: the desirable ability is reading different things at different, appropriate speeds.
Choosing only easy books avoids the problem instead of solving it, and the book is about reading demanding works.
questions.explain: The preface proposes variable-speed reading: read better, always, sometimes slower and sometimes faster.
questions.rule: The goal is the right speed, not the top speed.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Dev has one evening for a sports news site, a tenancy agreement he must sign, and a short poem a friend sent him. Which plans fit variable-speed reading? Select all that apply.
options: Skim the sports news quickly
Read the tenancy agreement slowly, clause by clause
Read all three at his fastest pace to save time
Give the poem a slow reading, perhaps twice
Read all three slowly to be safe
optionExplain: Right: light news can be read fast without losing what matters.
Right: a binding agreement repays slow, exact reading.
This saves minutes but risks missing a clause or the poem's sense; one top speed is what the preface rejects.
Right: a short poem often needs slow, repeated reading.
Caution feels responsible, but crawling through sports news wastes time and, as Pascal warned, too slow can lose the sense as well.
questions.explain: Each right plan matches the speed to what the text demands. A single speed for all three, fast or slow, misses the point of variable-speed reading.
questions.hint: Ask what each text needs, not what is quickest.
questions.rule: Let each text set its own pace.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: True or false: If Mia, fresh from a speed-reading course, reads a dense philosophy essay at the rate she reads a gossip column, the preface's view predicts she will miss much of the essay.
questions.explain: The condition that changed is the material: the pace that suits a column is too fast for close argument, and Pascal says reading too fast leaves us understanding nothing. The preface's answer is to slow down where the text demands it.
questions.rule: Harder material needs a slower pace.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Lena reasons that because speed hurts understanding, the slower she reads anything, the better she will understand it. Where does her reasoning go wrong?
options: It assumes understanding matters more than speed
It forgets that speed-reading courses improve comprehension
It ignores that reading too slowly can also lose the sense
It holds for fiction but not for nonfiction
optionExplain: The preface does put understanding first; that part of her reasoning is sound.
The preface treats the courses' promises with doubt, so this is no correction.
Right: Pascal's warning cuts both ways, too fast or too slowly, and the aim is sometimes faster, sometimes slower.
The preface makes no such split between fiction and nonfiction.
questions.explain: Lena turns a rule about appropriate speed into a rule about slowness. The preface warns against reading too slowly as well as too fast.
questions.rule: Too slow is also the wrong speed.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: A home cook opens a recipe post: a long personal story, then the ingredients and method. Following the preface's idea, how should she read it?
options: Slowly all the way through, so that no detail is missed
Quickly all the way through, since recipes are easy
Read only the story, then improvise the dish
Quickly through the story, slowly through the method
optionExplain: Thorough, but the story does not deserve that time; uniform slowness is a single speed too.
The method's quantities and steps are where a fast read causes mistakes.
This skips the part she needs most.
Right: each part gets the speed its content deserves.
questions.explain: Variable speed applies within one text as well as between texts. The filler can go fast; the parts that carry the substance go slow.
questions.rule: Speeds can change within a single text.
questions.teaches: The book later gives the formula: read every book no more slowly than it deserves, and no more quickly than you can with satisfaction and comprehension; even a good book has passages to read fast and others to read very slowly.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: According to the study quoted in the preface, what happens to most pupils' reading skill after about the sixth grade?
options: It keeps rising steadily through high school
It levels off and stops improving much
It declines as pupils read less
It jumps sharply when college reading begins
optionExplain: Many people assume this, since students keep reading more, but the study found the opposite.
Right: the improvement curves flatten out to a dead level after the fifth and sixth grade.
The study reports a flat line, not a decline.
College adds more reading, but the study says students stay at a sixth-grade level well into college.
questions.explain: Mursell found steady gains up to the sixth grade and then a flat line. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Reading gains usually stall after elementary school.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: True or false: Mursell concluded that reading skill flattens after the sixth grade because pupils reach their natural limit of efficiency.
questions.explain: He rules that out: with special tuition, older children and adults can make enormous improvement. The flat curve reflects missing instruction, not a ceiling.
questions.rule: The ceiling is in the teaching, not the reader.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Sort each claim: does it fit the account of Mursell quoted in the preface, or contradict it?

items.t: Reading improves steadily up to about the sixth grade
With special tuition, adults can improve enormously
Many pupils do poorly in high school because they cannot get meaning from the page
The sixth grade is the natural limit of reading efficiency
Most sixth-graders read well enough for all practical purposes
Reading skill keeps rising through high school

questions.explain: Mursell finds steady gains, then a flat line, and blames missing instruction rather than a natural limit. He also denies that sixth-grade skill is enough for practical purposes.
questions.rule: The flat curve is a failure of teaching, not of ability.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: A firm finds its new graduates handle emails well but struggle with dense technical standards. Following the preface, what is the most promising response?
options: Train them in reading complex documents at a higher level
Accept that adult reading ability is fixed by now
Rewrite the standards in plain language so no training is needed
Hire only graduates who scored highly on school reading tests
optionExplain: Right: the preface's evidence is that adults improve greatly with further instruction.
This is the natural-limit view the quoted study rejects.
Plainer documents may help, but this avoids the reading instead of building the higher skill the preface says adults can learn.
School reading tests mostly measure the elementary level, which these graduates already have.
questions.explain: The gap is in higher-level skill that was never taught, so teaching it is the fix. The preface says adults can make enormous improvement.
questions.rule: Missing higher skills can be taught to adults.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: True or false: If Mursell's account is right, an adult who receives special tuition in reading can still make large gains.
questions.explain: Mursell says it has been shown again and again that with special tuition older children and adults can make enormous improvement. Change the condition, add instruction, and the curve rises again.
questions.rule: Add instruction and the curve can rise again.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: A college reports that its first-year remedial reading course brought weak readers up to standard. On the book's view, has that course carried them to the higher levels the preface describes?
options: Yes: any reading course trains the higher levels
Yes, if the course also taught speed-reading
No: only private tutoring by a specialist can teach the higher levels
No: bringing readers up to basic competence is a different job
optionExplain: The book separates basic and higher instruction; a course can do one without the other.
The book counts speed-reading courses as mostly remedial too, so adding one does not help.
The book does not limit higher training to tutors; the point is what is taught, not who teaches.
Right: remedial work repairs the elementary level; the higher levels are distinct skills.
questions.explain: Remedial teaching fixes what the first six grades should have done. The higher levels are distinct skills that need their own instruction.
questions.rule: Fixing basic reading is not training higher reading.
questions.teaches: The book later states that remedial reading instruction is not instruction in the higher levels of reading, and that most speed-reading courses are remedial in this sense.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Mursell describes a typical high-school graduate. Which kinds of reading does he say leave this reader at a loss? Select all that apply.
options: A simple piece of fiction, such as a short story
A closely written exposition
A carefully and economically stated argument
Any text longer than a page or two
A passage requiring critical consideration
optionExplain: He says this reader can follow and enjoy simple fiction.
Right: close exposition is one of the three he names.
Right: a tight argument is another.
Mursell names kinds of writing, not lengths; a long simple story is within this reader's reach.
Right: passages that need critical thought are the third.
questions.explain: The graduate manages simple stories but fails at exposition, argument and critical passages. The card next says what skill is missing.
questions.rule: Stories can hide weak reading skill.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Tests showed the average high-school student was very poor at indicating the ____ of a passage, or the levels of emphasis and subordination in an argument.
questions.explain: Mursell names two failings: finding the central thought, and seeing emphasis and subordination. Both are about grasping how a text is built, not its words.
questions.rule: Find the central thought first.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: A reader summarises a council report on closing a branch library by listing, in order, that the building is old, visits have fallen, and the savings will fund a mobile library. By Mursell's test, what is missing?
options: More of the report's figures
The central claim and how the points serve it
A judgment on whether closing the library is the right choice
The names of the councillors involved
optionExplain: More detail adds to the list but still does not say what the list is for.
Right: a list in order shows no central thought and no subordination.
Judging comes later; first the reader must grasp what the report argues.
Names are detail, not the structure of the argument.
questions.explain: Retelling points in order is not the same as seeing which point is central and which ones support it. That is the skill Mursell found missing.
questions.rule: A list of points is not yet a grasp of the argument.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Sam reasons that since he reads three novels a month with ease, he must be a skilled reader of any book. Which step in his reasoning fails?
options: Three novels a month is too small a sample to judge by
Novels are harder to read well than arguments, so he is ahead
Skill can be shown only by a formal reading test, not by habit
Ease with simple fiction does not show skill with close argument
optionExplain: The number is not the problem; volume of reading proves little either way.
Mursell's account runs the other way: simple fiction is what the weak reader can manage.
Tests helped Mursell show the gap, but the flaw is in Sam's inference, not his lack of a test.
Right: Mursell's graduate enjoys fiction yet is lost with exposition and argument.
questions.explain: Sam generalises from the kind of reading that asks least to every kind. Mursell's reader is fine with stories and lost with arguments.
questions.rule: Skill with one kind of text does not prove skill with all.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: True or false: Mursell's test of central thought and subordination is the right measure for a reader enjoying a simple adventure story on holiday.
questions.explain: The test is for exposition and argument, where points are ranked and connected. A simple story read for enjoyment does not demand it, which is how fiction can hide the gap.
questions.rule: Use the central-thought test on exposition and argument.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: A hiring test gives candidates a policy memo and four statements, and asks which statement best expresses the memo's main idea. Which skill from Mursell's list is it testing?
options: Reading at high speed
Indicating the central thought of a passage
Remembering every detail and figure in the memo
Enjoying a simple piece of writing
optionExplain: The test has no time element as described; it asks about content.
Right: choosing the statement that best expresses the main idea is a test of central thought.
Details help, but the question asks for the main idea, not recall of specifics.
Enjoyment is what the weak reader can already manage; this asks for more.
questions.explain: Choosing the best statement of a main idea checks whether the reader found the central thought. Mursell's students failed exactly this.
questions.rule: Main-idea questions test central thought.
questions.teaches: Picking which of several statements best expresses the main idea of a passage is one of the standard reading-test formats the book describes in its appendix of exercises.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Which list gives the four levels of reading named in the preface?
options: Skimming, scanning, studying, reviewing
Literal, critical, creative, applied
Elementary, intermediate, advanced and expert reading
Elementary, inspectional, analytical, syntopical
optionExplain: These are familiar study-skill words, but not the book's levels.
This is a common school scheme, not Adler's.
Elementary is right, but the book's other three levels are inspectional, analytical and syntopical, not general grades like intermediate or expert.
Right: these four levels organize the whole rewritten book.
questions.explain: The four levels are elementary, inspectional, analytical and syntopical. The card next shows how they shape the book.
questions.rule: Four levels: elementary, inspectional, analytical, syntopical.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Put the four levels of reading in the order the preface lists them, first to last.
items: Elementary
Inspectional
Analytical
Syntopical
questions.explain: The preface lists them as elementary, inspectional, analytical and syntopical. This distinction is the controlling change in the book's organization.
questions.rule: The levels run from elementary to syntopical.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Match each part of the rewritten book to what the preface says it does.
pairs: Introduces the four levels of reading
Sets out the rules of analytical reading
Approaches different kinds of reading matter
questions.explain: Part One maps the levels, Part Two gives the analytical rules, Part Three applies them to kinds of reading, and Part Four adds syntopical reading. Only Part Two closely follows the 1940 book.
questions.rule: Levels, rules, kinds, syntopical: one part each.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: A reader wants help with a newspaper's advertisements and with a book of lyric poems. Which part of the rewritten book does the preface point her to for advice specific to these kinds?
options: Part One
Part Two
Part Three
Part Four
optionExplain: Part One introduces the levels; it does not treat kinds of reading matter.
Part Two gives general analytical rules, not advice for each kind.
Right: Part Three covers kinds from lyric poetry to journalism and even advertising.
Part Four is about reading several books on one subject.
questions.explain: Part Three, the largest addition, covers the different kinds of reading matter, including imaginative literature, current journalism and advertising.
questions.rule: Kinds of reading matter are Part Three's job.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: True or false: Since Part Three treats history separately, a reader of a history book can skip the analytical rules of Part Two.
questions.explain: Part Three applies the basic rules flexibly to each kind; it does not replace them. Skip Part Two and there is nothing for Part Three to adapt.
questions.rule: Advice for a kind builds on the general rules.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: A cookery course runs in four stages: knife skills, following recipes, adapting recipes, and planning menus that combine several cuisines. If it is built the way the four levels of reading are, what is true of the last stage?
options: It replaces the earlier stages with a new skill set
It can be taken first by talented students
It uses all the skills of the earlier stages
It matters less than the stages before it
optionExplain: Many picture levels as separate courses, but the book's levels do not replace one another.
Talent does not let you skip what the higher stage contains.
Right: each higher level includes those below it.
The highest level is the most demanding, not the least important.
questions.explain: The reading levels are cumulative, so the top one contains the rest. A menu planner still needs knife skills and recipes.
questions.rule: Higher levels contain the lower ones.
questions.teaches: The levels of reading are cumulative: each higher level includes the ones below it, which is why the book calls them levels rather than kinds.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: True or false: The preface treats the parody How to Read Two Books as pointing to a real problem of reading that the new edition takes up.
questions.explain: Adler says the problems suggested by the joking title are fully treated in the rewritten book. The card next says what that problem is.
questions.rule: Even a joke title can name a real problem.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: What problem does the preface say the title How to Read Two Books suggests?
options: How to read a number of related books in relation to one another
How to read two books in the time usually needed for only one of them
How to choose the better of two books on one subject
How to read one book twice for better recall
optionExplain: Right: the aim is to grasp what related books say about a common subject, where they agree and conflict.
That would be a speed problem; the preface means reading books in relation to one another.
Choosing between books is a different task from reading them against each other.
Rereading one book is valuable, but the joke is about more than one book.
questions.explain: The problem is reading several related books together so that their complementary and conflicting views on a common subject are grasped.
questions.rule: Read related books against one another.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Priya reads four articles on whether her city should build a new airport runway. Which actions fit the preface's aim for reading related works? Select all that apply.
options: Note where the articles agree on the noise figures
Note where two articles conflict on the jobs created
Read only the most persuasive article closely
Work out the common question they all address
Treat each article in turn as the final word
optionExplain: Right: finding the complementary points is half the aim.
Right: finding the conflicts is the other half.
This reads one work well but loses the relation between them.
Right: the books revolve around a common subject, so naming it comes first.
Taking each as final means the next one replaces it, and the comparison is never made.
questions.explain: The aim is to grasp what related works say about a common subject, both where they agree and where they conflict. That needs the common question and the points of agreement and disagreement.
questions.hint: Which actions put the articles side by side?
questions.rule: Find the common subject, then the agreements and the conflicts.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Suppose Priya reads the four articles weeks apart and does not set them side by side. What is she most likely to miss?
options: The basic facts that each article states on its own
Which of the four writers argues with the most control
The pleasure of reading each article at its own pace
How the articles complement and conflict with one another
optionExplain: She can still get each article's facts reading them one by one.
She can judge each writer's control one at a time; that is not what comparison adds.
Reading separately does not spoil enjoyment.
Right: the relations between the works only appear when they are read in relation to one another.
questions.explain: Change the condition, reading in isolation, and the specific gain of reading related works together disappears: the map of agreements and conflicts.
questions.rule: The relations between books appear only when you compare them.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: True or false: Reading several books in relation to one another removes the need to understand each book on its own terms.
questions.explain: You cannot compare what you have not understood. The higher level includes the lower ones, so each work still has to be read well.
questions.rule: Compare books only after you understand each.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: A journalist covering a new drug trial reads the press release and four news reports on it. Following the preface, what should her reading aim to give her?
options: The single most reliable report, to quote
A grasp of what the sources say in common and where they disagree
A careful count of how many of the sources call the new drug a breakthrough
The press release's wording, since it is the original
optionExplain: Picking one source is a choice, not a reading of the sources in relation to each other.
Right: that is the aim of reading related works together.
Counting agreement is not grasping it; she needs to know what they say and why they differ.
The original matters, but reading only it misses the other sources' agreements and conflicts.
questions.explain: The same aim works for news sources: set them in relation to one subject and see where they agree and conflict. From that she can build her own account.
questions.rule: Set sources against each other to see the whole subject.
questions.teaches: The book calls this fourth level syntopical reading: the reader places many works in relation to a subject and, with their help, builds an analysis of the subject that may not be in any one of them.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: How do the authors view radio and television in relation to reading?
options: They have made reading unnecessary for most people's needs
They spread so much distortion that serious readers should avoid them altogether
They have greatly improved our understanding of the world we live in
They do some jobs very well, but may not have improved understanding much
optionExplain: Some people feel this, and the authors report the feeling, but they do not share it.
The authors criticise packaged opinions, but they also praise broadcasting's strengths and do not say to avoid it.
This is the claim the authors call into question.
Right: they credit real strengths and doubt the gain in understanding.
questions.explain: The authors grant broadcasting real strengths but question whether it has much enhanced our understanding. The card next sets this out.
questions.rule: Information and understanding are different gains.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: True or false: By readers, the authors mean people who still get a large share of their information about and understanding of the world from the written word.
questions.explain: That is their definition. Speech and observation also teach, but curious people never found them enough, so they read too.
questions.rule: Readers learn much of what they know from the written word.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Ravi follows a far-off war through live television footage and knows what happened each day. Which of his needs has television served best, in the authors' terms?
options: Information about events
Understanding of why the war began
Practice in reading actively
Skill in judging arguments
optionExplain: Right: the authors credit television with the visual communication of news events, which has enormous impact.
This is the gain the authors doubt the media provide much of.
Watching footage is not reading, so it gives no practice in reading.
Footage of events presents no argument to judge.
questions.explain: Television is strong at conveying events. Whether Ravi understands the war is the question the authors raise.
questions.rule: Broadcasting is strong on events, weaker on understanding.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Sort each statement: something the authors grant to radio and television, or something they doubt or reject.

items.t: Television conveys news events with great impact
Radio informs us while we do other things
Radio can save a great deal of time
The new media have much improved our understanding of the world
Reading is no longer as necessary as it was
Speech and observation are enough for curious people

questions.explain: The authors grant the media's strengths at delivering news and information. They doubt the gain in understanding and deny that speech and observation were ever enough for the curious.
questions.rule: Grant the strengths, then ask about understanding.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: True or false: On the authors' view, a reader who wants understanding should give up television news entirely so as to read more books.
questions.explain: The authors praise television's news coverage and radio's time-saving. Their claim is that broadcasting does not do the work of understanding, not that it should be abandoned.
questions.rule: Use each source for what it does well.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Kate learns to change a bicycle tyre from a short video far faster than from the printed manual. By the authors' reasoning, what follows?
options: It did this job well; whether it built understanding is another question
Printed manuals are now obsolete for learning practical tasks
The video has given her an understanding of how bicycles work
The manual would have taught her more, since reading is a more active way to learn
optionExplain: Right: a new medium can do a job very well without settling the question of understanding.
The authors grant new media some functions, not that print is obsolete.
Knowing how to do one task is not the same as understanding the mechanism.
Active reading matters for understanding; for this practical task the video served well, a strength the authors grant.
questions.explain: The authors grant that newer media take over some jobs very well. What they question is whether they build understanding.
questions.rule: A medium can win at one job without replacing print.
questions.teaches: The authors compare this to photography, which took over some functions once served by painting: a new medium can take over certain jobs while the older one keeps others.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: True or false: The authors hold that the more facts you know about a subject, the better you will understand it.
questions.explain: They say knowledge is less of a prerequisite to understanding than people suppose, and too many facts can get in the way. The card next explains.
questions.rule: More facts are not automatically more understanding.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: The authors write that too many facts are often as much of an obstacle to understanding as too ____.
questions.explain: Both a flood and a shortage of facts can block understanding. That is why the authors say moderns are inundated with facts to the detriment of understanding.
questions.rule: Too many or too few facts can both block understanding.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Before buying a used car, Tom reads every forum thread, spec sheet and owner review he can find, and ends up less sure which model suits him. What does the chapter suggest went wrong?
options: He did not read enough reviews yet to be sure of his choice
The mass of facts got in the way of grasping what mattered
Car reviews are too biased to contain any useful facts
He should have let one trusted salesperson choose for him
optionExplain: More of the same would deepen the flood, not cure it.
Right: too many facts can be as much an obstacle to understanding as too few.
Bias may be real, but the trouble in the case is the sheer number of facts, not their quality.
Handing the judgment to someone else does not build his own understanding.
questions.explain: Tom treated more facts as more understanding. The authors warn that a flood of facts can bury the understanding it was meant to serve.
questions.rule: Ask what the facts mean before gathering more.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: A student argues that since knowledge is a prerequisite to understanding, whoever knows the most facts understands the most. Which step is faulty?
options: The premise that knowledge plays some part in understanding
The idea that understanding can be measured and compared between different people
The leap from needing some facts to more facts meaning more understanding
Nothing: the authors agree that more facts mean more understanding
optionExplain: The authors accept that knowledge is to some extent a prerequisite, so this premise is not the fault.
Comparing understanding may be hard, but that is not the faulty step.
Right: knowledge is less of a prerequisite than supposed, and past a point more facts obstruct.
The authors deny this: too many facts can be as much an obstacle as too few.
questions.explain: Needing some knowledge does not mean that more knowledge always means more understanding. The authors say too many facts can obstruct it.
questions.rule: Needing some facts does not mean the most facts win.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, someone who knows too few facts about a subject faces no obstacle to understanding it.
questions.explain: The warning cuts both ways: too many facts and too few can each be an obstacle. The rule against piling up facts does not license ignorance.
questions.rule: The warning against too many facts is not a case for too few.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: During a budget debate, Omar refreshes a live blog every few minutes and reads each update. By evening he can recite many figures but cannot explain the budget's main choice. What would the authors see in his day?
options: A good day of reading for understanding
A failure of memory he should train
A sign that he needed an expert's summary instead
Facts piling up to the detriment of understanding
optionExplain: He gained information, but the chapter's point is that this differs from understanding.
His memory is working; it is understanding that is missing.
A summary is someone else's understanding; the authors' diagnosis is a flood of facts without understanding.
Right: this is the flood of facts the authors describe.
questions.explain: Omar's updates gave him facts in quantity and no understanding. The authors also blame the way such media are built.
questions.rule: A stream of updates can bury the main point.
questions.teaches: The authors add that the same media are designed to make thinking seem unnecessary, though that is only an appearance: the work of understanding still has to be done.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: The authors compare a person who absorbs a ready-made opinion to which device?
options: A sponge soaking up water
A mirror reflecting light
A cassette played back on demand
A filter catching dust
optionExplain: A sponge is a common image for learning, but the authors want an image of replaying something unchanged.
A mirror reflects, but the authors stress storing a view and replaying it later.
Right: the opinion is inserted like a cassette and played back when it seems fitting.
A filter selects; the packaged opinion is taken whole.
questions.explain: The authors use the image of a cassette inserted into a player and replayed on demand. The card next explains the point.
questions.rule: A packaged opinion is stored and replayed, not formed.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the packaging of views in the media often works so well that the audience does not make up its own mind at all.
questions.explain: The aids are meant to make it easy to make up one's own mind, but they work so well that thinking is skipped. The person performs acceptably without having had to think.
questions.rule: Easy opinions can skip the thinking.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: After a news programme, Jo repeats its conclusion about a new railway line almost word for word. Asked what reasons support it, she cannot give any. In the authors' terms, what has happened?
options: She has formed her own view efficiently
She has played back a packaged opinion
She has read the issue actively
She has rejected the programme's view
optionExplain: Efficiency is the promise of packaging, but without reasons the view is not hers.
Right: she replays the conclusion without the thinking behind it.
Active reading would leave her able to give reasons.
She repeats the view rather than rejecting it.
questions.explain: Jo has the conclusion and none of the reasoning. That is the cassette the authors describe.
questions.rule: If you cannot give the reasons, the view is not yet yours.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Which signs suggest someone is playing back a packaged opinion rather than a view they thought through? Select all that apply.
options: They use a source's exact phrases but cannot explain them
They cannot say what evidence supports the view
They agree with a respected expert on the question
They can state the strongest objection and answer it in their own words
They repeat the view on cue, without reflecting on it
optionExplain: Right: borrowed words without understanding are a sign of a replayed opinion.
Right: no reasons means no thinking behind the view.
Agreement alone shows nothing; a thought-through view can agree with a good source.
Being able to handle an objection is a sign of real thinking.
Right: this is the play-back button the authors describe.
questions.explain: The marks of a packaged opinion are missing reasons and mechanical repetition. Agreement with a source is not one of them.
questions.hint: Look for missing reasons, not for agreement.
questions.rule: Missing reasons, not agreement, mark a packaged opinion.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: True or false: If you end up agreeing with a well-made documentary after checking its reasons for yourself, you are, on the authors' account, playing back a packaged opinion.
questions.explain: What makes an opinion packaged is skipping the thinking, not where the view came from. A conclusion you have worked through is your own even if it matches the source.
questions.rule: Thinking, not originality, makes a view your own.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: A consultancy hands a board a polished slide deck with charts and a recommended decision. What would the authors advise the board members to do before voting?
options: Vote for the recommendation, since experts prepared it
Vote against it, to be sure they are not swayed by clever packaging and charts
Work out for themselves whether the charts support the recommendation
Ask the consultants for a longer deck with more statistics
optionExplain: Expertise may be real, but adopting the view untested is playing back a package.
Rejecting it untested is no more thinking than accepting it untested, and the view may well be right.
Right: making up your own mind means testing the reasons, not taking the conclusion.
More data can be part of the package; a flood of facts does not replace thinking.
questions.explain: The board should do the thinking the package invites them to skip, then decide. The view may survive the test.
questions.rule: Test the reasons before adopting the recommendation.
questions.teaches: The book later makes this a reader's duty: once you understand a book, you must ask whether it is true and make up your own mind, since knowing the author's mind is not enough.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: True or false: The authors say their rules of reading apply to books alone, not to newspapers or advertisements.
questions.explain: The rules can be applied to printed material in general, down to advertisements. The card next lists the range.
questions.rule: The rules reach beyond books.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Which kinds of reading matter do the authors name as ones the rules can also be applied to? Select all that apply.
options: Newspapers
Pamphlets
Advertisements
Musical scores
Paintings
optionExplain: Right: newspapers head the authors' list.
Right: pamphlets and tracts are on the list.
Right: even advertisements are included.
Scores are read in a sense, but the authors' list is of printed reading matter in words.
Paintings are not reading matter in the authors' sense.
questions.explain: The list runs from newspapers and magazines through pamphlets, articles and tracts to advertisements: printed material in general.
questions.rule: Any printed matter can be read actively.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: If the rules apply to any printed matter, which readers is the book most particularly written for?
options: Readers of books whose main purpose is increased understanding
Readers who want to get through many more pages per hour than they do now
Newspaper readers who want more information, faster
Readers who read mostly for pleasure and entertainment
optionExplain: Right: the book is for readers, particularly of books, and most particularly those reading for understanding.
Speed is not the book's aim; the preface calls for appropriate speeds.
The rules help with newspapers, but information is not the book's main concern.
The authors say reading for entertainment needs no rules.
questions.explain: The rules reach all printed matter, but the book's focus narrows in steps: readers, then readers of books, then those who read books to understand more.
questions.rule: The book's focus is reading books for understanding.
questions.teaches: The chapter's first sentences say the book is, most particularly, for those whose main purpose in reading books is to gain increased understanding.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Leo receives a glossy brochure from a pension provider. Following the authors, how should he read it?
options: Actively, asking what it claims and whether the claims hold
Quickly and uncritically, since it is only a brochure
Not at all, since the rules are meant for books
As slowly as a treatise, line by line, reading it several times over
optionExplain: Right: the rules apply to pamphlets and advertisements too.
This treats non-book print as exempt from active reading, which the authors deny.
The authors say the rules apply to printed matter in general.
Active reading does not require treatise-level time for a brochure.
questions.explain: A brochure is printed matter, so the same active questions apply. The time spent can be much shorter than for a book.
questions.rule: Read a brochure actively, at the pace it deserves.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: True or false: Because the rules apply to a brochure as well as to a book, Leo should give the brochure as much time as a long treatise on economics.
questions.explain: The same rules can be applied with very different amounts of time and effort. The preface's call for variable speeds holds here too.
questions.rule: Same rules, different effort.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Nadia sees a widely shared social media post claiming her city will ban cars next year. What would applying the book's rules of reading involve?
options: Sharing it at once, since so many others have trusted it
Ignoring it, since a social media post is not a book
Reading it twice, slowly, so that she can memorize its exact wording
Asking what it claims, on what grounds, and whether it is true
optionExplain: Popularity is not a reason; this is close to playing back a packaged opinion.
The rules apply to printed matter in general, so the post is not exempt.
Memorizing words is not reading actively.
Right: these are the questions an active reader asks of any text.
questions.explain: A short post can be read with the same questions as a book. The rules shrink to fit it but still apply.
questions.rule: Ask a post the questions you would ask a book.
questions.teaches: The book later sums up the reader's obligation in four questions: what is it about as a whole, what is being said in detail and how, is it true, and what of it; they apply to anything worth reading, even an advertisement.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, it is possible to read in a completely passive way.
questions.explain: All reading is to some degree active; we cannot read with our minds asleep. The card next explains why the degree matters.
questions.rule: No reading is completely passive.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: According to the authors, a reader is better if he demands more of himself and of the ____ before him.
questions.explain: A reader is better in proportion to the range of activity and effort he brings. Demanding more of himself and of the text is how that shows.
questions.rule: Better readers demand more of themselves and the text.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Ali rereads a history chapter three times without pausing to think. Bea reads it once, asking what the author argues and noting points she doubts. On the authors' account, who read it better?
options: Ali, because he spent three times as long on it
Bea, because she demanded more of herself and the text
Neither, since rereading and questioning are equally good
Both equally, since all reading is to some degree active
optionExplain: Time spent is not the measure; his rereading made few demands on the text.
Right: her reading had a greater range of activity.
The authors rank readings by activity, and Bea's was more active.
All reading is somewhat active, but the authors stress that it can be more or less so.
questions.explain: The measure is activity and effort of mind. Bea asked more of the text, so she read better.
questions.rule: Activity of mind, not repetition, makes reading better.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: A tutor argues that since completely passive reading is impossible, every reader is equally active, so advice to read actively is empty. Where is the error?
options: Wholly passive reading is in fact possible for a tired reader
Activity cannot be seen from outside, so no one can rank it
Reading is only ever slightly active, whatever the reader does
Reading can be more or less active even if never wholly passive
optionExplain: The authors deny this: we cannot read with our minds asleep, so the tutor's premise is right.
Hard to observe is not the same as equal; the authors still rank readers by activity and effort.
The authors say the more active the better, so reading can be highly active.
Right: not being zero does not make everyone equal; activity is a matter of degree.
questions.explain: From some activity in all reading, the tutor infers equal activity in all reading. The authors' point is that activity comes in degrees, and more is better.
questions.rule: Never zero is not the same as always equal.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: True or false: The authors say reading a light novel purely for entertainment calls for the same demanding effort as reading a hard book for understanding.
questions.explain: Reading for entertainment is the least demanding kind and needs the least effort. The call for maximum activity is aimed at reading to understand.
questions.rule: The goal sets how much activity is needed.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Sam listens to a science podcast while washing up, and afterwards cannot say what the episode argued. Applying the chapter's idea to listening, what was missing?
options: Faster playback, so the episode held his attention
Better headphones, so he could hear every word
Activity of mind in receiving what was said
A transcript he could read later instead
optionExplain: Speed does not help a mind that is elsewhere.
He heard the words; the gap is in what he did with them.
Right: listening, like reading, can be more or less active.
A transcript would help only if read actively; the missing piece is his activity.
questions.explain: Sam received the sound but did little with it. Active listening, like active reading, means questioning and following what is said.
questions.rule: Listening, like reading, gains from activity.
questions.teaches: The book later gives one prescription for active reading: ask questions while you read, questions that you yourself must try to answer as you go.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Which comparison do the authors use for the reader?
options: A catcher in a game of baseball
A vessel being filled with water
An heir receiving a legacy
A judge handing down a verdict
optionExplain: Right: the reader is like a catcher, as active in receiving as the pitcher is in throwing.
This image makes the reader passive, which the authors reject.
The authors name receiving a legacy as the mistaken picture of reading.
A court's judgment is another passive image the authors reject, and the reader is the one receiving, not handing down.
questions.explain: The authors compare the reader to a baseball catcher. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: The reader is the catcher.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: True or false: In the authors' analogy, the passive element is the written work, like the ball, while writer and reader are both active.
questions.explain: The ball is the inert thing put in motion or stopped. The written work plays that part; writing and reading are the two activities.
questions.rule: Only the text is passive.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Match each part of the baseball analogy to its counterpart in reading.
questions.explain: The writer starts the process and the reader ends it; both act. The work itself, like the ball, is what passes between them.
questions.rule: Writer starts, reader ends, the text passes between.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: A student writes that reading is passive because the reader receives communication, as an heir receives a legacy. Which part of this do the authors reject?
options: That the reader is the one who receives communication
That receiving communication is like receiving a legacy
That the writer is the one who sends the communication
That writing, like speaking, is an active undertaking
optionExplain: The authors agree the reader receives; they call him the receiver.
Right: receiving communication is like catching a ball, not like inheriting.
The writer is the sender in their account too.
The authors agree that writing is active.
questions.explain: Receiving is not the mistake; picturing it as passive is. A catcher receives the ball by acting.
questions.rule: Receiving is itself an activity.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: In a meeting, Priti presents a plan and Leon listens. Using the catcher analogy, what should Leon be doing?
options: Waiting quietly for the plan to sink in
Preparing his own plan in his head while she talks
Judging the plan before she finishes
Working to take in each point as she makes it
optionExplain: Waiting for it to sink in is the passive picture the authors reject.
This stops the catch; his attention is on his own pitch.
Judging before receiving cuts the catch short.
Right: the catcher moves to receive what is sent.
questions.explain: The listener's job, like the catcher's, is active receiving. Leon must work to take in what Priti means.
questions.rule: Move to meet what is sent.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Before a meeting, Hana has ten minutes to skim a long report. Does the catcher analogy still apply to such quick reading?
options: Yes: quick reading is still an activity of receiving
No: skimming is passive by its nature
No: only slow reading counts as catching
Only if she takes written notes on each section as she goes
optionExplain: Right: speed changes how she catches, not whether she must.
Skimming done well is an effort, not passive.
The analogy concerns activity, not speed.
Notes can help, but the activity is in her mind, not in the notes.
questions.explain: The catcher's activity is not tied to a slow pace. Even a fast skim is an act of receiving that she must perform.
questions.rule: Fast reading is still active reading.
questions.teaches: The book later notes that inspectional reading, the quick, systematic skim, is always active: an effortful, not an effortless, undertaking.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: True or false: In the authors' view, writers are generally trying to make their meaning hard to catch.
questions.explain: The writer is not trying not to be caught, though it can seem so. The card next explains how writer and reader work together.
questions.rule: Writers want to be caught.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Successful communication occurs when what the writer wanted to have received finds its way into the ____'s possession.
questions.explain: Success is measured at the reader's end: did what the writer meant arrive? That needs both sides to play their part.
questions.rule: Communication succeeds when the meaning arrives.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: A manual for a new oven states each step precisely, with warnings set apart. In the authors' terms, what kind of writer produced it?
options: A writer with good control, easier to catch
A wild writer, whose meaning is harder to catch
A writer who is trying not to be caught
A writer who leaves all the work to the reader
optionExplain: Right: knowing exactly what to convey and conveying it precisely is control.
A wild writer lacks control; this manual shows plenty.
Clear warnings show a writer who wants to be caught.
Precision lightens the reader's load rather than handing it all over.
questions.explain: Control means knowing what you want to convey and conveying it precisely. Such writers are easier to catch, other things being equal.
questions.rule: Control on the writer's side eases the catch.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Sort each piece of writing: the work of a writer with control, or of a wild writer.

items.t: A contract clause that states one obligation exactly
An abstract that names its finding and method in two sentences
A recipe listing quantities and steps in order
An email that circles its request three times without stating it
A speech that changes topic in mid-sentence
A report whose conclusion contradicts its own summary

questions.explain: Control shows in knowing exactly what to say and saying it precisely. Wildness shows in circling, drifting and contradiction, which make the reader's catch harder.
questions.rule: Precision is control; drift is wildness.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: True or false: If a writer has excellent control, the reader no longer needs to read actively to receive the meaning.
questions.explain: Control makes the catch easier, other things being equal, but the catch is still made by the reader. Even a perfect pitch has to be caught.
questions.rule: A good pitch still has to be caught.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: A climate scientist writes a popular article on climate models, and a teacher reads it in order to explain it to her class. How do the authors describe the relation between the two people's skills?
options: The writer's skill matters and the reader's does not
The reader's skill matters and the writer's does not
The two skills converge on a common end
The two skills compete, each side trying to win
optionExplain: A clear writer helps, but the authors say success needs both sides.
A skilled reader helps, but the writer's control also counts.
Right: both work toward the same result, the meaning reaching the reader.
The writer is not trying to avoid being caught; it is not a contest.
questions.explain: Like pitcher and catcher, writer and reader succeed only as far as they cooperate. Their skills aim at one result.
questions.rule: Writer and reader work toward one end.
questions.teaches: The authors put it this way: the writer's skill and the reader's skill converge upon a common end, the same goal pursued from two sides.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: In what respect do the authors say the catcher analogy breaks down?
options: A catcher is active, but a reader is passive in receiving
Pitchers want to be caught, but writers try not to be
A ball is caught or not, but writing can be caught in part
A ball moves through the air, but a book stays on the page
optionExplain: The authors insist both are active; this is the view the analogy was built to refute.
Writers, like pitchers, are not trying to avoid being caught.
Right: a ball is a simple unit, while writing is complex and can be received more or less completely.
The ball's motion is not the point of difference the authors name.
questions.explain: A ball is caught or dropped; writing can be received in part. The card next explains what decides how much.
questions.rule: Writing is caught in degrees.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, how much a reader catches usually depends on the activity he puts in and on the skill of the mental acts he performs.
questions.explain: Both factors count: the amount of activity, and the skill with which the different mental acts are carried out.
questions.rule: Activity and skill set the size of the catch.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: After a talk on a change in tax law, two trainees compare notes. One got the headline change; the other got the change, its reasons and its exceptions. How would the authors describe the difference?
options: One caught the talk and the other dropped it
Both caught part of it, the second much more
Both caught it fully, in different words
Neither caught it, since neither got everything
optionExplain: This treats the talk like a ball, caught or dropped, which is where the analogy fails.
Right: communication is received more or less completely.
The first trainee missed the reasons and exceptions, so this overstates her catch.
Catching is not all or nothing; partial receipt still counts as receipt.
questions.explain: A complex message can be received in part. The second trainee caught more of what was intended.
questions.rule: Ask how much you caught, not whether you caught it.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Suppose the first trainee works much harder at following the next talk, but still has no skill at picking out reasons and exceptions. What would the authors expect?
options: A full catch, since effort alone decides it
No change, since skill alone decides it
A smaller catch, since straining makes listening harder
A larger catch, still limited by her lack of skill
optionExplain: Effort is one factor; the authors name skill as the other.
Activity counts too, so more effort should help somewhat.
Some think trying harder backfires, but the authors treat activity as raising the catch.
Right: the catch depends on activity as well as on skill in the acts involved.
questions.explain: Change one factor and the catch changes, but only as far as the other factor allows. Both activity and skill decide the amount.
questions.rule: Effort grows the catch only as far as skill allows.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Which factors does the chapter say affect how much of a piece of writing a reader catches? Select all that apply.
options: The amount of activity the reader puts in
The reader's skill in the mental acts involved
The writer's control, other things being equal
The length of the reader's past reading list
How fast the reader gets through the text
optionExplain: Right: the catch usually depends on the activity put into the process.
Right: it also depends on the skill with which the mental acts are done.
Right: a writer with control is easier to catch than a wild one, so effort alone guarantees nothing.
Having read a lot proves little; the authors look at activity and skill in this reading.
Speed is not among the factors the chapter names here; the preface asks for appropriate speeds.
questions.explain: The reader's activity and skill usually decide the catch, but the writer's side counts too. That is why even great effort does not guarantee a full catch.
questions.hint: Think of both the catcher and the pitcher.
questions.rule: Effort helps, but it does not guarantee a full catch.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: A juror listens to a witness's long, complicated testimony. Which statement fits the chapter's view of receiving communication?
options: She will catch more or less of it, depending on her activity and skill
She either understands the testimony or she does not: it is all or nothing
She cannot catch any of it without a written transcript to study
Her catch depends only on how well the witness tells the story
optionExplain: Right: complex communication is received in degrees, by activity and skill.
This is the ball picture, which fails for complex messages.
Listening is also catching; a transcript is not required.
The speaker's control matters, but so does the receiver's work.
questions.explain: Testimony, like writing, is complex, so it is received in degrees. The juror's activity and skill decide how much of it she takes in.
questions.rule: Complex messages are received in degrees.
questions.teaches: Because the catch grows with each mental act a reader can perform, the book goes on to break good reading into many separate acts and gives rules for performing them.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Given the same thing to read, which two things do the authors say make one person read it better than another? Select all that apply.
options: Reading it more actively
Performing each act involved more skilfully
Reading it at a faster pace
Having read more books in the past
Having more background in the subject
optionExplain: Right: the first factor is reading more actively.
Right: the second is performing each act more skilfully.
Speed is not one of the two factors; the preface asks for appropriate speeds.
Past reading may help, but the authors name activity and skill.
Background can help, but it is not one of the two factors the authors name.
questions.explain: The authors name two factors: more activity and more skill in each act. The card next shows how they relate.
questions.rule: Two factors: activity and skill.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Reading, like writing, is a complex activity that consists of a large number of separate ____, all of which must be performed in a good reading.
questions.explain: Reading is not one act done well or badly. It is many separate acts, and a good reading performs them all.
questions.rule: Reading is many acts, not one.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Mo works hard at a statistics textbook for hours, but has not learned to pick out the author's key terms or follow an argument step by step. By the chapter's account, what limits his reading?
options: Not enough hours spent working through the book
A subject too technical for a non-specialist
Missing skill in the separate acts of reading
A textbook too badly written to be read at all
optionExplain: He has plenty of activity; more hours would not supply the missing skill.
The chapter says reading skill can be improved; the gap here is skill, not the subject.
Right: effort without skill in the separate acts gains little.
Nothing in the case points to the writer; the gap is Mo's skill.
questions.explain: Mo supplies activity but not skill in the acts that make up good reading. Both are needed.
questions.rule: Effort needs skill in each act to pay off.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: A coach tells a book club that effort is all that matters: anyone who tries hard enough will read as well as anyone else. What do the authors add?
options: Skill in performing each separate act matters too
Effort matters little compared with natural talent
Reading well depends mostly on reading fast
Reading well depends mostly on knowing the subject
optionExplain: Right: the second factor is performing each act more skilfully.
The authors stress effort; they do not dismiss it for talent.
Speed is not one of the two factors.
Background helps, but the authors name activity and skill in each act.
questions.explain: Effort is half of the account. A reader also needs skill in each of the many acts a good reading includes.
questions.rule: Trying hard is half the job; skill is the other half.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: True or false: If two readers put in equal effort, the one who can perform more of the separate acts of reading is better able to read.
questions.explain: Hold effort fixed and skill makes the difference. The authors say the person who can perform more of the acts is better able to read.
questions.rule: With effort equal, more acts mastered means better reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: A tennis beginner practises the serve, the footwork and the backhand one at a time. What does the chapter's view of reading as many acts suggest about learning to read well?
options: Reading skill is a single gift that cannot be broken into parts
The separate acts can be learned and practised, then combined
Only the hardest act needs practice; the rest come by themselves
Practice adds little once you can read the words on a page
optionExplain: The authors say reading consists of many separate acts, so it can be broken down.
Right: a complex skill made of many acts is learned by mastering the acts.
All the acts must be performed in a good reading, not only the hardest.
The preface shows readers stall when training stops at the elementary level.
questions.explain: Reading, like tennis, is a complex skill made of separate acts. Each can be practised until they run together.
questions.rule: Learn the separate acts, then combine them.
questions.teaches: The book later compares learning to read to learning to ski: you learn the separate acts one at a time, with full attention, before they fuse into one smooth performance.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: True or false: The authors' first measure of success in reading is how much of what the writer intended to communicate the reader receives.
questions.explain: Success is first defined as receiving everything the writer intended. The card next shows why the authors find this too simple.
questions.rule: First measure: how much of the intended message you received.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: What reason do the authors give for calling that first measure of success too simple?
options: Writers seldom know exactly what they intend to say to readers
The reader's mind can stand in two relations to a book
Success also depends on how fast the reader reads
Readers can rarely know what a writer intended
optionExplain: The authors assume writers do intend something; skilled ones know exactly what.
Right: the measure ignores whether you understood the book before you began.
Speed is not the issue raised here.
The authors speak of readers receiving the intended message, so they think it can be known.
questions.explain: The measure hides two different relations between mind and book: understanding it all, or not. Those relations lead to different gains.
questions.rule: Ask which relation you stand in to the book.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Ana reads a rail company's refund policy and can state exactly what it entitles her to, as the company meant. By the first measure, how did her reading go?
options: It succeeded: she received what was intended
It failed: she gained no new understanding from it
It cannot be judged without a formal test
It failed: she read it without judging it
optionExplain: Right: by the first measure, receiving the intended message is success.
That point belongs to a fuller account, not to the first measure.
The measure needs no formal test, only what she received.
Judging comes later; the first measure asks only whether the intended message arrived.
questions.explain: Ana received what the writer intended, so the first measure scores her reading a success. Whether she gained understanding is a separate question.
questions.rule: The first measure looks only at what was received.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: True or false: If you received everything a writer intended, the first measure counts your reading a success even if you understood all of it before you began.
questions.explain: The measure only asks whether the message arrived. That is why it is too simple: it cannot tell a reading that stretched you from one that did not.
questions.rule: The first measure cannot see what you gained.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Which are gaps in judging a reading only by how much of the intended message you received? Select all that apply.
options: It hides whether you gained understanding or only information
It scores an easy book the same as one that stretched you
It ignores what the writer intended to communicate to you
It ignores the two relations a mind can have to a book
It treats a quick reading as better than a slow one
optionExplain: Right: the kind of gain is invisible to the measure.
Right: both readings count as success though only one could raise understanding.
The measure is built on what the writer intended, so it does not ignore it.
Right: this is the authors' own reason for calling it too simple.
The measure says nothing about speed.
questions.explain: The measure tracks receipt, not gain. It treats every complete receipt alike, whatever relation the reader had to the book.
questions.hint: What does the measure leave out, rather than what does it include?
questions.rule: Receipt is not the same as gain.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: A software engineer reads documentation for a tool she has used daily for years and finds every line familiar. By the authors' fuller account, which part of the first measure misleads here?
options: It says she failed, though she understood every line
It ignores whether she received what the writers of the documentation intended
It says she succeeded, though her understanding could not grow
It judges her by how fast she reads the documentation
optionExplain: She received the whole message, so the first measure counts it a success, not a failure.
Receipt is exactly what the first measure tracks.
Right: complete receipt of familiar matter adds information at most.
Speed plays no part in the measure.
questions.explain: Success by the first measure says nothing about growth. A text you already understand fully can only add information.
questions.rule: Full receipt of familiar matter is not growth.
questions.teaches: The second relation needs a book that has more to say than you understand: only then can a reading raise your understanding rather than add to your information.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a book you understand perfectly from start to finish cannot increase your understanding.
questions.explain: You may gain information from such a book, but not understanding. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Perfect ease means no growth in understanding.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: What do the authors say you may gain from a book that is completely intelligible to you?
options: Increased understanding, but no information
Both information and deeper understanding
Nothing, since an easy book has nothing to teach
Information, but not increased understanding
optionExplain: This reverses the authors' point.
Deeper understanding is exactly what such a book cannot give.
Ease rules out a gain in understanding, not in information; new facts can still be learned.
Right: your understanding was equal to the book before you began.
questions.explain: A book fully intelligible to you can add facts but cannot raise your understanding, which already matched it.
questions.rule: Easy books add information, not understanding.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
