questions.q: Sam reads a beginner's guide to chess. Every page is easy, and he learns the names of three openings he did not know. What did he gain, by the authors' account?
options: Information, within the understanding he already had
A deeper understanding of chess strategy
Nothing, since he knew it all before
Understanding, because the names of the openings were new to him
optionExplain: Right: new names at the same level of intelligibility are information.
Nothing in the guide stretched him, so his understanding stayed where it was.
He did gain something: the names were new information.
New facts are not the same as new understanding.
questions.explain: New items understood in the same light as old ones add information. Understanding would need something he could not at first grasp.
questions.rule: New facts in the old light are information.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Sort each reading experience: likely to add information only, or able to raise understanding.

items.t: A news report that is clear to you at once
A product manual you follow without effort
A list of new train times
A physics chapter you can follow only by hard work
An essay that makes you rethink a familiar topic
A history that throws new light on facts you knew

questions.explain: What is at once intelligible adds to your store of information. What at first exceeds you, or recasts what you knew, can raise understanding.
questions.rule: Difficulty that you can overcome is where understanding grows.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Raj breezes through a hard philosophy book and calls it easy, though he cannot explain any argument in it. Does the rule that easy books add only information fit his case?
options: Yes: the book felt easy to him, so it gave him information only
Yes, since he read every page and finished the whole book
No: hard books raise understanding in whoever reads them
No: he did not understand it, so his ease was not understanding
optionExplain: The rule applies to books you actually understand perfectly, not to books that only feel easy.
Finishing is not understanding; he cannot explain any argument.
A hard book raises understanding only if the reader does the work.
Right: feeling at ease is not the same as understanding perfectly.
questions.explain: The rule concerns books you truly understand throughout. A reader who misses what he does not understand only seems to be in that case.
questions.rule: Feeling at ease is not proof of understanding.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: True or false: If the chess guide had one chapter that puzzled Sam, working at that chapter could raise his understanding.
questions.explain: Change the condition so the book has more to say than he understands, and the second relation opens. Only then can reading raise his understanding.
questions.rule: Puzzlement marks where understanding can grow.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: An experienced lawyer reads a routine lease in her specialty and finds nothing in it surprising or unclear. What has the reading most likely given her?
options: A deeper grasp of the law of leases in general
Information about this lease, not new understanding
Nothing, since she already knew the law of leases
Understanding, because she read it carefully
optionExplain: Her grasp of the law already matched the document, so it could not deepen it.
Right: a document fully intelligible to her adds facts about this deal only.
She learned this lease's terms, which is information.
Care in reading does not create understanding the text cannot give her.
questions.explain: The lease was fully intelligible to her, so its gain is information about this deal.
questions.rule: Expert ease signals information, not growth.
questions.teaches: The authors say the same of newspapers, magazines and anything else at once thoroughly intelligible to us: such reading can increase our information but not our understanding.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: According to the authors, what feeling signals that a book is over your depth?
options: Boredom and restlessness
Puzzlement and perplexity
Pleasure and ease
Annoyance at the author
optionExplain: Boredom can come from many causes, including an easy book; the authors name another feeling.
Right: getting in over your depth brings a shock of puzzlement and perplexity.
Ease is the mark of a book already within your understanding.
Annoyance may follow, but it is not the signal the authors describe.
questions.explain: The authors name the shock of puzzlement and perplexity. The card next says who feels it.
questions.rule: Puzzlement marks the edge of your understanding.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: The authors say the shock of puzzlement and perplexity comes from getting in over our ____, if we are both alert and honest.
questions.explain: An alert reader notices the gap and an honest one admits it. Without both, a reader can go through a book over his depth without feeling it.
questions.rule: Be alert enough to notice and honest enough to admit.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Midway through a report on her company's pension scheme, Kim realises she cannot explain how the employer's share is calculated. What should she take from that moment, on the authors' view?
options: The report is badly written and not worth any more of her time and attention
She has read far enough, since she has the general idea
The report has more to say than she understands, so it can teach her
She should note the figure as a fact to remember and move on
optionExplain: Puzzlement can come from a poor writer, but nothing here suggests that; first assume the report can teach.
Stopping here gives up the very part that could raise her understanding.
Right: knowing she does not understand it all marks where it can increase her understanding.
Remembering is not understanding; the gap shows where the report can raise her understanding.
questions.explain: Kim understands enough to know she does not understand it all. That is the condition under which a text can raise understanding.
questions.rule: A noticed gap is a chance to learn.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Tom says he does not feel puzzled by anything he reads, so every book he reads must be within his understanding. What does the chapter suggest may be wrong with his inference?
options: He may not be alert or honest enough to feel the puzzlement
Feeling puzzled is itself a sign of poor reading skill
Puzzlement comes only with technical or scientific books
Puzzlement is felt by beginners, not by practised readers
optionExplain: Right: the shock of puzzlement comes only if the reader is both alert and honest.
The authors treat puzzlement as useful, not as a failing.
The authors tie puzzlement to being over your depth, in any subject.
The authors give no such exemption; even practised readers meet books over their depth.
questions.explain: No puzzlement can mean the books are easy, or that Tom is missing what he does not understand. The authors add the condition: alert and honest.
questions.rule: No puzzlement may mean no noticing.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, once a reader notices that a book has more to say than she understands, the book has done its work and she can stop.
questions.explain: Noticing shows where the book can teach her, but the job of reading is done only by going to work on the book herself, lifting herself from understanding less to understanding more.
questions.rule: Noticing the gap is where the work starts.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: In a geometry class, Ben is lost in a proof but tells the teacher it all makes sense. Which part of the chapter's advice is he failing?
options: Reading at the right speed
Being honest about where he is over his depth
Reading only books that are fully intelligible
Asking someone else to read for him
optionExplain: Speed is not his problem here.
Right: honesty about his puzzlement is what would let the proof teach him.
The chapter wants readers to tackle what is beyond them, not avoid it.
He has not asked for help; he has hidden the gap.
questions.explain: Ben feels lost but will not admit it, so the gap cannot become a place to learn. Admitting it is the first step.
questions.rule: Admit the gap before you try to close it.
questions.teaches: The authors name two easy ways out once you know a book is beyond you: hand the hard parts to someone else to explain, or decide they are not worth bothering about.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Faced with parts of a book over your head, which responses do the authors say fail to do the job of reading that the book requires? Select all that apply.
options: Having someone who reads better explain them
Deciding they are not worth bothering about
Working on the book with your own mind
Turning to a commentary to explain them first
Rereading the hard parts and thinking them through
optionExplain: Right: handing the hard parts to someone else is one of the two failed responses.
Right: dismissing what is over your head is the other.
This is the one way the authors say the job is done.
Right: a commentary counts as the someone else who explains.
This is working on the book yourself, which the authors endorse.
questions.explain: The two failed responses are handing off the hard parts and dismissing them; a commentary is a form of handing off. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Do not hand off or give up.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: In the authors' account, who might the someone else be that explains the troublesome parts?
options: Only a professional teacher or a tutor
Only the author himself, if he can somehow be reached
A person or another book, such as a commentary
Only a friend who has read the book
optionExplain: Teachers count, but the authors widen it beyond them.
The author is not mentioned; he is usually not available.
Right: the explainer may be a person or another book, a commentary or textbook.
Friends count, but so do books.
questions.explain: The handing-off can go to a person or to another book. Either way, the reader is not doing the job himself.
questions.rule: A commentary can be a way of handing off.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Stuck on a hard chapter of a book about economics, Ivo watches a ten-minute summary video and moves on. On the authors' account, what has he done?
options: Handed the hard part to someone else instead of reading it
Read the chapter actively, but through a new medium instead of print
Done the job of reading that the book requires
Decided the chapter was not worth bothering about
optionExplain: Right: the video is someone else explaining the part that troubled him.
He has not read the chapter at all; the video replaced it.
The authors say this job is done only by working on the book yourself.
He did think it worth bothering about; he got someone else to bother instead.
questions.explain: A summary video is another explainer. Ivo has the gist from someone else, not understanding won from the book.
questions.rule: A summary is someone else's reading, not yours.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Sort each response to a hard passage: doing the job of reading, or avoiding it.

items.t: Rereading the passage and working out its key words
Tracing how the passage connects to earlier chapters
Noting a question and coming back to it after thought
Reading a summary of the passage instead
Deciding the passage does not matter
Asking a friend what it means before trying it yourself

questions.explain: Each response on the left keeps the work in the reader's own mind. Each on the right hands it off or drops it.
questions.rule: Keep the work in your own mind.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: True or false: The authors allow that, in at least one kind of situation, asking for outside help with a difficult book is appropriate.
questions.explain: A footnote says there is one such situation, discussed in the chapter on reading philosophy. The warning is against help that replaces your own work, not against all help.
questions.rule: The rule against help has a stated exception.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Wen is puzzled by a clause in her employment contract. She has read it carefully several times, working at each phrase, and it still makes no sense. What does the book's later advice suggest?
options: Keep rereading it alone, however long it takes
Ignore the clause, since she understands the rest
Seek outside help now that she has done her best
Sign it and trust that the clause is standard
optionExplain: The book's later advice does not require endless solitary effort once you have done your best.
Dismissing it is one of the two failed responses.
Right: help sought after doing your best is not handing off.
This dismisses the clause as not worth bothering about, one of the failed responses.
questions.explain: The fault lies in reaching for help instead of working. Wen has done the work first, so help now builds on her own effort.
questions.rule: Do your best first; then help is fair.
questions.teaches: The book later gives a common-sense maxim: seek outside help when a work stays unintelligible after you have done your best to read it yourself, and doing all you can first means you need less and less help.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: True or false: In the authors' definition of the art of reading, the reader may draw on any outside help available, such as tutors and commentaries.
questions.explain: The definition says the mind works with nothing but the symbols of the text and no help from outside. The card next sets it out.
questions.rule: The art works with the text and your mind alone.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: In the art of reading as the authors define it, the mind passes from understanding less to understanding ____.
questions.explain: The mind raises itself by its own operations. The acts that cause this are the acts that make up the art of reading.
questions.rule: The art moves you from understanding less to understanding more.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Which reader is practising the art of reading as the authors define it?
options: Sam, who reads a plot summary of a novel instead of the novel
Lee, who reads a familiar magazine column in five minutes
Kai, who asks a tutor to explain each hard page as soon as he reaches it
Jo, who works through a hard essay alone until she grasps its argument
optionExplain: A summary is someone else's reading; Sam never works on the text.
A column at once intelligible to Lee cannot raise his understanding.
The tutor supplies the lift that the art asks the reader to supply.
Right: her own mind, working on the text alone, raises her understanding.
questions.explain: Only Jo works on a text above her with nothing but her own mind, and ends understanding more.
questions.rule: Own mind, the text, and a rise in understanding.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: A student claims that once you master the art of reading, understanding a hard book takes no real effort. What does the chapter say against this?
options: The authors call it a major exertion, a bootstrap climb
Hard books should be left to specialists in the field
Skill matters less than speed when a book is hard
Effort is needed for fiction, not for exposition
optionExplain: Right: the art makes the exertion productive, not unnecessary.
The authors say harder books are the ones that deserve this reading from any reader.
Speed is not the measure; the authors stress skilled operations.
The chapter is about reading for understanding, mostly in expository books.
questions.explain: Skill makes the climb possible, not effortless. The authors describe it as a major exertion.
questions.rule: Skill makes the climb possible, not easy.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a magazine you understand at once deserves the same bootstrap effort as a book that challenges your understanding.
questions.explain: The bootstrap kind of reading is what a book that challenges your understanding deserves. A text at once intelligible to you cannot raise your understanding, so it does not demand it.
questions.rule: Save the bootstrap effort for books above you.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: An engineer teaches herself a new programming language from a dense reference book alone, and by the end understands ideas she had not grasped before. Who deserves credit for her rise in understanding, on the authors' account?
options: The writer alone, since the knowledge was in the book
She does, by her own work, though the writer made it possible
She alone, since the book itself was only marks on a page until she read it
Her past teachers, since they taught her to read
optionExplain: The writer offered the lift, but the reader had to do the climbing.
Right: she raised herself by her own activity, and the writer made that possible.
The marks carried what the writer had to teach; without them there was nothing to climb.
Learning to read made it possible, but the rise came from her work on this book.
questions.explain: The reader raises herself by her own operations, but she needs a writer who has something to teach. Both parts are true.
questions.rule: You do the lifting; the writer supplies the height.
questions.teaches: The authors add that although the reader raises himself by his own activity, the rise is made possible, indirectly, by the writer who had something to teach him.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: In the authors' second sense of reading, how does the text compare with the reader at the start?
options: It is initially better or higher than the reader
It is fully intelligible to the reader
It is easier than what the reader usually reads
It covers a subject the reader already knows well
optionExplain: Right: the text is initially better or higher than the reader.
Full intelligibility marks the first sense, not the second.
Ease points to the first sense.
A familiar subject may still be treated in a new light, but familiarity is not the mark.
questions.explain: In the second sense, the text starts above the reader. The card next sets out both senses.
questions.rule: The second sense starts with a text above you.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Match each sense of reading to its description.
pairs: A text at once thoroughly intelligible to you
A text you do not at first completely understand
What the first sense can add
What the second sense can add
questions.explain: The first sense covers what is at once intelligible and adds information. The second covers what at first exceeds you and can add understanding.
questions.rule: First sense, information; second sense, understanding.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Sort each case: reading in the first sense or in the second sense.

items.t: A fan reads match reports on a team she follows closely
A cook reads a new recipe in a style she knows well
A commuter reads the morning headlines
A student works through a proof she cannot yet follow
A manager studies a book that recasts how she sees her market
A reader tackles an essay that challenges what he thought he understood

questions.explain: The first-sense cases are at once intelligible to the reader. The second-sense cases start above the reader and can raise understanding.
questions.rule: Ask whether the text starts above you.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Leo reads twenty new facts about Roman emperors, all of the kind he already knew and saw in the same light, and says his understanding of Rome has grown. In the authors' terms, what has he gained?
options: A new light on Roman history
Understanding, since twenty facts is a lot
More information, in the same light as before
Nothing, since the facts were not new
optionExplain: Nothing in the facts recast what he knew.
Quantity of facts is not understanding.
Right: more facts of the same kind, seen in the same light, are information.
The facts were new to him, so he gained information.
questions.explain: Learning in the second sense means understanding more, not remembering more of the same kind of information. Leo read in the first sense.
questions.rule: More of the same is information, not understanding.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors' account, the same book could be read in the first sense by one reader and in the second sense by another.
questions.explain: The first sense covers what is at once intelligible given our skill and talents, so it depends on the reader. A text easy for an expert can be above a beginner.
questions.rule: Which sense applies depends on the reader too.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: A chess player reads a book that reinterprets openings she has played for years, showing one principle that connects them. Which sense of reading does it call for?
options: The first, since she already knows the openings
The second, since the book offers understanding she lacked
Neither: books about games are read for entertainment, not understanding
The first, since she will learn some new moves
optionExplain: She knows the moves, but the book throws new light on them, which she does not yet have.
Right: like the history that recasts known facts, it is above her and can raise understanding.
A book can teach principles of any subject; the goal depends on the book and the reader.
Any new moves are a side gain; the main offer is the connecting principle.
questions.explain: A book that recasts familiar facts in a new light is better than its reader in the way that matters. It calls for reading in the second sense.
questions.rule: A new light on old facts calls for the second sense.
questions.teaches: The authors insist that such communication between unequals must be possible, or else no one could ever learn from another, either through speech or writing.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Which conditions do the authors say must hold for reading for understanding to take place? Select all that apply.
options: The writer understands more than the reader
The reader can overcome the gap to some degree
The reader already agrees with the writer
The book is written in plain, everyday words
The writer and reader share a profession
optionExplain: Right: the first condition is an initial inequality in understanding.
Right: the second is that the reader can partly overcome it.
Agreement is not a condition; understanding comes before any judgment.
Readable form matters, but plain words are not one of the two conditions.
A shared profession may help, but the authors do not require it.
questions.explain: The two conditions are an initial inequality and the reader's ability to narrow it. The card next explains them.
questions.rule: A gap, and the power to narrow it.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: In short, the authors say, we can learn only from our ____.
questions.explain: Learning in the sense of understanding more needs a writer who understands more than we do. We must know who such writers are and how to learn from them.
questions.rule: Learn from writers who understand more than you.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Which reading situation meets both of the authors' conditions?
options: An expert reads a beginner's pamphlet on her own field
A reader opens a book in a language he cannot read at all
A student reads a summary written by a classmate at her own level
A novice reads an expert's guide and grasps more each chapter
optionExplain: Here the reader is the superior one, so the first condition fails.
The gap is real, but he can close none of it, so the second condition fails.
No inequality in understanding, so the first condition fails.
Right: the writer is superior, and the reader narrows the gap.
questions.explain: Both conditions hold only when the writer knows more and the reader can climb toward him. The other cases each break one condition.
questions.rule: Check both conditions: a gap, and progress across it.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Ravi, with no grounding in physics, picks up a book on advanced quantum field theory and after a week understands none of it. Which condition failed?
options: The writer was not superior in understanding
Ravi could not overcome the inequality to any degree
The book was not in readable form for any reader
Ravi did not want to agree with the author
optionExplain: The writer is plainly superior; the first condition holds.
Right: a gap he can close none of means the second condition fails.
Physicists read it, so it is readable; the failure lies in Ravi's ability to close the gap.
Agreement is not a condition; understanding comes first.
questions.explain: Here the rule stops working: inequality is present, but Ravi cannot narrow it at all. A more approachable book could meet both conditions.
questions.rule: A gap you cannot narrow teaches nothing yet.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, reading for understanding requires the reader to reach full equality with the writer.
questions.explain: The reader overcomes the inequality in some degree, seldom perhaps fully, but always approaching equality. Partial progress counts.
questions.rule: Approaching the writer is enough; full equality is rare.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: A trainee pilot reads a dense manual by an experienced captain. Early on, many passages seem murky; by the end, the same passages make sense to her. On the authors' account, what changed?
options: The manual became easier as she read on
She got used to the manual's page layout and headings
She moved closer to the writer's understanding
The captain's control as a writer improved
optionExplain: The text stayed the same; the reader changed.
Familiar layout helps find things, but it does not make dense content make sense.
Right: as she approaches equality with the writer, communication becomes clear.
The words on the page did not change.
questions.explain: The passages did not change; her understanding did. As the gap narrows, what was murky becomes clear.
questions.rule: Clarity grows as the gap closes.
questions.teaches: The authors add that to the extent equality is approached, clarity of communication is achieved: clear communication is the result of the reader closing the gap.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: True or false: The authors claim that if you learn to read for understanding, reading for information will usually take care of itself.
questions.explain: The harder skill usually brings the easier one with it. The card next explains the claim and its hedge.
questions.rule: Learn the harder skill; the easier usually follows.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: The authors say that if you learn to read for understanding, reading for information will usually take care of ____.
questions.explain: That is why the book can focus on reading for understanding. Reading for information usually follows without separate training.
questions.rule: Focus on understanding; information usually follows.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Jas has trained hard at reading philosophy for understanding. She starts a job that requires reading industry news for facts. What do the authors expect?
options: She will need a separate course in reading for facts
She will read the news too slowly to keep up
She will find the news harder than philosophy
The news reading will usually come easily to her
optionExplain: The authors' claim is that such training is usually not needed.
Nothing in the claim predicts slowness; she can vary her speed.
News is at once intelligible to most readers; it is the easier kind.
Right: reading for information usually takes care of itself.
questions.explain: Her training in the harder skill should usually carry over to the easier one.
questions.rule: Skill in understanding carries over to reading for facts.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a mere recital of facts can sometimes itself lead to greater understanding.
questions.explain: The authors admit facts and insights are not always easy to tell apart, and that facts alone can sometimes bring understanding. The line is not sharp.
questions.rule: Facts and insights are not always separable.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Suppose a reader trains only at reading for information: skimming news, lists and reports. What does the chapter's claim say about her reading for understanding?
options: It will take care of itself, as information does
It will suffer, since fast reading spoils slow reading
Nothing is promised: the claim runs from understanding to information
It will improve faster than if she had trained at reading for understanding directly
optionExplain: This reverses the claim; the authors state it in one direction only.
The chapter says nothing of the kind; she can still learn to read for understanding.
Right: the claim is that understanding brings information, not the other way round.
The chapter gives no support for this.
questions.explain: The authors' claim goes one way: learn to read for understanding and information usually follows. Change the starting skill and the promise no longer applies.
questions.rule: The claim runs one way, from understanding to information.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: A violinist who practises hard concertos finds that easy folk tunes come to her with no separate practice. Which pattern from the chapter does this parallel?
options: The harder skill usually brings the easier one with it
Easy pieces should be mastered before hard ones
Both skills must be practised equally and separately
The easy tunes came by luck, not from the practice
optionExplain: Right: like reading for understanding, the harder skill usually carries the easier.
This reverses the order the authors favour.
The authors' claim is that the easier one usually needs no separate training.
The case suggests the practice carried over, the pattern the authors describe.
questions.explain: The pattern is one-way: master the demanding skill and the lesser one usually follows. The authors use the same one-way logic about the goals of reading.
questions.rule: Practise the harder skill; the easier usually follows.
questions.teaches: The authors make a similar one-way claim about goals: any book that can be read for understanding can probably be read for entertainment too, but not every book read for entertainment can be read for understanding.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: How do the authors describe reading for entertainment?
options: The hardest kind, needing the most rules
A waste of time for serious readers
The same as reading for information
The least demanding kind, needing no rules
optionExplain: This reverses their description.
The authors do not condemn it; they set it aside as needing no help.
They treat entertainment and information as different goals.
Right: it needs the least effort and has no rules.
questions.explain: Entertainment is the least demanding goal and has no rules. The card next places it among the goals.
questions.rule: Entertainment needs no rules.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: The authors call reading for entertainment the least demanding kind of reading, and say there are no ____ for it.
questions.explain: Because it needs the least effort and has no rules, anyone who can read at all can do it, and the book does not need to teach it.
questions.rule: Reading for fun needs no rules.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: By the authors' proposition, which of these can probably be read for all three goals: entertainment, information and understanding?
options: A timetable of the bus routes in your city
A book of crossword puzzles for the weekend
A great history that can raise understanding
A light comic strip in the Sunday paper
optionExplain: A timetable informs, but it holds little to understand or enjoy.
Puzzles entertain, but they offer little to understand more deeply.
Right: a book that can raise understanding can probably also inform and entertain.
A comic strip entertains, but the proposition does not reverse to give it the other goals.
questions.explain: The proposition starts from books that can be read for understanding: those can probably serve the other two goals as well.
questions.rule: Books for understanding can serve every goal.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: Lou reasons that because he enjoys a thriller, it must be capable of deepening his understanding too. What is wrong with his reasoning?
options: The proposition does not reverse: enjoyment is not depth
Enjoyment shows that the book is too shallow to teach
He should first check it is on a list of great books
Only nonfiction can be read for understanding
optionExplain: Right: not every book that can be read for entertainment can be read for understanding.
The authors do not say enjoyment shows shallowness; a deep book can entertain.
Lists are not the point; the flaw is reversing the proposition.
The book treats imaginative literature too as something that can be read for understanding.
questions.explain: Lou runs the authors' proposition backwards. Entertainment does not imply depth, though depth usually allows entertainment.
questions.rule: Enjoyable does not mean deep.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: True or false: The authors say a good book should not be read for entertainment.
questions.explain: They say outright that they do not urge readers to avoid reading good books for entertainment. Their concern is helping those who read for understanding.
questions.rule: A good book may be read for pleasure too.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: The Goals of Reading: Reading for Information and Reading for Understanding
questions.q: A film student watches a classic film for fun on Friday and studies it closely on Monday. Does the chapter's view of goals allow both uses of one work?
options: No: a work should be used for one goal, not several
Yes: a work rich enough for understanding can also be enjoyed
No: close study spoils a work for later enjoyment
Yes, but only if the Friday viewing for fun came after the close study
optionExplain: The authors show one book serving several goals.
Right: what can be taken for understanding can probably be taken for entertainment too.
The chapter says nothing of the kind.
Order is not part of the authors' proposition.
questions.explain: The same work can be approached with different goals, and each goal calls for a different way of reading.
questions.rule: One work, several goals, several ways of reading.
questions.teaches: The book later states that the goal a reader seeks, whether entertainment, information or understanding, determines the way he reads.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, being able to remember exactly what an author says is the same as being enlightened by him.
questions.explain: Remembering gives information. Enlightenment needs more, and the card next says what.
questions.rule: Memory alone gives information, not enlightenment.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: Which is the mark of being enlightened rather than only informed?
options: Knowing that something is the case, with its date and source
Being able to quote the author word for word on demand
Having read many books on the subject over the years
Knowing why it is so and how it connects with other facts
optionExplain: Knowing that it is so, even with details, is being informed.
Quoting exercises memory, which gives information only.
Breadth of reading is not the same as understanding what you read.
Right: enlightenment adds the why, the connections, and the likenesses and differences.
questions.explain: To be enlightened is to know what it is all about: why it is so and how it connects. That goes beyond knowing that it is so.
questions.rule: Enlightenment adds the why and the connections.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: Sort what each reader of a book on climate can say: does it show being informed, or being enlightened?

items.t: The book says sea levels rose last century
The author gives three figures for ice loss
The main claim appears in chapter four
The author argues that warming water expands, and that is why seas rise
This finding fits the ice data in chapter two, and here is how
The author's case differs from his rival's on one key point

questions.explain: The informed reader reports what the book says. The enlightened reader can say why, how points connect, and where cases are alike or different.
questions.rule: Reporting what was said is information; explaining it is enlightenment.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: True or false: On the authors' account, a reader who can explain an author's reasons but cannot recall what the author actually said is fully enlightened.
questions.explain: Being informed is a prerequisite to being enlightened: you should remember what the author said as well as know what he meant. Remove the first and the second is incomplete.
questions.rule: Enlightenment builds on being informed.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: A student memorises a philosopher's main sentences for an exam and says she has understood him. On the chapter's account, what has she gained?
options: Enlightenment, since she knows his main sentences
Information, gained by memory alone
Enlightenment, if she memorised the sentences in order
Understanding, since the sentences she learned are true
optionExplain: Knowing what he said is not knowing what he meant and why.
Right: exercising only memory yields information, not enlightenment.
Order is still memory; knowing what he means and why he says it is missing.
Even true sentences, merely remembered, give information only.
questions.explain: She knows what the author says, which is learning of a kind, but she has not shown she knows what he means or why he says it.
questions.rule: Memorised is not understood.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: A new hire memorises the company's safety rules; a colleague can say why each rule exists and how the rules fit together. Faced with a hazard the rules do not mention, which of them is better placed, by the chapter's distinction?
options: The new hire, because he knows every rule word for word
Neither, since a hazard that is not listed needs an outside safety expert
Both equally, since both of them know the same rules
The colleague, since knowing reasons reaches past the listed cases
optionExplain: Word-for-word recall covers only the listed cases.
Knowing why a rule exists is what lets someone reason about a new case.
They know the same rules, but only one knows why they hold.
Right: enlightenment includes why things are so and how they connect, which carries to new cases.
questions.explain: The informed person knows that the rules say something; the enlightened one knows why. Only the why reaches a case that is not on the list.
questions.rule: Knowing why lets you go beyond the list.
questions.teaches: The book later says that when a book has enlightened you and not only informed you, you should seek further enlightenment by asking what else follows from it.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: True or false: The authors treat being widely read and being well-read as the same thing.
questions.explain: They call that assumption an error. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Widely read and well-read differ.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: Match each term to its meaning in the chapter.
pairs: The ignorance of those who cannot read at all
The ignorance of those who have misread many books
Pope's name for the ignorantly read
The Greek-derived name for a mix of learning and folly
questions.explain: Montaigne's two ignorances bracket knowledge: one before learning to read, one after misreading many books. Pope and the Greeks name the second kind.
questions.rule: Doctoral ignorance comes from misreading many books.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: Which person best fits Montaigne's doctoral ignorance?
options: A reader who has read many books but misread them
A child who has not yet learned the alphabet
A reader who has read few books, each with care
A scholar who explains a few books well
optionExplain: Right: doctoral ignorance comes after reading, from misreading many books.
That is abecedarian ignorance, the kind that comes before knowledge.
Careful reading of a few books is the opposite case.
Explaining books well is a sign of reading them well.
questions.explain: Doctoral ignorance is the ignorance of the bookish but poorly read. It comes after much reading, not before any.
questions.rule: Much reading done badly breeds a learned ignorance.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: A dinner guest says he has read every bestseller of the last ten years, so he must be well-read. What is wrong with his claim?
options: Bestsellers are too easy to make anyone well-read
He needs to have read for longer than ten years
He confuses reading widely with reading well
He should have read classics instead of bestsellers
optionExplain: Easy books may add little, but the flaw is inferring quality of reading from quantity.
More time spent reading widely would not fix the inference.
Right: quantity of reading does not show quality of reading.
Which books are worth reading is a separate question; his inference fails either way.
questions.explain: He infers well-read from widely read. That is the error the authors warn against.
questions.rule: How much you read does not show how well you read.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: True or false: If someone reads many books and understands each one well, the authors' warning about bookful blockheads does not apply to her.
questions.explain: The warning is against reading too widely and not well. Wide reading done well is not the fault.
questions.rule: The fault is reading badly, not reading much.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: Kai has listened to five hundred episodes of a history podcast and can drop names and dates, but cannot explain why any event happened. Which of the chapter's labels fits him best?
options: Well-read, since he has absorbed so much history
Abecedarian, since he has not read the sources
Enlightened, since he knows so many names, facts and dates
A sophomore: learned in quantity, poor in understanding
optionExplain: Volume is not the measure; understanding is.
Abecedarian ignorance belongs to those who cannot read at all, which is not his case.
Knowing facts without the why is being informed, not enlightened.
Right: a mix of learning and folly, the Greeks' sophomore.
questions.explain: The same error can occur with any medium of instruction: a lot taken in, little understood.
questions.rule: Quantity without understanding is learned folly.
questions.teaches: To avoid this error, the authors turn to a distinction in kinds of learning, between learning by instruction and learning by discovery, which bears on reading and on education generally.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: What reason do the authors give for saying that learning by discovery must exist?
options: Teachers are often mistaken and must be checked
Many people have no teacher to learn from
Without it, teaching could never have begun
Discovery is quicker and surer than instruction
optionExplain: Teachers' errors are not the authors' argument.
True of many, but the authors' argument is about where knowledge could begin.
Right: if every teacher had to be taught, there would be no beginning to knowledge.
Speed and certainty are not the argument.
questions.explain: If every teacher had to be taught, there would be no beginning in the acquisition of knowledge. The card next sets out both kinds of learning.
questions.rule: Teaching depends on someone's earlier discovery.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: Sort each case: learning by instruction or learning by discovery.

items.t: Attending a lecture on volcanoes
Reading a textbook on genetics
Being talked through a tax return by a mentor
Working out why a plant wilts by testing how you water it
Finding a pattern in weather records you collected yourself
Reflecting on a problem until a solution comes to you

questions.explain: Instruction is being taught by someone else's speech or writing. Discovery is learning by research, investigation or reflection without being taught.
questions.rule: Taught by discourse, or found without a teacher.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: True or false: The authors hold that discovery is active learning and instruction is passive learning.
questions.explain: They call that a mistake. In both, the activity of learning goes on in the learner; there is no inactive learning.
questions.rule: All learning is active.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: An astronomer charts a comet's path from her own observations. Years later, a student learns the path from her published paper. Which labels fit the two cases, in order?
options: Discovery, then instruction
Instruction, then discovery
Instruction in both cases
Discovery in both cases
optionExplain: Right: she learned from the sky without a teacher; he learns from her writing.
This reverses them: observation without a teacher is discovery.
The astronomer had no one teaching her the path.
The student learns through someone's writing, which is instruction.
questions.explain: Learning from the world without a teacher is discovery; learning from someone's writing is instruction.
questions.rule: From the world, discovery; from a writer, instruction.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: True or false: The authors argue that if there were no learning by discovery at all, there could be no beginning in the acquisition of knowledge.
questions.explain: Remove discovery and every teacher must have been taught by an earlier teacher, without end. Some learning must happen without a teacher.
questions.rule: Knowledge starts with discovery.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: One cook invents a new sauce by experimenting at the stove; another learns the same sauce from the first cook's recipe card. Who is doing the learning, on the authors' account?
options: Only the inventor, since the recipe does the work for the second
Only the second, since the inventor already knew how to cook
Both, since in each case the learning goes on in the learner
Neither: they are using a skill, not gaining knowledge
optionExplain: The recipe helps, but the second cook still has to learn.
The inventor learned something new by discovery.
Right: learning, aided or not, happens in the one who learns.
Working out or taking in a new sauce is gaining knowledge, so it counts as learning.
questions.explain: Discovery and instruction differ in whether there is help, not in whether the learner is active.
questions.rule: Help or no help, the learner does the learning.
questions.teaches: The authors propose a better name for instruction to make this plain: aided discovery.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: Which two other arts do the authors say share teaching's special characteristic?
options: Music and painting
Law and the art of rhetoric
Architecture and engineering
Agriculture and medicine
optionExplain: These are arts, but not the ones the authors pair with teaching.
These aim to persuade or govern, not to help something grow.
Building arts make things; the authors chose arts that help living things grow.
Right: farmer and doctor help, but the growing or healing happens in the plant or patient.
questions.explain: The authors pair teaching with agriculture and medicine. The card next says what they share.
questions.rule: Teaching, farming and medicine help growth they cannot do.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: The authors suggest that a better name for instruction is ____ discovery.
questions.explain: Instruction is discovery with help. Unaided discovery is learning with no teacher at all.
questions.rule: Instruction is aided discovery.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: Match each art to what must happen in the one who is helped.
pairs: The plants or animals must grow
The student must do the learning
questions.explain: In each art the helper does much, but the essential change happens in the one helped: health, growth, knowledge.
questions.rule: The helper helps; the helped one grows.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: A parent hires an excellent tutor for a son who copies the tutor's worked answers into his book without thinking about them. By the authors' analogy, what is missing?
options: A better tutor, since this one is not getting through
More worked answers, so he has more examples to copy
A stricter timetable, so he spends more hours on it
The son's own learning: knowledge must grow in his mind
optionExplain: The tutor may be excellent; no tutor can do the learning.
More copying adds no growth.
Schedules do not make knowledge grow.
Right: as the patient must heal, the student must learn.
questions.explain: The tutor supplies aid, but the discovery must happen in the son. Copying skips the part only he can do.
questions.rule: No teacher can learn for you.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: True or false: Since the student must do the learning, the authors conclude that a good teacher makes no difference.
questions.explain: The doctor and the farmer do many things that matter. The teacher's help is real; it supports the learning rather than replacing it.
questions.rule: Help matters, though it cannot replace the learner.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: A personal trainer designs a perfect strength plan, but the client must lift the weights and build the muscle. Which point from the chapter does this parallel?
options: Help can matter, yet the growth happens in the one helped
A good enough plan makes hard effort unnecessary
The trainer's plan matters more than the client's effort
Clients who train alone do as well as those with trainers
optionExplain: Right: like the doctor, farmer and teacher, the trainer aids a growth only the client can achieve.
This is the passive picture of learning the authors reject.
The plan helps, but the growth happens only through the client's own work.
The analogy does not say help is useless; aid makes real differences.
questions.explain: The trainer, like the teacher, aids a change that has to happen in someone else.
questions.rule: Aid supports growth; it does not supply it.
questions.teaches: The authors then locate the real difference between aided and unaided discovery: it lies mainly in the materials the learner works on.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, reading and listening are, minor differences aside, the same art.
questions.explain: Both are ways of receiving communication from a teacher. The card next names the art and contrasts it with discovery.
questions.rule: Reading and listening share one art.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: The authors call reading and listening, taken together, the art of being ____.
questions.explain: Both are operations on discourse, written or spoken. That makes them one art, the art of being taught.
questions.rule: Reading and listening are the art of being taught.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: Sort each activity by what the learner works on: discourse, or nature and the world.

items.t: Following a lecture on economics
Reading a biography
Listening to a radio talk on gardening
Timing a pendulum's swings yourself
Watching ants to learn how they find food
Testing soil samples from your own garden

questions.explain: Lectures, books and talks are discourse, communicated by a teacher. Pendulums, ants and soil are the world, studied without a teacher.
questions.rule: Discourse is someone's communication; the world is not.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: On the authors' account, what mainly distinguishes learning by instruction from unaided discovery?
options: How hard the learner works
The materials the learner works on
Whether the learner is active
How fast the knowledge is gained by the learner
optionExplain: Both demand effort; that is not the main difference.
Right: instruction works on discourse, unaided discovery on nature or the world.
The authors say all learning is active.
Speed is not part of the distinction.
questions.explain: The difference lies mainly in the materials: discourse in one case, the world in the other.
questions.rule: The materials, not the effort, separate the two.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: A student says that since she learns mainly by listening to lectures, the rules of reading do not concern her. What would the authors reply?
options: She is right: listening has its own separate rules
Reading and listening are one art, so many rules apply
She is right, since a lecturer can answer her questions
The rules apply to her only if she takes written notes
optionExplain: The authors set aside the minor differences and treat both as one art.
Right: both are operations on discourse, the art of being taught.
A present teacher can answer, but that does not make the rules of being taught irrelevant.
Notes may help, but the rules apply because listening is itself the art of being taught.
questions.explain: Listening to lectures is learning from discourse, as reading is. Many of the book's rules carry over.
questions.rule: Rules for reading largely serve listening too.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: A detective examines footprints at a scene, then reads a witness's written statement. In the authors' loose sense of reading, what is she reading in each case?
options: Discourse, then the world
The world, then discourse
Discourse in both cases
The world in both cases
optionExplain: This reverses them: footprints are not anyone's communication.
Right: footprints belong to the world; a statement is discourse.
Footprints were not written to teach anyone.
The statement is someone's communication, so it is discourse.
questions.explain: Reading footprints is like unaided discovery, working on the world. Reading the statement is working on discourse.
questions.rule: Ask whether someone is telling you, or the world is showing you.
questions.teaches: The authors add that if thinking means using our minds to gain knowledge, it must take place in both activities: in reading and listening as much as in research.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: According to the authors, which of these does the art of reading call on? Select all that apply.
options: Keenness of observation
Range of imagination
An intellect trained in analysis
Memory alone, for what the text says
Agreement with the author's views
optionExplain: Right: keen observation is one of the skills reading shares with discovery.
Right: imagination is needed to construct what cannot be observed.
Right: a trained intellect is part of the art.
Memory is needed, but not alone; memory alone gives information only.
Agreement is not a faculty of learning; understanding comes before judging.
questions.explain: Reading uses the same skills as unaided discovery, including memory. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Reading uses every faculty discovery uses.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: If thinking means using our minds to gain knowledge or understanding, the authors say it must take place in reading and listening as well as in ____.
questions.explain: Instruction and discovery are the two ways of gaining knowledge, so thinking happens in both. The kinds of thinking differ, but both need it.
questions.rule: Reading is thinking, not a rest from it.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: Reading a poem about a harbour in winter, which activity shows the reader using imagination as the authors urge?
options: Counting the lines in each stanza
Picturing the scene the lines describe
Looking up the poet's date of birth
Reading it quickly to find its message
optionExplain: Counting observes the form, but it is not imagining.
Right: constructing what cannot be observed is the work of imagination.
Facts about the poet are information, not imagining.
A quick hunt for the message skips the slow attention and imagining a poem needs.
questions.explain: Imagination constructs what cannot be observed. A reader of a poem must do this, not only the poet.
questions.rule: Readers must imagine too.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: A student claims that the poet does the imagining, so the reader only needs to take in the words. What do the authors say against this?
options: The reader needs taste, not imagination, to judge a poem
The student is right: imagination belongs to the writer's side
Readers must imagine too, since reading uses discovery's skills
The student is right for poems but wrong for novels
optionExplain: Judgment comes later; first the reader must imagine what the poem presents.
This is the assumption the authors call a mistake.
Right: the authors name this assumption as a mistake.
The authors' example is a poem, so it fits poems most of all.
questions.explain: Many people assume only the poet needs imagination. The authors say the reader needs it as well.
questions.rule: Imagination is the reader's job as well as the poet's.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: True or false: The authors grant that reading a newspaper for information probably involves less thinking than trying to discover something.
questions.explain: They say one probably does less thinking when reading for information or entertainment than when discovering. The claim that reading needs hard thinking is about the effort to understand.
questions.rule: The more demanding the goal, the more thinking it needs.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.section: Reading as Learning: The Difference Between Learning by Instruction and Learning by Discovery
questions.q: An engineer reads a report describing a bridge in another country that she cannot visit. Which faculty does the chapter say she needs to construct what she cannot observe?
options: Imagination
Speed of reading
Memory of other reports
Trust in the report's figures
optionExplain: Right: imagination constructs what cannot be observed.
Speed does not build a picture of what is absent.
Memory helps, but constructing the unseen is the work of imagination.
Trust is not one of the faculties of learning the authors name.
questions.explain: Learning needs observing, remembering, and imagining what cannot be observed. A report on an unseen bridge calls for the last.
questions.rule: Imagine what the text describes but you cannot see.
questions.teaches: The book later adds that reading is harder to learn than a physical skill because its acts are mental: the beginning reader must, in a sense, think about his own thoughts.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, when you ask a book a question, you must answer it yourself.
questions.explain: A book cannot reply as a living teacher can. The card next explains what follows.
questions.rule: A book answers only through your own work.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: What reason do the authors give for putting reading ahead of listening?
options: Listening is harder than reading for most people to do well
Reading's teacher is absent; listening's is present
Books are more accurate than spoken lectures
Books are open to anyone, lectures are not
optionExplain: The authors do not rank them by difficulty in this way.
Right: the absent teacher cannot answer, so the reader must.
Accuracy is not the reason given.
Access is not the reason; it is the teacher's absence.
questions.explain: Listening is learning from a living teacher who can answer; reading is learning from one who cannot.
questions.rule: Reading means learning without a teacher to ask.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Reading a philosophy book alone, Femi wonders what the author means by a key word. What do the authors expect him to do?
options: Wait until he can ask the author in person
Work out the meaning himself from the text
Skip the word and read on regardless
Assume it has its everyday meaning
optionExplain: The author is absent; this question will not be answered that way.
Right: a book answers only as far as the reader does the thinking.
Skipping a key word dismisses what he does not understand.
Assuming does no thinking about how the author uses it.
questions.explain: With an absent teacher, Femi has to answer his own question by working on the text.
questions.rule: Answer your questions from the text.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Sort each situation: learning from a present teacher, or from an absent one.

items.t: Asking a lecturer a question after class
A tutor explaining a step you missed
A seminar leader answering on the spot
Reading a book on your own at home
Working through a manual with no one to ask
Rereading a classic years after leaving school

questions.explain: A present teacher can answer you. With an absent one, as in any book read alone, the answers must come from your own work.
questions.rule: Can anyone answer you? If not, the teacher is absent.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: True or false: The authors say that once a living teacher answers your question, you have no further work to do, whatever the question.
questions.explain: That holds only for a question of fact. If you seek an explanation, you still have to understand it, or nothing has been explained to you.
questions.rule: An explanation still has to be understood by you.

questions.unitTitle: The Activity and Art of Reading
questions.q: Mei learns from recorded video lectures by a professor who does not reply to messages. On the authors' reasoning, which situation is hers closer to?
options: A seminar with a living teacher present
A tutorial with constant feedback from a tutor
Reading a book, since no one can answer her
Unaided discovery, since no teacher takes part
optionExplain: She is listening, but there is no one present to ask.
There is no feedback in her case.
Right: what matters is that the teacher cannot answer, as with a book.
She works on discourse, so this is still instruction, not unaided discovery.
questions.explain: The key difference is whether the teacher can answer. A recording, like a book, leaves her to answer her own questions.
questions.rule: If the teacher cannot answer, treat it like a book.
questions.teaches: With an absent teacher, the book later advises reading a commentary only after reading the work yourself, since reading it first tends to make you see only the commentator's points.

questions.q: Two people read the same popular science article. One wants a talking point for dinner; the other wants to grasp how vaccines train the immune system. According to the authors, what should differ most between their readings?
options: The way each reads it, set by the goal each brings
Nothing: one text should be read the same way by everyone
Only their speed, since the words on the page are identical
Only how much each remembers a week later
optionExplain: Right: the authors hold that the goal a reader seeks determines how he reads, so different goals call for different readings.
This sounds fair to the text, but it ignores the reader's purpose, which the authors put first.
Speed may differ, but the authors' point is broader: the whole manner of reading changes with the goal.
Memory may differ as a result, but it is not what the authors say the goal decides.
questions.explain: The authors' first point is that the goal (entertainment, information or understanding) sets the way you read. The card next adds what decides how well you read.
questions.rule: Different goals, different ways of reading.

questions.q: According to the authors, the more ____ a reader puts in, the better, at least with books that are at first beyond the reader's powers.
questions.explain: Effectiveness depends on the effort and skill brought to the book, and the authors' rule is that more effort is better with books that start out beyond you.
questions.rule: More effort pays most on books that start out beyond you.

questions.q: Priya owns a cookbook she uses for weeknight dinners and a hard book on economics she wants to understand. Under the authors' effort rule, where should her greatest effort go?
options: Equally to both, to be fair to each author
To the economics book, which is at first beyond her
To the cookbook, since she opens it more often
To neither, since reading speed matters more than effort
optionExplain: Equal treatment sounds fair, but the rule ties effort to what a book can teach, and the two books differ greatly in that.
Right: the rule favours effort on books that can raise her from understanding less to understanding more.
Frequent use is not the test; a cookbook she already follows has little understanding left to give.
The authors make effort and skill, not speed, the measure of how well a reader reads.
questions.explain: The effort rule is strongest for books initially beyond the reader, because only they can raise understanding. The economics book is that kind of book for Priya.
questions.hint: Which book can raise her understanding?
questions.rule: Spend effort where there is understanding to gain.

questions.q: True or false: Once Priya fully understands the economics book, the authors' reason for pouring her greatest effort into it no longer applies to that book.
questions.explain: The rule rests on the book being beyond the reader, so that it can lift her to more understanding. When that gap is closed, the reason for maximum effort on that book is gone.
questions.rule: The effort rule follows the gap in understanding.

questions.q: A student first learns statistics in a class where the tutor answers questions on the spot, then later studies a new topic alone from a textbook. Which situation do the authors say calls most for knowing how to read well on your own?
options: Learning in the class, where the tutor sets a pace she must keep up with
Both equally, since in each case she learns from someone who knows more
Studying alone, where no one but the book can answer her questions
Learning in the class, since a live teacher demands closer attention than a page
optionExplain: Keeping pace is a real demand, but the tutor answers her questions, so less depends on her own reading skill.
Both are instruction from someone who knows more, which makes this tempting, but only the tutor is there to answer; alone, she must answer her own questions.
Right: with no one to answer her, she must raise and settle her own questions, which takes skill in reading.
Attention matters, but a present teacher carries the student past difficulties; the book alone cannot.
questions.explain: Both are learning by instruction, but the tutor is present and the textbook's author is absent. Alone with the book, the student has to answer her own questions, which is what calls for skill in reading.
questions.rule: Alone with a book, you must be your own teacher.
questions.teaches: Reading alone is still instruction (aided discovery), but from an absent teacher, so, as in unaided discovery, you must answer your own questions; most reading is done this way.

questions.q: Sort each item by how much effort the authors' rule suggests it deserves.

items.t: A treatise on ethics you find hard going
A bus timetable for tomorrow's trip
A paper built on ideas you have not met before
A news brief repeating facts you already know
A classic history whose argument puzzles you
A shopping list from a friend

questions.explain: Heavy effort pays where a text is beyond you and can raise your understanding. Where you follow everything at once, the rule stops: extra effort has nothing to close.
questions.rule: Match effort to how far a text is beyond you.

questions.q: True or false: In the authors' scheme, a reader who reaches the highest level of reading leaves the skills of the lower levels behind.
questions.explain: The authors call the levels cumulative: the highest level includes all the others and goes beyond them. The card next explains why they chose the word level.
questions.rule: Higher levels keep the lower ones.

questions.q: Put the four levels of reading in order, from the first to the highest.
items: Elementary reading
Inspectional reading
Analytical reading
Syntopical reading
questions.explain: Elementary reading comes first, then inspectional, then analytical, and syntopical reading is the fourth and highest, containing the other three.
questions.rule: Elementary, inspectional, analytical, syntopical.

questions.q: If the levels are cumulative, how might an inspectional reading of a book relate to a later analytical reading of the same book?
options: It should be forgotten, so that it does not bias the close reading
It can replace the analytical reading if it is done carefully enough
It has no link, since the two are separate kinds of reading
It prepares the ground: what the survey showed carries into the close reading
optionExplain: Fear of bias is understandable, but cumulative levels mean the lower work is kept and built on.
A higher level goes beyond a lower one, so a survey, however careful, cannot do the close reading's job.
Separate kinds is exactly what the authors deny when they choose the word level.
