Right: a lower level feeds the higher one; the survey's findings are used, not discarded.
questions.explain: Because each level contains the one below, what the inspectional survey found is kept and used as the starting point of the analytical reading.
questions.rule: Lower levels prepare the higher ones.
questions.teaches: Because levels are cumulative, the findings of a lower level are kept and built on at the higher level, not redone or thrown away.

questions.q: Lena, who is still learning Spanish, reads three Spanish articles on the same election to build her own view of what happened. Which statement fits the authors' idea of cumulative levels?
options: Her struggle with Spanish words is part of her high-level work, not separate from it
She works at the highest level now, so word recognition no longer matters
She should finish relating the articles first and deal with the words later
Her task is the fourth level, so it has nothing in common with a child's reading
optionExplain: Right: the highest level includes the elementary one, so her word work sits inside her larger task.
Working at a high level does not remove the lower skills; the authors say the higher includes the lower.
She cannot relate articles whose sentences she has not yet read; the lower level comes first.
A child's task, recognising words, is still present inside the fourth level, which is the point of cumulative levels.
questions.explain: Cumulative levels mean the elementary task of recognising words is still part of the highest kind of reading. Lena meets it openly because the language is foreign to her.
questions.rule: The top level still contains word recognition.

questions.q: A primary school teacher describes a child moving through four stages: getting ready to read, mastering simple words, growing vocabulary from context, and reading on her own. How do these relate to the authors' four levels?
options: They are the four levels under different names
They all fall inside the first level, elementary reading
They match the four levels one to one, stage by stage
They form a separate level below elementary reading
optionExplain: The count of four invites the match, but none of these stages involves surveying a book or relating many books.
Right: all four stages concern learning to recognise and read words, which is the work of elementary reading.
Reading on her own is not syntopical reading; a one-to-one match ignores what each level does.
There is no level below elementary reading in the authors' scheme; it is the first level.
questions.explain: Getting ready, word mastery, vocabulary from context and independent reading are steps in learning to read at all. That is elementary reading, the first level.
questions.rule: Stages of learning to read sit within the first level.
questions.teaches: The authors later describe four stages of learning to read, and all four are stages of the first level, elementary reading, not the four levels.

questions.q: True or false: A friend reasons that, because the levels are cumulative, every book must be read at all four levels; the authors' idea of cumulative levels supports this reasoning.
questions.explain: Cumulative describes how the levels relate: a higher one contains the lower ones. It does not require climbing to the top with every book; the reader picks the level the goal needs.
questions.rule: Cumulative is about inclusion, not a duty to climb.

questions.q: According to the authors, most speed reading courses work mainly on which kind of reading problem?
options: Judging whether an author's argument is sound
Relating several books on the same subject
Mechanical difficulties at the most basic level
Choosing which books are worth reading at all
optionExplain: Judging soundness is slow, careful work that speed training does not address.
Relating many books is the highest level, far from what speed drills train.
Right: overcoming mechanical difficulties at the first level usually speeds reading up, so speed courses concentrate there.
Choosing books is a matter of judgment and surveying, not of reading mechanics.
questions.explain: The authors say that fixing mechanical troubles at the elementary level usually lets us read faster, which is why most speed reading courses focus on it. The card next sets out that first level.
questions.rule: Speed courses work on the first level.

questions.q: At the elementary level, the question asked of the reader is: What does the ____ say?
questions.explain: Elementary reading asks what the sentence says, in the plainest sense: which words are on the page.
questions.rule: Level one asks what the sentence says.

questions.q: Tom, a fluent English reader, opens a German instruction leaflet for a new kettle. He knows little German. According to the authors, what must his first effort be?
options: Judge whether the instructions are sensible
Work out what kind of document it is
Compare it with the English leaflet's claims
Identify the actual words on the page
optionExplain: He cannot judge instructions he has not yet read; judging comes much later.
That is a surface question for a higher level, and he can hardly answer it before he can read the words.
Comparison needs both texts understood first, which is beyond him until the words are made out.
Right: in a language you know poorly, the first effort is to identify the words; meaning comes after.
questions.explain: A poorly known language sends even skilled readers back to elementary reading: recognise the words first, then struggle with what they mean.
questions.rule: In an unfamiliar language, words come before meaning.

questions.q: Sort each question a reader might ask: does it belong to elementary reading, or to a higher level?
groups: Elementary: what does the sentence say

items.t: What word do these letters spell?
Which words are printed on this line?
How is this unfamiliar word pronounced?
What is this whole book about?
Is the author's argument sound?
What are the main parts of this book?

questions.explain: Elementary questions stay with the words on the page. Questions about the whole book, its parts or its soundness belong to higher levels.
questions.rule: Elementary questions stay with the words.

questions.q: A law firm trains junior staff in speed reading so they get through contracts faster. In the authors' view, what is the limit of such training?
options: It speeds the mechanics, but hard clauses still need the pace understanding sets
It makes careful reading unnecessary, since fast readers absorb a contract in one pass
It sharpens judgment of whether a contract is fair, since speed frees attention for it
It harms understanding, since any pace above talking speed loses the meaning
optionExplain: Right: speed training works on the elementary level; it cannot remove the need to read a demanding text at the pace understanding requires.
This is the promise of many courses, but speed at the first level does not supply understanding.
Judging fairness is higher-level work that drills on reading mechanics do not touch.
Too harsh: the authors grant that overcoming mechanical problems usually lets us read faster without loss.
questions.explain: Speed reading addresses mechanical problems at the first level. How fast a contract should be read depends on what its clauses demand, which speed drills do not change.
questions.rule: Read as fast as understanding allows, no faster.
questions.teaches: Faster mechanics change how quickly you can take in words, not how quickly a given text should be read; the right pace is set by what the text demands of your understanding.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a student who reads a philosophy passage aloud without a single stumble over the words has finished the work of reading it.
questions.explain: Reading every word correctly answers only the elementary question of what the sentences say. What the passage means and whether it is true are questions for the higher levels.
questions.rule: Recognising every word is the start, not the end.

questions.q: You have fifteen minutes with a 400-page book that is new to you. Which aim best fits the time?
options: Understand every argument in the first chapter
Find out what the book is about and how it is organised
Memorise key facts from as many pages as possible
Decide whether the author's conclusions are true
optionExplain: Careful work on one chapter leaves you knowing nothing about the rest of the book.
Right: in a short time, the surface of a book can tell you its subject and structure.
Scattered facts do not tell you what the book as a whole is doing.
Judging truth needs a full understanding first, which fifteen minutes cannot give.
questions.explain: Fifteen minutes is far too short to get everything, but long enough to learn what the book is about and how it is built. The card next names this kind of reading.
questions.rule: Short time: aim at the whole, not the detail.

questions.q: Which questions belong to inspectional reading, according to the authors? Select all that apply.
options: What is the book about?
What are its parts?
Is the author's argument sound?
What kind of book is it?
What does this one sentence say?
optionExplain: Right: this is the typical question of inspectional reading.
Right: structure and parts are surface questions of the same sort.
Soundness is a judgment that needs a careful reading; the surface cannot settle it.
Right: after an inspection you should be able to say whether it is a novel, a history, a treatise and so on.
That is the question of elementary reading, the level below.
questions.explain: Inspectional questions are surface questions: what the book is about, what its structure and parts are, and what kind of book it is.
questions.rule: Inspection asks surface questions about the whole book.

questions.q: Which of these is inspectional reading in the authors' sense?
options: Opening a book at random pages until something catches your eye
Reading the first chapter slowly, then deciding about the rest
Checking the contents, preface and chapter openings in a planned order
Reading reviews of the book in place of the book itself
optionExplain: This is casual browsing, which the authors set apart from systematic skimming.
Slow reading of one chapter spends the limited time on a part, not on the surface of the whole.
Right: it examines the book's own surface with a system, which is what inspection means.
Reviews may help, but inspection examines the surface of the book itself.
questions.explain: Inspectional reading is skimming done systematically on the book itself. Random browsing and slow reading of one part both miss that.
questions.rule: Inspection is systematic, not random.

questions.q: Your manager hands you a 90-page market report and gives you ten minutes before a meeting. If you inspect it well, what should you be able to tell her afterwards?
options: Whether every figure in it is accurate, checked against the sources
A full account of the reasoning in each of its sections, in order
Which pages contain errors of reasoning, and why they mislead
Its subject, how its sections are arranged and what kind of report it is
optionExplain: Checking figures needs careful reading, not a ten-minute survey.
Following every section's reasoning is the work of thorough reading with time to spare.
Spotting errors means judging the argument, which comes after understanding it.
Right: subject, structure and kind are what the surface of a document can show in a short time.
questions.explain: Ten minutes is an inspectional reading: the aim is what the report is about, how it is built and what kind of document it is, not its accuracy or soundness.
questions.rule: A short survey yields subject, structure and kind.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a book twice as long could still be given an inspectional reading in the same fifteen minutes.
questions.explain: Inspection is defined by a set time, not by the book's length; the authors mention fifteen minutes for their book or even one twice as long. With more pages, the surface survey is thinner, but it is still inspection.
questions.rule: Inspection is set by time, not by length.

questions.q: A new hire is given her company's 200-page policy wiki and one hour before her first meeting. Which approach applies inspectional reading to it?
options: Scan the page list and headings to learn what it covers, how it is laid out and what kind it is
Read the first pages in full, since policy documents put the most important rules at the start
Search only for the few topics she expects to need, since the rest will not matter yet
Open pages at random to get a feel for the tone and style of the company's writing
optionExplain: Right: the same surface questions, subject, structure and kind, work on any long document with a visible surface.
Careful reading of the opening uses the hour on one part and leaves her blind to the rest.
Targeted searching can be useful later, but it skips the survey of the whole that inspection gives.
Random dipping is the casual browsing that the authors set apart from systematic skimming.
questions.explain: A wiki has a surface of its own: page lists, headings, summaries. Inspecting it systematically answers what it is about, how it is built and what kind of document it is, in the time she has.
questions.rule: Inspect any long document by its surface, not only books.
questions.teaches: Inspectional reading is not limited to books: any long document with a surface, such as headings, page lists or summaries, can be inspected with the same questions about subject, structure and kind.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, many quite good readers start a book on page one without even reading its table of contents.
questions.explain: The authors say most people, even many quite good readers, are unaware of the value of inspectional reading and plow straight in. The card next shows what this costs them.
questions.rule: Even good readers often skip the survey.

questions.q: Readers who plow through from page one must gain a superficial knowledge of the book at the same time as they try to ____ it.
questions.explain: Plowing through sets two tasks at once, learning the book's surface and understanding it, and the authors say this compounds the difficulty.
questions.rule: Do not learn the map and the meaning at once.

questions.q: Kofi has to learn a 300-page manual for new accounting software. Which plan fits the authors' advice?
options: Read every page in order, making sure each is clear before moving on
Look over the contents and section headings first, then read closely
Skip straight to the troubleshooting chapter, since it is most useful
Read only the index, then search for terms as problems arise
optionExplain: This feels thorough, but it is the plow-through approach that makes him learn layout and content together.
Right: the survey gives him the layout, so the close reading can focus on understanding.
Jumping to one chapter without a survey leaves him not knowing how it fits the rest.
The index helps a survey, but on its own it gives neither the layout nor the understanding he needs.
questions.explain: The authors' advice is to inspect before reading closely. A look at the contents and headings tells Kofi how the manual is built before he works through it.
questions.hint: Which plan separates learning the layout from understanding the content?
questions.rule: Map first, then read closely.

questions.q: Suppose Ben, the student who started his economics textbook at page one, had first spent five minutes on the table of contents. According to the authors' reasoning, what would change?
options: Little, since a contents page lists headings but cannot show how the argument runs
He would understand the chapters well enough to skip the hardest ones later
He would know something of the layout, so less attention would go on finding his way
He would have read out of order, which spoils a book meant to be read straight through
optionExplain: Headings alone do not give the argument, but they do show what the book covers and how it is laid out, which is the surface knowledge he lacked.
A survey prepares understanding; it cannot supply it, so no chapter can be skipped on its strength.
Right: even a brief look at the surface removes part of the double task, leaving more attention for understanding.
The authors' complaint is about readers who skip the contents; looking at the contents first is not reading out of order.
questions.explain: The difficulty comes from learning the layout and the meaning together. Any survey of the surface, even a short one, takes some of the first job off the close reading.
questions.rule: Even a short survey lightens the close reading.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a good inspectional survey of a hard book you want to understand makes the careful reading of it unnecessary.
questions.explain: Inspection gets the most from the surface in a short time, which is by definition too little to get everything. For a book you want to understand, the survey prepares the careful reading; it does not stand in for it.
questions.rule: The survey prepares the close reading; it does not replace it.

questions.q: Before listening to a 12-episode history podcast, Ravi reads the episode list and the host's opening summary. Which benefit does the authors' reasoning about plowing in predict?
options: He can skip the episodes whose titles he understands, since the list already covers them
He will remember the episode titles better, which is the main aim of any survey
He can judge the host's claims before hearing the evidence, which saves listening time
While listening, he can follow each episode's point instead of also working out where it fits
optionExplain: A title tells him what an episode covers, not what it says, so the survey cannot replace listening.
Remembering titles is a side effect; the aim of a survey is to grasp the whole and its parts.
Judging before understanding is backwards, and a list of titles holds no evidence to judge by.
Right: with the map in hand, his attention during each episode can go to understanding, not to finding his place.
questions.explain: The cost of plowing in is learning the layout and the content at once. A survey of the series removes the first job, so each episode gets his full attention.
questions.rule: Learn the map first, then give each part full attention.
questions.teaches: The cost of plowing in is not special to books: any long series of parts, such as a podcast or a course, is easier to follow once you have surveyed how the parts fit together.

questions.q: Francis Bacon wrote that some books are to be tasted, others swallowed, and some few chewed and digested. Which kind of reading do the authors link to chewing and digesting?
options: Thorough, active reading that makes a book yours
Skimming the surface of a book in a short, set time
Reading many books on one subject alongside each other
Recognising the words of each sentence as you go
optionExplain: Right: the authors say reading a book analytically is chewing and digesting it.
Skimming in a short time is closer to tasting: a first look at the surface.
Reading many books together is the fourth level, which the authors describe separately.
Word recognition is the first level, the start of reading, not its fullest form.
questions.explain: The authors use Bacon's image for the third level, analytical reading. The card next explains what makes it the best reading you can do.
questions.rule: Chewing and digesting means analytical reading.

questions.q: Inspectional reading is the best reading possible in a limited time; analytical reading is the best reading possible given ____ time.
questions.explain: The authors contrast the two levels by time: inspection is the best in a limited time, analysis the best and most complete with unlimited time.
questions.rule: Inspection: limited time. Analysis: unlimited time.

questions.q: Match each level of reading to its description.
pairs: the most from a book in a set, short time
the best, most complete reading with unlimited time
questions.explain: Elementary reading settles what sentences say; inspectional reading gets the most from the surface in a set time; analytical reading is thorough reading without a time limit.
questions.rule: Each level is defined by what it aims at.

questions.q: Four readers each work on a hard history book. Which one is doing analytical reading in the authors' sense?
options: Dev reads it slowly over a month but never asks what its author is claiming
Mia questions it in an orderly way until she can state its case herself
Sol gives it twenty minutes to learn its subject, its parts and its kind
Ivy reads the first lines of every chapter and then the final chapter
optionExplain: Dev has the time, but slowness without organised questions is not analytical reading; this is where the rule stops.
Right: organised questioning until the book becomes her own is what the authors describe.
That is a good inspectional reading, limited by time and by the surface.
Reading first lines is a piece of a survey, not a thorough reading.
questions.explain: Analytical reading is marked by active, organised questioning that ends with the book made your own. Time alone, as in Dev's case, does not make a reading analytical.
questions.hint: Which reader asks the book questions?
questions.rule: Organised questions, not hours, make a reading analytical.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, if a reader moves from analytically reading a plain introduction to analytically reading a dense treatise, the demands on her rise.
questions.explain: The authors say analytical reading makes more or less heavy demands depending on the difficulty of the text. A harder book asks more of the same method.
questions.rule: Harder text, heavier analytical demands.

questions.q: A new manager is handed twenty reports, three of which will shape next year's strategy. Using Bacon's image as the authors apply it, how should she read them?
questions.explain: Bacon's image sorts books by how much reading they deserve. Analytical reading, the chewing and digesting, goes to the few that need it; the rest get lighter reading.
questions.rule: Choose the level book by book.
questions.teaches: The level of reading is chosen text by text: one reading list can call for tasting most items, swallowing some and chewing and digesting only the few that deserve it.
options: Chew and digest all twenty, since every report deserves her best reading
Taste all twenty equally, since a quick look at each is fairest to the authors
Taste most, read some straight through, and chew and digest the three strategic ones
Chew and digest the longest ones, since length is the best sign of importance
optionExplain: Best reading for all sounds diligent, but analytical reading takes time and few texts deserve it.
Equal treatment ignores that three reports need understanding, which a taste cannot give.
Right: the level is chosen report by report, and only the few that deserve it get analytical reading.
Length does not show which reports matter; their role in the strategy does.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, analytical reading is hardly ever necessary if your goal is only information or entertainment.
questions.explain: The authors say analytical reading is preeminently for understanding and hardly ever needed for information or entertainment. The card next shows why the link matters.
questions.rule: Analytical reading serves understanding.

questions.q: According to the authors, analytical reading is preeminently for the sake of ____.
questions.explain: Of the three goals, entertainment, information and understanding, analytical reading belongs above all to understanding.
questions.rule: Analytical reading is for understanding.

questions.q: Sort each reading task by whether it calls for analytical reading, judged by the reader's goal.

items.t: A dense essay on free will you want to grasp
A recipe for tonight's dinner
A football score in the morning paper
A classic treatise on government that puzzles you
A holiday thriller read for fun
A paper on gene editing whose reasoning you want to follow

questions.explain: Tasks aimed at understanding something not yet grasped call for analytical reading. Reading for a fact or for fun hardly ever does.
questions.rule: Let the goal decide whether to read analytically.

questions.q: Hana starts a popular history book for entertainment, then finds she wants to understand why the empire it describes collapsed, which the book argues in depth. What does the authors' link between goals and levels suggest?
options: She should keep reading for fun, since a goal once set should stay fixed
She should switch to inspectional reading, since her time is now shorter
She should look for a different book, since one read for fun is the wrong tool
Her new goal of understanding now calls for analytical reading
optionExplain: Nothing in the authors' view fixes a goal for good; the goal guides the reading as it stands now.
Nothing in the case says her time is short, and inspection cannot give the understanding she now wants.
How a book was first picked up does not limit what it can teach; this book argues the very question she now cares about.
Right: once the goal becomes understanding, the level of reading should rise to match it.
questions.explain: The goal sets the way of reading. When Hana's goal changes from entertainment to understanding, the case for analytical reading appears.
questions.rule: When the goal changes, the reading should change.

questions.q: Tariq reads only books he can follow completely on first sight, and he reads them with great care. According to the authors, what can such reading give him?
options: Information, but no growth in his understanding
Growth in understanding, since he reads carefully
Understanding that deepens with each careful rereading of the same books
Skill at the fourth level, since he reads many books
optionExplain: Right: a book that is wholly clear to you at once can add facts but cannot raise your understanding.
Care is good, but understanding grows only when a book starts out above you.
Rereading feels like deepening, but if the book held nothing beyond him the first time, there is no gap left to close.
Reading many books does not by itself mean relating them to one subject.
questions.explain: Understanding grows only when a book is at first beyond you. Tariq's careful reading of easy books adds information without lifting his understanding.
questions.rule: Only books above you can raise your understanding.
questions.teaches: Care does not stand in for difficulty: the gain in understanding comes from the gap between the book and the reader, not from how slowly or carefully the reader goes.

questions.q: A graduate student has a shelf of twenty books on climate economics and two weeks. According to the authors' scheme, how can she decide which of them deserve analytical reading?
options: Read each one analytically in turn, in shelf order, until time runs out
Inspect each one first, then read analytically those that deserve it
Pick the longest books, since length usually signals depth of thought
Read only the reviews, then read the most praised ones analytically
optionExplain: This spends her best reading on whichever books come first, not on those that deserve it.
Right: a quick inspection of each book shows which ones need the full analytical treatment.
Length is no measure of whether a book can raise her understanding.
Reviews are second-hand; inspecting the books themselves tells her more about each.
questions.explain: Analytical reading is costly and meant for books that can raise understanding. Inspectional reading is the tool for sorting which books those are.
questions.rule: Inspect first to choose what to read analytically.
questions.teaches: With many books and little time, understanding is best served by spending a little time on every book first, then a lot of time on the few that repay it.

questions.q: A researcher reads ten books on sleep. In the authors' view, what would turn this into the highest level of reading?
options: Reading each book faster than the last, to cover more of the field
Writing a careful summary of each book as she finishes it
Building her own analysis of sleep from how the books relate
Choosing the single best book and rereading it closely
optionExplain: Speed is not what marks the highest level; it makes heavy demands even with easy books.
Summaries are useful, but separate summaries do not yet relate the books to each other.
Right: the highest level relates many books to one subject and builds an analysis from them.
Rereading one book is a single-book task, however careful.
questions.explain: The fourth level reads many books in relation to each other and to a shared subject, and goes on to build an analysis of that subject. The card next describes it.
questions.rule: Many books, related, toward your own analysis.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, syntopical reading makes very heavy demands on the reader even when the books read are relatively easy.
questions.explain: The difficulty lies in relating many books and building an analysis of the subject, not in the books themselves, so even easy books make it demanding.
questions.rule: The hard part is relating, not the books.

questions.q: Five diet books sit on your desk. Which task goes beyond comparison into syntopical reading?
options: Listing which of the five recommend fewer carbohydrates, and which do not
Making a table of when each was published and who wrote it
Choosing the one with the best reviews and following its plan closely
Using all five to map the questions they raise and build your own analysis
optionExplain: This is a real comparison, but it stops at setting the books side by side.
Publication dates are facts about the books, not about the subject they share.
Picking a winner ends the work with one book instead of relating all of them.
Right: it relates the books to a common subject and builds an analysis that no single book gives.
questions.explain: Comparison sets texts side by side. Syntopical reading uses them to build an analysis of the subject they revolve around.
questions.rule: Comparison is a step; analysis of the subject is the goal.

questions.q: Aisha reads four books on the history of the printing press for a talk. Which of her steps fit syntopical reading? Select all that apply.
options: Relating the books to each other on the questions they share
Relating all four to the subject of printing's effects
Building an analysis that none of the four states
Reading only the one with the clearest prose
Treating each book as a separate task with no link to the others
optionExplain: Right: placing the books in relation to one another is part of the definition.
Right: the books are related to the subject they all revolve around.
Right: the analysis may be in none of the books; that is what lifts it above comparison.
Clear prose is pleasant, but reading one book is not reading many in relation.
Separate tasks may be good analytical readings, but without links between them there is no syntopical reading.
questions.explain: Syntopical reading relates many books to each other and to one subject, and builds an analysis of the subject from them.
questions.rule: Relate the books, relate them to the subject, then analyse.

questions.q: A journalist sets out to read the major books on fairness in taxation, but finds that authors mean different things by fairness, and some books on her list are not really about her question. What does this show, according to the authors' later account of syntopical reading?
options: Settling the shared subject is part of the work, and may only come after reading
She chose the wrong subject and should restart with a narrower, clearer word
Syntopical reading works only for single historical events, not for ideas
She should adopt the meaning of fairness that most of the authors use
optionExplain: Right: when authors use one word in different senses, the reader has to work out what the shared subject really is, and that can take reading.
Narrowing may help later, but the clash of meanings is a normal part of the task, not a sign of failure.
The authors do say a historical event gives a clearer subject, but they show the method on ideas such as love.
A head count of authors does not settle the subject; it is the reader who must set the terms.
questions.explain: Different authors use the same word in different senses, so the subject cannot be fully fixed in advance. The syntopical reader has to establish the shared terms and questions herself.
questions.rule: In syntopical reading, the reader sets the terms.
questions.teaches: When authors use one word in different senses, setting their sentences side by side misleads; the syntopical reader must first work out what each means, and the shared subject may become clear only after the reading.

questions.q: Suppose Aisha could not yet follow the argument of any single book on her list. According to the authors' idea of cumulative levels, what would happen to her syntopical reading?
options: It would still succeed, since relating books needs no understanding of each
It would fail, since relating books rests on grasping each one
It would become easier, since she would bring no bias
It would still work if she relied on reviews to tell her what each book says
optionExplain: Relating books means relating what they say, which she cannot do without grasping it.
Right: the fourth level includes the lower ones, so it cannot stand without them.
Lack of understanding is not neutrality; it leaves her nothing to relate.
Second-hand accounts do not give her the books' arguments to relate; she still needs to grasp each one herself.
questions.explain: Because the levels are cumulative, syntopical reading rests on the reader's ability to grasp each book. Without that, there is nothing to relate.
questions.rule: The top level stands on the lower ones.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Which change would make teaching reading in a nation's schools harder, even if the teaching methods stayed exactly the same?
options: Fewer critics publish books attacking the way schools teach reading
Schools begin enrolling every child, however unmotivated or deprived
Cheaper printing puts many more books into every classroom in the land
Classes shrink to a handful of eager pupils from homes full of books
optionExplain: Less criticism might lower the pressure on schools, but it does not make the teaching itself any harder.
Right: teaching every child, however unmotivated or deprived, is far harder than teaching a keen few from reading homes.
More books would help, not hinder, reading instruction.
Small classes of eager pupils are the easiest case, the reverse of what makes teaching harder.
questions.explain: Who is being taught matters as much as how. The card next shows how the effort to teach everyone fed the worry about reading.
questions.rule: Teaching everyone is harder than teaching a motivated few.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, one of the trends behind the concern about reading was the American effort to make every citizen literate.
questions.explain: The first trend is the effort to educate all citizens, which at a minimum means making them all literate. The other two are changing methods and a tradition of criticizing the schools.
questions.rule: Trend one: schooling for everyone.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: A city's free adult literacy classes once drew only keen volunteers, and nearly all learned to read. Now the classes are required for everyone on a job scheme, and many struggle. Which trend does this most resemble?
options: The long tradition of criticizing schools
The repeated swings between methods
The effort to teach every learner
The spread of speed reading courses
optionExplain: Criticism may follow the struggles, but the change described is in who is being taught.
Nothing in the case says the method changed; the same classes are being given.
Right: moving from a motivated few to everyone is the change the authors describe in American schooling.
Speed reading is not part of this case and is not one of the three trends.
questions.explain: The classes did not change; the learners did. That is the shift from teaching a motivated minority to teaching everyone.
questions.hint: What changed: the lessons, the critics, or the learners?
questions.rule: Look at who is being taught before blaming the method.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: According to the authors, the American drive for universal literacy succeeded early, and this helped the nation become a highly developed ____ society.
questions.explain: The authors call the results remarkable: near-universal literacy came earlier in the United States than anywhere else and helped make it a highly developed industrial society. The problems came alongside that success.
questions.rule: The literacy drive succeeded broadly and still left hard problems.
questions.teaches: The authors say the United States reached near-universal literacy earlier than any other country, and that this helped it become a highly developed industrial society.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: A firm once trained only volunteers on new software. Now every employee must use it, and staff who cannot cope slow down their teammates. Which point of the authors does this parallel?
options: A weak reader in school becomes his teachers' and classmates' concern
Poor readers should leave school so that the others can make progress
Weak readers mostly lack physical readiness, such as eyesight or hearing
A better method of teaching would let every learner in the group succeed
optionExplain: Right: outside school a poor reader's problem is largely personal; inside a class it affects those around him, as the struggling staff affect their teams.
The authors draw no such conclusion; they support educational opportunity for all.
Readiness belongs to young children; nothing here points to eyesight.
The authors doubt any method is a cure for every learner.
questions.explain: The authors say a young person who reads poorly is hindered personally, but once he stays in school or goes to college his difficulty also concerns his teachers and fellow students. The software case has the same shape.
questions.rule: A learner's weakness becomes a group problem once the learner stays in the group.
questions.teaches: According to the authors, the problem grew urgent as more students stayed on in high school and college: outside school a poor reader's difficulty is mostly personal, but in school it concerns teachers and fellow students too.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: True or false: If schools solved every first-level problem the three trends raised, the authors would consider the nation's reading problem solved.
questions.explain: The three trends concern elementary reading. The authors hold that the higher levels were neglected and that remedies must work on all levels, so fixing the first level alone would not be enough.
questions.rule: Solving the first level is not solving reading.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: A teacher shows beginners whole words on cards and only later points out the letters inside them. What is this approach usually called?
options: The phonic method
The ABC method
The sight method
The syllable drill
optionExplain: The phonic method starts from the sounds of letters, not from whole words.
The ABC method starts from letter names and builds syllables.
Right: the sight method teaches recognition of whole words first.
Syllable drills build up from letters, the opposite direction.
questions.explain: Starting from whole words and working down to letters is the sight method. The card next contrasts it with methods that build words up from parts.
questions.rule: Whole words first is the sight method.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Match each method of teaching beginners with what pupils do first.
pairs: Name letters and combine them into syllables
Recognize words by the sounds of their letters
Sentence extension of the sight method
Read whole sentences, then words, then letters
questions.explain: The ABC and phonic methods start from letters or sounds. The sight method and its sentence extension start from larger units and work down.
questions.rule: Know each method by where it starts.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Sort each classroom activity by the family of method it belongs to.

items.t: Drilling syllables such as ab, ac, ad
Blending the sounds of each letter
Reciting letter names before any words
Flash cards of whole words with pictures
Reading a whole sentence before its words
Learning a word on sight, its letters later

questions.explain: Synthetic methods (ABC, phonic) assemble words from letters or sounds. Analytic methods (sight, sentence) begin with words or sentences and break them down.
questions.rule: Synthetic builds up; analytic breaks down.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: A language app first shows whole phrases with pictures, then switches to teaching each letter's sound and blending sounds into words. How has its approach changed?
options: From analytic, like the sight method, to synthetic, like phonics
From synthetic, like phonics, to analytic, like the sight method
From silent reading of phrases to reading the sounds aloud
No change: both stages start from whole units, so both are analytic
optionExplain: Right: whole phrases first is analytic; blending letter sounds is the phonic, synthetic way.
This reverses the direction: the app started with wholes and moved to parts.
The case is about which units are taught first, not about reading aloud or silently.
Blending letter sounds builds words up from parts, which is synthetic.
questions.explain: Starting from whole phrases is analytic; building words from letter sounds is synthetic. Changing the starting unit changes the family of method.
questions.hint: Where does each stage start: the whole or the parts?
questions.rule: Change the starting unit and you change the method family.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: True or false: The authors report that children who read aloud well did not necessarily read silently well.
questions.explain: It was found that ability to read orally did not necessarily mean ability to read silently, so oral instruction was not always enough when silent reading was the goal. This led to a heavy stress on rapid silent reading in the early 1920s.
questions.rule: Reading aloud and reading silently are different skills.
questions.teaches: Researchers found that skill in reading aloud did not guarantee skill in silent reading, which is why, from about 1920 to 1925, instruction stressed rapid silent reading almost exclusively.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: A school board member calls phonics a recent fad that pushed out the older methods. Based on the authors' history, what is the best reply?
options: Phonics is the newcomer; whole-word sight teaching is the older tradition
Phonics took over permanently in the 1920s, when sight methods were dropped
Phonics dates from the 1800s and never entirely left the curriculum
Phonics is the old ABC method of letter names, renamed for modern use
optionExplain: The sight method was promoted after about 1840; phonics arose in the same period as an alternative to the ABC method.
The 1920s and 1930s were the high point of the sight method, not of phonics.
Right: phonics arose in the mid-nineteenth century as a variant of the synthetic method and stayed in the curriculum even when sight methods were popular.
Both are synthetic, but phonics uses letter sounds where the ABC method uses letter names.
questions.explain: Phonics was proposed around the middle of the nineteenth century as a variant of the ABC method. Even at the height of the sight method it never entirely left the curriculum, and the pendulum later swung back toward it.
questions.rule: Check a method's history before calling it new.
questions.teaches: Phonics is not new: it arose in the mid-nineteenth century, and the authors say it never entirely left the curriculum even when whole-word methods were in fashion.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Which of these would you expect to come first as a child learns to read?
options: Comparing what two writers say on one subject
Working out new words from the sentences around them
Reading simple books alone
Being able to keep attention and follow directions
optionExplain: Comparing writers is the mark of the last stage, not the first.
Using context to work out words belongs to a middle stage.
Reading simple books independently comes at the end of the second stage.
Right: attention and following directions are part of readiness, which comes before any reading at all.
questions.explain: Before a child reads anything, certain kinds of readiness must be in place. The card next lays out the four stages in order.
questions.rule: Readiness comes before reading.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Put the four stages of learning to read in the order a child passes through them.
items: Reading readiness
Reading very simple materials
Rapid vocabulary growth and use of context
Refining skills and carrying ideas across texts
questions.explain: Readiness comes first, then simple materials, then vocabulary and context, and finally refinement, where ideas carry from one text to another.
questions.rule: Readiness, simple materials, vocabulary and context, refinement.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Maya, nine, reads science and history books for school and for fun, and works out new words from the sentences around them. She does not yet compare different authors on a topic. Which stage best fits her?
options: The first stage
The second stage
The third stage
The fourth stage
optionExplain: She is well past readiness; she is reading widely.
She has gone beyond very simple materials and sight words.
Right: vocabulary growth, using context, and reading in several subject areas for different purposes mark the third stage.
Comparing writers on one subject is the sign of the fourth stage, which she has not reached.
questions.explain: Using context clues and reading across subjects for school and pleasure belong to the third stage. The missing comparison of writers shows she is not yet in the fourth.
questions.hint: What can she not yet do?
questions.rule: Place the learner by the highest stage fully shown.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Which signs show that a reader has reached the fourth stage rather than the third? Select all that apply.
options: She compares how two writers treat the same subject
She uses an idea met in one article to understand another
She works out an unfamiliar word from the sentences around it
She reads on her own for fun, outside of any school assignment
She knows several hundred sight words and reads simple books
optionExplain: Right: comparing the views of different writers on one subject marks the fourth stage.
Right: carrying concepts from one piece of writing to another is the heart of the fourth stage.
Using context to unlock words is the skill of the third stage.
Discovering that reading can be done for fun belongs to the third stage.
Sight words and simple books belong to the second stage.
questions.explain: The fourth stage is marked by assimilating reading: carrying concepts across texts and comparing writers. Context clues and reading for pleasure come earlier.
questions.rule: Stage four connects texts; stage three unlocks words.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a fourteen-year-old who has reached the fourth stage has finished growing as a reader.
questions.explain: The fourth stage should be reached in the early teens, but the authors say readers should keep building on it for the rest of their lives. It is the end of elementary reading, not of growth.
questions.rule: The last stage is a base to build on, not a finish line.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: A literacy charity finds that many fifteen-year-olds in one town did not reach the fourth stage. Which explanations fit the causes the authors list? Select all that apply.
options: Economic or social deprivation at home
Parents who cannot read
Personal problems, such as revolt against the system
Starting reading lessons a few months after their classmates
Reading too often for fun
optionExplain: Right: the authors name economic, social and intellectual deprivation in the home.
Right: parental illiteracy is one form of intellectual deprivation they name.
Right: personal problems of all kinds, including total revolt against the system, are on their list.
The authors say a somewhat late start is not nearly so serious; it is starting too early that harms.
Reading for fun is a healthy sign of the third stage, not a cause of failure.
questions.explain: The authors list causes ranging from deprivation at home, economic, social or intellectual, including parental illiteracy, to personal problems. A slightly late start or reading for fun is not among them.
questions.rule: Failure to reach mature reading has many causes, at home and in the person.
questions.teaches: The authors list the causes of failing to reach the fourth stage as ranging from deprivation at home, economic, social or intellectual (including parental illiteracy), to personal problems such as revolt against the system.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Which is usually the bigger mistake when teaching a young child to read?
options: Starting lessons before the child is ready
Starting lessons a few months after the child is ready
Using picture books in the first lessons
Reading aloud to the child at bedtime
optionExplain: Right: starting too early tends to frustrate the child and can leave a lasting dislike of reading.
A somewhat late start is far less serious, though parents often worry about it.
Picture books are not a mistake in the authors' account.
Reading aloud at home is not a mistake in the authors' account.
questions.explain: Rushing a child who is not ready usually defeats itself. The card next explains what readiness involves.
questions.rule: Rushing is worse than waiting.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Match each kind of reading readiness with what it involves.
pairs: Taking in and remembering a whole word and its letters
Speaking clearly and ordering several sentences
Working with others, keeping attention, following directions
questions.explain: Readiness has four sides: the body, visual perception and memory, spoken language, and the personal habits needed to learn in a group.
questions.rule: Physical, intellectual, language, personal.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: A four-year-old speaks well in full sentences, cooperates well in groups and follows directions, but a check-up shows she cannot hear well. Which kind of readiness is missing?
options: Language readiness
Personal readiness
Intellectual readiness
Physical readiness
optionExplain: She speaks well in full sentences, which is the core of language readiness.
Cooperating and following directions show personal readiness is present.
Intellectual readiness concerns perceiving and remembering words, which the case does not question.
Right: good hearing is part of physical readiness.
questions.explain: Hearing and vision belong to physical readiness. The other three sides are present in this child.
questions.rule: Name the missing side of readiness before deciding to wait.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: A parent reasons: (1) my son's friends have started reading lessons; (2) he must keep up; (3) so he should start now, though his teacher says he is not ready; (4) any frustration will pass. Which steps go against the authors' advice?
options: Step 1 alone, because noticing what friends do is a factual mistake
Steps 3 and 4: starting before he is ready, expecting the upset to pass
None of them, since keeping pace with his peers is what matters most
Step 4 alone, because the frustration does pass, only more slowly
optionExplain: Noticing what friends do is not itself an error; acting on it against readiness is.
Right: starting an unready child is self-defeating, and the frustration can last into adult life.
The authors say a late start is far less serious than parents fear; keeping up is not the goal.
The authors warn the dislike may carry on into later schooling and adulthood, not that it passes.
questions.explain: The error is to override readiness for the sake of keeping up, and to assume the frustration is harmless. The authors warn it can last for years.
questions.rule: Readiness, not the peer group, sets the start.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, if a child ready at five and a half waits until seven to begin lessons, the harm is far less serious than if an unready child starts early.
questions.explain: Delaying beyond the readiness stage is not nearly so serious as jumping the gun, despite parents' fears that the child will fall behind. The limit is that a ready child should begin; waiting is the safer error, not a goal.
questions.rule: A late start costs less than an early one.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: A swimming school must decide when each four-year-old starts lessons. Following the way readiness for reading is judged, which approach fits best?
options: Start every child on the same birthday, so the class moves together
Wait until each child asks to start, so the wish comes from the child
Combine a short readiness test with the instructor's own judgement
Start each child as early as possible, so that they get ahead
optionExplain: A fixed age ignores the fact that readiness belongs to the child.
Waiting for the child to ask leaves the judgement to chance rather than to tests or a skilled teacher.
Right: reading readiness is assessed by tests and also estimated by teachers, who are often skilled at seeing when a pupil is ready.
Starting early is the jumping-the-gun error the authors warn against.
questions.explain: Reading readiness is judged two ways: by formal tests and by teachers' estimates. The same pairing suits any skill where starting too early backfires.
questions.rule: Judge readiness by tests and by a skilled teacher's eye.
questions.teaches: General reading readiness is assessed by tests and also estimated by teachers, who the authors say are often skilful at telling when a pupil is ready to learn to read.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Roughly how many words does a typical American child learn to read by the end of the first year of reading instruction?
options: About 30 to 40
About 300 to 400
About 3,000 to 4,000
optionExplain: Thirty or forty words is too few; children pass this number within weeks of starting.
Right: the authors give three hundred to four hundred words by the end of the first year.
Thousands of words belong to a much later point, after the rapid vocabulary growth of the third stage.
Ten thousand or more is far beyond a first-year reader.
questions.explain: A first-year reader typically masters a few hundred words. The card next shows what else happens in this second stage.
questions.rule: Stage two: a few hundred words, simple books.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: True or false: By the end of the second stage, pupils are expected to read simple books independently and with enthusiasm.
questions.explain: Independent, enthusiastic reading of simple books is the goal of the second stage. It comes after learning sight words and basic skills such as context clues and beginning sounds.
questions.rule: Stage two ends with simple books read alone and gladly.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: A first-grade teacher plans lessons for children in the second stage. Which activities belong there? Select all that apply.
options: Learning a set of common sight words
Noticing the beginning sound of a word
Guessing a word from the picture and the story
Comparing two authors' views on keeping pets
Studying how historians disagree about a war
optionExplain: Right: the stage usually begins with a few sight words.
Right: beginning sounds of words are one of the basic skills introduced.
Right: using context or meaning clues is another basic skill of this stage.
Comparing writers on one subject is the mark of the fourth stage.
Comparing historians belongs to the fourth stage, far beyond simple materials.
questions.explain: Sight words, beginning sounds and meaning clues are the tools of the second stage. Comparing writers comes two stages later.
questions.rule: Stage two tools: sight words, beginning sounds, meaning clues.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: A French child reads Le chat s'asseyait sur le chapeau and an English child reads The cat sat on the hat. What puzzle do the authors draw from this pair?
options: French is a harder language to learn to read than English is
Sight words cannot work in a language spelled like French
Some meaning is lost whenever a sentence is translated
Where meaning comes from, if different marks carry one sense
optionExplain: The authors make no comparison of difficulty between the languages.
Nothing in the example concerns teaching methods.
The point is the reverse: both children find the same meaning.
Right: if different marks carry the same meaning, the meaning cannot simply be in the marks, which deepens the mystery.
questions.explain: Two children, two sets of symbols, one meaning. The authors use this to sharpen the question of where meaning comes from.
questions.rule: Different symbols, same meaning: the mystery of reading.
questions.teaches: The authors point out that a French child finds the same meaning in entirely different symbols, which sharpens the question of where meaning comes from.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: A mother sees her six-year-old stare blankly at a page one week and read The cat sat on the hat a few weeks later. She asks how this happens. According to the authors, what is the honest answer?
options: No one really knows, though thinkers have studied it for ages
Psychologists have fully explained it through careful research
It comes from memorizing letter names, one by one, until done
It is the work of the phonic method, which builds the meaning
optionExplain: Right: the authors say no one really knows how a child discovers meaning in symbols, despite the efforts of philosophers and psychologists over two and a half millennia.
The authors say the opposite: the change remains unexplained.
Memorizing letter names was the ABC method; the authors do not say it explains the discovery of meaning.
The authors credit no teaching method with explaining how meaning is discovered.
questions.explain: The authors call the child's discovery of meaning in symbols almost magical, and say that no one really knows how it happens, though philosophers and psychologists have studied it for some two and a half thousand years.
questions.rule: We can describe the discovery of meaning, but not yet explain it.
questions.teaches: According to the authors, how a child comes to find meaning in symbols is still unexplained, although philosophers and psychologists have studied it for two and a half millennia.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: True or false: A child who reads simple books on her own with enthusiasm has mastered elementary reading.
questions.explain: That is the goal of the second stage only. Rapid vocabulary growth with context clues, and then the assimilation of the fourth stage, are still to come before elementary reading is mastered.
questions.rule: Stage two is a milestone, not the end of the first level.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: You meet an unknown word while reading, with no dictionary at hand. What is usually the most useful first move?
options: Skip the paragraph, since one word rarely matters much
Sound the word out, then carry on reading past it
Stop reading until you can look the word up
Work out its meaning from the sentences around it
optionExplain: Skipping loses the passage and the word together.
Sounding a word out may tell you how to say it, but not what it means.
Stopping breaks the reading, and the passage may already hold the answer.
Right: the surrounding words often suggest what the unknown word must mean.
questions.explain: The passage around a word is often the best clue to its meaning. The card next shows when readers learn to do this.
questions.rule: Look around a word before looking it up.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: True or false: In the third stage, children discover that reading can be something they do on their own, for fun or to satisfy curiosity, not only at school.
questions.explain: Along with vocabulary growth and context clues, the third stage brings reading for different purposes and in different subjects, including for pleasure and curiosity.
questions.rule: Stage three: more words, more purposes.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: The new manager was so parsimonious that she refused to buy pens and reused old envelopes. What does the context suggest parsimonious means?
options: Generous with gifts to her staff
Very careful not to spend money
Disorganized and forgetful at work
Strict about following office rules
optionExplain: Refusing to buy pens is the opposite of generosity.
Right: refusing small purchases and reusing envelopes point to someone who avoids spending.
Reusing envelopes shows care, not disorder.
Nothing in the sentence concerns rules; both details are about spending.
questions.explain: Both details in the sentence describe avoiding expense, so the context points to a meaning like stingy or very frugal.
questions.hint: What do the two details have in common?
questions.rule: Find what the surrounding details have in common.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Suppose the sentence had read only: The new manager was parsimonious. What changes for a reader who does not know the word?
options: Little: the word can still be worked out from the sentence
The word must now mean strict, as managers often are
The sentence becomes easier, with fewer distractions
There is too little context, so any guess needs checking
optionExplain: Without the details about pens and envelopes, nothing in the sentence points to a meaning.
There is no evidence for strict either; any meaning fits a bare sentence.
Fewer words here means fewer clues, not an easier task.
Right: context clues work only when the passage supplies them; here a dictionary or more reading is needed.
questions.explain: Remove the details and the clues go with them. Context can unlock a word only when the passage gives enough to go on.
questions.rule: No clues in the context, no unlocking from context.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Reading street signs, picture captions and a simple government form with ease needs ordinary vocabulary and some use of context, but no comparing of writers. Which stage's skill does it most likely need?
options: The third stage
The first stage
The second stage only
The fourth stage
optionExplain: Right: these everyday tasks need a working vocabulary and the use of context, the skills of the third stage; the authors report this is called functional literacy.
The first stage is readiness, before reading begins.
Second-stage readers manage very simple books; forms and signs ask for a wider vocabulary.
Nothing here requires carrying ideas across texts or comparing writers.
questions.explain: Everyday reading of signs, captions and simple forms rests on vocabulary and context. The authors report that this third-stage level, usually reached by about the end of fourth grade, is called functional literacy.
questions.rule: Everyday reading needs third-stage skill.
questions.teaches: Third-stage skill, typically reached by about the end of fourth grade, gives what is called functional literacy: by one common definition, the ability to read traffic signs or picture captions fairly easily and to fill out simpler government forms.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Which tasks go beyond what context clues alone can do? Select all that apply.
options: Comparing two historians' accounts of the same war
Pinning down the exact meaning of a contract term when several meanings fit the passage
Working out that a drought is a long dry spell from a description of cracked earth
Guessing that a word means stingy from a description of penny-pinching
optionExplain: Right: comparing writers is the work of the fourth stage, not of unlocking words.
Right: when the context fits several meanings, it cannot settle which one is meant; the guess needs checking.
This is the very kind of case context clues handle well.
The details point to one meaning, so context does the job here.
questions.explain: Context unlocks a word when the passage points to one meaning. It cannot choose among meanings the passage leaves open, and it does not compare whole texts.
questions.rule: Context unlocks words; it does not settle every meaning or compare texts.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: True or false: Comparing what two writers say on the same subject is a skill most children have by the age of seven.
questions.explain: At seven most children are still learning to read simple materials. Comparing writers comes much later; the card next shows when.
questions.rule: Comparing writers is a late skill.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: In the fourth stage the reader begins to ____ reading experiences, carrying concepts from one piece of writing to another.
questions.explain: To assimilate reading experiences is to carry concepts across texts and to compare different writers on the same subject.
questions.rule: Stage four: assimilate what you read.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: After reading two articles on sleep, Sam notices that one says naps help memory and the other says naps harm night sleep, and he works out where they differ. What is Sam doing?
options: Unlocking unfamiliar words through the context around them
Reading for fun, the discovery made in the third stage
Mastering the sight words of the second stage of reading
Comparing the views of different writers on one subject
optionExplain: Sam is not puzzling over a word; he is weighing two claims.
He may enjoy it, but the skill shown is comparison, not pleasure reading.
Sight words belong to the second stage.
Right: comparing writers on the same subject is the mark of the fourth stage.
questions.explain: Setting two writers side by side on one subject is assimilation, the fourth-stage skill.
questions.rule: Two writers, one subject, compared: stage four.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Which reader shows the fourth stage rather than only the third?
options: Ravi reads widely for fun in science, history and geography
Lena uses an idea from her biology text to grasp a news story
Omar works out hard words from the sentences around them
Ines knows four hundred sight words and reads simple books
optionExplain: Reading widely for pleasure and in several subjects is a third-stage discovery.
Right: carrying a concept from one piece of writing to another is assimilation.
Unlocking words through context is the third-stage skill.
Sight words and simple books belong to the second stage.
questions.explain: Only Lena carries a concept from one text into another. The other readers show earlier stages.
questions.rule: Stage four links texts; earlier stages read them one at a time.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reader who reached the fourth stage at fourteen and then stopped reading after school would fall short of the ideal they describe.
questions.explain: The authors say young people should reach the mature stage in their early teens and, ideally, keep building on it for the rest of their lives. Stopping leaves the ideal unmet.
questions.rule: The fourth stage is a foundation to keep building on.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: A journalist must become well informed on an unfamiliar subject by researching many books on her own. According to the authors, which reading skill does independent research like this call for?
options: Fourth-stage comparison, which is enough for any research
Syntopical reading, which a college degree ought to give
Remedial reading, since the subject is new and unfamiliar
Fast skimming of one good book, which covers the subject
optionExplain: Comparing writers at the fourth stage is still elementary reading; research across many books asks for a higher level.
Right: the authors say syntopical reading, among other things, enables independent research on almost any subject, and that a college degree ought to represent that competence.
Remedial reading repairs missing elementary skill; a new subject does not mean she lacks that skill.
One book cannot stand in for a subject researched across many books.
questions.explain: Fourth-stage readers compare writers. Independent research on almost any subject is, for the authors, one of the things syntopical reading makes possible, and they think a college degree should stand for it.
questions.rule: Comparing texts is elementary; independent research needs syntopical reading.
questions.teaches: According to the authors, syntopical reading, among other things, enables a reader to undertake independent research on almost any subject, and a college degree ought to represent this level of competence.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: True or false: Heavy emphasis on teaching young children the basics of reading can have the side effect of neglecting more advanced reading skills.
questions.explain: Effort spent on one level can leave the others slighted. The card next shows how the authors apply this to American schooling.
questions.rule: Focus on the basics can crowd out the rest.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: According to the authors, which seldom-noticed cause contributes to the failure to read well?
options: Too much reading for pleasure, which crowds out reading for school
So much focus on the early stages that higher levels were slighted
Dropping phonics from the curriculum in favour of whole words
Starting reading lessons too late, after the readiness stage
optionExplain: Reading for pleasure is a healthy third-stage discovery, not a cause of failure.
Right: the very emphasis on the first level has meant that the higher levels tended to be neglected.
The authors say phonics never entirely left the curriculum.
The authors say a late start is far less serious than an early one.
questions.explain: The authors say the emphasis on reading readiness and on methods for teaching the rudiments has led to the higher levels being slighted.
questions.rule: Attention to the first level has cost the higher levels.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: A company trains new staff hard in spelling and punctuation and not at all in following a long argument. By the authors' reasoning, what should it expect?
options: Staff who handle every kind of document well, since the basics carry over
Staff whose spelling slowly declines once the training ends
Staff who read long reports faster, since speed follows the basics
Staff who write correct sentences but struggle with long arguments
optionExplain: Training at one level does not give skill at the higher ones.
Nothing suggests the basics would decline; they were trained.
Sound basics may help speed, but speed does not give the skill to follow a long argument, which was never trained.
Right: work on the basics alone leaves the higher skills untrained.
questions.explain: Skill at the lowest level does not carry upward by itself. To cure the deficiency, effort is needed at every level.
questions.rule: Train every level you need, not only the bottom one.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: True or false: The authors conclude that schools should spend less effort on teaching the rudiments of reading.
questions.explain: The authors find the focus on the first level understandable, given how urgent its problems are. Their point is that the higher levels must be worked on as well, not that the first should get less.
questions.rule: Add the higher levels; do not drop the first.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: An education minister reasons in four steps. Which steps go against the authors' view? Select all that apply.
options: Step 1: first-level reading problems are urgent and widespread
Step 2: so all of the reading funds go to the first level
Step 3: once every child reads at level one, the problem is solved
Step 4: early reading instruction remains essential for every child
optionExplain: The authors agree: the first-level problems are urgent and extensive.
Right: putting everything into the first level is how the higher levels come to be slighted.
Right: the authors say the deficiencies cannot be cured without efforts on all levels.
The authors agree that the first task is to teach elementary reading.
questions.explain: Steps 1 and 4 match the authors. Steps 2 and 3 leave out the higher levels, which they say any real remedy must include.
questions.rule: Necessary is not sufficient: the first level is not the whole cure.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: A state decides its colleges should teach reading beyond the elementary level. Given how the higher levels have been slighted, what obstacle should it expect, according to the authors?
options: Most colleges lack the know-how, facilities or staff to teach it
Students no longer need reading help once they reach college
Higher reading is a talent, picked up alone rather than taught
Colleges already teach it widely, so the plan duplicates them
optionExplain: Right: the authors say most institutions of higher learning either do not know how to teach reading beyond the elementary level or lack the facilities and personnel to do so.
Many entering students need remedial help even at the elementary level, so the need is real.
The authors think courses in the higher levels could be set up; these levels can be taught.
The authors say instruction beyond the elementary level is offered in almost no colleges.
questions.explain: Because effort has gone into the first level, the skill to teach the higher levels is scarce. The authors say most colleges either do not know how to teach reading beyond the elementary level or lack the facilities and staff.
questions.rule: Neglect of the higher levels leaves few who can teach them.
questions.teaches: The authors say that most institutions of higher learning either do not know how to teach reading beyond the elementary level or lack the facilities and personnel to do so.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: True or false: The four stages of learning to read are the same thing as the four levels of reading that the book describes.
questions.explain: The stages and the levels are different things, though both come in fours. The card next shows how they fit together.
questions.rule: Four stages, four levels: not the same four.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Match each stage of elementary reading with the school years it typically corresponds to.
pairs: Vocabulary growth and use of context
About the end of fourth grade
Leaving elementary or junior high school
questions.explain: The stages follow the elementary curriculum: readiness before school, word mastery in first grade, context skills by the end of fourth grade, and the fourth stage at the end of elementary or junior high school.
questions.rule: The stages track the elementary school years.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Sort each item: is it a stage of elementary reading, or one of the higher levels of reading?

items.t: Reading readiness
Word mastery
Vocabulary growth and use of context
Carrying concepts across texts as a young teen
Inspectional reading
Analytical reading
Syntopical reading

questions.explain: All four stages of learning to read are stages of the first level. Inspectional, analytical and syntopical reading are the levels above it.
questions.rule: Every stage sits inside level one.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: A ten-year-old at the end of fourth grade reads street signs, picture captions and simple forms with ease. Which label fits her in the authors' account?
options: First grade literacy
Functional literacy
Ninth grade literacy
Analytical reading
optionExplain: She is beyond first grade literacy, which ends with simple books.
Right: third-stage skill, typically reached by the end of fourth grade, is called fourth grade or functional literacy.
Ninth grade literacy comes with the fourth stage, around the end of junior high school.
Analytical reading is a higher level, not a stage of elementary reading.
questions.explain: Vocabulary growth and use of context, reached at about the end of fourth grade, give fourth grade or functional literacy.
questions.rule: End of fourth grade: functional literacy.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: A healthy, normal child reaches word mastery only during second grade, a year later than the typical child. What do the authors' remarks suggest?
options: Something must be wrong, since the stages are tied to fixed grades
The child must have skipped part of the first stage of readiness
Grades fit the typical child, and many normal children differ
The child should repeat kindergarten to rebuild reading readiness
