optionExplain: The authors say many quite normal children are not typical in this sense, so a later date is no proof of a problem.
Reaching a stage late is no sign of a skipped stage; the order is the same.
Right: the grades give the typical timing, not a rule every normal child must meet.
Nothing suggests going back; the child is moving through the stages in order.
questions.explain: The authors stress that the match between stages and grades fits the typical child, and that many normal children do not fit it exactly.
questions.rule: Grades are typical timing, not deadlines.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: A language school says a learner who has finished its four elementary courses is ready for its intermediate course. Applying the authors' grade match to reading, what is a pupil who has finished all four stages ready for?
options: Analytical reading of any book, with no further training
Fourth grade work, since vocabulary growth ends there
Remedial reading courses of the kind colleges now offer
High school work, though still reading in a simple way
optionExplain: Analytical reading is a higher level that still has to be learned after the four stages.
The third stage is typically reached by the end of fourth grade; the fourth stage comes later, around leaving elementary or junior high school.
Remedial courses are for students who did not complete the stages; this pupil has.
Right: the authors say such a pupil is, in the simplest terms, mature enough to do high school work, though he reads in a relatively unsophisticated way.
questions.explain: The fourth stage is reached about the time a pupil leaves elementary or junior high school, so it prepares him for the next step in school: high school work.
questions.rule: Four stages done: ready for high school work, not yet for higher reading.
questions.teaches: The authors say that a pupil who completes the fourth stage is, in the simplest terms, mature enough to do high school work.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: A fifteen-year-old can read almost anything put in front of him, though in a fairly unsophisticated way. Is he a mature reader?
options: Yes, in every sense, since he can read almost anything
No, since he is still at the second stage of learning
In one sense yes; in the authors' fuller sense, not yet
No, because a mature reader is one who reads very fast
optionExplain: Reading almost anything in an unsophisticated way leaves something still to learn.
Reading almost anything is far beyond the simple books of the second stage.
Right: he has mastered elementary reading, yet does not know how to read beyond it.
Speed is not what the word mature measures here.
questions.explain: The word mature has two senses here. The card next separates them.
questions.rule: Mature can mean two different things.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: True or false: A pupil who has completed the fourth stage can read almost anything, though in a fairly unsophisticated way.
questions.explain: That is what mature means in the elementary sense: reading almost anything on your own, but without the skill of the higher levels.
questions.rule: Mature elementary reader: almost anything, unsophisticatedly.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: A college student reads her textbooks on her own but cannot say what an author's main argument is or how its parts fit together. In which sense is she a mature reader?
options: In the elementary sense only: she reads alone, not yet beyond it
In the full sense the authors intend, since she reads alone
In neither sense, since she cannot state the main argument
As a competent analytical reader, since she reads textbooks
optionExplain: Right: she has the independence of a mature elementary reader, without the skill of the higher levels.
Mature in the authors' sense means reading beyond the elementary level, which she cannot yet do.
Reading her textbooks alone shows she is mature in the elementary sense.
Not being able to state the main argument shows she is not yet an analytical reader.
questions.explain: Reading on your own is the mark of a mature elementary reader. Grasping an author's argument belongs to the higher levels.
questions.hint: Can she read alone? Can she read beyond the words?
questions.rule: Reading alone is not yet reading well.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: A reader who is mature only in the elementary sense picks up a closely argued book on economics. What does the authors' account lead you to expect? Select all that apply.
options: He can read the sentences on his own, without a teacher
He can follow the text, but in a fairly unsophisticated way
He can say what the book argues and judge whether it is sound
He can relate it to other books and build his own analysis
optionExplain: Right: a mature elementary reader can read on his own.
Right: he can read almost anything, but in a relatively unsophisticated manner.
Grasping and judging an argument belongs to the higher levels, which he has not yet learned.
Relating many books and building an analysis is the highest level, far beyond elementary maturity.
questions.explain: Elementary maturity gives independent reading of almost anything, in an unsophisticated way. Stating and judging the argument, or relating it to other books, needs the higher levels.
questions.rule: Elementary maturity reads the words alone; it does not yet read the argument.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: A carpentry manual starts with joints and takes for granted that readers can measure and saw. What parallel assumption do the authors make about their own readers?
options: That readers can already read analytically, so rules are a refresher
That readers have about ninth grade literacy, past all four stages
Only that readers can recognize letters, since it starts from scratch
That readers have taken a speed reading course before starting
optionExplain: The book exists to teach analytical reading, so it cannot assume its readers already have it.
Right: the authors assume ninth grade literacy, and say they could not assume less, since no one can learn from a how-to-do-it book until he can read it.
Letter recognition is far too little: the authors say they could not assume less than mastery of all four stages.
The authors make no such assumption; they regard most speed courses as remedial.
questions.explain: Any how-to book assumes the skills needed to use it. The authors assume their readers have passed all four elementary stages, about ninth grade literacy, because a book on reading must be readable by its readers.
questions.rule: A book that teaches reading must assume its readers can already read.
questions.teaches: The authors assume their readers have about ninth grade literacy, having passed all four stages; they could not assume less, because no one can learn from a how-to-do-it book until he can read it.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reader who is mature only in the elementary sense has achieved little of value.
questions.explain: Such a reader can read on his own and is prepared to learn more about reading. The authors build their whole book on this base; the distinction marks what is still to come, not that the base is worthless.
questions.rule: The first level is the foundation, not a failure.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Who usually helps a child through the early stages of learning to read?
options: Mostly themselves, by working out the words alone at home
Living teachers, who answer questions and ease difficulties
The authors of their books, through clear and simple writing
Classmates mainly, who explain new words to one another
optionExplain: Some children need less help than others, but a teacher is usually present.
Right: the four stages are typically attained with the help of living teachers.
Authors are absent; they cannot answer a child's questions.
Classmates may help, but the authors stress the teacher's role.
questions.explain: Elementary reading is usually learned with a teacher at hand. The card next shows what changes once the four stages are mastered.
questions.rule: Elementary reading is learned with help.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a child is prepared to move on to the higher levels of reading only after mastering all four stages of elementary reading.
questions.explain: Only after all four stages are mastered can the child read independently, learn on his own and move on to the higher levels.
questions.rule: All four stages first, then the higher levels.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: A twelve-year-old still needs a teacher's help with many words and cannot get through a simple magazine article alone. What do the authors' views suggest?
options: Start her on the rules of analytical reading, to stretch her
Withdraw all help at once, so she is forced to read alone
Treat her as ready for higher levels, since age is what counts
Keep helping her through the elementary stages for now
optionExplain: Higher levels presuppose that she can already read on her own.
Independence comes from mastering the stages, not from removing help before they are mastered.
Readiness for higher levels depends on mastery, not on age.
Right: she has not yet mastered the elementary stages, so help should continue until she can read alone.
questions.explain: Independent reading is the result of mastering the four stages, usually with a teacher's help. Until then the higher levels must wait.
questions.rule: Mastery, not age, opens the higher levels.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: Sort each situation: is it aided discovery or unaided discovery?
groups: Aided: a teacher is at hand

items.t: A teacher explains a hard word during class
A tutor smooths over a difficulty in a reading lesson
A child asks the teacher what a sentence means
An adult reads a philosophy book with no one to ask
A researcher works through papers on her own
A retiree studies a history book alone at home

questions.explain: Elementary reading is usually learned with a teacher present to answer questions. Reading beyond it is mostly done alone, where the learner must find the answers himself.
questions.rule: Elementary reading is aided; higher reading is mostly unaided.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: A violin student finishes all the beginner grades with a teacher and can now practise well on her own. By analogy with the authors' account of reading, what has she reached?
options: Full mastery, since the beginner grades cover the whole instrument
A point where she should repeat the beginner grades with help
The point where she can begin to become a really good player
A level of skill that will not need to grow any further
optionExplain: Beginner grades are a foundation; like the elementary stages, they do not cover everything.
She has mastered the basics and can work alone, so repeating them would hold her back.
Right: the authors say only after mastering the four stages can a reader begin to become a really good reader.
The authors want readers to keep building for life; mastery of the basics is a start.
questions.explain: Mastering the elementary stages lets a reader work independently, and only then can real growth as a reader begin. The violinist is at the same point: the start of becoming good, not its end.
questions.rule: Mastering the basics is where becoming good begins.
questions.teaches: According to the authors, only after mastering all four elementary stages can a reader begin to become a really good reader: mastery is where good reading starts, not where it ends.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, every child needs about the same amount of a teacher's help to pass through the four stages.
questions.explain: Children differ in their abilities, and some need more help than others. A teacher is usually there to answer questions and smooth over difficulties, as much as each child needs.
questions.rule: Children differ in how much help they need.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.section: Higher Levels of Reading and Higher Education
questions.q: True or false: A college course that helps freshmen catch up on basic reading skills is teaching the higher levels of reading.
questions.explain: Catching up on basic skills repairs the first level; it does not go beyond it. The card next draws this line.
questions.rule: Catching up is not moving up.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.section: Higher Levels of Reading and Higher Education
questions.q: According to the authors, remedial reading brings students up to the maturity in reading they should have reached by the end of ____ school.
questions.explain: Remedial reading only restores what elementary school should have given: mature elementary reading. It does not teach the higher levels.
questions.rule: Remedial reading restores the first level.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.section: Higher Levels of Reading and Higher Education
questions.q: A university advertises a course that raises freshmen's reading speed and basic comprehension until they can cope with their textbooks. How would the authors most likely classify it?
options: Training in analytical reading, since it uses textbooks
Remedial, as most such courses are, with some exceptions
Training in syntopical reading, since it covers many subjects
Graduate-level instruction, since it is taught at a university
optionExplain: Coping with textbooks is mature elementary reading, not analysis of a whole book.
Right: bringing students up to the level they should have had on leaving elementary school is remedial work.
Nothing in the course involves relating many books to a subject.
Its goal is the level that elementary school should have reached.
questions.explain: A course that brings students to where elementary school should have left them is remedial. The authors grant that a few such courses are exceptions.
questions.hint: Where does the course take students: to the first level, or beyond it?
questions.rule: Judge a course by where it leaves the student.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.section: Higher Levels of Reading and Higher Education
questions.q: Which courses would count as instruction beyond the first level, by the authors' standard? Select all that apply.
options: A course in reading a whole book thoroughly and analytically
A course in relating many books on a subject to build an analysis
A course that fixes slow word recognition, raising reading speed
A course that lifts students to eighth grade reading level
optionExplain: Right: analytical reading is one of the higher levels the authors want high schools to teach.
Right: syntopical reading is the level the authors want colleges to produce.
Word recognition is a first-level skill; fixing it is remedial.
Eighth grade literacy is the end of elementary reading, not beyond it.
questions.explain: Higher instruction aims at analytical and syntopical reading. Repairing word recognition or reaching eighth grade literacy stays within the first level.
questions.rule: Higher reading means analytical and syntopical reading.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.section: Higher Levels of Reading and Higher Education
questions.q: Suppose every student entering a college already reads at the mature elementary level. By the authors' standard, what should a good college then produce?
options: Students who read much faster, through speed reading training
Students who have gone over elementary reading once more
Competent syntopical readers, able to research on their own
Competent analytical readers, which is the most a college can do
optionExplain: Speed alone is the aim of many remedial courses, not of higher reading.
These students have already mastered elementary reading; repeating it is the remedial work they no longer need.
Right: the authors say a good college, if it does nothing else, ought to produce competent syntopical readers.
Analytical competence is the goal the authors set for a good high school; a good college should go further, to syntopical reading.
questions.explain: With remedial needs removed, the college is free to do its proper job: produce syntopical readers who can read any general material and research almost any subject.
questions.rule: A good college should produce syntopical readers.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.section: Higher Levels of Reading and Higher Education
questions.q: A firm finds that new engineers need four more years of on-the-job training before they can read technical specifications well, after sixteen years of schooling. What would the authors say about the parallel case in reading?
options: That is a normal time to learn to read at a high level
Reading at that level is a gift that schooling cannot give
Only graduate school has the means to teach such reading
Twenty years is far too long, and the fault can be fixed
optionExplain: The authors say the opposite: it should not take that long.
The authors propose courses in high schools and colleges, so they think it can be taught.
They object that students should not need graduate school to learn to read.
Right: the authors count twenty years of schooling, call it far too long, and say courses based on their largely common-sense program could fix it.
questions.explain: Twelve years of school, four of college and four of graduate school make twenty years. The authors say it should not take that long and that the fault can be corrected with courses based on their program.
questions.rule: If learning to read takes twenty years, the teaching has failed.
questions.teaches: The authors note that students often reach syntopical competence only after three or four years of graduate study, twenty years of schooling in all, and say this is wrong and correctable with courses based on their largely common-sense program.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.section: Reading and the Democratic Ideal of Education
questions.q: Which goal for a nation's reading do you think the authors set?
options: Functional literacy for everyone, which is enough
High reading skill for a small elite of good readers
Truly competent readers, on a base of literacy for all
Faster reading for every adult, to cope with more print
optionExplain: The authors want more than a nation of functional literates.
The authors support educational opportunity for everyone, not a select few.
Right: they want basic literacy for all first, and then truly competent readers.
Speed is not their goal; competence is.
questions.explain: The authors want both breadth and depth: basic reading for everyone, and competent reading beyond it. The card next shows how they hold the two together.
questions.rule: Basics for all, competence as the goal.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.section: Reading and the Democratic Ideal of Education
questions.q: True or false: The authors hold that, with large numbers of new students who read poorly, the first task is to teach them elementary reading.
questions.explain: As long as many new students cannot read well at the elementary level, the first task must be to teach them reading in its lowest, largest-common-denominator sense.
questions.rule: First things first: elementary reading.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.section: Reading and the Democratic Ideal of Education
questions.q: A city library can fund one new program this year, and many local adults cannot read street signs. Following the authors, which plan fits best?
options: A seminar on comparing great books for its best readers
Basic literacy classes now, as a first step, not the whole task
No program, since competent reading cannot be reached quickly
A speed reading course for everyone, to cover more ground
optionExplain: Higher reading matters, but the authors say the first task is the basics for those who lack them.
Right: the basics come first, while the goal of competent reading stays in view.
The authors keep the goal of competent reading in view; that it takes time is no reason to do nothing now.
Speed does not help adults who cannot yet read signs.
questions.explain: The authors put elementary reading first for those who lack it, but insist that it is not the whole task.
questions.rule: Start with the basics; keep the higher goal in view.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.section: Reading and the Democratic Ideal of Education
questions.q: Sort each skill: does it belong to functional literacy, or to the truly competent reading the authors call for?

items.t: Reading a traffic sign easily
Filling out a simple government form
Reading a picture caption
Analysing a whole book thoroughly
Relating many books to build your own analysis
Undertaking independent research on a subject

questions.explain: Functional literacy covers everyday reading of signs, captions and forms. Competent reading, as the authors use it, means the higher levels: analytical and syntopical reading.
questions.rule: Functional literacy is a floor, not the goal.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.section: Reading and the Democratic Ideal of Education
questions.q: A city aims to give every resident health care limited only by need, but does not yet know how to pay for it. Following the authors' reasoning about education, what should it do?
options: Drop the goal until someone shows exactly how to fund it
Limit care to those who already manage well on their own
Keep pursuing it: not knowing how is no reason to give up
Offer only the most basic care and call the task complete
optionExplain: The authors reject giving up an ideal because the way to reach it is not yet known.
The authors back opportunity for all, not only for those who already do well.
Right: the authors say that not yet knowing how to provide unlimited educational opportunity is no reason to give up the attempt.
The authors insist that the basic task, once done, is not the whole task.
questions.explain: The authors hold unlimited educational opportunity to be society's most valuable service, and say that not knowing how to provide it yet is no reason to give up. The same reasoning fits any ideal not yet within reach.
questions.rule: An ideal not yet reachable is still worth pursuing.
questions.teaches: The authors say that not yet knowing how to provide unlimited educational opportunity is no reason to give up the attempt.

questions.unitTitle: The First Level of Reading: Elementary Reading
questions.section: Reading and the Democratic Ideal of Education
questions.q: True or false: The authors' call for truly competent readers implies that higher education should be limited to students who already read well.
questions.explain: The authors back educational opportunity limited only by individual desire, ability and need, and accept that the first task is to teach the basics to those who lack them. Their call is to go further, not to shut anyone out.
questions.rule: Raise the goal without closing the door.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: The levels of reading are described as cumulative. Which statement fits that description?
options: Each level replaces the one below, which you can then forget
The levels are separate skills, each used for different books
Each higher level contains the skills of the levels below it
Each higher level is a faster version of the one below it
optionExplain: Moving up feels like leaving the old skill behind, but a cumulative series keeps every earlier skill in use.
Different books do call for different readings, but cumulative means the levels build on one another rather than standing apart.
Right: cumulative means each level includes the ones before it, so higher reading still uses the lower skills.
Speed changes between levels, but what makes them cumulative is that each contains the ones below, not that each is quicker.
questions.explain: Cumulative means each level builds on and includes the ones before it. The card next shows what that means for inspectional reading.
questions.rule: Each level of reading contains the levels below it.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: The first step of inspectional reading is systematic skimming; the second step is ____ reading.
questions.explain: Inspectional reading pairs systematic skimming (a quick, ordered look) with superficial reading (one straight-through reading that does not stop at difficulties).
questions.rule: Inspection is skimming, then superficial reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: True or false: To read a book inspectionally, you must already be able to make the best possible sense of every sentence in it.
questions.explain: The authors ask only that you make sense of a majority of the sentences and paragraphs, not necessarily the best sense of all of them. Getting the best sense of every sentence is the work of later, closer reading.
questions.rule: Inspection needs steady reading and some sense of most sentences, not perfect sense of all.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: Dana wants to inspect a technical manual written in Portuguese. She reads Portuguese slowly and has to look up a word in most lines. What does the cumulative view of the levels suggest?
options: Skim the manual faster to make up for the slow reading
Work on her Portuguese first, since she cannot yet read the text steadily
Skip skimming and give the manual an analytical reading instead
Read it superficially, since superficial reading passes over the hard words
optionExplain: Speeding up sounds like a fix, but skimming a text you cannot read steadily yields little: the trouble is at the elementary level.
Right: inspectional reading contains elementary reading, so a reader who stops on most lines must build that skill first.
Analytical reading contains inspectional and elementary reading too, so it demands even more of the skill she lacks.
Superficial reading passes over some difficulties, but it assumes most sentences make sense; here most lines stop her.
questions.explain: Because the levels are cumulative, a weakness at the elementary level blocks every level above it. Dana needs to read the language steadily before inspecting a book written in it.
questions.hint: Which level contains which?
questions.rule: Fix elementary reading before trying to inspect.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: Sort each activity into the step of inspectional reading it belongs to.

items.t: Looking over the table of contents
Reading the preface quickly
Sampling a few pages to decide whether to read on
Reading the whole book through once
Reading on past a paragraph you cannot follow
Leaving a puzzling footnote for later

questions.explain: Skimming is the quick, ordered look that decides whether a book deserves more time. Superficial reading is the one complete reading that does not stop at difficulties.
questions.rule: Skimming samples the book; superficial reading goes through all of it.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: A music student can read a score slowly, note by note, and now wants to grasp a piece's overall shape from a quick look. Reasoning by analogy with the levels of reading, what should she expect?
options: The quick overview will replace note reading, which she can then drop
The two skills are unrelated, so she can learn either one first
She should master full analysis of a piece before attempting any quick overview
Her note reading must be steady, and it stays at work inside the new skill
optionExplain: A new skill can feel like a replacement, but in a cumulative series the lower skill stays in use inside the higher one.
They look like separate tricks, but the overview depends on reading the notes, as inspection depends on elementary reading.
This reverses the order: the quick overview is the lower level, and full analysis builds on it.
Right: as with reading, the higher skill contains the lower one, so the lower one must be steady and is never discarded.
questions.explain: In a cumulative series, each higher skill contains the lower ones and needs them working smoothly. The same pattern runs on up through the levels of reading.
questions.rule: Higher skills contain lower ones; build from the bottom.
questions.teaches: The chain continues upward: inspectional reading is itself contained in analytical reading, and analytical reading in syntopical reading, so inspection skills return inside every higher level.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: True or false: A quick skim of a book can be worth the time even if you decide afterwards not to read the book.
questions.explain: A skim leaves you with something even when the answer is no: at least the book's main point and its kind. The card next shows what a skim is for.
questions.rule: A skim pays off whichever way you decide.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: According to the authors, what is the main aim of skimming a book?
options: To memorize the book's most important facts
To judge whether the author's conclusions are right
To get through the whole book faster than usual
To decide whether the book needs a more careful reading
optionExplain: Memorizing facts needs far more time than a skim, and it is not the decision a skim exists to make.
Judging an author comes much later, after the book has been understood; a skim cannot support that verdict.
A skim is fast, but it does not get through the whole book; it samples it to make a decision.
Right: the main aim is to discover whether the book requires a more careful reading.
questions.explain: Skimming is a sorting step. It tells you whether a book deserves a careful reading, and along the way what kind of book it is and what it mainly claims.
questions.rule: Skim to decide how much more time a book deserves.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: Which of these situations call for a skim, in the authors' sense? Select all that apply.
options: A friend lends you a promising book, and you have one evening to decide on it
You are halfway through a careful second reading of a book you already know well
With twenty minutes left in a shop, you wonder which of six histories to buy
You need one phone number from a directory and already know the name to look up
You must pick two of a dozen listed titles for close study this term
optionExplain: Right: you are unsure whether the book deserves careful reading, you suspect it might, and time is limited.
A careful reading is already under way; the decision a skim makes has been made.
Right: an open question about which books deserve your time, and a short time to settle it.
Looking up one known item is not deciding whether a work deserves reading, so it is not skimming in this sense.
Right: skimming the dozen is how you find the two that deserve close study.
questions.explain: Skimming fits when you do not yet know whether a work deserves careful reading and your time is limited. Where that decision is already made, or no reading is involved, a skim has nothing to decide.
questions.hint: In which cases is the question of whether to read carefully still open?
questions.rule: Skim when the worth of a book is an open question and time is short.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: Two years after skimming a book on negotiation and setting it aside, Omar takes a job full of hard bargaining. What should he make of his earlier verdict on the book?
options: It was final: a book set aside after a skim should stay set aside
It held for the time being, and the book may now deserve a careful reading
It was wasted effort, since he must now read the whole book from scratch anyway
It is enough on its own, since the skim already gave him the arguments
optionExplain: A skim's verdict can feel like a final ruling, but it measures the book against your present needs, which can change.
Right: what a skim yields may be all a book is worth to you for the time being; when your needs change, so may its worth.
The skim was not wasted: he already knows the book's kind and main contention, and where it fits.
A skim gives the main contention, not the arguments; careful reading is needed for those.
questions.explain: The authors say a skim may show that a book is worth no more to you for the time being. Omar's new job changes what the book is worth to him, so the old verdict can be reopened.
questions.rule: A skim's verdict is for now, not forever.
questions.teaches: The verdict of a skim is tied to your present purposes: a book worth only a skim today may deserve careful reading when your needs change.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: You come across a 40-episode podcast series on the history of medicine and have an hour to size it up. Applying the idea of skimming, what should you come away with?
options: Detailed notes on the main facts of every single episode
A verdict on whether the series' historians are accurate
The series' main claim, its kind, and whether to keep listening
The first five episodes heard in full, to give the series a fair chance
optionExplain: Full notes on forty episodes would take far longer than an hour, and they answer a different question.
Accuracy is a judgement that needs close study, which the skim helps you decide whether to give.
Right: the same yield as a skimmed book: the main contention, the kind of work, and a decision.
Hearing a few episodes in full spends the hour on one part and tells you little about the whole.
questions.explain: Skimming is defined by its purpose, not by paper. Any long work with parts and a main point can be sized up for its kind, its main contention and whether it deserves more of your time.
questions.rule: Size up any long work for its kind, main point and worth.
questions.teaches: Skimming is not limited to books: the authors speak of a book or other reading matter, and the same sizing-up works for any long work with parts and a main point.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: True or false: Once a skim has shown you an author's main contention, the skim also tells you whether that contention is true.
questions.explain: A skim can show what an author mainly claims, not whether the claim holds. Judging truth needs the careful reading that the skim helps you decide to give.
questions.rule: Skimming shows what is claimed, not whether it is true.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: In a quick look at a book, which part most often reveals the author's particular angle on the subject?
options: The subtitle and the preface
The copyright page
The page numbers of the chapters
The list of acknowledgments
optionExplain: Right: subtitles and prefaces are where authors usually state their scope, aim or angle.
The copyright page gives publishing facts, such as dates, which say little about the author's approach.
Chapter lengths hint at emphasis at most; they do not state an angle.
Acknowledgments name helpers and sometimes sources, but rarely state what the book sets out to do.
questions.explain: Authors tend to announce their approach in the subtitle and preface. The card next shows how the first skimming step uses them.
questions.rule: Look for the author's own statement of aim first.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: In the first skimming step, what should you look for on the title page and in the preface? Select all that apply.
options: Whether the book's arguments are sound
Signs of the book's scope
The author's special angle on the subject
The meaning of every technical term
Signs of the author's aim
optionExplain: Soundness is judged much later, after careful reading; the title page cannot tell you this.
Right: the step looks for indications of the scope of the book.
Right: the step looks for the author's special angle on the subject.
Defining every term would turn a quick look into slow study; terms come much later.
Right: the step looks for indications of the aim of the book.
questions.explain: The first step reads the title page and preface quickly for scope, aim and angle, so that you end it with a good idea of the subject.
questions.rule: Title and preface: scope, aim, angle.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: A book's title is Cold Light and its subtitle is A Field Guide to Glowing Animals of the Pacific. What does the subtitle tell a skimmer that the title did not?
options: The author's attitude to the animals, through the word glowing
Only marketing appeal, since subtitles exist mainly to sell books
The book's argument about how glowing evolved in the deep sea
Its scope (glowing Pacific animals) and its kind (a field guide)
optionExplain: A single descriptive word is not an attitude; the subtitle states no opinion about the animals.
Some subtitles are written to sell, but this one gives real information about scope and kind.
Nothing in the subtitle mentions evolution; that would be a guess.
Right: the subtitle narrows the subject and says what sort of book it is.
questions.explain: The title alone could be poetry or physics. The subtitle fixes the scope and the kind of book, which is what the first step looks for.
questions.hint: What did the title leave open?
questions.rule: Use the subtitle to fix scope and kind.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: True or false: If a book has a bare title page and no preface, you read the title page quickly and go on to the next skimming step.
questions.explain: The authors say to read the preface if the book has one. Without a preface you take what the title page gives and move on to the table of contents; the absence of a preface says nothing about the book's worth.
questions.rule: Use what the book offers, then move on.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: You must decide whether to read a long scientific paper. Which part of the paper does the job that the title page and preface do for a book?
options: The title and the abstract
The reference list at the end
The tables of data in the middle
The statement of who funded it
optionExplain: Right: the abstract is the author's own short statement of scope, aim and findings, like a preface.
References show what the paper draws on, which helps later, but they do not state its aim.
Data tables hold evidence, not a statement of what the paper sets out to do.
A funding statement names sponsors; it may raise questions, but it does not describe the paper's aim.
questions.explain: The first skimming step looks for the author's own statement of scope and aim. In a paper that job falls to the title and abstract.
questions.rule: Find the part where the author states scope and aim.
questions.teaches: The first step is defined by its job, not by page names: in other kinds of writing, look for whatever part states scope and aim, such as a paper's abstract or a report's foreword.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: Lena reads a book's title page and preface, files it among self-help books, and decides she now knows its main contention. Where does her reasoning go wrong?
options: She should not have placed the book in any category
She read the preface, which is written for reviewers
She treated a first guess as settled, without testing it
She should have started with the index, which is more reliable
optionExplain: Placing the book in a mental category is part of the step, so that is not her mistake.
Prefaces often state the author's aim for any reader; reading one is part of the step.
Right: the title and preface give a first idea; the contents, index and sampled pages confirm or correct it.
The authors' order starts with the title page and preface, so her starting point was right.
questions.explain: The first step gives a good idea of the subject and a provisional category. The main contention is something the whole skim, especially the last pages, has to confirm.
questions.rule: Treat the first step's verdict as provisional.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: What does a table of contents mainly show a reader who is skimming a book?
options: The author's qualifications
The book's structure
How hard the book is to read
Where each term is defined
optionExplain: Qualifications appear on the jacket or title page, not in the contents.
Right: the contents list the parts and their order, which is the book's structure.
Difficulty shows in the prose itself; chapter titles say little about it.
Finding where a term is treated is the index's job rather than the contents'.
questions.explain: A table of contents lays out the parts of a book in order. The card next shows how the second skimming step uses it.
questions.rule: The contents show the structure.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: The authors compare studying a book's table of contents to studying a ____ before taking a trip.
questions.explain: A road map shows the route and the stops before you set out; a table of contents shows the book's parts and their order before you read.
questions.rule: Use the contents as a map of the book.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: A cookbook's contents run: Stocks and Sauces, Soups, Fish, Meat, Vegetables, Baking. What has a skimmer learned from this list?
options: Which of the recipes the author considers the best
The author's views on healthy eating and diet
Its plan: chapters by kind of dish, starting from basics
Little, because cookbooks are consulted, not read through
optionExplain: Quality cannot be read off a list of chapter titles.
Views on diet would need the text itself; nothing in these titles states one.
Right: the list shows the plan of the book, which is what the contents step is for.
Even a book you consult rather than read through has a plan, and the contents show it.
questions.explain: The contents reveal how the book is put together: here, chapters by kind of dish, opening with the basics. That is the general sense of structure the step aims at.
questions.rule: Read the contents for the plan of the book.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: Full analytical tables of contents were once common and are now rare. Besides publishers' taste for mysterious chapter titles, what other reason do the authors suggest?
options: Printing long contents pages became too costly
Readers read contents pages less than they once did
Authors stopped planning their books in parts
Indexes took over the job of the table of contents
optionExplain: Cost is a reasonable guess, but the authors do not mention it.
Right: the authors suggest that one reason for the decline is that people no longer read contents pages as they used to.
Authors still plan their books, and the authors note that many spend considerable time on the contents.
An index does a different job, finding topics rather than showing structure, and the authors give no such reason.
questions.explain: The authors offer two possible reasons: readers read contents pages less than they once did, and publishers think a less revealing contents page is more seductive.
questions.rule: A neglected contents page is still worth reading.
questions.teaches: Another likely reason for the decline of full contents pages is that readers stopped reading them as much as they once did.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: When you size up something other than a book, which of these do the job of a table of contents? Select all that apply.
options: A syllabus listing each week's topic
The price printed on a report's cover
A report's list of numbered sections
A large website's main menu
The author's photograph on a jacket
optionExplain: Right: the syllabus lays out the parts of the course and their order.
The price tells you nothing about how the work is built.
Right: the section list is the report's map.
Right: the menu shows the parts of the site and how they are grouped.
A photograph may set an impression, but it shows nothing of the structure.
questions.explain: A table of contents is any list of a work's parts in order. Syllabuses, section lists and site menus play that role.
questions.rule: Look for the map of any structured work before entering it.
questions.teaches: The road-map idea carries over to any structured work: a syllabus, a report's section list or a site menu shows the parts and their order before you commit time.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: A nonfiction book's chapters are titled The Door, Smoke, Twelve Hours and After. How should this change your skim?
options: Read it anyway, then lean more on the index, blurb and sampled pages
Skip the contents, since titles like these tell you nothing
Read every chapter in full to find out what the titles mean
Treat the book as a novel, since only novels have chapter titles like these
optionExplain: Right: the authors still advise reading the contents, but teasing titles give a thin map, so other steps must carry more weight.
Even vague titles show the number and order of parts, and the authors say to read the contents even when titles are mysterious.
Reading every chapter turns the skim into a full reading, which defeats its purpose.
Publishers often give nonfiction mysterious titles to tempt readers, so the titles do not decide the kind.
questions.explain: Mysterious chapter titles weaken the contents step but do not cancel it. The skimmer reads it carefully and then relies more on the other steps to learn the structure.
questions.hint: What did publishers want from mysterious chapter titles?
questions.rule: When the map is vague, read it and check it against other clues.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: Which part of a nonfiction book gives the quickest estimate of the range of topics and authors it deals with?
options: The dedication
The opening paragraph
The copyright page
The index
optionExplain: A dedication names a person the author cares about, not the book's topics.
An opening paragraph sets out the first idea, but it cannot show the full range of topics.
The copyright page gives publishing details, not content.
Right: an index lists the topics and the authors referred to across the whole book.
questions.explain: An index gathers the topics and names treated anywhere in a book into one list. The card next shows how the third skimming step uses it.
questions.rule: The index shows the range of a book at a glance.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: What does the third skimming step ask you to do with a book's index? Select all that apply.
options: Estimate the range of topics covered
Note the kinds of books and authors referred to
Read every passage listed under every entry
Look up passages under terms that seem crucial
Memorize the main entries for later reference
optionExplain: Right: a quick estimate of the range of topics is the first use of the index.
Right: the kinds of books and authors cited tell you about the book's company and approach.
Reading every cited passage would take longer than the rest of the skim and turn it into a reading.
Right: for terms that seem crucial, look up at least some of the passages cited.
Memorizing entries spends effort on recall, while the step is about judging what matters.
questions.explain: The index step is a quick survey of topics and sources, followed by a few targeted look-ups under terms that seem crucial.
questions.rule: Survey the index, then sample the crucial entries.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: From the subtitle and contents, you know a nutrition book argues against low-fat diets. Its index lists insulin and saturated fat with many pages each, plus dozens of minor entries. What should you do next?
options: Look up a few passages under insulin and saturated fat
Read the passages under every entry, in alphabetical order
Skip the index, since the contents have already told you enough
Pick a few entries at random so that your choice is unbiased
optionExplain: Right: your general sense of the book from the first two steps tells you which terms are crucial, so you read some of their passages.
Working through every entry turns a quick step into a slow survey with no focus.
The contents show structure, but the index can lead you to the passage on which the book hinges.
Random picks ignore what you already know; the authors want you to judge importance from the earlier steps.
questions.explain: You choose crucial terms from the sense of the book gained in the first two steps, then read some of the passages cited for them. Those passages may contain the crux.
questions.hint: What do you already know from the first two steps?
questions.rule: Let earlier steps tell you which index terms to chase.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: Besides what the earlier steps told you, the authors point to one simple sign in an index that a term may be important. What is it?
options: The term is printed in capital letters
The term comes early in the alphabet
The term has many page references listed under it
The term is a word from another language
optionExplain: Printing style is a design choice, not a sign of how much the book discusses a term.
Alphabetical position has nothing to do with importance.
Right: a term that the book returns to again and again has a long list of page references.
Foreign words may be technical, but that alone says nothing about their weight in the book.
questions.explain: The authors invite readers to spot important terms by the number of references under them. A long list means the author keeps coming back to the term.
questions.rule: Many references under an entry hint that it matters.
questions.teaches: The number of page references under an index entry is a quick clue to how important that term is to the book.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: You must decide quickly whether a 90-page software manual deals with your problem of failed data backups. Applying the index step, what is the best move?
options: Read the manual from page one until backups come up
Read only the index, without opening any cited pages
Search other sources first, since manuals rarely explain much
Check the index for backup terms and read two cited passages
optionExplain: Reading from the start could take hours before you even know whether the manual covers backups.
The index shows that a term appears, but only the passages show whether the treatment helps.
This drops the step instead of applying it; the manual may well answer the question.
Right: the index shows whether and where the topic is treated, and two passages show how.
questions.explain: An index points to where a topic is treated. Reading a few of the cited passages tells you whether the work deals with it seriously enough to deserve more time.
questions.rule: Use the index to find, then the passages to judge.
questions.teaches: The index step also works from your side: when you know what you need, scanning the index and a few cited passages shows quickly whether a work treats it and where.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: True or false: When a book has no index, the authors' skimming method cannot be used on it.
questions.explain: The authors say to check the index if the book has one. Without one you skip that step; the title page, contents, blurb, pivotal chapters and last pages still give a skim to work with.
questions.rule: A missing step is skipped, not a reason to abandon the skim.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: True or false: A publisher's blurb is best ignored, since it is pure advertising that tells a reader nothing useful about a book.
questions.explain: Many blurbs, especially for nonfiction, try to state the book's main points. The card next shows how to use them, and what to do after the first four skimming steps.
questions.rule: A blurb can be a summary, not only an advert.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: Why do the authors think the blurb of an expository book is often worth reading?
options: Authors often help write it, summarizing their main points
Publishers are legally required to describe their books accurately
Blurbs are written by independent reviewers who have read the book
Blurbs list the argument of every chapter in turn
optionExplain: Right: many blurbs are written by the authors themselves, with publicity help, as summaries of their main points.
The authors mention no such rule; the value comes from who writes the blurb.
Review quotes may appear on jackets, but the authors point to blurbs written by the authors themselves.
A blurb is far too short for a chapter-by-chapter account; at best it states the main points.
questions.explain: According to the authors, it is not uncommon for authors to write their own blurbs and to try to sum up their main points. That makes the blurb worth a look.
questions.rule: A blurb may be the author's own summary.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: After the title page, preface, contents, index and blurb of a beekeeping book, Sam sees it is written for commercial firms running thousands of hives. He keeps two hives in his garden. What does the method suggest now?
options: Go on to the pivotal chapters, to finish all six steps
Give it an analytical reading anyway, to be fair to the author
Read the last pages first, in case they change his mind
Put it aside: the first four steps have answered his question
optionExplain: The later steps are for readers still unsure after four; Sam is not unsure.
Analytical reading is for books that deserve it; skimming exists to spare that effort on the wrong book.
The last pages help when the main contention is unclear, but his doubt is already settled by the book's audience.
Right: after four steps you may know enough to decide, and here the book does not fit his need.
questions.explain: The authors place a decision point after the first four steps: read the book carefully, drop it, or skim on. Sam already knows the book does not serve his purpose.
questions.hint: What do the first four steps let you decide?
questions.rule: After four steps, decide; do not finish the routine by habit.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: A blurb calls a book dazzling, essential and unforgettable, and says nothing at all about what it argues. What do the authors suggest this might tell you?
options: That publishers write the same puffery for every book
That the book itself may say nothing of importance
That the book is too deep to be summarized
That the publisher is hiding a controversial thesis
optionExplain: Some blurbs are puff, but treating them all alike throws away the clue that an empty one gives.
Right: the authors suggest that a blurb may say nothing because the book has nothing important to say.
Deep books can be summarized in a sentence or two; the authors do not read empty praise as a sign of depth.
A hidden thesis is a story the reader would be inventing; the authors draw a plainer inference.
questions.explain: A puff blurb is easy to spot at a glance, and that in itself tells you something. Perhaps the blurb says nothing because the book does not either.
questions.rule: An empty blurb is a clue in its own right.
questions.teaches: An empty blurb is itself evidence: if the summary says nothing of substance, that may be because the book says nothing of importance.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: You are choosing podcasts and read their show descriptions. Sort each line: does it give evidence about content, or is it empty praise?

items.t: Each season follows one city through a decade of change
Episodes compare three theories of inflation
Covers student budgeting, from rent to groceries
The most mind-blowing show you will ever hear
An essential listen for everyone
You will see the world differently forever

questions.explain: A useful description says what the work covers or claims. Lines that only praise give no content, and a description made only of such lines is a warning sign, as with a puff blurb.
questions.rule: Weigh what a description says, not how loudly it praises.
questions.teaches: Pure hype works like an empty blurb wherever you meet it: if a description says nothing of substance about a work, the work itself may have nothing of importance to say.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: True or false: A detailed, accurate-sounding blurb tells you what a book claims, but not whether those claims are sound.
questions.explain: Even an honest blurb is a summary written to sell the book. It tells you what to look for; judging whether the claims hold needs a careful reading.
questions.rule: A blurb tells you what to check, not what is proven.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: In a quick skim of a nonfiction book, which pages are most likely to hold the author's summing-up of what is new and important?
options: The first page of the second chapter
The pages at the exact middle of the book
The acknowledgments
The last two or three pages
optionExplain: An early chapter opening sets up the subject; the summing-up tends to come later.
The middle often carries the argument, but authors rarely pause there to sum up the whole.
Acknowledgments thank people; they seldom state the book's claims.
Right: authors tend to close by summing up what they think is new and important.
questions.explain: Most authors cannot resist stating at the end what they believe their book has achieved. The card next shows where else to look while skimming.
questions.rule: Look for the summing-up at the end.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: Put the six steps of systematic skimming in the authors' order.
items: Read the title page and preface
Study the table of contents
Check the index
Read the publisher's blurb
Look at the chapters that seem pivotal
Dip into pages and read the last few pages
questions.explain: The first four steps work on the parts of a book that describe the whole. If they leave you unsure, the last two sample the text itself, ending with the author's summing-up.
questions.rule: Describe the whole first, then sample the text.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: Ana has done the first four steps on a book about climate policy and is still unsure about it. The contents suggest chapters 3 and 8 carry the argument. What should she do next?
options: Read chapters 3 and 8 in full, start to finish
Read the opening and closing summaries of chapters 3 and 8
Start at chapter 1 and keep reading until she feels sure of it
Go back over the index more slowly for clues
optionExplain: Reading two whole chapters is more than a skim needs, and the summaries usually give the gist.
Right: step five looks at the pivotal chapters and reads any summary statements in their opening or closing pages.
Reading from the start abandons skimming and may use up her time before the argument appears.
The index has done its work; the next step is to look at the text of the pivotal chapters.
questions.explain: Step five uses the vague sense of the contents to pick the chapters that carry the argument, then reads their opening or closing summaries carefully.
questions.rule: Read the summaries of the chapters that carry the argument.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: While dipping into pages in step six, which of these fit the authors' advice? Select all that apply.
options: Reading a paragraph or two in several different chapters
Reading a few pages in a row where the argument surfaces
Settling into a whole chapter that looks interesting
Watching for signs of the main contention
Stopping to look up every unfamiliar name
optionExplain: Right: dip in here and there, a paragraph or two at a time.
Right: sometimes several pages in sequence, but never more than that.
A whole chapter is more than the authors allow; it turns sampling into reading.
Right: the point of dipping is to catch signs of the main contention.
Look-ups stall a skim; it is a quick search for the main thread.
questions.explain: Step six samples across the book, a paragraph or two, at most several pages in a row, always hunting for the main contention.
questions.rule: Sample widely and briefly, looking for the main point.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: A biography ends with a ten-page epilogue about its subject's grandchildren, written in a lighter tone. Where should a skimmer read for the author's summing-up?
options: The last pages of the epilogue, the end of the book
The last pages of the main part, before the epilogue
The opening pages of the epilogue, where it begins
The notes at the back, where sources are summed up
optionExplain: These are the last pages printed, but in this book they continue a side story rather than sum up.
Right: the authors say that if the last pages are an epilogue, read the last few pages of the main part instead.
The epilogue's opening starts the side story; it is not where the main work is summed up.
Notes support particular claims and point to sources; they rarely sum up the book.
questions.explain: The last-pages step aims at the author's summing-up. When a book ends with an epilogue, that summing-up sits at the end of the main part.
questions.hint: Why read the last pages at all?
questions.rule: Read the end of the main part, where the author sums up.
questions.teaches: If a book ends with an epilogue, read the last few pages of the main part instead, since that is where the author sums up.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: Ben reads the last three pages of a book, finds the author saying the book overturns fifty years of research, and concludes that it does. What is wrong with his reasoning?
options: He should not have read the last pages so early in the skim
The last pages only matter in novels, not in research books
He should have read the first pages for the conclusion instead
The last pages give the author's view, which may be wrong
optionExplain: Reading the last pages is part of the skim, so the timing is not the problem.
The authors recommend reading the last pages of any book you skim, especially expository ones.
Opening pages are worth a look too, but that does not fix his mistake of taking the author's word.
Right: the last pages give the author's judgment of what is new and important, which the authors warn may be mistaken.
questions.explain: The summing-up tells you what the author believes the book achieves. Whether it really overturns earlier research is a judgment that needs careful reading, not a skim.
questions.rule: The last pages state the author's view, not a proven fact.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: About how long should a systematic skim of a full-length book take?
options: A full afternoon
A few minutes, an hour at most
One evening for every hundred pages
As long as a careful first reading
optionExplain: An afternoon is the time of a long reading session, far more than a skim needs.
Right: a systematic skim is quick by design.
Scaling time with length treats skimming like reading; the skim samples rather than covers.
Skimming is what you do before deciding whether to give that time.
questions.explain: A skim is a fast, ordered sampling of a book. The card next shows what keeps it from becoming idle flipping.
questions.rule: A skim is measured in minutes.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: True or false: The authors describe skimming as a relaxed, passive kind of reading that needs little attention.
questions.explain: The authors call skimming a very active sort of reading: it is impossible without being alert, with all one's faculties awake and working.
questions.rule: Skimming is active work.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: Priya flips through a book on the beach, reading whatever catches her eye. After twenty minutes she cannot say what the book is about. In the authors' terms, what was missing?
options: More time, since an hour would have been enough
A dictionary close by for the harder words
A system that kept her on a thread of clues
A slower, more careful reading speed
optionExplain: More random flipping would not help; the trouble was the lack of method, not of minutes.
Nothing suggests the words stopped her; she had no thread to follow.
Right: having a system for following a general thread is what keeps a skim from drifting.
Slowing down would make her flip less, not search better.
questions.explain: Random browsing lets the mind wander. A system, with the detective's question about the main idea, keeps the reader alert and on a thread.
questions.hint: What does a detective have that a browser lacks?
questions.rule: Skim with a system and a question, not at random.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: Mira spends three hours on what she calls a skim, reading the first half of each chapter carefully. Where has she departed from the authors' advice?
options: She should have read the second half of each chapter instead
She skipped the table of contents, which is the most important step
No mistake: a longer skim is a more thorough skim
She went far past an hour and read long stretches in sequence
optionExplain: Which half she reads is not the issue; reading half-chapters at all is too much for a skim.
The question says nothing about the contents; her error shows in her time and her method.
Thoroughness belongs to careful reading; a skim that takes three hours has stopped being a skim.
Right: a skim takes at most an hour and samples only short stretches, a few pages at most.
questions.explain: Skimming is fast because it reads little of the book. Half of every chapter is a partial reading, and three hours is well past the authors' limit.
questions.rule: A skim samples; it does not read in long stretches.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: You have to size up a 60-page market research report before a meeting. Which habits show the detective attitude? Select all that apply.
options: Holding a guess about the main finding and testing it as you go
Treating the headings and the conclusion as clues
Reading the pages in order and waiting for the point to emerge
Noticing a chart that seems to contradict your guess
Skipping anything that does not fit your first guess
optionExplain: Right: a detective works with a theory of the case and checks it against the evidence.
Right: headings and conclusions are where clues to the main idea gather.
Waiting passively for the point is the opposite of hunting for clues.
Right: a clue against your guess is as useful as one for it.
Ignoring contrary evidence is how detectives go wrong; the guess must stay open to correction.
questions.explain: The detective attitude means reading with a question in mind, the main idea, and treating each detail as evidence for or against a working answer.
questions.rule: Read for clues to the main idea, including clues against your guess.
questions.teaches: The detective attitude works best with a working guess about the main idea, held loosely, so that every heading, chart or page becomes evidence for or against it.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.section: Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading
questions.q: True or false: A skim done alertly, with a system, within an hour, gives you as good an understanding of a book as a careful reading would.
questions.explain: A good skim tells you whether a book deserves more time, its kind and its main contention, and where to file it in your mind. Understanding what the book says needs the careful reading the skim helps you choose.
questions.rule: A skim gives a sketch, not an understanding.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: True or false: On a first reading of a hard book, the best approach is to stop and work out each passage you do not understand before reading on.
questions.explain: Stopping at every difficulty breaks the thread and often leaves you stuck in the opening pages. The card next gives the authors' rule for a first reading.
questions.rule: A first reading is for getting through the whole.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: According to the authors' rule for a first reading of a difficult book, what should you do at a passage you cannot grasp right away?
options: Read on and concentrate on what you do understand
Reread it until it becomes clear
Look it up in a reference work before going on
Take it as a sign the book is too hard for you
optionExplain: Right: go past the difficulty and you will soon come to things you understand.
Rereading feels diligent, but sticking at one block seldom solves it and can stall the whole reading.
Reference works have a place later; on a first reading they hold you up.
The authors warn against this conclusion: the fault lies in expecting too much from a first reading.
questions.explain: The rule for a first reading is to keep going and concentrate on what you understand, leaving difficulties for later.
questions.rule: Keep going; attend to what you understand.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Tom is on his first reading of a difficult history of the Byzantine Empire. Which actions fit the authors' rule? Select all that apply.
options: Skipping a footnote he cannot follow and reading on
Stopping to research each emperor he does not know
Pushing on past a confusing chapter on church councils
Concentrating on the chapters he does follow
Staying on a hard page until it makes sense
optionExplain: Right: footnotes that escape you should not halt a first reading.
Research looks responsible, but on a first reading it stops the flow of the whole book.
Right: past the hard point he will soon come to things he understands.
Right: pay attention to what you can understand.
Persistence seems a virtue, but sticking at one block seldom solves it and can stop the reading altogether.
questions.explain: Each right action keeps the reading moving and puts his attention on what he understands. Research and stalls belong, if anywhere, to a later reading.
questions.hint: Which actions keep him moving towards the end of the book?
questions.rule: Let no single difficulty stop a first reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Suppose Tom ignores the rule and refuses to go past page 30 until he understands a dense paragraph there. What do the authors expect to happen?
options: He will crack the paragraph within a day or two
He will understand the rest of the book better for the effort
He will likely stay stuck, since sticking seldom solves it
He will read faster once the paragraph is clear
optionExplain: Hard effort sometimes works, but the authors say that in most cases you will not puzzle it out by sticking to it.
He may never reach the rest of the book; that is the danger.
Right: the authors warn that a reader who lets one stumbling block stall him is lost.
Speed is not the issue; the risk is that he never gets past page 30.
questions.explain: The authors say that a stumbling block usually cannot be puzzled out by sticking to it. It is better understood on a second reading, after the whole book has been read once.
questions.rule: Sticking at one block rarely solves it.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: A new employee sits through her first week of meetings full of acronyms and project names she does not know. Applying the superficial-reading rule, what should she do?
options: Interrupt each speaker to ask what every acronym means
Follow what she can and note a few terms to ask about later
Stop attending until she has studied the company glossary in full
Conclude that she is not yet ready for these meetings
optionExplain: Asking about everything stalls the meeting and her grasp of its main business.
Right: she follows the whole, concentrates on what she understands, and leaves the rest for later.
Studying first sounds thorough, but she would miss the context that makes the terms make sense.
Like giving up on a hard book, this expects too much from a first encounter.
questions.explain: The rule fits any first encounter with a hard, unfamiliar whole. Much of what is obscure at first becomes clear once you have seen more of the whole.
questions.rule: Follow the whole first; collect the puzzles for later.
questions.teaches: Reading past difficulties works because later parts of a whole often throw light on earlier ones, so what baffled you at first may become clear in context.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: True or false: The superficial-reading rule forbids looking up words or footnotes at any stage of studying a difficult book.
questions.explain: The rule governs the first reading only. Looking things up and working through what you passed over belong to later, closer readings.
questions.rule: The rule is about the first reading, not about all study.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: A reader struggles with a hard classic, gives up in chapter 2, and decides it was a mistake to try it. Where would the authors place her mistake?
options: In choosing a book that was too hard for her
In not reading slowly and carefully enough
In expecting too much from a first reading
In skipping the introduction and preface
optionExplain: Choosing the book feels like the error, but the authors say trying a hard book was not the mistake.
Slower reading would make her stop at even more difficulties.
Right: the authors locate the mistake in the expectation, not in the choice of book.
