The introduction may help, but the authors point to a deeper mistake about what a first reading can do.
questions.explain: According to the authors, struggling with a hard book is normal; the error is demanding full understanding the first time. The card next explains what a partial reading is worth.
questions.rule: Blame the expectation, not the attempt.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: According to the authors, understanding ____ of a really tough book is much better than not understanding it at all.
questions.explain: The authors set a modest bar for a first reading: half of a really tough book is much better than none, which is what you get if the first hard passage stops you.
questions.rule: Half is far better than nothing.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Leo finishes a first reading of a hard book on cosmology, having followed about a third of it. What do the authors suggest about that third?
options: It is a base for returning to the parts he passed over
It shows he wasted his time and should choose an easier book
It does not count, since a third is not real understanding
It means he should read a summary instead of returning to the book
optionExplain: Right: what you understand on a first reading helps when you go back to the places you passed by.
The authors reject this conclusion; trying the hard book was not the mistake.
Partial understanding counts; the authors value half a tough book far above none.
A summary replaces the book instead of building on what he already grasped of it.
questions.explain: A complete first reading, however partial, gives a footing for the second. Leo's third is what will make the rest easier to reach.
questions.rule: What you grasp the first time supports the second time.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, you have a better chance of understanding a hard passage by returning to it on a second reading than by sticking at it on the first.
questions.explain: The authors say you will have a much better chance of understanding it on a second reading, and that this requires having read the book through at least once.
questions.rule: Hard passages yield to a second reading, after a full first one.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: On her first reading of a long Russian novel, Ines keeps losing track of characters who each go by several names. Applying the authors' advice, what should she do?
options: Stop and research each name before going on
Give up, since the novel is too confusing for her
Reread the first chapter until every name is fixed
Read on, follow the story, and sort out names later
optionExplain: Research at each name breaks up the story and makes her lose the whole.
Giving up is the mistake the authors warn against: expecting too much the first time.
Rereading one chapter until it is perfect stalls her, like sticking at any block.
Right: she gets the story whole first, and later readings can clear up the details.
questions.explain: The authors' advice to read straight through and accept partial understanding is not limited to expository books. A novel read through once gives the whole that later readings can fill in.
questions.rule: Get the whole story first; fix the details later.
questions.teaches: The read-through advice extends naturally to novels: following the story through once gives a frame in which confusing names and relations can be sorted out on a later reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Suppose the hard book is a research monograph written for experts in a field Leo has not studied. How does the authors' promise about difficult books apply?
options: It applies fully, since no book need ever cause despair
It covers books for the general reader, so it may not hold
It applies only if he reads the monograph very slowly
It means he should skip superficial reading and study it closely
optionExplain: The promise sounds universal, but the authors limit it to books intended for the general reader.
Right: a specialist work may need knowledge a first reading cannot supply, so the promise may not cover it.
Speed does not supply the missing background a specialist book assumes.
Nothing in the authors' limit says to drop the read-through; it limits what it can promise.
questions.explain: The authors say no book intended for the general reader need be a cause for despair. A monograph for specialists falls outside that promise, so reading through once may not be enough.
questions.rule: Note who a book was written for before trusting the promise.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: True or false: Looking up every unfamiliar word as you meet it on a first reading helps you understand a difficult book.
questions.explain: Constant look-ups chop a first reading into fragments, and the whole gets lost. The card next explains when reference aids help and when they hurt.
questions.rule: Timing decides whether aids help.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Which of these do the authors say can impede a reading when they are used too early? Select all that apply.
options: Discussing what you got from a quick first reading
Dictionaries
Reading the whole work once at one sitting
Encyclopedias and other reference works
Footnotes and scholarly commentaries
optionExplain: Discussion after a quick reading is what the authors recommend, not something to avoid.
Right: going to a dictionary for every word is one of the habits that, done prematurely, impedes reading.
Reading at one sitting is the authors' cure, not the problem.
Right: running to reference works for every allusion breaks up a first reading.
Right: studying footnotes and commentaries too early is the habit that spoiled Shakespeare for students.
questions.explain: All three aids are useful in their place. The authors' point is that used prematurely, before the whole has been read, they get in the way.
questions.rule: Aids help after the whole, not before.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: A teacher is planning a unit on a Shakespeare comedy. Which plan follows the authors' advice?
options: Students work through one scene a week, with the glossary and every footnote
Students read a plot summary in place of the play
Students read the play at one sitting, discuss it, then study it closely
Students learn the glossary words before they start reading
optionExplain: This is the scene-by-scene method the authors blame for spoiling Shakespeare for generations.
A summary replaces the reading rather than ordering it well.
Right: a quick reading of the whole first, discussion next, close study after.
Front-loading the glossary is premature use of aids in another form.
questions.explain: The authors want the whole play read first, at one sitting, and discussed. Close study then has something to build on.
questions.rule: Read the whole play first, then study its parts.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: What do the authors say happened to students who went through a play scene by scene with every footnote, without first reading it through?
options: They forgot the beginning and lost sight of the whole
They understood the play more deeply than quick readers
They read too fast to notice the language
They knew the plot well but missed the jokes
optionExplain: Right: the authors say these students never really read the play, because the whole slipped away.
Close study seems deeper, but without the whole first, it left them with fragments.
They read very slowly; speed was not the problem.
The authors say they lost the whole, plot included, not that they missed some jokes.
questions.explain: Scene-by-scene study with every aid stretches a play over weeks. The opening is forgotten before the end arrives, and the play is never grasped as a whole.
questions.rule: Slow piecemeal study can lose the whole.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Before her first opera, Zoe plans to pause the recording after every aria to read the full programme notes and background. Following the authors' reasoning, what does she risk besides losing the thread?
options: Hearing too much music in one long sitting to take it in
Losing her enjoyment, as glossary study did for Shakespeare
Learning the plot too well before she hears the music
Knowing the ending too early, which would spoil the suspense
optionExplain: Hearing the whole work in one sitting is what the authors' advice would recommend.
Right: the authors say the pedantic method spoiled the tremendous pleasure students could have had from Shakespeare.
Knowing the plot is no danger; the risk lies in the constant interruption.
Knowing the ending can reduce suspense, but the authors' warning concerns interruptions that spoil the pleasure of the whole.
questions.explain: Premature aids do more than break the thread. The authors say the scene-by-scene method spoiled the pleasure of Shakespeare for generations of students.
questions.rule: Meet the work whole before the notes.
questions.teaches: Interrupting a first reading costs enjoyment as well as understanding: the authors say the glossary-and-footnote method spoiled the pleasure of Shakespeare for generations of students.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Sort each action: does it fit a first reading of a difficult work, or does it belong after the work has been read through?

items.t: Reading on past a word you do not know
Leaving a footnote unread for now
Going on past an allusion you do not catch
Looking up words in the glossary
Reading a scholarly commentary
Checking an allusion in an encyclopedia

questions.explain: The authors do not forbid aids; they object to using them prematurely. The first reading gets you through the whole, and the aids then help with what you passed over.
questions.rule: First the whole, then the aids.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: A reader insists on fully understanding each page of a long economics book before turning it. What is she most likely to miss?
options: The book's big points
The details in its footnotes
The meaning of its technical terms
Some speed, but no understanding
optionExplain: Right: attention spent on every fine point leaves the main lines of the book unseen.
She is giving the details more attention, not less.
She is likely to work hard at the terms; the loss lies elsewhere.
It seems the only cost is time, but the authors say the cost is understanding of the big points.
questions.explain: Working page by page at every detail keeps a reader from seeing how the whole fits together. The card next shows the authors' example.
questions.rule: Details first can hide the main points.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Insisting on every fine point of an expository book during a first reading makes you miss the forest for the ____.
questions.explain: The forest is the book's big points; the trees are its fine points. Fixing on each tree hides the shape of the forest.
questions.rule: Do not lose the forest for the trees.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Raj reads a book arguing that clean water did more than medicine to raise life expectancy. He spends two weeks on chapter 2's tables of death rates. What is he most likely missing?
options: The meaning of the tables he is studying
The author's sources for the death-rate data
The main argument and how later chapters support it
Little, since the tables are the book's real evidence
optionExplain: He is studying the tables closely, so their meaning is what he is most likely to get.
Sources are a detail a careful reader checks later; they are not the big point he is missing.
Right: by stalling on one chapter's details he has not seen the whole argument the tables serve.
The tables are evidence for a thesis he has not yet followed through the book.
questions.explain: Evidence makes sense only in the light of the argument it serves. By stalling on the tables, Raj misses the big point that gives them their meaning.
questions.hint: What are the tables evidence for?
questions.rule: Get the argument before the evidence.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Which of these do the authors list among the big points of The Wealth of Nations that a page-by-page reader would miss? Select all that apply.
options: The market's role in setting prices
The exact figures in Smith's examples
The evils of monopoly
The reasons for free trade
The details of Smith's life
optionExplain: Right: the market's role in setting prices is one of the big points the authors name.
Exact figures are fine points, the trees rather than the forest.
Right: the evils of monopoly are on the authors' list of big points.
Right: the case for free trade is on the authors' list.
Smith's biography is not part of the book's argument at all.
questions.explain: The big points are the main claims that run through the book. Exact figures are fine points, and biography is outside the book's argument.
questions.rule: Big points are the claims the whole book makes.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Reading a 40-page tenancy agreement for the first time, Ama gets stuck on a clause about fixtures and fittings. Applying the forest-and-trees idea, what should she do?
options: Refuse to read on until that clause is clear
Sign it, trusting that standard clauses are fair
Ask the landlord for a shorter agreement
Read on for the main terms, then return to the clause
optionExplain: Stalling on one clause risks never seeing the agreement's main terms.
Signing on trust drops reading altogether, the opposite of the authors' aim.
A shorter document avoids the question instead of applying the idea.
Right: the main terms (rent, length, duties, ending it) frame the clause, which she can then study closely.
questions.explain: Seeing the whole agreement first shows where the clause fits and how much it matters. The detailed reading then has a frame to work in.
questions.rule: See the whole document before its hardest clause.
questions.teaches: Grasping the big points first gives a frame in which the fine points later make sense; without it, details pile up with nothing to hang on.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: True or false: Once a first reading has given you the big points of an expository book, the authors would have you leave its fine points alone for good.
questions.explain: The authors object to demanding the fine points too soon, not to the fine points themselves. A careful reading after the first one is where they are worked out.
questions.rule: Fine points wait; they are not abandoned.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: True or false: A book twice as long and twice as hard needs an inspectional reading that takes about four times as long.
questions.explain: Inspection is quick by design, because it samples a book and reads it through without stopping. The card next shows why its speed does not grow with the book.
questions.rule: Inspection stays quick as books grow.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: How did the authors define inspectional reading in Chapter 2, a definition this chapter keeps?
options: Reading every word at the fastest pace you can manage
Getting the most out of a book in a limited time
Memorizing the main facts of a book
Comparing several books on the same subject
optionExplain: Inspection is fast, but it reads less of the book rather than every word at speed.
Right: inspection aims at the most a book can give within a set, usually short, time.
Memorizing is no part of the definition; inspection looks for the book's kind, structure and main point.
Comparing several books on one subject is syntopical reading, the fourth level.
questions.explain: Inspectional reading is defined by its constraint, a limited time, and its aim, the most you can get from the book within it.
questions.rule: Inspection: the most from a book in limited time.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: A graduate student must size up a 1,000-page treatise and a 120-page essay before Friday. How should the time she spends inspecting each compare?
options: The treatise should take about eight times as long
The essay should take longer, since short books are denser
She should skip inspecting the treatise and start reading it
Both inspections should be quick, whatever the length
optionExplain: Scaling time with page count treats inspection like a full reading.
Density may matter for a careful reading, but inspection is quick for both.
A long treatise is exactly where a quick inspection saves the most time.
Right: a competent inspectional reader does both steps quickly, however long or difficult the book.
questions.explain: Inspection samples and reads through without stopping, so its time does not grow in proportion to the book. Both books can be sized up quickly.
questions.rule: Inspection time does not scale with length.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: The authors describe most speed reading courses as basically ____, since they teach reading mainly at the elementary level.
questions.explain: Remedial instruction repairs a basic skill. Speed courses train the eye and the uptake of words, an elementary skill, rather than the higher levels such as inspection.
questions.rule: Speed courses work at the elementary level.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: A council member receives a 300-page budget proposal the evening before a vote and has two hours. What does the idea of inspectional reading suggest?
options: Read the first 60 pages carefully, as far as time allows
Inspect the whole proposal quickly, within the two hours
Refuse to vote until she can read every page analytically
Run her eyes over all 300 pages at triple her usual pace
optionExplain: A careful reading of one fifth leaves her blind to most of the proposal.
Right: with the time fixed, inspection gets the most from the whole work.
Careful reading may be ideal, but the time is fixed; the question is how to use it well.
Racing every word is speed reading, an elementary skill, not inspection with its own steps and goals.
questions.explain: Inspection is designed for a fixed, short time. It covers the whole work selectively, which beats a careful reading of only its opening.
questions.rule: With fixed time, inspect the whole rather than read a part.
questions.teaches: When circumstances fix the time, inspectional reading gets the most from a work as a whole, which a careful reading of only its first part cannot.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: True or false: Since inspection should be fast whatever the book, an analytical reading of a long, difficult book should be fast as well.
questions.explain: Speed is a mark of the inspectional level. Analytical reading is usually much slower, because it aims at understanding the book, not at sizing it up.
questions.rule: Inspection is fast; analytical reading usually is not.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Which of these would the authors call the ideal reading speed?
options: As fast as possible, for everything
A steady, moderate pace for all material
Several speeds, and knowing when each fits
Slow for everything, to be safe
optionExplain: Speed saves time on some material, but it wastes the material that deserves slow reading.
One moderate pace is too slow for some things and too fast for others.
Right: the ideal is a range of speeds plus the judgment to choose among them.
Slowness wastes time on material that deserves only a quick reading.
questions.explain: No single speed suits everything people read. The card next explains what should decide the speed.
questions.rule: The ideal is many speeds, well chosen.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: True or false: The authors think many people read some things too fast and ought to read them more slowly.
questions.explain: Alongside their support for faster reading, the authors point out that many people also read some things too fast and should slow down.
questions.rule: Some reading is too fast, not only too slow.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Sort each item by the pace it deserves, following the authors' idea of varying speed.

items.t: A routine weekly newsletter from your gym
A weather report for tomorrow
The blurb for a film on a streaming site
The key clause of a contract you are about to sign
A hard proof in a geometry textbook
The central argument of a philosophy classic

questions.explain: Pace should follow the nature and complexity of the material. Routine, light items deserve little time; dense or consequential ones deserve slow reading.
questions.rule: Let the material set the pace.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: The authors sort books into three groups by how they deserve to be read. Which list matches their grouping?
options: Hardly worth a skim; worth a quick read; worth a slow, full reading
Fiction, nonfiction and poetry, each read at its own proper pace
Easy, medium and hard books, judged by their vocabulary
Short, medium and long books, judged by their page count
optionExplain: Right: many books hardly deserve a skim, some deserve a quick reading, and a few deserve slow reading for full comprehension.
Kind of book matters elsewhere, but this grouping is about what each book deserves.
Vocabulary affects difficulty, but the grouping is about worth, not word lists.
Length does not decide how a book deserves to be read.
questions.explain: The grouping sorts books by what they deserve: most little, some a quick reading, a few a slow reading that allows complete comprehension.
questions.rule: Sort by what the book deserves, not by its length.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Mo listens to every podcast at double speed to save time, including a lecture series on a hard subject he wants to master. Applying the authors' view of speeds, what is the best advice?
options: Keep double speed for everything, since a consistent habit is efficient
Fast playback for light shows, slower or paused for the lecture
Slow everything down to normal speed to be safe
Drop podcasts for the lecture and read a book instead
optionExplain: One fast speed is the mistake the authors warn about, moved from reading to listening.
Right: pace should follow the worth and difficulty of the material.
Normal speed for everything wastes time on light shows that deserve less.
Changing the medium avoids the question of pace instead of answering it.
questions.explain: The authors' ideal is many speeds, each matched to the material. The same judgment applies to anything taken in over time, listening included.
questions.rule: Choose the pace for each piece, in any medium.
questions.teaches: The varying-speed principle applies to listening and watching as well as reading: pace should follow the worth and difficulty of the material, not a fixed habit.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: A speed course doubles Hana's reading rate, and she now reads everything at that single new rate. What would the authors say is still missing?
options: Nothing, since faster reading is better reading
An even higher rate for difficult books
A wider vocabulary to match her new speed
The judgment to slow down when material deserves it
optionExplain: Faster saves time only on material that deserves a fast reading.
Difficult books usually call for slower reading, not faster.
Vocabulary is not the issue here; the issue is that one rate cannot fit all material.
Right: a good course teaches many speeds and when to use each, not one faster speed.
questions.explain: One speed, however fast, cannot fit everything. The authors want a reader who can vary the rate and knows when each rate is right.
questions.rule: A single fast speed is still a single speed.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: A student who reads very fast still struggles with a hard philosophy book. What is the most likely cause, according to the authors?
options: Her eyes have not been trained enough yet
The book is badly written and unclear
She does not know what to look for in it
She needs to read it even faster
optionExplain: Eye training addresses speed, which she already has.
Some books are badly written, but a fast reader struggling with a good one points elsewhere.
Right: the authors place the main obstacle in not knowing what to do with a difficult book.
More speed adds to what she already has without touching the real problem.
questions.explain: Speed does not supply the knowledge of what to look for. The card next explains what the authors see as the real obstacle.
questions.rule: Speed is not understanding.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: According to the authors, a fast reader is no better off if he does not know what he is ____ for and does not know when he has found it.
questions.explain: Speed helps only a reader who knows what he is looking for in a book and can tell when he has found it. That knowledge comes from the rules of reading.
questions.rule: Know what you are looking for.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: A company pays for a speed reading course so that its analysts will understand dense regulatory reports better. What does the authors' view predict?
options: They will read faster but may understand no better unless they learn what to look for
They will understand the reports fully, since speed brings understanding
Their understanding will collapse, since fast readers cannot comprehend
The reports will become easy, since their difficulty is mostly a matter of reading rate
optionExplain: Right: speed solves the time problem, not the problem of knowing what to do with a difficult text.
Speed and understanding are different achievements; the authors deny that one brings the other.
The authors do not say speed destroys understanding; they say it does not supply it.
The authors place difficulty in not knowing the rules of reading, not in the reading rate.
questions.explain: The obstacles to understanding are not ordinarily physical or psychological. A speed course trains the eye, not the reader's knowledge of what to look for.
questions.rule: Speed training does not teach what to look for.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Which problems can speed reading skills help with, according to the authors? Select all that apply.
options: Reading slowly a book that deserves only a fast reading
Not knowing the rules of reading
Wasting a lot of time on material not worth it
Not knowing what to look for in a hard book
Not knowing when you have found what you need
optionExplain: Right: the authors say speed reading skills can help solve this problem.
This is the deeper obstacle that speed does not touch.
Right: reading things not worth much time quickly saves that waste.
Knowing what to look for comes from the rules of reading, not from speed.
Recognizing what you have found is part of knowing what you are looking for, which speed does not give.
questions.explain: Speed answers one problem, wasting time on material that deserves little. The other problems belong to knowing how to read a difficult book.
questions.rule: Speed fixes wasted time, not lack of method.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: A junior programmer scrolls through code very fast but cannot find the bug in a large program. A senior colleague reads more slowly and finds it. Applying the authors' point, what best explains the difference?
options: The senior has sharper eyesight for small text
The junior should scroll even faster to cover more
The program is too long for anyone to search well
The senior knows what to look for and when it is found
optionExplain: Eyesight affects speed of scanning, which the junior already has.
More speed adds to the scanning without giving it a target.
The senior found the bug, so the length was not the barrier.
Right: knowing what you are looking for, and when you have found it, matters more than speed.
questions.explain: As with a difficult book, the barrier is not speed but knowing what to look for. The slower reader with a target outperforms the faster one without.
questions.rule: A clear target beats raw speed.
questions.teaches: A clear target makes slow searching efficient: knowing what you want lets you pass over most of the material quickly and stop only where it matters.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: True or false: The authors would agree that, because speed is not the main obstacle to understanding hard books, speed reading skills are worthless.
questions.explain: The authors are wholly in favour of faster reading where material deserves it, and say speed skills can solve the problem of reading slowly what deserves a fast reading. Speed is one tool, not the main key to hard books.
questions.rule: Speed is useful, but not the main key.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: True or false: In a careful, analytical reading, every part of a good book should be read at the same slow pace.
questions.explain: Even careful reading varies its pace within a book. The card next explains which parts go quickly and which slowly.
questions.rule: Careful reading still varies its pace.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Why is inspectional reading fast, according to the authors? Select all that apply.
options: You skip the book's hardest ideas for good
You read faster
You read only the first chapter
You read less of the book
You read differently, with different goals
optionExplain: Inspection passes over difficulties for now; it does not abandon them for good.
Right: the authors grant that you do read faster.
Inspection samples across the whole book, including the last pages, not only the start.
Right: you read less of the book when inspecting it.
Right: inspection reads differently, aiming to size the book up.
questions.explain: Speed is only part of it. Inspection is quick mostly because it covers less of the book, in a different way, for different ends.
questions.rule: Inspection is fast because it reads less, differently.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: During a careful reading of a law textbook, Ola reaches a page of transitional summary and then a dense section defining negligence. How should her pace change?
options: Keep the same careful pace throughout
Slow down for the summary and speed up for the definition
Quick through the summary, slow on the definition
Skip both, since neither is a main chapter
optionExplain: A single careful pace wastes time on the connecting material.
This reverses the advice: connecting material goes fast and difficult matter slow.
Right: interstitial material can be read quickly, while difficult matter deserves very slow reading.
Skipping is not the advice; in analytical reading you vary speed, you do not drop parts.
questions.explain: Within an analytical reading, interstitial material goes fast and the hard core goes slowly. The summary is connecting material; the definition is the core.
questions.rule: Fast on the connecting parts, slow on the core.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: You are reading a serious book on climate science analytically. Sort each part by the pace it deserves.

items.t: A recap of the previous chapter
A paragraph previewing what comes next
A story about the author's field trip that sets the scene
The definition of climate sensitivity
The argument for why feedback loops amplify warming
A key equation explained in words

questions.explain: Recaps, previews and scene-setting connect the main points and can be read quickly. Definitions, central arguments and key explanations are the difficult matter that deserves slow reading.
questions.rule: Find the core and give it the time.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: A journalist reviews a three-hour hearing transcript for a story. Applying the authors' idea of varied speed, what should she do?
options: Read the whole transcript at one pace, word by word
Speed through procedure and slow down for key testimony
Read only the first hour, where the main points usually are
Read every page as fast as she can, to cover it all
optionExplain: One pace wastes time on the procedural talk.
Right: the connecting stretches go fast, and the passages that carry the substance go slowly.
The key testimony may come at any point; the advice is to vary speed, not to cut the document short.
Racing through all of it risks missing the testimony that matters.
questions.explain: The advice about connecting material and hard core applies to any long document. Procedural exchanges connect; key testimony is the substance.
questions.rule: In any long document, vary the pace with the substance.
questions.teaches: Varied pacing within one work applies to any long document: procedural or connecting stretches go fast, and the passages that carry the substance go slow.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Arun decides that, because interstitial material can be read quickly, he will skip every passage that looks like filler during his analytical reading. What risk does he run?
options: No real risk, since filler adds little to a book
He will end up reading the whole book too slowly
He will understand the book better for the time saved
Missing a passage that looked like filler but mattered
optionExplain: Connecting material links the main points; dropping it can hide how they connect.
Skipping makes him faster, not slower; the risk lies elsewhere.
Saving time does not help understanding if something important was cut.
Right: judging filler can err, and the authors say interstitial material should be read quickly, not left out.
questions.explain: The authors say interstitial material can and should be read quickly. Skipping it is a different act, and a misjudged passage may carry something the argument needs.
questions.rule: Read connecting material quickly; do not drop it.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: What do the eyes of an untrained reader typically do along a line of print?
options: Stop several times per line, a word or two at each stop
Glide smoothly and steadily from left to right
Take in the whole line in a single glance
Read each word twice before moving to the next
optionExplain: Right: eye-movement films show untrained eyes stopping as many as five or six times per line.
It feels smooth from the inside, but the eye moves in jumps and stops.
Taking in a line at a glance is what the mind could manage, not what untrained eyes do.
Untrained eyes do go back sometimes, but not to every word.
questions.explain: Eyes move in jumps and see only when they stop. The card next names the habits that slow readers down.
questions.rule: Eyes read in stops, not in a glide.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Silently sounding the words while reading
A stop of the eyes on the line
The eyes going back to words already read
questions.explain: Sub-vocalizing ties reading to the speed of speech; fixations break a line into small pieces; regressions repeat ground already covered. And the eye sees only while it is still.
questions.rule: Know the three slow habits by name.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Filmed reading, Sara's eyes stop six times per line and go back to an earlier phrase every two lines. How would the authors describe her?
options: A careful, expert reader taking her time over each line of text
A reader whose eyesight is weak and needs correction
One with the fixations and regressions of an untrained reader
A reader who has stopped sub-vocalizing the words
optionExplain: Many stops can look careful, but they are the habit of untrained eyes, not a mark of expertise.
Eye stops and regressions are habits of reading, not signs of poor vision.
Right: five or six stops per line and a regression every two or three lines are the patterns the authors describe.
The film shows eye movements; it says nothing about whether she sounds out the words.
questions.explain: Her pattern matches the authors' description: up to six fixations per line and a regression every two or three lines.
questions.rule: Many stops and jumps back mark untrained eyes.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the eye takes in print while it moves across the line as well as when it stops.
questions.explain: The authors say the eye is blind while it moves; it can only see when it stops. That is why the number of stops matters.
questions.rule: The eye sees only when it stops.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Watching a foreign film, Noor's eyes stop on almost every word of the subtitles, and she keeps losing the end of a line before it vanishes. What best explains this?
options: The subtitles are badly translated, which makes them hard to follow
With a stop for nearly every word, each line takes many stops
She regresses too little and should go back more
Subtitles stay on screen too briefly for most viewers
optionExplain: Translation quality affects meaning, not how many times her eyes stop.
Right: with a stop for almost every word, a line takes more stops than the time on screen allows.
More jumping back would cost her even more time.
Many viewers read subtitles in the time given, so the trouble lies in her eye habits.
questions.explain: Since the eye sees only when it stops, a reader who fixates on almost every word needs many stops per line. Under time pressure, that limit shows at once.
questions.rule: Fewer, wider stops let the eye keep up.
questions.teaches: Because the eye sees only when it stops, the number of stops per line, not the speed of each jump, sets how much text a reader takes in per second.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Suppose a course cures Noor of fixating on every word and of regressing. What will that change, on the authors' account?
options: Her understanding of difficult arguments
Little, since eye habits barely affect reading speed
Her ability to judge whether the book is true
How fast she takes in words, not how well she understands
optionExplain: Understanding arguments is a matter of comprehension, which eye training does not supply.
The authors say these habits cut down reading speed, so curing them changes something real.
Judging truth needs understanding first, and eye training does not supply understanding.
Right: correcting fixations and regressions removes a limit on speed; comprehension is a separate problem.
questions.explain: Fixations and regressions are habits of the eye at the elementary level. Correcting them raises speed; comprehension depends on other skills.
questions.rule: Eye training speeds reading; it does not supply understanding.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: True or false: The mind can take in a whole sentence at a glance, provided the eyes supply it.
questions.explain: The mind works in larger units than the eye usually feeds it. The card next explains what follows for reading speed.
questions.rule: The mind can take in more than the eye gives it.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Once fixations and regressions are corrected, you can read as fast as your ____ will let you, not as slowly as your eyes make you.
questions.explain: With the eye habits corrected, the limit on speed moves from the eyes to the mind.
questions.rule: Let the mind set the limit.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: A reader's eyes stop five times per line, though she understands the light novels she reads with ease. What does the authors' account suggest is limiting her speed?
options: The difficulty of the novels
Her vocabulary
Her eyes, not her mind
Her mind's capacity
optionExplain: The novels are easy for her, so difficulty is not the limit.
She understands with ease, so her vocabulary is not holding her back.
Right: her mind could take in more, but her eyes feed it a word or two at a time.
Her easy understanding suggests her mind has capacity to spare.
questions.explain: When understanding is easy but speed is low, the eyes are the bottleneck. Correcting fixations would let her mind set the pace.
questions.rule: Easy understanding but slow reading points to the eyes.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Which statements fit the authors' account of fixations and regressions? Select all that apply.
options: The mind can grasp a sentence or a paragraph at a glance
Correcting them is the primary task that speed courses recognize
Correcting them is very hard and takes years of training
The mind, like the eye, must take in one word at a time
They are wasteful habits that cut down reading speed
optionExplain: Right: the mind can take in large units if the eyes supply them.
Right: all speed courses recognize this as the primary task.
The authors say the correction can be done quite easily.
This reverses the point: the mind, unlike the eye, does not need to read a word at a time.
Right: the authors call them wasteful because they slow reading.
questions.explain: The habits waste time because the mind can take in far more than a word at a time. Correcting them is the main and fairly easy task of speed training.
questions.rule: The eye is the bottleneck, and it can be fixed.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: After training, Ola's eyes no longer hold her back. She now turns to a dense philosophical argument. What should set her pace?
options: Her eyes' new top speed, since they are now trained
The fastest rate she reached during her training sessions
A fixed target of 400 words a minute for every text
Her mind, which needs a slower pace for hard material
optionExplain: Her eyes can now go fast, but speed of the eyes is no longer the limit that matters.
A training record was set on practice material, not on hard arguments.
A fixed target ignores the material, which the authors want to decide the speed.
Right: once the eyes are trained, the mind sets the pace, and the mind slows for difficult matter.
questions.explain: Removing the eye bottleneck does not make every text fast. It means the mind, working at the speed the material allows, sets the pace.
questions.rule: Trained eyes still follow the mind's pace.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: An experienced pianist reads a score a whole phrase at a time, while a beginner reads it note by note. How does this parallel the authors' account of reading?
options: The beginner's eyes take in too little to feed the mind
The pianist has faster fingers, which is all that differs
The beginner's hearing is untrained, so the score means less
Music is unlike reading, so the parallel fails
optionExplain: Right: as in the authors' account of reading, eyes that take in one small unit per stop hold back a mind that could take in more.
Fingers matter for playing, but the difference described is in how the score is read.
Hearing may differ too, but the case turns on the size of the units taken in.
Reading a score is reading by eye, so the authors' point about eye units applies.
questions.explain: The beginner's eyes feed one note at a time; the pianist's feed a phrase. The same eye bottleneck the authors describe in reading appears in reading music.
questions.rule: Larger units per glance free the mind.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the authors' point about eye units carries over to other reading by eye, such as reading music: taking in larger units per glance lets the mind set the pace.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Which tool do the authors say is usually all you need to break the habit of eye fixations?
options: An expensive reading machine
A metronome set to a fast beat
Your own hand
A ruler held under each line
optionExplain: Such devices exist, but the authors say they are usually not necessary.
A beat can pace you, but the authors point to something simpler that guides the eyes along the line.
Right: your own hand, used as a moving pointer, is usually enough.
A ruler marks the line but does not move ahead of your eyes to pull them along.
questions.explain: Complicated devices are rarely needed. The card next shows how to use your hand.
questions.rule: The simplest pacer is your hand.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Put the steps of the authors' hand-pointer method in order.
items: Put your thumb and first two fingers together
Sweep the pointer across a line a little faster than is comfortable
Force your eyes to keep up with your hand
Keep practising and increase the speed of your hand
questions.explain: You form the pointer, set it moving slightly too fast, make your eyes keep up, and then raise the speed over time.
questions.rule: Form, sweep, keep up, speed up.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Lena sweeps her hand across each line at a pace her eyes find easy, and after a month her reading speed has not changed. What is she doing wrong?
options: Her hand should move a little faster than is comfortable
She should use a ruler, which guides better than a hand
She should move her hand more slowly, to keep up easily
She should have stopped after the first week of practice
optionExplain: Right: the method works by setting a pace just beyond comfort and raising it with practice.
The tool is not the issue; the pace is.
Slowing down removes the push that the method depends on.
Stopping early would end the practice that builds speed.
questions.explain: A comfortable pace lets the eyes keep their old habits. The pointer must stay a little ahead of comfort, and get faster as the eyes adapt.
questions.hint: How fast should the hand move compared with the eyes' comfort?
questions.rule: Pace the hand just beyond comfort.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: True or false: The authors advise moving the pointer at whatever speed feels comfortable for your eyes.
questions.explain: The authors say to sweep the pointer a little faster than is comfortable for your eyes and force yourself to keep up. Comfort is what keeps old habits in place.
questions.rule: The pointer leads; the eyes follow.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Kai reads on a tablet app that moves a highlight steadily down the text, a little faster than he likes. Besides fixations, which bad habit is a steadily moving guide likely to curb?
options: Sub-vocalizing, the silent sounding-out of each word
Regressions, since the guide leaves no time to jump back
Skipping the index and blurb when skimming a book
Reading too slowly on the hardest passages of a book
optionExplain: Sub-vocalizing is a separate habit, and a moving guide is not aimed at it.
Right: a guide that keeps moving forward leaves no room for the eyes to go back.
Using the index and blurb belongs to skimming a book, not to habits of the eye.
Hard material deserves slow reading; the guide is not meant to speed that up.
questions.explain: Like the hand, a moving guide sets a forward pace. Eyes busy keeping up with it have no time to wander back, so regressions fall too.
questions.rule: A forward-moving pacer discourages jumping back.
questions.teaches: A moving pacer also curbs regressions: eyes that must keep up with a guide moving forward have no time to jump back to what they have read.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Sam has trebled his speed with the pointer and now sweeps it at top pace across a difficult philosophy text he wants to understand fully. What does the authors' wider advice say?
options: Carry on, since faster reading is better for every text
He should sweep even faster to push his limits further
Slow down: the text deserves slow reading, whatever his top speed
Keep the top speed, and reread later if anything is unclear to him
optionExplain: The authors reject one speed for everything; difficult matter deserves slow reading.
Speed training belongs to practice material, not to a text he must understand fully.
Right: the pointer removes an eye limit, but the material still decides how fast to read it.
Racing now and rereading later spends the first pass at a pace the text does not allow; the authors would have him slow down now.
questions.explain: The pointer is a tool for the eyes. The authors' wider advice is to read each thing at the speed it deserves, which for a hard text is slow.
questions.rule: Trained speed is a range, not a fixed setting.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: True or false: Being able to answer factual questions about what a text says shows that you have fully comprehended it.
questions.explain: Factual recall is only the first layer of comprehension. The card next explains what more is involved.
questions.rule: Recall of facts is not full comprehension.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: According to the authors, what does following your hand or another timer improve, besides reading rate?
options: Your vocabulary
Your memory for dates and names
Your concentration
Your judgment of arguments
optionExplain: A pacer moves the eyes; it does not teach new words.
Nothing in the method trains memory for particular facts.
Right: while you follow your hand, it is harder to doze, daydream or let your mind wander.
Judging arguments needs comprehension, which concentration alone does little for.
questions.explain: A pacer keeps attention on the page. That is concentration, which the authors equate with activity in reading.
questions.rule: Pacing helps concentration.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: A speed course reports that its graduates score 90 percent on comprehension quizzes asking who did what in a passage. What would the authors say about this evidence?
options: It shows only elementary comprehension: what the text says
It proves full comprehension rose along with speed
It proves the course has failed its students
It shows that the students' concentration has fallen
optionExplain: Right: who-did-what questions test the limited kind of comprehension, the ability to say what a text says.
The quiz asks only factual questions, which show the elementary layer.
The authors grant there is some basis for the claims; the evidence is limited, not worthless.
High factual scores fit improved concentration rather than reduced.
questions.explain: Factual quizzes measure the elementary ability to answer what a text says. The further questions that show higher comprehension are the ones speed courses seldom ask.
questions.rule: Ask what the test really measures.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Sort each task: does it show elementary comprehension (what the text says), or higher comprehension?

items.t: Naming the three examples the author gives
Stating the year in which the events took place
Listing the people mentioned in a chapter
Explaining what the author means by a key term
Showing how the conclusion follows from the reasons given
Saying what problem the book is trying to solve

questions.explain: Factual items answer what the text says. Explaining meanings, reasoning and purpose takes a reader beyond that elementary level.
questions.rule: Higher comprehension explains; elementary comprehension reports.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: A clinic checks that patients understand a consent form by asking them to repeat the risks it lists. Applying the authors' distinction, what does this check miss?
options: Whether the patients read the form quickly enough
Whether patients can explain what the risks mean for them
Whether the patients were concentrating while they read
Little, since repeating the risks shows full understanding
optionExplain: Speed is not what the clinic needs to know about.
Right: repeating the list shows what the form says; explaining meaning and reasons shows higher comprehension.
Concentration helps, but the authors say it alone does little for comprehension.
Repetition shows only the elementary layer of understanding.
questions.explain: Repeating what a text says is the elementary layer. Understanding shows when a reader can explain meaning and reasons.
questions.rule: Test understanding with why and what-it-means questions.
questions.teaches: Comprehension beyond the elementary shows when a reader can explain meanings and reasons, not only repeat what was said; a test of repetition measures only the first layer.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: True or false: Because concentration alone does little for comprehension, the authors treat concentration as unimportant in reading.
questions.explain: Concentration is another name for activity in reading, which the authors prize: the good reader reads actively, with concentration. It is necessary but not enough for comprehension.
questions.rule: Concentration is necessary, not sufficient.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: The Declaration of Independence is less than three pages long. In the authors' view, how long might a reading of its first two paragraphs for full comprehension take?
options: Days, weeks or even years
About five minutes, as for any short text
About an hour of careful attention
No longer than the rest of the document
optionExplain: Right: the authors say those paragraphs, properly read, might take days, weeks or even years.
Five minutes is enough to read the words, not to comprehend them.
An hour is a careful reading, but the authors suggest far more for full comprehension.
The authors say the opening paragraphs need far more than the rest.
questions.explain: Length is a poor guide to reading time. The card next shows how the authors divide the Declaration by the speed each part deserves.
questions.rule: Short is not the same as quick.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Sort each part of the Declaration of Independence by the pace the authors recommend.

items.t: The two pages of facts cited against the king
The closing pledge of lives, fortunes and honour
The first paragraph
The second paragraph
Words such as inalienable and consent

questions.explain: The list of facts and the closing flourish need only a general idea. The first two paragraphs, and their key words, carry the ideas and deserve slow, puzzled reading.
questions.rule: Lists and flourishes fast; core ideas slow.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: A company's annual report opens with two paragraphs on the firm's purpose, follows with forty pages of sales figures by region, and closes with the chair's stirring thanks. A reader wants to understand the firm's strategy. How should she pace it?
options: Slow on the opening statement, quick on the figures and the thanks
Slow on the figures, quick on the opening statement
One even pace from start to finish
Skip the opening, since statements of purpose are mostly empty rhetoric
optionExplain: Right: for her purpose, the statement of purpose is the core and the rest is support or flourish, as in the Declaration.
The figures support the strategy; for her purpose, a general idea of them is enough.
One pace ignores the difference between the core and the rest.
A statement of purpose can carry the central ideas, as the Declaration's opening does.
questions.explain: Like the Declaration, the report has a short core, a long body of supporting facts and a closing flourish. For understanding strategy, the core deserves the slow reading.
questions.rule: Find the short core and give it the time.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Suppose the reader of the Declaration is a scholar studying the circumstances in which Jefferson wrote. How does the authors' advice on the list of facts change?
options: It does not change: the facts can always be read quickly by anyone
The list can now be skipped, as he knows it already
Only the closing pledge now needs close reading
The facts may now deserve close reading, given the purpose
optionExplain: The authors make an exception for exactly this reader.
Skipping would remove the very material the scholar is studying.
The pledge is the rhetorical flourish; the change concerns the facts.
Right: the authors say a general idea of the facts is enough unless you are a scholar concerned with the historical circumstances.
questions.explain: The speed a passage deserves depends on why you read it. For a historian of the period, the facts are evidence and need close study.
questions.rule: Purpose can change what deserves slow reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: An app claims its users can finish any classic novel or treatise in an hour. Applying the authors' reasoning about the Declaration, what is the main flaw in this boast?
options: It treats speed as the goal, when comprehension is the issue
An hour is still too long for most busy readers
Classics should be read in print, not on a phone or tablet screen
Long texts are hard to follow on a small screen
optionExplain: Right: if two short paragraphs can need years, finishing a treatise in an hour says little about understanding it.
The issue is not that an hour is too long but that speed is the wrong measure.
The medium is beside the point; the flaw is treating speed as the goal.
Screens may be tiring, but the flaw lies in treating speed as the measure of reading.
questions.explain: The Declaration shows that comprehension, not speed, is the real issue. A boast about speed avoids the question of what a reader understands.
questions.rule: Ask what was understood, not how fast it was read.
questions.teaches: The authors conclude that the problem of speed reading is the problem of comprehension: the real task is to define understanding beyond the elementary level, which speed courses mostly do not attempt.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the Declaration's famous closing pledge deserves the same slow reading as its second paragraph.
questions.explain: Fame does not decide the pace. The authors treat the closing pledge as a rhetorical flourish that can be read quickly, while the second paragraph's ideas need slow reading.
questions.rule: Famous words are not always the core.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Which rule for the speed at which to read a book would the authors endorse?
options: As fast as you can, to get through more books
No slower than it deserves, no faster than you comprehend
At one steady pace, so you keep a rhythm
Fast for hard books, so you get through them
optionExplain: Top speed wastes books that deserve slow reading.
Right: this is the authors' formula, with a limit in each direction.
One steady pace ignores what different books deserve.
Hard books are where speed most costs comprehension.
questions.explain: A good rule has to limit speed in both directions. The card next gives the authors' formula.
questions.rule: Speed needs limits both ways.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Every book should be read no more slowly than it deserves, and no more quickly than you can read it with satisfaction and ____.
questions.explain: The upper limit on speed is set by satisfaction and comprehension; the lower limit by what the book deserves.
questions.rule: No slower than it deserves, no faster than you comprehend.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Which readers are following the authors' formula? Select all that apply.
options: A reader racing through a gripping thriller as fast as she still enjoys and follows it
A student speeding through a hard economics chapter too fast to follow its argument
A clerk spending an hour on a routine two-line office memo
A reader slowing right down for the hard core of a philosophy text
A reader going quickly through a trivial magazine
optionExplain: Right: she reads fast, but no faster than she can read with satisfaction and comprehension.
He breaks the upper limit: he reads faster than he can comprehend.
He breaks the lower limit: the memo deserves far less time.
Right: the hard core deserves slow reading, and slowing down keeps comprehension.
Right: the magazine deserves little time, and reading it fast honours that.
questions.explain: The formula has two limits. Too slow wastes time on what deserves little; too fast loses comprehension or satisfaction.
questions.hint: Check each reader against both limits.
questions.rule: Check both limits: deserves and comprehends.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Jon says that great reading speed is the mark of a great reader. What would the authors reply?
options: They would agree, since speed shows reading skill
They would say speed does not matter at all
Great speed is of value only for what is not worth reading
They would say that only slow readers ever truly understand books
optionExplain: The authors favour faster reading where it fits, but not speed as a badge of skill.
Speed does matter for material that deserves only a fast reading.
Right: this is the authors' summary verdict on great speed.
The authors want many speeds, not slowness as a virtue.
questions.explain: According to the authors, great speed is valuable only for what is not really worth reading. A great reader has many speeds and knows when to use each.
questions.rule: Speed alone is no mark of a good reader.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: A reader zips through a favourite poet's collection at great speed. She follows the literal sense of every line but takes no pleasure in any of it. Applying the formula, what should she conclude?
options: She read too fast: the formula also requires satisfaction
She read at the right speed, since she understood every line
Poetry is outside the formula, which is for prose
She should have skimmed instead of reading
optionExplain: Right: the upper limit is set by satisfaction as well as comprehension.
Understanding the literal sense meets only part of the upper limit.
The formula applies to every book.
Skimming would give even less of what she lost.
questions.explain: The formula limits speed by satisfaction and comprehension. Reading so fast that enjoyment vanishes breaks it, even if the words are understood.
questions.rule: Too fast to enjoy is too fast.
questions.teaches: Satisfaction is a separate test from comprehension: you can follow every word and still be reading too fast if the pleasure of the book is lost.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: True or false: Once you have found the right speed for a book, the formula says to hold that same speed from its first page to its last.
questions.explain: Different parts of a book deserve different speeds: connecting material can go quickly and difficult matter slowly. The formula applies passage by passage, not once per book.
questions.rule: Apply the formula as you go, not once.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: True or false: There is no point in skimming a book you have already decided to read carefully.
questions.explain: Even a book you will study closely is easier to read once you know its shape. The card next sums up the authors' advice.
questions.rule: Skimming helps even planned readings.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Which rule do the authors call the most important of all, the essence of inspectional reading?
options: Begin each skim with the index rather than with the title page
Read every book at the slowest speed it allows
Look up every unfamiliar word before reading on
Do not try to understand every page of a hard book at first
optionExplain: The index is one skimming step, not the essence of inspection.
The authors want many speeds, and inspection is fast.
Looking everything up is the habit the authors warn impedes a first reading.
Right: the authors call this the most important rule of all.
questions.explain: The essence of inspection is accepting partial understanding the first time. Trying to grasp every word and page defeats a first reading.
questions.rule: Do not demand everything the first time.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Yara must study a set textbook closely over a term. Before she starts chapter 1, what does the authors' summary advise?
options: Begin chapter 1 carefully, since skimming is only for books you may not read
Skim the whole textbook first for an idea of its form and structure
Read the last chapter carefully first, to see where it ends
Skip skimming, since a teacher has already chosen the book
optionExplain: Skimming is necessary for doubtful books but also worth doing for books you will read carefully.
Right: the authors say it is generally desirable to skim even a book you intend to read carefully.
The last pages are part of a skim, but a careful reading of the end first is not the advice.
Who chose the book does not change the value of seeing its form first.
questions.explain: Skimming has two uses: deciding whether to read a book, and seeing the form and structure of one you will read. Yara needs the second.
questions.rule: Skim to see the form of a book you will study.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Which attitudes fit the authors' summary advice for a first reading of a hard book? Select all that apply.
options: Racing through even the hardest book
Being willing to seem superficial
Insisting on mastering each page before moving on
Treating the first pass as preparation for a second
Putting off hard books until you feel ready
optionExplain: Right: the authors say to race through even the hardest book.
Right: do not be afraid to be, or to seem, superficial.
This is the opposite of the most important rule.
Right: the race-through prepares you to read the book well the second time.
Waiting is a form of expecting too much; the authors say no book for the general reader need cause despair.
questions.explain: The first reading of a hard book is quick, unafraid of superficiality, and aimed at preparing a good second reading.
questions.rule: Race first, read well second.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: A researcher has two weeks to survey thirty books on the history of vaccination for a review article. How does the authors' summary advice help her?
options: She should read all thirty analytically, one by one
She should read only the five newest books closely, since they are current
Skim all thirty, race through the best, study the few that matter
She should read random chapters to stay unbiased
optionExplain: Thirty careful readings will not fit in two weeks, and many books may not deserve one.
Newness is not the same as worth; skimming tests worth directly.
Right: skimming sorts the books, racing through gives a first grasp, and close reading goes where it pays.
Random sampling is the casual browsing systematic skimming replaces.
questions.explain: With many books on one subject, inspection is how a reader finds and prepares for the few that deserve close study.
questions.rule: With many books, inspect all and study few.
questions.teaches: Inspectional reading returns at the highest level: the authors say it plays an important role in syntopical reading, where many books on one subject must be surveyed.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: True or false: Racing through a hard book removes the need for a careful second reading if you want to understand it fully.
questions.explain: The race-through prepares you to read the book well the second time; it does not replace that reading. Seeming superficial is acceptable only because a better reading follows.
questions.rule: The race prepares the reading; it does not replace it.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Which part of a later, careful reading does a quick skim of a book most help to prepare?
options: Grasping the book's structure
Judging whether the book is true
Memorizing quotations from it
Comparing it with other books
optionExplain: Right: a skim shows the parts and their order, the beginning of grasping structure.
Judging comes last and needs full understanding, which no skim gives.
A skim reads too little for memorizing, and that is not its purpose.
Comparison belongs to syntopical reading; a skim of one book serves that book's reading first.
questions.explain: Skimming looks at the contents, the parts and the summaries, which is the raw material for seeing a book's structure. The card next links each inspectional step to a stage of analytical reading.
questions.rule: A skim is a first look at structure.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Match each inspectional step to what it anticipates in analytical reading.
pairs: The first step in interpreting the book's contents
Anticipations of steps in analytical reading
questions.explain: Skimming prepares the first stage of analytical reading, which deals with structure. Superficial reading prepares the second, which interprets the contents.
questions.rule: Skim for structure; read through for contents.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Lila skimmed a book on climate economics and noted from the contents that it moves from causes, to costs, to policies. When she later reads it analytically, where does this note help most?
options: In judging whether the author is right
In spotting printing errors and typos
In stating the structure in the first stage
Nowhere, since analytical reading starts afresh
optionExplain: Judging comes after understanding; the note concerns structure.
Error-spotting is not a stage of analytical reading.
Right: skimming anticipates the comprehension of a book's structure, the work of the first stage.
The levels are cumulative, so what inspection found carries forward.
questions.explain: Her note is a first sketch of the book's structure, which is exactly what the first stage of analytical reading must state.
questions.rule: Carry the skim's sketch into the first stage.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: Superficial reading prepares for the second stage of analytical reading. Which description fits that second stage?
options: Judging whether the author's conclusions are right
Interpreting the contents: its terms, propositions and arguments
Placing the book in a category with others of its kind
Comparing the book with other books on the same subject
optionExplain: Judging comes after interpretation, in a later stage.
Right: the second stage interprets the contents, which a first read-through begins.
Classifying the book belongs to the first stage, with structure.
Comparing books is syntopical reading, the fourth level.
questions.explain: The second stage of analytical reading interprets the book's contents. A straight-through first reading gives it a start: you already know what you understood and what you passed over.
questions.rule: A first reading starts the interpretation.
questions.teaches: The first stage of analytical reading asks what the book is about as a whole and how its parts are arranged; the second interprets what it says, through its terms, propositions and arguments.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: An engineer must review a 200-page technical specification in depth next week. Today she skims its sections and reads it through once without stopping at the hard parts. How does this help next week's review?
options: It replaces the review, which she can now skip safely
It wastes time she should have spent on the detailed review itself
It lets her judge the design's soundness already
She starts with a sketch of the structure and a first grasp
optionExplain: A skim and a first pass prepare a careful review; they do not replace it.
The preparation makes the detailed review faster and better aimed.
Judging soundness needs the detailed reading still to come.
Right: the skim anticipates the structure and the read-through begins the interpretation.
questions.explain: The inspectional steps prepare deep work on any complex document. A structural sketch and a first pass give the detailed review a map and a start.
questions.rule: Inspect before any deep review.
questions.teaches: The inspectional steps prepare deep work on any complex document, not only books: a structural sketch and a first pass make the detailed review faster and better aimed.

questions.unitTitle: The Second Level of Reading: Inspectional Reading
questions.q: True or false: A good skim gives you a finished outline of a book, so the structure stage of analytical reading can be skipped.
questions.explain: Skimming anticipates the grasp of structure; it does not complete it. The first stage of analytical reading still has to state the book's structure properly.
questions.rule: A sketch is not an outline.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: According to the authors, what mainly decides whether a reader stays awake over a book?
options: How bright the reading light is, since dim light strains the eyes
How comfortable the chair or bed is, since comfort invites dozing
Whether reading the book matters to the reader's goal
How short the chapters are, since short ones hold attention
optionExplain: Poor light is part of the authors' joke recipe for sleep, but candlelight readers stayed awake in dim light, so light is not the deciding factor.
Comfort helps you doze, but the authors note people stay awake in comfortable chairs and even in bed.
Right: what kept the candlelight readers awake was that it made a great difference to them whether they read the book.
Short chapters may feel easier, but the authors locate the cause in the reader's aim, not the book's layout.
questions.explain: The authors say staying awake depends largely on your goal in reading. The card next shows what that goal demands.
questions.rule: Your aim, more than your setting, keeps you awake.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, letting your mind wander during time set aside for reading to understand is as self-defeating as falling asleep.
questions.explain: The authors treat falling asleep and letting the mind wander as the same thing: both defeat the purpose of hours planned for reading for profit.
questions.rule: A wandering mind is a sleeping reader.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: A student blocks out two hours for a philosophy text, keeps checking her phone, and finishes the chapter unable to say what it argued. Which diagnosis fits the authors' view?
options: She picked the wrong time of day to read
She had no way of making her mind work on the text
Philosophy cannot be read in a two-hour block
She should have chosen a book read for pleasure
optionExplain: Timing can matter, but the authors place the failure in what the mind is doing, not the hour on the clock.
Right: the authors say such readers fail because they do not know how to make their mind do the work that earns the profit.
The length of the session is not the issue the authors raise; a reader can drift in ten minutes or two hours.
Switching to entertainment abandons the goal she set; the authors want her to meet it, not lower it.
questions.explain: She had a plan and a good book, so will and choice were present. What was missing is the know-how to keep her mind on the work, which is the authors' explanation for failed reading plans.
questions.hint: She had the plan and the book. What did she lack?
questions.rule: Failed reading plans usually lack method, not intention.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: Sort each reading situation by whether the authors' demand to read actively and stay awake applies to it.
groups: Reading for profit: the demand applies
Reading to relax or satisfy curiosity: it does not

items.t: Studying a book on economics to understand inflation
Working through a biography to grasp why a leader acted as she did
Rereading a classic novel to understand its view of justice
Paging through a thriller on a long flight to pass the time
Glancing at a magazine to catch up on celebrity gossip
Checking the sports page for last night's score

questions.explain: The authors ask for active, wakeful reading when the aim is to grow in understanding, and they say good books of fiction or nonfiction deserve it. Reading for entertainment or to satisfy curiosity is a different aim and does not carry the same demand.
questions.rule: The demand to stay awake comes with the aim of understanding.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
