questions.q: Ben moves from reading a dense book in bed to reading it in a quiet library, but he still has no aim beyond getting through it. Following the authors' argument, what should we expect?
options: He may still drift, since the room gives him no goal or skill
He will stay alert, because a library is built for study
He will understand more, because libraries reduce eyestrain
He will fall asleep faster, because libraries are quiet
optionExplain: Right: the authors say a comfortable library chair will put an expert napper to sleep any time; what changes wakefulness is the reader's aim and method.
A study setting looks helpful, but the authors joke that a comfortable library chair works as well as bed for dozing off.
Better light removes one discomfort, yet the authors show readers staying awake in dim light and sleeping in good light.
The authors do not claim quiet speeds sleep; they say the setting is not what decides it.
questions.explain: Changing the conditions does not change the cause. The authors tie wakefulness to whether the reading matters to you and whether you know how to work at it.
questions.rule: Change the aim and the method, not only the room.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: A manager has a long industry white paper to absorb before a strategy meeting and keeps losing her place. Applying the authors' reasoning, which change is most likely to keep her mind awake?
options: Printing it in a larger font so it is easier on the eyes
Reading it late at night, when the office is quiet and calm
Reading it faster so she finishes before attention fades
Setting questions for it to answer about what she needs
optionExplain: Larger type eases the eyes, but the authors show that physical conditions do not decide whether the mind works.
Quiet is a setting change; the authors' point is that settings do not supply a goal or a method.
Racing through gives the mind less to do, not more, so it is likely to drift just the same.
Right: a clear aim plus questions to answer gives her mind the work that keeps it awake, which is where the authors' prescription leads.
questions.explain: Her reading has a real purpose, so the authors' demand applies. A goal turned into questions gives the mind something to do, which is the remedy the next idea names.
questions.rule: Turn your purpose into questions the text must answer.
questions.teaches: Naming in advance what you need from a text is part of reading for profit: a stated aim tells you what to ask of the text and lets you see when your effort has been repaid.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: Which habit do the authors treat as the heart of active reading?
options: Asking questions and trying to answer them while reading
Reading every sentence slowly and carefully, without skipping
Rereading each chapter as soon as it ends, to fix it
Looking up every unfamiliar word the moment it appears
optionExplain: Right: the authors' one prescription for active reading is to ask questions you must try to answer as you read.
Slowness can help, but a slow reader can be as passive as a fast one; speed is not what the authors name.
Rereading may help later, but it is not the single prescription the authors give.
Checking words supports understanding, yet a reader can define every word and still ask the book nothing.
questions.explain: The authors boil active reading down to asking questions while reading and trying to answer them. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Active reading means questioning the book.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: According to the authors, the undemanding reader asks no questions, and so gets no ____.
questions.explain: The difference between demanding and undemanding readers comes down to asking: a reader who asks nothing receives nothing from the book.
questions.rule: No questions, no answers.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: Lena reads a newspaper investigation into hospital waiting times. Which approach best matches the authors' prescription?
options: Reading it twice quickly so that the facts sink in better
Highlighting every figure it reports so none is overlooked
Asking what it claims and how it backs that up, and answering
Writing down her feelings about hospitals before starting
optionExplain: Repetition without questions is still passive; two fast passes may leave the same blanks.
Marking numbers records details but asks nothing about what they show.
Right: she is asking questions while reading and working to answer them, which is the authors' one prescription.
Her prior feelings may matter later, but they are not questions put to the text in the course of reading.
questions.explain: The prescription has two parts: ask questions as you read and try to answer them. Only the third approach does both.
questions.rule: Question the text as you go, and answer as you go.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: Raj changes his method: he still jots a question after each section of a report, but leaves all of them unanswered until some later day. According to the authors, what has he given up?
options: Nothing, since asking is the whole of the prescription
The habit of reading the sections in their proper order
The chance to check his questions with a colleague first
The half that says to answer them in the course of reading
optionExplain: Asking feels like the active part, but the authors say the questions are ones you must try to answer while reading.
He still reads in order; the order of sections is not what changed.
Talking with a colleague may be useful, but the authors' prescription is about the reader answering for himself.
Right: the authors specify questions you yourself must try to answer in the course of reading; postponing every answer drops that half.
questions.explain: Questions alone do not make reading active. The authors pair asking with trying to answer, during the reading itself.
questions.hint: The prescription has two halves.
questions.rule: A question earns its keep when you try to answer it.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a quick inspectional reading of a book is passive, since it does not go deep.
questions.explain: The authors say inspectional reading is always active and effortful. What makes reading active is the questioning, not how slowly or deeply you go.
questions.rule: Active means questioning, not slow.
questions.teaches: Even quick inspectional reading counts as active reading: activity comes from questioning the book, not from depth or slowness.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: A client emails a long proposal for changes to a service agreement. Applying the demanding-reader habit, what should you do as you read it?
options: Read it once straight through and reply with first impressions
Ask what it proposes and why, and try to answer before replying
Count how many changes it asks for, to judge how big it is
Forward it to a colleague to read and summarise for you
optionExplain: A single straight read with first impressions is the undemanding approach; nothing has been asked of the text.
Right: questioning the proposal as you read, and answering, is the authors' prescription applied to a business text.
A count is a fact about the email, not an answer to what it claims or why.
Handing it on avoids reading altogether; the prescription asks you to do the questioning yourself.
questions.explain: The prescription is not limited to books. Any text you need to understand yields more when you question it and work out the answers.
questions.rule: Question any text you need to understand.
questions.teaches: Questioning puts the reader in charge: instead of waiting for a text to make its point, you decide what you need from it and check whether it delivers, which is what makes reading demanding rather than passive.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: Which of these are among the four basic questions the authors say a reader should ask of a book? Select all that apply.
options: What is the book about as a whole?
Is the book true, in whole or part?
How many copies has the book sold?
What of it?
Who published the book?
optionExplain: Right: this is the first of the four questions.
Right: this is the third question.
Sales figures are a natural thing to wonder about, but popularity tells you nothing about what a book says or whether it is true.
Right: this is the fourth question, about significance.
The publisher is a fact about the book's production, not about its meaning or truth.
questions.explain: Three of these are among the four questions; the fourth, what is being said in detail and how, is missing from the list. The card next sets out all four.
questions.rule: The questions concern meaning, truth and significance.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: Put the four basic questions in the order the authors give them.
items: What is the book about as a whole?
What is being said in detail, and how?
Is the book true, in whole or part?
What of it?
questions.explain: The two questions of understanding come first, then the question of truth, then the question of significance.
questions.rule: Whole, detail, truth, significance.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: A reader makes four notes on a book about how cities grow. Match each note to the basic question it answers.
pairs: It is about how cities grow, in three stages
What is the book about as a whole?
The author defines density and argues that it drives new ideas
What is being said in detail, and how?
The case on housing costs is weak, though the case on transport holds
Is the book true, in whole or part?
If this holds, my town's zoning plan needs a rethink
questions.explain: A one-line theme answers the first question, the author's terms and arguments answer the second, a verdict on parts answers the third, and consequences for the reader answer the fourth.
questions.rule: Each note should know which question it answers.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: A reader logs her work on a diet book. Step 1: decided the book is wrong about sugar. Step 2: worked out what the book is about as a whole. Step 3: listed its main arguments. Step 4: asked what it means for her meals. Which step is out of place?
options: Step 4, because significance is a matter for the author, not the reader
Step 1, since the truth question waits for the first two
Step 2, because the whole should come after the details
None, because the four questions can be asked in any order
optionExplain: The fourth question explicitly asks whether the book matters to you, so the reader's own concerns belong there.
Right: she judged the book's truth before finding out what it says, reversing the authors' order.
The authors put the whole first: you grasp the leading theme, then the detailed message.
The authors call the art of reading the habit of asking the right questions in the right order, so order matters.
questions.explain: Deciding the book is wrong is an answer to the third question. She gave it before answering the first two, so she judged something she had not yet understood.
questions.hint: Which step is a verdict?
questions.rule: Understand first, judge second.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the four questions sum up the whole of what a reader owes a book.
questions.explain: The authors say the four questions summarize the whole obligation of a reader. The many rules that come later are ways of answering them well.
questions.rule: Four questions, one whole obligation.
questions.teaches: The authors call the four questions a summary of the reader's whole obligation; every later rule of reading serves one of them.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: A book club picks a novel. One member insists on asking of it, unchanged, what assertions and arguments make up the author's message. What do the authors advise?
options: Use the questions unchanged, since they fit any book in the same form
Drop the questions, since a novel cannot be read actively
Adapt the questions, since as stated they suit expository books
Ask only the fourth question, since novels have no theme
optionExplain: The questions do reach fiction, but the authors say they need adapting first; a question about assertions and arguments fits a treatise better than a story.
The authors expect fiction to be read actively too; they adapt the questions rather than abandon them.
Right: the authors note that the four questions, as stated, apply mainly to expository works and need adaptation for fiction and poetry.
A novel has a whole and a structure worth grasping; the authors adapt all four questions, not just the last.
questions.explain: The authors' footnote says the questions as stated suit nonfiction and, adapted, also apply to fiction and poetry, with the adaptations given in later chapters.
questions.rule: Adapt the four questions before putting them to a story or poem.
questions.teaches: A novel does not set out assertions and arguments the way an expository book does, so the question about the author's message has to be reshaped before it fits a story.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a serious reader who fully understands a book may stop there without deciding whether it is true.
questions.explain: The authors say that once you understand a book, you are obliged, if reading seriously, to make up your own mind. The card next explains the timing.
questions.rule: Understanding brings a duty to judge.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: What reason do the authors give for making the truth question wait until the first two are answered?
options: You must know what is said before deciding if it is true
Judging truth takes much longer than understanding does
Truth is a matter of taste, so it is the less urgent question
The author's reputation has to be checked before anything else
optionExplain: Right: the authors say you cannot decide whether something is true until you know what is being said.
Time is not the reason; the problem is that judging comes out wrong without understanding.
The authors treat truth as something a serious reader must decide, not as a matter of taste.
Reputation is not part of the four questions; the order rests on understanding the text itself.
questions.explain: A judgment needs an object. Until you know what the book says, any verdict is about something other than the book.
questions.rule: Know what is said before deciding if it is true.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: Omar reads the first chapter of a book on transport policy and posts that its argument is wrong. He has not yet found out what its main proposals are. How does the authors' order of questions bear on his post?
options: It supports him, since first impressions are the most honest
It allows the post as long as he labels it provisional
It requires him to agree with the author until he finishes
It makes the post premature, as he does not yet know what it says
optionExplain: Honest impressions can still be about a book he has misread; honesty does not replace understanding.
A label does not fix the problem that he does not yet know the proposals he is judging.
Agreeing without understanding is as unjustified as disagreeing; the order delays every verdict, not only negative ones.
Right: he is answering the third question before the first two, so he is judging something he does not yet know.
questions.explain: The truth question depends on the first two. Omar does not yet know the book's main proposals, so his verdict has nothing solid to rest on.
questions.rule: No verdict before the first two answers.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: Which of these readers have met the authors' demand for the third question? Select all that apply.
options: A reader who restates a book's argument, then says which parts hold and which fail
A reader who summarises the author's view carefully and accurately, then stops there
A reader who understands a book and agrees with all of it, giving reasons
A reader who rejects a book after reading its title and its cover blurb
A reader who understands a book and concludes one key claim is unsupported
optionExplain: Right: she understood first and then judged the book true in part.
A careful summary is the work of the first two questions; knowing the author's mind is not enough for the third.
Right: agreeing is also a verdict, and she reached it after understanding.
Rejecting a book from its cover is a verdict without understanding, the error the order forbids.
Right: a partial verdict after understanding meets the question, which asks about truth in whole or part.
questions.explain: The third question needs both understanding and a verdict of one's own. That verdict can be agreement, disagreement or a judgment in part.
questions.rule: Understand, then decide, wholly or in part.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: True or false: If the text is a short newspaper editorial instead of a long book, the authors' order lets you judge whether it is true before working out what it says.
questions.explain: The order rests on a logical dependence, not on length: you still need to know what is said before deciding whether it holds. A shorter text makes the first two questions quicker to answer, not unnecessary, and the authors apply the four questions to articles as well as books.
questions.rule: Length changes the time, not the order.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: A friend asks whether the tenancy agreement she has been offered is fair. Following the authors' rule for the truth question, what should come first?
options: Judging it by what past tenants say about the landlord online
Comparing its length and layout with other standard leases
Working out what each clause commits her to, then judging it
Accepting it if similar leases are widely signed in her area
optionExplain: Reviews describe the landlord, not what this document says.
Length and layout say nothing about what the clauses require.
Right: understanding what the document says comes before judging it, just as with a book.
How widely a lease is used says nothing about whether this one is fair to her; she still has to know what its clauses require.
questions.explain: Judging a contract's fairness is a truth-style verdict. It needs an understanding of what the clauses actually require, which is the authors' order applied outside books.
questions.rule: Read what a document commits you to before judging it.
questions.teaches: Understand-then-judge applies to any document you must evaluate: judging a contract's fairness before working out what its clauses require is the same mistake as judging a book before knowing what it says.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: After understanding a book and deciding how far it is true, what do the authors say a reader should still ask?
options: Who the author's main rivals in the field are
What of it: why it matters and what follows
How the book compares with others by the same author
Whether the book is pleasant and easy to read
optionExplain: Rivals may be interesting background, but they are not part of the reader's four questions.
Right: the fourth question asks about significance, and what further follows.
Comparing an author's books is a later, syntopical kind of task, not the fourth question about this book.
Pleasure is a fair reaction, but the fourth question asks about importance, not enjoyment.
questions.explain: The last of the four questions is what of it. The card next shows what it asks.
questions.rule: After truth comes significance.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: A book has given you information. Which of these questions belong to the authors' fourth question? Select all that apply.
options: Why does the author think it is important to know this?
Is it important to me to know these things?
How many pages and chapters does the book have?
Is the author famous and respected in the field?
optionExplain: Right: the fourth question asks why the author thinks the information matters.
Right: it also asks whether the information matters to you.
Length is a fact about the book, not about the significance of what it says.
Fame is about the author's standing, not about why the information matters.
questions.explain: For information, the fourth question has two sides: why it matters to the author, and whether it matters to you.
questions.rule: Ask why it matters to the author and to you.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: Sort each question by which side of the fourth question it pursues.

items.t: Why does the author think these figures on obesity matter?
Do I need to know these dates for my own work?
Is this fact about sleep useful to me as a nurse?
If this explanation of habits is right, what does it imply for how I study?
What does this theory suggest about cases the author never mentions?
If memory works this way, what follows for how schools set tests?

questions.explain: Questions about why the information matters weigh its importance. Questions that carry an explanation into new cases seek what else follows, which the authors reserve for books that have enlightened, not only informed.
questions.rule: Information asks does it matter; enlightenment asks what follows.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: A reader finishes a well-argued report showing that long commutes lower wellbeing, and she accepts its case. Which next step best answers the fourth question?
options: Rereading the report's introduction to check its aims
Writing a summary of each section to record its points
Asking why it matters and what it implies for her move
Checking whether the report's statistics are correct
optionExplain: Rereading helps the first question, which she has already answered.
A summary records what was said, the work of the second question.
Right: she asks about significance for the author and for herself, and what follows from it.
Checking the figures belongs to the third question, which she has already settled by accepting the case.
questions.explain: She has understood and judged the report, so the remaining question is significance: why it matters and what follows for her.
questions.rule: Significance links the book to your own scheme of things.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: A reader skims the first pages of a book on diet and immediately overhauls his family's meals on the basis of what he thinks it will say. What risk does the authors' order of questions point to?
options: None, since significance is personal and needs no understanding
He may act on something the book never claimed, or on a claim that is false
He will find the rest of the book boring
He will agree with the author too readily on later chapters
optionExplain: Significance is partly personal, but it is the significance of what the book says, which he has not yet found out.
Right: skipping the first three questions means his what of it may rest on a misreading or a falsehood.
Boredom is a possible side effect, not the risk the order guards against.
His readiness to agree is a separate matter; the problem is acting before understanding or judging.
questions.explain: The fourth question depends on the first three. Acting on significance before knowing what the book says, and whether it is true, risks building on nothing.
questions.rule: Weigh significance only after understanding and judging.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: A government leaflet on fencing around home swimming pools is accurate and well argued, but you live in a flat with no pool. How does the fourth question apply?
options: Conclude it matters little to you, which still answers it
It does not apply, since the four questions are for books
You must find some way it matters to you, or you read badly
Doubt the leaflet's accuracy, since it is not relevant to you
optionExplain: Right: the fourth question asks whether it is important to you, and a modest answer is still an answer.
The authors apply the four questions to anything worth reading, including short texts.
The question asks whether it matters to you; it does not demand that the answer be yes.
Relevance and truth are separate questions; irrelevance to you says nothing about accuracy.
questions.explain: Significance has two sides, the author's and yours. A text can be true and important in general while mattering little to a particular reader, and recognising that answers the question.
questions.rule: What of it can honestly end in not much, for me.
questions.teaches: The fourth question can end in a modest answer: a true, well-argued text may matter a great deal to its author and little to you, and saying so still answers it.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the four basic questions are worth asking of an advertisement.
questions.explain: The authors say the questions apply to anything worth reading, a book, an article or even an advertisement. The card next shows how the levels of reading answer them.
questions.rule: Anything worth reading deserves the four questions.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: According to the authors, which of the four questions does inspectional reading tend to answer most accurately?
options: The last two: whether it is true and what of it
Only the fourth, since a quick look shows what matters
All four equally, since inspection covers the whole book
The first two: what it is about and what it says
optionExplain: Inspection helps with these too, but the authors say its answers here are less accurate.
The fourth question needs the first three, which a quick reading only partly supplies.
Inspection covers the whole book quickly, but the authors say it answers the first two more accurately than the last two.
Right: inspectional reading gives more accurate answers to the first two questions than to the last two.
questions.explain: A quick, structured look reveals what a book is about and roughly what it says. Judging truth and significance needs closer reading.
questions.rule: Inspection is strongest on the first two questions.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: After a quick inspectional reading of a book on urban gardening, Dev tells friends its advice is wrong. How should he treat that verdict, by the authors' account?
options: As settled, since inspection covers all four questions
As provisional, since inspection answers truth and significance less accurately
As meaningless, since inspection gives no help at all with truth
As more reliable than a later analytical verdict, since first readings are fresher
optionExplain: Inspection touches all four, but the authors say its answers to the last two are the least accurate.
Right: the authors say inspection helps with the last two questions but answers them less accurately than the first two.
The authors say inspection does help with the last two questions, only less accurately; it is not worthless.
Freshness is not accuracy; the authors rank the closer analytical answers higher.
questions.explain: Inspection helps with all four questions but is weakest on truth and significance. Dev's verdict is a hunch to test in an analytical reading.
questions.rule: Treat quick verdicts as hunches.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: Which readers have finished an analytical reading of a book by the authors' standard? Select all that apply.
options: Ana, who outlined the book and listed all of its arguments
Ben, who formed a view on its truth before outlining it
Cal, who outlined it, judged its arguments and saw why they matter
Dee, who read every page twice and took careful notes
Eve, who grasped its theme and arguments, judged it, and saw its use
optionExplain: Ana has answered the first two questions well, but the authors say an analytical reading is not done without the last two.
Ben has an answer to the third question, but he reached it before understanding, and he has none for the fourth.
Right: Cal has answers to all four, including the book's truth and its significance to him.
Rereading and note-taking are effort, not answers; Dee may still lack any view on truth or significance.
Right: Eve has answers to all four, from the book's theme and arguments to its truth and its use to her.
questions.explain: The authors say an analytical reading is not accomplished until you have answers to the questions of truth and significance, built on answers to the first two.
questions.rule: Analytical reading ends with truth and significance.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: True or false: Because what of it is probably the most important question in syntopical reading, a syntopical reader may answer it before the first three.
questions.explain: The authors say that even in syntopical reading the first three questions must be answered before the final one. Importance does not change the order.
questions.rule: The most important question can still come last.
questions.teaches: Importance and order are different things: the question that matters most in syntopical reading still depends on the three answered before it.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: An online ad for a meal-kit service says busy families save five hours a week. Using the four questions, which response is the most demanding?
options: Find what it claims and on what basis, judge it, then weigh it for you
Ignore it, since an ad is not worth reading with any care
Accept the figure, since advertising claims are regulated by law
Reject it at once, since ads routinely exaggerate their benefits
optionExplain: Right: this takes the four questions in order, from what is claimed to whether it is true to what of it for you.
The authors name advertisements among the things the questions apply to.
Accepting without asking skips the truth question entirely.
An instant rejection is a verdict reached before working out what the ad claims.
questions.explain: An ad states a claim and implies it matters to you. Asking the four questions in order separates what is claimed from what is shown and from what it means for you.
questions.rule: Put ads through the same four questions.
questions.teaches: An ad's pitch fuses two questions, is it true and what of it for you; taking the questions in order stops the promised benefit from standing in for evidence.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: According to the authors, why do many people fall asleep over good books?
options: They are unwilling to make the effort
Good books are too long to finish in one sitting
They do not know how to make the effort
They read at the wrong time of day
optionExplain: Unwillingness is the common guess, but the authors say the problem is not reluctance.
Length can be daunting, but the authors explain sleepiness by missing skill, not by how long the book is.
Right: the authors say people sleep over good books because they do not know how to make the effort.
Timing is part of the joke recipe for sleep, not the authors' explanation.
questions.explain: The authors locate the problem in missing skill, not missing will. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Tiredness over good books is usually a skill gap.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: Match each description to what the authors call it.
pairs: Remembering to ask the four questions as you read
The mark of a demanding reader
Answering the questions precisely and accurately
Reaching toward a hard book without the skill to succeed
questions.explain: The habit of asking marks the demanding reader; the trained ability to answer well is the art; unsuccessful stretching is what wears readers out.
questions.rule: Asking is the habit; answering well is the art.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: Kai, keen and determined, starts a hard book on statistics and gives up after two chapters, exhausted and annoyed. What does the authors' account suggest he needs most?
options: More determination to push through to the end
A quieter place to read without interruptions
An easier book, since this one is over his head
The skill to answer the questions the book raises
optionExplain: Kai already has determination; the authors say will alone is not enough.
The setting is not what the authors point to; his frustration comes from unsuccessful stretching.
Being over his head is what makes the book good for him; the authors want him to reach up, not step down.
Right: the authors say what tires readers is stretching unsuccessfully for lack of skill.
questions.explain: Kai has the will but not the skill. The authors' remedy is the art that lets a reader lift himself to a book's level.
questions.rule: Will without skill ends in frustration.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: Jo reasons: (1) This book is over my head. (2) Books over my head tire me when I lack the skill to reach them. (3) So the book is not good for me, and I should put it down. Where does her reasoning go wrong, by the authors' account?
options: Step 1, since no book is really beyond an adult reader
Step 2, since difficulty alone does not tire an unskilled reader
Step 3, since being over your head is what makes it good for you
Nowhere, since each step follows from the one before it
optionExplain: The authors say good books are over your head, so step 1 can be true.
The authors agree that books above your level weary you unless you can reach up to them.
Right: the authors say good books would not be good for you if they were not over your head; the fix is skill, not a different book.
Steps 1 and 2 hold, but the conclusion turns a call for skill into a reason to quit.
questions.explain: Jo's premises match the authors, but her conclusion does not follow. The authors treat difficulty as the source of a good book's value and lack of skill as the problem to fix.
questions.hint: Is difficulty the problem, or the reason the book is worth it?
questions.rule: A book over your head calls for skill, not retreat.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors' account, once Kai has built the skill through practice, the hard statistics book will stop demanding effort from him.
questions.explain: Skill turns unsuccessful stretching into successful stretching; the stretch remains, but the frustration goes. The authors also say you need both will and skill to keep reading actively, so effort does not disappear.
questions.rule: Skill keeps the stretch and removes the frustration.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: The Essence of Active Reading: The Four Basic Questions a Reader Asks
questions.q: An adult learning Spanish keeps picking up newspapers well above her level and quits each time, frustrated. Applying the authors' diagnosis, what change would help most?
options: Reading only texts she already understands with ease
Setting a stricter daily quota so she reads more often
Waiting until she feels more motivated to try again
Building techniques for hard text so her reaching succeeds
optionExplain: Easy texts end the frustration but also the growth; the authors value material that is over your head.
A quota adds will, which she already has; the missing piece is technique.
Motivation is will again; the authors say people fail for lack of skill, not lack of willingness.
Right: the authors place the cure in skill, which turns frustrated stretching into successful stretching.
questions.explain: Her problem has the shape the authors describe: plenty of will, not enough skill. Raising technique, not lowering the target, is their remedy.
questions.rule: Raise the technique, not the comfort level.
questions.teaches: The cure for frustration with hard material is to raise your technique rather than lower your target: skill is what makes reaching above your level pay off, in any field of learning.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: According to the authors, what completes your ownership of a book?
options: Writing in it until it becomes part of you
Paying for it in full
Shelving it in a personal library
Adding a bookplate with your name
optionExplain: Right: the authors say full ownership comes when you make the book part of yourself, best done by writing in it.
Payment gives a property right, which the authors call only the prelude to possession.
Shelving keeps the book, but keeping is not making it part of yourself.
A bookplate marks financial ownership, which the authors contrast with intellectual ownership.
questions.explain: The authors distinguish owning a book as property from owning it fully. The card next explains how the second comes about.
questions.rule: Buying is the prelude; writing completes ownership.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: The authors urge readers not only to read between the lines but also to ____ between the lines.
questions.explain: Reading between the lines is the old saying; the authors add writing between the lines, without which reading is unlikely to be most efficient.
questions.rule: Read between the lines, and write there too.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: Sort each act by the kind of ownership of a book it expresses, in the authors' terms.
groups: Full ownership: the book made part of you

items.t: Paying for the book at a shop
Pasting a bookplate inside the cover
Keeping the pages clean to protect resale value
Writing the questions a passage raises in the margin
Summing up a hard passage at the foot of the page
Recording a disagreement with the author beside the text

questions.explain: Buying, labelling and protecting a book concern it as property. Writing your questions, summaries and reactions in it is how the authors say a book becomes part of you.
questions.rule: Property is bought; full ownership is written.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: Mira reads a textbook as an e-book on a tablet, where she cannot use a pencil. Which practice keeps closest to the authors' advice?
options: Reading without notes, since the advice is about paper books
Using the annotation tool to record her questions and answers
Highlighting passages in colour so key parts stand out
Waiting to buy a paper copy before reading it at all
optionExplain: The pencil matters as a means of answering questions in writing; dropping the writing drops the point.
Right: the advice is to write your answers and reactions as you read, and annotations do that job.
Colour alone records that a passage caught her eye, not what she thinks about it.
Delay avoids the problem rather than applying the advice in the form she has.
questions.explain: The pencil is a sign of alert, written answering. Any tool that lets her write her questions and reactions while reading serves the same purpose.
questions.rule: The pencil stands for writing your thinking down.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: True or false: By the authors' reasoning, a reader who answers a book's questions in his head without writing anything has done real work, but has made that work harder than it needs to be.
questions.explain: The authors grant that answering could in theory be done in the mind only, but say it is much easier with a pencil in hand. Writing is the easier and more efficient route, not the only possible one.
questions.rule: Thinking in your head counts; writing makes it easier.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: An apprentice electrician is given her own printed wiring manual to study. Applying the authors' idea of ownership, what should she do with it?
options: Keep it spotless so it can be handed to the next apprentice
Memorise it page by page without marking it at all
Copy it out word for word into a separate notebook
Write her questions, cross-references and summaries in it
optionExplain: A clean manual stays someone else's text; the authors want the book made part of the reader.
Memorising stores the words without the questioning and reacting the authors want recorded.
Copying reproduces the author's words, not her own reactions and answers.
Right: writing her own thinking into the manual is how the authors say a book becomes yours.
questions.explain: Full ownership comes from writing your own thinking into the text. A working manual marked this way becomes a record of her understanding, not only a reference.
questions.rule: Make working texts yours by writing in them.
questions.teaches: Writing in a working manual turns a reference you consult into a record of your own understanding, which is the authors' fuller ownership applied to practical texts.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: Which of these do the authors give as reasons why marking a book is indispensable to reading it? Select all that apply.
options: It keeps you wide awake
It helps you remember the author's thoughts
It raises the book's value as a keepsake
It puts your thinking into words
It lets you skip any rereading
optionExplain: Right: the first reason is that marking keeps you not merely conscious but wide awake.
Right: the third reason is that writing your reactions helps you remember the author's thoughts.
A marked book may become a keepsake, but sentiment is not among the authors' reasons.
Right: the second reason is that active reading is thinking, and thinking tends to express itself in words.
Marking helps memory, but the authors do not promise it replaces rereading.
questions.explain: The authors give three reasons: wakefulness, expressing thought in words, and memory. The card next sets them out.
questions.rule: Mark to stay awake, to think in words, and to remember.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: According to the authors, a person who says he knows what he thinks but cannot ____ it usually does not know what he thinks.
questions.explain: The authors use this to explain why reading, which is thinking, should be expressed in written words: putting a thought into words tests whether it is there.
questions.rule: If you cannot say it, you may not yet think it.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: Nadia finishes an article on vaccine trials and feels sure she followed it, but when she tries to write a two-line summary in the margin, she cannot. What does the authors' second reason for marking suggest?
options: Her writing needs work, not her reading of the article
She probably does not yet know what she thinks about it
Margin summaries do not suit short texts like articles
She understood it fully but forgot it almost at once
optionExplain: Writing skill can be a factor, but the authors read a failure to express a thought as a sign the thought is not yet there.
Right: by the authors' second reason, inability to express what you think usually means you do not know what you think.
The authors' devices apply to anything worth reading, and a summary works for an article as for a book.
Losing it at once is unlikely if it was truly grasped; the more likely story is that it was never quite understood.
questions.explain: Writing exposed a gap her feeling of understanding hid. That is the second reason at work: thought tends to express itself in words, so failing to find the words is a warning.
questions.rule: A failed summary is a signal to reread.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: Match each situation to the reason for marking it shows.
pairs: A student marks as he reads so his attention does not drift
A reader tries to state a passage's point in a margin note
A reader looks at her notes a month later and recalls the argument
questions.explain: Each of the three reasons shows up in a different moment: during reading (wakefulness), in the act of writing (expressing thought) and later (memory).
questions.rule: Three reasons, three moments.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: True or false: If a reader marks a book only by copying the author's sentences word for word into the margins, the authors' second reason for marking is fully served.
questions.explain: The second reason is that your own thinking tends to express itself in words. Copying the author's words records his thought, not yours, so it does not test whether you know what you think.
questions.rule: Write your thinking, not the author's sentences.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: A team lead sits through a long briefing on a new project plan and wants to be sure she understood it. Applying the authors' second reason, which step tests her understanding best?
options: Rereading the slides that evening to refresh her memory
Recording the briefing so she can replay it later
Writing the plan in her own words in a few sentences
Asking a colleague whether he understood the plan
optionExplain: Rereading repeats the input without asking her to produce anything.
A recording preserves the words, not her grasp of them.
Right: putting the plan into her own words tests whether she knows what she thinks about it.
A colleague's understanding says nothing about hers.
questions.explain: The authors link thinking to expression in words. Writing a short account forces her own understanding into the open, where gaps show.
questions.rule: Write it in your own words to test your grasp.
questions.teaches: Putting a thought into your own words is a test of understanding wherever you learn, not only in books: failing to write it down is an early, cheap signal that understanding is missing.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, writing your disagreements in the margins of a book is a mark of disrespect to its author.
questions.explain: The authors say marking a book expresses your differences or agreements with the author and is the highest respect you can pay him. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Marking is respect, not vandalism.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: According to the authors, the learner has to be willing to argue with the teacher once he ____ what the teacher is saying.
questions.explain: Questioning starts at once, but argument waits for understanding. Then the reader is not only allowed but expected to argue.
questions.rule: Question at once; argue after understanding.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: Ali has followed a parenting book's case for limiting children's screen time and can restate it. He thinks it ignores children who use screens to keep in touch with distant family. What do the authors encourage him to do?
options: Keep quiet, since the author knows more than he does
Write the objection beside the passage as his reply
Stop reading, since he now disagrees with the book
Cross out the passage so he will not reread it later
optionExplain: The author presumably knows more, but the authors still want the learner to argue once he understands.
Right: he understands the case, so recording his difference is the conversation the authors describe.
Disagreeing with one point is no reason to stop; the conversation goes on.
Crossing out silences the author rather than answering him.
questions.explain: Ali has met the condition for arguing: he understands the argument. Marking his objection expresses his difference with the author, which the authors call the highest respect.
questions.rule: Once you understand, write your objection down.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: Pia writes the word nonsense beside the first sentence of a philosophy book, before reading any further. She says she is conversing with the author, as the authors recommend. What has she got wrong?
options: Nothing, since marking disagreement is the highest respect
She used a pen when the authors recommend a pencil
She argued before understanding what the author is saying
Philosophy books should not be marked at all
optionExplain: Marking disagreement is respect when it follows understanding; after one sentence there is nothing understood to disagree with.
The pencil is the authors' sign of alertness; the tool is not the error here.
Right: the authors say the learner argues once he understands; one sentence in, she cannot yet.
The authors recommend marking any book worth reading, philosophy included.
questions.explain: The conversation has an order: question first, then argue once you understand. Pia skipped the understanding, so her mark talks past the author.
questions.hint: What condition do the authors set for arguing?
questions.rule: A verdict on page one is not a conversation.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, if you already know more about a subject than a book's author, you probably should not be bothering with the book.
questions.explain: The authors presume the author knows more than you, and add that if he does not, you probably should not be bothering with his book. The conversation is worth having because there is something to learn.
questions.rule: Converse with books that can teach you.
questions.teaches: A conversation with a book is worth having only when the author presumably knows more than you; a book that cannot teach you may not merit demanding reading at all.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: A junior engineer reviews a senior colleague's design document. Applying the authors' conversation model, what should her review comments do?
options: Ask where she is unsure, then agree or object once she grasps it
Approve it without comment, since the colleague knows more
List every objection that occurs to her on a first quick read
Correct only spelling and formatting, to avoid seeming rude
optionExplain: Right: questions first, then agreement and objection after understanding, is the conversation the authors describe.
Knowing more does not end the conversation; the authors expect the learner to question and, once she understands, to argue.
Objections from a first quick read come before understanding, so they may miss the design's point.
Avoiding substance avoids the conversation; the authors call honest agreement and disagreement a form of respect.
questions.explain: The model fits any review of someone else's work. Questions come first; agreements and objections come after understanding; both show respect.
questions.rule: Review as a conversation: ask, understand, then argue.
questions.teaches: The conversation model fits any review of someone else's work: questions come first, agreement and objection come after understanding, and honest objection is a form of respect, not a breach of it.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: According to the authors, about how many passages in a whole book should get a star or asterisk in the margin?
options: One on every page
About ten or a dozen
Every passage you underline
About a hundred, one every few pages
optionExplain: A star on every page would make the mark mean nothing special.
Right: the authors reserve stars for the ten or dozen most important statements or passages.
Stars are meant to stand out from underlining, so starring every underlined passage defeats them.
A hundred is still far too many for the mark to pick out the book's core.
questions.explain: Stars are the strongest mark and are meant to be used sparingly. The card next sets out the other marks too.
questions.rule: Stars are for the dozen that matter most.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: Match each marking device to what the authors say it is for.
pairs: Stressing an underlined statement or a passage too long to underline
Star or asterisk in the margin
The ten or dozen most important passages
questions.explain: Underlining and circling mark points and terms, margin lines add emphasis or cover long passages, and stars single out the book's most important passages.
questions.rule: Each mark has its own job.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: A reader reaches a three-page passage that sets out the author's central argument. Which mark do the authors suggest for a passage too long to underline?
options: Underlining every sentence of it
Circling each paragraph
Vertical lines in the margin
A star beside every line
optionExplain: Underlining three pages buries the marks you make elsewhere.
Circling is for key words or phrases, not whole paragraphs.
Right: the authors suggest vertical lines in the margin for a passage too long to be underlined.
Stars are for the dozen top passages in the book, used sparingly, not for every line of one passage.
questions.explain: Vertical margin lines exist for this case: they point to a long passage without smothering it in underlining.
questions.rule: Long passage: margin line.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: Hugo stars 140 passages in a 200-page book so that he can find the important ones later. What has gone wrong?
options: Nothing, since more stars give better coverage of the book
He should have underlined those passages instead of starring
He should have put the stars at the top of each page
With so many, his stars no longer pick out the key passages
optionExplain: Coverage is not the goal; a mark that appears everywhere stops distinguishing anything.
Underlining has its own job, but the problem here is overuse, not the choice of mark.
Placement is not the issue; the number is.
Right: the authors say stars are to be used sparingly, for the ten or dozen most important passages.
questions.explain: The star's value lies in being rare. With 140 of them, Hugo cannot open the book at its core passages, which is the use the authors give the mark.
questions.hint: What does a star do if almost everything has one?
questions.rule: Overused marks pick out nothing.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: Sort each passage by the mark the authors' devices suggest for it.

items.t: A forceful sentence stating one chapter's main claim
A key term the author uses in a special sense
A supporting point that matters within one chapter
The passage that states the thesis of the whole book
One of the ten passages you would reread to recall the whole book

questions.explain: Underlining and circling cover major points and key terms throughout. Stars are reserved for the few passages that matter most to the book as a whole.
questions.rule: Underline the important; star the essential.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: An office worker flags emails so she can find the important ones later, but she now has 400 flagged messages. Which lesson from the authors' marking devices applies?
options: Keep the top flag for a handful, or it picks out nothing
Flag even more messages so that nothing important is missed
Stop flagging altogether, since marks do not help her
Use a different colour for every message she flags
optionExplain: Right: like the star, a top-priority flag works only if it is used sparingly.
More flags make the problem worse: a mark on everything marks nothing.
Marks help when used with restraint; the authors recommend them.
A colour per message removes the distinction the flag was meant to create.
questions.explain: The authors limit stars to the ten or dozen most important passages. The same logic governs any flagging system: the strongest mark must be rare to be useful.
questions.rule: The strongest mark must be rare.
questions.teaches: Marks of different strength work as a ladder: a common mark for what is important and a rare one for what is essential, so that each level still tells you something.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: Many readers write the abbreviation ____ before a page number in the margin, meaning compare or refer to.
questions.explain: Cf is the common abbreviation for compare. The card next shows how page references tie a book together.
questions.rule: Cf means compare.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: Match each marking device to what the authors say it records.
pairs: The steps of an argument in sequence
Other places with the same, related or contrary points
Writing at the foot of the page
A complicated discussion reduced to a simple statement
questions.explain: Numbers trace an argument's order, page references link scattered passages, and written notes record questions, summaries and the sequence of major points.
questions.rule: Number the steps, link the pages, write the summary.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: Across one chapter, an author gives five reasons for a four-day working week, spread over several pages. Which mark best records how her argument builds?
options: Circling the word reason each time it appears
Numbering each reason in the margin, 1 to 5
Starring each of the five reasons as important
Underlining the chapter title that names the topic
optionExplain: Circling a recurring word highlights vocabulary, not the order of the steps.
Right: numbers in the margin show a sequence of points made in developing an argument.
Stars are for the dozen most important passages in the whole book, not every step in one chapter.
The title does not show how the argument proceeds.
questions.explain: The authors give margin numbers exactly this job: tracking the sequence of points in an argument, even when they are pages apart.
questions.rule: Number the steps of an argument.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: On page 210 a historian says a reform failed; on page 45 she seemed to say it succeeded. Which of the authors' devices fits best?
options: Writing 45 on page 210 and 210 on page 45
Starring both passages as important ones
Underlining both passages so they stand out
Circling the word reform on both of the pages
optionExplain: Right: page numbers in the margin mark where else the author makes related or contradictory points, tying them together.
Stars mark importance, not a link between two places.
Underlining marks each passage separately; it does not connect them.
Circling marks a key term, but nothing in it points from one page to the other.
questions.explain: Cross-referenced page numbers are the device for points that belong together, including apparent contradictions, though many pages apart.
questions.rule: Link contradictions with page references.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: True or false: Writing other page numbers in the margin is useful only when the author repeats the same point, not when she contradicts herself.
questions.explain: The authors list three uses: places where the author makes the same point, a relevant one, or one in contradiction. Contradictions are among the most useful links to record.
questions.rule: Cross-reference agreements and contradictions alike.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: A student lends her marked history book to a study partner. Beside one passage she has written only 112, and he cannot tell what it means. Following the convention the authors mention, what would have made the mark clear?
options: Writing p. before it, so it reads as a page number
Copying out the passage from page 112 beside it
Circling the number so it stands apart from the text
Writing Cf before it, the usual sign for compare
optionExplain: Marking it as a page says where to look, but not why; Cf tells the reader to compare the two passages.
Copying the other passage takes space and reproduces the author's words instead of linking the two places.
A circle makes the number stand out but leaves its meaning a guess.
Right: many readers write Cf, meaning compare or refer to, before a cross-referenced page number.
questions.explain: A bare number could be a date, a count or a page. The sign Cf, which many readers use, tells any reader, including your later self, to compare or refer to that page.
questions.rule: Write Cf before a cross-referenced page.
questions.teaches: Shared conventions such as Cf make marks readable to others and to your future self: a bare number leaves the reader guessing, while Cf 112 says compare page 112.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: According to the authors, what is the best use of a book's front endpapers?
options: A decorative bookplate with your name and a design
An outline of the whole book, written after finishing
A list of the new vocabulary you met in the book
The date and place where you bought the book
optionExplain: A bookplate is a common choice, but the authors say it expresses only financial ownership.
Right: the authors reserve the front endpapers for an outline of the book as an integrated structure.
Vocabulary lists can help, but they are not what the authors recommend for this space.
Purchase details record the property, not your understanding.
questions.explain: The authors want the front endpapers to hold a record of your thinking about the whole book. The card next explains both endpapers.
questions.rule: Front endpapers: your outline of the whole.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: Sort each item by whether the authors place it on the back or the front endpapers.

items.t: A personal index of the author's points
Points listed in the order they appear
Page references for each point
An outline of the book as an integrated structure
The basic outline and the order of the parts
Written last, after the index is finished

questions.explain: The back holds a running index of points in order. The front, written after finishing, holds the outline of the whole as one structure.
questions.rule: Index at the back, structure at the front.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: Priya's front endpaper reads: p. 3, author defines habit; p. 17, cue, routine, reward; p. 40, keystone habits; and so on to p. 290. What would the authors say?
options: It is ideal, since it records every point in the book
It should be shorter, but is otherwise the right content
It is an index that belongs at the back, not an outline of the whole
It belongs on the title page, with her other first notes
optionExplain: Covering every point is the job of the back index; the front outline is about how the parts fit.
Length is not the problem; a shorter list is still a list rather than a structure.
Right: the authors say the front outline is not page by page or point by point but an integrated structure with an order of parts.
The title page suits structural notes from an inspectional reading, but this list is still an index, not an outline.
questions.explain: Priya has made a personal index, which the authors put on the back endpapers. The front outline should show the basic plan and how the parts are ordered.
questions.rule: An outline shows the whole, not a list of points.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: What reason do the authors give for preferring an outline to a bookplate on the front endpapers?
options: An outline helps whoever borrows the book from you next
An outline saves time when you come to reread the book
An outline raises the book's value if you ever sell it
The plate shows financial ownership; the outline, intellectual
optionExplain: Borrowers may benefit, but the authors' reason concerns the reader's own understanding, not other readers.
An outline may well save time later, but the authors' reason is the kind of ownership each one expresses.
Resale value belongs to the book as property, which is not what the authors care about here.
Right: the authors contrast the bookplate's financial ownership with the outline's intellectual ownership.
questions.explain: Both mark the book as yours, but in different senses. The outline shows you have made the book part of yourself.
questions.rule: A bookplate says you bought it; an outline says you understood it.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: True or false: If a reader cannot write a front-endpaper outline after finishing a book, the authors would take this as a sign that she does not yet understand the work as a whole.
questions.explain: The authors call the outline the measure of your understanding of the work. Being unable to write it shows the measure has not been met.
questions.rule: If you cannot outline it, you have not yet grasped it.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: How to Make a Book Your Own
questions.q: At the end of a twelve-week course, a student has a folder of notes taken lecture by lecture. Applying the endpaper idea, which final step best measures her understanding of the course?
options: Writing a one-page outline of how the course fits together
Rereading all the lecture notes in order, start to finish
Adding page numbers to every note so she can find things
Highlighting the terms that come up most often
optionExplain: Right: like the front endpaper outline, a structural summary of the whole tests whether she grasps how the parts fit.
Rereading is review, not a measure; it asks her to produce nothing.
Page numbers help finding, like the back index, but say nothing about the whole.
Repetition counts show frequency, not structure.
questions.explain: Her lecture notes are a running record like the back index. The front-endpaper step is the outline of the whole, which is what measures understanding.
questions.rule: End with an outline of the whole.
questions.teaches: An outline of the whole comes last for a reason: how the parts fit can only be seen once all of them have been met, which is why the authors place it after finishing.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: On a first quick look at a book, where do the authors suggest writing notes on its kind, subject and structure?
options: On the contents page or the title page
On the back endpapers, with the index
In a separate notebook kept for the purpose
On the last page of the final chapter
optionExplain: Right: the authors name the contents page, or perhaps the title page, which their marking scheme otherwise leaves unused.
The back endpapers hold the personal index made while reading analytically.
A notebook could work, but the authors suggest pages within the book.
The last page has no special role in the authors' scheme.
questions.explain: The contents and title pages are free in the marking scheme, and the contents page already shows the book's structure. The card next explains what these notes contain.
questions.rule: First-look notes go on the contents page.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: Put the three questions an inspectional reading answers in the order the authors give them.
items: What kind of book is it?
What is it about as a whole?
What is the structural order of the work?
questions.explain: The authors list kind first, then subject as a whole, then the structural order by which the author develops it. Structural notes record the answers.
questions.rule: Kind, subject, structure.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: Which of these notes on a contents page is a structural note?
options: Wrong about the minimum wage, which has risen since
Practical book on running a cafe, in five parts, plan to market
The author's prose is dull and hard going in places
The claim in chapter 3 about rising rents is out of date
optionExplain: This is a verdict on truth, which the authors say should wait for a careful reading.
Right: it answers kind, subject and structural order, the three inspectional questions.
A comment on style concerns neither structure nor the author's ideas.
Judging a claim's accuracy is substance, not structure.
questions.explain: Structural notes record kind, subject and order. Verdicts on claims or style are something else.
questions.rule: Structural notes map; they do not judge.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: During a twenty-minute inspectional reading, a reader writes these notes. Which go beyond what structural notes should hold? Select all that apply.
options: History of the Cold War, for general readers
Organised by decade, 1945 to 1991
The author is wrong about Cuba
Its account of the arms race is biased
About how the Cold War began and ended
optionExplain: This answers what kind of book it is, a proper structural note.
This records the structural order, a proper structural note.
Right: this judges the truth of a statement, which the authors say to put off until a careful reading.
Right: a charge of bias is a judgment of accuracy, again premature at this level.
This states what the book is about as a whole, a proper structural note.
questions.explain: Structural notes concern structure, not substance in detail. Verdicts on accuracy or truth belong to analytical reading.
questions.rule: At first look, map; do not judge.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: One reader will return to a book for an analytical reading this afternoon; another will not return for three months. How does the authors' advice on structural notes apply to the two?
options: Only the three-month reader should make notes at all
Neither needs notes, since an inspection takes so little time
Both should, but the case is strongest for the one who waits
Only the same-day reader, while it is all still fresh
optionExplain: The authors say you may and probably should make such notes in general, not only after long gaps.
Inspection is quick, but it answers important questions worth recording.
Right: notes are advisable in general and especially if days or months will pass before the analytical reading.
The same-day reader has the least risk of forgetting, so freshness argues more for the other reader.
questions.explain: The authors recommend recording inspectional answers while fresh, and stress it when there may be a long gap. Time changes how much the notes matter, not whether they are worth making.
questions.rule: The longer the gap, the more structural notes matter.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: A new developer spends an hour surveying an unfamiliar codebase before a week away. Which note best follows the structural-notes idea?
options: A list of bugs she suspects, to fix when she returns
Remarks on the quality of the coding style she saw
No notes, since she will relearn it anyway next week
A short map of what the system is, does, and how its parts fit
optionExplain: Suspected bugs are judgments on substance, premature after an hour's survey.
Style verdicts are judgments, not a map of structure.
Relearning from scratch wastes the survey; the authors advise recording answers while fresh.
Right: kind, purpose and arrangement are the structural answers, recorded for the deeper work later.
questions.explain: Her survey works like an inspectional reading. Recording kind, subject and arrangement while fresh lets her start next week from a map.
questions.rule: After a first survey, record the map.
questions.teaches: Structural notes suit any first survey of a large body of material: recording its kind, subject and arrangement while fresh lets later, deeper study start from a map instead of from scratch.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the notes you make during an analytical reading should be about your own concepts as well as the author's.
questions.explain: The authors say conceptual notes concern the author's concepts and also your own, as reading has deepened or broadened them. The card next sets this out.
questions.rule: Note how your own ideas change.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: What do the authors say conceptual notes concern?
options: The page layout and the chapter titles of the book
The reader's moods and feelings while reading
The facts and dates worth memorising for later use
The author's concepts, and the reader's own as they grow
optionExplain: Layout and titles belong to structure, the subject of structural notes.
Moods are reactions, not concepts.
Facts may appear, but the authors define conceptual notes by concepts, not memorisation.
Right: conceptual notes concern the author's concepts and the reader's own as they develop.
questions.explain: Conceptual notes track ideas, the author's and the reader's, rather than the book's layout.
questions.rule: Conceptual notes track ideas, both sides.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: Sort each note as structural or conceptual, in the authors' terms.

items.t: Theoretical book; three parts on causes, course and effects
About the economics of cities as a whole
Chapters 1 to 4 set up the problem; 5 to 9 propose solutions
By efficiency she means output per hour, not profit
Her case on wages convinces me; the case on rents does not
My idea of fairness has widened: she counts future generations too

questions.explain: Structural notes record kind, subject and order. Conceptual notes record the author's ideas, the reader's judgment of them, and changes in the reader's own ideas.
questions.rule: Structure versus concepts.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: True or false: During a quick inspectional reading of a book on nutrition, Ola writes that its claim about fasting is false. By the authors' advice, this is a well-timed conceptual note.
questions.explain: The authors say to put off judging the accuracy or truth of statements until you have read the book more carefully. Verdicts on truth belong to analytical reading, where conceptual notes are made; at the inspectional level the note is premature.
questions.rule: Truth verdicts wait for analytical reading.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: Kim is reading a third book on happiness after two others. Its author defines happiness in a way that conflicts with the first book's definition. Where should her conceptual note point?
options: Only to other pages within the third book itself
To the page in the first book with the other definition
Nowhere, since notes across books are not conceptual
To the contents page of the third book, with the plan
