optionExplain: Links within one book are useful, but here the related idea is in another book.
Right: the authors say syntopical notes may refer not only to other pages in that book but to pages in other books.
The authors say notes in syntopical reading tend to be conceptual too.
The contents page holds structural notes, not links between ideas.
questions.explain: When the reading spans several books, conceptual notes span them too. A note can send you to a page in another book.
questions.rule: In syntopical reading, link across books.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: A buyer reads three supplier proposals. In her notes on the second she writes: here delivery means arrival at our warehouse; proposal A meant dispatch from the factory. What kind of note is this, in the authors' terms?
options: A structural note on how the proposal is laid out
A dialectical note mapping a whole debate among them
A conceptual note that links a concept to another text
A personal index entry listing a point and its page
optionExplain: Layout is structure; this note is about meaning.
Dialectical notes map a whole discussion across texts; this note records one concept and one link.
Right: it records the writer's concept and refers to another document where the concept differs.
An index lists points in order with pages; this note compares meanings.
questions.explain: The note concerns concepts, what delivery means in each proposal, and points to another text. That is a conceptual note of the syntopical kind.
questions.rule: Notes on meaning are conceptual.
questions.teaches: Conceptual notes catch shifts in meaning between sources: when two writers use one word differently, a note recording each meaning is what makes a fair comparison possible.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: When reading several books on one subject, what might an expert reader map that no single author sets out?
options: The page count and length of each of the books
The publishing history and editions of each book
The shape of the discussion among all the authors
Each author's biography and career in the field
optionExplain: Page counts describe the books, not what they say.
Publishing history is background, not the content of the debate.
Right: an expert syntopical reader can note the shape of the discussion all the authors take part in, even unknowingly.
Biographies may explain a view, but they are not the discussion itself.
questions.explain: Several books on one subject form a discussion none of them lays out alone. The card next names notes that map it.
questions.rule: Several books make one discussion.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: The authors call notes on the shape of the discussion among several authors ____ notes.
questions.explain: Dialectical notes map the discussion engaged in by all the authors on a subject, and often need separate sheets because they concern several books.
questions.rule: Notes on the debate are dialectical.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: Which of these notes is dialectical?
options: Book A, chapter 3: by liberty the author means absence of restraint
Book B is a history in four parts, from 1600 to 1900
Book C's argument on page 40 is weak and rests on one case
On liberty: A and C say no restraint, B says self-mastery, D is silent
optionExplain: This records one author's concept, a conceptual note.
This records kind and structure, a structural note.
This judges one book's argument, a conceptual note.
Right: it sets out a question and where each author stands, mapping the discussion across books.
questions.explain: Dialectical notes organise the discussion around questions and positions across several authors, rather than around one book.
questions.rule: Dialectical notes are organised by question, not by book.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: Order the three kinds of notes from the one closest to a single book's structure to the one that maps a discussion across many books.
items: Structural notes
Conceptual notes
Dialectical notes
questions.explain: Structural notes record one book's kind and plan; conceptual notes record ideas, within one book or across several; dialectical notes map the discussion among all the authors.
questions.rule: Structure, concepts, discussion.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: True or false: A reader studying a single book analytically is in a position to make dialectical notes about it.
questions.explain: Dialectical notes concern the discussion among several authors, made when reading several books syntopically. With one book, the notes are conceptual.
questions.rule: One book, no debate to map.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: A council officer reads forty public submissions on a proposed bike lane. Applying the idea of dialectical notes, what should her summary look like?
options: A separate sheet of the questions in dispute and who takes which side
A one-line summary of each submission in the order received
A count of submissions for and against, to show the balance
A list of the most persuasive submissions, with her reasons
optionExplain: Right: organising by question and position maps the discussion, the work of dialectical notes.
Summaries in order received follow the sources one by one, which hides the shape of the debate.
A tally flattens the debate into one question and loses the others.
Picking favourites is judging before the discussion has been laid out.
questions.explain: Dialectical notes map a discussion by its questions and the positions taken, across all the contributors. A consultation has that same shape.
questions.rule: Map a many-voice debate by its questions.
questions.teaches: Dialectical notes suit any many-voice debate, such as a public consultation: organising by the questions in dispute, rather than by who said what, reveals a debate no single contributor set out.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, someone who can state all the rules of reading has the skill of reading.
questions.explain: The authors say knowing the rules of an art is not the same as having the habit, and the skill is the habit. The card next explains how the habit forms.
questions.rule: Knowing the rules is not having the skill.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: According to the authors, there is no other way of forming a habit of operation than by ____.
questions.explain: The authors say we learn to do by doing: the habit of operating comes only from operating, again and again.
questions.rule: Learn to do by doing.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: Match each phrase to what the authors say it means.
pairs: The art as something that can be taught
Rules to be followed in operation
The art as something learned and possessed
The habit that results from operating by the rules
Doing something as if you were born to it
Doing much better after practice what you once did badly
questions.explain: Rules are the teachable side of an art; the habit is the possessed side. Practice turns one into the other until the activity feels natural.
questions.rule: Rules are taught; habits are possessed.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: A reader can list the four basic questions perfectly, but in practice he reads novels and reports straight through without asking them. By the authors' account, what does he still lack?
options: Knowledge of the rules he is meant to follow
The habit of operating by them, formed by practice
A natural talent for reading that some people have
More books about reading to deepen his knowledge
optionExplain: He already knows the rules; listing them perfectly shows that.
Right: the skill is the habit of operating according to the rules, which only practice forms.
The authors explain skill by habit and practice, not by inborn talent.
More reading about rules adds knowledge he already has, not the habit he lacks.
questions.explain: Knowing rules is a condition of the skill but not the skill itself. Only operating by them, repeatedly, forms the habit.
questions.rule: Turn known rules into practised habits.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: Ella says: I will skip learning the reading rules and read a great deal instead; the skill will come by itself. Where does the authors' account disagree with her?
options: It does not; reading a great deal is enough on its own
Only in that she should read fewer, harder books instead
Skill is a habit of following rules, which she must first know
Only in that she needs a teacher beside her as she reads
optionExplain: Practice is needed, but the authors say it must be practice of rules; you cannot follow rules you do not know.
Book choice is a separate matter from how the skill is formed.
Right: the authors say knowing the rules is a condition of getting the skill, and skill is the habit of operating by them.
The authors do not make a teacher's presence the condition; the rules and practice are.
questions.explain: The authors' account needs both: rules to follow and practice in following them. Practice without known rules is not forming this habit.
questions.hint: What do the authors say about rules you do not know?
questions.rule: Practice needs rules to practise.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: A trainee chef has memorised every knife technique in a manual but has barely held a knife. In a busy kitchen she freezes, trying to recall each step. What does the authors' account of habit say she lacks?
options: Facility and readiness, which only practice brings
Knowledge of the techniques she has to use
A better manual with clearer step-by-step pictures
Self-confidence, which a pep talk could supply
optionExplain: Right: the authors say the difference before and after forming a habit is one of facility and readiness, and only operating forms it.
She knows the techniques; she recited them from the manual.
The manual gave her the rules; more rules would not supply the habit.
Confidence may follow, but the authors place the difference in the facility and readiness that practice forms, not in encouragement.
questions.explain: Freezing to recall steps is what knowing rules without a habit looks like. Practice brings the readiness that lets her act without stopping to recall.
questions.rule: Habit shows as readiness under real conditions.
questions.teaches: Readiness under real conditions is the test of a habit: a skill shows itself when you act well without stopping to recall the rules.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: A painter produces something entirely new. What do the authors say about whether she followed rules?
options: She followed none, which is why the work is original
She followed the traditional rules of composition exactly
She followed rules while learning, then left them behind
She followed the craft rules for preparing and applying paint
optionExplain: This is the common view the authors reject; it misses which rules she followed.
Original work may ignore traditional rules of composition; the authors do not claim she obeyed them.
Rules are not a stage left behind; the authors say the original painter must still follow the craft rules to make the work.
Right: the authors say there are rules for preparing canvas and mixing and applying paint, which she must have followed.
questions.explain: The authors separate rules of craft from traditional rules of art. The card next explains the difference.
questions.rule: Original work still uses craft rules.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, there are no final, unbreakable rules for making a painting, but there are rules for preparing canvas and mixing paints.
questions.explain: The authors grant that painting as a whole has no final rules, but the craft of handling materials does, and the painter must follow those.
questions.rule: No rules for the painting; rules for the paint.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: Sort each item by whether, in the authors' account, an original artist must follow it or may depart from it.
groups: Craft rules the maker must follow
Traditional conventions an original maker may break

items.t: How to weld steel so the joint holds
How to mix paints so they can be applied
How to prepare a canvas
That a portrait should look like its sitter
That a sculpture should stand on a pedestal
That a painting should tell a story

questions.explain: The authors say original work may obey little of the traditional rules of art, but the maker must still follow the rules for handling materials.
questions.rule: Conventions bend; craft rules hold.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: A reader says that great readers read by instinct, so he will ignore the rules and trust his gut. Using the authors' point about original artists, what is the best reply?
options: Fluent readers only seem rule-free; the rules have become habit
He is right, since great reading is a gift, not a craft
He should follow the traditional rules exactly, as the masters did
Instinct and rules cannot both play a part in good reading
optionExplain: Right: like the original artist, the fluent reader only looks rule-free; the rules have become habit.
The authors treat reading as an art with rules, learned through practice, not as a gift.
The authors do not demand rigid obedience to tradition; their point is that craft skill underlies even original work.
In the authors' view, rules practised long enough become second nature, which is what looks like instinct.
questions.explain: What looks like instinct in an expert is habit formed by operating according to rules. Ignoring the rules skips the craft that makes the expert's ease possible.
questions.rule: Ease that looks like instinct is practised craft.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: An experimental composer writes music unlike anything heard before. By the authors' reasoning, what must still be true of her?
options: She has no need of any musical training
She has followed every traditional rule of harmony
She has mastered the craft of her medium, like notation
She cannot be called skilled, since she broke with tradition
optionExplain: Originality does not remove the need to handle the materials of music.
Departing from traditional harmony is compatible with the authors' view; what is required is craft, not tradition.
Right: however original, she had to be skilled in her medium to produce the work, as the painter must handle paint.
The authors say an original maker must be skilled to produce the work at all.
questions.explain: The authors' claim travels from painting to any art: the maker of an original work must have followed the rules of handling the medium.
questions.rule: Originality presupposes craft.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.q: A poet writes without punctuation or capital letters. A student concludes that poets need not learn grammar. Following the authors, what is the flaw in the student's reasoning?
options: There is no flaw; original poets follow no rules at all
Breaking a convention still rests on command of the language
The poet is breaking the language's laws and should be corrected
The poem shows grammar was never a real rule of language
optionExplain: The authors reject the idea that original makers follow no rules.
Right: dropping a convention is not dropping the craft; the poet's skill with words is what lets the departure succeed.
The authors do not treat breaking conventions as an error; original work may obey few traditional rules.
Setting aside punctuation does not show the language has no rules; the poet still needs command of it to make the departure work.
questions.explain: Punctuation is a convention the poet may set aside; command of words is the craft she must have. The student confuses the two.
questions.rule: Breaking a convention is not skipping the craft.
questions.teaches: Mastery is what makes rule-breaking work: a maker who commands the craft can depart from convention and still produce something that holds together.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: From Many Rules to One Habit
questions.q: According to the authors, how does a beginner come to perform a complex skill like skiing or reading smoothly?
options: By learning each act separately, then combining them
By trying to do all the acts together from the start
By watching experts closely until the skill sinks in
By studying the rules thoroughly instead of practising
optionExplain: Right: the authors say you must learn the acts as separate acts before they can fuse into one performance.
Doing everything at once is what makes beginners awkward; the authors say you cannot fuse acts you have not mastered.
Watching shows what fluency looks like but does not form the habit in you.
Rules without practice give knowledge, not skill.
questions.explain: The authors use skiing to show the route: separate acts first, then a fused whole. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Separate first, together later.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: From Many Rules to One Habit
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, to forget the separate acts of a skill you must first learn them as separate acts.
questions.explain: The expert forgets the separate acts while performing, but only because he first learned each one separately.
questions.rule: You can only forget what you first learned.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: From Many Rules to One Habit
questions.q: Lea is new to analytical reading. On her first try she attempts to classify the book, outline it, find its terms and judge its arguments all at once, and ends up confused. What do the authors advise?
options: Keep trying everything at once until it finally clicks
Give up analytical reading, since it is too complex for her
Practise each act alone with full attention, then combine
Skip the separate steps and read for the overall gist
optionExplain: The authors say you cannot fuse acts until you are expert at each; repeating the overload will not fix it.
Complexity calls for patience, not surrender; the authors say it can be done.
Right: each separate act needs full attention at first, and practised parts later run together.
Reading for the gist abandons the acts instead of learning them.
questions.explain: Lea is trying to fuse acts she has not yet mastered. The authors' route is separate practice with full attention first.
questions.rule: Overloaded? Practise one act at a time.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: From Many Rules to One Habit
questions.q: A tennis coach tells a first-day beginner: forget about your grip, footwork and swing, and play the point. By the authors' account, what is wrong with this advice?
options: Nothing; experts do not think about the separate acts
Beginners should think only about winning the point
Grip and footwork matter little once you are on court
Acts can be forgotten only after being learned separately
optionExplain: True of experts, but the authors say they reached that state by first learning each act separately.
Attending to the goal is the expert's privilege, reached after the acts have fused.
They matter a great deal at the start; the question is when they can be left to habit.
Right: the authors say to forget the acts as separate acts you must first learn them as separate acts.
questions.explain: The coach gives the expert's state as the beginner's method. The authors' order is the reverse: learn the acts separately, then let them fuse.
questions.hint: What must happen before the acts can be forgotten?
questions.rule: The expert's ease is the end of the route, not the start.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: From Many Rules to One Habit
questions.q: Suppose Omar keeps practising each reading step separately and deliberately for years, keeping the steps apart instead of letting them run together. What does the authors' account suggest?
options: He will read as well as any expert, thanks to his care
He will fall short, since the acts must be forgotten to be done well
He will slowly lose his skill in each of the separate acts
He will need to learn the rules again from the beginning
optionExplain: The expert's mark is that the acts have fused; staying separate keeps him short of that.
Right: separate practice is a stage; the authors say performing well requires forgetting the acts as separate acts.
Nothing suggests practice erodes each act; the problem is that they never combine.
He knows the rules; what he lacks is their fusion into one performance.
questions.explain: The authors describe a route that ends with the acts fused. Staying in the separate stage keeps him at the beginner's level of attention.
questions.rule: Separate practice is a stage, not the goal.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: From Many Rules to One Habit
questions.q: A learner driver is working toward driving with ease. Put the stages in the order the authors' account of learning a complex skill predicts.
items: Working each control separately, such as mirrors, gears and steering, with full attention
Doing each control with more ease and less attention after practice
Combining the controls in one smooth drive
Watching the road ahead rather than the controls
questions.explain: Separate acts with full attention come first; practice brings ease; the acts then combine; finally attention is free for the road. Feeling clumsy at the first stage, even as an experienced passenger or reader, is part of the route, not a sign of failure.
questions.rule: Separate, ease, combine, look ahead.
questions.teaches: Awkwardness in the separate stage is normal even for adults who have long done something similar: the authors say relearning to read can be humiliating, like an adult learning to ski, and the awkwardness passes as the acts fuse.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: From Many Rules to One Habit
questions.q: What does the long list of rules for analytical reading indicate, according to the authors?
options: That reading is many separate habits to be kept apart
That most of the rules can be skipped
That the one habit of reading well is complex
That only experts can learn to read well
optionExplain: A long list suggests many habits, but the authors say it shows one complex habit, not a plurality of habits.
The rules describe parts of the habit; skipping them leaves gaps in it.
Right: the multiplicity of the rules indicates the complexity of the one habit to be formed.
The authors write to encourage learners; they say the habit can be formed.
questions.explain: The rules are many because the single habit has many parts. The card next shows what happens as they fuse.
questions.rule: Many rules describe one habit.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: From Many Rules to One Habit
questions.q: According to the authors, the multiplicity of the rules indicates the complexity of the ____ habit to be formed.
questions.explain: The many rules are parts of one complex habit, not many distinct habits; they coalesce as each becomes automatic.
questions.rule: One habit, many parts.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: From Many Rules to One Habit
questions.q: Sam opens the chapters on analytical reading, sees more than a dozen rules, and decides it is too much to learn. What would the authors say to him?
options: The rules are parts of one habit; past learning should make him patient
He is right, and should stay with inspectional reading only
He should learn all the rules in one evening to get it over with
He should pick the three rules he likes best and use those
optionExplain: Right: the authors say someone who has acquired one complex skill need not fear the array of rules, and patience recalled from other learning helps.
The authors write to encourage readers to go on; the length of the list is no reason to stop.
Cramming all the rules at once ignores the separate practice the authors describe.
Choosing a few leaves the habit incomplete; all the rules are parts of the one performance.
questions.explain: The authors expect the list to look daunting and answer with experience: complex skills always start with many rules, which fuse as each part becomes automatic.
questions.rule: Do not fear the array of rules.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: From Many Rules to One Habit
questions.q: Sort each thought by whether it shows a beginner's attention or an expert's, in the authors' account.
groups: Beginner: attention on the separate acts

items.t: Am I asking the four questions in the right order?
Where should my next margin note go?
Have I found the author's key terms yet?
What is this author really claiming about justice?
Does this argument change what I believe?
Can I take on this book I once thought too hard?

questions.explain: The beginner attends to himself and his skill in the separate acts. When the acts lose their separateness, attention turns to the goal: the book and what it means.
questions.rule: Technique first, then the goal.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: From Many Rules to One Habit
questions.q: The authors say learning to read well is harder than learning to ski. What reason do they give?
options: Books take far longer to finish than any ski run does
Reading has more rules than any other skill there is
Its acts are mental, so a beginner must watch his own thoughts
Ski instructors give clearer guidance than books on reading
optionExplain: Length is not the comparison the authors make.
The authors call reading much more complex than skiing, but their stated reason is its mental nature, not a count of rules.
Right: physical acts are easy to be conscious of; the beginning analytical reader must attend to mental acts, thinking about his own thoughts.
The authors say even the best ski instructor seems no help at first; their reason for reading's difficulty is that its acts are mental.
questions.explain: A skier can watch his knees; a reader has to notice what his mind is doing. Most people are not used to that, which makes the learning harder, though possible.
questions.rule: A reader's acts are mental, so watch your own thinking.
questions.teaches: Mental acts are harder to observe than physical ones, so a beginning reader must deliberately notice his own thinking, a kind of attention most people are not used to.

questions.unitTitle: How to Be a Demanding Reader
questions.section: From Many Rules to One Habit
questions.q: A nurse joining a new hospital faces a forty-step checklist for admitting patients and feels overwhelmed. Applying the authors' view, which outlook is most useful?
options: Each step is a separate habit to be kept apart from the others
The list is too long to master, so she should rely on colleagues
Only the first few steps matter much once she is on the ward
The steps are parts of one routine that will fuse with practice
optionExplain: The authors' point is the opposite: many rules describe one habit, not many separate ones.
Leaning on colleagues skips the separate learning the habit needs.
Every step is part of the whole performance; dropping some leaves it incomplete.
Right: like reading rules, the steps coalesce as each becomes automatic, freeing attention for the goal.
questions.explain: A long checklist is like a long list of reading rules: the steps describe one complex habit, and practised one by one they fuse into a single routine. The list remains the art as taught; the fused routine is the art as possessed.
questions.rule: A long checklist describes one practised routine.
questions.teaches: A checklist is the teachable form of a routine, not the routine itself: the written steps stay useful for learning and checking even after the performance no longer needs them one by one.

questions.q: Why do the authors state their rules of analytical reading in terms of whole books rather than articles?
options: A whole book poses the hardest problems a reader faces
Articles rarely hold arguments worth a careful, slow reading
Most of what serious readers read comes in book form
The rules were first built for students in book courses
optionExplain: Right: a long, difficult book is the hardest case, and a reader who can manage it can manage shorter pieces.
Many articles repay careful reading; the authors say their rules apply to them too.
Book reading may be common, but the authors give difficulty, not frequency, as their reason.
The authors give no such history; their reason is that the whole book is the hardest case.
questions.explain: The authors pick whole books because they pose the severest problems; what works there works on easier material. The card next shows how the rules carry over.
questions.rule: Train on the hardest case.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reader who can read a philosophical work well can also read an article in the same field.
questions.explain: The authors say that if you can read an expository book such as a history, a philosophical work or a scientific treatise, you can read an article or abstract in the same field.
questions.rule: Skill with the long form covers the short form of the same kind.

questions.q: Sort each pairing by the authors' reasoning: does skill with the first piece help with the second?

items.t: A novel, then a short story
An epic poem, then a lyric
A history book, then a history article
A scientific treatise, then an abstract in its field
A short story, then a long novel
A novel, then a chemistry paper

questions.explain: The authors claim that skill runs from harder to easier pieces of the same kind. They make no claim that short pieces prepare you for long ones, or that one kind prepares you for another.
questions.hint: Check two things: is the second piece easier, and is it the same kind?
questions.rule: Downward, within a kind.

questions.q: Suppose a reader has practised only on short stories and now faces a long, demanding novel. Going by the authors' reasoning, what should she expect?
options: The same ease, since stories and novels are one and the same kind
Less difficulty, since a novel has more room to explain
Ease with the plot, since short stories train plot reading best
More difficulty, since the authors' claim runs from long to short
optionExplain: Same kind is necessary for the transfer, but the authors also say the long form is the harder one.
More room to explain does not make a long book easier; the authors call the long form harder.
Nothing in the authors' reasoning singles out plot reading as what short stories train.
Right: the authors say the whole book poses the hardest problems, so skill gained on short pieces need not carry up to it.
questions.explain: The authors' claim is one-directional: master the harder, longer form and the shorter one comes easily. Reversing the direction removes the support for the claim.
questions.rule: The transfer runs downward, not upward.

questions.q: A two-page abstract in theoretical physics proves harder for one reader than a 300-page popular physics book. How does this fit the authors' reasoning?
options: It refutes them, since short pieces are meant to be easier to read than books
It shows the abstract is a different kind from the book
It fits, since they say shorter is almost always easier, not always
It shows the reader has not yet learned elementary reading
optionExplain: The authors hedge their claim, so one hard abstract does not refute it.
Both are expository physics; a difference in difficulty is not a difference in kind.
Right: the authors write that a short piece is almost always easier, which leaves room for exceptions like a dense abstract.
Struggling with technical physics says nothing about whether the reader can read words and sentences.
questions.explain: The authors say reading an article is almost always easier than a book on the same subject, which leaves room for a dense exception. When a short piece is that hard, it deserves the full method, not a trimmed version.
questions.rule: Shorter is usually, not always, easier.
questions.teaches: Difficulty, not length, sets how much of the method a piece needs: a short text that proves as hard as a book deserves the full analytical treatment rather than a lighter adaptation.

questions.q: A paralegal trained to analyse full, eighty-page contracts is asked to check a one-paragraph amendment. Which conclusion fits the authors' reasoning, by analogy?
options: Her contract skills cover it, with some adjustment for size
She needs new training, since amendments are their own legal kind
She can read it loosely, since one paragraph rarely misleads
Her skills will not help, since short texts hide more traps
optionExplain: Right: by analogy with books and articles, skill with the long, hard form carries to the short form of the same kind, adapted to fit.
An amendment is still contract language, the same kind she already reads.
A short text can still bind her client; the rules shrink to fit, they do not lapse.
Short texts can be tricky, but that is no reason to think her trained skill is useless on them.
questions.explain: By analogy, mastering the full contract prepares her for a clause of the same kind. She keeps the same questions and adapts them to the smaller text.
questions.rule: Master the whole, then adapt to the part.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the authors' reasoning fits any field: practising on the hardest complete form of a task, such as a whole contract, prepares you for its smaller forms of the same kind.

questions.q: True or false: In the authors' method, the first rule of analytical reading is to work out what kind of book you are reading.
questions.explain: Rule 1 is about classifying the book. The card next gives the rule in full and says how early to meet it.
questions.rule: Rule 1 is classification.

questions.q: Rule 1 says you should know what kind of book you are reading as early as possible, preferably before you ____.
questions.explain: The rule asks for the kind as early in the process as possible, preferably before you begin to read.
questions.rule: Classify before page one if you can.

questions.q: Which reader follows Rule 1 best?
options: Ana, who reads three chapters and then decides the kind
Cal, who decides the kind once finished, to sum it up
Ben, who decides the kind from the title, contents and preface
Dee, who goes by the shelf label in the shop where she bought it
optionExplain: Ana does classify, but three chapters in is later than the rule asks.
Classifying at the end is too late to guide the reading.
Right: Ben settles the kind before he begins, using the book's own front matter.
A shelf label is someone else's guess; it is no substitute for looking at the book itself.
questions.explain: Rule 1 asks for the kind as early as possible, preferably before reading begins, and the book's own front matter is what makes that possible.
questions.rule: Classify early, from the book itself.

questions.q: Rule 1 has a part you must meet and a part you should meet. Which is the part you should meet?
options: Know what kind of book you are reading
Know the kind as early as you can
Know whether the author is correct
Know the book's main argument
optionExplain: This is the part you must meet; without it, the rule fails altogether.
Right: knowing the kind is required; knowing it early, ideally before reading, is what you should aim for.
Truth is not part of Rule 1 at all; judging comes much later in analytical reading.
The main argument is not part of Rule 1; the rule concerns only the kind of book.
questions.explain: You must know the kind; you should know it early. The first is the core of the rule, the second is how well you meet it.
questions.rule: Must: the kind. Should: early.

questions.q: True or false: When a text has no title page, contents or preface, Rule 1 stops applying to it.
questions.explain: The rule asks for the kind as early as possible; front matter is only the easiest route. Without it, you read into the text just far enough to place it, then go on.
questions.rule: No front matter: classify from the first pages.

questions.q: A visitor reads the panel at the entrance of an unfamiliar exhibition to see whether it is a history of the building, a science display or an art show. Which part of Rule 1 does this match?
options: Judging the exhibition's quality before seeing it
Gathering the facts she needs to summarise it later
Choosing which rooms she can afford to skip entirely
Settling its kind before she begins, to guide her visit
optionExplain: The panel tells her the kind of show, not whether it is good.
Summarising comes after the visit; the panel serves the start.
Skipping rooms may follow, but the step she takes is classifying, not cutting.
Right: like a reader with front matter, she settles the kind at the start so it shapes what she looks for inside.
questions.explain: Reading the entrance panel is pigeonholing the exhibition before she starts. The kind tells her what to look for, and so how to spend her time, room by room.
questions.rule: Classify at the entrance.
questions.teaches: Classifying at the start also helps you plan your effort: once you know what kind of thing you face, you can judge roughly how much attention each part of it deserves.

questions.q: A book sets out one economist's speculations about the next fifty years, none of them proven. How would the authors classify it?
options: As fiction, since its claims are only unproven guesses
As neither, since opinion is not knowledge
As expository, since it offers its claims as true
As fiction, since it describes events yet to happen
optionExplain: Unproven is not invented: the economist offers the guesses as likely true.
The authors count opinions and speculations as knowledge in a broad sense.
Right: speculations offered as true in some sense make a book expository.
Writing about the future is not storytelling when the forecasts are offered as true.
questions.explain: The authors take knowledge broadly, so speculations claimed to be true make a book expository. The card next spells out the split.
questions.rule: Offered as true: expository.

questions.q: Which of these count as fiction in the authors' first split? Select all that apply.
options: A play
A book of theories about the origin of language
A lyric poem
A treatise on ethics
An epic
optionExplain: Right: the authors list plays among works of fiction.
Theories offered as true make a book expository, however uncertain they are.
Right: lyric poems are on the authors' list of fiction.
A treatise on ethics conveys knowledge in the broad sense, so it is expository.
Right: the epic is on the authors' list of fiction.
questions.explain: Novels, plays, epics and lyrics are the authors' examples of fiction. Theories and treatises offered as true are expository.
questions.rule: Fiction: novel, play, epic, lyric.

questions.q: Sort each book into the authors' first split.

items.t: A play about a family feud
A novel set in a mining town
An epic poem about a war at sea
Speculations about life on other planets, offered as likely
A critic's opinions on modern painting
A chemistry textbook

questions.explain: The play, novel and epic tell stories. The speculations, the critic's opinions and the textbook all offer claims as true in some sense, so all three are expository.
questions.hint: Is it telling a story, or offering claims as true?
questions.rule: Story or claims offered as true.

questions.q: Sam reasons: Step 1, the book is full of its author's opinions. Step 2, opinions are not knowledge. Step 3, so it is not an expository book. Which step goes wrong by the authors' definition?
options: Step 1, since opinions are hard to spot reliably in a book
Step 2, since knowledge is meant in a broad sense here
Step 3, since it does not follow from Steps 1 and 2
None, since opinion books are a kind of fiction
optionExplain: Spotting opinions may be hard, but Sam's observation is not where his reasoning fails.
Right: the authors count opinions claimed to be true as knowledge in their broad sense.
Step 3 does follow from Step 2; the trouble is that Step 2 is false.
Opinions offered as true tell no story, so they do not make a book fiction.
questions.explain: The authors construe knowledge broadly: opinions, theories, hypotheses and speculations claimed to be true all count, so Sam's Step 2 is the faulty premise.
questions.rule: Opinion offered as true still counts.

questions.q: A book on dream interpretation does not say outright that its theory is correct; it lays the theory out as an account of how dreams work. Is it expository?
options: No, because it never claims in so many words to be true
Yes, but only once its theory has been tested and confirmed by others
No, because a theory of dreams is a kind of imaginative writing
Yes, because offering it as an account of dreams claims truth
optionExplain: The claim need not be stated outright; presenting the theory as how things are already makes it.
Confirmation does not matter; untested theories offered as true count as knowledge in the broad sense.
The subject of dreams does not make the book a story; it offers an account, not a tale.
Right: the authors say the claim of truth may be made more or less explicitly, and an account of how things work implies it.
questions.explain: The authors say the claim to truth may be made more or less explicitly. Offering a theory as an account of how dreams work is such a claim, even if it is never announced.
questions.rule: The claim of truth can be implicit.
questions.teaches: The claim of truth may be implicit: a book need not announce that its theories are true; setting them out as an account of how things are is enough to make it expository.

questions.q: A podcast episode gives the host's theory of why a local restaurant failed, offered as the true explanation, with no invented story. Applying the authors' split, what is it?
options: Expository, because it offers its explanation as true
Fiction, because the host cannot prove the theory
Neither, since a spoken theory is only talk, not knowledge
Fiction, because podcasts are told in a storytelling voice
optionExplain: Right: the test is whether claims are offered as true, whatever the medium.
Lack of proof does not make a theory a story; it is still offered as true.
Knowledge is meant broadly; a theory offered as true counts, spoken or written.
A narrative tone does not turn a claimed explanation into fiction.
questions.explain: The test carries over: the episode offers a theory as the true explanation, so it is expository. Without front matter, a listener has to settle that from what the host says first.
questions.rule: The split works beyond books.
questions.teaches: A spoken work is often harder to classify than a book because it has no title page or preface to inspect, so its opening minutes have to do the work of the front matter.

questions.q: True or false: Once you know a book is expository, you also know in what particular way it will instruct you.
questions.explain: Expository is only the first split. A history, a philosophical work and a physics text are all expository, yet they instruct in quite different ways.
questions.rule: Expository is a first step, not the whole classification.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, how easily a book reads is a good sign of whether it is fiction.
questions.explain: The authors point to a book on relativity that is not fiction yet reads almost as easily as a novel. The card next shows why the line can blur.
questions.rule: Readability is not a test of kind.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say some novels carry so much social science, and some sociology so much fiction, that the two are hard to keep apart.
questions.explain: That is the authors' point: the blur comes from content crossing the line in both directions, not from any defect in the reader.
questions.rule: Content can cross the line both ways.

questions.q: A gripping, plain-language book explains how vaccines train the immune system, with no invented characters. A friend says it must be a novel because it reads like one. What is the best reply?
options: Agreed, since books this readable are written as stories by design
It may be a novel, since novels often explain science
Its ease proves nothing; it offers claims as true
It is neither, since popular science is a separate class
optionExplain: Readability is the very sign the authors warn against using.
Some novels carry science, but this book has no story and offers its account as true.
Right: readability does not decide kind; offering claims as true does.
Popular science still falls in the first split, on the expository side.
questions.explain: The authors' relativity example makes the point: an expository book can read like a novel. The test is what it offers, not how it reads.
questions.rule: Judge kind by what is offered, not by ease.

questions.q: Which of these are sound grounds for calling a book fiction? Select all that apply.
options: It is built as a story about invented characters
It is shelved with the novels in most bookshops
It reads easily and quickly from start to finish
Its events are offered as imagined, not as fact
It contains no statistics, tables or other data
optionExplain: Right: telling a story about invented people is what fiction does.
A shelf label is someone's judgment, which may be mistaken; it does not decide the kind.
Expository books can read easily, as the authors' relativity example shows.
Right: imagined events, not reported facts, mark a work as fiction.
Plenty of expository books, in philosophy for example, contain no data at all.
questions.explain: Sound grounds concern what the book does: tell a story of imagined events. Shelving, ease and the absence of data do not settle it.
questions.rule: Look at what the book does, not at its packaging.

questions.q: A sociologist's study invents a few composite families to illustrate its real findings, and says so. Does the invented material make the study fiction?
options: Yes, since any invented character makes a work fiction
Yes, since its findings can no longer be checked against real cases
No, since sociology is defined as a science
No, since its aim is still to offer findings as true
optionExplain: Invented material is the blur the authors describe; it does not alone decide the kind.
The composites illustrate the findings; the findings rest on the real study.
A field name does not decide kind; some novels look like sociology too.
Right: the study uses fiction as illustration, but what it mainly offers is findings claimed to be true.
questions.explain: The authors note that some sociology contains much fiction. Invented illustrations do not turn a study into fiction when its aim is still to offer findings as true.
questions.rule: Fictional illustration does not make a study fiction.
questions.teaches: Invented illustrations inside a study, such as composite cases, do not make it fiction: what decides is whether the work as a whole offers its findings as true.

questions.q: A website publishes a piece laid out like a news report, with quotes and a dateline, but the site is a known satire outlet and the events are invented. In the authors' first split, what is it?
options: Expository, since it follows the format of a news report
Fiction, since its events are invented despite the format
Expository, since satire makes real claims about the world it mocks
Neither, since satire mixes invented events with real opinions
optionExplain: Format is packaging; the report's events are made up.
Right: invented events make it fiction, however factual it looks.
Satire may hint at views, but the piece itself tells an invented story.
Satire may carry opinions, but the piece itself tells invented events, which is enough to place it as fiction.
questions.explain: Here the blur runs the other way: a story dressed as a report. The invented events, not the layout, decide the kind.
questions.rule: Format can mislead in either direction.
questions.teaches: Format can mislead in both directions: a piece laid out like a factual report may be invented, just as a novel may carry real social facts, so check what the piece offers as true.

questions.q: Two expository books both deal with crime: a history of a famous trial and a work arguing what punishment is fair. What matters most for a reader telling them apart?
options: Which of the two books is longer and more detailed
The kinds of problems they take up and their methods
Which author has the stronger reputation
Whether the two books reach the same conclusion
optionExplain: Length and detail do not tell you how a book instructs.
Right: the two books deal with different problems by different methods, which shapes how each should be read.
Reputation may help you choose a book, not classify it.
Conclusions come later; the kind of book can be known before you reach them.
questions.explain: A shared subject hides a difference in kind: one book recounts events, the other reasons about what is just. The card next explains why the way a book instructs matters.
questions.rule: Same subject, different ways of instructing.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a book on physics and a book on morals deal with different problems and use different methods to solve them.
questions.explain: The authors use exactly this pair to show that expository books instruct in different ways: different problems, different methods.
questions.rule: Different kinds, different problems and methods.

questions.q: Match each expository book to the kind of question it mainly sets out to answer.
pairs: How does nature behave in general?
A work on the nature of knowledge
What can be known, and how?
questions.explain: Each book instructs in its own way because it takes up a different kind of question. Seeing which question a book answers is what naming its way of instructing means.
questions.rule: Name the question the book answers.

questions.q: Jo has two expository books: a history of a famous trial and a treatise on fair punishment. Which of her plans go wrong, given that expository books instruct in different ways? Select all that apply.
options: Read both with the same questions in mind
Use her notes on one as a guide to the other
Ask first what problem each book takes up
Expect the history to narrate events
Expect the treatise to argue what ought to be
optionExplain: Right: the same questions will not fit a narrative and an argument about fairness.
Right: notes on one way of instructing will mislead her about the other.
A sound plan: naming the problem each book takes up is how she finds its way of instructing.
A sound plan: a history instructs by narrating.
A sound plan: a treatise on punishment argues about what should be done.
questions.explain: Being expository is shared; the way of instructing is not. Plans that treat the two books alike go wrong, while plans that ask how each instructs are sound.
questions.rule: Expository is a family, not a single kind.

questions.q: Three books are about money: one tells how coins first came into use in ancient Lydia, one measures how households actually spend, and one argues what a fair wage is. What does this show?
options: Books on one subject belong to one kind
Money books are always practical in the end, whatever they say
Only the first is expository, since it has facts
Subject alone does not fix the kind of book
optionExplain: The three share a subject yet instruct in quite different ways.
Two of them make no claim about what anyone should do.
All three offer claims as true, so all three are expository.
Right: one subject can be treated as a narrative of the past, a measurement of behaviour, or an argument about what is right.
questions.explain: The kind follows the treatment, not the topic. Money is handled here as a story of the past, as a study of behaviour, and as a question of fairness.
questions.rule: Classify by treatment, not by topic.
questions.teaches: Kind follows the treatment, not the topic: one subject, such as money or war, can be handled as a narrative of the past, a study of how things behave, or an argument about what is right.

questions.q: A new manager gets three documents about customer complaints: a timeline of one incident, a statistical study of complaint patterns, and a policy telling staff what to do. Which approach fits the authors' advice?
options: Read all three the same way, since they share a topic
Ask how each one instructs, to know what to look for
Read the policy only, since it is the one to act on
Read the statistics first, since numbers are most reliable
optionExplain: A shared topic hides three different ways of instructing.
Right: a narrative, a study and a set of directions each call for different questions.
The policy matters for action, but the others carry knowledge she needs to understand it.
Numbers are not automatically more reliable, and order is not the authors' point here.
questions.explain: The three documents instruct in different ways: a narrative, a study and a set of directions. Naming each one's way tells her what to look for, and the first two give her what she needs to judge the policy.
questions.rule: Ask how each document instructs.
questions.teaches: Knowing how each document instructs also suggests an order: reading the ones that give knowledge, such as a timeline or a data study, before the one that directs action lets you judge the directions.

questions.q: Which of these would the authors have you look at to classify a book before reading it? Select all that apply.
options: Reviews by other readers online
The number of pages in the book
The table of contents
The publisher's blurb
The title and subtitle
optionExplain: Reviews are other readers' verdicts, not the signals the authors list.
Length tells you little about what kind of book it is.
Right: the contents list is one of the signals the authors name.
Right: the authors say to read the blurb if the book has a dust jacket.
Right: title and subtitle come first on the authors' list.
questions.explain: The authors list the title, subtitle, contents, preface, index and blurb. The card next explains why these are the signals to read.
questions.rule: Classify from the front matter.

questions.q: The authors call the title, contents, preface and blurb the signal ____ the author waves to let you know which way the wind is blowing.
questions.explain: These are the signal flags the author waves. They exist to help you classify the book.
questions.rule: Front matter signals the kind.

questions.q: Pat skips the title page and preface of a new book, starts at chapter 1, and is soon puzzled about what kind of book it is. Where do the authors place the blame?
options: On Pat, since the author put the signals there to see
On the author, for not making the kind plain in chapter 1
On the bookseller, for shelving it in the wrong section
On the publisher, for a jacket that did not explain it
optionExplain: Right: the authors say it is not the author's fault if you will not stop, look and listen.
The author made the kind plain where readers are meant to look first: the front matter.
Shelving is no part of the authors' account; Pat had the book's own signals in hand.
Pat never read the jacket, so it cannot be blamed for what he missed.
questions.explain: The signals were there; Pat did not read them. The authors put the burden on the reader who will not stop, look and listen.
questions.rule: Missed signals are the reader's fault.

questions.q: True or false: When a secondhand book has lost its dust jacket, one of the signals the authors list, the publisher's blurb, has most likely gone with it.
questions.explain: The authors say to read the blurb if the book has a dust jacket. Without the jacket, the signals bound into the book, such as the title page, contents, preface and index, remain.
questions.rule: Lose the jacket, lose the blurb; the rest remain.

questions.q: A book's title is a single vague word, but its subtitle and contents point plainly to a history of shipping. What should you conclude?
options: Nothing yet, since the title is the main signal
That it is fiction, since vague titles suit novels
That it is a history, since the other signals settle it
That it is philosophy, since abstract titles often suggest it
optionExplain: The title is one signal among several; it does not outrank the rest.
A vague title is common in nonfiction too; the other signals point to history.
Right: when one signal is vague, the others can settle what it leaves open.
An abstract-sounding title proves nothing against a subtitle and contents that say history.
questions.explain: The signals work together. A vague title is filled in by a clear subtitle and a contents list.
questions.rule: Read the signals as a set.
questions.teaches: The signals work as a set: when one is vague or misleading, the others can settle or correct it, so read several before deciding.

questions.q: Before starting an unfamiliar podcast series, which of these plays the part the authors give to a book's front matter?
options: The show description, episode titles and host's intro
The number of listeners and the series' chart position
The sound quality and the running time of each episode
The adverts played in the first minutes of each episode
optionExplain: Right: like title, contents and preface, these are placed by the makers to tell you what kind of show it is.
Popularity is other people's verdict, not a signal of kind.
Production details say little about what kind of show it is.
Adverts are placed by sponsors, not by the makers to describe the show.
questions.explain: The description, episode list and opening introduction are the series' own signals, placed by its makers. Chart positions and adverts come from outside and say nothing about what the makers intended.
questions.rule: Find the maker's own signals.
questions.teaches: Signals placed by a work's makers outrank signals from outside, such as popularity or reviews, because only the makers know what kind of work they set out to produce.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, students asked what sort of book they had read usually answered with ease.
questions.explain: The authors report that it was often hard to get any kind of answer. The card next explains why the question still matters so much.
questions.rule: Few readers ask what sort of book they hold.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: The authors call asking what sort of book it is a good, almost ____ way to begin a discussion of a book.
questions.explain: The authors say the question is a good, almost indispensable way to begin.
questions.rule: Start with the kind.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: According to the authors, what is one reason many readers ignore titles and prefaces?
options: They do not think classifying the book is important
They believe titles are chosen by publishers to sell
They worry that prefaces give away the book's argument
They find titles and prefaces too short to be useful
optionExplain: Right: the authors say readers ignore these signals because they do not think it important to classify the book.
Some readers may think so, but the authors give a different reason.
The authors do not mention this worry.
Shortness is not the authors' explanation; neglect of classification is.
questions.explain: The authors trace the neglect to readers not following Rule 1: they do not see why classifying matters.
questions.rule: Ignoring titles comes from ignoring Rule 1.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: Asked in general terms what sort of book she has read, which answer by Mia meets the authors' aim?
options: A gripping read that I could not put down
A bestseller that everyone at work is reading
A long book with a lot of footnotes and maps
A history of the Irish famine, told year by year
optionExplain: This reports her reaction, not the kind of book.
Popularity says nothing about the kind of book.
Footnotes and maps fit many kinds of book; they do not name one.
Right: it places the book in a kind, a history, and says what it covers.
questions.explain: The question asks for a kind. Reactions, popularity and physical features do not answer it.
questions.rule: Answer with a kind, not a reaction.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: A reader goes through a whole book without once asking what sort of book it is. According to the authors, what is likely to happen?
options: He reads faster, since labels and categories no longer distract him
He catches the kind anyway by the last chapter
He grows more perplexed and cannot answer other questions
He judges more freshly, free of any category bias
optionExplain: Speed is not at stake; understanding is.
The authors expect his confusion to grow, not clear up on its own.
Right: the authors say he will become more perplexed and be unable to answer many other questions about the book.
Without a kind, he lacks a frame for his questions; the authors see no gain in freshness.
questions.explain: The kind of book frames every later question. Skip it, and the other questions go unanswered.
questions.rule: No kind, no frame for other questions.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: Which of these answer the question of what sort of book it is, rather than some other question? Select all that apply.
options: A practical guide to beekeeping
Five stars, highly recommended
A philosophical work on free will
Written by a Nobel prize winner
About three hundred pages long
optionExplain: Right: it names a kind, a practical guide, and its subject.
This is a verdict on quality, not a kind.
Right: it names a kind, philosophy, and its subject.
This is about the author, not the kind of book.
Length is a physical fact, not a kind.
questions.explain: Only answers that place the book in a category answer the question. Verdicts, authorship and length answer other questions.
questions.rule: Kind is not verdict, author or size.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: A committee meets to discuss a consultant's report. Half the members treat it as a plan to adopt; the others treat it as an account of last year's failures. What does the authors' advice suggest the chair should do first?
options: Vote on the report's recommendations straight away
Ask the group to settle what sort of report it is
Let each side argue its reading until one wins
Send the report back to be rewritten in plainer words
optionExplain: Voting before agreeing on the report's kind means voting on two different documents.
Right: like opening a book discussion, settling the kind first stops members talking past each other.
Arguing about details while disagreeing on the kind prolongs the confusion.
Rewriting may not help; the members first need to ask the right question about it.
questions.explain: By analogy, the committee is discussing two different documents until it agrees what sort of report it holds. That question comes first.
questions.rule: Agree on the kind before debating the content.
questions.teaches: By analogy, settling what sort of document is on the table is a good opening for any group discussion, because members who classify it differently will talk past each other.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: More than half of a group of well-read people got the title of Darwin's famous book wrong. What mistake did they make?
options: They called it The Descent of Man instead
They called it The Theory of Evolution
They added a word: The Origin of the Species
They gave its subtitle in place of the title
optionExplain: The Descent of Man is a later Darwin book; the error was subtler.
This was not the mistake the authors report.
Right: they added the, which changed what they thought the book was about.
The authors do not mention the subtitle; the error was one added word.
questions.explain: Most said The Origin of the Species. One small word changed what they thought the book was about. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Small words in titles matter.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Darwin's The Origin of Species has little or nothing to do with the development of the human species.
questions.explain: The authors say the book is about the proliferation of plant and animal species, mainly through natural selection; Darwin treated human origins in The Descent of Man.
questions.rule: The title says what the book is about.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: A book is titled A History of Bread in Medieval France. Read word by word, which expectations does the title support? Select all that apply.
options: It recounts past events
It is limited to France
It covers the Middle Ages
It gives recipes for home baking
It argues how we should eat today
optionExplain: Right: history promises an account of the past.
Right: France limits the place.
Right: medieval limits the period.
Bread is the subject, but history is the treatment; a recipe book would announce itself differently.
Nothing in the title promises advice about today.
questions.explain: Each word narrows the book: history sets the treatment, bread the subject, medieval the period and France the place.
questions.rule: Each word of a title narrows the book.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: Ken sees a book titled The Psychology of Crowds and notes: about how individuals cope with stress. His note ignores the title's word ____.
questions.explain: Ken let an assumption, that psychology is about one person's mind, push aside what the title says. Like the readers who added the to Darwin's title, he read his expectation instead of the words.
questions.rule: Let the title's words beat your assumptions.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: A reader believes Darwin's book is about the origin of human beings and starts reading it. What is the likely cost?
options: She will look for human origins and miss its account of species
None, since the book's real subject will soon correct her
She will read more slowly than usual, but understand the book in the end
She will judge the book false because it lacks evidence
optionExplain: Right: a misread title sets her looking for what is not there, so she may overlook what is.
The book may correct her, but only late and at a cost: she has already read part of it looking for the wrong thing.
Slowness is not the main cost; looking for the wrong thing is.
She might be disappointed, but the main cost lies in what she looks for, and so in what she notices.
questions.explain: Expectations steer attention. A wrong idea of the subject sends her hunting for human evolution and past the argument about how species multiply.
questions.rule: A misread title misdirects your attention.
questions.teaches: A misread title does harm beyond the title: it sets wrong expectations, so the reader searches the book for what is not there and misses what is.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: A new law is titled the Data Retention (Amendment) Act. A reader skims it as a brand-new data protection law. What has he missed by not reading the title word by word?
options: That the law is about data and not about privacy
That it changes an existing law, not a new one
That it was passed by a different parliament
That it is a draft bill and not yet in force at all
optionExplain: Data and privacy are closely linked; the missed word is elsewhere.
Right: the word Amendment marks it as a change to an earlier act, which sets its scope.
The title gives no information about which parliament passed it.
Nothing in the title marks it as a draft.
questions.explain: One bracketed word sets the scope: an amending act changes an existing law. Read loosely, the title suggests a different document.
questions.rule: Small words in official titles set the scope.
questions.teaches: In official titles, small or bracketed words such as Amendment often mark a document's scope, so word-by-word reading matters as much for laws and reports as for books.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: True or false: Once you have read a title carefully word by word, you can be sure what the book contains without checking the contents or preface.
questions.explain: A title is a compressed promise. Careful reading narrows your expectations, but a word may be used in an unusual sense, so check against the contents and preface.
questions.rule: Test the title against the front matter.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: A history is titled The Decline and Fall of a great empire. Where would you expect its first chapter to begin?
options: At the empire's high point, before the decline
At the empire's founding, to show how it first rose to power
At its final collapse, then looking back
With its neighbours, to set the wider scene
optionExplain: Right: a decline has to start from a height, so the book should open there.
A founding would suit a rise and fall; the title promises only the decline.
Some histories open at the end, but the title points to a narrative running from height to fall.
Setting the scene is possible, but the title says nothing about neighbours.
questions.explain: Decline implies a height to decline from. The card next shows how readers of Gibbon missed exactly this.
questions.rule: A decline starts at a peak.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: True or false: The well-read people the authors asked were puzzled partly because Gibbon's book does not discuss the Roman Republic.
questions.explain: They expected a rise and fall, so they looked for the Republic. The title, Decline and Fall, implied a start at the Empire's high point instead.
questions.rule: Read what the title says, not what you expect.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: A book is titled The Decline and Fall of the Hanseatic League. Put the chapters in the order the title implies.
items: The League at the height of its power
First signs of weakness
Loss of trade routes and member towns
The League's final end
questions.explain: Decline and fall runs from a high point, through weakening, to the end. That is the frame the title sets.
questions.rule: Decline and fall: height, weakening, end.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: Suppose Gibbon had called his book The Rise and Fall of the Roman Empire. What would readers then be right to expect?
options: The same opening, in the Age of the Antonines
A shorter book, since rise and fall is a narrower subject
An argument about how empires ought to be governed and kept strong
An account that starts earlier and shows how Rome grew
optionExplain: The Age of the Antonines fits a book on decline; a rise needs an earlier start.
Rise and fall is a wider span than decline and fall, not a narrower one.
Both titles promise a narrative; neither promises advice on governing.
Right: rise adds the growth to the story, so the book would have to begin before the high point.
questions.explain: Change one word of the title and the expected starting point moves. Rise pushes the opening back before the peak.
questions.rule: Change the title, change the frame.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: A reviewer complains that Gibbon's book says little about the early Roman Republic. Read in the light of the title, what is the best reply?
options: The title marks the Republic as outside the book's scope
The complaint is fair, since a good history covers all periods
The Republic is covered in the preface instead
The complaint shows the book is philosophy, not history
optionExplain: Right: a book on decline begins at the height, so the earlier rise is left out by design.
No book covers everything; the title tells you which part this one covers.
The authors say nothing of the Republic being covered in the preface.
Leaving out a period does not change a history into another kind.
questions.explain: The title sets the scope. What falls outside it is a choice made by the author, not a gap in the book.
questions.rule: A title tells you what is left out, too.
questions.teaches: A title also tells you what a book leaves out: a book on decline puts the earlier rise outside its scope, so that absence is a choice, not a gap to criticise.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: A company report is titled Winding Down the Leeds Office. What can a manager infer before reading it?
options: It explains why the Leeds office was opened
It starts from a running office and covers its closure
It compares Leeds with the company's other offices
It proposes ways to expand the Leeds office's work
optionExplain: Opening is the start of the office's story, which the title does not cover.
Right: winding down implies an office still working and a process that ends with its closure.
A comparison may appear, but the title promises a process at one office.
Expansion is the opposite of what winding down implies.
questions.explain: Process words set a start state and an end state. Winding down begins with a working office and ends with a closed one.
questions.rule: Process words in a title set start and end.
questions.teaches: By analogy, process words in any title, such as winding down, recovery or launch, tell you the starting state and the end state the document covers.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, writers generally try to make the kind of their book plain in the preface.
questions.explain: Authors think it important for readers to know what kind of book they hold, so they say so in the preface. The card next shows how to use this.
questions.rule: The preface states the kind.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: Einstein and Infeld's preface says a scientific book, even though popular, must not be read in the same way as a ____.
questions.explain: Their preface tells readers both the kind of book and how to read it: a popular scientific book still calls for a different reading from a novel.
questions.rule: Prefaces can say how to read the book.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: A book's only title is Water. Which part of the front matter would best show you what kind of book it is?
options: The cover picture, which shows what the book is about
The dedication, which shows whom it is for
The chapter headings, which amplify the title
The copyright page, which gives the date
optionExplain: A picture of water fits a novel, a science book or a guide equally well.
A dedication rarely says anything about the kind of book.
Right: the headings expand the one-word title into a picture of what the book does.
The date says when, not what kind.
questions.explain: A bare title leaves the kind open. The authors say the chapter headings amplify the significance of the main title.
questions.rule: Vague title: read the headings.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: Which of these preface statements would help you classify the book? Select all that apply.
options: Explains how tides work, for readers without maths
I thank my editor and my family for their patience
Each chapter ends with exercises in the methods
This book was written over five summers in Maine
Read it as an argument, not as a reference work
optionExplain: Right: it says what the book does and for whom, an explanatory book on tides.
Thanks tell you about the author's life, not the book's kind.
Right: exercises for practising methods mark a book that teaches a skill.
Where and when it was written says nothing about its kind.
Right: the author tells you what kind of book it is and how to read it.
questions.explain: Useful preface statements say what the book does and how to read it. Thanks and circumstances of writing do not.
questions.rule: Look for what the book does and how to read it.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: A book's blurb calls it an inspiring true story, but the author's preface says it is a study of how charities raise money. Which should weigh more in classifying it?
options: The blurb, since publishers know their market best
Neither, since the two cancel each other out
The blurb, since it is the first thing readers see
The preface, since it is the author's own statement
optionExplain: Publishers know how to sell a book; the author knows what kind of book was written.
Conflicting signals call for weighing them, not discarding both.
Being seen first does not make a signal more accurate.
Right: authors use the preface to make the kind plain, while the blurb is written by someone else.
questions.explain: By the authors' reasoning, the preface is where the author makes the kind plain. The blurb is a second-hand description, so the preface weighs more, to be checked against the contents.
questions.rule: Author's word over publisher's.
questions.teaches: When the publisher's blurb and the author's preface disagree about the kind, the author's own statement is the better guide, since the blurb is written by someone else.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: A government paper has the vague title Moving Forward. Its headings read: the shortage of nurses; its causes; three options; the option we recommend; costs. What kind of document is it?
options: A proposal recommending action on nurse numbers
A history of nursing in the country since about 1900
A statistical survey of what nurses are paid
A collection of nurses' personal stories of work
optionExplain: Right: the headings run from a problem to options to a recommended course, the shape of a proposal.
The paper looks at causes, but the headings move on to options and a recommendation.
Costs appear, but pay is not the subject and the paper ends in a recommendation.
Nothing in the headings suggests personal stories.
questions.explain: The headings turn an empty title into a clear picture: problem, causes, options, recommendation, cost. That is a proposal for action.
questions.rule: Headings amplify a vague title.
questions.teaches: By analogy, headings in any long document amplify its title: read in sequence, they turn a vague title into a picture of what the document does.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: According to the authors, what must a reader have before even the clearest title can help classify a book?
options: A summary of the book from a trusted source
Some knowledge of the author's life and times
A habit of reading the last chapter first
Broad categories of books already in mind
