optionExplain: A summary might help, but the authors name something the reader carries, not borrows.
Biography may help in other ways, but it is not what the authors say titles depend on.
Reading the end is part of inspection, not what makes a title useful.
Right: without categories in mind, titles and front matter have nowhere to place the book.
questions.explain: Titles inform only a reader with categories ready. The card next shows this with two famous titles.
questions.rule: Bring categories to the title.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: True or false: The authors say elements and principles mean much the same in the titles of Euclid's and James' books, though not in general.
questions.explain: In these two titles both words point to the basic truths of a science. The authors add that this does not hold in general.
questions.rule: Shared title words can mislead.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: A reader sees Elements of Geometry and Principles of Psychology and decides the two books have nothing in common. What is she missing, by the authors' account?
options: That geometry and psychology are both sciences
That both books were written as school textbooks
That both are works of philosophy rather than of science
That both authors wrote in the same century
optionExplain: Right: knowing both subjects are sciences shows how the books are of the same sort.
Being textbooks is not the authors' point and may not be true.
The authors call both sciences, not philosophy.
Euclid was ancient and James modern; dates do not link them.
questions.explain: The link is a category: both are sciences. Without that category in mind, the titles look unrelated.
questions.rule: Categories reveal what titles hide.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: Knowing that both are sciences shows how Euclid's and James' books are alike; to tell them apart you must also know there are different kinds of ____.
questions.explain: One category groups them, a finer one separates them: there are different kinds of science.
questions.rule: Categories at more than one level.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: Ivo knows no geometry at all. Can he still classify Euclid's Elements, by the authors' account?
options: No, since he must master geometry to classify the book
No, since only a trained mathematician can judge a geometry book
Yes, but only after reading the whole book once through
Yes, if he knows geometry is a science, without its content
optionExplain: Classifying needs the category, not mastery of the subject.
Judging the book is a later task; classifying it needs much less.
Classification is meant to come early, not after a full reading.
Right: the authors ask you to know that geometry is a science, not to know geometry.
questions.explain: Category knowledge differs from subject knowledge. You can place a book on a subject you have not learned if you know what kind of subject it is.
questions.rule: Know the category, not the content.
questions.teaches: Category knowledge is not subject knowledge: you can classify a book on geometry without knowing geometry, as long as you know what kind of thing geometry is.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: A wine list gives only region names, such as Rioja and Barolo. By analogy with the authors' point, why does it help some diners and not others?
options: Some carry categories that the names fit into
Some diners read more slowly than others
Some diners have tasted far more wine than others
Some diners have a better memory for names they have seen
optionExplain: Right: a label informs only someone with a scheme to place it in.
Speed is not what makes a label informative.
Tasting experience may build categories, but it is the categories that do the work.
Remembering a name is not enough; it informs only if it fits a scheme of categories.
questions.explain: Like a title, a region name is a label. It tells you something only if you carry categories to place it in, and each one placed makes the next easier.
questions.rule: Labels need a scheme.
questions.teaches: Categories and labels build on each other: each new label you manage to place also sharpens your scheme, so the reader who already carries categories learns more from every new title.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: True or false: When two titles share a key word such as principles, the books can be taken to be of the same kind.
questions.explain: The authors note that elements and principles match in Euclid's and James' titles but not in general. A shared word is a clue to check, not a classification.
questions.rule: Shared words are clues, not proof.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the titles The City of God, Leviathan and Social Contract make it easy to see that all three are political treatises.
questions.explain: The authors say it might not be easy to tell from these titles. The card next shows what would reveal it.
questions.rule: Titles do not always group books.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: The authors say a careful perusal of the chapter ____ would reveal the problems that the three political books have in common.
questions.explain: When titles hide what books share, the chapter headings show the problems they take up.
questions.rule: Headings reveal shared problems.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: Three books are titled Fire and Ice, The Quiet Shore and Long Division. How should you check whether they belong together?
options: Compare their covers and their publishers' series
Read the first page of each to compare their styles
Look through their chapter headings for shared problems
Wait until you have read all three in full
optionExplain: Covers and series are marketing choices, not signs of shared problems.
Style can be shared across very different kinds of book.
Right: the headings show which problems each book takes up.
Grouping should come early; waiting gives up the help the headings offer now.
questions.explain: Uninformative titles send you to the headings, which list the problems each book treats.
questions.rule: Group by problems in the headings.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: A reader writes a note on a set of three books. Which notes meet Rule 1? Select all that apply.
options: These are all political treatises
These three seem alike somehow
These are all works of mathematics
These three all ask who should rule
These three share chapters on law and citizens
optionExplain: Right: it names the kind the books share.
Sensing a likeness without naming the kind is grouping, not classifying.
Right: it names the kind.
A shared problem groups the books, but Rule 1 needs the kind named: political treatises.
Common chapter headings are evidence for a group, not the name of its kind.
questions.explain: Rule 1 asks you to know what the kind is. A note must name it; a vague likeness, a shared problem or shared headings only group the books.
questions.rule: Name the kind, do not just sense it.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: A reader plans to skip classifying and finish each book, trusting that its kind will be clear by the end. What do the authors say that bears on this plan?
options: It works, since a whole book will always reveal its kind
It works, though only for books on familiar subjects
It fails, since reading whole books takes far too long
A whole book may not show its kind without categories
optionExplain: The authors deny this: without categories, sometimes even the whole book will not tell you.
Familiarity may help, but the authors' point is about categories, not subjects.
Speed is a cost, but the deeper problem is that finishing may not reveal the kind at all.
Right: the authors say neither the title, the front matter nor sometimes the whole book reveals the kind unless you have categories to apply.
questions.explain: The authors say the whole book itself sometimes will not tell you its kind unless you bring categories. Finishing is no substitute for them.
questions.rule: Finishing a book does not classify it.
questions.teaches: According to the authors, without categories even reading the whole book may not tell you its kind, so finishing a book is no substitute for carrying categories.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: A listener has a playlist of songs she senses belong together but cannot name. A friend tells her they are all bossa nova. What does the name add, by analogy with the authors' point?
options: Nothing, since she had already grouped them
A link to what is known about that kind of music
A quicker way to find the songs again in her music app
Proof that her ear for music is reliable
optionExplain: Grouping is a start, but an unnamed group carries no knowledge with it.
Right: once named, the group connects to what is known about the kind, its history, rhythms and features.
Searching may be easier, but that is not what naming adds to understanding.
Naming confirms her grouping only in part; it does not prove anything about her ear.
questions.explain: A named kind brings knowledge with it. That is why Rule 1 asks you to know what the kind is, not only that books are alike.
questions.rule: A name links a group to knowledge.
questions.teaches: A named kind carries knowledge with it: once you can say what kind something is, you can bring to it what you know about that kind, which an unnamed group cannot give.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: Which of these is the main split in the authors' rough classification of books?
options: Old books versus modern books
Easy books versus difficult books
Popular books versus scholarly ones
Fiction versus expository works
optionExplain: Age matters for other questions, not for the authors' main split.
Difficulty varies within every kind, so it does not divide kinds.
A popular book can be expository, as the authors' relativity example shows.
Right: the main distinction is between fiction and works that convey knowledge.
questions.explain: The rough scheme begins with fiction versus expository works. The card next shows how it divides further and what it lacks.
questions.rule: First split: fiction or expository.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: Which of these are divisions of expository works in the authors' rough scheme? Select all that apply.
options: History
Philosophy
Lyric and epic poetry
Science and mathematics
Plays and other drama
optionExplain: Right: history is one division of expository works.
Right: philosophy is another.
Poetry, such as epic and lyric, falls on the fiction side.
Right: science and mathematics form the third division.
Plays fall on the fiction side.
questions.explain: Among expository works the authors distinguish history from philosophy, and both from science and mathematics.
questions.rule: Expository: history, philosophy, science and mathematics.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: Match each book to its slot in the authors' rough scheme.
pairs: An account of the Napoleonic wars
Proofs of theorems about prime numbers
A study of how stars form
An inquiry into what makes an action free
questions.explain: Each of these books fits the rough scheme without trouble, which is why the authors say most people can place most books in it.
questions.rule: Most books find a slot quickly.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: Ravi says: the rough scheme sorts most books well, so it needs no improvement. What do the authors say it still lacks?
options: A category for books of poetry and plays
Principles that justify the categories
A ranking of the categories by importance
More examples of books in each category
optionExplain: Poetry and plays already sit on the fiction side.
Right: the authors say the scheme has no principles of classification as yet.
The authors do not rank the categories.
Examples would illustrate the categories but not justify them.
questions.explain: Sorting most books is not enough. Without principles, the scheme cannot say why its lines fall where they do or settle the hard cases.
questions.rule: Categories need principles.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: A book on how to run a fair election fits none of fiction, history, philosophy, science or mathematics comfortably. What does this suggest, in the light of the authors' remarks?
options: The scheme lacks a principle that would place such a book
The book is badly written and should not be classified
The book must be fiction, since it fits no other slot
The scheme is useless and should be abandoned
optionExplain: Right: a book that fits no slot exposes the scheme's missing principle, here the line between knowing and doing.
Fitting badly is a fact about the scheme, not a verdict on the writing.
Fiction is a positive kind, storytelling, not a leftover bin.
The scheme works for most books; it needs a further distinction, not abandonment.
questions.explain: A book that tells you what to do has no natural home in the rough scheme. That gap is what the theoretical and practical distinction fills.
questions.rule: A misfit book exposes a gap in the scheme.
questions.teaches: A book that fits no slot, or two slots at once, is a sign that the scheme lacks a principle, not that the book is odd; here the gap is the line between knowing and doing.

questions.section: What You Can Learn from the Title of a Book
questions.q: An office files email in folders by sender: clients, suppliers, staff. Messages about a supplier's contract with a client keep landing in the wrong place. What does the authors' point about principles suggest?
options: Delete messages that fit more than one folder
Find a principle that decides where such messages go
Add a new folder for each new kind of awkward message that arrives
Let each person choose a folder by instinct
optionExplain: Discarding hard cases hides the problem without solving it.
Right: a scheme with a principle can settle borderline cases; a list of slots cannot.
Adding folders case by case multiplies slots without a principle behind them.
Instinct gives different answers for different people, the opposite of a principle.
questions.explain: Like the rough scheme of books, the folders handle easy cases and fail on hard ones. A principle of classification is what settles the borderline.
questions.rule: A principle settles the borderline cases.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any sorting scheme without a principle behind it handles the easy cases and fails on the hard ones; a principle is what tells you where a borderline item goes.

questions.q: True or false: In the authors' sense, a theoretical book is one whose ideas are visionary or of no practical use.
questions.explain: That is the hardheaded man's rough view. The authors polish it into a difference of ends, knowledge versus action. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Theoretical does not mean useless.

questions.q: According to the authors, what are the two ends a writer of an expository book may have in mind?
options: Pleasure and instruction
Truth and beauty
Facts and opinions
Knowledge and action
optionExplain: Pleasure and instruction is an old pairing for literature, not the authors' distinction here.
Truth and beauty concern other questions, not the theoretical and practical split.
Both theoretical and practical books may contain facts and opinions.
Right: polishing the rough view gives knowledge and action as the two ends.
questions.explain: Theoretical books aim at knowledge, something to be seen or understood; practical books aim at action, something that works.
questions.rule: Two ends: knowledge, action.

questions.q: Sort each book by the end it aims at.

items.t: A book explaining why the seasons change
A book on how bees communicate
A book on what caused the 2008 financial crash
A guide to training a puppy
A manual for repairing bicycles
A book urging readers to vote in every election

questions.explain: The first three aim at understanding something. The last three aim at something you will do: train, repair, vote.
questions.hint: Ask whether the book wants you to understand something or to do something.
questions.rule: Understand: theoretical. Do: practical.

questions.q: A businessman says: this book on economic policy will not make me money this year, so it is not practical. What part of the authors' view does he miss?
options: That economics books are theoretical by definition
That the practical is what works, now or in the long run
That a book is practical if it is easy to apply
That practical books avoid the subject of money
optionExplain: The authors say economics is usually practical, though some studies of it are theoretical.
Right: the authors say the practical has to do with what works, at once or in the long run.
Ease of application is not the test; the book's end is.
Practical books often deal with money; that is not the point.
questions.explain: The businessman equates practical with an immediate return. The authors keep the core of his view, what works, but drop the demand that it pay off at once.
questions.rule: Practical can mean the long run.

questions.q: True or false: If a book's explanation of why arches carry loads were rewritten as step-by-step instructions for building one, the book's end would change from knowledge to action.
questions.explain: The subject stays the same, but the end changes: the rewritten book aims at what you will do, so it becomes practical.
questions.rule: Change the end, change the class.

questions.q: A cooking podcast episode explains the chemistry of why bread rises and gives no recipe or tips. In the authors' terms, what kind of work is it?
options: Theoretical, since it aims at understanding
Practical, since baking is a practical activity
Practical, since listeners may bake better after it
Neither, since podcasts are not classified
optionExplain: Right: it aims at knowledge of why bread rises, not at telling you what to do.
The subject is practical, but this episode's end is understanding.
Listeners may benefit, but usefulness without aiming at action does not make a work practical.
The test of ends applies to any expository work, whatever the medium.
questions.explain: The end decides, not the subject. An explanation of rising dough aims at knowledge, even though baking is something people do.
questions.rule: A practical subject does not make a practical work.
questions.teaches: A practical subject does not make a practical work: an explanation of why bread rises aims at knowledge even though baking is an everyday activity, so the end, not the topic, decides.

questions.q: Practical books aim at action. Do they convey knowledge too, according to the authors?
options: No, they give step-by-step instructions rather than knowledge
No, since knowledge belongs to theoretical books
Yes, since intelligent action depends on knowledge
Only when they cite scientific research for support
optionExplain: Instructions rest on knowledge; the authors count practical books as expository.
Both kinds convey knowledge; they differ in what it is for.
Right: intelligent action depends on knowledge, so practical books convey it with a view to its use.
Citations are not the test; any intelligent guide to action conveys knowledge.
questions.explain: Intelligent action depends on knowledge, so practical books are expository too. The card next explains how they differ from theoretical ones.
questions.rule: Practical books convey knowledge for use.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a writer who limits himself to the knowledge itself thereby denies that the knowledge is useful.
questions.explain: Such writers do not deny its utility; they limit themselves to one kind of teaching and leave application to others.
questions.rule: Limiting the task is not denying use.

questions.q: The authors compare the distinction between theoretical and practical to the one between pure and ____ science.
questions.explain: Pure science seeks knowledge; applied science puts knowledge to use. That mirrors theoretical and practical books.
questions.rule: Pure and applied: theoretical and practical.

questions.q: Two nutrition books use the same facts about vitamins. Book A explains how the body uses them; Book B uses the facts to plan healthy meals. How do they differ?
options: In reliability, since B's facts are second-hand copies of A's
In kind, since A is science and B is fiction
In nothing, since the same facts make the same kind
In their end: A stops at knowledge, B applies it
optionExplain: B may rely on the same research; reliability is not the difference.
Neither book tells a story, so neither is fiction.
Shared facts do not make shared ends.
Right: both convey knowledge, but B does so with a view to its application.
questions.explain: Same knowledge, different ends. Book A is theoretical; Book B teaches the knowledge for use, so it is practical.
questions.rule: Same facts, different ends.

questions.q: A book teaches doctors how to diagnose and treat a disease and mentions no machines at all. Is it practical in the authors' sense?
options: No, since practical knowledge means technology only
No, since medicine counts as a branch of pure, not applied, science
Yes, since it applies knowledge to guide doctors' work
Yes, but only if it describes medical instruments
optionExplain: The authors say knowledge also serves to direct human conduct and skilled work, not only machines.
Medicine is listed by the authors among fields with manuals of practice.
Right: applying knowledge to direct conduct in a field of skill is practical, machines or not.
Instruments are beside the point; the book's end is action.
questions.explain: Applied knowledge covers directing conduct and skilled work as well as building machines. That is why the authors find the label science versus technology very inaccurate.
questions.rule: Practical is not the same as technological.
questions.teaches: The authors call the label science versus technology very inaccurate, because applied knowledge covers directing human conduct and skilled work, not only building machines.

questions.q: A sports scientist publishes a study of how muscles tire during sprints. A coach then writes a training plan based on it. How do the two texts relate in the authors' terms?
options: The study is theoretical; the plan converts it for use
Both are practical, since both of them concern sport
Both are theoretical, since both rest on the research
The plan is theoretical, while the study is practical
optionExplain: Right: one writer establishes knowledge, another applies it to a problem people want solved.
Sport is the shared subject; the two texts have different ends.
The plan rests on research but aims at what athletes should do.
This reverses the two ends.
questions.explain: The study stops at knowledge; the plan teaches that knowledge with a view to action. The two form a chain from knowing to doing.
questions.rule: Know which link in the chain you are reading.
questions.teaches: Theoretical and practical writing often form a chain: one writer establishes the knowledge, another converts it for use, and a reader should know which link a given text is.

questions.q: A book teaches you how to negotiate a pay rise. In the authors' terms, which kind of knowing does it mainly aim at?
options: Knowing how to do something
Knowing that something is the case
Knowing why people act as they do
Knowing who holds power at work
optionExplain: Right: it teaches you how to do something you want to do.
Facts about pay may appear, but the book's aim is a skill.
Motives may come up, but explaining them is not the book's aim.
Knowing who holds power may help, but the book teaches a skill.
questions.explain: A how-to book aims at knowing how. The card next sets out the authors' contrast with knowing that.
questions.rule: How-to books teach knowing how.

questions.q: To make knowledge practical, the authors say, we must convert it into rules of ____.
questions.explain: Practical books pass from knowing what is the case to knowing what to do about it: rules of operation.
questions.rule: Practical knowledge becomes rules of operation.

questions.q: Sort each statement by the kind of knowing it teaches.

items.t: Light bends when it passes into water
Inflation reduces what savings can buy
Most earthquakes occur along plate boundaries
To prune a rose, cut just above an outward bud
Draft the conclusion of a report before its summary
To ease a fever, rest and drink plenty of fluids

questions.explain: The first three state what is the case. The last three are rules of operation telling you what to do.
questions.rule: Is versus do.

questions.q: Tara classifies a gardening manual as theoretical because it contains many facts about soil. What is wrong with her reasoning?
options: Gardening manuals rarely contain any facts at all
The facts serve rules of operation, so it is practical
Facts about soil belong to history, not to theory
Nothing, since many facts make a book theoretical
optionExplain: Manuals often contain facts; that is not the error.
Right: a practical book uses knowing that in the service of knowing how.
Facts about soil are not history; the issue is what they are for.
A book full of facts can still be for action; the facts are means to the rules.
questions.explain: Practical books contain plenty of knowing that. What makes them practical is that the facts are converted into rules of what to do.
questions.rule: Facts in service of rules: practical.

questions.q: A theoretical book on sleep ends with a one-page appendix of tips for sleeping better. How should it be classified?
options: As practical, since it gives advice at the end
As both kinds at once, in roughly equal parts
As neither kind, since it mixes the two aims
As theoretical, since its main aim is knowing that
optionExplain: One page of tips does not change what the book as a whole is for.
A brief appendix does not make the two aims equal.
Mixing a little advice into a theoretical book does not take it out of the classification.
Right: classify by what the book as a whole is for, not by a single page.
questions.explain: A theoretical book may mention what follows for practice. The class goes with the book's main aim.
questions.rule: Classify by the whole, not the appendix.

questions.q: A software team keeps two documents: one describes how the system is designed and why; the other tells new staff how to deploy it. How do they map onto the authors' distinction?
options: Both are practical, since both are about software
Both teach that, since both describe the system
The guide teaches that, while the design document teaches how
The design document teaches that; the guide teaches how
optionExplain: Shared subject, different ends.
The deployment guide gives rules of operation, not just description.
This reverses the two.
Right: one explains what the system is and why; the other turns that into steps to follow.
questions.explain: Technical writing splits the same way as books: design documents teach that the system is so; how-to guides convert that into steps.
questions.rule: Design docs explain; guides instruct.
questions.teaches: By analogy, technical documentation splits the same way: design and reference documents teach that a system is so, while how-to guides convert that knowledge into steps.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, How to Read a Book is itself a practical book.
questions.explain: The authors say their book is practical, not theoretical: it teaches how to do something. The card next lists what else belongs in the class.
questions.rule: A guidebook is practical.

questions.q: Which of these do the authors place in the practical class? Select all that apply.
options: A manual of engineering practice
A treatise on ethics
A cookery manual
A study of how galaxies form
An inquiry into what numbers are
optionExplain: Right: manuals of practice in fields like engineering are practical.
Right: ethical treatises tell you what you should do, so they are practical.
Right: the authors name cooking among the fields with manuals of practice.
A study of galaxies aims at knowing that, so it is theoretical.
An inquiry into numbers aims at understanding, not at action.
questions.explain: Manuals and moral treatises both tell you what to do or how to do it. Studies of galaxies or numbers aim at understanding.
questions.rule: Manuals and moral treatises are practical.

questions.q: Sort each book into the practical or the theoretical class.

items.t: A guide to first aid
A treatise on what makes laws just
A book on the art of public speaking
An explanation of how vaccines work
A study of the structure of DNA
An inquiry into what time is

questions.explain: The first three tell you how to do something or what should be done. The last three aim at understanding what is so.
questions.rule: Should or how-to: practical.

questions.q: A cookbook assumes you want to bake a cake; a treatise on ethics argues whether you should pursue wealth at all. Both are practical. How do they differ?
options: The cookbook is practical, while the treatise is theoretical
One takes your goal as given; the other argues about it
The treatise gives the steps; the cookbook gives the reasons
They do not differ, since both tell you what to do
optionExplain: Both tell you what to do, so both are practical.
Right: a manual teaches how to do what you already want; a moral treatise argues about what you should want to do.
This reverses them: the cookbook gives steps, the treatise argues.
Both are practical, but they work at different points: the means and the goal.
questions.explain: The authors say practical books teach how to do something you want to do or think you should do. A manual serves a goal you bring; a moral treatise argues about which goals to pursue.
questions.rule: Manuals serve goals; treatises argue about them.
questions.teaches: The two families of practical book differ in where the goal comes from: a manual takes your goal as given, while a moral treatise argues about which goals you should pursue.

questions.q: All four books concern a city's budget. Which one is practical in the authors' sense?
options: A history of how the city spent its money
A study of what drives the city's costs
A novel about a mayor's crooked deals
A guide to how the city should spend its money
optionExplain: A history tells what was done, not what should be done.
Explaining what drives costs is knowing that.
A novel tells a story; it is fiction, not a practical book.
Right: it tells the city what it should do, so it is practical.
questions.explain: Same subject, four treatments. Only the guide tells anyone what to do.
questions.rule: Practical means telling what should be done.

questions.q: A country's highway code lists what drivers must and must not do, with brief reasons. Where does it fit in the authors' scheme?
options: Practical, since it is a rule book directing conduct
Theoretical, since it states facts about the roads
Theoretical, since it offers no method to be learned
Theoretical, since it records the rules that drivers follow
optionExplain: Right: the authors count rule books among practical works, alongside manuals and treatises.
Its statements are rules for drivers, not reports of what is so.
Directing conduct is enough; a practical work need not teach a method.
The code does not report what drivers do; it says what they must do, which directs conduct.
questions.explain: A code that says what to do and not do directs conduct. The authors place manuals and rule books together as practical works.
questions.rule: Rule books are practical.
questions.teaches: The authors count rule books among practical works, so codes and regulations, such as a highway code, belong in the practical class alongside manuals and moral treatises.

questions.q: A reader thinks an economics book's advice would not work in practice. According to the authors, how does that bear on whether the book is practical?
options: It shows the book is theoretical after all, not practical
It has no bearing on whether it is practical
It makes the book practical only in part
It means the book cannot be classified
optionExplain: Doubting the advice does not change the book's aim.
Right: the authors say whether a book is true or would work is irrelevant to whether it is practical.
The class does not come in parts according to how far you agree.
The book can be classified by its aim, whatever you think of the advice.
questions.explain: A practical book aims at action; your view of its advice is a separate matter. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Disagreement does not change the class.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a book on economics that is not true is still a practical book, though a bad one.
questions.explain: The authors say truth is irrelevant to whether the book is practical, though a book on economics that is not true is a bad book.
questions.rule: Wrong and practical can go together.

questions.q: Many modern readers call Kant's Critique of Practical Reason impractical because it bases right action on duty. What do the authors say these readers really mean?
options: That Kant's book is a work of science
That the book teaches knowing that
That the book is too hard to follow
That Kant is wrong in his basic approach
optionExplain: Nothing in their complaint concerns science.
The book is about how people should act, which is knowing how.
Difficulty is not what the complaint is about.
Right: impractical here is a verdict on Kant's view, not on the kind of book.
questions.explain: Calling Kant impractical expresses disagreement with his approach. The book remains practical because it is about how people should conduct themselves.
questions.rule: Impractical often means I disagree.

questions.q: Omar calls an ethics book theoretical because he thinks its advice is mistaken. Which replies to him are sound? Select all that apply.
options: Disagreeing with advice does not change the book's aim
A book that tells readers what to do is practical, right or wrong
He is right, since advice that is mistaken is really a kind of theory
He should not judge an ethics book at all until he has finished it
A wrong practical book is a bad practical book, not a theoretical one
He is right, since ethics is a branch of philosophy and so theoretical
optionExplain: Right: the book still aims at action, whatever Omar thinks of it.
Right: telling readers what they should do is what makes a book practical.
Mistaken advice is still advice; it tells readers what to do.
Judging is allowed at the right time; the problem is the inference he draws.
Right: the authors say a book that is not true is a bad book, not a different kind.
The authors class ethical works as practical, because they tell us how to live.
questions.explain: Omar confuses a verdict on quality with a classification. The book tells readers what they ought to do, so it stays practical even if its advice is wrong.
questions.rule: Verdict is not class.

questions.q: Sort each comment on a book by what it is about.

items.t: It tells readers what they should do
It explains how to run a small business
It aims at action, not knowledge
Its advice would fail in practice
Its case for duty is weak
It is a bad book on economics

questions.explain: Comments about aim place the book in a class. Comments about whether the advice is sound judge its quality, a separate question.
questions.rule: Keep kind and quality apart.

questions.q: Kant's Critique of Pure Reason examines how we in fact come to know things and what can and cannot be known, not how to know better. How should it be classified?
options: Practical, since it is about knowing, an activity
Practical, since Kant wrote his other critique on right conduct
Theoretical, since many readers disagree with Kant
Theoretical, since it asks how things are, not what to do
optionExplain: Knowing is an activity, but the book studies how it works rather than teaching how to do it.
An author's other books do not decide this book's class.
Disagreement never decides the class, either way.
Right: the authors call it a theoretical book par excellence; it is about what is and how we in fact know it.
questions.explain: The authors stress that the book is about how we in fact know, not how to know. Studying an activity is knowing that; teaching it would be knowing how.
questions.rule: A study of an activity can be theoretical.
questions.teaches: A book about an activity can still be theoretical: studying how we in fact know is knowing that, which is why the authors call Kant's Critique of Pure Reason a theoretical book par excellence.

questions.q: Critics call a city's climate plan unrealistic. A council member concludes that the plan is not a practical document. What is the best reply?
options: Agreed, since an unrealistic plan is only theory
Unrealistic judges the plan; it does not change its kind
The plan is fiction, since its targets are imagined ones
Agreed, unless the critics turn out to be mistaken
optionExplain: Theory aims at knowledge; a plan aims at action, realistic or not.
Right: to call advice unrealistic is already to treat it as advice.
Targets are goals for action, not invented stories.
The class does not depend on who wins the argument.
questions.explain: The criticism itself treats the plan as advice about what to do. It may be bad advice, but it is still practical.
questions.rule: Criticising advice presupposes it is advice.
questions.teaches: Calling advice unrealistic presupposes that it is advice: the criticism itself treats the document as practical, so it cannot also show that the document is not practical.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a sociological study that only reports how people behave, without judging it, is a practical book.
questions.explain: The authors call such studies neither ethical nor practical: they are theoretical works of science. The card next explains the line.
questions.rule: Reporting is theoretical.

questions.q: According to the authors, which kinds of economic study are theoretical rather than practical?
options: Studies that tell governments what to do
Studies that warn of the penalties that follow bad policy
Studies of how to organise a household budget
Reportorial, mathematical or statistical studies
optionExplain: Telling governments what to do is prescribing, which is practical.
Warning of penalties for not doing what one should belongs to practical works.
Organising a budget is a matter of how to act, so practical.
Right: the authors name reportorial, mathematical and statistical studies as theoretical.
questions.explain: Reporting, measuring and modelling economic behaviour aim at knowledge. Advising how to organise economic life aims at action.
questions.rule: Measure: theoretical. Advise: practical.

questions.q: Sort each book by whether it describes or prescribes.

items.t: A survey of how many hours teenagers spend online
A count of marriages and divorces by decade
A statistical model of how prices respond to demand
An argument that schools should ban phones
A plan for how a country should cut its debt
A case that companies ought to publish pay gaps

questions.explain: Surveys, counts and models report what is so. Arguments, plans and cases for change say what should be done.
questions.rule: Describe versus prescribe.

questions.q: True or false: A book measuring how many families fell below the poverty line each year and a book arguing for a minimum income belong to different classes, though both concern poverty.
questions.explain: The first reports, so it is theoretical; the second argues for what should be done, so it is practical. A shared subject does not make a shared class.
questions.rule: Same subject, different classes.

questions.q: A study surveys what people in ten countries believe is right and wrong about lying, without taking sides itself. Is it theoretical or practical?
options: Practical, since its subject is what is right and wrong
Practical, since readers may change their own views
Theoretical, since reporting opinions is still reporting
Neither, since opinions do not count as knowledge
optionExplain: The subject is moral, but the study does not itself say what anyone should do.
Readers may be moved, but the study's own aim is to report.
Right: describing what people think should be done is not saying what should be done.
Reports of opinion are knowledge in the authors' broad sense.
questions.explain: The study reports beliefs about right and wrong without endorsing any. Like any report of behaviour, it is theoretical.
questions.rule: Reporting shoulds is not prescribing.
questions.teaches: Describing what people approve of is still describing: a survey of moral opinions reports what people think should be done without itself saying what should be done, so it is theoretical.

questions.q: A newspaper page carries a news report on the latest unemployment figures and, beside it, an editorial on what the government should do. How do they map onto the authors' line?
options: The report describes and the editorial prescribes
Both prescribe, since both appear in one newspaper
Both describe, since both concern unemployment
The editorial describes the facts, and the report prescribes
optionExplain: Right: the report says what is the case; the editorial says what should be done.
Appearing side by side does not give them one aim.
Shared subject, different aims.
This reverses them.
questions.explain: News reporting and editorial comment split along the authors' line: describing what is versus prescribing what should be. The editorial's should cannot come from the report's figures alone.
questions.rule: News describes; editorials prescribe.
questions.teaches: An editorial can use the facts in a news report, but its conclusion needs more than facts: it also needs a judgment about what ought to be done, which no report supplies.

questions.q: According to the authors, what does anyone writing practically try to do besides advise you?
options: Entertain you with stories along the way
Prove the advice from first principles
Stay neutral about whether you follow it
Persuade you to follow the advice
optionExplain: Stories may appear, but entertaining is not what the authors name.
Practical writers may argue, but the authors stress persuasion, not proof.
The authors say the opposite: practical writers want you to follow the advice.
Right: practical writers try to persuade you to follow their advice.
questions.explain: Advice comes with an effort to get you to act on it. The card next explains why every practical book has this element.
questions.rule: Practical writers persuade.

questions.q: True or false: The authors admit that their own book tries to persuade readers, not only to teach them.
questions.explain: They say that besides trying to teach you to read better, they try to persuade you to make the effort.
questions.rule: Even a book on reading persuades.

questions.q: In a book on starting a vegetable garden, which passages are persuasion rather than instruction? Select all that apply.
options: Imagine the taste of a tomato picked from your vine
Plant tomatoes after the last frost, 60 cm apart
There is no better time to start than this spring
Water seedlings at the base, not on the leaves
Thousands of readers have changed their lives this way
optionExplain: Right: it appeals to your desire, urging you on rather than instructing.
This is a rule of operation, instruction.
Right: urging you to start now is exhortation.
This is a rule of operation, instruction.
Right: an appeal to what others did is meant to move you, not to teach a step.
questions.explain: Instructions tell you how; persuasion tries to get you to act. A practical book carries both.
questions.rule: Separate the how from the urging.

questions.q: Lena reasons: Step 1, this health book keeps urging me to change my habits. Step 2, so the author must be dishonest. Step 3, so I will stop reading it. Which step goes wrong?
options: Step 1, since health books never urge their readers
Step 3, since she should finish every book she starts
Step 2, since urging is normal in a practical book
None, since persuasion shows a book cannot be trusted
optionExplain: Urging is common in practical books; her observation is accurate.
Step 3 follows from Step 2; the faulty move is earlier.
Right: every practical book has an element of exhortation, so urging alone does not show dishonesty.
The authors say even their own book persuades; persuasion is part of practical writing.
questions.explain: Persuasion comes with practical writing. It is a reason to check the advice, not proof that the author is dishonest.
questions.rule: Urging is normal; check the advice.

questions.q: A book keeps urging you to act now and warns what you will lose if you wait. Before checking anything else, what does this suggest about its kind?
options: It is likely practical, since urging goes with advice
It is likely fiction, since urging the reader is a story device
It is likely theoretical, since it states consequences
Nothing, since urging appears in every kind of book
optionExplain: Right: practical writers try to persuade, so frequent urging is a clue that a book is practical.
Fiction tells a story; urging the reader to act is not its mark.
Stating consequences can be theoretical, but urging you to act on them is not.
A theoretical book tries to show what is so, and has less reason to urge you.
questions.explain: Since practical writers persuade and theoretical writers aim to show what is so, frequent urging is a useful early clue that a book is practical.
questions.rule: Urging is a clue to the practical.
questions.teaches: Persuasion is itself a clue to kind: a theoretical book tries to show that something is so and has less reason to urge you, so frequent urging suggests a book is practical.

questions.q: A charity's annual report explains how last year's donations were spent, then ends with a page urging readers to give again. How should a careful reader handle it?
options: Treat the whole report as an appeal, facts and all
Treat the whole report as neutral fact, the closing appeal included
Read the account for facts, and the last page as an appeal
Skip the account, since the appeal is the real purpose
optionExplain: The account may be accurate; treating it all as appeal throws away information.
The last page is meant to move you, not to inform you.
Right: noticing where informing stops and urging starts tells you how to read each part.
The account is where the facts are; skipping it leaves you with only the appeal.
questions.explain: Like a practical book, the report joins information and persuasion. Seeing the switch lets you weigh each part for what it is.
questions.rule: Find where informing turns into urging.
questions.teaches: By analogy, many documents join an informative part to a persuasive close; seeing where one turns into the other tells you where to read for facts and where to read for the appeal.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, since every practical book persuades, every practical book is a piece of oratory and nothing more.
questions.explain: Every practical book has some oratory, but the authors say oratory does not cover the whole of the practical. The card next shows the difference.
questions.rule: Some oratory is not all oratory.

questions.q: Match each piece of oratory to the kind of work the authors contrast it with.
questions.explain: In each pair, the first mainly urges and the second analyses a practical problem. Both are practical, but they are not the same kind of practical work.
questions.rule: Harangue versus treatise.

questions.q: Which of these is closer to a treatise than to oratory?
options: A report weighing three tax reforms and backing one
A rally speech chanting that taxes must fall now
A poster urging voters to throw out the government
A viral video mocking the finance minister's plans
optionExplain: Right: it analyses the problem, weighs options and then advises, the mark of a treatise.
Chanting a demand is harangue, not analysis.
A poster urges without analysing.
Mockery may persuade, but it offers no analysis of the problem.
questions.explain: A treatise analyses a practical problem and then recommends. Oratory mainly urges.
questions.rule: Analysis then advice: treatise.

questions.q: Which of these mark a practical treatise rather than mere oratory? Select all that apply.
options: It analyses the causes of the problem
It weighs other courses of action
It repeats one slogan many times
It works mainly by stirring anger
It gives reasons for what it recommends
optionExplain: Right: analysing causes is the work of a treatise.
Right: comparing options is analysis, not mere urging.
Repetition of a slogan is a device of oratory.
Stirring feeling is oratory's main tool.
Right: reasons for advice show analysis behind the persuasion.
questions.explain: A treatise analyses and argues before it advises. Slogans and stirred feelings are oratory's tools.
questions.rule: Look for analysis behind the urging.

questions.q: A long book analyses how factories treat their workers, in order to show what must change. A reader says the analysis makes it a theoretical book. What is the best reply?
options: Agreed, since any analysis is theoretical work
Agreed, unless its advice turns out to be sound
No, since the book is oratory, not analysis
No, since its analysis serves a practical end
optionExplain: Analysis appears in both kinds; what it is for decides the class.
Soundness of advice never decides the class.
The book analyses at length, so it is more than oratory.
Right: a treatise analyses a practical problem in order to advise, so its analysis serves action.
questions.explain: The authors set treatises against harangues, not against practical books. A treatise analyses so that it can advise, which keeps it practical.
questions.rule: Analysis for action stays practical.
questions.teaches: Analysis does not make a work theoretical: a practical treatise analyses a problem in order to advise, so its analysis serves a practical end.

questions.q: A chief executive sends staff a rousing email about a new direction and also circulates a strategy paper analysing the market. Which document gives the manager reasons that can be checked?
options: The email, since it shows the leader's true intent
Both equally, since both push the same direction
The email, since its confident tone shows the case is strong
The strategy paper, since it analyses the problem
optionExplain: The email shows enthusiasm, but gives little to check.
They push the same way, but only one offers analysis.
Confidence is a feature of the urging, not a reason; a tone cannot be checked the way an analysis can.
Right: like a treatise, the paper sets out the problem and reasons that can be evaluated.
questions.explain: The email is the oratory; the paper is the treatise. Only the paper sets out reasons and evidence the manager can test, however forceful the email sounds.
questions.rule: Check the reasons, not the tone.
questions.teaches: Force of tone is not a reason: how strongly a message urges you says nothing about how well its case is supported, so judge a decision by the reasons offered, not by the confidence of the call.

questions.q: Which title openings would the authors take as quick signs of a practical book? Select all that apply.
options: The Art of ...
How to ...
A History of ...
The Origins of ...
The Nature of ...
optionExplain: Right: the art of signals a book teaching a skill.
Right: how to signals a practical book at once.
A history narrates the past.
Origins suggests an account of how something came to be.
The nature of suggests an inquiry into what something is.
questions.explain: The authors name the art of and how to as phrases that let you spot a practical book at once. The card next adds field names.
questions.rule: The art of and how to: practical.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say economics, law and medicine in a title signal a practical book in many cases, but not in all.
questions.explain: The authors list ethics, politics, engineering and business as practical fields, and add economics, law and medicine in many cases.
questions.rule: Some field names are hedged.

questions.q: Sort each title by whether it signals a practical book.

items.t: The Art of Negotiation
How to Grow Orchids
Business Strategy for Small Firms
A History of Venice
The Origins of the Universe
The Nature of Light

questions.explain: The first two use practical phrases; the third names business, a practical field. The others signal history or inquiry.
questions.rule: Phrase or field signals the practical.

questions.q: Dan sees the title The Economics of Attention and files the book as practical without looking further. What is the weakness in his method?
options: Economics is not a practical field at all
Titles should be ignored when classifying books
Economics is practical in many cases, not all
He should have read the whole book before deciding
optionExplain: The authors say economics is usually practical; the issue is that it is not always so.
Titles are a good first sign; the problem is stopping there.
Right: the authors hedge economics, so the title is a sign to confirm, not a verdict.
Classifying should not wait for a full reading; a look at the front matter would do.
questions.explain: Some economics books are purely theoretical. Dan should check the front matter before settling the class.
questions.rule: Confirm a hedged sign.

questions.q: A book titled Winter explains how to keep bees alive through the cold months, but its title has no practical phrase or field name. What follows from the missing signal?
options: It must be theoretical, since no practical sign is present
It must be fiction, since the title is poetic
Nothing about its kind; you look for other signs
It cannot be classified until it is finished
optionExplain: Missing signs are not signs of the opposite.
A one-word title fits many kinds of book.
Right: a missing signal sends you to the subtitle, contents and text, not to the theoretical class.
The other front matter, or a short read-in, will usually settle it.
questions.explain: The authors say a title sometimes shows a book is practical. When it does not, the question stays open.
questions.rule: No signal is not a negative signal.
questions.teaches: The absence of a practical signal in a title proves nothing: many practical books carry no how-to phrase, so a plain title sends you to other signs rather than to the theoretical class.

questions.q: An online catalogue lists courses titled Masterclass: Pricing Your Product, Toolkit for New Landlords, and The Physics of Black Holes. By analogy with the authors' title signs, which look practical?
options: Only The Physics of Black Holes
All three, since all are courses
The masterclass and the toolkit
None, since a course title says nothing until you enrol
optionExplain: Physics names a field of inquiry, not a practical art.
Being a course does not fix the class.
Right: masterclass and toolkit, like how to, promise to teach a skill.
Titles are signals placed by the makers; you can read them before enrolling.
questions.explain: Words like masterclass and toolkit do the work that how to and the art of do in book titles. Because they promise a skill, they also set the test the course must pass.
questions.rule: Skill words signal the practical.
questions.teaches: A practical title promises a skill, so it also tells you how to judge the work afterwards: by whether you can now do what the title named.

questions.q: Locke wrote one book on human understanding and one on civil government. Judging from these subjects alone, which is likely to be practical?
options: The book on human understanding
Both, since a philosopher wrote both
Neither, since both are works of philosophy
The book on civil government
optionExplain: Any analysis of understanding would be theoretical.
The author's profession does not fix each book's class.
Being philosophical does not rule out being practical.
Right: problems of government are practical problems.
questions.explain: Government raises practical problems; understanding is a theoretical subject. The card next shows how Locke's wording confirms it.
questions.rule: Government: practical. Understanding: theoretical.

questions.q: Questions about the validity of something are theoretical, whereas questions about its end, the ____ it serves, are practical.
questions.explain: Locke asked about the certainty of knowledge in one book and the end, or purpose, of government in the other.
questions.rule: Validity: theoretical. Purpose: practical.

questions.q: Sort each question by the kind it raises.

items.t: How certain is our knowledge of the past?
Are eyewitness reports reliable?
Can memory be trusted as evidence?
What are prisons for?
What end should a school serve?
What is a constitution meant to achieve?

questions.explain: The first three ask whether some knowledge is valid. The last three ask what something is for.
questions.rule: Certain or for what?

questions.q: Kim reasons: Locke's stated aim and his title on government share the words origin and extent, so the two books must be of the same kind. What does she overlook?
options: That one asks about certainty, the other an end
That Locke wrote the two books decades apart from each other
That one book is a novel and the other a treatise
That titles say nothing about a book's kind
optionExplain: Right: the words that differ, certainty versus end, set the kind of question each book asks.
Dates do not bear on the class.
Neither book is a novel.
Titles say a good deal; Kim reads the wrong words in them.
questions.explain: The shared words hide the difference that matters: validity in one, purpose in the other.
questions.rule: Find the word that sets the question.

questions.q: A long book on the courts asks, in Part One, how reliable witness testimony is, and in Part Two, what punishment is for. Using the validity and purpose test, what can you say?
options: The whole book is practical, since courts are practical
The whole book is theoretical, since it starts with theory
Part One is theoretical and Part Two practical
Neither part can be classed, since they differ
optionExplain: The subject is practical, but Part One asks about validity.
The opening does not fix the class of the whole.
Right: the test sorts questions, so it can sort the parts of a book as well as whole books.
Different parts can each be classed by the questions they ask.
questions.explain: The test applies to questions wherever they occur. Applied part by part, it shows which parts of a book are theoretical and which practical.
questions.rule: Sort the parts by their questions.
questions.teaches: The validity and purpose test works on single questions, not only on whole books, so you can use it to see which parts of a book are theoretical and which practical.

questions.q: A hospital commissions two reviews: one asks whether its infection figures are accurate; the other asks what its infection targets are meant to achieve. How do they map onto the test?
options: The first asks about validity, the second about purpose
Both ask about purpose, since both concern targets
Both ask about validity, since both concern data
The first asks about purpose, the second about validity
optionExplain: Right: accuracy is a question of validity; what targets are for is a question of purpose.
Only the second asks what something is for.
Only the first asks whether something can be trusted.
This reverses them.
questions.explain: Asking whether figures can be trusted is a theoretical question. Asking what targets are for opens the practical question of what should be done.
questions.rule: Accuracy versus aim.
questions.teaches: By analogy, in audits and reviews, questions of accuracy belong to finding out what is so, while questions of purpose open the practical question of what should be done.

questions.q: A book's title and contents give no hint of its kind. Where do the authors suggest looking next?
options: Critics' reviews of the book in the press
The author's biography on the back flap
The first chapter only, read very slowly and closely
Its summaries, and the start and end of parts
optionExplain: Reviews are other readers' views, not the book's own signs.
A biography tells you about the author, not about this book's kind.
One chapter, read slowly, is both too narrow and too slow for classifying.
Right: summary passages and the beginnings and ends of the book and its parts carry the signs.
questions.explain: When the outside is silent, sample the inside at its most telling points. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Sample summaries, beginnings and ends.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say that, with the basic categories in mind, you should be able to classify a book without reading very far into it.
questions.explain: Attention to the words, plus categories in mind, lets you classify after a short read-in.
questions.rule: Classifying takes a short read, not a long one.

questions.q: Put these steps for classifying a puzzling book in the order the authors' advice suggests.
items: Read the title, subtitle and contents
Glance at the preface and index
Read summary passages and the start and end of major parts
Decide the kind from the words used in those passages
questions.explain: Start with the front matter; when it fails, read in at the summaries and the openings and closings; then classify from the words you found.
questions.rule: Outside first, then read in, then decide.

questions.q: A book's opening chapters are all theory, but its last part tells readers what they should do. What happens if a reader classifies it from the opening chapters alone?
options: She may misclassify it, having missed the practical close
She classifies it correctly, since openings set the kind
She classifies it as fiction, since it changes course
Nothing, since the parts of a book share one kind
optionExplain: Right: one sample can mislead, which is why the authors point to the end as well as the beginning.
Openings help, but a book can change character between parts.
Changing course does not make a book a story.
Books can be partly of one sort and partly of another.
questions.explain: Reading the beginning and the end of the book and its parts guards against a book that changes character.
questions.rule: Sample more than one place.

questions.q: Why are the beginning and end of each major part good places to look for signs of a book's kind?
options: Authors tend to put their best writing there
Those pages are the easiest ones to read quickly
Publishers place summaries there by rule
Authors often state aims and conclusions there
optionExplain: Quality of prose is not what makes them useful for classifying.
Ease is not the reason; telling content is.
No such rule exists; the summaries are the author's.
Right: openings tend to say what a part sets out to do, and endings what it has done, which shows the kind.
questions.explain: Openings and closings are where writers tend to state what they are doing and what they have shown. Those statements reveal whether the book aims at knowing or doing.
questions.rule: Aims and conclusions show the kind.
questions.teaches: Openings and closings of parts are where authors tend to state what they set out to do and what they claim to have done, which is why they carry the clearest signs of kind.

questions.q: You have a two-hour recorded lecture with no description. By analogy with the authors' advice, how can you classify it quickly?
options: Watch it all the way through, at double speed if need be
Sample its opening, summary slides and close
Read the comments left by other viewers
Judge it from the speaker's job title and fame
optionExplain: Even at double speed, this is an hour; classifying needs only samples.
Right: like reading a book's summaries and its beginnings and ends, these samples show the talk's aim.
Comments are others' reactions, not the talk's own signs.
A job title does not show what this talk is for.
questions.explain: The read-in method carries over: openings, summaries and closings reveal what a long talk sets out to do.
questions.rule: Sample the telling points.
questions.teaches: The read-in method works for recordings too: sampling the opening, any summary points and the close of a long talk reveals its kind without watching it all.

questions.q: Which word, used often, is a sign that a book is practical rather than theoretical?
options: Is
Ought
Because
Therefore
optionExplain: A steady is marks a theoretical book.
Right: frequent ought, like should, marks a practical book.
Because gives reasons, which both kinds do.
Therefore draws conclusions, which both kinds do.
questions.explain: Ought expresses what should be done, the mark of a practical book. The card next lists the other telltale words.
questions.rule: Ought marks the practical.

questions.q: Which word pairs do the authors name as betraying a practical book? Select all that apply.
options: should and ought
good and bad
ends and means
cause and effect
true and false
optionExplain: Right: these say what is to be done.
Right: these judge, which practical books do.
Right: these concern goals and ways of reaching them.
Cause and effect belong to explaining what is, the work of theory.
True and false concern what is so, which theoretical books try to show.
questions.explain: Should, ought, good, bad, ends and means are the authors' list. They belong to statements about what to do and what is better.
questions.rule: Should, ought, good, bad, ends, means.

questions.q: Sort each sentence by the kind of book it sounds like.

items.t: Managers should praise in public and criticise in private
The best way to learn a language is to speak it daily
Saving early is a better means than saving late
Water boils at a lower temperature at altitude
Most stars are found in galaxies
Children use grammar before they can explain it

questions.explain: Should, best way and better means mark statements about what to do. The others state what is the case.
questions.rule: Should and better versus is.

questions.q: Ian reads one sentence in a physics book saying an experiment ought to be repeated, and files the whole book as practical. What is wrong with his method?
options: Physics books never use the word ought at all
Ought is in fact a sign of a theoretical book
He should have checked the author's other books before deciding
One sentence does not show what a book keeps saying
optionExplain: Physics books can use ought; that is why one use proves little.
Ought is a practical word; the error is in how much weight he gives it.
Other books do not decide this one's class.
Right: the sign is frequency across the book, and its characteristic statements, not one sentence.
questions.explain: The authors speak of frequent occurrence and characteristic statements. A single ought in a physics book is not what the book keeps saying.
questions.rule: Weigh what the book keeps saying.

questions.q: A book uses no should or ought, but nearly every sentence is a command: mix the flour, rest the dough, bake for an hour. What kind of book is it?
options: Theoretical, since it never says should
Practical, since commands tell you what to do
Fiction, since it narrates a sequence of events
Neither, since commands make no claims
optionExplain: The words are missing, but the commands do their work.
Right: an imperative says what to do in every line, so it is a practical sign.
It narrates nothing; it instructs.
Commands are not claims, but they are exactly what practical books give.
questions.explain: A recipe written in commands is practical through and through. Imperatives carry the meaning of should without the word.
questions.rule: Commands are a practical sign.
questions.teaches: Commands do the work of should: a book written in the imperative, such as a recipe, says what to do in every line, so imperatives are signs of the practical too.

questions.q: A lease opens with recitals stating that the landlord owns the flat; its clauses say the tenant shall pay rent monthly. Which part plays the role of a practical book's should?
options: The clauses with shall, since they set duties
The recitals, since they state the facts
Both equally, since both are legal text
Neither, since every part of a lease states facts about the deal
optionExplain: Right: shall marks an obligation, what someone must do.
Recitals state what is so, the theoretical voice.
Both are legal, but only one sets what must be done.
The clauses do more than state facts: shall sets duties, what the tenant must do.
questions.explain: In legal drafting, shall plays the part of should, marking duties. Recitals state facts, like a theoretical book's is.
questions.rule: Shall marks duties.
questions.teaches: In contracts, shall and must play the role of should: they mark obligations, the practical part, while recitals state facts, the part that says is.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, telling a practical book from a theoretical one is as simple as telling coffee from milk.
questions.explain: The authors warn against supposing it is that simple. The card next explains why the signs need suspicion.
questions.rule: Classifying takes care.

questions.q: According to the authors, what are most books that claim to teach you how to think?
options: The best practical books available
Works of science in disguise
Practical books that rarely sell well
Terrible, in the authors' judgment
optionExplain: The authors' verdict is the reverse.
They present themselves as practical, not as science.
Sales are not the authors' concern; their verdict is on quality.
Right: the authors say most of them are terrible.
questions.explain: Understanding is mainly theoretical, so books promising to teach how to think borrow a practical form for a theoretical matter; the authors think most are terrible.
questions.rule: A practical form can wrap a theoretical matter.

questions.q: True or false: A book with How to in its title and economics as its field can still turn out to be a theoretical book.
questions.explain: Both signs point to practical, but signs can mislead: some economics books are purely theoretical, and a title phrase can be used loosely.
questions.rule: Two signs can both mislead.

questions.q: Which of these are reasons the authors give for mistrusting the signs? Select all that apply.
options: Some economics books are purely theoretical
Some books claim to teach how to think
Some authors confuse theory and practice
Titles are usually chosen by publishers
Practical books avoid the word is
optionExplain: Right: a mainly practical field can hold theoretical books.
Right: a mainly theoretical matter can be dressed as a how-to.
Right: an author who does not know the difference sends mixed signals.
The authors give no such reason.
Practical books use is often; that is why words must be weighed.
questions.explain: The authors' reasons are cases where field, form or author mislead. Publishers and the word is are not among them.
questions.rule: Field, form and author can all mislead.

questions.q: How should a reader treat the fact that a book's field is economics, given the authors' remarks?
options: As settling that the book is practical
As settling that the book is theoretical
As raising the odds that it is practical
As telling nothing at all about its kind
optionExplain: The authors say some economics books are purely theoretical, so it cannot settle it.
Economics is primarily and usually practical, the opposite of this.
Right: the field makes practical likely, until other signs say otherwise.
The field does tell you something: it shifts the likelihood.
questions.explain: The authors call economics primarily and usually practical. That makes the field a sign that shifts the odds, not one that settles the case.
questions.rule: Signs shift odds; they do not settle.
questions.teaches: A sign shifts the odds rather than settling the case: economics is primarily and usually practical, so a book on it is probably practical until other signs say otherwise.

questions.q: A job advert is titled Data Scientist, but the duties are all cold-calling customers to sell software. By analogy with the authors' warning, what should an applicant do?
options: Trust the title, since employers name roles precisely
Judge the role by its duties, not the borrowed name
Assume it is a science post with some sales work added on
Ignore the advert, since all titles mislead
optionExplain: Titles can borrow prestige, as how to think books borrow a practical form.
Right: like a book, a role is classified by what it does, not by the label it carries.
The duties show no science at all.
Some titles mislead, not all; suspicion means checking, not rejecting.
questions.explain: The title borrows a category the job does not belong to. As with books, check what the thing actually does.
questions.rule: Check the duties behind the title.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a name can borrow the standing of a category it does not belong to, as a job title can borrow scientist, so classify by what the thing actually does.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, some books are partly theoretical and partly practical.
questions.explain: The authors say you will find books that are partly of one sort and partly of another. The card next says what to do with them.
questions.rule: Some books mix the two.

questions.q: The authors give Spinoza's ____ as an example of a book that is partly of one sort and partly of another.
questions.explain: Spinoza's Ethics is the authors' example of a mixed book.
questions.rule: Spinoza's Ethics mixes the two.

questions.q: A gardening book spends its first half on plant biology and its second half on how to plan a garden. Which label fits best?
options: Practical, since a book takes the class of its ending
Partly theoretical and partly practical
Theoretical, since it begins with science
Unclassifiable, since it mixes the two
optionExplain: The ending does not decide the whole.
Right: the book is of both sorts, and the label should say so.
The opening does not decide the whole either.
Mixed is not unclassifiable; it calls for a qualified label.
questions.explain: Half explains what is so, half tells you what to do. A qualified label is the honest one.
questions.rule: A mixed book gets a mixed label.

questions.q: True or false: When a book mixes theory and practice, the authors say there is no longer any point in working out how the author approaches his problem.
questions.explain: The authors say the opposite: it remains to your advantage to detect the way an author approaches his problem, mixed book or not.
questions.rule: Mixed books still repay classifying.

questions.q: In a book on sleep, the first chapters explain how the body clock works and the last chapters tell readers how to fix poor sleep. How are the two parts most likely related?
options: They are unrelated books bound together
The advice is there to illustrate the theory
The theory is padding, put in to make the book look longer
The explanation grounds the advice that follows
optionExplain: A shared subject and order suggest a link.
This reverses the likely relation: here the theory comes first and the advice builds on it.
Calling the theory padding ignores that advice rests on knowledge.
Right: intelligent action depends on knowledge, so the theory supplies the basis for the advice.
questions.explain: Since intelligent action depends on knowledge, the theoretical part of a mixed book usually supports the practical part. Reading the theory well helps you judge the advice.
questions.rule: Theory often grounds the advice.
questions.teaches: In a mixed book, the theoretical part usually grounds the practical one: the explanation is there to support the advice, so understanding it well helps you judge the advice.

questions.q: A financial adviser spends the first half of a meeting explaining how pensions work and the second half recommending a plan. What does the authors' advice on mixed books suggest the client should do?
options: Notice the switch and test the plan by the explanation
Treat the whole meeting as advice she should follow as given
Treat the whole meeting as neutral, factual information
Ignore the explanation and judge the plan on its own
optionExplain: Right: knowing where explaining ends and advising begins lets her question the advice with what she has just learned.
The first half explains; treating it as advice blurs the two.
The second half recommends; treating it as neutral misses that it asks her to act.
The explanation is what lets her judge the plan.
questions.explain: Like a mixed book, the meeting moves from showing what is so to saying what to do. Seeing the switch lets her use the first half to examine the second.
questions.rule: Find where explaining turns into advising.
questions.teaches: By analogy, spoken advice often moves from explaining to recommending, and a listener who notices the switch can question the recommendation using the explanation just given.

questions.q: What do the authors call the essence of history?
options: Argument
Narration
Measurement
Prediction
optionExplain: Historians argue, but the authors name something else as essential.
Right: the authors say the essence of history is narration.
Measurement belongs more to science.
History looks back, not forward.
questions.explain: History tells what happened. The card next explains what else marks it.
questions.rule: History narrates.

questions.q: History is ____, a word built from the Greek words for time and place.
questions.explain: Chronos means time and topos place: history always deals with things at a particular date and place.
questions.rule: History is chronotopic.

questions.q: Which of these books are histories in the authors' sense? Select all that apply.
options: A month-by-month account of the 2008 financial crisis
How one village changed between 1800 and 1900
A study of the general laws by which gases expand
An inquiry into what makes any action fair or unfair
The story of a firm's founding last decade, year by year
optionExplain: Right: particular events, dated and placed, narrated as they changed.
Right: one place, a definite span of time, a story of change.
General laws hold at any time and place; that is not history.
A general inquiry into justice is not a narrative of particular events.
Right: recent events count; history need not be distant.
questions.explain: Histories narrate particular things at definite times and places. General laws and general inquiries are not narratives.
questions.rule: Particular, dated, placed, narrated.

questions.q: A book narrates, day by day, the events of last month's floods in one city. Can it count as history?
options: No, since history needs at least a century's distance
No, since recent events are journalism, not history
Yes, since history can concern what happened yesterday
Yes, but only once the events are long past
optionExplain: The authors set no such distance.
The authors' test is narration of particular past events, not their age.
