Right: the authors say the past may be the far past or only yesterday.
The book is history now; it does not have to wait.
questions.explain: History deals with the past, but not necessarily the far past. A narrative of last month's events in one city is chronotopic.
questions.rule: Recent past is still past.

questions.q: A history of the French Revolution pauses often to comment on what the events meant. Does the commentary change what kind of book it is?
options: Yes, it makes the book a work of philosophy
Yes, it makes the book a practical treatise
No, though the comment means the book is no longer pure history
No, historians often colour narrative with comment
optionExplain: Comment on significance is not a philosophical inquiry into general truths.
Comment on meaning does not tell the reader what to do.
Commentary does not make it less a history; it is a normal part of historical writing.
Right: the authors say historians often colour their narrative with comment on the significance of events.
questions.explain: The authors note that the historian narrates and often colours the narrative with comment on, or insight into, the significance of events.
questions.rule: Comment on meaning belongs to history too.
questions.teaches: The authors note that historians often colour their narrative with comment on the significance of events, so commentary inside a history does not turn it into philosophy or science.

questions.q: A hospital incident report narrates what happened on one ward on the night of 3 March, hour by hour. By the authors' account, what is it most like?
options: A history, since it narrates dated, placed events
A science, since hospitals rely on research
A philosophy, since it raises questions of blame
A manual, since it will guide future practice
optionExplain: Right: it tells particular events at a definite time and place, a chronotopic narrative.
The setting is scientific, but the report narrates one night's events.
Blame may follow, but the report itself narrates.
Lessons may be drawn later; the report itself narrates what happened.
questions.explain: An incident report is chronotopic: one ward, one night, events in order. It is read as a narrative of particulars, not as a set of general rules.
questions.rule: Case reports are chronotopic.
questions.teaches: By analogy, case histories and incident reports are chronotopic narratives: they tell particular events at a date and place, which is why they are read differently from guidelines stating general rules.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a scientist wants to find out how things happen for the most part or in every case.
questions.explain: The scientist seeks laws or generalisations, not the story of particular past events. The card next contrasts this with history.
questions.rule: Science seeks the general.

questions.q: According to the authors, the scientist seeks laws or ____.
questions.explain: The scientist seeks laws or generalisations about what happens at any time or place.
questions.rule: Laws or generalisations.

questions.q: Sort each book by whether it is history or science.

items.t: How the 1906 San Francisco earthquake unfolded
The voyage of the Beagle, 1831 to 1836
The cholera outbreak in Soho in 1854
Why earthquakes occur along fault lines
How natural selection changes populations
How cholera spreads through dirty water

questions.explain: The first three narrate particular events at a time and place. The last three seek what happens generally, wherever and whenever.
questions.rule: Particular events: history. General laws: science.

questions.q: Two books discuss the 1854 Soho cholera outbreak. Book A tells what happened street by street; Book B uses it as one case to show how cholera spreads. How do they differ?
options: A narrates particulars; B uses them toward a general law
A is fiction, while B is the true and scientific account of it
A is science, since it gives more exact detail
They do not differ, since they cover one outbreak
optionExplain: Right: A is history; B uses the case as evidence for what holds generally, which is science.
Both offer claims as true; neither is fiction.
Detail does not make science; seeking the general does.
A shared case can serve different aims.
questions.explain: The same facts serve a history in one book and a science in the other. What decides is whether the book is after the particular story or the general law.
questions.rule: Same case, different aims.

questions.q: Why can a claim in a scientific book be checked by new observations, while a claim in a history usually cannot be checked that way?
options: Scientists keep better records than historians do
Historians do not want their claims to be checked
Scientific claims are simpler than historical ones
Laws hold at any time or place; past events happened once
optionExplain: Record-keeping is not the point; the kind of claim is.
Historians do check claims, through the evidence the past left behind.
Scientific claims are not simpler; they are general.
Right: a general law can be tested again elsewhere and later; a particular past event cannot be rerun.
questions.explain: A law about what happens at any time or place can meet new cases. A particular event happened once, so it is checked through what it left behind.
questions.rule: General claims can meet new cases.
questions.teaches: By extension, because a scientific law holds at any time or place, it can be checked by new observations, while a historical event happened once and is checked through the records it left.

questions.q: One consultant writes a case study of how a single company turned itself around; another studies hundreds of firms to find what usually makes turnarounds succeed. By analogy, which is in the scientist's mode?
options: The single case study, since it is more detailed and concrete
Both, since both concern business success
The study of hundreds of firms seeking a pattern
Neither, since business is a practical subject
optionExplain: Detail about one case is the historian's mode.
Shared subject, different aims.
Right: looking for what holds for the most part across many cases is the scientist's aim.
Both may serve practice later, but as written both aim at knowledge.
questions.explain: The single case narrates particulars; the many-firm study seeks a generalisation. That mirrors history and science.
questions.rule: One case: history's mode. Many cases, one pattern: science's.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a case study works in the historian's mode, telling one particular story, while a study of many cases seeking a pattern works in the scientist's mode.

questions.q: Newton called his great work Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy. How do we class it today, according to the authors?
options: As philosophy, which is what its title says
As a history of the mathematics of its day
As one of the masterpieces of science
As a practical manual for engineers
optionExplain: The title says philosophy, but the word meant something different then.
It is not a narrative of past events.
Right: the authors say that for us it is one of the masterpieces of science.
It aims at knowledge of nature, not at instructions.
questions.explain: The word philosophy once covered what we now call physics. The card next explains why science titles mislead.
questions.rule: Old titles use old senses.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say the title of a scientific work is usually more revealing than the title of a history.
questions.explain: It is the other way round: history titles usually do the trick, while science titles often name only a subject.
questions.rule: Science titles reveal less.

questions.q: Match each subject or book to what the authors say about it.
pairs: Claimed by both at various times
questions.explain: Some subject names place a book at once; others are disputed, and older titles use the words in older senses.
questions.rule: Know whose subject it is.

questions.q: Lou learns that Aristotle called his Physics a scientific treatise, so he opens it expecting reports of laboratory experiments. What has he missed?
options: That Aristotle wrote about biology, not about physics
That Aristotle's Physics is in fact a work of history
That scientific treatises do not report experiments
That science has shifted; today we call it philosophy
optionExplain: The book is about physics; the issue is the word science.
It is not a narrative of past events.
Many scientific works report experiments; Lou's error is about the old use of the word.
Right: the authors say that by current usage we would regard Aristotle's Physics as philosophical.
questions.explain: Aristotle's science is not ours. Reading the old label in the modern sense sets the wrong expectations.
questions.rule: Read old labels in their own sense.

questions.q: A modern bestseller is titled My Philosophy of Investing and lists rules for picking shares. Does the word philosophy make it a philosophical book in the authors' sense?
options: No; the word is loose, and the book gives rules
Yes, since the author chose that word for it
Yes, since investing raises deep questions too
No, since books about money cannot count as philosophy
optionExplain: Right: here philosophy means a personal set of rules, and rules for picking shares make it practical.
An author's word choice can be loose; the book's aim decides.
Deep questions may exist, but this book gives rules, not an inquiry.
A theoretical book about money is possible; this one just happens to be practical.
questions.explain: Usage shifts in both directions. Here the word philosophy means a personal approach, and the book's rules mark it as practical.
questions.rule: A loose word is not a classification.
questions.teaches: Loose modern uses of philosophy, as in a philosophy of investing, often mean a personal set of rules, so the word in a title may even point to a practical book.

questions.q: In a museum, a case of 18th-century air pumps, prisms and magnets is labelled natural philosophy apparatus. What does the label most likely mean?
options: Tools used for staging philosophical debates
Instruments used in religious ritual and prayer
Decorations for a wealthy scholar's study
Equipment for what we now call physics
optionExplain: The word philosophy misleads a modern eye; these are experimental tools.
Nothing in the objects suggests ritual.
These are working instruments, not ornaments.
Right: as with Newton's title, natural philosophy then meant what we call physics.
questions.explain: Natural philosophy is the old name for physics, as Newton's title shows. Old labels need old meanings.
questions.rule: Read old records in their own terms.
questions.teaches: By analogy, old documents and labels of every kind use words in older senses, as natural philosophy once meant physics, so reading them needs the meanings of their time.

questions.q: One book on the mind reports observations made in a psychoanalyst's clinic; another asks you to examine your own thinking. Which is likely to be scientific, by the authors' test?
options: The one asking you to examine your thinking
The one reporting clinical observations
Both, since both study the human mind
Neither, since the mind is philosophy's subject
optionExplain: Examining your own thinking uses experience everyone has.
Right: clinical observation is special experience beyond ordinary life.
A shared subject does not settle the kind.
Psychology has been claimed by both; the subject does not decide.
questions.explain: The test is the experience a book relies on. The card next sets it out.
questions.rule: Special experience: science.

questions.q: If a theoretical book emphasises things outside your normal, routine, daily ____, it is a scientific work.
questions.explain: Science relies on special experience beyond daily routine; philosophy on the experience we all share.
questions.rule: Beyond daily experience: science.

questions.q: Sort each book by the authors' experience test.

items.t: Asks you to repeat an experiment with a pendulum
Reports what divers saw on the deep sea floor
Describes results from a particle accelerator
Asks whether you could have chosen otherwise
Asks you to reflect on what you mean by fairness
Appeals to your experience of recognising a face

questions.explain: Experiments, dives and accelerators are special experience. Choosing, judging fairness and recognising faces are experiences everyone has.
questions.rule: Lab, field or clinic: science. Common life: philosophy.

questions.q: The authors call Locke's Essay Concerning Human Understanding philosophical and many of Freud's writings scientific. What is the reason?
options: Locke wrote two centuries earlier than Freud
Freud wrote about the mind, Locke about knowledge
Locke drew on common experience, Freud on the clinic
Locke used mathematics and Freud did not use it
optionExplain: Date does not decide; the experience relied on does.
The authors call Locke's book a philosophical work in psychology, so both concern the mind.
Right: Locke makes every point from experience we all have of our own minds; Freud reports what he observed in the clinic.
Mathematics is not the difference the authors point to.
questions.explain: Both write about the mind. The difference is the experience each relies on: common for Locke, clinical for Freud.
questions.rule: Same subject, different experience.

questions.q: A history of the Second World War relies on archives that no ordinary reader has seen. Does the special-experience test make it a science?
options: Yes, since it relies on special, not common, experience
Yes, since an archive is a kind of historian's laboratory
No, since histories rely on everyone's common experience
No; the test only separates science from philosophy
optionExplain: The test sorts science from philosophy; it does not reach histories.
An archive is not a laboratory, and the test does not apply here anyway.
Histories do not rely on common experience; the test is simply the wrong one for them.
Right: the authors say the test applies only to books that are either science or philosophy.
questions.explain: The book narrates particular past events, so it is history. The experience test only separates science from philosophy.
questions.rule: Use the experience test only between science and philosophy.

questions.q: Darwin's facts came from years of fieldwork no ordinary reader has done. Does that make them impossible to check?
options: No; others who make a similar effort can recheck them
Yes, since only Darwin himself saw what he reported in his book
Yes, which is why the authors call his book philosophy
No, since any reader can check them from daily life
optionExplain: Right: the authors say such facts can be and have been rechecked by other observers making a similar effort.
Others have gone and looked; the facts are not private to Darwin.
The authors use Darwin as an example of science.
That is exactly what readers cannot do: the facts lie outside ordinary daily experience.
questions.explain: Special experience is not private experience. It takes effort beyond daily life, but other observers can make that effort and recheck the facts.
questions.rule: Special does not mean private.
questions.teaches: Special experience is not private: Darwin's field observations can be and have been rechecked by others who make a similar effort, so it is open to anyone willing to do the work.

questions.q: In a trial, a forensic chemist reports a laboratory analysis, while the judge tells jurors to use their own experience to judge whether a witness's story is plausible. How does this map onto the authors' test?
options: Both rely on special experience, since a court is formal
Both rely on common experience, since jurors decide
Chemist: special experience; jurors: common experience
Jurors: special experience; chemist: common experience
optionExplain: Jurors are chosen precisely because they bring ordinary experience.
The chemist's analysis lies outside the jurors' daily experience.
Right: the chemist reports what only lab work can show; the jurors judge from experience everyone has.
This reverses them.
questions.explain: Courts split evidence the way the authors split science and philosophy: expert special experience on one side, common experience on the other.
questions.rule: Experts bring special experience; jurors bring common experience.
questions.teaches: By analogy, courts split the same way: expert witnesses report special experience jurors lack, while on matters of everyday life jurors are asked to judge from their own experience.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, William James's Principles of Psychology is both a scientific and a philosophical work.
questions.explain: James appealed to both special and common experience. The card next shows how to classify such a book.
questions.rule: A book can draw on both experiences.

questions.q: The authors say James's Principles of Psychology is both scientific and philosophical, though primarily ____.
questions.explain: James reports much special experience, so the book is primarily scientific, though it also appeals to readers' own experience.
questions.rule: Classify by the dominant kind.

questions.q: Reading a chapter, you meet a point you can follow only by imagining a controlled experiment with rats in a maze. What does this tell you about that point?
options: It relies on common experience, so it is philosophical
It relies on special experience, so it is scientific
It is a historical point about experiments done in the past
It tells you nothing until the chapter is finished
optionExplain: A controlled maze experiment is not part of ordinary daily life.
Right: a controlled experiment lies outside routine experience, the mark of a scientific point.
The point concerns what happens generally, not a past event as such.
You can note the experience a point needs as soon as you meet it.
questions.explain: Noting the experience a point calls for classifies the point on the spot. Controlled experiments belong to science.
questions.rule: Note the experience each point needs.

questions.q: True or false: A psychology book that once asks readers to check a claim against their own experience is thereby a philosophical book.
questions.explain: James's book does this often and is still primarily scientific. Weigh the pattern of experience across the book, not one appeal.
questions.rule: One appeal does not set the class.

questions.q: Two books each ask you to imagine something: one, a ball rolled down a precisely angled plane and timed; the other, keeping or breaking a promise to a friend. Which relies on special experience?
options: Both, since each of them asks you to imagine a case you have not met
The promise, since it involves deep moral feeling
The timed ball, since such trials are outside daily life
Neither, since imagining something is not experience
optionExplain: Imagining is shared; what is imagined differs.
Promises are part of everyone's ordinary experience.
Right: a controlled, timed experiment is special experience even when you only imagine it, as with Galileo's inclined planes.
The authors count imagining Galileo's experiments as engaging special experience.
questions.explain: Being asked to imagine does not settle the test. What matters is whether the imagined case is a controlled experiment or a situation from ordinary life.
questions.rule: Ask what you are asked to imagine.
questions.teaches: Being asked to imagine does not settle the test: what matters is what you imagine, a controlled experiment beyond daily routine or a situation from ordinary life.

questions.q: A health podcast mixes reports of clinical trials with appeals to listeners' own experience of tiredness. How can the experience test help a listener?
options: It shows which claims she can check herself and which need data
It shows the podcast is unreliable, since it mixes evidence
It shows all the claims are scientific, since trials appear
It shows all the claims are philosophical, since she feels tired
optionExplain: Right: claims resting on common experience she can test against her own life; claims resting on trials need the experts' data.
Mixing kinds of evidence is normal; James did it too.
Some claims rest only on listeners' experience.
Some claims rest on trials she has not seen.
questions.explain: Noting which experience each claim rests on sorts them into those she can judge herself and those she must take from the evidence.
questions.rule: Sort claims by the experience behind them.
questions.teaches: By analogy, noting which claims rest on special evidence and which on common experience shows a listener which claims she can check herself and which depend on the experts' data.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, philosophy's armchair thinking is a lesser method than science's experiments.
questions.explain: The authors say the contrast should not be invidious: each method suits certain problems. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Different methods, not better and worse.

questions.q: The authors say the contrast between experimental science and armchair philosophy should not be ____, ranking one below the other.
questions.explain: An invidious contrast ranks one side below the other. The authors reject that: some problems need the armchair, others the laboratory.
questions.rule: The contrast is not a ranking.

questions.q: Sort each question by what it needs, following the authors' account.

items.t: Whether a promise made under threat binds you
What we mean when we call an act fair
Whether knowing something requires certainty
Whether a new drug lowers blood pressure
How deep the ocean floor is at a given point
Whether a bird species migrates in winter

questions.explain: The first three can be worked out by careful thought about common experience. The last three need observation beyond everyday life.
questions.rule: Fit the method to the problem.

questions.q: Ben says: philosophers only think and scientists only observe. What do the authors say?
options: Philosophers only think, but they think more deeply
Scientists only observe and leave thinking to others
Both observe and think, about different observations
Neither observes; both reason from definitions
optionExplain: The authors deny that the philosopher is a pure thinker.
The authors deny that the scientist is only an observer.
Right: both observe and think, but they think about different sorts of observation.
Both do observe: the philosopher common experience, the scientist special experience.
questions.explain: The difference is not thinking versus observing. It lies in which observations they think about and how they prove their conclusions.
questions.rule: Both observe; both think.

questions.q: A physicist hits on a new idea about light while daydreaming in an armchair. Does that make her eventual book philosophical?
options: Yes, since the idea came from armchair thinking
Yes, unless she rejects the idea on reflection
No, since physicists never think in armchairs
No; what counts is how she proves the idea
optionExplain: Where an idea came from does not set the kind of book.
Reflection does not change the kind either; proof does.
Physicists can think anywhere; that is not the point.
Right: the authors say that however they arrive at their conclusions, scientists and philosophers prove them differently.
questions.explain: The authors separate arriving at a conclusion from proving it. A scientist proves by pointing to special experience, wherever the idea first came.
questions.rule: Classify by how a conclusion is proved.
questions.teaches: How a conclusion was reached differs from how it is proved: a scientist may hit on an idea in an armchair, but must prove it by special experience, and the proof is what marks the kind.

questions.q: A store team asks two things about its returns policy: whether it is fair to honest customers, and whether it reduces fraudulent returns. Which needs special investigation?
options: Whether it reduces fraud, which needs data to settle
Whether it is fair, since fairness is hard to judge without figures
Both, since policy questions always need data
Neither, since staff can tell from experience
optionExplain: Right: how many fraudulent returns a policy prevents can only be known by gathering evidence beyond common experience.
Fairness can be hard, but it is weighed by reasoning from experience everyone has.
Some policy questions can be settled by careful thought.
Impressions from experience cannot measure a fraud rate.
questions.explain: By analogy, one question can be reasoned out from common experience; the other needs evidence no amount of reflection supplies.
questions.rule: Match the question to the method.
questions.teaches: By analogy, practical teams face both kinds of question: some can be settled by careful reasoning from common experience, others only by gathering special data, and treating one as the other wastes effort.

questions.q: According to the authors, what must a historian do because history is narrative in form?
options: Avoid any feature that resembles a story
Obey the rules for telling a good story
Reduce past events to general laws
Appeal only to the reader's own everyday experience
optionExplain: The authors say the reverse: the historian must write poetically.
Right: a narrative is a narrative, fact or fiction, so the historian must tell a good story.
General laws are the scientist's aim.
Appealing to common experience is the philosopher's method.
questions.explain: Narrative has its own rules, whether the story is true or invented. The card next explains why styles of argument differ by kind.
questions.rule: History must tell a good story.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say scientists and philosophers argue in different styles, not only from different kinds of experience.
questions.explain: Apart from the experiences they rely on, the authors say scientists and philosophers do not think in exactly the same way; their styles in arguing differ.
questions.rule: Different kinds, different arguing styles.

questions.q: Match each book to what a reader should mainly look for in it.
pairs: How one event led to the next
A law and the evidence for it
Claims to test against your own experience
questions.explain: Each kind carries its argument differently: narrative, law and evidence, appeal to common experience, or rules of action.
questions.rule: Know what each kind offers.

questions.q: Kai judges a history book poor because it tells a story instead of stating general laws. What has he missed?
options: That general laws are hidden in every story
That the book may be fiction after all
That a history is meant to tell a good story
That histories state facts and need no arguments
optionExplain: A history does not aim at general laws, hidden or not.
Telling a story does not make a history fiction.
Right: narrative is the typical form of history, so judging it by a science's standard misreads it.
A historian argues and interprets facts too, but in a different way from a scientist: through narrative, not general laws.
questions.explain: Kai applies a scientist's standard to a historian's book. The kind tells you which standard fits.
questions.rule: Judge each kind by its own standard.

questions.q: A reader skilled at following the plots of novels starts a history book. Given the authors' remark that a narrative is a narrative, what carries over?
options: Following how events connect into a story
Treating the events as imagined
Testing claims against everyday experience
Looking for the general law that lies behind the events
optionExplain: Right: following a narrative works the same way whether the story is true or invented.
The events are offered as fact; that does not carry over.
That is the way to read philosophy.
That is the way to read science.
questions.explain: Because history is narrative, some skills from reading fiction help: following plot and how events connect. The claims, though, remain claims of fact.
questions.rule: Narrative skills carry over; the claims stay factual.
questions.teaches: Because history is narrative, skills for reading fiction, such as following plot and how events connect, help in reading history, though its claims remain claims of fact.

questions.q: A doctor reads a patient's case history and then a study of a drug's effects across many patients. How should her way of following each change?
options: Both as stories of the particular events they report
Both for general findings only
Study as a story; case for general findings
Case as a story; study for general findings
optionExplain: The drug study seeks what holds generally, not a story.
The case history is about one patient's particular course.
This reverses them.
Right: the case history narrates one patient's events; the study argues for a general result from evidence.
questions.explain: A case history is narrative; a drug study argues for general findings. The case may raise a question, but only the study can answer it in general.
questions.rule: Match your reading to the kind of text.
questions.teaches: A case history can suggest a general finding but cannot establish it: one patient's story is evidence that a study across many cases must still test.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a visitor walking into a classroom could soon tell whether the class was history, science or philosophy.
questions.explain: The teacher's way of proceeding, words, arguments, problems and expected responses give it away. The card next draws the lesson for reading.
questions.rule: Kinds of teaching show themselves.

questions.q: Which clues do the authors say would reveal a class's subject? Select all that apply.
options: The kind of words the teacher uses
The type of arguments employed
The sort of problems proposed
The size of the room the class meets in
The time of day the class is held
optionExplain: Right: the words used are one of the authors' clues.
Right: the arguments are another.
Right: the problems proposed are another.
Room size says nothing about the subject.
Timetabling says nothing about the subject.
questions.explain: The authors list the teacher's way of proceeding, words, arguments, problems and expected responses. Room and time are not about the teaching.
questions.rule: Read the method, not the room.

questions.q: Why do the authors bring up the classroom comparison?
options: To show that kinds of teaching, and of reading, differ
To argue that books teach worse than people do
To show that classes are easier to classify than books
To urge readers to take classes before reading
optionExplain: Right: as teaching differs by kind, so the art of being taught, and so of reading, must differ.
The authors liken books to teachers; they do not rank them below teachers here.
Ease of classifying is not their point; the need to adjust is.
The comparison is about how to read, not a call to take classes.
questions.explain: The art of teaching differs by field, and the art of being taught must respond to it. Since books are teachers, reading must differ by kind too.
questions.rule: Different teaching, different learning.

questions.q: A reader with no background in either field picks up an introductory philosophy book and an advanced science book. Following the authors' remark about teachers, which is she likelier to manage?
options: The science book, since science is the more exact and orderly field
The philosophy book, since it relies on common experience
Both equally, since neither needs any background
Neither, since every kind needs earlier teaching
optionExplain: Exactness is not what helps a newcomer; prior preparation is.
Right: the authors say philosophers often prefer students untaught by colleagues, while scientists prefer students already prepared.
Advanced science usually assumes earlier teaching.
Philosophy's appeal to common experience makes earlier teaching less necessary.
questions.explain: The authors report that the philosopher usually finds it easier to teach students not taught by his colleagues, while the scientist prefers students already prepared. Philosophy appeals to experience everyone has.
questions.rule: Some kinds need more preparation than others.
questions.teaches: Different kinds need different preparation: the authors say philosophers often prefer students untaught by colleagues, while scientists prefer students already prepared, so a reader's background matters more for some kinds.

questions.q: True or false: A reader who follows a philosophy book as a story of events, as he would a history, is reading it in the appropriate manner.
questions.explain: He will look for a narrative and miss the arguments he should be testing against his own experience. Each kind needs its own manner of reading.
questions.rule: Wrong manner, missed argument.

questions.q: A new employee has a compliance briefing, a product demonstration and a strategy talk on one day. What does the authors' point suggest about how to listen?
options: Listen the same careful way to all three
Attend only to the one that seems most useful
Switch manner to suit each kind of session
Take full notes, since note-taking suits all three
optionExplain: One manner for all three misses what each offers.
Skipping sessions avoids the problem rather than handling it.
Right: rules to follow, a skill to watch and an argument to weigh each call for a different kind of attention.
Notes may help, but the point is to adjust the kind of attention.
questions.explain: As a student adjusts to history, science or philosophy, a learner can adjust to each kind of session, and does so best by deciding its kind in advance.
questions.rule: Adjust to the kind of teaching.
questions.teaches: Settling the kind of a session before it starts, from its title or agenda, lets a learner choose the right kind of attention from the first minute instead of finding it halfway through.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, grasping how a book is put together is an optional extra, useful mainly to scholars.
questions.explain: The authors call grasping a book's structure an essential part of apprehending any book. The card next shows the image they use for it.
questions.rule: Seeing the structure is part of understanding.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Sort each feature of a book: is it part of the skeleton or part of the surface?

items.t: The order in which the main parts build on each other
A vivid anecdote that opens chapter three
How each part serves the book's main aim
The author's jokes and turns of phrase
The division of the argument into major stages
A memorable photograph of a laboratory

questions.explain: The skeleton is the firm structure: the parts, their order and how they serve the whole. Anecdotes, style and illustrations are the flesh and clothes that cover it.
questions.rule: Structure is the bones; style and illustration are the flesh.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Nadia finishes a popular book on sleep. She can repeat ten fascinating facts from it but cannot say how its chapters are arranged or why. In the authors' image, what has she missed?
options: The facts themselves, which she ought to memorise more fully
The author's credentials, which decide what the book is worth
The structure under the facts she has remembered
Little, since a science book exists to hand over facts
optionExplain: She already has the facts; more of them would still be surface without the order that connects them.
Credentials are about the author, not the book's build; the X-ray demand is to see how the book itself is organised.
Right: she has the flesh but not the skeleton, the arrangement that makes the facts one book.
The authors say grasping structure is essential to apprehending any book, science included, so facts alone fall short.
questions.explain: Remembered facts are surface material. Without seeing how the parts are ordered, Nadia has not grasped the book as a built whole.
questions.rule: Facts without structure are flesh without bones.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the demand to see a book's structure applies to every book worth reading, poems included.
questions.explain: The authors say the structural rules apply to poetry as well as to science. What changes with the kind of book is how the rules are applied, not whether they apply.
questions.rule: Kind changes the application, not the demand.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A new office manager inherits a 40-page procedures manual. Carrying the X-ray idea over, what should she look for first?
options: Which pages have the most typing or layout errors
How its sections depend on one another to get work done
Which procedures are newest, since old ones may be stale
The longest section, since length shows what matters most
optionExplain: Errors are surface defects; fixing them tells her nothing about how the manual is organised.
Right: the manual's skeleton is the way its sections connect, which shows what must be read together.
Age might matter later, but it is a property of single parts, not the structure that ties them together.
Length is a surface feature; a short section can be the one everything else depends on.
questions.explain: A manual, like a book, has a skeleton: sections that depend on one another. Seeing those links first shows her which parts belong together.
questions.rule: Look for how sections depend on each other.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the X-ray habit works on any long working document: a manual or policy has a skeleton of dependent sections, and seeing it tells you which parts must be read together.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A student says: To find a book's skeleton I will skip its examples and stories, since they are only flesh. What is wrong with this plan?
options: Examples are the skeleton and the arguments are the flesh
Skipping works, but only for books under a hundred pages
The skeleton is printed in the index, so stories add nothing
X-ray reading looks through the surface; it still reads it
optionExplain: This reverses the image: examples cover the structure, they are not the structure.
Length is not the issue; at any length the bones are found by reading what covers them.
An index lists topics, not the ordered parts; the structure has to be found by reading.
Right: you need not tear the flesh off, but you find the bones by reading through it, not by skipping it.
questions.explain: The authors say you do not have to strip the book to reach its structure. You see the skeleton by reading the whole body with X-ray eyes.
questions.rule: Read through the surface, not around it.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: According to the authors, which books worth reading have a unity and an organization of parts?
options: Every book worth reading, whatever its kind
Only expository books, such as works of science
Only novels, plays and other stories with a plot
Only books whose authors announce a plan first
optionExplain: Right: the authors say every book worth reading, without exception, has a unity and an organization of parts.
A reasonable guess, since arguments look more organised than stories, but the authors include poetry and fiction.
Plot is one kind of unity, but the authors give unity to science and philosophy too.
Announcing a plan helps the reader, but the unity is in the book whether or not the author announces it.
questions.explain: The authors make the claim without exception for books worth reading. The card next explains how the unity differs from kind to kind.
questions.rule: Every worthwhile book has unity and parts.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the unity of a novel and the unity of a treatise on politics are of the same sort.
questions.explain: The authors say the unity of a novel is not the same as that of a political treatise, and their parts differ in sort and order. Both have unity, but not the same kind.
questions.rule: Same rules, different kinds of unity.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A reader picks up a well-regarded poetry collection and says: It is poetry, so there is no structure to look for. How would the authors respond?
options: Poetry worth reading has a unity too, of its own sort
They agree, since structure rules fit expository works only
Structure exists, but only the poet is able to identify it
Look for the same outline of argument a treatise has
optionExplain: Right: the claim covers every book worth reading, but the unity takes the form suited to poetry.
The authors say the rules apply to poetry as well as to science, so they would not agree.
The rules are addressed to readers; finding the structure is the reader's job, not the poet's privilege.
This expects the wrong form; a poem's parts are not ordered the way a treatise's arguments are.
questions.explain: The authors extend the structural rules to poetry. The reader should look for unity, but in the shape a poetry collection would have.
questions.rule: Expect unity, in the form the kind allows.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Which statements fit the authors' view of unity? Select all that apply.
options: A worthwhile book has an organization of parts
The structural rules apply to poetry and science alike
A novel's parts are ordered like a political treatise's
A book with no unity would be relatively unreadable
A worthwhile book's unity is plain at first glance
optionExplain: Right: the authors pair unity with an organization of parts in every book worth reading.
Right: they say the rules apply to poetry as well as to science, though applied differently.
They say the opposite: the parts of a novel and of a treatise differ in sort and order.
Right: they call such a book a mess and say bad books are relatively unreadable for this reason.
The authors ask for X-ray eyes because the structure is hidden under the surface, not plain at first glance.
questions.explain: Unity and organization belong to every worthwhile book, and the rules apply across kinds. What varies is the form, and the structure has to be looked for.
questions.rule: Unity is always there, but not always on the surface.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: If a volume turns out to be a loose set of unrelated magazine pieces, the expectation of a single unity may fail for it.
questions.explain: The authors say that parts not organically related make no whole, only a collection. The expectation of unity is a stance for books that hang together; a loose collection is where it can fail.
questions.rule: A mere collection may have no single unity.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: You are about to watch a six-part documentary series. Carrying over the authors' stance on unity, which expectation helps most?
options: Expect no plan, since series are made to entertain
Expect one main aim and ordered episodes, in the form TV uses
Expect its episodes to match a textbook's chapter scheme
Wait until the last episode to see whether a plan exists
optionExplain: Entertainment and structure are not opposites; well-made stories and films have plans too.
Right: expect a unity, but look for it in the shape a documentary series uses, not a book's.
This expects unity but in the wrong form, the mistake of carrying one kind's structure to another.
Waiting passively wastes the episodes; the stance is to search for the plan while watching.
questions.explain: Expecting unity makes you look for the plan from the start. Matching the expectation to the medium keeps you from looking for the wrong kind of order.
questions.rule: Expect a plan, shaped by the medium.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the expectation of unity carries over to other made works such as documentaries or courses: expect a plan, but in the form that medium uses rather than a book's.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Rule 2 says to state the unity of the whole book in a single sentence, or at most a few sentences making up a short ____.
questions.explain: The limit is a short paragraph. The card next explains what the statement has to cover.
questions.rule: One sentence, or a short paragraph at most.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: What does Rule 2 ask the reader to state?
options: What kind of book it is and its subject matter
What the whole book is about, put briefly
The major parts of the book in their proper order
The questions the author set out to answer
optionExplain: That is Rule 1, classifying the book; Rule 2 comes after it.
Right: Rule 2 asks for the unity of the whole, said as briefly as possible.
Setting out the parts is Rule 3, which builds on the unity.
Finding the author's questions is Rule 4, covered later in the chapter.
questions.explain: Rule 2 asks for one thing: what the whole book is about, in a sentence or a short paragraph.
questions.rule: Rule 2 is the unity in brief.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Readers describe a book on the history of salt. Which statements do what Rule 2 asks? Select all that apply.
options: It traces how salt shaped trade, empires and diets
A history book on salt, written for general readers
Chapter 4, on French salt taxes, is the most gripping
It shows salt's role in power, from Rome to Gandhi
It is well researched, lively and full of odd facts
optionExplain: Right: one sentence says what the whole book does, from start to end.
This classifies the book, the work of Rule 1, without saying what it is about as a whole.
This picks out one part; the rule asks for the whole book.
Right: a different wording, but it still says briefly what the whole book is about.
This is a verdict on quality; it does not say what the book is about.
questions.explain: A Rule 2 statement covers the whole book and says what it is about. Classification, a single chapter and praise all miss that target.
questions.rule: Whole book, briefly, what it is about.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Leo states the unity of a 12-chapter book using only chapters 1 to 3, because they are the strongest. What is the flaw?
options: He should use the weakest chapters, where problems lie
It is too short and ought to list all twelve chapters
It must wait until he has classified every chapter
The statement must cover the whole book, not its best part
optionExplain: Swapping strong chapters for weak ones still covers only part of the book.
Listing chapters is a list of parts, not a statement of unity; the length is not the problem.
Rule 1 classifies the book as a whole, not chapter by chapter, and it does not cure a partial statement.
Right: Rule 2 asks for the unity of the whole book, so three chapters cannot carry it.
questions.explain: The unity belongs to the whole book. A statement built from part of it describes that part, however good the part is.
questions.rule: A unity statement covers the whole.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: Even for a 900-page book, Rule 2 still asks for no more than a short paragraph.
questions.explain: The rule sets the limit at a sentence or a short paragraph whatever the book's length. A longer book makes the statement harder to write, not longer.
questions.rule: Book length does not stretch the limit.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A colleague who missed a 60-minute podcast episode asks what it was about. Following Rule 2, what is the best reply?
options: A minute-by-minute run through every topic it raised
One or two sentences giving its main point and its course
The name of the show, its host and its usual format
The most surprising fact the guest happened to mention
optionExplain: A full run-through is a list of parts, not the unity, and it takes far too long.
Right: a sentence or two on the main point and how it develops is Rule 2 applied to listening.
This classifies the show, like Rule 1, without saying what this episode was about.
One striking detail is a part, not the whole.
questions.explain: Rule 2 works on anything you take in as a whole. Being able to give the episode's point briefly shows you followed it as a whole, not as a string of moments.
questions.rule: If you can say it in two sentences, you followed it.
questions.teaches: Rule 2 doubles as a test of listening as well as reading: if you can give a talk or episode's point in a sentence or two, you grasped it as a whole rather than as a stream of moments.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: Saying that a book is a practical work on gardening is a statement of its unity in the sense Rule 2 wants.
questions.explain: That statement gives the book's kind and subject, which is Rule 1's work. The card next shows the other sense of about that Rule 2 needs.
questions.rule: Kind is not yet unity.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: In the everyday sense of about that Rule 2 uses, asking what a book is about means asking what?
options: What shelf of the library it belongs on
What subject matter it treats, and how
What the author is trying to do in it
What readers have said about it since
optionExplain: Shelving follows classification, the first sense of about and the work of Rule 1.
Subject matter and treatment are the first sense of about; they tell you the kind of book.
Right: like asking what a person is up to, it asks what the author is trying to do, which gives the theme.
Reception history is about readers, not about what the author set out to do.
questions.explain: The everyday sense asks what someone is up to. Applied to a book, it asks what the author is trying to do, which is the theme or main point.
questions.rule: About, for Rule 2, means what the author is up to.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Sort each statement: does it give the book's kind, or its theme?

items.t: A historical account of a nineteenth-century epidemic
It shows how a cholera outbreak led London to rebuild its sewers
A practical guide for first-time managers
It argues new managers fail by doing work instead of handing it on
A theoretical work in psychology
It claims memories are rebuilt each time we recall them

questions.explain: A kind statement would fit many books of that type. A theme statement says what this author is up to, so it fits this book.
questions.rule: Kind fits many books; theme fits one.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A student's report begins: This is a popular science book about the ocean. Her teacher asks her to state the book's unity instead. Which revision does that?
options: This is a popular science book on the ocean and its life
It shows how currents regulate climate and what warming does
This is an excellent and readable book on a vital subject
It has twelve chapters, opening with tides, closing with reefs
optionExplain: This restates the kind with more words; it still says nothing about what the author is up to.
Right: it says what the book is trying to show, which is its theme.
This is praise, a verdict on quality rather than a statement of what the book does.
This lists the parts' boundaries, a start on structure but not the unity.
questions.explain: Her first sentence gives the kind. The revision needed says what the author is trying to do, which only the currents statement does.
questions.rule: Replace the category with the aim.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: If a reader already has a good guess at a book's theme, Rule 1 no longer matters and the book's kind can go unexamined.
questions.explain: Rule 1 comes first and still matters. Without knowing the kind, a reader can misjudge what the author is up to, for instance reading a practical book as pure description.
questions.rule: Theme builds on kind; it does not replace it.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A friend describes a new restaurant as an Italian place. Using the two senses of about, which description tells you what this restaurant is up to?
options: It serves one region's home cooking, changed weekly
It is an Italian restaurant in the centre of town
It sits in the category of casual dining venues
It offers pasta, pizza and a short list of wines
optionExplain: Right: it names what this restaurant is trying to do, which sets it apart from others of its kind.
This repeats the category and adds a location; it fits many restaurants.
Another category, broader still; it says what sort of place it is, not what it aims at.
A menu list gives parts of the offer, not the aim that ties them together.
questions.explain: Italian place is a category, like a book's kind. The aim of serving one region's home cooking says what this one is up to.
questions.rule: A category says what sort; an aim says what this one does.
questions.teaches: The two senses of about apply beyond books: a category (Italian restaurant, crime novel) says what sort of thing something is, while its aim says what this one is up to, and only the aim tells it apart from others of its kind.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: When the authors call a book a work of art, what do they mean by art?
options: Beauty of style, as found in poetry and fine prose
Imaginative invention, as opposed to plain fact
Skill in making something, not only fine art
Decoration added to make a book attractive
optionExplain: A natural reading of art, but the authors warn against so narrow a sense; they include books of knowledge.
Invention fits fiction, yet the authors apply the word to science and philosophy too.
Right: they mean the skill of a maker; an author is a maker of books.
Decoration is surface; the authors mean the skill that shapes the whole thing.
questions.explain: The authors use art in the broad sense of skilled making. The card next shows what follows for a book's unity.
questions.rule: Art here means skilled making.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: According to the authors, in proportion as a book is good, its unity is more nearly perfect and more ____.
questions.explain: The authors say a better book has a more nearly perfect, more pervasive unity, and that this holds for books of knowledge as much as for fiction.
questions.rule: Better books have more pervasive unity.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Cookbook A builds a skill in each chapter that later chapters use. Cookbook B gathers posts from the author's blog in no particular order. How would the authors compare them as made things?
options: A has the more pervasive unity, which counts in its favour
B is better, since recipes can be cooked in any order
They are equal, since cookbooks are not works of art
Quality rests on the recipes, not on how they are arranged
optionExplain: Right: A's parts serve the whole, and the authors tie a book's goodness to how pervasive its unity is.
Free order of use is handy, but it does not make B a better-made book; its parts do not serve a whole.
The authors' broad sense of art covers any skilled making, cookbooks included.
Good recipes matter, but as a book, the authors judge it partly by how its parts are unified.
questions.explain: A book is a made thing, and the better it is made, the more its unity reaches every part. A's chapters work together; B's do not.
questions.rule: Parts that serve the whole mark a better-made book.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: In a book you are reading, one chapter could be cut and nothing else would need to change. On the authors' view, what does this suggest?
options: That chapter must be the book's real centre
The book must be fiction, where episodes stand alone
The book has no unity at all and is a mere collection
The unity is less than pervasive at that point
optionExplain: A chapter nothing depends on is the opposite of a centre; a centre is what the rest relies on.
Fiction is not exempt; the authors expect pervasive unity in novels and plays as well.
This overreaches: one loose chapter weakens the unity there but does not dissolve the whole book.
Right: in a pervasively unified book each part contributes, so a chapter that could go without trace shows a weak spot.
questions.explain: Pervasive unity means every part contributes to the whole. A chapter whose removal changes nothing is a sign the unity thins out there.
questions.rule: A part nothing depends on is a gap in the unity.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: A book whose unity you missed on a quick first skim may still turn out to be well made.
questions.explain: A skim can miss a unity that careful reading would find. The link between quality and unity is a mark to look for, not a verdict a first glance can deliver.
questions.rule: A unity not yet found may still be there.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A curator is planning a museum exhibition about rivers. Carrying over the idea of pervasive unity, which plan is strongest?
options: Show the most famous objects, whatever their link
Give every room its own theme to keep variety
Have every room develop one main story about rivers
Arrange objects by the date the museum got them
optionExplain: Fame draws visitors, but unlinked objects make a collection, not a whole.
Variety without a shared aim gives many shows under one roof, a multiplicity.
Right: each room serves the main story, so the unity runs through every part.
Acquisition date is the museum's history, not an order that serves a theme about rivers.
questions.explain: An exhibition is a made thing like a book. It is better made when each part serves one main aim.
questions.rule: Each part should earn its place by serving the aim.
questions.teaches: By analogy, pervasive unity is a design test for any made thing, such as an exhibition: each part should earn its place by serving the main aim, and a part that serves nothing weakens the whole.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, if your statement of a book's unity needs a great many words, you have probably seen something other than the unity.
questions.explain: The authors say too many words means you have seen a multiplicity instead of the unity. The card next explains the difference.
questions.rule: Many words signal many things, not one.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: If it takes too many words to state the unity, the authors say you have seen not the unity but a ____.
questions.explain: A multiplicity is the many things a book contains. The unity is the one thing that ties them together.
questions.rule: Too many words: a multiplicity.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Which statement about a book on climate and farming shows its unity rather than a multiplicity?
options: It covers soil, water, pests, crops, prices and policy
It argues farms must adapt to heat, and shows how
It is a book about climate and farming in coming decades
It deals with many problems facing farmers around the world
optionExplain: This is a list of contents joined by commas, the sign of a multiplicity.
Right: one main point, with the parts tied to it.
Short, but it only names the subject; it could fit any book on the topic.
Also short, but vague; it names many problems without saying what ties them together.
questions.explain: A unity statement gives one point and shows how the parts serve it. A list is a multiplicity, and a vague label leaves out the content.
questions.rule: One point, with the parts under it.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A reader sums up a travel memoir: She visits Peru, then Bolivia, then Chile, meets a healer, loses her passport, falls ill and learns Spanish. Which rewrite states the unity?
options: She tours three Andean countries and has many adventures
A travel memoir set in South America, told in twelve chapters
Losing her passport and falling ill teach her Spanish fast
A trip through the Andes teaches a burnt-out lawyer to let go
optionExplain: Shorter, but it still lists the journey without saying what it adds up to.
This gives the kind and the length, not what the book is doing.
This picks two episodes and links them; it is a part, not the whole.
Right: it names the one change the journey produces, which ties the events together.
questions.explain: The original is a sequence joined by then and and. The unity is the point the sequence serves: what the trip does to the traveller.
questions.rule: Find what the sequence adds up to.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: If you cut a long, list-like statement down to a very short one, such as It is a book about sleep, you have found the unity.
questions.explain: Shortness alone does not make a unity statement. It is a book about sleep could fit hundreds of books; it drops the content rather than finding the one point that ties it together.
questions.rule: Short and vague is not the same as unified.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A team lead's weekly update lists eleven tasks completed. Her manager asks what the team achieved this week. Applying the few-words test, which reply is best?
options: We closed eleven tickets across design, code and testing
We got payments ready for launch by fixing the last blockers
We worked on the payment project as planned this week
Here is the full list of tasks, with the hours for each
optionExplain: A count and a list of areas is still a multiplicity; it does not say what the tasks added up to.
Right: one sentence says what the week's work achieved as a whole.
Short but empty: it would fit any week on the project.
The full list is the multiplicity itself, which the manager has already seen.
questions.explain: The manager wants the unity of the week, not its contents. A few words that say what the tasks added up to pass the test.
questions.rule: Say what the work added up to.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the few-words test checks any report of work: if you can only list what was done, you have not yet seen what it added up to.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A reader says: I know what this book is about, I cannot put it into words. How do the authors view this?
options: It is normal, since real understanding is often wordless
It probably does not even fool the reader himself
It is fine for fiction but not for expository books
It shows the book is badly written, not the reader's fault
optionExplain: Many people believe deep understanding is wordless, but the authors reject that for a book's unity.
Right: the authors say such a reader probably does not even fool himself.
The authors make no such exception; the demand to state the unity applies to novels too.
Blaming the book may sometimes be fair, but here the reader claims to know the unity, and that claim is the problem.
questions.explain: The authors are blunt about this claim. The card next explains why expressing the unity is the test.
questions.rule: Know it means can say it.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: The authors say the reader who claims to know the unity but cannot say it probably does not even ____ himself.
questions.explain: The only way to know you have grasped the unity is to be able to express it. A reader who cannot is probably not even fooling himself.
questions.rule: Saying it is the proof.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Writing a one-sentence summary, Ayo stalls: she cannot say how the book's first half, on old trade routes, connects to its second half, on modern shipping. What is her best next step?
options: Reread to find what links the two halves, then try again
Write two separate summaries, one per half, and stop there
Trust her sense that she understands and move on
Copy the blurb's summary, since it states the main point
optionExplain: Right: the stall shows she has not yet seen the unity, so she goes back to look for it.
Two summaries describe two halves; they give up on the unity of the whole.
This is the felt-but-unsaid unity the authors reject.
Borrowed words would not show her own grasp of how the halves connect.
questions.explain: Failing to say the unity shows she has not grasped it yet. The fix is more reading, not settling for a feeling or someone else's words.
questions.rule: If you cannot say it, go back and look.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Ravi says: I can recite the blurb's one-line summary, so I have grasped the unity. What is wrong with his reasoning?
options: Unity must always take more than one sentence
He should have felt the unity before saying anything
Blurbs give a book's kind, so they never state a theme
Words borrowed from a blurb do not show his own grasp
optionExplain: The rule allows a single sentence; length is not his problem.
A feeling comes before nothing useful here; the authors put the weight on expressing it.
Some blurbs do state a theme; the trouble is that the words are not his.
Right: the test is whether he can state the unity he has grasped, not whether he can repeat someone else's.
questions.explain: Being able to produce a sentence is needed, not enough. A recited blurb shows memory of the blurb, not his own grasp of the book.
questions.rule: The words must come from your own grasp.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: If a reader can write a good statement of a book's unity but needs a few minutes of thought to produce it, the authors' test has still been met.
questions.explain: The test is whether you can express the unity, to yourself or to someone else. Taking time to find the words is fine; the failure the authors describe is never finding them.
questions.rule: Slow is fine; never is not.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A coding student says she understands how a recursive function works but cannot explain it. Carrying the authors' test over, what should she do?
options: Accept the feeling, since coding skill is often unspoken
Memorise a textbook definition and repeat it on demand
Write more recursive code without pausing to explain
Explain it step by step to find where it breaks down
optionExplain: This is the I know but cannot say claim the authors distrust.
Reciting a definition is borrowed wording, like a blurb, not a sign of her grasp.
Practice helps, but it skips the check of whether she can express how the function works.
Right: the attempt to explain tests the understanding, and the point where it stalls shows the gap.
questions.explain: Saying it is the proof of grasp. Trying to explain step by step both tests her and locates the step she has not understood.
questions.rule: Explain it to find the gap.
questions.teaches: By analogy, explaining aloud is a general check on understanding: the point where the explanation stalls marks the gap, which tells you exactly what to study next.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Aristotle summed up the Odyssey in a few sentences. What did he call everything his summary left out?
options: Subplot
Digression
Episode
Background
optionExplain: A reasonable guess for side stories, but Aristotle's word was episode.
Digression suggests wandering off topic; Aristotle's word was episode.
Right: the essence of the plot, he said; the rest is episode.
Background suggests setting; Aristotle's word was episode.
questions.explain: Aristotle separated the essence of the plot from the episodes. The card next shows how this states a story's unity.
questions.rule: Plot is the essence; the rest is episode.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: According to the authors, what did Aristotle hold to be the mark of every good story, novel or play?
options: A large number of exciting episodes and twists
A hero who changes greatly by the end
A single unity of action tying it all together
An ending that takes the reader by surprise
optionExplain: Many episodes are compatible with a good story, but they are not its mark; the Odyssey has them and still has one thread.
A changing hero is common in stories, but Aristotle's mark is the unity of action.
Right: a main thread of plot that ties everything together.
Surprise endings are a device, not the mark Aristotle named.
questions.explain: Aristotle's mark of a good story is a single unity of action, which is why its plot can be stated in a few sentences.
questions.rule: A good story has one main thread.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A novel: a young doctor arrives in a mining town, fights the company over unsafe water, loses her job, and is proved right when a flood strikes. Sort each element.

items.t: She arrives in the mining town as its new doctor
She fights the company over unsafe water
A flood proves her warnings right
A chapter on her landlady's love affair
A comic scene at the town fair
A letter from her college roommate

questions.explain: The arrival, the fight and the vindication make the few-sentence plot. The love affair, the fair and the letter are episodes placed along that thread.
questions.rule: Ask: would the summary need it?

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Suppose the chapter on the landlady's love affair were removed from that novel. What does the plot-and-episode distinction predict?
options: The novel would lose its single unity of action
The plot would stand, though the book may be poorer
The novel would become a different kind of book
The novel would be better, since episodes only distract
optionExplain: The unity of action lives in the main thread, which this chapter is not part of.
Right: the essence survives, but episodes carry much of a story's life, so something may be lost.
Kind depends on subject and treatment, which one episode does not change.
This treats episodes as worthless; the authors locate a story's quality largely in how the bones are dressed.
questions.explain: Removing an episode leaves the plot intact, since the plot is the essence. Whether the novel suffers depends on what the episode added.
questions.rule: Episodes can go without the plot going.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: Because the rest is episode, a reader who knows a story's plot has had most of what the story offers.
questions.explain: Episode means outside the essence of the plot, not worthless. The authors say good and bad stories with the same plot differ in how the author dresses up the bare bones; by that account, much of what a story offers lies beyond its bare plot.
questions.rule: Outside the plot is not outside the value.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A long magazine feature tells of a town's water crisis through a dozen residents' stories. Carrying over Aristotle's method, what should a reader do to grasp the whole?
options: State the main chain of events briefly, then place each story
Remember each resident's story as a separate piece
Focus on the most moving story, as it carries the point
Treat the residents' stories as the point, and skip the events
optionExplain: Right: the feature has a plot like a story's; once it is stated, each resident's account finds its place.
Separate pieces give a collection; the feature is built to be one account.
The most moving story is one episode; it does not show how the rest fit.
This reverses the method: the personal stories are hung on the chain of events, not the other way round.
questions.explain: A narrative feature has a main thread like any story. Finding it first shows what each personal account is there to illustrate.
questions.rule: Find the thread, then place the voices.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the plot test works on narrative journalism: a feature built from many voices still has a main chain of events, and finding it shows what each personal story is there to illustrate.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, two stories with the same essential plot can differ greatly in quality.
questions.explain: The authors say the difference between good and bad stories with the same plot lies in what the author does with it. The card next explains how few plots there are.
questions.rule: Same plot, different quality.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: To what formula do the authors reduce the plot of Tom Jones?
options: Hero leaves home, is tested, and returns changed
Boy meets girl, boy loses girl, boy gets girl
A crime is committed, investigated and solved
A man rises to power and then falls from it
optionExplain: A well-known story pattern, but not the one the authors give for Tom Jones.
Right: the authors call it the plot of every romance.
That is the frame of a detective story, not Fielding's romance.
That is a tragic pattern; the authors' formula for Tom Jones ends happily.
questions.explain: The authors reduce Tom Jones to boy meets girl, boy loses girl, boy gets girl, and note that this is the plot of every romance.
questions.rule: Tom Jones has the romance plot.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Two sports films share a plot: an underdog team trains, loses a key game, then wins the final. Critics love one and dismiss the other. On the authors' view, where does the difference lie?
options: In which film has the more original plot
In which plot holds more twists and turns
The weaker film must have a different plot
In how each film dresses the shared plot
optionExplain: The plots are the same by hypothesis, so originality of plot cannot separate them.
Twists belong to episode and treatment; the essential plot is the same in both.
This denies the setup; the authors' point is that many stories really share one plot.
Right: with the same bones, quality lies in what each maker did with them.
questions.explain: When the essential plot is shared, the authors locate the difference in how the bare bones are dressed: characters, scenes and craft.
questions.rule: Shared bones: judge the dressing.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Which statements follow from the authors' point that there are only a small number of plots? Select all that apply.
options: Many stories share one plot when stated at its essence
Quality lies largely in what is done with the plot
Two romances with the same plot are equally good
A story with a familiar plot is not worth reading
Stating the plot helps you see a story's unity
optionExplain: Right: at the level of essence, many stories reduce to one formula.
Right: the authors place the difference in how the author dresses the bare bones.
The authors say the opposite: stories with the same plot can be good or bad.
Every romance shares a familiar plot, and the authors recommend good novels such as Tom Jones.
Right: the plot is the unity of the narrative, which lets you place the parts.
questions.explain: Few plots means stories share skeletons, not that they are equal or stale. The plot gives the unity; the treatment gives the quality.
questions.rule: Plot gives unity; treatment gives quality.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: If a new novel's plot can be reduced to boy meets girl, boy loses girl, boy gets girl, that alone shows the novel is weak.
questions.explain: The authors use Tom Jones, a novel they recommend, as their example of this very plot. A familiar plot says nothing about quality; the dressing decides that.
questions.rule: A familiar plot is no verdict.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Two pop songs use the same four-chord progression. A listener asks why one became a classic and the other was forgotten. Carrying the authors' point over, which answer fits best?
options: The classic must use a hidden, richer progression
Popularity is luck, as the songs are the same underneath
What each writer built on the shared frame
The forgotten song copied the classic and lost out
optionExplain: This denies the shared frame, as if quality had to come from the skeleton.
Same skeleton does not mean same song; everything built on it differs.
Right: melody, words and arrangement are the flesh on a shared skeleton, where the difference lies.
Copying is a separate charge; sharing a common frame is normal and says nothing about who copied.
questions.explain: A chord progression is like a plot: a common skeleton. The worth of a song, like a story, lies in what is built on it.
questions.rule: Common frames; judge what is built on them.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the few-plots point holds for other arts built on shared frames, such as songs on common chord patterns: the frame gives the structure, while the worth lies in what is built on it.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Why do the authors quote an eighteenth-century title by Jeremy Collier?
options: Its long title tells you what the whole book is about
It shows how titles can mislead readers about content
It is an example of a book with no unity at all
Its title reveals that the book is a work of fiction
optionExplain: Right: the elaborate title tells the reader what the whole book is about.
A fair worry about titles in general, but the authors use Collier's as a helpful one.
The authors use it to show a unity the title makes plain, not one that is missing.
Collier's book was an attack on the stage, not fiction; the title says so.
questions.explain: Collier's long title is an example of an author telling you the unity up front. The card next shows how to use such help.
questions.rule: Some titles state the unity.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: The authors say eighteenth-century writers had the habit of composing ____ titles that told the reader what the whole book was about.
questions.explain: Elaborate titles like Collier's told the reader what the whole book was about. The authors say the author often helps in this way, sometimes through the title alone.
questions.rule: Elaborate titles can state the unity.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
