questions.q: From the title Why Bridges Fall: Engineering Failures and the Lessons They Taught, which draft unity statement is the best guess?
options: It is a history of the world's most beautiful bridges
It teaches readers how to design and build a bridge
It examines bridge failures to show what engineers learned
It argues bridges are more dangerous than other buildings
optionExplain: Beauty is not mentioned; the title is about failures.
The title promises lessons drawn from failures, not a design manual.
Right: the main title and subtitle together give subject and claim.
The title does not compare bridges with other structures.
questions.explain: The main title names the subject, failure, and the subtitle names what the book draws from it, lessons. Together they give a first unity statement.
questions.rule: Title plus subtitle gives a first draft.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: A short, catchy title usually tells you less about a book's unity than an elaborate title like Collier's.
questions.explain: Collier wrote when elaborate, descriptive titles were the habit. A one-word title may hint at the subject, but it rarely says what the whole book is about.
questions.rule: Catchy titles say less.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Mara reads the title Why Bridges Fall: Engineering Failures and the Lessons They Taught and submits it, reworded, as her unity statement without reading the book. What is the flaw?
options: Titles are chosen by publishers, so they cannot be used
She should have read the index instead of the title
A unity statement may not use any of the author's words
The title gives a first guess that the whole book must test
optionExplain: Publishers may shape titles, but the authors still treat a title as real help from the author.
The index shows topics, not the whole; it would not replace reading the book.
Borrowing apt words is fine; the problem is that she has not checked them against the book.
Right: the title is a starting hint, and the book may deliver more or less than it promises.
questions.explain: A title is the author's help, but finding the unity is the reader's job. A guess from the title needs the book to confirm or correct it.
questions.rule: A title is a hypothesis, not a finding.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: You receive a report titled Q3 Customer Churn: Causes and Three Proposed Fixes. What can you reasonably take from the title before reading?
options: Little, since report titles are written to sound good
Its full structure, section by section
A draft of its unity: why customers left and what to do
That it is a theoretical study of customer psychology
optionExplain: Some titles are promotional, but this one is descriptive and states subject and aim.
The title hints at two parts, but not the full structure; that needs the report itself.
Right: the title states the report's main point, a draft to test as you read.
Proposed fixes signal a practical report, not a theoretical study.
questions.explain: A descriptive title works like Collier's: it states what the whole is about. That gives a draft summary to check against the report.
questions.rule: Read a descriptive title as a claim.
questions.teaches: By analogy, descriptive titles of work documents, such as reports and memos, often state their unity outright, so reading the title as a claim gives you a draft summary to test.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a scientific or philosophical writer has good reason to keep the reader in suspense about the book's plan.
questions.explain: The authors say such a writer has no reason for suspense; the less suspense, the more likely the reader is to finish. The card next contrasts this with fiction.
questions.rule: Exposition has no need for suspense.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: The authors say that, like a ____ article, an expository book may summarise itself in its first paragraph.
questions.explain: A newspaper article puts its main point first. An expository book has no reason for suspense, so it may do the same.
questions.rule: Exposition can lead with its point, like news.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Sort each work: should you expect the plan stated early, or the unity to come clear only from the whole?
groups: Expect the unity to emerge from the whole

items.t: A philosophy book on free will
A mystery novel
A scientific report on bee decline
A historical novel about a shipwreck
A textbook on accounting
A play about a family feud

questions.explain: Expository works have no reason for suspense, so they often state their plan early. Stories build suspense, so their unity usually emerges from the whole.
questions.rule: Exposition early, fiction late.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: You have one evening to prepare a summary of a 400-page economics book. Where should you look first for the author's own statement of the plan?
options: The preface and the opening paragraphs
The last chapter, where the suspense resolves
The middle chapters, where the core argument sits
The reviews quoted on the back cover
optionExplain: Right: expository authors often state their plan in the preface or first paragraph.
This treats the book like a novel; exposition has no suspense to resolve.
The core argument may be there, but the author's statement of the plan is usually at the start.
Reviews are other readers' views, not the author's statement of the plan.
questions.explain: An expository author has every reason to state the plan early. The preface and opening are where to look first.
questions.rule: Look first where the author states the plan.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: An economist decides to hide her main conclusion until the last page, to build suspense. On the authors' account, what would you expect?
options: Readers would read every page more closely
Fewer readers would keep going to the end
The book would become a work of fiction
Readers would find the unity more quickly
optionExplain: Suspense works in stories; in exposition, not knowing the point makes the effort harder to sustain.
Right: the authors say the less suspense such a writer keeps you in, the likelier you are to finish.
Kind depends on subject and treatment, not on where the conclusion is placed.
Hiding the conclusion makes the unity harder to find, not easier.
questions.explain: The authors tie early statement of the plan to the reader's ability to sustain the effort. Hiding the point works against that.
questions.rule: In exposition, suspense costs readers.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A student reading a journal article skips the abstract so as not to spoil the findings. Carrying over the authors' point, what is she giving up?
options: An unbiased first reading of the paper's method
Suspense, which helps her remember the results
The method details, which only the abstract gives
The author's own early statement of the whole
optionExplain: Worrying about bias is reasonable, but the abstract is help, and she can still test it as she reads.
Suspense is a device for stories; the authors say it hinders reading exposition.
Abstracts summarise; the method details are in the body of the paper.
Right: the abstract is the author's summary of the whole, offered first, like a preface.
questions.explain: Expository writing has no spoilers to avoid. An abstract is the author's statement of the plan, there to help the reader.
questions.rule: In exposition, read the summary first.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the abstract of a research article does the job of an expository preface: a compact statement of the whole, placed first so the reader knows what the rest is for.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: According to the authors, who carries the final obligation to find a book's unity?
options: The reader
The author
The editor
The reviewer
optionExplain: Right: the obligation of finding the unity belongs finally to the reader.
The author's obligation is to have a unity; finding it is the reader's.
Editors shape books, but the authors do not give them this duty.
Reviewers may help, but the duty belongs to each reader.
questions.explain: The authors divide the work: the writer must have a unity, the reader must find it. The card next explains how far to trust the author's help.
questions.rule: Writers must have unity; readers must find it.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: The authors say you can honestly meet the duty of finding the unity only by reading the whole book.
questions.explain: The authors say the reader can discharge that obligation honestly only by reading the whole book, however helpful the preface is.
questions.rule: The whole book, not the preface, settles it.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A preface promises a fair comparison of three diets. In fact chapters 5 to 10 promote one of them. What should the reader's unity statement follow?
options: The preface, since the author knows his plan best
What the book does, which is promote one diet
A blend that splits the difference between the two
Neither, since such a book has no unity to state
optionExplain: The author knows what he intended, but the authors warn that plans go awry; the book shows what he did.
Right: the statement must fit the whole book as written, not the promise.
Averaging promise and performance describes neither; the reader states what is there.
The book still hangs together, as an argument for one diet; a broken promise is not a lack of unity.
questions.explain: The preface is a guide, but the unity belongs to the book as written. Where they part, follow the book.
questions.rule: Where preface and book differ, follow the book.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Which reading habits fit the authors' advice about prefaces? Select all that apply.
options: Reading the preface for the author's plan
Checking that plan against the whole book
Skipping the preface so as to avoid bias
Copying the preface's plan as the final statement
Revising the plan where the book went its own way
optionExplain: Right: the authors say not to be too proud to accept the author's help.
Right: the plan is a guide to be tested against the book.
This is the pride the authors warn against; the preface is help freely given.
This relies on the preface completely, which the authors also warn against.
Right: where the plan went awry, the reader's statement follows what the book did.
questions.explain: The authors steer between two errors: refusing the author's help and relying on it completely. Use the plan, then test it.
questions.rule: Accept the help; keep the duty.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: If an author's statement of plan turns out to fit the whole book well, the reader may adopt it, perhaps with small additions.
questions.explain: Testing the plan does not mean rejecting it. When it survives the test, using it is sound; the duty was to check, not to be different.
questions.rule: A plan that passes the test can be kept.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A software vendor's release notes say an update makes the app faster and simpler. Applying the authors' advice on prefaces, what should a team do?
options: Trust the notes, as the vendor knows the product best
Ignore the notes, since vendors tend to exaggerate
Use the notes as a guide, then test the update
Wait for user reviews and skip the notes entirely
optionExplain: Like trusting a preface completely: the maker's intentions may not match the result.
Like refusing the author's help out of pride: the notes still point to what to check.
Right: the maker's statement guides the check, and the product itself settles it.
Reviews are other people's findings; the notes are still useful help to start from.
questions.explain: Release notes are a maker's prospectus, like a preface. Use them to guide your own check of what the thing does.
questions.rule: Guide from the maker; verdict from the thing.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any maker's description of its own work, such as release notes or a product brief, is a prospectus: useful as a guide, but what the thing actually does is settled by checking the thing itself.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a historian's good opening summary is a starting point that the reader should enlarge after reading the whole book.
questions.explain: The authors call Herodotus' opening a good beginning but say not to stop there: after reading all nine parts, you will probably want to elaborate it. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Build on the author's summary.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: After reading Herodotus' history through, what do the authors suggest adding to his opening summary?
options: Every battle and every named person, in order
The main kings, heroes and decisive events
A verdict on whether Herodotus is reliable
The author's life and his reasons for writing
optionExplain: That would turn the statement into a multiplicity; the authors leave the rest of the detail out.
Right: Cyrus, Darius, Xerxes, Themistocles, the Hellespont, Thermopylae and Salamis.
Judging reliability is a later task; stating the unity comes first.
Herodotus' own reasons are already in his opening; the additions concern the history itself.
questions.explain: The authors elaborate Herodotus' summary with the chief figures and events, and leave out the rest.
questions.rule: Add the main actors and turning points.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A history of the Moon landing programme opens with a one-line summary. Sort each item: should it go into an elaborated unity statement, or stay out?

items.t: The decision to aim for the Moon within a decade
The 1969 landing of Apollo 11
The test fire that killed three astronauts
The menu at a launch-day breakfast
A contractor's office move in 1964
A technician's hobby of building model trains

questions.explain: The goal, the deadly setback and the landing are turning points in the thread of plot. Breakfasts, office moves and hobbies are detail the summary can leave out.
questions.rule: Turning points in, colour out.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: On the authors' account, the unity of a history is stated in the same way as the unity of which other kind of book?
options: A science treatise, as a set of laws
A practical book, as a list of steps
A philosophy book, as a set of definitions
A novel, as a single thread of plot
optionExplain: The authors do not liken history to a treatise of laws; history tells what happened.
Practical books aim at action; a history's unity is a story of events.
Definitions are not how the authors describe a history's unity.
Right: they say the rule elicits the same kind of answer in history and in fiction.
questions.explain: History and fiction are both narratives. The authors say their unity is stated the same way: as a thread of plot.
questions.rule: History and fiction share the plot form.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: If a reader keeps adding detail until every named person in Herodotus appears, the statement of the unity becomes more accurate.
questions.explain: Adding every name turns the unity into a multiplicity. The authors keep the main figures and events and leave the rest of the fascinating detail out.
questions.rule: More detail can mean less unity.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A fan is asked to sum up her club's long, dramatic season for a newcomer. Applying the authors' method for histories, which summary is best?
options: Every match result in order, with the scorers
Only the final score of the season's last match
Her own feelings at each match, in order
Its aim, key players and turning-point games
optionExplain: A full record is a multiplicity; the newcomer cannot see the thread.
One result is a part; it does not show how the season unfolded.
Her feelings may be vivid, but they describe her, not the season's thread of events.
Right: like Herodotus elaborated, it gives the thread with its main actors and turning points.
questions.explain: A season is a history in small. Its unity is a thread of plot, stated through the main actors and turning points.
questions.rule: Tell the thread, not the record.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any account of events over time, such as a season or a project's history, is unified by a thread of plot: state it through the main actors and turning points, not the full record.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Adam Smith states the plan of The Wealth of Nations at the start of the book. What do the authors note about that statement?
options: It is mistaken, so readers should ignore it
It is missing, so readers must find the plan alone
It runs several pages and can be put briefly
It is a single sentence, the ideal length
optionExplain: The authors call it an aid to the reader, not a mistake.
Smith does give the plan; the issue is its length.
Right: the plan of the work runs several pages, and the authors restate the unity in a paragraph.
It is far longer than a sentence; that is why the authors restate it.
questions.explain: Smith helps the reader with a statement of plan, but it is long. The card next shows the shorter version.
questions.rule: A long plan can be compressed.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: The authors' short statement of the unity of Aristotle's Ethics mentions goods besides virtue, such as health, wealth and friends.
questions.explain: Their statement stresses the virtues but adds that other goods, such as wealth, health, friends and a just society, are also needed for happiness.
questions.rule: A compressed unity keeps every major element.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A six-page project charter plans to move insurance claims from paper forms to a phone app, retrain the claims staff to support it, and cut handling time from ten days to two. Which compression states its unity best?
options: This project is about improving how the firm handles claims
Claims move to an app so customers can file them faster
The charter is detailed, clear and well argued throughout
Claims go to an app, staff retrain, handling falls to two days
optionExplain: Short, but vague: it names the subject and drops every element of the plan.
This keeps one element and drops the retraining and the two-day target, so it is not comprehensive.
This judges the document; it does not state its unity.
Right: one sentence keeps all three major elements of the plan.
questions.explain: A good compression is brief but keeps every major element. Only the last option keeps the app, the retraining and the two-day target.
questions.rule: Compress, but keep every major element.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Suppose a reader keeps shortening Smith's plan to save words. Which of these shorter versions drop a major part? Select all that apply.
options: An inquiry into how the division of labour creates wealth
An argument for free trade between nations
An inquiry into national wealth, price, capital, money and trade policy, arguing for free trade
An account of wages, profits and rent as the parts of price
Wealth from divided labour; price, capital, money; systems compared; free trade
optionExplain: Right: it keeps the starting point but drops price, capital, money and the case for free trade.
Right: it keeps the conclusion but drops everything the argument rests on.
This keeps every major element in one sentence, so it is a fair compression.
Right: it keeps one strand, price, and drops the rest of the plan.
Terse, but it keeps every major element, so nothing major is dropped.
questions.explain: Compressing must keep every major element. Each faulty version keeps one strand of Smith's plan and loses the others.
questions.rule: Shorter must not mean incomplete.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: The authors suggest that stating the unity of The Wealth of Nations, and doing the same for Marx's Das Kapital, would help a reader see how the two books relate.
questions.explain: The authors say a reader who did both would be well on the way to seeing the relation between two of the most influential books of the past two centuries.
questions.rule: Two unity statements let you compare two books.
questions.teaches: According to the authors, stating the unity of two books on one subject, such as Smith's and Marx's, puts a reader well on the way to seeing how the two relate.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Before an election debate, you have two party manifestos of about 60 pages each. Building on the authors' point about Smith and Marx, what prepares you best to compare them?
options: Count the pledges in each and compare the totals
Read the first page of each and stop there
Pick out the one policy you care most about
Compress each to a paragraph, side by side
optionExplain: Counting pledges compares quantity, not what each party is trying to do.
First pages may help, but stopping there skips checking the plan against the whole.
One policy is a part; it does not show how the two programmes differ as wholes.
Right: compressed unity statements set the two wholes next to each other.
questions.explain: Compressing each long plan into a paragraph makes the two comparable. Their main differences then show at a glance.
questions.rule: Compress both, then compare.
questions.teaches: By analogy, compressed unity statements make any two long documents comparable, such as rival manifestos or bids: side by side, their main differences show at once.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: What did the authors do with Locke's own summary of his Essay Concerning Human Understanding?
options: Kept it and added two subordinate qualifications
Rejected it and wrote a wholly new statement
Quoted it unchanged as the final word on the book
Shortened it to one brief phrase of a few words
optionExplain: Right: they called it excellent and added two qualifications for the first and third parts.
They did not quarrel with it; rejecting a sound statement wastes the author's help.
They did more than quote it; it did not cover every part.
Locke's statement was already brief; shortening was not the issue.
questions.explain: The authors kept Locke's excellent statement and added what it left out. The card next shows what they added.
questions.rule: Keep a sound statement; add what it misses.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Which two qualifications did the authors add to Locke's statement? Select all that apply.
options: No innate ideas: all knowledge comes from experience
Knowledge is impossible, so belief is all we have
Language as a medium of thought, its use and abuse
The mind is a machine run by physical laws
Ideas are inborn and only recalled by experience
optionExplain: Right: this covers the first part of the essay.
Locke's statement concerns the certainty and extent of knowledge; it does not deny knowledge.
Right: this covers the third part, on language.
Nothing in the authors' statement concerns the mind as a machine.
This reverses the first qualification: Locke denies innate ideas.
questions.explain: The two qualifications cover the parts Locke's own summary did not mention: the denial of innate ideas and the discussion of language.
questions.rule: Qualifications cover the parts left out.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: An author's summary of a gardening book covers soil and planting, but the last third of the book is about controlling pests. What should the reader's statement be?
options: The author's summary alone, since he knows best
The author's summary plus a clause on pests
A new statement about pests, dropping his
A list of every chapter, so nothing is missed
optionExplain: The author's summary misses a major part, so on its own it is incomplete.
Right: keep the sound statement and qualify it to cover the missing part.
Throwing out a sound statement loses the soil and planting parts instead.
A chapter list is a multiplicity, not a statement of unity.
questions.explain: This is Locke's case again: a good statement that misses a major part. The fix is a subordinate qualification, not a rewrite.
questions.rule: Qualify, do not replace.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: A good qualification adds a major part the author's statement missed, not a minor topic the reader happened to enjoy.
questions.explain: The authors added qualifications to do justice to whole parts of Locke's essay. Adding minor topics would turn the statement into a list.
questions.rule: Qualify for major parts only.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Suppose the author's statement of the unity already covers every major part of the book. What does this approach then call for?
options: Adding qualifications anyway, to show independence
Rewriting it in your own words regardless
Keeping it as it stands, with nothing added
Replacing it with a list of the major parts
optionExplain: Qualifications exist to cover gaps; with no gap, adding them only lengthens the statement.
Rewording a sound statement for its own sake adds nothing.
Right: qualifications answer omissions, so a complete statement needs none.
A list of parts is the work of outlining, not a better statement of unity.
questions.explain: The authors qualified Locke only where his statement fell short. Where nothing falls short, there is nothing to add.
questions.rule: No gap, no qualification.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A colleague's one-line meeting summary reads: agreed the Q4 budget. In fact the meeting also replaced the project lead. What should the minutes say?
options: Keep the budget line and add the change of lead
Leave it, since the chair wrote it after the meeting
Replace it with a full transcript of the meeting
Write only about the change of lead
optionExplain: Right: the summary is sound but misses a major item, so it is qualified.
Who wrote it does not change the fact that it leaves out a major decision.
A transcript is the whole multiplicity, not a summary.
Dropping the budget loses the part the summary had right.
questions.explain: A sound but incomplete summary is kept and qualified, just as the authors did with Locke.
questions.rule: Keep what is right; add what is missing.
questions.teaches: By analogy, qualifying a sound summary works for meeting notes and briefs: keep what is right and add any major item it omits, rather than discarding it or settling for it.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: The authors' statement of the unity of Darwin's Origin of Species is long. How do they defend it?
options: Darwin's own summary was even longer than theirs
Science books need one clause for each chapter
The book was an even bigger mouthful for readers
Long statements are more accurate than short ones
optionExplain: The authors do not compare their statement with one by Darwin.
The authors give no such formula; the clauses follow the main lines of the argument.
Right: they admit it is a big mouthful, but say the book was an even bigger one.
The authors prize brevity; length is allowed, not preferred.
questions.explain: The authors concede the length and point to the book's own size and difficulty. The card next says what keeps a long statement a unity.
questions.rule: A rich book may need more words.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: According to the authors, why did many nineteenth-century readers find the Origin hard going?
options: They did not trouble to find out what it was about
Its technical terms were unknown outside universities
Darwin held back his main claim until the last chapter
The book was too short to state its case in full
optionExplain: Right: the authors say readers did not go to the trouble of finding out what it was really about.
Vocabulary may have been a hurdle, but the authors name a different cause.
The authors make no such claim about Darwin's order of presentation.
The authors call the book a big mouthful, not too short.
questions.explain: The authors partly blame the readers: they never found out what the book was really about, which is what Rule 2 demands.
questions.rule: Not stating the unity makes a book harder.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A reader drafts a long unity statement for a book arguing that cities must redesign to cope with rising heat. Sort each clause.

items.t: showing how heat builds up on paved streets
comparing cooling schemes in three cities
proposing a building code that requires shade
with notes on the author's favourite parks
including a history of air-conditioning patents
and a list of the best summer festivals

questions.explain: Clauses about how heat builds, what has worked and what to require all serve the main claim. The others add topics, which pushes the statement toward a multiplicity.
questions.rule: Every clause must hang on the main claim.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: If you keep adding clauses until the statement fills a page, it still states the unity, provided each clause is true of the book.
questions.explain: Truth is not the only test. Rule 2 allows at most a short paragraph; past that, the statement has become a multiplicity, however accurate its parts.
questions.rule: True clauses can still add up to a list.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Reader A writes one long sentence whose clauses all hang on one claim. Reader B writes three short sentences on three unrelated topics. By the authors' standards, which is closer to a unity?
options: A, since its clauses serve one point
B, since short sentences are clearer
Both equally, since both are brief
Neither, since a unity must be one short sentence
optionExplain: Right: the authors' Darwin statement is long but unified, as A's is.
Short sentences on unrelated topics are a multiplicity, however clear each one is.
Brevity is shared, but only A ties its parts to one point.
The rule allows a few sentences or a short paragraph, not only one short sentence.
questions.explain: What makes a statement a unity is that its parts serve one point, not its sentence count.
questions.rule: Unity is in the tie, not the length.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A grant form asks for a project summary of up to 100 words. Carrying this idea over, what makes a summary near the limit still read as one piece?
options: It mentions as many activities as will fit
It repeats the key words for emphasis
Every clause supports one stated aim
It is cut to the fewest words the form allows
optionExplain: Filling space with activities makes a list, the multiplicity the authors warn about.
Repetition adds words, not unity.
Right: like the Darwin statement, length is fine when every clause serves the main point.
Brevity helps, but cutting to the bone can drop major elements; a short paragraph is allowed when every clause serves the aim.
questions.explain: A word limit allows a short paragraph, as Rule 2 does. What keeps it one piece is that every clause serves the aim, which you can test clause by clause.
questions.rule: Use the words, but tie them to one aim.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a near-limit summary can be tested clause by clause: write the main aim as one sentence first, then ask of each remaining clause whether it serves that sentence; the clauses that do not are where to cut.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Which reasons do the authors give for readers' failure to say briefly what a book is about? Select all that apply.
options: An inability to speak concise sentences
Neglect of the rule while reading
Ignoring the author's introductory words
Books being too long to sum up in a few words
A lack of formal schooling beyond the basics
optionExplain: Right: the authors blame a widespread inability to speak concise sentences.
Right: they also blame neglect of the rule in reading.
Right: many readers pay as little attention to introductory words as to titles.
Length is a real obstacle, but the authors show long books can be stated briefly.
The authors do not name formal education; the causes they give are habits anyone can change.
questions.explain: The authors name three causes: no practice at concise speech, neglect of the rule, and inattention to introductions. The card next turns each into a remedy.
questions.rule: Three causes, three habits to fix.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, many readers pay as little attention to an author's introductory words as they do to the title.
questions.explain: This is the third reason the authors give for readers' failure to state a book's unity, even when the author has helped.
questions.rule: Read the introduction; it is often the plan.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Jo starts every book at chapter 1, skipping the introduction, and later cannot say what the books argued. Which change addresses the cause the authors name?
options: Reading the introduction and title with care
Reading faster so as to finish more books
Underlining more passages in each chapter
Reading reviews after finishing each book
optionExplain: Right: the introduction is where authors often state the unity.
Speed does not touch the problem; she would miss the introduction faster.
Marking passages helps reading, but it does not recover the plan she skipped.
Reviews give other readers' views, not the author's own statement of the plan.
questions.explain: Jo's habit is the third cause the authors name. Reading the introductory words is the direct fix.
questions.rule: Do not skip the author's opening help.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Match each cause the authors give to the remedy that answers it.
pairs: Keep the unity question in mind
Read the opening pages with care
questions.explain: Each cause is a habit, so each has a matching habit to build: brief statement, steady attention to the unity, and careful reading of introductions.
questions.rule: Match the remedy to the cause.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: If a book has no introduction or preface at all, the reader is excused from stating its unity.
questions.explain: The author's help is welcome but not required. The obligation of finding the unity belongs finally to the reader, with or without an introduction.
questions.rule: No introduction, same duty.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A manager finds her team cannot sum up long customer emails in one line. Which of the authors' causes suggests a training drill, and what is it?
options: Lack of interest, fixed by bonuses for good summaries
Not putting things briefly, fixed by one-line drills
Too many emails, fixed by hiring more support staff
Poor typing speed, fixed by a keyboard course
optionExplain: Motivation may matter, but the authors' causes are about skill and habit, not interest.
Right: the first cause is a missing skill, and short regular practice builds it.
Volume affects time, not the ability to state a message's point.
Typing affects speed of writing, not the ability to find and state the point.
questions.explain: The authors' first cause is an inability to speak concisely. That is a skill, and skills improve with practice.
questions.rule: Brevity is a skill; drill it.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the authors' diagnosis implies that stating unity can be trained: brief, regular practice at one-line summaries attacks the first cause, an inability to put things concisely.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, there is one right way to state the unity of a book.
questions.explain: The authors say a unity can be stated in various ways and there is no one right way. The card next gives the marks of a better statement.
questions.rule: Many good statements are possible.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: By which marks do the authors say one statement of unity is better than another? Select all that apply.
options: Brief
Accurate
Imaginative
Comprehensive
Entertaining
optionExplain: Right: a better statement is briefer.
Right: it must be faithful to the book.
Imagination is not one of the marks; the authors sometimes accept the author's own words.
Right: it must cover the whole book.
Being entertaining is not one of the marks; plain statements can be excellent.
questions.explain: The authors name three marks: brief, accurate and comprehensive.
questions.rule: Brief, accurate, comprehensive.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A statement of a book on sleep says: It argues that coffee causes insomnia. The book covers why we sleep, what threatens sleep and how to protect it, with caffeine as one chapter. Which mark does the statement fail most?
options: Brief: it runs on for far too many words
Comprehensive: it covers one part only
Accurate: it misstates what that chapter says
Personal: it is worded in the author's style
optionExplain: It is very short; brevity is its one strength.
Right: it takes one part for the whole, so it is not comprehensive.
Nothing suggests the chapter is misstated; the trouble is what is left out.
Wording style is not one of the marks.
questions.explain: The statement is brief and may be accurate about caffeine, but it leaves out most of the book. Comprehensiveness is what it lacks.
questions.rule: A part stated well is still only a part.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: Two readers whose statements of the same book's unity use quite different words may both have done the job equally well.
questions.explain: The authors say quite different statements may be equally good. What counts is brevity, accuracy and comprehensiveness, not shared wording.
questions.rule: Different words can be equally good.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A reader cuts her statement from a paragraph to six words, and in doing so drops two major parts of the book. By the authors' marks, what has happened?
options: It has improved on every mark at once
It has gained accuracy by cutting words
It is unchanged, since its core idea remains
It gained brevity, lost comprehensiveness
optionExplain: Brevity improved, but losing major parts is a loss on another mark.
Cutting words does not make the statement more faithful; it makes it less complete.
Dropping two major parts changes how well it covers the book.
Right: the marks can pull against each other, and this cut traded one for another.
questions.explain: Brevity, accuracy and comprehensiveness have to be balanced. A cut that drops major parts buys brevity at the price of coverage.
questions.rule: Balance the three marks.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A teacher is marking students' one-paragraph summaries of the same article. Following the authors, how should she mark them?
options: Against brevity, accuracy and coverage
By how close each is to her own model summary
By length, giving more credit to longer ones
By how original each student's wording is
optionExplain: Right: the authors' three marks let her credit different but good summaries.
A model answer would penalise good summaries that are worded differently.
Longer is not better; brevity is one of the marks.
Originality is not a mark; a faithful plain summary can be excellent.
questions.explain: With no single right statement, the fair standard is the three marks, applied to each summary on its own terms.
questions.rule: Mark the qualities, not the match.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a marking scheme built on brevity, accuracy and coverage lets a marker credit very different summaries fairly, where a single model answer would penalise good ones worded differently.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Readers often state the same book's unity differently. What do the authors conclude from this?
options: Every reader's statement is equally valid
Wordings differ, but the book can check them
Only the author's own statement counts as correct
Statements of unity are matters of personal taste
optionExplain: A tempting conclusion from variety, but the authors deny that anything goes.
Right: readers differ, but the book is the same, so statements can be checked.
The authors themselves restate authors' plans differently, so this is not their view.
Taste would make checking impossible; the authors say there can be an objective check.
questions.explain: The authors accept different statements but insist on a check against the book. The card next explains what that check tests.
questions.rule: Different readers, same book.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, because a book is something different to each reader, anything goes when stating its unity.
questions.explain: The authors grant that readers differ but say this does not mean anything goes: the book is the same, and statements about it can be checked.
questions.rule: Variety is allowed; anything is not.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A book on remote work recommends hybrid schedules with set office days. Which readers' statements of its unity pass the check against the text? Select all that apply.
options: It argues hybrid work suits most teams, given set office days
It shows teams do well with a mix of home and office days
It argues offices should close and all work be done at home
It recommends fixed office days so hybrid teams stay close
optionExplain: Right: different wording, but faithful to the book's recommendation.
Right: faithful too; it stresses the mix rather than the set days.
The text recommends hybrid work, so a call to close offices contradicts it and fails.
Right: faithful; it puts the set days first, a difference of emphasis.
questions.explain: Three statements differ in wording and emphasis but agree with the text, so they pass. The one the text contradicts fails.
questions.rule: Emphasis may vary; fidelity may not.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: A student says: My statement is my own reading of the book, so no one can say it is wrong. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
options: Only teachers are allowed to judge a statement
Statements are judged by length, not fidelity
Personal readings are not allowed at all
The book is shared, so a reading can be checked
optionExplain: Anyone can check a statement against the text; it is not a matter of authority.
Length matters, but fidelity to the book is the check at issue here.
The authors allow personal wording; they deny that it is beyond checking.
Right: since the book is the same for every reader, any statement can be tested against it.
questions.explain: Owning a reading does not put it beyond correction. The shared text is the standard against which it is checked.
questions.rule: Your words, the book's standard.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Two careful readers disagree about a book's unity, and in places the text supports both readings. What can the check against the text still do?
options: Show which readings the text rules out
Prove that one of the two readers was careless
Leave it to the author's private intention
Show that both readings are worthless
optionExplain: Right: the check narrows the field even when it cannot pick a single winner.
Careful readers can differ when a text is unclear; disagreement is not proof of carelessness.
The check is against the book, not against guesses about the author's mind.
Two readings the text supports are not worthless; they may both be faithful.
questions.explain: The objective check tests fidelity. Where the text itself is unclear, it can rule readings out without forcing a single one in.
questions.rule: The text can rule out, even when it cannot pick.

questions.section: Of Plots and Plans: Stating the Unity of a Book
questions.q: Two journalists summarise the same court ruling in quite different words. How should an editor decide whether both are acceptable?
options: Check each against the ruling's text
Pick the one written by the senior journalist
Accept both, since summaries are opinions
Choose the one readers find more engaging
optionExplain: Right: the ruling is the same for both, so each summary can be tested against it.
Seniority is not a test of fidelity to the ruling.
A summary of a fixed text can be wrong; calling it opinion skips the check.
Engaging is good, but it does not show the summary is faithful.
questions.explain: A ruling, like a book, is a fixed text. Different summaries are fine if the text bears them out.
questions.rule: Check the summary against the source.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any summary of a fixed text, such as a court ruling or a contract, can be checked against that text: wording may vary, but fidelity to what it says is testable.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: Knowing how a book is one, its unity, is enough to have grasped it as a whole.
questions.explain: The authors say a book is a complex unity: you must know how it is many as well as how it is one. The card next gives the rule for the many.
questions.rule: One is not enough; see the many.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Rule 3 asks you to show how the major parts are ordered to one another and to the ____ of the whole.
questions.explain: Rule 3 asks for the parts and their relations: how they are ordered to each other and to the unity of the whole that Rule 2 stated.
questions.rule: Parts ordered to each other and to the unity.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: On the authors' account, what separates an organized many from a mere collection?
options: A collection has a larger number of parts
An organized many has fewer, longer parts
A collection is printed in one volume
Its parts are related and make up a whole
optionExplain: Number of parts is not the difference; a short collection is still a collection.
Size of parts is not the difference either.
Binding is not the issue; a collection can share a cover and still lack unity.
Right: if the parts were not related, there would be no whole, only a collection.
questions.explain: What makes a many organized is the relation among its parts. Without it, the parts form a collection, not a whole.
questions.rule: Related parts make a whole.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Which outline of a book on learning a new language does what Rule 3 asks?
options: Sounds, then words, then grammar that joins them
Vocabulary, grammar, listening, speaking and culture
Five chapters of roughly equal length, each with drills
The best part is the chapter on slang and idiom
optionExplain: Right: it gives the parts and shows how each prepares for the next.
A list of topics names parts but not how they relate.
This describes layout, not the order of the parts to one another.
A preference is a reaction, not an outline.
questions.explain: Rule 3 asks for parts in their order and relation. Only the second outline shows why each part comes where it does.
questions.rule: Show why each part comes where it does.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: If a volume is a set of unrelated essays by different writers, Rule 3 may find parts but no single order relating them to a whole.
questions.explain: Rule 3 assumes a complex unity. A true collection has parts that do not belong to one whole, which is where the rule runs out.
questions.rule: No whole, no order of parts to it.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: A recipe lists eight steps. Carrying Rule 3 over, what turns the list into an understood whole?
options: Timing how long each of the steps takes
Knowing which step is the most fun to do
Learning where each of the ingredients comes from
Seeing which steps prepare for which, and why
optionExplain: Timings help planning but do not show how the steps relate.
Enjoyment is a reaction, not structure.
Origins of ingredients are background, not the recipe's order.
Right: seeing what each step prepares for shows the order and the whole.
questions.explain: Like a book's parts, a recipe's steps are ordered to each other and to the dish. Seeing that order makes the list a plan.
questions.rule: See what each step prepares for.
questions.teaches: By analogy, Rule 3 turns a recipe's steps from a list into a plan: once you see which steps prepare for which, you know which can be reordered and which cannot.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: In the authors' analogy, a well-made book is most like which of these?
options: A heap of bricks
A single house of many rooms
A street of separate houses
A blueprint with no building
optionExplain: A heap has material but no order; the authors contrast it with a house.
Right: a book is like a single house, a mansion of connected rooms.
A collection of houses is many wholes, not one; the authors contrast it with a single house.
A blueprint is bare plan; a book, like a house, is the plan built and furnished.
questions.explain: The authors set a book beside a single house, not a heap of bricks or a row of houses. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A book is one house with many rooms.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: The authors say the rooms of a house are connected by doors, corridors and stairways, by what architects call a ____ pattern.
questions.explain: The traffic pattern is the set of connections between rooms. In a book, it is how the major parts relate to one another.
questions.rule: Find the traffic pattern between parts.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Reading a book on running a small shop, which observation finds a corridor between parts, in the authors' sense?
options: Pricing uses the costs worked out in the supplier part
The pricing chapter is set in a different typeface
The supplier chapter is the longest in the book
The staffing chapter reads well as a standalone piece
optionExplain: Right: one part depends on another, which is a functional connection.
Typeface is decoration, which the authors allow to differ between rooms.
Size is a feature of one room, not a link between rooms.
That shows the part's independence, the other half of the analogy, not a connection.
questions.explain: A corridor is a functional link: one part doing its job with something another part provides.
questions.rule: A corridor is a functional link.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Which features of the house analogy apply to a book's major parts? Select all that apply.
options: Each part has some independence
Each part may have its own inner structure
Parts must connect, or they add nothing to the whole
Every part must be about the same size and shape
Parts can be read in any order with the same sense
optionExplain: Right: like rooms, parts are independent in part.
Right: each room has its own structure and decoration.
Right: without functional connection a part would not add to the intelligibility of the whole.
The authors' rooms differ in size, shape and use.
Connections give an order; reading parts in any order can lose how they build on one another.
questions.explain: Parts are partly independent, may have their own structure, and must be connected. Uniform size and free order are not part of the analogy.
questions.rule: Partly independent, fully connected.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: In the house analogy, every major part must be connected to the others if it is to add its share to the whole.
questions.explain: The authors say each part must be related functionally to the others, or it would not contribute its share to the intelligibility of the whole. An unconnected room adds nothing to how the house works.
questions.rule: An unconnected part adds nothing to the whole.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: You have one hour in a large museum whose galleries form a sequence. Carrying over the house analogy, what helps most?
options: Walk into the nearest gallery and stay there
See the most famous object first, then leave
Learn how galleries connect, then pick a route
Try to see every gallery for a minute each
optionExplain: One room seen alone gives its partial function without its place in the whole.
A single highlight is one part, cut off from the rest.
Right: knowing the traffic pattern lets you choose some rooms and still know where they fit.
Rushing everything sees all the rooms but none of the connections.
questions.explain: With limited time, the traffic pattern is what lets you be selective without losing the whole.
questions.rule: Know the connections, then choose.
questions.teaches: By analogy, knowing the traffic pattern lets you use a large structure selectively: once you see how the parts connect, you can visit some of them and still know how they fit the whole.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the best books, though usually more complex, are also the most readable.
questions.explain: The authors say the best books have the most intelligible structure, which makes them the most readable. The card next explains the paradox.
questions.rule: Best built, most readable.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: How do the authors explain that a great book's greater complexity is also a greater simplicity?
options: It uses shorter words and simpler sentences
It leaves out hard material to spare readers
It restates its main point in every chapter
Its parts are better organized and unified
optionExplain: Style is not the point; great books can be hard sentence by sentence.
Great books are usually more complex, not less, so they do not drop hard material.
Repetition is not organization; the simplicity comes from how parts fit.
Right: better organization makes the complexity simpler to grasp.
questions.explain: The simplicity the authors mean lies in structure: the parts fit together better, so the whole is easier to grasp.
questions.rule: Simplicity comes from organization.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Sort each feature: does it make a book readable in the authors' sense, or not by itself?

items.t: Parts that build on each other toward one aim
A clear relation of each chapter to the whole
Well-organized, unified parts
Short sentences and everyday words
A breezy, chatty tone
A small number of pages

questions.explain: The authors tie readability to intelligible structure. Easy style and brevity can be pleasant, but they do not make the structure clear.
questions.rule: Readable means intelligible structure.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Book A on statistics is 600 tightly organized, demanding pages. Book B is 150 lively pages with no clear order. Which do the authors' views predict will be more readable?
options: A, since its parts are better organized
B, since shorter books are easier to read
Neither; both cover the same subject
B, since its stories make structure unneeded
optionExplain: Right: better organized parts make the complexity easier to grasp.
Length is not the authors' measure; structure is.
Same subject, different structure; the authors' measure is the structure.
Stories are flesh; without bones, the book is more bothersome to follow.
questions.explain: Readability, for the authors, follows from intelligible structure. A's organization outweighs B's shortness and charm.
questions.rule: Structure beats shortness.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: If a book is smooth and easy sentence by sentence, that shows it has an intelligible structure.
questions.explain: Easy sentences and clear structure are different things. A book can read smoothly line by line and still have no plan that ties its parts together.
questions.rule: Smooth style is not clear structure.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Two websites hold the same information. One has many pages but a menu showing how sections relate; the other has few pages linked at random. Carrying over the authors' point, which will users find easier?
options: The smaller one, as fewer pages mean less to read
The larger one, as its parts are better organized
Neither, since the information is the same
The smaller one, since random links aid exploring
optionExplain: Fewer pages do not help if users cannot see how they fit.
Right: organization does the work, as with the best books.
Same content, different structure; the authors' point is that structure decides readability.
Random links make the site a collection, which is more bothersome to use.
questions.explain: The authors' link between structure and readability carries over. A larger but well-organized site beats a small, disordered one.
questions.rule: Organization does the work.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the authors' point about readability carries to websites and manuals: a larger, well-organized structure can be easier to use than a small, disordered one, because organization does the work.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: According to the authors, what should a reader do with a lesser book whose plan is unclear?
options: Try to find some plan in it anyway
Give up, since no plan can be found
Impose a plan taken from a better book
Read only its best passages and stop
optionExplain: Right: to read such a book as well as it can be read, you must still look for its plan.
Giving up is tempting, but the authors say a book that hangs together has a plan.
Borrowing another book's plan puts in what this author did not.
Reading only highlights skips the whole that the authors ask you to find.
questions.explain: The authors ask the reader to look for the plan even in lesser books. The card next gives the condition.
questions.rule: Look for the plan anyway.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: The authors say that if a book is a complex unity to any degree, and not a mere ____, there must be a plan in it to find.
questions.explain: The condition is that the book hangs together at all. If it does, the authors say there must be a plan, and the reader must find it.
questions.rule: If it hangs together, it has a plan.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: A self-help book repeats itself and wanders. Which response follows the authors' advice?
options: Stop, since a wandering book can have no plan
List every tip as a separate, unrelated item
Find the main point and order chapters by it
Read only the opening and closing chapters
optionExplain: A wandering book can still hang together; the authors say to look.
A list of tips treats the book as a collection, giving up on its plan.
Right: reconstructing the plan around the main point is the reader's extra work.
Skipping the middle cannot show how the parts fit.
questions.explain: A lesser book puts more of the work on the reader. Finding the point most chapters serve recovers the plan the author half achieved.
questions.rule: Rebuild the half-made plan.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: If the volume is a scrapbook of unrelated newspaper columns, the authors' claim guarantees a single plan in it to find.
questions.explain: The claim is conditional: if a book hangs together, there is a plan. A scrapbook of unrelated pieces may be a mere collection, which fails the condition.
questions.rule: No unity, no plan to find.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Reading a messy book, a reader outlines its chapters around a theme the book does not raise anywhere. What has gone wrong?
options: She should have kept the chapter order exactly
Messy books cannot be outlined in any way
A theme may be taken only from the preface
She has made up an order the book lacks
optionExplain: Chapter order is a guide, but her fault is elsewhere: the theme is not in the book.
The authors say a book that hangs together can be outlined; messiness makes it harder, not impossible.
A theme can be found anywhere in the book; her theme is not in it at all.
Right: finding the plan means finding what is there, not supplying one.
questions.explain: Looking hard for a plan is right; inventing one is not. The order must be one the book itself supports.
questions.rule: Find the plan; do not supply it.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: A colleague gives a rambling 20-minute update with no agenda. Carrying over the authors' advice, what helps you most?
options: Treat each remark as unrelated to the rest
Find the point and rebuild the order
Hold on to only the last thing said
Assume there was no point and move on
optionExplain: This treats the talk as a collection, giving up on its plan.
Right: like a lesser book, the talk has a plan the speaker only half achieved.
The last remark is one part, not the whole.
If the talk hangs together at all, there is a point to find.
questions.explain: A rambling talk puts more work on the listener, as a lesser book does on the reader. Rebuilding its plan recovers the point.
questions.rule: Rebuild the speaker's half-made plan.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a listener can do for a rambling talk what a reader does for a lesser book: reconstruct the plan the speaker only half achieved, which takes more work but recovers the point.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Why do the authors give the unity and the parts as two separate rules?
options: The two rules apply to different kinds of books
Rule 3 is optional, meant for experts only
The structure is easier to grasp in two steps
The unity and the parts are unrelated
optionExplain: Both rules apply to any book; the authors split them for another reason.
Rule 3 is necessary, not optional.
Right: a complex unified structure is easier to grasp in two steps than in one.
The authors stress that the two are closely related.
questions.explain: The split is mainly for convenience. The card next gives a second reason.
questions.rule: Two steps make one structure easier.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Rule 2 directs attention to a book's unity and Rule 3 to its complexity.
questions.explain: The authors say the second rule points to the unity and the third to the complexity of the book.
questions.rule: Rule 2: unity. Rule 3: complexity.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Which reasons do the authors give for having two rules instead of one? Select all that apply.
options: A complex structure is easier to grasp in two steps
Rule 2 is for fiction and Rule 3 for exposition
The unity can be stated with no idea of the parts
Each major part usually has an inner structure
Different readers should do each of the steps
optionExplain: Right: this is the main reason, convenience.
Both rules apply to every kind of book.
The authors say you cannot grasp a whole without somehow seeing its parts.
Right: seeing the parts' own structure takes work beyond grasping the unity.
Both steps belong to the same reader.
questions.explain: Two reasons: convenience, and the fact that the parts have inner structures of their own that need further work.
questions.rule: Convenience, and parts within parts.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Ben states a book's unity and, in the same moment, names its four major parts. Has he done all that Rule 3 asks?
options: Not yet; each part's inner structure needs work
Yes; naming the four parts completes Rule 3
No; Rule 3 has to be done before Rule 2
Yes, as long as the four parts match the chapters
optionExplain: Right: the parts usually have their own structure, which Rule 3 also asks for.
Naming parts is a start; Rule 3 asks for more than an enumeration.
The order of the rules is not the problem; the unfinished parts are.
Matching the chapters does not supply the parts' inner structure.
questions.explain: The major parts may appear with the unity, but their inner structure does not. That is the authors' second reason for a separate Rule 3.
questions.rule: Seeing the parts is not yet outlining them.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: If a book's major parts each had no inner structure at all, the authors' second reason for a separate Rule 3 would lose its force.
questions.explain: The second reason rests on the parts being complex, with structures of their own. Without that, only the first reason, convenience, would remain.
questions.rule: The second reason depends on complex parts.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: A visitor learning a new city first grasps what kind of place it is, then its districts, then the streets within each. Which approach of the authors' does this mirror?
options: Start with details and let the whole emerge
Learn the districts in alphabetical order
Study only the district where you are staying
Unity first, then parts, then parts of parts
optionExplain: This reverses the authors' order; they start from the unity.
Alphabetical order ignores how the districts relate to each other.
One district alone is a part without the whole.
Right: the two-step approach, extended down to parts of parts.
questions.explain: Grasping a complex whole in steps, unity first and then the parts, is easier than trying to take it all in at once.
questions.rule: Whole, then parts, then parts of parts.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the two-step approach fits learning any complex place or system: take in the whole in one view, then the major parts, then each part's inner layout.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Rule 3 is satisfied once you have listed the book's major parts.
questions.explain: The authors say Rule 3 involves more than an enumeration of the parts. The card next explains what outlining adds.
questions.rule: Listing is not outlining.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: What do the authors mean by outlining a book's parts?
options: Listing the parts in the order they appear
Treating each part as a whole with its own parts
Copying the chapter headings into a notebook
Ranking the parts from most to least important
optionExplain: That is enumeration, which the authors say Rule 3 goes beyond.
Right: each part is a subordinate whole with a unity and complexity of its own.
Headings are the author's guide, not the reader's outline.
Ranking is a judgment of weight, not an account of each part's structure.
questions.explain: Outlining treats each part as a subordinate whole: it has a unity to state and parts of its own to find.
questions.rule: Each part is a smaller whole.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: A reader outlining a cookery book reaches its part on baking. Which next step follows the authors' method?
options: Move on, since the baking part is now named
Copy every baking recipe title into the outline
Say what baking covers, then find its sections
Judge whether the baking recipes really work
optionExplain: Naming the part is enumeration; the part still needs its own unity and parts.
A list of titles is a multiplicity, not the part's structure.
Right: treat the part as a whole, stating its unity and then its parts.
Judging comes later; this is about structure.
questions.explain: The same questions asked of the whole are asked of each part: what it is about, and what its own ordered parts are.
questions.rule: Ask the whole-book questions of each part.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Sort each outline line: does it only enumerate parts, or does it outline them?

items.t: Part 2: Vaccines
Part 2 shows vaccines train the body; it covers how, testing and boosters
Chapters 1 to 4, then 5 to 8, then 9 to 12
Part 1 sets the problem; its sections give causes, scale and costs
Five parts: history, theory, cases, policy, future
Part 3 answers part 1, splitting into short-term and long-term fixes

questions.explain: Enumeration names or counts parts. Outlining says what each part does and how it divides, treating it as a smaller whole.
questions.rule: Outlining says what each part does and how it divides.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: The descent into parts of parts should stop at the smallest units worth identifying.
questions.explain: The authors take the outline down to the least structural unit that is comprehensible and worth identifying. Below that, division adds length, not understanding.
questions.rule: Stop at the smallest units worth naming.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: A manager breaks a product launch into workstreams. Carrying over the outlining idea, what should she do with each workstream?
options: Give each its own goal and ordered tasks
List the workstreams by name and stop there
Give each the same number of tasks for fairness
Rank them by budget and drop the smallest
optionExplain: Right: each workstream is a subordinate whole, with its own aim and parts.
Naming them is enumeration; it leaves each workstream's structure unknown.
Equal counts impose a shape; the tasks should follow what each workstream needs.
Ranking and cutting is a decision about priorities, not an outline.
questions.explain: Treating parts as subordinate wholes means each one gets its own aim and its own ordered parts, the same questions at every level.
questions.rule: Same questions at every level.
questions.teaches: By analogy, treating parts as subordinate wholes is how plans of work are broken down: each workstream gets its own aim and ordered tasks, so the same two questions are asked at every level.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: In the authors' formula for outlining, what comes right after naming the book's major parts?
options: Judging whether each part is true
Writing the book's unity statement
Listing the book's key terms
Dividing each part into its sections
optionExplain: Judging truth belongs to a much later stage of reading.
The unity statement comes before the parts, from Rule 2.
Key terms belong to the next stage of reading, not to the outline.
Right: after the major parts come their sections, then the points in each.
questions.explain: The formula descends: whole, major parts, sections, points. The card next lays it out.
questions.rule: Parts, then sections.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Put the levels of the authors' outlining formula in order, from first to last.
items: The whole book is about so-and-so
The plan is carried out in a number of major parts
Each major part is divided into sections
Each section makes a number of points
questions.explain: The formula starts from the unity stated under Rule 2 and descends: major parts, then sections, then points.
questions.rule: Whole, parts, sections, points.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: In an outline of a guide to buying a first home, which line sits at the level of points within a section?
options: The book helps first buyers get a fair deal
Four parts: budget, search, offer and moving
The budget part has sections on saving and loans
Mortgage section's points: rates, fees, term
optionExplain: This is the unity of the whole book, the top level.
This names the major parts, the first step of the formula.
This divides a part into sections, the second step.
Right: within one section, it lists the points the author makes.
questions.explain: The formula has four levels: whole, parts, sections and points. Only the last line goes down to the points made inside a section.
questions.rule: Points sit inside sections.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: A reader's outline reads: Whole: about climate. Parts: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Sections: 1a, 1b, 1c. What is the main thing missing?
options: What each part and section is about
The page numbers of every section
A verdict on each part's argument
More parts, since five is too few
optionExplain: Right: the formula says what each part and section does, not only how many there are.
Page numbers locate parts but say nothing about what they do.
A verdict is criticism, which comes later.
The count comes from the book; nothing says five is wrong.
questions.explain: The formula asks at each level how many there are and what each is about. Counting alone gives a skeleton with no labels.
questions.rule: Count and characterise.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: Because the authors' formula mentions five parts, three sections and four points, a reader should look for those counts in the book.
questions.explain: The numbers in the formula are placeholders. The counts at each level come from the book being outlined.
questions.rule: The book sets the counts.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: A student must master a 40-page contract with numbered clauses. Carrying over the outlining formula, where should she start?
options: Read clause 1, then 2, then 3, to the end
Look up every legal term before starting
Its purpose, then parts, then their clauses
Start with the clauses that look most unusual
optionExplain: Reading in sequence gives the clauses but not how they group into parts.
Terms matter, but looking them up first does not show the structure.
Right: the formula's descent from whole to parts to points fits a contract.
Unusual clauses may matter, but picking them out first gives details without the structure they sit in.
questions.explain: A contract's numbering gives levels but not meanings. The formula asks what the whole is for and what each part and clause does.
questions.rule: Numbering is not yet an outline.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the outlining formula works on documents that are numbered but not explained, such as contracts: the numbering shows the levels, but the reader must still say what each part and clause does.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a good reader normally writes out a full outline of a book's parts, sections and points.
questions.explain: The authors say good readers may not write it all out or even put it into words. The card next explains what the rule asks of them.
questions.rule: Good readers need not write it all out.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: According to the authors, what does a good reader have, even without written notes?
options: A rough account of the book's structure
A memory of every point in every chapter
A full written outline kept for each book
A list of the book's most quotable lines
optionExplain: Right: asked for the structure, the good reader can approximate the formula.
Total recall is not what the authors describe; an approximation is enough.
The authors say good readers may not write it out at all.
Quotations are details, not an account of the structure.
questions.explain: The good reader's skill shows when asked: he can give an account of the structure that approximates the formula.
questions.rule: Be able to give an account on demand.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Which reader meets Rule 3 as the authors interpret it?
options: Kai copied the contents page into a notebook
Sam can sketch the main parts and their roles
Lia recalls vivid scenes but not how they fit
Max has a 20-page outline but cannot explain it
optionExplain: Copying the contents relies on the author's divisions without any account of his own.
Right: a rough account of the parts and how they work together approximates the formula.
Vivid scenes are flesh; without how they fit, there is no account of the structure.
A long outline he cannot explain is paper, not a grasp of the structure.
questions.explain: The rule is met by an approximate account of the structure that the reader can actually give.
questions.rule: An account you can give beats notes you cannot.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Which statements match the authors' view of approximating a rule? Select all that apply.
options: A good rule describes the ideal performance
Skill does not require being the ideal artist
Outlines are useless unless they are complete
A very rough approximation can be enough
Good readers need no sense of structure at all
