optionExplain: Right: the authors say a good rule always describes the ideal.
Right: one can be a good practitioner without being the ideal artist.
The authors say the opposite: a rough approximation should satisfy you.
Right: they say to be satisfied with a very rough approximation.
Good readers still approximate the rule; they do it without writing it out.
questions.explain: The rule states the ideal; skill is approaching it. A rough approximation is acceptable, but some grasp of structure is still required.
questions.rule: Aim at the ideal; accept the approximation.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: If a reader can say nothing about how a book's parts fit together, she can still claim a rough approximation of Rule 3.
questions.explain: An approximation is still an account of the structure. If she cannot say anything about how the parts fit, there is nothing being approximated.
questions.rule: Rough is not none.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: A music student is told her scales need only approximate a concert pianist's. Carrying over the authors' point about rules, what should she do?
options: Ignore the ideal, since she will not reach it
Aim at the ideal while accepting rough results
Stop practising as soon as she is roughly right
Practise only until she matches the pianist
optionExplain: Dropping the ideal removes the direction her practice needs.
Right: the ideal sets the direction; the approximation is what she can reach now.
Roughly right is acceptable now, but the ideal still points further.
Matching the ideal is not required for skill, so it is the wrong stopping rule.
questions.explain: The authors say a rule describes the ideal and skill approximates it. The ideal gives direction even when it is not reached.
questions.rule: The ideal points the way.
questions.teaches: By analogy, in any art the ideal described by a rule serves as a direction to aim at, so a learner measures progress by moving toward it rather than by reaching it.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: According to the authors, what decides how closely you should outline a book?
options: The book's kind and your purpose
The number of pages in the book
How famous the book's author is
How much free time you have that week
optionExplain: Right: the degree of approximation varies with the book and why you read it.
Length affects the work, but the authors name character and purpose.
Fame is not one of the authors' factors.
Time matters in practice, but the authors name the book's character and your purpose.
questions.explain: The authors tie the closeness of the outline to the kind of book and your reason for reading it. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Book and purpose set the closeness.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, even the best readers outline closely only relatively few books.
questions.explain: The authors say the best readers make a fairly close approximation for relatively few books, and are satisfied with a rough notion for most.
questions.rule: Close outlines for a few books.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Sort each reading situation: does it call for a close outline, or will a rough sense of the structure do?

items.t: A statute you must apply at work
A textbook for a final exam
A classic you will teach to a class
A light memoir read on a train
A popular book read for one fact
A thriller read for fun

questions.explain: Demanding books read for demanding purposes repay a close outline. Light books read for pleasure or a single fact need only a rough sense.
questions.rule: Match the closeness to book and purpose.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Two readers outline the same book, one closely and one roughly. On the authors' view, what is the same for both?
options: The time they spend on it
The rule they are following
The detail of their outlines
Their reasons for reading it
optionExplain: A close outline takes longer; time differs.
Right: the authors say the rule remains the same however closely it is followed.
Detail is exactly what differs between them.
Different closeness usually reflects different purposes.
questions.explain: Closeness varies; the rule does not. Both must know how to follow it.
questions.rule: One rule, many degrees.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Pat read a popular book on birds on holiday and kept a rough sketch of it. Now she must give a talk based on it. What follows from the authors' view?
options: Her outline can stay as rough as it was
She should switch to a different rule
She should outline it more closely now
She should outline only the first chapter
optionExplain: Her purpose has changed, and purpose helps decide closeness.
The rule stays the same; only how closely she follows it changes.
Right: a more demanding purpose calls for a closer approximation.
One chapter will not support a talk on the whole book.
questions.explain: Purpose is one of the two factors. A new, more demanding purpose calls for a closer outline of the same book.
questions.rule: New purpose, new closeness.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: You receive a one-page gym leaflet and a 30-page mortgage offer. Carrying over the authors' point, which plan fits?
options: Close outlines for both, to be on the safe side
Rough sketches for both, to save time and effort
Close for the leaflet, rough for the mortgage
Rough for the leaflet, close for the mortgage
optionExplain: Safe, but it spends close effort on a leaflet that does not need it.
This saves time on the leaflet but risks missing the mortgage's structure.
This reverses the stakes.
Right: the mortgage's character and what rides on it call for close reading.
questions.explain: What you will do with a document is part of your purpose. A large decision resting on it calls for a closer outline.
questions.rule: Higher stakes, closer outline.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the stakes of what you will do with a document are part of your purpose: the more a decision rests on it, the closer an outline it deserves.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a good outline of a book may include topics the author left out, if they belong to the subject.
questions.explain: The authors say your outline is of the book itself, not of its subject matter, so it adds nothing the author did not put there. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Outline the book, not the subject.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Why, according to the authors, does no book deserve a perfect outline?
options: Outlines take too long to be worth making
No book is perfect; each goes only so far
Readers are too busy to finish such an outline
A perfect outline would give away the ending
optionExplain: Time is one limit, but the authors say the limits are not only of time and effort.
Right: a book is finite and defective like all human work, so the outline can go only as far as it does.
The reader's limits are real, but the authors' point here is about the book's limits.
Endings are a concern for stories; the point applies to every book.
questions.explain: The limit lies in the book as well as in the reader. A book goes only so far, so its outline can go only so far.
questions.rule: The outline stops where the book does.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: A book on coffee covers growing and roasting in depth but barely mentions brewing. What should the reader's outline do about brewing?
options: Add a full brewing section from other sources
Show it as the slight part it is in the book
Expand brewing, since it matters most to drinkers
Drop brewing and roasting both, for balance
optionExplain: That outlines the subject of coffee, not this book.
Right: the outline follows the book's own treatment, thin parts included.
Importance to the subject does not put it into the book.
Dropping roasting removes a part the book treats fully.
questions.explain: An outline of the book reports what the book does. Where the author's treatment is thin, the outline shows that.
questions.rule: Thin in the book, thin in the outline.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Sort each feature: does it belong to an outline of the book, or to an outline of the subject?

items.t: Follows the author's own treatment
Stops where the book stops
Shows thin parts as thin
Fills gaps from other reading
Could be extended indefinitely
Adds topics the author skipped

questions.explain: The authors distinguish the two: a subject could be outlined without end, but a book's outline is bounded by what the book contains.
questions.rule: The book bounds its outline.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: If you notice a major gap in a book, you may record it as your own observation, provided you keep it apart from the outline of what the book contains.
questions.explain: The rule forbids putting into the book what the author did not put there. Noting the gap as your own remark does not do that, so long as the outline itself stays faithful.
questions.rule: Note gaps; do not fill them.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: A note-taker knows that an important topic was skipped at a meeting. Carrying over the authors' rule, what should the minutes do?
options: Write up the skipped topic as if discussed
Leave out everything that was not decided
Add her own view of the topic to the record
Record what was said; flag the gap apart
optionExplain: That puts into the record what the meeting did not contain.
Discussion without decisions still happened and belongs in the record.
Her view is not part of what was said.
Right: the record matches what was there, and the gap is noted separately.
questions.explain: Minutes, like an outline of a book, describe what was there. A sense of what was missing goes in a separate note.
questions.rule: Record what is there; note the rest apart.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any record of a discussion or document, such as minutes, should describe what was there; the recorder's sense of what was missing belongs in a separate note, not in the record.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, an outline of a book could in theory be longer than the book itself.
questions.explain: The authors say a full outline down to the smallest worthwhile units could be longer than the original. The card next gives examples.
questions.rule: A full outline can outgrow the book.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: What do the authors praise in Aquinas's commentary on Aristotle?
options: He corrects Aristotle wherever Aristotle erred
He sums up each of the books in a single sentence
He outlines each part and how it fits the whole
He rewrites Aristotle in plainer, simpler words
optionExplain: Correction is criticism; the authors praise his outlining.
A one-sentence summary is a unity statement, not the detailed outline they admire.
Right: he outlines each part and says how it fits, especially with the parts before and after.
Simplifying the language is not what the authors point to.
questions.explain: Aquinas opens each section with an outline and places the part within the whole. That is Rule 3 followed nearly to perfection.
questions.rule: Outline the part and place it in the whole.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Which works do the authors name as longer than the texts they deal with? Select all that apply.
options: Medieval commentaries on Aristotle
Modern commentaries on Kant's Critique
A variorum edition of a Shakespeare play
Abridged editions of Darwin's Origin
Study guides to Herodotus' history
optionExplain: Right: some great medieval commentaries on Aristotle are longer than his works.
Right: the authors cite the great commentaries on the Critique of Pure Reason.
Right: a variorum Shakespeare may be ten times as long as the play.
An abridgement is shorter than the original by design, and the authors do not mention one.
The authors mention no study guides to Herodotus.
questions.explain: These works include more than an outline: they interpret the author sentence by sentence, which is why they can outgrow the original.
questions.rule: Commentary is outline plus interpretation.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Reading chapter 6 of a textbook, which note best follows Aquinas's habit?
options: Ch. 6 is long and full of helpful diagrams
Ch. 6 is the most interesting in the book
Ch. 6 has three sections and a summary
Ch. 6 tests ch. 5's model; ch. 7 builds on it
optionExplain: Length and diagrams describe the surface, not the chapter's place in the whole.
Interest is a reaction, not structure.
This divides the chapter but does not place it among the others.
Right: it says how the part fits with the parts before and after.
questions.explain: Aquinas always says how a part fits the whole, especially its neighbours. Only the last note does that.
questions.rule: Place each part between its neighbours.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: The great commentaries show how far the outlining rule can be taken, not the length of outline every reader should write.
questions.explain: The commentaries show the rule followed close to perfection. Elsewhere the authors say a rough approximation should satisfy you.
questions.rule: The ideal is a measure, not a quota.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: A team is writing a guide to a large codebase, one page per module. Carrying over Aquinas's habit, what should each page include?
options: Its job and its links to the modules near it
Its full source code, pasted in for reference
The date and author of its last change
A list of every function it contains
optionExplain: Right: like Aquinas, each page says what the part does and how it fits its neighbours.
The full text is the thing itself, not a guide to its place.
History is useful but says nothing about how the module fits.
A list of contents enumerates; it does not place the module in the whole.
questions.explain: Aquinas gives every part a local map: what it does and how it connects to what comes before and after.
questions.rule: Give every part a local map.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a good guide to any large system gives each part a local map of its neighbours, as Aquinas did, so a reader who lands anywhere can see where that part fits.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: The authors outline the U.S. Constitution. What do they say about their division of it?
options: It is the only correct division of the document
It must follow the Articles exactly as numbered
It is too hard for ordinary readers to repeat
It is one of several reasonable ways to divide it
optionExplain: The authors say there are many other ways of doing the job.
They group Articles V to VII together, so they do not follow the numbering slavishly.
They invite readers to make their own division and go further.
Right: they call it only one way of doing the job.
questions.explain: The authors offer their outline as one of many. The card next shows it and some alternatives.
questions.rule: More than one good division.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: In the authors' suggested outline of the Constitution, which of these are major divisions? Select all that apply.
options: The Preamble
The Bill of Rights
Article IV, on the states
The delegates' signatures
Section 8 of Article I
optionExplain: Right: the Preamble, setting out the purposes, is their first division.
Right: the first ten amendments form their seventh division.
Right: Article IV, on states and the federal government, is their fifth.
Signatures are not among their divisions.
Section 8 is a subdivision of Article I, not a major division.
questions.explain: Their eight divisions run from the Preamble through the Articles to the Bill of Rights and later amendments. Sections of Articles are parts of parts.
questions.rule: Major divisions first; sections are parts of parts.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: A reader outlines her city's recycling rules and settles on a first division. Following the authors' lesson, what should she do next?
options: Treat her first division as settled and final
Copy the city's own headings exactly as given
Try another grouping and divide each part
Stop, since rules cannot be outlined
optionExplain: The authors present their own division as only one way.
Headings are a guide, not the reader's outline.
Right: try other divisions and go on to the parts of the parts.
The Constitution is a set of rules, and the authors outline it.
questions.explain: The authors invite readers to try their own divisions and go further into the parts of the parts. That is where new things show up.
questions.rule: Re-divide, then go deeper.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Which alternative divisions of the Constitution do the authors themselves mention?
options: Articles I to III as one; amendments by topic
Splitting the Preamble into several parts
Ordering the Articles by their length
Folding the Bill of Rights into Article I
optionExplain: Right: they mention grouping the first three Articles, and grouping amendments by the problems they address.
The Preamble is short and kept whole in their outline.
Length does not follow the document's joints.
The Bill of Rights is a separate division in their outline.
questions.explain: The alternatives they mention follow real joints: the three departments of government, and the problems the amendments address.
questions.rule: Alternatives must follow real joints.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: Since several divisions can be reasonable, grouping a document's parts by their length is as sound as grouping them by topic.
questions.explain: Several divisions can follow a work's real joints, but length is not a joint. A grouping of parts that do not belong together is a mistake, not an alternative.
questions.rule: Several good divisions, not every division.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: A team lead re-divides a long product backlog by customer problem instead of by software component, and spots links no one had seen. Which point of the authors' does this illustrate?
options: The old division was wrong and must go
Backlogs are better left as one undivided list
A new division can show what the old one hid
Components are the only sound way to divide it
optionExplain: Both divisions can be reasonable; the new one adds a view without making the old one wrong.
Without division, the links would be no easier to see.
Right: like regrouping the amendments by problem, a new principle reveals what you never saw.
The new grouping worked, so components are not the only sound division.
questions.explain: The authors say trying your own division reveals much you never saw. A new grouping principle can do that for any body of work.
questions.rule: Regroup to see anew.
questions.teaches: By analogy, re-dividing any familiar body of work by a new principle, such as by problem rather than by component, can show connections the usual division hides.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, your outline of a book's major parts should match its chapter divisions.
questions.explain: The authors say you need not follow the apparent structure shown by chapter divisions. The card next shows their example.
questions.rule: Chapters are not the outline.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: In the authors' outline of the Ethics, how do the six main parts relate to its ten books?
options: Each part matches one or two books exactly
They cut across the books, as pleasure does
The six parts cover only the first six books
Each of the ten books splits into six parts
optionExplain: Only the first part matches a single book; the rest do not line up.
Right: for example, pleasure is treated at the end of Book VII and the start of Book X.
The parts run through all ten books.
The six parts are of the whole, not of each book.
questions.explain: The authors' parts follow the argument, so they cross the book divisions.
questions.rule: Parts follow the argument, not the binding.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: A history of jazz has twelve chapters, one per decade. A reader finds its argument falls into three movements that cross decade lines. What should her outline follow?
options: The twelve chapters as printed
The three movements she found
Six pairs of chapters, as a compromise
The order of the book's photographs
optionExplain: The chapters are the apparent structure, which she need not follow.
Right: her outline follows the real parts, even where they cut across chapters.
Pairing chapters keeps the decade logic she found misleading.
Photographs are illustration, not structure.
questions.explain: Where the argument's parts cross the chapter lines, the outline follows the argument.
questions.rule: Follow the real parts.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Which statements match the authors' view of chapter divisions? Select all that apply.
options: Your major parts may cut across the chapters
The author's divisions may be better than yours
You make an outline in order to read well
Chapter divisions are best ignored as misleading
Only the author is really fit to outline a book
optionExplain: Right: the Ethics example shows parts crossing book lines.
Right: the authors say the apparent structure may be better than your outline.
Right: the author outlines to write well; the reader outlines to read well.
The authors say divisions may be better or worse; they are guides, not suspects.
Every reader is asked to make his own outline.
questions.explain: Your outline is your own work for reading well. It may cross the chapters, and the chapters may still be the better plan.
questions.rule: Make your own; respect theirs.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: The authors say that if the writer and the reader were both perfect, the reader's outline and the writer's would be the same.
questions.explain: The authors say a perfect writer and a perfect reader would produce the same outline. Discrepancies arise as either falls short of perfection.
questions.rule: Imperfection breeds discrepancy.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: A student revising from lecture slides finds the course's ideas fall into four themes, each spread over several lectures. Following the authors, how should she organize her notes?
options: By the four themes, noting their lectures
Lecture by lecture, in the order given
Alphabetically, by each key term used
By the length of each lecture's slides
optionExplain: Right: like outlining the Ethics, her notes follow the real parts and record where each appears.
Delivery order is the course's apparent structure, like chapter divisions.
Alphabetical order ignores how the ideas relate.
Slide count is a surface feature.
questions.explain: The lectures are the course's chapters. Her notes, like an outline, follow the real divisions of the subject as taught.
questions.rule: Organize by real parts, not by delivery.
questions.teaches: By analogy, revising by the real divisions of a course rather than its delivery order puts related material together, so the notes show the course's plan rather than its timetable.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: According to the authors, how should a reader treat a book's chapter headings?
options: As guides to your own work, not as the answer
As the book's true outline, to be copied
As decoration, to be ignored when outlining
As the publisher's choice, apart from the plan
optionExplain: Right: headings help, like titles and prefaces, but the outline is the reader's own work.
Copying them is relying on them passively, which the authors warn against.
The authors say not to ignore them; they did not in outlining the Constitution.
The authors treat headings as the author's help, part of the plan.
questions.explain: Headings are help from the author, to be used actively. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Headings guide; you outline.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, there is often more plan in a good book than meets the eye at first.
questions.explain: The authors say few authors execute their plan perfectly, yet good books often have more plan than the surface shows. You must look beneath it.
questions.rule: Look beneath the surface for more plan.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: A manual's headings are Setup, Use and Maintenance. You find that Use mixes daily tasks with rare emergency procedures. What should your outline do?
options: Copy out the three headings and stop there
Discard the headings and start from scratch
Keep the headings but split Use into two parts
Merge Use and Maintenance into one big part
optionExplain: Copying ignores what you found beneath the heading.
The headings mostly fit; discarding them throws away good help.
Right: use the headings as a guide and adjust where the real parts differ.
Merging hides a division the book does have and leaves the mixed part unsplit.
questions.explain: Headings are a starting point. Where one heading covers two real parts, the outline splits it.
questions.rule: Adjust the headings to the real parts.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Which uses of an author's headings fit the authors' advice? Select all that apply.
options: Using them as a first sketch of the parts
Checking them against what the chapters do
Copying them out as the finished outline
Ignoring them to avoid the author's bias
Splitting a heading that covers two real parts
optionExplain: Right: headings are help, a natural place to start.
Right: using them actively means testing them against the book.
That is relying on them passively.
The authors say not to ignore headings; they are meant to help.
Right: where the surface hides the real structure, the outline follows the structure.
questions.explain: Use headings as guides: start from them, test them and adjust them. Neither copying nor ignoring them fits the advice.
questions.rule: Start from, test, adjust.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: If careful reading shows that a book's headings match its real parts, the reader should still change them to make the outline her own.
questions.explain: Using headings actively means checking them, not changing them for the sake of it. When they match the real parts, keeping them is right.
questions.rule: Your own outline can agree with the author's.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: You must find your way around a government website whose menu reads Services, News and About. Carrying over the authors' advice, what helps most?
options: Trust the labels and do not look further
Ignore the menu and rely on search alone
Start from the menu, then check each section
Read every page in the order it is listed
optionExplain: That relies on the labels passively; Services may hide very different things.
Ignoring the menu throws away the maker's guide to the structure.
Right: the menu is a guide to use actively, checking what its labels contain.
Reading in order gives every page but no sense of the real divisions.
questions.explain: A site menu plays the part of chapter headings. It is help to use actively, since labels can hide or merge the real divisions.
questions.rule: Use the labels, then look inside.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any navigation scheme, such as a site menu or a filing system, is the maker's guide to structure: use it actively and check what its labels hold, since labels can hide or merge the real divisions.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a correct statement of a book's unity made after a quick glance shows that the reader knows the book's unity.
questions.explain: The authors say such a statement might be adequate, but the reader would not know it was. The card next explains what is missing.
questions.rule: A right guess is not yet knowledge.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: A unity statement made from a cursory glance might be adequate, but for you, the authors say, it would be a good guess, a lucky ____.
questions.explain: The authors liken it to a small child saying two plus two is four: the statement is true, but the child does not know what it means. A right guess is not yet knowledge.
questions.rule: A right guess is a lucky hit.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Two students give the same correct unity statement. One read the jacket; the other outlined the book. On the authors' view, how do they differ?
options: They are equal, since the statements match
The first did better, having saved time
The second's statement is more accurate
Only the second can show why it holds
optionExplain: The statements match, but only one is backed by a grasp of the parts.
Saving time bought a guess, not knowledge.
Both statements are the same, so neither is more accurate.
Right: the outline lets the second student show how the parts develop the theme.
questions.explain: The difference is not in the words but in the support. Outlining lets you show how and why the statement is right.
questions.rule: Same words, different grounds.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: Lea says: My teacher marked my one-line summary correct, so I know the book's unity. What does the authors' argument say about her reasoning?
options: A teacher's mark settles what she knows
Her summary must be wrong if it came quickly
A correct mark may reward a lucky hit
Unity statements cannot be marked at all
optionExplain: The authors say a better reader might award high marks, yet for the guesser it is still a guess.
A quick summary can be right; the issue is whether she can support it.
Right: the mark shows the statement is adequate, not that she knows why.
Statements can be checked against the book; the mark is not the issue.
questions.explain: The authors' point is exactly this case: someone who read better may award high marks, but from the guesser's side it is a lucky hit.
questions.rule: A right answer is not proof of grasp.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: True or false: If a reader outlines the parts and finds they do not develop the theme she first stated, the outline has given her reason to revise that statement.
questions.explain: The outline is meant to show how the parts develop the theme. If they do not, the statement of the theme is what needs another look.
questions.rule: The outline tests the unity.

questions.section: Mastering the Multiplicity: The Art of Outlining a Book
questions.q: A junior doctor names the right diagnosis at a glance but cannot say which findings support it. Carrying over the authors' point, what is missing?
options: A second doctor's agreeing opinion
A faster route to the same diagnosis
A record that the diagnosis proved right
Showing how the findings support it
optionExplain: Agreement from someone else is like the teacher's mark; it does not give her the grounds.
Speed is not the problem; the guess was already fast.
Being proved right later still leaves it a lucky hit at the time.
Right: like outlining a book, tracing the evidence turns a right guess into knowledge.
questions.explain: A correct conclusion without its supporting reasons is a lucky hit. Showing how the evidence leads to it is what makes it knowledge.
questions.rule: Show the grounds, not only the answer.
questions.teaches: By analogy, in any field a correct conclusion reached without its supporting reasons is a lucky hit: being able to show how the evidence leads to it is what makes it knowledge.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: How do the authors describe the relation between the rules for reading and for writing a book's structure?
options: Reciprocal: the author builds what the reader uncovers
Unrelated: writing is an art and reading an analysis
Identical: reader and writer do exactly the same thing
Opposed: good writers try to keep readers from the plan
optionExplain: Right: writing and reading are reciprocal, like teaching and being taught.
The authors call the reading rules rules of writing too, so they are related.
The rules are the same, but the authors say they are not followed in the same way.
Writers cover the skeleton, but so that the joints still show, not to hide the plan.
questions.explain: The author organizes, the reader uncovers. The card next shows how the two directions differ.
questions.rule: Writing builds what reading uncovers.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the reader starts with the skeleton and covers it, while the author tries to uncover it.
questions.explain: It is the other way round: the author starts with the skeleton and covers it; the reader tries to uncover the skeleton the book conceals.
questions.rule: Author covers; reader uncovers.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: Sort each task: is it the author's work or the reader's?

items.t: Starts from the skeleton
Covers the bones with flesh
Unifies and orders the parts
Searches for the unity
Uncovers the hidden skeleton
Works back from surface to plan

questions.explain: The same structure runs in two directions: the author builds and clothes it, the reader finds and uncovers it.
questions.rule: Same structure, opposite directions.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: According to the authors, why would telling readers to search for a book's unity be pointless if authors did not organize their books?
options: Readers would find the unity too easily
Authors would have to explain it in prefaces
Readers would need far more time to read
There would be no unity there to find
optionExplain: Without organization, finding a unity would be impossible, not easy.
Prefaces cannot supply a unity the book lacks.
More time would not produce a unity that is not there.
Right: the reader's search depends on the writer having unified and ordered the work.
questions.explain: The rules are reciprocal: the reader can only uncover what the writer organized.
questions.rule: No organization, nothing to find.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: True or false: A reader can recover a book's structure from the finished book alone, without the author's notes or drafts.
questions.explain: The reader works from the finished book, uncovering the skeleton it conceals. The structure to find is the one in the book, whatever the drafts looked like.
questions.rule: The structure is in the book.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: Carrying over the reciprocity of teaching and being taught, what should a student listen for in a well-planned lecture?
options: Every example, written down word for word
The main point and the order of its parts
The jokes and asides, which show what matters
The slide count, which reveals the structure
optionExplain: Transcribing the examples records the flesh and can miss the skeleton.
Right: the student uncovers what the lecturer organized, as a reader does with a book.
Asides are flesh; they rarely mark the main parts.
Slide count is a surface feature, like page count.
questions.explain: Teaching and being taught are reciprocal, like writing and reading. The listener recovers the unity and order the teacher built.
questions.rule: Listen for the plan, not only the words.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a student taking lecture notes does what a reader does with a book: recover the main point and the ordered parts the lecturer planned, rather than transcribe the surface.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the best expository book would be a bare outline of its subject.
questions.explain: The authors say the flesh is as much a part of the book as the skeleton. The card next explains what it adds.
questions.rule: A book is more than its outline.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: Which faults in covering the skeleton do the authors warn writers against? Select all that apply.
options: A puny skeleton buried under fat
Flesh so thin the bones show through
Joints that can still be detected
Parts whose motion shows how they join
optionExplain: Right: a good writer does not bury a puny skeleton under a mass of fat.
Right: nor should the flesh be so thin that the bones show through.
Detectable joints are a virtue: they let the reader find the structure.
This is also a virtue: the motion of the parts reveals the articulation.
questions.explain: Too much fat and too little flesh are the two faults. Detectable joints and visible articulation are what good covering allows.
questions.rule: Neither fat nor bare bones.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: A 300-page business book makes one small point and pads it with anecdotes. In the authors' terms, what is wrong?
options: Flesh so thin that the bones show through
Joints that can be seen between its parts
Too much structure and too little story
A puny skeleton buried under a mass of fat
optionExplain: The fault is the reverse: far too much covering, not too little.
Visible joints are a virtue, not the fault here.
The book has too little structure, not too much.
Right: a small point padded out is a puny skeleton under fat.
questions.explain: One small point under 300 pages of anecdote is the first fault the authors name: a puny skeleton buried in fat.
questions.rule: Length can hide a thin skeleton.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: Besides the fact that most readers cannot read outlines, why do the authors say a book should not be a bare outline?
options: Outlines hide the author's main point
Outlines cannot show any order of parts
The flesh adds life, an essential dimension
Bare outlines are harder for authors to write
optionExplain: An outline shows the main point plainly; hiding it is not the problem.
Showing order is exactly what an outline does.
Right: writing the book out from the outline gives it a kind of life it would not otherwise have.
The authors' reason concerns the book's nature, not the author's effort.
questions.explain: The deeper reason is that the flesh is part of the book. Spelling out the outline adds an essential dimension.
questions.rule: The flesh is part of the book.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: True or false: The authors say that if the flesh is thick enough and flabbiness is avoided, a book's joints will still be detectable.
questions.explain: Good covering hides the skeleton artistically without hiding the joints; the motion of the parts reveals how they connect.
questions.rule: Good flesh shows the joints.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: A documentary weaves interviews and footage around an argument in four stages. Carrying over the authors' point about flesh, how should a viewer treat the interviews?
options: As part of the work, showing its joints
As padding to skip to get at the argument
As the real argument, with stages as filler
As decoration unrelated to the structure
optionExplain: Right: the interviews give life to the stages, and how each advances the argument shows the joints.
Skipping the flesh treats it as fat; here it is part of the work.
This reverses skeleton and flesh.
Well-made flesh moves with the bones; it is not unrelated.
questions.explain: In a well-made work the flesh is part of the whole, and the movement of the parts reveals the structure beneath.
questions.rule: Watch how the flesh moves the bones.
questions.teaches: By analogy, in a well-made documentary or talk the illustrations are where the structure moves: watching how each interview advances a stage is how a viewer finds the joints.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: Which three qualities does the old maxim say a piece of writing should have?
options: Brevity, wit and grace
Accuracy, balance and depth
Unity, clarity and coherence
Simplicity, rhythm and force
optionExplain: Admired qualities, but not the maxim the authors recall.
Good qualities for an argument, but not the maxim.
Right: the authors call this a basic maxim of good writing.
Qualities of style, but not the three in the maxim.
questions.explain: The maxim is unity, clarity and coherence. The card next links each to the reader's work.
questions.rule: Unity, clarity, coherence.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: Match each quality in the maxim to what the authors say about it.
pairs: Comes from the distinctness of the parts
Comes from an orderly arrangement of parts
questions.explain: The reader finds the unity, and appreciates clarity and coherence by seeing the parts as distinct and ordered.
questions.rule: Find the one; see the parts distinct and ordered.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: In a city guidebook, the chapters on food and on markets overlap so much that a reader cannot tell where one ends and the other begins. Which quality is weak?
options: Clarity, since the parts are not distinct
Unity, since the guide has no single aim
Coherence, since the order is mistaken
Brevity, since the two chapters are long
optionExplain: Right: clarity lies in the distinctness of the parts, which is what fails here.
The guide may well have one aim; the problem is between two parts.
Order concerns which part comes first; here the parts cannot be told apart.
Length is not one of the three qualities in the maxim.
questions.explain: Clarity comes from distinct outlines. Parts that blur into each other weaken it.
questions.rule: Blurred parts weaken clarity.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: A report's sections are each distinct, but they come in a jumbled order, with conclusions before methods. Which quality is lacking?
options: Clarity of the parts
Unity of the whole
Brevity of the text
Coherence of order
optionExplain: The sections are distinct, so clarity is there.
Nothing says the report lacks one aim.
Brevity is not one of the three qualities.
Right: coherence is an orderly arrangement of parts, which the jumbled order lacks.
questions.explain: Distinct parts give clarity; an orderly arrangement gives coherence. Here the first is present and the second is not.
questions.rule: Distinct is clarity; ordered is coherence.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: True or false: A reader who cannot find distinct, ordered parts in a book may be facing a fault in the book rather than in her reading.
questions.explain: The maxim describes good writing, and many books fall short of it. Failing to find clarity and coherence may show that the book lacks them.
questions.rule: The lack may be in the book.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: You are reviewing a colleague's slide deck and want feedback grounded in the maxim. Which comment checks coherence?
options: Each slide should make one distinct point
The deck should serve one overall message
Each slide should follow from the one before
The fonts should match across all the slides
optionExplain: Distinct points check clarity.
One overall message checks unity.
Right: an order in which each part follows from the last is coherence.
Matching fonts is surface style, not one of the three qualities.
questions.explain: Coherence is the orderly arrangement of parts. Asking whether each slide follows from the one before tests it.
questions.rule: Coherence: does each part follow?
questions.teaches: By analogy, the maxim gives a reviewer three separate checks for any piece of work: one aim (unity), parts that do not blur (clarity), and an order with reasons (coherence).

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, most books are badly made, in the sense that their authors did not write them by these rules.
questions.explain: The authors say the very great majority of books are badly made in this sense. The card next explains when to conclude that a particular book is one of them.
questions.rule: Most books are badly made.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: According to the authors, when may a reader judge that a book is probably badly made?
options: When it is long and hard going at first
When skilled effort finds no unity or parts
When reviewers have criticised it in print
When the reader disagrees with its claims
optionExplain: Hard going at first is normal for good books too.
Right: after sufficient skill and effort, failing to find unity and parts points to the book.
Reviews are others' opinions; the test is the reader's own skilled effort.
Disagreement is about truth, not about how the book is made.
questions.explain: The test is skilled, honest effort to apply the two rules. If that fails, the book is very likely badly made.
questions.rule: Skilled effort fails: suspect the book.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: A beginner skims a famous philosophy book once, cannot see its plan, and calls it badly made. On the authors' view, what is wrong?
options: He should defer to the book's reputation
Philosophy books do not have plans to find
He should blame himself in every such case
He judged too soon, without skill or effort
optionExplain: Reputation does not decide; the authors say whatever its reputation.
Every book worth reading has a plan, philosophy included.
The authors warn against always assuming the fault is yours.
Right: the judgment comes after sufficient skill and real effort, not after one skim.
questions.explain: The authors warn against judging too quickly. One skim by a beginner is not the skilled effort the judgment requires.
questions.rule: Skill and effort first, verdict after.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: Which attitudes do the authors recommend when a book's structure will not come clear? Select all that apply.
options: Do not be too quick to blame the book
Do not assume the fault is always yours
Let the book's reputation settle the matter
Expect that the fault usually lies in the book
Refuse to judge how any book is made
optionExplain: Right: perhaps the fault is in you.
Right: the authors say not to always assume the fault is yours.
They say to judge whatever the book's reputation.
Right: since most books are badly made, the fault is usually in the book.
The authors say the rules can and should be used to tell well-made books from bad ones.
questions.explain: The authors steer between two errors: blaming the book too soon and never blaming it. Given how many books are badly made, the fault usually lies there.
questions.rule: Neither too quick nor never.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: True or false: If Ana's book is a celebrated bestseller, its fame should outweigh her skilled, careful finding that it lacks unity.
questions.explain: The authors say the judgment holds whatever the book's reputation. Skilled effort that finds no unity points to a badly made book, famous or not.
questions.rule: Reputation does not rebuild a book.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: An experienced engineer, after careful study, still cannot work out how a popular library's documentation is organized. Carrying over the authors' advice, what is a fair conclusion?
options: She must lack skill, since the library is popular
The documentation is likely poorly organized
Documentation does not need to be organized
She should stop using the library at once
optionExplain: Popularity is like reputation; it does not show the documentation is well made.
Right: skilled, careful effort that finds no structure points to the document.
Users need structure to find their way; disorganized documentation is a fault.
Judging how the documentation is made is not a verdict on the library's code.
questions.explain: The same test applies: experienced, careful effort that finds no organization suggests the fault is in the document.
questions.rule: Skilled readers stuck: suspect the text.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the skilled-effort test applies to any document judged by its users: when experienced readers who try hard cannot find its organization, the fault probably lies with the document, not with them.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, you can get the idea of a good novel by reading enough of it, without finishing it.
questions.explain: The authors say the idea of a good novel is in the whole and cannot be found short of reading the whole. The card next contrasts this with expository books.
questions.rule: A good novel's idea is in the whole.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: On the authors' account, why can a part of an expository book be read on its own more readily than a part of a novel?
options: Its parts can be much more autonomous
It is shorter than a novel on average
It has no unity of the whole to find
Its author wrote each part separately
optionExplain: Right: the parts of books conveying knowledge can be much more autonomous than those of stories.
Length is not the authors' reason.
Expository books have unity; their parts are simply more independent.
How the author worked is not the point; the parts' independence is.
questions.explain: The difference lies in how autonomous the parts are. In a story, the parts serve a whole that only the whole reveals.
questions.rule: Expository parts stand alone more easily.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: Sort each reading plan: can reading this part on its own work, or does it need the whole?

items.t: The chapter on vaccines in a book on medicine
A self-contained part of a political treatise
The section on sleep in a health manual
The first half of a detective novel
Three acts of a five-act tragedy
The opening chapters of a family saga

questions.explain: Relatively independent parts of expository books can be read well on their own. A story's idea lies in the whole, so its parts cannot stand in for it.
questions.rule: Exposition by parts; stories whole.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: True or false: Suppose a reader who has read only some chapters of Darwin's Origin carefully goes on to read all of it. On the authors' view, she can now try to carry out Rule 3 for the whole book, which reading the parts alone did not allow.
questions.explain: Parts read carefully can give the Origin's idea, but Rule 3 asks for the major parts of the whole and their order, which only a reading of the whole supplies. Change the condition, read the whole, and Rule 3 comes within reach.
questions.rule: Rule 3 needs the whole book.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: A student writes a report on a novel after reading half of it, saying the rest only adds detail. What does the authors' view say about this?
options: Half is enough if the half is read closely
Novels have no single idea to grasp
In a good novel the idea is in the whole
The report should cover only the half read
optionExplain: Close reading of half a story still misses what the whole holds.
A good novel has a unity of plot; the authors say its idea is in the whole.
Right: the authors say such a reader does not know what he is talking about.
Limiting the report to half still claims more than half a reading can give.
questions.explain: The claim that the rest only adds detail treats a novel like a set of autonomous parts. The authors say a good novel's idea is found only in the whole.
questions.rule: Do not judge a story by part of it.

questions.section: The Reciprocal Arts of Reading and Writing
questions.q: A podcast has two kinds of episodes: standalone interviews, and parts of an eight-episode story series. Carrying over the authors' distinction, which can be grasped from a single episode?
options: Episode four of the eight-part story series
Any episode, if heard carefully enough
A standalone interview, a whole in itself
Neither, since a podcast is one whole
optionExplain: One episode of a continuing story holds only part of its idea.
Care cannot supply what lies in the episodes not heard.
Right: a self-contained episode is like an autonomous expository part.
The interviews are wholes in themselves, not parts of one story.
questions.explain: The standalone interview is like an autonomous expository part. The story episode is like a chapter of a novel, whose idea lies in the whole.
questions.rule: Self-contained parts can stand alone; story parts cannot.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the authors' contrast between expository parts and story parts fits serial media: a self-contained episode can be grasped alone, but an episode of a continuing story holds its meaning only in the whole series.

questions.q: According to Rule 4, what should a reader find out about the author?
options: His life story and personal motives
The problems he set out to answer
His qualifications to write the book
His other books on similar subjects
optionExplain: Biography is not what the rule asks for; it concerns the book's questions.
Right: the author starts with questions, and the book contains the answers.
Credentials may matter elsewhere, but Rule 4 asks for the book's problems.
Other books may help later, but Rule 4 is about this book's questions.
questions.explain: Rule 4 asks for the author's problems: the questions the book sets out to answer. The card next explains the reader's part.
questions.rule: Find the questions the book answers.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, it is the reader's task to formulate the author's questions even when the author does not state them.
questions.explain: The authors say that whether or not the author states his questions, and especially if he does not, the reader must formulate them as precisely as possible.
questions.rule: Stated or not, formulate the questions.

questions.q: A reader finishes a book on bird migration. Which of these does what Rule 4 asks?
options: Is this a theoretical or a practical book?
What are the book's twelve chapters about?
Which bird does the author like best?
How do birds navigate so far, and why go?
optionExplain: That classifies the book, the work of Rule 1.
That asks for the parts, the work of Rule 3.
That asks about the author's tastes, not the book's problem.
Right: it states the questions the book sets out to answer.
questions.explain: Rule 4 asks for the questions the book answers. Only the last option states such questions; the others belong to other rules or to the author's tastes.
questions.rule: State the book's question as a question.

questions.q: Match each rule of the first stage of analytical reading to what it asks you to produce.
pairs: The kind of book and its subject matter
What the whole book is about, in brief
The major parts in their order and relation
The questions the book tries to answer
questions.explain: Each rule produces one thing: the kind, the unity, the ordered parts and the problems. Rule 4 restates the structure in terms of questions.
questions.rule: Kind, unity, parts, problems.

questions.q: True or false: If the author states his main question in the preface, Rule 4 leaves no work for the reader.
questions.explain: A stated question is help, like a stated plan, but the reader still has to formulate the questions precisely, including the subordinate ones, and check them against the book.
questions.rule: A stated question is a lead, not the end.

questions.q: You are handed a 30-page market analysis that states no purpose. Carrying over Rule 4, what should you work out first?
options: Who commissioned it, and their motives
Which of its charts look most striking
How long it took the team to prepare
The question the analysis tries to answer
optionExplain: Motives are about people; Rule 4 asks for the problem the document addresses.
Striking charts are surface; they may not be central.
Effort says nothing about what the analysis is for.
Right: inferring the question shows what the analysis is trying to settle.
questions.explain: A report without a stated purpose still answers some question. Working it out from what the data and conclusions address is Rule 4 applied.
questions.rule: Infer the question from what is answered.
questions.teaches: By analogy, Rule 4 works on reports that state no purpose: inferring the question from what the data and conclusions address lets you judge later whether the report actually answers it.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reader should be able to say which of the author's questions must be answered first if others are to be answered later.
questions.explain: The authors ask the reader to put the questions in an intelligible order, primary before secondary. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: Order the questions.

questions.q: When the main question of a book is complex, what else do the authors ask the reader to state?
options: The author's answer to each
Its subordinate questions
Questions the author ignored
The reader's own questions
optionExplain: Finding the answers comes later; Rule 4 is about the questions.
Right: a complex main question has parts, the subordinate questions.
Gaps can be noted later; Rule 4 asks for the questions the book does address.
The reader's questions matter, but Rule 4 asks for the author's.
questions.explain: A complex main question breaks into subordinate questions, and the reader should be able to state them.
questions.rule: Main question, then its parts.

questions.q: A book asks whether a town should build a new reservoir. Put its subordinate questions in the order in which they must be answered.
items: How much water will the town need in twenty years?
Can existing sources meet that need?
If not, which new source is best?
How should the chosen project be paid for?
questions.explain: Each question depends on the one before: need first, then whether current sources suffice, then which new source, then funding for it.
questions.rule: Ask what must be settled first.

questions.q: A book investigates why the Roman Republic fell. Which of these is its primary question?
options: What role did Caesar's army play?
How did the Senate answer the Gracchi?
What did grain shortages do to Rome?
Why did the Roman Republic fall?
optionExplain: A subordinate question: one possible part of the answer.
Another subordinate question about one episode.
Another subordinate question about one cause.
Right: the others are parts of answering this one.
questions.explain: The primary question is the one the others serve. Each subordinate question contributes part of the answer to why the Republic fell.
questions.rule: The primary question is the one the others serve.

questions.q: True or false: If a book pursues three questions side by side, none depending on the others, the reader should still force them into a strict first-to-last order.
questions.explain: The order the authors ask for is the one the questions actually have. Where questions are independent, inventing a dependence distorts the book.
questions.rule: Find the order; do not invent it.

questions.q: A team debugging a slow website lists four questions: whether it is slow for everyone, where the time goes, which change caused it, and how to fix it. Carrying over the authors' idea, why order these questions?
options: Each answer is needed before the next one
Questions look tidier in a numbered list
The fix matters most, so it should come first
Ordering lets each member take one question
optionExplain: Right: like a book's questions, each depends on answers to the ones before.
Tidiness is not the point; dependence is.
Jumping to the fix risks fixing the wrong thing; the fix depends on the earlier answers.
Splitting work is a separate matter and ignores how the questions depend on each other.
questions.explain: The authors ask which questions must be answered first for others to be answered later. In an investigation, that order is a working method.
questions.rule: Answer the prior questions first.
questions.teaches: By analogy, ordering questions by dependence is a working method for any investigation, such as debugging: answering the prior questions first keeps you from solving the wrong problem.

questions.q: According to the authors, what often happens to readers who fail to find the author's problems?
options: They read much more slowly than others
They agree with the author too easily
Their outline of the book is chaotic
They forget the book's title and author
optionExplain: Speed is not the consequence the authors name.
Agreement is a later question; the authors name a structural failure.
Right: their grasp of the main point is deficient and their outline chaotic.
Forgetting details is not what the authors describe.
questions.explain: Without the problem, the structure has nothing to organize it. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: No problem found, no order in the outline.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Rule 4 may be especially helpful with a difficult book because it is less familiar than the other two rules.
questions.explain: The authors say that since the rule is more unfamiliar than the other two, it may be even more helpful in tackling a difficult book.
questions.rule: For hard books, ask the question.

questions.q: A reader's outline of a book on economic policy is a list of topics that will not hang together. Which step do the authors' remarks suggest?
options: Ask what problem the book is trying to solve
Add more topics until nothing is left out
Copy out the chapter headings instead
Conclude that the book has no unity at all
optionExplain: Right: seeing the problem shows why the parts are there and how they fit.
More topics make the list longer, not more coherent.
Headings are a guide, but copying them does not supply the missing end.
That conclusion needs skilled effort first, and Rule 4 has not been tried.
questions.explain: A chaotic outline lacks the end the skeleton serves. Finding the problem supplies it.
questions.rule: The problem organizes the parts.

questions.q: According to the authors, which of these follow from neglecting Rule 4? Select all that apply.
options: A deficient grasp of the main point
An outline of the structure that is chaotic
Not seeing why the book has its unity
Reading too slowly to finish the book
Disagreeing with the author unfairly
optionExplain: Right: the conception of the main point may be extremely deficient.
Right: the outline of the structure will be chaotic.
Right: readers fail to see why the book has the unity it has.
Speed is not among the consequences the authors name.
Disagreement belongs to a later stage; the consequences named are structural.
questions.explain: All three consequences concern structure: the unity, the outline and the end they serve.
questions.rule: Miss the problem, miss the structure's point.

questions.q: True or false: Once you have stated the author's main question, you no longer need to outline the book's parts.
questions.explain: Rule 4 is useful alongside the other rules, not instead of them. A question unchecked against the parts can be as much a guess as an unchecked unity statement.
questions.rule: Use the three rules together.

questions.q: A paralegal faces a thick case file of letters, contracts and emails that seem unconnected. Carrying over the authors' point, what should organize her reading?
options: The date order of the documents
The length of each document in the file
Which documents mention sums of money
The legal question the case turns on
optionExplain: Date order is useful, but it does not show why each document matters.
Length says nothing about relevance.
Money may matter, but it is a filter, not the organizing question.
Right: once the question is clear, each document's place in the case shows.
questions.explain: As a book's parts line up once its problem is known, a file's documents line up once the question in dispute is clear.
questions.rule: Find the question; the pieces will place themselves.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a pile of documents organizes itself around the question it bears on: once the question in dispute is clear, each document's place becomes visible, as a book's parts do once its problem is known.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, it is a grave error to try to psychoanalyze Shakespeare from the evidence of Hamlet.
questions.explain: The authors give this as an example of the intentional fallacy. The card next separates it from Rule 4.
questions.rule: Do not psychoanalyze the author.

questions.q: What do the authors mean by the intentional fallacy?
options: Assuming an author always means what he says
Judging a book before finding its purpose
Thinking a book reveals its author's mind
Believing every book has a hidden message
optionExplain: Taking an author at his word is a different matter.
Hasty judgment is a real fault, but it is not this fallacy.
Right: the fallacy is thinking you can discover what was in the author's mind from the book.
Hidden messages are a different claim; the fallacy concerns the author's mind.
questions.explain: The intentional fallacy is reading the author's mind out of the work. Rule 4 asks for the work's problem instead.
questions.rule: The book is not a window into the author's mind.

questions.q: Sort each note: does it state the work's problem, or guess at the author's mind?

items.t: The poem asks whether love can survive distance
The essay tries to show why taxes should be simpler
The play explores what ambition does to loyalty
The poet was secretly unhappy in her marriage
The essayist resented paying taxes himself
The playwright feared his own ambition

questions.explain: The first group states what the work addresses, which the work itself can show. The second guesses at private feelings, which the work cannot establish.
questions.rule: The work, not the psyche.

questions.q: Which note on a novel about a failing farm follows Rule 4 without falling into the intentional fallacy?
options: The author must have grown up on a farm
The author was working out anger at his father
It asks if a family can keep both land and bonds
The author wanted to profit from rural nostalgia
optionExplain: A guess about the author's life, not the novel's problem.
A guess about the author's psychology, the fallacy itself.
Right: it states what the novel is trying to do, as the novel shows.
A guess about motives, which the book cannot establish.
questions.explain: Rule 4 asks what the work is trying to do. Only the third note answers from the work rather than guessing at the author.
questions.rule: Ask what the work tries to do.

questions.q: True or false: If the work is a poem rather than a treatise, the authors say there is no point asking what the author was trying to do.
questions.explain: The authors say that even with a poetical work it is often extremely helpful to say what the author was trying to do. The warning is against psychoanalyzing, not against asking about the work's aim.
questions.rule: Ask the aim, even of a poem.

questions.q: A manager receives a terse email proposing to cancel a project. Carrying over the authors' distinction, what should she analyse first?
options: What mood the sender must have been in then
The problem the email raises and its reasons
Whether the sender dislikes the project lead
What the sender's tone shows about his character
optionExplain: Mood is a guess about the sender's mind, like psychoanalyzing an author.
Right: the problem and reasons are in the email and can be answered.
Suspected dislike is another guess about inner life.
Tone may hint at things, but reading character from it is the same fallacy.
questions.explain: The email's problem and reasons are on the page. Guesses about the sender's mind are not, and arguing with them means arguing with someone you imagined.
questions.rule: Answer what was written.
questions.teaches: By analogy, reading any message for the problem it raises, rather than the sender's supposed mood, keeps a reply grounded in what was written and avoids arguing with a person you have imagined.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, knowing the kinds of questions anyone can ask about anything makes it easier to detect an author's problems.
questions.explain: The authors say that if you know these kinds of questions, you will become adept at detecting an author's problems. The card next gives the lists.
questions.rule: Know the questions to find the problem.

questions.q: According to the authors, what does knowing the kinds of questions anyone can ask about anything help a reader do?
options: Decide whether the author's answers are true
Detect the problems an author set out to solve
Classify the book before starting to read it
Find the book's key words and their senses
optionExplain: Judging the answers comes in a later stage; the lists serve Rule 4.
Right: the authors say knowing these questions makes you adept at detecting an author's problems.
Classifying is Rule 1's work; here the lists help find the book's questions.
Key words belong to the next stage of reading, not to Rule 4.
questions.explain: The lists are a tool for Rule 4: they help you spot which questions the book is trying to answer.
questions.rule: The lists help find the author's problems.

questions.q: A book on coral reefs takes up four questions. Match each with the kind of question on the authors' theoretical list.
questions.explain: Each of the book's questions is a particular case of a general question on the list: existence, kind, cause and consequence. Recognising the general form is how the list helps you spot what a book is asking.
questions.rule: Match the book's questions to the general kinds.
pairs: Do reef-building corals still grow in this sea?
What kind of organism builds a reef?
What kind of thing is it?
What follows for the fish that depend on them?

questions.q: A book on household money asks how much a family should aim to save, which budgeting methods reach that aim, and in what order to adopt them. Which is its main question, with the others subordinate?
options: Which budgeting method best suits a family's needs?
How should a family run its money to meet its goals?
In what order should a family adopt its methods?
How much should a typical family aim to save?
optionExplain: A question about means: one part of the answer, so subordinate.
Right: the questions of end, means and order are all parts of answering this one.
A question about the order of steps: subordinate to the main question.
A question about the end: an early subordinate question.
questions.explain: The practical list gives the subordinate questions: the end, the means and the order. The main question is the one they jointly answer.
questions.rule: The main question is the one the listed questions serve.

questions.q: True or false: If a book asks a question that does not appear on the authors' lists, it cannot have a problem in the sense of Rule 4.
questions.explain: The authors say the list is far from exhaustive. It is a prompt for detecting problems, not a test of whether a book has one.
questions.rule: The list prompts; it does not limit.

questions.q: The authors add a remark about using these question lists on novels, plays and poems. What do they say?
options: The lists do not apply to imaginative works
Only the practical questions apply to novels
Adapted, the questions help there too
Stories answer every question on both lists
optionExplain: The authors say the opposite: adapted, the questions are useful there too.
They do not limit novels to one list.
Right: the questions have to be adapted for imaginative literature, and there too they are useful.
No work answers every question; the lists are a prompt.
questions.explain: The lists were built for theoretical and practical knowledge. With imaginative literature they need adapting, but then they help find what the work is trying to do.
questions.rule: Adapt the questions for stories.
questions.teaches: According to the authors, the theoretical and practical question lists have to be adapted when applied to imaginative literature, and there too they are useful.

questions.q: A new analyst reads a vague report titled A Review of Remote Work and cannot say what it is trying to settle. How can the authors' question lists help her?
options: Use them to decide whether the report is right
Run down them to see which questions it takes up
Use them to label it theoretical or practical, and stop
Count how many listed questions it answers, to grade it
optionExplain: The lists serve understanding first; judging the report comes later.
Right: checking each listed question against the report shows which ones it actually addresses.
A label is a start, but Rule 4 wants the questions themselves, stated precisely.
The list is not a scorecard; a good report need not take up many of its questions.
questions.explain: The lists turn a vague topic into candidate questions. Checking each against the report shows which ones it takes up, which is Rule 4's work.
questions.rule: Run the list to find the questions.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the question lists work as a checklist for turning a vague topic into precise questions: running down them for an unfamiliar report shows which questions it actually takes up.

questions.section: The First Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Which of these belong to the first stage of analytical reading? Select all that apply.
options: Classify the book by kind and subject
State the unity of the whole book
Outline the major parts in order
Decide whether the book is true
Compare it with other books on its subject
optionExplain: Right: this is Rule 1.
Right: this is Rule 2.
Right: this is Rule 3.
Judging truth comes in a later stage, after understanding.
Comparing books on one subject belongs to a different, later kind of reading.
questions.explain: The first stage is classifying, stating the unity, outlining and finding the problems. Judging and comparing come later. The card next puts the four rules together.
questions.rule: Stage one: kind, unity, parts, problems.

questions.section: The First Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Put the four rules of the first stage of analytical reading in order.
items: Classify the book by kind and subject matter
State what the whole book is about, briefly
Enumerate the major parts in order and relation
Define the problems the author tries to solve
questions.explain: Rule 1 classifies, Rule 2 states the unity, Rule 3 outlines the parts and Rule 4 defines the problems.
questions.rule: Classify, unify, outline, define.

questions.section: The First Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: A reader has classified a book, stated its unity and outlined its parts, but has not asked what problems it addresses. What does the first stage still need?
options: Rule 1 again, in more detail
Rule 4: the author's problems
A verdict on the book's argument
A list of the book's key terms
optionExplain: Classification is done; repeating it does not complete the stage.
Right: the stage has four rules, and the fourth is missing.
A verdict belongs to a later stage.
Key terms belong to the next stage, interpretation.
questions.explain: The first stage has four rules. Without Rule 4, the reader may not see why the book has the unity and parts it has.
questions.rule: Four rules make the stage.

questions.section: The First Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: According to the authors, what single aim do the first four rules share?
options: Knowledge of whether it is true
Knowledge of the author's life
Knowledge of every term it uses
Knowledge of the book's structure
optionExplain: Truth is judged at a later stage.
The author's life is not the aim; the book is.
Terms belong to the next stage.
Right: together the four rules give knowledge of the book's structure.
questions.explain: The authors say the four rules are connected and form a group with a single aim: knowledge of the book's structure.
questions.rule: Stage one aims at structure.

questions.section: The First Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: True or false: Once you have applied the first four rules, you know whether the book's claims are true.
questions.explain: The first stage gives the structure: what the book is about as a whole. What exactly it says, and whether that is true, are questions for the later stages.
questions.rule: Structure first; truth later.

questions.section: The First Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: A reader says: I have stated the book's leading theme, so I have answered what it is about as a whole. On the authors' account, what is missing?
options: A verdict on whether the theme is true
How the theme is developed through sub-themes
The author's reasons for choosing the theme
A second statement of the theme in other words
optionExplain: Truth is a later question, not part of what the book is about.
Right: the first question asks for the theme and how it is developed in order through subordinate themes.
The author's private reasons are not what the question asks.
Restating the theme adds nothing about its development.
questions.explain: The first basic question has two halves: the leading theme, and its orderly development through essential subordinate themes. The reader has only the first.
