questions.rule: Theme plus its development.

questions.section: The First Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Taking over a project, a new lead first asks what kind of project it is, what it is for, what its main workstreams are, and what problems it is solving. Which part of the method does this mirror?
options: The first stage: getting the structure first
Judging the project before understanding it
Skimming the project's files at random
Reading the project's history in date order
optionExplain: Right: kind, aim, parts and problems are the four rules of the first stage.
Her questions are about understanding, not judging.
Her questions are systematic, not random.
Date order is a chronicle, not the structure she is after.
questions.explain: Her four questions match the four rules: classify, state the unity, outline the parts, define the problems. She gets the structure before changing anything.
questions.rule: Structure before action.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the first stage is a template for taking over any complex piece of work: kind, aim, parts and problems give you its structure before you change anything in it.

questions.section: The First Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, you must read a book through once for the first four rules and again for the later ones.
questions.explain: The authors say stage is not meant chronologically: the practised reader does all the stages at once. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Stages are not separate readings.

questions.section: The First Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: According to the authors, who accomplishes all the stages of analytical reading at once?
options: The beginning reader
The practised reader
The fastest reader
The occasional reader
optionExplain: A beginner may need to take the stages one at a time.
Right: the practised reader accomplishes all the stages at once.
Speed is not the authors' point; skill is.
An occasional reader may not attempt analytical reading at all; the authors credit practice.
questions.explain: Doing the stages together is a mark of practice. Beginners may need to separate them at first.
questions.rule: Practice merges the stages.

questions.section: The First Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: A beginner finds it too much to outline, interpret and judge a book all at once. On the authors' view, what is reasonable?
options: Taking the stages singly while learning
Giving up analytical reading as too hard
Skipping the structural rules altogether
Judging the book first, then outlining it
optionExplain: Right: the authors allow a chronological sense at the very beginning.
The difficulty is normal for a beginner, not a reason to stop.
Structure is a real stage toward reading analytically and cannot be skipped.
Judging before understanding reverses the proper order.
questions.explain: The authors allow that stage may be chronological at the very beginning of practice. With skill, the stages merge.
questions.rule: Separate stages while learning.

questions.section: The First Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Which statements match the authors' account? Select all that apply.
options: Inspecting first helps you apply the first four rules
Practised readers do all the stages at once
Your statement of the whole improves with later rules
Each stage needs a separate reading of the whole book
A good inspection does the first stage's work for you
optionExplain: Right: the authors say inspecting a book well beforehand helps you apply the rules.
Right: that is why stage is not meant chronologically.
Right: the answer improves in accuracy as you apply the later rules.
The authors say it is not necessary to read the book through again for each stage.
Inspection helps the first stage; it does not do its work.
questions.explain: Inspection prepares, the stages run together for the practised reader, and the statement of the whole keeps improving.
questions.rule: Prepare, combine, revise.

questions.section: The First Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: True or false: If, while working out a book's claims, you find your first statement of its unity was off, revising that statement fits the authors' account.
questions.explain: The authors say your answer to what the book is about will improve in accuracy as you apply the later rules. Revision is expected.
questions.rule: Later rules sharpen the first answer.

questions.section: The First Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: A learner driver practises steering, gears and mirrors separately; an experienced driver handles them all at once. Carrying over the authors' point, what does this suggest about the stages of reading?
options: Experts skip the steps that learners still need
The steps must stay separate to be done properly
Separate steps suit learning; skill combines them
Skill means doing the steps faster, one by one
optionExplain: Experienced drivers still check mirrors; they do it alongside everything else.
Skill combines the steps without dropping any.
Right: like the stages of reading, the parts are learned apart and performed together.
Speed alone is not the change; the steps run together.
questions.explain: The authors allow separate stages for beginners and describe the practised reader doing them at once, as an experienced driver does.
questions.rule: Learn apart, perform together.
questions.teaches: By analogy, as in driving, separate stages are scaffolding for a learner: practice folds them into one performance, so the stages describe the skill's parts rather than a fixed sequence of passes.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In analytical reading, where does coming to terms with an author fall?
options: At the end, once you have judged the book
As the first step after outlining the book
Before inspecting, as a way to choose a book
Only when two readers disagree about a book
optionExplain: Judging comes later; you cannot judge claims whose words you have not yet understood.
Right: once the structure is outlined, coming to terms opens the work of interpreting what the book says.
Choosing a book is the job of inspection; coming to terms belongs to reading it closely.
Disagreement can expose a failure to come to terms, but the step is part of every analytical reading.
questions.explain: Coming to terms is the first step beyond the outline, the start of interpreting what a book says. The card next shows why it comes first.
questions.rule: Outline first, then come to terms.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In analytical reading, coming to terms is the first step beyond the ____.
questions.explain: The first stage ends with an outline of the book's structure; coming to terms is the first step past it, into the book's meaning.
questions.rule: Coming to terms follows the outline.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: A reader who outlines a book on nutrition and then starts listing which of its claims she agrees with has skipped a step.
questions.explain: Between the outline and agreeing or disagreeing lies interpretation, and its first step is coming to terms with the author's key words. Without it she may be agreeing with meanings the author never intended.
questions.rule: Do not judge claims before coming to terms.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A student outlines a history of money, then argues with friends about its claims without settling what the author means by credit, which the author uses in a narrow sense. What is the likeliest result?
options: They reach agreement faster, since less is taken for granted
They understand the book better, since debate tests its claims
They argue over a claim the author may never have made
Nothing changes, since the outline already fixed the meanings
optionExplain: Fewer shared meanings means more room for talking past each other, not less.
Debate can test claims, but only claims the debaters have understood as the author meant them.
Right: if they read credit in a wider sense than the author's, the claim they dispute is theirs, not his.
An outline fixes the book's structure, not the meaning of its words.
questions.explain: Without coming to terms, readers attach their own meanings to the author's words. The claims they then argue about may not be the author's at all.
questions.rule: Unsettled terms make every later step unreliable.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A new nurse reads her hospital's handover protocol. She already knows its structure: arrival, checks, sign-off. What should she settle next, before following its instructions?
options: Whether it is longer than the last version she used
Who wrote it and when it was last revised
Whether colleagues follow it in practice
What it means by words like stable and urgent
optionExplain: Length tells her nothing about what the instructions require.
Authorship and dates matter for trust, but she cannot act on instructions whose key words she reads in her own sense.
How others behave is a separate question from what the protocol asks.
Right: words like stable and urgent carry the instructions; if she reads them in another sense she may follow every line and still act wrongly.
questions.explain: Knowing a text's structure is not knowing what it says. By analogy with reading a book, she must first share the protocol's meanings for its key words.
questions.rule: Structure first, then shared terms, then action.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any text meant to pass on knowledge or instructions, such as a protocol, needs shared terms first: a reader who takes one key word in another sense can follow every sentence and still act wrongly.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Mia reasons: Step 1, I outlined the book. Step 2, I came to terms with its key words. Step 3, so I now know that the author's position is correct. Which step goes wrong?
options: Step 1, because an outline should come after terms
Step 3, because shared meanings do not settle truth
Step 2, because terms come only after judging
No step, because shared terms show the author is right
optionExplain: The outline belongs to the first stage, so it rightly comes before terms.
Right: coming to terms tells her what the author means, not whether what he says is true.
Terms come before any judging; judging without them is the error.
Understanding an author's meaning is needed before judging him, but it is no proof he is right.
questions.explain: Coming to terms starts interpretation. Whether the author is right is a later question, which needs his meaning first but is not answered by it.
questions.rule: Understanding is not agreeing.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: If you and an author use exactly the same words, you have understood each other.
questions.explain: The same word can carry different meanings for writer and reader. The card next explains why a term is not the same as a word.
questions.rule: Same words do not guarantee same meanings.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: According to the authors, when an author uses a word in one meaning and the reader takes it in another, ____ have passed between them, but terms have not.
questions.explain: When the meanings differ, only the words have passed between them. Unresolved ambiguity leaves communication failed or, at best, incomplete.
questions.rule: Shared words without shared meanings are not terms.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Sort each case: did writer and reader come to terms, or share only the words?

items.t: A tenant takes major repairs to mean structural work, as the landlord does
A cook folds in the flour gently, as the recipe writer intended
A student reads energy in a physics text in the physicist's sense
A manager says finished to mean a draft; her team hears final
A reader takes theory in a science book as a guess; the author meant a tested explanation
A voter hears free care as no cost at all; the speaker meant no charge when treated

questions.explain: In the first three cases the reader takes the word in the writer's meaning, so a term is shared. In the last three the word is the same but the meanings differ, so only words passed between them.
questions.hint: Ask whether the reader's meaning matches the writer's, not whether the words match.
questions.rule: A term is shared only when the meaning is.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A reader shares nearly all of an author's meanings but misreads the one word on which the main argument turns. How do the authors' ideas describe this reading?
options: Total failure, since one of the words is misread
Full success, since nearly all meanings are shared
Partial success, with the gap where the argument turns
Partial success, with the gap in a minor detail of the text
optionExplain: Most meanings are shared, so it is not total failure; the authors allow for incomplete communication.
Counting shared meanings misses where the gap lies; one key word can carry the whole point.
Right: communication is partial, and the missing meaning is the one the main argument turns on.
One word can look like a detail, but this is the word the argument turns on, so the gap is central, not minor.
questions.explain: The authors say unresolved ambiguity leaves communication absent or at best incomplete. Here it is incomplete, and the failure sits in the word that matters most.
questions.rule: Weigh a misreading by where it falls, not by how many words it touches.
questions.teaches: Where a misreading falls matters more than how many words it touches: missing the word an argument turns on loses the argument itself, even when every other meaning is shared.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A doctor tells a patient that a test came back positive. The doctor means the condition was found; the patient hears good news. Why is this kind of gap especially hard to catch?
options: Patients do not listen closely when they are anxious
Both think they agree, since the word is the same
Doctors rarely explain the results of medical tests
The word positive has only one meaning in medicine
optionExplain: Anxiety may play a part, but the gap would arise even for a calm listener, because the word itself carries two meanings.
Right: a shared word gives both sides the feeling of agreement, so nothing prompts either to check the meaning.
Doctors may explain well or badly; the point here is why the gap goes unnoticed once the word is used.
In medicine the word has a fixed sense, but the patient brings the everyday sense, which is how the gap arises.
questions.explain: When the word is the same, each side assumes the meaning is too. That false sense of agreement is what keeps the ambiguity unresolved.
questions.rule: An unnoticed difference in meaning is the most dangerous kind.
questions.teaches: The most harmful ambiguity is the kind neither side notices: because the word is the same, both feel they agree, so nothing prompts them to check the meaning.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In which case is a difference between the author's meaning and the reader's least likely to matter?
options: The word in the book's title, which the author uses in a special sense
A common word the author has quietly made technical for his whole argument
A word the author defines with care in the opening chapter
An everyday word, used in its everyday sense, outside the main argument
optionExplain: A title word used in a special sense is likely to carry the book's main idea, so a gap there matters a great deal.
A common word made technical is a classic trap, since the reader thinks he already knows it.
A word the author takes care to define is one he thinks matters, so misreading it would matter too.
Right: everyday words used in everyday ways rarely mislead, and a small gap outside the argument changes little.
questions.explain: The worry is unresolved ambiguity in the words that carry the argument. An everyday word, used in an everyday way, outside the argument, rarely causes harm.
questions.rule: Concentrate on the words that carry the argument.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: What must a writer and a reader end up sharing for communication between them to have succeeded?
options: The same words, set out in the same order
A meaning that both of them now hold
Agreement that what was said is true
A feeling of having been understood
optionExplain: Words in the same order can still be read in different meanings.
Right: success means a common something, such as a piece of knowledge, now held by both.
Agreement is a further step; people can share a meaning and still disagree.
Feeling understood can happen when no meaning is shared at all.
questions.explain: Communication succeeds when something, such as a piece of knowledge, comes to be held in common. The card next traces this to the word itself.
questions.rule: Communication ends in something shared.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: The authors point out that the root of the word communication is related to the word ____.
questions.explain: Communication, like community, is related to common: it succeeds when something comes to be held in common.
questions.rule: To communicate is to make something common.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A coach tells the team to press high. Half the players press from kick-off; the other half wait for a signal. In the authors' terms, what did the whole team hold in common after the talk?
options: A shared plan, since they all heard the coach
Only the words press high
A meaning, since every player nodded
Agreement that pressing high is wise
optionExplain: Hearing the same words is not holding the same plan, as the split on the pitch shows.
Right: the words were common to all, but the meaning split in two, so only the words were shared.
Nodding shows a feeling of understanding, not a shared meaning.
They may all approve of pressing, but approval of a phrase is not a shared meaning of it.
questions.explain: With ambiguity, the only thing held in common is the words. The split in behaviour shows two meanings, so the plan was not communicated.
questions.rule: Shared words, split meanings: nothing communicated.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Two readers finish the same article. Both say they understood it, yet their summaries describe different main claims. What follows from the authors' test of communication?
options: Both have understood, since each feels sure of it
The article must be badly written, since readers differ
At most one of them shares the author's meaning
Both share the author's meaning in different words
optionExplain: Feeling sure is not the test; the test is a meaning held in common with the author.
Readers can differ because of their own reading, so the summaries alone do not prove the article is at fault.
Right: two different main claims cannot both be the author's one meaning, so at least one reader has missed it.
Different words could express one meaning, but here the summaries name different claims, not one claim reworded.
questions.explain: If communication succeeded, each reader would hold the author's meaning. Different claims show at least one did not, whatever they feel.
questions.rule: Where summaries part company, look for the failed meaning.
questions.teaches: When two readers' summaries of one text disagree, the point where they part company locates where a meaning failed to pass, which tells them which passage, and often which word, to go back to.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A tourist and a shopkeeper share no language. The shopkeeper types 12 on a calculator, the tourist hands over 12 euros, and both are satisfied. By the authors' test, did communication take place?
options: No, because they shared no words at all
Only partly, because gestures carry no knowledge
No, because a price is not knowledge
Yes, since a meaning became common to both
optionExplain: Shared words are not the test; a shared meaning is, and here one was reached without words.
A gesture or a number can carry a definite meaning, as this exchange shows.
The price is an item of information that both now hold, which counts.
Right: both now hold the same item of information, the price, which is what success requires.
questions.explain: The test is a common something, such as an item of information that both parties share. Here the price is shared, even though no words were.
questions.rule: Meanings, not words, are what must be shared.
questions.teaches: By analogy, communication needs a shared meaning rather than shared words: a number or a gesture can carry one, while identical words without a shared meaning carry nothing.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: Two people who disagree about whether a claim is true cannot have communicated about it.
questions.explain: They may hold the claim's meaning in common and differ only on its truth. A shared meaning is not the same as agreement.
questions.rule: Sharing a meaning is not agreeing with it.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Which is the most accurate definition of a term, in the authors' sense?
options: A word with only one dictionary meaning
A technical word that experts use
A word used in one meaning at a time
A word set in italics or bold type
optionExplain: Few if any words have only one dictionary meaning, so this would leave almost no terms.
Experts use many technical words, but a technical word can still be used ambiguously.
Right: a term is a word used unambiguously, in one sense at a time.
Italics may mark an important word, but type does not fix its meaning.
questions.explain: Almost every word has several meanings, so what matters is how it is used. The card next gives the authors' definition.
questions.rule: A term is a word used in one sense.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: According to the authors, a term is best defined as a word used ____.
questions.explain: Strictly there are no unambiguous words, but a word can be used unambiguously, in one sense at a time, and then it is a term.
questions.rule: Terms are words used unambiguously.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A fitness writer uses fit to mean able to run five kilometres, and holds to that meaning throughout the article. Fit has several dictionary meanings. Is it a term in this article?
options: Yes, because it keeps one meaning throughout
No, because the dictionary lists several meanings
No, because fit is an ordinary, everyday word
Yes, but only if a definition is printed
optionExplain: Right: the word is used in one definite sense, which is what makes it a term.
Having many dictionary meanings does not stop a word being used in one of them.
Everyday words can serve as terms when used in one definite sense.
A printed definition helps, but steady use in one sense is what makes the term.
questions.explain: Being a term depends on use, not on the word. Used in one sense throughout, fit works as a term here.
questions.rule: Use, not the dictionary, makes a term.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Halfway through, the fitness writer starts using fit to mean healthy in general, without signalling the change. What happens for the reader?
options: The word stays a term, since its spelling is unchanged
Fit may stop working as a term at the unmarked change
Nothing, since healthy and fit mean the same thing
The reader should discard the first half of the article
optionExplain: The spelling never makes a term; the use does, and the use has shifted.
Right: an unsignalled change of sense can leave the reader holding the wrong meaning from that point on.
Able to run five kilometres and healthy in general are different meanings; one can hold without the other.
The first half used the word definitely; it is the later passages that lose their footing.
questions.explain: A term holds only while writer and reader use the word in one sense. An unmarked change breaks that agreement for the reader.
questions.rule: An unmarked change of sense ends the term.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A contract opens: In this agreement, Delivery means arrival of the goods at the buyer's warehouse. What does this clause do, in the authors' language?
options: It shows the drafter distrusts the buyer
It makes the contract longer and harder for either side to use
It replaces the meaning delivery has elsewhere
It fixes one sense so the word can serve as a term
optionExplain: Distrust is not the point; the clause protects both sides from reading the word differently.
It adds a line but spares readers from guessing, which makes the contract easier to use.
It does not change the word in general, only how it is used inside this document.
Right: the clause makes every later use of delivery carry one meaning for writer and reader alike.
questions.explain: A definitions clause makes writer and reader agree to use the word in one sense for the length of the document, which is what a term needs.
questions.rule: Fixing a sense in advance turns a word into a term.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a definitions clause in a contract deliberately makes a word a term for the length of a document: it fixes one sense so that every later use can be read in it.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: An author who uses nature in one sense in chapter 2 and in a different, openly signalled sense in chapter 9 is using the word ambiguously.
questions.explain: A term needs one definite sense at a time, not one sense per book. If each use is definite and the change is signalled, the reader can follow, and both uses work as terms.
questions.rule: One sense at a time, not one sense forever.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: To find out what an author means by a key word, the best single source is a good dictionary.
questions.explain: A dictionary lists the senses a word can have, but not which one this author is using here. The card next shows where terms come from.
questions.rule: Dictionaries list senses; authors choose them.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: According to the authors, you cannot find terms in dictionaries, though the ____ for making them are there.
questions.explain: A dictionary supplies the materials, the possible senses. Terms themselves arise only when writer and reader use a word in one sense.
questions.rule: The dictionary holds materials, not terms.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A reader meets the word culture in an anthropology book, looks it up, and finds four senses. What should she do next?
options: See which sense fits the author's usage
Take the first sense, as the most common
Choose the sense she finds most useful
Assume the author means all four senses
optionExplain: Right: the dictionary gives candidates; the author's usage shows which one he means.
The first-listed sense is often the commonest, but the author may use a less common one.
Her preference is not the author's meaning; coming to terms means following his use.
An author may combine senses, but assuming all four without checking his usage is a guess.
questions.explain: Terms arise when the reader follows the writer's use of words. The dictionary narrows the field; the author's usage settles it.
questions.rule: Let usage choose among dictionary senses.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A writer uses a word in a sense that no dictionary records, but explains that sense in her text. Can the word work as a term?
options: Yes, if the reader follows the sense she has set
No, because a term needs a meaning recorded in some dictionary
No, because readers cannot learn new senses
Only after a dictionary adds the new sense
optionExplain: Right: terms are made in communication, so a sense fixed in the text and followed by the reader is enough.
Terms are not found in dictionaries at all, so a recorded entry is not what makes one.
Readers learn new senses from usage all the time; that is what following an author means.
A later entry would record the sense, but the term already exists once writer and reader share it.
questions.explain: Because terms arise in the act of communication, a sense need not be in any dictionary. What matters is that the writer fixes it and the reader follows.
questions.rule: Terms are made in use, not recorded beforehand.
questions.teaches: A sense need not appear in any dictionary to work as a term: if the writer fixes it in the text and the reader follows it, the term exists, because terms are made in communication rather than recorded in advance.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A new hire hears her team talk about the next sprint. She looks up sprint and finds: a short, fast run. Why does this not tell her what the team means?
options: Her dictionary must be an old edition
The team's sense comes from its own practice
The team is using the word carelessly
Workplace words have no fixed meanings at all
optionExplain: A newer edition might add a sense, but the team's meaning lives in how the team uses the word.
Right: the team has built a sense through its own use, which she learns by following that use.
The team may use the word quite precisely; it is only that the sense is theirs, not the dictionary's.
Their sense can be perfectly definite; she has not yet learned it.
questions.explain: Terms arise in communication. By analogy, a team, like an author, gives a word a sense through use, and a newcomer learns it by following that use.
questions.rule: Learn a group's terms by following its usage.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any group with its own practice, such as a workplace, a sport or a hobby, builds senses of words through use, and a newcomer learns them the way a reader learns an author's terms, by following how the words are used.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: In coming to terms with an author, a dictionary is of no use at all.
questions.explain: The dictionary holds the materials: the range of senses a word can have. It helps narrow the choice, even though only the author's usage settles it.
questions.rule: Use the dictionary for candidates, the text for the choice.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In which kind of writing might deliberate ambiguity be a strength rather than a fault?
options: A lyric poem
A legal contract
A chemistry textbook
A set of assembly instructions
optionExplain: Right: a poem can gain from several readings living in one line.
A contract that can be read two ways invites disputes.
A textbook exists to convey knowledge, which ambiguity blocks.
Instructions that can be read two ways lead to mistakes.
questions.explain: Works that convey knowledge need definite meanings; poems may thrive on several. The card next explains the difference.
questions.rule: Ambiguity can serve a poem.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: The authors state the rule about coming to terms for expository works, those that convey knowledge.
questions.explain: The authors say they are speaking of expository writers and books. Poetry and fiction are far less concerned with unambiguous words.
questions.rule: Coming to terms is a rule for expository works.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Sort each text: is ambiguity a fault here, or may it be intended?

items.t: A statistics textbook chapter on sampling
The user manual for a washing machine
A history of the Cold War
A love sonnet
The closing line of a novel
A song lyric about leaving home

questions.explain: The textbook, manual and history try to convey knowledge, so unclear words are a fault. A sonnet, a novel's last line and a lyric may use several meanings at once on purpose.
questions.hint: Is the text trying to convey knowledge?
questions.rule: Expository: avoid ambiguity. Imaginative: it may be the point.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Some thinkers, the philosopher Leibniz among them, tried to design an ideal language in which no word could be used ambiguously. What do the authors say would follow if they succeeded?
options: Reading would at last become effortless
There would be no more poetry
Expository books would grow much longer
Dictionaries would no longer be needed
optionExplain: Expository reading might ease, but the authors draw a different consequence.
Right: the authors remark that success would end poetry, which lives on the many meanings of words.
Length is not the point the authors make about such a language.
Dictionaries might change, but the authors' remark is about what would be lost.
questions.explain: Poetry can be richly ambiguous by design. A language of one-meaning words would remove what poetry works with, so the authors say there would be no more poetry.
questions.rule: Ambiguity is a loss for exposition and a resource for poetry.
questions.teaches: According to the authors, a perfect language of one-meaning words, the kind Leibniz and his followers tried to devise, would put an end to poetry, so the only course in expository works is to use real language as skilfully as possible.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A party's policy paper promises fair taxes and does not say what fair means, so that different voters can read in their own view. How should a reader trained by this chapter treat that ambiguity?
options: As a strength, since good writers are ambiguous on purpose
As a matter of style that does not affect the content
As a fault, since the paper claims to convey a proposal
As a sign that the paper is really a kind of poetry
optionExplain: Purposeful ambiguity is a virtue the authors allow to poets, not to works meant to convey knowledge.
In an expository text the key words are the content; a vague key word leaves the proposal unknown.
Right: the paper presents itself as conveying a proposal, so leaving its key word open is a fault to note.
Being vague on purpose does not make a policy paper imaginative writing; it still claims to inform.
questions.explain: What decides is what the text is trying to do. A policy paper claims to convey knowledge of a proposal, so a deliberately open key word counts against it.
questions.rule: Judge ambiguity by the job the text claims to do.
questions.teaches: Intended ambiguity is not always a poetic virtue: by analogy, in a text that claims to convey knowledge, such as a policy paper, deliberate vagueness is a fault to note, because it stops the reader learning what is actually proposed.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A biology chapter opens with an image: the cell is a busy city. Which response best fits the authors' ideas?
options: Read the chapter as poetry, since it opens with an image
Reject the chapter, since expository books must avoid all imagery
Enjoy the image, then look for the definite terms it rests on
Treat city as a technical word of biology from now on
optionExplain: One image does not change what the chapter is trying to do, which is to convey knowledge.
The demand is for definite terms where knowledge is conveyed, not a ban on every image.
Right: the image helps, but the chapter's knowledge rests on terms such as membrane and nucleus, which need definite meanings.
The image is a comparison, not a new technical sense of city.
questions.explain: The line between exposition and imagery is not sharp. Judge by what the passage is doing: here the image serves an expository chapter whose terms still need to be definite.
questions.rule: An image in an expository book serves its terms; it does not replace them.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: The fifth rule of reading has two parts. Which two?
options: Locate the important words
Fix the meanings the author gives them
Look each one up in a good dictionary
Count how often each one appears
Decide whether the author is right
optionExplain: Right: the first part is finding the words that make a difference.
Right: the second part is fixing, with precision, the meaning the author gives them.
A dictionary lists senses but cannot say which one the author uses.
Frequency can hint at importance, but counting is not part of the rule.
Judging truth comes later, after the author's meaning is understood.
questions.explain: The rule pairs a search for the important words with a precise reading of their meanings. The card next states it.
questions.rule: Find the words, then fix their meanings.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Put these steps of an analytical reading in the order the authors give them.
items: Outline the book's structure
Locate the important words
Determine what those words mean as the author uses them
questions.explain: Outlining ends the first stage. The fifth rule then opens the second: first locate the important words, then determine their meanings.
questions.rule: Outline, locate, determine.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Sam reads a housing report, highlights affordable, density and supply, and moves on to the conclusion. Which part of the fifth rule has he left undone?
options: Picking out the words in the report that matter most
Outlining the sections of the report
Judging whether the report is right
Fixing what the report means by those words
optionExplain: He has done this part: the highlighted words look like the ones that make a difference.
Outlining belongs to the first stage; the question is about the fifth rule.
Judging comes after interpretation, not as part of the fifth rule.
Right: affordable in particular can mean many things, and he has not settled the report's sense.
questions.explain: Sam has located the words but not determined their meanings. A list of key words with no meanings attached is half the rule.
questions.rule: Highlighting is half the rule.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A reader decides to fix a precise meaning for every word on the page, articles and prepositions included. What is the likeliest result?
options: Effort goes to words that need none, and the argument slips by
She comes to terms faster, since nothing at all is left unexamined
She discovers that most ordinary words are ambiguous here
The book becomes easier, since all its words are defined
optionExplain: Right: precision is needed for the important words; spreading it over every word wastes attention.
Examining everything is slower, and it hides which words make a difference.
Ordinary words used in ordinary ways rarely cause trouble.
Defining every word adds work without clearing the real difficulties.
questions.explain: The first part of the rule exists to pick out where precision is needed. Skipping it spreads effort thinly and can lose the argument.
questions.rule: Precision where it matters, not everywhere.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In a planning meeting, the director keeps saying the project must be lean. Carrying the fifth rule over to listening, what should you do?
options: Assume lean means cheaper, its usual sense
Treat lean as a key word and ask what she means
Let it pass, since a meeting is not a book
Repeat lean in your own reports to show you agree
optionExplain: The usual sense may not be hers; lean can mean fewer staff, fewer steps or a smaller budget.
Right: a word a speaker keeps leaning on is a key word, and in a meeting you can ask her directly what she means.
Words stand between speaker and listener just as they do between author and reader.
Repeating the word shares the word, not the meaning.
questions.explain: The same two parts apply: locate the word that matters, then fix its meaning. A live speaker, unlike a book, can be asked.
questions.rule: Find the speaker's key words and ask what they mean.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the fifth rule carries over to listening: note the words a speaker keeps leaning on and find out what they mean to the speaker, which in a talk or meeting you can often do by asking, as a reader of a book cannot.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: When reading a lyric poem, the fifth rule requires you to fix one precise meaning for each important word.
questions.explain: The rule is stated for expository works. A poem may be richly ambiguous on purpose, so forcing one meaning on each word can lose what it offers.
questions.rule: Rule 5 is for expository books.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: If every word had only one meaning and could not be used ambiguously, readers would still need to interpret what authors mean.
questions.explain: With perfect language a reader would see straight through the words to the writer's thought. The card next shows why real language needs two steps.
questions.rule: Imperfect language is why interpretation exists.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Match each item with what the authors say about it.
pairs: Deals with the words as such
Deals with meanings, that is, terms
questions.explain: Each interpretive rule has a step about words and a step about the thought behind them. Both are needed, since words and thought only communicate together.
questions.rule: Words carry thought; both steps are needed.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Reading a law article, you notice that the word reasonable carries the argument. That is the grammatical step. What is the logical step?
options: Working out what standard reasonable expresses here
Counting how often reasonable appears in the article
Checking that reasonable is spelled the same throughout
Finding a synonym for reasonable to use in your notes
optionExplain: Right: the logical step reaches the thought, here the standard of conduct the author means by the word.
Frequency stays at the level of words; it does not reach their meaning.
Spelling is about the word as such, the grammatical side.
A synonym is another word; it helps only once you know the meaning it must match.
questions.explain: The grammatical step finds the word; the logical step moves to the term, the meaning the author gives it.
questions.rule: From word to meaning is the logical step.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: The authors say skill in reading and writing is gained through two arts, grammar and logic. Why both?
options: Both join language to thought, from either side
Grammar is for writing, and logic is for reading
Grammar teaches spelling, and logic teaches debate
Both are needed to pass exams in reading and writing
optionExplain: Right: grammar treats language in relation to thought, and logic treats thought in relation to language, so each art serves both reading and writing.
Both arts serve both activities; a writer needs logic and a reader needs grammar.
Spelling and debate are narrow pieces of the arts, not what links them to reading.
The authors' point concerns skill in communication, not exams.
questions.explain: Reading and writing join language to thought. Grammar and logic are the arts that study that joint, from either side, so skill in both comes through them.
questions.rule: Grammar and logic are the arts of words joined to thought.
questions.teaches: According to the authors, grammar and logic, as arts, deal with language in relation to thought and with thought in relation to language, which is why skill in both reading and writing is gained through them.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A translator renders a German contract into English word by word, giving each word its commonest English equivalent. Which step has he skipped?
options: The grammatical step, since he ignored the rules of German grammar
The logical step: he never asked what each word meant
Neither step, since every word has been carried over
Both steps, since he only consulted a word list
optionExplain: He dealt with the words closely; what he neglected was their meaning in context.
Right: by matching words without grasping the thought, he may carry over the words and lose the meaning.
Carrying over every word is the grammatical step alone; the thought may not survive it.
A word list is a grammatical tool; he did take the grammatical step, but not the logical one.
questions.explain: Word-for-word work stays at the grammatical step. The logical step asks what each word means here, which a common equivalent may not capture.
questions.rule: Translate thoughts, not only words.
questions.teaches: By analogy, word-for-word translation shows what happens when the logical step is skipped: the words are carried over but the thought may not be, because each language's words carry their own range of senses.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: The logical step cannot be taken without the grammatical one, since the thought reaches a reader only through the words.
questions.explain: Thought cannot be communicated without language. The logical step works on the words the grammatical step has found, so it depends on it.
questions.rule: The thought reaches you only through the words.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: When a difficult book is not getting its meaning across, who do the authors think must put in the effort?
options: The writer alone, since he chose the words
The reader alone, since the book itself cannot change
Both writer and reader, each from his own side
A teacher who explains the book to the reader
optionExplain: The writer must try hard, but the authors say he cannot do the job by himself.
The reader must work, but a writer who made no effort would leave him little to work with.
Right: communication needs effort from both sides, like crews tunnelling toward each other.
A teacher can help, but the authors describe communication between writer and reader, with each doing a share of the work.
questions.explain: The authors treat communication as joint work against the barrier of language. The card next shows what the reader's share is.
questions.rule: Both sides must work.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a skilled enough writer can achieve communication without any matching skill on the part of readers.
questions.explain: As teaching needs a matching activity of being taught, writing needs matching skill in reading. No author can communicate alone.
questions.rule: Writing skill needs reading skill to meet it.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Which of these readers of a hard philosophy book are meeting the author halfway? Choose all that apply.
options: One who rereads a passage to see how a key word is used
One who marks the words that give him trouble
One who stops at page ten, saying the author should write more plainly
One who works through the author's definitions before the argument
One who reads it at newspaper speed and hopes it sinks in
optionExplain: Right: following the author's use of a word is the reader's side of the work.
Right: marking troubling words locates where his share of the work lies.
Plainer writing might help, but stopping leaves the author tunnelling alone.
Right: the definitions are the author's effort to reach him, and working through them meets it.
Reading at newspaper speed treats the book's words as if they needed no work.
questions.explain: Meeting the author halfway means active work on his words: following usage, marking difficulties, using his definitions. Giving up or reading passively leaves the author to do it all.
questions.rule: Halfway means active work on the author's words.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: The authors add that tunnelling crews meet only if they make their calculations by the same principles of engineering. What does this add to the halfway picture?
options: That the reader should dig faster than the writer
That the writer must do most of the calculating
That a meeting is a matter of luck more than skill
That effort must follow rules both sides share
optionExplain: Speed is not the point; crews digging fast in different directions still miss each other.
The picture gives both crews the same task; neither does the calculating for the other.
The point is the reverse: the meeting is planned by shared principles, not left to chance.
Right: effort meets only when both sides work by the same rules, here the rules of writing and reading.
questions.explain: Two crews can each work hard and still miss. They meet when both follow the same principles; reader and writer likewise meet when both follow rules for using words.
questions.rule: Shared rules make shared effort meet.
questions.teaches: Effort alone does not bring writer and reader together: like tunnellers who must calculate by the same principles, they meet only when both follow the same rules, which is why the rules of reading mirror those of good expository writing.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A software team writes setup instructions with a glossary of its terms. A new developer skips the glossary, gets stuck, and reports that the instructions are unclear. What does the halfway idea suggest?
options: The team should rewrite them so no glossary is needed
He should use the glossary before judging the text
Instructions should be so plain that no effort is needed
He should ask a colleague and skip the text in future
optionExplain: Rewriting may help later readers, but he has not yet used the help already offered.
Right: the glossary is the writers' side of the tunnel; using it is his side.
Some effort is part of any reading that teaches something new.
Asking can help, but abandoning the text does not meet its writers anywhere.
questions.explain: The team did part of the work by defining its terms. By analogy, the reader's part is to use that help before deciding the text is at fault.
questions.rule: Use the help a text offers before blaming it.
questions.teaches: By analogy, documentation, like a book, assumes a reader who does part of the work: before blaming a text for being unclear, check whether you used the help it offered, such as its glossary or its definitions.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Which reader has gone past meeting the author halfway, into a mistake?
options: One who rereads a hard passage to follow a key word
One who notes where the author defines his words
One who asks what a key word means in each passage
One who credits his own meaning to the author
optionExplain: Rereading to follow usage is the reader's proper share.
Noting definitions uses the author's own effort to be clear.
Asking which sense is in use at each place is coming to terms.
Right: the reader's effort aims at the author's meaning; supplying one of his own for a vague word and calling it the author's is not meeting him.
questions.explain: Meeting halfway is working toward the author's meaning. A reader who supplies his own meaning and attributes it to the author has stopped meeting him.
questions.rule: Aim at the author's meaning, not your own.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: A single word can stand for several different terms within one book.
questions.explain: One word can carry several meanings, and each definite use of it is a different term. The card next shows how to keep them apart.
questions.rule: One word, possibly several terms.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In the authors' scheme, if X is the word reading and a, b and c are three of its meanings, then Xa, Xb and Xc are one word but three ____.
questions.explain: The word X stays the same, but each definite sense makes a different term, provided writer and reader know which is in use.
questions.rule: One word, three senses, three terms.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A health article uses fat for body fat in one section and for fat in food in another, and says which at each change. In the section on diet, a sentence says that cutting fat lowers cholesterol. Which reading is the author's?
options: Body fat, the commoner everyday sense
Both senses at once, since the word itself is the same
Fat in food, the sense the diet section signals
Neither, since fat is too common to be a term
optionExplain: Commonness is no guide; the author has signalled which sense each section uses.
One word can carry two terms, but here each use is definite, and the diet section uses one.
Right: the author signalled the sense for that section, and the reader follows it.
Common words can be terms when used in one definite sense.
questions.explain: Coming to terms means reading each use in the sense the author gives it at that place. Here the section tells you which sense applies.
questions.rule: Read each use in the sense in play at that place.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: An author uses a word in sense a in some chapters and sense b in others; a reader who takes it in sense b everywhere still shares the author's terms in every chapter.
questions.explain: Minds meet only in Xa or Xb, not in X. Wherever the author means a and the reader thinks b, they share the word but not the term.
questions.rule: Fixing one sense for every use misses the author's changes.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: An author writes early on that reading is easy and later that reading is hard. Before calling this a contradiction, what should a reader check?
options: Whether the author changed his mind between chapters
Whether a later edition quietly corrected one of the two claims
Whether reading carries the same sense in both places
Whether other critics have noted the contradiction
optionExplain: A change of mind is possible, but the first thing to rule out is a change of term under one word.
Editions can matter, but the text in hand may already be consistent once the senses are separated.
Right: easy may apply to reading for information and hard to reading for understanding, two terms under one word.
Critics may help, but the reader can check the senses himself first.
questions.explain: One word can carry several terms. If reading means Xb in one claim and Xc in the other, the two claims do not clash at all.
questions.rule: Check the terms before charging a contradiction.
questions.teaches: An apparent contradiction may be two terms under one word: before charging an author with inconsistency, check whether the word carries the same sense in both places.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In a company database, a field called date holds the order date in one table and the delivery date in another. Reports mixing the tables come out wrong. What lesson from this chapter fits?
options: One name carrying two meanings causes errors no one sees
Databases should store fewer dates, to avoid this kind of confusion
The delivery date should be dropped as less important
Reports should be checked by hand every single month
optionExplain: Right: like a word carrying two terms, the shared name hides the difference until results go wrong.
Both dates are needed; the trouble is the shared name, not the number of dates.
Dropping data does not fix the naming; it loses information.
Checking by hand might catch errors, but the cause is one name for two meanings.
questions.explain: The field name works like a word with two terms. By analogy, naming each meaning separately, such as order date and delivery date, removes the ambiguity.
questions.rule: Give each meaning its own name where you can.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the one-word-many-terms problem is why database designers and programmers give each field a precise name, such as order date and delivery date: one name carrying two meanings produces errors nobody notices.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: An essay uses freedom on one page to mean absence of restraint and on the next to mean self-mastery, with no signal and no apparent reason. What fits the authors' ideas best?
options: Assign the senses by guessing which the author probably meant
Treat freedom as one term, since the essay uses one word
Assume the sense you find more persuasive in each place
Note that the word is being used ambiguously there
optionExplain: Guessing assigns letters the text does not support.
One word is not one term; the essay shows two senses.
Choosing by persuasiveness puts your meaning in place of the author's.
Right: when an author slides between senses without signalling, the honest finding is ambiguity.
questions.explain: Labelling senses works only when each use is definite. Where the author slides without signal, the reader can report the ambiguity but not settle it.
questions.rule: Where the author slides, report the ambiguity.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Of all the words in a typical expository book, how many are important in the authors' sense?
options: Most of them, since authors choose each word with care
About half of them, the nouns and the verbs
A small share, those used in a special way
Only the few words that appear in the title
optionExplain: Care in choosing words does not make most of them special; most are used as anyone uses them.
Most nouns and verbs are ordinary words used in ordinary ways.
Right: the important words are the few the author uses in a special way.
Title words may be important, but key words appear throughout the book.
questions.explain: Most words are used as everyone uses them and need no special work. The card next shows how to pick out the rest.
questions.rule: Few words are key words.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the important words in a book are those the author uses in a special way.
questions.explain: Words used as the proverbial man in the street uses them give no trouble. The ones used specially are important for the author and for the reader.
questions.rule: Special use marks a key word.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In a personal finance article, sort each word as it is used: ordinary, or special?

items.t: month, in pay the bill each month
house, in save up to buy a house
spend, in spend less on coffee
liquidity, defined as how fast an asset turns into cash
compound interest, explained as interest earned on interest
risk, used to mean the spread of possible returns

questions.explain: Month, house and spend are used as anyone uses them. Liquidity, compound interest and risk are given special senses that carry the article's advice.
questions.hint: Would a friend in conversation use the word in this sense?
questions.rule: Work on the specially used words.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Eddington trusted readers to follow reading from pointer readings to reading nature. What do the authors say about a reader who could not follow such shifts among ordinary senses?
options: He could not talk with friends or do his daily business
He would need a technical dictionary of physics at his side
He would read more carefully than most people
He would have to skip the book's first chapters
optionExplain: Right: following shifts among ordinary senses is part of everyday speech, so the authors say such a reader could not manage daily life.
A technical dictionary helps with special senses, not ordinary ones.
Missing ordinary shifts is not care; it is a gap in everyday skill.
The difficulty would arise on every page, not in particular chapters.
questions.explain: Everyone follows shifts among the ordinary senses of words all day. That is why ordinary words are not where a reader's work lies.
questions.rule: Ordinary shifts are handled by everyday skill.
questions.teaches: The authors observe that following shifts among a word's ordinary senses is a skill everyone uses daily; a reader who lacked it could not talk with friends or carry on his daily business, so ordinary words are no real obstacle.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Energy appears in a self-help book, in have more energy in the mornings, and in a physics textbook, in energy is conserved. In which book is it likely to be an important word?
options: Both books, since it is the same word
Neither book, since energy is a common word
The self-help book, since energy is its central promise
The physics book, where it is used specially
optionExplain: The same word can be ordinary in one book and special in another; importance follows the use.
Common words can be used specially, as energy is in physics.
The promise uses energy as anyone would, in its everyday sense, so it needs no special work there.
Right: physics gives energy an exact sense, while the self-help line uses it as anyone would.
questions.explain: Importance belongs to how a book uses a word. The authors make the same point about reading, ordinary for Eddington and important in their own book.
questions.rule: A word's importance depends on the book using it.
questions.teaches: A word can be ordinary in one book and special in another: the authors note that reading is ordinary in Eddington's book but important in theirs, so importance belongs to the use in a given book, not to the word.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Which is the weakest reason for treating a word in a book as ordinary?
options: The author uses it in passing, with no stress
Its meaning shifts only in the ways it does in daily talk
Context makes its everyday sense plain each time
It is a familiar word you use every day yourself
optionExplain: Use in passing, without stress, is a fair sign of ordinary use.
Shifts like those in everyday talk are what ordinary use looks like.
Context that makes the everyday sense plain is good evidence.
Right: a familiar word can be used in a special sense, so familiarity alone proves little.
questions.explain: The test is how the author uses the word, not how familiar it is to you. Familiar words can be given special senses without warning.
questions.rule: Familiar is not the same as ordinary in this book.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: In a book written centuries ago, a word that looks ordinary to you may not have been used in today's ordinary sense.
questions.explain: Ordinary usage changes with time and place. The card next explains why old books and translations need extra care.
questions.rule: Ordinary is relative to time and place.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: According to the authors, which of these make it harder to tell an author's ordinary words from his special ones? Choose all that apply.
options: The book was written long ago
The author uses archaic senses on purpose
The book is translated from another language
The book is printed in a small typeface
The book runs to more than five hundred pages
optionExplain: Right: in older books it is harder to know how most people of that time used a word.
Right: deliberately archaic words or senses complicate the matter further.
Right: translation adds another layer between you and the author's usage.
Type size affects comfort, not which words are ordinary.
Length makes reading longer, not ordinary words harder to spot.
questions.explain: Your sense of ordinary usage comes from living now. Age, archaism and translation all weaken that guide.
questions.rule: Age, archaism and translation call for extra care.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A reader studies an English translation of an ancient Greek work on ethics in which virtue appears on every page. What extra care does this chapter suggest?
options: Assume virtue means moral goodness, as it does in English today
Skip virtue, since translators choose words freely
Swap virtue for a word that sounds more modern
Ask whether virtue carries the author's sense or today's
optionExplain: Today's sense is exactly what may mislead in an old, translated book.
Translators choose with care, and a word on every page is likely a key word.
A modern-sounding word only hides the question of what the author meant.
Right: age and translation both mean today's ordinary sense may not be the author's.
questions.explain: In an old and translated book, today's sense of a word is a weaker guide. A word that recurs on every page deserves the question of what it meant for the author.
questions.rule: Check old key words against the author's time, not yours.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: If the same book were written by a living author for readers today, your own sense of ordinary usage would be a more reliable guide to which of its words are ordinary.
questions.explain: Contemporary writers use most words as people now use them, and you know that usage because you are alive today.
questions.rule: Your own usage guides you best with books of your own time.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A British report says a committee will table a motion. An American reader takes this to mean the motion will be set aside, its sense in American usage. What has gone wrong?
options: The British writer has used the word carelessly
An ordinary sense in one place is not ordinary in another
The American has misread an old, archaic sense of the word table
Reports should avoid all words with two meanings
optionExplain: In British usage the phrase means to put the motion forward for discussion, so the writer used it ordinarily.
Right: the phrase is ordinary in both countries, but with different senses, so place matters as well as time.
Both senses are current; nothing archaic is involved.
Most words have more than one meaning, so this would be impossible.
questions.explain: The authors warn that words are not equally familiar at different times and places. By analogy, two places sharing a language can still differ in a word's ordinary sense.
questions.rule: Ask whose ordinary usage a writer follows.
questions.teaches: The same caution applies across places as well as times: by analogy, a word can be ordinary in different senses in two countries sharing a language, as table a motion is in British and American English.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Which response to an old book overdoes the caution this chapter recommends?
options: Checking a key word that reads slightly oddly in context
Asking whether a title word meant then what it means now
Looking up the old sense of every word, even of and the
Noting where the translator explains a choice of word
optionExplain: A key word that reads oddly is exactly where care pays off.
Title words often name the book's main ideas, so their old sense matters.
Right: most words in an old book read as they always have; the care is for words that matter.
Translators' notes are help offered for precisely this problem.
questions.explain: The extra care is aimed at important or odd-looking words. Most words in an old book need no special work.
questions.rule: Aim old-book caution at the words that matter.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: On a typical page of an expository book, which words can mostly be read as you would read them in everyday talk?
options: Only the articles, prepositions and conjunctions
Articles, prepositions and nearly all nouns and verbs
Only the words in the headings and the captions
Only the short words of one or two syllables
optionExplain: Articles and prepositions are ordinary, but so are most nouns and verbs.
Right: almost every word on a page is used as anyone would use it.
Headings may hold key words; the ordinary words are spread throughout.
Length is no guide; many short words are key words and many long ones are ordinary.
questions.explain: Most of the words on a page need no special work. The card next shows how few carry the meaning.
questions.rule: Most words on a page are ordinary.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Of the few important words in the opening of their chapter on terms, the authors say the most important is ____.
questions.explain: The authors list word, term, ambiguity and communication, and say that term is the most important, the others mattering in relation to it.
questions.rule: One key word is central; the rest relate to it.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A passage reads: Herd immunity arises when enough people are immune that a disease cannot spread; the threshold depends on how contagious the disease is. Which words carry its meaning? Choose three.
options: herd immunity
threshold
contagious
enough people
arises when
depends on
optionExplain: Right: herd immunity is the idea the passage explains.
Right: threshold names the point the explanation turns on.
Right: contagious is what the threshold depends on.
Enough people is a plain phrase used as anyone would use it.
Arises when is a link between ideas, used in its everyday sense.
Depends on links ideas but carries no special sense.
questions.explain: Most of the words are ordinary. Herd immunity, threshold and contagious carry the meaning, with herd immunity at the centre.
questions.rule: Find the few words that do the work.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: The authors say word, ambiguity and communication matter in relation to term. What does this suggest about how to record an author's key words?
options: List them alphabetically so none is missed
List them in the order they first appear in the text, page by page
Put the central word first and note how each relates to it
Give each the same weight, since all are key words
optionExplain: Alphabetical order hides how the words depend on one another.
First appearance is a weak guide; the central word may appear late.
Right: recording relations to the central word turns a list into a map of the author's ideas.
The authors rank them: term first, the others important in relation to it.
questions.explain: If one word is central and the rest matter through it, a record that shows those relations captures more of the author's thought than a flat list.
questions.rule: Record key words with their relations.
questions.teaches: A record of key words is more useful when it shows their relations: putting the central word first and noting how each other word bears on it turns a list into a map of the author's ideas.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: After a lecture on inflation, one student has two pages of verbatim notes. Another has five words, inflation, expectations, wages, prices, credibility, joined by arrows showing how each bears on inflation. Whose notes better hold the lecture's substance?
options: The verbatim notes, since nothing is left out
Both equally, since both record the lecture
Neither, since only a recording keeps the substance
The five linked words, since they hold its key terms
optionExplain: Verbatim notes keep the words but bury the few that matter among the many that do not.
They record very different things: one the words, the other the structure of ideas.
A recording keeps every word, but finding the key ones is still the listener's work.
Right: if the speaker's terms are well chosen, the key words and their links hold most of the meaning.
questions.explain: By analogy with a page, a talk's meaning rests on a few key words. Capturing them and their relations compresses the talk without losing its substance.
questions.rule: Key words with links compress a talk.
questions.teaches: Picking out the few words that carry a talk lets you compress it without losing its substance: by analogy with a page, the key words and their links hold most of the meaning of the many words around them.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: The word that appears most often on a page is the most important word on it.
questions.explain: Articles and prepositions appear most often and are ordinary. A key word is marked by special use, not by frequency.
questions.rule: Frequency is not importance.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: When you do not fully understand a passage, what is the likeliest cause, according to the authors?
options: Not knowing how the author uses certain words
Reading too slowly to keep hold of the thread
The passage being printed too densely on the page
A factual error made somewhere by the author
optionExplain: Right: the authors trace most failures to understand to words the author uses in a way you do not know.
Slowness is rarely the problem with hard expository books.
Layout can tire you, but it does not hide meaning.
Errors happen, but the first suspect is your grasp of the author's words.
questions.explain: The authors say that failing to understand a passage is probably due to not knowing how the author uses some words. The card next turns this into a method.
questions.rule: Misunderstanding usually points to words.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, you cannot locate the key words of a passage without making an effort to understand it.
questions.explain: The authors say you cannot locate the key words without trying to understand the passage. The trouble you meet in trying is what points to them.
questions.rule: Understanding and finding key words go together.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A history of medicine says that doctors balanced a patient's humours by bleeding. The sentence puzzles you. What does this chapter suggest?
options: Skip it as a detail of old-fashioned medicine
Assume humours means moods, its everyday sense
Mark humours as a word the author may use specially
Stop reading until you can find a medical dictionary
optionExplain: The puzzle may hide one of the book's key words, so skipping it loses a lead.
The everyday sense makes the sentence strange, which suggests the author means something else.
Right: the word that will not fit its everyday sense is the one to mark.
Marking and reading on lets the context help; stopping cuts you off from it.
questions.explain: The sentence stops you because one word does not fit its everyday sense. That makes humours a candidate key word worth marking.
questions.rule: Mark the word that stops you.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: According to the authors, if you fully understand a passage, you will already know which of its words are the most ____.
questions.explain: Understanding a passage includes knowing which words carry it. The paradox is that you need key words to understand, and understanding to find them.
questions.rule: Full understanding reveals the key words.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A student's economics textbook says: Demand for salt is inelastic, so a sharp rise in its price barely changed sales. She is stuck on this one sentence. What does this chapter suggest she do first?
options: Reread the whole chapter from the start, slowly
Skip to the chapter summary and hope it explains
Look for the word she may be reading in the wrong sense
Copy the sentence into her notes so she can learn it by heart
optionExplain: Rereading everything spreads her effort over pages she already follows, when the block is in one sentence.
A summary may repeat the word without explaining it, and skipping leaves the block in place.
Right: inelastic is used in a special economic sense; once she marks it and works out that sense, the sentence opens up.
Learning the sentence by heart keeps the words without the meaning she is missing.
questions.explain: When a passage will not yield, the likely cause is a word used in a way the reader does not know. Here inelastic, meaning that sales respond little to price, is the word to mark.
questions.rule: Name the word behind the block.
questions.teaches: Naming the word that blocks a sentence turns a vague feeling of being lost into a precise question, one that can then be checked against the author's definition or his other uses of the word.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: You stall on four passages. Which stall is least likely to point to a key word?
options: One where an everyday word is used in an odd way
One where a word in italics will not fit its usual sense
One where a word's usual sense makes the claim absurd
One where an 80-word sentence of plain words loses you
optionExplain: An everyday word used oddly is a classic sign of special use.
Italics plus a poor fit with the usual sense strongly suggest a key word.
If the usual sense makes nonsense, the author probably means another.
Right: a long sentence of plain words is a problem of construction, not of a word's sense.
questions.explain: Trouble can come from sentence length or a missing step as well as from words. A long sentence of ordinary words points to construction, not to a key word.
questions.rule: Not every stall is a word problem.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: The words that give a reader trouble are likely to be important words for the author too.
questions.explain: Likely, but not certain. The card next explains why the reader's list and the author's list differ.
questions.rule: Troubling words are likely key words.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: According to the authors, from the reader's point of view the most important words are those that give you ____.
questions.explain: The authors say that, for the reader, the most important words are the ones that give trouble, and they are likely, though not certain, to matter for the author.
questions.rule: For you, trouble marks importance.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Several words trouble a reader of a book on climate. Sort them by what the clues suggest.
groups: Likely a key word for the author too
Likely important only for the reader

items.t: albedo, which the author keeps returning to
feedback, which the author says he uses in a special sense
forcing, which appears in a chapter title
ubiquitous, used once in passing
erstwhile, in an anecdote in the preface
perspicacious, praising a colleague in the acknowledgements

questions.explain: Words the author returns to, stresses or puts in titles are likely his key words. Words that appear once in passing are more likely gaps in the reader's vocabulary.
questions.hint: Does the author give the word weight, or does it pass by once?
questions.rule: Check troubling words for signs of the author's stress.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A word that troubled you turns out to be an ordinary word you had not met, used in its everyday sense. What is the sensible next step?
