options: Study it as closely as the author's own key words, to be safe
Settle it quickly, then return to the key words
Ignore it, since it is not a key word
Treat it as a key word, since it troubled you
optionExplain: Close study is for specially used words; an everyday word needs less.
Right: a quick lookup settles an ordinary word and saves effort for the key words.
It still blocks the passage until settled, so it is important for you.
Trouble made it important for you, not a key word of the author's.
questions.explain: Troubling words need different kinds of work. An unfamiliar ordinary word needs a quick fix; a specially used key word needs the slower work of coming to terms.
questions.rule: Quick fix for new ordinary words; real work for key words.
questions.teaches: Troubling words call for two kinds of work: an unfamiliar ordinary word needs only a quick lookup, while a specially used key word needs the slower work of coming to terms, so sorting them early saves effort.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A book club compares the words that troubled each member. Five of six were stopped by the same word; one member alone was stopped by another. Which word is the stronger candidate for one of the author's key words?
options: The word that stopped five members
The word that stopped only one member
Both equally, since each troubled someone
Neither, since a group cannot judge key words
optionExplain: Right: a word that stops most careful readers is more likely used in a special sense than missing from one person's vocabulary.
A word that stops one reader is more often a gap in that reader's vocabulary.
Each matters for the reader it troubled, but the evidence of special use differs.
A group can pool clues; the final test is still the author's usage.
questions.explain: A word that troubles many readers is likely used specially by the author. A word that troubles one reader is more often a personal gap. By analogy, pooling trouble gives better evidence.
questions.rule: Shared trouble points to the author's special use.
questions.teaches: By analogy, when several readers compare the words that troubled them, a word that stopped many is a strong candidate for one of the author's key words, while a word that stopped only one is more often a gap in that reader's vocabulary.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Raj reasons: Step 1, the word habitus troubled me. Step 2, so it is important for me. Step 3, so it must be one of the author's central terms. Which step goes wrong?
options: Step 1, since trouble should be ignored
Step 2, since trouble does not make a word important
Step 3, since likely does not mean certain
No step, since troubling words are the author's key words
optionExplain: Noticing trouble is exactly what the authors advise.
For the reader, trouble does make a word important.
Right: a troubling word matters to Raj, and is likely, not certain, to be one of the author's key words.
Troubling words are likely key words, but the authors say they may not be.
questions.explain: Steps 1 and 2 follow the authors. Step 3 turns likely into certain; Raj should check the author's use before deciding.
questions.rule: Likely key word is not certain key word.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A reader meets one of an author's key words and already understands it in exactly the author's sense. What should she do with it?
options: Study it at length, since it is a key word
Look it up anyway, to be thorough about it
Move on: she has already come to terms on it
Treat it as unimportant for the rest of the book
optionExplain: Study is for words not yet understood; this one already is.
A lookup adds nothing when she already shares the author's sense.
Right: understanding it in the author's sense means the term is already shared.
It stays important to the book; it simply needs no more work from her.
questions.explain: A key word you already share with the author needs no more effort. The card next explains where the effort should go.
questions.rule: Understood key words need no more work.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, only where you fail to come to terms do you have work still to do.
questions.explain: Key words you already understand in the author's sense are already terms between you. The remaining work lies where that sharing is missing.
questions.rule: Work where terms are missing.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A reader plans her time on a hard book about genetics. Sort each word by whether it needs more work.

items.t: allele, a key word she cannot yet explain
expression, which the author uses in a special sense she is unsure of
linkage, which she can explain only as an everyday word
gene, which she can explain in the author's sense
cell, used as in her school biology, as the author uses it
inherit, used in its plain sense throughout

questions.explain: Key words she cannot explain, or can explain only in an everyday sense, need work. Words she already holds in the author's sense need none.
questions.hint: Can she state the author's meaning, not only some meaning?
questions.rule: Sort key words by whether you share the author's sense.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A key word felt easy, but when asked to restate the author's meaning, a reader gives his everyday sense, which the author does not use. What does this show?
options: The author used the word carelessly
The word was never a key word at all
He had come to terms, but forgot
Feeling easy hid a missing term
optionExplain: The author's use may be quite definite; the reader did not follow it.
It is still a key word; the problem is the reader's sense of it.
Giving a different sense shows the term was never shared.
Right: the word felt easy because he read it in his own sense, so the term was missing all along.
questions.explain: No trouble is good evidence only when your sense matches the author's. His everyday sense fails to fit the author's uses, and a single such misfit shows the term was never shared.
questions.rule: Hunt for a use your sense cannot explain.
questions.teaches: One passage where your sense of a key word makes the author's sentence odd or false is enough to show the term is not shared, so scanning a word's uses for such a misfit is a fast check on a word that feels easy.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A student uses flashcards for an exam. Which way of spending study time best matches this chapter's advice on effort?
options: Go through every card equally often
Spend most time on the cards she gets wrong
Spend most time on the cards she likes best and enjoys
Study only the cards she already knows well
optionExplain: Equal time spends effort on what she already knows.
Right: effort goes where understanding is missing, as the chapter advises for terms.
Liking a card says nothing about whether she knows it.
Reviewing known cards feels good but leaves the gaps open.
questions.explain: Effort belongs where understanding has not yet been reached. By analogy, study time belongs on the cards she misses.
questions.rule: Put effort where understanding is missing.
questions.teaches: By analogy, effective study of any kind puts effort where understanding is missing, as flashcard systems do by showing the cards you miss more often than the ones you already know.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Which key word most needs checking, even though it caused you no trouble?
options: A common word the author says he uses in a special sense
A word you have already explained in the author's sense
A word used exactly as it is in everyday conversation
A preposition that occurs on nearly every page
optionExplain: Right: a common word given a special sense can feel easy while you read it in your own sense.
Having explained it in the author's sense, you have already come to terms on it.
An everyday word used in its everyday sense needs no work.
Prepositions are ordinary words and rarely carry special senses.
questions.explain: Lack of trouble counts only when your sense matches the author's. A common word given a special sense is where that match most often fails.
questions.rule: Check familiar words the author uses specially.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Which of these could signal that a word is one of an author's important words? Choose all that apply.
options: The word is printed in italics
The author discusses its several senses
The author defines the thing it names
The word falls at the start of a line
The word has an unusual spelling
optionExplain: Right: italics are one way an author marks a word for you.
Right: discussing a word's senses shows it matters to him.
Right: defining the thing a word names stresses the word.
Where a word falls on a line is set by the printer, not the author's stress.
An odd spelling may reflect age or origin, not importance.
questions.explain: Authors stress important words by typography, by discussing their senses, or by defining what they name. The card next sets out these positive signs.
questions.rule: Look for the author's own signals.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Finding key words because they bother you is a negative method. What is the first positive sign the authors name?
options: How long the paragraph around the word happens to be
Explicit stress the author puts on the word
How often the word turns up in the index
Whether the word appears in a footnote
optionExplain: Paragraph length says little about any single word.
Right: the author may stress a word by typography, by discussing its senses, or by defining what it names.
The index can help, but the authors' first sign is the author's own stress in the text.
Footnotes can hold anything; position in a note is no sign of importance.
questions.explain: The first and most obvious positive sign is the explicit stress an author places on certain words and not others.
questions.rule: Explicit stress is the first positive sign.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Match each kind of stress with an example of it in an economics book.
pairs: Growth is set in italics on first use
A paragraph contrasts three ways writers use capital
Saying how he will use it
In what follows, rent means income from land alone
A market is any place where buyers meet sellers
questions.explain: Each example is the author marking a word for you, in one of the ways the authors list: type, discussion of senses, announced use, or a definition of the thing named.
questions.rule: Type, discussion, announced use, definition: four kinds of stress.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: An author spends two pages discussing the senses of justice and says which one he will use. Beyond marking the word, how does this help the reader?
options: It proves that justice is the book's only key word
It shows the author is unsure of what he means
It supplies the meaning, the rule's second part
It saves the reader from reading later chapters
optionExplain: One word discussed at length is a key word, but not the only one.
Discussing senses shows care, not doubt; he ends by choosing one.
Right: the discussion both locates the word and tells you how he will use it.
Later chapters still use the word; the discussion helps you follow them.
questions.explain: The fifth rule has two parts: locate the word and fix its meaning. A discussion of senses does both, which is why it repays slow reading.
questions.rule: A discussion of senses serves both parts of Rule 5.
questions.teaches: Explicit discussion of a word's senses serves both parts of the fifth rule at once: it marks the word as important and supplies the author's meaning, so such passages are worth reading slowly.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A modern biology textbook prints new words in bold, defines them in the margin, and repeats them in a glossary at the end of each chapter. What are these, in this chapter's language?
options: Explicit stress, built into the book's design
Decoration meant to make the pages livelier
Signs that the textbook has no technical words
Help that a good reader should ignore
optionExplain: Right: bold type, margin definitions and glossaries are the author's signals in a systematic form.
Bold type may look lively, but here it marks words the author wants you to master.
The reverse: the devices exist because the field has many technical words.
Using the author's help is meeting him halfway, not a weakness.
questions.explain: Typography, definitions and announced uses are the authors' positive signs. By analogy, textbooks build them into every chapter.
questions.rule: Use a textbook's design as a map of its key words.
questions.teaches: By analogy, modern textbooks build explicit stress into their design, with bold type on first use, margin definitions and chapter glossaries: the same signals the authors describe, in a systematic form.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: Every word an author prints in italics is one of his key words.
questions.explain: Italics have other uses, such as marking a foreign phrase like ad hoc or the title of a book. Check that a marked word carries the argument, not only that it is marked.
questions.rule: Ask why a word is marked, not only whether.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: In Euclid's geometry, a word can be basic even though Euclid does not define anything it names.
questions.explain: Words such as equals, whole and part are not defined, yet they are basic. The card next shows how you can tell.
questions.rule: Basic words need not be defined.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: How, according to the authors, can you tell that equals, whole and part are important in Euclid?
options: Euclid defines each of them first
They occur in Euclid's axioms
They are printed in italics
They are hard words to understand
optionExplain: These words name nothing that Euclid defines; that is the point of the example.
Right: they occur in the axioms, the primary propositions stated at the start.
The authors do not mention typography for these words.
They are common words, which Euclid seems to use in their common way.
questions.explain: Words that occur in the opening principles are basic, whether or not they name something defined.
questions.rule: Words in the axioms are basic.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A club's constitution defines member, officer and quorum, then states one principle: decisions need a majority of the members present. Which words are basic by Euclid's two signs? Choose three.
options: member
quorum
majority
welcome, from a note on the cover page
newsletter, mentioned once in an appendix
optionExplain: Right: member names a defined thing and also appears in the principle.
Right: quorum names a defined thing.
Right: majority is undefined but appears in the opening principle.
A cover note is not a definition or a principle.
A passing mention in an appendix carries no weight.
questions.explain: Defined things (member, quorum) and words in the opening principle (majority) are basic. Words outside the definitions and principles are not marked by these signs.
questions.rule: Defined things and words in principles are basic.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A reader opens a philosophy book laid out like Euclid, with numbered definitions and axioms on its first pages. What does the chapter predict about finding its key words?
options: They will be hidden, since philosophers avoid definitions
The opening pages will point to many of them
The definitions will be decorative and can be skipped
Its key words will all be new, coined words
optionExplain: This book sets out its definitions openly; the layout itself is the clue.
Right: in the geometrical manner, defined things and words in the axioms are the basic terms.
In this layout the definitions are where the basic terms are fixed.
The words may be common ones, used in fixed senses, as with Euclid.
questions.explain: A book written in the geometrical manner shows its basic terms at the start, in its definitions and axioms.
questions.rule: A geometrical layout shows its key words early.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A statute opens with an interpretation section defining its terms, followed by a section of general principles. How can a reader use Euclid's two signs here?
options: Skip both sections and go straight to the operative rules
Treat only the defined terms as important
Read only the general principles, since they summarize
Treat defined terms and words in the principles as basic
optionExplain: The rules depend on the defined words; skipping the definitions leaves them open to misreading.
Undefined words in the principles can be basic too, as with Euclid's equals.
The principles use the defined terms, so they cannot be read alone.
Right: the statute copies Euclid's layout, so both signs apply.
questions.explain: Like Euclid, the statute fixes its terms first and then states principles. By analogy, both signs point to its basic words.
questions.rule: Look to definitions and principles in any document laid out like Euclid.
questions.teaches: By analogy, many modern documents, such as statutes, standards and technical specifications, copy Euclid's layout, opening with definitions and general principles, so the same two signs point a reader to their basic words.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: Euclid's basic words count as basic because they are hard to understand.
questions.explain: Point, line, equals and part are common words that may give you no difficulty. They are basic because the propositions rest on them, not because they are hard.
questions.rule: Basic does not mean difficult.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Why can't every expository author set out his terms at the start, as Euclid does?
options: Publishers object to long opening definitions
The geometrical method does not fit every field
Readers dislike books that open with rules
Only mathematics has a technical vocabulary
optionExplain: Publishing habits are not the reason the authors give.
Right: the method of exposition and proof that works in mathematics does not suit every field.
Readers' tastes are not the issue; the subject matter is.
Every field has a technical vocabulary; only the way it is presented differs.
questions.explain: Some thought any subject could be set out like geometry, but the authors say the method does not fit every field. The card next shows what follows for readers.
questions.rule: Not every field can be written like Euclid.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: According to the authors, every field of knowledge has its own technical ____.
questions.explain: This is what all exposition has in common. Euclid shows his technical vocabulary at once; in most books the reader must find it.
questions.rule: Every field has a technical vocabulary.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A gardening book does not list its terms. Sort each word as it is used there.

items.t: pH, as a measure of how acid the soil is
hardening off, moving seedlings outdoors by stages
deadheading, removing spent flowers
water, as in water the beds each evening
garden, as in my small back garden
spring, the season

questions.explain: pH, hardening off and deadheading carry fixed senses that the advice depends on. Water, garden and spring are used as anyone uses them.
questions.hint: Does the advice depend on a fixed sense of the word?
questions.rule: Find the technical words the author did not list.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Elasticity appears in a physics textbook and in an economics textbook, as a technical word in each. What does the idea of field vocabularies suggest?
options: The word has one technical sense shared by both fields
Only one of the two books can be using it correctly
Each field may give it its own technical sense
Technical words cannot appear in more than one field
optionExplain: Fields build their vocabularies separately, so a shared sense cannot be assumed.
Both can be correct within their own fields.
Right: each field's vocabulary is its own, so the same word may be technical in two senses.
Many words are technical in several fields.
questions.explain: In physics, elasticity is a material's power to return to shape; in economics, how strongly demand or supply responds to price. Knowing a book's field tells you which technical sense to expect.
questions.rule: Know the field to know the technical sense.
questions.teaches: Because each field has its own technical vocabulary, the same word can be technical in two fields with different senses, as elasticity is in physics and in economics; knowing a book's field tells you which sense to expect.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A nurse writes a leaflet for patients about managing diabetes. What does this chapter suggest she do before writing?
options: Use the words she uses at work, since they are precise
Avoid every word longer than two syllables
Leave out the technical ideas altogether
Spot the words patients will find technical
optionExplain: Precise to her, but technical to patients; precision does not help a reader who lacks the vocabulary.
Length is a poor proxy; some short words are technical and some long ones ordinary.
Patients need the ideas; the task is to make the words reachable.
Right: words that feel ordinary to an insider are technical to lay readers, so she must spot them first.
questions.explain: Every field has a technical vocabulary, and insiders stop noticing it. By analogy, a writer for outsiders must find it as a reader must.
questions.rule: Insiders must spot their own technical words.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a writer explaining her own field to outsiders must spot its technical vocabulary too, because words that feel ordinary to an insider are technical to a lay reader.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Which is the weakest sign that a word belongs to a book's technical vocabulary?
options: The book's argument keeps resting on it
It carries a fixed sense within the field
The author treats it as a word of his field
It is long, rare, or Greek in origin
optionExplain: An argument resting on a word is a strong sign it is technical.
A fixed sense within a field is what makes a word technical.
An author's treating a word as his field's own is good evidence.
Right: technical words can be short and common, and long rare words can be used ordinarily.
questions.explain: A technical vocabulary is marked by fixed senses that the argument relies on, not by how a word looks. Ordinary-looking words can be technical.
questions.rule: Judge technical words by use, not looks.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Before reading the first chapter, which of these could help you guess a book's technical words?
options: Its price and its number of pages
The colour and design of its cover and jacket
The size and style of its typeface
Its title, chapter headings and preface
optionExplain: Price and length say nothing about the vocabulary.
Cover design is chosen to sell, not to point to terms.
Typeface is the printer's choice, not a sign of terms.
Right: titles, headings and prefaces often name the book's main ideas.
questions.explain: What a book is about, and how it is divided, points to its technical words. The card next explains how.
questions.rule: Titles and headings point to terms.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the rules for analysing a book's structure can help you separate its technical words from its ordinary ones.
questions.explain: Knowing the kind of book, what it is about as a whole and its major parts helps separate the technical vocabulary from ordinary words.
questions.rule: Structure helps you find terms.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A book is called The Economics of Water, with chapters headed Scarcity, Pricing and Allocation. Which words should a reader expect to be technical? Choose three.
options: scarcity
allocation
pricing
throughout
afterwards
especially
optionExplain: Right: a chapter heading in an economics book is a strong lead.
Right: allocation heads a chapter and is a word economists use technically.
Right: pricing heads a chapter and is likely given a fixed sense.
Throughout is a linking word, used ordinarily.
Afterwards is an ordinary word of time.
Especially is an ordinary word of emphasis.
questions.explain: The title and headings name the main ideas, so their words are the first candidates for the technical vocabulary. The text must then confirm them.
questions.rule: Headings suggest technical words.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Two readers open Darwin. One has studied some biology; the other has not. What does the chapter predict?
options: The biologist has leads; the other relies more on the book's clues
Both find the technical words equally fast, since Darwin defines them all
The reader without biology finds them faster, having fewer assumptions
Neither can find them until a teacher points them out
optionExplain: Right: prior knowledge gives leads, and the book's kind, title and headings help a reader without it.
Darwin does not lay out his terms as Euclid does, so readers must find them.
Fewer assumptions can help with misreadings, but prior knowledge gives leads to which words are technical.
The book's own structure gives any reader clues; a teacher is not required.
questions.explain: Prior knowledge gives leads toward technical words. A reader without it is not helpless but leans more on structure, title, headings and preface.
questions.rule: Prior knowledge gives a head start, not the only way in.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: You are about to listen to a ten-part podcast series on the history of banking. What could you use, before the first episode, to spot its technical words?
options: The host's voice and speaking speed
Episode titles and show notes
The number of listener reviews
The length of each episode
optionExplain: Voice and pace tell you about delivery, not vocabulary.
Right: episode titles and notes work like chapter headings and a preface.
Reviews tell you about popularity, not terms.
Length says nothing about which words carry the series.
questions.explain: By analogy with titles, headings and prefaces, a series' episode titles and notes reveal its main ideas and so its likely technical words.
questions.rule: Use any structure on offer to find terms.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any material with a structure offers the same clues as a book's title and headings: episode titles and show notes for a podcast, slide headings for a lecture, section names for a report.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Lena knows physics well. Reading a philosophy book that uses energy, she takes it in the physicist's sense without checking how the author uses it. What is her error?
options: Using prior knowledge at all, since it biases reading
Reading philosophy when she trained in physics
Treating a lead from prior knowledge as a definition
Noticing energy as a possible technical word
optionExplain: The authors recommend using prior knowledge; the error lies in how she uses it.
Training in another field is no barrier to reading philosophy.
Right: her knowledge rightly flags energy, but the author may use it in his own sense.
Flagging the word is the right first move.
questions.explain: Prior knowledge points to candidate technical words. The author's use decides their meaning, which may differ from the field she knows.
questions.rule: Prior knowledge is a lead, not a definition.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: Finding one of an author's technical words tends to lead you to others.
questions.explain: Technical words are tied together in an author's analysis, so one tends to call up the next. The card next shows how to use this.
questions.rule: Technical words come in families.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Which of these do the authors list among Adam Smith's important words? Choose three.
options: labor
capital
rent
species
selection
point
optionExplain: Right: labor is on the authors' list for Smith.
Right: capital is on the list.
Right: rent is on the list.
Species is Darwin's technical word, not Smith's.
Selection belongs to Darwin's list.
Point is one of Euclid's basic words.
questions.explain: Starting from wealth, the authors list labor, capital, land, wages, profits, rent and more for Smith. Species and selection belong to Darwin, point to Euclid.
questions.rule: One technical word leads to its family.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Reading a book on music theory, you mark harmony as a technical word. Which words is it most likely to lead you to?
options: chord, interval and consonance
concert, ticket and audience
page, chapter and table of contents
loud, soft, fast and slow
optionExplain: Right: these are tied to harmony in the analysis of music, so they belong to the same family.
These words concern going to music, not its theory, and are used ordinarily.
These are words about the book, not its subject.
These are everyday descriptions that rarely carry special senses.
questions.explain: A technical word leads to others tied to it in the author's analysis. Harmony is analysed in terms of chords, intervals and consonance.
questions.rule: Follow the ties between technical words.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A reader's list of an author's technical words falls into three clusters of words that call for each other. What might the clusters tell her?
options: That the author repeats himself across chapters
Which parts of the book's analysis belong together
That her list is too long and should be cut
That the author's vocabulary is poorly organized
optionExplain: Clusters reflect connections between ideas, not repetition.
Right: words that call for each other usually belong to the same part of the analysis, which can check her outline.
The clusters say nothing about length; they show structure.
Clusters are a sign of organization, not of disorder.
questions.explain: Technical words lead to one another because they are tied in the author's analysis. Their clusters therefore sketch the analysis itself.
questions.rule: A list of key words sketches the theory.
questions.teaches: A well-made list of an author's technical words works as a sketch of his theory: words that call for each other usually belong to the same part of his analysis, which can confirm or correct your outline.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A student starts researching sleep science knowing only the phrase circadian rhythm. How can the family idea help her search?
options: Search only for circadian rhythm, to stay focused
Avoid technical phrases, since they narrow results
Use what each result links to it as new search terms
Search everyday words like tired, since they are common
optionExplain: One phrase alone misses the related words the field uses.
Technical phrases make searches more precise, not less useful.
Right: words that turn up tied to circadian rhythm, such as melatonin, are the family to search next.
Everyday words bring up everyday results, not the field's vocabulary.
questions.explain: One technical word leads to the others tied to it. By analogy, each one found becomes a search term that surfaces more of the family.
questions.rule: Use each technical word to find its neighbours.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a technical word makes a good search term: looking it up in an index or a search engine tends to surface the related technical words that belong with it, which then become the next search terms.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: Once your list of an author's technical words is complete, you have come to terms with him.
questions.explain: A list does the first part of the fifth rule, locating the words. Coming to terms also needs the second part: fixing what each word means as the author uses it.
questions.rule: A list locates terms; it does not interpret them.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Which kind of word is most likely to mislead a reader?
options: A common word an author has made technical
A newly coined word that no one has seen
A word borrowed from a foreign language
A long word taken from a scientific field
optionExplain: Right: the reader thinks he already knows it, so he reads it in its everyday sense.
A coined word is strange to everyone, so readers know they must look for its meaning.
A foreign word stands out and invites a lookup.
A scientific word looks technical, so readers expect a special sense.
questions.explain: Strange words announce themselves; familiar words used specially do not. The card next explains why this matters.
questions.rule: Familiar words used specially mislead most.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, most good authors give an explicit warning when they turn a common word into a technical one.
questions.explain: Good authors foresee that readers will treat a familiar word as ordinary, so they warn when they give it a special sense.
questions.rule: Watch for the author's warning.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Sort these words from a philosophy book as they are used there.

items.t: substance, in the substance of a thing persists through change
idea, which the author says he will use for any object of thought
will, discussed for a whole chapter as a power of the mind
chair, in I sat in my chair by the fire
letter, in I received a letter from a friend
morning, in I wrote this in the morning

questions.explain: Substance, idea and will are common words given weight, warnings or long discussion, so they are likely technical. Chair, letter and morning appear in passing in their everyday senses.
questions.hint: Is the familiar word carrying more than its everyday weight?
questions.rule: A familiar word given weight is likely technical.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A philosopher coins a new word, while another takes the everyday word care and makes it technical. Why is the coined word less likely to mislead?
options: Coined words are always defined in a glossary
Readers trust coined words more than common ones
Its strangeness tells readers to seek its meaning
Coined words have only one meaning in any book
optionExplain: Some coined words come with glossaries, many do not; that is not the reason.
Trust is not the issue; awareness of not knowing is.
Right: no one thinks he already knows a coined word, so its difficulty is out in the open.
A coined word can also be used loosely; its advantage is that it is visibly unfamiliar.
questions.explain: A common word made technical hides its difficulty behind familiarity. A coined word shows its difficulty, so readers look for the author's meaning.
questions.rule: Strange words announce themselves; familiar ones hide.
questions.teaches: A coined word announces its own difficulty, since no reader thinks he already knows it, while a common word made technical hides its difficulty behind familiarity, which is why it misleads more.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In contract law, consideration means something of value given in exchange for a promise. A tenant reads that his lease is void for lack of consideration and thinks it means a lack of thoughtfulness. What has happened?
options: The lease uses consideration carelessly
Legal words have no fixed meaning
The tenant has misread a newly coined legal word
He read a technical sense as an everyday one
optionExplain: The lease uses the word in its exact legal sense; the trouble lies in how the tenant read it.
Consideration has a fixed legal sense; that is the problem for the tenant.
Consideration is a common word, not a coined one; that is why he fell into the trap.
Right: the law has made a common word technical, and he read it in its everyday sense.
questions.explain: By analogy with philosophy, law turns common words into technical ones. A lay reader then meets the same trap: a familiar word read in the wrong sense.
questions.rule: In law, as in philosophy, familiar words may be technical.
questions.teaches: By analogy, law is full of common words made technical, such as consideration in contract law, so a layperson reading a legal document meets the same trap as a reader of philosophy.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: An author uses natural on page after page in a sense that does not fit its everyday meaning, but gives no warning. What can the reader do?
options: Read it in the everyday sense, since no warning was given
Infer the special sense from how the word behaves in context
Conclude the word must be ordinary, since it is common
Stop reading, since the author has broken the rules
optionExplain: The poor fit with the everyday meaning is itself the warning sign.
Right: without a warning, the shifted use has to be worked out from the contexts.
Commonness is exactly what makes a technical use easy to miss.
Not every author warns; the reader can still do the work.
questions.explain: Most good authors warn, but not all. Where no warning is given, the reader infers the special sense from how the word is used.
questions.rule: No warning? Infer the sense from use.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: When an author argues against the way other writers use a word, that word is probably important to him.
questions.explain: Authors do not argue about words that make no difference to them. The card next explains this clue.
questions.rule: Disputed words matter to the author.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: According to the authors, one clue to an important word is that the author ____ with other writers about it.
questions.explain: When an author explains how others have used a word and why he uses it otherwise, the word makes a great difference to him.
questions.rule: A quarrel marks a key word.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Which passage most strongly signals a key word by this clue?
options: Happiness, as people often say, is hard to find
The word happiness comes from an old English word for luck
Happiness is the word I chose for my book's title
Others call happiness pleasure; I call it activity
optionExplain: A common saying uses the word in passing.
A note on origin may interest, but it does not dispute anyone's use.
A title word is a lead, but this passage does not show a quarrel.
Right: the author sets his use against others' and promises to defend it.
questions.explain: The clue is an author telling you how others use a word and why he uses it differently. Only the last passage does that.
questions.rule: Look for others' usage set against the author's.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Besides marking a key word, how does an author's quarrel help with the second part of the fifth rule, fixing the word's meaning?
options: It lists every possible sense the word can have
It shows the rejected sense beside the adopted one
It proves that the rival writers' usage is mistaken
It saves you from reading the rest of the book
optionExplain: A quarrel usually sets out one or two rival senses, not every sense.
Right: seeing what he rejects next to what he adopts lets you define his term by contrast.
A quarrel shows his choice, not that the rival is wrong.
His later uses still need following; the quarrel gives you a head start.
questions.explain: A quarrel puts the author's sense next to the one he turns down. The contrast makes his meaning easier to pin down.
questions.rule: Define a disputed term by what it is set against.
questions.teaches: A quarrel over a word helps fix its meaning as well as locate it: seeing the sense an author rejects beside the one he adopts lets you define his term by contrast.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: At a council meeting, one member says: My opponents call this plan affordable housing, but by affordable they mean 80 percent of market rent; I mean rent no more than a third of a typical income. What does this chapter suggest about the debate?
options: The word dispute marks the real disagreement
The member is stalling, since words matter less than numbers
Both sides agree, since they use the same word
The debate is pointless, since words can mean anything
optionExplain: Right: the quarrel shows the key word, and settling its senses turns a vague fight into a clear choice.
The numbers are inside the definitions, so the word dispute is about the numbers.
Using the same word is exactly what hid the disagreement.
Each side has stated a definite sense; the debate can now proceed.
questions.explain: By analogy with books, a speaker who disputes others' use of a word is showing what matters most to him. Here the two senses of affordable are the two policies.
questions.rule: A word dispute often marks the real disagreement.
questions.teaches: By analogy, in public debate a dispute over a word often marks where the real disagreement lies: settling what each side means by the word can turn a vague fight into a clear choice.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: When an author argues against other writers' use of a word, that shows his own use is the better one.
questions.explain: A quarrel shows the word matters to the author. Whether his use is better is a later judgment, made after you understand both uses.
questions.rule: A quarrel shows importance, not correctness.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Which best describes an author's special vocabulary?
options: The small set of words that carry his main ideas
All the technical words used in his field
Only the new words he has invented himself
Every word he defines anywhere in the book, however minor
optionExplain: Right: the special vocabulary is the few words expressing his leading concepts.
A field's vocabulary is larger than the words carrying one author's ideas.
Invented words may belong, but so may traditional ones.
Some defined words are minor; the test is whether a word carries his main ideas.
questions.explain: An author's special vocabulary is the relatively small set of words for his leading concepts. The card next explains what goes in it.
questions.rule: Special vocabulary: the words for the main ideas.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, an author's special vocabulary may include words used in the way that has become traditional in his field.
questions.explain: Some of his key words may be used in a very special way and others traditionally. Either way, if they carry his main ideas, they belong to his special vocabulary.
questions.rule: Traditional or new, key words carry the argument.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Sort these words from a book on sleep.

items.t: circadian rhythm, used in its standard scientific sense throughout
sleep pressure, which the author builds her argument on
sleep debt, the author's own coinage, defined in chapter 1
pillow, mentioned in a tip about comfort
bedroom, used in its everyday sense
Tuesday, in an anecdote about a bad night

questions.explain: Circadian rhythm (traditional), sleep pressure (central) and sleep debt (new) carry her argument, so they form her special vocabulary. Pillow, bedroom and Tuesday are ordinary words in passing.
questions.hint: Does the word carry the argument?
questions.rule: Traditional or new, the carrying words are special.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Why does an author with something original to say tend to use some of his key words in a very special way?
options: Original authors like to sound difficult
Publishers ask for new words to sell books
No ready-made words fit his new ideas
Traditional words are banned in original work
optionExplain: Difficulty for its own sake is not the reason; the ideas themselves need new uses.
Marketing plays no part in the authors' account.
Right: a new idea has no ready word, so he stretches an existing one or coins one.
Original authors often use traditional words too, as the card says.
questions.explain: Saying something new means naming ideas that have no settled word. So an original author must give some words new senses, and those are where readers most need to come to terms.
questions.rule: New ideas bring new uses of words.
questions.teaches: Originality and special usage go together: an author saying something new has no ready-made words for it, so he must stretch an existing word or coin one, and those are the places where readers most need to come to terms.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A new employee reads her company's strategy document. Phrases such as operational excellence, the flywheel and customer obsession recur throughout. What does this chapter suggest?
options: Skip them, since slogans like these have no content
Look them up in a good dictionary of business terms
Treat every phrase in the document as equally weighty
Master these few phrases, since they carry the plan
optionExplain: They may sound like slogans, but if the plan rests on them, they carry its content.
Some are trade terms, but the flywheel is the firm's own; only the document shows its sense.
A special vocabulary is small; treating everything as weighty hides the few that matter.
Right: a few phrases, some from the trade and some the firm's own, carry the whole plan.
questions.explain: By analogy, an organisation's documents have a special vocabulary: a few phrases, traditional and new, that carry the argument. Mastering them unlocks most of the plan.
questions.rule: Find the few phrases a plan rests on.
questions.teaches: By analogy, an organisation's strategy documents have a special vocabulary too: a few phrases, some borrowed from the trade and some the firm's own, carry the whole plan, and an employee who masters those few understands most of it.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A reader lists sixty words as the special vocabulary of a 200-page book. What does this chapter suggest?
options: The list is probably too long to be his special vocabulary
The list is about right, since long books need many terms
The list is too short, since every defined word belongs
The number does not matter as long as the words are hard
optionExplain: Right: the special vocabulary is a relatively small set; sixty words probably mixes in minor and ordinary ones.
Length does not multiply leading concepts; a long book develops a few ideas at length.
Defined words that do not carry main ideas do not belong.
Hardness is no test; the test is whether a word carries the main ideas.
questions.explain: The special vocabulary is the relatively small set of words for an author's leading concepts. A very long list has probably swept in words that are minor, or only unclear to the reader.
questions.rule: Keep the special vocabulary small.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the trouble with most readers is that they look up too many words.
questions.explain: The authors say the opposite: most readers do not pay enough attention to words to locate their difficulties. The card next explains the remedy.
questions.rule: Most readers attend too little to words.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: According to the authors, the outstanding fault of the non-active reader is his inattention to ____.
questions.explain: Inattention to words leads to a failure to come to terms. The non-active reader does not notice which words he has not understood.
questions.rule: Attend to words, or fail to come to terms.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A reader finishes a hard chapter on monetary policy in twenty minutes, marks nothing, and feels it went well. What does this chapter suggest?
options: She has read it well, since the feeling of ease is reliable
She probably read hard words as if they were plain
She should reread it at once, more slowly, without marking
She is a gifted reader for whom marking is unnecessary
optionExplain: Ease can come from reading difficult words at newspaper level, so it is not a reliable sign here.
Right: a chapter that can teach her something should contain words she had to work on; marking none suggests she did not notice them.
Slower reading without marking repeats the fault; she needs to note her difficulties.
Talent is not the issue; the habit of noting difficult words is.
questions.explain: A book that can increase understanding contains words not fully clear to the reader. Marking nothing suggests she did not distinguish the words she understood from those she did not.
questions.rule: No marks on a hard chapter is a warning sign.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, if you read a book that could enlighten you as if all its words were as plain as a newspaper's, you might as well be reading a newspaper.
questions.explain: The book cannot enlighten you if you do not try to understand it. Treating every word as ordinary means making no headway toward interpretation.
questions.rule: Newspaper-level reading gets newspaper-level results.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Before signing an insurance policy, a buyer reads it and circles excess, exclusion and pre-existing condition, which she cannot explain. How does this chapter's habit help her?
options: It slows her down, which is a cost with no benefit
It proves the insurer is hiding something from her
It shows exactly which questions to ask before signing
It means she should refuse to sign the policy at all, to be safe
optionExplain: The slower pass buys her knowledge of where her understanding stops.
Unclear words show her gaps, not the insurer's intent.
Right: the marked words are where her understanding stops, so they become her questions.
Unclear words call for answers, not for refusal.
questions.explain: Marking the words you do not understand shows where to work. By analogy, in a binding document those words become the questions to settle before committing.
questions.rule: Marked words become your questions.
questions.teaches: By analogy, before signing any document that binds you, marking the words you cannot explain, such as excess or exclusion in an insurance policy, shows exactly which questions to ask before you commit.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A reader goes through a light magazine article on holiday packing and marks no words. Is this the fault of inattention the authors describe?
options: Yes, since every text has words that need marking
Yes, since the authors say all reading must be marked
No, since magazine articles are never worth reading
Not necessarily, since the text may teach nothing new
optionExplain: A text that adds nothing to your understanding may have no difficult words at all.
The authors' warning concerns books that can increase understanding.
Many articles are worth reading; this one simply poses no word problems.
Right: the fault is failing to notice difficult words that are there; an easy text may have none.
questions.explain: The fault is inattention to words that need work. A text that teaches nothing new may contain none, so finding none is not always a failure.
questions.rule: No marks is a fault only when there were words to mark.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: You have marked a word an author uses often. What is the most useful first question to ask about it?
options: Does he use it in one sense or in several?
Can I find a synonym to put in its place?
Is it listed in a standard dictionary?
Do other authors in the field use it often?
optionExplain: Right: whether the word stands for one term or several shapes everything you do next.
A synonym helps only once you know which sense to match; if the word has several senses, one synonym will misread some uses.
The dictionary gives candidates, but not how this author uses the word.
Other authors' habits do not settle this author's usage.
questions.explain: A marked word stands either for one term or for several. The card next explains why this comes first.
questions.rule: First ask: one sense or several?

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, if an author uses a word in several senses, the word stands for several terms.
questions.explain: A word used in a single sense stands for a single term; a word used in two or more senses stands for several terms.
questions.rule: Several senses, several terms.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A reader has checked how a book uses each of these words. Sort them.

items.t: gravity, meaning the same force in every chapter
point, used as Euclid uses it, the same each time
inflation, always the general rise in prices
culture, sometimes the arts and sometimes a way of life
power, sometimes energy per second and sometimes political control
interest, sometimes a charge on loans and sometimes a concern

questions.explain: A word used in a single sense throughout stands for one term. A word that shifts between senses stands for several, and each use must be read in its own sense.
questions.hint: Does the word keep the same meaning across the book?
questions.rule: Sort marked words by how many senses they carry.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A reader checks a word's first five uses, all in chapter 1, finds one sense, and decides it is a single term. How firm is that decision?
options: Firm, since five uses are plenty to go on
Provisional, since later chapters may shift it
Firm, since authors keep their senses fixed
Worthless, since no sample can show anything
optionExplain: Five uses from one chapter can all agree while later chapters shift the sense.
Right: a sample from one chapter is a start; uses from across the book are needed before deciding.
Many authors shift senses from place to place, as the card says.
A sample can show a great deal if it is drawn from across the book.
questions.explain: Whether a word has one sense or several is a pattern across the whole book. A judgment from one chapter should be checked against uses elsewhere.
questions.rule: Sample uses from across the book.
questions.teaches: Deciding whether a word has one sense or several needs a sample of uses from across the book: the first few uses may agree while later chapters shift, so a judgment drawn from one chapter is provisional.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A survey report uses satisfied in every chart. In one chart it means very satisfied; in another it means at least somewhat satisfied. Why does the one-sense-or-several question matter here?
options: Because satisfied is a vague word that should be banned
Because charts should not use words at all
Because the report's authors must be dishonest
Because figures that look comparable are not
optionExplain: The word can be used precisely; the trouble is that it carries two senses here.
Charts need labels; the labels need definite senses.
Two senses may come from carelessness, not dishonesty.
Right: one word stands for two terms, so a reader who assumes one sense compares unlike figures.
questions.explain: By analogy, a report's key measure is a key word. If it stands for two terms, numbers that seem to measure the same thing do not.
questions.rule: Check a measure's word for one sense or several.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a report's key measure, such as satisfied in a survey, should be checked for one sense or several: if it means very satisfied in one chart and at least somewhat satisfied in another, figures that look comparable are not.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A reader finds that labour keeps one sense throughout a book on economics, and concludes it will keep that same sense in every economics book. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, since economists all agree on their terms
One sense in this book says nothing of other books
Labour cannot have a single sense in any book
She should have used a dictionary instead
optionExplain: Writers in a field often use words differently, especially where the vocabulary is unsettled.
Right: one sense or several is a fact about this book's usage, not about the word.
A word can keep a single sense within one book, as she found.
A dictionary lists senses but cannot say which a given author uses.
questions.explain: Whether a word carries one meaning or many is settled book by book. Another author may give the same word other senses.
questions.rule: Settle senses book by book.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: An author uses one word in three senses. Which step helps most in following him?
options: Choosing the sense you like and keeping it
Counting how often each sense appears
Replacing the word with a symbol everywhere
Noting where each sense is used, and why
optionExplain: Keeping one sense means misreading every place he uses another.
Frequency does not tell you which sense a given use carries.
One symbol for three senses repeats the problem in a new form.
Right: seeing where each sense occurs, and what prompts it, lets you follow his shifts.
questions.explain: Following a many-sensed word means tracking where each sense is used and what in the context calls for it. The card next sets out the steps.
questions.rule: Track where each sense appears.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Put the authors' procedure for a marked word in order.
items: Decide whether the word has one meaning or many
If many, see how the meanings are related
Note where each sense is used and what in the context explains the shift
questions.explain: First settle one or many; if many, relate the meanings; then track each sense through the text and look for the reason for each shift.
questions.rule: One or many, relate, then track.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In a book on health, positive means a test result showing a condition in some passages and a hopeful outlook in others. Which context clue best tracks the shift?
options: Whether the passage is about tests or about attitudes
Whether the word falls early or late in the chapter
Whether the sentence containing it is long or short
Whether the passage includes numbers or tables
optionExplain: Right: the subject of the passage tells you which sense is in play.
Position in a chapter does not decide the sense.
Sentence length has nothing to do with which sense is meant.
Numbers often go with test results, but a passage on outlook may cite figures too; the subject is the surer clue.
questions.explain: The reason for a shift usually lies in what the passage is about. Test results call for one sense, patients' outlook for the other.
questions.rule: Let the passage's subject show the sense.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A reader has found that state means both a nation and its apparatus of government, and that the second is part of the first. How does knowing this relation help with a new, unclear use?
options: It shows that the two senses are really the same
It lets her place the use by asking which side it leans to
It means she can safely ignore the difference between them from now on
It proves the author is using the word ambiguously
optionExplain: Related senses are still different senses.
Right: with the relation in mind, she asks whether the use concerns the whole nation or its governing part.
The difference matters; claims about the apparatus need not hold of the nation.
Related senses used definitely are not ambiguity.
questions.explain: Senses that share a core can be told apart by asking which side of the core a use leans to. Knowing the relation turns a guess into a question with two answers.
questions.rule: Use the relation between senses to place new uses.
questions.teaches: Seeing how a word's senses are related lets you place a new use: when senses share a core, as nation and government do for state, an unclear occurrence can be settled by asking which side of that core it leans to.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A learner of French meets passer meaning to pass, to spend time, to take an exam and to stop by. How does this chapter's procedure help?
options: Learn one translation and use it everywhere
Avoid the verb until its meaning settles
Relate its senses and note each one's contexts
Memorize the four senses in alphabetical order
optionExplain: One translation will misread three of the four uses.
A common verb cannot be avoided, and its senses never settle into one.
Right: relating the senses and tracking their contexts lets her follow the verb as flexibly as a native speaker.
A list without contexts does not tell her which sense a given sentence uses.
questions.explain: By analogy, a many-sensed word in a foreign language is followed the same way as an author's: relate the senses and note what in each context calls up which.
questions.rule: Relate senses and track their contexts.
questions.teaches: By analogy, learners of a foreign language can follow a many-sensed word, such as French passer, the same way: group its related senses and note which contexts call up each, rather than memorizing one translation.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: When a word's sense shifts and the context gives no clue, the reader should assume the author planned the shift for a reason.
questions.explain: Some shifts are everyday senses slipping in by habit, and some are lapses by a careless author. Where the context offers no clue, there may be no reason to find.
questions.rule: Not every shift is designed.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: According to the authors, how do you find the meaning of a word you do not understand?
options: Ask someone who is an expert in the subject
Look it up in a dictionary as soon as it appears on the page
Use the surrounding words you already understand
Skip it and hope the book explains it later
optionExplain: An expert may help, but the authors describe a method the reader can use alone.
A dictionary lists senses but cannot say which the author means.
Right: the meanings of the familiar words around it fix the meaning of the strange one.
Skipping gives up the materials the context already offers.
questions.explain: The authors' answer is to work from the meanings of the other words in the context. The card next explains why this is the only way.
questions.rule: Work from the words you know.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: The authors admit that working out a word's meaning from its context can seem circular at first.
questions.explain: They grant it may seem to go round in circles, but say there is no other way, and that patience and practice show it works.
questions.rule: Circular at first, workable with practice.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A report says: The old bridge was friable; chunks of its concrete crumbled at a touch. From the context, friable means easily ____.
questions.explain: You know chunks, crumbled and at a touch. Together they fix friable: easily crumbled.
questions.rule: Familiar neighbours fix a strange word.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: An essay says: Unlike pleasure, which comes and goes with circumstances, happiness in my sense belongs to a whole life and cannot be had in a moment. What does the author mean by happiness?
options: A quality of a life taken as a whole
A strong feeling of pleasure in the moment
Whatever a person happens to want
Good fortune that comes from circumstances
optionExplain: Right: the familiar words whole life and cannot be had in a moment fix the sense.
The author sets happiness against momentary pleasure.
Nothing in the context ties happiness to wants.
Circumstances are linked to pleasure, which he contrasts with happiness.
questions.explain: The context uses words you know: unlike pleasure, whole life, cannot be had in a moment. They fix the author's special sense of happiness.
questions.rule: Read the contrast and the familiar words around a term.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A word appears in four passages. Each passage, read alone, leaves two or three possible meanings. What is the best way to use them?
options: Pick the meaning the first passage suggests
Compare them, keeping meanings that fit all four
Choose the meaning that appears most interesting
Give up, since no passage settles it alone
optionExplain: The first passage alone leaves several meanings open.
Right: each context rules out some meanings, so together they narrow the field further than any one can.
Interest is no guide to what the author means.
No single passage settles it, but together they may.
questions.explain: Each context excludes some candidate meanings. Comparing a word's uses across passages narrows it down more than any single passage can.
questions.rule: Let several contexts narrow a meaning.
questions.teaches: Several uses beat one: each context rules out some candidate meanings, so comparing a word's uses across passages narrows it further than any single passage can.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A new slang word turns up in a teenager's group chats, in no dictionary yet. How do the friends come to understand it?
options: From the familiar words around it in many messages
They wait until a dictionary records it
They ask the person who first used it to define it
They do not; slang words have no definite meaning
optionExplain: Right: hearing it in many messages, they fix its meaning from the words they know around it.
Dictionaries record slang long after people already understand it.
Some may ask, but most learn it from use without any definition.
Slang can be quite definite within the group that uses it.
questions.explain: By analogy, people learn new words from context all the time. Familiar words in many settings fix the meaning of the new one.
questions.rule: Everyday word learning works through context.
questions.teaches: By analogy, people pick up new slang the same way a reader finds an author's meanings: hearing a word in several conversations, they fix its sense from the familiar words around it long before any dictionary records it.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Ben opens an advanced text in which nearly every sentence has two or three words he does not know. He tries to work out each from context and gets nowhere. What best explains this?
options: The method of context does not work for adult readers
He should have read faster to see more context
Context helps only when most of it is understood
The text must be badly written, since context fails
optionExplain: Adults use context constantly; the method is fine.
Speed gives no more understood words to work from.
Right: with too many unknown words, there are not enough familiar ones to fix the rest; easier reading may come first.
A text can be well written for experts and still too dense for a beginner.
questions.explain: Context works by using the words you understand. When too few are understood, the method has too little to work with.
questions.rule: Context needs enough known words.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: For a definition to help you, you must already understand the words used in it.
questions.explain: A definition is stated in words; if they are unclear to you, so is the defined word. The card next shows how a good definition works.
questions.rule: Definitions rest on words you know.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Euclid defines a point as that which has no ____.
questions.explain: Euclid fixes the meaning of point by defining the thing it names, using words he assumes you already understand.
questions.rule: A point is that which has no part.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A glossary defines a sinecure as a post that pays a salary but needs little or no work. A reader knows post, salary and work. What can she now say about sinecure?
options: It is a paid job with almost nothing to do
It is a job that pays very badly for hard work
It is any well-paid job in government service
It is an unpaid post held for the honour of it
optionExplain: Right: the familiar words salary and little or no work build the meaning.
This reverses the definition: the salary is paid and the work is light.
The definition says nothing about government; the point is pay without work.
The definition says the post pays a salary.
questions.explain: She works from meanings she already has, post, salary and work, and builds the defined word from them.
questions.rule: Build a defined word from the words you know.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Euclid's point is that which has no part. If no physical thing lacks parts, what follows about Euclid's point, according to the authors?
options: It must be a very small physical thing
It cannot be a physical thing at all
It can be seen only under a microscope
It is a word without any meaning
optionExplain: Any physical thing, however small, has parts on this assumption, so a point cannot be one.
Right: something with no parts cannot be physical if every physical thing has parts.
Being seen under a microscope would make it physical, with parts.
The definition gives point a definite meaning; it names something non-physical.
questions.explain: Working through the definition with words you know shows what kind of thing a point is: if physical things all have parts, a partless thing is not physical.
questions.rule: Follow a definition to its consequences.
questions.teaches: A definition can carry consequences beyond itself: the authors note that if no physical thing lacks parts, Euclid's point cannot be physical, so working through a definition can show what kind of thing a term names.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Some learners' dictionaries write every definition using a fixed core vocabulary of about two thousand common words. Why does this design make sense, in the light of this chapter?
options: It keeps the dictionary short and cheap to print
It shows off how few words English really needs
It ensures each definition rests on words learners know
It avoids having to define the difficult words at all, which saves space
optionExplain: Length may change, but the purpose is understanding, not cost.
English has a huge vocabulary; the design serves learners, not a claim about English.
Right: a definition helps only if its own words are understood, so the dictionary limits them to common ones.
Difficult words are defined; they are defined in easy words.
questions.explain: A definition works only through words the reader already has. By analogy, a learners' dictionary turns that point into a rule for every entry.
questions.rule: Define in words the reader already has.
questions.teaches: By analogy, learners' dictionaries define every entry using a small core vocabulary, so each definition rests on words the reader already knows: the authors' point about definitions turned into a design rule.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: A definition stated in words that are themselves unfamiliar to you will bring you to terms with the defined word.
questions.explain: A beginner told that entropy measures the microstates compatible with a macrostate learns nothing if those words are strange. The definition passes the difficulty along until its own words are understood.
questions.rule: Unclear definitions pass the difficulty along.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: When readers say a hard book in their own language is all Greek to them, the authors think they have usually not really tried to understand it.
questions.explain: The authors say giving up would be fair only if the book really were in a foreign language. The card next explains why a reader has what is needed.
questions.rule: Hard is not foreign.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: If every word of a book were strange to you, as in a wholly foreign language, you could make no ____.
questions.explain: Without any familiar words there is no context to work from. A book in your own language is not like that.
questions.rule: Familiar words make progress possible.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: A reader of a book in her own language on game theory who meets three unfamiliar words a page already has all the materials she needs to begin interpreting them.
questions.explain: Most words on each page are familiar, and they form the context for the strange ones. The job is hard but possible.
questions.rule: The familiar words are the materials.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A reader complains that a book is full of words he does not readily understand. What do the authors suggest this difficulty indicates?
options: The book is probably badly or carelessly written
The book is meant only for specialists in the field
He should put it down and read something easier
The book may be able to teach him something new
optionExplain: Hard words can come from good writing about new ideas.
Difficulty does not settle who a book is for.
Difficulty alone is no reason to drop a book that can teach him.
Right: a book that can enlighten you probably contains words you do not readily understand.
questions.explain: The authors argue that a book's power to give new insight indicates it will contain words you do not readily understand. Difficulty is the price of learning something new.
questions.rule: Difficult words can signal a book worth reading.
questions.teaches: According to the authors, a book's power to enlighten you is itself a sign that it will contain words you do not readily understand: some difficulty is the price of learning something new from it.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: An engineer is handed a medical research paper and says it is all Greek. What does this chapter suggest about reading outside her field?
options: She should not try without a medical degree
Its ordinary words give her a foothold
She should read only the abstract and stop
She should translate every term before starting
optionExplain: A degree helps, but the familiar words already give her a way in.
Right: the technical terms sit among ordinary words that let her begin to interpret them.
The abstract is a start, but the context in the full paper helps fix its terms.
Working from context as she reads is the method; translating everything first is not needed.
questions.explain: By analogy, a paper outside your field is not in a foreign language. Its ordinary words surround its technical ones and give a newcomer the context to work from.
questions.rule: Outside your field, start from the ordinary words.
questions.teaches: By analogy, reading outside your own field is rarely all Greek: a specialist paper is written mostly in ordinary words, and these give a newcomer a foothold on its technical ones.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: When is it most reasonable to set a hard book aside for an easier one on the same subject?
options: When the first page has a word you do not know
When too little of it is familiar to make progress
When it takes longer to read than a newspaper
When it contains any technical words at all
optionExplain: One strange word is normal in a book that can teach you.
Right: if too few words and too little background are familiar, an easier book can supply them first.
A book that teaches should take longer than a newspaper.
Technical words are expected; the familiar words around them are the way in.
questions.explain: The job is possible, not always possible today. When too little is familiar, an easier book can build the context the hard one needs.
questions.rule: Set a book aside only when too little is familiar.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: What do the authors compare the work of finding a book's meanings to?
options: Putting together a jigsaw puzzle
Climbing a ladder rung by rung
Following a recipe step by step
Looking words up in an index
optionExplain: Right: meanings are fitted by trial and error, each fitted piece helping with the rest.
A ladder is strictly ordered; the authors stress trial and adjustment instead.
A recipe gives fixed steps; the authors say there is no rule of thumb.
An index points to places, but does not fit meanings together.
questions.explain: The authors use the picture of a jigsaw: pieces fitted by trial, the picture growing clearer as more fit. The card next develops it.
questions.rule: Finding meanings is like a jigsaw.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In the authors' jigsaw picture, a word in place is a ____.
questions.explain: A word in place is fixed by the meaning you and the author share, which is what a term is.
questions.rule: A placed word is a term.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: Halfway through a hard book, words tend to fall into place more easily than at the start, partly because fewer remain to be placed.
questions.explain: Each word placed makes the next easier: fewer pieces remain, and the picture they show is clearer.
questions.rule: Each fitted word helps the next.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A reader refuses to read past page one until she has fixed the meaning of its hardest word. What is the likely result?
options: She will understand the rest of the book faster
It will be harder, with few pieces in place
She will discover the word needs no work
Nothing different, since order does not matter in a jigsaw
optionExplain: Early on, few terms are in place, so the hardest word is at its hardest.
Right: placing a piece is easier when more of the picture is already in place.
The hardest word usually needs the most work.
Order matters: the more pieces fitted, the easier the remaining ones.
