questions.explain: In a jigsaw, the hardest pieces are easier to place once more of the picture is done. Holding up all reading for one word removes the context that would help.
questions.rule: Let the picture grow before forcing hard pieces.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A crossword solver is stuck on a long, hard clue. Following the jigsaw idea, what should she do?
options: Keep at the hard clue until it is solved
Look up the answer and move on
Start again with a different crossword
Fill easier clues that cross it, for letters
optionExplain: Staring at one clue ignores the help that placed answers give.
Looking it up skips the work and the skill.
A new puzzle brings the same problem back.
Right: easy answers supply letters for the hard one, as placed terms help fix the remaining ones.
questions.explain: By analogy, placed pieces constrain the remaining ones. Crossing answers give the hard clue letters, as known terms give a hard word its context.
questions.rule: Place what you can, and let it help with the rest.
questions.teaches: By analogy, crossword solvers work as the jigsaw idea suggests: easy answers supply letters for hard ones, so starting with what you can place, rather than with the hardest clue, speeds the whole grid.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Which word needs the least trial and error to place?
options: A word the author never explains, used in a special sense
A word whose sense shifts between chapters without warning
A word the author defines plainly on first use
A word that fits two different readings of a passage
optionExplain: An unexplained special word has to be placed by trial against its context.
Unmarked shifts make placing harder, not easier.
Right: a plain definition hands you the piece already fitted.
A word that fits two readings needs more trial to settle.
questions.explain: Trial and error is for words the author leaves you to place. A plain definition does much of the fitting for you.
questions.rule: Plainly defined words come already fitted.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, when you cannot make an author's words fit together, the fault may lie with the author rather than with you.
questions.explain: No book is ideally good, and some authors use words ambiguously. The card next explains how to tell which case you are in.
questions.rule: The misfit may be the author's.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Why, according to the authors, do errors in placing meanings tend to get corrected?
options: The author points them out in later chapters
Teachers or fellow readers usually catch them
While they remain, the picture cannot be completed
Dictionaries warn readers about the commonest mistakes of this kind
optionExplain: Authors rarely know which errors a reader has made.
Many readers read alone; the correction comes from the text itself.
Right: a wrongly placed meaning blocks the rest from fitting, so the error shows itself.
Dictionaries list senses, not a reader's misplacements.
questions.explain: A wrong meaning stops other pieces fitting. That failure is what reveals and corrects it.
questions.rule: Misfits reveal errors.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A meaning you assigned stops fitting. Put the steps the chapter suggests in order.
items: Notice that a new passage does not fit your reading
Try a different sense for the word
Recheck earlier passages under the new sense
If no sense makes the words fit, conclude the author was imprecise
questions.explain: Readjust your own readings first, checking that the new sense fits throughout. Only when no reading works do you conclude the author used words ambiguously.
questions.rule: Readjust first, blame the author last.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A reader took risk, in a finance book, to mean the chance of losing money. Then the author called a bond that cannot lose money, but whose returns swing widely, risky. She readjusts to risk as variation in returns. What should she do next?
options: Recheck earlier passages that used risk
Carry on, since only later passages are affected
Decide the author contradicted himself
Use both senses wherever risk appears
optionExplain: Right: earlier passages read under the old sense may now read differently.
A change in a term's sense affects every place it appears, before and after.
The new sense makes the bond passage fit, so there may be no contradiction.
Using both senses at once brings back the ambiguity she has just resolved.
questions.explain: Readjusting one word can force a series of readjustments. Earlier passages must be read again under the new sense to see whether the whole picture now fits.
questions.rule: A new sense must be checked backwards too.
questions.teaches: Readjustment runs backwards as well as forwards: when a new reading of a word fits, recheck the earlier passages that used it, since they may now read differently.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Assembling flat-pack furniture, you reach a step where a panel will not fit. What does this chapter's approach suggest?
options: Force the panel, since the picture shows it there
Blame the instructions at once and improvise
Retrace your steps before blaming the instructions
Give up and return it, since the kit must be faulty
optionExplain: Forcing a misfit hides the error that caused it.
Instructions can be wrong, but your earlier steps are the first suspect.
Right: check your own work first; blame the instructions only if a careful retrace still fails.
Giving up leaves the error, wherever it lies, unfound.
questions.explain: By analogy with a book, a misfit may be yours or the author's. Retracing your own steps comes first; the instructions are at fault only if that fails.
questions.rule: Retrace before you blame.
questions.teaches: By analogy, following any set of instructions has the same two-way check: when a step will not work, first retrace your earlier steps, and blame the instructions only when a careful retrace still fails.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: The first time an author's words seem not to fit together, a reader should conclude that the author is imprecise.
questions.explain: Misfits usually come from the reader's own wrong placements at first. Blaming the author too soon stops you readjusting and learning; conclude imprecision only after honest readjustment fails.
questions.rule: Do not blame the author first.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: An author who uses one of his key words in two different senses is, for that reason, using it ambiguously.
questions.explain: Using a word in several senses is common and can be done well. The card next explains what makes a use ambiguous.
questions.rule: Several senses are not yet ambiguity.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: According to the authors, to use a word ambiguously is to use it in several senses without distinguishing or ____ their meanings.
questions.explain: Ambiguity is a failure to distinguish or relate the senses, not the mere number of senses.
questions.rule: Ambiguity: senses not distinguished or related.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Sort each author: offering terms, or using the word ambiguously?

items.t: A biologist says she uses species in two senses and tags each use
An essayist uses nature for the physical world and for human character, each made plain by context
A historian defines revolution narrowly, then broadly, explaining why
A columnist uses freedom in three senses and never shows which
A report uses growth for sales and for profit interchangeably
A manifesto uses the people for all citizens and for its own voters, unannounced

questions.explain: The first three authors distinguish their senses, by announcement, by context or by explanation, so readers can follow. The last three slide between senses without signal, which is ambiguity.
questions.hint: Can a reader tell which sense is meant at each use?
questions.rule: Distinguished senses are terms; undistinguished ones are ambiguity.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Ana reasons: Step 1, the author uses law for laws of nature and for laws passed by parliaments, and distinguishes them carefully. Step 2, so he is using law ambiguously. Step 3, so I cannot come to terms with him. Which step goes wrong?
options: Step 1, since no author uses law in two senses
Step 3, since terms need no effort from her
No step, since two senses always mean ambiguity
Step 2, since distinguished senses are not ambiguity
optionExplain: Authors often use key words in several senses; Step 1 is a fair report.
Step 3 follows from Step 2; the error is earlier, and terms do need her effort.
This is the very confusion the authors correct.
Right: an author who distinguishes his senses is offering terms, so Step 2 is the mistake.
questions.explain: Ambiguity means senses left undistinguished. Since the author distinguishes them, he offers terms, and Ana can come to terms with him.
questions.rule: Distinguished senses can be terms.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Why might a careful author keep one word for two related senses, distinguishing them, rather than coin a new word for the second?
options: It keeps the link between the ideas in view
It saves him the trouble of inventing a word
It makes his book seem harder and deeper
It lets him avoid ever defining either sense
optionExplain: Right: one word with distinguished senses reminds the reader that the two ideas are related, which a fresh word would hide.
Saving effort may play a part, but the point concerns what the reader learns.
Seeming difficult is no aim of a good expository author.
He still has to distinguish the senses, which is a kind of defining.
questions.explain: Related senses share something. Keeping one word, with the senses kept apart, tells the reader the ideas belong together, while still letting him tell them apart.
questions.rule: One word, distinguished senses, can show a real connection.
questions.teaches: Several related senses of one word can carry a real connection between ideas: keeping one word for both, with the senses distinguished, reminds the reader that the ideas are related, which a fresh word would hide.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A good dictionary numbers a word's senses and gives an example sentence for each. In the authors' terms, what does this do?
options: It makes the word ambiguous by listing many senses
It shows which sense every author will use
It keeps the senses apart for the reader
It removes the need to read the word in context
optionExplain: The authors do call most dictionary words ambiguous in the sense of having many meanings, but a numbered entry does not blur those senses; it separates them for the reader.
It shows the senses available, not which one a given author chooses.
Right: numbered senses with examples let a reader make the matching discrimination, as a careful author does.
The reader still needs the context to see which numbered sense is in use.
questions.explain: By analogy, a well-made entry separates each sense and shows it in an example sentence, much as a careful author distinguishes the senses of a critical word and lets context show which is in use.
questions.rule: Distinguishing senses is what makes them usable.
questions.teaches: A dictionary's example sentences work like an author's contexts: each fixes one sense by surrounding the word with familiar words, which is why the example often makes a sense clearer than the bare definition.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: An author shifts a word's sense between two chapters without announcing it, but the context of each chapter makes the sense plain. Is this ambiguity?
options: Yes, since every shift must be announced
No, since the context distinguishes the senses
Yes, since one word should have one sense
No, since key words cannot be ambiguous
optionExplain: Announcement is one way to distinguish senses; context is another.
Right: if the context lets the reader tell the senses apart, the author is offering terms.
One word may carry several terms, as the chapter stresses.
Key words are the ones most often used ambiguously by careless authors.
questions.explain: What matters is whether the reader can tell the senses apart. Context can do that as well as an announcement.
questions.rule: Context can distinguish senses as well as labels.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: A single use of a word can stand for several of its related meanings at once and still be a term.
questions.explain: A word can cover all, some or one of its related senses in a given use. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: A use can combine related senses.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: With a, b and c standing for reading to be entertained, for information and for understanding, match each use of reading with its symbol.
pairs: Reading books that instruct rather than entertain
Reading that enlightens rather than informs
questions.explain: Reading any book covers all three senses; reading books that instruct drops entertainment; reading that enlightens keeps only understanding.
questions.rule: All, some or one sense: Xabc, Xbc, Xc.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A sports article uses football for every code of the game, soccer, rugby and American football, in one paragraph, and for soccer alone in another, each time making the scope plain. Are both uses terms?
options: No, since a term must have one narrow sense
Only the narrow use, since the wide one is vague
Only the wide use, since it covers everything
Yes, since each use is definite in its scope
optionExplain: A term may cover several related senses at once, as Xabc does.
The wide use is definite in what it covers, so it is not vague.
The narrow use is definite too, so it is also a term.
Right: one use takes in all the codes and one takes in soccer only, and both are definite.
questions.explain: A word can stand for all, some or one of its related senses. As long as each use is definite, each is a term.
questions.rule: Wide or narrow, a definite use is a term.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: If a third paragraph uses football so that it could mean either all the codes or soccer alone, with nothing to decide, that use is still a term.
questions.explain: A combined use is a term only if it is definite. A use that could take in all the senses or one, with nothing to decide between them, is ambiguous.
questions.rule: Indefinite scope means ambiguity.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Moving from Xabc to Xbc to Xc, the authors narrow reading by adding conditions: instruct rather than entertain, then enlighten rather than inform. How can a reader tell that a given passage uses the narrow sense Xc?
options: By taking the word's first dictionary sense
By context that marks the added conditions
By choosing the narrowest sense where possible
By choosing the broadest sense unless told otherwise
optionExplain: The dictionary lists the senses; it cannot say which one this passage uses.
Right: a phrase such as rather than informs marks which conditions are in play, and so which use is meant.
A blanket preference for the narrowest sense would misread the passages that mean Xabc.
A blanket preference for the broadest sense would misread the passages that mean Xc.
questions.explain: Each narrower sense adds conditions to the broader one. The reader can know which use is in play only from the surrounding words that mark those conditions; a narrower use stays a term only if the context marks them.
questions.rule: Context must mark which conditions apply.
questions.teaches: Narrower senses nest inside broader ones by adding conditions, and a narrower use stays a term only if its context marks which conditions apply; without that mark the reader cannot tell Xc from Xabc.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Two friends argue whether a tomato is a fruit. One means fruit as botanists use it; the other means fruit as cooks use it. What would settle the argument?
options: Asking which width of fruit each is using
Deciding which friend knows more about plants
Looking up fruit and taking the first sense
Agreeing that the question has no answer
optionExplain: Right: the botanical sense is wider than the culinary one; once each width is named, both friends can be right.
Expertise does not decide which sense is in use.
The first dictionary sense may not be the one either friend means.
There are clear answers once the sense is fixed: yes botanically, usually no in cooking.
questions.explain: By analogy, fruit is used at different widths in different settings. Naming the width in play turns an apparent disagreement into two compatible claims.
questions.rule: Name the width of a word before disagreeing.
questions.teaches: By analogy, everyday categories like fruit are used at different widths in different settings, botanical in one place and culinary in another; asking which width is in play settles apparent disagreements such as whether a tomato is a fruit.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: When a careful author switches from one word to another, he is signalling a different meaning.
questions.explain: Good authors often vary their words to avoid repetition while keeping the same meaning. The card next shows how to tell.
questions.rule: A new word need not be a new meaning.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: When an author uses different words with the same meaning, two or more words express a single ____.
questions.explain: This is the reverse of one word carrying several terms: here several words carry one term.
questions.rule: Several words, one term.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A self-help book speaks of grit on one page, perseverance on the next and staying power later, each time meaning continuing toward a goal despite setbacks. How many terms are there?
options: Three terms, one for each word used
Two terms, since staying power is a phrase
None, since the author is inconsistent
One term, expressed by three words
optionExplain: Different words can express one meaning, as here.
A phrase can express a term just as a word can; it is the meaning that counts.
Varying words while keeping one meaning is good practice, not inconsistency.
Right: all three words carry the same meaning, so there is one term.
questions.explain: The contexts give all three words the same meaning. The words differ, but there is one term to grasp.
questions.rule: Count terms by meanings, not words.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Legal drafters and scientists often repeat the same key word, even when it reads clumsily. Why, in the light of this chapter?
options: Their fields forbid the use of any synonyms
Because their readers dislike variety in style
So readers do not take a new word as a new term
Because their key words have no synonyms
optionExplain: There is no such ban; the choice is made for clarity.
Readers' taste is not the reason; precision is.
Right: in exact writing, a change of word may be read as a change of meaning, so repeating the word removes the doubt.
Most key words have near-synonyms; the drafters avoid them on purpose.
questions.explain: Synonyms make prose livelier but raise the question whether the term has changed. Where precision matters most, writers often pay in clumsiness to keep that question closed.
questions.rule: In exact writing, repeat the key word.
questions.teaches: A writer's wish to avoid repetition can mislead readers: variation for style alone may look like a distinction, so careful technical and legal writers often prefer repeating a key word to swapping in synonyms.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A library catalogue files some books under car, others under automobile and others under motor vehicle, with no links between them. What problem does this chapter predict?
options: Readers searching one word miss books on the same idea
The catalogue becomes too short to be useful
Each heading will attract a different kind of reader with different needs
Nothing, since the three words mean different things
optionExplain: Right: one term filed under three words is scattered, so a search on one finds only a third.
Splitting headings makes no catalogue shorter.
The headings name one idea; readers of each want the same books.
Here the three words serve as synonyms for one idea.
questions.explain: By analogy, one term expressed by several words is split up unless the words are linked. Catalogues and search tools use synonym lists for this reason.
questions.rule: Link the words that share a term.
questions.teaches: By analogy, catalogues and search tools use synonym lists so that one idea filed under several words is found together; without them, a search on one word misses the same term under another.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: A historian who switches from revolution to rebellion, after explaining that a rebellion seeks new rulers while a revolution seeks a new order, is using the two words as synonyms.
questions.explain: Here the change of word marks a distinction the author has drawn, so the words express two terms. A change of word must be checked against context, not assumed either way.
questions.rule: Some word changes mark real distinctions.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: A term can be expressed by a phrase of several words as well as by a single word.
questions.explain: A phrase that works as a unit can refer to something as a word can. The card next shows why authors use phrases for this.
questions.rule: Phrases can express terms.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: According to the authors, a phrase is in general less likely to be ____ than a single word.
questions.explain: Each word in a phrase sits in the context of the others, which restricts their meanings, so a phrase leaves less room for ambiguity.
questions.rule: Phrases restrict their own meanings.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: An economics article uses growth, then growth in output per person, then the rise in what the average person produces over time. What should a reader infer?
options: One term, with the phrases pinning down growth
Three different terms, one for each wording
That the author cannot decide what he means
That only the shortest wording is a term
optionExplain: Right: like the authors with reading, this writer expresses one term by a word and two phrases, each narrowing it further.
The wordings differ but the meaning stays the same.
Restating a key word in longer phrases is a sign of care, not indecision.
Phrases can express terms just as words can.
questions.explain: A writer who wants his meaning sure replaces a word with a fuller phrase. All three wordings express one term.
questions.rule: Longer phrases can pin down a key word.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In one article, free trade means trade without tariffs; in another passage it means trade without any regulation at all. What does this show?
options: A phrase can carry two terms, like a word
Phrases are always ambiguous and should be avoided
The two passages must be by different writers
Only single words can be used in two senses
optionExplain: Right: the relations between words and terms hold for phrases, so one phrase may express several terms.
Phrases are usually less ambiguous than words, not always ambiguous.
One writer can use a phrase in two senses, as with any key word.
Phrases can shift sense too, depending on how their words are used.
questions.explain: One phrase may express several terms, depending on how its words are used. A key phrase needs the same checking as a key word.
questions.rule: Check key phrases as you check key words.
questions.teaches: Even a phrase can carry two terms: free trade may mean trade without tariffs or trade without any regulation, so a key phrase needs the same checking for one sense or several as a key word.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A help-desk script replaces reboot with turn the device fully off, wait ten seconds, then turn it on again. Why might the writers make this change?
options: To make the script longer and more formal
Because reboot is a word with no meaning
To avoid using any technical vocabulary
A phrase leaves less room for a private sense
optionExplain: Length is a cost here, not the aim.
Reboot has a meaning; callers may not share it.
Avoiding jargon is part of it, but the deeper reason is that the phrase fixes exactly what to do.
Right: callers may take reboot as a quick restart; the phrase restricts its meaning to one definite action.
questions.explain: By analogy with an author's elaborate phrases, the script trades a word for a phrase whose parts restrict one another, leaving callers less room to misread it.
questions.rule: Swap a word for a phrase when the meaning must be sure.
questions.teaches: By analogy, writers of instructions for the public often replace a single technical word with a descriptive phrase, because a phrase restricts its own meaning and leaves less room for a reader's private sense.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: Replacing a key word with any longer phrase makes the author's meaning more definite.
questions.explain: A phrase like the general sort of thing that matters to people is built from vague words and pins down nothing. Phrases help when their words restrict one another.
questions.rule: A phrase is only as definite as its words.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: What is the difference between an author's vocabulary and his terminology, as the authors use these words?
options: Vocabulary is common words; terminology is technical words
Vocabulary is his words; terminology is his meanings
Vocabulary is for speech; terminology is for writing
They are two names for one list of key words
optionExplain: Both columns can include common and technical words; the split is between words and meanings.
Right: vocabulary lists the important words, terminology the important meanings, the terms.
The distinction has nothing to do with speech and writing.
The point is that the lists differ, since words and terms do not match one to one.
questions.explain: The authors separate the words an author uses from the meanings they carry. The card next shows how to use the two lists.
questions.rule: Vocabulary: words. Terminology: terms.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, if you list an author's important words in one column and their meanings in another, a single word may be linked to several terms.
questions.explain: The columns show two kinds of link: one word to several terms, and one term to several words.
questions.rule: Links run both ways.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: In a book on money, a reader's columns link money to two meanings, a medium of exchange and wealth in general, and link currency and cash to the first meaning only. Which statements follow? Choose two.
options: Money stands for two terms in this book
Currency and cash express one term
Currency and money are synonyms throughout
Cash stands for two terms in this book
The book uses exactly three terms
optionExplain: Right: money is linked to two meanings, so it carries two terms.
Right: both words link to the same meaning, so they express one term.
Only where money means a medium of exchange; where it means wealth, currency is not a synonym.
Cash is linked to one meaning only.
The columns show two meanings, so two terms, not three.
questions.explain: Reading the links: one word (money) carries two terms, and two words (currency, cash) share one. The book uses two terms in all.
questions.rule: Read the links in both directions.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A reader keeps only one column: a list of the author's important words. What is she likely to miss?
options: Which words in the book are the important ones to study
How often each key word appears in the book
Where one word carries two terms, or two words one
Which chapters the key words appear in
optionExplain: A list of words does record which words are important.
Frequency is not what the second column adds.
Right: without a column of meanings, she cannot see the links between words and terms.
Location is not what the columns are for.
questions.explain: The relation between vocabulary and terminology appears only when both are written down. A word list alone hides both kinds of link.
questions.rule: Two columns show what one hides.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A software team starts a project glossary listing names in one column and meanings in another. Early on, it shows user meaning both a customer and a staff member, while account and profile mean the same thing. What has the two-column layout done?
options: Created confusion that was not there before
Exposed both kinds of link before they cause errors
Shown that the team should stop using the word user
Proved that account and profile must be merged in code
optionExplain: The confusion was already in the team's usage; the glossary only revealed it.
Right: one name for two things and two names for one thing are now visible and can be settled.
The team can keep user if it distinguishes the two senses.
The glossary shows a shared meaning; what to do in code is a separate decision.
questions.explain: By analogy with vocabulary and terminology, separating names from meanings shows where one name covers two things and where two names cover one.
questions.rule: Separate names from meanings to see the links.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a project glossary that lists names and meanings in separate columns lets a team see at a glance where one name covers two things and where two names cover one, before the confusion reaches the work.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A reader cannot link the word spirit, in a book she is reading, to any definite meaning, though she has tried hard. What should her columns show?
options: The dictionary's first sense, to keep the table full
A guess at the meaning she finds most likely
Every sense of spirit, linked to the word at once
A marked gap, rather than a forced link
optionExplain: A dictionary sense is not the author's meaning; filling the cell hides the problem.
A guess entered as a link looks like knowledge she does not have.
Linking every sense records ambiguity as if it were terminology.
Right: an honest gap shows where coming to terms failed, possibly through the author's imprecision.
questions.explain: The columns record your reading. Where no definite meaning can be found, a marked gap is more useful than a neat but false link.
questions.rule: Mark gaps; do not force links.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: The authors think the habit of finding a book's important words and coming to terms is a small change with a large effect.
questions.explain: The authors close the chapter by saying that seldom does such a small change in habit have such a large effect. The card next explains what lies beyond the habit.
questions.rule: Small habit, large effect.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: Which topics do the authors say practising this rule will make you want to know more about? Choose three.
options: Literal and metaphorical uses
The emotive use of words
Defining words versus things
The history of book printing
Techniques for faster reading
optionExplain: Right: the authors name the literal and metaphorical use of words.
Right: they name the emotive use of words, to arouse feeling or move to action.
Right: they name the difference between defining words and defining things.
Printing history is not among the topics they list.
Faster reading is not one of these questions about words.
questions.explain: The authors list metaphor, abstract and concrete words, names, definition and emotive language as subjects practice will make you curious about.
questions.rule: Practice raises questions about words.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A campaign leaflet calls an inheritance tax a death tax. In the authors' terms, what use of words is at work?
options: The emotive use, meant to stir feeling
The technical use, meant to be precise
The metaphorical use, meant as poetry
The ordinary use, meant to inform plainly
optionExplain: Right: the phrase is chosen to arouse feeling and move people, not to convey knowledge.
Death tax is not a technical term of tax law; it is chosen for effect.
A leaflet aims to persuade, not to make poetry.
It names the tax by its most alarming association, which is not plain information.
questions.explain: The authors distinguish the emotive use of words, to arouse emotions or change minds, from the communication of knowledge. The leaflet's label is emotive.
questions.rule: Notice words chosen to move rather than inform.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: An economics book keeps calling prices signals. Does this metaphor stop a reader from coming to terms with the author?
options: Yes, since expository books must use only literal words
Yes, since metaphors are always ambiguous in exposition
Not if the author fixes what the metaphor stands for
No, since metaphors need no interpreting at all
optionExplain: Expository authors use metaphors often; the question is whether they are definite.
A metaphor can be used in one definite sense, like any word.
Right: treat signals like any key word and ask what definite meaning it carries here.
A metaphor needs interpreting as much as any key word.
questions.explain: A figure of speech in an expository book can work as a term if its meaning is fixed. The reader asks of it what he asks of any key word.
questions.rule: Ask of a metaphor what you ask of any key word.
questions.teaches: A metaphor in an expository book can still serve as a term if the author fixes what it stands for, so the question to ask of a figure of speech is the same as of any key word: what definite meaning does it carry here?

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: A headline says a minister slammed a report. The article shows she questioned one figure in it. What does this chapter help a reader notice?
options: That the article must be inaccurate
The emotive use of a word in the headline
That slammed is a technical word in politics
That headlines should not be read at all
optionExplain: The article may be accurate; the headline's word is what overstates.
Right: slammed is chosen to excite, while the article reports milder criticism.
Slammed has no technical sense in politics; it is used for effect.
Headlines can be useful once their emotive words are discounted.
questions.explain: By analogy, headlines often use emotive words where the story reports something milder. Spotting the emotive use is the first step to finding what was said.
questions.rule: Discount emotive words to find the claim.
questions.teaches: By analogy, news headlines often use emotive words, such as slammed or blasted, where the article reports milder criticism; noticing the emotive use is the first step to finding what was actually said.

questions.unitTitle: Coming to Terms with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, studying grammar and logic in the abstract, apart from any reading practice, is the most practical way to improve your reading.
questions.explain: The authors say the study of grammar and logic is practical only to the extent you relate it to practice. Questions born of your own reading make such study pay.
questions.rule: Study language through questions from practice.

questions.q: In an expository book, what is a proposition?
options: A judgment the author declares, affirming a truth or denying a falsehood
An offer the author makes about what the book will do for its readers
A question the author raises at the start of a chapter for readers to ponder
A recommendation the author makes about how readers should act afterwards
optionExplain: Right: in a book a proposition expresses the author's judgment, what he affirms as true or denies as false.
That is the business sense of proposition, an offer or intention; the authors contrast it with the book sense.
Questions state problems; a proposition is an answer the author declares, not a question he poses.
A recommendation about action sounds like an offer of guidance, but the authors define a book's proposition as a declaration of knowledge.
questions.explain: The authors call a book's proposition a declaration of the author's judgment: what he affirms or denies. The card next contrasts it with a trader's proposition.
questions.rule: A proposition declares what the author judges to be so.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a proposition in a book declares the author's intentions, much as a trader's proposition declares an offer.
questions.explain: The authors draw the contrast the other way: a trader's proposition declares an intention to act, while a book's proposition declares knowledge, a judgment that something is or is not so.
questions.rule: Traders declare intentions; authors declare judgments.

questions.q: Which of these sentences from a book about sleep express propositions in the authors' sense? Choose two.
options: Adults who sleep under six hours show slower reaction times.
In the next chapter I hope to persuade you to rethink your evenings.
A single long lie-in does not fully repay a week of short nights.
Have you ever wondered why so many of us wake at three in the morning?
I wish every school in the country started its day an hour later.
optionExplain: Right: the author affirms something as a fact about sleep and reaction times.
It sits in an expository book, but it states the author's plan for the book, not a judgment about sleep.
Right: a denial is a judgment too; the author declares that something is not the case.
A question can introduce a topic, but it states a problem rather than an answer, so it declares no judgment.
A wish reveals the author's hopes, not his judgment of what is true about sleep.
questions.explain: Propositions affirm or deny something about the subject. The plan, the question and the wish tell you about the author's aims and feelings, not what he judges to be so.
questions.rule: Affirmations and denials are propositions; plans, questions and wishes are not.

questions.q: A housing book states that rent controls reduce the supply of rental homes. What if the author rewrote the sentence as a question: do rent controls reduce the supply of rental homes?
options: It would still be the same proposition, since the words have not changed
It would become a stronger proposition, since questions invite agreement
It would no longer declare a judgment; it would state a problem instead
It would become an argument, since a question asks the reader for reasons
optionExplain: The words are nearly the same, but the author no longer affirms anything; sentence form changes what is declared.
A question may draw readers in, but it asserts nothing, so there is no judgment to be stronger.
Right: a question poses a problem; a proposition is an answer the author affirms or denies.
Asking for reasons does not supply any; an argument needs statements, some of which support another.
questions.explain: Turning the claim into a question removes the author's affirmation. What remains is a problem the book might answer, not a declared judgment.
questions.rule: No affirmation or denial, no proposition.

questions.q: An article on remote work reads: Some critics claim remote work destroys team culture. The evidence points the other way. Which judgment about remote work is the author putting forward as true?
options: That remote work destroys team culture, since that claim is stated first
That the evidence does not support the claim that remote work harms culture
None, because the author only reports what critics have said about remote work
Both views equally, since the author sets out the two sides for readers
optionExplain: Coming first does not make a claim the author's own; here it is attributed to critics.
Right: this is what the author affirms in his own voice; the critics' claim is reported in order to be rejected.
The author does more than report: the second sentence declares his own judgment.
The author does not hold both; he presents the critics' view and then denies it.
questions.explain: The first sentence reports someone else's claim; the second declares the author's own judgment against it. Only what the author himself affirms or denies is his proposition about the subject.
questions.rule: Find the author's own voice before naming his proposition.
questions.teaches: A sentence that reports another person's claim is not the author's proposition about the subject; his proposition is what he himself affirms or denies, often in reply to the claim he reports.

questions.q: A cookbook page contains four sentences. Which one is a proposition about cooking?
options: Preheat the oven to 200 degrees before you start on the filling.
Shall we try a lighter version without the butter next time?
I hope you enjoy this dish as much as my family always has.
Salting meat an hour ahead of cooking helps its surface brown.
optionExplain: This tells you what to do, not what is so; a command declares no judgment, though it may rest on one.
This is a question; it raises a possibility rather than affirming anything.
This expresses a hope; it reveals the writer's feeling, not a claim about food.
Right: the writer affirms something as true about how meat behaves, which is a judgment about cooking.
questions.explain: Only the salting sentence affirms something about how cooking works. By analogy with the authors' point about wishes and intentions, a command such as a recipe step is not a proposition either, though a proposition about cooking usually stands behind it.
questions.rule: Behind a command, look for the judgment that justifies it.
questions.teaches: By analogy with wishes and intentions, a command such as a recipe step is not a proposition, but a proposition about how things work usually stands behind it, and that is what a careful reader looks for.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, you find out whether a book keeps the promises of its preface by looking at the propositions the author makes.
questions.explain: The preface states intentions; the propositions are what the author actually declares. The card next shows how to set one against the other.
questions.rule: Promises are checked against propositions.

questions.q: According to the authors, the author of an expository book usually promises at the start to ____ the reader about something.
questions.explain: An expository author usually promises to instruct. Whether he does is shown by the propositions he goes on to declare, not by entertainment, source lists or calls to action.
questions.rule: Expository books promise instruction.

questions.q: A personal finance book's preface promises to show why index funds beat stock picking for ordinary savers. The chapters contain the author's life story, interviews with traders, and lists of questions to ask a broker. What should a reader conclude so far?
options: Unclear until the reader decides whether index funds are better
Kept, because the subject of every chapter is investing money
Kept, because the interviews with traders count as the promised explanation
Not kept yet: no chapter declares why index funds beat stock picking
optionExplain: Whether index funds really are better is a later question; whether the promise was kept depends on what the author declared.
Staying on topic is not delivering; a book can be about investing and still never make the promised claim.
Interviews are material, but unless the author draws a judgment from them, nothing has been explained.
Right: the promise was an explanation, and no proposition explaining why index funds win has appeared.
questions.explain: The test is to set the promise beside the propositions. Life stories, interviews and questions are not judgments about why index funds win, so the promise is still unmet.
questions.rule: Topic is not delivery; look for the promised propositions.

questions.q: A reader reasons: (1) The preface promises to explain why bees are declining. (2) The author sounds expert and sincere throughout. (3) Therefore the book keeps its promise. Which step goes wrong?
options: Step 1: a preface cannot promise an explanation of a cause
Step 2: an author's sincerity cannot be sensed from the page
Step 3: sounding sincere is not the same as declaring an explanation
None: an expert who sounds sincere throughout has delivered what he promised
optionExplain: Prefaces do promise explanations; the authors say expository authors usually promise to instruct.
Tone can be sensed, and the authors say we usually trust the author's honesty; the trouble lies in what the reader infers from it.
Right: the promise is kept only if the book contains propositions explaining the decline; tone cannot stand in for them.
Expertise and sincerity make delivery more likely, but only the propositions show whether it happened.
questions.explain: Honesty is a reasonable starting assumption, but the question is what the author declared. The reader must find the propositions about the bees' decline.
questions.rule: Judge delivery by what was declared, not by tone.

questions.q: True or false: If a book has no preface or introduction, the reader has no propositions to look for in it.
questions.explain: The preface only gives you a yardstick. The author's propositions are in the body of the book whether or not he announced them in advance.
questions.rule: No preface, still propositions.

questions.q: A research team's grant proposal promised to find out whether a new reading programme improves children's spelling. Their final report is forty pages long. Borrowing the authors' approach, what should a reviewer do first?
options: List the report's findings and see which answer the spelling question
Count the pages and data tables to see how much work the team put into it
Reread the proposal to judge how well the aims were worded
Check whether the team sounds confident in its conclusion
optionExplain: Right: the findings are the report's propositions, and they are what must answer the promised question.
Volume of work is easy to measure but says nothing about whether the question was answered.
The wording of the aims matters, but the check is what the report delivers against them.
Confidence is tone; a confident report can still leave the promised question open.
questions.explain: Like a preface, a proposal states intentions. The reviewer sets them beside the findings the report actually affirms.
questions.rule: Hold any stated aim against the claims actually delivered.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any statement of aims, such as a grant proposal, a project brief or an agenda, can be checked the same way: list the concrete claims or results actually delivered and set each against the aims, ignoring length and tone.

questions.q: According to the authors, how does the order of reading compare with the order in business dealings?
options: It matches it: the reader finds the proposition, then comes to terms
It reverses it: the reader comes to terms before finding the proposition
It skips a step: a reader needs the propositions but not the terms
It merges them: terms and propositions are found together in one single step
optionExplain: That is the business order; the authors say reading generally reverses it.
Right: traders hear the proposition and then come to terms; readers usually need the terms first.
Propositions are made of terms, so skipping the terms leaves the proposition unclear.
The two steps support each other, but the authors still give them as separate rules in a usual order.
questions.explain: The authors say the order of reading reverses the order of business. The card next explains why terms usually come first.
questions.rule: Readers usually come to terms first.

questions.q: In the authors' list, Rule 5 concerns words and terms, and Rule 6 concerns sentences and ____.
questions.explain: Rule 6 moves from words to sentences, and from terms to the propositions that sentences express.
questions.rule: Words carry terms; sentences carry propositions.

questions.q: A legal article states that consent obtained under pressure is not consent. Before deciding what the writer claims, what should a reader settle?
options: Whether the writer of the article is a qualified practising lawyer
Which sense of consent each of the two uses of the word carries
Whether the courts in the reader's own country would agree
How many examples the writer gives later in the same article
optionExplain: The writer's credentials may matter for trust, but they do not tell you what the sentence asserts.
Right: the sentence uses consent twice, probably in two senses, and the claim depends on which senses they are.
Agreement by courts is a question of judging the claim, which comes after understanding it.
Later examples may help with the meaning, but the first job is to fix the senses of the key word.
questions.explain: The sentence turns on the word consent. Until you know the sense of each use, you cannot tell whether it states a substantive claim or a contradiction.
questions.rule: Fix the key word's senses before reading the claim.

questions.q: A legal article says that consent obtained under pressure is not consent. Suppose a reader, without settling the senses of consent, paraphrases it at once as: consent under pressure is a contradiction. What risk does the authors' order warn of?
options: He may agree too quickly, since contradictions are easy to accept
He will understand it faster, since paraphrasing is the goal of reading
He will reach the right meaning, since the words of the sentence are plain
He may report a proposition the writer never made, by guessing the terms
optionExplain: Contradictions are usually rejected, not accepted; the risk is misreporting the claim, not agreeing with it.
Paraphrase is a good test of understanding, but only after the terms are known; a quick paraphrase can be wrong.
Plain words can carry special senses; that is exactly why terms must be settled.
Right: without the writer's senses for consent, the reader supplies his own and may state a claim the writer never declared.
questions.explain: A proposition is built from terms. Guessing the terms means guessing the proposition, so the paraphrase may describe the reader's idea rather than the writer's.
questions.rule: Guess the terms and you guess the proposition.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, only the key words of a sentence need settling before you read its proposition; ordinary words can keep their everyday sense.
questions.explain: Coming to terms is about the key words. Ordinary words can be read in their everyday sense, and the order is usual rather than fixed.
questions.rule: Settle the key words, not every word.

questions.q: A company policy says staff who work remotely must be reachable during core hours. Before deciding what the policy requires of her, what should an employee pin down first?
options: Whether the policy was drafted by the legal team or by HR
Whether other companies have similar rules about remote staff
What the company counts as working remotely and as core hours
How strictly managers have enforced the rule in the past
optionExplain: Authorship might hint at intent, but the meaning still depends on how the key phrases are used.
Comparing companies may be interesting, but it does not tell her what this policy says.
Right: the requirement turns on these two phrases; change either sense and the policy demands something different.
Enforcement history is about practice, not about what the sentence requires.
questions.explain: The proposition is only as clear as its key phrases. Working remotely and core hours are the words the requirement turns on, so they are settled first.
questions.rule: Settle first the words the claim turns on.
questions.teaches: The words worth settling first are the ones a claim turns on: change the sense of one of them and the proposition changes, while the remaining words can usually be read in their ordinary sense.

questions.q: According to the authors, what is an author's proposition to a reader if no reasons support it?
options: A personal opinion, telling you more about the author than the subject
A fact, since honest authors only declare what they know to be true
A hypothesis, which the reader should test by experiment before going on
A conclusion, which the reader must accept on trust to keep reading
optionExplain: Right: the authors say propositions are only expressions of personal opinion unless supported by reasons.
Honesty means the author believes it, not that it is known; belief without reasons is still opinion.
Testing may come later, but the authors' first point is that unsupported claims remain opinion.
A conclusion is something reasons lead to; with no reasons, there is nothing to make it a conclusion.
questions.explain: Without reasons, a proposition tells you what the author thinks, not why you should think it. The card next shows where the reasons come in.
questions.rule: Unsupported propositions are opinions.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the seventh rule of analytical reading deals with arguments, the reasons an author gives for his propositions.
questions.explain: Rule 6 finds the propositions; Rule 7 finds the arguments that support them, so the reader learns why the author thinks they should be accepted.
questions.rule: Rule 7 is about reasons.

questions.q: Sort these sentences from opinion columns by whether a reason is offered for the claim.

items.t: Cities should ban cars from their centres.
Cities should ban cars from their centres, since road deaths fell where it was tried.
A four-day week raises output.
Because tired staff make more errors, a shorter week can raise output.
Homework does little for young children.
Young children gain little from homework, as studies find no link with their test scores.

questions.explain: Words such as since, because and as introduce a reason. The bare claims tell you what the writer thinks; the others also tell you why.
questions.rule: Look for the because behind each claim.

questions.q: You are reading a famous scientist's memoir mainly to learn what kind of person she was. What happens to the authors' demand that you find her reasons?
options: It stays, since every reading needs reasons for each of its claims
It grows, since famous people must justify every claim they make
It weakens, since her bare opinions are what you came to learn
It vanishes, since a memoir contains no propositions of any kind
optionExplain: The authors limit the demand: it applies unless you are exclusively interested in the author himself.
Fame does not change the logic; the demand depends on the reader's interest, not the author's status.
Right: the authors make the demand for readers interested in the subject, not those interested only in the author's personality.
Memoirs do contain propositions; the point is that here her opinions themselves are the object of interest.
questions.explain: The authors tie the demand for reasons to an interest in the subject. When the person is the subject, knowing her opinions is itself the goal.
questions.rule: Your interest decides whether bare opinions are enough.

questions.q: A medical review concludes that a drug probably reduces the risk of stroke. What does the word probably tell you about the argument?
options: The author admits the argument has failed to establish anything
The author defends only a probability, a legitimate kind of argument
The claim is a bare opinion, since the author offers no certainty at all
The claim is proven, since only doctors write reviews of that kind
optionExplain: Claiming probability is not failure; the authors note that sometimes no more than a probability can be defended.
Right: the authors say some arguments defend truth and others only a probability; this one claims the second.
Opinion means no reasons are given; a probable conclusion can be well supported by reasons.
The author's profession does not turn probably into proven; the word itself limits the claim.
questions.explain: The strength a conclusion claims is part of the proposition. An argument for a probable conclusion should be read as such, not faulted for failing to prove certainty.
questions.rule: Note how strong a claim the author makes.
questions.teaches: How strong a conclusion claims to be, certain or probable, is part of the proposition itself; an argument for a probable conclusion is not defective because it stops short of certainty.

questions.q: A reference letter says only that Priya is the best analyst the referee has ever managed. A hiring manager applies the authors' advice. What should she look for next?
options: Nothing more, since a sincere referee's judgment is already evidence
Whether the referee is senior enough for the praise to settle the matter
Whether this praise is stronger than in the other candidates' letters
The grounds for the praise, such as projects, results or comparisons
optionExplain: Sincerity shows the referee believes it; the authors want to know why we should be persuaded.
Seniority may make the claim worth checking, but rank is not a reason inside the argument.
Comparing strength of praise compares opinions; it still leaves out why anyone should accept them.
Right: the praise is a proposition; what she needs is the reasons for accepting it.
questions.explain: The letter states a judgment without support. The manager should ask what the referee rests it on, not how senior or emphatic he is.
questions.rule: Ask what the claim rests on, not who made it.
questions.teaches: A source's rank or sincerity is not a reason within the argument; it may make a claim worth examining, but the grounds for the claim still have to be found.

questions.q: Which of these expressions usually signal that a reason is being given or a conclusion drawn? Choose three.
options: because
therefore
at the same time
it follows that
on the other hand
optionExplain: Right: because introduces a reason for something said.
Right: therefore introduces what is concluded from what came before.
This marks things happening together or a second point, not a reason or a conclusion.
Right: it follows that introduces a conclusion drawn from earlier statements.
This marks a contrast between two points, which is not the same as supporting one with the other.
questions.explain: Because, therefore and it follows that relate statements as reason and conclusion. The card next shows how these words mark the joints of an argument.
questions.rule: Connecting words reveal reasoning.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the word because in an argument signals that a reason is being given.
questions.explain: The authors use because as their first example of a word that relates statements: this is said because of that.
questions.rule: Because marks a reason.

questions.q: A council report reads: The bridge closed for repairs last spring. Since then, traffic on Elm Street has doubled. Because Elm Street now carries the bridge's traffic, the city should add a traffic light there. Which statement do the others support?
options: The bridge closed for repairs last spring
The city should add a traffic light on Elm Street
Traffic on Elm Street has doubled since then
Elm Street now carries the bridge's traffic
optionExplain: This is background that starts the chain; nothing in the passage is offered as a reason for it.
Right: the facts about the bridge and the traffic are offered as grounds for this recommendation.
Since then here marks time, not a reason; the doubling is a ground, not the conclusion.
Because introduces this statement as a reason, so it supports the conclusion rather than being it.
questions.explain: Because attaches a reason to the recommendation about the traffic light, which is the point the passage argues for. Since then marks time, not reasoning.
questions.rule: Ask which statement the others are offered to support.

questions.q: In the sentence the streets are wet, so it rained overnight, what does the word so introduce?
options: An example illustrating the first part
The reason why the streets became wet
A second fact listed in time order
The conclusion drawn from the wet streets
optionExplain: Rain does not illustrate wet streets; it is the inference drawn from them.
Rain is the cause of the wet streets, but in this sentence it is what the speaker concludes, not the ground offered.
So can join events in sequence, but here the speaker infers the rain from the streets.
Right: so points forward to what is inferred; the wet streets are the evidence.
questions.explain: Because and since come before reasons; so and therefore come before conclusions. The two kinds of word point in opposite directions.
questions.rule: Reason words point back to grounds; conclusion words point forward.
questions.teaches: Signal words fall into two kinds that point in opposite directions: because and since introduce a premise, while so, therefore and hence introduce a conclusion.

questions.q: Since usually signals a reason, but suppose it is followed by a point in time. In which sentences does the connecting word NOT signal a reason? Choose two.
options: Since 2010, the town has built three new schools.
Since the town's population doubled, it needed more schools.
She has lived in this street since she was born.
Because the vote was close, a recount was ordered.
optionExplain: Right: since here marks a point in time; no reason is being given.
Here since gives the reason the town needed more schools.
Right: since she was born says how long, not why.
Because gives the reason for the recount.
questions.explain: The same word can mark time or a reason. Signal words are clues; you still have to check whether one statement is offered as support for another.
questions.rule: Check that a signal word is really doing the work of reasoning.

questions.q: A phone review reads: The battery lasts two days. However, the phone weighs more than its rivals, although the camera is excellent. What work do however and although do here?
options: They signal conclusions drawn from the battery life
They give reasons for concluding the phone is worth buying
They mark contrasts and concessions rather than reasons
They introduce examples that illustrate the weight
optionExplain: Conclusion words such as so or therefore would do that; however and although do not.
The review may lead to a verdict, but these words weigh points against each other rather than supply reasons.
Right: however and although set one point against another; neither offers a ground for a conclusion.
An example word would be for instance; these words mark a turn, not an illustration.
questions.explain: Contrast words show the writer weighing considerations. A verdict may follow from the balance, but the words themselves are not reason or conclusion signals.
questions.rule: Contrast words weigh points; they do not give reasons.
questions.teaches: Contrast words such as however, but and although mark where a writer sets one point against another or concedes something; they do not by themselves give a reason, though a conclusion may follow from the balance.

questions.q: True or false: A single short statement, such as a claim that taxes are too high, counts as an argument by itself.
questions.explain: An argument needs more than one statement: some giving grounds, one being concluded. The card next spells out what makes statements an argument.
questions.rule: One statement alone is a claim, not an argument.

questions.q: According to the authors, an argument is a set of statements of which some provide the grounds or ____ for what is to be concluded.
questions.explain: The defining feature of an argument is the relation of support: some statements give grounds or reasons for another. A quarrel, a lone forceful claim or a list of facts lacks that relation.
questions.rule: Grounds plus conclusion make an argument.

questions.q: A tourism report says: The museum should open on Mondays. Most cruise passengers arrive on Mondays. The rival galleries all close that day. Which statement do the others support?
options: The rival galleries all close that day
Most cruise passengers arrive on Mondays
The museum should open on Mondays
None; they are three separate claims
optionExplain: This is a second ground: with rivals shut, the museum would have the day to itself.
This is a ground: it explains why Monday opening would pay.
Right: the facts about arrivals and rivals are offered as grounds for opening on Mondays, even though they come after it.
There is no signal word, but the second and third statements make sense only as support for the first.
questions.explain: The conclusion comes first and the premises follow. Premises are the source of the conclusion wherever they appear in the text.
questions.rule: The conclusion need not come last.

questions.q: Sort these passages by whether they express an argument.
groups: An argument: some statements support another
Not an argument: no support relation

items.t: Bees pollinate crops. Bee numbers are falling. So crop yields are at risk.
Bees pollinate crops. Some bees live alone. Honey keeps for years.
Our rent rose a fifth and my pay did not, so we must move.
The flat has two bedrooms, a balcony and a view of the river.
Since the ice is thin, no one should skate on the lake today.
The lake froze in December and thawed in March.

questions.explain: A topic in common is not enough. In the arguments, some statements are offered as grounds for another; in the others, statements stand side by side with no claim of support.
questions.rule: Same topic is not the same as support.

questions.q: An author argues: Every member of the club pays dues. Sam is a member. So Sam pays dues. What happens to the support for the conclusion if you remove either premise?
options: It turns into a different but equally good argument
It survives, because one premise is enough for this conclusion
It grows stronger, because fewer premises mean fewer errors
It collapses, because the two premises work only together
optionExplain: What remains is a single claim with nothing it is offered to support, not another argument.
Neither premise alone links Sam to paying dues, so one is not enough.
Fewer premises can mean fewer chances of error, but here they also remove the support itself.
Right: without the rule about members, Sam's membership proves nothing; without his membership, the rule says nothing about Sam.
questions.explain: These premises support the conclusion jointly. Missing one leaves a gap, so a reader must find every premise an argument uses.
questions.rule: Find all the premises, not just the most striking one.
questions.teaches: Premises often work jointly: each alone gives no support, and the conclusion follows only from them together, so a reader must find all of them, not only the most striking one.

questions.q: A history textbook says the old bridge collapsed because its bolts had rusted. No one doubts that the bridge collapsed. What is the because doing here?
options: Giving a reason to believe the bridge fell
Explaining why an accepted event happened
Stating a wish for better bridge repairs
Marking a contrast between design and use
optionExplain: No one needs persuading that the bridge fell, so the rusted bolts are not offered as grounds for believing it.
Right: the collapse is not in question; the sentence tells you its cause.
Nothing in the sentence expresses a hope; it states a cause.
Because does not mark contrast; words such as but or however do.
questions.explain: Here because explains a fact everyone accepts. An argument aims to make you accept its conclusion; an explanation aims to make you understand something already accepted.
questions.rule: Ask whether because supports a claim or explains a fact.
questions.teaches: Because can introduce an explanation of something already accepted rather than a reason to believe it: an argument tries to make you accept its conclusion, an explanation tries to make you understand a fact.

questions.q: An argument is valid. What does that tell you about its conclusion?
options: It follows from the premises, but may be false if a premise is false
It is true, because a valid argument cannot reach a false conclusion
It is probable, because validity is a matter of degree in arguments
It is the author's opinion, because validity only measures his sincerity
optionExplain: Right: validity concerns whether the conclusion follows; the truth of the premises is a separate matter.
A valid argument can reach a false conclusion when a premise is false; validity alone does not guarantee truth.
Probability is a different strength of claim; validity is about whether the conclusion follows from the premises.
Sincerity is about the author's honesty, not about the link between premises and conclusion.
questions.explain: A valid conclusion follows from its premises, which is not the same as being true. The card next separates the two questions.
questions.rule: Following is not the same as true.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a conclusion that follows validly from its premises may still be false.
questions.explain: The authors say that a valid conclusion is not necessarily true, since one or all of its premises may be false.
questions.rule: Valid conclusions can be false.

questions.q: A leaflet argues: All natural remedies are safe. This herbal tea is a natural remedy. So this tea is safe. Which description fits the argument best?
options: Valid, but the first premise is doubtful, so the conclusion is not secured
Invalid, because the conclusion does not follow from the two premises
True, because the conclusion follows from the premises that are given
Neither valid nor invalid, since it is about health and safety rather than logic
optionExplain: Right: granting both premises, the conclusion follows; but some natural substances are harmful, so the first premise is open to doubt.
The conclusion does follow if the premises are granted; the weakness lies in a premise, not the link.
Following from the premises does not make the conclusion true when a premise may be false.
Arguments on any subject can be valid or invalid; the topic does not exempt them.
questions.explain: The structure is valid, so the question becomes whether the premises are true. The claim that all natural remedies are safe is doubtful, so the conclusion is not established.
questions.rule: A sound-looking structure can carry a weak premise.

questions.q: Suppose a valid argument turns out to have a conclusion you know to be false. What can you infer?
options: All of its premises are false together
The argument must be invalid after all
At least one of its premises is false
Nothing, since validity is unrelated to truth
optionExplain: One false premise is enough to explain a false conclusion; the others may be true.
The argument was given as valid; a false conclusion does not change whether it follows.
Right: if all the premises were true, a valid argument would carry the truth to its conclusion, so one must be false.
Validity does connect premises and conclusion: true premises in a valid argument cannot yield a false conclusion.
questions.explain: Validity means the conclusion cannot be false while every premise is true. So a known false conclusion lets you work back to a faulty premise.
questions.rule: A false conclusion from valid reasoning exposes a false premise.
questions.teaches: A valid argument with a false conclusion must have at least one false premise, so a known false conclusion lets you work backwards to look for the faulty premise.

questions.q: Match each case to what it shows about the conclusion.
pairs: The premises are true and the conclusion follows
A premise is false but the conclusion follows
Valid, yet the conclusion is not secured
The premises are true but the conclusion does not follow
True grounds that give the conclusion no support
questions.explain: Both questions must be answered yes for a conclusion to be secured: the premises true and the conclusion following from them. A no to either leaves it unsupported.
questions.rule: A secured conclusion needs true premises and a valid link.

questions.q: A colleague says prices should be cut because the chief executive's astrologer advised it. You also think prices should be cut, for reasons about competition. Applying the authors' point, how should you treat his argument?
options: Accept the astrologer, since a true conclusion proves its premises
Accept his argument, since you already hold its conclusion
Reject the conclusion, since his argument for it is weak
Reject his reasoning while agreeing with his conclusion
optionExplain: A true conclusion can come from false or irrelevant premises, so it proves nothing about them.
Agreeing with a conclusion is no reason to accept the reasoning someone offers for it.
A weak argument does not make its conclusion false; you have your own reasons for it.
Right: his premise gives no real support, so the argument fails even if the conclusion is right.
questions.explain: The link from premises to conclusion and the truth of the conclusion are separate. A conclusion can be right while the argument for it is worthless.
questions.rule: Judge the reasoning apart from whether you like the conclusion.
questions.teaches: A true conclusion can be reached by bad reasoning: agreeing with a conclusion is no reason to accept the argument offered for it, and a weak argument does not make its conclusion false.

questions.q: In what order do the authors' rules of interpretation take the units of a book?
options: Sentences, then words, then whole chapters
Paragraphs first, then sentences, then single words last
Words, then sentences, then groups of sentences
Groups of sentences, then words, then sentences
optionExplain: Chapters are units of structure; interpretation starts with words and builds upward.
This runs the wrong way: it breaks larger units of language into smaller ones, while interpretation builds up from words to larger units.
Right: the rules build up from simpler to more complex units of language.
This scrambles the order; the rules move steadily from smaller to larger units.
questions.explain: Interpretation builds from words to sentences to groups of sentences, matching terms, propositions and arguments. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Interpretation builds upward.

questions.q: Match each unit of language with the unit of thought the authors pair it with.
questions.explain: Terms are found through words, propositions through sentences, and arguments through collections of sentences.
questions.rule: Words, sentences, paragraphs; terms, propositions, arguments.

questions.q: A student has looked up every unfamiliar word in a philosophy essay but still cannot say what the essay claims. According to the authors, what has she left out?
options: Reading the author's biography to learn his general opinions
Looking up the words in a second, more detailed dictionary
Reading the sentences and paragraphs as units of their own
Memorising the key words so that she can recall them later
optionExplain: Biography may hint at views, but it does not tell her what this essay asserts.
Better definitions still stop at the level of words; the claim is in how the words combine.
Right: claims live in sentences and arguments in groups of sentences; word meanings alone do not deliver them.
Memorising words is still work at the word level; it does not reach the propositions.
questions.explain: A book consists of groups of words and groups of sentences as well as words. Knowing the words is necessary but not adequate.
questions.rule: Words are necessary, not enough.

questions.q: True or false: A reader who understands every sentence in a chapter is bound to see how the chapter's argument runs.
questions.explain: An argument is a relation among propositions. A reader can grasp each sentence and still miss which ones support which, so each level of understanding can fail on its own.
questions.rule: Each level of reading can fail on its own.
questions.teaches: Understanding can fail at each level independently: knowing every word does not guarantee grasping the sentence, and grasping every sentence does not guarantee seeing the argument that connects them.

questions.q: Suppose an author packs a whole argument, premises and conclusion, into one long sentence. What does that show about the authors' ladder of units?
options: The reader should treat it as a term, since it is the smallest unit present
The author has broken a rule, since arguments must be written in paragraphs
The sentence holds only one proposition, since it is a single sentence
The units guide attention, but grammar and logic do not match exactly
optionExplain: A term is a word used in a definite sense; a sentence with premises and a conclusion is far more than that.
There is no such rule; the authors themselves note that one complex sentence can express several propositions forming an argument.
A single sentence can express several propositions, and here it expresses a whole argument.
Right: the ladder tells you where to look, but an argument can live inside one sentence.
questions.explain: The grammatical ladder is a guide, not a fixed map. Here a single grammatical unit carries a whole logical argument.
questions.rule: Grammatical units guide you to logical ones; they do not define them.

questions.q: Someone learning Spanish has memorised three thousand words but cannot follow a radio interview. By analogy with the authors' point, what does she most need to practise?
options: Memorising another three thousand words
Taking whole sentences and exchanges as units
Slowing the audio until each word is clear
Listening only for the words she knows best
optionExplain: More words help, but she already has many; the gap is at the level of sentences and exchanges.
Right: meaning in speech, as in books, lives in sentences and longer stretches, which have to be practised as units.
Hearing each word clearly still leaves her working word by word.
Catching familiar words gives fragments, not the claims and replies the speakers are making.
questions.explain: By analogy, vocabulary is the word level. Following an interview needs the larger units, sentences and stretches of talk, practised in their own right.
questions.rule: Practise each level of language as a unit.
