questions.teaches: By analogy, learning a language or a field works level by level too: drilling vocabulary does not teach you to follow a conversation, because sentences and longer stretches of talk must be practised as units of their own.

questions.q: Outlining moves from the whole book down to its parts. In which direction does interpretation move?
options: Down from the whole book to its chapters
Up from terms to propositions to arguments
Across, comparing the book with others
Down from arguments to propositions to terms
optionExplain: That is the direction of outlining, which interpretation reverses.
Right: interpretation builds larger units of thought out of smaller ones.
Comparing books belongs to syntopical reading, not to interpreting one book.
That reverses it: interpretation starts with terms, the smallest units, and builds up to arguments.
questions.explain: Outlining works down; interpretation works up from terms. The card next shows where the two movements meet.
questions.rule: Outline down, interpret up.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, outlining and interpretation meet at the level of propositions and arguments.
questions.explain: Dividing a book far enough gives you points that are propositions; building up from terms gives you propositions and arguments. That is where the two processes meet.
questions.rule: The two movements meet at propositions and arguments.

questions.q: Put these steps of working down from the whole book in order.
items: State what the whole book is about
Divide the book into its major parts
Divide each part into its subordinate sections
Say which points are made in each section
questions.explain: Outlining goes from the whole to the parts to their divisions. The last step, naming the points made, is where you reach propositions, the level interpretation builds up to.
questions.rule: Divide until you reach the points made.

questions.q: Suppose your outline of a chapter lists four points, but your interpretation finds two propositions and an argument that does not touch the other points. What is the most useful next step?
options: Ignore the gap, since the two processes are meant to give different results
Keep the outline, since structure matters more than propositions do
Keep the interpretation, since sentences are more reliable than outlines
Reread that chapter, since the mismatch marks where one of them is wrong
optionExplain: The processes move in opposite directions but should arrive at the same propositions.
Neither process outranks the other; the authors want both completed and in agreement.
Interpretation can misread too; preferring it without checking throws away the cross-check.
Right: the two processes should meet; where they do not, one of them has gone wrong in that part.
questions.explain: Agreement between outline and interpretation supports both. Disagreement is useful too: it marks the part of the book to reread.
questions.rule: A mismatch tells you where to reread.
questions.teaches: When the outline and the interpretation disagree, the mismatch is useful in itself: it marks the exact part of the book to reread, because one of the two readings has gone wrong there.

questions.q: True or false: An outline and an interpretation that agree can still both be wrong, if both were done carelessly.
questions.explain: Agreement is good evidence, not proof. A careless outline can match a careless interpretation, so the meeting point is a check rather than a guarantee.
questions.rule: Agreement supports a reading; it does not prove it.

questions.q: A treasurer plans a festival budget by category, then separately adds up every receipt. By analogy with the authors' point, what do the two methods give her when their totals agree?
options: A reason to stop adding up receipts in future years of the festival
Little, since the total of the receipts is the only figure that really counts
Each method confirms the other, as top-down and bottom-up work meeting
Proof that the festival made a profit, since the books are balanced
optionExplain: Agreement this year does not make next year's checking unnecessary.
The receipts matter, but a plan that matches them shows both were done carefully.
Right: like outlining and interpreting, planning down and adding up arrive at one result from opposite directions.
Matching totals show consistency, not profit; profit depends on income as well as spending.
questions.explain: By analogy, any large piece of work can be checked from both ends. When a top-down plan and a bottom-up count agree, each is evidence for the other.
questions.rule: Check big work from both ends.
questions.teaches: By analogy, many large tasks can be checked by working both top-down and bottom-up, as with a budget planned by category and totalled from receipts; agreement between the two is evidence that both were done well.

questions.q: Which of these are units of thought rather than units of language, in the authors' scheme? Choose two.
options: A sentence printed in the book
A proposition asserted by the author
A paragraph set off by an indent
An argument linking several claims
A word chosen for its sound
optionExplain: A sentence is a grammatical unit: it belongs to language.
Right: a proposition is a logical unit, something thought and declared.
A paragraph is a unit of writing, set off by the writer's layout.
Right: an argument is a logical unit made of propositions.
A word is the smallest unit of language, not of thought.
questions.explain: Sentences, paragraphs and words belong to language; propositions and arguments belong to thought. The card next explains why the difference matters.
questions.rule: Language carries thought; it is not the thought.

questions.q: According to the authors, sentences and paragraphs are grammatical units, while propositions and arguments are ____ units.
questions.explain: Propositions and arguments are logical units, units of thought and knowledge, expressed through the grammatical units of sentences and paragraphs.
questions.rule: Grammatical units express logical ones.

questions.q: Two news sites report: The minister resigned on Tuesday. On Tuesday the minister stepped down. How many propositions do these reports contain?
options: Two propositions, because the two verbs are different
Two propositions, one for each of the two sentences
One proposition, expressed in two different sentences
None, because both are reports rather than judgments
optionExplain: Resigned and stepped down are different words for the same act.
Counting sentences counts units of language, not units of thought.
Right: different words, same claim about the minister.
A report of a fact is still a declaration that something is the case.
questions.explain: Two sentences can carry one proposition. What matters is what is asserted, not how many sentences assert it.
questions.rule: Count claims, not sentences.

questions.q: A student's grammatically broken sentence says the earth is flat; a classmate's clumsy run-on sentence says it is round. Suppose the first student then fixes her grammar. What does the authors' distinction let you say about the two claims?
options: Grammar is a test of sentences; truth is a test of propositions
The first claim is false mainly because its grammar is wrong
The second claim is less true because its sentence is so badly written
Neither has a proposition, since both sentences are faulty
optionExplain: Right: well or badly formed describes the sentence; true or false describes the proposition it carries.
The flat-earth claim is false whatever its grammar; good grammar would not make it true.
Clumsy writing does not reduce the truth of the proposition that the earth is round.
Faulty sentences can still carry propositions, as both of these do.
questions.explain: Sentences are judged by grammar and style, propositions by truth. Keeping the two apart stops you blaming or praising a claim for its wording.
questions.rule: Judge sentences by form and propositions by truth.
questions.teaches: Truth and falsity belong to propositions, while correctness of form belongs to sentences: a well-made sentence can carry a false proposition, and a clumsy one a true proposition.

questions.q: True or false: Because the proposition is what matters, a reader of a contract can safely ignore its exact wording.
questions.explain: You reach the proposition only through the sentence, and in contracts small changes of wording can change the commitment. The distinction does not license careless reading of the words.
questions.rule: Reach the thought through the words, not around them.

questions.q: A company report shows a bar chart of sales rising in each quarter, with no caption. Using the authors' distinction, what does the chart contain?
options: No proposition, since there is no sentence on the chart to carry one
A proposition, carried by a chart instead of a sentence
Only terms, since it has labels but no verbs at all
An argument, since several figures appear in it
optionExplain: Sentences are one vehicle for propositions, not the only one.
Right: the chart asserts that sales rose each quarter; the claim does not need a sentence to be made.
The labels are words, but the chart as a whole makes a claim about sales.
Several figures make one claim here; nothing is offered as a reason for anything else.
questions.explain: If a proposition is the thought and the sentence only its vehicle, other vehicles can carry it too. A chart can declare that something is the case.
questions.rule: Look for the claim, whatever carries it.
questions.teaches: By extension, propositions can be carried without sentences: a chart, table or map can assert that something is the case, and a reader should state that claim in words to examine it.

questions.q: According to the authors, what is the greatest error a reader can make in applying the rules about terms, propositions and arguments?
options: Judging the author's claims before checking his qualifications
Reading too slowly to keep the whole argument of the book in mind at once
Looking up words in a dictionary instead of working from context
Assuming each unit of language matches exactly one unit of thought
optionExplain: Judging too early is a fault the authors discuss later, but it is not this one.
Speed matters elsewhere in the book, but it is not the error named here.
Dictionaries have their uses; the error the authors single out is about matching language to thought.
Right: the authors name the assumption of a one-to-one relation between language and thought as the greatest error.
questions.explain: The authors warn against supposing a one-to-one relation between elements of language and of thought. The card next shows the buttons-and-buttonholes picture.
questions.rule: Language and thought do not pair off neatly.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, one word can express several terms, and one term can be expressed by several words.
questions.explain: This is the case that introduces the error: words and terms do not stand in a one-to-one relation, and neither do sentences and propositions.
questions.rule: Words and terms do not pair off one-to-one.

questions.q: Which of these situations show that language and thought do not match one-to-one? Choose three.
options: One sentence in a treaty commits both parties to two separate duties
An author states one claim in chapter 2 and again, reworded, in chapter 9
A writer uses right to mean correct here and a legal claim there
A simple sentence with unambiguous words states one single claim
A paragraph states exactly one argument from premise to conclusion
optionExplain: Right: one sentence, two propositions.
Right: two sentences, one proposition.
Right: one word, two terms.
Here the match holds; that can happen, but it shows no mismatch.
This is a case where paragraph and argument coincide, which shows no mismatch.
questions.explain: Mismatches run both ways: one unit of language can carry several units of thought, and several units of language can carry one. The last two options are cases where the match happens to hold.
questions.rule: Mismatches run both ways.

questions.q: A student summarises a ten-sentence passage by writing one shortened line for each sentence. What do the authors suggest about this method?
options: It is the most faithful method, since each sentence is one claim
It copies the language; the claims may need more or fewer lines
It is too long, since a summary needs one line per paragraph
It works as long as each line keeps the author's word order
optionExplain: That assumes the one-to-one match the authors warn against.
Right: a line per sentence follows units of language; the number of claims can differ from the number of sentences.
A line per paragraph is the same error one level up: paragraphs and arguments do not match either.
Keeping the word order keeps the language, which is not the same as stating the thought.
questions.explain: A summary should follow the propositions and arguments, not the sentences. Some sentences carry two claims; some carry none worth keeping.
questions.rule: Summarise claims, not sentences.
questions.teaches: A summary that keeps one line per sentence of the source copies the language rather than the thought; a good summary may need fewer or more lines than the source has sentences.

questions.q: What if a passage is made of short, simple sentences whose words are used unambiguously?
options: Each must hold several propositions, since none can be one-to-one
The warning fails, since simple sentences hold no propositions
Each likely holds one proposition, though that is found, not assumed
It cannot contain an argument, since all its sentences are simple
optionExplain: The warning is against assuming the match, not a claim that matches never happen.
Simple sentences do express propositions; that is the usual case.
Right: the authors say a simple sentence with unambiguous words usually expresses one proposition; the reader confirms it rather than assuming it.
An argument can run across several simple sentences; simplicity of each does not prevent it.
questions.explain: Here the match often holds. The rule warns against assuming it, so the reader still checks each sentence.
questions.rule: The match can hold; check rather than assume.

questions.q: A customer survey asks people to answer yes or no to whether they are satisfied with our prices and our service. What problem do the authors help you see?
options: One sentence asks two things, so one answer cannot judge either
The question is too short to give useful information on service
Yes or no answers are less reliable than ratings on a scale
Customers may not know what the word service means here
optionExplain: Right: a customer happy with service but not prices has no honest answer, and a yes or no cannot be split.
Length is not the trouble; a short question about one thing would work.
Scales may be better, but even a scale cannot fix a question that asks two things at once.
Service is an everyday word here; the trouble is that the sentence carries two questions.
questions.explain: By analogy, the one-to-one error can happen in writing as well as reading. One sentence carrying two questions makes every answer ambiguous.
questions.rule: One question per sentence when you need one answer.
questions.teaches: Writers can make the one-to-one error too: a double-barrelled survey question puts two questions in one sentence, so a single answer cannot be read as a verdict on either.

questions.q: True or false: Every sentence in an expository book expresses a proposition.
questions.explain: Some sentences ask questions, and others express wishes or intentions. The card next shows what they are good for.
questions.rule: Not every sentence is a proposition.

questions.q: According to the authors, how are propositions related to questions?
options: They are questions in disguise
They are the answers to questions
They are the reasons for asking
They are questions readers must ask
optionExplain: A proposition affirms or denies; it does not ask.
Right: questions state problems, and propositions are the answers.
Reasons support propositions; they are not what a proposition is.
Readers do ask questions, but the propositions are the author's answers.
questions.explain: Questions state problems; propositions are declarations that answer them. That is why their sentences are called declarative.
questions.rule: Questions pose; propositions answer.

questions.q: Sort these sentences from a book about city trees.

items.t: Street trees lower summer temperatures by several degrees.
Which trees survive best beside busy roads?
I intend to show that planting costs are repaid within a decade.
Roots seldom damage pavements when the right species is chosen.
If only every city kept a register of its trees.
Shade from trees cuts the energy used for air conditioning.

questions.explain: The declarative sentences affirm something about trees. The question states a problem, the intention describes the author's plan, and the wish expresses a hope.
questions.rule: Declaratives can carry knowledge; questions, wishes and intentions cannot.

questions.q: A columnist ends a paragraph by asking who would trust a bank that hides its fees. How should a reader treat this sentence?
options: As a real question the columnist wants readers to research
As a disguised proposition: no one should trust such a bank
As a wish that banks would publish all their fees openly
As a statement of the columnist's plan for the article
optionExplain: The columnist does not expect readers to investigate; the answer is assumed.
Right: the question form expects one answer, so the columnist is asserting it.
A wish may lie behind it, but the sentence asserts something about trust.
Nothing in it describes what the article will do.
questions.explain: Grammatical form can mislead. A rhetorical question asserts its expected answer, so the reader restates it as the proposition it implies.
questions.rule: Restate rhetorical questions as the claims they make.
questions.teaches: A rhetorical question has the form of a question but asserts an answer; a reader should restate it as the proposition it implies before deciding what the author holds.

questions.q: True or false: Once questions, wishes and intentions are set aside, the sentences left in a chapter are its key propositions.
questions.explain: Many declarative sentences are background, examples or side remarks. The test removes sentences that cannot carry the author's knowledge; finding the important ones is a further step.
questions.rule: Declarative is necessary, not sufficient, for a key proposition.

questions.q: A research abstract says: We asked whether sleep loss affects memory. We hoped to inform school policy. We found that one night without sleep cut recall by a third. Which sentence states a proposition about sleep and memory?
options: We found that one night without sleep cut recall by a third
We asked whether sleep loss affects memory in any way
We hoped to inform school policy on homework and exams
None, since all three describe what the researchers did
optionExplain: Right: this affirms something about sleep and memory; it is the paper's answer.
This states the research question, a problem rather than an answer.
This states the researchers' intention, not knowledge about sleep.
All three mention the researchers, but only the finding declares something about sleep and memory.
questions.explain: The question and the aim frame the study; the finding is its proposition. Reading the findings tells you what the paper claims.
questions.rule: In a paper, the findings are the propositions.
questions.teaches: In a research paper, the research question and aims frame the work while the findings are its propositions, so a reader who wants the paper's claims looks to the findings first.

questions.q: True or false: The same sentence, word for word, can express two different propositions in two places in a book.
questions.explain: If a key word in the sentence shifts its sense, the proposition shifts with it even though the sentence does not. The card next shows the authors' example.
questions.rule: Same words, possibly different claims.

questions.q: According to the authors, the same sentence can express different propositions if there is a shift in the ____ that its words express.
questions.explain: Words are ambiguous; when a word expresses a different term, the sentence containing it expresses a different proposition.
questions.rule: A shift in terms is a shift in proposition.

questions.q: A fitness app says on one screen that its users get stronger, meaning they lift heavier weights, and on another that its users get stronger, meaning they feel more confident. A reviewer finds data showing users lift heavier weights. What does the data support?
options: Both claims, since the sentence is the same on each screen
Only the first claim, about lifting heavier weights
Neither claim, since the app uses the word loosely
Only the second claim, since confidence follows strength
optionExplain: The sentence is the same but the propositions differ, so evidence for one is not evidence for the other.
Right: the data bears on the proposition about weights, not on the one about confidence.
Loose use does not void both claims; the data does support one of them.
Confidence may follow strength, but the data measured weights, not feelings.
questions.explain: Two propositions share one sentence. Evidence attaches to propositions, so it supports only the claim it measures.
questions.rule: Evidence attaches to propositions, not to sentences.

questions.q: Suppose an argument uses the word law in both premises: laws of nature cannot be broken; speed limits are laws; so speed limits cannot be broken. What has gone wrong?
options: The conclusion is true, since the police enforce speed limits
The second premise is false, since speed limits are not really laws at all
Nothing, since the conclusion follows from two true premises
The word law shifts sense between the premises, so they do not connect
optionExplain: Enforcement shows speed limits are often broken, which is why the conclusion is false.
Speed limits are laws in the legal sense; the trouble is that it is a different sense from the first premise.
It looks valid, but the premises use law in two senses, so they share a word, not a term.
Right: a law of nature describes what happens; a speed limit prescribes what should. The shared word hides two terms.
questions.explain: The premises seem to connect through the word law, but they use two terms. An argument whose key word shifts sense can look valid while proving nothing.
questions.rule: Check that a key word keeps its term through an argument.
questions.teaches: An argument whose key word shifts sense between premises can look valid while proving nothing, because the premises share a word but not a term.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, most repeated sentences in a careful book express the same proposition each time.
questions.explain: The check for shifting terms is for key sentences whose words have more than one sense. Most repetitions mean the same thing.
questions.rule: Check repetitions of ambiguous key words; do not suspect them all.

questions.q: An election slogan reads: make our streets safe again. Voters worried about crime, about traffic and about crumbling pavements all cheer it. Using the authors' point, what best explains its wide appeal?
options: It works like a question, so each voter answers it in his own personal way
It states one clear claim that all these voters happen to share
Readers take safe in different senses, so each hears a different claim
Its words are too plain to be read in more than one way by anyone
optionExplain: It is a call to action, not a question; its appeal comes from the open sense of safe.
The voters' worries differ, so they are not agreeing on one proposition.
Right: one sentence carries several propositions, and each voter supplies the one he likes.
Plain words can still be ambiguous; safe covers crime, traffic and repairs here.
questions.explain: Ambiguity lets one sentence promise different things to different readers. Agreement with the sentence may hide disagreement about the propositions.
questions.rule: Ask which proposition a popular sentence is committing to.
questions.teaches: A slogan can draw its appeal from ambiguity: each reader supplies the sense he prefers, so the sentence seems to promise more than any single proposition it could express.

questions.q: How many propositions can a single grammatical sentence express?
options: None, since only paragraphs carry claims
Exactly one, since a sentence is one thought
One or several, depending on how it is built
Two at most, one for each main clause
optionExplain: Sentences are the usual vehicle of propositions; paragraphs are more often the vehicle of arguments.
That is the one-to-one assumption the authors warn against.
Right: a simple sentence usually carries one; a compound sentence carries two or more.
A complex sentence can carry three or more; the authors find three in one from Machiavelli.
questions.explain: A compound sentence is really a collection of sentences, so it can express several propositions. The card next works through an example.
questions.rule: Compound sentences carry several propositions.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the sentence they quote from Machiavelli's The Prince says three things, although it is grammatically a single sentence.
questions.explain: The authors find a recommendation about fear, a reason for it, and a condition for avoiding hatred, all in one sentence.
questions.rule: One sentence, three propositions.

questions.q: A health article says: Regular walking lowers blood pressure, and because it costs nothing, doctors should prescribe it before medication. Which propositions does the sentence contain? Choose three.
options: Regular walking lowers blood pressure
Walking costs nothing
Doctors should prescribe walking before medication
Medication does not lower blood pressure
Walking is the only way to lower blood pressure
optionExplain: Right: the first clause affirms this.
Right: the because clause asserts it as a reason.
Right: this is the recommendation the sentence argues for.
Prescribing walking first does not deny that medication works; the sentence never says this.
The sentence says walking lowers pressure, not that nothing else does.
questions.explain: The and and the because split the sentence into three claims. The wrong options read in claims the sentence does not make.
questions.rule: List what is asserted, and only that.

questions.q: Suppose a reader breaks this sentence only at its connecting words: the new vaccine, which was tested on only two hundred people, should be offered to everyone over sixty. She finds one proposition. What has she missed?
options: The which clause's claim about testing on only two hundred people
A second conclusion that the vaccine should be offered to all ages
A reason why people over sixty are most at risk from the disease
Nothing, since a sentence without and or because holds one claim
optionExplain: Right: the which clause asserts something that could be true or false on its own, and it matters to the recommendation.
The sentence limits the offer to people over sixty; it says nothing about all ages.
No reason about risk is stated; the reader would be adding it.
Claims can sit inside clauses as well as at joins, as the which clause shows.
questions.explain: Connecting words are one place to split a sentence, but a which or who clause can carry a separate claim too. Here it states a fact a critic might use against the recommendation.
questions.rule: Look inside which and who clauses for hidden claims.
questions.teaches: Propositions can hide inside which and who clauses as well as at the joins marked by and or because, so splitting a sentence only at its connecting words can miss a claim.

questions.q: True or false: The word and can join two things inside a single claim, so a sentence containing it may express only one proposition.
questions.explain: And can join two claims, but it can also join two things in one claim, as in a sentence saying that salt and pepper sit on the table. Look at what is asserted, not only at the joining word.
questions.rule: And joins things as well as claims.

questions.q: A rental agreement says the deposit will be returned within 30 days, provided that the flat is left clean and no rent is owed. A tenant reads it as a plain promise to return the deposit within 30 days. What has she missed?
options: Nothing, since such conditions are standard wording with no legal effect
The conditions, which add separate requirements that limit the promise
The date, since 30 days is only a suggestion in such agreements
The tone, since provided that shows the landlord's distrust of her
optionExplain: Standard wording still carries meaning; these conditions decide whether she gets the deposit.
Right: each condition is a further proposition, and the promise holds only if they are met.
The date is stated firmly; the gap in her reading is the conditions.
Tone is not the point; provided that adds requirements, whatever the landlord feels.
questions.explain: Provided that adds two propositions that restrict the main one. Reading only the main clause changes what the sentence asserts.
questions.rule: Read the conditions as claims in their own right.
questions.teaches: Condition words such as provided that, unless and only if add propositions that limit the main claim; skipping them changes what the sentence asserts.

questions.q: A sentence makes three claims. You think one is false and two are true. What does the authors' advice suggest you do?
options: Accept the whole sentence, since most of it is true
Reject the whole sentence, since part of it is false
Agree with two claims and disagree with the third
Hold back all judgment until the author rewrites it
optionExplain: Majority does not decide; the false claim stays false.
One false claim does not make the others false; rejecting all three is too coarse.
Right: the authors say you may disagree with one proposition in a sentence and agree with the others.
You can judge now, once you have separated the claims; there is no need for a rewrite.
questions.explain: A sentence with several propositions calls for several verdicts. The card next shows the authors' example.
questions.rule: Several claims, several verdicts.

questions.q: According to the authors, unless you recognize the distinct propositions in a complicated sentence, you cannot make a ____ judgment on what the writer is saying.
questions.explain: A discriminating judgment separates what you accept from what you reject. Without seeing the distinct propositions, you can only judge the sentence as a whole.
questions.rule: Discriminate the claims before judging them.

questions.q: An editorial says the new stadium will bring jobs, so the city should pay for it out of the schools budget. A reader agrees the stadium will bring jobs but opposes cutting school funds. How does separating the propositions help her?
options: It shows she must reject both, since they form a single argument
It shows she must accept both, since one is a reason for the other
She can accept the jobs claim while rejecting the funding proposal
It shows the editorial makes no claims, only recommendations
optionExplain: Being linked in an argument does not make two claims stand or fall together in every case.
A reason can be true and still too weak to carry the conclusion.
Right: a true reason does not force the conclusion; jobs may not justify taking money from schools.
The editorial does claim something about jobs and recommends something about funding.
questions.explain: Separating the claim about jobs from the proposal about funding lets her judge each. Accepting a premise does not commit her to every conclusion drawn from it.
questions.rule: Accepting a reason is not accepting every conclusion drawn from it.

questions.q: An editorial argues that a new stadium will bring jobs, so the city should pay for it from the schools budget. Suppose a reader rejects the claim that the stadium will bring jobs. What happens to the funding proposal in her eyes?
options: It loses the support that claim gave it, though other reasons might remain
Nothing at all, since the two propositions are wholly independent of each other
It is shown false, since the reason offered for it is itself false
It becomes stronger, since there are fewer claims left to question
optionExplain: Right: a premise and its conclusion are linked, so rejecting the premise removes that support, but the conclusion could have other grounds.
Premise and conclusion are not independent: the conclusion was resting on the premise.
A false reason weakens the case; it does not prove the conclusion false.
Removing a reason leaves the proposal with less support, not more.
questions.explain: Separating claims does not make them independent. Rejecting a premise takes away the support it gave, without proving the conclusion false.
questions.rule: Rejecting a premise weakens, but does not refute, its conclusion.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, separating the propositions in a sentence belongs to understanding it, and comes before deciding whether you agree.
questions.explain: You must understand what is said before agreeing or disagreeing. Separating the propositions is part of that understanding; the verdicts come afterwards, in criticism.
questions.rule: Separate first; judge afterwards.

questions.q: A manager proposes moving to a four-day week and cutting everyone's pay by ten percent. The team is split. Borrowing the authors' advice, what is a useful first step?
options: Vote on the whole proposal, since it was put forward as a package
Separate the two proposals so the team can see where it agrees
Drop the proposal, since one of its parts is disputed by the team
Adopt the proposal, since most staff want a four-day week
optionExplain: A single vote forces people to accept or reject parts they feel differently about.
Right: some may welcome the shorter week and oppose the pay cut; splitting shows exactly where the dispute lies.
A disputed part is a reason to examine it, not to drop the parts people accept.
Popularity of one part says nothing about the other part.
questions.explain: By analogy, a compound proposal works like a compound sentence. Splitting it lets people agree where they can and argue only over the rest.
questions.rule: Split compound proposals before debating them.
questions.teaches: By analogy, in a discussion, splitting a compound proposal into its parts lets people agree where they can and argue only about the part that is really in dispute.

questions.q: How many claims does the sentence the shop sold the painting to a museum in 1952 make?
options: Several: about the seller, the buyer, the object and the date
One, since it is a single simple sentence with one main verb
Two, one carried by the subject and one carried by the verb
None, since it reports a past event rather than a judgment
optionExplain: Right: each could be true or false on its own; the sale might have happened in another year, or to a collector.
One verb does not mean one claim; the authors show simple sentences can carry several.
Claims are not counted by parts of speech but by what could be separately true or false.
A report of an event is still an assertion that something happened.
questions.explain: A simple sentence can assert several things at once. The card next shows how lawyers read such sentences.
questions.rule: Simple grammar can hide several claims.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, even a grammatically simple sentence sometimes expresses two or more propositions.
questions.explain: The authors' lease example shows it: one simple sentence asserts who signed, what was signed and when.
questions.rule: Read simple sentences closely too.

questions.q: A witness says: The red van left the depot at noon. Which of these are claims the sentence makes, each of which could be challenged on its own? Choose three.
options: That the vehicle was red
That it left at noon
That it left from the depot
That the driver was speeding
That the van was stolen
optionExplain: Right: the colour is asserted and could be wrong.
Right: the time is asserted and could be wrong.
Right: the place it left from is asserted and could be wrong.
Nothing in the sentence says how fast it went.
The sentence says nothing about how the van came to be there.
questions.explain: Each modifier, red, the depot, at noon, adds a claim that could be false while the others are true. Speeding and theft are not asserted at all.
questions.rule: Each modifier can carry its own claim.

questions.q: Take the sentence John Doe signed the lease on March 24. Suppose a lawyer denies it, stating that her client did not sign the lease on March 24. What could this denial be denying?
options: Only the date, since dates are what lawyers usually dispute
Only that the client ever signed any document at all
Any of its claims: the signing, the document or the date
Nothing definite, since a denial asserts nothing
optionExplain: Dates are often disputed, but the denial could also be about the signing or the document.
That is one reading, but the client may have signed on another day.
Right: since the sentence makes several claims, its denial is unclear about which one is false.
A denial is a judgment too; the trouble is that it is unclear which claim it targets.
questions.explain: A sentence carrying several claims has a correspondingly vague denial. To know what is denied, you must know which claim is meant.
questions.rule: Ask which embedded claim a denial targets.
questions.teaches: Denying a sentence that makes several claims is ambiguous: the denial may target any one of them, so a careful reader asks which claim is actually being rejected.

questions.q: True or false: A careful reader should split a key sentence into as many grammatical parts as possible, since more parts make a fuller reading.
questions.explain: Split a sentence only into claims that could be separately true or false and that matter to the author's point. Splitting into grammatical details gives noise, not understanding.
questions.rule: Split into claims that matter, not into words.

questions.q: A politician says that last year her government built 10,000 new homes in the north. A fact-checker finds 10,000 homes were built, but spread across the whole country. Which verdict best reports each separate claim?
options: Unclear, since a single sentence cannot be split
True, since the main figure of 10,000 is correct
False, so the 10,000 figure should be withdrawn
Partly true: the number is right but the place is wrong
optionExplain: Sentences can be split into claims, which is exactly what the fact-checker needs to do.
The figure is right, but the claim about the north is part of what was asserted.
The figure was right; calling the whole sentence false would withdraw a true claim along with the false one.
Right: the sentence makes separate claims about number and place, and only one holds.
questions.explain: Treating the sentence as several claims gives a precise verdict. A single true or false would misreport what was right and what was wrong.
questions.rule: Give a verdict claim by claim.
questions.teaches: Fact-checking works claim by claim: a sentence can be right in its main figure and wrong in a detail, and an honest verdict says which part is which.

questions.q: True or false: Two sentences that share no key words can still express the same proposition.
questions.explain: Different words can express the same terms, and the same terms in the same relation make the same proposition. The card next gives the authors' example.
questions.rule: Different words can carry one claim.

questions.q: The authors compare two sentences: teaching and being taught are correlative functions, and initiating and receiving communication are related processes. What do the two sentences have in common?
options: They share a sentence form but not a proposition
They express opposite propositions about teaching
They express the same proposition in different words
They show that one word can carry two different terms
optionExplain: Their wording differs entirely; what they share is the proposition.
Nothing in either sentence contradicts the other; both describe the same paired activities.
Right: the authors say a reader who grasps their terms will see the two say the same thing.
This example shows the reverse: several words carrying the same terms.
questions.explain: Teaching and being taught are the same activities as initiating and receiving communication, and correlative means related. Same terms, same relation, same proposition.
questions.rule: Match terms and relation to spot a restatement.

questions.q: Which sentence expresses the same proposition as the sentence most voters distrust the parliament?
options: Most of the electorate has little faith in the legislature
Some voters distrust the parliament more than they distrust courts
Every voter distrusts the parliament and all of its members
Most members of parliament distrust the voters who elect them
optionExplain: Right: electorate, little faith and legislature carry the same terms as voters, distrust and parliament, with the same quantity, most.
This compares two institutions and speaks of some voters, a different proposition.
Every is stronger than most, so the proposition changes.
This reverses who distrusts whom, though it reuses the same words.
questions.explain: The matching sentence changes every word but keeps the terms, the quantity and the relation. The others keep more words but change what is asserted.
questions.rule: Shared words do not mean a shared proposition.

questions.q: Suppose the second sentence in each pair is a reworded version of the first. Which pairs express DIFFERENT propositions, despite their similar wording? Choose two.
options: All drivers must carry a licence. Most drivers must carry a licence.
The museum opens at nine. Opening time at the museum is nine o'clock.
Prices rose because wages rose. Wages rose because prices rose.
She wrote the report. The report was written by her.
optionExplain: Right: all and most make different claims; one word changes the proposition.
These reword the same claim about opening time.
Right: the same words, but the direction of cause is reversed.
Active and passive forms of one claim express the same proposition.
questions.explain: Sameness is judged by what is asserted. Changing a quantity word or the direction of a relation changes the proposition even when most words stay.
questions.rule: A small change of wording can be a large change of claim.

questions.q: True or false: When an author restates the same proposition in new words at several points in a book, the repetition can be a clue that he treats it as important.
questions.explain: By inference, authors are likely to return to what matters most to them. If so, recognizing restatements, which needs the skill on the card, helps you find the propositions the book turns on.
questions.rule: Restated claims are often central claims.
questions.teaches: By inference, a proposition an author restates in fresh words at several points is often one he regards as central, so recognizing restatements helps you locate his key propositions.

questions.q: A student copies no sentence from a published essay but restates each of its main claims in her own words, in the same order, without credit. Using the authors' point, how should her essay be described?
options: It is a summary, which only needs credit when it quotes directly
It is original work, since none of its sentences matches the published essay
It is a translation, which by its nature needs no credit at all
It borrows the essay's propositions, so the ideas still need credit
optionExplain: Summaries of another's ideas need credit whether or not they quote.
Originality lies in the propositions, not the sentences, and these are the essay's.
Even a translation carries another writer's propositions and needs credit.
Right: new sentences, same propositions; the ideas are borrowed even though the words are not.
questions.explain: By analogy, credit attaches to propositions, not to wording. Restating claims in new sentences leaves them someone else's claims.
questions.rule: Ideas belong to their author whatever the wording.
questions.teaches: Restating a claim in other words does not make it a new idea: credit belongs to the proposition rather than the wording, which is why paraphrase without citation still counts as borrowing.

questions.q: According to the authors, how much grammar does a reader need for analytical reading?
options: Enough to see how the words in sentences are ordered and related
None, since meaning comes through without attention to form
Full technical command of syntax, with formal sentence diagrams
Only spelling and punctuation, since these show the writer's care
optionExplain: Right: the authors want readers concerned with the order of words and their relations, without demanding everything about syntax.
The authors call some knowledge of grammar indispensable.
They say you need not understand everything about syntax.
Spelling and punctuation are surface features; the authors point to how words relate in sentences.
questions.explain: Some grammar is indispensable, but not a technical mastery. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Some grammar, not all of syntax.

questions.q: According to the authors, you cannot begin to deal with terms, propositions and arguments until you can get beneath the surface of ____.
questions.explain: Terms, propositions and arguments are the elements of thought. While words, sentences and paragraphs stay opaque and unanalyzed, they block communication instead of carrying it.
questions.rule: See through the language to the thought.

questions.q: One report says the board only approved the merger in March. Another says the board approved only the merger in March. What do they assert differently?
options: The first stresses timing; the second says nothing else was approved
Nothing, since the two sentences contain exactly the same words
The first says the merger was rejected before it was approved
The second says the board held no other meeting that year except in March
optionExplain: Right: the position of only decides what it restricts, the time or the thing approved.
Same words in a different order can make different claims.
Nothing about an earlier rejection is asserted; only suggests lateness at most.
Only attaches to the merger, not to the meetings.
questions.explain: The word only restricts whatever it sits next to. Attending to word order is the kind of grammar the authors have in mind.
questions.rule: Word order can change the claim.

questions.q: Compare two sentences: the students, who failed, retook the exam; and the students who failed retook the exam. What does the difference in commas change?
options: The first says the students retook the exam more than once
Nothing, since commas change only the rhythm of a sentence, not its claim
The first says all the students failed; the second picks out those who failed
The second says that none of the students in the class failed
optionExplain: Neither sentence says how many times the exam was retaken.
Here the commas change which students the claim is about.
Right: with commas the clause describes all the students; without them it picks out the ones who failed.
The second picks out the students who failed and says they retook it; it does not say none failed.
questions.explain: Punctuation is part of the grammar a reader must see through. With commas the clause describes all the students; without them it picks out only the students who failed.
questions.rule: Punctuation can change what is asserted.
questions.teaches: Punctuation belongs to the grammar a reader must see through: a pair of commas can turn a clause that picks out certain members of a group, here the students who failed, into one that describes all of them.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reader must be able to name the parts of speech and diagram sentences formally before reading analytically.
questions.explain: The authors ask for attention to how words are ordered and related, not for formal analysis or technical terms. Grammar serves understanding; it is not the goal.
questions.rule: Attend to grammar; do not worship it.

questions.q: A news report says the council told the developers that they would have to pay for the new road. A resident and a developer read it differently. Where does the difference most likely lie?
options: In whether the report states a fact or an opinion
In what the word road means in a planning report
In whether the council has the legal right to give such orders
In whom they refers to, the council or the developers
optionExplain: Fact or opinion, the reader still has to know who is said to pay.
Road is plain here; the ambiguity is in the pronoun.
That is a question of law, not of what the sentence says.
Right: they could point to either noun, and the claim about who pays changes with it.
questions.explain: Pronouns are a common place where grammar decides meaning. Until the reference of they is settled, the sentence carries two possible propositions.
questions.rule: Settle what each pronoun points to.
questions.teaches: Pronouns are a frequent source of ambiguity: when it or they could point to two nouns, the sentence carries two possible propositions until the reader settles the reference from context.

questions.q: Which of these did the authors give as Rule 6 of analytical reading?
options: Mark the most important sentences and discover their propositions
Find the important words in a book and come to terms with the author
Find out what the author's solutions to his problems are
State the unity of the whole book in a sentence or two
optionExplain: Right: Rule 6 moves from sentences to the propositions they contain.
That is Rule 5, which comes just before.
That is Rule 8, the last rule of interpretation.
That belongs to the first stage of analytical reading, not to Rule 6.
questions.explain: Rule 6 deals with sentences and propositions, after Rule 5 on words and terms. The card next sets out Rules 6 and 7.
questions.rule: Rule 6: key sentences, their propositions.

questions.q: Put these rules of analytical reading in order, from Rule 5 to Rule 7.
items: Find the important words and come to terms
Mark the most important sentences and find their propositions
Locate or construct the basic arguments from connected sentences
questions.explain: The rules build up from words to sentences to connections of sentences, matching terms, propositions and arguments.
questions.rule: Terms, then propositions, then arguments.

questions.q: A reader opens a textbook on plate tectonics and applies Rule 6. What does she do?
options: Marks the main claims and works out what each one asserts
Marks every unfamiliar word and looks each one up in a dictionary
Marks the chapter headings and copies them into an outline
Marks the passages she enjoys most and rereads them for pleasure
optionExplain: Right: Rule 6 has two parts, marking the important sentences and discovering their propositions.
Looking up words is closer to Rule 5's work on terms.
Outlining headings belongs to the first stage, the structure of the book.
Enjoyment is not the test of importance in Rule 6.
questions.explain: Rule 6 asks for both steps: find the key sentences, then find what each asserts.
questions.rule: Mark, then interpret.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Rules 6 and 7 apply in the same way to a novel as to a textbook.
questions.explain: The authors say these rules apply primarily to expository works. For novels, plays and poems the rules about propositions and arguments are quite different.
questions.rule: These rules are made for expository books.

questions.q: Suppose a novel contains a chapter in which the narrator sets out, essay-style, a theory of why empires fall. How might a reader apply Rules 6 and 7 there?
options: Use them on every sentence, since the book contains an argument
Use them on that essay-like chapter, reading the story by other rules
Avoid them entirely, since the book as a whole is a novel
Use them only on the dialogue, where the characters state their opinions
optionExplain: One expository chapter does not make the whole novel a treatise.
Right: the chapter is expository in kind, so its propositions and arguments can be traced, while the story needs different handling.
The book's overall kind does not stop one part from being expository.
Characters' opinions are part of the story; they are not the author's propositions.
questions.explain: The rules fit expository writing wherever it appears. A mixed book needs the reader to judge which parts are which.
questions.rule: Apply the rules to the expository parts of a mixed book.
questions.teaches: Some books mix kinds: an expository passage inside a novel can be read for propositions and arguments, while the story around it calls for the different rules the authors give for imaginative works.

questions.q: A satirical news site runs an article solemnly arguing that cities should ban walking to ease traffic. Reading it with Rule 6, what should a reader take as the writer's proposition?
options: That traffic is not a real problem, since the piece is a joke
That cities should ban walking, since the article says so plainly
No proposition at all, since satire is written only to make people laugh
The point the irony implies, such as that car-first planning is absurd
optionExplain: Joking about a problem is different from denying it exists.
The literal sentence is not the writer's judgment, just as a character's speech is not a novelist's.
Satire amuses, but it usually makes a point about its target.
Right: the literal claim is a mask; the writer's judgment is what the absurdity points to.
questions.explain: In satire the literal sentences are not the writer's claims. The proposition lies in what the irony implies, which the reader must state in plain words.
questions.rule: In irony, the proposition is what is implied, not what is said.
questions.teaches: In satire and irony the literal sentences are not the writer's propositions; the reader must state the judgment the irony implies before applying the rules about propositions.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, because a book has only a few key sentences, a reader can skip most of the others.
questions.explain: The authors say you have to understand every sentence. The card next explains how pace divides the work.
questions.rule: Few key sentences, but every sentence understood.

questions.q: According to the authors, most sentences in a book, like most words, cause no difficulty, and you read them relatively ____.
questions.explain: Easy sentences are read relatively quickly but still understood; skipping them is not the advice. The few hard sentences get slow, careful reading.
questions.rule: Quick, not skipped.

questions.q: A reader gives every sentence of a thirty-page economics chapter the same slow, careful attention and runs out of time halfway. What do the authors suggest?
options: Stop and choose an easier book on the same subject instead
Skip to the chapter's last page, where the key sentences sit
Read every sentence faster, at one quicker speed throughout
Read the easy majority faster and save care for the hard few
optionExplain: The difficulty is pace, not the book; varying speed should solve it.
Key sentences can appear anywhere; skipping leaves most unread.
A uniform faster speed would rush the sentences that need care.
Right: uniform slowness wastes effort on sentences that need none.
questions.explain: Varying pace gives each sentence what it needs. One speed for everything, slow or fast, misallocates effort.
questions.rule: Vary pace by difficulty.

questions.q: A student short of time reads only the sentences she highlighted on a first pass and skips the rest. What risk does she run that a quick reader of every sentence does not?
options: Learning less vocabulary, since new words appear mostly in plain sentences
Missing claims the key sentences rest on, hidden in plain ones
Missing the author's examples, which matter more than his key claims
Forming opinions too early about whether the author is right
optionExplain: New words can appear anywhere, and vocabulary is not the main loss; the danger is a skipped premise or definition the key sentences need.
Right: a skipped sentence may hold a premise or definition the key sentences depend on.
Examples help, but the authors rank the leading claims and their reasons above illustrations; the real risk is losing a claim the key sentences rest on.
Early judgment is a separate fault; it is not caused by skipping.
questions.explain: Quick reading still takes in every sentence, so a buried premise gets noticed. Skipping cannot catch it.
questions.rule: Skimming is not skipping.
questions.teaches: Skipping sentences is not the same as reading them quickly: a skipped sentence may hold a premise or definition the key sentences depend on, which quick reading would still catch.

questions.q: True or false: If an easy-looking sentence, read at speed, turns out to state the author's main conclusion, the reader should slow down and reread it.
questions.explain: Pace follows what a sentence needs, not a plan made in advance. A sentence that proves important gets the careful reading, even if the reader first took it at speed.
questions.rule: Change pace when a sentence proves important.

questions.q: A small-business owner must read a fifteen-page supplier contract tonight. Applying the authors' point by analogy, how should she spend her attention?
options: Read standard clauses at pace; slow down on payment and liability
Read only the payment clause, since the rest is standard legal wording
Read every clause at the same slow speed to be completely safe
Skim the whole contract once and sign if nothing stands out
optionExplain: Right: every clause gets read, and the ones carrying money and risk get the slow, careful reading.
Skipping clauses risks missing a term that changes the payment clause.
Uniform slowness may leave her too tired for the clauses that matter.
Skimming risks missing what does not stand out but still binds her.
questions.explain: By analogy, effort goes where difficulty and stakes are highest. Every clause is still read, and the definitions deserve care too, since a defined word carries its meaning into every clause that uses it.
questions.rule: Spend effort where the stakes are.
questions.teaches: In a contract the definitions section deserves slow reading even though it looks like boilerplate, because a defined word carries its special meaning into every clause that uses it.

questions.q: From the reader's point of view, which sentences in a book are likely to matter most?
options: Those that contain surprising facts or vivid stories
Those you agree with most strongly on a first reading
Those you understand only enough to know there is more
Those printed at the very start of each chapter
optionExplain: Surprising facts catch interest, but interest and importance are not the same.
Agreement tells you about your views, not about which sentences carry the author's meaning.
Right: the authors say the sentences important for you are the ones needing an effort of interpretation.
Position can help, but the authors' test here is the effort a sentence demands.
questions.explain: The sentences that resist your understanding are the ones to slow down for. The card next explains why they tend to be the author's key sentences too.
questions.rule: What resists you is likely to matter.

questions.q: According to the authors, the sentences important for you are those that require an effort of ____ because, at first sight, they are not perfectly intelligible.
questions.explain: These sentences need work to understand. You grasp them just well enough to know there is more, so you read them slowly.
questions.rule: Effort of interpretation marks a key sentence.

questions.q: While reading a book on monetary policy, which reactions mark a sentence as important for you, in the authors' sense? Choose two.
options: I follow it, but I sense it says more than I have grasped
I have to reread it to see how its parts fit together
I find it amusing and want to quote it to a friend
I already knew this fact before I opened the book
I strongly disagree with it and want to argue back
optionExplain: Right: partial understanding with a sense of more is exactly the authors' mark.
Right: needing to reread to see how it fits is an effort of interpretation.
Amusement shows interest, not a need for interpretation.
A familiar fact needs no effort to understand.
Disagreement may follow later, but it is a reaction to a claim, not a sign that you need to work out its meaning.
questions.explain: The test is the effort of understanding a sentence demands, not how you feel about it.
questions.rule: Effort, not feeling, marks the key sentence.

questions.q: True or false: If two careful readers of the same book, one new to the subject and one expert, each mark the sentences that need an effort of interpretation, their lists may differ.
questions.explain: Difficulty depends on what a reader already knows. A sentence obscure to a newcomer may be plain to an expert, so each reader's list reflects their background as well as the book.
questions.rule: Your hard sentences reflect you as well as the book.
questions.teaches: Difficulty is relative to the reader: two readers of the same book may mark different sentences, so a list of hard sentences reflects the reader's background as well as the author's emphasis.

questions.q: A sentence is hard to follow only because it uses a rare word in passing, in a side remark about the author's travels. What does the authors' limit suggest?
options: Stop reading, since the author writes too obscurely to follow
Treat it as a key sentence, since every hard sentence is a key one for you
Skip it, since side remarks need not be understood at all
Look up the word, but do not treat the side remark as a key sentence
optionExplain: One hard word in a side remark is no reason to abandon a book.
That treats the clue as a proof; some sentences are hard for reasons unrelated to importance.
Every sentence should be understood, even ones read quickly.
Right: difficulty is a clue, and here the cause is a passing word in a digression, not a key judgment.
questions.explain: Difficulty points to key sentences only when the difficulty lies in the thought. A rare word in a digression needs a dictionary, not slow interpretation.
questions.rule: Ask why a sentence is hard before treating it as key.

questions.q: In a training lecture you follow most points easily, but one remark about how the new pricing model works leaves you half sure. By analogy with the authors' point, what should you do?
options: Ask about a detail you already understand, to confirm you have it
Ask about that remark, since it probably carries the central point
Let it go, since most of the lecture was easy to follow
Note the speaker's jokes, since those show what really matters
optionExplain: Confirming what you know adds little; the gap is elsewhere.
Right: the half-understood remark is the listener's key sentence, and asking about it reaches the core fastest.
Ease elsewhere does not settle the one point you only half grasp.
Jokes may hold attention, but they rarely carry the central point.
questions.explain: By analogy, in talk as in books, the point you half follow is likely to be the important one. A question there pays off most.
questions.rule: Ask about what you half understand.
questions.teaches: By analogy, in a lecture or meeting the remark you only half follow is the one to ask about; a question there usually reaches the speaker's central point faster than one about details you already grasp.

questions.q: From the author's point of view, which sentences in his book are the most important?
options: Those stating the judgments his whole argument rests on
Those telling how he first came to his point of view
Those reviewing what other writers have said on the topic
Those defining the particular words he has chosen to use
optionExplain: Right: the authors say these are the sentences that matter from the author's side.
The story of how he arrived at his view is surrounding discussion.
Comment on others' work supports the argument but is not its core.
Discussing his words helps, but the authors class it with the surrounding discussion.
questions.explain: The core is the set of judgments the argument rests on. The card next shows how to separate them from everything else.
questions.rule: The core is the judgments the argument rests on.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the heart of an author's communication lies in his major affirmations and denials and the reasons he gives for them.
questions.explain: Everything else, history, consequences, comments on others, surrounds this core.
questions.rule: Affirmations, denials and reasons are the heart.

questions.q: A book argues that remote work raises productivity. Sort these sentences from it.
groups: Core: main affirmation, denial or reason

items.t: Remote workers finish more tasks per week than office workers.
Time saved on commuting is mostly spent on work.
Open-plan offices do not increase collaboration.
I first noticed this while running a small design firm.
Several economists dismissed the idea in the 1990s.
In this book I use productivity to mean output per hour.

questions.explain: The core sentences affirm or deny something the argument depends on. The author's story, the history of the debate and his remarks about his words surround that core.
questions.rule: Separate the claims from their setting.

questions.q: An author argues that remote work raises productivity. Suppose that in a later chapter replying to critics he writes: I do not claim that all remote work raises output; I claim it does so for tasks needing long concentration. What does this sentence do for the reader?
options: It is surrounding discussion, so it can be read quickly
It retracts the book's main thesis in the face of the critics' objections
It states the author's key proposition in an exact, limited form
It describes the critics' view rather than the author's
optionExplain: Replies to critics are surrounding discussion in general, but this sentence states the core claim.
He narrows the claim, but he still affirms it; nothing is withdrawn.
Right: in answering critics the author has to say exactly what he holds.
He mentions what critics attribute to him only to deny it; the second half is his own view.
questions.explain: Replies to critics often state the core claim in its sharpest form, because a defence must say precisely what is being defended.
questions.rule: Look for key propositions in the author's replies to critics.
questions.teaches: Replies to critics often restate an author's key propositions in their sharpest form, because to defend a view he must say exactly what he holds and what he does not.

questions.q: True or false: Even after the main sentences are raised in relief, the surrounding discussion can still help you understand them.
questions.explain: Surrounding discussion can explain a key sentence or show why it matters. Raising the main sentences in relief means letting them stand out, not discarding the rest.
questions.rule: Relief means standing out, not standing alone.

questions.q: A founder's ten-minute pitch covers her childhood, a story about a customer, and two claims: the sensors cut warehouse losses by a fifth, and they pay for themselves within a year. Which parts should an investor raise in relief?
options: All parts equally, since a pitch is short enough to weigh whole
The childhood story, which shows her commitment to the venture
The customer story, since stories are what persuade investors
The two claims about losses and payback, which the pitch rests on
optionExplain: Weighing all parts equally blurs the claims into the stories.
Commitment matters to investors, but it is setting, not the claim to be tested.
Stories persuade, which is a reason to separate them from the claims they decorate.
Right: these are the affirmations everything else supports; if they fail, the pitch fails.
questions.explain: By analogy, a pitch has a core and a setting like a book. The investor tests the claims; the stories only frame them.
questions.rule: Find the claims under the stories.
questions.teaches: By analogy, anecdotes and personal history make a talk persuasive but are not its claims; a listener who separates the two can say exactly what was asserted and test it.

questions.q: Which of these can signal that a sentence is one of the author's leading propositions? Choose three.
options: The author says this point is important
It is set in italics or in bold type
It follows a marker such as I answer that
It sits in a footnote listing sources
It is the longest sentence on its page
optionExplain: Right: some authors tell you when a point is important.
Right: typographical devices can make leading sentences stand out.
Right: Aquinas uses this phrase to mark where he argues his own point.
Source notes support the text; they rarely carry the leading claims.
Length is no sign of importance; long sentences are often digressions.
questions.explain: Authors and formats can flag their leading sentences. The card next describes such signals and how readers misuse them.
questions.rule: Use the author's own signals.

questions.q: In Aquinas's Summa Theologica, according to the authors, what marks the place where he begins to argue his own point?
options: The words I answer that
A numbered list of objections
The question heading the section
A summary at the end of the part
optionExplain: Right: the authors say his own argument begins with these words.
The objections state views opposing his answer; they come before his argument.
The question opens the section; it states the problem, not his answer.
The authors describe no such summary as his marker.
questions.explain: Each section opens with a question, then objections, then I answer that, where Aquinas argues his own position.
questions.rule: In Aquinas, I answer that marks the author's own argument.

questions.q: Suppose a management book prints one sentence per chapter in a shaded box, and the author writes that it is the most important idea in the chapter. A reader keeps going without stopping. According to the authors, what has he done?
options: Followed good practice, since stopping breaks concentration
Read efficiently, since boxes usually hold side material
Ignored a signal that makes the leading sentence stand out
Done nothing wrong, since every sentence counts the same
optionExplain: Stopping at a key sentence is what the authors recommend.
Some boxes do hold side material, but this author says the box holds the chapter's main idea.
Right: the authors describe readers who ignore such clear signs and read on instead of examining the sentence.
Treating every sentence as equal is what turns a book into a blur.
questions.explain: The author did the reader's work of locating the sentence. The reader's part is to stop and examine it.
questions.rule: When the author points, stop and look.

questions.q: A student quotes a sentence from the objections in an article of Aquinas as Aquinas's own view. What has the format told the reader that the student missed?
options: Objections come before I answer that, so they state views he opposes
Objections are where Aquinas states his own conclusions most fully and plainly
Objections summarise the whole argument of the article
Objections give the definitions he will use in his answer
optionExplain: Right: the objections oppose the answer Aquinas defends, so quoting them as his view reverses his position.
His conclusions come after I answer that, not in the objections.
The objections state opposing views, not a summary of his own argument.
They are arguments against his answer, not definitions.
questions.explain: A format marks role as well as importance. In Aquinas, a sentence's place tells you whether it is his view or one he means to answer.
questions.rule: Read a format for each sentence's role.
questions.teaches: A book's format can show a sentence's role as well as its importance: in Aquinas the objections come before I answer that, so a sentence there is a view he means to answer, not his own.

questions.q: True or false: An author may set a sentence in italics for reasons other than marking a leading proposition, such as a striking phrase or a new word.
questions.explain: Authors emphasise for many reasons. A marked sentence is a clue, and still needs your own judgment of its role.
questions.rule: Emphasis is a clue, not a guarantee.

questions.q: Match each marker phrase to what it usually introduces in its kind of writing.
pairs: We hold that, in a court judgment
The court's ruling on the legal question
We find that, in a research report
A view the author will answer
questions.explain: Like Euclid's labels and Aquinas's I answer that, many kinds of writing have stock phrases that mark their leading propositions or the views opposed to them.
questions.rule: Learn the markers of each kind of writing.
questions.teaches: Many kinds of writing have their own marker phrases for leading propositions, such as we hold that in a court judgment or we find that in a report; learning a genre's markers speeds up finding its key sentences.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, noticing that you are puzzled by a passage is a sign of poor reading that you should try to avoid.
questions.explain: The authors treat perplexity, noticed and admitted, as an essential part of reading. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Noticing puzzlement is part of good reading.

questions.q: The authors say that ____ is the beginning of wisdom in learning from books as well as from nature.
questions.explain: Wonder opens the questions that let a book teach you something new.
questions.rule: Wonder starts learning.

questions.q: Suppose a reader finishes a chapter on climate economics feeling she understood all of it, having asked herself no questions along the way. What do the authors suggest?
options: She may have gained little new insight, since she raised no questions
She read it perfectly, since nothing in the chapter puzzled her at all
The chapter was too easy, so she should switch to a harder book
She should reread it at the same pace to fix it in her memory
optionExplain: Right: the authors warn that without questions about meaning, a book gives no insight beyond what you already have.
Feeling no puzzlement may mean she read past the hard sentences, not that she mastered them.
The chapter may be easy, but the card's point is about her questioning, not the book.
Rereading at the same pace without questions repeats the same reading.
questions.explain: A reader who never asks what a passage means may be confirming what she knew. Questions are what let the book teach.
questions.rule: No questions, no new insight.

questions.q: One reader writes confused in the margin. Another writes a question asking how lower interest leads to higher saving here. What makes the second note more useful?
options: It shows the reader disagrees with the author's main claim
It is longer, and longer margin notes hold more information for rereading
It names a specific question, which gives the rereading a direction
It records an answer, while the first note records nothing
optionExplain: The note asks how the claim works; it does not dispute it.
Length is not the point; a long vague note helps no more than a short one.
Right: a precise question tells the reader what to look for when rereading.
The note is still a question, not an answer.
questions.explain: A vague sense of confusion gives no direction. Turning it into a specific question makes the puzzle workable.
questions.rule: Turn confusion into a specific question.
questions.teaches: Writing a puzzle down as a specific question, such as how one claim leads to another, makes it workable; a vague note of confusion gives no direction for rereading.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, some confusion clears up as you read on, so not every unfamiliar phrase needs to stop you at once.
questions.explain: Some confusion comes from fatigue or haste, and some clears as you read on. The aim is to locate the real puzzles, not to halt at every bump.
questions.rule: Work on the real puzzles, not every bump.

questions.q: A chess learner replays only games she understands and skips positions she cannot explain. Applying the authors' point by analogy, what is she giving up?
options: Nothing, since skipping hard positions spares her needless frustration
Time she could spend playing faster games against stronger players
The pleasure of replaying games she enjoys and already understands
The positions that could teach her something she does not yet know
optionExplain: Frustration is the price of the puzzle that teaches; avoiding it keeps her where she is.
Faster games are another activity; the loss is in what she skips.
She keeps that pleasure; what she gives up is learning.
Right: the positions she cannot explain are where her new understanding would come from.
questions.explain: By analogy, the puzzles you avoid are the ones that would extend you. Studying only what you already follow confirms what you know.
questions.rule: Study what puzzles you, not only what you follow.
questions.teaches: By analogy, in any field the problems you cannot yet explain are where new understanding lies; studying only what you already follow confirms what you know without extending it.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, you must finish marking all the important words in a book before you look for its important sentences.
questions.explain: The authors say the rules need not be followed in their stated order. The card next shows how words and sentences lead to each other.
questions.rule: Words and sentences lead to each other.

questions.q: According to the authors, terms constitute propositions, and propositions contain ____.
questions.explain: Because terms are the parts of propositions, knowing the terms gives you the proposition, and understanding the proposition gives you the terms. That is why either step can lead to the other.
questions.rule: Terms build propositions.

questions.q: Reading a book on ecology, you have marked the words resilience and disturbance. How can these marks help next?
options: They show which claims in the book are true and which are false
They tell you which chapters you can safely skip over entirely
They make it unnecessary to read the sentences around those words with care
They point to sentences using those terms, as candidate key sentences
optionExplain: Truth is a later question; the marks help with finding what is said.
Marked words help you find sentences, not decide what to skip.
Every sentence still has to be understood; the marks direct attention.
Right: the authors say marked words lead you to the sentences that deserve attention.
questions.explain: Marked words are the first step of interpretation preparing for the second: they lead you to the sentences that use them.
questions.rule: Let marked words guide you to sentences.
