options: Note where each remark came from, so she can check she altered no link
Keep only the most recent remark, since an official's views change over time
Rewrite the remarks into one smooth quote that reads well
Add her own linking remarks wherever the position seems thin
optionExplain: Right: tracking sources lets her, and others, verify that the assembled position is the official's.
Earlier remarks may be essential parts of the position.
A merged quote hides where each piece came from and may change the meaning.
Her own links would make it her construction, not the official's.
questions.explain: By analogy, an argument built from scattered pieces must stay checkable. Recording where each piece came from guards against altered or invented links.
questions.rule: Keep a record of where each piece came from.
questions.teaches: When the pieces of an argument come from different places, noting where each came from lets you check later that you have not altered or invented a link, which is what margin numbers do inside one book.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reader who has not worked through a book can make full use of the author's final summary of its argument.
questions.explain: The authors say the reader who has worked through the book deserves the summary; the one who has not cannot use it. The card next explains how to use summaries.
questions.rule: Summaries reward those who did the reading.

questions.q: Darwin ends The Origin of Species with a chapter that sums up his whole argument, entitled Recapitulation and ____.
questions.explain: Darwin's last chapter recapitulates the argument of the book, help the authors say a reader who has worked through the book deserves.
questions.rule: Good books summarize themselves.

questions.q: A chapter of a policy book ends with a five-point summary. How should a reader use it?
options: Memorise the five points as the chapter's settled conclusions
Read only the summary, since it contains the whole argument
Skip it, since a summary adds nothing to a chapter already read
Look back over the chapter to find where each point was argued
optionExplain: Memorising conclusions without their reasons is the verbal learning the authors warn against.
A summary gives conclusions without the steps that support them.
It helps a great deal: it shows which sentences to gather.
Right: the authors advise looking back to find the materials gathered into the summary.
questions.explain: A summary is a map back to the argument. Tracing each point to its place in the chapter shows the sentences that compose it.
questions.rule: Use the summary as a map back to the text.

questions.q: Suppose that, checking a summary against its chapter, a reader finds the summary's fourth point was asserted in the chapter but not argued for anywhere. What has she learned?
options: That she misread the chapter, since summaries are exact
Where the argument is thinner than the summary suggests
That point four is false, since no argument in the chapter supports it
That the whole summary is unreliable and should be ignored
optionExplain: Summaries can simplify or overstate; the check exists to catch that.
Right: the summary presents point four as a result, but the chapter only asserts it.
An unsupported claim may still be true; it is just not established here.
One gap does not discredit every point; it marks one claim to watch when judging the book.
questions.explain: Comparing summary and text does more than locate arguments. A point summarized but never argued marks a gap worth noting for later judgment.
questions.rule: Check each summary point for its argument.
questions.teaches: Checking a summary against its chapter can reveal points that were asserted but never argued, showing where the author's case is thinner than his summary suggests.

questions.q: Sort these features of books by their effect on finding the arguments.

items.t: A summary at the end of each chapter
Knowing from inspection where the summaries are
Labelled propositions, as in Euclid
Diffuse paragraphs in a loosely built book
One argument scattered over a whole chapter
A book that does not encourage the search at all

questions.explain: Summaries, inspection and clear formats point you to arguments. Loose construction spreads them out and sometimes leaves the search fruitless.
questions.rule: Use every aid; expect loose books to make you search.

questions.q: A board member reads only the executive summary of a sixty-page report before voting on its recommendation. By analogy with the authors' point, what is she missing?
options: The steps and evidence behind each summarised point
Nothing, since the summary contains the full argument
The authors' names, which show how far to trust them
The page layout, which shows which points matter most
optionExplain: Right: the summary gives conclusions; the body gives the reasons she should weigh.
A summary leaves out the steps by design.
Authorship may matter, but it is not what the summary omits.
Layout is not the missing piece; the argument is.
questions.explain: By analogy, an executive summary is a map, not the territory. A vote should rest on checking the evidence for the points that matter.
questions.rule: Read past the summary for what you must decide.
questions.teaches: Executive summaries work like an author's summaries: useful as a map, but a decision should check the body's evidence for each summarised point that matters to it.

questions.q: According to the authors, what is one familiar trick of orators and propagandists?
options: Leaving unsaid relevant steps that might be challenged if stated
Stating every premise at length so that listeners lose the thread
Using numbered lists so that their arguments seem more rigorous
Quoting opponents fairly so as to appear even-handed and calm
optionExplain: Right: the authors name leaving relevant, challengeable things unsaid as a familiar trick.
Long-winded premises can confuse, but the authors' point is about omission.
Formatting tricks are not what the authors describe.
Fair quotation is not a trick the authors mention.
questions.explain: Omitting a step that would be challenged hides the weak point. The card next explains why readers should make every step explicit.
questions.rule: Watch for what is left unsaid.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, steps in an argument can sometimes be omitted without harm, because readers can supply them from common knowledge.
questions.explain: Not every omission misleads. The danger is the omitted step that is relevant and open to challenge.
questions.rule: Some omissions are harmless.

questions.q: A school leaflet says that students who take music lessons get higher grades, so music lessons improve grades. Which unstated step does the argument need?
options: That nothing else, such as family income, explains both
That music lessons are enjoyable for most students
That higher grades lead students to take up music in the first place
That all students should be offered music lessons
optionExplain: Right: if a third factor explains both, the lessons need not cause the grades.
Enjoyment is irrelevant to whether lessons raise grades.
This would reverse the claimed cause; it is not a step the argument needs.
This is a further conclusion, not a missing premise.
questions.explain: Moving from together to causes needs the unstated premise that nothing else explains the link. Making it explicit shows what to check.
questions.rule: Name the premise that turns a pattern into a cause.

questions.q: To find a missing premise, ask what would have to be ____ for the conclusion to follow from the premises that are stated.
questions.explain: The gap between the stated premises and the conclusion is exactly the unstated premise. Asking what would close it is the quickest way to find it.
questions.rule: Ask what would close the gap.
questions.teaches: The surest way to find a missing step is to ask what would have to be true for the conclusion to follow from the stated premises; the answer is the unstated premise.

questions.q: True or false: The more steps of an argument a reader writes out, trivial ones included, the better the reading.
questions.explain: Spelling out trivial steps buries the argument. Make explicit the steps that carry weight or could be disputed.
questions.rule: Make explicit the steps that matter.

questions.q: A campaign leaflet says the city's air is dangerously polluted, so diesel cars must be banned this year. Which unstated step is most worth checking?
options: That diesel engines emit some pollutants when they run
That air pollution harms people's health over time
That at least some of the city's pollution comes from road traffic
That a diesel ban this year would cut the pollution by much
optionExplain: True and uncontroversial; it does not show the ban would help much.
This is needed too, but it is well established and rarely disputed.
Also needed, but widely accepted; the size of the effect is the real question.
Right: the argument needs the ban to work, and that is the step most open to dispute.
questions.explain: By analogy, the missing premise worth naming is the one hardest to defend. Here it is that the proposed action would actually solve the problem.
questions.rule: Name the hardest unstated step.
questions.teaches: In everyday persuasion, the unstated premise most worth naming is often the hardest to defend, such as the claim that a proposed action will actually work; naming it shows where to look for evidence.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, any good argument can be put into a nutshell.
questions.explain: The authors say so directly. The card next explains what this asks of the reader.
questions.rule: Good arguments fit in a nutshell.

questions.q: According to the authors, arguments may be built upon arguments, but the units of reasoning are single ____.
questions.explain: Find the single arguments and the larger chains they form will not be missed. Chapters and paragraphs are units of writing, not of reasoning.
questions.rule: Single arguments are the units of reasoning.

questions.q: A passage argues: because smaller classes let teachers give each child more feedback, and feedback speeds learning, schools should cut class sizes in the early years. Which is the best nutshell?
options: Small classes let teachers give more feedback, which children enjoy receiving
Early class sizes should be cut, since parents and teachers prefer them
More feedback in small classes speeds learning, so cut early class sizes
Feedback speeds learning, so teachers should give more of it at all ages
optionExplain: This drops the link to learning and the conclusion.
This replaces the premises with a reason the passage never gives.
Right: it keeps both premises and the conclusion in brief.
This keeps one premise but changes the conclusion and drops class size.
questions.explain: A nutshell is short but keeps the premises and the conclusion. Dropping or replacing a premise changes the argument.
questions.rule: A nutshell keeps premises and conclusion.

questions.q: In a chain of three arguments, the first conclusion is a premise of the second, and the second's conclusion a premise of the third. A reader finds the first argument weak. What follows for the third conclusion?
options: It loses support, since it rests on the first through the second
Nothing, since each argument in a chain stands on its own
It is proved false, since the chain began with a weak link
It gains support, since the later arguments in the chain are stronger
optionExplain: Right: a weak early link weakens everything built on it.
In a chain, later arguments rest on earlier conclusions; they do not stand alone.
Weak support is not disproof; the conclusion may have other grounds.
Strong later links cannot make up for a weak foundation.
questions.explain: Because each conclusion feeds the next argument, a weak early argument weakens all that is built on it. Seeing the single arguments shows where the chain is weakest.
questions.rule: A chain is only as strong as its weakest link.
questions.teaches: A weak argument early in a chain weakens every later conclusion that depends on it, so the first links of a long chain deserve the closest checking.

questions.q: True or false: A nutshell that leaves out one of the premises an argument needs still represents the argument fairly, since nutshells are meant to be short.
questions.explain: A nutshell trims detail, not premises. Dropping a needed premise misrepresents how the conclusion is supported.
questions.rule: Trim detail, not premises.

questions.q: A law student must summarise a forty-page court judgment for class. Applying the authors' point, what should her summary contain?
options: Every fact of the case, in the order the judge gave them
The question, the ruling and its reasons, in brief
The judge's most memorable phrases, quoted at length
Her own view of whether the ruling was right or wrong
optionExplain: Facts in full order are detail; the reasoning is what must be kept.
Right: this is the judgment's argument in a nutshell.
Memorable phrases are not the argument.
Her view comes after understanding the ruling and its reasons.
questions.explain: By analogy, briefing a case reduces a long judgment to its single arguments: the question, the answer and the reasons.
questions.rule: Brief long reasoning to question, answer and reasons.
questions.teaches: Law students brief cases the same way: reducing a long judgment to the question decided, the ruling and its key reasons is a nutshell of its single arguments.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reader must study formal logic before he can find the arguments in a book.
questions.explain: The authors say you need not know arguments as a logician does; books that instruct are written for general readers. The card next explains what is needed instead.
questions.rule: Attention, not formal logic.

questions.q: The authors say the human mind is by nature as sensitive to arguments as the eye is to ____.
questions.explain: The comparison makes two points: the sensitivity is natural, and like the eye, the mind must be open and awake to use it.
questions.rule: The mind sees arguments as the eye sees colours, when open.

questions.q: A reader spots the sentence therefore the dam should not be built at the end of a section. According to the authors, what should he do next?
options: Look back for the reasons offered for that conclusion
Treat it as the section's whole argument and move on
Look only ahead, to see where the conclusion leads
Decide at once whether he agrees with the conclusion
optionExplain: Right: having found the conclusion first, he looks for the reasons.
A conclusion alone is not an argument; its reasons are missing.
The conclusion may feed a later argument, but first he needs the reasons for this one.
Agreement comes after understanding the argument.
questions.explain: Therefore marks a conclusion. Found first, it sends the reader back to the statements that support it.
questions.rule: Found the conclusion? Look for the reasons.

questions.q: Suppose a reader takes in two premises, about rising sea levels and the low height of a town's sea wall, and before the next paragraph guesses that the author will conclude the wall must be raised. What does making this guess do for her?
options: It replaces reading the conclusion, which she can now skip
It biases her, so she should avoid guessing where the arguments lead next
It tests whether she is following, as the text will confirm or not
It shows that she disagrees with the author before reading on
optionExplain: The guess must be checked; the author may conclude something else.
A guess held loosely and checked against the text is a test, not a bias.
Right: seeing where the reasons lead, then checking, tests her grasp of the argument.
Anticipating a conclusion is not disagreeing with it.
questions.explain: Seeing where reasons lead lets you predict the conclusion. The text then confirms or corrects you, which shows whether you are really following.
questions.rule: Predict the conclusion, then check it.
questions.teaches: When you find the reasons first, predicting the conclusion before you reach it is a useful check: the text will confirm or correct the guess and show whether you are following the argument.

questions.q: True or false: Because the mind is by nature sensitive to arguments, a reader will notice a book's arguments even when reading half asleep.
questions.explain: The sensitivity works only in a mind that is awake, as the eye sees only when open. Natural capacity is no excuse for inattention.
questions.rule: Natural sensitivity needs an awake mind.

questions.q: A legal system lets twelve citizens with no training in logic decide a case after hearing both sides argue. Which assumption does this share with the authors?
options: People are moved by stories rather than by arguments
Arguments are too hard for anyone but trained experts
Logic is needed for writing arguments, not judging them
Ordinary attentive people can follow and weigh arguments
optionExplain: Stories do persuade, but the system asks jurors to weigh the arguments.
If that were assumed, juries would be made of logicians.
Juries judge without formal logic, but that is not a claim about writing.
Right: like the authors, the jury system trusts an attentive general mind to follow reasoning.
questions.explain: By analogy, trial by jury rests on the same view the authors hold: an awake general mind can follow arguments without formal training.
questions.rule: Attentive general readers can follow arguments.
questions.teaches: Trial by jury rests on the same assumption as the authors: ordinary people who pay attention, without formal training in logic, can follow and weigh the arguments put before them.

questions.q: An argument cites cases from fifty hospitals as evidence for a general claim about hospitals. What is this kind of argument usually called?
options: Inductive
Deductive
Circular
Rhetorical
optionExplain: Right: it reasons from particular facts to a generalization.
Deductive arguments reason from general statements, not from particular cases.
A circular argument assumes its conclusion; this one rests on cases.
Rhetorical describes persuasive style, not the direction of support.
questions.explain: Particular facts offered as evidence for a generalization make an inductive argument. The card next contrasts it with the deductive kind.
questions.rule: Cases to a general claim: inductive.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, what matters most is the ability to tell inductive from deductive arguments, not the names themselves.
questions.explain: The authors say the names are not important; being able to discriminate between the two kinds is.
questions.rule: Tell them apart; the names matter less.

questions.q: Sort these arguments by how they support their conclusions.
groups: From particular facts to a generalization
From general statements to a further one

items.t: Every swan seen in ten countries was white, so swans are generally white.
Twenty trials found the drug lowered blood pressure, so it lowers blood pressure.
Sales rose in each store that cut prices, so price cuts raise sales.
All mammals breathe air; whales are mammals; so whales breathe air.
Any tax on a good raises its price; this is a tax on sugar; so it raises sugar prices.
Whatever is scarce gains value; clean water is growing scarce; so it will gain value.

questions.explain: The first three reason from observed cases to a general claim. The last three reason from general statements to a further general claim.
questions.rule: Ask what the conclusion rests on: cases or general truths.

questions.q: From 500 observed cases, researchers conclude that a bird species migrates south every winter. Suppose one flock then stays north for a winter. What does this show about their inductive conclusion?
options: It still stands, since 500 cases outweigh a single flock
It was deductive, so its general premises must have been false
It went beyond its evidence, so a new case could overturn it
It was not an argument, since it rested on observation
optionExplain: A clear counterexample tells against an every-winter claim, however many cases came before.
It reasoned from cases, so it was inductive, not deductive.
Right: an inductive generalization claims more than the cases observed, so a new case can count against it.
Observed facts offered as grounds make an argument.
questions.explain: Induction generalizes beyond its cases, so new cases can overturn it. A deductive conclusion, by contrast, is only as secure as its general premises.
questions.rule: Inductive conclusions stay open to new cases.
questions.teaches: An inductive conclusion goes beyond its evidence, so a new case can overturn it, while a deductive conclusion is only as secure as the general premises it starts from.

questions.q: Harvey wrote that the circulation of the blood had been shown by reason and experiment. What does this tell you about the support he offered?
options: He relied on reasoning, with experiment only as decoration
He supported it both by reasoning and by experiment
He relied on experiment, since reason cannot prove facts
He gave no support, since he only asserted the result
optionExplain: Harvey names both as showing the result; neither is mere decoration.
Right: the authors cite Harvey as a case where both methods support one proposition.
He names reason as well as experiment.
Saying how a result was shown points to support, not bare assertion.
questions.explain: Some propositions can be supported both by reasoning from general truths and by experimental evidence. Harvey claims both.
questions.rule: Note whether a scientific claim rests on reasoning, experiment or both.

questions.q: A mechanic reasons that a car which cranks but will not start most likely lacks fuel or spark, then tests the spark plug and finds it dead. How does this fit the authors' advice?
options: Neither, since repair work involves no arguments at all
Pure induction, since he looked at one particular car
Pure deduction, since the test added nothing to the reasoning
Reasoning from general knowledge, then confirming by a test
optionExplain: Diagnosis is full of argument: general premises, particular evidence, conclusion.
He started from general knowledge of engines, not from cases alone.
The test decided between fuel and spark, so it added a great deal.
Right: he reasons from how engines work, then checks by experiment, as Galileo illustrated demonstrations by experiment.
questions.explain: By analogy, practical expertise often uses both kinds of support: general reasoning to narrow the possibilities, and a test on the particular case to settle them.
questions.rule: Reason to a hypothesis, then test it.
questions.teaches: Everyday expertise often combines the two kinds of support: a mechanic or doctor reasons from general knowledge to a likely cause, then tests the particular case to confirm it.

questions.q: True or false: In a well-made argument, every proposition, including the starting points, has been proved.
questions.explain: Not everything can be proved; an argument has to start somewhere. The card next explains where.
questions.rule: Every argument starts from something unproved.

questions.q: According to the authors, why can not everything be proved?
options: Some propositions are too complex for any reader to follow
If every proposition needed proof, no proof could ever begin
Proof is possible only in mathematics, not in any other field of study
Authors lack the space to prove everything in one book
optionExplain: Complexity is not the reason; even simple proofs need starting points.
Right: proofs need starting points that are not themselves proved.
The authors discuss proof and evidence in many fields, not only mathematics.
Space is not the issue; the limit is logical.
questions.explain: Just as not everything can be defined, not everything can be proved. Axioms, assumptions or postulates are needed to begin.
questions.rule: Proof needs unproved starting points.

questions.q: A book on voting contains these three sentences. Match each to its role in the argument.
pairs: For this book, let us assume that voters act in their own interest
An assumption agreed with the reader
The whole electorate is larger than any one district within it
As shown in chapter 3, turnout falls when voting is costly
A proposition proved in the argument
questions.explain: The first is announced as an assumption, the second cannot be denied, and the third is offered as already shown by argument.
questions.rule: Sort starting points from proved points.

questions.q: Suppose two economists reason validly to opposite conclusions about minimum wages. Where is their disagreement most likely to lie?
options: In their logic, since valid reasoning cannot give opposite results
In their starting assumptions, which valid steps carry through
In their wording, since they must really mean the same thing
Nowhere, since both of the conclusions can be true together
optionExplain: Valid reasoning can give opposite results from different starting points.
Right: valid reasoning preserves whatever it starts from, so opposite conclusions point back to different premises.
Wording can mislead, but opposite conclusions usually reflect different premises.
Opposite conclusions cannot both be true.
questions.explain: If both arguments are valid, the conclusions differ because the starting points differ. Comparing assumptions is the quickest way to find the real disagreement.
questions.rule: When valid arguments clash, compare their starting points.
questions.teaches: When two authors reach opposite conclusions by valid steps, their disagreement lies in their starting assumptions, so comparing assumptions is the quickest way to locate it.

questions.q: True or false: If an author does not list his assumptions, he is being dishonest with his readers.
questions.explain: The authors say an author may just as honestly leave the reader to find his assumptions. Finding them is part of the reader's work.
questions.rule: Unlisted assumptions are for the reader to find.

questions.q: In chess, nobody proves that a bishop moves diagonally; players reason from that rule to plans and tactics. Which kind of starting point does the rule resemble?
options: An assumption agreed by all who play, from which conclusions follow
A self-evident truth about the game that no one anywhere could possibly deny
A conclusion proved earlier in the long history of chess
A guess that players test in each game by experiment
optionExplain: Right: the rule binds because players accept it, as writer and reader agree on an assumption.
Its opposite is not seen to be false; a different game could let bishops move otherwise.
Rules are laid down, not proved from earlier truths.
Players do not test the rule; they reason from it.
questions.explain: By analogy, game rules are agreed starting points. Within the game conclusions follow from them, but they hold only for those who accept them.
questions.rule: Agreed rules are starting points, not truths.
questions.teaches: The rules of a game, like the defined terms of a contract, work as agreed assumptions: conclusions follow within them, but they bind only those who accept the starting rules.

questions.q: Which proposition is true only because of how its words are defined?
options: A father of a father is a grandfather
The whole is greater than its parts
Water boils at lower heat on mountains
Most large cities grow along rivers
optionExplain: Right: grandfather is defined as a parent's father, so the truth comes from the definition.
The authors argue this one expresses our understanding of wholes and parts, not a definition.
This is a fact learned from experience, not from definitions.
This is a historical generalization, true or false by the facts.
questions.explain: Some truths hold because of how words are defined. The card next contrasts them with self-evident truths about things.
questions.rule: Some truths come from definitions.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a proposition is self-evident when its opposite is immediately seen to be false.
questions.explain: That is the authors' test: you cannot think an uncut page is less than half of it.
questions.rule: Self-evident: the opposite is seen at once to be false.

questions.q: Sort these propositions using the authors' distinction.
groups: True by definition of the words

items.t: A bachelor is an unmarried man.
A week has seven days.
A parent's parent is a grandparent.
A whole is greater than any one of its parts.
If A is taller than B and B taller than C, then A is taller than C.

questions.explain: The first three hold because of how the words are defined. The last two express an understanding of how things are related, whatever words are used.
questions.rule: Ask whether the truth comes from a definition or from the things.

questions.q: To check whether a statement is a tautology, a reader sets aside the special definition behind one of its words. What result would show it was true only by definition?
options: It becomes harder to understand than it was before
Its truth survives whatever words are used for it
Its truth disappears once the definition is set aside
It turns into a question rather than a statement
optionExplain: Difficulty is not the test; whether the truth survives is.
That is the mark of the self-evident kind, which holds whatever words we use.
Right: if the truth depended on the stipulation, removing it removes the truth.
Setting aside a definition does not change the sentence's form.
questions.explain: A tautology's truth rests on a verbal stipulation, so it does not survive without it. A self-evident truth about things survives any change of words.
questions.rule: Remove the definition and see whether the truth survives.
questions.teaches: A practical check for a tautology is to set aside the stipulated definition: if the proposition's truth vanishes with it, the truth was put in by definition rather than found in the things.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, propositions that moderns call tautologies add nothing to our knowledge.
questions.explain: The authors hold that some so-called tautologies, such as the whole is greater than its parts, really instruct. This is their position, which they say Locke and some moderns missed.
questions.rule: According to the authors, some self-evident truths instruct.

questions.q: An accounting textbook states that assets equal liabilities plus equity, with equity defined as what is left after liabilities. A student calls this a discovery about how firms succeed. What do the authors suggest?
options: It is a guess that auditors test against each firm
It is self-evident about firms, like the whole and its parts
It is a finding from studying many firms' accounts
It holds by definition of equity, so it explains no success
optionExplain: Auditors check figures against it, but the identity itself cannot be falsified.
Its truth comes from defining equity, not from seeing its opposite as false about things.
No study could find otherwise, because the definition guarantees it.
Right: since equity is defined as the remainder, the equation cannot fail, and so it tells nothing about why firms prosper.
questions.explain: By analogy, many practical identities are true by definition. They organise figures usefully but do not by themselves explain anything.
questions.rule: Identities organise facts; they do not explain them.
questions.teaches: Many identities in practical fields, such as assets equal liabilities plus equity in accounting, are true by the definition of their terms; they organise facts but do not by themselves explain them.

questions.q: After working out a book's terms, propositions and arguments, what do the authors ask the reader to determine next?
options: How the book compares with others on the same subject
Whether the author's prose style is pleasant to read aloud
Which of his problems the author solved and which he did not
Whether the reader agrees with each of the author's terms
optionExplain: Comparing books belongs to syntopical reading, not this rule.
Style is not part of the rules of interpretation.
Right: Rule 8 asks what the author's solutions are.
Agreement belongs to criticism, and terms are not things to agree with.
questions.explain: The last step of interpretation checks the author's problems against what his arguments achieved. The card next sets out the questions.
questions.rule: Interpretation ends with the author's solutions.

questions.q: Which questions belong to Rule 8, according to the authors? Choose three.
options: Which problems did the author succeed in solving?
Did he raise new problems in solving them?
Which failures did the author himself recognise?
Which of his claims do I personally agree with?
How many pages does he give to each problem?
optionExplain: Right: the first of the authors' questions.
Right: solving one problem can raise others.
Right: of the unsolved problems, which did he know he had failed on.
Agreement belongs to the next stage, criticism.
Page counts measure attention, not solutions.
questions.explain: Rule 8 asks three questions: what was solved, what new problems arose, and which failures the author knew about.
questions.rule: Solved, newly raised, knowingly unsolved.

questions.q: A book on poverty set out to explain why it persists and how to reduce it. It gives a strong explanation, offers no workable remedy, and in its last chapter admits the remedy is beyond it. How should a reader record its solutions?
options: Neither problem solved, since the remedy is still missing
Both problems solved, since the book addresses each of them
Explanation solved; remedy unsolved, and the author knows it
Remedy solved, since the author discusses it at some length
optionExplain: The explanation was achieved; one gap does not cancel it.
Addressing a problem is not solving it.
Right: one problem solved, one not, and the author admits the failure.
Discussing a problem at length does not solve it, and the author says so himself.
questions.explain: Rule 8 sorts the problems: what was solved, what was not, and whether the author knew. Here each problem lands in a different place.
questions.rule: Record each problem's fate separately.

questions.q: Suppose an author writes in his closing pages that whether his proposed mechanism works in large firms remains an open question. What should a reader make of this sentence?
options: It marks a problem he knows is unsolved, the edge of his book
It is a weakness best hidden when summarising the book for other readers
It shows the whole book is unreliable and can be set aside
It is a polite phrase that can be passed over as filler
optionExplain: Right: it answers the third question of Rule 8 directly: a failure he recognises.
Hiding it would misreport what the book achieved.
Admitting a limit is a sign of a careful writer, not grounds for rejecting everything.
A sentence that marks what is unsolved carries real information.
questions.explain: An author's own admission of an open question tells you where his solutions stop, so you do not treat that question as settled.
questions.rule: Value the author's admissions of what remains open.
questions.teaches: An author's admission that a question remains open is valuable: it marks the frontier of his book and keeps the reader from treating an unsolved problem as settled.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Rule 8 is where the reader begins to argue with the author about whether he is right.
questions.explain: Through Rule 8 the reader is still following the author. The authors say that only from this point on does the reader get the chance to argue with him.
questions.rule: Follow through Rule 8; argue afterwards.

questions.q: A team's end-of-project report is to be reviewed. Borrowing Rule 8, which questions should the reviewer ask?
options: How many hours each member worked on each of the tasks
Goals met, new problems raised, and failures the team admits
Whether the report's layout is clear and well designed
Whether the team stayed within the original budget
optionExplain: Hours worked describe effort, not what was achieved.
Right: these mirror the three questions of Rule 8.
Layout matters for reading, not for judging results.
Budget is one concern, but it does not ask what problems were solved.
questions.explain: By analogy, Rule 8's three questions work for any report on an attempt to solve problems.
questions.rule: Ask what was solved, what arose, what was admitted.
questions.teaches: Rule 8's three questions work for reviewing any report of work on problems, such as a project report: which goals were met, which new problems arose, and which failures the authors admit.

questions.section: The Second Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Which basic question does the second stage of analytical reading help you answer?
options: What of it, and why does it matter?
What is the book about as a whole?
Is the book true, in whole or part?
What is being said in detail, and how?
optionExplain: That is the fourth question, asked after the book is understood.
That is the first basic question, answered in the first stage.
That is the third question, for the stage of criticism.
Right: Rules 5 to 8 supply the materials for this second question.
questions.explain: The second stage interprets the contents: what is said in detail, and how. The card next lists its four rules.
questions.rule: Stage two: what is said in detail, and how.

questions.section: The Second Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Match each rule of the second stage with its task.
pairs: Come to terms by interpreting key words
Grasp leading propositions from important sentences
Know the arguments from sequences of sentences
questions.explain: The four rules move from words to sentences to sequences of sentences, and end by checking the author's solutions.
questions.rule: Terms, propositions, arguments, solutions.

questions.section: The Second Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Suppose a reader has listed a book's key terms and marked its important sentences, but cannot say how its claims support one another. Which rule should she work on next?
options: Rule 8, deciding which problems were solved
Rule 5, coming to terms with the key words
Rule 4, stating the problems the author tackles
Rule 7, finding or constructing the arguments
optionExplain: Rule 8 depends on knowing the arguments, so it comes after Rule 7.
She has already listed the key terms.
Rule 4 belongs to the first stage; her gap is in the arguments.
Right: how claims support one another is the work of Rule 7.
questions.explain: Terms and propositions are in hand; the support relations among claims are arguments, the business of Rule 7.
questions.rule: Support among claims is Rule 7's work.

questions.section: The Second Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: A reader wants a one-page record showing she has completed the second stage on a book. What should it contain?
options: A plot summary of each chapter in the order it appears
Terms, propositions, arguments in brief, problems solved or not
Her verdict on whether the author is right, with her reasons for it
A list of the author's other books and their reception
optionExplain: A chapter-by-chapter summary follows structure, not the interpretation of contents.
Right: one part for each rule's product.
A verdict belongs to the third stage, criticism.
Other books are outside the work of interpreting this one.
questions.explain: Each of Rules 5 to 8 yields something that can be written down. Together they make a compact record of what the book says.
questions.rule: Record the product of each rule.
questions.teaches: A practical record of the second stage fits on a page in four parts: key terms with their senses, leading propositions in your own words, the main arguments in nutshells, and the problems marked solved or unsolved.

questions.section: The Second Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: True or false: Once a reader has completed Rules 5 to 8 on a book, she has shown that she agrees with it.
questions.explain: The second stage yields understanding of what is said. Whether it is true is the next question, and she may end up disagreeing.
questions.rule: Understanding is not agreement.

questions.section: The Second Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Asked to critique a colleague's proposal, a manager first restates its key terms, its main claims, its reasoning and what it claims to solve. By analogy with the authors' point, what does this first step achieve?
options: She will criticise the proposal actually made, not a misreading of it
It delays the critique, which makes the colleague feel more at ease
It replaces the critique, since a fair summary is feedback enough
It shows that she agrees with the proposal before she raises any objection
optionExplain: Right: like the second stage, it makes sure she understands before she judges.
Comfort may follow, but the purpose is accurate understanding.
Understanding prepares the critique; it does not replace it.
Restating a proposal is not agreeing with it.
questions.explain: By analogy, the second stage comes before criticism in any review. Restating the proposal guards against attacking something never proposed.
questions.rule: Restate before you critique.
questions.teaches: In any review, such as of a colleague's proposal, restating its terms, claims, reasoning and what it claims to solve before criticising guards against attacking a proposal that was never made.

questions.q: A book cannot reply to its reader. According to the authors, what does that mean for the conversation between them?
options: The conversation ends when the author's last page ends
The book is a lecture, so the reader should only listen
The reader may reply freely, since no one can object
The reader has the last word and must use it with care
optionExplain: The author's part ends there, but the reader's turn begins.
The book can look like a lecture, but the authors say the reader has a turn and an obligation to take it.
Freedom to reply is real, but the absent author is exactly why the reply needs discipline.
Right: the reader speaks last, and because the author cannot defend himself, the reply must be disciplined.
questions.explain: The authors say the reader has the last word, and an undisciplined reader can spoil the exchange because the author cannot protest. The card next shows what that turn asks.
questions.rule: The reader speaks last, so he must speak well.

questions.q: According to the authors, in the conversation between a book and its reader, the ____ has the last word.
questions.explain: The author has had his say in the book; then it is the reader's turn, and nothing comes after it.
questions.rule: The author speaks first; the reader speaks last.

questions.q: Lena reads an article proposing school uniforms. After the second paragraph she posts a reply attacking the proposal and stops reading. Which fault in the conversation does her reply show?
options: She disagreed, when a reader's turn is meant for agreeing with him
She replied at all, when a reader's part is to listen
She replied in writing rather than talking it over
She took her turn before the author had finished his say
optionExplain: Disagreement is a legitimate reply, once the author has been heard.
Replying is the reader's right and duty; the fault is in the timing.
The medium of the reply is not the issue; the conversation with a book is written anyway.
Right: she interrupted an author who cannot ask her to wait until he has finished.
questions.explain: The orderly conversation has each side speak in turn. Lena answered before the author finished, which is the interruption the author cannot prevent.
questions.rule: Let the author finish before you take your turn.

questions.q: Suppose the author of a book were sitting beside you as you read, free to interrupt you. By the authors' reasoning, what would change?
options: Nothing, since a reader's duties are fixed by the text itself, not by the author
He could protest a misreading, so his defence would not rest on you alone
You would lose your turn, since the author would now have the last word
You would no longer need to understand him before you replied to him
optionExplain: The text does not change, but the card's reason for extra care is the author's absence, and that would be gone.
Right: the reader's discipline matters so much because the absent author cannot ask him to wait or say he was misread.
A present author could protest, but the reader would still answer after hearing him.
Understanding before replying is needed in any serious conversation, with a present speaker too.
questions.explain: The card stresses the reader's obligation because the author cannot defend himself. A present author could protest a misreading, so the fairness of the exchange would no longer rest on the reader alone.
questions.rule: The absent author is why the reader's discipline matters.

questions.q: A city council publishes a draft plan, invites written comments for a month, and then closes the consultation without replying to each one. By analogy with the authors' point, why does the care taken in each comment matter?
options: Short comments are read first, so brevity matters more than care
Comments are counted, so the side that sends more of them wins the vote
The planners cannot answer each comment, so a misreading may stand
The plan is final, so comments serve only as a record of mood
optionExplain: Length is not the point; a short comment can still misread the plan.
Counting comments may happen, but it does not make a careless comment fair to the plan.
Right: like an author, the planners have spoken and cannot reply, so a comment that misreads the plan goes uncorrected.
If comments changed nothing there would be no consultation; the point is that misreadings cannot be challenged.
questions.explain: A one-way consultation puts the commenter where the reader of a book stands: the other side cannot answer. A careful commenter can supply the missing check himself by stating what he takes the plan to be before objecting, so any misreading shows.
questions.rule: Where the other side cannot reply, state what you are replying to.
questions.teaches: When the other party cannot reply, a responder can supply the missing check himself: opening a comment with his reading of the proposal makes any misreading visible to whoever reads it, which the planners could not otherwise point out.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reader who delivers a verdict on a book after each chapter, before reading the rest, takes his turn too early.
questions.explain: The reader's turn comes after the author has had his whole say. Questions may arise along the way, but a verdict delivered mid-book interrupts an author who cannot ask the reader to wait.
questions.rule: Questions may come early; verdicts come after the author has finished.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the manners that matter most when talking back to a book are the conventions of social politeness.
questions.explain: The authors say social conventions are not really important. What matters is an intellectual etiquette, without which conversation turns into bickering. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: The etiquette that matters is intellectual, not social.

questions.q: According to the authors, without intellectual etiquette, conversation is ____ rather than profitable communication.
questions.explain: Intellectual etiquette is what turns an exchange into profitable communication; without it, the talk is bickering.
questions.rule: No etiquette, no profit: only bickering.

questions.q: In an online forum about bread baking, someone posts a method with a very short rise. Which reply best keeps the intellectual etiquette the authors describe?
options: Thank you so much for sharing, what a lovely recipe and photo
I think the long rise matters more than you say, and here is why
This method is wrong and anyone who bakes bread knows it
I have not tried it myself, but that short a rise sounds far too short
optionExplain: It is perfectly polite, but it offers nothing that either side could learn from.
Right: it engages the post and offers reasons, so both sides can learn something.
It is blunt, but the deeper fault is that it gives no reasons and invites a quarrel.
It is mild, but it judges without trying the method or giving any grounds.
questions.explain: Intellectual etiquette is measured by whether the exchange can produce learning. A reply that engages the claim and gives reasons does; a courteous compliment or a bare verdict does not.
questions.rule: Etiquette shows in reasons offered, not in courtesy alone.

questions.q: Sort each habit by whether it belongs to intellectual etiquette or to social politeness.

items.t: Waiting until you understand before objecting
Thanking the speaker for their time
Addressing the reasons the other side gave
Using a courteous form of address
Replying to what was said, not to what you assumed
Opening a reply with a compliment

questions.explain: Intellectual etiquette governs how ideas are exchanged so that something is learned. Courteous forms are pleasant but, as the authors say, not really important to the profit of the talk.
questions.rule: Ask whether a habit helps learning, not whether it sounds nice.

questions.q: Two colleagues debate whether to adopt a new software tool. Each repeats his position more loudly, and neither asks about the other's reasons. If they kept this up for another hour, what do the authors lead you to expect?
options: More bickering and no more learning, however long it ran
Agreement, since a long enough talk wears down resistance
A clearer case on both sides, since repetition sharpens views
A decision for the louder colleague, which ends the bickering
optionExplain: Right: without the etiquette, more time yields more bickering, not more profit.
Fatigue can end a talk, but giving in from weariness is not learning.
Repetition can make a case firmer in the mind, but not better grounded.
Volume may settle who gets his way, but nothing has been learned.
questions.explain: The profit of conversation is something learned, and that needs the etiquette. Lengthening an exchange that lacks it only prolongs the bickering.
questions.rule: Time does not turn bickering into learning.

questions.q: A journal editor gives peer reviewers rules: summarise the paper's claim first, tie each objection to a specific passage, and make no remarks about the authors' character. By analogy with the authors' point, what are these rules?
options: Limits that stop reviewers from disagreeing with the paper
Social politeness, meant to spare authors' feelings at the cost of rigour
A written intellectual etiquette that keeps review from bickering
Formalities that matter little, since good papers survive review
optionExplain: The rules let reviewers disagree; they only govern how disagreement is expressed.
Sparing feelings may be a side effect, but the rules are about how objections are made, not softening them.
Right: each rule makes the exchange about the ideas, so that both sides can learn from it.
Even a good paper can be harmed by a review that bickers instead of engaging.
questions.explain: The rules govern how ideas are exchanged: understand first, object to specific passages, leave persons out. That is an intellectual etiquette written down.
questions.rule: Groups that trade criticism often write their etiquette down.
questions.teaches: By analogy, groups that exchange criticism often write their intellectual etiquette down, as in reviewing guidelines that require summarising a claim before objecting and tying each objection to a passage.

questions.q: You finish a serious book and are not convinced by it. According to the authors, what do you owe its author?
options: Silence, since a negative verdict helps no one
Nothing, since only success earns a reader's respect
Agreement, since he made the effort to teach you
A considered judgment, with grounds for your doubt
optionExplain: A reasoned negative verdict is one of the replies the author is owed.
Success is the author's aim, but the authors say the effort deserves respect even when it fails.
Respect for effort is not agreement; you may still disagree on grounds.
Right: the author's effort deserves a considered judgment, with grounds if you cannot agree.
questions.explain: The authors say that even an unconvinced reader owes the author a considered judgment. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Unconvinced is fine; unconsidered is not.

questions.q: According to the authors, which replies can count as a considered judgment from a reader who has understood a book? Select all that apply.
options: Agreeing with it
Disagreeing on stated grounds
Suspending judgment on stated grounds
Putting it aside and forgetting it
Praising it faintly without reasons
optionExplain: Right: being taught and convinced is the outcome the author hoped for.
Right: if the reader cannot agree, he should have grounds for disagreeing.
Right: suspending judgment also needs grounds.
This feels harmless, but the authors call it worse than faint praise: no consideration at all.
Faint praise says something, but without reasons it is not a considered judgment.
questions.explain: The card allows agreement, or disagreement or suspended judgment with grounds. Forgetting the book gives it no critical consideration.
questions.rule: Agree, or give grounds for disagreeing or suspending.

questions.q: A book-club member has read and understood a history of the railways. Asked what she made of it, she says only that it was not for her and moves on. What has she left out?
options: A second reading, which must come before any opinion
Praise for the author, which must come before any doubt
A full summary of the book, which would stand in place of a judgment
Grounds for her verdict, which the author's effort deserved
optionExplain: She has already understood the book; what is missing is her reasons.
The card asks for grounds, not a ritual of praise before criticism.
A summary shows understanding, but the card says reading is completed by judging.
Right: she gave a verdict but no grounds, so it is not a considered judgment.
questions.explain: Not for me is a verdict with no grounds. The card asks an unconvinced reader for grounds for disagreeing or suspending judgment.
questions.rule: A verdict without grounds is not a considered judgment.

questions.q: Jon reasons: the author set out to convince me; he failed; so his effort counts for nothing and I owe him no response. Which step is wrong?
options: Admitting that the author failed to convince him
Treating failure to convince as voiding his debt
Thinking that the author set out to convince
Expecting a book of this kind to try to teach
optionExplain: Being unconvinced is an honest result, not a mistake.
Right: the authors say the effort deserves respect even when it fails, so a considered judgment is still owed.
Authors of books that convey knowledge do aim to convince or persuade.
That is the card's own description of such a book.
questions.explain: Jon's first two steps are sound. The error is the last one: failure to convince does not cancel the respect owed to the effort.
questions.rule: Failure to convince does not cancel the debt.

questions.q: A teacher returns a student's essay arguing that the voting age should be lowered, marked only with a C and no comments. By analogy with the authors' point, what has the teacher withheld?
options: Praise, which ought to soften any low grade given
Agreement, which the student's effort earned anyway
The grounds for not being convinced by the argument
A rewrite of the essay showing the position the student should take
optionExplain: The card is about grounds, not about softening a verdict.
Effort deserves a considered reply, not automatic agreement.
Right: the student tried to convince a reader, and a bare grade gives no considered judgment.
A rewrite replaces the student's work; what is owed is a judgment of it.
questions.explain: The essay is an attempt to convince, and the teacher is its reader. A bare grade is a verdict without the grounds the card says an unconvinced reader owes.
questions.rule: Any serious attempt to convince is owed grounds, not a bare verdict.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the debt runs to any serious attempt to convince, not only to published authors: the reader of a student's essay or a colleague's memo owes grounds for being unconvinced, not a bare mark.

questions.q: True or false: By the authors' view's standard, someone who only leafs through a book in a shop for two minutes does not yet owe its author a considered judgment.
questions.explain: The debt follows the work of understanding a book that tries to teach. Deciding not to read a book is not a judgment on what it says.
questions.rule: The verdict is owed after understanding, not after a glance.

questions.q: Francis Bacon gave advice on what a reader should aim at. Which aim did he recommend?
options: To find faults and refute the author
To weigh and consider what is said
To believe and take what is said on trust
To gather material for conversation
optionExplain: Bacon warned against reading to contradict and confute.
Right: Bacon set weighing and considering against the other three aims.
Bacon warned against reading to believe and take for granted.
Bacon warned against reading to find talk and discourse.
questions.explain: Bacon rejected reading to contradict, to believe, or to find talk, and recommended weighing and considering. The card next sets out the four aims.
questions.rule: Weigh and consider.

questions.q: Match each aim of reading in Bacon's advice with what it does.
pairs: Looks only for faults to refute
Takes what is said for granted
Examines what is said on its merits
questions.explain: Bacon names three wrong aims and one right one. Only weighing and considering examines the book itself rather than using it for something else.
questions.rule: Three wrong aims, one right one.

questions.q: Before a dinner party, Tara skims an article on deep-sea mining, picking out surprising facts to mention, without asking whether they are sound. Which aim in Bacon's advice does this show?
options: Reading to contradict and confute
Reading to find talk and discourse
Reading to believe and take for granted
Reading to weigh and consider
optionExplain: She is not hunting for faults to refute.
Right: she is gathering material for conversation.
She does take the facts on trust, but her aim is something to talk about, not to settle what is true.
She does not ask whether the facts are sound, so she is not weighing them.
questions.explain: Tara's aim is talk: facts to mention at dinner. Weighing would mean asking whether they are sound.
questions.rule: Reading for talk uses the book; weighing examines it.

questions.q: Four people read the same diet book. Which one is weighing and considering it?
options: Gus notes the most surprising claims to share at the gym
Eve hunts each chapter for lines she can mock in her review
Fay underlines each claim and adopts the plan the same day
Dev checks each claim against its cited studies; two fail
optionExplain: He reads to find talk.
She reads to contradict: the verdict came before the reading.
She reads to believe, taking the claims for granted.
Right: he examines the claims on their merits, and finding faults after weighing is no breach of the advice.
questions.explain: Dev and Eve both end up finding faults, but only Dev began by examining the claims. Weighing concerns the aim and method, not whether the verdict is favourable.
questions.rule: Faults found by weighing differ from faults hunted for.

questions.q: A juror hears the prosecution's case in a fraud trial. By analogy with Bacon's advice, how should she listen?
options: Weigh the evidence as it comes, without starting from a verdict
Look for holes from the start, since the accused needs defending
Accept the case as given, since the prosecutor knows the facts
Note striking moments, since those are what jurors will discuss
optionExplain: Right: like a reader, she should examine the case on its merits before deciding.
That is reading to contradict: the verdict is fixed before the evidence is heard.
That is reading to believe: the case is taken for granted.
That is reading to find talk: material for discussion rather than judgment.
questions.explain: The juror faces a case laid before her, as a reader faces a book. Hearing only one side invites reading to believe, which is why a trial hears the defence before the jury deliberates.
questions.rule: The verdict comes after weighing, not before hearing.
questions.teaches: Weighing needs both sides: a case heard from one side only invites reading to believe, which is why trials hear the defence in full before the jury deliberates, a procedural guard against fixing a verdict early.

questions.q: True or false: A reader who weighs a book carefully and then concludes that its main argument fails has broken Bacon's advice not to read to contradict.
questions.explain: The advice concerns the aim a reader brings, not the verdict he reaches. Disagreement that comes out of weighing is the result of weighing, not a breach of it.
questions.rule: Bacon's advice governs the aim, not the verdict.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, every book, however good, has some fault that a reader can find.
questions.explain: The authors say it is certain that no book is so good that no fault can be found with it. The card next explains the attitude they are rejecting.
questions.rule: Every book can be faulted somewhere.

questions.q: The authors say it is certain that there is no book so ____ that no fault can be found with it.
questions.explain: They turn Cervantes' saying around: whatever one thinks about finding good in bad books, faults can be found in good ones.
questions.rule: No book is so good as to be faultless.

questions.q: A reader of a classic history finds a claim that conflicts with evidence she knows well. She decides that, since the book is a classic, she must be the one who is wrong, without checking. What do the authors call this?
options: False piety toward the book
Teachability toward the author
Weighing and considering its claim
Intellectual etiquette toward the author
optionExplain: Right: she lets the book's reputation stand in for checking, the halo the authors reject.
Teachability is active judgment, not deference without checking.
Weighing would mean checking the claim against the evidence, which she skipped.
Etiquette governs how she replies; it does not require her to assume she is wrong.
questions.explain: Deciding she must be wrong because the book is famous treats it as beyond criticism. The authors call that false piety.
questions.rule: Reputation is not a reason to stop checking.

questions.q: Which of these thoughts, in a reader who has worked through a great book, express false piety? Select all that apply.
options: It is a classic, so this gap must be my misreading
So famous an author cannot have overlooked this
I have checked twice and still see a gap here
I should understand this chapter before judging it
Who am I to find fault with a book like this?
optionExplain: Right: fame is used in place of checking.
Right: the author's reputation is treated as proof he made no error.
This is careful judgment, not piety: she has checked and kept her finding.
Understanding first is the authors' own rule, not false piety.
Right: it treats the reader's standing, not the evidence, as settling the matter.
questions.explain: False piety lets a book's reputation silence a reader's finding. Checking a finding, or understanding before judging, is good practice.
questions.rule: Piety is false when reputation replaces evidence.

questions.q: Suppose a reader has worked through a great book until she understands it, and she now sees a real flaw in one argument. On the authors' view, what should she do?
options: Keep quiet, since a great book outranks her judgment
State the flaw, since the book's fame does not shield it
Drop the whole book, since one flaw spoils all of it
Assume the flaw is deliberate, since great authors plan it all
optionExplain: That is the false piety the authors reject.
Right: once she understands, the reputation of the book is no reason to stay silent.
A flaw in one argument is a point to criticise, not a reason to discard what the book teaches.
That treats the author as faultless, which is false piety in another form.
questions.explain: The authors are certain no book is faultless. A reader who has understood and found a flaw should say so; the book's standing does not change that.
questions.rule: Understood and flawed: say so.

questions.q: A junior doctor sees that a clinical guideline written by eminent experts recommends a dose that conflicts with a newer trial she has read closely. By analogy with the authors' point, what should she do?
options: Keep silent, since juniors are not peers of the guideline's authors
Ignore the trial, since eminent authors will have weighed it
Stop following the guideline at once, since one fault discredits it
Raise the conflict with her reasons, since eminence is no proof
optionExplain: Standing to raise a reasoned point comes from understanding it, not from rank.
Perhaps they did, but assuming so without checking is false piety toward experts.
One conflict is a reason to question that point, not to throw out the whole guideline unilaterally.
Right: an expert text earns a careful hearing, not immunity, so an informed conflict should be raised.
questions.explain: The guideline is like a great book: respected, and still capable of error. Expert texts also age; one written before a newer trial can have been sound for its time and still need revising, so her objection is about evidence, not the experts' competence.
questions.rule: Authority earns a hearing, not immunity, and expert texts can age.
questions.teaches: Expert texts age: a guideline written before newer evidence appeared can have been faultless for its time and be wrong now, so a reader's informed objection may concern dates, not the authors' competence.

questions.q: According to the authors, what happens to the relation between reader and author once the reader understands a good book?
options: The reader is bound to accept what he understood
The reader stays a pupil and should not judge
The author loses his authority on the subject
The reader rises almost to the author's level
optionExplain: Understanding opens the way to judgment, not to automatic acceptance.
That holds before understanding; afterwards the reader may and should judge.
The author keeps his knowledge; it is the reader who has risen.
Right: understanding raises the reader almost to equality with the author.
questions.explain: The authors say a reader who understands has raised himself almost to the author's level. The card next shows what follows from that.
questions.rule: Understanding makes the reader nearly a peer.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reader who understands a book but declines to use his critical powers does the author an injustice.
questions.explain: The author has worked to make the reader his equal, so he deserves to be engaged as a peer. Holding back at that point wrongs him.
questions.rule: Having understood, criticize.

questions.q: Kai has worked through a book on urban planning until he can restate each argument. He doubts its chapter on traffic but thinks a mere reader should not object to a professor. What would the authors say?
options: He should first read the reviews to see if experts share his doubt
He should wait until he holds a degree in planning himself
He should defer, since a superior book is beyond his criticism
Understanding has made him nearly a peer, so he should object
optionExplain: Reviews give other people's judgments; the authors want his own.
Standing comes from understanding the book, not from credentials.
That was true only until he understood it.
Right: having understood, he is fit to talk back, and holding back wrongs the author.
questions.explain: Kai has done the work of understanding, which the authors say raises him almost to equality. His objection is now owed, not presumptuous.
questions.rule: Understanding, not rank, confers the right to object.

questions.q: Sort each reader by whether, on the authors' reasoning, he is still a pupil who should hold back criticism or a peer who should now give it.

items.t: Has read half the book and dislikes its tone
Can restate the author's main argument in his own words
Feels sure the author is wrong after the first chapter
Knows what the key terms mean and how the claims connect
Is clever and widely read but has only skimmed this book
Has traced each argument and seen which problems were solved

questions.explain: What moves a reader from pupil to peer is understanding this book. Strong feelings, partial reading and general cleverness do not.
questions.rule: Understanding this book is what makes you a peer.

questions.q: An apprentice carpenter has learned his master's joinery method thoroughly and now sees a way it wastes timber. By analogy with the authors' point, what should he do?
options: Leave and work alone, since a pupil who sees faults has outgrown his master
Keep quiet, since a pupil's place is to follow the method he was taught
Say so, since making him the master's equal was the aim of the teaching
Wait for the master to notice, since a teacher should find his own faults
optionExplain: Seeing a fault calls for talking back, not for breaking off the conversation.
That was right while he was learning; now that he understands the method, silence wastes what he was taught.
Right: teaching aims to make the learner a peer, and an informed objection shows it has worked.
That leaves the master without the reply his teaching has earned.
questions.explain: The apprentice stands where an understanding reader stands. His teacher worked to raise him to his own level, so a reasoned objection is the fruit of the teaching.
questions.rule: An informed objection is the success of teaching.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any teaching aims to make the learner a peer, so a well-taught learner's informed objection is a sign that the teaching succeeded, not disloyalty to the teacher.

questions.q: Suppose a reader is brilliant in another field but has not yet understood this particular book. On the authors' reasoning, what standing does he have to criticize it?
options: A pupil's, since standing comes from understanding this book
A peer's, since his ability elsewhere makes him the author's equal
A peer's, as long as he feels strongly that the author is wrong
A critic's by right, since anyone may judge any book at any time
optionExplain: Right: near-equality is earned by understanding this book, and he has not yet done that.
Ability elsewhere may help him understand, but it does not replace understanding.
Strength of feeling is not understanding.
Nothing stops him from judging, but the authors say a superior book should not be criticized until it is understood.
questions.explain: The card ties the change from pupil to peer to understanding the particular book. Talent in another field does not skip that step.
questions.rule: Talent elsewhere does not replace understanding here.

questions.q: Which reader would the authors call the most teachable?
options: The one who works hardest to make up her own mind
The one who accepts whatever the author says
The one who defers to the expert on every claim
The one who copies the book's conclusions exactly into her notes
optionExplain: Right: the authors say the most teachable reader is the most critical.
Acceptance looks teachable, but the authors call it subservience.
Deference may come from respect, but without one's own judgment it is pliability.
Copying conclusions is training at best, not being taught.
questions.explain: Teachability is the effort to make up one's own mind, not passive acceptance. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: The most teachable reader is the most critical.

questions.q: According to the authors, teachability is often confused with ____.
questions.explain: People wrongly think a passive, pliable person is teachable. The authors call that subservience, and say teachability is active.
questions.rule: Teachable is not subservient.

questions.q: The authors distinguish being trained from being taught. What marks the difference?
options: Whether the learner uses his own independent judgment
Whether the learner remembers what he was shown
Whether the teacher is an expert in the subject
Whether the lesson is practical rather than theoretical
optionExplain: Right: no one is really teachable who does not freely use his power of independent judgment.
Memory matters to both, but a trained person can remember without judging.
Expertise of the teacher does not decide whether the learner is taught.
Either kind of lesson can be received by training or by being taught.
questions.explain: Someone without independent judgment can perhaps be trained, but not taught. The difference lies in the learner's own active judgment.
questions.rule: Taught means judging for yourself; trained means complying.

questions.q: Which response to a book on personal finance shows teachability as the authors define it?
options: Refusing to change any habit, since her money is her own business and no author's
Adopting every rule in it at once, since the author is an expert
Testing its budgeting rule on her own accounts, then rejecting one part
Rereading it until she can recite each rule word for word
optionExplain: That is independence without listening; she has not let the author teach her.
That is pliability: acceptance without her own judgment.
Right: she uses her own judgment on what the author teaches, keeping some and rejecting some.
Recitation shows memory, not judgment.
questions.explain: Teachability means hearing the author and then using one's own judgment. Testing the rule and rejecting part of it does both.
questions.rule: Teachability is judgment applied to what you were taught.

questions.q: True or false: On the authors' account, a reader who argues with a book from its first page is more teachable than one who waits to understand it before judging.
questions.explain: The authors say the teachable reader makes up his mind finally, after the teacher has been heard and understood. Arguing from page one is premature, not more active.
questions.rule: Active judgment comes after understanding, not instead of it.

questions.q: A manager says she wants a team that is easy to teach, and hires the candidates who agreed with everything she said in their interviews. By the authors' account of teachability, what has she selected for?
options: Expertise, since people who agree know the right answers
Teachability, since agreeable people learn the fastest
Independence, since agreeing with everything shows a mind already made up
Pliability, which makes people trainable but not teachable
optionExplain: Agreement with the interviewer says nothing about knowledge.
Agreeableness can look like teachability, which is exactly the confusion the authors describe.
Agreeing with everything suggests the opposite of independent judgment.
Right: agreeing with everything is the passive, pliable stance the authors say is mistaken for teachability.
questions.explain: The manager confused agreeableness with teachability. By the authors' account, the teachable recruit would be the one who listened and then tested what she said.
questions.rule: Agreeableness is not teachability.
questions.teaches: By the authors' account, agreeableness is a poor sign of teachability in people as well as readers: someone who agrees with everything may be pliable, while a teachable learner shows it by testing what he hears.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reader who puts great effort into criticizing a book has thereby shown that he is teachable.
questions.explain: The authors say sheer amount of effort is not an adequate measure of teachability. The card next explains what else is needed.
questions.rule: Effort alone does not prove teachability.

questions.q: According to the authors, teachability requires that a teacher be fully heard and, more than that, ____ before he is judged.
questions.explain: Hearing is not enough: the teacher must be understood before the reader judges him.
questions.rule: Heard, then understood, then judged.

questions.q: Max spends a weekend writing a long rebuttal of a book on minimum wages, without first working out the author's key terms or main argument. What do the authors say his rebuttal lacks?
options: The method of judging, which effort alone cannot supply
Enough effort, since a weekend is too short for a rebuttal
Passion, since a rebuttal needs strong feeling to persuade
Agreement, since a rebuttal should begin with concessions
optionExplain: Right: he skipped understanding, so his effort went into judging something he has not grasped.
His effort was large; the fault is where it went.
Feeling does not replace understanding the author.
Concessions are not required; understanding is.
questions.explain: Max worked hard but skipped hearing and understanding the author. The card says a reader must know how to judge, not only try hard.
questions.rule: Hard work on the wrong step is still the wrong step.

questions.q: A reviewer writes: I read this book three times and spent a month on my review, so my verdict on it must be sound. Which assumption is faulty?
options: That a review deserves time and care
That reading a book three times can help
That effort guarantees a sound verdict
That a verdict on a book can be sound
optionExplain: Time and care are good; they just do not guarantee soundness.
Rereading can help understanding; it is not the faulty step.
Right: effort is not an adequate criterion; the reviewer must also know how to judge.
Verdicts can be sound; the question is what makes them so.
questions.explain: The reviewer infers soundness from effort. The authors say a reader must know how to judge, so effort alone proves nothing about the verdict.
questions.rule: Effort is no proof of a sound verdict.

questions.q: A new restaurant critic eats at one place four times and writes 3,000 words, but has no idea what makes a dish well made. By analogy with the authors' point, what is wrong with her review?
options: Nothing, since four visits make for a thorough judgment
Her effort is real, but judging also needs a learned method
Her visits were excessive, since critics should go once
Only chefs may judge food, so her verdict counts for nothing
optionExplain: Thoroughness of effort is what the card says is not enough.
Right: as with books, judging food well needs standards learned for the purpose, not only hours.
The number of visits is not the problem; her lack of standards is.
Diners can judge food; the card's point is that a judge must know how.
questions.explain: Like a reader who tries hard without knowing how to judge a book, the critic spends effort without standards. With standards, fewer visits would serve; without them, more visits add little.
questions.rule: Every kind of criticism needs its own learned standards.
