questions.teaches: Effort and standards are not interchangeable: a critic with good standards can judge well from less exposure, while extra hours without standards add little, so method multiplies effort rather than replacing it.

questions.q: True or false: Even a reader who knew the rules for judging a book perfectly would still have to hear the author out before he could judge the book fairly.
questions.explain: Method is needed, but it applies to a book already heard and understood. The authors put hearing and understanding before judgment whatever the reader's skill.
questions.rule: Skill in judging does not replace hearing the author out.

questions.q: Grammar, logic and rhetoric are the three traditional liberal arts. Which one do the authors say governs the third stage of analytical reading, criticism?
options: Logic
Grammar
Rhetoric
All three in equal measure
optionExplain: Logic, with grammar, underlies the first two stages; criticism goes beyond understanding.
Grammar, with logic, underlies the first two stages.
Right: skill in the third stage depends on the remaining art, rhetoric.
All three cooperate in reading, but the authors assign each to particular stages.
questions.explain: Grammar and logic serve understanding; rhetoric serves critical judgment. The card next shows how the three fit together.
questions.rule: Grammar and logic to understand; rhetoric to judge.

questions.q: Match each item with its role in the authors' account of the three arts.
pairs: Skill in the first two stages
Matched by a reader aiming at understanding
The etiquette of the third stage
Makes the reader polite and effective
questions.explain: Grammar and logic give understanding; rhetoric governs the critical response. The writer's and reader's skills mirror each other, and the etiquette serves effectiveness as well as politeness.
questions.rule: Each art has its stage; etiquette has two purposes.

questions.q: A reader has worked out a pamphlet's key terms and how its claims connect. She now asks how far its case ought to move her. In the authors' scheme, which art is she now using?
options: Logic, the art of following arguments
Grammar, the art of reading words
Rhetoric, the art of the third stage
Personal taste, which lies outside the arts
optionExplain: Logic served her in seeing how the claims connect, which she has already done.
Grammar served her in finding the key terms, which she has already done.
Right: deciding how to respond to an attempt to convince or persuade is rhetorical work.
The authors treat critical judgment as governed by an art with rules, not left to taste.
questions.explain: Terms and connections are the work of grammar and logic. Judging how far the case should move her is the third stage, governed by rhetoric.
questions.rule: How far should it move me? is a rhetorical question.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the etiquette of the third stage serves to make a reader effective in talking back, not only polite.
questions.explain: The authors note that etiquette always serves two purposes, though this is not generally recognized: it makes the reader polite, and it makes him effective.
questions.rule: Etiquette makes talking back polite and effective.

questions.q: A film critic first describes what a documentary claims and how it builds its case, and only then discusses how far its case should move viewers. By analogy with the authors' point, what is she doing?
options: Using rhetoric alone, since critics judge effects
Using rhetoric first, then grammar and logic
Using logic alone, since films have no grammar
Using grammar and logic first, then rhetoric
optionExplain: She does judge effects, but only after the work of understanding.
Her order is the reverse: understanding first, response second.
A film's statements can be followed like a text's; she is understanding before judging.
Right: she understands what the film says and how, then judges her response to it.
questions.explain: Describing claims and how the case is built is understanding; discussing how far it should move viewers is critical response. A film runs at its own pace and cannot be reread at will, so the understanding step may need notes or a second viewing.
questions.rule: Understand before judging, even when the medium will not wait.
questions.teaches: In media that set their own pace, such as film or a live talk, the grammar-and-logic work is harder because you cannot reread at will, so notes or a second viewing may be needed before the rhetorical question can be asked fairly.

questions.q: Suppose a reader had mastered rhetoric but not grammar and logic. By the authors' view's scheme, what would go wrong when he criticized a book?
options: Nothing, since criticism needs only the third art
He would respond skilfully to a case he had not understood
He would understand the book but be unable to respond
He would be unable to tell convincing from persuading
optionExplain: The third art depends on the other two having done their work.
Right: rhetoric works on what grammar and logic have made clear; without them it has no sound material.
That would be the opposite case: grammar and logic without rhetoric.
That distinction is part of rhetoric, which he has; his gap is in understanding.
questions.explain: Grammar and logic prepare the way for a critical reaction. Without them the reader's skilful response would be to a book he has not understood.
questions.rule: Rhetoric without understanding responds to the wrong book.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, rhetoric concerns orators and propagandists, not the writers of ordinary serious books.
questions.explain: In its most general sense, the authors say, rhetoric is involved wherever people communicate. The card next explains its two aims.
questions.rule: Rhetoric is in all serious communication.

questions.q: Sort each piece by whether its aim, in the authors' sense, is to convince or to persuade.

items.t: A paper arguing that a fossil is 50 million years old
A charity appeal asking you to donate today
A proof that there are infinitely many primes
A campaign speech urging you to vote
An essay explaining why tides occur
A eulogy meant to stir grief and gratitude

questions.explain: One convinces about what is true and persuades about what ultimately affects action or feeling. The fossil, the primes and the tides are matters of truth; the appeal, the speech and the eulogy aim at acts or feelings.
questions.rule: Convince about truth; persuade about action or feeling.

questions.q: A book on economics spends ten chapters explaining how inflation arises, then a final chapter urging readers to support a particular tax policy. Which description fits?
options: It convinces throughout, since the end rests on theory
It persuades throughout, since economics is political
It convinces in the body and persuades at the end
It does neither, since explaining involves no rhetoric
optionExplain: The final chapter rests on theory, but its aim is action.
Political relevance does not turn an explanation into a call to act.
Right: the explanation aims at accepting a truth, the final chapter at action.
Explaining seeks agreement that something is true, which is convincing.
questions.explain: The ten chapters aim at assent to an account of inflation; the last aims at what readers do. Many books combine the two, the first preparing the second.
questions.rule: Sort a book's parts by what each aims at.

questions.q: A writer calmly lays out evidence that regular exercise lowers blood pressure, and ends: so you should start walking daily. Which part persuades, in the authors' sense?
options: The closing advice to start walking daily
The calm tone in which the evidence is set out
The evidence linking exercise and blood pressure
The careful definition of blood pressure used
optionExplain: Right: it aims at action, which is what persuading concerns.
Tone does not decide the aim; a calm piece can still persuade.
The evidence aims at accepting a truth, which is convincing.
A definition serves understanding, not action.
questions.explain: The distinction is about the end in view. Only the closing advice aims at what the reader will do.
questions.rule: Judge the aim, not the tone.

questions.q: A company's annual report explains, with figures, why sales fell, and asks shareholders to approve a new strategy at the vote. By the authors' distinction, how should a shareholder read it?
options: Skip the explanation, since only the request for her vote matters
Treat it all as persuasion, since the company wants something from her in the end
Treat it all as convincing, since figures make every part theoretical
Judge the explanation as a truth claim, and the request as a call to act
optionExplain: The request depends on the explanation, so skipping it leaves her unable to judge the request.
The company wants her vote, but its explanation still makes claims that are true or false.
Figures support the explanation; the request still aims at action.
Right: the two parts have different aims and call for different questions.
questions.explain: The report convinces about why sales fell and persuades about how to vote. The request can be sound only if the explanation is true, so both need judging, each on its own terms.
questions.rule: In a mixed document, judge the truth claims before the call to act.
questions.teaches: Documents that mix convincing and persuading, like an annual report that explains results and then asks for a vote, are best read in two parts, since the call to act is only as sound as the explanation it rests on.

questions.q: True or false: In the authors' general sense of rhetoric, a historian who only describes what happened at a battle, asking nothing of the reader, is still engaged in rhetoric.
questions.explain: Any serious writer wants not only to be understood but to be agreed with. The historian wants her account accepted as true, which is an attempt to convince.
questions.rule: Wanting to be believed is already rhetoric.

questions.q: A reader follows an essay closely and sees why its author wrote it, but takes no view on whether it is right. According to the authors, what is missing?
options: Responsiveness: following what was said
Responsibility: taking a position of her own
Etiquette: replying politely to the author
Agreement: accepting the author's conclusion
optionExplain: She has followed what was said and noted its intention, so she is responsive.
Right: she has followed the essay but not taken a position.
Politeness is not the issue; she has not replied at all.
A position of her own could be disagreement; agreement is not required.
questions.explain: Following the essay and noting its purpose is responsiveness. Taking a position is the further step of responsibility. The card next explains both.
questions.rule: Follow, then take a position.

questions.q: Match each phrase with the authors' account of it.
pairs: Follows what is said and notes the intention behind it
Takes a position on what is said
Holding another answerable for your judgment
To be a slave rather than a free man
Arts named for the free mind that judges for itself
questions.explain: Responsiveness is following; responsibility is taking a position that is your own. The authors tie this freedom to the name of the liberal arts.
questions.rule: Responsive follows; responsible decides.

questions.q: Asked his view on a book about school testing, Sam says the author is a leading expert, so whatever he concludes is Sam's view too. What is Sam failing to be?
options: Responsive, since he did not follow the book
Responsible, since his position is not his own
Teachable, since he refuses to accept the book
Courteous, since he brings up the author's rank and title
optionExplain: He may have followed it well; the fault is in whose judgment he holds.
Right: he has made the author answerable for his judgment.
He accepts the book entirely; the trouble is that he accepts it on authority.
Mentioning rank is not discourteous; the issue is his borrowed judgment.
questions.explain: Sam holds the author's conclusion because of who the author is. The authors say a position must be your own; treating another as answerable for it gives up your freedom.
questions.rule: A borrowed verdict is not a position of your own.

questions.q: Which readers are responsive but not yet responsible? Select all that apply.
options: Can summarise the claim and its purpose, but has no view on it
Knows the author wrote to change a policy, and leaves it there
Has a firm view but cannot say what the author argued
Has followed the argument and decided where it fails
Reports the author's case accurately and defers to it
optionExplain: Right: following and noting purpose without a position is responsiveness alone.
Right: noting the intention is responsive; stopping there takes no position.
This reader has a view but has not followed the author, so is not even responsive.
This reader is both responsive and responsible.
Right: deferring hands the judgment to the author.
questions.explain: Responsiveness is following what is said and why. Responsibility adds a position of one's own; the third reader has a view without responsiveness, the fourth has both.
questions.rule: Responsiveness first, then responsibility.

questions.q: A voter follows a referendum campaign closely and understands each side's case. On polling day she votes as her favourite newspaper advises, without forming a view. By the authors' view, what has she done?
options: Been responsive but handed her responsibility to the paper
Been responsible, since she chose which paper to trust
Been neither, since she understood neither side's case
Been both, since following a campaign closely is already taking a stand
optionExplain: Right: she followed the debate but borrowed the judgment behind her vote.
Choosing whom to follow is still letting another decide the question itself.
She did understand both cases, so she was responsive.
Following is responsiveness; a stand needs a judgment of her own.
questions.explain: Understanding each case is responsiveness. Voting as the paper advises, without a view of her own, hands the judgment to someone else.
questions.rule: The act can be yours while the judgment is borrowed.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a citizen who understands a public debate but takes her position from someone else has been responsive without being responsible: the vote is hers, but the judgment behind it is borrowed.

questions.q: True or false: On the authors' view, a reader who ends up agreeing fully with an author, for reasons she has examined and accepts, has failed to take a position of her own.
questions.explain: Her position matches the author's, but she holds it for reasons she accepts. Being responsible concerns whose judgment it is, not whether it differs from the author's.
questions.rule: Agreement can be a position of your own.

questions.q: On the reader's side, what do the authors say rhetorical skill is?
options: Knowing how to write persuasively, in turn, about what we have read
Knowing how to react to those who try to convince or persuade us
Knowing how to spot the emotional words a writer uses
Knowing how to resist each attempt to change our minds
optionExplain: That is the writer's skill applied to a review, not the reader's skill as a receiver.
Right: the reader's skill mirrors the writer's skill of convincing or persuading.
Spotting emotional words may help, but the skill is in reacting to the whole effort.
Resisting is one possible reaction; the skill is reacting rightly.
questions.explain: A writer's rhetorical skill is to convince or persuade; a reader's is to react to such attempts. The card next sets the two side by side.
questions.rule: The reader's rhetoric is skill in reacting.

questions.q: For a speaker or writer, the authors say, rhetorical skill is knowing how to convince or ____.
questions.explain: Convincing and persuading are the writer's final aims, and the other parts of communication serve them.
questions.rule: The writer aims to convince or persuade.

questions.q: A charity’s appeal is written with great clarity: every fact is easy to follow and well ordered. What do the authors suggest a reader do with that clarity?
options: Treat it as a sign that the charity's case is sound, and give
Use it to understand the claims, then judge how far they move her
Distrust it, since clear writing is a sign of manipulation
Ignore it, since only the emotional appeal is rhetorical
optionExplain: Clarity serves the writer's aim of convincing; it is not proof.
Right: clarity lets her understand, and understanding prepares her critical reaction.
Clarity also serves honest writers; suspicion of it is not a reaction to the case.
Clarity is part of how the appeal works, since it serves the aim of persuading.
questions.explain: Clear writing helps the reader understand, which is what prepares a critical reaction. The reaction itself must then weigh the claims, not the clarity.
questions.rule: Use clarity to understand, not as a verdict.

questions.q: A reader reasons: this author writes with great clarity; clear writing comes from grammatical and logical skill; so his conclusions are true. Which step goes wrong?
options: Reading closely enough to notice the author's clarity
Linking clear writing with grammatical and logical skill
Noticing that the author writes with great clarity
Treating clarity as proof that the conclusions are true
optionExplain: Close reading is needed for understanding; it is not the faulty step.
The authors do link intelligible writing with grammar and logic.
Noticing clarity is a fair observation.
Right: clarity is a means to the writer's end of convincing, not evidence of truth.
questions.explain: Grammar and logic make writing intelligible, and intelligibility serves the aim of convincing. That a case is clearly put does not show that it is true.
questions.rule: Clear is not the same as true.

questions.q: A patient reads a drug maker's leaflet that explains its treatment in plain, well-ordered prose. By analogy with the authors' point, what should her reaction rest on?
options: Understanding its claims, then asking how far they hold up
Trusting it, since medical leaflets are checked for accuracy
Rejecting it, since the company profits from her choice
Following her doctor, since patients cannot judge such claims
optionExplain: Right: the leaflet is an attempt to persuade, so she understands, then reacts deliberately.
Checks may exist, but trusting by default hands over her judgment.
Knowing the source's interest is a reason for care, not grounds for rejection.
Her doctor can help, but the card's point is that her reaction should be her own.
questions.explain: Knowing who is trying to persuade her calls for a deliberate reaction: understand the claims, then weigh them. Neither automatic trust nor automatic rejection is a reaction to the case.
questions.rule: A source's interest calls for care, not automatic rejection.
questions.teaches: By analogy, knowing who is trying to convince you, such as a company describing its own product, is a reason to react deliberately, not to reject: the claims still have to be understood and then weighed.

questions.q: True or false: On the authors' view, a reader with strong rhetorical skill may end by being convinced by the author's case.
questions.explain: The skill is in reacting rightly to an attempt to convince or persuade, not in resisting it. When the case is sound, the right reaction is to be convinced.
questions.rule: Skilled reaction can end in being convinced.

questions.q: According to the authors, what should you be able to say before you agree or disagree with a book?
options: I have read the leading reviews of it
I understand, with reasonable certainty
I have read it all the way to the end
I know where the author stands on it
optionExplain: Reviews give others' judgments, not your own understanding.
Right: Rule 9 asks for I understand before any of the three critical positions.
Finishing is needed, but reaching the end does not prove you understood.
Knowing the author's conclusion is less than understanding his book.
questions.explain: Rule 9 puts understanding first: I understand comes before I agree, I disagree or I suspend judgment. The card next states the rule.
questions.rule: I understand comes first.

questions.q: Rule 9 says you must be able to say I understand before you can say which of these? Select all that apply.
options: I agree
I disagree
I suspend judgment
I have finished reading
I have a question
optionExplain: Right: agreeing is a critical position that needs understanding first.
Right: disagreeing needs understanding first.
Right: suspending judgment needs understanding first.
Finishing is part of reading, not a critical position.
Questions help you reach understanding; they are not verdicts.
questions.explain: Rule 9 governs the three critical positions: agree, disagree, suspend judgment. Finishing and asking questions are part of reaching understanding.
questions.rule: All three verdicts wait on understanding.

questions.q: Ali has read a book on criminal justice twice and can state its main question, its key terms and its central argument. He now thinks the author is wrong about prisons. What does Rule 9 say about his position?
options: He must wait until he finds experts in the field who share his view
He has earned the right to disagree, and owes his criticism
He must suspend judgment, since he could still be wrong
He should agree for now, since the author knows more
optionExplain: Rule 9 asks for his understanding, not for support from others.
Right: having understood, he has the right and the duty to criticize.
Any judgment could be wrong; that is no reason to withhold one he can ground.
The author's greater knowledge does not cancel a reader's duty to judge once he understands.
questions.explain: Ali can say I understand with reasonable certainty. Rule 9 then gives him the right to turn critic and the duty to do so.
questions.rule: Understanding earns the right and imposes the duty.

questions.q: Suppose a reader can honestly say she understands a book, but chooses to write nothing about whether it is true. By Rule 9, what has she done?
options: Done all that reading asks, since understanding is the goal
Followed the rule, which forbids premature judgment
Broken the rule by judging before understanding
Earned the right to criticize but skipped the duty
optionExplain: The authors say active reading is completed by criticism, not by understanding alone.
Her judgment would not be premature; she has understood.
She has not judged at all, so she has not judged too early.
Right: understanding brings both the right and the duty to criticize.
questions.explain: Rule 9 cuts both ways: no judgment before understanding, and a duty to judge after it. She has met the first half and skipped the second.
questions.rule: After understanding, silence is a failure too.

questions.q: True or false: Rule 9 asks for reasonable certainty of understanding, not complete certainty, before a reader agrees or disagrees.
questions.explain: The rule asks for reasonable certainty. Complete certainty would put judgment off indefinitely, and the rule is meant to delay criticism, not cancel it.
questions.rule: Reasonable certainty, not perfect certainty.

questions.q: A city planner is asked to approve or reject a consultant's traffic forecast model. Applying Rule 9 by analogy, what should she be able to say first?
options: That the model's results match what she expected
That the consultant has a good record on the past models she built
That she understands what the model assumes and predicts
That the model has been used by other cities
optionExplain: Matching expectations is a reaction, not understanding.
A good record is a reason for trust, not understanding of this model.
Right: its assumptions and predictions are what she must understand before approving or rejecting it.
Use elsewhere is evidence about others' judgments, not her own understanding.
questions.explain: Approving or rejecting is a verdict, so Rule 9 applies. For a model, understanding means knowing what it assumes and what it predicts.
questions.rule: Know what it assumes and predicts before you sign off.
questions.teaches: By analogy, Rule 9's test of understanding for a technical work, such as a forecast model, is being able to state what it assumes and what it predicts, the counterparts of a book's premises and conclusions.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, an expert reader can combine all three stages of analytical reading into a single pass.
questions.explain: An expert can combine the first two stages almost completely, but he must still wait until he understands before he criticizes. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Experts fuse two stages, not three.

questions.q: According to the authors, the third stage of analytical reading must follow the other two in ____.
questions.explain: The first two stages can overlap, but criticism comes after them in time.
questions.rule: Criticism follows in time.

questions.q: Rosa outlines a report and interprets its key terms in the same reading, and as she goes she also marks each claim as right or wrong. What do the authors say about her method?
options: It is all fine, since an experienced reader combines every stage
Combining the first two stages is fine, but the verdicts are too early
It is all premature, since outlining must be finished before interpreting begins
The verdicts are fine as she goes, since she can revise them later
optionExplain: Experts combine the first two stages, not the third.
Right: outlining and interpreting may overlap; judging must wait until she understands.
The first two stages interpenetrate, so doing them together is not premature.
Planning to revise does not make a verdict before understanding sound.
questions.explain: Outlining and interpreting can run together. Marking claims right or wrong is criticism, which must follow understanding.
questions.rule: Combine the first two stages; hold the third.

questions.q: Suppose a reader is a leading expert in a book's subject. On the authors' account, what changes for her?
options: Nothing, since experts and beginners read in exactly the same way
She may judge as she reads, since her expertise shows errors at once
She may skip the first two stages, since she knows the subject well
She fuses the first two stages more fully, but still waits to judge
optionExplain: Experts do read differently: they combine the first two stages almost completely.
The authors say the expert, no less than the beginner, waits until he understands.
Knowing the subject is not knowing what this author says about it.
Right: expertise lets the first two stages merge, but not the third.
questions.explain: Skill changes how smoothly the first two stages run together. It does not change the order: criticism waits for understanding.
questions.rule: Expertise speeds understanding; it does not skip it.

questions.q: A building surveyor walks through a house, noting its layout and how each system connects, and writes her pass or fail report only after seeing the whole. By analogy with the authors' point, why does the verdict wait?
options: A fault in one room may be explained by another part of the house
Surveyors are paid by the hour, so waiting adds to the fee
A verdict written early is more honest, so she ought not to wait for the end
Her report must follow a standard order that starts with layout
optionExplain: Right: like a book's parts, a house's systems explain one another, so judging one part early can mislead.
Fees have nothing to do with when a fair verdict can be given.
Early verdicts feel candid, but they may judge something not yet understood.
Report format is a convention; the reason to wait is understanding the whole.
questions.explain: Mapping the whole can run as one pass, but the verdict needs the whole in view. What looks like a fault in one place may be explained elsewhere.
questions.rule: Map the whole before judging any part.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any inspection that ends in a verdict, such as a house survey, separates mapping the whole from judging it: an apparent fault in one part may be explained by another, so the verdict waits for the map.

questions.q: Sort each activity by whether it can run together with the others in one pass, or must wait until you understand the book.
groups: Can run together in one pass

items.t: Dividing the book into its major parts
Finding the author's key terms
Deciding the author is wrong about a claim
Picking out the leading propositions
Concluding that you agree with the main argument
Suspending judgment on the conclusion

questions.explain: Outlining and interpreting interpenetrate. Agreeing, disagreeing and suspending judgment are the third stage, which follows them.
questions.rule: Understanding can be fused; verdicts wait.

questions.q: True or false: To criticize a book is to find fault with it.
questions.explain: The authors call this a popular misconception: agreeing is as much a critical judgment as disagreeing. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Criticism is not the same as fault-finding.

questions.q: According to the authors, to agree without understanding is ____, and to disagree without understanding is impudent.
questions.explain: Both agreement and disagreement are empty without understanding; the authors call the first inane and the second impudent.
questions.rule: Inane to agree, impudent to disagree, without understanding.

questions.q: Ivy and Jack finish a book on four-day weeks. Ivy cannot state its argument and praises it warmly; Jack cannot state it either and attacks it. According to the authors, how do their judgments compare?
options: Both are empty, since neither rests on understanding
Ivy's is sound, since agreeing with a book is not really judging it
Jack's is sound, since criticism needs no grounding
Neither is a judgment, since neither found a flaw
optionExplain: Right: Ivy's agreement is inane and Jack's disagreement impudent.
Agreeing is a critical judgment, and it can be just as wrong.
Disagreement needs understanding as much as agreement does.
Both took a position; finding a flaw is not what makes a judgment.
questions.explain: Both took a critical position, and both positions lack understanding. The authors condemn them equally.
questions.rule: Praise and attack are equally empty without understanding.

questions.q: A reader says he is not a critic of a book, since he agrees with all of it. What is wrong with this?
options: He must disagree with something in order to read fairly
Nothing, since being a critic means finding fault with it
Agreeing is itself a critical judgment, and may be wrong
Agreeing with all of a book shows he did not read it
optionExplain: Fairness does not demand disagreement; it demands understanding.
That is the popular misconception the authors correct.
Right: agreement is one of the three critical positions and needs the same care.
Full agreement can follow a careful reading.
questions.explain: He has made a judgment: he agrees. The authors say agreement is as much a critical act as disagreement, and can be as wrong.
questions.rule: Agreeing is criticizing too.

questions.q: A restaurant has 200 five-star reviews online, many of which say nothing about the food. By analogy with the authors' point, how should a reader treat them?
options: As reliable, since praise needs no grounds to be fair
As verdicts that need grounds as much as bad reviews do
As beside the point, since only faults are informative
As proof of quality, since so many people agree
optionExplain: That treats agreement as if it were not a judgment.
Right: praise is a verdict, and without grounds it is as empty as blame without grounds.
That treats criticism as fault-finding only.
Many ungrounded verdicts do not add up to a grounded one.
questions.explain: Approval is a critical judgment like disapproval. Many ungrounded verdicts add up to no more evidence than one, since each may share the same lack of understanding.
questions.rule: Scrutinise praise as you would blame.
questions.teaches: Numbers do not supply grounds: many ungrounded verdicts, positive or negative, add up to little more evidence than one, since each may rest on the same lack of understanding, so one reasoned review can outweigh a hundred bare ratings.

questions.q: True or false: A reader who only remarks that a book's prose is graceful has taken none of the three critical positions on its claims.
questions.explain: The three positions are judgments on what the book says. A remark on style, however fair, neither agrees nor disagrees with the author's claims.
questions.rule: Style remarks are not verdicts on claims.

questions.q: A reader says she suspends judgment on a book's main claim. In the authors' view, what is she doing?
options: Declining to take any position on the claim
Taking the position that it has not been shown
Agreeing with the claim, with some reservations
Postponing reading until she has more time
optionExplain: It can look like declining, but the authors count it as an act of criticism.
Right: suspending judgment is a critical position that the case is not made either way.
Reservations about a claim she accepts would be qualified agreement.
That is a decision about reading, not a judgment about the claim.
questions.explain: The authors treat suspending judgment as a critical act: saying that something has not been shown. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Suspending says: not shown.

questions.q: According to the authors, suspending judgment takes the position that something has not been ____.
questions.explain: To suspend judgment is to say you are not convinced or persuaded either way, because the case has not been shown.
questions.rule: Suspend means not shown either way.

questions.q: Which statement is a suspended judgment in the authors' sense?
options: I have not read far enough to have any view on this book
The book shows the trend, but not that the policy caused it
I agree with most of it, though the style is heavy going
Who can say, when every view here is as good as another
optionExplain: That is not yet understanding, so it is no critical position.
Right: it names what has and has not been shown.
That is agreement with a remark on style.
That denies that the case could be shown at all, rather than saying it has not been.
questions.explain: A suspended judgment says what has not been shown. Only the first statement does that about the book's claim.
questions.rule: Name what has not been shown.

questions.q: A student writes: I suspend judgment on this book, since I have not understood its argument yet. Which part of the statement conflicts with the authors' point?
options: Writing anything about the book before the seminar
Admitting that she has not yet understood the argument
Choosing not to agree or disagree with the book until later on
Calling it suspended judgment when she has not understood
optionExplain: Writing notes is fine; the problem is the claim to a critical position.
Honest admission is good; it is the label that is wrong.
Holding back from verdicts before understanding is what Rule 9 asks; the timing is not the problem.
Right: suspension is a critical position and needs understanding behind it.
questions.explain: Not yet understanding calls for more reading, not a verdict. Suspending judgment is a position taken after understanding.
questions.rule: Not understanding is not suspension.

questions.q: A peer reviewer writes: I cannot recommend acceptance or rejection until the authors report results for the control group. By the authors' view, what has she done?
options: Suspended judgment and said what has not been shown
Avoided judging, since she refused to recommend
Rejected the paper, since she found a fault in it
Accepted the paper, since she raised no objection
optionExplain: Right: she names the missing evidence, which makes her suspension a position.
Declining to recommend can look like avoidance, but she stated what is missing.
She has not said the paper is wrong, only that its case is not yet made.
Asking for missing results is not acceptance.
questions.explain: Her report takes the position that the case has not been shown, and says exactly what would show it.
questions.rule: A good suspension names what would settle it.
questions.teaches: A well-made suspension of judgment names the evidence that would settle the matter, as a reviewer's request for missing control-group results does; that turns holding back into a concrete next step.

questions.q: True or false: If a reader has understood a book and finds its case fully made, she may keep suspending judgment as the safest course.
questions.explain: Suspension says the case has not been shown. If she finds it shown, holding back avoids the duty to judge rather than taking a position.
questions.rule: When the case is made, suspension becomes avoidance.

questions.q: A critic attacks your proposal. What test do the authors suggest for whether his criticism deserves an answer?
options: Ask him what experience he has on the subject
Ask him to state your position in his own words
Count how many separate objections he raises
Ask whether others in the room agree with him
optionExplain: Experience may help, but it does not show that he understood this proposal.
Right: if he cannot restate your position satisfactorily, he does not understand it.
Many objections can all rest on one misreading.
Agreement from others says nothing about whether he understood you.
questions.explain: The authors' test is whether the critic can state your position in his own words. The card next explains why the test is needed.
questions.rule: Can he state your view? Then listen.

questions.q: According to the authors, why did they bother to state Rule 9 explicitly? Select all that apply.
options: Many people identify criticism with disagreement
Few people obey it in practice, though many praise it
It contradicts what most readers believe about books
It applies only to experts, who often forget it
Readers rarely finish the books they criticize
optionExplain: Right: that error is the first reason they give.
Right: like the golden rule, it gets more lip service than intelligent obedience.
The authors say the rule seems like common sense, so it agrees with what readers believe.
The rule applies to every reader; the expert waits like the beginner.
Unfinished reading is one way to break the rule, but not a reason they give for stating it.
questions.explain: The authors give two reasons: criticism is confused with disagreement, and the rule is praised more than practised.
questions.rule: Common sense is not the same as common practice.

questions.q: After a talk on urban trees, a listener says he does not really follow her argument, but thinks it is wrong. By the authors' account, how should the speaker treat this?
options: Answer it in full, since every objection deserves a reply
Ask him to restate her position; if he cannot, set it aside
Concede the point, since a listener's doubt shows a flaw
Repeat the whole talk, since he must have missed its opening part
optionExplain: The authors say there is no point in answering critics who admit they do not understand.
Right: criticism not based on understanding is irrelevant, and the test shows whether it is.
A doubt that rests on not following shows nothing about the argument.
Repeating may help him understand, but it does not make his objection relevant.
questions.explain: He has admitted he does not understand. The authors' polite response is to ask him to state the position; criticism without understanding can be ignored.
questions.rule: Objections without understanding are irrelevant.

questions.q: A reviewer defends his attack on a book: I quoted the author's exact sentences, so I must have understood him. What is wrong with this defence?
options: Reviewers need not understand a book, only rate it
Nothing, since exact quotation proves careful reading
He ought to have quoted far more sentences to be fair
Quoting is not restating the position in his own words
optionExplain: The authors complain about exactly such reviewers.
Quotation shows he copied accurately, not that he understood.
More quotation still would not show understanding.
Right: the test asks for the critic's own words, which show whether he grasped the meaning.
questions.explain: Anyone can copy sentences. The restating test asks for the position in the critic's own words, because only that shows the meaning was grasped.
questions.rule: Own words, not quoted words.

questions.q: A counsellor asks each partner in a quarrel to restate the other's complaint, to the other's satisfaction, before replying to it. By analogy with the authors' point, what does this achieve?
options: Each reply is aimed at the complaint actually made
It delays the argument until both partners have calmed down
It forces each partner to agree with the other
It lets the counsellor decide who is right
optionExplain: Right: the restatement makes sure each partner answers what the other actually said.
Calm may follow, but the purpose is understanding.
Restating a complaint is not agreeing with it.
The counsellor is not judging; she is making sure each understands the other.
questions.explain: Restating to the other's satisfaction is the authors' test built into the conversation. Replies then meet the real complaint, not a misreading.
questions.rule: Let the other side confirm your restatement before you reply.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the restating test can be built into a disagreement as a rule of procedure, as counsellors and mediators do: no reply until the other side agrees that its view has been stated fairly.

questions.q: True or false: A critic who restates your position well in his own words may still be wrong in his criticism of it.
questions.explain: Passing the test shows he understands, which makes his criticism relevant. The authors say such a critic's dissent should seriously disturb you, but understanding is not the same as being right.
questions.rule: Understanding makes criticism relevant, not right.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, with a good book you should be quick to say that you understand it, so that you can move on to judging.
questions.explain: The authors say you ought to hesitate before saying I understand about a good book, since much work is usually needed first. The card next explains.
questions.rule: With good books, I understand comes slowly.

questions.q: With a good book, the authors say, you ought to ____ before you say I understand.
questions.explain: The presumption is that a good book needs much work before you can say I understand honestly and with assurance.
questions.rule: Hesitate before I understand.

questions.q: After one reading of a dense book on game theory, Bea feels she gets it. What do the authors suggest before she says she understands?
options: Wait a month, since understanding comes with time alone
Trust the feeling, since a sense of clarity is reliable
Read a summary online, which will confirm her grasp
Check the feeling, for example by restating the argument
optionExplain: Time without work does not produce understanding.
A feeling of clarity after one reading of a good book is what the authors warn against trusting.
A summary tells her what someone else understood.
Right: I understand is a claim to be earned and checked, and restating tests it.
questions.explain: The feeling is a starting point, not a verdict. She must judge herself honestly, and restating the argument is one way to do it.
questions.rule: Test the feeling of understanding before you trust it.

questions.q: The authors found that students often agreed with positions they could not express in their own words. What does that show about their agreement?
options: It was sound, since agreeing needs less than disagreeing
It was all words, with no understanding underneath it
It was polite, since students defer to the books they read
It was harmless, since agreement does the author no injury
optionExplain: Agreeing needs as much understanding as disagreeing.
Right: their discussion, like their reading, was all words.
Deference may explain it, but it does not make it understanding.
Agreement without understanding is still an empty judgment, and can mislead the reader himself.
questions.explain: Being unable to state a position in your own words shows you have not understood it. Agreement then is words only.
questions.rule: If you cannot say it, you cannot agree with it.

questions.q: A new lab employee is asked whether she understands the safety procedure, and says yes after one quick read to avoid looking slow. By analogy with the authors' point, why is that risky?
options: The procedure is too long to be understood in any time
Her supervisor is bound to test her on every step at once
Only she can check the claim, and she has not checked it
Saying no would have counted as a critical judgment
optionExplain: The procedure can be understood; she has not done the work yet.
A test might catch the gap, but the card's point is that she is the judge.
Right: as with a reader, the judgment of understanding is hers alone, and pressure pushed her to make it early.
Saying she does not yet understand would have been honest, not a verdict on the procedure.
questions.explain: Like a reader, she is the judge of her own understanding. A quick yes made to look capable is the premature I understand the card warns against.
questions.rule: Pressure to say yes is the enemy of an honest I understand.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any claim of understanding that no one else will test, such as a new employee's yes to a safety briefing, rests on self-judgment alone, so social pressure to answer yes quickly is the main threat to its honesty.

questions.q: True or false: On the authors' view, a short, simple instruction leaflet deserves the same long hesitation before saying I understand as a great book does.
questions.explain: The authors tie the presumption of much work to good books. A simple text may be honestly understood with far less effort.
questions.rule: Hesitation scales with the book.

questions.q: You cannot follow the central chapter of a famous book. According to the authors, where does the fault most likely lie?
options: With the author, for writing obscurely
With you, the reader, at least at first
With the translator, if there is one
With the subject, too hard to explain
optionExplain: That may turn out to be true, but only after your hardest effort.
Right: with good books, failure to understand is usually the reader's fault.
Translation can matter, but the authors' presumption is about the reader.
Good authors make hard subjects intelligible; the presumption favours the book.
questions.explain: The presumption favours a good book. The card next explains when I don't understand starts to count against the book.
questions.rule: With good books, presume the fault is yours first.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, saying I don't understand is itself a critical judgment.
questions.explain: It is a judgment, but it reflects on the book only after the reader has tried his hardest; until then it reflects on him.
questions.rule: I don't understand is a judgment too.

questions.q: Which remark about a hard book on economics best fits the authors' advice?
options: This book is unreadable, and I gave up after the first chapter
After three readings I lose the thread at chapter six; it may be me
The author cannot write, which is why I could not follow him
I didn't understand it, so there is no point in judging it
optionExplain: A verdict after one chapter blames the book before the reader has tried his hardest.
Right: it follows real effort, locates the difficulty, and concedes the fault may be the reader's.
It assumes the fault is the author's, against the presumption.
Not understanding calls for more work, not for giving up on judging.
questions.explain: The remark follows effort and keeps the tone the authors ask for: it allows that the fault may not be the author's.
questions.rule: Locate the difficulty, and allow that it may be yours.

questions.q: According to the authors, which conditions make a reader's I don't understand begin to count against the book? Select all that apply.
options: He has tried his hardest to understand it
He has done everything that can be expected of him
He found the opening chapters dull
He read it once, quickly, and was confused
Other readers say they find it hard as well
optionExplain: Right: only after his hardest effort does the judgment reflect on the book.
Right: if he has done all that can be expected, the book may be unintelligible.
Dullness is a reaction, not evidence of unintelligibility.
One quick reading is far short of his hardest effort.
Others' difficulty may share his cause; it does not replace his own effort.
questions.explain: The authors set one condition, stated two ways: full effort, everything that can be expected. Dullness, haste and company do not meet it.
questions.rule: Only full effort shifts the fault to the book.

questions.q: A software engineer cannot make sense of a widely used library's documentation. By analogy with the authors' point, what should she do before posting that the documentation is unintelligible?
options: Work through it hard, then report exactly where she gets lost
Post at once, since a confused user is proof the docs are poor
Drop the library, since good tools need no explanation at all
Ask one colleague, since two readers settle the matter for good
optionExplain: Right: effort first, then a precise report that allows the fault may be hers.
Confusion alone does not show where the fault lies.
Complex tools need documentation; the question is whether hers is intelligible.
A colleague's view helps, but it does not replace her own effort.
questions.explain: The presumption favours widely used documentation, as it favours a good book. A careful report of where she loses the thread helps the authors and tests whether the fault is hers.
questions.rule: A useful I don't understand says exactly where.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a well-made I don't understand pinpoints where the reader loses the thread, as a good report on unclear documentation does; a precise location helps the author and tests whether the fault is the reader's.

questions.q: Suppose the book is not a good one but a hastily written self-help book full of undefined jargon. After a careful reading, what do the authors allow?
options: The reader should reread it until she understands every page
The reader must still blame herself, since with books the reader is at fault
The reader may fairly blame the book, since the presumption is weaker
The reader may not judge it, since she did not understand it
optionExplain: Some books cannot be understood because they are unintelligible; endless rereading assumes otherwise.
The authors say failure is usually the reader's fault with good books, not with every book.
Right: the presumption favours good books especially; after real effort, a poor one may be judged unintelligible.
I don't understand, after real effort, is itself a judgment the reader may make.
questions.explain: The presumption shifts the burden to the reader, most of all with good books. After careful effort, a reader may conclude a poor book is unintelligible.
questions.rule: The presumption is strongest for good books.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a book is harder to judge fairly when it depends on other works by the same author.
questions.explain: When a book depends on an author's other works for its full meaning, the authors say to be slower to claim understanding. The card next gives their examples.
questions.rule: A book in a system is harder to judge alone.

questions.q: Match each work with the companion work the authors say a fair judge of it should also know.
pairs: His works on psychology, logic and metaphysics
His Theory of the Moral Sentiments
questions.explain: Each of these authors could not say everything in one work, so judging one book alone risks judging what you do not fully understand.
questions.rule: Know the companion works before judging one part.

questions.q: A reading group is assigned three chapters of a twelve-chapter book on education. One member wants to write a review rejecting the book's thesis. What do the authors advise?
options: Go ahead, since three chapters are enough to show the author's whole view
Be more hesitant, since judging from part of a book is less sure
Refuse to say anything until every chapter has been read
Judge the author instead, since the book is not fully known
optionExplain: Style is not thesis; the remaining chapters may develop or qualify it.
Right: reading only part makes it harder to be sure of understanding the thesis.
She can comment on what the chapters say, labelled as partial; it is the verdict on the whole that waits.
Judging the person instead of the book is not a fix for partial reading.
questions.explain: Partial reading makes understanding the whole less certain, so a verdict on the book's thesis calls for more hesitation.
questions.rule: Part read, verdict slowed.

questions.q: Which reader most needs the caution about an author's related works?
options: One judging a cookbook with self-contained recipes
One judging a standalone guide to pruning roses
One judging a newspaper editorial on a single bill
One judging a sequel whose key terms are set in book one
optionExplain: Self-contained recipes need no companion volume.
A standalone guide does not lean on other works by its author.
An editorial on one bill is usually meant to stand alone.
Right: the sequel depends on its predecessor for the meaning of its terms.
questions.explain: The caution applies in proportion to how much a book leans on the author's other works. A sequel that uses terms defined earlier leans heavily.
questions.rule: The more a book leans on others, the slower the verdict.

questions.q: A journalist quotes one clause of a long supply contract to show that a company exploits its suppliers. Another clause, which she did not read, caps the suppliers' losses. By analogy with the authors' point, what went wrong?
options: She judged a part whose meaning depended on parts she skipped
She quoted the contract, when she ought to have paraphrased it
She judged a contract, which is not a matter for journalists
Nothing, since one harsh clause is enough to condemn a contract
optionExplain: Right: like a book in a system, a clause gets its force from other parts of the document.
Quoting is not the fault; reading only one clause is.
Anyone may judge a contract they have understood.
A clause's effect can be changed by limits set elsewhere, as here.
questions.explain: The clause's meaning depended on another part of the same document. Judging it alone is judging something not fully understood.
questions.rule: Read interlocking documents as wholes.
questions.teaches: By analogy, documents built of interlocking parts, such as contracts or statutes, are read as wholes: a clause's force often depends on definitions and limits elsewhere, so quoting one clause can misstate what the document does.

questions.q: True or false: On the authors' view, a reader of a self-contained book should read the author's other works before judging it.
questions.explain: The caution applies when a book depends on other works for its full meaning. A self-contained book can be understood, and judged, on its own.
questions.rule: Caution follows dependence.

questions.q: You realise halfway through an argument that you are probably wrong. According to the authors, what is the point of winning it anyway?
options: It protects your reputation, which matters most in debate
None worth having; honesty serves better in the longer run
It tests the other side's case, which is useful to them
It keeps the discussion lively, which helps both sides learn
optionExplain: A win may help your standing briefly, but the authors say honesty pays better in the longer run.
Right: the authors see no point in winning when you know or suspect you are wrong.
Testing a case is useful when you believe your objection; pressing one you suspect is wrong tests nothing.
Liveliness is not learning; a debate kept alive by a position you doubt teaches no one.
questions.explain: The authors say there is no point in winning an argument you know or suspect you should lose. The card next states Rule 10.
questions.rule: A win you suspect is wrong is worth nothing.

questions.q: Rule 10: when you disagree, do so reasonably, and not disputatiously or ____.
questions.explain: The rule concerns the manner of disagreement: reasonably, not as a contest to be won.
questions.rule: Disagree reasonably, not contentiously.

questions.q: In an online debate about a new stadium, Mo notices that his opponent's traffic data are sound and his own are out of date. Which response fits Rule 10?
options: Switch to attacking the opponent's spelling to keep the upper hand
Concede the traffic point and go on to what is still in dispute
Keep citing his own data, since the audience will not check them
Leave the debate without saying anything more about the data
optionExplain: Changing the subject to win is contentiousness.
Right: he gives up the point he now thinks is wrong and keeps disagreeing only where he has grounds.
That is winning while suspecting you are wrong, which the rule rules out.
Leaving avoids the contest but also hides what he has learned.
questions.explain: Rule 10 asks him to disagree reasonably. Conceding the point he has lost, while continuing where he still has grounds, does that.
questions.rule: Concede what you have lost; argue only what you can ground.

questions.q: Sort each move by whether it is reasonable or contentious disagreement.

items.t: Objecting on grounds you can state, after understanding
Pressing a point you suspect is wrong to save face
Holding firm on a point the evidence still supports
Raising side issues to avoid conceding the main one
Conceding one point while disputing another
Opposing a point only because the other side holds it

questions.explain: Reasonable disagreement follows the truth as far as the reader can see it, firm where the grounds are firm. Contentious disagreement aims at winning, whatever the truth.
questions.rule: Firmness on good grounds is reasonable; firmness to win is not.

questions.q: A defence lawyer must argue her client's case in court even when she privately suspects the other side is right. By analogy with the authors' point, does Rule 10 condemn her?
options: Not as such: she plays an assigned role, not her own verdict
Yes, since arguing any side you suspect is wrong breaks it
No, since winning is the true aim of any serious argument
Yes, since a lawyer ought to argue for the side that is right
optionExplain: Right, by analogy: Rule 10 is advice for a reader's own judgment; an advocate's side is assigned within a procedure built to test both sides. The authors do not discuss advocates; this is our extension.
That stretches the rule to assigned roles, which the authors do not discuss; by analogy, an advocate is not answering for her own verdict.
The authors reject the view that winning is what matters.
Courts assign advocates to each side so that the truth can be tested; she is not the judge.
questions.explain: The authors write Rule 10 for a reader judging a book, who answers for his own verdict; they say nothing about advocates. By analogy only, it does not cover someone whose assigned role is one part of a larger procedure for finding the truth.
questions.rule: Rule 10 governs your own judgment, not an assigned role.
questions.teaches: By analogy, Rule 10 governs a person's own search for truth, not every assigned role: an advocate or a debater given a side argues it by design, and the procedure as a whole, not the speaker, is meant to find the truth.

questions.q: Suppose winning an argument you suspect is wrong would earn you a promotion. According to the authors, how does that change things?
options: It changes nothing, since winning brings no benefit of any kind
It settles the matter, since practical gains in a career outweigh the truth
It may pay for a short time, but honesty is better in the longer run
It makes the argument reasonable, since the stakes are now real
optionExplain: The authors admit a contentious win may get you ahead for a short time.
The authors put the truth above winning, whatever it pays.
Right: the authors grant a short-term gain but call honesty the better policy in the slightly longer run.
High stakes do not make a position you suspect is wrong into a reasonable one.
questions.explain: The authors concede that contentious winning can pay in the short run. Their claim is that honesty serves better in the slightly longer run.
questions.rule: Short-term gain does not make a dishonest win worth it.

questions.q: In Plato's Symposium, Agathon admits he cannot refute Socrates. How does Socrates reply?
options: Then let us change the subject, to be fair
Then you must agree with me in everything
Say rather that you cannot refute the truth
Then you have lost and I have won the debate
optionExplain: He does not avoid the point; he redirects it to the truth.
Socrates claims nothing for himself; he credits the truth.
Right: Socrates says he himself is easily refuted; what Agathon cannot refute is the truth.
Socrates refuses to treat the exchange as a contest he has won.
questions.explain: Socrates moves the credit from himself to the truth. The card next shows how Aristotle echoes this.
questions.rule: You yield to the truth, not to the arguer.

questions.q: Aristotle, quoted by the authors, says that piety requires us to honour ____ above our friends.
questions.explain: Friends and truth are both dear, but for lovers of wisdom truth comes first.
questions.rule: Truth above friends.

questions.q: A city councillor has backed a project for years alongside a close ally. An independent audit she has studied shows the project is failing. Which response fits the authors' view?
options: Attack the auditors, since the audit hurts a friend
Stand by the project, since loyalty to a long-standing ally is a duty
Accept the audit's finding, though it costs her ally's support
Say nothing, since neither loyalty nor truth must yield
optionExplain: Attacking the messenger protects the friend at the truth's expense.
Loyalty is real, but Aristotle ranks truth above friends.
Right: she honours the truth above a relationship she values.
Silence avoids choosing, but the truth is what she now owes.
questions.explain: The audit is the truth as far as she can tell. Aristotle's maxim ranks it above loyalty to an ally.
questions.rule: When truth and loyalty part, follow truth.

questions.q: Agathon says he cannot refute Socrates and will assume Socrates is right. What does Socrates' correction add to that?
options: That what Agathon yields to is the truth, not Socrates himself
That Agathon should keep arguing until he finds a refutation
That nobody has ever managed to refute Socrates in argument
That assuming something true is the same as knowing it
optionExplain: Right: Socrates says he is easily refuted; the truth is what cannot be.
Socrates does not urge more contest; he redirects the credit.
Socrates says the opposite: he is easily refuted.
Socrates' point is about whom Agathon yields to, not about assuming and knowing.
questions.explain: Agathon frames the exchange as losing to Socrates. Socrates reframes it as yielding to the truth, which no one need feel beaten by.
questions.rule: Credit the truth, not the person.

questions.q: A sports analyst confidently predicted a team would win the league, and it finished tenth. By analogy with the authors' point, how should she treat her earlier prediction on air?
options: Defend it, since keeping to past views shows integrity
Explain that the season was unusual in every way
Avoid the topic, since viewers forget predictions
Say plainly where her reasoning went wrong
optionExplain: Consistency is not integrity when the evidence has turned.
Unusual seasons happen, but blaming them shields the view rather than testing it.
Silence protects her pride at the expense of the truth.
Right: her own past view is something dear to her, and the truth ranks above it.
questions.explain: A view you have stated publicly touches you closely, much as a friend does. The maxim asks you to give it up when the truth requires.
questions.rule: Your own past views rank below the truth too.
questions.teaches: Honouring truth above what is dear applies to one's own past positions as well: an earlier public view touches a person closely, and the maxim asks her to give it up when the evidence turns.

questions.q: True or false: On the authors' view, being unable to answer an argument on the spot does not by itself prove its conclusion true.
questions.explain: The maxim asks you to yield to the truth when you see it. Having no answer yet may only mean you need time to examine the argument.
questions.rule: No answer yet is not the same as no answer.

questions.q: A reader approaches a book as a battle to be won. According to the authors, what will he read it for?
options: Facts he can use in his work
Evidence that he is mistaken
Something he can disagree with
Passages he can quote in praise
optionExplain: That is reading for use, not for combat.
That is the opposite of a battle stance.
Right: the reader who treats conversation as battle reads only to find something to disagree with.
Praise is not what a combatant seeks.
questions.explain: In a battle you win only by disagreeing successfully, so the reader hunts for disagreement. The card next explains why it is so easy.
questions.rule: Battle readers hunt for disagreement.

questions.q: For the contentious, the authors say, a ____ to pick a quarrel over can be found, even if it is really a chip on the reader's own shoulder.
questions.explain: A contentious reader can always find something to quarrel over, even if it is really a chip on his own shoulder.
questions.rule: The contentious always find a bone.

questions.q: Which reader is picking a bone, in the authors' sense?
options: Pip reads a book on veganism twice before deciding it is mostly right
Oli finishes a book on veganism and disputes its land-use figures, with sources
Nia skims a book on veganism for a slip to mock, as she dislikes vegans
Quin notes questions about a book on veganism to raise once he finishes
optionExplain: Careful agreement is not bone-picking.
He disagrees after finishing and gives grounds; that is reasonable disagreement.
Right: she reads only to find something to quarrel over, and the chip is on her own shoulder.
Questions held for later serve understanding.
questions.explain: Bone-picking is reading in order to quarrel. Nia's aim was fixed before she read; Oli's disagreement came out of reading.
questions.rule: Quarrels sought first are bones; faults found after are criticism.

questions.q: A critic says: I found a sentence on page three that is wrong, so I have shown that the book is wrong. Which flaw do the authors point to?
options: An early slip, found before understanding, does not judge the book
Page three is too early in any book to hold its main argument
He ought to have found at least three wrong sentences first
Critics should leave individual wrong sentences out of their reviews altogether
optionExplain: Right: it is the empty victory the authors describe, won from the first few pages.
Some books state their thesis early; the fault is judging the whole from one slip.
More slips found the same way would still not judge the book.
Noting a wrong sentence is fine; treating it as a verdict on the book is not.
questions.explain: A glance at the first few pages is enough for the empty satisfaction of seeming to show an author up. It is not a judgment of the book.
questions.rule: One early slip is a pretext, not a verdict.

questions.q: On a comment thread, a reader answers a long article by quoting one clumsy sentence from its first paragraph. By analogy with the authors' point, why is this kind of reply so common?
options: It is rare: most commenters read articles to the very end
It is fair: a clumsy sentence shows the whole piece is weak
It is useful: other readers need warning about weak writing
It is easy: the writer is absent, and one line will do
optionExplain: The question grants it is common; the card explains why.
One sentence does not show the quality of the argument.
A warning based on one line misleads more than it helps.
Right: like the reader in his study, the commenter can seem to win without engaging the argument.
questions.explain: The writer cannot defend himself in the thread, and one quoted line gives the look of a win. That is the easy, empty victory the card describes.
questions.rule: Easy wins against an absent author are empty.
questions.teaches: By analogy, comment threads give every reader the book-reader's easy victory at scale: the writer is absent, one quoted line suffices, and the reply can look like a win without any engagement with the argument.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reader who, after understanding a book, shows that its central argument fails is picking a bone.
questions.explain: The authors want readers to show where an author is wrong. Bone-picking is a quarrel sought first; this is a fault found after understanding.
questions.rule: Faults found after understanding are fair criticism.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the only profit in a conversation with an author is what you can learn from him.
questions.explain: The authors say the only profit in conversation, with living or dead teachers, is what one can learn from them. The card next draws out what that means for agreeing.
questions.rule: The profit is what you learn.

questions.q: According to the authors, you win only by gaining ____, not by knocking the other fellow down.
questions.explain: The only profit in conversation is what you learn, so the only win is knowledge gained.
questions.rule: The win is knowledge.

questions.q: Ben finishes a book on nuclear power, finds its safety evidence convincing, and feels irritated at having to agree. What do the authors say about his irritation?
options: It is the price of honesty, and shows that he read fairly
It is a sound instinct, a sign that the book may be biased
It is an emotional problem, a sign of a habit of disputing
It is a reason to keep reading until he finds a flaw
optionExplain: Admitting the point is honest; the irritation is something else.
Irritation is not evidence about the book.
Right: the authors say a reader who feels whipped by agreeing has an emotional, not intellectual, problem.
Hunting for a flaw to escape agreement is bone-picking.
questions.explain: Ben admitted the point, which honesty requires. Feeling beaten by it shows a disputatious habit, which the authors call an emotional problem.
questions.rule: Feeling beaten by agreement is an emotional problem.

questions.q: Which attitudes fit the authors' advice? Select all that apply.
options: Being as ready to agree as to disagree
Letting the facts alone decide which
Disagreeing at least once to show independence
Feeling beaten whenever you have to agree
Agreeing to be polite when you are unsure
optionExplain: Right: readiness to agree matches readiness to disagree.
Right: the truth about the case is the one consideration.
Disagreeing for show lets something other than the facts decide.
That is the emotional problem of the disputatious reader.
Politeness is not a reason to agree; the facts are.
questions.explain: The card asks for equal readiness and a single deciding consideration, the facts. Display, wounded pride and politeness are other motives.
questions.rule: Ready either way; decided by the facts.

questions.q: A scientist runs an experiment designed to refute a rival's hypothesis, and the results support it. By analogy with the authors' point, how should she count the outcome?
options: As void, since a test meant to refute cannot confirm
As a loss, since her experiment failed in the purpose it was designed for
As a draw, since neither of them was proved right
As a gain, since she now knows more about what is true
optionExplain: A test can support what it was designed to challenge.
She failed to refute, but she did not fail to learn.
The results did support the rival's hypothesis.
Right: the profit of inquiry, as of conversation, is what you learn.
questions.explain: Like a reader who ends up agreeing, she has gained knowledge. Counting it as a defeat is the disputatious habit in another setting.
questions.rule: A result that proves you wrong is still a gain.
questions.teaches: By analogy, in research a result that supports a rival's view is a gain in knowledge, not a defeat; a scientist who counts it as a loss shows the same emotional problem the authors find in disputatious readers.

questions.q: Suppose that, weighing the facts, a reader finds the author wrong on his central claim. On the authors' view, what should she do?
options: Agree anyway, since readiness to agree is the virtue at stake
Disagree, since the facts, not a wish to agree, should decide
Suspend judgment, since disagreeing risks contentiousness
Say nothing, since showing him wrong is knocking him down
optionExplain: Readiness to agree means being open to it, not agreeing against the facts.
Right: readiness to agree is not a lean toward agreeing; the facts decide.
Disagreement on good grounds is reasonable, not contentious.
The authors want readers to show where an author is wrong when he is.
questions.explain: The card asks for readiness either way, with the facts deciding. Here they point to disagreement, so she should disagree.
questions.rule: Ready to agree does not mean bound to agree.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, all rational people can agree, even when they do not.
questions.explain: The authors say all rational people can agree, not that they do. The card next explains why the difference matters.
questions.rule: Can agree, not do agree.

questions.q: Match each feature of human nature with the role the authors give it in agreement and disagreement.
pairs: The source of our power to agree
Among the causes of most disagreements
An imperfect medium, clouded by emotion and interest
questions.explain: Rationality makes agreement possible; our animal nature, with its passions, prejudices and imperfect language, causes most disagreement.
questions.rule: Reason unites; passion and imperfect language divide.

questions.q: Two colleagues disagree about whether remote work lowers productivity. One says: we will not agree, so let's drop it. What does the third maxim say about this?
options: It turns the dispute into futile agitation by giving up hope
It is wise, since some disputes come down to temperament
It is polite, since pressing on would become contentious
It is honest, since rational people do not in fact agree
optionExplain: Right: the maxim warns against disagreeing hopelessly; without hope of resolution, disagreement is futile.
Temperament may play a part, but the question is about evidence on productivity.
Pressing on with reasons and in hope is not contentious.
The authors say rational people can agree even when they do not.
questions.explain: Productivity can be studied, so the issue is resolvable in principle. Dropping it as hopeless is what the third maxim warns against.
questions.rule: Do not disagree hopelessly.

questions.q: Suppose a disagreement arises because both sides feel strongly and use a charged word in different ways. On the authors' account, what does that suggest?
options: It shows one side is irrational and can be ignored
It cannot be resolved, since feelings are beyond argument
Its causes are feeling and language, which reason can overcome
It is a deep disagreement lodged within reason itself
optionExplain: Feeling strongly does not make a person irrational; both sides share the obstacle.
The authors trace such disputes to obstacles that reason can work past.
Right: passion and imperfect language cause most disagreements, and to the extent people are rational these obstacles can be overcome.
Deep disagreements are rare and hard to identify; this one has ordinary causes.
questions.explain: The authors name passion, prejudice and imperfect language as the usual causes of disagreement. They are obstacles to understanding that reason can overcome.
questions.rule: Ordinary causes of disagreement have ordinary cures.

questions.q: Diplomats from two countries in a long border dispute meet again, though talks have failed for years. By analogy with the authors' point, what makes the new talks worth holding?
options: The chance to restate both positions for the record
The belief that the issue can still be resolved
The hope that one side will tire and give in at last
The duty to be seen talking, whatever comes of it
optionExplain: Restating positions without hope of resolving them is ritual.
Right: talks held in the hope of resolution can make progress; without it they are futile agitation.
Giving in from weariness is not agreement reached by reason.
Talks held only for show are the futile agitation the authors describe.
questions.explain: The maxim says disagreement is worth pursuing only in the hope of resolving it. The same holds for negotiation: hope turns meetings into work.
questions.rule: Talks without hope of agreement are ritual.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any long negotiation depends on the hope the authors describe: talks held without believing agreement is possible become ritual, while the same talks held in hope can make progress.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, if two rational people have argued for years without agreeing, that shows they cannot agree.
questions.explain: The authors separate can agree from do agree. Years of disagreement show only that the obstacles have not yet been removed.
questions.rule: Not yet agreed is not unable to agree.

questions.q: Two people disagree because they use a key word in different senses. According to the authors, what kind of disagreement is this?
options: Apparent, and curable by coming to terms
Real, and curable only by more evidence
Deep, and lodged within reason itself
Emotional, and out of reach of argument
optionExplain: Right: disagreement from misunderstanding is only apparent, and certainly curable.
More evidence will not help while they mean different things.
Deep disagreements are rare; this one has a plain cause.
A difference in word use is open to argument and agreement.
questions.explain: Disagreement from misunderstanding is apparent: once the words are agreed, it may vanish. The card next adds a second curable kind.
questions.rule: Different senses make apparent disagreement.

questions.q: Match each kind of disagreement with what the authors say about it.
pairs: Hard to be sure of or to describe
questions.explain: The first two cover the great majority of disagreements and are curable, though often with difficulty. The third may exist but is hard to pin down.
questions.rule: Misunderstanding and ignorance are curable.

questions.q: A tourist tells a local guide that the old bridge was built by the Romans. The guide, who has studied the town's records, says it is medieval. By the authors' view, what kind of disagreement is this?
options: Unequal knowledge, curable by the guide's instruction
Apparent, curable by agreeing on what a bridge is
Deep, since the past cannot be known with certainty
