Emotional, since the tourist likes his Roman story
optionExplain: Right: the guide knows records the tourist does not, so instruction can cure it.
They mean the same bridge; the difference is in what they know about it.
Historical records allow the question to be settled well enough.
He may like the story, but the root is a gap in knowledge.
questions.explain: Both mean the same bridge, so this is not misunderstanding. The guide knows more, so the cure is instruction.
questions.rule: A knowledge gap is cured by teaching.

questions.q: Sort each disagreement by its likely cause.

items.t: They mean different things by the word inflation
One has read the trial results and the other has not
One takes rich to mean wealthy, the other full-flavoured
A newcomer disputes a rule whose reason the veterans know
They agree on the facts but read a key sentence differently
One is unaware of a law passed last year

questions.explain: Differences in meaning or reading are misunderstandings, cured by coming to terms. Differences in what each knows are cured by instruction.
questions.rule: Ask whether the gap is in meaning or in knowledge.

questions.q: In a design review, a junior engineer disagrees with a senior colleague about a load calculation. By the authors' view, what should the senior engineer keep in mind?
options: Her experience settles it, since she knows more overall
She may be the one who misunderstands or lacks a fact
The junior lacks knowledge, so needs only to be taught
The dispute is apparent, so a definition will settle it
optionExplain: Knowing more overall does not mean knowing more on this point.
Right: disagreement is an occasion for being taught as well as for teaching.
That assumes the gap is on the junior's side, which is what needs checking.
It may be apparent, but that too needs checking, not assuming.
questions.explain: The card asks anyone who disagrees to keep in mind that he may be the one misunderstanding or ignorant. Rank does not decide where the gap lies.
questions.rule: Check your own side of the gap first.
questions.teaches: Seniority predicts who usually knows more, not who knows more on this point: in a disagreement across ranks, the senior party should test whether she is the one missing a fact before treating it as a chance to teach.

questions.q: True or false: The authors allow that some disagreements may lie deep in reason itself, beyond the two curable kinds.
questions.explain: They grant that such deeper disagreements may exist, though they are hard to be sure of. Their claim covers the great majority of disagreements, not all.
questions.rule: Most disagreements, not all, have the two curable causes.

questions.q: Two people end an argument by agreeing that each is entitled to his own opinion. According to the authors, what has their conversation produced?
options: Real agreement, since both accept the same principle
A fair result, since opinions are like private property, owned by each
No gain in knowledge: each keeps the views he began with
A resolution, since the dispute no longer continues
optionExplain: They agree only to stop; the original question is untouched.
That is the view the authors reject: opinions as inviolable property.
Right: on that view, conversation cannot increase anyone's knowledge.
Ending a dispute is not resolving it.
questions.explain: The authors compare such talk to a game no one wins and no one loses. The card next explains their alternative.
questions.rule: Agreeing to differ settles nothing.

questions.q: The authors compare conversation on the everything-is-opinion view to a ____ game in which no one keeps score.
questions.explain: Opinions go back and forth, no one wins, and everyone is satisfied because no one loses.
questions.rule: Opinion ping-pong teaches no one.

questions.q: In a debate about whether a vaccine causes a rare side effect, one side says: that's your truth, and I have mine. What do the authors suggest instead?
options: Vote on it, since a majority is the fairest way to end a dispute
Accept the standoff, since each person's view is his own property
Treat it as a question of knowledge that evidence can settle in time
Drop it, since a dispute this heated must really be about taste
optionExplain: A vote settles what people prefer, not what is true.
That is the property view of opinion the authors reject.
Right: whether a vaccine causes a side effect is a matter of fact, open to evidence.
Heat is no sign of taste; the question is factual.
questions.explain: The question is about what happens, so knowledge is at stake. The card says such issues can be resolved, in the long run, by fact and reason.
questions.rule: Factual questions are not anyone's private truth.

questions.q: Extending the authors' distinction (they do not themselves discuss tastes), sort each question by whether it is a matter of knowledge that fact and reason can settle, or a matter of personal preference.

items.t: Whether a bridge design can carry a given load
Whether mint ice cream tastes nicer than vanilla
Whether a drug lowers blood pressure
Which colour to paint your own bedroom
Whether a city's population grew last decade
Whether you enjoy jazz more than opera

questions.explain: The authors' maxim covers matters of knowledge, where evidence bears on the answer. By extension, not as the authors' own statement, questions of personal taste may be no more than opinion.
questions.rule: The maxim governs knowledge; taste lies outside it, by extension.

questions.q: Suppose two scientists disagree about a real issue and a decade of work has not settled it. On the authors' view, what follows?
options: The dispute must be only apparent and will vanish once terms are set
It is a matter of opinion, since ten years of work has not settled it either way
One of them is being contentious and should give way to the other
Be patient: real issues are resolved in the long run by fact and reason
optionExplain: The question says the issue is real, not a misunderstanding.
Slow resolution does not turn knowledge into opinion.
Long disagreement can be honest; nothing shows either is contentious.
Right: the maxim of rationality about disagreements is to be patient for the long run.
questions.explain: The authors say real issues can be resolved in the long run, of course. A decade without resolution calls for patience, not for giving up.
questions.rule: Real issues take the long run.

questions.q: A school debate club scores rounds on style and confidence, and not on whether the arguments hold up. By the authors' view, what kind of conversation does this scoring encourage?
options: Inquiry, since debaters must research both sides first
Ping-pong of opinions, where no one needs to learn anything
Agreement, since scoring forces debaters to converge
Resolution, since a winner is named at the end of each round
optionExplain: Research may happen, but the scoring does not reward getting it right.
Right: if nothing rewards finding the truth, opinions just bounce back and forth.
Scoring style pushes debaters apart, not together.
Naming a winner is not resolving the issue.
questions.explain: Even with a winner named, the issue is not resolved if only style counts. Such scoring rewards the ping-pong the authors describe.
questions.rule: How a discussion is scored shapes what it produces.
questions.teaches: By analogy, how a discussion is scored shapes it: if nothing rewards finding out what is true, the exchange tends toward the ping-pong of opinions even when someone is declared the winner.

questions.q: You find yourself disagreeing with a claim in a book. According to the authors, what should you check first?
options: That the author is an expert on this subject
That other readers share your disagreement
That you have not misunderstood the claim
That your view is backed by a published source
optionExplain: The author's standing is not the first question.
Others' agreement does not show you understood the author.
Right: the maxim first requires the reader to be sure the disagreement is not owing to misunderstanding.
Sources matter later, once you know what you disagree with.
questions.explain: A disagreement that rests on a misreading is not with the author at all. The card next sets out the steps that follow.
questions.rule: Rule out misunderstanding first.

questions.q: Put these steps for handling a disagreement with a book in the order the authors give.
items: Make sure the disagreement is not owing to misunderstanding
Decide whether the point is knowledge or mere opinion
Treat a question of knowledge as one that can be resolved
Learn from the author, or justify your criticism of him
questions.explain: First rule out misunderstanding; then sort knowledge from opinion; then pursue an issue of knowledge, which may change your mind or justify your criticism.
questions.rule: Misunderstanding, then knowledge or opinion, then resolution.

questions.q: A reader disagrees with a book that declares, giving no reasons at all, that modern music is worthless. On the authors' view, what is that statement?
options: An apparent disagreement, which a definition will remove
A claim of knowledge, which must be refuted with evidence
The author's personal opinion, telling more about him than music
A self-evident truth, which needs no supporting reasons
optionExplain: Nothing suggests the reader misunderstands the words.
A claim offered without any reasons is not presented as knowledge.
Right: a proposition without reasons can be treated only as personal opinion.
Whether modern music has worth is not a self-evident truth.
questions.explain: Without reasons, the statement can be treated only as the author's opinion. Reacting to it tells the reader about the man, not the subject.
questions.rule: No reasons, no knowledge claim.

questions.q: A reader writes: I disagree with chapter 3, so the author must be wrong, and I will say so in my review. Which step has she skipped?
options: Checking that she has not misunderstood chapter 3
Finding other critics who disagree with it
Reading the author's earlier books first
Contacting the author to ask what he meant
optionExplain: Right: the maxim's first step is to rule out misunderstanding.
Other critics' views do not show that she understood.
Earlier books matter only if this one depends on them.
Asking the author may be impossible; the check is hers to make.
questions.explain: She moves from disagreeing to concluding the author is wrong. The first step, making sure the disagreement is not a misreading, is missing.
questions.rule: Disagreeing is not yet showing the author wrong.

questions.q: A doctor disagrees with a medical paper's conclusion. She confirms she read its methods correctly, sees that it gives data, and writes to the journal with data of her own. By the authors' view, what is the best outcome she can hope for?
options: The journal prints her letter, which ends the matter for good
The paper is retracted, which shows that she has won the argument outright
The authors concede at once, which confirms her expertise
Either she learns from the authors' reply or they learn from her
optionExplain: Printing the letter starts the exchange; it does not resolve the issue.
Retraction may follow, but winning is not the aim.
A quick concession without reasons would teach no one.
Right: an issue of knowledge pursued in hope ends with someone instructed.
questions.explain: She has ruled out misunderstanding and found an issue of knowledge. Unlike a dead author, these authors can reply, so either side may be instructed.
questions.rule: With a living author, the hoped-for exchange can happen.
questions.teaches: Unlike a dead author, a living one can reply, so a reasoned objection to a published paper can complete the exchange the authors can only hope for with books: either side may end up instructed.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reader who disagrees with a dead author's reasoned claim has no way to answer him, since that author's mind can no longer be changed.
questions.explain: The authors say such a reader may, metaphorically at least, instruct the author, and can hope that were the author alive and present, his mind could be changed.
questions.rule: Even a dead author can be answered with reasons.

questions.q: According to the authors, what must accompany any critical judgment a reader makes?
options: A comparison with other books
A summary of the whole book
A note on the author's motives
Reasons for the judgment
optionExplain: Comparisons can help, but the rule asks for reasons, whatever their source.
A summary shows understanding, which comes before judgment, but it is not a reason for the verdict.
Motives concern the man, not whether his claims are true.
Right: Rule 11 asks for reasons behind any critical judgment.
questions.explain: Without reasons, a verdict treats a matter of knowledge as opinion. The card next states Rule 11.
questions.rule: Every verdict needs reasons.

questions.q: Rule 11: respect the difference between knowledge and mere personal opinion, by giving ____ for any critical judgment you make.
questions.explain: Reasons are what separate a judgment that claims knowledge from a bare opinion.
questions.rule: Reasons mark knowledge off from opinion.

questions.q: Match each situation with what Rule 11 asks of the reader.
pairs: Actively share the author's reasons for the point
Give your own grounds for disagreeing
You treat knowledge as if it were opinion
questions.explain: Agreement can borrow the author's reasons, if they are actively held; disagreement needs the reader's own grounds. Without either, a judgment is mere opinion.
questions.rule: Agree for his reasons; disagree for yours.

questions.q: Which comment on a book about rural policy best follows Rule 11?
options: I disagree: this author has long been biased against farmers
I disagree: the survey asked only city people, so it misses farmers
I disagree, and I expect most readers will feel the same way
I disagree; the conclusion does not ring true to me at all
optionExplain: That is about the man, not the book's reasoning.
Right: it gives a ground that bears on the claim and that others can check.
Expected agreement from others is not a reason.
A feeling that something is untrue is a motive, not a ground.
questions.explain: Only the first comment gives a reason bearing on the book's claim. The others offer the author's character, a prediction of others' views, or a feeling.
questions.rule: A ground bears on the claim, not on the author or your feelings.

questions.q: A reader says: I agree with the author's conclusion, though I could not tell you why he thinks it is true. What does Rule 11 say is missing?
options: A second reading of the conclusion
Grounds of his own for disagreeing
Active sharing of the author's reasons
Agreement from other readers too
optionExplain: Rereading the conclusion alone will not supply the reasons.
He agrees, so his own grounds for disagreeing are not what is needed.
Right: agreement needs the reader to share the author's reasons actively.
Others' agreement does not supply his reasons.
questions.explain: Agreeing is enough only when the reader actively shares the author's reasons. Agreeing without knowing them is opinion, not knowledge.
questions.rule: Agreeing without the reasons is opinion.

questions.q: A member of a hiring panel votes against a candidate, saying only that she did not feel right for the role. By analogy with Rule 11, what should the panel ask for?
options: Grounds that bear on the role, which others can weigh
A second vote, to confirm that her feeling holds
Nothing, since each member's feeling is her own
A note of the feeling, to file with the decision for the record
optionExplain: Right: reasons let the panel weigh and test her verdict.
Repeating a feeling does not ground it.
That is the view that everything is opinion, which leaves the panel nothing to weigh.
Recording a feeling does not turn it into a reason.
questions.explain: Like a reader's verdict, a panel vote is a judgment. Without reasons it can only be counted, not weighed.
questions.rule: Reasons can be weighed; feelings can only be counted.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any group decision built from individual verdicts, such as a hiring panel's, works better when each verdict carries reasons: reasons can be weighed and challenged by the others, while bare feelings can only be counted.

questions.q: True or false: Under Rule 11, a reader who agrees with an author is expected to find new reasons of his own, different from the author's.
questions.explain: When the reader agrees, it suffices that he actively shares the author's reasons. Own grounds are required when he disagrees.
questions.rule: Agreement may rest on the author's reasons, actively held.

questions.q: According to the authors, what separates knowledge from mere opinion?
options: Agreement among most of the people one knows
Complete certainty that it can never be revised
Strong personal conviction that it is right
Evidence that other reasonable people would accept
optionExplain: Agreement among acquaintances is not evidence.
The authors say most knowledge is subject to correction.
Conviction without evidence is exactly what they call opinion.
Right: knowledge, for the authors, is opinion that can be defended with objective evidence.
questions.explain: The line is drawn by evidence, not certainty or conviction. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Knowledge is defensible; opinion is unsupported.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether it is knowledge or mere opinion in the authors' sense.

items.t: A claim backed by evidence others are likely to accept
A claim resting only on personal feeling
A defended belief that new evidence might still correct
A judgment held from prejudice, with no support
A self-evident proposition
A hunch the speaker cannot explain to anyone

questions.explain: Knowledge is supported judgment, correctable or, in the case of self-evident propositions, undeniable. Opinion is unsupported judgment resting on feeling or prejudice.
questions.rule: Supported or unsupported: that is the line.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, knowledge can be subject to correction and still differ from mere opinion.
questions.explain: Correctability does not remove the distinction. Knowledge is supported by the weight of evidence; opinion has nothing behind it but feeling or prejudice.
questions.rule: Correctable is not the same as unsupported.

questions.q: A nutritionist says, citing several large trials, that a diet lowers cholesterol, and adds that future studies could revise this. On the authors' view, what is her claim?
options: Opinion: since it might be revised, she cannot know it
Knowledge: defensible by evidence, though open to correction
Certainty: since the trials were large, it cannot be wrong
Prejudice: since she is a nutritionist, she is biased
optionExplain: Being revisable is the normal state of knowledge, not a mark of opinion.
Right: she has evidence others can accept and holds it subject to correction.
Large trials give weight, not certainty.
Her profession is not evidence of prejudice.
questions.explain: Her claim has objective evidence behind it and is held open to correction. That is knowledge as the authors define it.
questions.rule: Evidence plus openness to correction is knowledge.

questions.q: A judge decides a civil case on the balance of probabilities, knowing new evidence could emerge later. By analogy with the authors' point, what is her verdict?
options: Absolute knowledge, since a court's ruling is final
Mere opinion, since she admits she cannot be sure
A grounded judgment, held open to later correction
A guess, since the future may overturn any finding
optionExplain: Finality is a legal rule, not proof of certainty; appeals exist.
Lack of certainty does not make a judgment unsupported.
Right: it rests on the weight of present evidence and can be revisited.
A judgment from weighed evidence is not a guess.
questions.explain: The verdict rests on the weight of the evidence, like knowledge in the authors' sense, and legal procedures allow it to be corrected.
questions.rule: Weighed evidence, open to correction.
questions.teaches: By analogy, institutions such as courts build the authors' idea of correctable knowledge into their procedures: a verdict rests on the weight of present evidence, and appeals or retrials allow it to be corrected.

questions.q: Suppose new evidence overturns something a scientist claimed, on good evidence, to know. On the authors' view, what was her earlier claim?
options: Knowledge in their sense, which has now been corrected
Mere opinion all along, since it turned out false
Prejudice, since she ought to have foreseen the evidence
A self-evident truth, which new evidence cannot touch
optionExplain: Right: it was a defended belief supported by the evidence of its day; the authors expect such correction.
Opinion means unsupported, and her claim was supported.
Evidence not yet found cannot be blamed on her.
Self-evident propositions are undeniable; this one was overturned.
questions.explain: The authors say we know subject to correction. A claim supported by the weight of evidence was knowledge, even if later evidence revises it.
questions.rule: Correction does not turn past knowledge into opinion.

questions.q: According to the authors, what turns a disagreement from an issue that is only stated into one that is defined?
options: Repeating it in writing
Stating it more firmly
Giving reasons for it
Finding others who share it
optionExplain: Writing it down records the issue without defining it.
Firmness adds force, not definition.
Right: reasons define the issue, and in that lies all hope for resolution.
Company is not a reason.
questions.explain: The third maxim asks for reasons so that issues are defined, not only stated. The card next sums up the three maxims.
questions.rule: Reasons define issues.

questions.q: Match each rule with what it asks of the critical reader.
pairs: Complete the task of understanding before judging
Do not disagree disputatiously or contentiously
Give reasons, treating disagreement on knowledge as remediable
questions.explain: The three general maxims set the conditions of critical reading and the manner of talking back.
questions.rule: Understand, disagree reasonably, give reasons.

questions.q: After a careful reading of a book on policing, a reader calmly writes her verdict but gives no reasons for it. Which maxim has she not yet met?
options: Rule 10, avoiding contentiousness
Rule 9, understanding before judging
Rule 11, giving reasons for her judgment
None, as her verdict was calm and informed
optionExplain: Her calm tone suggests she is not contentious.
Her careful reading meets the condition of understanding.
Right: without reasons, her verdict does not define an issue.
Calm and informed meets two maxims, not the third.
questions.explain: Understanding and calm cover Rules 9 and 10. Rule 11 still asks for reasons.
questions.rule: All three maxims, not two.

questions.q: Ama and Ben both disagree, calmly, with a book they understand. Ama writes that its conclusion is wrong; Ben writes which step he rejects and why. By the authors' account, what does Ben's version add?
options: A defined issue, where hope of resolution lies
A harsher verdict, which is more convincing
A longer review, which shows more effort
Nothing new, since both reach the same verdict on the book
optionExplain: Right: his reasons define the issue, so it can be examined and resolved.
His verdict is no harsher; it is more precise.
Length and effort are not the point.
The verdicts match, but only Ben's reasons give the issue a shape that can be examined and resolved.
questions.explain: Ama states the issue; Ben defines it. The authors say all hope for resolution lies in reasons that define issues.
questions.rule: A stated issue can only be repeated; a defined one can be resolved.

questions.q: A software team adopts three norms for code review: read the whole change before commenting, comment on the code and not the coder, and give a reason with every objection. By analogy, how do these map onto the authors' maxims?
options: They match none, since code is not a book
They match Rule 9 alone, said three ways
They match Rule 11 alone, said three ways
They match Rules 9, 10 and 11 in turn
optionExplain: The maxims concern any serious exchange of judgment, not books alone.
Only the first norm is about understanding first.
Only the third norm is about reasons.
Right: understand first, avoid contention, give reasons.
questions.explain: Reading the whole first is Rule 9; aiming at the work, not winning against the person, is Rule 10; reasons with objections is Rule 11.
questions.rule: The three maxims travel to any review.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the three maxims form a portable code for any review of others' work, such as code review: read the whole before commenting, aim at the work rather than at winning, and attach a reason to every objection.

questions.q: True or false: A reader who follows the three maxims has thereby shown that her criticism of a book is correct.
questions.explain: The maxims set the conditions and manner of fair criticism. A reasoned, courteous disagreement can still be mistaken, which is why the reasons are offered for others to examine.
questions.rule: Fair is not the same as correct.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A reader finishes a hard book and is unsure what its main argument was. According to the authors, what should she do next?
options: Go back to work on the book before making any critical remark
Give a provisional verdict, labelled as only a first impression
Read reviews by experts and adopt their verdict for the time being
Disagree with the parts she found confusing and accept the rest
optionExplain: Right: a reader who cannot say she understands should keep quiet and return to the book.
A labelled first impression is still a judgment of something she has not yet grasped.
Borrowing a verdict skips the understanding that any verdict of her own would need.
Confusion is not a ground for disagreeing; it is a sign she has not understood yet.
questions.explain: The authors make understanding the condition of every critical remark. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: No understanding, no verdict: go back to the book.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reader must be able to say I understand before giving any verdict at all on a book, whether agreement, disagreement or suspended judgment.
questions.explain: Every critical remark depends on the first remark being I understand. Without it, there is nothing definite to judge.
questions.rule: I understand comes before every verdict.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: In a book club, which of these members are ready, by the authors' test, to give a verdict on a history of the printing press?
options: Ana, who can state its central claim and the evidence offered for it
Ben, who knows the period well and disliked the book's tone
Cleo, who can say how its chapters build to the author's conclusion
Dev, who skimmed it and found nothing he would object to
Eli, who read every page closely but cannot say what it argues
optionExplain: Right: stating the claim and its support is the test of understanding.
Knowing the period and disliking the tone do not show he grasped what this book says.
Right: tracing how the parts lead to the conclusion shows she understands the book.
Finding nothing to object to after a skim is not understanding what it argues.
Close reading is effort, but he still cannot state what the book says.
questions.explain: The test is not effort, expertise or mood. It is whether the reader can say what the book claims and how it argues.
questions.rule: Ready to judge means able to state the claim and its support.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A reader cannot honestly say she understands a book on climate economics. Going back to work on it, where should she start?
options: With the chapters she enjoyed most, since interest aids memory
With a different book on the subject that is easier to read
With the earlier rules: outline, key terms, propositions, arguments
With the last chapter, where the author states his final verdict and sums up the case
optionExplain: Enjoyment is a poor guide; the gap may lie in parts she skimmed.
An easier book may help later, but it does not mend her reading of this one.
Right: the failure lies somewhere in the first two stages, so she checks each.
Conclusions read without their arguments do not yield understanding.
questions.explain: Understanding is what the first two stages produce. When it is missing, one of their steps was left unfinished, so that is where to look.
questions.rule: Find the unfinished earlier step.
questions.teaches: Going back to work has a direction: a failure to understand usually traces to one unfinished earlier step, such as an unclear outline, a vague key term or an argument not yet found, so you return to that step rather than reread at random.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: If, after rereading, the reader can now state the book's argument in her own words, the advice to keep quiet still applies to her.
questions.explain: Keeping quiet is the advice for a reader who does not understand. Once she can say I understand, she is expected to go on and agree, disagree or suspend judgment.
questions.rule: Understanding ends the silence and starts the judging.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A committee member does not yet follow a motion on the pension fund. By analogy with the authors' point, which response fits best?
options: Vote against it, since an unclear motion is likely a weak one
Vote for it, trusting colleagues who seem to understand it
Propose an amendment to the parts she found hardest to follow
Abstain for now and ask for the motion to be explained again
optionExplain: Unclear to her is not the same as weak; she has not shown any defect in it.
Voting for it is also a verdict on something she has not grasped.
Amending what she cannot follow judges the motion before she understands it.
Right: like going back to the book, she seeks understanding before any verdict.
questions.explain: Voting for or against are both verdicts. Holding back while she seeks understanding is the committee version of keeping quiet and rereading.
questions.rule: Abstain until you understand.
questions.teaches: By analogy, in any vote or review, holding back until you understand differs from voting against: abstaining admits a gap in your grasp, while a no vote claims to have found a fault.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, saying I don't understand this book can sometimes be a fair criticism of the book.
questions.explain: It can, but only when the reader shows that the trouble lies in the book itself. The card next shows what that takes.
questions.rule: I don't understand can be a criticism, if supported.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Which of these can a reader point to in support of the charge that a book is unintelligible?
options: Its parts do not hang together
It uses a key word in shifting senses
It covers a subject new to the reader
Its structure is disorderly
It is longer than most books on the topic
optionExplain: Right: parts that do not connect are a fault in the book.
Right: equivocation in important words is one of the named sources of trouble.
A new subject makes reading harder for this reader; it is not a fault in the book.
Right: a disorderly structure is a fault the reader can show.
Length is not a defect of intelligibility.
questions.explain: The supports are all features of the text: disorderly structure, disconnected parts, irrelevance, equivocation. Features of the reader's situation do not count.
questions.rule: Point to the book's faults, not your own difficulty.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A reader cannot follow a policy paper on housing. Which statement turns her difficulty into a supported criticism?
options: The paper uses too much jargon for a general reader like me.
Affordable means below-market in part 1 and subsidised in part 3.
I read the paper twice and still could not see where it was going.
Other readers in my office also found the paper hard to follow.
optionExplain: Jargon unfamiliar to her is her difficulty; it does not show a defect in the paper.
Right: she locates an equivocation in a key word, a fault in the text itself.
Effort and confusion describe the reader, not a located source of trouble.
Shared confusion is still confusion; it does not say where the paper goes wrong.
questions.explain: Only the second statement locates the trouble in the paper. A key word that shifts sense is a defect the author can be shown.
questions.rule: Locate the trouble in the text.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A book's central term, freedom, shifts sense between two chapters. Why can this one shift make much of the book hard to follow, not only those chapters?
options: Readers tend to lose patience after one confusing passage and skim the rest
A shifted term makes the book's subject matter different in each of its parts
The publisher's editors would then have missed other errors throughout the book
Every later argument using the term may rest on both senses and fail to connect
optionExplain: Impatience is a fact about readers; the question is about the book's own reasoning.
The subject stays the same; what changes is the meaning of one key term.
Editing lapses elsewhere are a guess; the shift itself is the source of trouble.
Right: arguments built on the term inherit the shift, so confusion spreads.
questions.explain: An important word is used throughout a book's arguments. If it shifts sense, the steps that rely on it stop connecting, which spreads the confusion.
questions.rule: One shifting key word can confuse a whole argument.
questions.teaches: Equivocation in a key word produces a train of confusions: every argument that relies on the word may use it in both senses, so one shift can undermine much of a book.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: If a reader finds a book on quantum physics very hard going, that difficulty alone supports the charge that the book is unintelligible.
questions.explain: Difficulty may lie in the reader. The charge holds only when he can show disorder, disconnection, irrelevance or equivocation in the book itself.
questions.rule: Hard is not the same as unintelligible.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A user cannot assemble a bookshelf from its manual. By analogy with the authors' point, which complaint gives the maker something to fix?
options: The manual is confusing and I gave up halfway through it.
I am not good with tools, so a video would suit me better.
Step 6 needs part H, but part H is fitted in step 9.
The pictures are small, and I prefer instructions in text.
optionExplain: Confusing names the user's state, not where the manual goes wrong.
This describes the user's skills, not a fault in the manual.
Right: it locates disorder in the steps, a fault the maker can repair.
A preference is not a located defect.
questions.explain: A located complaint names a defect in the text itself, here steps out of order. That makes the complaint a real criticism and tells the writer what to change.
questions.rule: A located complaint is a usable one.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a located I don't understand also helps the writer: naming where the text fails tells the author what to repair, while bare confusion gives nothing to act on.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A reader understands a book and agrees with all of it. According to the authors, how much of the analytical reading is left to do?
options: None: the analytical reading is done
A search for flaws the author missed
A summary of how the author argued
A check against the book's reviews
optionExplain: Right: thorough agreement after understanding completes the reading.
The extra steps are for disagreement or suspended judgment, not thorough agreement.
Stating how the author argues belongs to interpretation, already done.
Reviews are not part of the analytical reading the authors describe.
questions.explain: Understanding plus thorough agreement means the reader has been enlightened and convinced. The card next explains what changes when he does not agree.
questions.rule: Understand and agree thoroughly: the reading is done.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: The authors say the extra steps of criticism are needed only in cases of disagreement or ____ judgment.
questions.explain: Thorough agreement ends the reading. Only disagreement or suspended judgment calls for further steps, and disagreement is the more usual case.
questions.rule: Extra steps for disagreement or suspended judgment.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Two readers of a book on urban planning both disagree with it. Lia traced each argument; Max traced them and also tested each premise and step. Who has met the arguments?
options: Max, since he tested the premises and steps, not only traced them
Lia, since tracing an argument already shows where it fails
Both, since anyone who disagrees after reading has met the arguments already
Neither, since meeting an argument requires writing a reply
optionExplain: Right: meeting an argument means testing it, not only following its course.
Tracing is following; finding where an argument fails takes testing it.
Disagreeing is a verdict; it does not show the arguments were tested.
A written reply may record the meeting, but the meeting is the testing itself.
questions.explain: Following an argument shows how it goes. Meeting it asks whether its premises and steps hold, which is what a verdict must rest on.
questions.rule: Follow, then meet: test premises and steps.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A reader understands a book and agrees with every chapter except one argument she doubts. What do the authors imply about her reading?
options: It is done, since agreeing with nearly all of it counts as thorough
It is undone, and she must reread the whole book from the start
It is done except for the doubted argument, which she must meet
It is done, but her agreement with the rest is now in question
optionExplain: Thorough agreement means all of it; one doubted argument breaks that condition.
Her understanding stands; only the doubted argument calls for more work.
Right: the extra steps apply to the point where she disagrees or holds back.
Doubting one argument does not by itself unsettle agreement with the others.
questions.explain: The work ends only with thorough agreement. Where she doubts, the further steps of criticism apply, and only there.
questions.rule: Further steps go where the doubt is.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: By the authors' logic, agreement reached without testing an author's arguments is not the significant agreement the authors have in mind.
questions.explain: The authors say only meeting the arguments, not following them, leads to significant agreement or disagreement. Untested agreement is acceptance, not a judgment.
questions.rule: Agreement counts when it survives testing.
questions.teaches: Agreement can be shallow too: agreeing with an author you have only followed is acceptance, and it becomes a judgment of your own only after you have tried the arguments and found them sound.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Two reviewers approve a colleague's change to a payment system. One read it for flow; the other tried inputs that might break it. By analogy, whose approval carries more weight?
options: The first, because a smooth read shows the code is well written
Both equally, because each reviewer gave the change a full reading
The first, since reviewers should not redo testing the author has already done
The second, because the approval rests on testing the change itself
optionExplain: A smooth read is following; it does not test whether the change holds up.
Reading fully is not the same as testing; the two approvals rest on different work.
Relying on the author's own testing is following his work; the reviewer's own attempt to break it is what gives an approval weight.
Right: like meeting an argument, trying to break the change gives the approval weight.
questions.explain: By analogy with meeting an argument, an approval means as much as the testing behind it. The second reviewer tried to make the change fail and could not.
questions.rule: An approval weighs what its testing weighs.
questions.teaches: By analogy, in any review an approval is worth as much as the attempt to find fault behind it: approval after real testing is a judgment, approval after a smooth read is a courtesy.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Someone says that whenever two people truly understand each other, they can no longer disagree. What do the authors think of this view?
options: It is right: all disagreement comes from some misunderstanding
It is wrong: understanding makes disagreement more likely
It is right for facts, but wrong for questions of value
It is wrong: it confuses two different senses of agreement
optionExplain: This is the error the authors name: thinking all disagreement is misunderstanding.
Understanding makes real disagreement possible, not more likely.
The authors treat both theoretical and practical claims as open to real dispute.
Right: agreeing about meaning is not agreeing about truth.
questions.explain: The view runs together agreement about words and agreement about what is so. The card next separates them.
questions.rule: Understanding each other is not agreeing with each other.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Match each sense of agreement with what it is about.
pairs: How the words are used to express ideas
Whether what is said is true or probable
questions.explain: Understanding is agreement about language; judgment is agreement about the world. Mixing them up leads to the belief that understanding rules out disagreement.
questions.rule: Meaning first, truth second.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Two economists both state a book's thesis on minimum wages in the same words and accept each other's summary. One thinks the thesis is true, the other false. What is going on?
options: One of them has misread the book, since they reach different verdicts
Neither has finished reading, since a finished reading yields agreement
They disagree only about words, since their summaries differ slightly
They agree in understanding the book but disagree in judging it
optionExplain: Their matching summaries show they read it the same way; the split is elsewhere.
A finished reading yields understanding; the verdict can still go either way.
Their summaries agree, so the dispute is not about meaning.
Right: shared understanding, different judgments about truth.
questions.explain: They have the first kind of agreement, about meaning. Their split is in the second kind, about whether the thesis is so.
questions.rule: Same understanding, different verdicts: a real disagreement.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: By the authors' distinction, two readers can agree that a book's conclusion is true while meaning different things by it.
questions.explain: The two senses can come apart in either direction. If the readers take the conclusion's words in different senses, their agreement about truth hides a lack of agreement about meaning.
questions.rule: Check meaning before trusting agreement too.
questions.teaches: The two senses can separate the other way: readers can agree on a conclusion while meaning different things by it, a false agreement that hides a disagreement and also needs shared understanding to expose.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Which of these disagreements is about the first sense of agreement, meaning, rather than the second, truth?
options: Whether the book's evidence on sleep and memory is strong enough
Whether the author's advice on screens at night should be followed
Whether the author uses rest to include naps or only night sleep
Whether the book's claim about teenage sleep needs is accurate
optionExplain: The strength of evidence is a question of truth, the second sense.
Whether advice should be followed is a practical judgment, the second sense.
Right: it asks what the author means by a word, the first sense.
Accuracy of a claim is a question of truth, the second sense.
questions.explain: Only the dispute over what rest covers is about meaning. The others presuppose the meaning and ask whether the claims hold.
questions.rule: Ask: is this about meaning or about truth?

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Two doctors read the same trial report and agree exactly on what it claims. One will change her prescribing; the other will not. By analogy with the authors' point, what does this show?
options: Shared understanding leaves each reader's judgment as her own to make
One doctor must have misread the report, since their actions differ
The report must be badly written, since it produced two responses
Their difference is about words, since prescribing is a practical matter
optionExplain: Right: agreeing on what the report says does not settle each doctor's verdict on it.
They agree on what it claims, so the split is not a misreading.
A clear report can still divide readers who judge its evidence differently.
Practical claims can be right or wrong; their split is about judgment, not words.
questions.explain: The doctors share the first kind of agreement. The second, about whether the report's claims should be acted on, is each one's own judgment.
questions.rule: Understanding is shared; judgment is your own.
questions.teaches: Agreement in understanding is reached jointly, but agreement in judgment is made by each reader for himself, so two readers with exactly the same understanding of a text may still reach opposite verdicts.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: You object to a writer's claim that all people are equal, taking it to mean equal in talent. She meant equal in legal rights. What becomes of your objection?
options: It is irrelevant, since it answers a claim she did not make
It still stands, since talent and rights are closely linked
It wins the argument, since her wording invited the misreading
It turns into agreement, since you accept equal legal rights
optionExplain: Right: an objection to a misread claim misses the claim actually made.
Whatever the link, your objection was about talent, which she never claimed.
Unclear wording may explain the misreading; it does not make the objection hit.
Whether you accept equal rights is a new question, not settled by dropping the objection.
questions.explain: A disagreement built on a misreading does not touch the author's real position. The card next shows what is left once the reading is corrected.
questions.rule: Objecting to a misread claim misses the real one.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a genuine disagreement about facts or policy requires that both sides first share an understanding of what is being said.
questions.explain: Agreement about the use of words is the condition of any real agreement or disagreement about the facts. Without it, the parties argue past each other.
questions.rule: Shared meaning first, then real dispute.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A reader attacks an essay's call for free public transport, assuming it means abolishing fares for everyone. The essay proposes free travel for people under eighteen. Which statement describes the situation correctly?
options: Her objection is irrelevant until she judges the proposal as made
Her objections on cost apply, since any free scheme costs money
Her objection is real, since the essay's title invited her reading
Her objection is settled, since the essay's scheme is smaller
optionExplain: Right: she must first take the proposal in the author's sense, then judge it.
The costs of abolishing all fares are not the costs of the scheme proposed.
A misleading title may explain the misreading; it does not make the objection relevant.
A smaller scheme may or may not survive her judgment; that remains to be decided.
questions.explain: Her objection targets a proposal the essay did not make. Once she reads it correctly she may agree or disagree, and only then is there a real issue.
questions.rule: Judge the proposal as the author made it.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Once the reader corrects her misreading and reconsiders free travel for under-eighteens, which outcomes are open to her, according to the authors' point?
options: Agreeing with the proposal as actually made
Disagreeing with it, now on a real issue
Keeping her old objection, now as a real issue
Suspending judgment for good, as the dispute was verbal
optionExplain: Right: with the reading corrected, she may find the actual proposal sound.
Right: a disagreement with the claim as made is a real issue.
Her old objection was aimed at abolishing all fares; it does not become real by being kept.
The verbal part is cleared up; nothing forces her to hold back on the real claim.
questions.explain: Correcting the misreading does not decide the verdict. It makes a real verdict possible, for or against.
questions.rule: Correction opens the real question; it does not answer it.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A reviewer realises his main objection to a book rested on a misreading. What should he do with it, by the authors' logic?
options: Keep it, and add a note that the author's wording was unclear
Withdraw it openly, then judge the claim the author actually made
Move it quietly to the corrected claim, as the point stays similar
Drop the review, since one error shows he cannot judge this book
optionExplain: Keeping an objection to a claim never made keeps an irrelevant disagreement.
Right: an irrelevant objection should be dropped in the open, and the real claim judged.
Shifting the objection silently hides that it was aimed at the wrong target.
One misreading, once corrected, does not disqualify him from judging.
questions.explain: An objection to a misread claim is irrelevant and should go. Saying so openly keeps the record honest, and the corrected claim gets its own judgment.
questions.rule: Withdraw misread objections openly.
questions.teaches: When you find an objection rested on a misreading, the honest course is to withdraw it openly and judge the real claim afresh, rather than quietly carrying the old objection over to the corrected claim.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: An online thread rages over a council plan to ban cars. Half the posters think it covers the whole city; the plan covers two downtown streets. By analogy, what does the heat of the thread show?
options: That the plan touches a real issue, since people care so strongly
That most posters oppose car bans, whatever the plan's real scope
That the council chose its wording badly and should withdraw the plan
Nothing about whether the dispute is real; many argue a misread plan
optionExplain: Strong feeling is not evidence that the parties disagree about the same claim.
Their opposition is to a citywide ban, which is not what the plan proposes.
Poor wording may explain the confusion; it says nothing on the plan's merits.
Right: heat can surround an irrelevant dispute as easily as a real one.
questions.explain: Many posters are disputing a plan nobody proposed. However heated, their disagreement is irrelevant to the actual plan until they read it correctly.
questions.rule: Heat does not make an issue real.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the intensity of a dispute is no evidence that it is a real issue: people can argue fiercely over a claim nobody made, so check the shared reading before measuring the disagreement.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A reader feels strongly that a book is wrong but cannot say where. What do the authors suggest may be happening?
options: She has found a flaw that she has not yet put into words
She is treating strong feelings as if they were reasons
She has read the book closely enough to sense its errors
She disagrees with the book's tone but not with its claims
optionExplain: Possible, but until she can state it, a felt flaw is not yet a reason.
Right: the authors warn you may think you have reasons when you only have feelings.
Close reading would let her point to the place; she cannot.
That may be so, but she believes the book is wrong, a claim about substance.
questions.explain: A strong feeling that cannot be turned into a statable point is not yet a reason. The card next gives the first condition of good controversy.
questions.rule: A feeling you cannot state is not yet a reason.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: The first ideal condition of good controversy is to ____ the emotions you bring to a dispute or that arise during it.
questions.explain: Acknowledging emotions keeps them from passing as reasons. People are animals as well as rational, so feelings are always present.
questions.rule: Acknowledge the feelings in play.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A reader lists objections to a book arguing for a four-day work week. Sort each into a reason that could be shown or a feeling stated as an objection.

items.t: The trial it cites had no control group
The idea sounds lazy to me
Its cost figures omit overtime pay
The author seems smug about it
Chapter 4 contradicts the claim in chapter 2
I would hate working longer days

questions.explain: Reasons point to something in the book that can be checked: evidence, figures, consistency. Feelings report the reader's reaction, which may be real but is not a showing that the author is wrong.
questions.rule: A reason points to the book; a feeling points to you.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: Acknowledging that you feel strongly against a book's conclusion means your objections to it should be discarded.
questions.explain: Acknowledging a feeling separates it from the reasons; it does not cancel them. An objection with evidence behind it keeps its force whatever the reader feels.
questions.rule: Name the feeling; keep the reasons that stand.
questions.teaches: Strong feeling and good reasons can coexist: acknowledging an emotion does not discredit the objections that come with it, it lets you see which of them stand on evidence once the feeling is set aside.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A reader begins a book calmly, but grows irritated by the author's mocking tone in chapter 3. What does the first condition ask of her from then on?
options: To acknowledge the irritation too, so it does not pose as an objection
To stop reading until the irritation has passed, then start again
Nothing new, since the condition covers only feelings brought to the book
To treat her irritation as a sign that the argument is weak there
optionExplain: Right: a feeling arising mid-book must be named like one brought to it.
Pausing may help, but the condition asks her to acknowledge the feeling, not wait it out.
The condition covers emotions that arise during a dispute as well as those brought to it.
A mocking tone and a weak argument are different things; the feeling is not evidence.
questions.explain: The first condition includes emotions that arise in the course of a dispute. Irritation at tone can easily pass itself off as an objection to the argument.
questions.rule: Name feelings that arise, not only those you bring.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A team lead must judge a proposal from a rival department and notices resentment. By analogy with the authors' point, what is a good first step?
options: Hand the review to someone else, since feelings spoil any judgment
Approve the proposal, to make up for any unfairness the resentment causes
List the reasons apart from the resentment, and see which still stand
Keep the resentment private and trust that it will not affect the review
optionExplain: Handing it off may sometimes be wise, but the card's point is that feelings can be acknowledged.
Approving to compensate lets the feeling decide the verdict, in the other direction.
Right: separating reasons from feelings shows how much of the case survives without them.
Unacknowledged feeling is the danger the card names.
questions.explain: Acknowledging the resentment and listing reasons apart from it shows what the judgment rests on. Overcompensating or ignoring the feeling both leave it in charge.
questions.rule: Separate reasons from feelings on paper.
questions.teaches: By analogy, in workplace judgments writing the reasons apart from the feelings works as a check: whatever case survives once the feelings are set aside is what the verdict should rest on, in either direction.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: In the authors' usage, what is a prejudice?
options: A belief held against a group of people, which a reader must drop
A prejudgment: something taken as settled before the reading began
An emotion that arises during a dispute and clouds a reader's view
A conclusion reached too early from evidence the author presented
optionExplain: That is the common social sense; here the word is about any assumption brought to a book.
Right: the authors use the word in its literal sense, a prejudgment.
Emotions are the first condition; prejudices are assumptions, the second.
That is a hasty judgment about the book, not an assumption brought to it.
questions.explain: A prejudice here is a prejudgment, an assumption held before reading. The card next explains why you must make yours explicit.
questions.rule: Prejudice means prejudgment.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, good controversy should not be a quarrel about assumptions.
questions.explain: Disputants are entitled to different assumptions. A dispute that turns into a contest of starting points never reaches the argument itself.
questions.rule: Argue about the case, not the starting points.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A book on ethics opens by asking readers to assume that animals can feel pain, and builds its argument from there. A reader doubts the assumption. What do the authors advise?
options: Put the book aside, since its argument rests on a doubtful premise
Grant the assumption and follow the argument where it leads
Reject each conclusion, since each depends on the assumption
Read on, but count each chapter as weak until the premise is proved
optionExplain: Setting the book aside refuses the author's openly stated request.
Right: an explicitly requested assumption should be honoured so the case gets a hearing.
Rejecting conclusions because of the starting point is a quarrel about assumptions.
Marking every chapter weak in advance denies the case a fair hearing.
questions.explain: The author has openly asked for the assumption. Honouring it lets the reader judge the argument he actually built.
questions.rule: Honour openly requested assumptions.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A reader writes: (1) I believe markets allocate goods best. (2) This book assumes they often fail. (3) Its assumption is a bias, while mine is plain fact. (4) So its case does not deserve a hearing. Where does the reasoning go wrong first?
options: Step 1, since a reader should hold no beliefs about markets
Step 2, since the reader may have misread the book's assumption
Step 4, since a hearing is owed only to books one agrees with
Step 3, since it treats the reader's own prejudgment as fact
optionExplain: Holding beliefs is unavoidable; the condition is to make them explicit.
Possible, but nothing in the step shows a misreading.
Step 4 does go wrong, but it follows from the error made in step 3.
Right: refusing to see one's own assumption as an assumption blocks a fair hearing.
questions.explain: The reader does not acknowledge her own prejudgment as one. That is why she cannot admit the author is equally entitled to his, and denies the case a hearing.
questions.rule: Your assumptions are assumptions too.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A reader meets several starting points in a book on school reform. Sort each into one to honour while following the case, or one to examine as part of the argument.
questions.explain: The authors speak of honouring an explicit request to take something for granted. A premise the author slips in without stating it is not such a request, and it can be examined as part of his argument.
questions.rule: Honour stated requests, examine hidden premises.
groups: Examine as part of the argument

items.t: Let us assume, for this book, that class sizes stay fixed
I ask the reader to grant that budgets will not rise
An unstated premise that test scores measure learning
Take it as given, for now, that teachers are well trained
A step that quietly treats all parents as able to choose schools

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: In a debate class the motion asks which transport plan would be best if the city had no budget limit. One student answers only that real cities have budget limits. By analogy with the authors' point, what has she done?
options: Answered well, since realism matters more than a hypothetical
Won the debate, since she exposed a false premise in the motion
Refused the hypothetical, so she gives no answer to the question asked
Made a fair start, since questioning the premise is the first step of any answer
optionExplain: Realism may matter elsewhere, but the motion asked what follows from the assumption.
The premise was granted openly for the exercise; exposing it wins nothing.
Right: rejecting the requested assumption ends the exercise instead of engaging it.
Denying the premise is not a start on the question; it leaves it untouched.
questions.explain: The motion openly asks for an assumption. Quarrelling with it, like quarrelling with an author's stated assumption, never reaches the question that was posed.
questions.rule: Grant the hypothetical, then argue.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a hypothetical's value lies in what follows from it: refusing to grant it ends the exercise rather than winning it, so the place to object to an assumption is apart from the argument that uses it.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reader should become free of partisanship before disagreeing with a book.
questions.explain: The authors say controversy without partisanship is impossible. What they ask is an attempt at impartiality. The card next explains what that attempt looks like.
questions.rule: Not free of sides: trying to see the other side.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Put the authors' three ideal conditions for good controversy in the order they give them.
items: Acknowledge the emotions you bring or that arise
Make your own assumptions explicit
Attempt impartiality by taking the other's point of view
questions.explain: Emotions, assumptions, impartiality: each guards against a different way of mistaking something else for a reason.
questions.rule: Emotions, assumptions, impartiality.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A reader strongly opposed to nuclear power must judge a book in favour of it. Which plan best meets the third condition?
options: Read only the chapters on safety, where her doubts are strongest
Read it through first as its author would want it read, then judge
Read it alongside a book against nuclear power, for balance
Ask a friend who supports nuclear power to judge it in her place
optionExplain: Reading only where she objects keeps her partisan view in charge.
Right: taking the author's point of view first is the attempt at impartiality.
A second book may help later, but it does not make her read this one sympathetically.
Handing it over avoids the attempt instead of making it.
questions.explain: Impartiality is attempted by seeing the matter from the author's side before judging. Balance from another book does not replace reading this one sympathetically.
questions.rule: Read from the author's side before judging.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: After reading a book as sympathetically as she can, a reader still disagrees with its main claim. What do the authors imply about her disagreement?
options: It is suspect, since true sympathy would have led her to agree
It is contentious, since disagreeing is always a form of partisanship
It is irrelevant, since sympathetic readers should suspend judgment
It is likely civil, since it comes after seeing the author's view
optionExplain: Sympathy is a way of reading, not a commitment to agree.
Partisanship is unavoidable, but contentiousness comes from failing to read sympathetically.
Nothing requires suspending judgment; sympathy prepares the judgment.
Right: disagreement after a sympathetic reading is aimed at the author's real case.
questions.explain: The authors link contentiousness to a failure to read sympathetically. A reader who has tried to see the author's side and still disagrees has earned a civil disagreement.
questions.rule: Sympathy prepares a verdict; it does not fix it.
questions.teaches: Sympathetic reading is a step, not a verdict: reading an author generously does not commit you to agreeing, it makes sure that any disagreement is aimed at his best case rather than a weak version of it.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, if a reviewer could not read a book sympathetically, her disagreement with it is probably more contentious than civil.
questions.explain: Failing to read sympathetically does not make every point wrong. It makes the disagreement likely to generate heat rather than light.
questions.rule: No sympathy, likely contention.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A debating student is assigned to argue for a policy she opposes. By analogy with the authors' point, what is she most likely to gain?
options: A change of mind, since arguing a side tends to make one believe it
Nothing of use, since arguing against belief is a form of pretence
A clearer view of where her own side's case is weakest
Better speaking skill, but no better grasp of the issue itself
optionExplain: She may or may not change her mind; that is not what the exercise reliably gives.
Taking another's point of view is the attempt at impartiality, not a pretence.
Right: taking the other side's view shows the points her side must answer.
Arguing the other side engages the substance, not only the delivery.
questions.explain: Arguing the other side is a disciplined way of taking the opponent's point of view. It shows the strongest objections her own position faces.
questions.rule: Argue the other side to test your own.
questions.teaches: By analogy, arguing the side you oppose, as debaters do when assigned it, is a practical form of impartiality: it shows the strongest objections your own position must answer.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A critic rebuts a version of an author's thesis that is far weaker than the one the author defends. What do the authors call this lapse?
options: Suspending judgment unfairly
Knocking over a straw man
Quarrelling about assumptions
Charging the author as uninformed
optionExplain: Suspending judgment is holding back a verdict, not rebutting a weaker version.
Right: a straw man is a weaker version set up to be knocked down.
That lapse is about refusing the author's starting points.
Being uninformed is a legitimate charge, if supported; this is a misaimed attack.
questions.explain: Rebutting a weaker version than the author holds is knocking over a straw man. The card next lists this and the other lapses the authors confess to.
questions.rule: Rebut the position held, not a weaker one.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Which lapses do the authors admit they themselves have committed in controversy?
options: Attacking a book rather than criticizing it
Denouncing where they could not support a denial
Praising books they had not finished reading
Proclaiming their own prejudices as superior
Refusing to read books they expected to dislike
optionExplain: Right: one of the lapses they confess.
Right: condemning without support is on their list.
Not on their list; their lapses are all in adverse criticism.
Right: treating one's own prejudices as superior is on the list.
Not on their list; their lapses concern how they argued, not what they read.
questions.explain: The authors confess to attacking instead of criticizing, straw men, unsupported denunciation and proclaimed prejudice. That candour is why they offer easier prescriptions.
questions.rule: Know the lapses: attack, straw man, denunciation, proclaimed prejudice.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A review says: this author is a well-known crank, and his book on diet should be ignored. Which lapse does it show most directly?
options: A straw man, since it restates the diet claims in a weaker form
An attack, since it targets the author instead of his book
A quarrel about assumptions, since it rejects his starting point
An incomplete analysis, since it does not cover each chapter
optionExplain: It does not restate the book's claims at all, weak or strong.
Right: it condemns the author and offers no criticism of anything he wrote.
It never engages his assumptions; it dismisses him personally.
Incomplete analysis is a remark about a book, not a fault of this review.
questions.explain: Calling the author a crank says nothing about what the book claims or how it argues. That is attacking, not criticizing.
questions.rule: Criticize the work, not the worker.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: What separates denying an author's claim from denouncing it, in the authors' terms?
options: A denial is polite in tone, while a denunciation is harsh
A denial comes from experts, while a denunciation comes from others
A denial concerns facts, while a denunciation concerns values
A denial is supported by reasons, while a denunciation is not
optionExplain: Tone is not the difference; a supported denial can be stated sharply.
Anyone can deny with support, and experts can denounce without it.
Both can concern either facts or values.
Right: the lapse is denouncing where you could not support a denial.
questions.explain: The authors fault denouncing where a denial could not be supported. What makes a denial legitimate is the support behind it, not its tone or source.
questions.rule: A denial carries its support; a denunciation does not.
questions.teaches: Denying and denouncing differ in support, not in tone: a sharply worded denial with reasons is fair criticism, while a mild-sounding condemnation without reasons is still denunciation.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: By the authors' view, a severe criticism that targets what the author actually wrote and gives reasons for each denial counts as an attack.
questions.explain: Severity is not the test. Criticism becomes an attack when it misses the real position or condemns without support.
questions.rule: Severe is not the same as unfair.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A restaurant review reads: the chef is lazy and arrogant. By analogy with the authors' point, how could the reviewer turn this into criticism of the work?
options: Add more adjectives, so readers see how strongly she feels
Mention that other diners agreed with her view of the chef
Name what was wrong with the dishes and why, such as overcooked fish
Soften the tone, so the chef is more likely to read the review and take it to heart
optionExplain: More adjectives intensify the attack without adding a reason.
Agreement from others is still about the chef, not the food.
Right: specific faults in the dishes, with reasons, are criticism of the work.
A softer tone does not turn a personal attack into a criticism of the work.
questions.explain: Describing the chef is attacking the person. Pointing to faults in the dishes, with reasons, criticizes the work itself, which the reader of the review can check.
questions.rule: Point to faults in the work.
questions.teaches: By analogy, in any review, comments on the maker's character give readers nothing to check, while a fault named in the work itself, with its reason, can be tested and acted on.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Which of these do the authors list among the remarks a disagreeing reader can make to an author?
options: You are uninformed
You are biased in your sources
You are illogical
You are behind the times
Your analysis is incomplete
optionExplain: Right: lacking relevant knowledge is the first remark.
Bias is not on the list; the remarks concern knowledge, reasoning and completeness.
Right: faulty reasoning is the third remark.
Age is not a defect on the list; an old book can be sound.
Right: incompleteness is the fourth remark.
questions.explain: The four remarks are uninformed, misinformed, illogical and incomplete. The card next sets them out.
questions.rule: Four remarks: uninformed, misinformed, illogical, incomplete.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Put the four adverse remarks in the order the authors number them.
items: You are uninformed
You are misinformed
You are illogical
Your analysis is incomplete
questions.explain: The authors number them in this order, and later treat the first three apart from the fourth.
questions.rule: Uninformed, misinformed, illogical, incomplete.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A reader criticizes a book on running injuries. Match each criticism with the remark it makes.
pairs: It does not know the newer studies on shoe cushioning
It states that stretching prevents most injuries, which trials contradict
Its conclusion on mileage does not follow from its own data
It never deals with injuries in older runners, though it set out to
questions.explain: Missing knowledge, false assertion, faulty inference and an unfinished task are four different defects, matching the four remarks.
questions.rule: Name which defect you mean.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Which of these objections to a book fits none of the four adverse remarks?
options: Its prose is dull and the chapters are much too long
Its figures on crime rates are wrong for the years it covers
It ignores a major study that bears on its conclusion
Its last chapter contradicts what it argued in the first
optionExplain: Right: dull prose may be a fair complaint, but it is not one of the four remarks.
Wrong figures make the author misinformed.
Ignoring a relevant study makes the author uninformed.
A contradiction is a kind of illogic.
questions.explain: The four remarks concern knowledge, reasoning and completeness. Style is a different kind of complaint and is not a ground for disagreeing with what the book says.
questions.rule: Style is not one of the four remarks.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Why might confining yourself to the four remarks make criticism less driven by emotion or prejudice?
options: Each tells the author what the reader feels about his work
Each is milder in tone than the remarks readers usually make
Each can be made without reading the whole of the book
Each names a kind of defect that someone else could check
optionExplain: They state defects in the work, not the reader's feelings.
Tone is not the point; the remarks can be sharp.
They all presuppose a reader who understands the book.
Right: a named defect turns a mood into a claim others can test.
questions.explain: Each remark claims something specific about the book that can be verified or refuted. A feeling cannot pass that test.
questions.rule: A checkable claim is harder to fake with feeling.
questions.teaches: Confining criticism to the four remarks turns a mood into a claim that can be checked: each remark names a kind of defect that another reader, or the author, could verify or refute.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: An investor reviews a startup's business plan. Which of her criticisms fit one of the four remarks, used by analogy?
options: It omits the new competitor that entered the market last year
Its founders seem too young and untested to run a company
Its revenue forecast does not follow from its own growth figures
I have a bad feeling about this whole sector of the market
It sets out to cover the European launch but never does
optionExplain: Right: missing relevant knowledge, by analogy uninformed.
This targets the people, not a defect in the plan.
Right: a forecast that does not follow is, by analogy, illogical.
A feeling is not one of the four remarks.
Right: an announced task left undone is, by analogy, incomplete.
questions.explain: By analogy, the four remarks fit any reasoned document. They also differ in what would settle them: missing data or wrong figures are answered from outside the plan, while a forecast that does not follow can be checked from the plan alone.
questions.rule: Know what evidence would settle each remark.
questions.teaches: The four remarks differ in what would settle them: a charge of being uninformed or misinformed is answered by evidence from outside the document, while a charge of illogic can be checked from the document alone.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, it is enough to tell an author he is illogical, as long as you are sure it is true.
questions.explain: The authors require you to say exactly where the author goes wrong and to give reasons. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Being sure is not enough; show where and why.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
