questions.q: The authors note that no book can be totally ____, so a charge of faulty reasoning must say exactly where the reasoning fails.
questions.explain: No book is uninformed or misinformed about everything, and none is totally illogical. A charge that names no place says nothing definite.
questions.rule: No book is wrong everywhere, so say where.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Which criticism of a book on climate policy meets both demands the authors set?
options: The author is careless with numbers throughout the book.
Chapter 3 uses the 2010 emission figure as the 2020 one, inflating his trend.
The author is wrong about carbon taxes, as most economists who study them would agree.
The book is illogical, and anyone who reads it carefully will notice.
optionExplain: Throughout names no place, and no reason is given.
Right: it names the exact point and gives the reason it matters.
It names a topic, but an appeal to what most think is not a reason.
It neither names the place nor gives a reason.
questions.explain: The second criticism names where the author goes wrong and shows why. The others are labels, with or without a vague appeal.
questions.rule: Name the place and give the reason.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: A reader who shows that an author is misinformed on one point is then barred from also charging him with being illogical on another.
questions.explain: The defects are not mutually exclusive. Each charge needs its own specification and support, but making one does not prevent making another.
questions.rule: Charges can combine; each needs its own support.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A critic names the exact page and reasoning behind her charge. Besides convincing readers, what does this precision make possible?
options: It lets others check her charge, and correct her if she is wrong
It stops the author from replying, since the point is now settled
It makes the review longer, which signals effort to the reader
It turns the charge into a fact that needs no further support
optionExplain: Right: a precise charge exposes itself to checking, which disciplines the critic too.
Precision invites a reply; it does not prevent one.
Length is not the point of being precise.
A precise charge still rests on the reasons given for it.
questions.explain: A charge tied to a place and a reason can be tested by anyone. That is fair to the author and also guards against the critic's own mistakes.
questions.rule: Precise charges can be checked, both ways.
questions.teaches: Specifying a criticism exposes the critic as well as the author: a charge tied to a place and a reason can be checked and, if it is wrong, corrected, which a vague charge escapes.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A tenant writes to her landlord. By analogy with the authors' point, which complaint is most likely to get a useful response?
options: The flat is badly maintained and has been for a long time.
Several neighbours agree that the building is neglected.
The bathroom fan has not worked since March, so mould is growing.
I expected much better when I signed the lease last year.
optionExplain: A general charge invites a general denial.
Agreement from others still names no specific fault.
Right: a specified fault with its consequence can be checked and fixed.
Disappointed expectations name no fault in the flat.
questions.explain: A specified complaint gives the landlord a definite fault to check and a reason it matters. A sweeping one is easy to deny.
questions.rule: Specify the fault and its effect.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a sweeping complaint invites a sweeping denial, while a specified one with its consequence must be either fixed or answered on its merits.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A reader says an author is uninformed. According to the authors, what must the missing knowledge be?
options: Knowledge the reader has and the author lacks
Knowledge available when the author wrote
Knowledge relevant to the author's problem
Knowledge that experts in the field share
optionExplain: The reader must have it to state it, but irrelevant knowledge does not count.
Darwin lacked genetics that came later; the charge does not require it was available.
Right: unless the knowledge bears on his problem, the remark has no point.
Shared expertise may be irrelevant to this author's problem.
questions.explain: The defining condition is relevance to the problem the author is trying to solve. The card next explains how to support the charge.
questions.rule: Uninformed means lacking relevant knowledge.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: To support the charge that an author is uninformed, every critic must state the knowledge he lacks and show how it makes a difference to his conclusions.
questions.explain: Stating the missing knowledge shows it exists; showing its effect on his conclusions shows it was relevant.
questions.rule: State it and show its effect.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A 1990s book argues that a disease cannot yet be treated because its cause is unknown. The cause was later found and a treatment followed. Which criticism follows the authors' view?
options: The author was careless, since a diligent researcher should have foreseen the discovery
The book is worthless now, since medicine has moved on
The author lacked knowledge of the cause, which overturns his conclusion
The author was illogical, since his conclusion did not follow
optionExplain: The charge is about the book's knowledge, not the author's diligence.
One gap does not make a book worthless; the charge must be specific.
Right: it states the missing knowledge and shows how it bears on the conclusion.
Given what was known, his reasoning held; the defect is the missing knowledge.
questions.explain: The criticism names the knowledge the author lacked and shows that it would have changed his conclusion. That is the full support the card asks for.
questions.rule: Name the gap and its effect on the conclusion.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A reader finds gaps in a book arguing that a town's flooding comes from new housing. Sort each gap by whether it supports the charge that the author is uninformed.
questions.explain: Each supporting gap is knowledge that bears on the cause of the flooding and could change his conclusion. The others are facts he lacks that make no difference to it.
questions.rule: No difference to the conclusions, no charge.

items.t: He lacks the river gauge data showing rainfall rose sharply
He does not know the town's founding date
He lacks the drainage survey showing blocked culverts
He does not know the mayor's party
He lacks records of which streets flooded before the housing was built

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: Charging Darwin with being uninformed about genetics is a claim about the limits of his book, not an accusation that he was lazy.
questions.explain: The knowledge came largely from later work. The charge marks what the book lacks and how it matters, whatever the author could have done.
questions.rule: Uninformed describes the book's knowledge, not the author's effort.
questions.teaches: Calling an author uninformed is not blaming him: the missing knowledge may not have existed when he wrote, so the charge marks a limit of the book rather than a failing of character.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A 2012 workplace safety manual gives no guidance on a solvent later found to be harmful. By analogy with the authors' point, how should a reader treat the manual?
options: Discard it, since a manual with one gap cannot be trusted at all
Use it, but check where later knowledge changes its guidance
Follow it fully, since its authors followed the best advice of the time
Report the authors, since they should have tested every solvent
optionExplain: One relevant gap is a specific defect, not a reason to reject everything.
Right: name the missing knowledge and see which guidance it changes.
The authors' good faith does not fill the gap in what the manual knows.
The gap may not have been knowable then; blaming is not the point.
questions.explain: Like an uninformed book, the manual lacks knowledge that bears on its conclusions. The reader names the gap and checks its effect, without discarding the rest.
questions.rule: Find where later knowledge changes the guidance.
questions.teaches: By analogy, practical guidance ages the way books do: a manual written before a hazard was known is uninformed through no fault of its authors, so a careful reader checks its date and what has been learned since.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, in philosophy a later author can be uninformed about a distinction that earlier philosophers had already established.
questions.explain: The authors say philosophy can lose knowledge as well as gain it over time. The card next gives their example.
questions.rule: In philosophy, later does not guarantee better informed.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: In the authors' example, Hume showed no grasp of the distinction between images and ____, though earlier philosophers had made it clear.
questions.explain: The ancients separated sensing and imagining from understanding. The authors say Hume, in the eighteenth century, revealed his ignorance of this distinction.
questions.rule: Hume's gap: images versus ideas.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A reader wants to check whether a 1990s geology textbook is uninformed. Following the authors' point, where should she look first?
options: At ancient writings on the earth, which may hold lost insights
At the textbook's own index, to see which topics it omits
At later research, which tends to expose gaps in science
At reviews written when the textbook first came out
optionExplain: That route fits philosophy better; in science knowledge tends to grow.
Omitted topics are not gaps unless they are relevant and known elsewhere.
Right: in science, later observation and investigation usually reveal what was lacking.
Reviews from the same time share the same state of knowledge.
questions.explain: In science and history, later research usually reveals an author's gaps. So she checks what has been learned since.
questions.rule: Science: check later research.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Now the same reader turns to a recent book of moral philosophy. What changes in her check for gaps?
options: She should also ask what earlier philosophers had already settled
Nothing, since newer work in every field builds on the older
She should skip the check, since philosophy has no facts to lack
She should look only at the oldest works, since philosophy declines
optionExplain: Right: a recent philosopher may lack a distinction earlier ones had made.
The authors say philosophy can lose as well as gain over time.
Philosophy has knowledge to lack, as Hume's case shows.
Loss is as likely as gain, not certain; later work also adds.
questions.explain: In philosophy, knowledge does not reliably accumulate. A careful check looks backward as well as forward.
questions.rule: Philosophy: check earlier thinkers too.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: By the authors' reasoning, the date of a philosophy book does not by itself tell you whether it is better informed than an older one.
questions.explain: If loss is as likely as gain, a newer philosophy book may lack what an older one had. You have to check the particular distinction.
questions.rule: Check the distinction, not the date.
questions.teaches: In fields where knowledge can be lost, newness is no proxy for being informed: a recent author can know less than an ancient one about a given distinction, so the check is made point by point, not by date.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A builder restoring an old stone wall finds that modern manuals omit a lime-mortar technique described in a 19th-century guide. By analogy with the authors' point, what does this suggest?
options: The old guide is outdated, since manuals improve over time
A craft can lose knowledge, so the older guide may correct the new
The technique must be poor, or modern manuals would include it
The two sources cancel out, so he should rely on his own judgment
optionExplain: That assumes knowledge only grows, which the card questions outside science.
Right: like philosophy, practical knowledge can drop out of later sources.
Omission may reflect loss, not judgment that the technique failed.
He can weigh them; disagreement between sources does not cancel both.
questions.explain: By analogy with philosophy, knowledge in a craft can be lost over time. The older guide may supply what later manuals lack.
questions.rule: Older sources can correct newer ones.
questions.teaches: By analogy, practical crafts can lose knowledge as philosophy can: a technique known to earlier makers may vanish from later manuals, so an older source can sometimes show where a newer one is uninformed.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: What distinguishes calling an author misinformed from calling him uninformed?
options: Misinformed means he asserts what is not the case
Misinformed means he lacks some relevant knowledge
Misinformed means his reasoning does not follow
Misinformed means he leaves his task unfinished
optionExplain: Right: the misinformed author makes assertions contrary to fact.
That is being uninformed, the first remark.
That is being illogical, the third remark.
That is incompleteness, the fourth remark.
questions.explain: Uninformed is a lack; misinformed is a positive error, asserting something false. The card next explains how to support the charge.
questions.rule: Misinformed: asserting what is not so.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: To support the charge that an author is misinformed, you must argue the truth or greater ____ of a position contrary to his.
questions.explain: Showing an author wrong means arguing for the contrary, as true or at least more probable than his claim.
questions.rule: Argue the contrary is true or more probable.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A book claims that most heat leaves a house through its windows and builds its advice on that. A reader thinks this is wrong. What would support her charge?
options: Citing heat-loss measurements showing walls and roofs lose more
Saying the claim sounds exaggerated to anyone who owns a house
Pointing out that the author is not trained as a building engineer
Noting that the book never discusses floors as a source of loss
optionExplain: Right: evidence that the contrary is true supports the charge.
An impression is not an argument for the contrary position.
Credentials are about the author, not about whether the claim is true.
An omission would make the author uninformed, not misinformed.
questions.explain: The charge needs an argument that the contrary is true or more probable. Measurements of where heat goes do that.
questions.rule: Support the charge with evidence for the contrary.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: A history of a war that does not mention a treaty which shaped the outcome, but makes no false statement about it, is misinformed about the treaty.
questions.explain: Misinformed requires asserting what is not so. A relevant omission with no false claim is a lack of knowledge, which makes the author uninformed.
questions.rule: No false assertion, no charge of misinformed.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A critic charges an author with being misinformed about the cause of a recession. What does making this charge commit the critic to?
options: Nothing beyond showing that the author's account has doubtful parts
Defending a contrary account, which can be criticized in its turn
Proving the author was careless in gathering his evidence
Offering a full theory of recessions to replace the author's
optionExplain: Doubt is not enough; the charge requires arguing the contrary.
Right: the critic takes on a position of her own, open to the same scrutiny.
The charge concerns the claim's truth, not the author's care.
Only the contrary to the point at issue is needed, not a whole theory.
questions.explain: Supporting the charge means arguing that a contrary claim is true or more probable. The critic now holds a claim of her own that others can examine.
questions.rule: Charging error means defending a contrary claim.
questions.teaches: The charge of misinformation shifts some burden to the critic: arguing for a contrary position commits her to a claim of her own, which can itself be examined for being uninformed, misinformed or illogical.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A news site published a wrong unemployment figure. By analogy with the authors' point, what should a good correction contain?
options: A note that the figure was wrong, with an apology to readers
A promise that future stories on this topic will be checked more carefully before release
A statement that the reporter has been reminded to check facts
The accurate figure and its source, and what it changes in the story
optionExplain: Saying it was wrong without the contrary figure leaves readers with no true claim.
Future care does not correct the present error.
This is about the reporter, not the claim and its effect.
Right: it supports the contrary and shows how it bears on the conclusions.
questions.explain: Like supporting a charge of misinformation, a good correction states the true figure with its source and traces its effect. If the conclusion rested on the figure, the conclusion itself must be revisited.
questions.rule: Correct the fact, then recheck what rests on it.
questions.teaches: When a corrected fact carried the conclusion, fixing the figure is not enough: the conclusions built on it must be reconsidered, which in journalism can mean retracting a story rather than correcting it.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, an author's factual error deserves criticism even when none of his conclusions depends on it.
questions.explain: The authors say a factual error should be pointed out only if it is relevant to the author's conclusions. The card next contrasts two cases.
questions.rule: Criticize errors that bear on conclusions.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Match each of the authors' examples with how much the error matters.
pairs: Aquinas on the matter of the heavens
Spinoza on democracy as more primitive
Aristotle on the female role in reproduction
Leads to unsupportable conclusions on procreation
questions.explain: Aquinas's error leaves his account of matter and form untouched, while Spinoza's and Aristotle's errors carry into their conclusions.
questions.rule: Same kind of error, different weight.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A book argues that a city's bridges need urgent repair. It misstates the year one bridge opened, and it overstates traffic loads by half. Which error deserves the main criticism?
options: The opening year, since dates in a history are easy to check
The traffic loads, since the case for urgent repair rests on them
Both equally, since any error weakens the author's credibility
Neither, since a book with sound aims can survive small slips
optionExplain: Easy to check is not the test; relevance to the conclusion is.
Right: the load figure supports the main conclusion, so it carries the weight.
The card weighs errors by what they support, not by their effect on reputation.
The load error is not small for this argument; it is central.
questions.explain: Trace which conclusions depend on each error. The opening year supports nothing about repair; the loads support the whole case.
questions.rule: Weigh an error by the conclusion it carries.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A book makes one false claim about a city's population. Its chapter on schools ignores the figure, but its chapter on housing builds on it. How should a reader weigh the error?
options: As minor, since one chapter does not depend on it
As irrelevant, since population figures are often revised
As fatal to the book, since an error in one place affects all
As damaging to housing but harmless to schools
optionExplain: The housing chapter depends on it, so it is not minor there.
Revision does not excuse the error where conclusions depend on it.
The schools chapter does not use the figure, so it is unaffected.
Right: relevance is judged against each conclusion that depends on the error.
questions.explain: An error's weight depends on the conclusion in question. The same false claim can be harmless to one argument and decisive for another.
questions.rule: Judge relevance conclusion by conclusion.
questions.teaches: An error's relevance is judged against each conclusion separately: the same false claim can be harmless to one argument in a book and fatal to another, so criticism should say which conclusion it affects.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: An error of limited relevance to an author's main conclusion can be ignored entirely in a careful criticism.
questions.explain: Limited relevance is not none. Such an error may still bear on a lesser conclusion and is worth pointing out there.
questions.rule: Point out an error wherever it is relevant.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A fact-checker reviews a magazine story on a new drug. It misnames the city where the company is based and misreports the trial's success rate. By analogy with the authors' point, how should she rank them?
options: Equally, since a fact-checker's duty is to every fact
The city first, since readers notice local errors most
The success rate first, since the story's claims rest on it
Neither, since both can be fixed with a short note
optionExplain: Both should be fixed, but they do not carry equal weight for the story.
Noticeability is not relevance to the story's claims.
Right: the trial figure supports the headline claim about the drug.
A note may fix the city; the rate may undo the story's conclusion.
questions.explain: By analogy, errors are triaged by what they support. To do that she must first state the story's central claim, that the drug works, and only then can she see that the success rate carries it and the city does not.
questions.rule: State the main claim, then rank the errors.
questions.teaches: Triaging errors presupposes knowing the main claim: a fact-checker must first state what a story argues before she can tell which errors it rests on, so understanding again comes before judging.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: According to the authors, if an author is misinformed on some point, what else is true of him on that same point?
options: Nothing else follows about him
He is also illogical on it
His analysis is also incomplete
He is also uninformed on it
optionExplain: The authors say something does follow: the lack that goes with the error.
Illogic is a fault of reasoning, a different defect.
Incompleteness concerns the whole work, not one false claim.
Right: whenever a man is misinformed in some respect, he is also uninformed in it.
questions.explain: Asserting a falsehood about something implies lacking the true knowledge of it. The card next shows why the two still differ.
questions.rule: Misinformed implies uninformed on the same point.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Sort each effect by the defect that produces it.

items.t: Certain problems cannot be solved
Wrong conclusions are reached
Certain conclusions cannot be supported
Untenable solutions are offered

questions.explain: A gap leaves conclusions unsupported or problems unsolved. A false supposition drives the author to conclusions and solutions that are wrong.
questions.rule: Gaps block; errors mislead.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A nutrition book lacks any data on children and so cannot say what children should eat. Another assumes children need the same protein as adults and recommends adult portions. Which describes them correctly?
options: Both are misinformed, since both give poor advice about children
Both are illogical, since neither reasons well about children
The first is misinformed, the second uninformed, since the second lacks data
The first is uninformed; the second is misinformed
optionExplain: The first makes no false claim; it only cannot answer.
Neither fault is in the reasoning; both are in the premises.
This reverses them: the false supposition is the second book's.
Right: a gap leaves the problem unsolved; a false supposition yields a wrong solution.
questions.explain: The first book's defect is negative and leaves the problem unsolved. The second's is positive and produces an untenable recommendation.
questions.rule: Gap: no answer; error: wrong answer.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: By the authors' distinction, how would repairing an uninformed book differ from repairing a misinformed one?
options: Both are repaired the same way, by adding more evidence
The first needs facts added; the second needs a premise removed
The first needs a new conclusion; the second needs only a footnote
Neither can be repaired, since both defects lie in the premises
optionExplain: Adding evidence fills a gap, but it leaves a false premise in place.
Right: a gap is filled, while an error must be taken out with what was built on it.
A false premise that leads to wrong conclusions needs more than a footnote.
Premises can be corrected; the defect is not fatal by nature.
questions.explain: A negative defect is mended by supplying what is missing. A positive one has already produced wrong conclusions, so those must be undone as well.
questions.rule: Fill gaps; remove errors and what rests on them.
questions.teaches: The two defects call for different repairs: an uninformed account can often be extended by adding what it lacks, while a misinformed one must have the false premise removed and the conclusions built on it reworked.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: If an author's premises are all true and well supported but his conclusion does not follow from them, the charge of a defect in his premises fits.
questions.explain: Both uninformed and misinformed attack premises. A conclusion that fails to follow from sound premises is a fault of reasoning, a different charge.
questions.rule: Sound premises, bad inference: not a premise defect.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A detective lacks a key witness in one case, and relies on a false alibi in another. By analogy with the authors' point, which is likely to do more harm to the investigation's conclusion?
options: The false alibi, since it points the investigation the wrong way
The missing witness, since the case cannot be closed without it
Both equally, since each is a defect in the evidence
Neither, as long as the detective reasons carefully from what he has
optionExplain: Right: a false premise leads to a wrong conclusion, not only an unsupported one.
A missing witness leaves the case open, but does not point it wrongly.
Both are defects in the evidence, but they work differently.
Careful reasoning from a false alibi still reaches a wrong conclusion.
questions.explain: By analogy, a gap leaves the conclusion unsupported, while a false premise drives it to a wrong answer, which careful reasoning cannot fix.
questions.rule: A false lead misleads; a missing one stalls.
questions.teaches: By analogy, in any investigation a missing clue stalls the case while a false clue misdirects it, so a false premise is often more dangerous than a missing one: careful reasoning cannot correct it.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: An author argues: every good school has dedicated teachers; this school has dedicated teachers; so this school is good. What is wrong with the argument?
options: Its premise about good schools is false
Its key term changes meaning midway
Its two premises contradict each other
Its conclusion does not follow
optionExplain: The premise may well be true; the problem is the step to the conclusion.
Dedicated is used in one sense throughout.
The premises are compatible; neither denies the other.
Right: having what good schools need does not make a school good.
questions.explain: Good schools needing dedicated teachers does not mean dedicated teachers make a school good. The card next names this fallacy.
questions.rule: Needing X does not mean X is enough.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Match each term with its meaning.
pairs: A conclusion that does not follow from its reasons
Two claims by the author that are incompatible
questions.explain: Illogic means a fallacy, and the authors name two general sorts: the non sequitur and inconsistency.
questions.rule: Two sorts of fallacy: non sequitur and inconsistency.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A report says: a city cannot thrive without good transport; Riverton has good transport; so Riverton will thrive. Which reply exposes the fallacy?
options: Riverton's transport is not as good as the report claims
The report's authors work for a transport company
Some cities thrive with poor transport, so the first premise is false
Transport may be needed for thriving without ensuring it
optionExplain: This attacks a premise, not the step from the reasons to the conclusion.
This is about the authors, not the reasoning.
This also challenges a premise; the inference would still fail if the premise were true.
Right: the conclusion treats a requirement as a guarantee.
questions.explain: Like Machiavelli's argument, the report moves from what thriving depends on to what guarantees it. That step does not follow.
questions.rule: A requirement is not a guarantee.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Both Machiavelli's argument and the transport report share one pattern. What is it?
options: From A sometimes brings B, they conclude A always does
From B needs A, they conclude that A brings B
From A and B occurring together, they conclude A causes B
From most A being B, they conclude that all A are B
optionExplain: That is overgeneralising, a different slip.
Right: they treat a necessary condition as if it were sufficient.
That confuses correlation with cause, a different slip.
That is also overgeneralising, not this pattern.
questions.explain: Good laws need arms, so arms bring good laws; thriving needs transport, so transport brings thriving. Each turns what is needed into what is enough.
questions.rule: Needed is not the same as enough.
questions.teaches: A common form of non sequitur treats a necessary condition as a sufficient one: from B requires A it concludes that A produces B, which does not follow.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: If a reader shows that an author's conclusion does not follow from his reasons, she has shown that the conclusion is false.
questions.explain: A non sequitur shows the reasons do not establish the conclusion. The conclusion may still be true for other reasons.
questions.rule: Not shown is not the same as false.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A reader who knows no medicine meets this argument in a medical paper: every patient who recovered had taken the drug, so taking the drug brings recovery. Can she test the step with a parallel argument like the authors' health and happiness one?
options: Yes: a parallel tests only the form, so it works on any subject
No: a parallel works only on political arguments like Machiavelli's
No: she must first learn medicine to judge the step
Yes, but only once she has shown the premise to be false
optionExplain: Right: a parallel such as every recovered patient had drunk water, so drinking water brings recovery, keeps the form and gives an absurd result.
Machiavelli was only the authors' example; the move depends on the form, not the topic.
Judging the premises may need medicine, but the step from reasons to conclusion is a matter of form.
The test leaves the premise alone; it asks whether the conclusion follows even if the premise is true.
questions.explain: A parallel argument keeps the form and swaps the content for something plainly true and plainly false. Since it tests only the form, a reader can use it on an argument about any subject, without knowing that subject.
questions.rule: A parallel argument works on any subject.
questions.teaches: The parallel-argument test can be used on any argument, in any field, even one the reader knows nothing about, because it checks only the form: keep the form, give it plainly true premises, and see whether the conclusion comes out plainly false.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: An author can be illogical even if every one of his arguments, taken alone, reaches its conclusion validly.
questions.explain: Two claims argued well in different places can still be incompatible. The card next shows the authors' example.
questions.rule: Valid parts can make an inconsistent whole.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: In the authors' example, why is Hobbes's account of sensory qualities inconsistent with his view of bodies?
options: What holds of all bodies holds of brain atoms, yet he gives them qualities
Because he cites no evidence that atoms in the brain are moving
Because he uses the word body in two different senses in the two places he discusses it
Because his view of bodies was later shown to be false by physics
optionExplain: Right: bodies without qualities cannot also, as brain atoms, be qualities.
Lack of evidence would be a premise problem, not inconsistency.
The authors do not say body shifts sense; the conflict is real.
Later physics may bear on truth, but the charge is incompatibility.
questions.explain: He says the world of bodies has no qualities, then makes sensory qualities motions of certain bodies. What holds of all bodies must hold of these.
questions.rule: What is true of all is true of each group.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A management book says in chapter 2 that people are motivated only by money, and in chapter 7 that the best teams work for shared purpose regardless of pay. What should a critic charge?
options: A non sequitur, since chapter 7 does not follow from chapter 2
Misinformation, since the chapter 2 claim is false
Inconsistency, since both claims cannot be true at once
Incompleteness, since the book covers motivation unevenly
optionExplain: A non sequitur concerns a conclusion and its reasons; these are two separate claims.
That may also be true, but the clear fault here is that the claims conflict.
Right: if only money motivates, no team works for purpose regardless of pay.
Uneven coverage is not the problem; the two claims contradict each other.
questions.explain: The two claims are incompatible. Whichever is false, the book cannot hold both.
questions.rule: Two incompatible claims: charge inconsistency.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: If the critic finds that chapter 2's only money refers to poorly paid jobs, a case chapter 7 does not address, the charge of inconsistency may fall.
questions.explain: Inconsistency is between claims, not sentences. If the two passages concern different things, both claims may be true and the contradiction vanishes.
questions.rule: Check the terms before charging contradiction.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Showing that two of an author's claims are inconsistent proves that they cannot both stand, but not ____ of them is false.
questions.explain: An inconsistency proves that not both can stand. Deciding which to give up needs further argument, about premises and evidence.
questions.rule: Inconsistency shows one must go, not which.
questions.teaches: Finding an inconsistency does not tell you which claim is false: it shows only that not both can stand, so deciding which to give up needs further argument, often a charge of misinformation against one of them.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A company handbook says in one section that all staff may work from home on Fridays, and in another that all managers must be on site every weekday. Managers are staff. By analogy with the authors' point, what is the problem?
options: The handbook is uninformed about how managers actually prefer to organise their week
Its two rules are inconsistent for managers, who are covered by both
Its rule on Fridays does not follow from its rule on weekdays
There is no problem, since each section is clear on its own
optionExplain: Preferences are not the issue; the rules conflict.
Right: what holds for all staff holds for managers, so both rules cannot be followed.
Neither rule is offered as a reason for the other.
Clarity of each section is what makes the clash between them visible.
questions.explain: Like Hobbes's case, what is said of all staff applies to managers too. The two rules cannot both be obeyed on Fridays.
questions.rule: A rule for all applies to each group.
questions.teaches: By analogy, rules and policies can be inconsistent the way arguments are: when a rule for everyone collides with a rule for a subgroup, those in the subgroup cannot obey both, and only the writer can say which prevails.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: According to the authors, how often do really good books make obvious slips in reasoning?
options: Often, since even great authors write fast
As often as other books, but readers forgive them
Never, which is what makes them really good
Rarely, and their slips are usually well hidden
optionExplain: The authors say the opposite: obvious slips are few in good books.
They are less frequent in good books, not equally frequent.
The authors say slips occur, though hidden.
Right: few obvious slips, and those that occur are elaborately concealed.
questions.explain: Obvious fallacies are rare in good books. The card next explains what that means for the critic.
questions.rule: In good books, fallacies hide.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a book may safely lack cogency in respects that do not affect its major conclusions.
questions.explain: The charge of illogic matters only so far as major conclusions are affected. Irrelevant lapses do not undermine the book.
questions.rule: Press only slips that touch major conclusions.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A book argues for a four-day school week. In a side remark it reasons badly about the history of the calendar; its main argument, from attendance data, is valid. Which steps should a critic take?
options: Note the side slip briefly, as a minor point
Judge the main argument on its own merits
Lead the review with the side slip, as the headline
Reject the book, since one fallacy taints its logic
Treat the main argument as suspect because of the slip
questions.explain: Cogency matters where major conclusions depend on it. A slip in a side remark is noted but does not decide the verdict.
questions.rule: Weigh slips by the conclusions they touch.
optionExplain: Right: the slip is real and can be noted, in proportion.
Right: the main argument stands or falls on its own reasoning.
The side slip does not affect the major conclusion, so it should not lead.
One irrelevant slip does not undo a valid main argument.
Suspicion is not a showing; the main argument has to be faulted on its own terms.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A student believes he has found a glaring logical blunder at the centre of a classic book. Given the authors' point, what should he do first?
options: Publish it at once, since classics deserve close scrutiny like any other book
Check whether he has misread the argument before charging it
Assume the blunder is a printing error and move on
Drop it, since great books contain no real fallacies
optionExplain: Scrutiny is right, but a glaring blunder in a classic calls for a check first.
Right: obvious slips are rare in good books, so his own reading is the likelier suspect.
A printing error is a guess; his reading should be checked first.
Fallacies do occur in good books, though they are usually hidden.
questions.explain: If obvious slips are rare in good books, a glaring one is more likely a misreading. He should check his understanding before charging.
questions.rule: A glaring flaw in a great book: recheck your reading.
questions.teaches: Because good books rarely contain obvious slips, an apparent blunder at the centre of one is more often a sign of the reader's misreading, so the first step is to recheck understanding before making the charge.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: Finding a real fallacy in a book shows that the book's main conclusion is unsupported.
questions.explain: Only if the fallacy lies in the reasoning for that conclusion. A slip in a side argument leaves the main case standing.
questions.rule: Say which conclusion the fallacy affects.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A reviewer finds an invalid step at line 12 of a 30-line mathematical proof. By analogy with the authors' point, which parts of the proof does the flaw undermine?
options: The steps that depend on line 12, and the conclusion if it does
All 30 lines, since one invalid step spoils the whole proof
Only line 12 itself, since every other step is separately valid
Nothing, if the final result is known to be true from elsewhere
optionExplain: Right: a flaw affects what rests on it, not what comes before or apart from it.
Steps before line 12, or independent of it, are not affected.
Later steps that use line 12 inherit its flaw.
A true result can still be badly proved; the proof as given is flawed.
questions.explain: A faulty step undermines only what depends on it. The charge should trace the dependency to the conclusion.
questions.rule: Trace what depends on the faulty step.
questions.teaches: In any chain of reasoning, a single invalid step undermines only what depends on it: steps before it or apart from it stand, so tracing dependencies shows exactly which conclusions fall.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: According to the authors, which case is the main concern of the charge that an author is illogical?
options: Leaving some premises unstated
Reasoning well from false premises
Reasoning poorly from false premises
Reasoning poorly from true premises
optionExplain: Unstated premises can be supplied; that is not the fallacy the authors mean.
Reasoning well from false premises is not illogic; the fault is in the premises.
Possible to note, but the authors call it less important.
Right: poor reasoning from good grounds is the main concern.
questions.explain: The charge of illogic matters most when the grounds are good and the reasoning fails. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Illogic matters most from good grounds.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, an author who fails to draw conclusions that his evidence implies is reasoning incompletely.
questions.explain: The authors note this connection: leaving implied conclusions undrawn makes the reasoning incomplete, though their main concern is poor reasoning from good grounds.
questions.rule: Undrawn conclusions: incomplete reasoning.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Sort each case by whether the charge of illogic is the main criticism or a lesser one.
groups: Main concern: bad reasoning from good grounds
Lesser: bad reasoning from bad grounds

items.t: Accurate crime data, but a conclusion they do not support
Invented survey figures, and a leap beyond even those
Well-tested premises, then a step that does not follow
A false premise about tax rates, followed by a slip in inference

questions.explain: When premises are sound, a fallacy is the decisive fault. When they are already false or inadequate, the fallacy is real but adds less.
questions.rule: Sound grounds make the fallacy decisive.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Why might finding bad reasoning from false premises be less important than finding it from true ones?
options: Because false premises make every inference drawn from them invalid as well
Because the conclusion is already unsupported by the false premises
Because readers rarely notice bad reasoning from false premises
Because authors cannot be blamed for errors in their premises
optionExplain: Validity concerns the step, not the truth of the premises.
Right: the false premises already fail to support it, so the fallacy adds little.
Noticeability is not the reason; importance is about what the charge adds.
Authors can be faulted for their premises; that is the charge of misinformation.
questions.explain: If the premises are false, the conclusion has already lost its support. Showing the reasoning also fails adds less than showing it fails from good grounds.
questions.rule: A fallacy matters most where it is the only fault.
questions.teaches: A fallacy counts for most when it is the only thing wrong: if the premises are already false, the conclusion has lost its support, so exposing the bad reasoning as well adds comparatively little.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: An author starts from sound premises and reaches a false conclusion by an invalid step. The authors say he is in a sense misinformed. Why do they still separate this from being misinformed?
options: Because he did not assert the conclusion, only suggest it
Because his conclusion is true, while a misinformed author's is false
Because his error comes from bad reasoning, not from lacking knowledge
Because misinformed applies only to errors of historical fact
optionExplain: He did assert it; that is why he is, in a sense, misinformed.
His conclusion is false here; the difference is in where the error comes from.
Right: the source of the error differs, and that is worth distinguishing.
Misinformed applies to any assertion contrary to fact.
questions.explain: Both end in a false assertion, but one comes from faulty inference and the other from defects such as insufficient knowledge. The distinction shows where the fault lies.
questions.rule: Same false result, different source.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A cook uses fresh, correct ingredients but the cake collapses because she mixed them in the wrong order. By analogy with the authors' point, what should she change next time?
options: The method, since the ingredients were sound and the process failed
The ingredients, since a failed cake suggests something was off
Both, since any failure means the whole recipe is suspect
The oven, since uneven heat is a common cause of a cake collapsing in the middle
optionExplain: Right: good grounds with a bad process means the process is at fault.
The ingredients were sound; changing them would not fix the fault.
Changing both hides what actually went wrong.
Nothing points to the oven; the order of mixing is the known fault.
questions.explain: Like bad reasoning from good grounds, the fault is in the process. Diagnosing the source shows what to fix.
questions.rule: Find whether grounds or process failed.
questions.teaches: By analogy, diagnosing where a wrong result came from tells you what to repair: a failure from sound inputs and a faulty process calls for fixing the process, while bad inputs call for new inputs.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A reader understands a book and cannot show that the author is uninformed, misinformed or illogical on any relevant point. According to the authors, what follows?
options: She is free to agree or disagree, as she chooses
She may disagree if the conclusion seems unlikely to her
She should suspend judgment until experts weigh in
She must agree with the author as far as he has gone
optionExplain: The authors deny this freedom: it is not her privilege to choose.
Seeming unlikely is not a supported criticism.
Suspension responds to incompleteness, not to deference to experts.
Right: failing all three criteria obliges agreement, as far as the author has gone.
questions.explain: Without a supported charge against his knowledge or reasoning, nothing grounds disagreement. The card next explains the obligation.
questions.rule: No supported fault, no disagreement.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reader who understands a book keeps the right to disagree with it even when he cannot support any of the first three critical remarks.
questions.explain: The authors say the reader has no freedom of will here. Without support for one of the first three remarks, he must agree as far as the author has gone.
questions.rule: Agreement is compelled, not chosen.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: After careful study, a reader of a book on sleep finds its data sound and its reasoning valid, though its conclusion clashes with her habits. Which responses fit the authors' advice?
questions.explain: With no fault found in premises or reasoning, agreement follows. A clash with her habits is a reason to reconsider them, not the book.
questions.rule: Sound and valid: agree.
options: Agree with the book's conclusion
Reconsider her habits in its light
Withhold agreement until her habits change
Disagree, citing her own experience of sleep
Set the book aside as unsuited to her life
optionExplain: Right: sound data and valid reasoning oblige agreement.
Right: the clash is a reason to rethink her habits, not the book.
Her habits do not bear on whether the argument holds.
Experience is not a supported criticism unless it shows a premise false.
Setting it aside dodges the verdict the argument compels.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A year later, a new study shows that one of the book's key premises was false. What becomes of her agreement?
options: It stands, since she was obliged to agree at the time
It can be revised, since the author now proves misinformed
It turns into suspended judgment, since the book is incomplete
It was a mistake, since she should have foreseen the study
optionExplain: The obligation held while no fault could be shown; now one can.
Right: a newly supported charge reopens the question on that point.
A false premise is a charge of misinformation, not incompleteness.
She could not have shown the fault before the study existed.
questions.explain: The obligation depends on not being able to support the first three remarks. Once one can be supported, disagreement on that point becomes possible.
questions.rule: New grounds can reopen agreement.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: By the authors' logic, the obligation to agree binds a reader to the arguments as she can judge them now, not forever.
questions.explain: The obligation rests on her inability to support any of the first three remarks. If new knowledge supplies support later, the obligation lifts on that point.
questions.rule: Agreement answers the case as it stands.
questions.teaches: The obligation to agree is tied to the state of the evidence: it binds you to the arguments as they stand, and later knowledge that supports a charge of being uninformed or misinformed reopens the question.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A scientist checks a rival lab's study that contradicts her hypothesis. She finds the data sound and the analysis valid. By analogy with the authors' point, what should she do?
options: Accept the study's result, since she can find no fault in it
Keep her hypothesis, since one study cannot outweigh her own work
Ignore the study until her own lab repeats it with her methods
Reject the study, since its result runs against her careful theory
optionExplain: Right: sound evidence and valid reasoning compel acceptance, even against her view.
Her own work counts, but unless she can fault the study, she cannot reject it.
Repetition is useful, but ignoring the result until then dodges the verdict.
Clashing with her theory is not a fault in the study.
questions.explain: By analogy, a researcher who can find no fault in data or analysis is bound to accept the result. That is how evidence changes minds.
questions.rule: Can't fault it? Accept it.
questions.teaches: By analogy, in science a researcher who can find no fault in a study's data or analysis is bound to accept its result, even against her own hypothesis; that obligation is what lets evidence change minds.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A reader says: I can find nothing wrong with your premises or your reasoning, but I do not agree with your conclusion. According to the authors, what is he really expressing?
options: A disagreement he has not yet put into words
Dislike of the conclusion, not disagreement
A reasonable suspension of judgment
A fair criticism of the book's completeness
optionExplain: If he could put it into words, it would be a criticism; as stated, it is not.
Right: the authors say all he can mean is that he does not like the conclusion.
Suspension responds to incompleteness, not to finding no fault at all.
He makes no charge about what the book leaves undone.
questions.explain: Rejecting a conclusion while admitting no fault in its grounds is an expression of emotion or prejudice. The card next draws the consequences.
questions.rule: No fault in the grounds, no disagreement with the conclusion.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: According to the authors, which responses are open to a reader who can find no fault in an author's premises or reasoning?
options: Admit that he has been convinced
Disagree with the conclusion all the same
Ask whether he really understood the book
Treat his dislike as a ground for rejecting the book
Reject the conclusion as a matter of personal privilege
optionExplain: Right: if convinced, he should admit it.
That is the dislike the authors rule out.
Right: honest lingering doubt suggests he may not have understood.
Dislike is emotion, not a ground.
The authors deny that agreement is a privilege to grant or withhold.
questions.explain: Either he admits he is convinced, or, if honestly unconvinced, he reconsiders whether he understood.
questions.rule: Admit conviction, or recheck understanding.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reader who cannot fault a book's premises or reasoning but still honestly feels unconvinced should ask whether she really understood it.
questions.explain: The authors suggest that honest doubt without a supported criticism may mean the reader should not have said she understood. Rechecking is the honest course.
questions.rule: Doubt without grounds: recheck understanding.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A reader reasons: (1) I understand the book. (2) I can fault none of its premises. (3) I can fault none of its steps. (4) So I may still reject its conclusion, since my verdict is my own. Which step is the error?
options: Step 1, since no reader fully understands a book
Step 2, since every book has some faulty premise
Step 3, since valid steps can still mislead
Step 4, since sound grounds compel the conclusion
optionExplain: Understanding can be good enough to judge; the authors assume a reader can reach it.
Not every book has a faulty premise; this one, she finds, does not.
Valid steps from sound premises do not mislead.
Right: with no supported fault, the authors say she must agree.
questions.explain: Steps 1 to 3 leave nothing to disagree with. Calling the verdict her own does not license rejecting a conclusion she cannot fault.
questions.rule: Your verdict is your own, but it must follow the grounds.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Why might admitting you have been convinced be a mark of a good reader rather than a defeat?
options: Because it shows the book has changed what you understand and believe
Because it ends the reading quickly and saves time for other books
Because authors appreciate readers who agree with them in public
Because it avoids conflict with other readers who admire the book and its author
optionExplain: Right: being moved by argument is the purpose of reading to learn.
Saving time is not the reason; agreement is no shortcut.
The author's pleasure is not what makes it creditable.
Avoiding conflict would be agreeing for the wrong reason.
questions.explain: Reading for understanding aims at learning from the author. Conceding to a sound argument is that learning taking place.
questions.rule: Conceding to good argument is learning.
questions.teaches: Admitting you have been convinced is part of reading well, not a loss: reading to understand aims at being changed by sound argument, and a reader who never concedes has stopped learning from books.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A voter studies a policy and can find no fault in its evidence or reasoning, but rejects it because a party she opposes proposed it. By analogy with the authors' point, what is her rejection?
options: A reasoned disagreement, since parties have track records
A suspension of judgment pending more evidence
Dislike of the source, not disagreement with the policy
A fair criticism, since motives matter in politics
optionExplain: A track record might prompt a closer look, but she found no fault in this case.
She has not suspended judgment; she has rejected the policy.
Right: the source is not a premise; rejecting on that basis is dislike.
Motives may matter elsewhere, but she found no fault in the policy itself.
questions.explain: Like rejecting a conclusion whose grounds you cannot fault, rejecting a sound policy for its source expresses prejudice, not a judgment of the policy.
questions.rule: Judge the case, not who made it.
questions.teaches: By analogy, rejecting a proposal because of who made it, while finding no fault in its evidence or reasoning, is prejudice about the source rather than disagreement with the proposal.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, saying that a book is incomplete is a worthwhile criticism by itself, since few books cover everything.
questions.explain: Anyone can say it of any book, so the bare remark adds nothing. The card next says what turns it into a real criticism.
questions.rule: Incomplete needs specifics to mean anything.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Which of these, according to the authors, can make an author's analysis incomplete?
options: He has not solved all the problems he started with
He has not seen all the implications of his materials
He uses technical terms that some readers do not know
He has failed to make distinctions relevant to his task
He writes about a subject that later authors also treated
optionExplain: Right: unsolved original problems are one form of incompleteness.
Right: missing implications and ramifications is another.
Unfamiliar terms are a matter of reading difficulty, not completeness.
Right: failing to make relevant distinctions is a third.
Later treatment of a subject does not show this book left its task undone.
questions.explain: The forms of incompleteness all concern the author's task: problems unsolved, materials underused, implications unseen, distinctions not made.
questions.rule: Incompleteness is measured against the task.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A book sets out to explain how cities can cut traffic deaths. It covers drivers and road design but says nothing about cyclists, though they make up a third of the deaths. Which criticism follows the authors' view?
options: The book is incomplete, as all books are in some way
It is illogical, since its conclusions about road deaths leave out the cyclists
It is misinformed about the causes of traffic deaths
It leaves unsolved part of its own problem, the cyclist deaths
optionExplain: True of every book, so it says nothing in particular.
Its reasoning about what it covers may be valid; the gap is in scope.
It asserts nothing false about cyclists; it says nothing about them.
Right: it names the exact part of the author's own problem left undone.
questions.explain: A precise charge names which part of the author's own task is unfinished. Cyclist deaths are part of the problem he set himself.
questions.rule: Name the unfinished part of the author's task.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A book sets out to explain how bread rises. Sort each omission by whether it supports a charge of incompleteness.
questions.explain: Incompleteness is measured against the author's own problem. Omitting what that problem does not require is a choice of scope, not a failure to finish.
questions.rule: Outside the task is not incomplete.

items.t: The role of yeast in producing gas
The history of bakeries in medieval towns
How gluten traps the gas in the dough
The price of flour in different countries
Why dough rises more slowly when cold

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: The authors say that to a Christian who believes in personal immortality, Epictetus's account of happiness is incomplete. What does this example show about the charge?
options: That the charge can only come from religious readers
That Epictetus was misinformed about the nature of happiness
That it may depend on the reader's own view, and should say so
That any account of happiness will seem incomplete to some reader or other
optionExplain: The example uses a religious reader, but the point is about standpoint generally.
The charge is incompleteness, not a false assertion.
Right: what counts as missing can rest on the reader's beliefs, and a fair charge states them.
That would make the charge empty, the very thing the card warns against.
questions.explain: Here the missing element is one the reader believes in and the author does not treat. Such a charge rests on the reader's standpoint, which should be made explicit.
questions.rule: State the standpoint behind the charge.
questions.teaches: A charge of incompleteness can rest on the reader's own convictions, as in the authors' Epictetus example: what looks missing depends on what the reader believes belongs in the account, so a fair charge says from which standpoint it is made.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A laptop review says in its opening that it will test battery life, screen and keyboard. It tests the battery and screen only. A reader complains it ignored the speakers. By analogy, which complaint about completeness holds?
options: The keyboard, since the review promised it and did not test it
The speakers, since a full review should cover every feature
Both, since any untested feature makes a review incomplete
Neither, since reviewers may test whatever they choose
optionExplain: Right: the keyboard was part of the task the review chose and left undone.
The review never set out to test speakers; that was outside its task.
Only features within the task count; the speakers were not.
Choice of scope is allowed, but the review chose the keyboard and did not test it.
questions.explain: By analogy with the card, completeness is judged against the task the reviewer announced. Announcing the tests also protects the reviewer: he can be faulted for the skipped keyboard, but not for speakers he never promised.
questions.rule: A stated task both binds and protects.
questions.teaches: A stated plan cuts both ways: announcing what a work will do commits the author to it and exposes gaps, but it also shields him from charges about what he never set out to do.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A reader finds a book sound in everything it argues but leaving one of its main problems unsolved. According to the authors, what is the fitting verdict?
options: Disagree, since an unsolved main problem defeats the book
Suspend judgment on every part until the gap is filled
Agree with all of it, since what it argues is sound
Agree in part, and suspend judgment on the whole
optionExplain: Incompleteness is not, strictly, a ground for disagreement.
The sound parts must be accepted; suspension is for the whole.
Full agreement ignores the unsolved problem.
Right: accept what is shown; hold back on the whole.
questions.explain: What the book shows soundly is accepted. Its incompleteness affects only the verdict on the whole. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Sound but incomplete: agree in part, suspend on the whole.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the charge that a book is incomplete is not, strictly speaking, a basis for any disagreement with it.
questions.explain: It is adverse only in marking the limits of what the author achieved. Disagreement needs one of the first three remarks.
questions.rule: Incomplete marks limits; it does not refute.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A book on food waste argues soundly about households and restaurants, but its promised chapter on farms is missing. The reader should agree with the parts on households and restaurants and ____ judgment on the whole.
questions.explain: The sound parts compel agreement. The missing chapter leaves the whole unestablished, so the verdict on it waits.
questions.rule: Accept the parts; wait on the whole.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A reader agreed with a food-waste book's sections on households and restaurants and suspended judgment on the whole. Suppose she now shows that its figures on restaurant waste are false and its restaurant conclusions rest on them. How does her verdict change?
options: It stays the same, since incompleteness already decided it
She may now disagree on the restaurant conclusions, on that ground
She must now reject the whole book, including households
She must suspend judgment on the households part as well, since one error taints it
optionExplain: A new supported charge of misinformation changes the verdict on that point.
Right: a supported charge of misinformation grounds disagreement where it applies.
The household argument is untouched by the restaurant figures.
The households part still stands on its own grounds.
questions.explain: Incompleteness alone leads to suspension. A supported charge of misinformation, where it applies, grounds disagreement on that point.
questions.rule: Disagree where a first-three charge applies.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: By the authors' logic, suspended judgment on an incomplete book can be lifted if another work later fills the missing part soundly.
questions.explain: Suspension responds to a task left undone. If the gap is filled, the reason for holding back on the whole is answered.
questions.rule: Suspension waits on the missing part.
questions.teaches: Suspended judgment is provisional: it waits on the part left undone, so when another work fills the gap soundly the verdict on the whole can be given.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A drug was tested thoroughly in adults and worked well; it has not been tested in children. By analogy with the authors' point, what should a careful doctor conclude?
options: It works for adults; judgment on children is suspended
It works for everyone, since the trial found no problems
It should not be trusted, since the trial is incomplete
It probably works for children too, being the same drug
optionExplain: Right: agree within the evidence, suspend beyond it.
The trial says nothing about children; extending it is unwarranted.
Incompleteness does not undo what was shown for adults.
Children may respond differently; the evidence does not cover them.
questions.explain: By analogy, the trial supports agreement for the cases it covered and suspended judgment for those it did not. Naming the uncovered group also says exactly what study is needed next.
questions.rule: Suspension names the missing evidence.
questions.teaches: Suspended judgment points to the next inquiry: by naming exactly what the evidence does not cover, it says what study or reading would settle the question.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Two books on the same economic question are both free of errors and reason well. According to the authors, what makes the deepest comparison between them?
options: Which one makes more valid and significant distinctions
Which one is more recent and cites newer research
Which one is clearer and easier for a beginner to read
Which one has been praised by more reviewers in the field
optionExplain: Right: completeness, measured by valid and significant distinctions, is the profoundest comparison.
Recency may matter for information, but it is not the measure the authors name.
Clarity matters, but it is not the authors' measure of the deepest comparison.
Praise is not one of the four criteria.
questions.explain: Beyond truth and logic, the authors measure completeness by distinctions. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: The deepest comparison counts valid distinctions.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: According to the authors, the number of distinct terms in an account is correlative with the number of ____ it makes.
questions.explain: Each distinction needs its own term. That is why coming to terms with an author pays off when you compare books.
questions.rule: Distinct terms mark distinctions.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Two books on sleep both get the facts right. One treats all sleep as one state; the other separates deep sleep, dream sleep and light sleep and shows each has different effects. By the authors' view, which account is more complete?
options: The second, for its more valid and significant distinctions
The first, since a simpler account is easier to check
Neither, since both are free of factual errors
The first, since extra distinctions only complicate the subject
optionExplain: Right: it draws real distinctions that make a difference to the subject.
Ease of checking is not the measure of completeness.
Being error-free is the same for both; completeness separates them.
These distinctions are significant, since the states have different effects.
questions.explain: Both are sound, so completeness decides. The second makes distinctions that are valid and matter.
questions.rule: More valid, significant distinctions, more complete.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: A book that introduces many new labels for small differences that do not matter to its subject is more complete than one with fewer, significant distinctions.
questions.explain: Only valid and significant distinctions count. Labels for differences that make no difference add terms without adding completeness.
questions.rule: Count significant distinctions, not labels.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A reader compares a short book on the causes of the 2008 crash with a long survey of all economic history, and counts more distinctions in the survey. What is wrong with concluding that the survey is more complete?
options: Nothing, since more distinctions always means more complete
They answer different problems, so the counts are not comparable
Short books are better at making distinctions than long ones
Surveys borrow their distinctions, so they should not be counted
optionExplain: The count only means something between accounts of the same subject.
Right: completeness is relative to a task, so the books must share the problem.
Length is not the issue; matching the problem is.
Borrowed or not, a valid distinction counts; the problem is the mismatch.
questions.explain: The comparison applies to related books in the same field treating the same subject. A survey and a focused study set different tasks.
questions.rule: Compare like problems with like.
questions.teaches: Comparing books by completeness requires matched tasks: a focused study and a broad survey answer different problems, so counting their distinctions side by side misleads unless both treat the same question.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A birdwatcher compares two field guides for her region. One lumps three similar warblers under one entry; the other separates them by song and wing bars. By analogy with the authors' point, which guide is more complete for her purpose?
options: The first, since fewer entries make it quicker to use
The first, since experts still disagree on how finely warblers should be split
Neither, since field guides are judged by their pictures
The second, since it draws distinctions she can act on in the field
optionExplain: Speed of use is a convenience, not completeness for identifying birds.
Some disputes exist, but these distinctions are drawn on observable features.
Pictures help, but the comparison here is about the distinctions drawn.
Right: valid, significant distinctions are what let her tell the birds apart.
questions.explain: By analogy, a guide's completeness shows in the significant distinctions it supports. Separating look-alike species is what an identification guide is for.
questions.rule: Completeness shows in usable distinctions.
questions.teaches: By analogy, in practical guides completeness shows as distinctions a user can act on: a guide that separates look-alike cases serves its purpose better than one that lumps them.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: A charge that a book is incomplete looks back to an earlier step of analytical reading. Which one?
options: Classifying the book by kind
Skimming the table of contents
Finding the key words of the book
Listing problems and solutions
optionExplain: Classification matters, but completeness is measured against problems and solutions.
Skimming is inspectional; completeness rests on analytical steps.
Terms matter for comparing distinctions, but not as the measure of the task.
Right: completeness is judged against the problems stated and the solutions found.
questions.explain: Completeness asks how well the author stated and solved his problems. The card next shows how the stages connect.
questions.rule: Completeness looks back to problems and solutions.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Match each stage of analytical reading with its last step.
pairs: Know the problems the author tries to solve
Know which problems he solved and which not
Judge the completeness of his analysis
questions.explain: Each stage ends on the author's problems: stating them, checking their solutions, and judging how adequately both were done.
questions.rule: Each stage ends on the problems.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: Interpreting a book on water policy, a reader marked two of its three problems solved and one unsolved and unadmitted. Now judging completeness, what does she ask?
options: Whether the author is a recognised expert on water policy
Whether the book's facts were up to date when it was published
Whether the book's tone was fair to the authorities it criticised
Whether the problems were well stated and the gap matters
optionExplain: Expertise is about the author, not the adequacy of his work.
Currency of facts is a question for the charge of being uninformed.
Tone is not part of the completeness judgment.
Right: completeness looks at the statement of problems and their solutions.
questions.explain: Completeness touches outlining (were the problems well stated?) and interpretation (how far were they solved?). Her notes from both feed the judgment.
questions.rule: Ask how well the problems were stated and solved.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: True or false: A reader who skipped stating the author's problems while outlining can still fairly charge the book with incompleteness.
questions.explain: Completeness is measured against the author's problems. Without a statement of them, the reader has nothing to measure the book's achievement against.
questions.rule: No list of problems, no measure of completeness.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.q: The authors say completeness also asks how adequately the author stated his problems. How can a book that solves every problem it states still be incomplete?
options: It cannot, since solving every stated problem is completeness itself
Its readers may want it to cover topics it never meant to treat
Its problems may have been framed too narrowly for the task it chose
Its solutions may have been reached by reasoning that is invalid
optionExplain: The card says completeness also judges how well the problems were stated.
Wishes for other topics fall outside the author's task.
Right: a task stated too narrowly leaves out what the undertaking needed.
Invalid reasoning is the charge of illogic, not incompleteness.
questions.explain: Completeness has two sides: how well the problems were stated and how far they were solved. A well-solved but badly framed set of problems can still fall short of the undertaking.
questions.rule: Check the framing as well as the solving.
questions.teaches: A book can solve every problem it states and still be incomplete, if the problems were framed too narrowly for its undertaking; completeness judges the framing as well as the solving.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
