questions.q: A team reviews a finished project. By analogy with the authors' point, what should the review start from?
options: The goals, which were met, and whether they were right
The final results, judged by how impressive they look
The opinions of the people who worked hardest on it
The budget, since a project within budget is complete
optionExplain: Right: like the three stages, it moves from stated problems to solutions to their adequacy.
Without the goals, there is nothing to measure the results against.
Effort is not a measure of whether the task was done.
Budget is one constraint; it says nothing about whether the goals were met.
questions.explain: By analogy, a review judges completeness against the stated goals, checks which were met, and asks whether the goals were well framed. Without the original goals on record, the goals tend to be restated afterwards to fit the results.
questions.rule: Record the goals before judging the results.
questions.teaches: When the original problems were never recorded, reviewers tend to restate the goals after the fact to fit what was achieved, which hides incompleteness; that is a practical reason to state problems early.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: How many rules do the authors give for the third stage of analytical reading, criticism?
options: Four: one for each adverse remark
Seven: three maxims and four criteria
Three: one for each ideal condition
Eight: four maxims and four criteria
optionExplain: The four remarks are only the criteria; three maxims come first.
Right: rules 9 to 15, three maxims of etiquette and four criteria.
The three ideal conditions are not the numbered rules.
There are three maxims, not four.
questions.explain: The third stage has seven rules. The card next lists them in their two groups.
questions.rule: Third stage: three maxims, four criteria.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Sort each rule into its group.

items.t: Do not begin criticism until you can say I understand
Show wherein the author is misinformed
Do not disagree disputatiously or contentiously
Show wherein the author is illogical
Give good reasons for any critical judgment
Show wherein the analysis is incomplete

questions.explain: The maxims govern how you conduct criticism; the criteria name the points you can make.
questions.rule: Maxims for conduct, criteria for content.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: A reader halfway through a book on nutrition posts a long rebuttal of it online. Which rule of the third stage has she broken first?
options: Rule 12: show wherein the author is uninformed
Rule 9: understand the book before criticizing it
Rule 15: show wherein the analysis is incomplete
Rule 11: give good reasons for any critical judgment
optionExplain: This is a criterion she might later use; it is not what she has broken.
Right: she has not finished understanding the book, so criticism is premature.
The same: a criterion, not the maxim she has broken first.
She may also lack reasons, but she has broken Rule 9 before that.
questions.explain: Rule 9 comes first: no criticism before outline and interpretation are complete. Halfway through, she cannot yet say I understand.
questions.rule: Rule 9 first: understand before criticizing.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: A reviewer is courteous, waits until she understands, and gives reasons, but her only complaint is that the author's conclusion is unwelcome. What does the authors' grouping reveal?
options: Her review is sound, since it follows all three maxims
Her review is incomplete, which is the fourth criterion
She has broken the maxims, since an unwelcome conclusion is not a good reason
She has followed the maxims but offers none of the criteria
optionExplain: Following the maxims governs conduct; it does not supply grounds.
The incompleteness criterion is about the book, not her review.
Her conduct is fine; the problem is the content of her complaint.
Right: good conduct with no criterion means no grounds for disagreement.
questions.explain: The maxims and the criteria do different jobs. Perfect manners with no criterion leaves a disagreement without grounds.
questions.rule: Good manners do not supply grounds.
questions.teaches: The maxims and the criteria are separable: a review can follow every maxim and still make no criterion-based point, or make valid points contentiously, so a good criticism needs both conduct and grounds.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: True or false: If a reader can support none of rules 12 to 14 on a book but can support rule 15, the rules let her disagree with the book as a whole.
questions.explain: Only rules 12 to 14 are criteria for disagreement. With rule 15 alone, she must agree at least in part and may suspend judgment on the whole.
questions.rule: Rule 15 alone: suspend, not disagree.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: A lawyer prepares to answer an opposing brief. By analogy with the three stages, which plan is soundest?
options: Draft the rebuttal first, then read the brief to find support for it
Attack every claim in the brief, since any concession weakens her case
Map the brief and its reasoning, then attack only where it fails
Focus on the opposing lawyer's past losses to cast doubt on the brief
optionExplain: A rebuttal drafted first risks attacking claims the brief never made.
Attacking everything ignores the duty to grant what cannot be faulted.
Right: structure, then interpretation, then criticism on the four criteria.
This attacks the person, not the brief.
questions.explain: By analogy, the three stages fit any adversarial reading: understand the opposing case fully, then criticize only where it can be shown to fail.
questions.rule: Map, interpret, then attack where it fails.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the three stages fit adversarial reading such as a lawyer studying an opponent's brief: an attack drafted before mapping and interpreting the brief tends to hit claims it never made and to waste force on points that cannot be faulted.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the question Is it true? can be asked of every kind of writing, including poetry.
questions.explain: The authors say it applies to every kind of writing, in one or another sense of truth, poetical included. The card next lists those senses.
questions.rule: Every kind of writing faces the question of truth.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: By which standards do the authors say books should be judged, as against those many reviewers use?
options: Truth
Novelty of approach
Clarity
Sensationalism
Power to enlighten
optionExplain: Right: truth is the highest standard they name.
Novelty is one of the standards they say reviewers wrongly favour.
Right: clarity is on their list.
Sensationalism is one of the standards they deplore.
Right: the power to enlighten is on their list.
questions.explain: The authors set truth, clarity and the power to enlighten against novelty, sensationalism, seductiveness and force.
questions.rule: Truth, clarity, enlightenment.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: A reviewer praises a new book as daring, shocking and impossible to put down, but says nothing about whether its claims hold. According to the authors, what is missing from the review?
options: A judgment of the book's truth
A summary of the book's plot or structure
A comparison with the author's earlier books
An account of the author's life and motives
optionExplain: Right: the review praises force and novelty but never asks whether it is true.
A summary may help, but the authors' complaint is about the standard of judgment.
Comparisons are not the missing standard.
The author's life is not the measure of the book.
questions.explain: The authors say the highest praise is for truth. A review that praises only shock and pace has judged by other standards.
questions.rule: Judge by truth before force.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: If the question of truth applies to mathematics, history and poetry alike, what follows for how a reader asks it?
options: The same test must be applied to all three, so that verdicts can be compared
Only mathematics can be judged, since the others lack proof
The sense of truth, and so the test, must fit the kind of work
Poetry must be judged by whether its events happened
optionExplain: The authors speak of different senses of truth, so one test cannot fit all.
The authors apply the question to all kinds, not only to proofs.
Right: a proof, a history and a poem are true in different senses.
That applies the historical sense to poetry, the mismatch to avoid.
questions.explain: The authors name several senses of truth. By extension, each kind of work is tested in its own sense: steps for a proof, evidence for a history, a different kind of truth for a poem, taken up later in the book.
questions.rule: Fit the test of truth to the kind of work.
questions.teaches: Because truth has several senses, the test must fit the work: by extension, a proof is checked by its steps and a history by its evidence, while a poem's truth is of another kind that the authors take up later.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: True or false: The authors present their complaint about reviewers favouring novelty and sensation as a proven fact about all recent books.
questions.explain: It is their judgment of the reading culture of their time, offered as a lament and even a guess about what would follow. A reader can weigh it like any other opinion with reasons.
questions.rule: Separate the authors' standard from their lament.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: A health claim goes viral, shared a million times in a day. By analogy with the authors' point, what does its spread tell you about whether it is true?
options: That it is probably true, since so many people found it convincing
That it is true for those who shared it, which is what matters
That it is probably false, since viral claims are usually wrong
Little, since sharing rewards novelty and force rather than truth
optionExplain: Many shares show appeal, not that the claim has been checked.
Truth is not relative to who shares a claim.
Spread does not show falsehood either; the claim must be checked.
Right: popularity measures the qualities the authors set apart from truth.
questions.explain: By analogy, shares reward the novelty and force the authors distinguish from truth. The claim has to be tested on its evidence.
questions.rule: Popularity is not evidence.
questions.teaches: By analogy, measures of attention such as shares and clicks track a piece's novelty and force, the qualities the authors set apart from truth, so popularity is no evidence that a claim is accurate.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: A digest of the year's science news presents twenty findings. According to the authors, what has the digest already done besides reporting facts?
options: Selected the facts by some judgment of their significance
Checked each finding against the original studies before including it
Removed any interpretation, leaving the bare facts
Arranged the findings in order of when they appeared
optionExplain: Right: a digest must select by some principle of interpretation.
Checking is possible, but the authors' point is about selection.
The authors say facts seldom come without interpretation, and digests least of all.
Order of appearance may be used, but choosing which twenty is already a judgment.
questions.explain: Choosing which facts to include already judges what matters. The card next explains why that makes What of it? unavoidable.
questions.rule: Selecting facts is interpreting them.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the question What of it? arises only if what you have read is true in some sense.
questions.explain: Unless what you read is true in some sense, the authors say you need go no further. If it is, you must face the last question.
questions.rule: Truth first, then significance.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: A newspaper's page on crime lists five stabbings in a month and no other figures. The reports are accurate. Which steps fit a reader asking what significance these facts have?
questions.explain: The facts are true, so the reader goes on to significance. Part of that is noticing the significance already implied by the selection.
questions.rule: Ask what the selection implies.
options: Ask what principle chose these facts for the page
Compare them with figures for other months and places
Conclude that crime is rising, as the facts are accurate
Dismiss the page, since selected facts are untrustworthy
Adopt the paper's implied view, as it has better sources
optionExplain: Right: the selection implies a significance that must be weighed.
Right: significance needs context the selection left out.
Accurate facts can carry a misleading significance; rising needs comparison.
The facts are accurate; the task is to judge what they mean.
Better sources do not settle what significance the facts should carry.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Why does asking what principle chose a set of facts help a reader decide their significance for herself?
options: It shows whether the facts themselves are accurate
It reveals whether the writer can be trusted in general
It separates the facts from the verdict built into them
It tells her which facts she can safely forget
optionExplain: Accuracy is checked by evidence; selection is a different matter.
General trust is about the writer, not the meaning of these facts.
Right: once the selector's judgment is visible, she can make her own.
Forgetting is not the aim; weighing is.
questions.explain: Facts arrive with a significance built in by whoever chose them. Seeing the principle lets her separate the two and attach her own judgment.
questions.rule: Separate the facts from the chooser's verdict.
questions.teaches: Naming the principle that selected a set of facts separates the facts from the significance already attached to them, which frees the reader to weigh them herself rather than inherit the selector's judgment.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: True or false: Once a reader has settled what a book's facts signify, the question What of it? is finished for good.
questions.explain: In reading for enlightenment, the authors say the inquiry has no end: What of it? is renewed at every stage of learning.
questions.rule: Significance keeps growing with learning.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: A manager's weekly dashboard shows sales, website visits and new sign-ups, but not customer complaints. All figures are accurate. By analogy with the authors' point, what should she ask?
options: Whether the figures are correct, since accuracy is all that matters
How to raise the shown figures, since they are what the firm tracks
Whether to replace the dashboard, since selection makes it biased
Why these measures were chosen and what that choice implies matters
optionExplain: They are accurate; the open question is their significance.
Chasing the chosen figures accepts the built-in judgment without asking.
Every dashboard selects; the point is to see the principle, not discard it.
Right: the choice of measures carries a judgment of what matters.
questions.explain: By analogy with a digest, a dashboard selects facts by some judgment of significance. Reading it intelligently means seeing that judgment.
questions.rule: Ask why these measures were chosen.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any dashboard or report built from chosen measures carries a judgment of what matters, and reading it intelligently means asking what was left out as well as what the figures show.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: According to the authors, why would interpretation be unnecessary if language were perfect?
options: Because the words would show the meaning plainly
Because readers would agree with everything they read
Because books would no longer need any structure
Because authors would make no errors of fact
optionExplain: Right: interpretation answers the opacity of language.
A clear meaning can still be disputed; agreement is a separate matter.
Structure answers complexity, not imperfect language.
Errors of fact answer to criticism, not interpretation.
questions.explain: Interpretation is needed because language is a relatively opaque medium. The card next matches each stage to a feature of communication.
questions.rule: Interpretation answers opaque language.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Match each feature of human communication with the stage of reading it makes necessary.
pairs: Language is a relatively opaque medium
Error and ignorance limit truth and knowledge
questions.explain: Each obligation of the reader answers a feature of discourse: complexity, opacity, error, and the gap between information and understanding.
questions.rule: Each stage answers a feature of communication.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: A reader faces a long, carefully argued report written in clear, plain language by a source with a mixed record of accuracy. Where should most of her effort go?
options: Outlining and criticism, since it is long and the source is uneven
Interpretation, since every text is hard to interpret
None of the stages, since clear language from a source means it can be trusted
Seeking significance, since that is always the hardest question
optionExplain: Right: length calls for outlining, and an uneven record calls for criticism.
Its language is plain, so interpretation will take less work here.
Clarity eases interpretation but does nothing about errors.
Significance comes after the earlier questions are answered.
questions.explain: The features that call for each stage are present in different degrees. This report is complex and possibly in error, but not opaque.
questions.rule: Spend effort where the text's difficulties lie.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: True or false: By the authors' logic, a short memo in plain words still calls for criticism if its author might be mistaken.
questions.explain: Brevity and plain words reduce the work of outlining and interpretation. They do nothing about error, so the need for criticism remains.
questions.rule: Simple and clear does not mean true.
questions.teaches: Because each stage answers a different feature of communication, the amount of work per stage varies with the text: a short, plain memo needs little outlining or interpretation but as much criticism if its author can be wrong.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: Suppose a text were written in a perfectly clear language but its author were often mistaken. Which stage of reading could the reader largely drop?
options: Criticism, since a clear text can be taken at its word
Interpretation, since the meaning would be plain
Outlining, since clarity removes complexity
None, since every stage is needed equally for any text
optionExplain: Errors remain, so criticism is still needed.
Right: perfect language would remove the need for interpretation.
Clarity of language does not make a long argument simple.
The stages answer different features; removing one feature removes one need.
questions.explain: The authors tie interpretation to the opacity of language. Remove that and interpretation shrinks, while criticism still answers to error.
questions.rule: Remove a difficulty, remove its stage.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: A team receives a contract translated from another language. Its structure is simple and the supplier is reliable. By analogy with the authors' point, which stage needs the extra effort?
options: Outlining, since every contract has a complex structure
None, since a reliable supplier means the contract can be signed
Criticism, since a foreign supplier is likely to be wrong
Interpretation, since translation makes the language more opaque
optionExplain: The structure here is simple, so outlining is light.
Reliability does not remove the need to know what the words mean.
Nothing suggests the supplier is wrong; the stated difficulty is language.
Right: translation adds opacity, which is what interpretation answers.
questions.explain: By analogy, the feature that makes this text harder is the language, so the reader's extra effort goes into interpreting key terms.
questions.rule: Match the effort to the difficulty.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a translated document raises the opacity of language, so its extra reading effort belongs to interpretation, such as checking how key terms were rendered, before criticism of what it says.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: According to the authors, how many people have read books in the ideal way their rules describe?
options: Few people, and those few have read few books that way
Most serious readers, given enough time and a good set of rules
Only professional scholars in their own fields
Most great writers, who read everything of their day
optionExplain: Right: the rules describe an ideal that is rarely met.
The authors say few, not most, have done it.
The authors do not limit it to scholars.
Great writers often read fewer books, but read them well.
questions.explain: The rules describe an ideal performance. The card next explains why an ideal rarely met still matters.
questions.rule: The rules describe an ideal.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: The authors quote Hobbes as saying that if he read as many books as most men do, he would be as ____ as they are.
questions.explain: Hobbes's remark makes the authors' point: being well-read is about the quality of reading, not the number of books.
questions.rule: Well-read means read well.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: A student has a semester and a list of forty recommended books on political thought. Following the authors, what is the best plan?
options: Inspect all forty, then read a few of the best analytically
Read all forty quickly, so she knows something of each
Pick the five shortest, so she can finish them carefully
Read summaries of all forty and skip the books themselves
optionExplain: Right: inspection sorts them, and the few that merit it get full reading.
Superficial acquaintance with many is what the authors warn against.
Length is not merit; the shortest may not deserve close reading.
Summaries are not reading the books at all.
questions.explain: Reading by merits means inspecting widely and reading well the books that deserve it. Quantity without quality is what the authors deplore.
questions.rule: Inspect many, read few well.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: How does skill at inspectional reading serve the ideal of analytical reading, given the authors' point?
options: It replaces analytical reading for most books worth reading well
It lets a reader skip the analytical rules for books already familiar
It sorts books by merit, freeing time for those that deserve it
It counts toward being well-read by raising the number of books read
optionExplain: For books worth reading well, inspection prepares; it does not replace.
Familiarity is not understanding; the rules still apply.
Right: inspection decides what deserves full effort, which makes that effort possible.
The authors judge well-read by quality, not by count.
questions.explain: Most books should only be inspected. Doing that well is what lets a reader give the few deserving books the full treatment.
questions.rule: Good inspection buys time for analytical reading.
questions.teaches: Reading by merits makes inspection part of the ideal, not a lesser substitute: deciding quickly which books deserve full reading is what frees the time to read those few as the rules require.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reader who falls short of the ideal described by the rules is not a good reader.
questions.explain: The authors say you are a good reader to the degree you approach the ideal. Falling short is normal; the ideal is a measure, not a pass mark.
questions.rule: Good is a matter of degree.

questions.unitTitle: Agreeing or Disagreeing with an Author
questions.section: The Third Stage of Analytical Reading
questions.q: A violin student can either sight-read fifty pieces once this term or master five pieces thoroughly. By analogy with the authors' point, which choice builds more skill?
options: Sight-reading fifty, since breadth exposes her to more styles and composers
Splitting time equally, since both approaches count the same
Neither, since skill depends on talent more than practice
Mastering five, since deep work on a few builds the skill itself
optionExplain: Breadth has value, but the card's analogy favours depth for building skill.
The card holds that depth on the deserving few counts for more.
The card treats skill as something you approach by practice.
Right: like reading one book well, mastering a few pieces develops the skill.
questions.explain: By analogy, the ideal is approached by applying the full method to a single work, not by passing quickly over many.
questions.rule: Depth on a few builds skill.
questions.teaches: By analogy, in learning any skill, deep work on a few examples builds more ability than a quick pass over many, as a musician learns more from mastering a few pieces than from sight-reading many.

questions.q: A reader looks up an unfamiliar word in a dictionary while reading a history of Rome. In the authors' terms, what kind of reading is the look-up?
options: Extrinsic, since the dictionary is outside the book
Intrinsic reading, since it serves the book being read
Inspectional reading, since it is a quick look-up
Syntopical reading, since two books are in use at once
optionExplain: Right: any aid lying outside the book being read is extrinsic, whatever its purpose.
The look-up does serve the book, but what makes reading intrinsic is that it stays within the book itself.
Speed is not the test; inspectional reading is about skimming a book, not consulting another one.
Syntopical reading compares several books on one subject; a dictionary consulted for a word is an aid, not a second book on Rome.
questions.explain: The dividing line is whether the help comes from inside the book or from outside it. The card next draws that line.
questions.rule: An aid from outside the book makes the reading extrinsic.

questions.q: The authors call reading a book in itself, apart from all other books, ____ reading.
questions.explain: Intrinsic reading stays within the book; extrinsic reading reads it in the light of other books and outside sources.
questions.rule: Intrinsic means within the book.

questions.q: A reader is working on a treatise about city planning. Sort each activity by the kind of reading it belongs to.
groups: Extrinsic: drawing on something outside it

items.t: Outlining the treatise from its own headings and text
Working out a key term from how the author uses it
Restating the main argument in her own words
Checking a date in an encyclopedia
Comparing the treatise with an earlier work it replies to
Reading a scholar's essay about the treatise
Recalling the traffic in her own town to test a claim

questions.explain: Outlining, finding terms and restating work on the book itself. Encyclopedias, other books, commentaries and your own experience all come from outside the book, so using them is extrinsic.
questions.rule: Ask where the help comes from: the book or outside it.

questions.q: True or false: A reader who goes back to an earlier chapter of the same book to make sense of a later one has moved to extrinsic reading.
questions.explain: The whole book is the context for each of its parts, so using one chapter to read another stays within the book. Reading becomes extrinsic only when the help comes from outside it.
questions.rule: Using the book to read the book is still intrinsic.

questions.q: Suppose a reader concludes that because a commentary is an extrinsic aid, consulting one at any stage would betray the authors' method. What is wrong with this conclusion?
options: The method forbids dictionaries but allows commentaries
Extrinsic aids can help and are sometimes needed
A commentary counts as intrinsic once you own the book
Extrinsic aids belong to inspectional reading only
optionExplain: The method treats both as outside aids with a proper time and place; neither is singled out as forbidden.
Right: the authors held aids back to teach intrinsic reading first, not to ban them; for some books they are needed for full understanding.
Ownership does not change where the help comes from; a commentary is still another writer's work about the book.
Aids serve analytical reading too; nothing in the method confines them to skimming.
questions.explain: Calling an aid extrinsic describes its source, not its value. The authors say outside help can be useful and sometimes necessary.
questions.rule: Extrinsic is a description, not a ban.

questions.q: A judge must decide what a disputed clause in a lease means. Which approach mirrors the order of intrinsic reading before extrinsic reading?
options: Ask the two parties what they meant, then read the lease
Look up each word of the clause in a legal dictionary first
Check how other courts read similar clauses, then read this lease
Study the whole lease for the clause's meaning, then outside evidence
optionExplain: The parties' accounts are outside evidence, and each side may describe the clause to suit itself; starting there reverses the order.
A dictionary is an outside aid; consulting it word by word before reading the whole document breaks the clause away from its context.
Other cases may help later, but reading them first lets other documents shape your view of this one before you have read it.
Right: the document as a whole is the first context for any clause; outside evidence comes in for what the text leaves unclear.
questions.explain: Intrinsic-first means working from the text as a whole before going outside it. The same order appears in how lawyers read documents.
questions.rule: Read the text as a whole before going outside it.
questions.teaches: By analogy, courts often read a contract first within its own four corners and admit outside evidence of what it means only when the text alone leaves the meaning unclear.

questions.q: True or false: Even a careful reader brings what she already knows from life and from other books to every book she reads.
questions.explain: What you already know enters your reading whether you intend it or not. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: You cannot switch off what you already know.

questions.q: The authors point out that no one starts a reading career by reading ____; we have all read other books first.
questions.explain: Every reader comes to analytical reading with earlier reading behind them, so earlier books shape how any new book is read.
questions.rule: Every reader arrives with earlier reading.

questions.q: Reading an article claiming that working from home lowers stress by ending the daily commute, a reader thinks of her own two-hour commute. What is she doing?
options: Leaving intrinsic reading for an unrelated activity
Reading syntopically, since she uses two sources
Measuring the article's claim against her experience
Making the error of judging before reading on
optionExplain: Her thought bears directly on the article's claim, so it is part of reading it, not a separate activity.
Syntopical reading compares several books on one subject; recalling her own commute is experience, not a second text.
Right: readers measure a writer's statements against what they know from life; she is doing it with a relevant experience.
Relating a claim to experience can help understanding; it becomes an error only if it replaces what the author says.
questions.explain: Bringing life experience to a claim is normal and useful. The skill is to do it deliberately and to notice when a judgment rests on it.
questions.rule: Measure claims against what you know, on purpose.

questions.q: Suppose two equally skilled readers read the same essay on fairness, one widely read in ethics and one who has read little. What do the authors' remarks lead you to expect?
options: The wider reader can test the essay against more of what she knows
The less-read reader will judge better, being free of influence
The wider reader must set her knowledge aside to read intrinsically
Both will reach the same judgment, since they use the same rules
optionExplain: Right: earlier reading is part of what a reader measures an author's statements against, so wider reading gives more to test with.
Having less to measure with is not freedom from bias; it gives the reader less to test the essay against.
The authors do not ask anyone to forget their reading; intrinsic and extrinsic reading fuse in practice.
The rules are the same, but readers measure an author against what they already know, and that differs between them.
questions.explain: Since readers measure an author's statements against other things they know, what they know changes what they can test. Wider reading is an advantage, used with care.
questions.rule: What you already know is part of your equipment.

questions.q: A reader of a history of vaccination rejects the author's account of an early trial because it conflicts with a story his grandfather told him. Which criticisms fit the authors' advice? Select all that apply.
options: He let a belief override the account before understanding it
He should keep every family memory out of his reading
He could treat the story as a question to check, not a verdict
He should have read a commentary before the trial chapter
He was wrong to think about anything outside the book
optionExplain: Right: outside knowledge is a measure; here it replaced the author's account before he had grasped it.
Experience enters reading anyway and can help; the card asks for deliberate use, not a ban.
Right: the story can prompt him to check the author's evidence, which uses experience without letting it rule.
A commentary first would add another outside voice before reading, the opposite of what the method advises.
No book can be read in isolation, so thinking beyond the book is not the fault; the fault is how he used it.
questions.explain: Bringing experience to a book is unavoidable and useful. It goes wrong when an outside belief settles the matter before the author has been understood.
questions.rule: Let outside knowledge test the book, not replace it.

questions.q: A doctor sees one blood test showing slightly high sugar in a patient. How does the authors' point about reading in isolation carry over to her task?
options: Wait for a specialist's commentary before forming a view
Read the result against the patient's history and other findings
Treat the result alone, since each test should stand on its own
Repeat the test until two results agree, then act on them
optionExplain: Waiting for someone else's view first is the habit of leaning on outside help before using her own knowledge.
Right: like a book's claims, a single result is understood by measuring it against everything else she knows about the patient.
Taken alone, one figure is easy to misjudge; it gains its meaning from what else is known.
Repeating the test may help, but it still treats the number in isolation from the rest of the picture.
questions.explain: A reader measures an author's statements against what she knows from many sources, and specialists read single findings the same way. The risk is reversed too: knowledge used to prejudge evidence distorts it.
questions.rule: Read any single piece of evidence in the light of what else you know.
questions.teaches: By analogy, medicine names the danger on the other side: a doctor who settles on a diagnosis early can read every later finding to fit it, so outside knowledge should test new evidence, not decide it in advance.

questions.q: A reader hits a hard passage in a philosophy book. Which first move fits the authors' advice?
options: Find a summary online so as not to misread it
Ask a friend who has read it to explain the passage
Put the book aside for an easier one on the topic
Reread and work on it before looking anything up
optionExplain: A summary feels safe, but reaching for it first skips the effort that builds your own skill.
A friend is outside help too; asking before trying replaces your effort with theirs.
Changing books avoids the difficulty instead of working on it.
Right: the authors want you to do all you can alone before seeking help.
questions.explain: The authors' principle is to do your best alone before seeking outside help. The card next gives their reason.
questions.rule: Try first, then seek help.

questions.q: True or false: The authors claim that readers who consistently do all they can alone before seeking help will find they need less and less outside help.
questions.explain: Doing the work yourself exercises the skill, so over time fewer passages need outside help.
questions.rule: Effort first makes help less needed.

questions.q: Ravi is learning to read commercial contracts. Whenever a clause puzzles him, he emails a lawyer friend before thinking it through. What does the authors' principle predict about his reading?
options: He will soon need no help, since the answers teach him all
He will read better, since early help prevents his mistakes
Nothing will change, since asking has no effect on skill
He will keep needing help, his own skill unused
optionExplain: Answers do inform him, but he never practises working out a clause himself, so the skill of doing it stays weak.
He may avoid some mistakes, but he also avoids the practice that would let him read contracts without help.
The authors' claim is the opposite: how you use help shapes how much you will need it.
Right: the principle ties less need for help to doing your own best first; skipping that step keeps him dependent.
questions.explain: The payoff of trying first is a growing ability to manage alone. Asking at once keeps the need for help high.
questions.rule: Help taken before trying keeps you dependent.

questions.q: A reader says: The authors told me to do my best alone, so I will stop using dictionaries altogether. What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: The authors want dictionaries first and commentaries last
The advice sets when to use aids, not whether to use them
The advice applies to novels but not to other books
Nothing; refusing every aid is what the authors require
optionExplain: The authors put all aids after your own effort; they do not rank dictionaries ahead of the book.
Right: the authors warn against reading with a dictionary in hand, but they do not ban going to one for strange words.
The principle is stated for reading in general, not for one kind of book.
The authors say outside help can be useful and sometimes needed; refusing it is not their rule.
questions.explain: Doing your best first is a rule about order. After your effort, a dictionary, commentary or other aid may be exactly what is needed.
questions.rule: Order the help; do not refuse it.

questions.q: Sort each habit: does it follow do-your-best-first, or does it lean on aids too soon?

items.t: Rereading a puzzling chapter before searching for help
Noting a question to look up after finishing the chapter
Looking up a word that still blocks a key sentence after trying the context
Reading a plot summary before starting the novel
Opening a study guide beside the book on page one
Checking every unfamiliar name the moment it appears

questions.explain: The first group tries the book first and saves help for what remains. The second puts help ahead of any effort, which is the habit the authors warn against.
questions.rule: Help belongs after the attempt, not before it.

questions.q: A beginner learning bicycle repair asks the shop owner to do each repair while she watches. By analogy with the authors' principle, what would serve her learning better?
options: Attempt each repair first and ask about what defeats her
Watch more repairs before she touches a bicycle herself
Read the full manual before attempting any repair at all
Ask for a written guide so she never needs the owner
optionExplain: Right: trying first exercises the skill, and the owner's help then fixes the exact step she could not manage.
Watching feels like learning, but like reading a summary first, it lets someone else do the work.
A manual is still help taken before any attempt; it shifts the reliance from the owner to the page.
A guide is another aid; her dependence moves to the paper instead of shrinking.
questions.explain: The authors' reason for trying first is that skill grows by use. Help that does the work leaves the skill unpractised, while a small hint after an attempt keeps the learner doing most of it.
questions.rule: Attempt the task, then use help to fix what the attempt missed.
questions.teaches: By analogy, good teachers of a skill give the least help that will unblock a learner, a hint rather than the answer, so the learner still does most of the work; help can come in small steps rather than all or nothing.

questions.q: Which of these do the authors count as extrinsic aids to reading? Select all that apply.
options: The book's own table of contents
Your own relevant experience
Commentaries and abstracts
Dictionaries and encyclopedias
The author's own preface to the book
optionExplain: The table of contents is part of the book itself, so using it is intrinsic reading.
Right: relevant experience is the first of the four kinds of extrinsic aid.
Right: commentaries and abstracts are the third kind.
Right: reference books are the fourth kind.
The author's preface belongs to the book; reading it first is a rule of intrinsic reading.
questions.explain: An aid is extrinsic when it lies outside the book. The card next lists all four kinds.
questions.rule: Outside the book means extrinsic.

questions.q: Put the four kinds of extrinsic aid in the order in which the authors discuss them.
items: Relevant experience
Other books
Commentaries and abstracts
Reference books
questions.explain: The chapter moves from experience, through other books and commentaries, to reference books such as dictionaries and encyclopedias.
questions.rule: Experience, other books, commentaries, reference books.

questions.q: Which situation meets the authors' maxim for seeking outside help?
options: On page three, the first technical term appears
After two careful readings, a section is unclear
Before starting, a reader wants to know how it ends
Midway, the reader wants to check that others agree
optionExplain: A term on page three may be explained a few pages later; the reader has not yet done her best.
Right: both conditions hold: a full effort has been made, and part of the book is still unintelligible.
Wanting to know the ending is not a difficulty in understanding; nothing has been tried.
Agreement is a question of judgment, not of understanding, and the maxim concerns what remains unclear.
questions.explain: The maxim has two conditions: a real effort with the rules of intrinsic reading, and something still unclear after it.
questions.rule: Both conditions: full effort, and something still unclear.

questions.q: Suppose that after her best effort, the only thing still unclear to a reader is one technical word that the context does not explain. Which kind of aid fits this difficulty?
options: A commentary that interprets the whole book
An earlier book the author was answering
Her common experience of daily life
A dictionary or other reference book
optionExplain: A commentary answers far more than she asked and brings another reader's interpretation along with it.
Related books help with ideas and context, but they are a long road to the meaning of one word.
Experience helps her test and picture claims, but it cannot supply a technical definition she has never met.
Right: a narrow question about a word fits a reference book, which is built to answer such questions.
questions.explain: The maxim says when to seek help; the difficulty itself suggests which aid. A single word is a job for a reference book.
questions.rule: Match the aid to the difficulty.

questions.q: True or false: Since the maxim says to seek help only after your best effort, you should keep your life experience out of your reading until that point.
questions.explain: Experience enters reading all along; the maxim is about deliberately seeking outside help to understand what remains unclear. Shutting out experience is neither possible nor what the authors ask.
questions.rule: The maxim times the search for help; it does not shut out experience.

questions.q: A computer help desk asks every caller to describe what they have already tried before it offers help. How does this echo the authors' maxim?
options: It holds that callers should solve every problem alone
It holds that help should come first, so effort is not wasted
It aims help at what remains after the caller's own effort
It mainly lets the desk avoid answering hard questions
optionExplain: The desk does help; asking what was tried is a step before helping, not a refusal.
The desk does the opposite: it puts the caller's attempt before its help.
Right: the account of what was tried shows exactly what is still unsolved, so the help fits the real difficulty.
The question narrows the problem; it does not dodge it.
questions.explain: The maxim puts outside help after a full effort. Asking what has been tried applies the same order from the helper's side.
questions.rule: Help fits best when it starts where the effort stopped.
questions.teaches: By analogy, asking what has already been tried is how a good helper applies the maxim from the other side: the record of a person's own effort shows which difficulty remains and what kind of help fits it.

questions.q: True or false: For an experience to count as common in the authors' sense, every human being must share it.
questions.explain: Common experience is what most people meet in ordinary life, even if some never do. The card next draws the line between common and special.
questions.rule: Common is not the same as universal.

questions.q: According to the authors, what is the best example of special experience?
options: An experiment in a laboratory
Growing up within a family
Reading a difficult book
Travelling abroad on holiday
optionExplain: Right: a laboratory experiment is experience few people have unless they go out of their way to get it.
Family life is the authors' example of common experience: most people share it in ordinary life.
Reading is something many people do, and it is not the experience the authors use to define special experience.
Holidays abroad are part of many ordinary lives and are not sought as research; the authors' special cases are deliberate inquiry.
questions.explain: Special experience must be actively sought. The laboratory is the clearest case, though field research also counts.
questions.rule: Special experience is sought on purpose.

questions.q: Sort each experience as common or special in the authors' sense.

items.t: Being taught in a school
Grieving for a relative
Shopping for food
Having parents
Measuring radiation inside a reactor
Recording bird songs on a remote island for a study
Observing bacteria grown in a lab culture

questions.explain: The first four come to most people in ordinary life, even if not to all. The last three must be sought out by deliberate effort, in a laboratory or the field.
questions.rule: Ask whether it comes with ordinary living or through deliberate effort.

questions.q: True or false: Because a small number of people are born without a sense of smell, the smell of rain counts as special experience.
questions.explain: Common experience is what most people meet in the ordinary course of life, not what every person has; orphans lack family life, yet family life is common. Special experience is what must be deliberately sought.
questions.rule: A few exceptions do not make an experience special.

questions.q: An anthropologist studies a remote valley no outsider has visited. Suppose that, years later, thousands of researchers and tourists visit it every year. What happens to the experience of the place, on the authors' account?
options: It stays special, since research first produced it
It becomes universal, since anyone may now go
It is unchanged, since special names a method
It stops being unique and loses its specialness
optionExplain: How the experience was first gained does not fix its status for ever; what matters is how hard it is to come by now.
Easier access does not make it shared by everyone; universal is not even the authors' test for common.
Special describes how rare and hard to get an experience is, not only the method used to get it.
Right: the authors note that if many scientists invaded such a region, it would cease to be unique.
questions.explain: Special experience is defined by being unavailable without special effort. When many people can easily have it, that status fades.
questions.rule: Special status depends on how hard the experience is to get.
questions.teaches: Special experience depends on how hard it is to come by: the authors note that if large numbers of scientists invaded a remote region, it would cease to be unique, so what is special can lose that status.

questions.q: A team designs a phone app for older users. One designer says her own years of using phones are enough to go on; a colleague wants to watch chosen older users try the app in planned sessions. What kind of experience does the colleague want?
options: Common experience, since nearly everyone uses phones
Special experience, sought through planned sessions
Universal experience, since all users share it
Extrinsic reading, since the test lies outside the app
optionExplain: The designer's own phone use is common experience; the colleague wants something ordinary use does not supply.
Right: watching chosen users in planned sessions is experience gained on purpose, which is what makes it special.
Universal is not one of the two kinds, and the sessions involve a chosen few, not everyone.
Extrinsic reading is about aids to reading a book, not a kind of experience.
questions.explain: The designer offers common experience; the colleague wants special experience, gathered deliberately to answer a question ordinary life does not answer.
questions.rule: Some questions need experience gathered on purpose.
questions.teaches: By analogy, design teams use both kinds: everyday experience of products is common, while watching chosen users in planned testing sessions is special experience gathered for a question that everyday life does not answer.

questions.q: Which experience matters most when you judge whether a novel is true to life?
options: Common experience of ordinary life
Special experience gained through research
Knowledge of the author's own biography
Familiarity with criticism of the novel
optionExplain: Right: the authors say judgments of a novel's verisimilitude rest almost wholly on common experience.
Research helps with science and parts of history, but a story's truth to life is not tested in a laboratory.
An author's life may be interesting, but it does not tell you whether the story fits life as people live it.
Critics' opinions are another outside aid, not the experience that tests a story against life.
questions.explain: A novel is true or not true to our experience of life as most people live it. The card next maps each kind of book to its kind of experience.
questions.rule: A novel is tested against ordinary life.

questions.q: Match each kind of book with the experience the authors say is most relevant to reading it.
pairs: Common experience of life as most people live it
questions.explain: Fiction and philosophy rest on common experience, science on special experience, and history on both, since it is part story and part research.
questions.rule: Fiction and philosophy: common; science: special; history: both.

questions.q: A philosopher's essay argues that true friendship means wishing a friend well for the friend's own sake. A reader wants to test this principle. What should she mainly draw on?
options: Her own friendships and daily observation
A commentary on the essay, read before the essay
A survey of experimental studies of friendship
The essayist's private letters about his friends
optionExplain: Right: a philosopher appeals to common experience, so her own life is the proper testing ground.
Reading a commentary first puts another reader's view between her and the essay; it is not a test of the principle.
Studies are special experience; the authors say philosophy's principles are tested without it.
The author's private life does not test a general principle about friendship.
questions.explain: Philosophers refer you to your own common sense and observation. A reader can test a principle about friendship against the friendships she knows.
questions.rule: Test philosophy against your own life.

questions.q: Which of these books call mainly for special experience to follow and judge their arguments? Select all that apply.
options: A novel about a marriage under strain
A report of trials comparing two treatments
An essay on whether lying is ever right
A geologist's account of drilled rock samples
A dialogue about what makes an action fair
optionExplain: A novel is judged against common experience of how people live and feel.
Right: the trial results are evidence few readers could gather themselves; judging the argument means following that evidence.
This is a philosophical question, tested against common sense and daily observation.
Right: the samples are special evidence gained by fieldwork; the argument rests on them.
A dialogue about fairness appeals to ordinary experience of fair and unfair action, so it is philosophical.
questions.explain: Scientific reports rest on evidence gained deliberately, so following them needs the special experience they describe. Novels and philosophical works appeal to experience every reader has.
questions.rule: Arguments from reported evidence need special experience.

questions.q: Suppose a historian's account of a 17th-century trade dispute rests on archive letters that few readers could ever see. Which part of the reading can a reader manage with common experience alone?
options: Checking that the letters say what the historian reports
Following the story of the dispute
Judging whether the archive is complete
Fixing the exact dates of each shipment
optionExplain: Checking the letters needs access to them, which is special experience the reader lacks.
Right: as a story with characters and complications, history calls on the common experience used in reading novels.
Judging the archive means knowing what survives and what is missing, which is research, not common experience.
Dates come from the documents; common experience cannot supply them.
questions.explain: History is part story and part research. The story side is open to common experience; the research side rests on the historian's special experience.
questions.rule: In history, the story is yours to judge; the sources are the historian's.

questions.q: A reader picks up a collection of poems about grief. Which experience does the authors' account suggest she bring to understanding them?
options: Special experience, such as studies of mourning
A history of the period in which they were written
A critic's reading, before she reads the poems
The common experience of loss most people share
optionExplain: Studies of mourning are special experience, which the authors tie to science, not to poetry.
Historical context can help some poems, but it is a different aid from the experience the poems appeal to.
A critic first would put another reader's view ahead of her own response; it is not experience she brings.
Right: the authors say the philosopher, like the poet, appeals to the common experience of mankind; her own experience of loss helps her grasp what the poems say.
questions.explain: The authors set poets beside philosophers: both appeal to experience most people share. Grief is common experience, so that is what she brings to understanding the poems.
questions.rule: Bring common experience to understanding poems.
questions.teaches: Poetry, like philosophy, appeals to experience most people share, so a reader brings her common experience of loss to understanding poems about grief, rather than special research.

questions.q: True or false: If you can repeat the author's own example of a point, that shows you have understood the point.
questions.explain: Repeating an example shows memory. Supplying a new one shows understanding. The card next explains the test.
questions.rule: Your own example, not the author's.

questions.q: If you cannot supply a concrete example of the author's point, the authors advise you to go back and ____ the discussion again.
questions.explain: Failing to find an example is a signal that the point has not been grasped, so the remedy is to read that discussion again.
questions.rule: No example: read again.

questions.q: A management book claims that useful feedback is specific rather than general. Which response best shows that a reader has grasped the claim?
options: She repeats the book's own example about a sales pitch
She agrees that specific feedback sounds sensible
She learns the book's definition of specific feedback by heart
She rewrites a vague note so it names the confusing slide
optionExplain: Repeating the author's example shows she remembers it, not that she can find the principle elsewhere.
Agreement comes after understanding and is no evidence of it; she could agree with words she has not grasped.
A memorised definition can sit in the mind without any grasp of what it applies to.
Right: she produces a fresh case of her own, which shows the claim has met her experience.
questions.explain: The test is a concrete example of your own. Turning a vague note into one that names the exact problem is such an example.
questions.rule: A fresh case of your own shows grasp.

questions.q: A reader has finished a chapter on supply and demand. Which of these suggest she has understood its main point? Select all that apply.
options: She can recite the labels on the chapter's diagram
She explains why tickets cost more when a show sells out
She feels confident after reading the chapter twice
She invents a case about umbrella prices on a rainy day
She recalls the author's example about wheat prices
optionExplain: Labels can be learned without grasping what the diagram shows.
Right: she applies the point to a case the author did not give.
Confidence is a feeling, not a demonstration of understanding.
Right: an invented case that fits the principle is her own concrete example.
Recalling the author's case shows memory of the chapter, not grasp beyond it.
questions.explain: Only new examples of her own show that the principle has connected with her experience. Recitation, confidence and recall can all occur without understanding.
questions.rule: Count new examples, not recall or confidence.

questions.q: Asked for an example of Aristotle's mean, one reader gives an example her teacher used in class: thrift between meanness and waste. Another works out her own: patience with a slow colleague, between snapping and leaving the problem unspoken. Which shows more grasp?
options: The first, since a teacher's example is sure to be right
Both equally, since both fit Aristotle's principle
The second, since she found the case herself
The first, since thrift is closer to Aristotle's own list
optionExplain: Being correct is not the test; a borrowed example can be right without the reader grasping why.
Both fit, but only one shows the reader can find the principle at work for herself.
Right: she produced the case from her own thinking, which a repeated example cannot show.
Closeness to Aristotle's cases makes an example safer, not better evidence of grasp.
questions.explain: The teacher's example is borrowed, even though it is not the author's. What the test looks for is a case the reader produced herself.
questions.rule: Borrowed from anyone is still borrowed.
questions.teaches: Examples from a teacher, a textbook or a friend are borrowed too: the line the test draws is not between the author's examples and everyone else's, but between cases you were given and cases you found yourself.

questions.q: True or false: No example copied from a study guide, however apt, shows by itself that the reader has grasped the author's point.
questions.explain: A copied example needs only memory, so it cannot show grasp however well it fits. Only a case the reader works out herself passes the test.
questions.rule: Only your own example counts as evidence.

questions.q: A cookbook says that acid balances richness in a dish, and illustrates with lemon on fried fish. Which example shows the most understanding of the principle?
options: Lime on fried fish instead of lemon
Lemon on fried fish with extra salt
Vinegar to cut a creamy stew
Fried fish served with no lemon at all
optionExplain: Swapping lime for lemon keeps the author's case almost unchanged, so it shows little beyond memory.
Adding salt changes the seasoning but still copies the author's case and does not apply the principle anew.
Right: a different acid and a different rich dish keep the principle while changing every surface detail.
Leaving out the acid is not an example of acid balancing anything.
questions.explain: An example far from the author's own, yet still fitting the principle, shows you hold the principle itself. A near copy shows little more than recall.
questions.rule: The further your example from the author's, the better the test.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a strong example changes the surface details while keeping the principle: a case drawn from a different area than the author's shows more understanding than one that copies his case with small changes.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: Apart from lacking reading skill, why do the authors think many readers of great books soon feel inadequate?
options: They expect a book to make sense without its relatives
Great books are written for specialists only
They read too slowly to keep the argument in mind
They read translations that lose the original sense
optionExplain: Right: readers try to understand a book without having read the others to which it is closely related.
The authors present great books as readable by ordinary readers who read well; specialism is not their reason.
Speed is a separate matter; the authors' second reason concerns what readers have read before.
Translation can cause trouble, but it is not the reason the authors give here.
questions.explain: Great books are often related, and one may assume knowledge of another. The card next gives the authors' example.
questions.rule: Related books help explain each other.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: True or false: The authors suggest that readers struggle with The Federalist Papers partly because they have not first read the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution.
questions.explain: The Federalist Papers argue about documents and ideas that came before them. Without those, much of the argument floats free.
questions.rule: Read what a book is answering.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: A student starts a famous economist's reply to an earlier economist's theory of unemployment and keeps losing track of what is being denied. What do the authors suggest?
options: Read the earlier work that the reply answers
Push on, since a good reply should stand alone
Read a newer textbook that skips the debate
Switch to a summary of the reply instead
optionExplain: Right: the reply's points are directed at the earlier theory, so knowing that theory makes them intelligible.
Some books stand alone, but a reply is built on what it answers; pushing on leaves the targets unknown.
A textbook that ignores the debate cannot show what this reply denies.
A summary of the reply has the same gap: it still assumes the earlier theory.
questions.explain: When a book is a response, the work it responds to is part of its meaning. Reading that work first removes the student's difficulty.
questions.rule: A reply needs the thing it replies to.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: A reader refuses to start Locke until she has read every book Locke read, and every book those authors read. What is the flaw in her plan?
options: Locke read nothing worth reading, so there is no need
Related books matter for novels, not for political works
The demand has no end; read the books closely tied to this one
The authors say related books should come after, not before
optionExplain: The authors say great authors were great readers; dismissing his reading contradicts that.
The authors say the reverse: related reading matters most for philosophy and history.
Right: the advice is to read the closely related books that make a work intelligible, not to chase every source back for ever.
For great books the authors advise reading the earlier, related books, since they make the later one intelligible.
questions.explain: Related reading serves understanding of the book in hand. Followed without limit, it would postpone that book indefinitely.
questions.rule: Read the close relatives, not the whole family tree.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: A reader feels lost in a great book. Sort each symptom by its more likely cause.
groups: Weak reading of the book itself

items.t: Cannot tell what earlier position the author keeps attacking
Misses references to a document the book assumes you know
Is puzzled by terms borrowed from a predecessor
Never worked out the main question the book asks
Cannot outline the book's main parts
Skipped the author's own definitions of key words

questions.explain: Related books supply what the book assumes from outside. They cannot supply what the reader failed to do with the book itself, such as finding its question, parts and terms.
questions.rule: Related reading fixes outside gaps, not inside ones.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: A law student reads a court judgment that overturns an earlier ruling and cannot see what it is correcting. What does the authors' reasoning suggest?
options: Memorise the new judgment's conclusion and move on
Ignore the earlier ruling, since it is no longer law
Read newspaper reactions to the new judgment
Read the earlier ruling the judgment overturns
optionExplain: Knowing a conclusion without its target leaves the reasoning unread.
It no longer binds, but it is still what the new judgment is responding to.
Reactions are commentary on the judgment, not the earlier text it addresses.
Right: the judgment answers the earlier ruling, so the earlier ruling is the related text that makes it intelligible.
questions.explain: A later text that answers an earlier one takes much of its meaning from it. That holds for court rulings as much as for great books.
questions.rule: To read an answer, know the question it answers.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a later text that answers an earlier one takes much of its meaning from it: a judgment overturning a precedent is hard to follow until you know what the precedent held.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: True or false: When a later great book was influenced by an earlier one, reading the earlier first can make the later easier to understand.
questions.explain: A later writer is often influenced by an earlier one, so reading the earlier first can make the later intelligible. The card next states the maxim.
questions.rule: Order matters for related books.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: The authors compare reading related books to using a whole book to interpret its parts: related books supply an even larger ____.
questions.explain: Within one book, the whole is the context for the parts. Related books extend that context outward, beyond the covers of the book.
questions.rule: Related books are a larger context.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: A reader wants to read an eighteenth-century theory of the social contract and a nineteenth-century critique of it. Which plan follows the authors' maxim?
options: The critique first, since it is newer and corrects the theory
The theory first, so that the critique's targets are known
The shorter book first, to build some reading momentum
Alternate chapters of each, so both stay fresh in mind
optionExplain: Newer is not clearer: a critique read first attacks positions the reader has not yet met.
Right: the critique answers the theory, so the theory makes the critique intelligible.
Length is not the relation that matters; influence and response are.
Alternating keeps both in view but gives neither its proper order, so the critique's targets stay half-known.
questions.explain: Read related books in an order that makes the later ones intelligible. A critique depends on the work it criticises.
questions.rule: Read the influence before the work it shaped.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: Which of these use context in the sense the authors describe? Select all that apply.
options: Using a chapter's argument to fix what a word means
Using the author's fame to decide what he meant
Using an earlier treatise to see what a book answers
Using the book's layout to judge which parts matter
Using a key sentence's neighbours to interpret it
optionExplain: Right: within a book, the larger argument is the context for a word.
Fame says nothing about what a particular sentence means; it is not context.
Right: related books extend the context beyond the book itself.
Layout can signal emphasis, but it is not the context of meaning the card describes.
Right: surrounding sentences are the closest context for any sentence.
questions.explain: Context is the surrounding text that fixes meaning: the sentence, the chapter, the whole book and, beyond it, related books. The same principle works at each scale.
questions.rule: Context works at every scale, from sentence to library.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: Suppose two books on the same subject were written in the same year by authors who had not read each other. What does the maxim about order offer here?
options: Little: the maxim rests on influence
Read the one with the earlier publication month
Read the longer first, since it sets the context
Read neither until a third book links them
optionExplain: Right: order helps because a later book draws on an earlier one; without that relation there is no order to respect.
A few months' gap means nothing if neither author read the other; order serves influence, not dates alone.
Length gives no reason why one should explain the other.
There is no need to wait; each can be read well, and compared later if useful.
questions.explain: The maxim about order exists because later books draw on earlier ones. Where neither draws on the other, order gives little help.
questions.rule: Order matters where influence runs.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: A reader opens a research paper whose first section says it extends a method introduced in an earlier paper. How does the authors' maxim apply?
options: Read the paper alone, since a paper must be self-contained
Skip the earlier paper, since the new one replaces it
Read the earlier paper first, so the extension makes sense
Read a news story about the paper before either
optionExplain: Papers aim to be clear, but one that extends a method assumes the method, so reading it alone leaves gaps.
An extension builds on the earlier work; it does not restate all of it.
Right: the earlier paper is the influence that makes the later one intelligible.
A news story is commentary on the new paper and does not explain the method it builds on.
questions.explain: Research papers state what they build on, which tells the reader what to read first. That is the maxim about order, written into the paper itself.
questions.rule: Follow the trail a text gives to what it builds on.
questions.teaches: By analogy, research papers make the order explicit: their opening sections and reference lists name the earlier work they build on, which shows a reader what to read first.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: According to the authors, what is one good way to understand a great author?
options: Read the books that the author himself read
Read only his single most famous work
Read a biography before reading his works
Read his works in order of difficulty
optionExplain: Right: great authors were great readers, and their books answer the books they read.
One book, however famous, does not show whom he was answering.
A biography tells you about his life, not about the ideas his books answer.
Difficulty is a reader's concern; it does not reveal the author's conversation partners.
questions.explain: Great authors were great readers, so their books are replies in a conversation. The card next explains how to join it.
questions.rule: Read what the great authors read.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: True or false: The authors say the great books can be read from the present into the past as well as from the past into the present.
questions.explain: Both directions respect chronology. The authors add that past to present has certain advantages, being more natural.
questions.rule: Either direction respects the sequence.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: A reader is puzzled by a twentieth-century philosopher who keeps arguing with Descartes without explaining him. What would help her join the conversation?
options: Read Descartes, the voice the philosopher is answering
Read the philosopher's later critics before anything else
Read a dictionary of philosophical terms in place of both
Read only the philosopher, to avoid outside influence
optionExplain: Right: reading the book an author was answering is one way to understand him.
Later critics answer the philosopher; they do not supply the earlier voice he is answering.
Definitions may help with words, but not with what is being argued against.
Avoiding his partner in the conversation leaves her hearing only one side of it.
questions.explain: The philosopher is speaking in a conversation with Descartes. Hearing the earlier voice makes the later one intelligible.
questions.rule: Hear the earlier voice to follow the reply.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: Sort each reading plan by whether it respects the chronology of the conversation.

items.t: Plato, then Aristotle, then Aquinas
A modern essay, then the older work it answers, then that work's source
Books on justice from ancient Athens to today, in order
Books on justice chosen by their cover design
The shortest books on a subject first, whatever their dates
A random chapter from each of five books on justice

questions.explain: Going forward or backward in time both respect the order in which the voices spoke. Choosing by cover, length or chance ignores it.
questions.rule: Forward or backward, follow the order of time.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: Suppose a reader switches from going present to past to going past to present through the same set of books. What do the authors say about the forward direction?
options: It loses the thread, since the replies come first
It has certain advantages, being more natural
It is the only order that respects chronology
It is worse, since recent books explain older ones
optionExplain: Going forward, each book comes before the replies to it, so nothing is out of order.
Right: the authors say the order from past to present has certain advantages through being more natural.
The authors allow either direction; both observe chronology.
Recent books can shed light on older ones, but the authors do not rank the backward order above the forward one.
questions.explain: Both directions respect chronology. The authors give the forward direction a slight edge as the more natural one.
questions.rule: Forward is more natural; backward still respects time.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: A colleague forwards you the twelfth reply in a long email thread and asks your view. What does the idea of a conversation in time suggest you do first?
options: Answer the last message, since it is the newest view
Ask the sender to summarise the thread in one line
Wait until the thread has finished
Read the earlier messages it is answering
optionExplain: The last message replies to earlier ones; read alone, its points may be aimed at things you have not seen.
A one-line summary is a digest written by one participant, who may leave out what you need.
