Waiting does not help you understand; the meaning is already in the earlier messages.
Right: the later message takes its meaning from the exchange before it.
questions.explain: Any running exchange is a small conversation in time. A late message is clearest in its place, and the later replies in turn show which parts of the earlier messages mattered.
questions.rule: Read a reply in its place in the exchange.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a reply also changes how the earlier message reads: once you know what was objected to, you see which parts of the original carried weight, so an exchange can be read in both directions.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: For which kind of book do the authors say reading related books matters most?
options: Novels and stories
Plays and drama
Philosophy
Science textbooks
optionExplain: The authors say related reading is probably least important for novels.
Plays, like novels, can be read in isolation if they are really good.
Right: philosophers are great readers of each other, so their books answer one another.
The authors say the need applies more to history and philosophy than to science.
questions.explain: Philosophers read and answer one another, so a philosophy book is often a reply. The card next ranks the kinds of books.
questions.rule: Philosophy needs its relatives most.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: Order these kinds of book from where related reading matters most to where it matters least, according to the authors.
items: Philosophy
History
Novels and plays
questions.explain: Philosophy comes first because philosophers read each other; history also needs related reading; good novels and plays can be read in isolation.
questions.rule: Philosophy, then history, then novels and plays.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: A book club plans two months: one on a celebrated novel and one on a classic of moral philosophy. Where should they add related reading?
options: Before the novel, since fiction draws on earlier novels
Before both equally, since all great books need it
Before the philosophy book, since it answers others
Before neither, since great books stand alone
optionExplain: Novels have literary ancestors, but a really good novel can be read in isolation.
The authors say the need differs by kind; treating all books alike spends effort where it helps least.
Right: philosophy is where related reading matters most, since philosophers answer each other.
Many great books do not stand alone; philosophy especially depends on its relatives.
questions.explain: Spend related reading where it pays: most on philosophy, least on good fiction.
questions.rule: Put related reading where the kind of book needs it.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a really good play can be read with understanding in isolation from the works related to it.
questions.explain: The authors say novels and plays, if they are really good, can be read in isolation. Related reading matters least for them.
questions.rule: A good play can stand alone.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: A literary critic writing a study of a novel reasons: good novels can be read in isolation, so I need read nothing but this novel. What would the authors say?
options: He is right, since novels need no related reading
He should read a plot digest of the novel as well
He should first read the novelist's philosophy
A critic will want to go beyond the novel
optionExplain: What suffices for an ordinary reader does not suffice for a critic, as the authors note.
A digest of the same novel adds nothing he lacks; he has read the novel itself.
Nothing suggests the novelist's philosophy is the needed context; this guesses at a relative.
Right: the authors say the literary critic will not want to confine himself to reading novels in isolation.
questions.explain: The ranking describes what an ordinary reader needs. A critic's aims reach further, so he reads novels in relation to others too.
questions.rule: Least need is not no use.

questions.section: Other Books as Extrinsic Aids to Reading
questions.q: A chemistry student learns from a current textbook and does not read Lavoisier or other founders first. Reasoning from why philosophy needs related reading, why might science need it less?
options: Scientists do not read one another's work
Later books restate earlier results
Old science books are too difficult to read today
Science has no history worth knowing
optionExplain: Scientists do read each other's work; the difference lies in how later books treat earlier ones.
Right: by inference, a current textbook carries much of what the founders established, so the reader gets it without reading them.
Difficulty may be real, but it does not explain why related reading matters less for understanding.
Science has a rich history; the point concerns what a learner needs to read to understand a current book.
questions.explain: Philosophers answer each other, so their earlier books stay part of the argument. By inference, science absorbs and restates its earlier results, so a current book carries much of them.
questions.rule: Related reading matters most where earlier books stay part of the argument.
questions.teaches: By inference from the authors' reason, science needs related reading less because later science books restate earlier results, so a current textbook carries much of what its predecessors established.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, commentaries on a book should be used freely, since their writers are experts.
questions.explain: The authors advise using commentaries sparingly, partly because commentators are not always right. The card next gives the reasons.
questions.rule: Commentaries: sparingly.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: The authors say commentaries and abstracts should be used wisely, which is to say ____.
questions.explain: Wise use of commentaries means sparing use. The first reason the authors give is that commentators can be wrong.
questions.rule: Wise use is sparing use.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: A study guide says a poem is a lament for a dead friend. A student who has read the poem finds that it mocks fashionable mourning customs. Which response fits the authors' view?
options: Test the guide against the poem itself
Accept the guide, since its writer is an expert
Ask her teacher which reading to adopt
Keep both, since a poem can mean anything
optionExplain: Right: a commentary is one reader's account; her own reading of the poem is the check on it.
Expertise does not prevent error; handbooks are sometimes badly wrong.
A teacher may help, but handing over the decision skips the check she can make herself with the poem.
A poem can bear several readings, but not any reading; a lament and a mockery cannot both fit the same lines.
questions.explain: Because commentators can be wrong, the book itself is the test of a commentary. She can catch the guide's error because she knows the poem.
questions.rule: Check the commentary against the book.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: In fairness to student handbooks, which points do the authors concede? Select all that apply.
options: They are usually more accurate than scholarly work
They are often invaluable for passing examinations
They can replace reading the book for most students
Some teachers use them in their own teaching
They are written by the books' own authors
optionExplain: The authors say the opposite: handbooks are often particularly misleading.
Right: the authors grant that handbooks are often invaluable for passing examinations.
The authors warn that depending wholly on a handbook and never reading the book can lead to bad trouble.
Right: while some teachers are irritated by handbooks' errors, others use them in their teaching.
Handbooks are written by others about a book; that is what makes them commentary.
questions.explain: The authors balance their warning: handbooks help with exams, and some teachers use them. The concession does not change the advice to use them sparingly.
questions.rule: Useful for some purposes is not reliable for all.
questions.teaches: The authors concede that handbooks are often invaluable for passing examinations and that some teachers use them in their own teaching, even though other teachers are irritated by their errors.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: A reader reasons: commentators are sometimes wrong, so I will refuse every commentary, however good. What is the flaw?
options: Commentaries from universities are reliable
Some commentaries are enormously useful
Handbooks err but scholarly commentaries do not
Books are wrong more often than their commentators
optionExplain: The publisher does not guarantee accuracy; any commentator can be wrong.
Right: the authors grant that some commentaries are enormously useful; the advice is sparing use, not none.
The authors single out handbooks, but they say commentators in general are not always right.
The question is not who errs more; the book is the thing you are trying to understand.
questions.explain: That commentators can be wrong is a reason to use them sparingly and check them, not to refuse them all.
questions.rule: Sometimes wrong is a reason to check, not to refuse.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: A podcast says a new 300-page government report recommends closing rural clinics. A listener who reads the report finds it recommends merging them. What does this case share with the authors' warning?
options: The report must have changed after release
Podcasts are less reliable than print
Government reports are too long to read
A secondhand account can misstate its source
optionExplain: Possible, but the simpler explanation is that the account misread the report.
The medium is not the point; print handbooks also err.
Length is a reason people rely on summaries, not a reason the summary is right.
Right: like a commentary, the podcast is one account of a text, and only the text shows where it went wrong.
questions.explain: Any account of a document is one reader's version and can be wrong, and an account of an account can drift further. Reading the source is what lets you catch the error.
questions.rule: Check secondhand accounts against the source.
questions.teaches: By analogy, errors can grow along a chain of accounts: a story based on a press release based on a report may drift further from the source at each step, so go to the earliest source you can.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: True or false: If a commentary is correct in everything it says, reading it cannot limit your understanding of the book.
questions.explain: A correct commentary may still leave out important meanings, and its points tend to crowd out the ones it does not raise. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Correct is not complete.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: Even when a commentary is right, the authors warn, it may not be ____: you may find important meanings in the book that its writer did not find.
questions.explain: The first reason for caution is that commentators can be wrong; the second is that even right ones are incomplete and tend to narrow your view.
questions.rule: Even right commentaries leave things out.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: Two readers study a novel about a family business. One reads only an accurate guide that discusses greed and loyalty. The other reads the novel first. What do the authors suggest?
options: The second may find meanings the guide leaves out
The first will grasp more, since the guide prevents misreading
Both will grasp the novel equally, since the guide is accurate
The second will misread it, lacking expert help
optionExplain: Right: a reader of the book itself can discover meanings the commentator did not.
The guide may prevent some errors, but it also limits what the first reader notices.
Accuracy does not make the guide complete; the first reader sees only what it covers.
Reading without help can involve errors, but it also leaves the whole book open to view.
questions.explain: A correct commentary limits a reader to its points. The reader who meets the novel directly can find more.
questions.rule: The book holds more than any account of it.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: Two correct commentaries cover the same points. One states every reading as settled; the other notes where other readings are possible. Which is less likely to narrow your understanding?
options: The settled one, since its certainty saves effort
Neither, since both are correct on every point
The one noting where other readings are possible
Both equally, since they cover the same points
optionExplain: Certainty saves effort, but that is how it narrows: it tells you there is nothing more to look for.
Being correct does not prevent narrowing; the card says even correct commentaries limit understanding.
Right: by flagging open questions it sends the reader back to the book instead of closing the matter.
Coverage is the same, but the way they present it differs, and the authors single out self-assured commentaries.
questions.explain: The authors say a very self-assured commentary especially tends to limit understanding. By inference, one that marks its readings as open does so less.
questions.rule: Prefer commentary that points you back to the book.
questions.teaches: By inference, a commentary that marks its readings as open, noting other possible interpretations, narrows less than a self-assured one, because it sends the reader back to the book.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: Sort each case by the problem it shows: a commentary that is wrong, or a correct one that is incomplete.

items.t: A guide says the hero dies, but he survives in the last chapter
A handbook misdates the war in which the novel is set
A summary gets the author's conclusion backwards
A guide rightly explains the economic argument but ignores the moral one
An introduction traces the poem's imagery accurately and never mentions its rhythm
A study guide rightly explains three themes and stops there

questions.explain: The authors give two reasons for caution. Some commentaries misstate the book; others state it correctly but only in part, which still narrows a reader who relies on them.
questions.rule: Ask two questions of a commentary: is it right, and is it all?

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: A museum audio guide describes three details of a large painting. Visitors who play it at once tend to look at those three details and move on. What would the authors' point suggest?
options: Play guides only for paintings by famous artists
Play the guide twice to fix the details
Skip the painting and read the guide's script
Look at the painting first, then play the guide
optionExplain: Fame does not change what a partial account does to attention.
Replaying fixes the guide's points more firmly and narrows the view further.
The script without the painting replaces the work with an account of it.
Right: looking first lets visitors find what the guide leaves out, then use the guide for questions.
questions.explain: A guide directs attention to a few points, as a commentary does. Looking first keeps the rest of the painting in view.
questions.rule: Meet the work before the guide to it.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any guided tour, such as a museum audio guide, directs attention to a few points, and visitors tend to see only what the guide names unless they look for themselves first.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: A new edition of a classic opens with a long introduction by a scholar. When do the authors advise reading that introduction?
options: Before the book, to learn what to look for
Halfway through, once the plot is clear
After reading the book itself
Not at all, since it is commentary
optionExplain: It seems helpful to know what to look for, but that is how an introduction narrows what you see.
Midway still lets the scholar's points shape the rest of your reading.
Right: the authors say not to read another person's commentary until after you have read the book.
The authors do not ban introductions; they set their place after the book.
questions.explain: A scholar's introduction is commentary, and commentary comes after the book. The card next gives the reasons.
questions.rule: Commentary after the book.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, you should read an author's own preface before his book, but a scholar's introduction to it only afterward.
questions.explain: The author's preface belongs to the book, so reading it first is a rule of intrinsic reading. A scholar's introduction is commentary, so the rule of extrinsic reading puts it after.
questions.rule: Author's preface first; others' introductions after.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: A student is assigned a hard book of political theory that comes with a critic's introduction. Which plan follows the authors' maxim?
options: Critic's introduction, then the book, to be guided through it
Critic's introduction in place of the author's preface
Author's preface, then the book, then the critic's introduction
The book alone, skipping all prefaces and introductions
optionExplain: Being guided sounds safe, but it sets the critic's points as the frame for the whole reading.
This swaps a part of the book for commentary on it, the reverse of the rules.
Right: the author's own preface belongs to the book; the critic's introduction comes after, for questions still open.
Skipping the author's preface drops a part of the book; skipping the critic loses help with leftover questions.
questions.explain: The two rules work together: read the author's preface with the book, and read others' commentary after it.
questions.rule: Preface with the book; commentary after it.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: Suppose a reader reads a critic's introduction first, and it stresses the book's theme of revenge. What do the authors predict?
options: She will tend to see the critic's points and miss others
She will reject the critic's view out of contrariness
She will grasp the book more fully than otherwise
She will read faster and miss nothing
optionExplain: Right: read first, an introduction tends to make you see only the points the critic made.
Some readers react against critics, but the authors expect the opposite effect: following the critic's lead.
The introduction adds one reader's view, but read first it tends to narrow, not widen, her reading.
Speed may rise, but the authors' concern is what she will fail to notice.
questions.explain: An introduction read first sets the frame for everything after it. Points outside that frame, which may be equally important, tend to be missed.
questions.rule: Read first, commentary becomes a filter.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: Sort each text by when the authors would have you read it.
groups: Before or with the book: part of it
After the book: commentary on it

items.t: The author's own preface
The author's own introduction
The author's table of contents
A scholar's critical introduction
A study guide's chapter summaries
An editor's essay on how the book was received

questions.explain: What the author wrote belongs to the book and is read with it. What others wrote about the book is commentary and comes after.
questions.rule: Who wrote it decides when to read it.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: A film fan likes to read long critical reviews. By analogy with the authors' maxim, when would a detailed review serve her best?
options: Before the film, so she knows what matters
After the film, to compare views
Instead of the film, to save the time
During the film, on her phone, to follow along
optionExplain: Knowing what matters in advance is the very thing that makes viewers watch for the critic's points only.
Right: after the film she has her own view and can meet the critic on equal ground.
A review in place of the film is the handbook problem: an account with no first-hand knowledge to check it.
Reading during the film splits attention and lets the review steer what she notices.
questions.explain: The maxim fits any work and its commentary. A review read first steers attention; read afterward it becomes a second view to compare.
questions.rule: Experience the work, then read the critics.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the maxim fits other works too: a detailed critical review read before a film tends to make viewers watch for the critic's points, while read afterward it lets them compare their view with the critic's.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: According to the authors, where do you stand if you read a scholar's introduction before reading the book?
options: Better placed than he was
On equal terms with him
At his mercy
Protected from misreading
optionExplain: He has read the book, perhaps many times; you have not read it at all.
Equal terms come from having read the book yourself, which you have not yet done.
Right: without your own reading, you cannot judge what he tells you.
His guidance may prevent some errors, but you cannot tell which of his points are themselves errors.
questions.explain: Reading the book first is what lets you weigh a commentator's claims. The card next explains the difference.
questions.rule: Read first, or you cannot weigh what you are told.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: If you read the book first and the introduction afterward, the authors say you approach its writer on essentially ____ terms.
questions.explain: Both of you have read and understood the book, so you can meet his understanding with your own.
questions.rule: Read first, meet as equals.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: A student has read a novel and then reads a handbook claiming the heroine marries for money. She remembers the heroine refusing a rich suitor. What can she do that a handbook-only reader cannot?
options: Trust the handbook, since it was written for students
Assume the novel must have two endings
See that the handbook is wrong on this point
Learn both versions by heart for the exam
optionExplain: Being written for students does not make a handbook right; the authors say handbooks can be badly wrong.
Inventing a second ending protects the handbook instead of checking it against the book.
Right: a handbook cannot hurt a reader who knows the book and can see where it is wrong.
Learning both avoids deciding, when she has the evidence to decide.
questions.explain: Having read the book, she can check the handbook. A reader who knows only the handbook has nothing to check it against.
questions.rule: Knowing the book lets you catch the handbook.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: Suppose a reader who has read a book finds that a commentator reads a key chapter quite differently from her. What is the most useful next step?
options: Reread the chapter to see what it supports
Keep her reading, since she formed it first
Adopt his reading, since he has read it more often
Find a third commentator to break the tie
optionExplain: Right: the disagreement points to exactly where the book needs another look, and the text decides.
Having read first does not make her right; equal terms cut both ways.
He may well be right, but deferring at once gives up the equal footing she earned by reading the book.
A third opinion adds another outside voice; the book itself is the better judge.
questions.explain: On equal terms, neither side wins by authority. A disagreement marks the place to go back to the book.
questions.rule: Let disagreement send you back to the text.
questions.teaches: By inference, meeting a commentator on equal terms turns disagreement into a guide: where your reading and his differ is exactly where to reread the book to see which reading it supports.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: True or false: Meeting a commentator on equal terms means assuming he knows no more about the book than you do.
questions.explain: The equality lies in both having read the book, not in equal knowledge. A scholar may know far more of its background, and a reader on equal terms can learn from that while still judging it.
questions.rule: Equal footing is not equal knowledge.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: A couple buying a house receive a long surveyor's report and a one-page summary from their agent. Which couple is better placed to judge the agent's summary?
options: One who read only the agent's summary
One who read the surveyor's full report first
One who asked the agent to explain it again
One who read summaries of other houses too
optionExplain: With only the summary, they depend entirely on how the agent chose to present it.
Right: knowing the source lets them see where the summary softens or leaves out a problem.
A fresh explanation still comes from the same source; it cannot reveal what that source left out.
Other summaries show how agents write, not what this report says.
questions.explain: As with a book and its handbook, knowing the original lets you judge the account of it, especially when the account's author has a stake in your reading.
questions.rule: Know the source before you trust its summary.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a summary is written by someone with their own interests: knowing the source matters most when the person summarizing gains from how you read it, as an agent may gain from a smooth sale.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reader who regularly relies on commentaries becomes a better reader in general.
questions.explain: The authors say the opposite: a commentary may help with one book, but the habit makes you a worse reader in general. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: The habit of commentaries weakens the reader.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: According to the authors, what happens to a reader dependent on commentaries who cannot find one?
options: He reads more slowly but still well
He writes a commentary of his own
He is totally lost
He turns to a dictionary and manages
optionExplain: The authors expect worse than slowness: the habit leaves him unable to manage alone.
Writing a commentary needs the very skill that dependence fails to build.
Right: the authors say such a reader will be totally lost without a commentary.
A dictionary helps with words, not with understanding a book as a whole.
questions.explain: Dependence leaves the reader's own skill undeveloped, so without the usual support he cannot manage.
questions.rule: Dependence leaves you lost without support.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: A new manager reads every industry report only through a consultant's summary. One week a report arrives with no summary. What do the authors suggest will happen?
options: She will struggle, having not practised reading reports
She will read it easily, since the summaries trained her
She will read it as well as the consultant would
Nothing, since reports and summaries need different skills
optionExplain: Right: the habit of reading through someone else's account leaves her own skill unused.
Summaries gave her conclusions, not practice in finding them; they trained her to read summaries.
The consultant built the skill by doing the reading; she did not.
The point is that she practised only one of the two, and it is the wrong one for this job.
questions.explain: Each report read through a summary leaves her own reading skill where it was. When the support is gone, the gap shows.
questions.rule: Support you always use becomes support you cannot do without.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: Which of these build the kind of dependence the authors warn against? Select all that apply.
options: Reading a guide before every chapter of each assigned book
Consulting a commentary on one passage left unclear after a full reading
Turning to commentary at the first difficulty in any book
Reading a scholar's essay after finishing the book to compare views
Never starting a book that lacks a study guide
optionExplain: Right: a guide before every chapter puts outside help ahead of your own work every time.
This is the use the authors approve: after your best effort, for a question that remains.
Right: reaching for help at the first difficulty means your own skill is never tested.
Comparing views after your own reading is meeting the commentator on equal terms, not dependence.
Right: refusing books without guides shows the reader can no longer manage alone.
questions.explain: Dependence is help used in place of your own effort, by habit. Help used after your effort, for what remains, does not build it.
questions.rule: Help after effort is use; help instead of effort is dependence.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: True or false: Suppose a student drops study guides for a year, doing her own best reading first and using a guide only for leftover puzzles. The authors' principles predict she will come to need guides less and less.
questions.explain: The authors say that if you consistently do all you can by yourself before seeking help, you will need less and less of it. That principle is the cure for dependence.
questions.rule: Effort first, and the need for help shrinks.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: A driver uses turn-by-turn directions for every trip, even around her own town. One day her phone dies. By analogy with the authors' warning, what is likely?
options: She finds her way easily, having driven the roads often
She is no worse off, since driving skill is unaffected
She is better off, having learned the routes from the app
She has trouble, having built little sense of the routes
optionExplain: She has driven the roads, but following each instruction, she may not have learned how they connect.
Handling the car is unaffected; finding the way is the skill the app replaced.
The app gave instructions, not understanding of the routes; it did the finding for her.
Right: like a reader who leans on commentaries, she reached each place without building the skill of finding it.
questions.explain: Following directions gets you to each destination, as a commentary gets you through each book. In both cases the skill underneath is left unpractised.
questions.rule: A tool that does the work for you can leave you helpless without it.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the same trade appears with navigation apps: following directions turn by turn gets you to each place but builds little sense of the routes, so a driver who always relies on them is lost when they fail.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: For which purposes do the authors say abstracts and plot digests are useful? Select all that apply.
options: Jogging your memory of a book you have read
Replacing a long book you lack time to read
Deciding whether a book bears on a syntopical project
Learning a book's argument before you read it
Preparing to discuss a book you will not read
optionExplain: Right: a digest can bring back the contents of a book you have already read.
This is the use the authors rule out: an abstract can never replace reading the book.
Right: in syntopical reading, an abstract can show whether a work is likely to be germane.
Reading a summary first works like a commentary read first: it frames the book before you meet it.
Discussing a book from its digest treats the summary as the book, which the authors warn against.
questions.explain: The authors name two uses only: recalling a book already read, and sorting books for syntopical reading. The card next explains both.
questions.rule: Abstracts: to recall or to sort, not to replace.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: True or false: The authors say the ideal abstract for jogging your memory is one you made yourself while reading the book analytically.
questions.explain: Ideally you made your own abstract during analytical reading. If you did not, a published abstract or digest can still be an important aid to memory.
questions.rule: Your own abstract is the best reminder.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: A student read a long history carefully last term and has an exam on it tomorrow. Which use of a digest fits the authors' advice?
options: Reading a digest to refresh what she already read
Reading a digest of a different history in its place
Reading a digest of only the chapters she skipped
Learning the digest's wording by heart for the exam
optionExplain: Right: jogging the memory of a book already read is the first use the authors allow.
A digest of another book cannot jog her memory of this one.
For skipped chapters the digest would replace reading, which is the use the authors rule out.
Memorising the wording puts the digest's account in place of her own understanding.
questions.explain: She has read the book, so a digest can bring its contents back. Using it for parts she never read would be replacement, not reminder.
questions.rule: A digest reminds; it does not stand in.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: Sort each use of an abstract or digest by whether it fits the authors' two uses.
groups: Fits one of the two uses

items.t: Rereading a digest of a novel finished last year
Scanning abstracts to choose which of thirty books bear on a topic
Reviewing your own summary before a talk on a book you read
Discussing a book in class having read only its digest
Writing an essay on a novel from its plot summary
Reading a digest to decide whether you agree with the book

questions.explain: Recalling a book you read and sorting books for a project are the two uses. Discussing, writing about or judging a book from its digest treats the summary as if it were the book.
questions.rule: Recall and sort: yes. Replace: no.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: A reader uses a published digest to recall a novel she read years ago. The digest says a character dies in chapter ten, but she remembers him leaving the country instead. What should she do?
options: Trust the digest, since her memory has faded
Check the novel itself to see which is right
Trust her memory, since she read the book
Read a second digest to break the tie
optionExplain: Memory does fade, but digests can also be wrong; trusting it by default puts the account above the book.
Right: a digest is a kind of commentary and can err; where it clashes with memory, the book settles it.
Having read the book is an advantage, but years later her memory may be the one at fault.
A second digest is another outside account and may copy the first one's error.
questions.explain: Used as a reminder, a digest still carries the risks of any commentary. The book itself is the final check.
questions.rule: When a digest and your memory clash, go to the book.
questions.teaches: A digest used as a reminder carries the same risk as any commentary: it can be wrong, so where it clashes with your memory of the book, the book itself settles the matter.

questions.section: How to Use Commentaries and Abstracts
questions.q: Law reports open each case with a headnote, a short summary. A lawyer researching a point has fifty cases. Which use of headnotes matches the authors' second use of abstracts?
options: Citing a headnote in court as what the case decided
Reading only headnotes to learn the law of the area
Ignoring headnotes and reading all fifty in full
Using headnotes to choose which judgments to read
optionExplain: A headnote is someone's summary; citing it as the decision replaces the source with an account of it.
Learning the law from summaries alone is replacement, the use the authors rule out.
Reading everything is thorough but gives up the sorting help a summary can give.
Right: headnotes help decide whether a case bears on the question, after which the judgment itself is read.
questions.explain: The second use of abstracts is sorting: judging what is worth reading for a project. The reading itself is still done on the source.
questions.rule: Use summaries to choose sources, then read the sources.
questions.teaches: By analogy, law reports open with headnotes summarising each case, and lawyers use them to choose which cases to read, but rely on the judgment itself, not the headnote, for what the case decided.

questions.q: True or false: A reference book cannot help a reader who has no idea at all of what she wants to know.
questions.explain: A reference book cannot cure total ignorance; you need enough knowledge to ask it a question. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Reference books need a question.

questions.q: The authors picture the ignorance a reference book can help with as a circle of darkness surrounded by ____.
questions.explain: You can bring light into the dark circle only if what surrounds it is already lit: you must know enough to see what you do not know.
questions.rule: Knowledge around the gap lets you fill it.

questions.q: Which reader is best placed to use an encyclopedia well?
options: One who senses history matters but has no topic
One who hopes it will tell him what to think of empire
One who wants to know when the Suez Canal opened
One who plans to read it through from A to Z
optionExplain: A vague sense with no topic is the fog the authors describe; there is no question to put.
What to think is a matter of judgment, not something a reference book can do for him.
Right: she knows what she wants, so she can ask the book an intelligible question.
Reading it through treats it as a book to absorb, not a source for answering questions.
questions.explain: A reference book serves the reader who can put a definite question to it.
questions.rule: A definite question opens a reference book.

questions.q: Asked to write about a period she knows nothing of, a student opens an encyclopedia at random and reads entries, hoping a topic will appear. What is the main problem?
options: She has no question for the work to answer
Encyclopedias are written for experts only
She should read entries in alphabetical order
She should have used a dictionary instead
optionExplain: Right: without some idea of what she wants to know, she is wandering in a fog the book cannot clear.
Encyclopedias serve general readers, but only readers who can ask them something.
The order of reading does not supply the missing question.
A dictionary would not help either; the trouble is not the kind of reference book.
questions.explain: A reference book answers questions; it does not supply them. She needs enough knowledge to frame a question first.
questions.rule: No question, no help from a reference book.

questions.q: True or false: Suppose a reader's question starts vague, something about how bees find flowers. According to the authors, she should look nothing up until she can state the question exactly.
questions.explain: The authors require some idea, however vague, of what you want to know, not an exact question. Looking up bees can sharpen her question; only total fog defeats a reference book.
questions.rule: A vague question is a start; no question is not.

questions.q: Two people search a medical database. One types fatigue. The other, who has read about her condition, types iron deficiency anaemia in runners. Why does the second get more useful results?
options: The database favours longer search entries
She knows enough to name what she wants
Short searches are blocked by the database
Medical databases serve only medical staff
optionExplain: Length alone does not help; a long query of the wrong words would fail too.
Right: her prior knowledge lets her put an intelligible, specific question to the database.
Short searches run, but a single vague word matches far too much to be useful.
Anyone can search; what matters is knowing enough to ask well.
questions.explain: A search tool, like a reference book, answers the question it is given. Knowing enough to frame the question is the searcher's job.
questions.rule: Search tools answer only the question you can ask.
questions.teaches: By analogy, search engines and databases work the same way as reference books: they return useful results only to a query that names what you want, so the searcher must already know enough to choose the right words.

questions.q: Before using a reference work you have not used before, what do the authors advise reading first?
options: Its longest entry, to judge its quality
A critic's review of the work
Entries on words you already know
The editor's advice on how to use it
optionExplain: One entry shows its style but not how the work is arranged.
A review may judge the work but will not teach you to use it.
Testing familiar entries shows something, but the editor's explanation is faster and fuller.
Right: the authors say not to use a reference book before getting the editor's advice on how to use it.
questions.explain: Each reference work is arranged in its own way, and the editor explains it. The card next sets out what else you must know.
questions.rule: Read the instructions first.

questions.q: Put the first three things you must know to use a reference book in the authors' order.
items: What you want to know
Which kind of reference book answers it
How the particular work is organized
questions.explain: You need a question, then the right kind of book for it, then the know-how to find the answer in that book.
questions.rule: What, where, how.

questions.q: Match each question with the kind of reference work most likely to answer it.
pairs: When a poet was born and died
What an old word once meant
How a type of volcano forms
questions.explain: Each reference work is a specialist. Knowing which kind answers which kind of question is the second requirement.
questions.rule: Each reference work is a specialist.

questions.q: A reader uses the right kind of reference work, reads its instructions, and finds the entry on a festival. It describes the festival's history, but she wanted to know why it falls on a different date each year. What do the authors suggest?
options: Accept the entry, since she used the right book correctly
See it misses her question, look further
Conclude that her question cannot be known
Read the entry again until it answers her
optionExplain: Using the book correctly gets her to the right page, but the page may still not answer what she asked.
Right: she still has to judge whether what she found answers what she asked.
Nothing suggests the date rule is unknowable; this entry does not cover it.
Rereading cannot add what the entry does not contain.
questions.explain: The three requirements get you to the right place; judging the answer against your question is still your job.
questions.rule: Check that the answer fits the question.

questions.q: Why do the authors say the rule of reading the preface first applies with special force to reference books?
options: The preface lists answers to the most common questions
Reference books have no other text worth reading closely
Compilers cannot foresee every need
Their entries cannot be read without the editor's permission
optionExplain: Prefaces explain arrangement and symbols, not the answers themselves.
The entries are well worth reading; the preface matters because it explains how to find them.
Right: the compiler arranges the book for readers' expected needs but cannot anticipate all of them, so the instructions bridge the gap.
Entries are open to anyone; the editor's advice is guidance, not permission.
questions.explain: Making a reference book is an art too: the compiler fits the arrangement to expected needs. Since he cannot foresee them all, his advice on use is essential reading.
questions.rule: The editor's advice explains the arrangement.
questions.teaches: There is a matching art of making reference books: the compiler should anticipate what readers will seek and arrange the book to fit, but cannot foresee every need, which is why his advice on use matters so much.

questions.q: A new employee must find one figure in a large company database with dozens of tables. Which approach fits the third requirement?
options: Read the database's guide to its tables first
Search every table one by one until it appears
Email a colleague for the figure each time
Assume it is laid out like her last firm's
optionExplain: Right: knowing how this particular store is organized is what lets her find things in it.
Searching blindly may work eventually, but it ignores how the store is organized.
Asking each time leaves her unable to use the database herself, the habit of dependence.
Every store has its own arrangement; assuming it matches another is the mistake the third requirement guards against.
questions.explain: The third requirement is knowing how the particular work is organized. Any large store of information has its own arrangement and, usually, a guide to it.
questions.rule: Learn the arrangement of each store you use.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any large organized store of information, such as a company database or an archive, has its own arrangement and usually its own guide, and learning that arrangement is the first step in using it.

questions.q: Which of these questions could you expect a reference book to answer?
options: Whether lying is ever morally right
Which party will win the next election
When a famous composer was born
How much wealth a person needs to be happy
optionExplain: A moral question is one people do not agree on, so reference books cannot settle it.
A question about the future is not something people agree on, so it is not there.
Right: dates of birth are matters people agree can be known.
This is like Tolstoy's question of how much land a man needs: no reference book answers it.
questions.explain: Reference books hold what people generally agree on. The card next draws the line.
questions.rule: Reference books hold the agreed.

questions.q: According to the authors, only those things about which people generally and conventionally ____ are to be found in reference books.
questions.explain: Reference books report what is generally agreed: dates, definitions, histories. Unsupported opinions have no business there.
questions.rule: Agreement decides what belongs in a reference book.

questions.q: Sort each question by whether a reference book could properly answer it.
groups: A reference book could answer it
No reference book can settle it

items.t: The date a famous bridge opened
The definition of photosynthesis
A short history of the bicycle
Whether capital punishment is fair
Whether house prices will fall next year
What a good life consists of

questions.explain: Dates, definitions and histories are matters of general agreement. Moral questions and questions about the future are not, so reference books cannot settle them.
questions.rule: Dates, definitions, histories: yes. Morals and the future: no.

questions.q: The authors say the history of reference books is interesting in itself. Why?
options: It shows how views of what is knowable changed
It shows which publishers made the most money
It shows that older reference books were better
It shows which words fell out of common use
optionExplain: Right: since reference books hold what is thought knowable, their history records changes in that opinion.
Sales are not the authors' interest; they care about what reference books reveal about knowledge.
The authors do not rank older reference books above newer ones.
Word histories belong to dictionaries; the point here is about what was thought knowable at all.
questions.explain: Reference books contain only what their makers think can be known. So their changes over time record shifts in what people thought knowable.
questions.rule: What reference books include shows what an age thinks knowable.
questions.teaches: Because reference books hold only what is thought knowable, their history records changing opinions about what can be known; the authors note that our time assumes the physical world is orderable, which was not always so.

questions.q: A reader finds a sentence in a reference book stating that one economic policy is the wisest. She concludes the matter is settled. What is wrong with her conclusion?
options: Nothing, since reference books contain no errors
Policy questions concern the future, so the book is right
She should have checked the word policy in a dictionary
Opinions creep in, and this one does not show agreement
optionExplain: Reference books can contain errors; the authors say unsupported opinions sometimes creep in.
Questions about the future are among those people do not agree on, which is why they do not belong there.
The word is not the problem; the sentence states an opinion as if it were settled.
Right: a judgment about which policy is wisest is a matter of opinion, and its presence in a reference book does not make it agreed.
questions.explain: Reference books are meant to hold what is generally agreed. An evaluative claim found there may be an opinion that crept in.
questions.rule: Finding an opinion in a reference book does not make it agreed.

questions.q: Almanacs print tide tables and eclipse dates years ahead. How can this fit the authors' claim that questions about the future are not found in reference books?
options: It cannot; almanacs break the authors' rule
These are agreed results of settled laws
Tides and eclipses are about the past, not the future
Almanacs are not reference books at all
optionExplain: The tables fit once you see the reason behind the rule: what matters is agreement.
Right: by inference, the authors' line falls between what is agreed and what is not; predictions from settled laws are agreed.
The tables are about future dates; the point is that people agree on them.
Almanacs are a common kind of reference book; ruling them out dodges the question.
questions.explain: The authors exclude the future because people do not agree about it. Where predictions follow from laws everyone accepts, there is agreement, so they can appear.
questions.rule: The test is agreement, not tense.
questions.teaches: By inference, the authors' line falls between what is agreed and what is not, rather than strictly between past and future: predictions computed from settled laws, such as tide tables and eclipse dates, are agreed and appear in reference works.

questions.q: According to the authors, what is a dictionary primarily?
options: A guide to correct spelling
A rulebook for correct usage
An educational instrument
A record of current slang
optionExplain: Spelling is one thing a dictionary gives, but treating it as a spelling book is the misuse the authors warn against.
Some makers tried to dictate usage, but the authors call that conflict a side-issue to the dictionary's educational purpose.
Right: from the first glossaries on, dictionaries were made mainly to help people read and learn.
Slang is only one of the kinds of usage a dictionary records.
questions.explain: However it is constructed, the authors say, a dictionary is primarily an educational instrument. The card next shows why that matters.
questions.rule: A dictionary is made to educate.

questions.q: The first dictionaries, the authors say, were glossaries of ____ words, made to help Romans read the Iliad and the Odyssey.
questions.explain: Romans learning Greek culture needed help with the archaic vocabulary of Homer, so the first dictionaries were made to teach reading.
questions.rule: Dictionaries began as aids to reading.

questions.q: A student uses her dictionary only to check how words are spelled. According to the authors, what is she missing?
options: Nothing, since spelling is its main purpose
The pronunciation marks for each word
The history in the order of a word's meanings
The power to settle arguments about ideas
optionExplain: The authors say that using a dictionary only for spelling is using it poorly.
Pronunciation is the other narrow use the authors mention; adding it still misses the history.
Right: the order and relation of meanings record the growth of the language, which a spelling check ignores.
Dictionaries cannot settle arguments about ideas; that is not what she is missing.
questions.explain: Knowing what kind of book a dictionary is changes how you use it. Its educational value lies in the meanings, their order and their relations.
questions.rule: Read the order of meanings, not only the spelling.

questions.q: On the authors' account, why did the ancient Greeks have no dictionaries?
options: They were not educated by foreign masters
They had not yet invented the alphabet
Their language had too few words to need one
Their scholars kept word lists secret
optionExplain: Right: the authors cite Santayana's remark that even the learned Greeks were not educated by sitting at the feet of foreign masters, so they needed no glossaries.
The Greeks wrote with an alphabet; that is not the authors' explanation.
Greek had a rich vocabulary; size is not the authors' point.
Nothing in the book suggests secret word lists.
questions.explain: Education in the sense of learning from another culture begins, for the authors, with the Romans, who went to school to Greek teachers. Dictionaries arose to serve that kind of education.
questions.rule: Dictionaries serve learners reaching into another culture's words.
questions.teaches: The authors tie dictionaries to learning from foreign masters: the Greeks, never schooled in another people's culture, made none, while the Romans, who learned from Greek teachers, needed glossaries to read Greek literature.

questions.q: True or false: In any dictionary, the first meaning listed under a word is its oldest one.
questions.explain: Some dictionaries list senses in historical order, others put the most common sense first. The front matter says which, so read it before drawing conclusions from the order.
questions.rule: Check how a dictionary orders its senses.

questions.q: A modern student finds that she needs a glossary to read Chaucer, though she reads novels with ease. How does this connect with the authors' history of dictionaries?
options: It shows modern readers read worse than Romans did
It shows the original use of dictionaries continues
It shows glossaries are only for poetry
It shows Chaucer wrote in a foreign language
optionExplain: Needing a glossary for an old text is no sign of weak reading; the Romans needed one for Homer.
Right: as the Romans needed glossaries for Homer's archaic words, readers today need one for Chaucer.
Glossaries serve any text with old or technical vocabulary, not poetry alone.
Chaucer wrote in English, but in an older stage of it with archaic words and senses.
questions.explain: Dictionaries began as glossaries for reading old literature. Readers of Chaucer, or of Shakespeare, still use them for the same purpose.
questions.rule: Old texts still call for glossaries.
questions.teaches: The authors note that many of us today need a glossary to read Shakespeare, or if not Shakespeare, Chaucer, as the Romans needed one for Homer: the first use of dictionaries is still with us.

questions.q: True or false: On a first reading of a difficult book, the authors recommend looking up each unfamiliar word as you meet it.
questions.explain: Looking up many words at the start breaks the thread of the book. The card next says which words to look up and when.
questions.rule: A first reading is not a word hunt.

questions.q: Which kinds of vocabulary do the authors say the dictionary is primarily meant to help with? Select all that apply.
options: Technical words
Words whose spelling you doubt
Archaic words
Familiar words in obsolete senses
Words you already use every day
optionExplain: Right: technical words are one of the kinds the authors list.
Spelling is the narrow use the authors warn against treating as the dictionary's main job.
Right: archaic words are on the authors' list.
Right: familiar words used in obsolete senses are on the list too.
Everyday words in their current senses need no dictionary.
questions.explain: The primary use is help with books whose vocabulary includes technical words, archaic words, literary allusions, or familiar words in obsolete senses.
questions.rule: Technical, archaic, allusive, obsolete: the dictionary's targets.

questions.q: On a first reading of a hard history, sort each unfamiliar word: look it up now, or read on and save it.

items.t: A term the whole thesis rests on that the context does not explain
A technical word in the chapter's main claim, wholly new to you
A word used in every chapter's conclusion, still unclear after context
An old name for a coin in a passing anecdote
A rare word for a colour in a description of a dress
An unfamiliar place name in a list of ports

questions.explain: During a first reading, the test is importance to the author's general meaning. Words in the main claims qualify; words in passing details can wait.
questions.rule: Look up what the general meaning depends on.

questions.q: Suppose a reader looks up every new word in the first chapters of a hard book. What do the authors predict?
options: She will grasp each chapter more fully
She will lose track of the book's unity and order
She will build her vocabulary fastest this way
She will finish sooner with fewer puzzles
optionExplain: Each sentence may become clearer, but the whole, which is what the first reading is for, slips away.
Right: the authors say too many look-ups at the start make you lose track of the book's unity and order.
Her word list may grow, but the authors' concern is understanding the book.
Constant stopping slows a first reading and fragments it.
questions.explain: A first reading aims at the whole book. Stopping for every word breaks it into pieces.
questions.rule: Too many look-ups early cost you the whole.

questions.q: Of the four kinds of hard vocabulary the authors list, which is a reader least likely to notice needs looking up?
options: Technical terms of a field
Archaic words no longer used
Old senses of familiar words
Allusions to other literature
optionExplain: Technical terms usually look unfamiliar, so the reader knows to check them.
An archaic word looks strange, which itself prompts a look-up.
Right: the word looks known, so the reader feels no puzzle and misreads it without noticing.
An allusion often feels like a reference to something, which can prompt a question.
questions.explain: The other three kinds usually announce themselves as strange. A familiar word in an obsolete sense does not, so the misreading slips through.
questions.rule: Beware familiar words in old texts.
questions.teaches: By inference, familiar words used in obsolete senses are the hardest of the four kinds to catch, because the reader feels no puzzle: the word looks known, so the misreading passes unnoticed.

questions.q: An adult learning Spanish reads a short novel in Spanish for pleasure. Which approach to unknown words matches the authors' advice for a first reading?
options: Look up only the words that block the story
Look up every unknown word before reading on
Read only books with no unknown words
Translate each page fully into English first
optionExplain: Right: like a first reading, she keeps the whole in view and stops only where the general meaning depends on a word.
Stopping for every word breaks up the story, as it breaks up a hard book.
Avoiding all unknown words removes the difficulty instead of reading through it.
Full translation turns reading the novel into reading her own version of it.
questions.explain: The same filter works in a new language: keep reading for the whole, and stop for words the story depends on.
questions.rule: Stop for the words the whole depends on.
questions.teaches: By analogy, language teachers recommend extensive reading on the same principle: learners reading a story in a new language look up only the words that block the plot, so they keep the whole in view.

questions.q: Two people argue whether a policy is fair. One reads out a dictionary's definition of fairness. Does this settle the argument?
options: Yes; the dictionary is the final authority on meaning
No; it records how the word is used, not what is fair
Yes, provided the dictionary is a recent edition
No; dictionaries do not define abstract words
optionExplain: Lexicographers are authorities on usage, not, the authors say, the final founts of wisdom.
Right: the dispute is about the thing, whether the policy is fair, and the dictionary is about words.
A newer edition records newer usage; it still does not judge the policy.
Dictionaries do define abstract words; the problem is what a definition can settle.
questions.explain: A definition reports how a word is used. The argument is about whether a policy deserves the word. The card next explains the difference.
questions.rule: Definitions do not settle disputes about things.

questions.q: The authors sum up their negative rules: the dictionary is a book about ____, not about things.
questions.explain: Every proper use of a dictionary follows from this: it answers questions about words, not about the things words name.
questions.rule: A dictionary is about words.

questions.q: Which of these disputes could a dictionary properly settle?
options: Whether hate speech should be protected
What decimate meant in ancient Rome
Whether a fair wage is set by the market
Whether democracy is the best government
optionExplain: This is a moral and political question about a thing, not about a word.
Right: this is about the history of a word's use, which a dictionary records.
This concerns how wages work and ought to work, not how a word is used.
This is a disputed judgment about governments, beyond any definition.
questions.explain: Questions about a word's use or history are the dictionary's business. Questions about what is right or true of things are not.
questions.rule: Usage questions belong to the dictionary.

questions.q: Sort each question: is it about a word, or about the thing a word names?

items.t: How the word liberal was used in the 1800s
Whether the word irregardless appears in standard dictionaries
Whether the word bank has a sense meaning a riverside
Whether liberal policies reduce poverty
Whether a particular war was justified
Whether the death penalty deters crime

questions.explain: The first three ask how words are used or recorded. The last three ask what is true or right about the world, which no dictionary can settle.
questions.rule: Ask whether the dispute is about the word or the thing.

questions.q: A student memorizes a list of 500 impressive words he has not met in his reading. Then he meets one of them, used in its full sense, in a book. What does the authors' rule suggest he gains at that moment?
options: A meaning tied to a use he can see
Nothing new, since he already knew the definition
Only a spelling check on the word
A reason to memorize a longer list
optionExplain: Right: meeting the word in use connects its meaning with something real, which the list never did.
Knowing a definition is not the same as having the word connected with experience, which the list lacked.
The encounter offers far more than spelling; it shows the word at work.
Longer lists repeat the mistake the authors call swallowing the dictionary.
questions.explain: The authors warn against memorizing words unconnected with any experience. Meeting a word in a real use supplies the connection the list lacked.
questions.rule: Words become yours when you meet them in use.
questions.teaches: By inference, words become your own by meeting them in use: a word learned from its role in something you are reading has its meaning connected with experience from the start, which a memorized list cannot give.

questions.q: A court must decide whether the word vehicle in a 1950 park rule covered bicycles, as people used the word then. May a dictionary of that era properly help?
options: No; dictionaries cannot settle any legal dispute
No; only the judge's sense of fairness can decide
Yes; here the question is how a word was used
Yes; it also shows whether the rule is fair
optionExplain: The authors' rule targets disputes about things; this dispute turns on usage, which dictionaries record.
Fairness may matter elsewhere in the case, but this question asks what the word meant to people in 1950.
Right: a question about a word's usage at a time is the dictionary's proper business.
The dictionary can inform the usage question, but whether the rule is fair is a question about things.
questions.explain: The rule against quoting dictionaries applies to disputes about things. Where the dispute really is about usage, a dictionary is the right tool.
questions.rule: When the dispute is about usage, consult the dictionary.
questions.teaches: By analogy, judges do consult dictionaries when the question is what a word in a law ordinarily meant when it was passed, a question about usage, but not to decide whether the law is fair.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the authors' four ways of looking at words?
options: Words as statements of fact
Words as parts of speech
Words as conventional signs
Words as physical things
optionExplain: Right: statements of fact combine words; single words are not facts. Facts come up with encyclopedias, not dictionaries.
This is the second way: words play grammatical roles.
This is the fourth way: words are man-made and so have histories.
This is the first way: words are written marks and spoken sounds.
questions.explain: The four ways are physical things, parts of speech, signs and conventions. The card next shows what each one asks.
questions.rule: Four ways: physical, grammatical, sign, convention.

questions.q: Match each way of looking at words with the question it leads you to ask a dictionary.
pairs: How is it spelled and pronounced?
What grammatical role can it play?
What does it mean, and what words are related?
Where did it come from, and is this sense current?
questions.explain: Each aspect of a word gives one kind of question: form, grammar, meaning, history.
questions.rule: Form, grammar, meaning, history.

questions.q: A reader looks up mean in a novel and finds a dozen senses: unkind, stingy, average, intend and more. How should she decide which sense the novelist intends?
options: See how the author uses it
Check the word's etymology
Take the first sense listed
Check the list of abbreviations
optionExplain: Right: the dictionary shows the senses the word can bear; the context shows which one is meant.
Etymology tells the word's history, not which sense this writer chose.
The first sense may be the oldest or the commonest, not the author's.
Abbreviations explain the entry's labels; they do not pick a sense for the novel.
questions.explain: The dictionary answers questions about the word. Which of its senses a writer uses is settled by his context.
questions.rule: The dictionary offers senses; the context chooses.

questions.q: Sort each name as concrete or abstract, in the authors' sense.
groups: Concrete: points to something we can sense
Abstract: grasped by thought, not observed

items.t: apple
thunder
granite
fairness
courage
friendship

questions.explain: Concrete names point to things we can see, hear or touch. Abstract names refer to aspects of things we understand by thought but cannot observe with the senses.
questions.rule: Concrete: sensed. Abstract: thought.

questions.q: A dictionary gives bank as the side of a river and, separately, as a business that keeps money, with no link between the two. What does this show about words as signs?
options: The dictionary has made an error
Words can bear unrelated meanings
One sense must be slang for the other
The two senses must share a root
optionExplain: Listing both is correct; the word does carry both senses.
Right: meanings may shade into one another, but a word can also carry two or more totally unrelated sets of meanings.
Neither sense is slang; both are standard.
Shared roots are a question of history; the point here is that the meanings themselves are unrelated.
questions.explain: As signs, words can have many meanings. Sometimes these shade into each other; sometimes, as with bank, they are wholly separate.
questions.rule: Some senses shade; some stand apart.
questions.teaches: A word's meanings may shade from one into another, or a word may have two or more sets of totally unrelated meanings, as bank does for a riverside and a business that keeps money.

questions.q: A programmer looks up a function in a language's documentation. Which part matches the authors' fourth question, about words as conventional?
options: Its exact spelling and capitals
Where it may appear in a line of code
What it computes and related functions
Its version history and retired uses
optionExplain: Spelling and form match the first question, words as physical things.
Its place in a statement matches the second question, grammatical role.
What it does and its relations match the third question, words as signs.
Right: like a word's etymology and obsolete senses, its history shows how the convention has changed.
questions.explain: The four questions fit any man-made system of signs: form, role, meaning and history.
questions.rule: Form, role, meaning and history fit any system of signs.
questions.teaches: By analogy, good software documentation answers the same four kinds of question about a function: how it is written, where it fits in a statement, what it does, and how it has changed between versions.

questions.q: What do the authors say about using an encyclopedia only to look up dates and places?
options: It is the proper use of an encyclopedia
It is risky, since dates are often wrong
It under-uses an educational tool
It is fine if the edition is recent
optionExplain: Looking up simple facts is a use, but the authors call relying on it alone under-use or misuse.
The authors' worry is not accuracy here but how little of the encyclopedia such a reader uses.
Right: encyclopedias are educational as well as informational tools.
Recency does not change the point: the reader still ignores what the work can teach.
questions.explain: Like a dictionary used only for spelling, an encyclopedia used only for dates is under-used. The card next shows what else it offers.
questions.rule: An encyclopedia teaches, not only informs.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a reader who fails to use an encyclopedia's index has only himself to blame if the work does not serve his needs.
questions.explain: The index gathers discussions of one subject from across the volumes and partly reveals how the work arranges knowledge, so skipping it wastes the work.
questions.rule: Start from the index.

questions.q: A student wants to understand why the Black Death changed the lives of European workers. Which approach fits the authors' view?
options: Read the entry under Black Death and stop
Read the volume in order from A to the B entries
Start from the index, follow related entries
Look up only the year the plague began
optionExplain: One entry may give the facts of the plague but not their relations to labour, prices and law.
Reading in alphabetical order follows the masking arrangement, not the structure of knowledge.
Right: the index gathers scattered discussions, and the relations among them give understanding.
A single date is information, not the understanding she wants.
questions.explain: Understanding comes from facts in relation. The index brings together widely separated discussions of one subject.
questions.rule: Follow the index to related facts.

questions.q: The authors describe an ideal encyclopedia that no one had yet made. Which features would it have? Select all that apply.
options: Articles in alphabetical order
A topical key, like a table of contents
No index, since an outline replaces it
One article per university department
Its editors' views on disputed topics
optionExplain: Right: separate articles in alphabetical order keep things easy to find.
Right: a topical key or outline would show how the articles relate, as a table of contents does for a book.
The ideal adds a topical key; it does not drop the means of quick access.
Department-sized articles would show structure but lose the easy access of alphabetical entries.
Unlabelled editorial opinion is what an honest encyclopedia avoids, whatever its arrangement.
questions.explain: Alphabetical order makes things easy to find; topical order shows how they relate. The authors' ideal has both.
questions.rule: Easy access plus visible structure.
questions.teaches: A table of contents is a topical arrangement of a book and an index an alphabetical one; the authors' ideal encyclopedia would have alphabetical articles plus a topical key, which they knew of no encyclopedia offering.

questions.q: Suppose an encyclopedia were arranged by topic instead of alphabetically. What would change, on the authors' account?
options: It would hold fewer facts, since topics take space
Arrangement would make no difference to understanding
Its articles would turn into opinions rather than facts
Relations would stand out, but readers find it unfamiliar
optionExplain: Arrangement changes order, not the number of facts the work can hold.
The authors say understanding depends on seeing relations, which arrangement can hide or show.
Arranging facts by topic does not turn them into opinions.
Right: topical works highlight relations, but they have disadvantages, including that most readers are not used to them.
questions.explain: Alphabetical order obscures the relations among facts; topical order highlights them, at the cost of unfamiliarity.
questions.rule: Arrangement can hide or show relations.

questions.q: In a large library, the catalogue lets you search titles alphabetically, while the shelves group books by subject. A reader wants to understand a whole field. What do the authors suggest?
options: Search the catalogue title by title in order
Browse the shelves for that subject
Read the catalogue from beginning to end
Borrow only the single most popular title
optionExplain: Alphabetical searching finds known items but hides how they relate.
Right: the shelves reveal the subject order beneath the alphabetical catalogue, showing books in relation.
Reading a catalogue through is like reading an encyclopedia through: vain.
One popular book gives one view, not the shape of the field.
questions.explain: Like an encyclopedia, a library has an underlying order beneath its alphabetical finding aid. Seeing that order shows items in relation.
questions.rule: Look for the order beneath the alphabet.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any large collection has an underlying order beneath its finding aids: a library's shelves follow subject classes even though its catalogue lets you search by title.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, encyclopedias should be used to end arguments about matters of fact as quickly as possible.
questions.explain: Facts should not be argued about at all, and an encyclopedia can end such disputes. The card next sets out which disputes it cannot end.
questions.rule: Disputes of fact: look it up.

questions.q: Why do the authors advise reading more than one encyclopedia on a subject you care about?
options: One encyclopedia takes too long to read
Each one covers only a few subjects
Encyclopedias often disagree on facts
Older ones are out of date and wrong
optionExplain: You do not read an encyclopedia through, so its length is not the point.
Encyclopedias aim to cover all knowledge; coverage is not the reason.
Right: unlike dictionaries on words, encyclopedias often disagree in their accounts of facts.
Older editions may be revised, but the authors advise reading ones from different times, not discarding the old.
questions.explain: Since encyclopedias often disagree about facts, comparing several, from different times, gives a truer picture.
questions.rule: Compare encyclopedias; they disagree.

questions.q: Sort each dispute by whether an encyclopedia could properly end it.

items.t: The year a city was founded
The boiling point of mercury
Which of two countries is larger in area
Whether the city was wisely sited
Whether mercury mining is worth its harms
Which of two countries has the finer culture

questions.explain: Dates, measurements and areas are matters of fact. Wisdom, worth and fineness are matters of judgment on which people differ.
questions.rule: Facts can be looked up; judgments cannot.

questions.q: Suppose two encyclopedias, one from 1910 and one from 2010, give different numbers of soldiers at an ancient battle. What does the authors' advice suggest?
options: The older one must be wrong, so discard it
Neither can be trusted, so avoid them
Accounts of facts get revised; weigh both
The numbers are opinions, so either will do
optionExplain: Newer is not always right; the older account may rest on evidence the newer one dropped.
Disagreement is a reason to compare, not to abandon encyclopedias.
Right: encyclopedias from different times can differ, which is why the authors advise reading more than one.
The number of soldiers is a factual question even when sources differ on it.
questions.explain: The authors advise reading encyclopedias written at different times precisely because accounts of facts differ and change.
questions.rule: Differences between sources call for comparison.

questions.q: True or false: Two colleagues argue whether their city's crime rate is high. Once an encyclopedia gives them the rate, their argument should be over.
questions.explain: The rate is a fact the encyclopedia can supply, but whether it counts as high is a judgment. A dispute that looks factual can hide a disagreement of judgment, and the encyclopedia ends only the factual part.
questions.rule: Separate the fact from the judgment about it.

questions.q: A fact-checking team receives two claims: the city's budget rose ten percent last year, and the mayor is the worst in decades. How would the authors' distinction guide them?
options: Rate both claims as true or as false
Rate only the second, the more important
Decline both, since politics is opinion
Check the first; call the second opinion
optionExplain: Rating an opinion true or false treats a judgment as if it were a fact.
Importance does not make a judgment checkable.
The budget figure is a matter of fact even in politics, and can be checked.
Right: the budget claim can be settled from records; the verdict on the mayor is a matter of opinion.
questions.explain: Disputes of fact can be ended by agreed records; disputes of opinion cannot. Fact-checkers draw the same line.
questions.rule: Check facts; label opinions.
