questions.teaches: By analogy, professional fact-checkers settle claims of fact by going to agreed records and comparing sources, and they treat claims of opinion as opinion rather than rating them true or false.

questions.q: According to the authors, what must an honest encyclopedia do with opinions it reports?
options: Present them as facts if its editors hold them
Leave out every mention of them
Give only the view most likely to be true
Label them as opinions
optionExplain: An encyclopedia containing its editors' unsupported opinions is, the authors say, dishonest; holding a view does not make it fact.
An encyclopedia may report opinions, for instance the disagreements on a moral question.
Choosing the likeliest view takes sides; the authors allow opinions to be reported only when labelled as such.
Right: it may report that some hold one view and others another, provided it labels them.
questions.explain: Facts are what is generally agreed. Opinions may appear only when labelled as such. The card next gives all four points about facts.
questions.rule: Opinions must be labelled.

questions.q: Match each of the authors' points about facts with the question it leads you to ask.
pairs: What does this fact signify for my question?
Is this generally agreed, or an opinion?
Is this agreed, or only a theory?
questions.explain: Each point about facts becomes a question to put to an encyclopedia: significance, agreement, reality and revisability.
questions.rule: Significance, agreement, reality, revision.

questions.q: An encyclopedia article says one diet is the healthiest way to live, with no note of other views. Which point about facts does it break?
options: That facts are propositions made of words
That a fact's significance needs explaining
That facts may change over time
That facts are agreed and opinions labelled
optionExplain: The sentence is a proposition; that point is not what it violates.
Explaining significance is a reader's need, not the fault in this sentence.
Facts may change, but the problem here is presenting a contested view as settled now.
Right: a disputed judgment stated as fact, unlabelled, is the dishonesty the authors describe.
questions.explain: An encyclopedia should report what is generally agreed, and label any opinion it reports.
questions.rule: An unlabelled opinion is a fault.

questions.q: Sort each statement: a fact in the authors' sense, or not yet a fact?
groups: A fact in the authors' sense
Not yet a fact: theory or opinion

items.t: Lincoln was born in 1809
Gold's atomic number is 79
Water boils at 100 C at sea level
A historian's guess about Lincoln's private feelings
A new hypothesis about dark matter, still disputed
An editor's view that one president was the greatest

questions.explain: Facts are agreed singulars or relatively unquestioned generalizations. Guesses, disputed hypotheses and evaluations are not facts until generally agreed, and opinions never are.
questions.rule: Agreed singulars and generalizations are facts; guesses are not.

questions.q: An encyclopedia article on Aristotle's school describes his view of the heavens, which no one now holds. Does this break the rule that encyclopedias report facts?
options: Yes; such views belong in history books instead
Yes; only views held true today may appear
No; old theories may appear under their school
No; any theory counts as fact once printed
optionExplain: History books do treat old theories, but the authors expressly allow encyclopedia articles on a school to describe them.
This is the general rule, but the authors make an exception for theories tied to an article's subject.
Right: the authors allow describing a theory no longer held when it belongs to a person or school that is the subject of an article.
Printing a theory does not make it a fact; that is why the exception needs stating.
questions.explain: It is a fact that Aristotle held this view, even though the view itself is no longer believed. Articles on people and schools may describe such theories.
questions.rule: Reporting what someone held is not asserting it.
questions.teaches: The authors allow one exception: an encyclopedia may describe a theory no longer held, or not yet validated, in an article on the person, school or topic it belongs to, as with Aristotle's views on celestial matter.

questions.q: A physicist and a person raised in a culture with a very different picture of nature compare what they take as facts. On the authors' account, which must they agree on?
options: That two plus two is four
Facts about the causes of illness
Facts about subatomic particles
Nothing, since all facts are cultural
optionExplain: Right: the authors say people with very different pictures of reality must still agree on some facts, such as two plus two being four.
Causes of illness are among the matters cultures picture differently.
The authors say such a person may not accept the physicist's facts about nuclear particles.
Facts are only to some extent conventional; some are shared by all.
questions.explain: Facts are partly shaped by culture and theory, but not wholly. Some, like simple arithmetic, hold across every picture of reality.
questions.rule: Facts are partly, not wholly, conventional.
questions.teaches: The authors note that people with very different pictures of reality must still agree on some facts, such as that two plus two is four or that a whole is greater than any of its parts, while disagreeing on others.

questions.q: On the authors' account, which of these would you NOT expect to find in an encyclopedia?
options: Facts about a famous poet's life
The full text of the poem itself
The date a poem was first printed
A list of the poet's major works
optionExplain: Facts about poets are the kind of thing an encyclopedia holds.
Right: an encyclopedia contains no poetry or imaginative literature, though it may hold facts about it.
A publication date is a fact and belongs there.
A list of works is factual information an encyclopedia includes.
questions.explain: An encyclopedia gives facts about imaginative works, not the works. The card next names this and one other omission.
questions.rule: Facts about poems, not poems.

questions.q: Which striking omissions do the authors find in an encyclopedia? Select all that apply.
options: Arguments
Dates of historical events
Imaginative literature
Facts about poets
Accounts of how knowledge is arranged
optionExplain: Right: apart from reporting widely accepted arguments, it contains no arguments.
Dates are exactly what encyclopedias contain.
Right: it holds no imaginative literature, only facts about it.
Facts about poets are included.
The authors say an encyclopedia can give insight into the order and arrangement of knowledge; that is one thing it does offer.
questions.explain: Without arguments, it lacks a major element of expository writing; without imaginative works, it lacks what feeds the imagination. Understanding needs both.
questions.rule: No arguments, no poems.

questions.q: A student wants to judge whether a philosopher's argument for free will holds up. Where should she mainly go?
options: An encyclopedia entry on his conclusions
The philosopher's own book, to follow it
A dictionary definition of free will
A list of thinkers who wrote on the topic
optionExplain: An entry reports conclusions and perhaps the course of the argument, but she needs to weigh the reasoning herself.
Right: judging an argument means following it step by step in the work itself.
A definition concerns the words, not the argument about the thing.
A list tells her who wrote, not whether the reasoning holds.
questions.explain: An encyclopedia can tell her that the argument exists and what it concludes. Judging it needs the argument itself.
questions.rule: To judge an argument, read the argument.

questions.q: Sort each item by whether an encyclopedia can give it to you.

items.t: The dates of a war
Who wrote on a subject, and when
How a field of knowledge is divided
Following a proof step by step yourself
The feel of a war as a novel conveys it
Weighing a disputed argument's premises

questions.explain: Facts and the arrangement of knowledge are the encyclopedia's strength. Reasoning through arguments and experiencing imaginative works require the works themselves.
questions.rule: Facts from the encyclopedia; understanding from the works.

questions.q: True or false: Because an encyclopedia contains no arguments, it cannot tell you anything about an argument such as Darwin's case for natural selection.
questions.explain: An encyclopedia may report the course of arguments that are widely accepted or of historical interest. What it does not give is the argument itself to follow and weigh.
questions.rule: Reporting an argument is not making it.

questions.q: A student reads a detailed encyclopedia entry on a symphony: its date, its four movements, its first reception. What does the authors' point suggest she still lacks?
options: More facts about the composer
A longer and more detailed entry
Hearing the symphony itself
A dictionary of musical terms
optionExplain: More facts add information but not the experience of the work.
A longer entry is still facts about the work.
Right: as with poetry, facts about an imaginative work do not give what the work itself gives.
Terms help describe the music but do not replace hearing it.
questions.explain: An encyclopedia offers facts about imaginative works, not the works. That holds for music as for poetry.
questions.rule: Facts about a work are not the work.
questions.teaches: By analogy, facts about any work of the imagination, such as the date and structure of a symphony, do not give what the work itself gives; an encyclopedia can point to the experience but not supply it.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: According to the authors, what is the main drawback of making the rules of an art very general?
options: They become too many to learn and keep in mind
They become harder to understand in themselves
They grow remote from the actual situations of use
They stop applying to most of the particular cases in a field
optionExplain: A fair worry about rules, but generality works the other way: the more general, the fewer rules.
The authors say the reverse: general rules are easier to understand by themselves.
Right: generality buys fewer, clearer rules at the price of distance from the case at hand.
General rules are meant to cover many cases; the trouble is fitting them to each one, not their reach.
questions.explain: General rules are fewer and easier to grasp, but further from the details of real use. The card next shows what this means for reading particular books.
questions.rule: Generality trades closeness to the case for clarity.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the fifteen rules of analytical reading apply to novels and poems in the same way as to expository books.
questions.explain: Novels, plays and poems do not proceed by terms, propositions and arguments, so the authors give a parallel set of rules for them.
questions.rule: The fifteen rules are for expository books.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Priya has used the analytical rules on a biology textbook and now opens a book of household repair guides. Which approach fits the authors' advice?
options: Keep the four questions and adjust the rules to a manual
Apply each rule exactly as she did for the biology book
Set the rules aside, since repair guides are not real books
Switch to the parallel rules meant for imaginative works
optionExplain: Right: the four questions carry over, and the rules are adapted to the kind of book.
Consistency sounds rigorous, but the authors warn that you cannot read a book in general; a manual is a particular sort.
A repair manual is an expository, practical book, so the rules still apply in adapted form.
Those rules are for fiction and poetry; a repair manual is expository.
questions.explain: A repair manual is expository but practical. The four questions still apply, and the rules are fitted to what such a book does.
questions.rule: Same questions, adapted rules.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Sort each item by which rules of reading the authors would have you use.
groups: Expository rules, adapted to the kind

items.t: A cookbook
A history of the French Revolution
A treatise on ethics
A sonnet sequence
A stage play
A collection of short stories

questions.explain: Books that convey knowledge, practical or theoretical, take the expository rules in adapted form. Stories, plays and poems do not argue by terms and propositions, so they get their own rules.
questions.rule: Expository or imaginative decides which rule set.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: After the repair guides, Priya picks up a collection of poems. What part of her reading method carries over, according to the authors?
options: The fifteen rules, applied as for the repair guides
The search for the poet's key terms and main propositions
The outline of arguments, made shorter for a poem
The four questions, though answered in a different way
optionExplain: The fifteen rules are for expository books; poems need the parallel rules.
Poems do not proceed by terms and propositions, so this search misfires.
A poem has no logical arguments to outline, however short the outline.
Right: the four questions apply to any book, and the rules for imaginative literature are developed from them.
questions.explain: The four questions fit every book, fiction or not. What changes for a poem is the rules developed from them, because a poem's content is not logical.
questions.rule: The four questions travel to every book.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: A cooking teacher can give students 200 exact recipes or 10 general techniques. By the authors' reasoning about general rules, what trade-off does the choice involve?
options: Techniques are more numerous, but easier to fit to each dish
Techniques are fewer and clearer, but harder to fit to each dish
Recipes are fewer and clearer, but harder to fit to each new dish
No trade-off, since both cover the same set of dishes
optionExplain: This reverses the count: general rules are the fewer ones.
Right: general techniques are fewer and easier to grasp, but each must be fitted to the dish at hand.
This gives the recipes the virtues and costs of general rules; exact recipes are many and close to each dish.
Covering the same dishes does not make them equal; where the fitting work falls differs.
questions.explain: General techniques are like general rules: few and clear, but the cook must fit each one to a particular dish. Exact recipes need less judgment but there are many more of them.
questions.rule: General guidance moves the fitting work to the learner.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any teacher chooses between many specific instructions and a few general ones: the general ones are quicker to learn, but they put more of the work of fitting them onto the learner.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a well-written practical book can solve the practical problem it deals with.
questions.explain: However good the book, a practical problem is solved only by doing something. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Books help; action solves.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: According to the authors, a practical problem can be solved only by ____ itself.
questions.explain: A theoretical book can answer its own question, but a practical problem is about something to be done, so only doing it solves it.
questions.rule: Nothing short of the doing solves it.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: A reader finishes a highly rated book on budgeting and announces that her money problems are solved. By the authors' account, when is her problem solved?
options: When she has understood every chapter of the book
When she manages her money well in daily practice
When she can explain the method well to a friend
When she has drawn up a full budget plan from the book
optionExplain: Understanding solves a theoretical problem, but hers is practical.
Right: the problem is solved only by the action of managing money well.
Being able to explain the method shows understanding, not the action that solves the problem.
A plan is a step toward action, but the problem is managing money, which the plan does not yet do.
questions.explain: The problem is how to handle money, so only handling it well solves it. Understanding, explaining and planning prepare for that action.
questions.rule: Solved means done, not understood.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Which readers face a problem that, on the authors' account, only their own action can solve? Select all that apply.
options: Lin, who reads a swimming manual in order to learn to swim
Omar, who reads a swimming manual to write a history of coaching
Bea, who reads a negotiation guide before asking for a raise
Raj, who reads a physics book to learn why ice floats
Kim, who reads an Olympic history to prepare for a quiz
optionExplain: Right: learning to swim is a practical problem, solved only by swimming.
The manual is practical, but Omar's interest is theoretical: he wants to understand coaching, not to swim.
Right: getting a raise is a practical problem that only asking, and asking well, can solve.
Why ice floats is a theoretical question; understanding answers it.
Knowing the history for a quiz is a matter of knowledge, not action.
questions.explain: What counts is the reader's problem. A practical book read with a theoretical interest, as Omar reads it, leaves nothing to do but understand.
questions.rule: The reader's interest decides whether action is owed.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Suppose the budgeting reader rereads the book until she knows it by heart but changes nothing in how she spends. What follows on the authors' account?
options: Her problem is solved, since she now knows the method fully
Her problem is half solved, since knowledge is half of the whole task
Her problem has turned theoretical, since she only studies it
Her problem remains, since nothing has yet been done about it
optionExplain: Knowing the method by heart is still knowledge; the practical problem is untouched.
Knowledge helps, but the authors give no half credit: nothing short of the doing solves it.
Her money problem is still practical; changing how she reads does not change the problem.
Right: more reading adds knowledge, but the problem is solved only by acting.
questions.explain: Rereading improves her grasp of the book, not her finances. The practical problem waits on action.
questions.rule: More reading is not more solving.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Sam has bought six books on getting fit this year and exercised twice. What does the authors' point about practical books suggest about his reading?
options: More reading cannot solve his problem and may stand in for acting
He needs a better book that will at last solve the problem
His reading was wasted, since books cannot help with fitness
He has finished the theoretical half, so action will now follow by itself
optionExplain: Right: only exercise solves his problem, and buying more books can postpone it.
No book can solve a practical problem, so a seventh will not either.
The authors say practical books can help by suggesting what to do; the help is real but incomplete.
Reading does not guarantee action; six books and two workouts show the gap.
questions.explain: Since only action solves a practical problem, collecting more advice can become a way of not acting. The books help only if he exercises.
questions.rule: Do not let reading replace the doing.
questions.teaches: By analogy, reading more and more practical books can become a substitute for action, postponing the only thing that solves the problem.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: According to the authors, who could give you fully concrete advice for a practical situation you face?
options: The author of the best book on the subject
Any expert who has studied a great many such cases
Someone in exactly the same situation as you
A teacher who knows the general rules well
optionExplain: Even the best author cannot foresee each reader's concrete situation.
Studying many cases yields general rules, not advice fitted to your case.
Right: only someone in exactly your situation could give advice that concrete.
Knowing the rules well still leaves the fitting to the particular case.
questions.explain: Concrete advice needs knowledge of the exact situation, which no author of a book has. The card next shows what that leaves for the reader.
questions.rule: Concrete advice needs your exact situation.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: True or false: The authors say the practical judgment that comes immediately before an action is highly particular and is seldom put into words.
questions.explain: Action is always here and now, so the judgment that precedes it is particular. It could be expressed, but it seldom is, and it is almost never found in books.
questions.rule: The last judgment before action is particular.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: A gardening book says to water deeply but less often. Ana gardens on sandy soil in a hot, windy spot. Which of these must she add herself to use the rule? Select all that apply.
options: Her knowledge of how fast her sandy soil drains
Her judgment of how deep and how often suits her plot
A new general rule that will fit every garden
The author's own knowledge of her particular plot
A guarantee that the rule works in every climate
optionExplain: Right: knowledge of her own situation is the first thing the reader adds.
Right: judging how the rule applies to her case is the second.
More general rules would sit even further from her case.
The author cannot have this; that is why the reader must supply it.
No general rule comes with such a guarantee, and adding one is not the reader's job.
questions.explain: The reader adds knowledge of the case and judgment of how the rule fits it. Neither can come from the book.
questions.rule: Add knowledge of the case and judgment of the fit.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Tom reasons: Step 1, this negotiation book gives general rules. Step 2, general rules cannot tell me the exact words to use with my landlord. Step 3, so the book is no use for my case. Which step goes wrong?
options: Step 1, since such books give exact scripts for each case
Step 2, since a good enough book would give the exact words
Step 3, since the rules help once he fits them to his case
None, since a book that lacks his case cannot help him
optionExplain: Practical books give general rules; his first step is accurate.
The authors say no author can foresee each reader's situation; Step 2 is accurate too.
Right: general rules are meant to be applied by the reader to his own case.
The authors expect books to give rules, not cases; usefulness comes through the reader's judgment.
questions.explain: Tom is right that the rules are general and right that they do not give exact words. The mistake is concluding they are useless: applying them is his part of the work.
questions.rule: General is not useless; applying is your part.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: A first-aid manual's rules for burns are written for small kitchen burns. Your case is a large chemical burn. What does the authors' account of general rules suggest?
options: Ask whether your case is of the sort the rules cover
Apply the rules with extra care, since they are general
Follow them exactly, since general rules fit every case
Use whichever rule seems closest, applied in full
optionExplain: Right: rules cover situations of a sort, so the reader must first judge whether the case belongs to it.
Care in applying does not help if the rules were written for a different sort of case.
General rules cover many situations of the same sort, not every situation.
Choosing the nearest rule skips the question of whether any of them fits.
questions.explain: The authors say practical rules apply to many situations of the same sort. Judging whether a case is of that sort is part of what the reader adds.
questions.rule: First ask whether the rule covers this sort of case.
questions.teaches: General rules cover situations of the same sort, so part of the reader's judgment is deciding whether a case is of that sort at all.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: An experienced nurse makes a quick decision about a patient and, when asked, cannot fully explain why. What does the authors' account of practical judgment suggest?
options: Her decision rested on luck, since she cannot state a rule
She must be following a written rule she has forgotten
Her training failed, since good practice is all written down
Such particular judgment is seldom put into words
optionExplain: Being unable to state a rule does not make a judgment lucky; particular judgment is rarely spelled out.
Her judgment fits this patient; it is not a forgotten general rule.
The authors say this kind of judgment is almost never found in books, so it cannot all be written down.
Right: the judgment immediately before action is particular and seldom expressed, so this is what one would expect.
questions.explain: The judgment that precedes action is about this case, here and now, and seldom put into words. Skilled practice often shows it without explaining it.
questions.rule: Expect skilled judgment to outrun words.
questions.teaches: By analogy, because particular judgment is seldom put into words, skilled practitioners often cannot fully explain their decisions, so such judgment is learned largely by practice.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: A practical book explains why its rules work by appeal to laws of physics. What kind of knowledge are those explanations, according to the authors?
options: Practical knowledge, since the book itself is practical
Theoretical knowledge, the theory behind the practice
Rhetoric, meant to persuade more than to inform
Historical knowledge of how the rules came about
optionExplain: The book is practical, but its explanatory principles are items of theoretical knowledge.
Right: the principles underlying rules are usually scientific, the theory of the thing.
Explanations can persuade, but laws of physics state what is so; they are knowledge, not oratory.
Laws of physics explain why the rules work, not where they came from.
questions.explain: The principles beneath practical rules are usually theoretical knowledge. The card next shows how they sit inside a practical book.
questions.rule: Principles behind rules are theory.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: The principles that make the rules of good procedure what they are, taken together, are what the authors call the ____ of the thing.
questions.explain: We speak of the theory of bridge building or of contract bridge, meaning the principles that make the rules of good procedure what they are.
questions.rule: The principles together are the theory.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Sort each sentence from a car owner's manual into rule or principle.

items.t: Check tyre pressure once a month
An underinflated tyre flexes more and heats up
Brake before the bend, not in it
A tyre has less grip for braking while cornering
Change the oil every 10,000 km
Oil breaks down with heat and lubricates less well

questions.explain: Rules direct what to do; principles state what is the case and explain why the rule is good procedure.
questions.rule: Rules direct; principles explain.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Which sentence from a book on public speaking states a principle rather than a rule?
options: Pause for a moment after each main point
Listeners recall ideas best in small groups
Open your talk with a question to the audience
Keep each slide to a single idea at most
optionExplain: This tells the speaker what to do, so it is a rule.
Right: it states something that is so about listeners, which can explain rules such as keeping points few.
A direction to the speaker is a rule, however good.
This directs the speaker; the reason for it would be the principle.
questions.explain: A principle says what is the case; a rule says what to do. The statement about memory could explain several of the rules.
questions.rule: Is it a fact that explains, or a direction?

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: If a practical book gave only its rules and left out every principle, what would its reader lose?
options: The rules themselves, since rules cannot exist without stated principles
Its practical character, since a book needs principles to be practical
Little, since following a rule does not need its reasons
The reasons for the rules, and with them a basis for adapting them
optionExplain: Rules can be stated and followed without their principles; a cookbook does it on every page.
A book of bare rules is still practical; it is the rule-book kind.
A rule can be followed blind, but then the reader cannot tell when or how to adjust it.
Right: principles make rules intelligible, and a reader who knows why a rule works has grounds for adjusting it when the case changes.
questions.explain: Principles make the rules intelligible. This suggests that a reader who knows why a rule works is better placed to adapt it when circumstances change.
questions.rule: Knowing why lets you adjust how.
questions.teaches: Knowing the principle behind a rule gives a reader grounds for adapting the rule when circumstances change, while knowing only the rule allows following it but not adjusting it.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Principles of how loads spread through a structure appear in manuals for bridge builders and for scaffold erectors, each with different rules. What does this show?
options: One body of theory can yield different rules for different jobs
Rules come first, and principles are drawn from them later
The two manuals must contradict each other somewhere in their details
The principles are practical knowledge, since manuals use them
optionExplain: Right: the same principles of load can underlie different rules for different practices.
Here the shared principles explain both sets of rules, so they are not drawn from either one.
Different rules for different jobs need not conflict; each fits its own practice.
Principles stay theoretical knowledge even when a practical book uses them.
questions.explain: Principles are theoretical, so they are not tied to one practice. The same theory can produce different rules for different jobs.
questions.rule: Principles travel further than rules.
questions.teaches: By analogy, one body of theory can underlie several practices and generate different rules for each, which is why principles carry further than any single set of rules.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: According to the authors, where are most of the great practical books found?
options: Among cookbooks, manuals and other books of rules
In the natural sciences, as books of experimental method
In economics, politics and morals, as books of principles
Among popular guides to success, habits and self-improvement
optionExplain: Rule-books are the most familiar practical books, but the authors say there are few great ones.
Books of scientific method can be useful, but the authors place the great practical books elsewhere.
Right: most of the great books in economics, politics and morals deal with the principles that generate rules.
Popular guides are mostly rule-books, the kind the authors say has few great examples.
questions.explain: The authors split practical books into books of rules and books of principles, and place most great practical books in the second group. The card next sets out the split.
questions.rule: Great practical books are mostly books of principles.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: True or false: The authors say one practical book can contain both rules and principles, so the two kinds differ in emphasis rather than sharply.
questions.explain: The distinction is not sharp and absolute; both may be found in one book, and the point is relative emphasis.
questions.rule: The two kinds differ in emphasis.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Sort each practical book by its main emphasis.

items.t: A handbook for passing the driving test
A book of knitting patterns
A step-by-step guide to filing taxes
A treatise on what justice requires of a state
A work on what a fair economy aims at and why
A study of what makes a human life go well

questions.explain: Handbooks, patterns and step-by-step guides mainly say what to do. Works on justice, a fair economy or a good life mainly set out the principles from which such directions would follow.
questions.rule: Ask which the book mainly offers.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: A cookbook opens with a long chapter on the chemistry of flavour and then gives 300 recipes. How should it be sorted?
options: As a book of principles, since it opens with a chapter of theory
As a theoretical book, since chemistry is a science
As a rule-book, since its chemistry serves the recipes
As neither kind, since it mixes rules and principles
optionExplain: The opening chapter is theory, but it is there for the sake of the recipes.
Chemistry is theoretical knowledge, but here it is part of a practical book.
Right: the emphasis falls on the recipes, and the chemistry serves them.
Mixing is normal; the authors sort by relative emphasis, not by purity.
questions.explain: Most practical books mix the two. What decides the pile is which part serves the other; here the theory is there for the recipes.
questions.rule: Sort by which part serves the other.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: A reader wants one practical book in economics or politics worth reading slowly several times. Given the authors' remarks on great practical books, where should she look first?
options: Among the books of practical principles in the field
Among the manuals that give the most detailed rules
Among the newest guides, since rules date quickly
Among the shortest books, since great rules are brief
optionExplain: Right: most great practical books in these fields deal with principles, so that is where to look.
Detailed rules make a useful manual, but the authors say great rule-books are few.
Newness is not the authors' test; they sort great books by kind, not by date.
Brevity is not what the authors associate with great practical books.
questions.explain: Great rule-books are rare, and most great books in economics, politics and morals deal with principles. A reader looking for depth will usually find it there.
questions.rule: Look for depth among books of principles.
questions.teaches: Since great rule-books are few, a reader looking for a practical book that rewards repeated analytical reading will usually find it among the books of principles.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: A company's procedures manual from 1995 is now mostly obsolete, while its founding statement of purposes still guides decisions. By analogy with the two kinds of practical book, what best explains the difference?
options: The procedures were badly written, while the purposes were written with care
Statements of purpose are vague, so they can never be shown to be out of date
Procedures are theoretical, so they date as knowledge advances over the years
Rules fit their circumstances; principles can yield new rules
optionExplain: Good drafting does not stop procedures dating; even well-written rules are tied to the circumstances they were made for.
Vagueness is a risk, but a statement that still guides decisions is doing real work, not escaping test.
Procedures say what to do, so they are practical rules, not theory.
Right: rules are fitted to circumstances of a sort, while principles generate rules, so they can produce new ones when circumstances change.
questions.explain: Rules are made for situations of a certain sort, so they age as those situations change. Principles generate rules, so they can be applied afresh.
questions.rule: Rules date; principles regenerate rules.
questions.teaches: By analogy, rule-books tend to date faster than books of principles: rules are fitted to the circumstances of their time, while principles can generate new rules when circumstances change.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: A book reads like a theoretical treatise but deals with how people ought to govern themselves. How would the authors classify it?
options: As theoretical, since its sentences state what is so
As practical, since it is about conduct done well or badly
As history, since government is studied through its past
As half and half, since its style and its topic point different ways
optionExplain: Declarative sentences are common in books of practical principles; style does not decide.
Right: the nature of its problems gives it away as practical.
Government can be studied historically, but this book asks how people ought to govern.
The authors classify by the problems, which point one way here.
questions.explain: A book of practical principles can sound like theory. Its problems, about conduct that can be better or worse, show it is practical. The card next explains the test.
questions.rule: The problems give it away.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: According to the authors, a book of practical principles gives itself away because it concerns a field of human behaviour in which people can do ____ or worse.
questions.explain: Its problems concern conduct that can be done better or worse, which marks it as practical however theoretical it looks.
questions.rule: Better or worse marks the practical.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Which of these books are practical in the authors' sense, though each might read like theory? Select all that apply.
options: A treatise on what makes a punishment fair
A survey measuring how often citizens vote
A study of what a good friendship requires
An account of how the planets were formed
A work on what a central bank should aim for
optionExplain: Right: punishing justly or unjustly is conduct that can be better or worse.
Measuring how often people vote describes behaviour; it does not address how to do better.
Right: friendship is a field where people can do better or worse.
Planet formation is not human conduct at all, so the book is theoretical.
Right: running a central bank is a practice that can be done well or badly.
questions.explain: Each practical book concerns a field where people act better or worse. Describing behaviour, or explaining nature, stays theoretical.
questions.rule: Ask whether the field allows better or worse.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Dev reasons: Step 1, this book on ethics gives almost no commands. Step 2, a book without commands is theoretical. Step 3, so this book is theoretical. Which step goes wrong?
options: Step 1, since ethics books are full of commands
Step 2, since books of principles also lack commands
Step 3, since one book cannot settle a whole field
None, since commands are what make a book practical
optionExplain: Many ethics books do give few commands; his observation may well be accurate.
Right: books of practical principles state what is so, yet are practical because of their problems.
Step 3 follows if Step 2 were true; the fault lies in Step 2.
Commands mark a rule-book, but a book of principles is practical without them.
questions.explain: Commands are a sign of a rule-book, not a requirement for being practical. A book of principles is practical because its problems concern conduct.
questions.rule: No commands does not mean theoretical.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: A book argues that some ways of furnishing a home are better than others, and explains why. A reader thinks taste is wholly personal. How should the reader classify the book?
options: As theoretical, since taste cannot be done better or worse
As theoretical, since it explains rather than commands
As unclassifiable until the dispute about taste has been settled
As practical, since the author treats it as better or worse
optionExplain: That is the reader's view of taste, not the author's; classification follows the problem the author takes on.
Explaining why is what books of practical principles do.
The reader can classify the book now by the problem it addresses, and judge it later.
Right: the author treats furnishing as a field where one can do better or worse, so the book is practical.
questions.explain: The test asks what problem the author takes on. Whether the reader accepts that taste admits better and worse is a question for the later judgment of the book.
questions.rule: Classify by the author's problem; judge later.
questions.teaches: The better-or-worse test follows the author's treatment of the field: if the author treats a field as one where people can do better or worse, the book is practical even if the reader doubts that the field allows it.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: You classify a book on hospital management as practical principles, because hospitals can be run better or worse. Which words are most likely to be among its key terms?
options: Efficient, safe and humane care, the marks of running a hospital well
Building dates, staff numbers and bed counts, its most frequent facts
The names of the hospitals it uses as examples throughout the book
Technical medical names for the diseases that the hospitals treat
optionExplain: Right: the book's problem is how to run a hospital better, so the words naming doing well are likely its key terms.
Frequent facts are not thereby key terms; they describe rather than carry the book's problem.
Examples illustrate the argument; their names are not the terms it turns on.
Medical vocabulary belongs to the field, but the book's problem is management, not disease.
questions.explain: A practical book's problem is how to do better in its field, so the words that name doing well or badly are likely to carry its argument.
questions.rule: Words for doing well are likely key terms.
questions.teaches: In a book of practical principles, words that name doing well or badly in its field, such as efficient, just or healthy, are likely to be its key terms, since the book's problem is how to do better.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a rule in a practical book can be stated as an ordinary declarative sentence rather than as a command.
questions.explain: A stitch in time saves nine is a statement, yet it carries the same rule as the command to take a stitch in time. The card next shows how to spot rules in either form.
questions.rule: Rules come in statements too.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: According to the authors, what marks a sentence as a rule, whatever its grammar?
options: It is written in the imperative, as a command
It appears in a numbered list of directions to follow
It recommends something as worth doing for an end
It is set apart in a box or printed in bold
optionExplain: The imperative is the most direct form, but the authors show that statements can carry rules too.
Lists are a common layout for rules, but layout is not what makes a rule.
Right: a rule recommends something as worth doing to gain an end.
Typography may highlight rules, but the authors identify rules by what they recommend.
questions.explain: Grammar and layout vary. What every rule does is recommend something as worth doing for the sake of an end.
questions.rule: A rule recommends something for an end.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Which sentences from a book on personal finance are rules, though some are worded as statements? Select all that apply.
options: Pay yourself first, before any bills, each month
A good saver keeps three months of expenses in cash
Inflation is a rise in the general level of prices
The prudent investor spreads money across many funds
Interest rates rose sharply during the 1970s
optionExplain: Right: a command, the most direct form of a rule.
Right: the word good recommends keeping a cash reserve as worth doing.
This defines a term; it recommends nothing.
Right: prudent recommends spreading money as worth doing, for safety.
This reports history; it recommends nothing.
questions.explain: Commands and statements with words like good or prudent recommend something for an end. Definitions and history do not.
questions.rule: Watch for words that recommend.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Sort each sentence from a gardening book into rule or not a rule.

items.t: The wise gardener mulches before summer
Good pruning removes dead wood first
Water early, before the sun is high
Roses belong to the same plant family as apples
Most garden soils in this region are clay
Slugs feed mainly at night

questions.explain: Rules recommend something as worth doing, by command or by words like wise and good. Facts about plants, soil or pests recommend nothing on their own, though they may explain a rule.
questions.rule: No recommendation, no rule.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: A management book says: Effective managers give feedback within a day. How can a reader check that this is a rule and see what it asks of her?
options: Count how often the author repeats the sentence
Look up whether most managers actually do this
Restate it as a command and name the end it serves
Check whether it appears in the chapter summary
optionExplain: Repetition shows emphasis, not whether the sentence recommends anything.
That would test it as a report; the sentence recommends rather than reports.
Right: give feedback within a day, in order to manage effectively, shows both the recommendation and its end.
Placement may show importance, but not whether the sentence is a rule.
questions.explain: If a statement can be turned into a command for the sake of an end without changing its point, it was a rule. The restatement also shows what to do.
questions.rule: Turn it into a command to test it.
questions.teaches: Restating a declarative rule as a command, and naming the end it serves, is a quick way to check that you have found a rule and to see what it asks you to do.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: A school leaflet says: Smart parents read to their children every night. In the authors' terms, what is this sentence?
options: A rule recommending nightly reading to children
A report of what smart parents happen to do
A definition of what the word smart means
A principle explaining why reading helps children
optionExplain: Right: smart works like good, recommending nightly reading as worth doing.
It looks like a report, but nobody surveyed smart parents; the word smart recommends.
It does not define smart; it uses the word to praise an action.
A principle would explain why reading helps; this sentence gives no reason.
questions.explain: Praise words turn an apparent description into a recommendation. Spotting them lets a reader see advice for what it is and ask for its reasons.
questions.rule: Praise words often carry rules.
questions.teaches: By analogy, advice often hides in apparent reports: words such as smart, responsible or healthy turn a description into a recommendation, and spotting them lets a reader ask for the reasons behind it.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: According to the authors, which kind of argument for a practical rule is usually the more persuasive?
options: An appeal to the principles behind the rule
A list of the experts who follow the rule
An account of how long the rule has been used
Showing the rule working in concrete cases
optionExplain: Principles explain a rule well, but the authors call this appeal usually less persuasive.
Authority can impress, but it is not one of the two sorts the authors name.
Age of a rule is not one of the two sorts of argument the authors name.
Right: illustration in concrete cases is usually the more persuasive.
questions.explain: Seeing a rule work persuades more readily than hearing why it works. The card next shows what each sort is good for.
questions.rule: Cases persuade; principles explain.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Match each part of a rule-book to what it does.
pairs: Explains the reason for a rule
Shows a rule working in practice
questions.explain: In a rule-book the rules are the main propositions, and the arguments try to show they are sound, by explaining or by illustrating.
questions.rule: Rules, then two sorts of support.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Sort each passage from a book on better sleep by the sort of argument it gives for its rules.

items.t: Screen light delays the body's release of melatonin
Caffeine blocks the brain's signal that tiredness is building
The body clock sets itself by regular light and timing
A nurse who switched off screens at nine fell asleep faster within a week
One reader found a fixed wake-up time ended years of poor sleep
A student who cut afternoon coffee slept an hour longer

questions.explain: Statements about how the body works explain why the rules should help. Stories of particular people show the rules working.
questions.rule: Why it works, or that it worked.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Suppose a book supports its rule with many success stories and no explanation at all. What would the reader find harder as a result?
options: Believing the rule worked for the people in the stories
Seeing the reason why the rule works at all
Remembering the rule, since stories distract from it
Finding the rule, since stories bury it in detail
optionExplain: Stories are the more persuasive sort, so belief comes easily.
Right: without an appeal to principle, the reason for the rule stays unexplained.
Stories often make rules more memorable, not less.
The rule may still be stated plainly; what is missing is its reason.
questions.explain: Illustration persuades but does not explain. Without principles, the reader knows the rule works for some people but not why.
questions.rule: Stories without principles leave the why out.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: A diet book offers twenty glowing stories from readers who lost weight. What question should a careful reader ask about this kind of support?
options: Whether the stories are written in a lively way
Whether readers for whom it failed were left out
Whether the author has tried the diet himself
Whether there are more than ten such stories
optionExplain: Liveliness adds to persuasion, not to evidence.
Right: the author chose the cases, so the failures may be missing.
The author's own success would be one more story, open to the same doubt.
More stories chosen the same way do not answer whether failures were left out.
questions.explain: Illustrations are cases the author selected. Many successes prove little if the failures were never reported.
questions.rule: Ask what cases were left out.
questions.teaches: Success stories in a practical book are selected by the author, so a careful reader asks whether cases where the rule failed have been left out.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: A cycling coach wants riders to adopt a new pedalling drill. Which support would back the drill most fully, by the authors' account of the two sorts of argument?
options: Race results from several more riders who used the drill
A detailed account of the muscle mechanics alone
A record of the coach's years of experience and titles
Results of riders who used it, and the mechanics behind it
optionExplain: More cases add persuasion but still leave the reason unexplained.
Mechanics explain the drill but are usually less persuasive and do not show it working.
Experience and titles are authority, not either of the two sorts of argument.
Right: cases show the drill works and principles show why, so each covers the other's gap.
questions.explain: Each sort has a strength the other lacks. Used together, a case shows the rule works and a principle explains why.
questions.rule: Combine showing with explaining.
questions.teaches: The two sorts of argument complement each other: a case shows that a rule works and a principle shows why, so together they support a rule more fully than either does alone.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: A reader studies a book of political principles as pure theory, without asking what actions follow from it. According to the authors, how well has she read it?
options: Poorly, since she has not read it as practical
Well, since principles are theoretical knowledge
Well for understanding, poorly only for criticism
Well, if she can state each principle accurately
optionExplain: Right: the authors say failing to read a practical book as practical is reading it poorly.
Principles are theoretical in form, but in a practical book their significance lies in the actions they lead to.
The authors say such a reader does not really understand the book, so understanding fails too.
Stating principles accurately is part of the job, but not the part that makes it a practical reading.
questions.explain: A practical book read as theory is not really understood. The card next shows what reading it as practical involves.
questions.rule: Read practical books as practical.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the significance of practical principles is found in the rules and actions they lead to.
questions.explain: Rules are made intelligible by principles, and principles are made significant by the rules and actions they recommend.
questions.rule: Principles matter through what they recommend.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: A public health book argues that infections spread fastest where people crowd together indoors. Which of a reader's notes show it being read as practical? Select all that apply.
options: Rule implied: ventilate shared rooms in winter
Infections spread fastest in crowded indoor spaces
For my office: open the windows during long meetings
The author cites forty studies on indoor crowding
optionExplain: Right: a rule the principle implies, though the author may not state it.
This restates the principle; accurate, but it does not yet draw out a rule.
Right: this works out how the derived rule applies in a particular case.
This records the evidence, which matters for judging the principle, not for drawing rules from it.
questions.explain: Reading as practical means deriving the rules a principle implies and working out how to apply them. Restating the principle or its evidence stops short.
questions.rule: Derive the rule, then its application.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: A book on economic principles argues that high taxes reduce investment. Mia's notes say: The author says to abolish all taxes. What went wrong?
options: She derived a rule, which a careful reader should leave alone
She read a theoretical book as if it were a practical one
She credited the author with a rule his claim does not imply
Nothing, since rules derived from a book belong to its author
optionExplain: The authors want readers to derive rules from practical principles.
A book on economic principles concerns a field where people can do better or worse; reading it as practical is right.
Right: abolishing all taxes does not follow from the claim, and she reported her inference as the author's words.
A rule the reader derives is the reader's inference and should be marked as such.
questions.explain: Deriving rules is the right move, but the rule must follow from the principle and be labelled as the reader's own inference.
questions.rule: Derive carefully, and label what you derived.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: If you cannot derive any rule at all from a book's principles about a field of conduct, what might that tell you?
options: That the book is theoretical after all and so needs no rules
That the author has failed, since every book of principles must state its rules
That you have not grasped the principles, or they are too vague to act on
That the rules must be printed in an appendix you have not reached
optionExplain: A book about a field of conduct is practical by its problems, whether or not you can draw rules from it.
Books of principles often leave rules unstated; that is why the reader reads between the lines.
Right: principles get their significance from the rules they lead to, so finding none points to a gap in understanding or in the principles.
Unstated rules are usually not printed anywhere; deriving them is the reader's task.
questions.explain: Practical principles are significant through the rules they lead to. If none can be drawn, either the reader's grasp or the principles themselves need a second look.
questions.rule: No rules derivable is a signal worth heeding.
questions.teaches: If no rule can be drawn from a book's practical principles, either the reader has not yet understood them or the principles are too vague to guide action; both are worth noticing before judging the book.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: A landlord and a tenant both read a court ruling that an agreement made under heavy pressure is not freely agreed. Each derives rules for their own dealings. What should we expect?
options: Different rules, each fitted to their side of the dealing and faithful to it
The same rules, since a principle implies one set of rules for everyone
No rules at all, since a court ruling is theory rather than practice
Rules that favour whichever of the two read the ruling more carefully
optionExplain: Right: each applies the same principle to a different situation, so faithful derivations can differ.
A principle can imply different rules for people in different situations.
A ruling bears on how people should deal with each other, so it is practical.
Care in reading matters, but the difference here comes from their situations, not from who read better.
questions.explain: Deriving rules means applying principles to a situation. Different situations can yield different rules from one principle, all of them faithful to it.
questions.rule: One principle, many faithful rules.
questions.teaches: Deriving rules from principles depends on the reader's situation, so two readers of the same principle can derive different rules that are equally faithful to it.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: According to the authors, which conditions must a rule of conduct meet to be practically true? Select all that apply.
options: It works, getting you to the end it promises
It leads to an end you rightly desire
It is stated in the form of a command
It is accepted by most experts in the field
optionExplain: Right: the first condition is that the rule works.
Right: the second is that its working leads to the right end.
Rules can be stated as commands or as statements; form is not a test of truth.
Expert approval may be evidence, but it is not one of the authors' two conditions.
questions.explain: Practical truth has two conditions: the rule works, and it leads to an end rightly desired. The card next explains them.
questions.rule: Works, and leads to the right end.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, practical truth is judged in the same way as theoretical truth, by comparing a claim with how things are.
questions.explain: Theoretical truth is a matter of fit with how things are. Practical truth adds a second test: whether the rule leads to an end rightly desired.
questions.rule: Practical truth is not theoretical truth.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: A book's cramming rules really do raise exam scores overnight. A student values lasting understanding over scores. How would the authors have her judge the rules?
options: As practically true, since the rules do work
As practically true, since high scores are the goal of study
As theoretically false, since cramming does not cause understanding
As practically false for her, as they serve an end she rejects
optionExplain: Working is only the first test; the rules must also lead to an end she rightly desires.
That assumes her end is scores; she has another end in view.
The book claims cramming raises scores, which is true; the question is practical, not theoretical.
Right: they pass the first test and fail the second, given the end she rightly seeks.
questions.explain: The rules work, so they pass the first test. They lead to an end she does not seek, so they fail the second for her.
questions.rule: Working is not enough.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Sort each case by which test of practical truth the rules fail.
groups: Fails the first test: does not work
Fails the second test: wrong end

items.t: A diet whose steps do not cause weight loss
Study rules that do not improve recall at all
Exercises that build no strength in the muscles named
A proven way to get rich fast, for a reader who rejects wealth as a goal
Effective tips for gaining a huge online following, for a reader who thinks fame is not worth having
Reliable speed-reading drills, for a reader who values slow, careful reading

questions.explain: Rules that do not deliver fail the first test. Rules that deliver, but toward an end the reader does not rightly desire, fail the second.
questions.rule: Does it work, and is the end right?

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Suppose a book aims at an end you rightly desire, but its rules do not in fact achieve it. How would the authors' two tests judge the rules?
options: As practically true, since the end is the right one
As practically false, since they fail the test of working
As half true, to be weighed against other books
As theoretically true, since the end is worth having
optionExplain: A right end does not make rules true if they do not reach it.
Right: practical truth needs both conditions, and these rules fail the first.
The authors give two conditions to be met, not a score to be averaged.
Whether an end is worth having is a practical question, not a theoretical truth about the rules.
questions.explain: Both tests must be passed. A good aim cannot rescue rules that do not work, and working rules cannot rescue a wrong aim.
questions.rule: Both tests, not either.
questions.teaches: The two tests are jointly required: a right end cannot rescue rules that do not work, any more than sound means can rescue a wrong end.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: A hospital's new scheduling rule cuts waiting times as promised, partly by sending patients home earlier than their doctors think wise. How do the two tests apply?
options: It is practically true, since it meets the target it promised
Doubtful on the second test: this may not be the right end
It is theoretically false, since the waiting figures must be wrong
It is beyond the two tests, which apply only to rules in books
optionExplain: Meeting the target passes the first test only.
Right: the rule works, but whether shorter waits won at patients' expense is the right end is exactly the second test.
Nothing suggests the figures are wrong; the rule does what it promised.
The tests concern rules of conduct, wherever they are written down.
questions.explain: The rule works, so the question belongs to the second test. That test looks at everything the rule's working brings about, including early discharges, not only the target it names.
questions.rule: Judge the whole result, not only the target.
questions.teaches: The second test looks at what a rule's working actually brings about, side effects included, not only at the target it names.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: According to the authors, what does your main judgment of a practical book turn on?
options: The soundness of the means it proposes
The author's standing among experts in the field
How well its rules are worded and set out
The ends or goals it asks you to pursue
optionExplain: Means matter, but the authors say the main judgment is about ends.
Reputation is not the authors' criterion for judging a practical book.
Clarity helps understanding, but judgment concerns the goals.
Right: in judging a practical book, everything turns on the ends.
questions.explain: We care about means only for ends we want. The card next explains why the ends decide.
questions.rule: Ends first.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reader has little practical interest in even very sound means to an end he does not care about.
questions.explain: The authors say we have no practical interest in the soundest means to ends we disapprove of or do not care about.
questions.rule: Sound means to an unwanted end leave us cold.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: A book offers proven methods for the greenest possible lawn. Maya wants to turn her lawn into a wildflower meadow. On the authors' account, how is she likely to judge the book?
options: As practically irrelevant to her, however sound its methods
As practically true, since its methods are proven
As theoretically false, since lawns are not meadows
As a poor book, since it says nothing at all about meadows or wild gardens
optionExplain: Right: she does not seek its end, so its sound means have no practical interest for her.
Proven methods pass the test of working, but she does not share the end.
The book's claims about lawns may be true; her judgment is practical, not theoretical.
A book is not poor for lacking a goal it never set; her judgment is about its end, not its coverage.
questions.explain: Her judgment turns on the end. Not sharing it, she finds the book practically irrelevant, whatever the quality of its methods.
questions.rule: No shared end, no practical interest.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Sort each step by the kind of book whose judgment it belongs to, according to the authors.

items.t: Compare your basic assumptions with the author's
Ask whether the account fits how things are
Ask whether you share the goal the author proposes
Ask whether the proposed means would reach that goal

questions.explain: A theoretical book is judged by its truth to how things are and by comparing basic assumptions. A practical book is judged mainly by its ends, then by its means.
questions.rule: Assumptions for theory, ends for practice.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: Two economists agree that a reform will both reduce inequality and slow growth. One praises the book proposing it; the other calls it practically false. What best explains this?
options: One of them must have misread the evidence
One of them has not understood the means the book proposes
They weigh the ends, equality and growth, differently
The book must be ambiguous about its main claims
optionExplain: They agree on the evidence about what the reform does.
They agree on what the reform would do, so both grasp the means.
Right: agreeing on the facts, they differ over which end matters more, and that decides the practical judgment.
They read the book's claims the same way; the difference lies in their own ends.
questions.explain: Their disagreement is about ends, as in the authors' example of Marx and Burke. More evidence about the means would not settle it.
questions.rule: Agreement on facts can coexist with opposite verdicts.
questions.teaches: Two readers who agree on every fact in a practical book can still judge it oppositely, because their disagreement lies in ends, which evidence about means cannot settle.

questions.section: The Two Kinds of Practical Books
questions.q: A city plan gives a well-costed route to more parking downtown. A councillor wants fewer cars in the centre. By the authors' reasoning, where should her debate with the planners begin?
options: With the costings, since numbers are the most objective part
With the timetable, since delays raise every cost
With the end: whether more parking is the right goal
With the maps, since details reveal hidden flaws
optionExplain: The costings concern means, which matter little while the end is in dispute.
Timing is a matter of means, secondary while the goal is disputed.
Right: she rejects the end, so arguing about the means would miss her real objection.
Details of the means do not touch the disagreement about the goal.
questions.explain: As with a practical book, the main question is the end. Arguing over costs and maps while disagreeing on the goal wastes the debate.
questions.rule: Settle or face the ends first.
questions.teaches: By analogy, in planning and policy debates, arguing over means is wasted effort while the parties disagree about ends; the productive debate starts with the goal.

questions.q: The two major questions for a practical book ask what the author's objectives are and what ____ he proposes for achieving them.
questions.explain: Objectives and means: what the author wants, and how he proposes to get it. The card next explains why both are needed.
questions.rule: Ends and means.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the ends and means are usually easier to find in a book of principles than in a book of rules.
questions.explain: The authors say it may be harder in a book of principles, where ends and means are likely to be less obvious.
questions.rule: Principles hide ends and means more.

questions.q: A guide to cutting household waste is being analysed. Sort each item into the author's objectives or the means proposed.

items.t: A home that sends almost nothing to landfill
A household budget freed from needless spending
Buy staples in bulk
Compost food scraps
Repair before replacing

questions.explain: Objectives are the states of affairs the author wants; means are the actions proposed to reach them.
questions.rule: What for, and how.

questions.q: Leo starts judging a book on city planning by attacking its proposals for bus lanes, without saying what the author wants cities to become. What has he skipped?
options: Finding the author's objectives, which the means serve
Checking the author's credentials as a city planner
Counting the proposals to see which ones dominate
Comparing it with other books on rural planning
optionExplain: Right: bus lanes are means; without the objectives he cannot judge whether they serve them, or whether he shares the end.
Credentials may interest a reader, but they are not one of the two questions.
Counting proposals does not tell him what they are for.
Comparison comes later, and still needs the author's objectives first.
questions.explain: Means make sense only in light of the ends they serve. Leo has answered neither question before judging.
questions.rule: Find the ends before attacking the means.

questions.q: A treatise on justice does not state what it wants readers to do or bring about. How can a reader find its objectives?
options: Conclude that it has none, and read it as theoretical
Look only in the preface, where aims are usually stated
Infer them from reviews written by other readers
Ask what its principles would bring about if acted on
optionExplain: A book on justice concerns conduct that can be better or worse; unstated objectives are still objectives.
Prefaces can help, but books of principles often leave their aims implicit throughout.
Reviews can mislead and are no substitute for working it out from the book.
Right: asking what the principles would bring about if followed reveals the end they serve.
questions.explain: In a book of principles, ends are often implicit. Picturing what acting on the principles would bring about is a way to make them explicit.
questions.rule: Ask what acting on it would produce.
questions.teaches: When a book of principles does not state its objectives, the reader can infer them by asking what state of affairs its principles would bring about if acted on.

questions.q: An advertisement for a fitness tracker shows people hiking happily on a mountain. Applying the two questions to the advertiser, which reading fits best?
options: Objective: making viewers healthier; means: images of hikes
Objective: a sale; means: tying the tracker to a happy, active life
Objective: promoting hiking; means: showing a tracker on a hike
Objective: describing the product; means: a picture of it in use outdoors
optionExplain: Health is the end offered to the viewer, not necessarily the advertiser's own objective.
Right: the advertiser's objective is a sale, and the hiking scene is the means of winning you to it.
The hikes are a setting; the advert is about the tracker.
An advert that only described would list features, not stage a happy scene.
questions.explain: Asked of the author himself, the two questions can expose a gap between the end offered to you and the author's own end.
questions.rule: Ask what the author wants, not only what he offers.
questions.teaches: In persuasive communication the author's own objective can differ from the end he offers you: an advertisement offers you health or happiness, but its objective is a sale.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, appeals to the reader's emotions are out of place in a good practical book.
questions.explain: The authors see nothing wrong in a practical author appealing to the emotions, since people must be moved to act. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Practical writing appeals to feeling.

questions.q: According to the authors, nobody makes serious practical judgments or acts without being moved somehow from below the ____.
questions.explain: Practical thinking and action are not affairs of the mind alone; the emotions cannot be left out.
questions.rule: Action involves feeling.

questions.q: In a book urging readers to cycle to work, which passages appeal to the heart rather than the mind? Select all that apply.
options: Picture yourself gliding past a line of stalled cars
Cycling eight kilometres burns about 250 calories
Your children deserve to grow up breathing clean air
In one city study, bike lanes cut commutes by a fifth
Feel the morning air and arrive at work awake and proud
optionExplain: Right: it invites you to imagine a pleasing scene, appealing to feeling.
This is a factual claim offered to the mind, true or false.
Right: it works on love and guilt about your children.
This is evidence for the mind to weigh.
Right: it appeals to how cycling will make you feel.
questions.explain: Appeals to the heart invite you to picture, feel or care. Claims and evidence are offered to the mind; a practical book uses both.
questions.rule: Tell heart appeals from mind appeals.

questions.q: Nadia notices that a book on giving to charity tugs at her feelings. Since practical authors must move readers, she decides that every appeal in it deserves her assent. Where does her reasoning go wrong?
options: In noticing the appeal, since a charity book has no reason to move readers
In moving from appeals being normal to every appeal deserving assent
In assuming practical authors must move readers, which the authors deny
Nowhere, since appeals in practical books are there to be accepted
optionExplain: A charity book has every reason to move its readers; her observation is likely accurate.
Right: that appeals are natural explains them; whether one deserves assent depends on whether the arguments support its end.
The authors say practical writers must move readers, so this premise is their view.
The authors warn that a reader who does not see this is likely to be sold a bill of goods.
questions.explain: Her two premises are sound. The slip is moving from appeals are normal to appeals should be accepted.
questions.rule: Normal is not the same as deserving assent.

questions.q: Given why practical authors persuade, where in a practical book would you expect the strongest appeals to feeling?
options: In the technical details of the means it proposes
In the definitions of key terms near the start
Spread evenly, since persuasion has no reason to cluster
Where the author presents the ends he wants you to adopt
optionExplain: Means can be argued for on their merits; the author's main need to move you lies elsewhere.
Definitions set up terms; they are rarely where an author needs to stir you.
Persuasion has a purpose, winning you to the end, so it tends to gather where the end is at stake.
Right: since your judgment turns on accepting his goal, the author has most reason to move you where he presents it.
questions.explain: The author must win you to his ends, so his appeals tend to gather where those ends are presented. Those passages deserve the closest watch.
questions.rule: Watch most closely where the ends are urged.
questions.teaches: Because a practical author must win you to his ends, his appeals tend to gather where he presents those ends, so passages about goals deserve the closest watch for oratory.

questions.q: A budget proposal contains no emotional language, only figures, but it opens with the most alarming one. Given the authors' view of practical writing, what should a reader expect?
options: That it may persuade through the choice and order of its facts
That it has no oratory, since it uses no emotive words
That the alarming figure proves the proposal is needed
That figures belong to theory, so the proposal is not practical
optionExplain: Right: a practical document aims to win you to its ends, and leading with alarm is one way to move you.
Oratory does not need emotive words; arrangement can do the work.
One figure, however alarming, is a means of persuasion before it is proof.
A proposal urges action, so it is practical whatever its figures.
questions.explain: Every practical document aims to win you to its ends. When the words are neutral, the persuasion can lie in which facts are chosen and where they are put.
questions.rule: Persuasion can live in arrangement.
questions.teaches: By analogy, even a document that looks purely technical, such as a budget proposal, can persuade through the choice and order of its facts, not only through emotional language.

questions.q: According to the authors, what kind of oratory is really insidious?
options: Oratory that appeals to the strongest emotions
Oratory found in books of political theory
Oratory that stays hidden and undetected
Oratory used by the most skilled writers
optionExplain: Strength of feeling is not the danger the authors name; a strong appeal you notice can be weighed.
