Political books do persuade, but the authors locate the danger in concealment, not subject.
Right: only hidden and undetected oratory is really insidious.
Skill makes oratory effective, but the authors' point is about whether it is noticed.
questions.explain: An appeal you see can be weighed; one you do not see works on you unchecked. The card next shows how a reader brings it to light.
questions.rule: Hidden oratory is the dangerous kind.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reader who knows a practical book's terms, propositions and arguments will be able to detect its oratory.
questions.explain: Knowing the argument lets the reader see which passages make an emotive use of words rather than adding to the case.
questions.rule: Knowing the argument exposes the oratory.

questions.q: In an article for banning cars from a town centre, which sentences make an emotive use of words rather than adding to the argument? Select all that apply.
options: Air pollution there exceeds the legal limit on 90 days a year
Only selfish drivers would choke our children for convenience
Car-free zones in two nearby towns cut asthma admissions
The greedy car lobby wants our streets as its private car park
Delivery vans would still be allowed in before 8 a.m.
optionExplain: A checkable claim that supports the case.
Right: selfish and choke our children work on feeling and add no premise.
Evidence offered to the mind, whatever its strength.
Right: greedy lobby and private car park are labels meant to stir resentment.
A detail of the proposal, part of its means.
questions.explain: With the argument in view, the emotive passages stand out: they push the reader without adding evidence or reasons.
questions.rule: Ask what each passage adds to the case.

questions.q: Which reader is best protected against a practical book's propaganda, on the authors' account?
options: One who avoids practical books that use emotional language
One who reads fast so that the appeals have less time to work on him
One who has outlined its argument and marks where it moves him
One who trusts only authors he already agrees with
optionExplain: Every practical book has some oratory, so avoidance would mean not reading them.
Speed gives the mind less chance to catch the appeals, which is what makes them insidious.
Right: knowing the argument lets him recognize the oratory for what it is.
Agreement makes a reader less likely to notice appeals, not more.
questions.explain: Recognition is the protection, and recognition comes from knowing the argument well enough to see what is not argument.
questions.rule: Outline the argument, then mark the appeals.

questions.q: A reader takes in a stirring book without ever stating its argument, and weeks later finds she strongly supports its cause. What does the authors' account predict?
options: She may not know why she feels or thinks as she does
She can explain exactly why she supports the cause
Her support will soon fade, since unexamined views do not last
Her support is well founded, since the book moved her deeply
optionExplain: Right: propaganda taken in unawares works like a drug; afterwards you do not know why you feel as you do.
Without having stated the argument, she has no clear reasons to give.
The authors say such appeals can put the mind out of business, not that they wear off.
Being moved is not the same as having good reasons.
questions.explain: What reaches the heart without passing through the mind leaves feelings whose source is hidden. That is why the authors call undetected oratory insidious.
questions.rule: Unexamined appeals leave unexplained convictions.

questions.q: True or false: Once a reader has spotted emotive language in a practical book, he should conclude that the argument it accompanies is weak.
questions.explain: Recognizing an appeal tells you what to weigh. Emotive language can sit beside a sound argument, so spotting it does not refute the case.
questions.rule: Spotting the appeal is not refuting the case.

questions.q: A podcast host makes a stirring case for a new diet. How can a listener test how much of its force comes from the argument itself?
options: Listen again and note how strongly she feels on each hearing
Check how many listeners have left glowing reviews online
Compare the host's tone with that of other podcast hosts
Restate the case in plain words and see what force remains
optionExplain: Feelings measure the appeal, not the argument.
Popularity shows the appeal worked, not that the case is sound.
Tone is part of the oratory; comparing tones does not separate it from the argument.
Right: what survives a plain restatement is the argument; what disappears was the wording.
questions.explain: Stating the argument in neutral words separates it from the oratory. Whatever force is lost was coming from the delivery, not the reasons.
questions.rule: Restate it plainly to find the argument.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a plain, neutral restatement of a persuasive case is a test for oratory: whatever force disappears in the restatement was coming from the wording rather than from the reasons.

questions.q: According to the authors, how much sales resistance should a reader of practical books have?
options: Total, so that no appeal can sway him at all
Enough to stop hasty, thoughtless acceptance
None, since appeals are part of practical books
Only toward authors whose politics he dislikes
optionExplain: The authors say a reader deaf to all appeals might as well not read practical books.
Right: resistance is good when it prevents buying hastily and thoughtlessly.
Appeals are part of practical books, but the authors still want them weighed.
Resistance aimed only at disliked authors leaves the reader open to the appeals he likes.
questions.explain: The authors want resistance to haste, not to every appeal. The card next explains the balance.
questions.rule: Resist haste, not every appeal.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a reader who is totally deaf to all appeals might as well not read practical books.
questions.explain: Practical books aim to move you to act; a reader who refuses all appeals cannot be moved by any of them.
questions.rule: Total deafness defeats practical reading.

questions.q: A book urges readers to start saving for retirement and paints a bleak picture of a poor old age. Which response fits the authors' advice?
options: Ignore the picture entirely, since appeals to fear are illegitimate
Notice the fear, then ask whether the argument supports saving now
Let the fear decide, since the author knows the subject better
Stop reading, since a book that frightens readers cannot be trusted
optionExplain: The authors see nothing wrong in appeals to feeling; ignoring them all is the deafness they warn against.
Right: notice the appeal and weigh it against the argument before acting.
Letting the feeling decide is the hasty buying sales resistance is meant to prevent.
An appeal to fear does not by itself show the author is untrustworthy.
questions.explain: Weighing means noticing the appeal and checking it against the case. Neither swallowing it nor refusing it does that.
questions.rule: Notice, then weigh against the argument.

questions.q: Sort each reader's response by whether it weighs the appeal or fails to.

items.t: Asks whether a moving story fits the book's argument
Notes an appeal to guilt and checks what it supports
Lets an appeal count once the argument behind it holds
Adopts a plan because the closing chapter was inspiring
Refuses to consider a plan because it stirred feelings
Buys the course advertised on the last page at once

questions.explain: Weighing connects the appeal to the argument. Accepting it at once and refusing it on sight both skip that step.
questions.rule: Both credulity and deafness skip the weighing.

questions.q: Two books urge action with equally strong appeals: one to try a new recipe tonight, one to sell your house and move abroad. By the logic of the authors' advice, how should your sales resistance differ?
options: The same for both, since the appeals are equally strong
Higher for the recipe, since small choices invite carelessness
Zero for both, since both books are practical and meant to move us
Higher for the move, since a hasty choice there costs far more
optionExplain: Equal appeals do not mean equal stakes; the cost of acting hastily differs greatly.
Small choices can be made lightly because a mistake costs little.
Practical books are exactly where resistance is needed, though not total.
Right: resistance guards against hasty buying, and haste matters most where the action is costly or hard to undo.
questions.explain: Sales resistance exists to prevent hasty, thoughtless action. The more an action costs and the harder it is to reverse, the more weighing it deserves.
questions.rule: Raise resistance with the stakes.
questions.teaches: Sales resistance can be set by the stakes: the more costly or irreversible the action urged, the more the appeals should be checked against the argument before acting.

questions.q: A fundraising email says a donation-matching offer ends at midnight tonight. What does healthy sales resistance suggest?
options: See that the deadline urges haste, and weigh the cause first
Give at once, since any delay would lose the matched sum
Delete it, since a deadline proves the email is manipulation
Forward it to friends and let their replies decide for you
optionExplain: Right: pressure to act at once is itself an appeal, and noticing it gives you back the time to weigh.
Rushing is what the deadline invites; it skips the weighing.
A deadline may be genuine; rejecting on sight is the deafness the authors warn against.
Handing the decision to others avoids weighing it yourself.
questions.explain: A deadline works against weighing by demanding haste. Seeing that lets you weigh the cause on its merits, then decide.
questions.rule: Pressure to hurry is an appeal too.
questions.teaches: Pressure to act at once is itself an appeal against weighing; noticing it, and taking the time to weigh the case, is sales resistance at work.

questions.q: According to the authors, for which of these books does the author's life and times matter most to understanding and judging it?
options: A treatise proving theorems in geometry
A reference table of physical and chemical constants
A political tract on how a state ought to be ruled
A textbook setting out the rules of algebra
optionExplain: In mathematics the reasoning is good or not, whatever kind of man the author is.
A table of constants stands or falls by measurement, not by its compiler's life.
Right: for political, moral and economic books the authors say you should know the writer's character, life and times.
Algebra's rules hold or not regardless of who sets them out.
questions.explain: The more a book concerns action and carries oratory, the more the author's situation bears on it. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Practical books bring the author into view.

questions.q: Match each book to the background the authors say throws light on it.
pairs: Italian politics of his day and the Medici
The English civil wars and dread of disorder
No background needed to judge the reasoning
questions.explain: Each practical work is lit up by its author's situation; a mathematical treatise is judged by its reasoning alone.
questions.rule: Know the setting of a practical book.

questions.q: You are reading a 1930s book urging a country to grow all its own food. Which background would the authors want you to know?
options: The typeface and publisher of the first edition
Nothing beyond the text, since the argument is all that counts
The author's circumstances, such as war fears or blockade
How later critics ranked the book among its rivals
optionExplain: Printing details rarely bear on what the author wanted readers to do.
That holds for a mathematical treatise, but this is a practical book, where the author's situation matters.
Right: the author's life and times help explain the ends he urges.
Later reputation says little about the author's own situation and aims.
questions.explain: In a practical book the author's situation helps explain his ends. Fear of war or blockade would explain an urgent call for self-sufficiency.
questions.rule: Ask what the author's world pressed on him.

questions.q: Sara learns that an economist wrote a policy book while holding shares in an industry it favours, and concludes the policy must be wrong. What is her error?
options: She let his background stand in for testing his argument
She should not have looked into the author's life at all
She should have checked his statistics and proofs instead
None, since an author with an interest must be wrong
optionExplain: Right: the background may explain his ends and deserve attention, but it does not show his argument fails.
For an economic book, the authors want you to know the author's situation.
His proofs, if any, are part of the argument; the error is in how she used the background.
Having an interest calls for care, but it does not make every conclusion false.
questions.explain: Knowing the author's situation helps you understand and weigh his recommendations. Using it to skip the argument is a different, faulty move.
questions.rule: Background informs judgment; it does not replace it.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, to judge a proof in a mathematical treatise you should first learn about the author's character.
questions.explain: The authors say you need know nothing about the author of a mathematical treatise: his reasoning is either good or not.
questions.rule: In mathematics the reasoning stands alone.

questions.q: An opinion piece urges cutting the rules on short-term holiday lets. A note says the writer runs a holiday-rental firm. How should a reader use this?
options: As a sufficient reason to reject the piece outright
As irrelevant, since only the argument ever matters
As evidence that the current rules must be harming the public
As a clue to his ends, while still weighing his argument
optionExplain: An interest is a reason for care, not a refutation.
In practical writing the writer's situation matters, as the authors argue for books.
His interest tells you about him, not about the rules.
Right: like an author's life and times, the writer's position helps you see which ends he is likely pursuing.
questions.explain: Knowing who is writing, and from what position, helps you understand a practical argument's ends without settling whether it is right.
questions.rule: Know the writer's position; still weigh the case.
questions.teaches: By analogy, knowing who employs or funds the writer of an opinion piece or report serves the same purpose as knowing an author's life: it shows which ends he is likely pursuing, without settling whether he is right.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: According to the authors, in reading a practical book, which part of finding out what it is about becomes the dominant one?
options: Classifying the book by its subject matter
Finding out what the author wants you to do
Counting the parts of its outline in order
Learning when and where the book was written
optionExplain: Classifying comes first, but it is not the part the authors say becomes dominant.
Right: the author's problems become the main concern, and in a practical book that means what he wants you to do.
The outline is still needed, but it is not the dominant task.
Background can help, but it is not part of answering the first question in the authors' scheme.
questions.explain: In a practical book, the author's problems come down to what he wants you to do. The card next shows how the first two questions are adapted.
questions.rule: Find what he wants you to do.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: Match each item to what it becomes or requires when the book is practical.
pairs: Find out what the author wants you to do
Find out how he proposes that you do this
Still requires an outline of the structure
questions.explain: The first two questions keep their usual work, outline and interpretation, but the adapted Rules 4 and 8 become the main tasks.
questions.rule: What he wants, and how.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: A booklet urges parents to fund school trips through a monthly scheme in which each family gives a small sum. Which pair applies the adapted Rules 4 and 8?
options: Wants me to: read about fundraising; how: by studying this booklet
Wants me to: fund school trips; how: a monthly scheme of small gifts
Wants me to: understand school budgets; how: through its cost tables
Wants me to: run one large gala; how: by selling tickets to it
optionExplain: Reading is how you learn the author's aim, not the aim itself.
Right: the end is funding the trips, and the means is the monthly scheme.
Understanding budgets would be a theoretical aim; the booklet asks for action.
This invents an aim and means the booklet does not propose.
questions.explain: The adapted rules ask for the action the author wants and the means he proposes for it.
questions.rule: State the action and its means.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: Before its adaptation for practical books, Rule 8 asked you to say which of the author's ____ he solved and which he did not.
questions.explain: Rule 8 asked which problems the author solved. For a practical book this becomes how he proposes that you achieve his aim.
questions.rule: Rule 8 concerns the author's solutions.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: After careful reading, a reader can state what a book wants her to do but finds no workable account of how. In terms of the original Rule 8, what has she found?
options: That she has misread, since every practical book supplies means
That the book is theoretical, since it offers no means
That the book's end must be the wrong one to seek
That the author has left his main problem unsolved
optionExplain: She read carefully; books can fail to supply workable means.
The book still aims at action, so it is practical, however weak its means.
A good end can lack good means; the gap is in the means, not the end.
Right: the adapted Rule 8 asks how; finding no answer is finding the main problem unsolved.
questions.explain: Rule 8 asked which problems were solved. When the means are missing, the practical problem the book set itself remains unsolved.
questions.rule: No workable means, problem unsolved.
questions.teaches: The adapted Rule 8 also tests the author: if you cannot find how he proposes you reach his aim, the book has left its main problem unsolved, which is what the original Rule 8 asked you to notice.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: Before reading the details of a long email from your manager, you write one line: she wants me to brief the new client by Friday. How does that line help with the rest?
options: Each later paragraph reads as part of how, or as background
It replaces any need to read the rest of the email closely
It tells you whether you agree with the end she is pursuing
It shows you the tone she wants you to take with the new client
optionExplain: Right: with the action stated, each passage either says how to do it or is background to it.
The how is still in the details; the line guides the reading rather than replacing it.
Stating the end is understanding it; agreeing with it is a later judgment.
Tone may matter, but the line states the action, not the manner.
questions.explain: Once the action wanted is stated, the rest of a practical text sorts itself: passages either tell you how, or support and surround that.
questions.rule: State the ask first, then read for the how.
questions.teaches: Stating the action wanted in one line early gives a test for the rest of a practical text: each passage either tells you how to do it, or is background to it.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, judging whether a practical book is true is mainly a matter of checking its claims against the facts.
questions.explain: Facts still matter, but the main question is whether its ends and means accord with what you think right to seek and the best way to seek it. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Practical truth turns on ends and means.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: According to the authors, what does the third question mainly ask of a practical book? Select all that apply.
options: Whether its ends accord with what you think right to seek
Whether its means are the best way to seek those ends
Whether its account of the world fits your experience, and no more
Whether the author is well known and respected in the field
Whether its rules are worded as commands or as statements
optionExplain: Right: the end must accord with your conception of what is right to seek.
Right: the means must accord with your view of the best way to seek it.
That is the test for a theoretical book; for a practical one it is not the main consideration.
Reputation is not part of the third question.
Wording has nothing to do with whether a rule is true.
questions.explain: For a practical book, the question of truth becomes: are the ends right, and are the means the best way to them?
questions.rule: Right end, best way.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: A book proposes cutting road deaths by lowering every speed limit to 20 mph. A reader agrees fewer deaths is right to seek but thinks redesigned streets would do better at less cost. How does she answer the third question?
options: True, since she shares its end
False, since its end is the wrong one
Partly: a right end, but not the best means
Not yet, since it is a purely factual matter
optionExplain: Sharing the end answers only half the question; she doubts the means.
She accepts the end; her doubt is about the way.
Right: the end accords with her view, but the means do not seem the best way.
Facts bear on the means, but the third question also asks about the right end and best way.
questions.explain: The third question has two parts. Here the end passes and the means do not, so her verdict is split.
questions.rule: Judge the end and the means separately.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: Sort each question by the kind of book whose test of truth it belongs to.

items.t: Does its account fit what I know of the world
Does it describe the events as they happened
Do its explanations match my experience
Is the end it urges right to seek
Is its way the best way to reach that end
Would I choose these means for this goal

questions.explain: A theoretical book is compared with how things are. A practical book is compared mainly with your conception of the right end and the best way.
questions.rule: Fit with the world, or fit with the right.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: A reader who has not yet thought about what a good education aims at is judging a book on school reform. What does the authors' version of the third question suggest about her position?
options: She can judge it fully by checking all of its facts
She is the fairest judge, since she brings no view of her own to it
She lacks part of the standard, and should think about ends first
She should adopt its ends, since she has none of her own
optionExplain: Facts help with the means, but the main test needs a view of the right end.
Having no view leaves her nothing to measure the book's ends against.
Right: the third question compares the book with her conception of the right end, which she has yet to form.
Adopting the book's ends without thought would skip the judgment altogether.
questions.explain: The third question measures a practical book against your own view of what is right to seek. Without one, you can check means but not ends.
questions.rule: Think about the end before judging a book on it.
questions.teaches: Because the third question compares a practical book with your conception of what is right to seek, a reader who has never thought about the ends in a field cannot fully judge a practical book about it.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: A surgeon recommends an operation that will very likely succeed. Applying the authors' practical third question, what else should the patient weigh?
options: Whether its result is what she wants, by the best route
Only how often the operation succeeds in patients like her
Whether the surgeon has published research on the operation
Whether the operation is new or long established in practice
optionExplain: Right: whether the result is the end she rightly seeks, and this the best way to it, is hers to judge.
Success rates show the means work, but not whether the end and the way are right for her.
Publications bear on the surgeon's expertise, not on her ends.
Age of the method bears on the means, not on whether she wants its end.
questions.explain: An expert can tell her whether the means will work. Whether the end, and this way to it, accord with what she rightly seeks remains her judgment.
questions.rule: Experts judge the means; you judge the end.
questions.teaches: By analogy, expert advice can settle whether means will work, but whether the end and the way suit what you rightly seek is a judgment left to the person advised.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: According to the authors, which of the four questions changes most when the book being read is practical?
options: The first, about what the book is about as a whole
The second, about what is being said and how
The third, about whether the book is true
The fourth, about what of it
optionExplain: The authors say the first question does not change very much.
The second also changes little: terms, propositions and arguments are still needed.
The third changes somewhat more than the first two, but not the most.
Right: the fourth changes most, because agreement now implies action.
questions.explain: The fourth question changes most: agreeing with a practical book means acting on it. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: What of it changes most.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the adjustments a theoretical book calls for do not necessarily imply action on the reader's part.
questions.explain: A theoretical book may change your general view of things, but such adjustments need not lead to any action.
questions.rule: Theory adjusts views; practice calls for action.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: After reading a book on composting, Raj agrees that cutting food waste is worth while and that home composting would do it. What does the authors' account say should follow?
options: Nothing yet, since agreement is a matter of thought
That he begins composting, as the book recommends
That he reads two more books on the subject first
That he adjusts his general view of waste and stops
optionExplain: For a theoretical book that might do, but agreement with a practical book implies action.
Right: accepting both the end and the means, he can hardly refuse to act.
More reading postpones the action his agreement already implies.
Adjusting views is the response to a theoretical book; here action is implied.
questions.explain: Raj accepts the end and the means. On the authors' account, that agreement implies acting as the book recommends.
questions.rule: End plus means accepted: act.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: Sort each case by whether, on the authors' account, the reader's agreement implies action.

items.t: Accepting a language guide's goal of fluency and its daily-practice method
Agreeing with a fitness book's goal and trusting its plan
Accepting a history's account of the 1918 flu
Agreeing that a physics book explains the tides correctly
Admiring a book's goal while doubting its methods
Accepting a theory of how memory works

questions.explain: Only full agreement with a practical book, ends and means both, implies action. Agreement with a theoretical book, or with the end alone, does not.
questions.rule: Practical book, both accepted: action implied.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: Suppose Raj agrees that cutting food waste is worth while but doubts that home composting would make much difference. What follows on the authors' account?
options: He is still committed to composting, since he shares the end
He is not committed to the book's means, though he shares its end
He must give up the end as well, since end and means stand or fall together
He should adjust his general view of waste and leave it there
optionExplain: The commitment needs acceptance of the means as well as the end.
Right: without accepting the means, the implication to act on them does not follow.
Ends and means can be judged separately; doubting one need not mean rejecting the other.
He may well look for better means to an end he still holds.
questions.explain: Agreement implies action only when both end and means are accepted. Doubting the means leaves him free of this book's method, though not of its end.
questions.rule: Doubt the means, and the commitment to them lapses.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: After a book on negotiating, Lee says he agrees with it but cannot say what he would do differently at his next meeting. What does this suggest?
options: He agrees fully, since agreement is a matter of thought
The book is theoretical, since it suggests no action
He should adjust his view of negotiation and stop there
He may not yet grasp the means well enough to accept them
optionExplain: Agreement with a practical book implies action, so it shows in what one would do.
A book on negotiating aims at action; Lee's difficulty is with him, not the book's kind.
That is the response to a theoretical book.
Right: if he cannot name a first step, he may not have understood, and so cannot yet accept, the means.
questions.explain: Agreement with a practical book should translate into some concrete action. If none comes to mind, the means may not have been understood well enough to accept.
questions.rule: Name the first step to test your agreement.
questions.teaches: Agreement with a practical book can be tested by a concrete first step: if you cannot name what you would do first, you may not yet have understood the means well enough to accept them.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: A reader says he accepts a practical book's goal and its method, yet does nothing about them. What do the authors conclude?
options: He does not really agree with the end or accept the means
He agrees, but is too lazy or tired to act
He agrees, but the book failed to move his feelings
He agrees in theory, which is all a book can ask of him
optionExplain: Right: if he really accepted both, he could not reasonably fail to act.
The authors say it is not only laziness or tiredness.
Feeling may play a part, but the authors locate the problem in what he really accepts.
For a practical book, agreement implies action, so agreement in theory alone is not real agreement.
questions.explain: Real acceptance of both end and means would lead to action, so inaction shows one was not really accepted. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Inaction shows something was not accepted.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: According to the authors, a reader who really agreed with both the ends and the means could not ____ fail to act.
questions.explain: If the reader truly accepted both, failing to act would make no sense; inaction points to a hidden reservation.
questions.rule: Full agreement leaves no reason not to act.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: Mo says a book convinced him that regular budgeting is worth while and that a monthly spreadsheet would achieve it. Six months later he has no spreadsheet. What should he ask himself, following the authors?
options: How he could find more free time in each month
Whether a different book would motivate him better
Whether he really accepts the end, or the spreadsheet
Whether the author's examples were vivid enough to move him
optionExplain: Time is the excuse the authors look past; the question is what he really accepted.
Another book does not address what he really accepts.
Right: the authors' test sends him back to which of the two he did not really accept.
Vividness concerns persuasion, not what he actually accepts.
questions.explain: The authors treat inaction as evidence about agreement. Mo should check whether his doubt lies with the end or with the means.
questions.rule: Ask which you did not really accept.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: Jo agreed that exercise is good and that the book's plan would work, but she did not start it. She concludes: I agree, I am only weak-willed, so my agreement needs no rechecking. What is wrong with her conclusion?
options: It concedes too much, since agreeing with a book has no bearing on action
Nothing, since will and agreement are wholly separate matters in practice
It blames her will alone, when inaction suggests she did not accept both
It is wrong only in calling herself weak, since the plan must be at fault
optionExplain: For a practical book the authors tie agreement closely to action, so agreement does bear on what she does.
The authors treat inaction as evidence about agreement, so the two are connected.
Right: the authors say inaction is not only weakness or tiredness; it shows the end or the means was not really accepted.
She accepted that the plan would work; the authors' test points back at what she really accepted, not at the plan.
questions.explain: Jo explains her inaction by will alone. The authors' test asks her to recheck whether she really accepted the end or the plan.
questions.rule: Do not blame will alone; recheck agreement.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: Kai agrees that cooking at home is healthier and that the book's weekly plan works, yet keeps ordering takeaway. Applying the authors' test, what might his inaction reveal?
options: That another end, such as free evenings, ranks higher
That cooking at home is not really healthier after all
That he agrees fully, since new habits take time to form
That the book's recipes must be badly written or dull
optionExplain: Right: he may not really hold the book's end as highly as he says, because another end outranks it in practice.
His inaction says something about him, not about the facts of nutrition.
The authors do not accept time or habit as the whole explanation.
Nothing suggests the recipes are at fault; he accepted the plan as working.
questions.explain: Inaction can show that the book's end, though granted in words, gives way in practice to another end the reader holds more strongly.
questions.rule: Look for the end that wins in practice.
questions.teaches: Inaction can point to an end the reader holds more strongly, such as comfort or free time, which outranks the book's end in practice even though he grants the book's end in words.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: A company board approves a new strategy and the plan to carry it out. A year later nothing has changed. Which questions follow the authors' test? Select all that apply.
options: Did the members really accept the goal of the strategy
Did they really believe the plan would reach that goal
Were the minutes of the approving meeting well written
Was everyone too busy to act, and nothing more
Would a louder launch event have made the difference
optionExplain: Right: the test asks whether the end was really accepted.
Right: it also asks whether the means were really accepted.
The minutes record the approval; they do not explain the inaction.
The authors refuse to treat busyness or tiredness as the whole explanation.
A louder launch adds persuasion but does not ask what was really accepted.
questions.explain: The test works on groups as well as readers: approval with no action invites the question of whether the end or the means was really accepted.
questions.rule: Endorsement without action is a question, not an answer.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the test applies to groups: when an organisation endorses a goal and a plan but nothing happens, the honest question is whether the endorsement of the end or the means was real, not only whether people were busy.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: A reader agrees that a recipe's dish is good and its method sound, but does not cook it. According to the authors, how should this case be understood?
options: As proof that agreement does not imply action at all
As disagreement, since anyone who agrees must cook it
As irrelevant, since recipes are not practical writing at all
By asking if the end is meant for him, or if he excuses himself
optionExplain: The authors treat it as an apparent exception that does not overturn their point.
Whether he must cook depends on whether the end is meant for him.
A recipe is a plain case of practical writing, a set of rules.
Right: the authors distinguish universal from selective ends, and warn that the reader may be fooling himself.
questions.explain: The authors answer the mousse case with a distinction between universal and selective ends, plus a warning about self-deception. The card next sets it out.
questions.rule: Ask whom the end is for.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, when a practical book's end is universal, the implication to act applies to every reader who accepts its ends and means.
questions.explain: A universal end is meant for all human beings, so no reader can excuse himself by belonging to the wrong class.
questions.rule: Universal ends bind every reader.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: Sort each book by whether its end is universal or selective.

items.t: A book arguing that everyone should read better
A book urging all people to deal honestly with others
A book urging everyone to wash their hands before meals
A guide to passing the bar exam
A manual for new beekeepers
A guide for parents of newborn twins

questions.explain: Universal ends are meant for everyone; selective ends for a class, such as law students, beekeepers or parents of twins.
questions.rule: For all, or for a class.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: Which reader may fairly decline to act on a practical book whose end and means he accepts?
options: A reader of a book on reading better who prefers to skim
A non-pilot reading a guide to landing light aircraft
A reader who agrees everyone should exercise, and that walking works, but never walks
A citizen who agrees all should vote but leaves it to others
optionExplain: Reading better is a universal end, so the implication applies to him.
Right: the guide's end is selective, meant for pilots, and he honestly does not belong to that class.
If everyone should exercise, the end includes him; agreeing and still not walking is self-excuse, not non-membership.
If all should vote, the end includes him; leaving it to others is self-excuse.
questions.explain: Only a reader honestly outside a selective end's class may decline. The others are leaving the action to someone else.
questions.rule: Only real non-membership excuses.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: Suppose a reader decides she is outside a book's intended class mainly because acting would be inconvenient. On the authors' account, what is likely?
options: That she is correctly outside the intended class
That she is fooling herself about her motives
That the book's end has thereby become universal
That she has found a real flaw in the means
optionExplain: Inconvenience is not what decides membership of a class.
Right: the authors warn that readers may misread their own motives in deciding the end does not apply to them.
Her reasoning does not change whom the book's end is meant for.
Inconvenience to her is not a flaw in the means as means.
questions.explain: Deciding you are outside the class is where self-deception creeps in. Inconvenience is a motive, not a reason for non-membership.
questions.rule: Check the motive behind I am not the audience.

questions.section: What Does Agreement Entail in the Case of a Practical Book?
questions.q: Twenty residents agree that their shared path should be cleared of snow and that shovelling would do it. Nobody shovels. Which reading fits the authors' analysis?
options: None of them thinks a clear path is worth having
The end is selective, so none of them is obligated
The means are unsound, since shovelling is slow work
Each grants end and means but leaves the doing to others
optionExplain: They agreed the path should be cleared; what they avoid is the doing.
A path all of them use is an end for all of them.
They agreed shovelling would work; slowness does not make it unsound.
Right: this is the let someone else do it move, multiplied by twenty.
questions.explain: The authors describe conceding the end and the means while leaving the action to someone else. In a group, everyone can make that move at once.
questions.rule: In groups, watch for everyone leaving it to someone else.
questions.teaches: By analogy, shared tasks such as a group project or a neighbourhood clean-up invite the same move on a larger scale: everyone concedes the end and the means, and each leaves the action to someone else.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Many readers who enjoyed a novel cannot say what they liked about it. What do the authors suspect this usually shows?
options: Good readers of fiction seldom make good critics
They have not read it below its surface
Pleasure in fiction is private and cannot be shared
Novels please through effects no one can name
questions.explain: The authors suspect that a reader who cannot say what he liked has probably not read below the obvious surface. The card next shows why this is only part of the answer.
optionExplain: This is the view the authors call at best a half-truth: criticism depends on how fully you grasped the work.
Right: the authors suspect that readers who cannot say what they liked have stayed near the surface.
The authors expect a good reader to give an account of his pleasure, so they do not treat it as private.
The authors say beauty is hard to analyse, not impossible; the rules aim to show the sources of delight.
questions.rule: Not saying why often means not reading deeply.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, imaginative literature primarily pleases rather than teaches, and knowing why one is pleased is harder than being pleased.
questions.explain: The authors say it is much easier to be pleased than taught, but much harder to know why one is pleased. Beauty is harder to analyse than truth.
questions.rule: Being pleased is easy; knowing why is hard.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: After a book club meeting on a novel, which of these comments show a reader has gone below the surface? Select all that apply.
options: The ending worked because the sister's silence built up
I loved it; it was a really good read from start to finish
The village felt real through its small daily routines
Everyone I know enjoyed it, so it must be a good novel
It kept me reading late, which is all I ask of a novel
questions.explain: A reader who has gone below the surface can point to what in the work caused the pleasure. Reporting enjoyment, or other people's, does not do that.
optionExplain: Right: it names something in the book, the build-up of the sister's silence, as the cause of the effect.
This reports enjoyment but says nothing about what in the book produced it.
Right: it points to details in the work that produced the sense of a real place.
Others' enjoyment is no account of what in the book pleases; it does not reach the work at all.
This says the book pleased, not why; being kept reading is the effect, not its cause.
questions.rule: Name what in the work caused the effect.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Mia reasons: Step 1, I enjoyed this novel enormously. Step 2, I cannot say what in it I liked. Step 3, so I am a good reader of fiction who happens not to be a critic. Which step goes wrong?
options: Step 1, since enjoyment is no sign of having read a novel
Step 2, since anyone who enjoys a novel can say why
None, since reading well and criticizing are separate skills
Step 3, since saying why depends on a full reading
questions.explain: Mia's first two steps are honest reports. Her conclusion treats good reading and the ability to give an account as unrelated, which the authors call at best a half-truth.
optionExplain: The authors accept that such readers did enjoy the book; the doubt is about how deeply they read.
The authors report that many readers cannot say why, so Step 2 is a plausible report, not the error.
This is the view the authors call at best a half-truth, because criticism depends on the fullness of apprehension.
Right: the authors suspect that being unable to say what you liked shows the reading stayed near the surface.
questions.rule: An account of pleasure rests on a full reading.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: True or false: On the authors' account, a reader who cannot explain her pleasure in a poem the moment she finishes it has thereby shown that she read it badly.
questions.explain: The authors stress that beauty is harder to analyse than truth, so explaining a pleasure takes reflection. A pause before the words come is not proof of a poor reading; lasting inability is the warning sign.
questions.rule: Explaining beauty takes time; lasting silence is the warning.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A listener says a piece of music moves her deeply but she cannot say why. Applying the authors' point by analogy, what would help her most?
options: Accepting that musical pleasure lies beyond words
Reading what critics have said about the piece
Listening again for what in the music causes it
Comparing her reaction with how her friends reacted
questions.explain: By analogy with the authors' point about novels, the gap between enjoying and knowing why closes by attending again to the work itself. Learning to name what one hears is part of that.
optionExplain: The authors grant beauty is hard to analyse, not that its causes cannot be found.
A critic's account can help later, but it puts another listener's reasons in place of her own discovery.
Right: by analogy, the work is to find what in the piece, such as a theme's return, causes the pleasure.
Others' reactions describe their experience, not what in the music caused hers.
questions.rule: Return to the work to find the source of the effect.
questions.teaches: By analogy, in music or painting, as in fiction, the feeling that something works comes before the ability to explain it, and attending again to the work, often with the art's own vocabulary, is how enjoyment becomes an account.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: According to the authors, what does a work of imaginative literature mainly try to communicate?
options: Knowledge about experiences the reader has had
A moral lesson dressed in the form of a story
The author's opinions, presented indirectly
An experience the reader can have by reading
questions.explain: Expository books convey knowledge about experience; imaginative ones communicate an experience itself. The card next shows what follows from that.
optionExplain: That is the aim the authors give to expository books.
Stories can teach, but the authors say their primary aim is not a lesson.
The authors do not treat fiction as disguised opinion; that would make it a kind of argument.
Right: imaginative works try to communicate an experience itself, one had only by reading.
questions.rule: Fiction gives an experience; exposition gives knowledge.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Match each item with what the authors connect it to.
pairs: The powers by which we experience
The powers by which we know
questions.explain: Expository works aim at knowledge and appeal mainly to the intellect; imaginative works aim at experience and appeal mainly to the imagination.
questions.rule: Knowledge goes with intellect, experience with imagination.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Sort each work by its main aim.

items.t: A guide to train routes across Japan
A short story about a night train journey
A lyric poem about grief after a funeral
A report on the causes of rail accidents
A play about a family during a strike
An essay arguing for cheaper rail fares

questions.explain: The guide, report and essay tell you about experience or argue a claim. The story, poem and play offer an experience you have by reading them.
questions.rule: Ask what the work offers you, not what it is about.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A student says: since novels appeal to the imagination, reading them involves no thinking at all. Which reply fits the authors?
options: Agreed, since thinking belongs only to expository reading
No, the difference is one of emphasis, not a total split
No, novels appeal mainly to the intellect after all
Agreed, since imagination and judgment never work together
questions.explain: The authors contrast imagination and intellect as a matter of emphasis. Fiction leans on imagination, but reflection is never absent.
optionExplain: The authors say we cannot think without imagination, and the reverse holds too; the split is not total.
Right: the authors say the matter is only one of emphasis; imagination and reflection work together.
The authors say fiction appeals primarily to the imagination, not the intellect.
The authors deny that sense experience is ever wholly divorced from rational insight.
questions.rule: Imaginative and intellectual: a difference of emphasis.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Two books share a subject: one is a history of a famous battle, the other a novel set during the same battle. What does the authors' distinction say about how to read them?
options: Read both for facts, since they share the same subject
Read the novel too for the battle's causes and results
Read the history for knowledge, the novel for experience
Read both as stories, since each tells events in order
questions.explain: What decides how to read a work is its aim. The same battle can be the subject of knowledge in one book and of an experience in another.
optionExplain: A shared subject does not make the aims the same; the novel is not offering a record to check.
Causes and results are what the history is for; the novel aims to let you live through events.
Right: the aim, not the subject, decides how to read: knowledge from one, an experience from the other.
Both may narrate, but the history offers its account as knowledge, while the novel offers an experience.
questions.rule: The aim, not the subject, decides how to read.
questions.teaches: The same subject can be treated in both ways, so the subject matter of a book does not tell you which kind it is; only its aim does.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Ravi reads a novel the way he reads a textbook, noting facts and arguments to remember. What is he most likely to miss?
options: The experience the novel exists to give
The author's main thesis about society
The facts the novel teaches most directly
The definitions of the novel's key terms
questions.explain: Reading for knowledge catches what a novel offers least. The experience, which is its main gift, slips past a reader looking only for facts and arguments.
optionExplain: Right: the novel's aim is an experience, and a fact-gathering reading passes over it.
This assumes the novel has a thesis to extract, which is the textbook habit Ravi already has.
Gathering facts is what his textbook method does catch; it is not what he will miss.
Key terms belong to expository reading; looking for them is part of his mistake, not what he misses.
questions.rule: Read a novel for the experience it gives.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: The authors compare a good reader of expository books to a bird of prey, ready to pounce. What do they recommend for reading a story?
options: The same alertness, aimed at details of the plot
An openness that lets the story act on you
A quick, light reading that keeps it relaxing
Reading with a critic's notes close at hand
questions.explain: The authors keep active reading for fiction, but of a different kind: one that lets the story act on the reader. The card next names it.
optionExplain: Pouncing alertness is what the authors say does not suit a story.
Right: with fiction, the authors want the reader to let the story move him.
The authors still want active, attentive reading; lightness is not the point.
Another reader's notes put judgment before experience, which the authors advise against.
questions.rule: A story needs openness, not pouncing.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: The authors call the right kind of activity for reading fiction passive action or, better, active ____.
questions.explain: Active passion means acting so as to let the story act on you: you stay attentive while allowing it to move you.
questions.rule: Fiction calls for active passion.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Reading a poem about a lost child, Lena feels tears coming and stops herself to list the poem's images instead. What would the authors advise?
options: List the images first, since feelings cloud judgment
Let the feeling come, since that effect is the poem's aim
Put the poem aside until she can read it without feeling
Skip to a calmer poem and return to this one later
questions.explain: The poem aims to move her, so stopping the feeling is resisting the work. The authors want the reader to let it do its work.
optionExplain: Analysis has its place later, but resisting the effect now blocks what the poem is trying to do.
Right: the authors' main negative rule is not to resist the effect the work has on you.
Reading without feeling is reading against the poem's purpose.
Avoiding the effect is another way of resisting it.
questions.rule: Do not resist the effect a work has on you.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Which of these fit what the authors call active passion? Select all that apply.
options: Following the story with full attention
Letting a tense scene frighten you
Checking each event against the facts as you go
Refusing on principle to feel for a villain
Letting yourself be absorbed in the setting
questions.explain: Active passion combines attention with openness. Checking facts or refusing feeling are ways of holding the work at arm's length.
optionExplain: Right: active passion is still active; it takes full attention.
Right: being moved by the scene is the story doing its work on you.
This is the pouncing alertness suited to expository books, applied where it blocks the story.
Holding back feeling on principle is resisting the work's effect.
Right: absorption in the story's world is part of being open to it.
questions.rule: Attentive and open, not on guard.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, active passion means letting your attention go slack so that the story washes over you.
questions.explain: The authors insist reading fiction is active, though in a different way. You act so as to let the story act on you, which takes attention, not slackness.
questions.rule: Open is not slack.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Theo, a music student, must analyse the structure of a symphony for class, but he also wants to experience it. By extension of the authors' advice, which plan fits best?
options: Analyse it on the first hearing, to save time later
Hear it through openly once, then again to analyse it
Skip the open hearing, since analysis is the assignment
Feel and analyse together, switching every few minutes
questions.explain: Openness and analysis are both active, but they get in each other's way when mixed. Taking them in turn, experience first, keeps both.
optionExplain: Analysing from the start holds the music at arm's length, so the experience to be analysed is never had.
Right: receiving the work first and studying how it was made afterwards lets each activity do its own job.
The analysis would then describe effects he never let the music have on him.
Switching back and forth keeps breaking the openness that active passion needs.
questions.rule: Receive first; analyse on a second pass.
questions.teaches: By extension, receiving a work and studying it need not compete: a reader or listener can take them in turn, first an open reading or hearing, then a second pass to see how the effects were made.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: What attitude do the authors take to the idea that imaginative literature is escapist?
options: They welcome it, since escape is fiction's main use
They treat escape as harmless and beside the point
They see a wish to escape as a sign of a weak reader
They reject plain escape but allow a deeper kind
questions.explain: The authors accept that we need to get away from the world sometimes, but not in the ordinary escapist sense. The card next says where they think fiction should take us.
optionExplain: The authors call escapism in the ordinary sense contemptible.
They do not treat it as beside the point; they redirect it to a deeper reality.
They grant that we need to get away from the world from time to time.
Right: if we escape, they say, it should be to a deeper, greater reality.
questions.rule: Escape, if at all, to something deeper.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the goal of the rules for reading a great literary work is a profound experience, and the rules should clear away what stops us from feeling deeply.
questions.explain: The authors make the profound experience the goal of the rules. The rules serve that goal by removing obstacles to feeling.
questions.rule: The rules clear the way for deep feeling.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Ana says she reads novels only to forget the world for an hour and does not think of them afterwards. Which response fits the authors' view?
options: A great novel can take her to a deeper reality, her inner life
Forgetting the world is exactly what fiction is for
She should read only expository books, which shape the world
She reads correctly, since fiction teaches nothing anyway
questions.explain: The authors do not condemn getting away; they point it somewhere. A great novel offers more than forgetting: it can show us our own inner life.
optionExplain: Right: the authors want escape, if any, to be into our inner life and unique vision of the world.
This is escapism in the ordinary sense, which the authors find contemptible as an account of fiction.
The authors say we need to get away from the world sometimes, and fiction serves that need.
The authors say we can learn from fiction, derivatively, through the experience it gives.
questions.rule: Fiction's escape should lead inward, not nowhere.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Which of these describe the deeper reality the authors say great imaginative literature leads to? Select all that apply.
options: The reader's inner life
The reader's own unique vision of the world
A dream world that replaces daily life
The facts of the author's own biography
A part of ourselves we do not usually touch
questions.explain: The deeper reality is inward: our inner life and our own vision of the world. It is neither a substitute world nor facts about the author.
optionExplain: Right: the authors name the reality of our inner life.
Right: they also name our own unique vision of the world.
Replacing daily life is the ordinary escapism they reject.
The deeper reality is the reader's, not the author's life story.
Right: discovering this reality satisfies a part of us we do not ordinarily touch.
questions.rule: The deeper reality is the reader's inner life.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Mo finishes a novel many readers call great and feels nothing much. Given the goal the authors set for the rules, what is the most useful first question?
options: Whether great novels are overpraised by most readers
Whether something in his reading stopped him feeling
Whether he should force himself to feel more on rereading
Whether the novel is true to the facts of life
questions.explain: The rules are meant to clear away what stops deep feeling, so a flat response is first a reason to look at the reading: haste, distraction, resistance. Judging the work comes later.
optionExplain: Possible in the end, but the rules point first at obstacles in the reading.
Right: since the rules exist to remove what blocks deep feeling, a flat response first sends him to check his reading.
Forced feeling is not the experience the work offers; it is a different way of not receiving it.
The authors say fiction is not judged by the standards of factual truth.
questions.rule: A flat response: check the reading first.
questions.teaches: Because the rules exist to remove obstacles to feeling, a flat response to a great work is first a reason to examine one's own reading, such as haste, distraction or resistance, before blaming the work.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A song Nell loved at seventeen moves her in a new and deeper way at forty-five, though not a note has changed. By analogy with the authors' account, what best explains this?
options: The song has gained meaning from its later fame
The inner life the song reaches has changed
Her memory of the song has faded and misleads her
Older listeners feel music less sharply than the young
questions.explain: The authors place the deeper reality in our inner life and our vision of the world. When that changes, the same work can reach something new.
optionExplain: Fame changes what others say about a song, not what it reaches in her.
Right: by analogy, a great work reaches the listener's inner life and vision, which grow and change over the years.
She is hearing it again now; the new response is to the song itself.
This contradicts the case: she is moved more deeply, not less.
questions.rule: A changed reader meets the same work anew.
questions.teaches: By analogy, because a great work reaches the reader's or listener's own inner life, returning to it at a different stage of life can give a different and often deeper experience, though the work itself is unchanged.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a good poem or story tries to say everything relevant as explicitly as possible, leaving nothing between the lines.
questions.explain: That is the ideal of expository writing. Imaginative writing relies as much on what it implies as on what it says; the card next explains why.
questions.rule: Fiction leaves much between the lines.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: According to the authors, the imaginative writer uses ____ as the units of his construction, as the logical writer uses words sharpened to a single meaning.
questions.explain: Metaphors carry several meanings at once, which is why the imaginative writer builds with them. The logical writer needs words with one meaning each.
questions.rule: Metaphors are the building blocks of imaginative writing.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: In a short story, a son repaints his late father's fence every spring and does not speak of him. A reader says that since no sentence describes the son's feelings, the story says nothing about grief. What fits the authors' view?
options: The story implies the grief; the whole says what no sentence states
The reader is right, since a story's meaning is in its sentences
The story is weak, since good writing states its point plainly
The grief is the reader's own invention, not part of the story
questions.explain: The story carries its meaning in the repeated, silent act. Looking only for statements misses what it implies.
optionExplain: Right: imaginative writing relies on implication, and the whole says what none of its words say.
That treats the story like expository writing, where everything relevant should be stated.
Plain statement is the ideal of exposition; in fiction implication is a strength.
The repeated act in the story supports the reading; it is implied, not invented.
questions.rule: In fiction, read what is implied as well as what is said.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Sort each text by how it should carry its meaning, according to the authors' contrast.

items.t: A tenancy agreement
A laboratory report
A love sonnet
A story that ends on a silent gesture
Assembly instructions for a desk
A play in which a lie reveals a character

questions.explain: Texts that convey knowledge or instruction aim to leave nothing between the lines. Poems, stories and plays work as much through what they imply.
questions.rule: Exposition states; imaginative writing implies.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A study guide turns a poem into a plain prose paraphrase, line by line. Given what the authors say about imaginative language, how should a reader treat the paraphrase?
options: As the poem's real meaning, minus decoration
As useless, since poems cannot be discussed in prose
As a guide that leaves out much of the poem
As a better version, since it removes ambiguity
questions.explain: If the whole poem says more than any of its words, a line-by-line paraphrase can point the way but cannot hold what is implied. It is a help, not a substitute.
optionExplain: This assumes the metaphors are decoration, when the authors make them the units that carry meaning.
The authors themselves discuss poems in prose; a paraphrase can help, as long as it is not taken for the poem.
Right: much of the meaning lies in what is implied and in how the words work together, which plain prose drops.
Removing ambiguity removes the richness the poet sought; it is a gain only in expository writing.
questions.rule: A paraphrase guides; it does not replace the poem.
questions.teaches: By extension, a prose paraphrase of a poem loses much of its meaning, because that meaning lies in implication and in how the metaphors act on each other, so a paraphrase can guide a reading but never stand in for it.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: By analogy with the authors' contrast, in which case should a listener most carefully avoid reading between the lines?
options: A friend's short reply after an argument
A song lyric about leaving a hometown
A pharmacist's directions for a medicine
A eulogy given by a close family friend
questions.explain: By analogy, whether to read between the lines depends on the speaker's aim. Instruction should be explicit; a poem or a personal remark may mean more than it says.
optionExplain: Everyday talk between friends often carries meaning by implication, so listening for it is reasonable.
A lyric is imaginative writing; implication is part of how it works.
Right: directions aim to convey knowledge, so every relevant point should be explicit; guessing at hidden meaning risks harm.
A eulogy often works through images and memory, so implied meaning is part of it.
questions.rule: Read between the lines only where the aim invites it.
questions.teaches: By analogy, everyday speech also carries meaning by implication, but whether to read between the lines depends on the speaker's aim: a personal remark may invite it, while instructions and directions should not need it.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Which of these do the authors tell readers not to look for in imaginative literature?
options: Terms, propositions and arguments
Characters, incidents and settings
Beginnings, crises and climaxes
Metaphors and implied meanings
questions.explain: Terms, propositions and arguments are logical devices, suited to expository books. The card next shows what a reader of fiction does instead.
optionExplain: Right: these are logical devices, and the authors say not to look for them in poetry and fiction.
These are the very elements a reader of fiction must get to know.
These belong to the structure of a story, which the authors want readers to follow.
Metaphor and implication are how imaginative writing carries meaning.
questions.rule: Do not hunt for logical devices in fiction.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: True or false: The authors cite the poet Mark Van Doren's remark that in poetry and drama, statement is one of the obscurer mediums.
questions.explain: Van Doren's point is that poems and plays do not work mainly by stating. What a lyric says cannot be found in any one of its sentences.
questions.rule: In poetry, statement is an obscure medium.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A reading group plans its work on a short story. Which tasks fit the authors' advice? Select all that apply.
options: Listing the main propositions the story asserts
Following closely what happens to the characters
Noticing what the ending implies without saying
Outlining the premises of the author's argument
Choosing the sentence that states the story's thesis
questions.explain: The group should read closely, but for what the story does: its people, events and implications. Propositions, premises and a thesis sentence are tools for expository books.
optionExplain: Propositions are logical devices; looking for them treats the story as an essay.
Right: close attention to characters and events is what the story asks for.
Right: imaginative writing relies on what is implied as much as on what is said.
An argument with premises is a logical device the authors say not to look for in fiction.
What a story says cannot be found in any one of its sentences.
questions.rule: Read stories closely, but not for logic.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Kofi reasons: Step 1, this poem has no sentence that states a claim. Step 2, so it has no propositions to extract. Step 3, so it says nothing worth reading. Which step goes wrong?
options: Step 1, since every poem states its claim somewhere
Step 2, since propositions can be found in any text
None, since meaning in writing lives in its claims
Step 3, since the whole says more than any statement
questions.explain: Kofi's first two steps agree with the authors. The error is assuming that without propositions there is no meaning; a poem's meaning lies in the whole.
optionExplain: Many poems state no claim; the authors say what a lyric says cannot be found in any one sentence.
The authors say propositions are logical devices that poems do not work through.
That is the expository assumption the authors reject for imaginative literature.
Right: the whole, its words acting on each other, says something that will not fit inside propositions.
questions.rule: No propositions does not mean no meaning.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, since fiction contains no terms or propositions, a reader of fiction need not attend closely to its details.
questions.explain: The authors say fiction has elements analogous to terms, propositions and arguments, and they give rules for reading them. The ban is on logical devices, not on close reading.
questions.rule: No logic-hunting is not careless reading.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A picture book without words shows a lost dog finding its way home. A reviewer complains it makes no claims. What does the authors' rule suggest by analogy?
options: The book has no meaning to discuss, since it states nothing
The reviewer should look harder for the claims it hides
Pictures cannot carry meaning without words beside them
Its meaning lies in the whole experience, not in claims
questions.explain: If even a lyric's meaning is not in its sentences, a work with no sentences can still mean a great deal. Its meaning is in the experience it gives as a whole.
optionExplain: Stating nothing is no bar to meaning in imaginative work; the whole says what statements cannot.
Hunting for hidden claims is the logic-seeking habit the rule warns against.
The book tells a whole story through its pictures, so this underrates them.
Right: by analogy, the work communicates an experience, and that is where its meaning lies.
questions.rule: Meaning need not live in statements.
questions.teaches: By analogy, works with no sentences at all, such as wordless picture books or instrumental music, can still convey a whole experience, which shows that an imaginative work's meaning need not live in statements.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: According to the authors, in what way do imaginative books teach?
options: Primarily, by stating truths in a vivid, memorable way
Not at all, since their whole aim is to please
Derivatively, by creating experiences to learn from
Through the moral the author states at the end
questions.explain: Fiction teaches by giving an experience the reader can think about. The card next shows what that asks of the reader.
optionExplain: Teaching primarily, by stating, is how the authors describe expository books.
The authors say stories teach as well as please, though in a different way.
Right: imaginative books teach derivatively, through the experiences they create.
This treats the story as a lesson with a stated conclusion, which is the expository pattern.
questions.rule: Stories teach through the experience they create.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Match each item with the authors' account of it.
pairs: Comments on experiences we have or can get
Doing our own thinking about the experience
questions.explain: Expository books teach primarily, by commenting on experience; imaginative books teach derivatively, by creating it. So the reader's work differs.
questions.rule: Fiction: think for yourself; philosophy: understand the author first.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: After a play about a family torn apart by an inheritance, Jo asks her friend what the author's lesson was. Which approach fits the authors?
options: Think over the play's experience and see what she learns
Find the speech in which the author states his moral
Look up the author's interviews to learn his intended lesson
Decide the play has no lesson, since plays only entertain
questions.explain: The play teaches by giving her an experience; what she learns comes from her own reflection on it. Asking for the author's lesson looks for the wrong kind of teaching.
optionExplain: Right: to learn from fiction, the reader does her own thinking about the experience.
A play cannot speak in the author's person; looking for a stated moral treats it as exposition.
This puts the author's thinking in place of her own, which is the expository approach.
The authors say plays especially can teach, through the experience they create.
questions.rule: Ask what you learn, not what the author argued.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Which of these is learning from a book derivatively, in the authors' sense?
options: Memorising the dates given in a historian's account of a war
Following each step of a philosopher's proof of his claim
Reflecting on a novel's jealous husband to grasp one's own envy
Accepting an essay's conclusion once its reasons are clear
questions.explain: Learning derivatively means learning from an experience the work created, by one's own thinking. The other options learn from an author's stated thinking.
optionExplain: Taking in a historian's account is learning from exposition, which teaches primarily.
Following a proof means understanding the author's thinking, the primary way of learning.
Right: the reader learns by reflecting on an experience the novel created.
Being persuaded by reasons is learning from an expository work.
questions.rule: Derivative learning comes from reflecting on a created experience.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: True or false: On the authors' account, if two readers draw different lessons from the same novel, at least one of them must have misread it.
questions.explain: What we learn from fiction comes from our own thinking about the experience, so different readers can reach different, defensible lessons. With an expository book, both must first understand the same doctrine.
questions.rule: Lessons from fiction are the reader's own.
questions.teaches: Because learning from fiction is the reader's own thinking about the experience, different readers can draw different, defensible lessons from the same story, whereas an expository book's doctrine must first be understood the same way by all.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A hospital trains staff with a realistic role-play of breaking bad news to a family. By analogy with the authors' account, what makes such training teach?
options: The trainer's lecture on the correct steps beforehand
The realism of the actors, which makes it memorable
Repeating the scene until it feels routine
The staff thinking over what happened afterwards
questions.explain: By analogy, a role-play teaches the way fiction does: it creates an experience, and learning follows from thinking it over. That is why such training usually ends with discussion.
optionExplain: A lecture teaches primarily, by stating; the role-play is meant to teach another way.
Realism gives the experience, but the learning comes from reflecting on it.
