Repetition builds habit; it is not the reflection on experience the analogy points to.
Right: as with fiction, the created experience teaches when the learner does her own thinking about it.
questions.rule: Created experience teaches through reflection.
questions.teaches: By analogy, simulations and role-plays teach the way fiction does, through an experience, which is why such training usually ends with a debrief in which learners think over what happened.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: According to the authors, what is the truth of a good story?
options: Its plausibility as a likely story
Its accuracy about real places and events
The moral truth it teaches its readers
Its match with the reader's own life
questions.explain: A story must be a likely story, not a verified one. The card next shows when factual errors do and do not matter.
optionExplain: Right: the authors call a story's truth its verisimilitude, its intrinsic plausibility.
Factual accuracy is the standard for books that offer knowledge, such as histories.
The authors do not make a story's truth depend on a lesson.
A story need not match the reader's life; it must be likely in its own world.
questions.rule: A story's truth is its plausibility.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: The authors call the truth of a good story its ____, its intrinsic probability or plausibility.
questions.explain: Verisimilitude means being like the truth: a likely story, one that could have happened in the world the author has made.
questions.rule: Verisimilitude is a story's kind of truth.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A reviewer complains that the dragons in a fantasy novel could not fly, given real physics. What would the authors say is the fair question?
options: Whether the author consulted experts in physics
Whether a book with impossible creatures is worth reading
Whether the dragons are plausible in the novel's world
Whether readers already know dragons are not real
questions.explain: The novel does not offer itself as physics, so physical accuracy is the wrong test. What matters is whether its dragons fit the world it has made.
optionExplain: Expert checking is a standard for treatises, not for stories.
The authors do not dismiss stories for departing from fact; they ask for plausibility.
Right: the story must be true only in the sense that it could happen in the world it creates.
What readers know of the real world is beside the point; the test is the story's own world.
questions.rule: Test a story against its own world.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: By the authors' standards, sort each complaint.

items.t: A history of Rome gives the wrong year for a battle
A novel set in Rome moves a battle by a year, plausibly
A medical textbook puts an organ in the wrong place
A play invents a king who never reigned
A novel's hero suddenly acts against all we know of him, for no reason
A thriller's convincing heist uses a lock that does not exist

questions.explain: Factual errors count against books that offer themselves as knowledge. In fiction, invented facts are fine if plausible, but events that break the story's own logic fail its standard.
questions.rule: Fact for treatises, plausibility for stories.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A novelist defends an unconvincing scene by saying it happened to her in real life, exactly as written. What does the authors' standard imply?
options: The scene stands, since real events are the best evidence
The scene fails if it is not plausible within the story
The scene should be cut, since fiction must not use real life
The scene is fine, since a story's events need no test
questions.explain: The standard runs both ways: invented facts can pass if plausible, and real events can fail if the story does not make them likely. What happened in life does not settle it.
optionExplain: This applies the standard of factual truth, which the authors say does not govern fiction.
Right: the test is plausibility in the story's world, and a true event can still fail it.
Nothing in the authors' standard forbids real material; it must only be made plausible.
Stories do have a test, verisimilitude; the scene is judged by it.
questions.rule: True to life is not the same as likely in the story.
questions.teaches: Factual accuracy does not rescue a story: an event that really happened can still be implausible in the story's world, and then it fails the standard of verisimilitude.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A lawyer watching a courtroom television drama is annoyed that it gets trial procedure wrong. By the authors' standard, what is the fair question about the drama?
options: Whether its procedure would survive in a real courtroom
Whether lawyers were hired to advise on the scripts
Whether viewers might learn wrong ideas about the law
Whether the slip breaks the drama's own plausibility
questions.explain: By analogy, the drama offers a story, not a treatise on law. A factual slip counts against it only if it breaks the story's plausibility on its own terms.
optionExplain: That is the standard for a legal guide, which the drama does not offer itself as.
Advisers might help accuracy, but accuracy is not the standard for fiction.
A real concern about effects, but it judges the drama as if it were teaching law.
Right: by analogy, the drama fails only if the error makes its story implausible on its own terms.
questions.rule: Judge drama by plausibility, not expertise.
questions.teaches: By extension, factual accuracy matters to fiction only as a support for plausibility: a slip harms a story when it breaks belief in the story's world, and does no harm when the story stays convincing.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Once we understand a philosophical book, what do the authors say we should test it against?
options: The findings of laboratory experiments
The common experience that inspired it
The views of later philosophers on it
The life and character of its author
questions.explain: A philosophical book draws on common experience, so that is where we test it. The card next shows why a play cannot be tested this way.
optionExplain: Special experience from the laboratory is the test for science, not for philosophy.
Right: the authors say a philosophical book is tested against the common experience that was its inspiration.
Later views may help, but the authors name common experience as the test.
The author's life is beside the point; the test is the experience the book is about.
questions.rule: Philosophy is tested against common experience.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Which questions do the authors suggest asking of a philosophical book you have understood? Select all that apply.
options: Is this true?
Have we felt this?
Is this obvious now, though it was not before?
Is the author widely admired by other experts?
Does this agree with my favourite writer's view?
questions.explain: Each of the authors' questions checks the theory against experience we share. If the answers are mostly yes, we are bound to agree.
optionExplain: Right: the authors' first test question is whether the book is true.
Right: they ask whether we have felt what the book describes.
Right: they ask whether the point is obvious now, though it was not before.
Reputation is not a test against experience.
Agreement with another writer is not the test the authors propose here.
questions.rule: Test a theory by asking whether experience bears it out.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Watching a play about a general who murders his king to take the throne, Nadia says it rings false because she has felt no such ambition. What fits the authors' view?
options: She is right to test the play against her own feelings
The play is false only if ambition never leads to murder
The play's general and his world are unique, not a theory
She should first check whether such a king ever existed
questions.explain: Her life is not the test of the play's truth. The play presents one unique character and world, not a claim about ambition in general.
optionExplain: That is the test for a philosophical book, which the authors say we cannot apply to poetry.
This still treats the play as a general claim about ambition to be checked.
Right: like Othello, the general is not every ambitious man; the play is unique, not a claim to test.
Historical checking is the standard for histories, not for plays.
questions.rule: Do not test a unique story against your own life.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Sort each work by how the authors would have you check it.

items.t: A treatise on what friendship requires
A lyric about one lover's jealousy
An essay claiming people fear loss more than they value gain
A novel about the ruin of one family
A philosophy of happiness
A play about a jealous general

groups: Do not test against your own life
questions.explain: Expository works make general claims about experience, which we can check against our own. Stories and poems present unique worlds that are not offered as claims.
questions.rule: Theories meet experience; stories present unique worlds.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Suppose a reader really were a Moor married to a Venetian lady he suspected. According to the authors, could he then test Othello against his own experience?
options: Yes, since his life would match the play's situation
Only if he had also been deceived by a false friend
Yes, as long as he first understood the play fully
No, since Othello is not every Moor; the play is unique
questions.explain: The authors push the case to the limit: even a reader in Othello's place would not be Othello. The work is unique, so it cannot be checked like a general claim.
optionExplain: Matching the situation is not enough; the authors say the character is still not every Moor.
Even then his life would not be Othello's; most such couples never meet an Iago, and the play is one of a kind.
Full understanding is needed before any judgment, but it does not turn the play into a theory.
Right: the authors say that even then the play would be unique, so no one's life is its test.
questions.rule: A unique work has no general test case.

questions.section: How Not to Read Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A listener says a song about one woman's particular heartbreak is false, because his own breakup felt nothing like it. By analogy with the authors' view, what is the flaw?
options: Songs should be tested against many listeners, not one
He treats one person's story as a general claim
He has not checked the singer's real life story
The song is false only if the singer made it up
questions.explain: By analogy, a song about one heartbreak is not a claim that all heartbreaks feel this way. A different experience does not refute it; the fair question is whether it is convincing in its own terms.
optionExplain: Testing against more listeners still treats the song as a general claim about heartbreak.
Right: by analogy, the song presents one particular experience, which a different experience cannot refute.
The singer's biography is a question of fact, not the standard for a song.
Whether the singer invented it is a question of fact; a song is judged as a likely story in its own terms, not as a record.
questions.rule: A different life does not refute a particular story.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a song or film about one person's particular experience is not a generalization, so a listener whose experience differs has not refuted it; the fair question is whether it convinces in its own terms.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: What can a novelist do that, according to the authors, a playwright cannot do?
options: Show characters acting on one another
Build a plot with many characters
Speak to the reader in his own person
Arouse strong emotion in an audience
questions.explain: A play tells its story only through what characters say and do. The card next shows why knowing the kind changes how you read.
optionExplain: Plays are made of characters acting and reacting on one another.
Plays, like novels, have complicated plots with many characters.
Right: the playwright narrates only through actions and speeches, while the novelist can speak in his own voice.
Plays move audiences as strongly as novels do.
questions.rule: A playwright cannot speak in his own person.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Match each kind of imaginative work with the authors' description.
pairs: Tells its story mainly through one emotional experience
Complex plot, and the author may speak in his own voice
Narrates entirely through actions and speeches
questions.explain: The lyric centres on one emotional experience; novels and plays have complicated plots, but only the novelist can comment in his own person.
questions.rule: Know the kind: lyric, novel or play.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Reading the script of a play, Priya keeps waiting for the author to explain why the heroine betrays her friend. What would help her most?
options: Reading a summary that states the author's view of the heroine
Inferring the motive from what characters say and do
Accepting that the play leaves the motive unknowable
Looking for the narrator's comments in the stage directions
questions.explain: Because a playwright cannot speak in his own person, a reader must find motives in the characters' words and deeds. Knowing the kind tells her where to look.
optionExplain: A summary puts someone else's account in place of her own reading of the play.
Right: in a play everything is narrated through actions and speeches, so motives must be read from them.
The motive is shown, not stated; a playwright's silence is not the same as an unknowable motive.
Stage directions are not a narrator speaking in the author's person, as in a novel.
questions.rule: In a play, read motives from words and deeds.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A passage reads: She still had not forgiven him, though she did not yet know it. Which kind of work does this manner of telling point to?
options: A novel, since a narrator comments on a character
A play, since it reports a character's feeling
A lyric, since it centres on a single emotion
A play, since an actor could speak these words
questions.explain: Only a narrator can tell us what a character does not yet know about herself. That is the novelist's privilege.
optionExplain: Right: a voice telling us what the character does not know is the novelist speaking, which a play cannot do.
Plays show feelings through action and speech, not through a report from outside the characters.
A lyric centres on one emotional experience, usually the speaker's own, not a narrator's comment on another person.
An actor speaks as a character; this sentence describes her from outside, as a narrator does.
questions.rule: A commenting narrator marks a novel.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a play narrates entirely through actions and speeches, yet there are some interesting exceptions to this, which they discuss later.
questions.explain: The authors state the rule and in the same breath mention interesting exceptions to it. The kinds guide the reader's expectations; they are not sealed boxes.
questions.rule: Kinds guide expectations; they admit exceptions.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: An audiobook of a novel is performed by a cast of actors, one voice for each character, so it sounds much like a radio play. By the authors' account of kinds, what should a listener still expect?
options: No narrator, since actors now speak every line
A narrator who may speak in the author's person
A single emotional experience, as in a lyric
Only actions and speeches, as in any play
questions.explain: The kind lies in how the work narrates, not in how it is delivered. A novel read by many voices is still a novel, with a narrator who can comment.
optionExplain: The performance adds voices, but the novel's narrating passages are still there to be read aloud.
Right: the work is still a novel, and its manner of narrating, including the novelist's own voice, is unchanged by the medium.
A novel has a complex plot with many characters; the performance does not turn it into a lyric.
Sounding like a play does not make it one; a play has no narrator, while this novel keeps its own.
questions.rule: Kind is set by the manner of narrating, not the medium.
questions.teaches: A work's kind lies in its manner of narrating, not its medium: a novel performed by a cast still has a narrator who can speak in the author's person, and a play read silently still tells everything through action and speech.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: According to the authors, where does the unity of a story lie?
options: In its central theme or message
In its most important character
In its setting and atmosphere
In its plot
questions.explain: A story conveys a concrete experience, so its unity is a matter of what happens, not of a stated message. The card next shows how to state it.
optionExplain: A theme stated as a message is a proposition, which belongs to expository unity.
Characters are elements of the story; the unity ties them together.
Setting matters, but the authors place the unity elsewhere.
Right: the authors say the unity of a story is always in its plot.
questions.rule: A story's unity is in its plot.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, you have grasped a story's unity when you can summarise its plot in a brief narration rather than as a proposition or argument.
questions.explain: An expository book's unity is stated as a problem or the propositions that solve it. A story's unity is stated by narrating its plot briefly.
questions.rule: Narrate the plot to state the unity.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Which statement of a novel's unity follows the authors' rule?
options: The novel argues that wealth should be shared fairly
A miser hoards gold, loses his only friend and dies alone
The novel is about greed, friendship and loneliness
The novel shows that greed corrupts even good people
questions.explain: The rule asks for a narration of the plot. Topic lists and theses are the expository way of stating unity.
optionExplain: This turns the story into an argument, which is the slip the rule warns against.
Right: a brief narration of what happens is how the authors want a story's unity stated.
A list of topics names what the book is about but does not state its unity.
This is a proposition about the story, not a narration of its plot.
questions.rule: Narration, not thesis or topic list.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Ben reasons: Step 1, a story's unity is in its plot. Step 2, I can summarise this novel's plot in two sentences. Step 3, so I now have what the novel offers and need not read it. Which step goes wrong?
options: Step 1, since a story's unity lies in its message
Step 2, since no novel's plot fits in two sentences
Step 3, since the plot only frames the experience
None, since the unity is all a reader needs from a novel
questions.explain: The plot summary states the unity, but it is only the framework of the experience. Knowing the frame is not having the experience.
optionExplain: The authors place a story's unity in its plot, so Step 1 is sound.
The authors ask for exactly such a brief narration, so Step 2 can be done.
Right: the plot stands for the unity, but the experience the novel re-creates in you is had only by reading.
The authors say the unity properly lies in the experience, which a summary does not give.
questions.rule: A plot summary frames the experience; it is not the experience.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: In a novel, two brothers spend long chapters arguing about whether God exists. How do the authors' rules have you state the novel's unity?
options: As the conclusion the stronger brother reaches
As the author's own position on God's existence
As the main question the brothers' debate raises
As a narration of what happens to the brothers
questions.explain: Arguments spoken by characters are things that happen in the story. The novel's unity is still the brief narration of its plot.
optionExplain: Picking a winner treats the debate as the author's argument, not as part of the story.
The novelist's own view is not stated as the story's unity; the plot is.
A question and its answer state an expository book's unity, not a story's.
Right: even arguments inside a novel are events in its plot, so the unity is still a narration.
questions.rule: In a novel, debates are events in the plot.
questions.teaches: Even when characters in a novel argue at length about ideas, the novel's unity is still its plot: the debates are events in the story, not propositions the author asserts.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A screenwriter must describe her new film in one sentence for producers. By analogy with the authors' rule, which description states the film's unity best?
options: A film about loyalty, risk and second chances in later life
A retired pilot flies a last rescue for his estranged daughter
A film proving that it is not too late to change your life
A moving, beautifully shot drama made for adult audiences
questions.explain: By analogy, a one-sentence narration of the plot states a film's unity. The industry's logline does exactly this.
optionExplain: A list of themes says what the film is about but not what happens.
Right: a brief narration of who acts and what is at stake states the plot's unity.
This is a thesis, the expository way of stating unity.
This describes the film's qualities and audience, not its unity.
questions.rule: State a film's unity as a narrated plot.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the film industry's logline, one sentence saying who wants what and what stands in the way, is a brief narration of plot and so states a film's unity in the authors' sense.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: In your own words, explain how the authors say the plot of a story is related to the experience the story gives.
questions.a: The plot is not the experience itself but its framework or occasion. It stands for the story's unity, which properly lies in the experience the work re-creates in the reader, much as a logical summary stands for the argument of an expository book.
questions.rule: The plot stands for the unity; the experience is the unity.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the place where a narrative begins is not necessarily its first page.
questions.explain: The authors say you must know where a narrative begins, which is not necessarily on the first page. The card next shows what else to trace.
questions.rule: The first page need not be the beginning.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Put these parts of a narrative's structure in the order the authors give.
items: Where the narrative begins
The crises that lead up to the climax
The climax itself
The aftermath within the narrative
questions.explain: A story moves in time from its beginning through crises to a climax, and then to what happens after the climax within the narrative.
questions.rule: Beginning, crises, climax, aftermath.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A novel opens at a woman's funeral, then goes back to her childhood and follows her life up to her death. Where does the narrative's temporal scheme begin?
options: At the funeral, since that is the first page
With her childhood, where the story's events start
At her death, since that is the novel's climax
With whatever event the reader finds most moving
questions.explain: The authors separate the first page from the beginning of the narrative. Here the events start with her childhood and move forward from there.
optionExplain: The first page is not necessarily where the narrative begins.
Right: the story's progress in time starts with her childhood, though the book opens later.
Her death may be a turning point, but it is not where the story's progress starts.
The structure lies in the story's order of events, not in the reader's response.
questions.rule: Find the start of the events, not of the book.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Sort each description by whether it fits the parts of an expository book or the parts of a story.

items.t: Partial solutions to parts of the problem
Details of characterization and incident
Ordered logically
Fitted into a temporal scheme
Sections that often make sense read alone
Chapters that lose meaning when wrenched from the whole

questions.explain: Expository parts solve parts of a problem, in logical order, and can often stand alone, as the first book of Euclid's Elements does. Story parts develop a plot in time and depend on the whole.
questions.rule: Logic orders exposition; time orders a story.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A student writes: The aftermath of this novel is that the heroine probably remarries and moves abroad, as the last chapter hints. Which point about the authors' term corrects the student?
options: Aftermath means the crises that come before the climax
The aftermath is what happens in the story after the climax
Novels have no aftermath in this sense; only plays have one
The aftermath must be stated plainly on the last page
questions.explain: The student guesses at events beyond the story's end. The authors' aftermath is what happens within the narrative after the climax.
optionExplain: Crises lead up to the climax; the aftermath comes after it.
Right: the authors say no one can know what happens after the story is over, so the aftermath is only what the narrative shows.
The authors apply the term to narratives in general.
The aftermath can take many pages; the point is that it lies within the narrative.
questions.rule: The aftermath is inside the story.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: You read only the first of Euclid's thirteen books of the Elements, and only the third act of a five-act play. According to the authors, what should you expect?
options: Both to make sense, since each is a well-made part
Neither to make sense, since all parts need their whole
The act to make sense, the book of Euclid not
Euclid's book to make sense, the act much less
questions.explain: Because expository parts are logically ordered partial solutions, they can stand alone more often. Parts of a story serve a plot in time and lose meaning out of it.
optionExplain: Parts of fiction often become relatively meaningless when wrenched from the whole.
The authors say the first book of Euclid can be read by itself.
This reverses the authors' contrast between expository and fictional parts.
Right: expository parts are more independently readable; an act of a play depends on the whole.
questions.rule: Expository parts stand alone more than story parts.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: At a dinner, Leo tells a funny story about a missed train but gives away the ending before the build-up. By analogy with the authors' account, why does it fall flat?
options: Its parts no longer lead in time to the climax
It has no real problem to solve, so no unity
Anecdotes need a moral to make them work
Listeners judge a story by its facts, not its order
questions.explain: By analogy, an anecdote has a beginning, crises and a climax. Telling the climax first breaks the temporal scheme the effect depends on.
optionExplain: Right: by analogy, an anecdote's punchline is its climax, and the crises must build to it in order.
Its unity is its plot, which it still has; the trouble is the order of the parts.
A moral is a proposition; the anecdote works through its structure, not a lesson.
Order matters to a story's effect; the facts were the same either way.
questions.rule: A story's effect depends on its order in time.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a well-told joke or anecdote has the same temporal structure in miniature, with the punchline as its climax, which is why giving the ending away first ruins it.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: In the authors' analogy between expository and imaginative works, what in fiction plays the part that terms play in an expository book?
options: Its characters and incidents
Its central theme or idea
Its setting or background world
Its plot taken as a whole
questions.explain: The authors match terms with the elements of fiction: its characters and incidents. The card next shows what to do with them.
optionExplain: Right: characters, incidents and their thoughts, speeches, feelings and actions are fiction's elements, like terms.
A theme stated as an idea is closer to a proposition, which the authors say not to look for.
The background connects the elements; it is not one of them.
The plot is what moves the elements, not an element itself.
questions.rule: Characters and incidents are fiction's terms.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, you have not grasped a story until you are familiar with its characters and have lived through its events.
questions.explain: Coming to terms with fiction means becoming acquainted with its people and what happens to them, closely enough to have lived through it.
questions.rule: Know the people; live through the events.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A book club member can recite a novel's plot outline but cannot say what any character wanted or feared. What, on the authors' account, is missing from her reading?
options: A statement of the novel's thesis
Acquaintance with its characterization
Knowledge of the author's life and times
A firm judgment of whether it is good
questions.explain: An outline without the characters' inner lives is the frame without the people. The rule asks her to know them closely.
optionExplain: A thesis is a logical device the authors say not to look for in fiction.
Right: knowing what characters want and fear is part of becoming acquainted with them.
Background on the author may help, but it is not the acquaintance the rule asks for.
Judgment comes after understanding; what is missing is earlier than that.
questions.rule: An outline is not acquaintance.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Which of these are elements of fiction in the authors' sense? Select all that apply.
options: A character's spoken words
An incident at a wedding
A character's secret fear
The author's thesis about marriage
A definition of love stated by the author
questions.explain: The elements of fiction are incidents, characters and their thoughts, speeches, feelings and actions. Theses and definitions belong to exposition.
optionExplain: Right: speeches are among the elements of fiction.
Right: episodes and incidents are elements.
Right: characters' feelings are elements too.
A thesis is a proposition, a logical device, not an element of the story.
A definition belongs to expository writing; it is a term in the logical sense, not a story element.
questions.rule: Elements are people, deeds and happenings.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Near the end of a novel a quiet maid steals the family's jewels. Tom finds this unmotivated, but he skimmed the early scenes in which the household mocks her. What does the rule suggest?
options: The novel is weak, since the theft comes from nowhere
The theft should be read as the author's comment on class
He skipped details of character that prepare the act
Late surprises in novels need no preparation at all
questions.explain: Acquaintance with characters includes the small details that build motive. A turn that seems unmotivated may show a gap in the reading, not in the book.
optionExplain: The motive is in the book; it seems to come from nowhere only because he skipped it.
This turns an incident into a proposition, which the authors warn against.
Right: small details of characterization often prepare later events; skimming them breaks the chain.
Surprises in good stories are usually prepared; the authors want the reader to know the characters well.
questions.rule: Small details of character prepare later events.
questions.teaches: Small details of characterization often prepare later events, so a reader who skims them may find a later turn unmotivated when the gap lies in the reading, not in the book.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: In a television drama, a doorman appears in only a few scenes, but each time the main characters treat him differently. By extension of the authors' rule, why pay attention to him?
options: He may turn out to be the hidden hero later
Minor parts are filler that viewers can skip
How others treat him shows the main characters
Every minor character carries the show's message
questions.explain: Minor characters are elements too. Authors often use them to show the main characters, so getting to know them is part of coming to terms with the story.
optionExplain: Possible, but the rule's reason does not depend on a later twist.
Minor characters are elements the author manipulates too; skipping them loses part of the acquaintance.
Right: minor characters often reveal the main ones by contrast or by how they are treated.
A message is a proposition; minor characters serve the story, not a thesis.
questions.rule: Minor characters reveal the major ones.
questions.teaches: By extension, minor characters are elements too: authors often use them to reveal the main characters by contrast or by how they are treated, so skipping them leaves the acquaintance incomplete.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: According to the authors, what connects the elements of a story, as propositions connect terms?
options: The author's own comments on the action
The moral lesson the story points toward
The book's division into chapters and parts
The scene or background they stand against
questions.explain: The world of the story, its scene and background, is what holds characters and incidents together. The card next shows how to enter it.
optionExplain: A novelist may comment, but the authors name something else as the connection.
A moral is a proposition, which the authors say not to look for.
Chapters are parts of the book, not what connects the story's elements.
Right: the elements stand out in relief against the total scene or background.
questions.rule: The scene connects fiction's elements.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: If you become at home in a story's world, its elements cease to be isolated pawns moved about mechanically on a ____.
questions.explain: Without a sense of the world, characters seem moved like pieces. Inside it, they become members of a living society.
questions.rule: Enter the world and the pawns come alive.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: In a science fiction novel, the first chapters show a colony's water rationing and its strict laws. Kai skims them to reach the action. What is he most likely to miss later?
options: Why the characters' choices weigh so much there
The author's thesis about scarcity in the real world
The scientific errors in how the colony is designed
The order in which the author wrote the chapters
questions.explain: The setting is what connects the elements. Skipping it leaves the action unexplained, like pawns moved about on a board.
optionExplain: Right: without the world's conditions, characters' acts lose their weight and connection.
A thesis is not what the setting supplies; the world gives the story's connections, not a claim.
Scientific accuracy is not the standard for fiction; plausibility within the world is.
Composition order is beside the point; the setting connects the story's elements.
questions.rule: Skip the world, and the action loses its weight.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Which reader is at home in a story's world in the authors' sense?
options: One who stays coolly distant to judge the characters fairly
One who notes where the setting departs from real history
One who shares the characters' hopes and fears like a friend's
One who skips the description to follow the main action
questions.explain: Being at home means living in the world as a member of its society, sharing its happenings as a friend would.
optionExplain: Distance while reading holds the world at arm's length; judgment comes later.
Checking against history applies a standard that does not govern fiction.
Right: the authors want the reader to befriend the characters and share their fortunes by sympathetic insight.
Skipping the world leaves the elements unconnected.
questions.rule: Join the world; befriend its people.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors' approach, becoming a sympathetic member of a story's world means giving up any later judgment of the work.
questions.explain: The authors place judgment after the reader has had the experience the work offers. Sympathy while reading is a step toward fair judgment, not a replacement for it.
questions.rule: Sympathy first, judgment after.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Ken moves to a country whose customs are new to him. The first months are slow and tiring, but later daily life starts to make sense. By analogy with the authors' rule, what does this suggest about a novel set in an unfamiliar world?
options: Its slow opening chapters are a fault the author should fix
Its early effort is often the price of becoming at home there
It should be read only by those who know such worlds already
Its strange customs can be skipped to reach the main story
questions.explain: By analogy, the work of becoming at home comes first and pays off later. Slow early chapters in a strange world are often that work, not a flaw.
optionExplain: Slowness can be a fault, but in an unfamiliar world it is often the reader still learning its laws.
Right: by analogy, becoming at home in a strange world takes effort first, and the story connects once the world is known.
The authors ask every reader to become a member of the story's world; prior knowledge is not required.
The customs are part of the scene that connects the elements; skipping them leaves the pawns on the board.
questions.rule: Entering a strange world costs effort at first.
questions.teaches: By analogy, becoming at home in an unfamiliar fictional world costs effort at the start, so slow early chapters are often the price of entry rather than a fault, and the story usually connects once the world is known.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: According to the authors, what did Aristotle call the soul of a story?
options: Its characters
Its language
Its plot
Its theme
questions.explain: Plot is the story's life, its movement. The card next shows how a reader follows it.
optionExplain: Characters are elements the plot moves; they are not what Aristotle named.
Language matters greatly in imaginative writing, but it is not what Aristotle named.
Right: the authors quote Aristotle that plot is the soul of a story, its life.
A theme is closer to a proposition, which is not the life of a story.
questions.rule: Plot is the soul of a story.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Match each part of an expository book with its analogue in fiction, as the authors set them out.
pairs: The unravelling of the plot, a dynamic connection
questions.explain: Elements are like terms, the setting connects them as a proposition does, and the plot moves them as an argument moves from reasons to conclusions.
questions.rule: Elements, setting, plot: fiction's terms, propositions, arguments.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Fifty pages into a thriller, Rosa reads the last chapter to learn who did it, then goes back to the middle. What does she lose, on the authors' account?
options: Nothing, since the solution is the plot's whole point
Her feel for the plot's unfolding, its pace and suspense
The author's argument about crime and its causes
The chance to check the novel's facts about police work
questions.explain: To follow a plot is to move with it. Jumping to the end replaces the story's life with its outcome.
optionExplain: The plot is the story's movement, not only its result.
Right: knowing the end first takes her finger off the narrative's pulse.
A thriller does not argue; looking for an argument is the wrong habit.
Factual checking is not the standard for a story.
questions.rule: Move with the plot, not ahead of it.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Kim reasons: Step 1, this chapter of the novel is slow and quiet. Step 2, so nothing in it moves the plot forward. Step 3, so I can skip it. Which step goes wrong first?
options: Step 1, since every chapter of a good novel is fast
Step 3, since skipping is wrong even when a chapter is idle
Step 2, since slow passages are part of the plot's beat
None, since the plot lives only in its events
questions.explain: Kim's mistake is equating slow with idle. Being sensitive to a narrative's beat includes its quiet stretches, which often prepare later turns.
optionExplain: Good novels vary their pace; a slow chapter is no fault.
Step 3 follows from Step 2; the earlier inference is where the error lies.
Right: a slow chapter can be gathering what comes next; the pulse includes its quiet beats.
Sensitivity to the beat means attending to pace as well as events.
questions.rule: Quiet is not idle.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the setting of a story is its dynamic connection, as an argument is in an expository book.
questions.explain: The authors call the setting a static connection, like a proposition. The plot's unravelling is the dynamic connection, like an argument.
questions.rule: Setting is static; plot is dynamic.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Ali watches only the highlights of a football match, while Ben watches the whole game. By analogy with the authors' point, what does Ben have that Ali lacks?
options: The final score and the names of all the scorers
The rhythm of pressure that gives the goals meaning
An expert's analysis of the tactics each side used
A fair verdict on which team deserved to win the game
questions.explain: By analogy, highlights are like a plot summary: decisive moments without the beat that leads to them. Following the whole keeps a finger on the pulse.
optionExplain: Highlights give both of these; they are outcomes, not the match's life.
Right: by analogy, the full match carries the pulse, the build-up that makes the key moments matter.
Watching more is not the same as expert analysis.
A verdict might come from either; what Ben has first is the experience of the match's movement.
questions.rule: The pulse lives in the build-up, not only the peaks.
questions.teaches: By analogy, highlights of a match, like a plot summary, show its decisive moments but not the rhythm of pressure that gives them meaning; following the whole is what keeps a finger on the pulse.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: True or false: The authors say that their interpretive steps for fiction should enrich, not spoil, the pleasure of reading a novel.
questions.explain: The authors expect the steps to enrich your pleasure by showing you its sources. The card next adds a caution about how to use them.
questions.rule: Analysis should enrich enjoyment.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: The authors warn that their analogy between expository and fictional rules is like a ____ that will disintegrate if you press it too hard.
questions.explain: An analogy, like a metaphor, works by likeness in some respects. Forced to match point by point, it breaks down.
questions.rule: Press an analogy too hard and it breaks.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A student sets out each chapter of a novel as a premise and the last chapter as the conclusion, as if the book were a proof. What is the problem, on the authors' account?
options: Novels have no structure, so outlines distort them
Each chapter should be one term, not one premise
The last chapter is the climax, not the conclusion
He presses the plot-argument analogy far too hard
questions.explain: The plot is like an argument in being the story's movement, not in having premises and a conclusion. Forcing that match is the misuse the authors warn against.
optionExplain: Novels have a structure in time; the authors ask readers to trace it.
This still forces the novel into logical units, only different ones.
This swaps one label for another without fixing the forced fit; the climax need not be the last chapter either.
Right: the plot is like an argument only loosely; treating chapters as premises breaks the analogy.
questions.rule: Plot resembles argument; it is not one.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Which statements fit what the authors say about their interpretive steps for fiction? Select all that apply.
options: They trace a growing awareness of the writer's artistry
They should enrich, not spoil, the pleasure of reading
Each character must match exactly one defined term
They help you know why you like a work, not only that you do
They show that a novel is a kind of argument in disguise
questions.explain: The steps are a loose guide toward appreciating the writer's art and the sources of your pleasure. They do not turn fiction into logic.
optionExplain: Right: the authors say the steps outline how one becomes aware of the writer's achievement.
Right: they say the steps should enrich your pleasure.
This presses the analogy point by point, which the authors warn against.
Right: you will know not only what you like but also why.
The analogy is loose; it does not make a novel an argument.
questions.rule: A loose guide toward knowing why you enjoy.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Lena worries that once she understands how a favourite novel achieves its effects, rereading it will feel flat. What does the authors' view suggest?
options: She is right; analysis and enjoyment cannot coexist
She should avoid analysis of novels she loves
Knowing the sources of delight should deepen it
Rereading matters little, since the plot is known
questions.explain: The authors expect understanding to add to enjoyment. Seeing how the effects are made adds delight in the craft to the first delight.
optionExplain: The authors say the steps should enrich, not spoil, enjoyment.
Avoiding analysis keeps her from knowing why she likes the novel.
Right: the authors expect intimate knowledge of the sources of delight to enrich the pleasure.
Knowing the plot is not having the experience; rereading can give more, not less.
questions.rule: Understanding the craft adds a pleasure.
questions.teaches: On the authors' view, understanding how a work produces its effects adds a second pleasure, delight in the craft, to the first, so a well-understood work can be richer on rereading, not flatter.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A choir director borrows a football coach's methods and insists every singer have a fixed position, a set play and a scored match each week. By analogy with the authors' caution, what is going wrong?
options: Choirs and teams share nothing, so nothing should be borrowed
He forces a useful analogy to match point by point
He should borrow from music teachers alone instead
He has not borrowed enough of the coach's methods
questions.explain: By analogy, rules carried from one field to another help at the level of roles and purposes. Forced to match in every detail, they mislead.
optionExplain: Teams and choirs do share much, such as teamwork and practice; the analogy can help.
Right: an analogy guides by broad likeness, and pressing every detail makes it fall apart.
Other sources are fine, but the problem is how he uses this one.
Borrowing more would press the analogy even harder.
questions.rule: Borrow the likeness, not every detail.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any set of rules borrowed from one field for another, such as coaching methods used in a choir, guides well by its broad likeness but misleads when every detail is forced to match.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: According to the authors, what is the one character that every lyric poem has, however short?
options: The speaker of the poem
The person the poem addresses
The poet's beloved or muse
The reader of the poem
questions.explain: Even a lyric with no story has someone whose experience it is. The card next shows what else the rules find in a lyric.
optionExplain: Right: the authors say there is always at least one character, the speaker.
Many lyrics address someone, but not all do.
Some lyrics concern a beloved; many do not.
The reader has the experience but is not a character in the poem.
questions.rule: Every lyric has a speaker.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the rules for reading stories apply in some degree to every lyric poem, even one that tells no story.
questions.explain: The authors say the rules do not cease to apply to non-narrative lyrics, though the connection is much less close.
questions.rule: The rules reach the lyric, loosely.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A short poem reads, line by line: I notice the first frost on the window. I remember my mother scraping the glass each winter. I lift my own hand to scrape it. I feel warm, despite the cold. Match each part of the experience with the lines that carry it.
pairs: Noticing the frost, in the first line
The memory and the lifted hand, in lines two and three
Warmth despite the cold, in the last line
questions.explain: The poem tells no story, yet the experience it re-creates moves in time: it begins with noticing, passes through memory and action, and ends in a changed feeling.
questions.rule: Even a short lyric moves from beginning to end.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Why, according to the authors, does even the shortest lyric have a beginning, middle and end?
options: Because any experience, however brief, takes time
Because lyrics are written in three equal stanzas
Because every lyric secretly retells a story
Because poets plan their poems in three parts
questions.explain: The lyric re-creates an experience, and experience takes place in time. That is why even a few lines move from a beginning to an end.
optionExplain: Right: a lyric represents an experience, and every experience has a temporal sequence.
Stanza form varies; the authors' point does not depend on it.
The authors speak of lyrics without a narrative line, so no hidden story is needed.
The point is about the experience the poem represents, not the poet's method.
questions.rule: Experience is temporal, so the lyric is too.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Omar reasons: Step 1, this three-line poem tells no story. Step 2, so it has no characters. Step 3, so the rules about getting to know characters do not help me. Which step goes wrong first?
options: Step 1, since every poem tells a story
Step 2, since the speaker is a character
Step 3, since the rules apply anyway
None, since a short poem has no people
questions.explain: A poem can tell no story and still have a character: its speaker. Getting to know the speaker is how the rules about characters apply.
optionExplain: Many lyrics tell no story; the authors grant this.
Right: the authors say there is always at least one character, the speaker of the poem.
Step 3 follows from Step 2; the earlier inference is where it goes wrong.
The speaker is a person in the poem, whose experience it is.
questions.rule: No story does not mean no character.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A song is sung to someone whom the singer addresses only as you, a person who does not speak at all. By extension of the authors' point about a lyric's cast, how should a listener treat this person?
options: As the listener, since the song speaks to whoever hears it
As a second character, known only through the speaker's words
As no one, since the speaker is the lyric's only character
As the singer's real partner, whose life the song records
questions.explain: The speaker is the one character every lyric has, but not necessarily the only one. Someone addressed is known through how the speaker talks to and about them.
optionExplain: The listener receives the experience, but the person addressed belongs to the song's situation.
Right: a lyric's cast can include people present only through the speaker's words, and getting to know them is part of reading it.
The authors say there is at least one character, the speaker; that does not rule out others.
Treating the song as a record of real life applies the standard for history, not for a lyric.
questions.rule: Look for who else the speaker's words call up.
questions.teaches: By extension, a lyric's cast can include people present only through the speaker's words, such as someone addressed, and getting to know them is part of reading the poem.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: What do the authors say you must do before criticizing a work of imaginative literature?
options: Fully appreciate the experience the author tried to give
Read what established critics have said about the work
Check the work's facts against the history of its period
Decide what main argument the author is putting forward
questions.explain: Appreciation is to fiction what understanding is to an expository book: the condition for fair criticism. The card next defines it.
optionExplain: Right: the maxim for fiction is not to criticize until you fully appreciate what the author tried to make you feel.
Critics' views are not the first step; your own appreciation is.
Factual accuracy is not the standard for fiction.
Fiction does not put forward arguments in the expository sense.
questions.rule: Appreciate before you criticize.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: By ____, the authors mean having the experience the author tried to produce for you by working on your emotions and imagination.
questions.explain: Appreciation is the fictional counterpart of understanding: having the experience the work was made to give.
questions.rule: Appreciation means having the intended experience.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A viewer walks out of a film after twenty minutes and posts a one-star review of it. What would the authors say about the review?
options: It is fair, since twenty minutes show a film's quality
It is fair, since dislike needs no full viewing
It is unfair only if the reviewer is not an expert
He has not had the experience, so cannot yet judge
questions.explain: The maxim puts appreciation before criticism. Leaving early may be reasonable, but it gives no basis for a verdict on the work.
optionExplain: A film, like a novel, gives its experience as a whole; a fraction is not enough.
The authors ask for an honest effort to appreciate before likes and dislikes are expressed.
Expertise does not replace having the experience the work offers.
Right: without an honest effort to appreciate the work, he is not yet competent to criticize it.
questions.rule: No experience, no verdict.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Match each item with what the authors pair it with.
pairs: Understand before you agree or disagree
The active reading a novel needs
questions.explain: The critical maxim keeps its shape across kinds of book: first understanding or appreciation, then judgment. Both require active reading.
questions.rule: Understanding for exposition, appreciation for fiction.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors' maxim, a reader who has made an honest effort to appreciate a novel will end up liking it.
questions.explain: Appreciation is the condition for judging, not a guarantee of a favourable judgment. After a full reading, a reader may like the work or not.
questions.rule: Appreciation enables judgment; it does not fix its result.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Tom tries one cautious bite of a dish from a cuisine he has not eaten before and declares the whole cuisine bad. By analogy with the authors' maxim, what has he skipped?
options: An honest effort to have the experience offered
A study of the cuisine's long history and origins
The opinions of food critics about the dish
A check of whether the dish is healthy to eat
questions.explain: By analogy, judging comes after an honest effort to receive what the thing offers. An unfamiliar cuisine, like an unfamiliar kind of book, may take several tries.
optionExplain: Right: by analogy, an unfamiliar art may need several honest tries before one has had the experience it offers.
History may help, but it is not the experience itself.
Critics' views cannot replace his own appreciation.
Health is a different question from judging the food as an experience.
questions.rule: Give the unfamiliar an honest trial before judging.
questions.teaches: By analogy, an unfamiliar cuisine or musical tradition may take several honest tries, and some learning of its ways, before one has had the experience it offers and can judge it fairly.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Henry James said we must grant the artist his subject, his idea, his donné. To what did he say our criticism applies?
options: Only to what the artist makes of it
Mainly to the subject he chose
To whether his subject is true to life
To his reasons for choosing the subject
questions.explain: The starting point is granted; the making is judged. The card next shows how this works.
optionExplain: Right: James says our criticism is applied only to what the artist makes of his donné.
The subject is what James says we must grant, not criticize.
Truth to life is not the standard for a story's chosen world.
The author's reasons are beside the point; what he makes of the subject is judged.
questions.rule: Grant the subject; judge the making.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reader has a right to criticize all that the author does with his chosen setting, though not the choice of setting itself.
questions.explain: The setting is part of the world the author creates, which the good reader grants. What the author does with that city and its people is fully open to criticism.
questions.rule: Grant the setting; judge what is done with it.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Which complaint about a novel set in a medieval monastery respects the authors' corollary?
options: The monks' rivalries never become convincing
A modern office would make it more relevant
Monasteries are too remote from readers' lives
The author should have chosen a livelier era
questions.explain: Fair criticism works inside the world the author chose. Only the first complaint is about what he made of it.
optionExplain: Right: this criticizes what the author made of his monks, which is fair.
This questions the chosen world instead of judging what was done with it.
This also rejects the donné rather than the handling of it.
Choosing the period is the author's right; the complaint refuses the donné.
questions.rule: Criticize the handling, not the choice.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Sort each complaint about a novel.

items.t: It should have been set in a big city
The city in it never feels like a real place
Why write a whole book about a dying man?
The dying man's fear is named but never felt
Talking animals are a childish premise
The talking animals break the rules their world set up

groups: Criticizes what the author made of it
questions.explain: Choices of setting, subject and premise belong to the donné. How the city, the man's fear and the animals are handled is open to criticism.
questions.rule: Premise granted; execution judged.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A fantasy novel establishes that every spell costs its caster a year of life. In the last chapter the hero casts a great spell at no cost, with no explanation. What does the authors' corollary allow a reader to say?
options: Nothing, since the author's world must be granted
That magic is a childish premise for a serious book
That the novel should not have used magic at all
That the author broke the rules of his own world
questions.explain: The reader grants the world, including its rules. Holding the author to those rules is criticism of what he made, not of his donné.
optionExplain: Granting the world means granting its rules too, so breaking them is fair to criticize.
This rejects the premise, which the corollary asks the reader to grant.
This also refuses the donné rather than judging what was made of it.
Right: once the world's rules are granted, breaking them without reason is a fault in what the author made.
questions.rule: Grant the world, then hold the author to it.
questions.teaches: Granting the donné includes holding the author to it: once a world's rules are set, breaking them without reason is a fault in what the author made, not part of what the reader granted.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A painter is commissioned to paint a small still life of lemons. A critic complains that it should have been a grand landscape. By analogy with the authors' corollary, what would fair criticism ask?
options: Whether lemons are a worthy subject for a serious painter
Whether a landscape would have sold for more money
Whether still lifes are out of fashion among critics
How well the painter handled the lemons and the light
questions.explain: By analogy, the subject of a commissioned still life is its donné. Fair criticism asks how well the painter used it, not whether he should have painted something else.
optionExplain: This questions the chosen subject, the painter's donné.
Price is not a judgment of the work, and it still refuses the subject.
Fashion is not a standard for criticizing what was made.
Right: by analogy, fair criticism accepts the subject and judges what the artist made of it.
questions.rule: Judge the work on the subject it took.
questions.teaches: By analogy, in any art made to a chosen brief or form, such as a still life or a sonnet's fixed shape, fair criticism accepts the subject or form and asks how well the artist used it.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: According to the authors, what do we chiefly consider when criticizing imaginative literature?
options: Its beauty
Its truth
Its moral lesson
Its accuracy
questions.explain: The word belles-lettres points to beauty, and so do the authors. The card next shows how beauty relates to pleasure.
optionExplain: Right: in criticizing belles-lettres, the authors say, we consider chiefly their beauty.
Truth is the concern of criticism of expository books.
The authors do not make a moral lesson the chief standard for fiction.
Factual accuracy is not the standard for a story.
questions.rule: Fiction is judged chiefly by its beauty.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Match each item with the authors' account of it.
questions.explain: Arguments make claims, which we accept or reject. Stories give experiences, which we like or dislike and judge for their beauty.
questions.rule: Agree with arguments; like or dislike stories.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Ruth says she disagrees with a novel about a family's long feud, because feuds are pointless. According to the authors, what is the right kind of response to the novel?
options: Agreeing or disagreeing with the novel's view of feuds
Checking whether feuds really last so long in life
Asking whether the author approves of feuds
Saying whether she liked it, and later why
questions.explain: Ruth answers the novel as if it argued a thesis. According to the authors, fiction is liked or disliked, not agreed with.
optionExplain: The authors say we do not agree or disagree with fiction.
Factual checking is not the standard for a story.
This still treats the novel as stating a position.
Right: the response to fiction is liking or disliking, followed by reasons.
questions.rule: Answer a story with liking, not agreement.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Which remarks are the kind of critical response the authors expect to fiction? Select all that apply.
options: I liked it very much
I disliked the way it ended
I disagree with what the novel says
The novel is false about Victorian London
It grew more beautiful as I knew it better
questions.explain: The fitting responses are liking, disliking and judgments of beauty. Agreement and factual truth belong to expository books.
optionExplain: Right: liking is the first form of a judgment of fiction.
Right: disliking, here of the ending, is the same kind of response.
The authors say we do not agree or disagree with fiction.
Factual truth is not the standard for a story.
Right: beauty, tied to pleasure in a work known well, is what criticism of fiction chiefly considers.
questions.rule: Like, dislike, beauty: the vocabulary of judging fiction.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: The authors relate a work's beauty to the pleasure it gives when we know it well. What follows about a reader's first impression of a poem?
options: It is weak evidence, since judgment grows with knowing
It is the best evidence, since it is the most direct
It is no evidence, since beauty has nothing to do with pleasure
It is decisive, since a poem's effect is strongest at first
questions.explain: Beauty is tied to the pleasure a work gives when it is known well. So a first impression is a starting point, and a work's standing can change as the reader comes to know it.
optionExplain: Right: if beauty goes with pleasure in a work known well, a first impression says little yet.
Directness is not the authors' test; knowing the work well is.
The authors tie beauty to pleasure, so pleasure is evidence, once the work is known.
A first effect may be strong, but the authors tie beauty to pleasure in a work known well.
questions.rule: Judge beauty from a work known well.
questions.teaches: Since beauty is tied to the pleasure a work gives when known well, a first impression is weak evidence about it, and a work's standing can rise or fall as the reader comes to know it.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A comedian performs as a character who boasts about cheating at cards. Meg finds the character's views repellent. By analogy with the authors' view of fiction, what has she not yet done?
options: Judged the routine itself, by whether it is good
Shown that the comedian himself is dishonest
Proved that cheating at cards is really wrong
Disagreed with the routine, as she ought to
questions.explain: By analogy, the character's boasts belong to the world the routine creates. Disliking them is part of the experience; the judgment of the routine still waits.
optionExplain: Right: by analogy, rejecting a character's views is part of the experience; the work is still judged by whether it is good.
The character's views belong to the performance's created world, not to the performer's own claims.
Whether cheating is wrong is not the question about the routine, which makes no claim to be tested.
The authors say we do not agree or disagree with fiction; by analogy, the same holds for a performed character.
questions.rule: Rejecting a character's views is not judging the work.
questions.teaches: Disagreeing with a character's opinions is not disagreeing with the work: by analogy, in fiction and performance alike, the views a character voices belong to the created world, and the work is still judged by whether it is good.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: According to the authors, the reasons a reader first gives for liking or disliking a novel are most likely to be about what?
options: The reader's own preferences and prejudices
The novel's real artistic virtues and faults
The author's intentions in writing the book
The views of critics the reader has heard
questions.explain: A first judgment of taste says as much about the reader as about the book. The card next shows how to move past it.
optionExplain: Right: the authors say first reasons are more likely to be about you than about the book.
Reaching the book's virtues is the goal of later, objectified criticism.
The authors do not say first reasons concern the author's intentions.
The authors locate first reasons in the reader's own tastes, not in others' views.
questions.rule: First reasons tend to describe the reader.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Put the authors' steps toward criticizing a work of fiction in order.
items: Read the work actively until you appreciate it
Say whether you like or dislike it, and why
Point to what in the book caused those reactions
Say what is good or bad in the book, and why
questions.explain: Appreciation comes first, then a judgment of taste, then the work of objectifying it by pointing to the book, which leads to a judgment of good and bad.
questions.rule: Appreciate, react, point to causes, judge the book.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Sort each reason a reader gives for a judgment of a novel.

items.t: I always enjoy stories set by the sea
The storm scene's short sentences build real panic
I cannot stand books with talking animals
The narrator's jokes undercut each sad scene too early
It reminded me of my grandmother, so I loved it
Each chapter ends on a question the next one answers

questions.explain: Reasons about the reader report preferences and associations. Reasons about the book point to things in it that cause the reaction, which is what objectifying means.
questions.rule: Point to the book, not to yourself.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: A reviewer writes: Step 1, I disliked this novel. Step 2, that is because I dislike long descriptions. Step 3, so the novel is badly written. Which step goes wrong?
options: Step 1, since a reviewer should not admit dislike
Step 2, since a reviewer should give no reasons
Step 3, since his reason is about him, not the book
None, since a reviewer's taste is the book's measure
questions.explain: Steps 1 and 2 are an honest judgment of taste. Step 3 treats a preference as a fault in the book without pointing to anything in it.
optionExplain: The authors expect the first judgment to be one of liking or disliking.
Giving reasons is part of the first judgment of taste.
Right: his reason describes his preference; to judge the book he must point to something in it.
The authors ask readers to pass beyond taste to what is good or bad in the book.
questions.rule: A preference is not a flaw in the book.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Why does pointing to features of a book make a critical judgment easier to discuss with other readers than a report of taste?
options: Features cannot be disputed once they are named
Readers with similar taste will agree in any case
Reports of taste concern only the reader's mood
Others can examine the same features and test it
questions.explain: A preference can only be reported; a feature can be examined. Pointing to the book turns a private reaction into a claim others can test.
optionExplain: Readers can still dispute what a feature does or how much it matters.
Shared taste explains agreement among some readers, not why the claim can be tested by all.
Taste has some critical relevance, the authors say; it is not only a mood.
Right: an objectified judgment points to something in the book that another reader can go and check.
questions.rule: Objectified judgments can be checked by others.
questions.teaches: Objectified judgments can be discussed and tested: once a judgment points to something in the book, another reader can go and look, which a report of personal preference does not allow.

questions.section: General Rules for Reading Imaginative Literature
questions.q: Over a year, a new wine taster keeps asking what in each wine she enjoyed: its acidity, its balance, its finish. By analogy with the authors' account, what is she building?
options: A standard for judging wine that others can share
A list of personal likes that no one can question
A habit that will spoil her enjoyment of wine
A record that will replace the need to taste
questions.explain: By analogy, asking what in the thing caused the pleasure turns taste into a standard. That is how the authors say good taste in literature develops.
optionExplain: Right: by analogy, discerning the causes of pleasure gradually builds a standard of criticism.
She is moving from likes toward causes in the wine, which others can examine.
The authors expect knowing the sources of delight to enrich it.
A standard guides judgment; it does not replace the experience.
questions.rule: Trace pleasure to its causes to build a standard.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a trained palate in wine or food grows the way the authors describe literary taste growing: by repeatedly asking what in the thing caused the pleasure, until the causes form a standard others can share.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: When a reader asks of a novel what it is about as a whole, what kind of answer do the authors look for?
options: A list of the themes the author believed in
A summary of the author's life and motives
A statement of the unity of its plot
The propositions the novel argues for
optionExplain: Themes sound like what a book is about, but the authors ask for the plot's unity, not the author's beliefs.
A life story may explain where a novel came from, but it does not say what the novel itself is about.
Right: for a story, play or poem, the whole is grasped by stating the unity of its plot.
Propositions belong to expository books; a novel tells a story rather than arguing for claims.
questions.explain: For imaginative works the first question is answered by describing the unity of the plot. The card next shows how the second and third questions change too.
questions.rule: The whole of a story is the unity of its plot.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a lyric poem can be said to have a plot, in the broad sense of an action or movement.
questions.explain: The authors construe plot broadly, so that it includes the action or movement of a lyric poem as well as the plot of a story.
questions.rule: Plot, broadly taken, includes a poem's movement.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Dev finishes a six-episode podcast drama and wants to show he has answered the second question about it. What should he be able to do?
options: Retell its key incidents and each main character's part in his own words
State in two sentences the single thread that ties all six episodes together
Explain whether the drama is a likely story and why it moved him so much
Quote the best lines of dialogue in the order in which they were spoken
optionExplain: Right: the second question is answered by discerning the characters' roles and recounting the key incidents in your own words.
This is a fine answer, but to the first question: it states the unity of the plot.
This belongs to the third question, the reasoned judgment of poetical truth.
Quoting lines in order shows memory, not that he can recount the incidents in his own words.
questions.explain: The second question asks what is said in detail and how; for a story that means the characters' roles and the key incidents, retold in your own words.
questions.rule: Second question: characters and incidents, in your own words.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Sort each note a reader made on a novel by the question it answers.

items.t: The plot comes down to a son's long journey home
The aunt is the one who sets every misunderstanding going
Retelling the shipwreck scene in my own words
The ending feels earned, because the hero's choices led there
It satisfied my mind as well as my heart
The closing chapter is beautiful, and I can say why

questions.explain: Plot, characters and incidents describe what the work is and says. Likelihood, satisfaction of heart and mind, and beauty are the parts of a reasoned verdict on poetical truth.
questions.rule: Understand the plot and people first; then judge poetical truth.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A reviewer ends her notes on a film script with three words: beautiful, likely, satisfying. By the authors' standard, what is missing?
options: A statement of the script's practical lesson
A check that the events really happened
A list of the propositions the script asserts
Reasons for each of those three judgments
optionExplain: A practical lesson belongs to the fourth question, which the authors say works differently for imaginative works.
