Poetical truth is about likelihood within the story, not whether the events took place.
A script tells a story; it is not built from propositions the way an expository book is.
Right: the authors ask of each judgment, can you say why? Bare verdicts are not yet a reasoned judgment.
questions.explain: Her three words cover the right ground, but the authors want a reasoned judgment: for each verdict, the reader should be able to say why.
questions.rule: A verdict needs its reasons.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A friend says a wordless ballet has no plot, so the first question cannot be asked of it. Using the authors' broad sense of plot, what is the better reply?
options: Only works made of words have unity, so the friend has a fair point here
Its unity lies in its movement, which can be described like a plot
Its unity lies in the choreographer's life, not in the dance
Skip to the third question, since the first one does not fit
optionExplain: The authors' broad sense of plot already covers a lyric, which has no story; words are not what makes unity.
Right: if a lyric's movement counts as plot, a dance's movement from beginning to end can be stated as its unity too.
The maker's life may be interesting, but the first question asks about the work as a whole.
Judging truth or beauty before grasping the whole reverses the order of the questions.
questions.explain: Plot in the broad sense is the action or movement of a work. A ballet moves from a beginning to an end, and that movement can be described as its unity.
questions.rule: Find the movement, and you can state the unity.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the broad sense of plot reaches beyond literature: a work without words, such as a ballet, still moves from a beginning to an end, and the unity of that movement can be stated.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, once you have read a novel well, you are obliged to act on what it shows, or to change your views because of it.
questions.explain: That obligation holds for expository books you agree with. For a novel, play or poem, strictly speaking no action is called for. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Agreement obliges action only for expository books.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: According to the authors, when you have answered the first ____ questions about a story, play or poem, your responsibilities as its reader are discharged.
questions.explain: Plot, characters and incidents, and poetical truth: once those three questions are answered, a reader has done everything a story asks.
questions.rule: Three questions finish a story.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Lena can state a family saga's plot, retell its key scenes and explain why it rings true. A classmate says she is not finished until she decides what to change in her life. What would the authors reply?
options: She must first draw the saga's moral and live by it
Her reading is complete; nothing more is required of her
She must find a practical book that agrees with it
She must decide whether the author's views on family are right
optionExplain: A moral to live by treats the saga like a practical book, which the authors say a story is not.
Right: answering the first three questions discharges a reader's duties to a story.
Pairing a novel with a practical book is not a step the authors ask for; the story stands on its own.
This treats the saga as a set of claims to accept or reject; its truth is poetical, and she has judged that already.
questions.explain: The classmate is applying the expository version of the fourth question. For a story, a reader who has answered the first three questions has read it well.
questions.rule: No practical upshot is owed to a story.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Sort each book by what the fourth question asks of a reader who has read it well and agrees with it.
groups: Action or a change of view

items.t: A guide to saving money whose ends and methods you accept
A study of the climate whose conclusions convince you
A first aid manual you agree with
A novel about a family farm
A comedy written for the stage
A sonnet about an old friendship

questions.explain: Agreement with a practical book calls for action, and conviction by a theoretical book calls for a change of view. Stories, plays and poems ask nothing further once they are read well.
questions.rule: Expository: act or adjust. Imaginative: nothing owed.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Suppose the reader agrees with a theoretical book on economics rather than a practical one. What does the fourth question then require, according to the authors?
options: Nothing, since only practical books ask for action
Going out to apply its findings in her business
The first three questions only, as with a novel
Mental action: adjusting her views to fit it
optionExplain: Tempting, since no deed is required, but the authors say a theoretical book still calls for mental action.
Doing something is the response to a practical book; a theoretical one asks for a change of mind.
Stopping after three questions is the rule for imaginative works, not for an expository book you agree with.
Right: a convincing theoretical book requires the mental action of accepting its conclusions and adjusting your views.
questions.explain: Change the kind of book and the answer changes. A theoretical book you accept asks you to adjust your views; a story asks for nothing of that kind.
questions.rule: Theoretical agreement asks for a change of mind.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A book club leader ends every meeting on a novel by asking members to list three action points from it. By the authors' account, what is the leader doing?
options: Asking a story the expository form of the fourth question
Answering the third question about poetical truth
Following the authors' advice for reading novels with a message
Checking that members grasped the unity of the plot
optionExplain: Right: action points are what a practical book you agree with calls for; a novel read well asks for none.
Action points are not judgments of likelihood, satisfaction or beauty.
The authors give no such advice; even a story's buried message is something other than the story itself.
A list of things to do says nothing about whether the plot has been grasped as a whole.
questions.explain: Treating each novel as a source of things to do turns the fourth question into its expository form, which the authors say a story does not require.
questions.rule: A novel does not owe you action points.
questions.teaches: By the authors' account, a book club or class that ends each novel by listing action points is asking the fourth question in its expository form, which a story read well does not require.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: According to the authors, why have stories such as Animal Farm been banned and censored so often?
options: Stories are harder for censors to read through and approve quickly
Their authors broke the publishing laws of their own countries
A story can carry a political point more powerfully than an essay
Readers mistook the invented events in them for factual reports
optionExplain: Length and difficulty are not the reason the authors give; they point to the force of the story itself.
The authors say nothing about broken laws; they explain bans by what the stories can do to readers.
Right: the authors say a story is sometimes a better way of getting a point across than an expository work.
Readers of a fable about farm animals are not misled about the facts; they are moved by the point.
questions.explain: Sometimes a story gets a political, economic or moral point across better than an expository work. The card next asks whether that power is the heart of the matter.
questions.rule: Stories can carry points with unusual force.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: The authors quote E. B. White: a despot fears an eloquent writer preaching freedom less than a drunken ____ whose joke may take hold.
questions.explain: White's remark explains why imaginative works have so often been banned: a story or a joke can take hold of people in a way argument may not.
questions.rule: Censors fear the joke that takes hold.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A short story about a family drowning in debt leads many readers to support a change in lending law. How would the authors describe this effect?
options: Proof that those readers have read the story well
A sign the work is an expository book in disguise
Real and often powerful, but not what makes it a good story
A misuse of fiction that careful readers should learn to resist
optionExplain: Acting on a story shows it moved them, but reading it well means answering the first three questions.
A story that makes a point is still a story; the authors' examples, like Animal Farm, remain fiction.
Right: the authors grant that stories move readers to act, while denying that this is of their essence.
The authors do not condemn the effect; they only say it is not the essence of the work.
questions.explain: The effect is genuine, and the authors give examples of it. But whether a story is good, and whether it was read well, does not depend on what readers did afterwards.
questions.rule: The effect is real but beside the story's worth.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A critic argues: this novel changed no laws and started no movements, so it is a weaker story than Animal Farm. Which step goes wrong by the authors' account?
options: It measures a story by its practical consequences
It compares two novels written in quite different countries
It assumes Animal Farm had political influence
It judges a novel before a second reading of it
optionExplain: Right: practical consequences are not of the essence, so they cannot rank one story above another.
Comparing books across countries is not the problem; the yardstick is.
The authors themselves call Animal Farm a powerful attack on totalitarianism, so this assumption is fair.
Rereading may help, but the flaw is in what the critic measures, not when.
questions.explain: The critic ranks stories by what they caused. Since leading to action is not essential to imaginative writing, its absence is no weakness in the story.
questions.rule: Do not rank stories by what they caused.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors' reasoning, if the attack on tyranny in a fable were rewritten as a factual report, the point could reach readers with less force.
questions.explain: The authors claim a story is sometimes a better way of getting a point across than an expository work; they say Solzhenitsyn's novel tells more than a hundred factual studies. Change the form and the force can change.
questions.rule: The same point can land harder as a story.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: An authoritarian government bans a satirical comedy show while letting dry policy critiques circulate. Which reasoning from the chapter best explains the choice?
options: Comedy is easier to prove false than a careful, documented argument
Policy critiques are read only by officials and experts
Satire breaks rules of public taste that reports keep
A joke that catches on can spread further than an argument
optionExplain: Satire is not a set of claims to disprove; its danger lies in how it spreads, not in being false.
Some critiques reach wide audiences; the chapter's reasoning concerns the force of a joke, not readership.
Taste may matter to censors, but the chapter explains bans by the power of imaginative work to move people.
Right: this is White's point, that a despot fears the joke that may take hold more than eloquent preaching.
questions.explain: White's remark explains the pattern: a memorable joke can take hold and travel in a way that reasoned argument often does not.
questions.rule: Memorable stories and jokes travel.
questions.teaches: By analogy with E. B. White's remark, satire in any medium, from cartoons to comedy sketches, can alarm those in power more than reasoned critique, because a memorable joke spreads and sticks.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: In the phrase fine art, what does the word fine mean according to the authors?
options: Being refined in style
Being an end in itself
Being finished with care
Being made by trained artists
optionExplain: A natural guess, but the authors explicitly reject refined as the meaning.
Right: fine comes from finis, end; the work is its own end.
Finished sounds close to finis, but the authors reject this reading too.
Training says who made the work, not what kind of thing it is.
questions.explain: The authors trace fine to the Latin for end: the work is an end in itself. The card next draws out what that means for reading.
questions.rule: Fine means end in itself.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: The word fine in fine art comes from the Latin ____, which means end.
questions.explain: Finis means end. A work of fine art is an end in itself and does not move toward some result beyond itself.
questions.rule: Finis: the work is its own end.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Which of these works fits the authors' sense of fine art most closely?
options: A pamphlet written to win votes at an election
A lyric poem written to be read for itself
A leaflet explaining how to leave a building
A cookbook written to teach weeknight dinners
optionExplain: A pamphlet is a means to a further result, the votes.
Right: the poem aims at no result beyond itself; reading it is the point.
A safety leaflet exists for the action it produces, a safe exit.
A cookbook serves the cooking that follows; it is a practical book.
questions.explain: The pamphlet, leaflet and cookbook all serve results beyond themselves. The poem is meant to be experienced for its own sake.
questions.rule: Ask whether the work serves a result beyond itself.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Which statements fit the authors' account of a work of fine art? Choose all that apply.
options: Its real value lies in the action it leads readers to
It does not move toward a result beyond itself
It must be polished to a high and careful finish
It is its own excuse for being, in Emerson's words
It is worth reading only if it teaches a lesson
optionExplain: This describes a practical work, which the authors contrast with fine art.
Right: this is what being an end in itself means.
The authors reject finished as the meaning of fine.
Right: the authors borrow Emerson's remark about beauty for imaginative works.
A lesson is a further result; a work of fine art needs none to justify it.
questions.explain: A work of fine art aims at nothing beyond itself and needs no further justification. Polish and lessons are beside the point of the word fine.
questions.rule: Fine art needs no further justification.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Suppose a novelist wrote a book mainly to change a law, and the law changed. On the authors' account, what decides whether the book succeeds as fine art?
options: Whether the law was in fact changed afterwards
Whether the novelist's purpose in writing it was a worthy one
Whether readers felt moved to act on its point
Whether it works as a story experienced for itself
optionExplain: The change in the law is a practical consequence, which the authors say is not of the essence.
A worthy purpose concerns the author's aims, not whether the work succeeds as a story.
Moving readers to act is the effect the authors call inessential to imaginative writing.
Right: as fine art the novel is judged as the thing it is, a story, not by the result it achieved.
questions.explain: Changing the conditions changes nothing in the test. A novel succeeds as fine art by what it is as a story, whatever results it brought about.
questions.rule: Judge the work, not its results.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A school board keeps novels in the curriculum only after a study shows that reading fiction raises test scores. By the authors' reasoning about fine art, what does this defence of novels concede?
options: It judges novels as means, by a result beyond themselves
It shows novels are practical books after all, like manuals
It proves fiction is fine art, since its value can be measured
It concedes nothing, since any good result counts in their favour
optionExplain: Right: valuing novels for test scores treats them as tools for a further end, which on the authors' view is not what they are.
A side effect does not turn a story into a practical book; manuals are written for the action they produce.
Measurable usefulness is the mark of a means, the opposite of the authors' fine art.
Good results may be real, but resting the case on them judges the novel by something beyond itself.
questions.explain: The defence may be true and politically useful, but it argues on the ground the authors call inessential: what fiction leads to. On their view a novel's first claim is as an end in itself.
questions.rule: Defending art by its side effects treats it as a means.
questions.teaches: By extension, defending literature only by its useful side effects, such as better test scores or greater empathy, judges it as a means; on the authors' view such benefits, however real, are beside its essence as an end in itself.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: According to the authors, if a novel makes you want to go out and do something, what should you ask yourself?
options: Whether the author meant readers to take that action
Whether other readers felt the same urge after reading
Whether an implied statement in it produced the feeling
Whether the strength of the urge proves the novel is a great one
optionExplain: The author's intentions are not the authors' test; the question is what in the work produced the feeling.
Other readers' reactions say nothing about where your own urge came from.
Right: the authors advise asking whether a buried statement in the work is behind the feeling.
Moving readers to act is not of the essence of imaginative writing, so the urge proves nothing about greatness.
questions.explain: The authors suggest tracing the urge to an implied statement in the work. The card next explains why that matters.
questions.rule: Trace an urge to act to its source.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, poetry, properly speaking, is the realm of statement.
questions.explain: The authors say poetry is not the realm of statement, although many stories and poems have statements buried in them.
questions.rule: Poems may hold statements, but are not made of them.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: After a play about a factory fire, Mia feels driven to campaign for safety inspections. Following the authors' advice, what should she conclude?
options: She has read the play well at last, since it changed what she does
She should suppress the urge, since a story asks nothing of her
She is reacting to a buried claim, which is fine, not to the play
She has misread a play that was never about safety at all
optionExplain: Reading the play well means experiencing it and answering the first three questions, not being changed by it.
The authors do not ask readers to suppress such urges; they ask readers to see where they come from.
Right: reacting to an implied statement is quite right, but it is a response to something other than the play.
The play may well contain such a claim; the point is that the claim is not the play.
questions.explain: Mia's urge is a fair response to a statement buried in the play. Seeing that keeps her clear about what she is reacting to, and about what reading the play itself involves.
questions.rule: React to the statement, knowing it is not the story.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Sort each reaction a reader had to a novel by what it responds to.

items.t: Being gripped by the tension of the trial scene
Feeling the grief of the final chapter
Finding the ending satisfying to heart and mind
Deciding to give money to a refugee charity
Writing to a newspaper about prison conditions
Concluding that wealth corrupts, and changing jobs

questions.explain: Being gripped, grieving and finding the ending satisfying are ways of experiencing the novel. Decisions to act follow from claims the reader has drawn out of it.
questions.rule: Experiencing a story differs from acting on its claims.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: On the authors' account, a story containing no implied statement at all could still be read well.
questions.explain: Statements are something other than the story itself, which subsists in its own right. To read it well, the authors say, all you have to do is experience it.
questions.rule: A story needs no message to be read well.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A charity's short film tells the moving story of one child and ends with a donation link. Using the authors' distinction, what is the clearest description of what the film asks of viewers?
options: It uses a story to carry a statement that calls for action
It is fine art, so it asks nothing of its viewers at all
It is a pure story, so the donation link is beside the point
It is an expository argument with no real story in it
optionExplain: Right: the story is a vehicle; the call to give comes from the claim it carries.
A film built to produce donations aims at a result beyond itself, unlike the authors' fine art.
The link shows the film is built around a claim; ignoring it misses what is being asked.
There is a real story; it serves a statement rather than standing alone.
questions.explain: The film tells a story in order to carry a claim, that this child needs help and you can give it. The call to act comes from that claim, which is what a viewer would need to weigh.
questions.rule: When a story carries a call to act, weigh the call as a claim.
questions.teaches: By extension, a work can use a story as a vehicle for a statement, as charity films and advertisements do; then the call to act comes from the statement, and judging the call means judging that statement, not the story.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: What is the authors' first piece of advice for reading a story?
options: Read it slowly, savouring each chapter
Read a summary of it before you begin
Read it twice before forming any view
Read it quickly and with total immersion
optionExplain: Savouring sounds like loving attention, but the authors warn that drawing a story out loses its unity.
A summary may orient you, but it is not the authors' first advice and replaces the story's own unfolding.
Rereading can help later, but the first advice concerns how to read it the first time through.
Right: speed keeps the plot whole, and immersion catches the details.
questions.explain: The authors' first advice is to read a story quickly and with total immersion. The card next shows what each half of the advice is for.
questions.rule: Quickly, and with total immersion.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Ideally, the authors say, a story should be read at one ____.
questions.explain: One sitting is the ideal. When a long novel makes that impossible, compress the reading into as short a time as you can.
questions.rule: Approach the one-sitting ideal.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Omar has a 300-page thriller and a free fortnight. Which plan best fits the authors' advice?
options: Read ten pages a day so that he can enjoy it for longer
Read it over two or three long sessions close together
Read the first half, pause for a week, then finish it
Skim it in an hour, then decide whether to read it
optionExplain: Spreading the reading out risks forgetting what happened, so the unity escapes.
Right: a few close sessions compress the reading and keep the plot's unity in mind.
A week's gap in the middle invites forgetting exactly where the plot needs holding together.
Skimming may suit an expository book, but it loses the details that immersion is meant to catch.
questions.explain: Omar cannot always read in one sitting, but he can compress the reading into a few close sessions, keeping both the whole and the details.
questions.rule: Compress the reading of a story.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Match each way of reading a story with what the authors say it does.
pairs: Lets you see the unity of the story
Reading in scattered bits over weeks
questions.explain: Speed and intensity do different jobs: speed holds the whole, intensity catches the parts. Losing either costs the matching half of the reading.
questions.rule: Speed for unity, intensity for details.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Suppose a reader races through a novel in one evening, but with half her mind on her phone. By the authors' account, what is she most likely to miss?
options: The rough unity of the plot as a whole
The details of its characters and incidents
The chance to read it at a single sitting
The author's statements buried deep in the story
optionExplain: Her speed is what protects the unity, so this is the part she is least likely to lose.
Right: the authors tie seeing the details to reading intensely, which she is not doing.
She did read it at one sitting; the sitting was not the problem.
Buried statements are not what the authors link to intensity; the details of the story are.
questions.explain: Speed without intensity keeps a rough sense of the whole but lets the details pass by. Change the condition from intense to distracted and the details are what go.
questions.rule: Fast is not enough; read intensely too.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Ines must set a long novel aside for a week halfway through. By the authors' reasoning about why speed matters, which step would best limit the damage of the break?
options: Start the whole novel over again from the first page after the week
Skip ahead to the ending so that the break no longer matters
Read a few pages a day during the week to keep in touch
Before resuming, restate the plot so far in a few sentences
optionExplain: Starting over works against compressing the reading and doubles the time it takes.
Jumping to the end replaces the unfolding of the plot instead of protecting it.
A trickle of pages spreads the reading out further, which is what loses the unity.
Right: the danger of a gap is forgetting what happened; restating the plot rebuilds the unity before going on.
questions.explain: The authors want speed because gaps make you forget what happened. When a gap cannot be avoided, recalling the plot's thread before resuming repairs some of the loss.
questions.rule: After a forced break, recap the plot before going on.
questions.teaches: When a story must be interrupted, restating the plot so far before resuming, as television series do with a recap, partly restores the unity that the gap erodes.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, stretching out the reading of a novel you love is a sign that you are reading it especially well.
questions.explain: The authors suspect such readers are satisfying their feelings about the characters more than reading the book. The card next explains the cost.
questions.rule: Savouring is not the same as reading well.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Readers who draw out a beloved novel are, the authors suggest, satisfying their more or less ____ feelings about its events and characters.
questions.explain: The authors say such readers are probably satisfying more or less unconscious feelings, rather than reading the book.
questions.rule: Lingering can feed hidden feelings.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Priya loves a novel so much that she reads one chapter a week to make it last all year. By the authors' account, what risk does she run?
options: Losing the plot's unity while she indulges her feelings
Reading too fast to notice the fine details of each chapter
Judging the characters before she understands them
Missing a political statement buried in the novel
optionExplain: Right: spreading the reading out loses the whole, and the lingering serves her feelings.
Her pace is the opposite of too fast; one chapter a week is very slow.
Slowness does not make her judge sooner; the problem lies elsewhere.
Buried statements are a separate matter from how long the reading takes.
questions.explain: A year-long reading stretches the plot past what memory can hold together, and the authors suspect the stretching serves her feelings rather than her reading.
questions.rule: Stretching the reading costs the whole.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A reader says: I allow myself one page a night of this novel, because I love the characters too much to let them go. Which point from the authors does this miss?
options: Characters should not be loved until they are judged
A novel should be read once and then put away
Lingering feeds feelings and costs the plot's unity
Loving the characters proves the story is poetically true
optionExplain: The authors ask readers to let characters into their hearts; love is not the fault here.
The authors say nothing against rereading; the issue is how the first reading is paced.
Right: the authors suspect the lingering serves feelings, and the slow pace lets the unity slip.
Affection is not the test of poetical truth, and it is not what the reader is claiming anyway.
questions.explain: The reader's love of the characters is fine; the problem is letting it set a pace at which the story's unity cannot hold.
questions.rule: Do not let fondness set the pace.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: Finishing a novel in two long sittings and returning a month later to favourite scenes is a different matter from the savouring habit the authors warn against.
questions.explain: The authors' warning is about drawing out the reading itself so that the whole slips away. Here the whole was grasped first; returning to scenes afterwards is a different matter.
questions.rule: Grasp the whole first; returning later is fine.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A listener saves the last track of a beloved album for months so that the album will not be over. By analogy with the authors' point about savouring, what is going on?
options: He is listening with the total immersion the authors ask for
He is judging the album before he understands it
The delay serves his feelings at the cost of the whole
He is treating the album as a practical work
optionExplain: Immersion means letting the work act on you in full; holding back its end is the opposite.
He is not judging the album at all; he is postponing its end.
Right: like the savouring reader, he trades experiencing the whole for a feeling about it.
A practical work aims at a result beyond itself; nothing here is about use.
questions.explain: Holding back the end keeps a pleasant feeling alive, but it means the album is never heard as the whole it was made to be.
questions.rule: Holding back the end trades the whole for a feeling.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the savouring trap appears in any art taken in over time: holding back the end of a series or an album to make it last trades the experience of the whole for a feeling about it.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: According to the authors, when may you disapprove of something a character in a novel does?
options: Not before you understand why he does it
As soon as it breaks your own moral code
Only after you have read what critics say
Only if the author signals disapproval too
optionExplain: Right: understanding why comes first, and the authors add that even then disapproval may not follow.
Your own code may be sound, but judging at once means judging from your world, not his.
Critics are not the gate the authors set; your own understanding of the character is.
The author's signals are not the test; the reader's understanding of the character's reasons is.
questions.explain: Understand first, judge later, if at all. The card next shows what living in a character's world involves.
questions.rule: Understand why before you disapprove.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, reading a story with total immersion includes suspending your disbelief about its events.
questions.explain: Immersion means letting the story work on you: let the characters into your mind and heart and suspend your disbelief about the events.
questions.rule: Immersion suspends disbelief.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: In a novel set on a whaling ship, the captain has a sailor flogged. Lucy, who abhors cruelty, wants to put the book down in disgust. What would the authors advise first?
options: Stop reading, since the book endorses cruelty
Skip ahead to see whether he is punished later
Judge him by modern law in order to stay objective
Find out why he acts so, from inside his world
optionExplain: Showing an act is not endorsing it, and stopping means judging before she understands.
Checking for punishment is a way of judging early, and it breaks the story's unfolding.
Modern law is her world's standard; the authors ask her to live in his world first.
Right: try to live in the captain's world, where his act may become understandable, before disapproving.
questions.explain: The authors ask Lucy to understand why the captain acts before she disapproves, by living in his world rather than hers.
questions.rule: Enter the character's world before judging him.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Sort each reader's response by whether it lives in the story's world or judges from the reader's own.

items.t: Asking what a duel meant to men in that society
Accepting that ghosts walk in this novel's town
Feeling the heroine's fear as the soldiers arrive
Dismissing the plot because animals cannot talk
Condemning a character on page five for an act not yet explained
Calling the hero foolish because nobody you know would act so

questions.explain: Entering the society, accepting its premises and feeling with its people are immersion. Rejecting premises, condemning before explanation and measuring by your own acquaintances judge from outside.
questions.rule: Judge a story from inside its world.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Suppose Lucy reads to the end, understands fully why the captain acts as he does, and still finds his cruelty abhorrent. What does the authors' advice now allow her?
options: Only to approve, since she now understands him
To disapprove, now that she has understood first
No view at all, since stories ask for no judgment
Only a view of the author, not of the captain
optionExplain: Understanding is not approving; the authors only say disapproval must wait for it.
Right: the rule was not before you understand; having understood, she may judge, though the authors hint she may not need to.
Stories ask no action of you, but the authors still want reasoned judgments about them.
Nothing in the advice limits her to judging the author; the advice concerns the character.
questions.explain: Immersion postpones judgment rather than banning it. The authors' words are do not disapprove before you understand why, if then: after understanding, the question is open.
questions.rule: Understanding first; then judgment is open.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A visitor to a village festival abroad sees adults throwing flour at passers-by and decides the custom is plain rudeness. By analogy with the authors' advice on characters, what should he do first?
options: Complain to the organisers that the custom is rude
Learn what the custom means there before judging it
Join in at once so as not to seem a stranger
Judge it by his own country's manners, which are fixed
optionExplain: Complaining at once is disapproving before understanding, the error the authors warn against.
Right: as with a character, understand the reasons inside that world before disapproving.
Copying without understanding is not the same as grasping why people act as they do.
Judging by his home manners is living in his world, not theirs.
questions.explain: The authors' rule for characters works for any unfamiliar world: understand why people act as they do there, and judge afterwards, if at all.
questions.rule: Understand a world from inside before judging it.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the rule to live in a character's world before judging carries over to meeting another culture: understand the reasons inside that world first, and judge, if at all, afterwards.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: What do the authors compare the crowd of characters at the start of a big novel to?
options: Reading a telephone directory page by page
Learning a play's cast list by heart
Studying a family tree before a wedding
Arriving at a party full of strangers
optionExplain: A directory has no one who matters more than anyone else; a novel's crowd sorts itself by importance.
Learning every name by heart is what the authors say you need not do.
Studying relationships in advance is a sensible-sounding plan, but the authors' image is of people emerging as you go.
Right: at a party, as in a novel, the people who matter emerge from the crowd after a while.
questions.explain: The authors liken a novel's crowd to a party or a new town, where individuals soon stand out. The card next draws the lesson.
questions.rule: A novel's crowd sorts itself as at a party.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a good reader of a big novel tries to remember every character introduced.
questions.explain: Many characters are background figures who set off the main ones. The authors say we should not expect to remember them all.
questions.rule: Let background figures stay in the background.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Ana is forty pages into a family saga with thirty named characters and is ready to quit, sure she cannot keep them straight. What would the authors tell her?
options: Read on; the important ones will stand out in time
Chart every character fully before going further
Start again and memorise each name as it appears
Switch to a shorter novel with fewer people to keep track of
optionExplain: Right: as at a party, the people who matter emerge from the crowd as she reads.
A chart sounds thorough, but it treats background figures as if they all mattered equally.
Memorising every name is the burden the authors tell her she need not carry.
Giving up on a big novel is the fainthearted reaction the authors want her to avoid.
questions.explain: The important characters emerge as the story goes on, much as friends emerge from a crowd of new colleagues. Ana needs patience, not a memory feat.
questions.rule: Read on and let the important ones emerge.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Ana wants to know early which of the saga's thirty characters will matter. By the authors' party analogy, which signals suggest a character is one of the important ones? Choose all that apply.
options: Her name is the hardest one to pronounce
She returns at the turning points of the plot
She is the first person named in chapter one
Other characters keep talking about her
She appears once, described at great length
optionExplain: Strange names are what overwhelm readers at first; they say nothing about importance.
Right: as at a party the person you keep meeting stands out, a character who recurs when the plot turns is one who matters.
Being named first is no guarantee; some early figures are background.
Right: the people others keep mentioning are the ones worth knowing, at a party or in a novel.
A long description can mark importance, but a figure who never returns is background however fully drawn.
questions.explain: At a party the people who matter are the ones you keep meeting and hearing about. In a novel that means the characters who keep returning, especially when the plot turns.
questions.rule: Importance shows in recurrence.
questions.teaches: By extension of the party analogy, the characters who matter reveal themselves by recurring, by being talked about and by acting at the plot's turning points, so a reader can watch for those signals instead of memorising everyone.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Suppose Ana finishes the saga but still cannot say who the main characters were or what each of them did. What does that suggest?
options: She has read it well, since background names can be let go
The novel has too many characters to have any unity
The second question about the novel is still open
She should have quit at page forty, as she meant to
optionExplain: The permission covers background figures only, not the people who carry the story.
A big cast does not destroy unity; the authors expect the important figures to emerge.
Right: letting go of background figures is fine, but the main characters and their roles must be clear by the end.
Quitting would have left her knowing even less; the fix is closer reading, not stopping.
questions.explain: The advice to relax about names has a limit: by the end you should know who matters and what each did. If not, the characters' roles, which the second question asks about, are still unclear.
questions.rule: By the end, know who matters.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Jo starts following a football league with twenty teams and hundreds of players, and tries to learn every squad before watching a match. By analogy with the authors' advice, what would serve Jo better?
options: Finish learning every squad before the first match
Follow only one team and ignore the rest of the league
Watch matches and let the key teams and players emerge
Wait for the season to end and read its summary
optionExplain: Memorising everyone first is the same burden the authors lift from the reader of a big novel.
Narrowing to one team avoids the crowd rather than letting it sort itself.
Right: as in a big novel, following the action lets the figures who matter stand out.
A summary replaces the experience of following the season as it unfolds.
questions.explain: A crowded new field sorts itself the same way a novel's cast does: follow what happens, and the important people become visible.
questions.rule: Follow the action and let the key figures emerge.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the party principle fits any crowded new field, such as a sports league or a long-running drama: follow the action and the figures who matter will emerge, rather than memorising every name up front.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a well-made story should make clear from its first pages how all of its events relate.
questions.explain: The authors say a story should not be clear at the beginning; like life, it becomes clear looking back. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Stories come clear in hindsight.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: According to the authors, you must ____ a story in order to be able to say that you have read it well.
questions.explain: Because a story's events come clear only looking back, a reader who stops partway cannot claim to have read it well.
questions.rule: Finish the story.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Halfway through a mystery novel, Ben cannot see why a scene in a lighthouse was included. What does the authors' advice suggest?
options: Keep reading; its place may come clear looking back
Reread the scene until its point is clear, then go on
Treat the scene as padding the author forgot to cut
Look up a summary to learn why the scene matters
optionExplain: Right: a scene's relation to the rest often shows only once the story is finished.
Stopping to force clarity treats a story like a hard passage of argument; the story itself may supply the answer later.
Judging the scene useless before the end is judging before the whole is in view.
A summary hands over the relations the reader is meant to discover by finishing.
questions.explain: Ben is halfway through; the relation of events is something a reader grasps looking back. The authors would have him read on.
questions.rule: Read on; the relations come later.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A reader reasons: the author drew heavy attention to a stolen letter in chapter one, but I cannot yet see why, so the novel is badly made. What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: Heavy flagging is itself the sign of a weak author
A stolen letter cannot carry a novel's plot alone
The reader should judge the novel only after a second reading
Flags show what matters; why it matters can come later
optionExplain: The authors describe flagging as help authors give, not as a weakness.
Nothing in the reasoning needs the letter to carry the plot alone; the fault is judging too soon.
A second reading may help, but the flaw is judging before finishing the first.
Right: authors flag what is essential, and the reason it matters is understood looking back.
questions.explain: The reader noticed the flag, which is good, and then demanded its meaning at once. The author marked it as essential; why it is essential is the kind of thing that shows only looking back.
questions.rule: Notice the flags; wait for their meaning.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: By the authors' reasoning, a reader who stops a novel two-thirds through cannot yet say she has read it well, even if she understood every page so far.
questions.explain: Understanding each page is not the same as grasping how the events relate, which comes only looking back from the end. Stopping short leaves that relation unseen.
questions.rule: Page-by-page clarity is not the whole.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A juror finds the first days of a trial confusing: witnesses appear whose relevance is unclear. By analogy with the authors' point about stories, what attitude helps most?
options: Decide now which witnesses matter and ignore the rest
Hold judgment until the case is in, then look back
Assume the confusing witnesses do not bear on the verdict
Rely on the closing speeches to sort out the evidence
optionExplain: Deciding early which parts matter is the anxiety the authors warn against, and it may discard what proves essential.
Right: as with a story, how the parts relate may appear only once everything has been presented.
Unclear relevance now is not irrelevance; the relations may show later.
Closing speeches are one side's account; looking back over the evidence oneself is the parallel to the authors' reader.
questions.explain: A trial, like a story, unfolds in sequence. Its parts often make sense only when the whole has been presented and the juror looks back over it.
questions.rule: Things told in sequence come clear at the end.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any account unfolded in sequence, such as a trial, can be fully clear only in retrospect: holding judgment until it is complete lets the relations among its parts appear.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: What do the authors say about asking what happens to characters after a novel ends?
options: It is a good test of how well you grasped the plot
It is meaningless; they have no life outside the book
It is worthwhile whenever the author has left the ending open
It belongs to the third question, poetical truth
optionExplain: Grasping the plot means grasping what the book contains, not inventing what follows.
Right: the story stops on its last page, and any answer is only as good as the next reader's.
An open ending is still the ending; the authors' point holds for any story.
Poetical truth concerns the story as told, not an invented sequel.
questions.explain: The authors call such speculation meaningless, because the characters have no life outside the book. The card next shows why the limits matter.
questions.rule: Characters live only inside the book.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: The authors say that a story, like life, goes on after its last page.
questions.explain: Life goes on; the story does not. That is where, the authors say, a story stops being like life.
questions.rule: The story ends where the book ends.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A book group spends an evening debating whether the heroine of a novel later regretted her marriage, which the book does not show. How would the authors judge the debate?
options: Useful: it tests whether they grasped her character
Required: the third question calls for such a verdict
Fruitful: the author left that question open for her readers
Idle: any answer is only as good as the next reader's
optionExplain: Grasping her character means reading what she does in the book, not inventing her future.
A verdict on poetical truth is about the story as told, not about events after it.
The story's limits are part of its shape; the authors do not treat what follows as an invitation.
Right: the book contains no such regret, so no answer can be better grounded than another.
questions.explain: The debate is about events outside the book. The authors call such speculation meaningless, since the characters have no vitality beyond the last page.
questions.rule: Do not debate what the book does not contain.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Sort each activity by whether it reads what the story contains or speculates beyond its pages.

items.t: Working out her childhood from the memories she recounts
Tracing how the war changed the brothers between chapters
Noticing what the final scene implies about her choice
Imagining the heroine's life ten years after the ending
Writing a prequel about her parents' courtship
Guessing whom the hero would have married had he lived

questions.explain: Memories told in the book, changes shown between chapters and what an ending implies are all inside the story. Life after the end, a prequel or an alternative fate are not.
questions.rule: Inside the book: read it. Outside: leave it.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Suppose another writer publishes an authorised sequel to a classic novel. By the authors' reasoning, how does the sequel bear on the original?
options: It adds nothing to the original, which is complete
It settles what the original's ending meant
It completes a story the first author had left unfinished
It shows that the original's ending had failed
optionExplain: Right: the original's characters have no life beyond its last page, so a sequel is a different work.
The sequel writer's view of what came next is only as good as any other reader's.
The original is limited in time by design; the authors see those limits as part of why it satisfies.
A sequel's existence says nothing about whether the original ending worked.
questions.explain: Authorisation does not change the point. A sequel is a new story; it cannot reach back and alter a work whose limits are part of its shape.
questions.rule: A sequel is another work, not more of the first.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Fans of a film demand to know what the hero did in the years before the film begins. By analogy with the authors' view, what is the best description of their question?
options: It shows the film failed to explain its hero
It is the first question the film itself raises
It asks about events the work does not contain
It can be settled by asking the director
optionExplain: A hero can be fully understood from what the film shows; leaving years out is not a failure.
The first question asks what the work is about as a whole, not what it leaves out.
Right: the film's world begins and ends with the film; its unshown past is outside the work.
Even the maker's answer would be a new story, not something the film contains.
questions.explain: The hero has no years outside the film. What fans imagine there may be fun, but it is not part of the work they watched.
questions.rule: A work's world ends at its edges.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the authors' view extends to film and television: prequels and spin-offs may be new works in their own right, but they cannot settle anything about the original, whose world ends at its edges.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: According to the authors, why does fiction seem to be a necessity for human beings?
options: It is the easiest way to pass on factual knowledge to people
It trains readers for harder expository books
It satisfies unconscious as well as conscious needs
It gives a truer picture of society than research
optionExplain: Fiction is not mainly a carrier of facts; the authors locate its necessity in the needs it meets.
Fiction may sharpen a reader, but the authors' reason is about needs, not practice.
Right: fiction reaches the unconscious as well as the conscious mind, which expository writing does not.
The authors grant stories great force, but they do not rest fiction's necessity on accuracy.
questions.explain: The authors say fiction meets unconscious as well as conscious needs. The card next shows how that can colour our judgment.
questions.rule: Fiction reaches the unconscious.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, expository writing touches the unconscious mind as fiction does.
questions.explain: The authors contrast the two: expository writing touches the conscious mind, while fiction touches the unconscious as well.
questions.rule: Exposition speaks to the conscious mind.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Tom raves about a novel in which a kind, poor clerk inherits a fortune, but he cannot say what is good about the writing. By the authors' account, what may be going on?
options: A hidden wish of his own is being satisfied
He has grasped its poetical truth by intuition
He is reacting to an implied political statement
He has read it quickly and with full immersion
optionExplain: Right: the authors' own example is pleasure at a sympathetic character's inheritance, which we do not admit we would like.
Poetical truth calls for a reasoned verdict; Tom cannot give reasons.
Nothing in an inheritance plot need carry a political claim; the pull here is personal.
Immersion helps a reading, but it does not explain liking a book he cannot defend.
questions.explain: Tom likes the book without knowing why, which is the sign the authors point to. The pleasure may come from his own unadmitted wish rather than from the novel's art.
questions.rule: Unexplained liking may be a private wish.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Which of these are among the unconscious needs the authors say novels can satisfy? Choose all that apply.
options: Admiring the precision of the author's prose style
Joy when a sympathetic character inherits money
Learning facts about a distant country's customs
Identifying with characters who love more richly
Identifying with a conqueror, a victim, or both
optionExplain: Admiring prose is a conscious judgment of craft, not an unconscious need.
Right: we do not admit we want the money; we say we like the book.
Facts feed the conscious mind; the authors' list is about hidden wishes.
Right: the authors suggest we would all like to love more richly than we do.
Right: the authors name unconscious sadism and masochism, satisfied by identifying with either side.
questions.explain: Inheritance, freer love and identification with conqueror or victim are the authors' examples. Admiring prose and learning facts are conscious responses.
questions.rule: Hidden wishes can pass for literary taste.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Suppose two readers react to the same novel, one delighted and one irritated, and neither can say why. What do the authors' remarks suggest about these reactions?
options: The book must be mediocre, since its readers disagree so sharply
The delighted reader has read it more fully
Both are reasoned verdicts on its poetical truth
Each may reflect private feelings more than merit
optionExplain: Disagreement between readers says little about quality when neither can give reasons.
Delight is not a sign of fuller reading; it may be a wish being met.
A verdict without reasons is not a reasoned one.
Right: like and dislike for kinds of people can both make us feel more strongly than the book merits.
questions.explain: The authors' point cuts both ways: unexplained dislike can come from the unconscious as easily as unexplained delight.
questions.rule: Unexplained dislike is as suspect as unexplained delight.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A sports film in which your home town's underdog team wins the cup leaves you elated. By analogy with the authors' point, what should you ask before calling it a great film?
options: Whether the real team ever won such a match
Whether your own wish is doing the film's work
Whether other fans of the team liked it too
Whether the director came from the same town
optionExplain: A film's poetical truth does not depend on real results.
Right: identification can inflate a verdict, so the elation may be about you rather than the film.
Other fans share your wish, so their liking is no independent check.
Where the director came from says nothing about the film's merit.
questions.explain: As with sympathetic heirs in novels, a story that rewards people you identify with can feel better than it is. Separate that pull from the film's own merits.
questions.rule: Check your loyalties before praising a story.
questions.teaches: By analogy, loyalty and identification inflate verdicts on any story, a film included: a fan's delight at a home-town win is evidence about the fan before it is evidence about the work.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: What do the authors mean by poetic justice in a story?
options: Villains punished in the most poetic and fitting way possible
Characters rewarded or punished by their true merit
A happy ending for every sympathetic character
The author's verdict on the society of the time
optionExplain: Poetic here means belonging to poetry and fiction, not a fancy style of punishment.
Right: the author, like a god to his characters, gives each what he truly deserves.
Sympathetic characters may still suffer; the test is merit, not happiness.
A verdict on society is a statement the story may carry, not the justice done to its characters.
questions.explain: Poetic justice is the story's putting right of what life leaves unjust: characters get what they deserve. The card next explains why it matters to readers.
questions.rule: Poetic justice: each according to true merit.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, one irritating feature of a bad story is that rewards and punishments fall with no rhyme or reason.
questions.explain: Where outcomes follow from nothing in the characters, the story fails the need that poetic justice meets.
questions.rule: Random fates mark a bad story.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: In a novel, a hard-working nurse is killed by a falling sign in the last chapter, a death connected to nothing before it. By the authors' standard, what is the likely complaint?
options: The story is sad, and good stories end happily
Real life contains no such random accidents
The author should have punished a villain instead
Her fate follows from nothing she is or did
optionExplain: Sadness is not the fault; tragedies are sad and still satisfy.
Life does contain such accidents; that is exactly the injustice stories are expected to put right.
Punishing someone else would not answer the complaint, which is that this outcome is unconnected to merit.
Right: a fate with no rhyme or reason is what the authors call irritating in a bad story.
questions.explain: The death is random within the story. Poetic justice needs outcomes that follow from what the characters truly are, and this one follows from nothing.
questions.rule: Fates should follow from the characters.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Sort each ending by whether it shows poetic justice or an outcome with no rhyme or reason.

items.t: A liar is at last trapped by his own lies
A patient farmer's care of his land saves him in the drought
A proud general's pride leads him into the fatal battle
A villain wins a lottery in the final chapter
The kind sister dies of a fever first mentioned on the last page
The hero's rival is struck by lightning out of nowhere

questions.explain: In the first group the outcome grows from what the character is and does. In the second, chance from outside the story decides, so nothing is earned.
questions.rule: Justice is earned inside the story.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Suppose a novel lets a cruel landlord die rich and at peace, yet makes clear what his cruelty cost him inwardly. How does the authors' standard apply?
options: It may satisfy, if it convinces us justice was done
It fails, since he is not punished in outward ways
It succeeds, since the ending is realistic
It does not apply, since stories are ends in themselves
optionExplain: Right: the test is whether the storyteller convinces us that justice has been done, not the form it takes.
Outward punishment is one form of justice, not the only one the authors allow.
Realism is not the test; stories are meant to put right what life leaves unjust.
Being an end in itself does not exempt a story from satisfying us; poetic justice is part of how it satisfies.
questions.explain: Change the outward ending and the question stays the same: has the story convinced us that each got his true deserts? Inner cost can carry that conviction.
questions.rule: The test is conviction, not the form of the punishment.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Viewers of a long-running TV drama are furious when a beloved character is killed off because the actor left the show, with no link to the plot. By the authors' reasoning, what best explains the anger?
options: Viewers object to any death of a sympathetic character
They wanted the drama to imitate the randomness of real life more closely
Her fate broke the justice the story had led them to expect
They judged the series before it had finished
optionExplain: Viewers accept deaths that are earned by the story, as in tragedy; the trouble is this one was not.
Real life is where random deaths happen; viewers wanted the story to do better than life.
Right: her death follows from nothing inside the story, so it has no rhyme or reason.
Their complaint is about a specific outcome, not a premature verdict on the whole.
questions.explain: The character's fate was decided by something outside the story, an actor's departure. Inside the story it has no cause, which is the failure of poetic justice the authors describe.
questions.rule: Outside forces should not decide a character's fate.
questions.teaches: By analogy, audiences of serial dramas feel poetic justice violated when outside pressures, such as an actor leaving, decide a character's fate: the outcome then follows from no merit inside the story.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: According to the authors, what does the tragic hero gain, even when he does not wholly deserve his fate?
options: A reward in some later life or world
The pity of the other characters
An understanding of why it befalls him
A chance to undo his mistake at the end
optionExplain: Tragedy does not compensate the hero with a reward; that would be ordinary poetic justice.
Pity may surround him, but the authors point to what he himself comes to know.
Right: the hero at least comes to understand his fate, and we share that understanding.
Tragic heroes usually learn too late to undo anything; their understanding comes after ruin.
questions.explain: The tragic hero comes to understand his fate. The card next explains why readers value that so much.
questions.rule: Tragedy gives understanding, not reward.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: The authors cite a story by Sherwood Anderson whose title, I Want to Know ____, could be the title of many stories.
questions.explain: I Want to Know Why names the desire tragedy satisfies: to understand why things happen as they do.
questions.rule: We want to know why.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: In a play, an honest judge is ruined by a slander he believed; in the last scene he sees how his own pride let it work. What, by the authors' account, does the audience gain?
options: His insight, without sharing his suffering
Proof that honesty is rewarded in the end
A warning never to enter public office
Relief that the slanderer is caught at last
optionExplain: Right: the hero learns why, after his ruin, and the audience shares the insight at no such cost.
The judge is ruined; the play shows understanding, not reward.
A practical warning treats the play as advice; the authors point to shared insight.
The scene described says nothing of the slanderer; what it gives is the judge's understanding.
questions.explain: The judge comes to understand his fate, too late to escape it. The audience takes away that understanding without the ruin that bought it.
questions.rule: Share the hero's insight, not his suffering.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Which contrast best captures the difference between ordinary poetic justice and the justice of tragedy, as the authors describe them?
options: A happy ending, versus a sad but random ending
Heroes who win in the end, versus villains who learn too late
Justice in novels, versus justice on the stage
Merit rewarded or punished, versus a fate understood
optionExplain: A random ending is the failure of justice, not the tragic form of it.
In tragedy it is the hero, not the villain, who comes to understand.
Both kinds of justice appear in novels, narrative poems and plays.
Right: in most stories people get what they deserve; in tragedy the hero may not, but comes to understand.
questions.explain: Ordinary poetic justice deals out deserts. Tragedy may deal out more than is deserved, and offers instead the hero's understanding of his fate.
questions.rule: Tragedy swaps deserts for understanding.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: On the authors' account, if a tragic hero were destroyed without ever grasping why, the play would lose what lets the audience share his insight.
questions.explain: The satisfaction the authors describe comes from sharing the hero's understanding. Take away his learning why, and only the suffering remains.
questions.rule: No understanding, no tragic insight to share.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A documentary about a failed company ends with its founder explaining, frankly and painfully, the choices that sank it. By analogy with the authors' account of tragedy, why might viewers find this ending satisfying despite the loss?
options: They enjoy seeing a powerful man brought down
They share his hard-won insight without its cost
They learn that the company deserved to fail
They expect him to build a new firm afterwards
optionExplain: That pleasure exists, and the authors mention such hidden wishes, but it is not what the ending's clarity provides.
Right: like the tragic hero, the founder learns why after the ruin, and viewers gain the insight free.
Deserving is the logic of ordinary poetic justice; the satisfaction here comes from understanding.
A comeback would be a different story; the ending's force lies in what he now sees.
questions.explain: The ending offers what tragedy offers: the clear insight of one who paid dearly for it, which viewers can share without paying.
questions.rule: Hard-won insight can be shared at no cost.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a candid account of a real failure, such as a founder's post-mortem, offers what tragedy offers: the insight of one who paid for it, shared by those who did not.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: According to the authors, what marks the great stories that live on for centuries?
options: They satisfied the private tastes of first readers
They meet deep needs shared by almost everyone
They are faithful records of life in their time
They teach a clear moral that applies anywhere
optionExplain: Private tastes pass with the readers who held them; the authors look for what everyone needs.
Right: great stories satisfy needs nearly all people share, such as a belief in justice.
Faithful records may be valuable history, but the authors locate greatness in the needs a story meets.
A moral is a statement; the authors speak of needs met, not lessons taught.
questions.explain: The great stories satisfy the deep needs of almost everybody, which is why they last. The card next sets this against private needs.
questions.rule: Great stories meet shared needs.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a book you like without really knowing why may be satisfying needs that are particular to you.
questions.explain: That unexplained liking is the authors' sign of a book meeting your own particular unconscious needs.
questions.rule: Unexplained liking may be private.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Kai loves a novel about a lonely chess prodigy because he was one, but friends find it dull. Grace loves an ancient epic that readers everywhere have loved for centuries. By the authors' account, which love more likely signals a great story?
options: Kai's, since his personal tie to it is stronger
Neither, since liking tells nothing about greatness
Both equally, since each love is sincere
Grace's, since the need it meets is widely shared
optionExplain: A strong personal tie is exactly what may make a book seem better to one reader than it is.
The authors do connect greatness to what readers find satisfying, when the satisfaction is widely shared.
Sincerity is not in doubt; the question is whose needs the book meets.
Right: lasting appeal to readers everywhere is the authors' sign of a need almost everyone shares.
questions.explain: Kai's love rests on a private match with his own life. Grace's epic meets needs shared so widely that it has satisfied readers for centuries.
questions.rule: Wide and lasting appeal signals shared needs.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Sort each source of a reader's satisfaction by the kind of need it meets.
groups: A need shared by almost everyone

items.t: The hero grew up in your own home town
A rival you dislike on sight comes to grief
The heroine reminds you of your sister
A world in which justice is done
Sharing a hero's understanding of his fate
Relief from anxiety about why the good suffer

questions.explain: Hometowns, likenesses and private dislikes belong to one reader. Justice, understanding and relief from anxiety are the needs the authors say nearly all people share.
questions.rule: Ask whose need the story is meeting.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Suppose a novel delighted a whole generation by flattering its tastes, then was forgotten within twenty years. What would the authors' distinction suggest?
options: It met a passing need rather than a lasting one
It was a great story that later readers misread
Its popularity proves it met universal needs
It failed because it grew too long for later tastes
optionExplain: Right: the needs of almost everybody do not fade in twenty years; what pleased one generation was narrower.
Possible in a single case, but the authors' test points to what lasts across generations.
Wide popularity in one period is not the same as meeting needs common to all people.
Length is not in question; the story's appeal was tied to one generation's tastes.
questions.explain: Great stories go on satisfying readers for generations. A book whose appeal dies with one generation's tastes was meeting something narrower.
questions.rule: Lasting appeal is the authors' sign of shared needs.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A music critic notices that a song she adores reminds her of her first summer abroad. Following the authors' distinction, what should she do before ranking it among the great songs?
options: Rank it highly, since sincere feeling is the critic's best guide
Drop it, since any personal feeling rules a song out of fair judgment
Separate her memory's pull from what it gives listeners generally
Ask the songwriter what the song was meant to make people feel
optionExplain: Sincere feeling may be private; that is the very thing the distinction asks her to examine.
Personal feeling does not disqualify a song; a song she loves for private reasons may also be great.
Right: like a reader of fiction, she separates a private association from what the work offers nearly everyone.
The maker's intention does not tell her whose needs the song meets.
questions.explain: Her delight may come from a private memory. The authors' distinction asks her to look past it to what the song gives listeners in general before calling it great.
questions.rule: Set private association aside when judging greatness.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a critic of any art can separate the pull of personal association from what a work offers nearly everyone, and should rest a claim of greatness on the second.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: How do the authors describe the place of the great epic poems in the Western tradition?
options: The most widely read books after the Bible
Honoured in their own day, but forgotten since then
Perhaps the most honoured, probably the least read
Read mainly by scholars, and honoured by few
optionExplain: The authors pair the epics with the Bible as the backbone of a reading program, but say they are little read.
The epics are still honoured; the authors' point is that honour has outlasted reading.
Right: the authors call this a paradox that needs comment.
The authors say the epics are highly honoured; it is the reading that is rare.
questions.explain: The epics are honoured more than they are read. The card next explains what makes them so rare and so demanding.
questions.rule: Much honoured, little read.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: The authors take the honour paid to the great epics as a sign that they are easy and pleasant to read.
questions.explain: The honour reflects how rare a finished epic is. The authors say plainly that these poems are certainly not easy to read.
questions.rule: Honoured is not the same as easy.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A poet works on a verse epic for twenty years and dies with it still unfinished. How does this fit the authors' account of epics?
options: It fits: few epics begun are ever completed
It is unusual: most epics begun are completed
It shows modern poets lack the gift for epics
It shows epics are best left without an ending
optionExplain: Right: hundreds of epics have been begun and few completed, so an unfinished one is the common case.
The authors say the reverse: very few have been completed successfully in 2,500 years.
The authors' unfinished examples include famous poets; the difficulty lies in the form, not one era.
Unfinished epics, like Byron's Don Juan, are cases of a task not done, not a chosen form.
questions.explain: Hundreds of epics have been started, and some grew long without being finished. A poet dying with one incomplete fits the authors' judgment that a long epic is the hardest thing to write.
questions.rule: Few epics are ever finished.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Which of these are among the five great epics the authors name? Choose all that apply.
options: Byron's Don Juan
Virgil's Aeneid
Wordsworth's Prelude
Milton's Paradise Lost
Dante's Divine Comedy
optionExplain: Don Juan is the authors' example of an epic that grew long without ever really being finished.
Right: the Aeneid is one of the five.
The Prelude is the authors' other example of a long epic never really finished.
Right: Paradise Lost is one of the five, and the only one with no prose translation.
Right: the Divine Comedy is one of the five.
questions.explain: The five are the Iliad, the Odyssey, the Aeneid, the Divine Comedy and Paradise Lost. The Prelude and Don Juan illustrate how often epics are left unfinished.
