questions.rule: Five finished epics; many unfinished ones.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Among the many people who begin writing a complete dictionary of a language alone, few ever finish, and those who do are celebrated. By analogy with the authors' view of epics, what does the celebration track?
options: How many copies of the finished work are sold
How old the language being described is
How easy the finished work is to consult
How rarely so vast a task is completed well
optionExplain: Sales measure popularity; the authors note the epics are honoured even though little read.
The age of the subject does not explain why finishing is honoured.
Ease of use is beside the point; the epics are honoured while being hard to read.
Right: as with epics, honour follows the rarity of carrying a huge undertaking through to a fine finish.
questions.explain: The authors measure an epic's difficulty by how few are completed, and honour the poet who finishes. The same logic explains honour for any vast solo work carried through.
questions.rule: Honour tracks how rarely a vast task is finished well.
questions.teaches: By analogy, honour for any vast undertaking, such as a one-person dictionary, tracks how rarely it is completed well, the same measure the authors use for the difficulty of an epic.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: According to the authors, what mainly makes the great epics hard to read?
options: Their being written in verse rather than in plain prose
Their elevation, their lofty approach to the subject
Their many references to forgotten local history
Their great length compared with modern novels
optionExplain: Verse is the obvious suspect, but the authors note prose translations exist for all but Paradise Lost.
Right: the authors locate the difficulty in the epics' elevation and the demands it makes.
Unfamiliar references can slow a reader, but the authors do not name them as the main difficulty.
Length is not the authors' explanation; they point to the way the epics approach their subjects.
questions.explain: The authors say the difficulty lies in the epics' elevation, not mainly in their verse. The card next shows what that demands and what it repays.
questions.rule: Elevation, not verse, makes epics hard.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, prose translations are available for every one of the five great epics.
questions.explain: The authors make one exception: Paradise Lost. For the other four, prose translations exist, which is why verse cannot be the main difficulty.
questions.rule: All but Paradise Lost come in prose.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Rosa picks up a prose translation of the Odyssey, expecting it to read as easily as a modern novel now that the verse is gone. What does the authors' account predict?
options: It will read easily, since verse was the main barrier
It will still demand great attention and imagination
It will lose its value once the verse is removed
It will be harder, since prose hides the story's unity
optionExplain: The authors say verse is not the main source of difficulty.
Right: the elevation, and the demands it makes, survive translation into prose.
The authors recommend prose translations without suggesting they lose the work's value.
The authors say nothing about prose hiding unity; the demand comes from elevation.
questions.explain: Removing the verse removes one obstacle but not the main one. The epic's elevation still asks for attention, involvement and imagination.
questions.rule: Translation does not lower the demands.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Which statements match what the authors say about the rewards of reading the great epics? Choose all that apply.
options: They come mostly from the beauty of the verse
They can be gained from a quick skim of the story
They are at least as great as those of any other books
They are smaller than those of the finest novels
They go only to readers who do a good job
optionExplain: The authors do not single out the verse; the rewards come from a good, analytical reading.
A skim is less than a good job, and the authors say such readers miss the rewards.
Right: the authors rank them at least as high as any books, certainly any other fiction.
This reverses the authors' claim about other works of fiction.
Right: the rewards are not gained by readers who do less than a good job.
questions.explain: The authors put the epics' rewards at the top of all reading, and attach a condition: they come only from reading the epics well.
questions.rule: Great rewards, for good readers only.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Suppose a reader skims the Aeneid in an afternoon so that she can say she has read it. By the authors' account, what will she gain?
options: Most of it, since knowing the story is the main reward
Half the reward, for half of the effort
Enough to stand with the poets who read Virgil
Little, since the rewards come from reading it well
optionExplain: Knowing the story is not the reward the authors describe; that comes from an analytical reading.
The authors do not describe the rewards as proportional; a poor reading misses them.
Having turned the pages is not having read Virgil as the poets did.
Right: the authors say the rewards are not gained by readers who do less than a good job.
questions.explain: Change the effort and the reward does not shrink in proportion; it goes missing. The authors tie the epics' rewards to a good, analytical reading.
questions.rule: A skim of an epic earns little.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A modern war film's hero comes home in disguise and tests his household before revealing himself, echoing a famous ancient story. By the authors' remark that every good poet has read the great epics, what does knowing the Odyssey give a viewer here?
options: The ability to see the echo and what the film does with it
A reason to dismiss the film as borrowed and so unoriginal work
Nothing more, since a film must stand on its own merits
Proof that the director studied the classics at university
optionExplain: Right: because later writers have read the epics, a reader who knows them can recognise echoes and see how the new work changes the old.
Echoing a classic is how writers in the tradition work; recognising it opens the film rather than condemning it.
The film can stand alone, but a viewer who knows the source sees more in it.
The echo says nothing certain about the director's schooling; what matters is what it adds to the viewing.
questions.explain: The authors say Homer, Virgil, Dante and Milton are the authors every good poet, and many other writers, have read. Knowing them lets you catch echoes of them in later work and see what is made of them.
questions.rule: Knowing the epics unlocks later echoes.
questions.teaches: Because later writers have absorbed Homer, Virgil, Dante and Milton, a reader who knows the epics catches allusions and echoes throughout later literature and film that others miss, and can see what the new work makes of them.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a play should be read in an entirely different way from a story.
questions.explain: A play is a story, and so far as it is one it should be read like a story. The card next shows where the reader of a play must do more.
questions.rule: A play is read first as a story.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A novel abounds in description and a play has almost none, so the reader of a play must be more active in creating the ____, the world in which the characters live and move.
questions.explain: With no description to lean on, the reader of a play builds the background for himself. Otherwise, the authors say, the problems are essentially those of reading a story.
questions.rule: No description: build the world yourself.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A script's opening stage direction reads only: A kitchen. Morning. What does the authors' advice ask of the reader?
options: Wait until one of the characters describes the kitchen in full
Treat the setting as unimportant to the story
Build the room and its mood from that line and the talk
Look up how the first production staged the scene
optionExplain: Characters in plays rarely describe their own surroundings; waiting may leave the room empty.
The setting is part of the world the characters live in, and the reader must supply it.
Right: the reader actively creates the background the play does not describe.
A past production is one answer, but the authors ask the reader to do the work.
questions.explain: With a bare stage direction, the reader must build the setting and atmosphere from the few words given and from what the characters say and do.
questions.rule: A bare direction is a cue to imagine.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Sort each task by whether it is the same as reading a story or extra work that a play demands.

items.t: Stating the unity of the plot
Sorting out the characters and their roles
Living in the characters' world before judging
Picturing a setting the text barely names
Supplying the atmosphere a narrator would describe
Imagining the places where the characters move

questions.explain: Plot, characters and immersion are common to all stories. Building the background is the extra work a play's lack of description demands.
questions.rule: Same story questions, more world-building.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Suppose a reader, told a play is set in a royal palace, pictures it on a spaceship because that seems more exciting. What has gone wrong?
options: Nothing, since the reader is free to create the background
She should picture no setting at all, to stay faithful
Her background no longer fits the words she was given
She has judged the play before understanding its plot
optionExplain: The freedom to create a background is the freedom to fill gaps, not to replace what the play states.
Picturing nothing loses the world the characters live in; the fix is a setting that fits.
Right: the reader creates the background, but it must fit the play's words and actions.
Her error is in the setting she imagines, not in an early verdict.
questions.explain: Creating the background means filling what the text leaves open. A palace on a spaceship contradicts what the text says, so it reads a different play.
questions.rule: Fill the gaps, but keep to the text.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A transcript of a court hearing records every word spoken and nothing else. By analogy with the authors' point about plays, what work falls to its reader?
options: Picturing the room and the people the record leaves out
None, since the words alone are the whole of the hearing
Reading only the parts where the judge speaks
Judging the witnesses before following the hearing
optionExplain: Right: like the reader of a play, the reader of a transcript must supply the setting the record omits.
The words are all there, but the room, the faces and the atmosphere are not.
Leaving out speakers loses part of the exchange without supplying what is missing.
Judging first reverses the order of understanding and judging.
questions.explain: A transcript, like a play, gives speech without description. Its reader supplies the courtroom and the people, as the reader of a play supplies the background.
questions.rule: Supply what the medium leaves out.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any record made only of speech, such as a hearing transcript, leaves the setting out, so its reader supplies the room and the people as the reader of a play supplies the background.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: What do the authors say you are reading when you read a play in a book?
options: The purest form of the work, free of actors
A complete work, since every word is there
A sketch the director is meant to rewrite
An incomplete work, lacking its performance
optionExplain: Some readers prefer the text, but the authors say the work the author intended is the acted play.
The words are all there, but the physical dimension is not.
The lines are fixed; what the page lacks is performance, not finished wording.
Right: the complete play is apprehended only when it is acted on a stage.
questions.explain: A play on the page lacks the performance its author intended. The card next shows how a reader makes up for it.
questions.rule: A read play lacks its performance.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: The authors compare a play to ____, which must be heard to be complete.
questions.explain: Like music, which must be heard, a play lacks a physical dimension when read in a book, and the reader must supply it.
questions.rule: A play, like music, needs performing.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Leo reads a comedy and finds a scene flat: two characters swap short lines while a third hides under a table. What does the authors' point suggest he try?
options: Skip it, since a flat scene is most likely filler
Picture it acted, with the hiding and timing seen
Read a critic's account of why the scene is meant to be funny
Judge it weak, since the words alone fall flat
optionExplain: The flatness may come from the missing performance, not from the scene.
Right: much of the scene lives in the physical dimension the page lacks.
A critic's account replaces Leo's own work of imagining the scene acted.
Words alone are not the complete play; judging them alone judges an incomplete work.
questions.explain: The comedy of a hidden character depends on what an audience sees and hears. Supplying that dimension may show what the bare lines hide.
questions.rule: If a scene falls flat, stage it in your head.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Match each work with what makes it complete, according to the authors' comparison.
pairs: The text on the page, description included
questions.explain: Music and plays need a performance to be complete; a reader of either must supply it. A novel carries its description on the page.
questions.rule: Know which works need performing.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, no reader staging a play in his head is free to question what the characters are to say, since their words are before him.
questions.explain: The authors say we cannot question what we are to hear, since the play's words are before us. What the reader supplies is how it looks and sounds.
questions.rule: Imagine the staging, not new words.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: An architect's plans for a concert hall are laid out on a table. By analogy with the authors' view of plays, how should a client read them?
options: As the finished work, since every measurement is given
As a work completed by picturing the hall in use
As less telling than photographs of other halls
As a document that only builders need to grasp
optionExplain: Every measurement can be there while the experience of the space is not, as every word of a play can be there without its performance.
Right: like a play, the plan is completed elsewhere, and reading it well means imagining that realisation.
Other halls show other buildings; the plan must be read for this one.
The client too must grasp the plan, by imagining the building it describes.
questions.explain: A plan, like a play, is meant to be realised in another medium. Reading it well means supplying the missing dimension: people moving through the finished hall.
questions.rule: Read a plan by imagining it realised.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any work made to be realised in another medium, such as an architect's plan or a screenplay, is read well only when the reader supplies the dimension it lacks by imagining it realised.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: What exercise do the authors suggest for reading a play well?
options: Write a summary of each act
Learn the major roles by heart
Compare it with a film version
Imagine directing actors in it
optionExplain: Summaries help with the plot, but they do not supply the physical dimension.
Memorising roles is an actor's task; the authors ask the reader to direct.
A film shows someone else's choices; the authors want the reader to make them.
Right: telling imagined actors how to say lines and play scenes supplies the missing performance.
questions.explain: The authors suggest pretending to direct the play. The card next explains when and how.
questions.rule: Direct the play in your head.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Put these steps for reading a play in the order the authors suggest.
items: Read the play through to grasp it as a whole
Work out its characters and key incidents
Imagine actors before you, awaiting instructions
Tell them how to say key lines and play the climax
questions.explain: Directing comes after you have found out what the play is about as a whole and in detail. Then the imagined actors get their instructions.
questions.rule: Understand first, then direct.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Reading a family drama, Sam reaches the line: So you knew all along. How would directing the play in his head help him?
options: Deciding how it is said forces him to decide what it means
It lets him skip the line until a film settles its tone
It lets him rewrite the line so that its meaning becomes plain
It lets him leave its tone open, since the words suffice
optionExplain: Right: whether the line is spoken in anger, relief or grief changes the scene, so choosing a delivery is choosing an interpretation.
Waiting for a film hands the decision to someone else.
The words are fixed; the director decides how they are said, not what they are.
Leaving the tone open is the partial reading the authors warn about.
questions.explain: A line like this can be furious, broken or relieved. Telling an imagined actor how to say it makes Sam decide what is happening in the scene.
questions.rule: Choosing a delivery is choosing a meaning.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A student says: this playwright gives detailed stage directions for everything, so there is no point in directing the play in my head. What would the authors say?
options: Right: directing is for plays that lack directions
Right: detailed directions already make the reading complete
Wrong: staging is worth it however explicit the playwright
Wrong: stage directions are unreliable guides
optionExplain: Missing directions make directing more pressing, but the authors want it for every play.
Directions on the page still have to be seen and heard in the reader's mind.
Right: the authors say mental staging is always desirable, no matter how explicit the playwright was.
The authors do not question stage directions; they ask the reader to realise them.
questions.explain: Even the fullest directions are words on a page. The reader must still picture the performance, which is why the authors call staging always desirable.
questions.rule: Stage every play, however detailed its directions.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, directing a play in your head should come first, before you have worked out what the play is about as a whole.
questions.explain: The authors place directing after you have discovered what the play is about, as a whole and in detail. Staging without that grasp has nothing to stage.
questions.rule: Grasp the whole before you stage it.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A manager is given a script for a difficult conversation with an employee. By analogy with the authors' advice on plays, what would help most in preparing?
options: Reading the script once silently and trusting the words
Memorising every line so that she can recite it exactly as written
Rehearsing in her head how each key line is said, and why
Rewriting the script so that tone no longer matters
optionExplain: A silent reading leaves the spoken dimension, where tone lives, unexamined.
Exact recital is an actor's memory task; it does not settle how the lines should land.
Right: as with a play, deciding the delivery of key lines shows what they will mean to the listener.
Tone matters in any spoken exchange; rewriting cannot remove it.
questions.explain: A script for speaking, like a play, is incomplete until it is voiced. Deciding how the key lines are said is how she discovers what they will mean.
questions.rule: Rehearse how key lines are said.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any text meant to be spoken, such as a speech or a scripted conversation, is understood best by deciding how each key line should be delivered and why.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: In the authors' Hamlet example, what question about the action does Shakespeare leave the reader to decide?
options: Whether Hamlet overheard the plan to spy on him
Whether Ophelia ever truly loved Hamlet at all
Whether the king knew that Polonius was hiding there
Whether the ghost of Hamlet's father was real
optionExplain: Right: whether Hamlet overheard Polonius changes the meaning of his later talk with Polonius and Ophelia.
Ophelia's feelings are much discussed, but they are not the authors' example.
The king is in on the plan; he hides with Polonius.
The ghost raises its own questions, but the authors' example concerns what Hamlet overheard.
questions.explain: Shakespeare left no stage direction saying whether Hamlet overheard the plotting. The card next explains why the reader must decide.
questions.rule: Some plays leave the staging to you.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Shakespeare's stage directions settle whether Hamlet overheard Polonius.
questions.explain: Shakespeare left no stage directions on the point. The reader, or director, must decide.
questions.rule: No direction: the reader decides.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: In a modern play, a wife tells her husband she saw the letter. The text does not say whether she is telling the truth. Following the authors, how should a reader handle this?
options: Leave it open, because the playwright chose to leave it open
Assume she is bluffing, since characters often bluff in plays
Pass over it, since unstated facts are not the reader's concern
Decide from the evidence, since the choice shapes the scenes
optionExplain: The authors say the reader or director must decide; leaving it open leaves the scenes unread.
A blanket assumption is not a decision from the evidence of this play.
The unstated fact is central to understanding, so it is very much the reader's concern.
Right: as with Hamlet, what is true here changes the meaning of what follows, so the reader must decide.
questions.explain: Whether she saw the letter changes how every later exchange reads. The authors' advice is to decide, on the evidence, as a director would.
questions.rule: Settle open facts that change the meaning.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Suppose a reader decides that Hamlet did overhear Polonius's plan to spy on him. How does Hamlet's sudden harshness to Ophelia then read?
options: As proof that he really has gone mad for love of her, as Polonius says
As his response to knowing she is being used against him
As an outburst with no link to anything before it
As a sign that Ophelia herself devised the plan
optionExplain: That is Polonius's theory, which the overheard plan gives Hamlet reason to play up, not proof of it.
Right: if he heard the plan, he may know she is part of a trap, and his words take that meaning.
Having overheard the plan is precisely a link to what came before.
The plan was Polonius's; overhearing it would tell Hamlet so.
questions.explain: Change the decision and the scene changes. If Hamlet overheard, his harshness answers a trap he knows about; if not, it means something else.
questions.rule: The decision changes how the scene reads.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Which of these may a reader of a play have to decide for himself when the text is silent? Choose all that apply.
options: Whether a character overheard a conversation
What words a character speaks in the next line
How a key line is to be spoken
Whether a character is lying when the text is silent
In which order the scenes of the play should come
optionExplain: Right: the authors' Hamlet example is exactly this.
The words are before the reader; what he decides is how they are seen and heard.
Right: telling actors how to say a line is part of directing in your head.
Right: like overhearing, it changes what the following scenes mean.
The order of scenes is fixed by the text.
questions.explain: The reader decides what the text leaves open, such as who heard what, who is lying, and how lines are said. The words and their order are given.
questions.rule: Decide what is open; accept what is given.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Reading an email chain, you notice a manager's curt reply might mean she had already seen a complaint forwarded earlier, or might not. By analogy with the authors' Hamlet point, what is the useful move?
options: Treat the reply as meaningless until she explains it herself
Decide which reading the evidence supports, then reread
Assume the harsher reading in order to be safe
Set the question aside, since tone cannot be known
optionExplain: Waiting for an explanation postpones understanding; the evidence may already settle it.
Right: what she knew when she wrote changes the meaning of the whole exchange, as with Hamlet's overhearing.
A safe assumption is not a reasoned one.
Tone is uncertain, but the evidence of the chain can often decide what she had seen.
questions.explain: As with Hamlet, the meaning of a reply turns on what its writer knew. Settling that on the evidence lets the rest of the chain be read properly.
questions.rule: Settle who knew what, then reread.
questions.teaches: By analogy, in any record of exchanges, such as an email chain, what one party knew when they spoke can change the meaning of everything they said; settling it on the evidence is part of understanding the exchange.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: According to the authors, what should you do when reading a play by Bernard Shaw?
options: Skip the stage directions for the dialogue
Read it only after seeing it performed
Ignore his comments and judge the play alone
Read the preface he wrote for it
optionExplain: Shaw's very full stage directions were written for readers, so skipping them loses help.
Shaw hoped his plays would be read; one was published before it was ever acted.
Judging a play without the author's own aid is the turning away the authors warn against.
Right: Shaw's prefaces explain the plays, and skipping them throws away an important aid.
questions.explain: Shaw wrote long prefaces telling readers how to understand his plays. The card next sets this among the rare cases of a playwright speaking directly.
questions.rule: Read Shaw's prefaces.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Match each writer with the way the authors say he spoke directly to his audience or readers.
pairs: A novelist addressing the reader directly
An actor stepping out of character for a political speech
Long prefaces and very full stage directions
questions.explain: Novelists like Fielding can address readers at will. Playwrights usually cannot, which is what makes Aristophanes' speeches and Shaw's prefaces interesting exceptions.
questions.rule: Novelists can speak directly; playwrights rarely do.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A new play is published with a long introduction by its author explaining what she meant by the ending. A reader skips it to keep the play pure. By the authors' reasoning, what does he lose?
options: An aid the author gave for understanding the play
Only background on the author's life and times
Only a summary he could have written for himself
Nothing, since a play's words speak for themselves
optionExplain: Right: like Shaw's prefaces, the introduction is the author speaking directly to readers about the play.
The introduction explains the play's meaning, not only the author's life.
An explanation of the ending from its author is more than a summary of events.
The words of a play are incomplete without staging, and the author has offered further help.
questions.explain: The authors treat a playwright's own explanation as an important aid. Skipping it on principle is turning your back on help the author chose to give.
questions.rule: Use the author's own aid when it exists.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Later playwrights have imitated the devices of Aristophanes and Shaw. How do the authors judge the imitations?
options: More effective, since modern audiences expect them
Gone entirely, since modern theatre has dropped them
Still in use, though less effective than the originals
Equally effective, since a device works the same anywhere
optionExplain: The authors make the opposite judgment of the imitators.
The authors say the devices are still used; no useful artistic device is ever really lost.
Right: the authors say such devices are still used but not as effectively as by Aristophanes and Shaw.
The authors' judgment is that the imitators used them less well.
questions.explain: The devices survive: actors still step out of character and playwrights still write prefaces. But the authors judge none has done it as well as the originals.
questions.rule: Useful devices survive, unevenly used.
questions.teaches: The authors note that no useful artistic device is ever really lost: playwrights still step out of character or write explanatory prefaces, though in their view rarely as effectively as Aristophanes and Shaw.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: By the authors' account, even after reading Shaw's preface to a play, a reader still has reason to imagine the play performed.
questions.explain: A preface explains the play, but the play on the page still lacks its performance. The authors call mental staging desirable however explicit the playwright was.
questions.rule: A preface aids staging; it does not replace it.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A film's director records a commentary track explaining her choices. By analogy with the authors' advice on Shaw, how might a viewer best use it?
options: As the final word that settles every meaning
As a distraction, since films should speak for themselves
As an aid to understanding the film from its maker
As useful only to students of film-making
optionExplain: An aid explains; it does not take over the viewer's own work of understanding.
Refusing the maker's own help is what the authors call turning your back on an aid.
Right: like a Shaw preface, it is the maker speaking directly to the audience about the work.
Shaw's prefaces were written for ordinary readers, and a commentary can serve ordinary viewers.
questions.explain: A director's commentary does for a film what Shaw's prefaces do for his plays: it lets the maker speak directly about the work. Used well, it helps; it does not replace watching.
questions.rule: Makers' commentaries are aids, not substitutes.
questions.teaches: By analogy, makers' commentaries in other media, such as a director's commentary or an artist's statement, are aids to understanding of the kind Shaw's prefaces are, and like a preface they explain the work rather than replace experiencing it.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: According to the authors, what should you try first when a passage of Shakespeare's verse is hard to follow?
options: Read it aloud, slowly and with expression
Look up the hard words in the glossary
Read a modern prose version of the scene
Skip it and come back after the act ends
optionExplain: Right: speaking the passage as if to an audience clears up many difficulties.
The glossary has its place, but the authors put it after reading aloud.
A prose version replaces Shakespeare's words rather than helping you hear them.
Skipping keeps the whole moving, but the authors suggest a way through the passage itself.
questions.explain: The authors' first resort for opaque verse is the reader's own voice. The card next gives the order of steps.
questions.rule: Voice first, notes later.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: According to the authors, you should turn to the glossary or notes only after reading a puzzling passage ____ has failed.
questions.explain: Reading aloud, slowly and with expression, comes first. The notes are the fallback.
questions.rule: Notes only after reading aloud fails.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A student reaching a knotty speech in Macbeth at once reads the footnote to every line. What would the authors suggest instead?
options: Read the footnotes more slowly to absorb them
Skip the speech and follow the plot instead
Find a plain summary of the speech online
Say the speech aloud as if to an audience first
optionExplain: Slower note-reading keeps the notes in charge of the passage.
Skipping avoids the speech rather than understanding it.
A summary replaces the words instead of helping you understand them.
Right: speaking it with expression may make the speech clear without breaking it into footnotes.
questions.explain: Going straight to the notes reverses the authors' order. Reading the speech aloud slowly, with expression, often clears it, and the notes remain if it does not.
questions.rule: Try your voice before the footnotes.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Put these steps for reading a Shakespeare play in the order the authors advise.
items: Read the play through, as near to one sitting as you can
Read a puzzling passage aloud, slowly and with expression
Turn to the glossary or notes if that fails
questions.explain: The whole comes first, then the reader's own voice on hard passages, and the notes last of all.
questions.rule: Whole, then voice, then notes.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Suppose a passage stays opaque after Lena reads it aloud slowly and with expression, because one word has changed its meaning since 1600. What does the authors' advice allow now?
options: Reading it aloud again until it clears
Turning to the glossary or notes
Skipping it, since notes are to be avoided
Replacing the word with a modern one
optionExplain: Repetition will not reveal a meaning that has changed; that is what the glossary is for.
Right: the notes come after reading aloud has failed, and here it has.
The authors do not forbid notes; they only put them after reading aloud.
Swapping in a modern word guesses at the meaning instead of finding it.
questions.explain: Reading aloud clears many difficulties but cannot recover a lost meaning. Once it has failed, the authors' advice sends you to the notes.
questions.rule: When voice fails, use the notes.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Reading her grandmother's letters from the 1930s, Ada finds sentences that look garbled on the page. By analogy with the authors' advice, what might she try before a dictionary?
options: Typing them into a translation tool at once
Reading them aloud slowly, as if to a listener
Asking a historian to explain each phrase
Skipping the hard sentences to finish sooner
optionExplain: A tool is a later resort, like the glossary; her own voice comes first.
Right: writing close to speech often comes clear when it is spoken, as opaque verse does.
An expert, like the notes, is the fallback, not the first step.
Skipping avoids the difficulty rather than clearing it.
questions.explain: Letters written close to speech often make sense when spoken. The authors' order applies: the reader's voice first, reference help after.
questions.rule: Speak it before you look it up.
questions.teaches: By analogy, older informal writing such as family letters, which was written close to speech, can often be untangled by reading it aloud before reaching for reference tools.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, most plays are not worth reading.
questions.explain: The authors say most plays are not worth reading because they are incomplete on the page. The card next names the exceptions.
questions.rule: Most plays were made to be acted.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Most plays are not worth reading, the authors say, because they are ____: they were meant to be acted, not read.
questions.explain: A play on the page lacks its performance. For most plays that leaves a reader with too little to repay the effort.
questions.rule: Incomplete on the page, most plays give little.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Which of these do the authors name among the few great plays? Choose all that apply.
options: The melodramas of the nineteenth century
Molière's comedies
The tragedies of Sophocles
The farces of the Roman stage
The plays of Shakespeare
optionExplain: The authors do not name these; their list is short and selective.
Right: Molière's comedies are on the authors' list.
Right: the Greek tragedians Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides head the list.
The authors do not name Roman farces among the great plays.
Right: Shakespeare's plays are on the list.
questions.explain: The authors' list: the Greek tragedians, Shakespeare, Molière's comedies, and a very few moderns.
questions.rule: A short list of very great plays.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A reading group must pick a play for a month of close reading: a recent hit comedy praised mainly for its performers, or Sophocles' Antigone. By the authors' view, which suits close reading, and why?
options: The comedy, since recent plays are easier to stage mentally
Either one, since every play is incomplete on the page
The comedy, since its success shows it works on stage
Antigone, a great play whose insights repay the work
optionExplain: Ease of staging is not the authors' test; the depth of insight is.
All plays are incomplete, but only the great ones repay a reader for it.
Success on stage shows it works as theatre, not that it rewards reading.
Right: the few great plays hold insights rich enough to repay the effort of reading.
questions.explain: All plays are incomplete on the page, so the question is which ones repay the reader's extra work. The authors put the Greek tragedies among the few that do.
questions.rule: Read the plays that repay the extra work.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Suppose the hit comedy is wonderful in the theatre but thin on the page. What does the authors' view imply?
options: It may be worth seeing, though not worth reading
It must be a poor play, since it reads thinly
It is a great play, since great plays are incomplete
It shows reading is the truest test of any play
optionExplain: Right: the authors' judgment that most plays are not worth reading rests on their being made for the stage.
Reading thinly is what the authors expect of most plays; it is not a verdict on the theatre.
Incompleteness belongs to all plays; it is not what makes the few great.
The authors say the complete play exists only on the stage, so reading is not its truest test.
questions.explain: The authors' reason, that plays are made to be acted, cuts both ways: a play thin on the page can still be fine where it was meant to be.
questions.rule: Not worth reading is not the same as not worth seeing.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A friend plans to read the published screenplays of a dozen recent blockbusters. By analogy with the authors' view of plays, what is a fair caution?
options: Screenplays are complete works on the page, unlike plays
Only the screenplays of old classic films are worth reading
Most were made for the screen and give little on the page
Reading them first will spoil the experience of the films
optionExplain: A screenplay lacks its performance as much as a play does.
Age is not the test; depth of insight is.
Right: like most plays, most screenplays are incomplete without performance, and only a few repay reading.
Spoilers are a separate matter from what the reading itself repays.
questions.explain: A screenplay, like a play, is made to be performed. By the authors' reasoning, most will be thin on the page, and only a rare few will reward reading for their own sake.
questions.rule: Scripts made for performance seldom reward reading.
questions.teaches: By analogy, most scripts written for performance, screenplays included, are incomplete on the page, so only the few with deep insights reward reading for their own sake.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: According to the authors, which kind of play is probably the hardest for beginning readers?
options: Shakespeare's histories
Molière's comedies
Greek tragedy
Modern realist drama
optionExplain: Shakespeare's verse can be opaque, but the authors single out Greek tragedy.
Molière is on the authors' list of great plays, but not named as hardest.
Right: the authors call Greek tragedy the toughest nut to crack for beginners.
The authors do not single out modern drama as especially hard.
questions.explain: The authors single out Greek tragedy as the toughest for beginners. The card next gives their three reasons.
questions.rule: Greek tragedy is the hardest start.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Which obstacles do the authors name for readers of Greek tragedy? Choose all that apply.
options: Most companion plays in each group of three are lost
No reliable translations into English exist
We know almost nothing of how the plays were staged
The plays use metres that modern ears cannot hear
We know their stories only through the plays
optionExplain: Right: only the Oresteia survives as a whole group.
The authors do not mention translation as an obstacle.
Right: this makes staging the plays mentally almost impossible.
Metre is not among the authors' reasons.
Right: the audience knew the stories already; we meet them in the plays.
questions.explain: Lost companion plays, unknown staging and unfamiliar background stories are the authors' three obstacles.
questions.rule: Three gaps: lost plays, lost staging, lost background.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Ravi reads Oedipus Rex knowing nothing of the Oedipus story beforehand. By the authors' account, how does his position differ from that of the original audience?
options: They saw the play as a comment on a familiar tale
They found the play's ending a complete surprise
They knew how earlier actors had played the roles
They needed the play to learn the story of Oedipus
optionExplain: Right: the audience knew the story as we know Washington and the cherry tree; Ravi meets the play as the primary story.
The opposite: the audience knew the story already, so the ending was no surprise.
The authors' point concerns the familiar story, not knowledge of earlier performances.
That describes Ravi, not the original audience.
questions.explain: The first audience brought a familiar tale to the play and watched Sophocles comment on it. Ravi must take the play as the story itself and imagine the familiar tale behind it.
questions.rule: The first audience knew the story already.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A student concludes: since we cannot know how the Greeks staged their tragedies, there is no point in reading them. What would the authors say?
options: Sound: a play cannot be read without knowing its staging
Sound, unless a modern production is consulted first
Mistaken: the original staging is in fact well recorded
Mistaken: the plays' power triumphs over such obstacles
optionExplain: Unknown staging makes reading harder, but the authors still urge reading the plays well.
A modern production is not the authors' remedy; they rely on the plays' own power.
The authors say the reverse: we know almost nothing about the staging.
Right: the authors grant the obstacles but say the plays are powerful enough to triumph over them.
questions.explain: The student treats an obstacle as a barrier. The authors admit the gap in our knowledge and still say the plays triumph over it.
questions.rule: Obstacles are not reasons to stop.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Greek tragedy tells us much about life as we still live it, besides forming a framework for later plays such as Racine's and O'Neill's.
questions.explain: The authors say the plays tell us much about life as we still live it, and that they form a framework for many later plays.
questions.rule: Greek tragedy speaks to present life.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A modern reader finds a century-old newspaper cartoon baffling, though it delighted readers at the time. By analogy with the authors' third obstacle, what is the likely reason?
options: Old cartoons were drawn with much less skill than modern ones are
It commented on events its first readers knew and we do not
Its first readers were less demanding than readers now
Cartoons lose their meaning when printed in black and white
optionExplain: Skill is not the issue; the missing background is.
Right: like Greek tragedy, it was a comment on a story its audience already knew.
Nothing suggests the first readers were less demanding; they had knowledge we lack.
Colour is beside the point; the cartoon's meaning depended on shared knowledge.
questions.explain: The cartoon took for granted a story its first readers knew. Later readers must reconstruct that background, as we must for the tales behind Greek tragedy.
questions.rule: Recover the background a work took for granted.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any work that comments on a story or event its first audience knew, such as an old political cartoon, is harder for later readers, who must reconstruct the background the work took for granted.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: According to the authors, what is the essence of tragedy?
options: A hero's fatal flaw of character
Time, or rather the lack of it
The cruelty of the gods to mortals
A conflict between duty and love
optionExplain: A familiar idea, and the authors do call heroes fallible, but the essence they name is the lack of time.
Right: every tragic problem could be solved with enough time, and there is never enough.
The gods appear in many tragedies, but the authors locate the essence elsewhere.
Such conflicts occur, but the authors' answer is time.
questions.explain: The authors say the essence of tragedy is the lack of time. The card next shows the question this leads to.
questions.rule: Tragedy: never enough time.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: The authors say the question to ask of any Greek tragedy is whether we would have been able to see ____ what should have been done.
questions.explain: Seeing the right course at leisure is easy. The authors' question is whether we would have seen it in time, as the hero had to.
questions.rule: Would I have seen it in time?

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: In a tragedy, a general receives a forged order at dawn and must march or refuse before noon; he marches, and his army is destroyed. Following the authors, what question should the reader ask?
options: Why did the general not check the order with more care?
Which of the gods arranged the forgery, and for what end?
What would a wise general have done with a month to think?
Would I have seen through the forgery in the time he had?
optionExplain: This judges from leisure, assuming there was time to check, which is what tragedy denies.
Divine causes may interest a reader, but the authors' question is about seeing in time.
With a month there would be no tragedy; the point is what could be seen by noon.
Right: the authors' question puts the reader under the same pressure of time as the hero.
questions.explain: The general had a morning, not a month. The authors' question asks whether the reader, under that pressure, would have done better.
questions.rule: Judge the choice inside the time allowed.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A reader writes: the heroine's choice was foolish; anyone could see she should have waited for her brother's letter. By the authors' account, where does the judgment slip?
options: It ignores that she had no time to weigh the choice
It assumes that the heroine is a fallible person
It judges a character after finishing the play
It wrongly treats the brother's letter as part of the plot
optionExplain: Right: the reader sees at leisure what she had to decide in a moment.
The authors agree tragic heroes are fallible; that is not the slip.
Judging after finishing is what the authors recommend.
The letter is part of the plot; the slip is in ignoring the pressure of time.
questions.explain: Anyone could see it, reading at leisure. The authors ask whether we would have seen it in time, which the reader's judgment skips.
questions.rule: Hindsight is easy; ask about foresight.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: If the hero of a Greek tragedy had been given as much time as he needed to weigh his choice, the authors' account implies his problem could have been solved.
questions.explain: The authors say every problem in a Greek tragedy could have been solved with enough time, but there is never enough. Supply the time and the hasty, wrong decision, and with it the tragedy, need not happen.
questions.rule: Enough time would undo the tragedy.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A review of a hospital emergency finds that a doctor made the wrong call within ninety seconds. By analogy with the authors' tragic question, what should reviewers ask before blaming her?
options: Whether the right call is plain now that the case is being reviewed
Whether she is more fallible than the other doctors on staff
Whether they would have seen the right call in ninety seconds
Whether the patient's family accepts the outcome of the case
optionExplain: What is plain afterwards is the hindsight the authors' question guards against.
Fallibility is shared by all; the issue is what could be seen in ninety seconds.
Right: like the tragic question, it judges the choice inside the time she had.
The family's view matters for other reasons but does not test the decision.
questions.explain: Reviewers know the outcome and have hours to think. The tragic question asks what anyone could have seen in the time the doctor had.
questions.rule: Judge rushed decisions by the time available.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the authors' tragic question guards against hindsight bias in any review of decisions made under time pressure: ask what could have been seen in the time available, not what is plain afterwards.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: According to the authors, what did tragic actors on the Greek stage wear on their feet?
options: Bare feet, to seem humble before the gods
Soft slippers, so as to move silently
Buskins that raised them several inches
The same sandals that the chorus wore
optionExplain: Humility is not what the staging aimed at; the protagonists were raised up.
Silence was not the point; height was.
Right: the buskins lifted the protagonists above the ground, and above the chorus.
The chorus did not wear buskins, which is what made the contrast.
questions.explain: Tragic actors wore buskins that raised them several inches. The card next explains what this means for reading.
questions.rule: Protagonists stood taller.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the members of the chorus wore buskins as the protagonists did.
questions.explain: Only the tragic actors wore buskins; the chorus did not, though they sometimes wore masks. The contrast in height was the point.
questions.rule: No buskins for the chorus.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: You are reading a chorus's lament in a Greek tragedy, followed by the king's reply. Following the authors, how should you picture the two speakers?
options: The chorus at your own height, the king as a giant
Both at your own height, as ordinary people
Both as giants, since all of them wore masks
The chorus as giants, the king at your height
optionExplain: Right: the chorus speak as people of your stature; the protagonists as figures larger than life.
This loses the contrast the staging was built to show.
Masks were shared, but buskins were not; height marked the difference.
This reverses the staging: the protagonists wore the buskins.
questions.explain: The buskins made the protagonists tower over the chorus. Reading with that contrast keeps the king larger than life and the chorus at your own scale.
questions.rule: Chorus your size; heroes giants.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Match each element of Greek staging with what the authors say about it.
pairs: Raised on buskins, larger than life
No buskins, of the reader's own stature
Worn by the actors, and sometimes by the chorus
questions.explain: Buskins separated the protagonists from the chorus; masks were worn on both sides. Height, not masks, carried the contrast.
questions.rule: Height carried the contrast.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Suppose a modern production put every speaker, chorus included, on raised shoes. By the authors' reasoning, what would be lost?
options: The masks that hid the faces of the actors
The lack of time that drives the tragic plot
The audience's knowledge of the old stories
The contrast between ordinary people and giants
optionExplain: Masks are untouched by the change in shoes.
The pressure of time is in the plot, not the footwear.
What the audience knows does not depend on shoes.
Right: the significance lay in the difference in height, which raising everyone erases.
questions.explain: Raising everyone removes the difference that the authors call highly significant. The chorus would no longer stand at the audience's own scale.
questions.rule: The meaning was in the difference.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: In many medieval paintings, saints and kings are painted far larger than the ordinary people around them. By analogy with the authors' advice on Greek staging, how should a viewer read the difference in size?
options: As a mistake in the painter's sense of perspective
As a sign of stature rather than of bodily height
As showing that those figures stood nearer the viewer
As decoration that carries no meaning of its own
optionExplain: Calling it an error misses a deliberate convention.
Right: like buskins, the size marks who is larger than life.
Nearness is how modern perspective uses size; here size marks importance.
The size is chosen to mean something, as the buskins were.
questions.explain: As buskins made tragic heroes tower over the chorus, a painter's scale can show importance. Reading it as meaning, not error, is the same move.
questions.rule: Read deliberate scale as meaning.
questions.teaches: By analogy, other arts use size to mark importance, as medieval paintings enlarge saints and kings; reading such scale as meaning rather than error is the same move as hearing tragic heroes as giants.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: What is the simplest definition of poetry that the authors offer?
options: It is any language that rhymes
It is what poets write
It is an overflowing of feeling
It is words that praise a subject
optionExplain: Rhyme is one of the definitions the authors call too narrow.
Right: the authors call this the simplest definition, though some would dispute it.
This is the broad definition the authors set aside for their purpose.
Praise is another definition they call too narrow.
questions.explain: The simplest definition is that poetry is what poets write. The card next sets out the broader and narrower definitions the authors reject.
questions.rule: Poetry: what poets write.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Sort each definition of poetry by how the authors judge it.

items.t: Poetry is any spontaneous overflowing of the personality
Poetry can be made by anyone, as action, sound or feeling
Poetry must rhyme
Poetry must praise its subject
Poetry must rouse readers to action
Poetry must use a special poetic diction

questions.explain: The overflow view lets anything count; the rhyme, praise, action and diction views each shut out much real poetry. The authors steer between them.
questions.rule: Steer between too broad and too narrow.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A friend says an unrhymed poem in plain modern words cannot be a real poem. How would the authors answer?
options: That is right; poetry needs rhyme or poetic diction
Any words at all are poetry, so the friend's question is idle
Only the poet can say whether it counts as a poem
That definition is too narrow; rhyme is not required
optionExplain: This is the narrow definition the authors reject.
This swings to the over-broad side; the authors want words in orderly, disciplined arrangement.
The authors trust readers to recognise poems in nearly every case.
Right: rhyme and poetic diction are among the definitions the authors call too narrow.
questions.explain: Requiring rhyme or poetic diction leaves out much that most people would accept as poetry. Words arranged in an orderly, disciplined way are what count.
questions.rule: Rhyme is not the test.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A student argues: a sunset filled me with overwhelming feeling, so the sunset was a poem. By the authors' account, where does this go wrong?
options: For them a poem is made of words, ordered and disciplined
Sunsets cannot in fact stir strong feelings in people
Only feelings that are written down in rhyme count as poetry
The student should first have stated the poem's plot
optionExplain: Right: the student uses the broad overflow definition, which the authors set aside.
The feeling is real; the question is whether feeling alone makes a poem.
This swaps one error for another, the over-narrow rhyme test.
Stating a plot assumes there is a poem to read, which is the point in question.
questions.explain: The student treats any strong feeling as poetry, the broad definition the authors find has a kernel of truth but is too wide. For them, poetry consists of words.
questions.rule: Feeling alone is not a poem.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the central core of poetry is something they deliberately do not try to state precisely.
questions.explain: The authors say that trying to state the core precisely would get them into trouble, so they do not try. Agreement on nearly all cases is enough for their purpose.
questions.rule: A working definition, not a precise one.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: In a debate on whether chess is a sport, one person says any competition counts and another says only contests of physical strength count. By analogy with the authors' handling of poetry, what is the sensible approach?
options: Adopt the broadest definition so nothing is left out
Adopt the narrowest definition so the term stays strict
Work from the central cases most people agree on
Refuse to discuss it until a precise definition exists
optionExplain: Over-broad definitions make the term cover almost anything.
Over-narrow definitions shut out cases nearly everyone accepts.
Right: like the authors with poetry, steer between too broad and too narrow and rely on the agreed core.
The authors manage without a precise definition; agreement on most cases is enough.
questions.explain: Both debaters push a definition to an extreme. The authors' way with poetry is to work from the central cases reasonable people accept, without forcing a precise boundary.
questions.rule: Work from the agreed core of a term.
questions.teaches: By analogy, many working terms, like sport or music, are best handled as the authors handle poetry: avoid definitions that are too broad or too narrow, and rely on the central cases nearly everyone recognises.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: According to the authors, what is the first rule for reading a lyric poem?
options: Work out the first line fully before going any further
Read about the poet's life before reading the poem
Read it through without stopping, understood or not
Mark every word you do not know as you come to it
optionExplain: This is the habit the authors say defeats readers of modern poetry.
Background is the authors' last concern, not their first rule.
Right: the poem's unity is found only in the whole, so read all of it at once.
Marking words keeps you stopping; the first rule is not to stop.
questions.explain: The first rule is to read the poem through without stopping. The card next explains why stalling at the start does so much harm.
questions.rule: First, read it through without stopping.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the essence of a lyric poem is usually to be found in its first line or first stanza.
questions.explain: The authors say the essence is almost never in the first line or stanza; it is found only in the whole.
questions.rule: The essence lies in the whole.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Mei opens a modern poem and cannot make sense of its first stanza. She rereads it six times and gives up. What would the authors have advised?
options: Read on to the end, then return with the whole in view
Look up every word of the stanza before rereading it
Choose an older poem, since modern ones are too hard
Paraphrase the first stanza in prose before going on
optionExplain: Right: the whole poem may explain the stanza that baffles her in isolation.
Word-by-word lookup is another way of stalling at the start.
The authors say even modern poetry demands less work than people think, read the right way; older poems can be as involved.
Paraphrasing before reading on still treats the first stanza as if it held the poem's essence.
questions.explain: Mei did what the authors describe: stopping at the first stanza and concluding the poem is beyond her. Reading through first would give her the whole that the stanza belongs to.
questions.rule: Do not stall on the opening.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: After reading a poem straight through, Mei finds that three of the five lines that puzzled her now make sense. By the authors' reasoning, what should she make of the two still puzzling her?
options: They show she read too fast and must start all over again
They can be ignored, since the whole has now been grasped
They prove the poem is badly made at exactly those two places
They are likely the real difficulties, worth close work now
optionExplain: Starting over is unnecessary; the read-through has done its job by sorting the easy puzzles from the hard.
A good poem deserves close work after the read-through; the remaining puzzles are where to begin it.
Lingering difficulty may mean the lines are rich, not faulty; many apparently simple poems are complex beneath the surface.
Right: much early puzzlement dissolves once the whole is known, so what remains marks the places that need work.
questions.explain: The read-through lets the whole explain many parts. Whatever still puzzles her afterwards is not a reading accident but a real difficulty, and that is where her close work should go.
questions.rule: What still puzzles after the whole is the real difficulty.
questions.teaches: A first read-through also sorts difficulties: much early puzzlement dissolves once the whole is known, so the lines that still resist mark where close work on the poem should begin.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Suppose Mei reads the poem straight through and comes away with only a vague sense of what it is about. Which statements fit the authors' account of where that leaves her? Choose all that apply.
options: She has finished, since a read-through is all a poem asks
She has a first grasp of the whole to build on
She has failed, since a vague sense is no grasp at all
She can go on working at and rereading the poem
She must read a critic's account before going further
optionExplain: A good poem can be worked at and reread for a lifetime; the first reading is only the start.
Right: the read-through gives a sense of the whole, even a vague one, which later work builds on.
A vague grasp of the whole is what a first read-through is expected to give.
Right: the authors say a good poem can be worked at and thought about over and over.
The authors put commentaries last; her own rereading comes next.
questions.explain: The first read-through is meant to give a sense of the whole, not full understanding. From there the work on the poem can begin.
questions.rule: A vague whole is a good start.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Hearing a jazz piece for the first time, Theo stops the recording after every phrase to work out what the saxophone is doing, and gives up bored. By analogy with the authors' first rule for lyrics, what would serve him better?
options: Studying music theory before he listens again
Hearing the piece through once to sense its shape
Choosing simpler music that makes sense at once
Reading notes on each phrase before he plays it
optionExplain: Theory may help later, but it keeps him from the whole piece now.
Right: like a poem, the piece's unity may only appear when it is taken in whole.
Switching to easier work is the give-up reaction the authors describe in poetry readers.
Phrase-by-phrase notes are another way of stopping at every step.
questions.explain: Stopping at every obscure phrase is the poetry reader's mistake in another art. Taking the whole piece in first gives each phrase a place.
questions.rule: Take dense short works in whole first.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any short, dense work whose meaning lies in its whole shape, such as a piece of jazz, should first be taken in uninterrupted; stopping at each obscure moment destroys the unity that would explain it.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, reading a lyric poem aloud is a pleasant extra but not important for understanding it.
questions.explain: The authors call reading a lyric aloud essential, not optional. The card next explains what the voice does.
questions.rule: For a lyric, reading aloud is essential.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: For poetic drama like Shakespeare's, reading aloud was helpful; for a lyric poem, the authors call it ____.
questions.explain: The authors rank reading aloud higher for lyrics than for plays: helpful for drama, essential for a lyric.
questions.rule: Helpful for drama, essential for lyrics.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Kim reads a poem aloud and keeps stumbling on one line, where her stress falls on a word the rhythm does not want stressed. By the authors' account, what may the stumble be telling her?
options: The poet's metre is faulty at that point in the poem
She has misread the line, and the rhythm exposes it
She should go back to silent reading for that line
The line is unimportant and can be passed over
optionExplain: Blaming the metre skips the more likely cause, her own reading.
Right: the ear catches a misplaced emphasis, and the rhythm shows where the emphasis belongs.
Silent reading is where such misreadings slip past unnoticed.
A stumble marks a place to look harder, not a place to skip.
questions.explain: The authors say the ear is offended by misplaced emphasis that the eye would miss, and that rhythm guides the stress to where it belongs. The stumble is information.
questions.rule: A stumble aloud flags a misreading.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Which effects of reading a poem aloud do the authors describe? Choose all that apply.
options: It makes a misunderstood phrase harder to glide over
It lets you skip the first silent read-through
Your ear catches emphasis your eyes might miss
Rhythm and rhyme guide where the emphasis belongs
It removes the need to reread the poem later
optionExplain: Right: having to say a phrase exposes whether you understand it.
Reading aloud is the second rule; the first read-through still comes first.
Right: the authors say the ear is offended by a misplaced emphasis.
Right: rhythm and rhyme make you place the emphasis where it belongs.
A good poem deserves many return visits; reading aloud does not end the work.
questions.explain: Speaking exposes misunderstanding, the ear hears wrong stress, and rhythm and rhyme guide emphasis. Reading aloud comes after the first read-through and does not end the work.
questions.rule: The voice tests understanding.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Suppose Kim reads the poem aloud fast, in a flat monotone, while thinking about dinner. What do the authors' reasons for reading aloud suggest?
options: Full benefit, since speaking the words aloud is what counts
More benefit, since the speed keeps the unity whole
Some harm, since poems are better read in silence
Little gain, since the voice helps only with attention
optionExplain: Speaking without attending lets phrases slip past, as silent reading does.
Speed served the first read-through; this reading is for catching emphasis and meaning.
The authors call reading aloud essential for lyrics.
Right: the benefits come from noticing what speaking reveals, which inattention throws away.
questions.explain: Each benefit the authors list depends on noticing: a phrase you cannot glide over, an emphasis that offends the ear. Mumbling on autopilot notices nothing.
questions.rule: Read aloud with attention.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A student proofreads her essay by reading it aloud and catches clumsy sentences she missed on screen. By analogy with the authors' account, why does this work?
options: Speaking forces attention to each phrase and its stress
Hearing her own voice makes the essay sound better
Reading aloud is slower, so she reads less of the essay overall
Speech reveals spelling errors the screen conceals
optionExplain: Right: as with a poem, the voice cannot glide over a clumsy phrase, and the ear notices bad emphasis.
If anything, a flattering voice would hide faults; she is finding them.
She reads the whole essay; the gain is in how closely, not how much.
Speech is poor at catching spelling; it catches phrasing and stress.
questions.explain: The authors' reasons for reading poems aloud carry over: speaking slows the eye's gliding, and the ear hears awkward emphasis.
questions.rule: The ear checks what the eye skims.
questions.teaches: By analogy, reading aloud works as a check on any prose, not only poems: phrasing and emphasis that the eye glides over become audible when spoken.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: What kind of questions do the authors say you should usually ask of a lyric poem?
options: Logical ones, such as what premises it argues from
Historical ones, such as when the poet wrote it
Rhetorical ones, such as why some words stand out
Grammatical ones, such as how each term is defined
optionExplain: Logical questions suit expository books, which argue; a lyric does not.
Dates and context may help, but they are not the questions the authors put first.
Right: the questions for a lyric are usually rhetorical, though they may also be syntactical.
Defining terms belongs to coming to terms with an expository book.
questions.explain: The questions you ask of a lyric are usually rhetorical. The card next shows how they lead you to the key words.
questions.rule: Ask a poem rhetorical questions.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, you come to terms with a poem in the same way as with an expository book.
questions.explain: The authors say you do not come to terms with a poem, though you must still discover its key words.
questions.rule: Key words, yes; coming to terms, no.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: In a poem, the word gone ends three of the stanzas and falls on the strongest beat each time. What does the authors' advice suggest about it?
options: It needs a precise definition agreed between reader and poet
It is filler chosen to keep the rhyme scheme going
It is likely a key word, marked by rhythm and repetition
It matters less than the words in the first line
optionExplain: Defining and agreeing on terms belongs to expository reading, not to a poem.
Rhyme marks words as important; it is not evidence that they are filler.
Right: repetition and rhythmic stress are two of the signals the authors name.
The essence of a poem is almost never in its first line alone.
questions.explain: A word that recurs and takes the strongest beat is being pushed forward by the poem itself, which is how the authors say key words announce themselves.
questions.rule: Repetition and stress mark key words.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Sort each question by whether it suits a lyric poem or an expository book.
groups: A question for an expository book

items.t: Which words does the rhythm stress?
Which words recur across the stanzas?
Do the stanzas form a sequence of ideas?
What premises does the author start from?
How does the author define this term?
Does the conclusion follow from the reasons?

questions.explain: Rhythm, recurrence and the sequence of stanzas are rhetorical questions for a lyric. Premises, definitions and conclusions are logical and grammatical questions for an expository book.
questions.rule: Rhetorical for poems, logical for exposition.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Suppose a poem has no rhyme and no regular rhythm. By the authors' list of questions, how might its key words still stand out?
options: Through repetition, or stanzas that share ideas
They cannot, since key words need rhyme or rhythm
Through a glossary of the poet's private terms
Through the poet's own list of them in a preface
optionExplain: Right: repetition and stanzas returning to the same ideas are signals that do not depend on rhyme or metre.
Rhythm and rhyme are two signals among several, not the only ones.
A glossary treats key words as terms to define, which is not how the authors find them.
Outside help is not the method; the poem's own patterns are.
questions.explain: Remove rhyme and rhythm and the other questions remain: which words repeat, and which ideas recur from stanza to stanza.
questions.rule: Without rhyme, look for repetition and recurring ideas.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Listening to a famous speech, you notice one phrase returns at the start of sentence after sentence, each time on a rising beat. By analogy with the authors' rhetorical questions, what should you conclude?
options: The speaker ran short of ideas and repeated herself
The phrase must be defined precisely before the speech can be followed
Repeated phrases are ornaments with no meaning of their own
The phrase is likely central, marked by repetition and rhythm
optionExplain: Deliberate repetition on a stressed beat is a device, not a lapse.
Defining terms is the expository move; here the phrase's place in the speech is what matters.
Repetition is how the phrase is made to matter.
Right: the same signals that mark a poem's key words mark a speech's central phrase.
questions.explain: A speech built on a refrain uses the rhetorical signals the authors point to in poems: repetition and rhythm push a phrase forward as the centre.
questions.rule: Repetition and rhythm mark the centre.
questions.teaches: By analogy, rhetorical marking works in speeches as in poems: a phrase that repetition and rhythm push forward, as in a speech built on a refrain, is usually where the speaker's meaning gathers.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: According to the authors, what do most good lyric poems contain?
options: A story with a clear beginning and end
Some kind of conflict, named or implied
A moral stated in the closing lines
A regular pattern of rhyme and metre
optionExplain: A lyric has a movement, but not usually a story with a plot of events.
Right: the authors say most good lyrics hold a conflict, sometimes stated, often only implied.
