Poetry, the authors say, is not the realm of statement; a stated moral is not what they look for.
Rhyme is one of the definitions of poetry the authors call too narrow.
questions.explain: The authors find some kind of conflict in most good lyrics. The card next shows how to find it when it is not named.
questions.rule: Look for the conflict.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Shakespeare's Sonnet 138 is about love and time, even though the word time does not appear in it.
questions.explain: Sonnet 138 is the authors' example of an implied conflict: love against time, with no mention of time.
questions.rule: A conflict can be present without being named.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Marvell's To His Coy Mistress opens with these words to the lady: Had we but world enough, and time, this coyness, lady, were no crime. What conflict does this opening announce?
options: Duty against private desire
Love against the shortness of time
Wealth against poverty in a vast world
Youth against the wisdom of age
optionExplain: Duty plays no part in the opening; the lack of time is the obstacle.
Right: the authors say Marvell makes the love and time conflict clear right at the beginning.
World here means space and time enough for slow courtship, not wealth.
The poem urges haste because time is short, not because age is wiser.
questions.explain: If there were world enough and time, coyness would be no crime; there is not, so love must hurry. The conflict is named in the first line.
questions.rule: Some poems name their conflict at once.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Sort each poem, described in brief, by whether its conflict is named or only implied.

items.t: Summer and Winter speak by name as rivals
The speaker cries that Time will take his love away
Death and a lover argue with each other by name
A rose in a vase, with no mention of age
A crowded beach at dusk, with no word of death
A lover's white lies, in lines that do not name time

questions.explain: When the antagonists appear by name, the conflict is stated. When only images such as a fading rose or dusk carry it, the reader must find the implied conflict.
questions.rule: Named conflicts are easy; implied ones need finding.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Suppose a reader decides that every lyric he meets, including a comic poem about a lost umbrella, is about love and time. What has gone wrong?
options: Nothing has, since most great lyrics are about love and time anyway
He should look for the conflict in the first line alone
He read too quickly to notice the poem's rhyme scheme
He imposes a common conflict instead of finding the poem's own
optionExplain: Most is not all, and a comic poem may hold a quite different conflict.
The essence of a poem is almost never in its first line alone.
Rhyme may mark key words, but the error is in forcing one theme onto every poem.
Right: love against time is frequent, not universal; the conflict must come from the poem's words.
questions.explain: The authors say a great many lyrics, perhaps most, concern love and time. Treating that as true of all poems replaces reading with a formula.
questions.rule: Find the poem's conflict; do not impose one.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: An untitled photograph shows a child's elaborate sandcastle at the water's edge as the tide comes in. By analogy with the authors' advice on implied conflict, what is the photograph likely about?
options: The beauty of passing things set against time
The photographer's skill with light on wet sand
A family holiday on one particular afternoon
The rules about building on public beaches
optionExplain: Right: like an implied conflict in a lyric, the image sets a fragile, lovely thing against what will erase it, without naming either.
Skill is on display, but the rising tide points to a subject beyond technique.
It may record a holiday, but the incoming tide makes the castle's passing the subject.
Nothing in the image raises rules or regulations.
questions.explain: A sandcastle about to meet the tide does what the authors' lyrics do: it carries the conflict between transient beauty and time through an image rather than words.
questions.rule: Images can carry an unnamed conflict.
questions.teaches: By analogy, visual art can carry the same implied conflict as lyrics: an image of a sandcastle meeting the tide sets the beauty of passing things against time without naming either.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a poem's title can help reveal a conflict that the poem itself does not name.
questions.explain: In the authors' MacLeish example, the title supplies the link to love and time that the poem leaves unstated. The card next shows how.
questions.rule: The title can carry the theme.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: MacLeish's poem You, Andrew Marvell does not use the word ____, yet its title calls up Marvell's theme of world enough and time.
questions.explain: The poem mentions neither time nor a lover. The title, by recalling Marvell, brings in the conflict between love, or life, and time.
questions.rule: A title can import a theme.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A poem titled After the Harvest describes an empty field under a low sky and does not mention age or death. Following the authors' advice, what should a reader do with the title?
options: Ignore it, since only the lines of the poem carry its meaning
Take it as proof that the poem is about farming
Weigh it as a clue to an implied theme of endings
Read about the poet's farm before going further
optionExplain: The authors' MacLeish example shows the title is part of the evidence.
A title is a clue to weigh, not proof; it must fit what the poem says.
Right: after the harvest suggests something completed and passing, which may point to the implied conflict.
Background on the poet is not the authors' first resort; the title and the lines are.
questions.explain: The lines leave the subject implicit, so the title becomes evidence. It suggests endings and passing time, which the reader can test against the empty field and low sky.
questions.rule: Weigh the title against the lines.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: A reader says of You, Andrew Marvell: the poem is about geography, since it names Persia, Baghdad, Crete and Spain. What has the reader missed?
options: The rhyme scheme, which marks the places as key
The poet's life, which explains the journey
The title, which points to the conflict with time
The places are real, so it is a travel account
optionExplain: Rhyme may mark words, but it does not show what the places are doing in the poem.
The authors read the poem through its title and images, not the poet's biography.
Right: the places trace the shadow of night moving across the world, and the title ties that to Marvell's love and time.
Real places can serve a poem's theme; naming them does not make it a travel account.
questions.explain: The places are stations of the advancing night. Read with the title, which recalls Marvell, they become part of a conflict between life and time.
questions.rule: Read the details in the light of the title.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: A reader who has not heard of Marvell's poem gets the full force of the clue in MacLeish's title.
questions.explain: An allusion points somewhere only for a reader who knows what it names. Without Marvell, the clue loses much of its force, though the poem's images of advancing night still carry the theme.
questions.rule: An allusion needs its source known.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: An abstract painting of swirling greys hangs with the title Grief. By analogy with the authors' point about titles, what does the title do?
options: It points the viewer to a subject the image leaves open
It is a label with no bearing on the work itself
It replaces the need to look closely at the painting itself
It proves the painter was grieving while painting it
optionExplain: Right: like MacLeish's title, it supplies a subject the work itself leaves implicit.
Treating the title as a mere label ignores evidence the artist chose to give.
The title guides looking; it does not substitute for it.
A title tells us what the work is about, not the artist's state at the time.
questions.explain: An abstract image leaves its subject open. The title, like MacLeish's, is part of the work and directs the viewer to what the image is about.
questions.rule: Titles are part of the work.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the titles of artworks, especially abstract ones, often carry part of the meaning, pointing to a subject the image itself leaves open, so a careful viewer weighs the title with the work.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: According to the authors, what do readers of lyric poems often wrongly believe?
options: That a poem should be read once, and quickly
That rhyme is the key to every poem's meaning
That modern poems are easier than older ones
That they need much knowledge of the poet's life
optionExplain: The authors do want a first read-through without stopping, but they also want many return visits.
Rhyme can mark key words, but the authors do not make it the key to meaning.
The authors say many readers think modern poetry especially difficult, not easier.
Right: the authors say readers think they must know more about poets and their times than they really have to.
questions.explain: Readers often lean on biography and criticism out of doubt about their own reading. The card next says what matters more.
questions.rule: Context is not the first need.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a vast knowledge of a poem's context guarantees that the poem itself will be understood.
questions.explain: Context may help, but it is no guarantee. To be understood, the poem must be read, over and over.
questions.rule: Context is no guarantee.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Before reading a short lyric by Emily Dickinson, Raj plans to read two biographies and a volume of criticism. What would the authors suggest?
options: Finish the biographies first, since context must come before text
Read the poem itself, over and over, using those as help
Skip the poem, since the criticism will summarise it
Read only the criticism that matches his first view
optionExplain: The authors say readers overrate how much context they need before reading.
Right: the poem must be read, repeatedly; background is valid help, not a precondition.
A summary of a poem is not the poem; it must be read to be understood.
Choosing criticism to confirm a view still puts commentary in place of reading.
questions.explain: Raj is about to do what the authors describe: putting faith in biography and criticism ahead of the poem. Almost anyone can read a poem who will go to work on it.
questions.rule: Read the poem first and often.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Sort each habit by whether it follows the authors' advice or is what they warn against.

items.t: Rereading a poem many times over the years
Using a biography as one help among others
Returning to a poem after a long break
Reading criticism in place of the poem
Doubting you can read a poem without an expert
Treating the poet's biography as the poem's meaning

questions.explain: Rereading, return visits and background used as help fit the authors' advice. Letting commentary or biography stand in for the poem, out of self-doubt, is what they warn against.
questions.rule: Background helps; it does not replace.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: Suppose Raj reads a poem many times one year, sets it aside for two years, and then returns to it. By the authors' account, what might he find?
options: That he must start again, having forgotten it all
That he has learned more about it in the interval
That a poem once understood has nothing more to give
That his first readings were wrong in every respect
optionExplain: The authors expect return visits to build on earlier ones, not start from scratch.
Right: the authors say that during vacations from a poem we may learn more about it than we realise.
A good poem keeps yielding new things for the rest of your life, the authors say.
Return visits deepen a reading; nothing suggests they overturn it completely.
questions.explain: The authors treat a great poem as a lifetime companion: return visits, with time between them, keep revealing more.
questions.rule: Time away can deepen a poem.

questions.unitTitle: Suggestions for Reading Stories, Plays, and Poems
questions.q: At a concert, Zoe spends the whole symphony reading the programme notes, barely listening to the orchestra. By analogy with the authors' advice on poems, what is she missing?
options: Nothing, since notes explain more than listening can
More notes, since context guarantees understanding
A shorter piece, so that she could hear more works
The music itself, which no notes can hear for her
optionExplain: Notes are valid help, but they cannot do the listening for her.
The authors say a vast knowledge of context is no guarantee of understanding.
Hearing more works briefly is not the same as hearing any of them well.
Right: as with a poem, background helps, but understanding comes from attending to the work, again and again.
questions.explain: Zoe has swapped the work for its context. By the authors' reasoning, background is help, but the work itself must be attended to, repeatedly.
questions.rule: Attend to the work, not only its notes.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the authors' warning about context applies to concerts: programme notes can help, but no amount of background substitutes for listening to the work itself, again and again.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a collection of documents published with no commentary can still tell a story.
questions.explain: The authors hold that even a bare collection of documents tells a story implicitly. The card next shows what they mean by history.
questions.rule: Even documents tell a story.

questions.q: The authors hold that the essence of history is ____, a point they see hinted at in the last five letters of the word.
questions.explain: The last five letters of history spell story. The authors take narration to be what every history, even a set of documents, has in common.
questions.rule: History is narration.

questions.q: Which of these fit the narrower sense of history the authors use in this chapter? Select all that apply.
options: A transcript of one interview with a retired dock worker
A formal account of how a city rebuilt itself after a great fire
A narrative of the rise and fall of a colonial trading company
A soldier's private diary kept during a long siege
A textbook setting out the general laws of supply and demand
optionExplain: An interview transcript can be called a history of what the speaker saw, but it is source material, not the formal narrative the authors mean.
Right: a formal narrative of a past series of events is history in the authors' sense.
Right: it narrates a past series of events, more or less formally.
A diary may be called a history of its time, but it was written with a different intention and is not a formal narrative account.
General laws that hold at any time are the business of science, not a narrative of particular past events.
questions.explain: The authors keep to narrative accounts, presented more or less formally, of past events. Diaries and transcripts can be called histories in a loose sense, but they are not what this chapter is about.
questions.rule: History here means a formal narrative of past events.

questions.q: A museum publishes a box set of court records about a 1790s riot, sorted by date, with no introduction. What would the authors say about calling it a history of the riot?
options: It does not count, since a history needs an author who narrates
It counts only once a historian adds an essay that arranges and explains the records
It counts, since the records chosen already tell a story implicitly
It does not count, since records are facts and facts cannot be read
optionExplain: This fits the narrower sense, but the authors widen it: the story can be implicit in the collection itself.
An essay would make the story explicit, but the authors hold the story is already there without it.
Right: in the authors' view a collection, as a collection, tells a story, even if no one states it.
The facts themselves cannot be read, but the records are a written record, which can be read.
questions.explain: The authors say even a collection of documents tells a story, explicit or not; otherwise it would not be called a history of its time.
questions.rule: A collection's story can be implicit.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, if an editor deliberately prints documents in random order to avoid suggesting any meaning, the collection stops telling a story.
questions.explain: The authors say the story is implicit in the documents whether they are ordered or not. Refusing to arrange them does not remove it.
questions.rule: Order or no order, the story is there.

questions.q: A team keeps an unsorted folder of every email about a failed product launch. Two new managers read it to learn what went wrong. What does the authors' view of history suggest about their reading?
options: They can come away with different stories, since each supplies the order
They will agree, since the emails are facts and facts speak for themselves
They learn nothing until someone writes a formal account of the launch
They should read only for single facts, since the folder makes no claims
optionExplain: Right: the folder implies a story, but with no stated order each reader has to reconstruct it, and they may do so differently.
The emails are records, not a finished story; turning them into an account of what went wrong takes interpretation.
The authors hold that a collection already tells a story implicitly, so the readers can learn from it before anyone writes it up.
On the authors' view the collection, as a collection, tells a story, so reading for isolated facts misses it.
questions.explain: If even an unarranged collection tells a story, the reader must draw it out. With no narrator to fix the order, two readers can reconstruct different stories from the same folder.
questions.rule: An unarranged record leaves the story to the reader.
questions.teaches: By extension, a reader of an unarranged record supplies the narrative order herself, so two readers of the same documents can come away with different stories.

questions.q: Compared with a jury deciding what happened in a recent car accident, how hard do the authors think it is to know what happened in history?
options: About as hard, because all knowledge of the past rests on memory
Easier, because historians have centuries of records to compare with one another
Easier, because time lets the strong feelings around events settle
Much harder, because historical witnesses lack the court's safeguards
optionExplain: Both rest on memory, but the court can test memory in ways the historian cannot.
Old records can be many, but their writers were not questioned, and many guessed or assumed.
Distance may cool feelings, but it also removes the witnesses who could be questioned.
Right: historical testimony comes without living witnesses, rules of evidence or cross-examination.
questions.explain: The authors argue that if a juror struggles with a recent event, a historian faces a harder task. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Old testimony is untested testimony.

questions.q: Which safeguards does a court have that historical testimony usually lacks, according to the authors? Select all that apply.
options: Cross-examination of what each witness says
A guarantee that no witness will tell a lie
A judge who decides every question of fact
Living witnesses who saw the events take place
Rules that forbid witnesses to guess or estimate
optionExplain: Right: courtroom testimony is cross-examined; historical testimony never is.
A witness is not supposed to lie, but the court offers no guarantee; that is why it cross-examines.
In the authors' example the jury decides what happened, which is why jurors face the doubt they describe.
Right: court cases concern recent events with living witnesses, while most historical witnesses are dead.
Right: a witness in court may not guess, estimate or suppose except under strict conditions.
questions.explain: The authors list living witnesses, strict rules of evidence and cross-examination. Even with all three, jurors are left with some doubt.
questions.rule: Courts test testimony; history inherits it untested.

questions.q: According to the authors, the law does not expect jurors to be absolutely sure; a doubt should affect the verdict only if it is ____.
questions.explain: The law assumes some doubt will always remain and asks only whether it is reasonable, strong enough to trouble the conscience. That gives a working standard short of certainty.
questions.rule: Act on the evidence, short of certainty.
questions.teaches: The law's standard of reasonable doubt shows a way to act on evidence without certainty: a reader of history can likewise accept a well-supported account while keeping the leftover doubt in view.

questions.q: A popular book quotes a medieval king's exact deathbed words, citing a chronicle written by a monk forty years later. How should a reader who follows the authors treat the quoted words?
options: As reliable, since a chronicle is a written record made in the same period
As uncertain, since the monk was not questioned and may have guessed
As invented, since nothing said centuries ago can be known at all
As reliable, since the monk had no reason to lie about the words
optionExplain: Being written down at the time does not test the testimony; the monk may not have known what was said.
Right: the source was written long after, was never cross-examined, and may rest on hearsay or guesswork.
Elusive does not mean unknowable; the right response is doubt in proportion, not dismissal.
Lying is only one risk; a witness can be honest and still be guessing or misinformed.
questions.explain: Historical witnesses may guess and are never cross-examined, so precise reported words from a late source deserve caution rather than trust or dismissal.
questions.rule: Weigh how the witness could have known.

questions.q: A student argues: (1) Juries cannot be absolutely sure about recent events. (2) Historians work with even weaker evidence. (3) So no historical claim deserves belief. Where does the reasoning go wrong?
options: Step 1, because cross-examination does in fact make jurors certain
Step 3, because harder to know is not the same as impossible to know
Step 2, because old records are checked more strictly than courtroom testimony
Nowhere, since the conclusion follows from the first two steps
optionExplain: The authors say the opposite: even with cross-examination a juror is seldom absolutely sure.
Right: the first two steps show historical facts are elusive, not that none can be believed; some, like agreed dates, are close to certain.
The authors stress that historical witnesses gave evidence under no rules at all, so step 2 stands.
The steps support more doubt about history, but the conclusion leaps from doubt to total disbelief.
questions.explain: Steps 1 and 2 match the authors. Step 3 overreaches: the authors themselves say some historical facts, such as the date of the attack on Fort Sumter, are about as certain as anything.
questions.rule: Elusive is not the same as unknowable.

questions.q: An investigator studies a factory accident from thirty years ago. Her only sources are retired workers interviewed last year. Applying the authors' comparison, what is her strongest reason for caution?
options: The workers had a strong motive to lie about what caused the accident
Interviews are a less formal kind of source than written company records
Thirty years is too short a time to judge any past event without bias
No one has tested the accounts the way cross-examination tests testimony
optionExplain: The question gives no sign of a motive; assuming one smuggles in a suspicion the evidence does not support.
Formality is not the issue; written records can also guess or err, and the authors' concern is untested testimony.
The authors' worry runs the other way: the further from the event, the weaker the evidence tends to be.
Right: the witnesses are alive, but their memories, recorded decades later, have not been tested by cross-examination.
questions.explain: Living witnesses are an advantage only if their accounts can be tested. Memories gathered decades later, unquestioned, share the weaknesses the authors find in historical testimony.
questions.rule: A living source is not yet a tested one.
questions.teaches: By extension, memories recorded long after an event lack the test of cross-examination even when the witness is still alive, so a living source is not automatically a tested one.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, once we know exactly when a war started and ended, we have learned a good deal about it.
questions.explain: The authors ask how much we have learned from exact dates and answer: not much. The card next shows what is missing.
questions.rule: A date is not an explanation.

questions.q: Having granted that Fort Sumter was fired on, on April 12, 1861, what do the authors call the obvious next question?
options: Why the fort was fired on in the first place
Who gave the order for the first shot that day
How many soldiers were holding the fort then
Whether the calendars of the time were correct
optionExplain: Right: the authors move at once from the date to the question of cause.
Who gave the order is a further fact; the authors' next question is about cause.
The size of the garrison is another detail of what happened, not why it happened.
The authors treat errors in every calendar as very unlikely; the date is the settled part.
questions.explain: The authors grant the date and immediately ask why Sumter was fired on, and whether war could still have been avoided.
questions.rule: After when, ask why.

questions.q: The authors report that even the start and end of the Civil War have been disputed. Which of these views do they mention? Select all that apply.
options: It really began with Lincoln's election in the fall of 1860
It began five, ten or twenty years before the attack on Sumter
It really ended with Lincoln's assassination after the surrender
It really began with the first great battle at Gettysburg
It ended only when the last Union troops left Fort Sumter
optionExplain: Right: the authors mention dating the war from Lincoln's election.
Right: others claim it began as much as five, ten or twenty years earlier.
Right: one view ends it with Lincoln's assassination, five days after Lee's surrender.
Gettysburg came in the middle of the war; the authors mention no one dating its start from there.
The authors mention no such view; they note fighting went on after the surrender in places word had not reached.
questions.explain: Each rival dating reflects a view of what the war was really about. Starting it with an election, for instance, treats the political break as its cause.
questions.rule: Where you start a story says what you think caused it.
questions.teaches: Where an event is said to begin and end is itself an interpretation: dating a war from an election rather than the first shots already implies a view of its causes.

questions.q: A company history gives the exact date the firm went bankrupt and the day its doors closed, and says little else. By the authors' standard, what is the main thing missing?
options: A second source to confirm that the two dates are entirely accurate
A list of every employee who lost a job on the day the doors closed
An account of why the firm failed and whether it could have been saved
A fuller timeline giving the dates of every board meeting held in its final year
optionExplain: Checking dates makes the frame more secure, but the dates are already the least informative part.
More detail about the day adds facts, not understanding of why it happened.
Right: like the questions about Sumter, the missing part is cause and whether the outcome could have gone otherwise.
More dates make a longer timeline; they still do not explain the failure.
questions.explain: The authors' Sumter questions are why it happened and whether it could have been avoided. Dates, however many, do not answer them.
questions.rule: Ask what caused it and whether it had to happen.

questions.q: True or false: The authors' point about the Civil War dates implies that a reader of history can safely skip over the dates.
questions.explain: The authors treat agreed dates as among the few near-certain facts. Their point is that dates frame the story; understanding comes from asking why.
questions.rule: Dates frame; they do not explain.

questions.q: A patient's chart shows a new pill started on Monday and a rash appeared on Tuesday. Following the authors' approach to dates, how should the doctor read this?
options: As proof that the pill caused the rash, since it came first
As unreliable, since dates in a chart are elusive like old ones
As a sequence that raises, but does not settle, the cause
As unimportant, since only the cause matters and not the order
optionExplain: Coming first is not the same as causing; the timeline alone cannot show cause.
Recent, recorded dates are the kind of fact the authors treat as close to certain.
Right: the dates are a firm frame, and the question of why the rash appeared is still open.
Order matters as the frame for any account of cause; it is not enough, but it is needed.
questions.explain: A dated sequence sets up the question of cause but does not answer it. The doctor still has to ask why, as the reader of history asks why after the dates.
questions.rule: Before is not because.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a timeline is not an explanation in any field: knowing that one thing came before another does not show that it caused the other.

questions.q: Many forts have been fired on over the centuries. In the authors' view, what made the firing on Fort Sumter a significant historical fact?
options: The war that followed it, which people still care about
Its exact date, which every source of the time agrees on
The number of shots fired, which was unusually high
Its careful record in official documents of the time
optionExplain: Right: the authors suggest it matters because of what it led to and because we care about that.
The date is certain, but many equally certain attacks are forgotten.
The authors say nothing about the number of shots; size is not what makes a fact significant here.
Good records make a fact certain, not significant.
questions.explain: The authors ask whether the attack would still matter if war had been avoided. The card next explains their answer.
questions.rule: Significance comes from what follows.

questions.q: True or false: The authors suggest that if war had been avoided after the attack, the firing on Sumter might not count as a significant historical fact.
questions.explain: They point out that we care nothing about many attacks on forts we know nothing of. Without the war, Sumter might have been one of them.
questions.rule: No consequence, little significance.

questions.q: A local history gives a chapter to a well-documented flood that damaged a few barns and changed nothing, and one line to a smaller flood that led the town to move uphill. How does the authors' reasoning judge this?
options: The first flood deserves more space, as it is better documented
Both deserve equal space, since both are equally certain facts
Neither belongs in a history, since floods are natural events
The second flood looks more significant, given what it led to
optionExplain: Documentation makes a fact certain; it does not make it matter.
Equal certainty does not mean equal significance, as the Sumter argument shows.
Natural events can be historical facts when they shape what people do afterward.
Right: significance comes from consequences, and the second flood reshaped the town.
questions.explain: By the Sumter reasoning, a fact matters for what it led to. The flood that moved the town has the larger place in the town's story.
questions.rule: Weigh facts by what they led to.

questions.q: Suppose new research shows that a minor treaty, long ignored, shaped a border dispute that is still going on. On the authors' reasoning, what happens to the treaty's standing?
options: It stays minor, since its date and terms have not changed at all
It becomes significant, because of what it is now seen to lead to
It becomes doubtful, since no one thought it important until now
It stays minor until a court rules on its legal force in the dispute
optionExplain: Date and terms fix what the treaty was, not how much it matters.
Right: its significance depends on its place in the larger story, which the research has changed.
Being overlooked does not make a fact less certain; certainty and significance are separate.
Legal force is a separate question; historical significance comes from consequences.
questions.explain: If significance rests on what an event led to, discovering new consequences raises an event's standing even though the event itself is unchanged.
questions.rule: New consequences, new significance.

questions.q: Sort each statement about a city fire by whether it helps settle that the fire happened or helps show why the fire matters.

items.t: Two diaries agree on the date of the fire
The fire led to the city's first building code
A newspaper of that week reports the fire
Debates on safety still cite the fire today
Insurance records list the houses that burned
The rebuilt centre set the city's later layout

questions.explain: Diaries, newspapers and insurance records make the fire a secure fact. Its consequences and the attention it still draws are what make it significant.
questions.rule: Certainty and significance are different questions.

questions.q: A family historian has verified hundreds of names and dates back to 1700 but cannot say what any of it means for the family. What does the authors' Sumter argument suggest she add?
options: More names and dates, until the record is entirely complete
The story of which events changed the family's path, and why
A second check on every date, to make each fact more certain
A list of world events printed beside each family date, to give them context
optionExplain: A longer list adds certain facts but no more significance.
Right: significance comes from a fact's place in a larger story, which her list lacks.
Her facts are already verified; more certainty does not tell her what matters.
Placing dates side by side shows coincidence in time, not which events shaped the family.
questions.explain: Her record is accurate but has no story. Significance comes from which facts led to what, which only a narrative can show.
questions.rule: Accuracy is not yet history.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a record can be fully accurate and still not be a history: accuracy settles what happened, while significance comes from the story the facts are placed in.

questions.q: If history had to be grouped with either fiction or science, where do the authors say it is more often placed?
options: With fiction, since historians make up most of their facts
With science, since historians work from gathered evidence
With science, since both look for laws that hold everywhere
With fiction, though historians do not make up their facts
optionExplain: This gets the grouping right for the wrong reason; the authors say a good historian does not make up the past.
Historians do use evidence, but the authors say history is more often classed with fiction than science.
Seeking general laws is the mark of science; history tells of particular events.
Right: history is usually classed nearer fiction, but the authors deny that the historian invents the past.
questions.explain: The authors place history between fiction and science, closer to fiction, while denying that historians invent facts. The card next explains the distinction.
questions.rule: Nearer fiction, but not invented.

questions.q: The authors say that if history is allowed to sit between the two main kinds of books, it is usually admitted to be closer to ____ than to science.
questions.explain: History lies between fiction and science but nearer fiction, because it tells a story. That is a likeness of form, not a licence to invent facts.
questions.rule: Between the two, nearer fiction.

questions.q: The authors warn against saying too strongly that a novelist makes up his facts. What is their reason?
options: A fictional world is built from elements of ordinary experience
Most novels are based on real events that the author once witnessed firsthand
Publishers check novels for accuracy before they are printed
Readers refuse to believe any story set in an unfamiliar world
optionExplain: Right: the novelist learns through ordinary senses, and his world must not be wholly unlike ours.
The authors make no claim that novels retell witnessed events; their point is about the materials of imagination.
The authors say nothing of publishers checking fiction; the point concerns how any imagined world is made.
The authors say characters must use our words to be believed, but they do not say unfamiliar settings are rejected.
questions.explain: The authors argue that a made-up world is built from ordinary experience. They push the point to dreams: even there, the strange events are made of everyday elements in new combinations.
questions.rule: Imagination rearranges experience.
questions.teaches: The authors go further: even in the most fantastic dream, the creatures and events are everyday elements put together in strange new ways, so no imagined world is made from nothing.

questions.q: A history of a shipwreck opens with the captain pacing the deck the night before and builds suspense toward the sinking. A reader objects that this is fiction, not history. How would the authors respond?
options: The reader is right, since a history ought to read like a plain report of findings
The scene is fine, since histories are a kind of fiction in any case
Story form suits history; the question is whether the facts bear it out
The scene is fine, since suspense is what most readers want in a book
optionExplain: The authors see narration as the essence of history, so story form is no fault in itself.
History is closer to fiction, not a kind of it; the historian is bound to accuracy.
Right: history tells a story, so narrative shape is expected, while the facts must still hold.
What readers want does not decide the matter; the test is whether the scene is faithful to the facts.
questions.explain: Because history is narrative, a dramatic opening is fair. What matters is whether the evidence supports the scene, such as records of the captain's movements.
questions.rule: Judge the story by the facts, not by its form.

questions.q: True or false: Since history is closer to fiction than to science, a reader should hold a historian to the facts no more than a novelist.
questions.explain: The placement is about the form of history, not its duty to the truth. A good historian considers himself bound by accuracy, and a reader may judge him on it.
questions.rule: History owes the facts; fiction does not.

questions.q: A true-crime podcast opens with a vivid scene of the victim's last evening, down to what she was thinking as she locked her door. Applying the authors' view of history as story bound by facts, what should a listener ask?
options: Whether the scene is gripping enough to justify the rest of the series
Nothing, since story devices show that the whole podcast is invented
Which details rest on evidence and which the teller reconstructed
Whether the podcast's host has worked as a police detective in the past
optionExplain: How gripping it is says nothing about whether it is true.
Story devices do not prove invention; histories use them too, bound by the facts.
Right: story form is fair, but a vivid scene can contain details, such as her thoughts, that no evidence could supply.
The host's background may help, but the question is which parts of this scene rest on evidence.
questions.explain: The podcast tells real events in story form, which is fair. But a vivid scene feels known even where it is reconstructed, so the listener sorts evidence from reconstruction.
questions.rule: Vividness is not evidence.
questions.teaches: By extension, story devices can lend a false sense of certainty: a vivid, detailed scene feels known even when its details, such as a person's private thoughts, are reconstructed rather than recorded.

questions.q: According to the authors, what must every historian do, however careful about accuracy?
options: Make up something, such as a pattern or the actors' motives
Leave out every interpretation and set down only what the record shows
Check each fact against at least two independent sources
Admit openly that nothing about the past can be known
optionExplain: Right: the authors say the historian must always make up something, a pattern or motives.
A history with no interpretation at all would be a list; the authors say every historian adds something.
Checking sources is good practice, but the authors' point is about what the historian adds, not how he checks.
The authors call historical facts elusive, not unknowable, and they expect historians to aim at accuracy.
questions.explain: The authors grant that a good historian does not invent the past, yet he must still supply something the record lacks. The card next says what.
questions.rule: The historian always adds something.

questions.q: According to the authors, which of these might a historian supply that the record does not give by itself? Select all that apply.
options: The dates on which the main events occurred
The documents surviving from the period
A general pattern found in the events
A pattern imposed on events from a theory
Reasons why the people in the story acted
optionExplain: Dates come from the record; they are among the near-certain facts, not something the historian supplies.
Surviving documents are the record itself, which the historian works from.
Right: the historian may find a pattern in events.
Right: or impose one on them.
Right: or suppose he knows why the people did what they did.
questions.explain: The authors name two things: a general pattern, found or imposed, and the motives behind actions. Dates and documents belong to the record.
questions.rule: Pattern or motives: those are the historian's.

questions.q: Two historians agree that a city's population fell by half between 1340 and 1360. One says plague drove people out; the other blames famine. What does the authors' point say about this disagreement?
options: One of them must have misread the population figures
Their disagreement shows that the population figures are unreliable
Neither is writing history, since causes cannot be shown
They share the record but supply different causes for it
optionExplain: They agree on the figures; the dispute is over why, not what.
Disagreement about cause does not touch the figures both accept.
Assigning causes is part of what historians do; the authors expect it rather than ruling it out.
Right: the fall in population is the record; the cause is what each historian brings to it.
questions.explain: The shared figures are the record. Plague and famine are explanations each historian has supplied, which a reader can weigh against the evidence.
questions.rule: Same record, different supplied causes.

questions.q: A reviewer praises a history because the author adds nothing of his own and lets the events speak for themselves. Using the authors' view, what is wrong with the praise?
options: Praise should go to the histories that add the most opinion to the record
Every historian supplies a pattern or motives of his own
A history that adds nothing of its own would count as a work of science
The reviewer should first have checked whether the author's sources exist
optionExplain: The authors do not reward opinion for its own sake; the point is to see what was supplied, not to want more.
Right: on the authors' view, events cannot be turned into a history without some supplied pattern or motives.
Science seeks general laws; a history without interpretation would be a bare chronicle, not science.
Checking sources is a fair step, but it does not touch the reviewer's mistaken idea that nothing was added.
questions.explain: Events do not arrange or explain themselves. The reviewer has missed the parts the historian supplied, which are the parts most worth examining.
questions.rule: Events do not speak for themselves.

questions.q: True or false: Because the historian supplies the pattern or the motives, a careful reader should treat those parts of a history as baseless.
questions.explain: Supplied is not the same as unsupported. A motive or pattern can be argued well from the evidence; the reader's task is to notice it and weigh it.
questions.rule: Notice and weigh, do not discard.

questions.q: A sports analyst says the team lost its season because the coach lost the players' trust. What would best test this explanation the analyst has supplied?
options: Checking again how many games the team lost over the whole season
Seeking other signs that should follow if trust truly broke
Asking whether other analysts have repeated the same explanation
Asking whether the analyst once played for a rival club himself
optionExplain: The losses are the record the explanation is meant to explain; recounting them does not test it.
Right: if lost trust caused the defeats, other things should follow, such as public friction or a late-season slump.
Repetition spreads an explanation without testing it.
His background may colour his view, but it does not test whether the explanation fits the facts.
questions.explain: A supplied explanation can be weighed by asking what else would be true if it were right, and then looking for it.
questions.rule: Test an explanation by what else it predicts.
questions.teaches: By extension, a supplied explanation can be tested by asking what else would be true if it were right, and checking for those further signs in the record.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a historian who rejects every grand theory of history is thereby freed from explaining why things happened.
questions.explain: Such a historian, the authors say, is likely to be forced to assign causes and motives instead. The card next sets out the two ways historians work.
questions.rule: No theory still means causes.

questions.q: Which example do the authors give of a general theory that a historian might make a history fit?
options: That economic interest drives every war
That great men alone shape events
That history repeats itself in cycles
That Providence rules human affairs
optionExplain: Economic theories of history exist, but this is not the example the authors give here.
This is a familiar theory of history, but not the one the authors name.
Cyclical theories exist too, but the authors' example is Providence.
Right: the authors' example of a general theory or philosophy is that Providence rules human affairs.
questions.explain: The authors mention a historian who believes Providence rules human affairs and makes his history fit that belief.
questions.rule: A theory can shape the whole account.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a historian who resolves to report only events, with no pattern imposed from above, is likely to end up assigning causes and motives.
questions.explain: Refusing a general pattern does not remove the need to explain. The authors say such a historian is likely to be forced to assign causes for events and motives for actions.
questions.rule: Drop the theory, and causes take its place.

questions.q: Sort each statement from a history by whether it fits events to a general theory or assigns a cause to one event.
groups: Fits events to a general theory
Assigns a cause to one event

items.t: Every revolution in the book is a stage of class struggle
The famine is blamed on a late frost that spring
Each ruler's fall is divine punishment for pride
The treaty failed because one envoy fell ill
The nation's rise is the unfolding of its destiny
A strike spread because a rumour reached the mills

questions.explain: Class struggle, divine punishment and destiny are general patterns applied across events. A late frost, a sick envoy and a rumour are causes assigned to particular events.
questions.rule: One pattern for all, or one cause per event.

questions.q: A historian writes in his preface that he holds no theory and only sets down what happened. Following the authors, where should a reader look for what he has supplied?
options: In the causes and motives he gives for events along the way
Nowhere, since he has promised to add nothing of his own
Only in the preface, where he states his intentions and method openly
In the dates, which he must have chosen to suit his story
optionExplain: Right: a historian without a stated theory is likely to supply causes and motives event by event.
The authors hold that every historian must make up something, whatever he promises.
The preface states his aim, but his contributions are spread through the narrative.
Dates are among the firmest facts; the supplied part is in the explanations.
questions.explain: Rejecting a general pattern moves the historian's contribution into the many causes and motives he assigns. That is where to look.
questions.rule: No stated theory: check the causes.

questions.q: A company's annual report explains every result of the year, good and bad, as proof that its long-term strategy is working. Applying the authors' distinction, how is the report working?
options: It assigns a separate cause to each event, one at a time
It reports the year's events with no explanation at all
It fits each event to one pattern decided in advance
It holds that the causes of results cannot be known
optionExplain: Separate causes would differ from event to event; here one pattern explains them all.
The report explains everything, through its strategy story.
Right: every result, good or bad, is made to fit the same overarching story.
Far from calling causes unknowable, it claims one cause for everything.
questions.explain: The report works like a historian with a general theory. When good and bad results alike confirm the pattern, the pattern is doing the explaining, not the events.
questions.rule: Beware a pattern that fits every outcome.
questions.teaches: By extension, a pattern that fits every outcome, good or bad, is a warning sign: if no event could count against it, it tells the reader little about the events themselves.

questions.q: According to the authors, what must a historian assume to avoid both finding a pattern in events and assigning motives?
options: That every event has one clear and simple cause
That only economic forces move human affairs
That human purposes are absent or undiscoverable
That the records of the past are complete and true
optionExplain: One simple cause per event is still assigning causes, which is one of the two positions.
An economic theory is a general pattern imposed on events, the first position.
Right: only by denying knowable purposes can a historian avoid both a pattern and assigned motives.
Complete records would not remove the need to explain; the historian would still supply a pattern or motives.
questions.explain: The authors say the only escape is to assume people do not act for purposes or that their purposes cannot be found. The card next shows who held this view.
questions.rule: No knowable purpose, no pattern.

questions.q: The authors cite the novelist ____ as holding that the causes of human action are too many and too hidden for anyone to know why anything happened.
questions.explain: Tolstoy was a novelist, not a historian, but the authors note that many historians, especially modern ones, have shared his view.
questions.rule: Tolstoy: the causes are too hidden to know.

questions.q: Match each position on history with what a historian holding it does.
pairs: Fits events to a scheme such as Providence
Reports events and gives causes one by one
Holds that why anything happened is unknowable
questions.explain: The authors describe two ways of supplying what the record lacks, a pattern or causes, and a third position that denies causes can be known at all.
questions.rule: Pattern, causes, or no pattern: know which.

questions.q: A history of a plague year describes events in rich detail but says again and again that why people fled, stayed or panicked lay too deep in hidden impulses for anyone to know. Which position is this?
options: The no-pattern view, which holds such causes cannot be known
The general-pattern view, fitting events to an overall theory
The assigned-causes view, giving motives one event at a time
No position at all, since the historian declines to explain
optionExplain: Right: holding that motives are too hidden to know is Tolstoy's position.
No overall scheme is offered; the historian denies that causes can be found.
The historian refuses to assign motives rather than assigning them one by one.
Declining to explain on these grounds is itself a theory of history, which shapes the account.
questions.explain: The historian's repeated claim that motives are unknowable is the no-pattern view. It is a theory, not the absence of one.
questions.rule: Refusing to explain can be a theory.

questions.q: True or false: A historian who says the cause of one riot is uncertain for lack of evidence, while explaining the rest of the period, holds the no-pattern view of history.
questions.explain: Leaving one question open is ordinary caution. The no-pattern view holds that the causes of human action cannot be known at all, not that one cause lacks evidence.
questions.rule: One open question is not the no-pattern view.

questions.q: After a product unexpectedly sells out, a marketing team decides that buyers' choices are too many and too hidden to explain, so there is nothing to learn from it. How does this compare with the authors' positions?
options: It takes the pattern view, fitting the event to a theory
It assigns a cause, namely the buyers' hidden motives
It takes no position, since it offers no explanation
It takes the no-pattern view, leaving no lesson to draw
optionExplain: No general scheme is applied; the team denies there is an explanation to find.
Calling motives hidden is a reason not to name a cause, not the naming of one.
Holding that causes are unknowable is itself a position, with consequences for what the team does next.
Right: like Tolstoy, the team holds causes unknowable, and so gives up on learning anything from the event.
questions.explain: The team adopts the no-pattern view. If causes cannot be known, nothing can be learned about what to repeat, so the view also ends the inquiry.
questions.rule: No causes, no lessons.
questions.teaches: By extension, the no-pattern view has a practical cost: if causes cannot be known, no lesson can be drawn about what to repeat or avoid, so a reader should notice when the view is used to end an inquiry.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the first rule of reading history is to read more than one account of the event or period that interests you.
questions.explain: The authors call reading more than one account the first rule of reading history. The card next gives their reason.
questions.rule: More than one account.

questions.q: What reason do the authors give for reading more than one account of a historical event?
options: Older histories are often out of date and full of errors of fact and dating
Theories of history differ, and each shapes the account it yields
No single book can hold all the facts of a period or an event
Comparing styles helps a reader find the best writer to follow
optionExplain: Errors are a risk, but the authors' reason is that theories differ, not that books age.
Right: because the historian's theory affects the account, one account gives one theory's version.
Length is not the issue; even a complete account would carry its author's theory.
The authors are concerned with getting at the truth, not with choosing a favourite stylist.
questions.explain: The authors reason from the differences between theories of history: since theory shapes the account, understanding needs more than one.
questions.rule: Different theories, different accounts.

questions.q: For which of these readers does the authors' reasoning make reading several accounts especially important? Select all that apply.
options: A citizen of a country still divided by the legacy of a civil war
A reader browsing a history of medieval fashion for pleasure
A collector curious about the date a famous coin was minted
A town council deciding whether to rebuild a dam that failed in 1950
A voter weighing a border dispute that began with a war a century ago
optionExplain: Right: like the authors' Civil War example, the event shaped the world the citizen lives in.
Several accounts would still help, but the authors stress the rule most where the event has practical significance.
A minting date is a single fact, not an account shaped by a theory of history.
Right: how the earlier failure is explained bears on a practical choice the council must make.
Right: the past war bears directly on a decision the voter faces now.
questions.explain: The authors press the rule hardest where the event has practical significance for the reader, as the Civil War does for Americans.
questions.rule: The more it matters, the more accounts you need.

questions.q: A reader has finished one well-reviewed history of a revolution and feels she now understands it. Following the authors, what should she do next?
options: Reread the same book slowly to catch what she missed the first time
Read another account, ideally from a different side or school
Check the book's dates against a reliable encyclopedia entry
Accept it, since the reviewers have already compared the accounts
optionExplain: Rereading deepens her grasp of one account but still leaves her with one historian's view.
Right: a second account from another viewpoint shows what the first historian supplied.
Dates are the firmest part; the theory shaping the account is the part to test.
Reviews report others' judgments; reading other accounts is how she gets her own.
questions.explain: One account, however good, gives one historian's theory. The first rule asks her to read another before she claims to understand.
questions.rule: One good book is still one view.

questions.q: Suppose a reader reads three histories of a war, all by members of the same faction of historians. How well does this meet the authors' first rule?
options: Fully, since three accounts are more than the one required
Fully, since historians of one school check one another's work
Poorly, since three is too few for any useful comparison
Poorly, since one faction's shared outlook shapes all three
optionExplain: The rule aims at different viewpoints, not a count of books.
Checking within a school may catch errors of fact, but it will not test the school's shared theory.
Three accounts from different viewpoints could serve well; the trouble is their shared outlook, not their number.
Right: the authors warn against seeing an event through one faction of historians, whatever the number of books.
questions.explain: The point of the rule is to see past one theory. Three books from one faction share a theory, so they give little more than one.
questions.rule: Count viewpoints, not books.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a careful reader of the only surviving history of an event can still be confident of learning what really happened.
questions.explain: The authors say that when we cannot read more than one history, we must admit we have little chance of learning what really happened. Care in reading cannot supply the missing comparison.
questions.rule: One account cannot be checked, however carefully read.

questions.q: Two coworkers each give their manager an account of a heated meeting. Applying the authors' first rule, what does comparing the two accounts let her do?
options: Separate what both report from what each one has added
Decide which of the two coworkers is more honest in general
Average the two versions into a single fair account
Skip the meeting notes, since two accounts are enough
optionExplain: Right: agreement points toward what happened; differences show each teller's contribution.
Comparing two accounts of one meeting does not settle anyone's general honesty.
Splitting the difference can produce a version neither saw; comparison is for finding agreement and contribution.
Notes are another account; more viewpoints help rather than being made unnecessary.
questions.explain: Where the two accounts agree, the manager is probably near the record. Where they differ, she sees what each coworker supplied, as with two histories.
questions.rule: Agreement points to the record; difference shows the teller.
questions.teaches: Comparing accounts shows where they agree, which points toward the record, and where they differ, which reveals what each teller has supplied.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, every narrative history has to be written from some point of view.
questions.explain: The authors grant that every narrative history has a point of view, and draw a lesson for readers. The card next gives it.
questions.rule: Every history stands somewhere.

questions.q: Since every narrative history has a point of view, the authors say that to get at the truth we ought to look at an event from more than one ____.
questions.explain: The authors accept that no narrative history stands nowhere. Their remedy, prompted by a history claiming to be impartial from the South's point of view, is to look from more than one viewpoint.
questions.rule: To get at the truth, change viewpoint.

questions.q: A reader finds a history of a colonial war built entirely from the colonisers' records and letters. What would the authors advise?
options: Discard it, since a one-sided history is of no use to a reader
Trust it, since letters and records are firsthand sources
Read it, note its viewpoint, and find an account from another side
Rely on it, since writers inside events know the most about them
optionExplain: A history with a viewpoint can still be accurate and useful; the remedy is comparison.
Firsthand sources from one side still carry that side's viewpoint.
Right: its viewpoint is a reason to add other accounts, not to throw it away.
Insiders may know much, but they see from one place; the authors want more than one.
questions.explain: Every history has a viewpoint. The authors' remedy is to look at the event from more than one, not to reject the history in hand.
questions.rule: Add viewpoints; do not discard them.

questions.q: Which of these statements fit the authors' view of point of view in history? Select all that apply.
options: Good historians write narratives that stand nowhere at all
A history can have a point of view and still be accurate
Seeing an event from several viewpoints helps get at the truth
A history that has a point of view must be inaccurate
The goal is to find the one history written from no viewpoint
optionExplain: The authors say every narrative history has to be written from some point of view, good ones included.
Right: the authors expect good historians to be accurate, though every narrative has a viewpoint.
Right: to get at the truth, the authors say, look at the event from more than one viewpoint.
A viewpoint limits what one account shows; it does not make the account false.
Since every narrative history has some viewpoint, such a book may not exist; the aim is several viewpoints.
questions.explain: Viewpoint is unavoidable in narrative history, and it is compatible with accuracy. The remedy for its limits is to add viewpoints, not to hunt for a history without one.
questions.rule: Viewpoint is unavoidable; one viewpoint is not enough.

questions.q: Suppose one historian tells the same battle twice, once from each army's side, in alternating chapters. How does this bear on the authors' advice?
options: It meets the advice fully, so no other account is needed
It defeats the advice, since mixing viewpoints confuses the reader
It helps, but both sides are still told through one author's choices
It has no bearing, since viewpoint only matters between books
optionExplain: One author telling both sides still supplies the pattern and motives for both.
Seeing more than one side is what the authors recommend, not a source of confusion.
Right: two viewpoints in one book widen the view, but one historian still selects and explains both.
Viewpoint matters within a book too; that is why this design helps.
questions.explain: Telling both sides is a step toward the authors' aim, but each side is still filtered through one historian. Another author would still add something.
questions.rule: Two sides in one book is still one author.

questions.q: A transport department publishes a report on the new tram line it built, then a second, updated report. Applying the authors' advice on viewpoint, what should a resident do before judging the tram?
options: Find accounts from other standpoints, such as riders and shop owners
Accept the two reports, since together they give two viewpoints
Reject both reports, since a builder can never judge its own work
Wait for a third report, since more data from the department will settle it
optionExplain: Right: other viewpoints come from people who stood elsewhere, not from more reports by the same party.
Two reports from one department share one standpoint; they are one viewpoint told twice.
A party to events can still be accurate; the remedy is adding viewpoints, not rejecting this one.
More from the same source adds detail, not a new viewpoint.
questions.explain: The department's reports, however many, are written from one standpoint. A new viewpoint needs someone who stood elsewhere.
questions.rule: A new viewpoint needs a new standpoint.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a second report from the same source adds length but not a new viewpoint; what widens the picture is an account by someone who stood elsewhere.

questions.q: When only one history of an event can be read, what do the authors say the reader must admit?
options: That single history must be the definitive account
The event is not worth reading about until more is written
The reader must personally check all of that history's sources
There is little chance of learning what really happened
optionExplain: Being the only account does not make it final; it makes it uncheckable.
The authors say finding out what happened is not the only reason to read history.
Exhaustive checking is the professional's duty, not the lay reader's.
Right: with one account, the reader cannot see past that historian's version of events.
questions.explain: One account leaves the reader with one version of events. The card next shows why that need not stop a reader.
questions.rule: One account, little certainty.

questions.q: Match each kind of reader of history with how the authors describe their reading.
pairs: Checks every source against the others
questions.explain: The authors place the lay reader between the professional, who must leave no stone unturned, and the amateur, who reads only to be amused.
questions.rule: The lay reader stands between the two.

questions.q: A retired engineer reads the one available history of the building of a canal in the 1800s, for her own interest. By the authors' account, what is a fair expectation?
options: She must find and compare its sources before trusting any of it
She can learn from it while holding its version of events loosely
She should read it for fun only, since one account proves nothing
She can take it as fact, since no other account contradicts it
optionExplain: Cross-examining every source is the professional's task, not the lay reader's.
Right: a lay reader admits the limits of one account and still reads it for what it offers.
That is the amateur's stance; the lay reader reads seriously even when certainty is out of reach.
With only one account, nothing is available to contradict it, which is not the same as confirmation.
questions.explain: As a lay reader she need not check every source, but with one account she should not claim to know exactly what happened. She can still learn much.
questions.rule: Read seriously, claim modestly.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a lay reader of history has the same duty as a professional historian to check every source against the others.
questions.explain: The authors say only the professional writing a history is required to cross-examine his sources exhaustively. The lay reader stands between him and the amateur.
questions.rule: Exhaustive checking is the professional's job.

questions.q: A lay reader who has read the only history of a famine learns that a second, very different account has now appeared. Following the authors, what changes?
options: Nothing, since a lay reader needs only one account of any event
The first rule now applies, so she should read the second as well
She should drop the first, since newer accounts replace older ones
She should wait for historians to decide which account is right
optionExplain: The lay reader's lighter duty concerns exhaustive checking, not reading a second account that is at hand.
Right: reading more than one account is the rule whenever it can be done.
Newer is not automatically better; the value lies in comparing the two.
Comparing the accounts herself is how she gets nearer the truth; she need not wait for a verdict.
questions.explain: One account was a limit forced on her. Once another exists, the authors' first rule asks her to read it and compare.
questions.rule: When a second account appears, read it.

questions.q: A traveller finds only one detailed account of a remote village's past, written by a visiting missionary a century ago. Which stance fits the authors' advice?
options: Ignore it, since a single source is worse than having none
Accept it in full, since no other source contradicts it
Correct it while reading, changing whatever seems unlikely
Read it with interest, as one man's version of the facts
optionExplain: The authors read Thucydides though nothing can be checked against him; a single source still teaches.
Nothing contradicts it only because nothing else exists; that is not confirmation.
A reader can doubt what seems unlikely, but rewriting the account replaces one version with a guess.
Right: it is worth reading, with its account of events held as one observer's version.
questions.explain: A sole source cannot be checked, so its facts stay provisional. Its silence of contradiction comes from the lack of other sources, not from proof.
questions.rule: Uncontradicted is not confirmed.
questions.teaches: Absence of contradiction is not confirmation: when a source is the only one, nothing contradicts it only because nothing else exists.

questions.q: Why, according to the authors, is Thucydides' history of a war fought 2,500 years ago still worth reading?
options: It has influenced how later leaders saw their times and acted
It is a perfect record of everything that happened in the war it describes
The war it tells of still shapes the borders of modern Greece
It was the very first work of history that anyone ever wrote
optionExplain: Right: later leaders compared their situations to Athens and Sparta, so the book helped shape later history.
The authors say we read him not because he described perfectly what happened.
The authors say the opposite: the war can have little real effect on our lives today.
The authors call it the only major contemporary history of that war, not the first history ever written.
questions.explain: The authors stress the book's effect on later history rather than its precision about the war. The card next explains how.
questions.rule: Some histories made history.

questions.q: According to the authors, how did later leaders use Thucydides' history? Select all that apply.
options: As a pattern of conduct to follow
As a legal code for ending wars
As proof that wars can be avoided
As an excuse for what they did
As a justification of their choices
optionExplain: Right: and even as a pattern of conduct.
The authors mention no legal use; leaders drew comparisons, not rules of law.
Thucydides hoped others would avoid the mistakes he saw, but the authors do not say leaders used him as such proof.
Right: the authors say leaders used Thucydides as an excuse.
Right: and as a justification.
questions.explain: Leaders who found themselves in situations like those of Athens or Sparta used Thucydides as an excuse, a justification and a pattern of conduct.
questions.rule: Leaders read history and acted on it.

questions.q: An old history of a nation's founding, taught in its schools for generations, is still quoted by leaders to justify their decisions. By the authors' reasoning about Thucydides, why read it today?
options: To learn exactly what happened at the nation's founding
To enjoy it as a story, since its facts are now settled
To understand how it has shaped and still shapes events
To check whether its style meets present-day standards
optionExplain: An influential history may not be a perfect record; its value lies partly elsewhere.
Reading for enjoyment alone is the amateur's stance, and it misses the book's influence.
Right: like Thucydides, it matters for how it has influenced later action.
Style is not the point; the book's effect on later events is.
questions.explain: A history that leaders quote has become part of the history that followed. Reading it helps a reader understand their choices.
questions.rule: Read what the actors read.

questions.q: True or false: If a history has strongly influenced later events, that shows its account of the past is accurate.
questions.explain: The authors read Thucydides not because he described perfectly what happened but because he shaped what happened after. Influence and accuracy are separate questions.
questions.rule: Influential is not the same as accurate.

questions.q: Suppose no later leader had ever read Thucydides. On the authors' reasoning, which reason for reading him would be weakened?
options: That his account tells of the war that it describes
That his is the only major contemporary history of that war
That his account helped to shape what happened after it
That his account teaches lessons about human conduct
optionExplain: The book would still tell of the war; that is not the reason in question.
It would still be the only major contemporary history; that fact does not depend on readers.
Right: the influence argument depends on later people having read and acted on the book.
Lessons about how people act would remain in the book whether or not leaders had used them.
questions.explain: The argument from influence rests on later readers. Remove them and that reason goes, though the book's other values remain.
questions.rule: Influence depends on readers.

questions.q: A famous account of an old price war, in which two firms ruined each other, is widely read. Today two rival firms' leaders both know it well and see their contest in its terms. What does the authors' Thucydides point suggest could happen?
options: The leaders may act out the old pattern, making the story come true again
Nothing, since an account of the past cannot affect what people do now
The leaders will avoid the old mistakes, since they know how it ended
The account will lose its value, since present conditions are different
optionExplain: Right: later leaders used Thucydides as a pattern of conduct; a story read as a pattern can be repeated.
The authors argue the opposite: Thucydides changed history by shaping later leaders.
Thucydides hoped readers would avoid mistakes, yet the authors note similar errors keep being made.
Changed conditions do not stop leaders from acting on the pattern the story gives them.
questions.explain: Leaders who compared themselves to Athens and Sparta used Thucydides as a pattern. A story believed as a pattern can steer actions so that the pattern recurs.
questions.rule: A believed story can repeat itself.
questions.teaches: By extension, an influential account can help bring about what it describes: leaders who see their situation in its terms may act out its pattern and so repeat it.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a good history can teach something that holds beyond the time and place it describes.
questions.explain: The authors say any good history is also universal. The card next shows in what sense.
questions.rule: Good history reaches beyond its period.

questions.q: Aristotle wrote that poetry is more ____ than history, meaning that it is more general, true in all times and places.
questions.explain: More philosophical here means more universal. History is tied to particular events, so it is less universal than poetry, but the authors hold that any good history is universal too.
questions.rule: More philosophical means more general.

questions.q: A reader finishes a history of an ancient city's ruinous war and says she learned nothing useful, since the city no longer exists. What do the authors say she has missed?
options: The exact dates and order of the war's main battles
The economic causes the historian ought to have stressed
The second account she needed to find out the truth
Human mistakes that recur in other times and places
optionExplain: Dates are the part tied to that time and place; they are not the main lesson.
Judging the historian's emphasis comes later and does not answer her complaint that nothing applies.
A second account would help with what happened, but her complaint is about usefulness, which the universal answers.
Right: the main thing a good historian teaches is how people act, including mistakes that are made again.
questions.explain: She read only for what happened, so the city's disappearance seemed to empty the book. The authors point to the recurring human mistakes it shows.
questions.rule: The city is gone; the mistakes are not.

questions.q: Sort each point from a history of an ancient war by whether it is tied to that time and place or could mean something beyond it.
groups: Tied to that time and place

items.t: The name of the general who lost the battle
Overconfidence led a strong city to overreach
The city fell in the summer of a certain year
Allies deserted a leader who ignored their interests
The fleet sailed from one particular harbour
Fear of a rival's growth pushed both sides to war
