questions.explain: Names, dates and harbours tie the history to its events. Overreaching, deserting allies and fear of a rival are human patterns that recur, which is where the universal lies.
questions.rule: Look for the pattern of conduct, not the particulars.

questions.q: A leader argues: in an ancient war a city lost by attacking too soon, so we must not act first in our dispute. Following the authors' idea of the universal in history, what is the weakness?
options: Ancient wars hold no lessons at all for disputes in the present day
History is tied to its events, so check the lesson against how now differs
Nothing, since a good history is universal and its lessons apply directly to today
A lesson drawn from a war cannot carry over to a non-military dispute
optionExplain: The authors hold that good histories do teach the present; the problem is applying a lesson without care.
Right: good history is universal, but less so than poetry, because it stays tied to particular events.
This forgets that history is less universal than poetry; the lesson needs fitting to the new case.
The authors find lessons about how people act in general, not only in war.
questions.explain: The leader treats one ancient outcome as a rule for today. The authors' Aristotle point cuts both ways: history teaches beyond its time, but it is tied to events, so the fit must be checked.
questions.rule: Universal lessons still need fitting.

questions.q: An engineering firm keeps reports of bridge failures from a century ago, involving materials no one now uses. A young engineer asks why she should study them. Applying the authors' idea, what is the best answer?
options: The old materials may well come back into use one day, so she should know them
The human errors behind them, such as ignored warnings, still recur
Learning the dates of famous failures is part of her training
The firm needs someone to check whether the old reports are true
optionExplain: A possible return of old materials is a weak, speculative reason; the lasting value is elsewhere.
Right: the materials are tied to their time; the judgments and mistakes of the people involved are not.
Dates are the particulars; they are the least transferable part.
Checking the reports may be useful, but it is not why the failures teach her anything.
questions.explain: Like a good history, an old failure report holds a universal part, the human errors, beneath technical particulars that have aged.
questions.rule: Particulars age; human errors recur.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the universal part of a past case is usually the human element, such as haste, pride or ignored warnings, while the technical particulars are what age; reading for the human element lets old cases inform new practice.

questions.q: The authors call history the story of what led up to now. What follows for a reader, in their view?
options: Only recent history is worth reading if the aim is to understand the present
History can tell us about the past but nothing about the future
The present should be studied first, to explain the past
Even ancient history can teach about the present and the future
optionExplain: The authors draw the opposite conclusion, using a historian over two thousand years old.
Since the present partly determines the future, history can teach something about the future too.
The authors' point runs from the past toward now, not the reverse.
Right: the authors say even Thucydides can teach us something about the present and the future.
questions.explain: If history leads up to now, and now shapes the future, an old history can bear on both. The card next spells this out.
questions.rule: History points toward now.

questions.q: Put in order the steps of the authors' reasoning that an ancient historian can teach us about the future.
items: History is the story of what led up to now
The present, and the future, are what chiefly interest us
The future will be partly determined by the present
So a historian of long ago can teach something about the future
questions.explain: History leads up to the present; the present partly determines the future; so a history can tell us something about both.
questions.rule: Past to present to future.

questions.q: Match each piece of the authors' advice with the aim it serves.
pairs: Get nearer to what really happened
Learn about people in all times, especially now
Admit the limits of one account
Claim no more than the evidence allows
questions.explain: The first suggestion serves the truth about events; the second serves understanding of people now. Admitting the limits of one account keeps the first honest when it cannot be met.
questions.rule: Two suggestions, two aims.

questions.q: A reader has time for only one history of a city's long decline. Using the authors' two suggestions, what can she still get from it?
options: Insight into how people act, though not certainty about events
Certainty about events, since there is no rival account to doubt
Nothing reliable, since the first suggestion cannot be met
Entertainment only, since one account is for amateurs
optionExplain: Right: the second suggestion works even with one account; the first, about events, does not.
A lack of rival accounts leaves events less certain, not more.
The suggestions serve different aims; failing the first does not cancel the second.
The lay reader reads seriously even with one account; amusement alone is the amateur's stance.
questions.explain: With one account she cannot be sure what happened, but she can still learn how people act, which is the main thing a good historian teaches.
questions.rule: One account still teaches how people act.

questions.q: A reader studies only the parts of a history that echo this week's headlines and skips the rest as irrelevant. Given the authors' second suggestion, what does this approach get wrong?
options: Nothing, since the present is the whole reason to read history
It breaks the first suggestion, which is to read every page
It narrows how people act in all times to what looks like now
It ignores the past, which matters more than the present
optionExplain: The present matters most to the authors, but they also want lessons about all times and places.
The first suggestion is about reading more than one history, not about reading every page.
Right: the second suggestion asks how people act in all times and places, especially now, not only where the past mirrors now.
The authors do not rank the past above now; they ask how people act in all times, especially now.
questions.explain: Reading toward the present is the authors' advice, but only reading what already looks familiar shrinks it. Conduct in unfamiliar settings can also teach about now.
questions.rule: Read for all times, especially now, not only now.

questions.q: A new head teacher finds a rule that pupils may not use the back stairs, which seems pointless to her. Applying the authors' view of history as the story of what led up to now, what should she do first?
options: Scrap the rule, since a rule with no visible purpose has no purpose
Keep the rule, since anything the school inherited must be right
Find out what past events led to the rule before deciding on it
Ask the pupils whether they would like the rule to be dropped
optionExplain: A purpose she cannot see may lie in events she does not know.
Knowing the history informs the decision; it does not settle it in the rule's favour.
Right: the present, rules included, is what the past led up to, so the rule's history may explain it.
Pupils' wishes matter, but they do not tell her why the rule exists.
questions.explain: If the present is what the past led up to, a puzzling feature of the present may have a history that explains it. Learning it comes before changing it.
questions.rule: Learn why it is there before removing it.
questions.teaches: By extension, knowing what led up to now explains present arrangements that look pointless to a newcomer: a rule without a visible purpose often has a history that gave it one.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, because history is closer to fiction, it should be read like a novel rather than as an expository work.
questions.explain: The authors say histories can be read as expository works and therefore should be. The card next explains what that involves.
questions.rule: History is read as exposition.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: The authors say that although most histories are closer to fiction, they can be read as ____ works, and therefore should be.
questions.explain: A history tells a story but also makes claims to be understood and judged, so the questions asked of any expository book apply.
questions.rule: Expository, though story-shaped.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: A reader works through a history of a famine using the authors' four questions. Put her steps in order.
items: Find what period and place the history covers
Work out how the story is told and what is basic to it
Judge whether the account is believable and well sourced
Ask what the history suggests for famine relief now
questions.explain: The order follows the four questions: what it is about, what is said and how, whether it is true, and what of it.
questions.rule: About, said, true, what of it.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: A reader finishes a history of the printing press and asks only whether she enjoyed it. Following the authors, what has she skipped?
options: The four questions of any expository book, adapted to history
A comparison with novels set in the same period and place
A check of the author's credentials before she began reading
Nothing, since enjoyment is the fitting test for a story
optionExplain: Right: the authors want histories read as expository works, with all four questions asked.
Novels might add colour, but the authors' questions concern the history's own subject, telling, truth and significance.
Knowing the author can help, but it does not replace understanding and judging the book.
History is closer to fiction, but the authors still say to read it as exposition.
questions.explain: Enjoyment is fine, but a history makes claims. The four questions ask what those claims are, whether they are true and why they matter.
questions.rule: Enjoy it, then question it.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: True or false: The authors say the four questions apply to history exactly as to any other expository book, and get the same kinds of answers.
questions.explain: The authors say the questions must be asked a little differently of history, and the answers will be of slightly different kinds.
questions.rule: Same questions, adjusted for history.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: A museum exhibition on a city's industrial past puts a huge photo of smiling factory workers at the entrance and a small panel on child labour in a back corner. Applying the authors' approach to history, what should a visitor ask?
options: Whether the objects on display are genuine pieces from the period
Nothing, since an exhibition presents objects rather than claims
How many visitors the museum hopes the exhibition will attract
What the arrangement itself claims, as well as what the panels say
optionExplain: Authenticity matters, but genuine objects can still be arranged to tell a particular story.
Chosen and arranged objects do make claims about the past, like a written history.
Visitor numbers say nothing about what the exhibition claims or whether it is true.
Right: placing one image first and largest and another out of the way is a way of saying what matters most.
questions.explain: An exhibition tells a story of the past and so can be read as exposition. Its layout does part of the telling, as a historian's choice of what is basic does in a book.
questions.rule: In a display, arrangement argues.
questions.teaches: By analogy, in a display the arrangement does part of the arguing: what is placed first, largest or out of the way works like a statement of what matters, so the question of what is being said applies to layout as well as text.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: What do the authors say readers of history often fail to note?
options: The dates on which the main events took place
The limits the author sets on his subject
The details of the author's life and career
The number of sources listed at the back
optionExplain: Dates are usually the most noticed part of a history, not the most neglected.
Right: readers often do not note carefully what limitations the author sets himself.
The author's life can matter, but the authors' point here concerns the book's subject.
The authors do not raise counting sources; their concern is knowing the subject and its limits.
questions.explain: The authors find it surprising how often readers skip finding a history's subject and especially its limits. The card next shows why that matters.
questions.rule: Find the limits first.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, an author cannot be blamed for not doing what he did not try to do.
questions.explain: This is why the reader must know what a history is not about before criticising it. Faulting a book for missing what it never aimed at is unfair.
questions.rule: Judge a book by its aim.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: A history of shipbuilding in one port from 1800 to 1850 says almost nothing about the port's music halls. A reviewer calls this a serious flaw. How would the authors judge the complaint?
options: It is fair, since a good history covers all of a port's life
It misfires, since music halls lie outside the stated subject
It is fair, since any omission reveals the author's bias
It misfires, since a reviewer should judge only the writing, not the coverage
optionExplain: Every history has a particular and limited subject; no history covers everything.
Right: the author set shipbuilding as his subject and cannot be blamed for not writing about music halls.
Leaving out what lies beyond the subject is the setting of limits, not bias.
The authors expect criticism of content too; the point is to judge it against what the book set out to do.
questions.explain: Music halls lie outside a history of shipbuilding. The complaint judges the book by a task it never took on.
questions.rule: Do not fault a book for its chosen limits.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: A history of shipbuilding in one port from 1800 to 1850 leaves out the port's music halls, and also ignores a long strike by the port's shipwrights. On the authors' view, how does the strike omission differ from the music halls?
options: It is no fault, since an author may set whatever limits he likes
It is no fault, since strikes belong to labour history, not shipbuilding
It matters only if the author promised in advance to cover strikes
It may be a fair criticism, since the strike bears on the subject itself
optionExplain: The authors hint that some omissions should not be made, as with a Civil War history that ignores the frontier.
A shipwrights' strike is part of how ships were built in that port, whatever label it also carries.
A promise is not needed; what counts is whether the omitted matter bears on the subject.
Right: a strike by the shipwrights shapes shipbuilding, so leaving it out weakens the chosen subject.
questions.explain: The rule protects an author's chosen limits, not omissions within them. A strike that halted the shipyards bears on shipbuilding itself.
questions.rule: Limits excuse what is outside, not what is inside.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: Before criticising a history for leaving something out, which questions should a reader following the authors ask? Select all that apply.
options: What did the author set out to cover?
Does the omitted matter bear on that subject?
Did the author state limits that exclude it?
Would the book have been more interesting with it?
Did some other history of the period include it?
optionExplain: Right: knowing what the history is about comes first.
Right: an omission matters if it bears on the chosen subject.
Right: knowing what the history is not about is needed before criticising it.
A reader's interest is not the test; the author's aim is.
Another book's choices do not set this author's task.
questions.explain: The fair test is the book's own subject and limits. Interest and other books' choices do not decide whether an omission is a fault.
questions.rule: Ask about the aim before the omission.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: A reviewer pans a cookbook for beginners because it has no recipes for advanced pastry. Applying the authors' rule for histories, what is the strongest reply?
options: The book set out to teach beginners, so that is no fault
Every cookbook ought to cover all levels of skill to be useful
The reviewer should have read more cookbooks before judging
Reviews of cookbooks do not need to be fair to their authors
optionExplain: Right: the book's stated aim sets the fair test, as a history's limits do.
No book covers everything; a beginners' book has chosen its limits.
Wider reading might help, but the key point is the book's own aim.
Fairness to the author's aim is exactly what the authors ask of criticism.
questions.explain: Like a history, the cookbook has a limited subject. Criticising it for not doing what it never tried to do misses the mark.
questions.rule: Judge by the aim, in any field.
questions.teaches: By analogy, judging any work by a standard it never aimed at, such as a beginners' guide by experts' standards or a summary by the depth of a treatise, is a common unfair criticism; the work's stated aim sets the fair test.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the general outline of a history is largely set by time, so the reader does not have to search for it.
questions.explain: Because the story happened in time, its outline is given. What the reader must find is how the historian chose to tell it. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Time gives the outline.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: Which ways of dividing a history into chapters do the authors mention? Select all that apply.
options: By the alphabetical order of the main figures
By the archives the author consulted
By years
By decades or generations
By aspects such as economics, wars and religion
optionExplain: That arrangement suits a reference book, not a story told in time.
Sources support the story; the authors do not mention organising a history by archive.
Right: chapters can follow years.
Right: or decades or generations.
Right: or headings of the author's own choosing, such as economic history, wars, religious movements and literature.
questions.explain: The authors contrast chronological divisions with divisions by aspect. Each is a choice about how to tell the story.
questions.rule: By time or by aspect.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: A history of a nation's twentieth century opens with four chapters on farming and industry, then turns to its wars and literature, explaining each by economic change. What do the authors' questions suggest?
options: The author has divided the book by decades and generations
The author has no view of what mattered most in the period
The author treats the economy as the most basic aspect
The author has erred, since wars ought to come before economics
optionExplain: The chapters follow aspects, not periods of time.
The arrangement and the explanations show a clear view of what is basic.
Right: leading with the economy and explaining the rest by it shows what he takes as fundamental.
The reader may disagree with his choice, but the first task is to see it, not to rank aspects.
questions.explain: Both the order and the way other aspects are explained point to the economy as basic for this historian.
questions.rule: What explains the rest is what he thinks basic.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reader who disagrees with a historian about which aspect is most basic can learn little from him.
questions.explain: The authors say we may not agree with his judgment about what is basic, but we can still learn from him. Seeing his choice helps us understand him.
questions.rule: Disagree with the emphasis, still learn.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: Suppose a historian reorganises the second edition of his book from chapters by decade into chapters by theme, with religion first. What should a reader of the new edition ask?
options: Whether the dates of the events in the book have changed
Whether the story still happened in the order of time
Whether religion is now what he treats as most fundamental
Whether he has now read more than one source per event
optionExplain: Reordering chapters does not alter dates; it changes the telling.
The events still happened in time; the reorganisation concerns how they are told.
Right: a change in the way of telling may signal a change in what he takes as basic.
Sources are a separate matter; the new arrangement bears on emphasis.
questions.explain: Moving from time to theme, with religion first, changes how the story is told. The authors' question is what that says about what he now treats as fundamental.
questions.rule: A new arrangement may mean a new emphasis.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: A biology textbook's first and longest section is on genetics, and its later sections on ecology and behaviour keep explaining things through genes. Applying the authors' question about histories, what can a student infer?
options: The author treats genetics as most fundamental to the subject
The book is ordered by when each idea was first discovered
The author thinks ecology and behaviour lie outside biology
The textbook is a history of biology rather than a science book
optionExplain: Right: the aspect used to explain the others shows what the author takes as basic.
Nothing suggests a chronological order; the sections are arranged by aspect.
Ecology and behaviour are included; they are explained through genetics.
Organising by aspect does not make a book a history.
questions.explain: As with a history divided by aspect, the book's order and its explanations reveal what its author treats as fundamental.
questions.rule: Find the aspect that explains the others.
questions.teaches: By analogy, in any book that divides its subject into aspects, the aspect used to explain the others reveals what the author takes as fundamental, and spotting it helps a reader understand and later judge the whole.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: A reader finds a history's portrait of its hero hard to believe, since no real person would act so nobly. What kind of criticism is this, in the authors' terms?
options: A charge that the historian misused his sources
A complaint that the book strays beyond its subject
A finding that the history is really a novel
A judgment that the history lacks verisimilitude
optionExplain: Misusing sources is the authors' second form of criticism; this reader questions how people act.
The portrait is within the subject; the doubt is about its likeness to real people.
An unlikely portrait does not make a history fiction; it may make it a poor history.
Right: doubting that people act as the history says is the criticism of verisimilitude.
questions.explain: The authors call this judging that a history lacks verisimilitude. The card next explains when the judgment is fair.
questions.rule: Do people act that way?

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: The authors' first form of criticism of history is to judge that a work lacks ____, the quality of seeming true to how people really act.
questions.explain: Verisimilitude means likeness to truth. A history lacks it when its people act in ways real people do not.
questions.rule: Verisimilitude: true to life.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, even a history whose every statement is documented from relevant sources can lack verisimilitude.
questions.explain: The authors say we can still feel the historian has misunderstood or misjudged his sources through some failure in his grasp of human nature.
questions.rule: Documented is not the same as lifelike.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: A history of a peasant revolt shows every rebel acting from pure religious devotion, with no mention of hunger, debt or land. What may a reader who has understood it fairly say, following the authors?
options: It must have misread its sources, since all revolts concern land
Its people seem unlike real people, so it may lack verisimilitude
It is beyond criticism, since its sources are all documented and relevant
It is a work of fiction, since its picture seems so unlikely
optionExplain: Whether sources were misread is a different charge, and the claim that all revolts concern land is too sweeping.
Right: rebels moved by nothing but devotion seem unlike real people, which is the verisimilitude criticism.
The authors say a documented history can still lack verisimilitude.
An unlikely portrait makes a weak history, not a novel.
questions.explain: Like the older historians who left out economics, this account gives its people motives too pure to be believed. That is a fair verisimilitude criticism, once the book is understood.
questions.rule: Doubt motives too pure to be real.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: A reader skims the first chapter of a history, finds the king too generous to believe, and dismisses the book for lacking verisimilitude. What has gone wrong, by the authors' account?
options: He used the wrong form of criticism, since only sources count
He judged before understanding what the history says
Nothing, since an unlikely portrait is reason enough to stop
He should have checked the book's dates before anything else
optionExplain: Verisimilitude is a legitimate criticism; the authors rank it as the more important one.
Right: the authors allow the verisimilitude judgment only after understanding what is said.
The portrait may be explained later; judging from one chapter skips understanding.
Dates are not the issue; the fault is judging before understanding.
questions.explain: The criticism is valid in form but premature. A reader must first understand the history, which a skim of one chapter cannot give.
questions.rule: Understand first, then ask if it is lifelike.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: A company's official history says every decision its founders made was for customers, and not for profit. Applying the authors' verisimilitude test, and their own example, what should an employee keep in mind?
options: Accept it, since an official history is drawn from company records
Reject it, since founders of companies are moved only by profit
Leave the question aside, since no one's motives can be judged
Doubt is fair, though her sense of human nature has a date too
optionExplain: Records can be documented and still be misjudged; verisimilitude is a separate test.
Assuming pure self-interest is the opposite error, the very assumption the authors note in present-day readers.
The authors expect readers to judge how people act; the point is to do it with care.
Right: the account may lack verisimilitude, but her judgment of how people act is itself a view of her time.
questions.explain: The authors' own example shows readers of their day assuming self-interest. Her doubt is fair, but she should hold it as a judgment shaped by her time, not as a certainty.
questions.rule: Your sense of human nature has a date too.
questions.teaches: The verisimilitude test cuts both ways: the reader's own sense of how people act, such as the assumption that everyone acts from self-interest, belongs to a time as well, so it should be held as a judgment, not a certainty.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the criticism that a historian misused his sources is more important than the criticism that his history lacks verisimilitude.
questions.explain: The authors rank verisimilitude first. The card next explains the second criticism and why it comes second.
questions.rule: Verisimilitude ranks first.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: According to the authors, a good historian must combine the talents of the storyteller and the ____.
questions.explain: The storyteller's talent is a sense of what is likely to have happened; the scientist's is care with what witnesses and sources say did happen.
questions.rule: Storyteller and scientist.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: Sort each complaint about a history by the form of criticism it makes.

items.t: People do not act the way this history says
The author never read a key memoir of the period
The hero is far too noble to be believed
The author has the date of the treaty wrong
The motives given ignore self-interest entirely
A relevant archive was left unexamined

questions.explain: Complaints about how people act concern verisimilitude. Complaints about unread books, wrong facts or unexamined archives concern the use of sources.
questions.rule: How people act, or what the sources say.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: A specialist reviewing a new history of a shipwreck finds the author ignored the ship's surviving logbook, which she has read. By the authors' account, what can she conclude?
options: He has neglected his sources, which is a real fault in a history
Nothing, since only verisimilitude counts as criticism of history
The history lacks verisimilitude, which is the more serious fault
The logbook lies outside the subject the author chose to cover
optionExplain: Right: with special knowledge she can see he misused his sources; we expect a historian to be informed.
Verisimilitude ranks higher, but the authors count misuse of sources as a real criticism too.
Ignoring a logbook is a fault of sources, not of how people are shown to act.
The ship's own logbook is central to a history of its wreck, not outside it.
questions.explain: This is the second form of criticism, open especially to readers with special knowledge. It is ranked below verisimilitude but is still a real fault.
questions.rule: An uninformed historian falls short.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: One history of a rebellion has small factual slips but portrays its people believably. Another is accurate in every detail but shows its leaders acting as no one would. By the authors' ranking, which has the more serious fault?
options: The first, since factual slips spoil any history
Both equally, since any fault ruins a history
The second, as lack of verisimilitude weighs more
Neither, since small slips and odd portraits are normal in any long history
optionExplain: Slips matter, but the authors rank the failure to grasp how people act higher.
The authors rank the two criticisms rather than treating them as equal.
Right: the authors call the verisimilitude criticism the more important of the two.
Both are real faults in the authors' view; the question is which weighs more, and they rank verisimilitude first.
questions.explain: Accuracy of detail cannot make up for a failure to know what people are likely to do. That is why the authors put verisimilitude first.
questions.rule: Getting people wrong outweighs small slips.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: A claims investigator gets an account of a theft that matches every receipt and date, yet says the thief left expensive items behind and took only a cheap one. Applying the storyteller-and-scientist standard, what should she do?
options: Accept it, since the receipts and dates all check out
Reject it, since unusual behaviour proves the account false
Ask whether the story is likely, not only if papers fit
Request more receipts, since documents settle such questions
optionExplain: Fitting documents is the scientist's half; the storyteller's sense of the likely is missing.
Unlikely is not impossible; the oddity calls for inquiry, not a verdict.
Right: like a good historian, she weighs both what the records say and what people would likely do.
More documents test the same half again; the question raised is about likelihood.
questions.explain: The account passes the documentary check but raises a question of likelihood. Both talents are needed to judge it.
questions.rule: Check the papers and the plausibility.
questions.teaches: By analogy, an account can pass every documentary check and still fail the test of likelihood, so investigators in any field weigh both what the records say and what people would plausibly do.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: Which kind of literature do the authors suggest may have the greatest effect on what people do?
options: History
Satire
Utopian writing
Lyric poetry
optionExplain: Right: the authors say perhaps no kind of literature has a greater effect on the actions of men than history.
The authors say satires have little effect on action.
Pictures of philosophical utopias, the authors say, seldom inspire action.
The authors do not credit lyric poetry with this effect on action.
questions.explain: The authors single out history for its effect on action. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: History moves people to act.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: According to the authors, history suggests the ____, since it describes things that have already been done.
questions.explain: If something has been done, perhaps it can be done again, or perhaps avoided. That is how history bears on action.
questions.rule: What was done may be done again.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: Why, according to the authors, do satires and pictures of ideal societies move people to act less than history does?
options: They are read by far fewer people than histories are
They are harder to understand than histories are
Their authors seldom hold any political power
They show the ideal, not what was actually done
optionExplain: The authors give no argument from readership; their point is about what each kind shows.
Difficulty is not the authors' reason.
Statesmen read history, but the authors' reason concerns the books, not their authors' power.
Right: describing the ideal does not show it can be done; history shows things that were done.
questions.explain: History describes actions actually taken, which suggests what is possible. Satire and utopias describe what ought to be, which seldom moves people to act.
questions.rule: What was done moves people more than what is imagined.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: A health minister planning a nationwide vaccination drive reads histories of earlier campaigns. By the authors' answer to the last of the four questions, what should she look for?
options: The exact dates of earlier campaigns to cite in her speeches
What was done before that might be done again, or avoided
The ideal programme described by public-health theorists
Proof that her campaign is certain to succeed this time
optionExplain: Dates are the least useful part for action.
Right: history suggests the possible, what can be repeated and what should be avoided.
An ideal programme is the kind of writing the authors say seldom moves action.
History suggests what is possible; it does not prove success.
questions.explain: The practical value of history lies in what it shows was possible. She reads to repeat what worked and avoid what failed.
questions.rule: Read history for what can be done.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: True or false: On the authors' view, if a policy succeeded once in history, history shows it will succeed when tried again.
questions.explain: The authors say history suggests the possible: what has been done perhaps can be done again. Perhaps is not will; conditions may differ.
questions.rule: Possible, not certain.

questions.section: Questions to Ask of a Historical Book
questions.q: A startup founder reads one famous success story and copies its strategy step by step, without asking why it worked or how other firms fared. In the authors' terms, what has gone wrong?
options: He read history at all, when he needed business theory
He acted on some history, but not enough to read it well
He read about business, when history concerns politics
He chose a story too recent to learn anything from
optionExplain: The authors hold that history, which shows what was done, moves action better than theory.
Right: like the leaders the authors mention, he acted with some knowledge of history but not enough.
The authors stress political action, but what history suggests about the possible applies more widely.
Recent history can teach; the problem is how little and how carelessly he read.
questions.explain: One success story shows something was possible once. Without knowing why it worked, or how often the same move failed, he is acting on too little history.
questions.rule: A little history is a risky guide.
questions.teaches: By extension, a single success story is a risky guide to action: knowing what worked once, without knowing why or how often it failed elsewhere, is the partial knowledge of history the authors warn against.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a biography poses many of the same problems as a history.
questions.explain: A biography is ordinarily a narrative of a life, a kind of history, so it shares history's problems. The card next adds what is special to it.
questions.rule: A life is a history.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: Which questions do the authors say a reader must ask of a biography, besides those asked of any book? Select all that apply.
options: What are the author's criteria of truth?
Is the subject of the book still alive?
Did the subject approve of the book?
How does its length compare with other lives?
What is the author's purpose?
optionExplain: Right: and his criteria of truth.
This bears on which kind of biography it can be, but it is not one of the two questions.
Approval matters for authorized biographies, but it is not one of the two questions the authors name.
Length tells little about purpose or truth.
Right: the authors name the author's purpose.
questions.explain: The authors ask of a biography what they ask of a history: what is the author trying to do, and by what standard does he decide what is true.
questions.rule: Purpose and criteria of truth.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: Why do the authors say biography has a mixed character?
options: It mixes the lives of several people in one
It is written partly by its subject, partly by others
It joins history to the science of personality
It is a story, yet the story of a real person
optionExplain: Some biographies cover a group, but that is not the mixture the authors mean.
That describes some memoirs, not what makes every biography mixed.
The authors say nothing of a science of personality here.
Right: being a story and being about a real person give it a mixed character.
questions.explain: A biography has a storyteller's form and a historian's subject. That mixture is why both kinds of question apply.
questions.rule: Part story, part history.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: A reader picks up a biography of a famous singer written by her longtime manager. Following the authors, what should the reader ask first?
options: What the manager meant the book to do, and what he counts as true
Whether the singer's records are still in print and selling well
How many other biographies of the singer have been written, and by whom
Whether the book reads as smoothly as a good novel would
optionExplain: Right: purpose and criteria of truth matter all the more when the author was close to the subject.
Her current sales say nothing about how far to trust the book.
Other biographies help later, but the first questions concern this author.
Readability is pleasant, but the authors' questions concern purpose and truth.
questions.explain: A manager may write to praise, to settle scores or to record. Knowing his purpose and his standard of truth tells the reader how to read the book.
questions.rule: Ask why and by what standard.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: True or false: Once a biographer states his purpose in the preface, the reader can trust the book to serve that purpose.
questions.explain: A stated purpose is a starting point. The reader still checks it against what the book does, since a biographer may state one aim and pursue another.
questions.rule: Check the stated aim against the book.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: A book follows the four members of a rock band from their school days to the band's break-up. Applying the authors' account of biography, how should a reader treat it?
options: As fiction, since it tells the band's rise and fall as a story
As something other than biography, which covers one life only
As a biography of a group, read with the questions for history
As a reference work, since it records albums and tours
optionExplain: Story form does not make it fiction; it is about real people.
The authors count narratives of a group of people as biography too.
Right: the authors' account of biography extends to the life of a group of people.
Lists of albums may appear, but the book is a narrative of lives, not a work for looking things up.
questions.explain: The authors describe biography as the narrative of the life of a man or woman or of a group of people, so a band's story raises the same questions.
questions.rule: A group can have a biography.
questions.teaches: A biography need not be about one person: the authors include narratives of a group of people, such as a family or a band, which raise the same questions as history.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: According to the authors, which of these cannot be the subject of a definitive biography?
options: A person who wrote no books
A person with many earlier lives
A person who is still living
A person who lived long ago
optionExplain: A subject need not be a writer; letters and other sources serve.
Earlier lives usually come first; they do not rule a definitive one out.
Right: the authors say definitive biographies cannot be written about living persons.
Long-dead subjects are the usual case for a definitive biography.
questions.explain: A life still being lived cannot be treated finally. The card next describes what a definitive biography is.
questions.rule: Definitive lives are of finished lives.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: According to the authors, what goes into writing a definitive biography? Select all that apply.
options: Approval of the text by the heirs
Going through all the sources
Reading all the subject's letters
Examining much of the history of the time
Long interviews with the subject
optionExplain: Approval by heirs marks an authorized biography, a different kind.
Right: all sources are gone through.
Right: all letters are read.
Right: a great deal of contemporary history is examined.
A definitive biography cannot be of a living person, so the subject cannot be interviewed.
questions.explain: Exhaustive work on all the sources, letters and history of the time is what the definitive biographer does.
questions.rule: All the sources, all the letters, the whole time.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a definitive biography is usually the first biography written about its subject.
questions.explain: The authors say definitive biographies are seldom written until several non-definitive ones have appeared first.
questions.rule: Definitive lives come later.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: A reader wants to understand the politics of a king's reign and finds a definitive biography of his chief minister. How do the authors suggest she read it?
options: As history of the minister and his times, seen through his eyes
As a portrait of character, setting the politics of the reign to one side
As useless for the reign, since it centres on a single person
As a reference book to dip into for single facts and dates
optionExplain: Right: a definitive biography is a slice of history, the person and his times.
Character matters, but the authors say to read it as history, politics included.
Centring on one person is the point of the form; it still shows the times.
It is a narrative to be read as history, not a work to consult for scattered facts.
questions.explain: The authors call a definitive biography a slice of history and say to read it as history. It can teach her much about the reign.
questions.rule: A definitive life is a slice of history.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: Suppose a trunk of a famous poet's letters is found decades after her definitive biography appeared. What follows, on the authors' account?
options: Nothing, since a definitive biography is final by definition
The definitive biography becomes an authorized one instead
The letters can be ignored, since her life is now settled
New biographies may follow, since definitive names an aim
optionExplain: The authors note that other lives of Johnson appeared after Boswell's definitive one.
Authorized means commissioned by heirs or friends; new letters do not change that.
A definitive biographer reads all the letters; newly found ones are what later biographers will read.
Right: as with Johnson, other biographies can appear after a definitive one.
questions.explain: Definitive describes an aim at finality. New sources, like the poet's letters, can call for new biographies, as happened even after Boswell.
questions.rule: Definitive aims at final; it can be overtaken.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: A student uses a definitive biography of a general as her only source for the history of the war he fought in. Applying the authors' rules, what is the weakness?
options: A definitive biography is too unreliable to be used as a history
It shows the war through one man's eyes, so other accounts are needed
Biographies may not be read as history, only as stories of a life
There is none, since a definitive biography has checked every source
optionExplain: The authors trust definitive biographies more than any other kind and say to read them as history.
Right: the times are seen through the subject's eyes, so the first rule of reading more than one account still applies.
The authors say a definitive biography should be read as history.
Thoroughness about the general's life does not give other viewpoints on the war.
questions.explain: A definitive biography is trustworthy history of its subject and his times, but its standpoint is his. For the war as a whole, other accounts are still needed.
questions.rule: One life's view of the times is still one view.
questions.teaches: Because a definitive biography sees the times through its subject's eyes, it gives the period from one standpoint, so the first rule of reading history, more than one account, still applies to the times it describes.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: A biography is commissioned by its subject's family, who open all his papers to the author. What do the authors say about trusting it?
options: Trust it fully, since the author was allowed to see all the material
Read it as possibly biased, showing how the family want him known
Disregard it, since a commissioned book can hold no truth at all
Treat it as definitive, since it draws on every one of his letters
optionExplain: Access is a real advantage, but it does not remove the sponsors' interest in the picture.
Right: an authorized biography presents its subject in the best light his family and friends can give.
The authors say authorized biographies can be very good and tell much; the caution is about trust, not worth.
Using the papers is not what makes a biography definitive; its aim and independence differ.
questions.explain: The family's commission shapes the picture. The card next explains what such a book can and cannot give.
questions.rule: Commissioned lives show the sponsors' picture.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, an authorized biography can sometimes be very good, because its author is given access to material others cannot see.
questions.explain: Those who control the material open it to the authorized biographer, an advantage other writers seldom have.
questions.rule: Access is the authorized biography's strength.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: If an authorized biography gives the picture its sponsors want, what would a reader need to do to get at the subject's real life, by the authors' account?
options: Read the authorized biography again, more slowly and with more care
Ask the heirs directly what they chose to leave out of the book
Trust only the passages the heirs would have found unflattering
Read all the accounts, ask those who were there, and judge for herself
optionExplain: Rereading improves understanding of the picture, not knowledge of what lies outside it.
The heirs are the interested party; asking them repeats the source of the bias.
Unflattering passages may be more credible, but they are a small and still selected part.
Right: the authors compare it to reading one side's war reports; the truth needs all of them, witnesses and one's own judgment.
questions.explain: The authors liken an authorized biography to one side's war communiques. A definitive biography has already done the comparing; with an authorized one, the reader must do it.
questions.rule: One side's report needs the other sides.
questions.teaches: The authors compare an authorized biography to the communiques of one side in a war: to get at the truth, read all the communiques, ask people who were there, and use your own mind on the muddle, work a definitive biography has already done.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: An authorized life of a 1950s film star leaves out her divorce, while her charity work fills three chapters. What can the reader fairly learn from this?
options: Something about what her circle, and that era, thought fit to show
That the star was never divorced, since the book is well sourced
That the book is worthless as evidence, since it leaves out a known fact
That charity was the most important part of the star's life
optionExplain: Right: an authorized biography shows what interested persons wanted known and what its time found acceptable.
Access to sources does not mean everything found is told.
The authors say such books tell much, about their sponsors and their time, even when they leave things out.
The space given reflects what the sponsors wanted known, not necessarily what mattered most in her life.
questions.explain: The selection itself is evidence: about the star's circle and about what the 1950s thought presentable. It is not evidence about her private life.
questions.rule: What is shown tells about who shows it.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: Sort each item by whether, on the authors' account, a reader can learn it from an authorized biography or should not expect it there.

items.t: What its sponsors want the public to know
The customs and manners of its time
Attitudes that were acceptable then
The subject's real private life
An even-handed account of his errors
The trust owed a definitive biography

questions.explain: An authorized biography teaches about its sponsors and its time. It is written to show the subject in the best light, so the private truth and an even-handed account lie elsewhere.
questions.rule: Learn the picture and its time, not the private life.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: A candidate's campaign film tells her life story but says nothing of her ten years at one particular company. Applying the authors' view of authorized biography, what does the gap suggest?
options: It proves she did something wrong during those years
It means those years did not matter in her life
It may hint at what her campaign thinks would harm her
It shows the film is a full and final account of her
optionExplain: A gap is a reason to look further, not proof of wrongdoing.
Sponsors leave out what they would rather not show, which is not the same as what did not matter.
Right: a sponsored life leaves out what its sponsors think unhelpful, so the gap is a clue to where to look.
A full account would include the years; their absence marks a sponsored picture.
questions.explain: Like an authorized biography, the film shows its subject as her supporters want her seen. What it omits, by implication, points to what they would rather not show.
questions.rule: A sponsored gap is a place to look.
questions.teaches: Omissions in a sponsored life can be read by implication: what the sponsors leave out hints at what they think would harm the subject, which tells the reader where to look elsewhere.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Plutarch's Lives is read more for its view of life than for its information about its subjects.
questions.explain: Plutarch wrote to help readers become great and avoid the errors of the great. The card next sets didactic lives beside ordinary ones.
questions.rule: Didactic lives teach a view of life.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: Match each kind of biography with how the authors suggest reading it.
pairs: Read as history of a life and its times
Read as the picture its sponsors want known
Expect accuracy and the feel of a real life
Read chiefly for the view of life it teaches
questions.explain: The four kinds differ in purpose and in the trust they deserve, so each is read differently.
questions.rule: Know the kind before you trust the life.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: A popular biography of a jazz pianist, neither commissioned nor exhaustive, makes the reader feel she is in 1950s New York clubs. By the authors' standards, what else should she expect of it?
options: That it is the last and complete word on the pianist's life
That it shows the pianist in the light his heirs and friends wanted him seen
That its facts are accurate, though it is not the final word
That it teaches a moral lesson about how to live a good life
optionExplain: That is the aim of a definitive biography; an ordinary one is not exhaustive.
That marks an authorized biography; this one was not commissioned.
Right: from an ordinary biography we expect accuracy and the feel of a real life, not definitive trust.
A moral purpose marks a didactic biography; nothing suggests one here.
questions.explain: It gives the feeling of a real life in another time and place; the authors also expect an ordinary biographer to know his facts.
questions.rule: Ordinary lives owe accuracy.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: According to the authors, what did Plutarch himself say happened to his purpose as he wrote the Lives?
options: He found that he himself was profiting more and more from the lives
He came to doubt his facts and turned from biography to history
He found that his readers paid no attention to his moral lessons
He decided to write only about Romans and to leave out the Greeks
optionExplain: Right: he set out to instruct others and found he was gaining profit and stimulation himself.
The authors report no such doubt; the change was in who profited.
The authors say nothing of his readers ignoring him; the Lives proved deeply influential.
The Lives covers both Greeks and Romans.
questions.explain: Plutarch said that, as the work went on, he more and more drew profit and stimulation himself from living with these men.
questions.rule: A teacher of lives can learn most.
questions.teaches: A didactic writer can become his own best reader: Plutarch set out to instruct others but found that he himself profited more and more from the company of the lives he wrote.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: True or false: Because a didactic biography is read for its view of life, a reader need not care whether its facts are accurate.
questions.explain: Plutarch's Lives is often the only account of its subjects, so its facts still matter and need the care owed any single account. A moral aim can also bend the story.
questions.rule: Lessons do not excuse errors.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: A young entrepreneur models her career on a famous founder as portrayed in a bestselling biography. Applying the authors' Plutarch example, what is worth noticing?
options: She is learning about the real founder, since the book sold so widely
She is reading wrongly, since a biography should not be a model
She is safe, since a moral biography shows only good conduct
She copies the biographer's portrait, which may differ from the man
optionExplain: Sales measure popularity, not faithfulness to the life.
The authors say a biography can inspire action; the point is to know what is being imitated.
A didactic life shows the errors of the great as well, and its portrait is still a portrait.
Right: later conquerors modelled themselves on Plutarch's Alexander, a portrait, not the man himself.
questions.explain: As with Plutarch's Alexander, the model she follows is the biographer's version. Knowing that lets her ask whether the portrait and the man match.
questions.rule: Imitators copy the portrait.
questions.teaches: By analogy with conquerors who modelled themselves on Plutarch's Alexander, people who take a biography as a model imitate the biographer's version of the subject, not necessarily the person who lived.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, it is questionable whether anyone has ever written a wholly true autobiography.
questions.explain: The authors doubt any autobiography is wholly true, though they also say none is wholly false. The card next gives both sides.
questions.rule: No self-portrait is the whole truth.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: Which reasons do the authors give for doubting that an autobiography can be wholly true? Select all that apply.
options: With no one to contradict him, the author is tempted to distort
Publishers cut autobiographies heavily to fit a length
Few authors keep diaries to work from when they write
Knowing your own life is harder than knowing another's
The life is not yet complete when it is written
optionExplain: Right: the temptation to tell less or more than the truth is almost irresistible when no one can contradict you.
The authors say nothing of publishers' cuts; their reasons lie in the author.
Diaries are not mentioned; the difficulty is self-knowledge and temptation, not lack of notes.
Right: if another's life is hard to know, one's own is harder.
Right: every autobiography is written about a life not yet finished.
questions.explain: Self-knowledge is hard, the life is unfinished, and nobody can contradict the author. Secrets and illusions do the rest.
questions.rule: Hard to know, unfinished, uncontradicted.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: The authors say an autobiographer is tempted to tell either less or more than the truth, and that telling ____ than the truth may be the commoner fault.
questions.explain: Concealment is expected, but the authors suggest embellishment, telling more than the truth, may be even more common.
questions.rule: Watch for embellishment as well as concealment.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: A celebrity's autobiography describes a childhood of heroic hardship that her siblings remember as fairly comfortable. In the authors' terms, what kind of distortion is most likely here?
options: Telling less than the truth, to hide a secret she cannot share
Telling more than the truth, which may be the commoner fault
No distortion at all, since she knows her own life the best
Deliberate fiction, since an autobiography is a kind of novel
optionExplain: Concealment is the other temptation, but here she adds drama rather than holding something back.
Right: heightening the hardship adds to the truth rather than hiding it.
The authors say knowing one's own life is harder than knowing another's.
Embellishment is not invention of a whole world; it is a real life told with more than the truth.
questions.explain: Her account adds hardship her siblings do not recall. That is telling more than the truth, the fault the authors think may be commoner.
questions.rule: Embellishment is telling more than the truth.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: Suppose an autobiographer could be questioned by people who knew him while he wrote. Which of the authors' reasons for doubt would be weakened most?
options: The difficulty of knowing one's own life even from the inside
The temptation that comes from no one contradicting him
The incompleteness of a life that is still being lived
The illusions about himself that he cannot see as illusions
optionExplain: Self-knowledge stays hard however many people ask questions.
Right: the temptation is strongest when no one can contradict you; questioners would supply contradiction.
The life would still be unfinished.
Questioners might expose some illusions, but the authors present them as nearly impossible for the author himself to recognise.
questions.explain: Contradiction checks the temptation to distort. The other difficulties lie in the nature of self-knowledge and of an unfinished life.
questions.rule: Contradiction checks distortion.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: An applicant's personal statement describes her as a natural leader who meets every deadline. Applying the authors' view of autobiography, how should a hiring manager read it?
options: As accurate, since no one knows her work better than she does
As worthless, since applicants tend to present themselves too favourably
As a reference, carrying the weight of another's judgment
As showing how she wants to be seen, while checking its claims
optionExplain: The authors say knowing oneself is harder than knowing others.
Embellishment is likely, but no self-portrait is wholly untrue; it still shows what she wants to present.
A reference is another's account; a personal statement is the applicant's own.
Right: it is a self-portrait no one can contradict, so it tells something true about her aims while its claims need checking.
questions.explain: A personal statement is a small autobiography written where no one can contradict it. It invites embellishment, yet still shows how she wants to be seen.
questions.rule: Self-description reveals the self it wants to show.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any self-description written where no one can contradict it, from a personal statement to a profile page, invites embellishment, yet still reveals what the writer wants to be seen as.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: What do the authors claim about books that are not autobiographies, such as Plato's Republic?
options: Much of them is autobiographical, revealing something of their authors
They reveal nothing of their authors, since they treat other subjects
They should be read mainly for what they show of their authors' lives
They are autobiographies in disguise and should be read as such
optionExplain: Right: the authors say there is a great deal of Plato in the Republic, as of Milton in Paradise Lost.
The authors hold that no one keeps himself entirely out of his book.
The author's character should never be the primary consideration.
They reveal their authors in part, but they remain books about their subjects and are read for what they say.
questions.explain: Every book is written by a living person and carries traces of him. The card next explains how much attention those traces deserve.
questions.rule: Every book has an author in it.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, discovering the author's character should be a reader's primary consideration in reading a book.
questions.explain: The authors say we may read partly to discover the author's character, but this should never be the primary consideration; overdone, it becomes a fallacy.
questions.rule: The author's character comes second.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: The authors say that even if Plato and Aristotle had agreed completely, they could not have written the same books, because they were different ____.
questions.explain: Words are found and written by a particular living person, so agreement in doctrine would not make two writers' books the same. Each writer's self enters his words.
questions.rule: Different writers, different books.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: A student writing on a famous economics treatise spends her essay speculating about the author's unhappy marriage and barely states his argument. By the authors' advice, what has gone wrong?
options: Nothing, since every book is partly autobiographical
She ought to have read his autobiography before the treatise
She hunted his secrets and missed what he says plainly
She should not have thought about the author at all
optionExplain: Books are partly autobiographical, but that makes the author a secondary interest, not the main one.
Another book would not fix the problem; she has neglected the treatise's own argument.
Right: the authors warn against spending so long on a writer's secrets that you miss what he says plainly.
The authors allow interest in the author within reasonable limits.
questions.explain: Interest in the author is fair within limits. Her essay reverses the order, putting speculation before the argument the book plainly makes.
questions.rule: What he says plainly comes first.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a work as impersonal as the Summa Theologica reveals nothing at all about its author.
questions.explain: The authors say we may discover something of Thomas Aquinas even in such an apparently unrevealing work. Traces are fainter in some books but not absent.
questions.rule: Even impersonal books carry their authors.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: A code reviewer decides early that a colleague is careless, then finds faults in nearly every line, including some that others judge sound. Applying the authors' advice about the author in a book, what has gone wrong?
options: She has looked too closely at the code and should skim it instead
Nothing, since the code reveals its maker and she has read it well
Her view of the maker has begun to shape her reading of the work
She should have reviewed the colleague's earlier code before this
optionExplain: Close reading is not the fault; reading through a fixed view of the maker is.
The work does show its maker, but here the impression is driving the judgment, not following from it.
Right: the maker's character came first for her, and now colours how she reads the work.
More of his code would feed the same impression; the fix is to judge this work on its own terms first.
questions.explain: The authors put the work first and the author's character second. Reverse the order, and the impression of the maker colours the judgment of the work.
questions.rule: Judge the work before the maker, or the maker will judge it for you.
questions.teaches: By extension, an early impression of a maker can bias the judgment of the work itself, so reading what a work plainly says before guessing at its author also protects the judgment.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: To know the truth about a person's life, what do the authors advise reading?
options: As many biographies as you can find, including his own account
Only his autobiography, since he knew his own life best
Only the definitive biography, since it is meant to be final
Only the authorized biography, since it had full access
optionExplain: Right: the authors advise reading as many biographies as you can, and his own account if he wrote one.
The authors doubt any autobiography is wholly true; it is one account among several.
A definitive biography is the most trustworthy single life, but the authors still advise reading as many as you can.
Access does not remove an authorized biography's bias.
questions.explain: As with any history, more than one account is needed. The card next gives the authors' full summary.
questions.rule: Many lives, including his own.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: The authors advise taking all autobiographies with a grain of ____.
questions.explain: No autobiography is wholly true, so the reader discounts the self-portrait while still learning from it.
questions.rule: Season the self-portrait with doubt.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: A reader plans to study the life of a famous scientist. Which steps fit the authors' summary advice? Select all that apply.
options: Read several biographies of her
Read her own memoir, with caution
Understand each book before disputing it
Rely on whichever biography is shortest
Prefer her memoir wherever it differs
optionExplain: Right: read as many biographies as you can find.
Right: include her own account, taken with a grain of salt.
Right: never argue with a book until you fully understand it.
Length is no guide to truth; several accounts are the guide.
The memoir is the account most in need of salt, not the one to prefer.
questions.explain: The authors' advice combines the first rule of history, caution toward self-portraits, and understanding before judging.
questions.rule: Several lives, salted memoir, understanding first.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, biography can be read as a cause of history as well as a record of it.
questions.explain: The authors say to read biography as history and as the cause of history, as Plutarch's Alexander shaped later conquerors.
questions.rule: Lives make history as well as record it.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: Suppose an inventor's autobiography and two biographies disagree about who first had his key idea. Following the authors, what should a reader do?
options: Accept the autobiography, since the inventor was there himself
Accept the biographies, since autobiographies are always false
Split the difference, taking a middle position between the accounts
Weigh the self-account cautiously and compare it with the others
optionExplain: Being there is not enough; the temptation to tell more than the truth is strongest where no one can contradict.
The authors say no autobiography is wholly false; it is weighed, not thrown out.
Averaging is not judging; the self-account needs extra caution, especially on a point that flatters him.
Right: the self-account is evidence taken with a grain of salt, set against the other lives.
questions.explain: The disagreement is what comparison is for. The autobiography gets extra caution, especially on a point that flatters its author.
questions.rule: Compare, and salt the self-account.

questions.section: How to Read Biography and Autobiography
questions.q: A young reader devours biographies of founders who left college and grew rich, and plans to leave college too. Given the authors' remark that a biography usually tells a more or less successful life, what should she weigh?
options: Founders' biographies are authorized, so their facts are largely invented
Those who took the same path and failed seldom get biographies written
Inspiration from a life should be resisted, since one life cannot teach another
Several founders' lives agreeing proves the path works for most who try it
optionExplain: Some may be authorized, but authorized does not mean invented, and that is not the main gap here.
Right: biographies are mostly of lives that succeeded, so her shelf overstates how often the path works.
The authors say a biography can inspire action; the point is to weigh what the inspiration rests on.
Agreement among success stories cannot show how many tried the same path and failed.
questions.explain: Biographies are usually written about more or less successful lives. A shelf of them shows the path's winners, not its odds.
questions.rule: A shelf of success stories is a biased sample.
questions.teaches: Because biographies are usually written about more or less successful lives, a shelf of them is a biased sample: those who took the same path and failed rarely get a biography, so inspiration should be checked against how often the path succeeds.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the four questions must be asked of anything you read, even when full analytical reading is not needed.
questions.explain: The authors relax the rules of analytical reading for much everyday reading, but not the four questions. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: The questions always apply.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: The authors say we have an obligation, as human beings and as ____, to try to understand the world around us.
questions.explain: History did not stop long ago; the world keeps changing, and understanding it is a duty, which is why current-events reading still gets the four questions.
questions.rule: Understanding the present is a citizen's duty.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: Sort each activity by whether, on the authors' account, it can be relaxed for an ordinary news article or must be kept for everything you read.

items.t: Making a full outline of the article
Asking what the article is about
Writing out each argument step by step
Asking whether its claims are true
Asking what follows from it for you
Rereading it several times for its structure

questions.explain: Outlining, writing out arguments and repeated rereading belong to full analytical reading, which much news does not need. The four questions stay.
questions.rule: Relax the rules, keep the questions.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: A reader scans headlines on a news app each morning and stops at a long piece on interest rates. What do the authors' rules ask of her?
options: A full analytical reading, since every text deserves the same effort
At least the four questions, whether or not she reads it analytically
No questions at all, since news is read only for its information
Only a check of the source's reputation, since that settles how far to trust it
optionExplain: The authors say analytical reading is not always necessary.
Right: the four questions are asked of anything; full analytical reading is optional.
Even reading for information calls for the four questions, in the authors' view.
Knowing the source helps, but it does not replace asking what the piece says, whether it is true and what follows.
questions.explain: She can skip the full apparatus of analytical reading, but not the questions: what it is about, what it says, whether it is true, and what of it.
questions.rule: Every article gets the four questions.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: Suppose the same report on interest rates is reprinted in a history book thirty years later. On the authors' view, how does the reader's basic problem change?
options: It disappears, since time has confirmed the facts
It grows, since history is less reliable than news
It changes kind, since history needs no questions
Little, as both pose the problem of knowing facts
optionExplain: Time can bring more accounts, but it does not by itself confirm the facts.
The authors do not rank news above history; they say the problem is the same.
The four questions apply to history as to any expository book.
Right: the authors say current events pose the same problem as history.
questions.explain: Whether read as news or as history, the report raises the same question: how do we know that what we are told is true?
questions.rule: News and history share one problem.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: A manager receives a two-paragraph company-wide email announcing a reorganisation. Applying the authors' advice on current events, how should she read it?
options: Briefly, still asking what it says, if true, and what follows
With full analytical reading, outlining its structure in detail
Without questions, since internal announcements state plain facts
Only for the date on which the change is due to take effect
optionExplain: Right: a short text needs little time per question, but the questions still apply.
Two paragraphs do not call for the full rules of analytical reading.
An announcement is a report of current events written by someone; it still invites the questions.
The date is one fact; what the change means for her is the question that matters most.
questions.explain: The email is current-events reading in miniature. The four questions take a minute, not an hour, but they are still asked.
questions.rule: Short texts get short questions, not none.
questions.teaches: By extension, the effort scales with the text: a short notice may need only a moment per question, so asking the four questions of everything need not make reading slow.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: According to the authors, what is the most important thing to know when reading any report of current events?
options: When it was published, and how recently
Where it appeared, and how widely it sold
Who wrote it, and what kind of mind he has
How long it is, and how much detail it gives
optionExplain: Recency matters for news, but it does not tell you how the report was shaped.
Circulation shows reach, not how the events were filtered.
