Right: the authors say the most important thing is who is writing the report, meaning the kind of mind he has.
Length and detail can come from any kind of mind; they do not reveal the filter.
questions.explain: Every report passes through a reporter's mind. The card next explains why that makes the writer the key question.
questions.rule: Ask who wrote it.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: Ideally, the authors say, a reporter is a clear ____ through which reality shines, but the human mind is not like that.
questions.explain: The human mind reflects poorly and filters what passes through it, separating out what it takes to be untrue.
questions.rule: Not a clear glass, a filter.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: The authors say a reporter's mind filters out what it takes to be untrue. How do they judge this filtering?
options: Improper, since a reporter ought to pass on everything he hears and let readers judge
Harmless, since a reporter's sense of what is true is reliable
Proper, though the reporter may be mistaken about what is untrue
Dishonest, since it shows the reporter is pursuing an agenda
optionExplain: The authors call the filtering proper; passing on everything would include what he believes false.
The authors warn that the reporter may be mistaken, so the filter is not harmless.
Right: a reporter should not report what he thinks false, but his judgment can be wrong.
Filtering what one believes false is honest; the risk is error, not deceit.
questions.explain: The filter is proper and unavoidable. The danger is that it can filter wrongly, which is why the reader needs to know the kind of mind behind it.
questions.rule: Proper filtering can still err.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: Two reporters cover the same council meeting. One, a business writer, stresses the budget; the other, an education writer, stresses school closures. Following the authors, what explains the difference?
options: Each mind filtered the same events in its own way
One of the two must have misreported the meeting
The meeting must have had two separate agendas
Reporters choose their emphasis more or less at random
optionExplain: Right: different minds pass the same reality through different filters.
Both may be accurate; they differ in what their minds selected.
One meeting can be filtered into two different stories without two agendas.
The emphasis follows each writer's kind of mind, which is why the authors want to know it.
questions.explain: The reporters' interests shaped what each one noticed and stressed. Knowing each writer's beat tells the reader what kind of filter shaped each report.
questions.rule: Different filters, different stories.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: Suppose a report is published with no byline and nothing about who wrote it. Following the authors, what becomes harder?
options: Understanding what the words of the report mean
Reading the report for its basic information
Telling whether it is a report of current events
Judging what filter the report has passed through
optionExplain: The words can still be understood; what is lost is knowledge of the mind that chose them.
The information can still be read; the reader knows less about how it was filtered.
Its subject still shows whether it concerns current events.
Right: without knowing the writer, the reader loses the main clue to the kind of mind behind the report.
questions.explain: The authors' first concern is the writer's mind. Without a name or background, the reader must infer the filter from the report itself, which is harder.
questions.rule: No writer, no easy view of the filter.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: True or false: On the authors' view, because a reporter's mind is a filter, a reader is wise to set news reports aside as distorted.
questions.explain: The authors call filtering proper; a reporter should leave out what he thinks false. The point is to know the filter, not to set reports aside.
questions.rule: Know the filter; do not reject the report.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: You hear about a client meeting from a colleague who heard about it from the manager who attended. Applying the authors' idea of the filter, how does this differ from hearing the manager's own account?
options: It is more reliable, since two people have now checked the account
The account has passed through two filters on its way to you, not one
It is the same, since the facts of the meeting have not changed
It is worthless, since secondhand accounts of meetings are rumours
optionExplain: Passing a report on is not checking it; each teller filters it again.
Right: the manager filtered the meeting, and your colleague then filtered the manager's account.
The meeting is unchanged, but what reaches you has been shaped twice.
A secondhand account can still be useful; the point is to allow for the extra filter.
questions.explain: Each mind a report passes through acts as a filter. A relayed account carries the filtering of every teller between you and the event.
questions.rule: Each relay adds a filter.
questions.teaches: By extension, a report relayed through several people has been filtered at each step, so the further a reader stands from the event, the more filters lie between.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, it is mostly safe to assume that a book about current events wants to prove something.
questions.explain: The authors say it is safe, for the most part, to assume every current-events book has something to prove. The card next shows where to find it.
questions.rule: Current-events books argue.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: According to the authors, the main thesis of a current-events book is often stated in its blurb or, if not there, in the author's ____.
questions.explain: Current-events books usually announce what they want to prove early: in the blurb, or else in the preface.
questions.rule: Check the blurb and the preface.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: Which questions about audience do the authors suggest asking of a current-events book? Select all that apply.
options: Is it written for readers of a certain age?
Is it for readers who know the author's earlier books?
Is it written for those in the know?
Is it for a small group able to act quickly?
Is it written for everyone?
optionExplain: The authors do not raise age; their concern is knowledge and power to act.
Familiarity with the author is not among the audiences the authors name.
Right: the authors ask whether the book is for insiders, and whether you are one.
Right: or for a small group who can do something, and quickly.
Right: or for everyone.
questions.explain: The authors' three audiences are insiders, a small group able to act, and the general public. Knowing which tells you whether you are among the intended readers.
questions.rule: Insiders, actors, or everyone.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: A short book on a hospital merger opens with a preface addressed to the hospital's board, who must vote within a month. A curious general reader picks it up. What do the authors' questions suggest?
options: She must read it, since every current-events book is for everyone
She is outside the intended audience and may decide not to read it
She should skip the preface, since it does not affect the content
She should assume it proves nothing, since it is written for insiders
optionExplain: The authors list several possible audiences; not every book is for everyone.
Right: the book is for a small group able to act quickly; she may not want to read it.
The preface is where she learns whom the book addresses, which bears on how to read it.
A book for insiders still wants to prove something, to them.
questions.explain: The preface shows the book is aimed at the board. A reader outside that audience may choose not to read it, or read it knowing it was not meant for her.
questions.rule: Know whom the book is talking to.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: Suppose a current-events book's blurb and preface state no thesis at all. Following the authors, what should the reader assume?
options: It wants to prove nothing and does no more than report the facts
It is likely a neutral survey, since arguing books announce their thesis early
It cannot be understood until the author explains his aim
It still probably wants to prove something, to be found by reading
optionExplain: An unstated thesis is not an absent one.
Blurbs and prefaces are shortcuts; silence there does not make a book neutral.
The reader can discover the thesis from the book itself.
Right: the authors say it is mostly safe to assume such books want to prove something; the reader must find it.
questions.explain: The blurb and preface are shortcuts. When they are silent, the presumption that the book argues something still holds, and the reader looks for it in the text.
questions.rule: No stated thesis is not no thesis.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: A think-tank report on energy prices opens with a summary saying government subsidies must end. Applying the authors' first two questions, how should a reader proceed?
options: Take the summary as the thesis to test, and ask whom the report addresses
Skip the summary, since conclusions belong only at the end of a report
Accept the summary, since think tanks are staffed by experts
Treat the report as neutral data, since it deals in prices
optionExplain: Right: knowing what is to be proved, and to whom, lets the reader read the evidence as a test of the claim.
The summary is the shortcut to the thesis, like a blurb or preface.
Expertise does not remove the aim to prove something; the thesis still needs testing.
A report that opens with a call to end subsidies is arguing, not only reporting.
questions.explain: The summary works like a blurb: it names the thesis. Reading with that thesis in mind lets the reader check each point against it.
questions.rule: Know the claim, then test it.
questions.teaches: Knowing the thesis before reading turns the evidence into a test: the reader can watch whether each point supports the claim instead of being carried along by it.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: When the authors ask what special knowledge a current-events author assumes, what words do they say might fit better than knowledge?
options: Training or degrees
Facts or figures
Opinion or prejudice
Sources or contacts
optionExplain: The question is about what the reader is assumed to share, not the author's credentials.
Facts are what the author reports; the assumptions lie beneath them.
Right: the authors say opinion or prejudice might have been a better choice of word.
Sources come up under the fifth question, not this one.
questions.explain: What an author assumes his readers know is often what he assumes they believe. The card next explains why that matters.
questions.rule: Assumed knowledge is often assumed opinion.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: True or false: According to Basil Willey, as the authors quote him, people find it easy to become aware of their own habitual assumptions.
questions.explain: Willey says it is almost insuperably difficult; doctrines felt as facts are seen to be doctrines only after great effort, and are easier to see in another age.
questions.rule: Our own assumptions feel like facts.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: A reader finds herself furious after a few pages of a book on immigration. Following the authors, what should she check first?
options: Whether the publisher has a reputation for producing honest books
Whether the book's statistics have gone out of date since it appeared
Whether she rejects assumptions the author expects her to share
Whether she has looked at the book's index and notes before reading
optionExplain: The publisher's reputation does not explain why she reacts as she does.
Old figures might mislead, but irritation after a few pages more often signals a clash of assumptions.
Right: the authors say a reader who disagrees sharply with the author's assumptions may only be irritated.
Inspecting the book helps in general, but the authors' point here is about assumptions.
questions.explain: Her anger may come from the author's assumptions, not his facts. Seeing that lets her decide whether to read on and how to weigh what she reads.
questions.rule: Irritation can signal a clash of assumptions.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: Which words in a news story are most likely to call for the control of responses the authors recommend? Select all that apply.
options: Extremist
Radical
Tuesday
Kilometre
Regime
optionExplain: Right: extremist provokes a strong response before any facts are weighed.
Right: radical stirs feelings that depend on the reader and the time.
A day of the week provokes no special response.
A unit of measure carries no emotional charge.
Right: like the authors' example of Communist, regime carries a charge beyond its plain meaning.
questions.explain: Charged words provoke responses before judgment. The authors ask readers to control these responses, or at least notice them.
questions.rule: Notice the words that move you.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: Suppose a reader a century from now reads an article full of words that stir strong feelings today. What do the authors' remarks suggest?
options: The words may not provoke in her the responses they provoke now
The words will provoke even stronger responses as time passes
The words will mean nothing at all to a reader of that time
The words carry a fixed charge that will be the same for her
optionExplain: Right: the authors note that certain words provoke responses now that they might not provoke a century hence.
The authors suggest the charge fades with distance, not that it grows.
The meaning may survive; it is the special response that may not.
The authors' point is that the charge belongs to a time, not to the word forever.
questions.explain: A word's charge belongs partly to its time. That is why reading about our own time is hardest: we feel the charge most.
questions.rule: Charged words belong to their time.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: A new employee from another country notices that her colleagues treat long working hours as a sign of dedication, a view seldom questioned there. Applying Willey's point as the authors use it, why can she see this more easily than they can?
options: She is more perceptive than any of her new colleagues
Her colleagues are hiding what they really believe
Long hours are plainly wrong, as any outsider can see
She stands outside their habits, as a later age does
optionExplain: Ability is not the point; her position outside their habits is.
Doctrines felt as facts are held sincerely, not hidden.
Seeing an assumption does not settle whether it is wrong.
Right: assumptions are easier to see from a distance, whether of time or of place.
questions.explain: Willey says doctrines felt as facts are easier to see in another age. Her outsider's position gives her a similar distance.
questions.rule: Distance reveals assumptions.
questions.teaches: By analogy, distance in place works like distance in time: an outsider to a group can often see its doctrines felt as facts, so asking outsiders is one way to find one's own.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reporter with no bias who wants only to tell the truth can still mislead his readers.
questions.explain: A sincere reporter may be uninformed about things kept secret, perhaps without knowing it. The card next explains this danger.
questions.rule: Good will is not full knowledge.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: The authors sum up their advice on reading current events in the Latin warning Caveat ____, let the reader beware.
questions.explain: Caveat lector warns that a contemporary author, or his sources, may have an interest in how you understand what you read.
questions.rule: Let the reader beware.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: A reporter writes in good faith that a treaty negotiation has failed, not knowing that a secret agreement was reached. In the authors' terms, what is his problem?
options: He is biased toward one side of the negotiation he describes
He is uninformed rather than biased, a perilous case
He uses special language that provokes strong responses
He wrote for insiders rather than for the general public
optionExplain: Nothing suggests bias; his good faith is given.
Right: he means well but lacks the facts, and if he does not know it, his readers are in special peril.
Charged words are the fourth question; his trouble is missing information.
His audience does not explain the error; his lack of information does.
questions.explain: The fifth question asks whether the reporter really knows. Here bias is absent, yet the report is wrong, because secret actions were hidden from him.
questions.rule: Ask whether he could know.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: A news article about a company's layoffs relies entirely on a statement from the company's press office. Following the authors, what should a reader ask?
options: Whether the article uses words with a strong emotional charge
Whether the source has an interest in how readers understand it
Whether the article is long enough to be fully trustworthy
Whether the reporter is someone the reader knows personally
optionExplain: Charged words matter, but the main concern here is the interested source.
Right: the authors warn that the sources of an author's information may have an interest in your reading.
Length does not tell whether the source has a stake in the story.
The authors care about the kind of mind behind the report, not personal acquaintance.
questions.explain: Even if the reporter is fair, the press office has an interest in how the layoffs are understood. Caveat lector covers the sources as well as the author.
questions.rule: Beware the source's interest too.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, readers need to be as wary of Aristotle, Dante or Shakespeare as of any contemporary book.
questions.explain: The authors say readers do not have to be wary when reading Aristotle, Dante or Shakespeare. The warning is aimed at contemporary writing, where an author or his sources may have a stake in your reading.
questions.rule: The warning is for contemporary writing.

questions.section: How to Read About Current Events
questions.q: A detailed online review praises a new phone. The reviewer seems honest, but the site earns a fee when readers buy through its links. Applying Caveat lector, what should a reader do?
options: Trust the review, since the reviewer seems honest, careful and well informed
Disregard the review, since any review with links must be false
Look only at the star rating, since written reviews can mislead
Allow for the site's interest in her buying, while weighing the review
optionExplain: The reviewer's honesty does not remove the site's interest in a sale.
The authors say an author may have an interest, not that every such text is false.
The rating comes from the same interested channel.
Right: an interest can stand behind an honest writer; the reader allows for it without dismissing the review.
questions.explain: The reviewer may be sincere, but the site profits from a favourable reading. Knowing that interest and allowing for it is what the warning asks.
questions.rule: Know who profits from your reading.
questions.teaches: By analogy, an interest can sit behind an honest writer: the writer may be sincere while the outlet publishing him profits from a certain reading, so Caveat lector applies to the channel as well as the author.

questions.q: How do the authors judge a good condensation of an average, mainly informational magazine article?
options: Usually adequate, and sometimes better than the original
Worse in every case, since all condensing loses something
Of no use, since information has to be read in full
Acceptable only when the original is read as well
optionExplain: Right: for the average informational article, the authors say a condensation is usually adequate and often better.
The authors reserve the warning about loss for the very best writing.
Digests exist because there is too much information to read in full, and the authors praise them for it.
Reading the original is advised for the best writing, not for the average article.
questions.explain: The authors value digests for informational material. The card next shows where they stop being enough.
questions.rule: Digests suit the average article.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the people who write news magazines and digests are first of all skilled readers.
questions.explain: The authors say these writers have developed reading for information far beyond the average reader; the writing comes second.
questions.rule: Good digesting starts with good reading.

questions.q: Sort each piece of writing by whether, on the authors' view, a digest of it usually serves or the original should be read.

items.t: A routine report on quarterly sales figures
A celebrated essay by a great writer
A roundup of this week's transport news
A masterly argument on the nature of justice
A notice of changes to tax filing dates
A famous speech admired for its thought

questions.explain: Mainly informational pieces condense well. The best writing, like Montaigne's essays, cannot be condensed without loss.
questions.rule: Condense information; read the best in full.

questions.q: A student reads a two-page summary of a classic essay instead of the essay and feels she knows it. By the authors' account, how should the summary have been used?
options: As a full substitute, since the core was kept
As the final word on what the essay means
As a spur to go and read the essay itself
As a test of whether the essay has any value
optionExplain: The best writing cannot be condensed without loss, so no core is enough.
The summary is one reader's condensation, not the authority on the essay.
Right: a summary of the best writing works well only if it leads the reader to the original.
A classic essay's value is not in question; the summary's role is to lead to it.
questions.explain: For first-rate writing, the authors say a summary serves only if it impels us to read the original.
questions.rule: A summary of the best should send you to it.

questions.q: Suppose a news magazine's editors are poor readers of the reports they condense. What happens to the value of their digest, by the authors' account?
options: It stays the same, since clear writing is what matters most
It rises, since less skilled readers keep in more detail
It falls, since a digest is first of all a work of reading
It stays the same, since the facts themselves do not change
optionExplain: The authors put plain, lucid writing second, after reading.
Poor reading is more likely to miss the core than to keep more of value.
Right: the authors say the skill behind a digest is first of all a skill in reading.
The facts stay the same, but which of them reach the reader depends on the editors' reading.
questions.explain: A digest is only as good as the reading behind it. Poor readers cut the wrong things, however well they write.
questions.rule: A digest is as good as its editors' reading.

questions.q: A book-summary app offers ten-minute versions of business bestsellers and of great works of philosophy alike. Applying the authors' view of digests, how should a reader use it?
options: For informational books it may serve; for great works, as a pointer
For every book alike, since each summary keeps the essential core
For no book at all, since summaries lose the point of what they cover
For the great works only, since those are too long to read in full
optionExplain: Right: condensation suits mainly informational writing; for the best books it should lead to the original.
The best books cannot be condensed without loss, so the core is not enough.
For mainly informational writing, the authors say condensation is usually adequate.
Length is not the test; the more a book rewards understanding, the more a summary loses.
questions.explain: The authors' line falls between informational writing and the best writing. A summary app fits the first and can only point toward the second.
questions.rule: Match the summary to the kind of text.
questions.teaches: The worth of a summary depends on the kind of text: the more a text's value lies in its thought rather than its facts, the more a summary of it loses.

questions.q: Which kind of reading do the authors say is sometimes the most demanding and difficult of all?
options: Reading lyric poems
Reading textbooks
Reading old letters
Reading digests
optionExplain: The authors find lyric poetry demanding in its own way, but this claim is about digests.
Textbooks are not the subject of this claim.
Old letters come up as historical sources, not as the hardest reading.
Right: the authors say reading digests is sometimes the most demanding and difficult reading you can do.
questions.explain: It sounds backwards, since digests are meant to save effort. The card next explains why the authors say it.
questions.rule: Short can be hard.

questions.q: According to the authors, the greater the condensation, the more important it is to know the character of the ____.
questions.explain: Heavy condensation means heavy selection, so whoever did the selecting matters more and more.
questions.rule: Know the condensor.

questions.q: Two digests of the same 600-page government report: one runs to 400 pages, the other to a single page. By the authors' reasoning, which calls for more care, and why?
options: The 400 pages, since there is far more text to check
The single page, since far more selection has occurred
Both equally, since both of them are digests
Neither, since a government report is factual and facts survive condensing
optionExplain: Length to check is not the issue; the amount omitted is.
Right: the more condensed the digest, the more critical the question of what was left out.
The authors distinguish light from heavy condensation; 1,000 to 900 is not 1,000 to one.
Facts can be selected and omitted like anything else, and heavy condensation omits most of them.
questions.explain: Going from 600 pages to one leaves almost everything out. The authors say that is when the question of omission becomes critical.
questions.rule: More cut, more care.

questions.q: Reading a heavily condensed digest with no access to the original, which steps fit the authors' advice? Select all that apply.
options: Read it quickly, since its editors did the hard work
Find out who did the condensing and how they lean
Infer from the digest itself what was likely left out
Read it with the care its editors gave the sources
Assume the condensor kept everything important
optionExplain: The editors saved us extent of reading, not the work of reading.
Right: the greater the condensation, the more the condensor's character matters.
Right: without the original, the reader reads between the lines of the condensation.
Right: the digest profits us only if we read it as well as its editors read the originals.
That trust is what the authors' warning about the condensor is meant to check.
questions.explain: Heavy condensation shifts the work onto the reader: knowing the condensor, inferring omissions and reading for understanding.
questions.rule: The digest saves pages, not thought.

questions.q: True or false: On the authors' reasoning, a digest that cuts 1,000 pages to 900 calls for as much concern about omissions as one that cuts them to ten.
questions.explain: The authors say we need not worry much when 1,000 pages become 900; the question of what was left out becomes critical as the condensation grows.
questions.rule: Concern grows with condensation.

questions.q: A director reads only a half-page executive summary of a 200-page safety audit before approving a plant restart. Applying the authors' view of digests, what should she do?
options: Approve it, since the summary was written by the audit's experts
Ask who wrote the summary and what such audits tend to qualify
Reject it, since a summary of an audit can never be relied on
Count the summary's points to judge how thorough the audit was
optionExplain: Expert authorship does not remove the selection that a half page requires.
Right: a heavy condensation calls for knowing the condensor and inferring what was left out.
The authors find digests valuable; the remedy is careful reading, not rejection.
The number of points says little about what was cut.
questions.explain: Two hundred pages cut to half a page is extreme selection, and a serious decision rests on it. That is when the condensor and the omissions matter most.
questions.rule: The heavier the cut and the decision, the harder you read.
questions.teaches: By analogy, an executive summary is a heavy condensation whose omissions carry most risk when a decision rests on it, so a decision-maker who cannot read the whole should at least question its author about what was cut.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the major scientific books written before about 1900 were aimed mainly at other specialists.
questions.explain: They were written for a lay audience, though their authors also welcomed specialist readers. The card next shows what this means for you as a reader.
questions.rule: The old classics were written for the educated public.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: According to the authors, science today tends to be written by experts for ____.
questions.explain: Modern scientific communication assumes so much specialized knowledge that outsiders usually cannot read it at all.
questions.rule: Modern science is written by experts for experts.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Marco wants to understand the foundations of physics but finds current physics journals unreadable. What do the authors' remarks suggest he try?
options: A recent research review written for working physicists in the field
Waiting until he has completed a degree in physics
A classic such as Newton's, written with lay readers in mind
Leaving physics for a field still written for everyone
optionExplain: A review sounds like a shortcut, but it is still expert writing for experts and assumes the training Marco lacks.
Training would help, but the authors' point is that the classics are open to an intelligent reader without it.
Right: the great classics were written for an educated lay audience, and the authors say none is impossibly difficult.
The authors note that other fields are drifting toward expert-only writing too, and in any case the classics answer his interest in physics.
questions.explain: The classics were written before science was walled off by specialization, so they are the part of serious science still open to a lay reader willing to work.
questions.rule: When current work is closed, go to the classics.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: A nurse wants to read about how historians work, but finds recent history monographs written in shorthand for other historians. Following the authors' reasoning about science, where is she likely to find readable accounts?
options: In older narrative works written for a general audience
In the newest monographs, since they are the most accurate
In conference papers, since they are shorter than books
Nowhere, since history has become an expert-only field
optionExplain: Right: the authors say historians are only beginning to adopt expert shorthand, while the traditional narrative was written for everyone.
Recency may bring accuracy, but these are the works written in shorthand for specialists, the ones she cannot read.
Length is not the barrier; conference papers are expert-to-expert communication too.
The authors describe a drift, not a closed field: the older narrative tradition remains open to her.
questions.explain: The authors describe the same move from writing for everyone to writing for specialists in history. Where a field is making that move, its older narrative works are the ones a general reader can enter.
questions.rule: In a field turning specialist, older works for everyone stay open.
questions.teaches: By extension, the move from writing for everyone to writing for specialists is a trend across fields, so in any field making it, the date and form of a work can tell you whether it was meant for a general reader.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: True or false: The authors say they cannot help a lay reader read specialized monographs on narrow, abstruse research topics.
questions.explain: They say their advice may sometimes apply to such monographs, but that they cannot help you read them, partly because they are not qualified. Their advice is for classics and popularizations.
questions.rule: The chapter's advice targets classics and popularizations.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Suppose the leading researchers in a field began writing their serious work for the general public again. By the authors' account, what would a lay reader gain?
options: Faster progress in the field, since lay readers could join the research
Nothing, since popularizations already cover the same results
Freedom from the effort that reading science demands
Direct access to the field's serious work, not only reports of it
optionExplain: The authors say the opposite tends to hold: expert-to-expert writing is what speeds research.
Popularizations report results through someone else; reading the work itself is a different and fuller access.
The classics were written for lay readers and still take effort; openness removes the barrier of training, not the work.
Right: the lay reader falls back on popularizations only because the serious work is closed; open it, and he can read the source.
questions.explain: The authors say the general reader must fall back on popularizations because he cannot become expert in every field. If serious work were written for all, he could read it directly, as readers of Galileo or Darwin once did.
questions.rule: Popularizations fill the gap that specialization leaves.
questions.teaches: By extension, a popularization is a second-best route forced by specialization: where serious work is written for everyone, the reader can go to the source instead of relying on someone's account of it.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: What do the authors call the most helpful advice for a lay reader of a scientific classic?
options: Learn the book's mathematics before starting
State the problem the author tried to solve
Read a modern textbook on the subject first
Memorize the book's main experimental results
optionExplain: Mathematics is a real obstacle, but the authors treat it later and even advise skipping much of it.
Right: they single out the rule of stating the author's problem.
Background helps, but the authors' chief advice is about the classic itself, not a substitute for it.
Results matter less to a lay reader than the problem they answered.
questions.explain: The authors pick out one familiar rule of analytical reading as most useful here. The card next shows which and why.
questions.rule: Start a scientific classic from its problem.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the rule of stating the author's problem applies only to scientific and mathematical books.
questions.explain: It is a rule for all expository works; the authors say it is particularly relevant to science and mathematics.
questions.rule: The rule is general; science is where it matters most.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it states a problem or only names a subject.

items.t: Why does a prism spread white light into colours?
What path does the blood take after leaving the heart?
Does a heavy body fall faster than a light one?
Light and colour
The heart and the blood
Motion in the seventeenth century

questions.explain: A problem is a question the author tries to answer, so it can be answered rightly or wrongly. A subject heading tells you what the book is about but not what it is trying to find out.
questions.rule: A problem is a question; a subject is a heading.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Leena starts Gilbert's book on magnets and gets lost in the descriptions of experiments with lodestones. Following the authors' advice, what should she do first?
options: Reread each experiment slowly until every detail is perfectly clear
Work out what question about magnets Gilbert set out to answer
Check a modern physics text to correct his outdated results
Skip ahead to the last chapter to collect his conclusions
optionExplain: Patience helps, but details stay confusing until she knows what they are meant to show.
Right: once she knows Gilbert's problem, each experiment has a place in his answer.
Correcting results serves a modern student, not a lay reader trying to follow the book.
Conclusions without the question they answer are hard to understand or judge.
questions.explain: Experiments are evidence for an answer to some question. Finding the question first lets Leena see what each experiment is for.
questions.rule: Find the question before sorting the evidence.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: An engineer reads a design document and first states its problem: pages must load in under a second for a million users. Beyond orienting her reading, what does this statement give her?
options: A full list of the design's technical choices
Proof that the chosen tools are up to date
A summary she can use instead of the document
A test of whether the design actually solves it
optionExplain: The choices are in the document; the problem statement gives the purpose they serve, not the list.
A problem statement says nothing about how modern the tools are.
Knowing the problem is a start, not a substitute for the solution the document describes.
Right: a well-stated problem says what success looks like, so she can later check whether the design delivers it.
questions.explain: A precise statement of the problem also fixes what would count as solving it. That lets her judge, after reading, whether the design answers the problem it set itself.
questions.rule: A well-stated problem is also a test of the answer.
questions.teaches: A good statement of a problem also tells you what would count as solving it, so stating the problem first lets you judge later whether the author's answer actually addresses it.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: A student writes: The problem of Newton's Optics is light. What is wrong with this as a statement of the author's problem?
options: It names a subject, not a question Newton tried to answer
It is too short to count as a statement of anyone's problem
It should give Newton's conclusions rather than his topic
It treats an old book as if it were still modern science
optionExplain: Right: light is what the book is about; the problem is what Newton wanted to find out about it.
Length is not the test; a short question can state a problem well.
Conclusions come later; the rule asks for the question the conclusions answer.
The statement says nothing about modernity; its fault is that it asks no question.
questions.explain: A problem can be answered; a subject cannot. Something like how white light is made up and why a prism splits it would state a problem.
questions.rule: If it cannot be answered, it is not yet a problem.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a lay reader reads the scientific classics chiefly to understand the history and philosophy of science.
questions.explain: That is the purpose the authors give, rather than mastering the subject as it stands today. The card next explains what it involves.
questions.rule: Classics are not current textbooks.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: According to the authors, which should a lay reader become aware of in reading the scientific classics? Choose two.
options: The errors later scientists found in each book
The personal quarrels among the great scientists
The problems the great scientists were trying to solve
The background against which those problems arose
The current state of research in the same field
optionExplain: Later corrections can be interesting, but the authors stress the problems and their background, not a list of errors.
The Newton industry does study personality, but the authors' advice to readers centres on problems.
Right: awareness of the problems is the main way to meet the layman's responsibility.
Right: the authors add the background of the problems to the problems themselves.
Current research is what a modern specialist needs; the lay reader's aim is historical and philosophical.
questions.explain: The authors name two things: the problems the great scientists tried to solve, and the background of those problems.
questions.rule: Know the problem and what lay behind it.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Aisha is reading an eighteenth-century treatise that treats heat as an invisible fluid. Which response fits the authors' purpose for lay readers?
options: Stop reading, since a disproved theory has nothing left to teach
Correct each passage against a modern physics text as she reads
Ask why a heat fluid seemed to answer the puzzles of its day
Take the treatise as a reliable guide to how heat behaves
optionExplain: A theory can be wrong and still show what the problem was and how science moved past it.
Correcting it treats the book as a faulty textbook; that serves current knowledge, not history.
Right: the problems the theory answered, and their background, are what the lay reader reads for.
Old classics are often superseded; trusting this one for current facts mistakes its use.
questions.explain: A superseded theory still shows what puzzled scientists and how they tried to answer it, which is the history the lay reader is after.
questions.rule: Read old science for its problems, not its facts.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Sort each reading aim by whether a scientific classic suits it or a modern text would serve better.

items.t: Seeing what puzzled chemists around 1780
Learning why an old theory once seemed convincing
Following how a key idea first took shape
Preparing for a chemistry examination next month
Looking up the accepted value of a constant
Learning current laboratory safety rules

questions.explain: Aims about how science developed and what problems it faced suit the classics. Aims about current knowledge or practice need a modern source.
questions.rule: Historical aims go to classics; current aims go to modern texts.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Reading the debates over a long-replaced law, a lawyer notices that its phrase reasonable care still appears in statutes today. By analogy with reading superseded science, what does this show?
options: Today's law must still be the same as the old law
The old law was right after all and never needed replacing
Old answers leave traces in the terms still in use
Legal language has no connection with legal history
optionExplain: A surviving phrase does not mean the surrounding law is unchanged; the law was replaced.
Keeping a phrase is not endorsing the whole old law; the phrase can be put to new use.
Right: terms often outlive the law or theory that coined them, and the old view explains what they carry.
The surviving phrase is direct evidence of the link between today's language and its history.
questions.explain: Superseded work explains present language. Knowing the old problem and answer helps a reader see why a term still in use means what it does, much as old scientific terms survive their theories.
questions.rule: Old answers survive in today's words.
questions.teaches: Superseded work explains present language: terms often outlive the theory or law that coined them, so knowing the old view helps a reader see why today's words carry the meanings they do.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Aisha's nephew must pass a school physics test next week and asks to study from her eighteenth-century heat treatise. What does the authors' purpose for lay readers imply?
options: He needs a modern text, since his aim is current knowledge
He should use the treatise, since classics teach best
He should read the treatise alongside its preface only
He should use it, provided he states the old author's problem first
optionExplain: Right: the historical purpose fits a lay reader; an exam tests the subject as it stands today.
Classics teach the history and philosophy of science best, not the current subject.
A partial reading still teaches the old theory, not what the test will ask.
Stating the problem helps him understand the book, but the book still teaches a superseded theory.
questions.explain: When the condition changes from understanding science to mastering its present content, the classic is the wrong tool; the authors make the same point about Lavoisier and a school examination.
questions.rule: Change the aim, and the right book changes.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Which do the authors name as the central aim of education since Socrates?
options: Passing on the settled results of each science
Training skills that are useful in working life
Teaching students to distrust every authority
Freeing the mind through the discipline of wonder
optionExplain: Settled results matter, but the authors place the aim in what education does to the mind, not in what it transmits.
Useful skills are a common goal of schooling, but not the aim the authors name.
Questioning is part of wonder, but distrust of all authority is not the aim they name.
Right: the authors tie the historical study of science to this aim.
questions.explain: The authors name the freeing of the mind through the discipline of wonder. The card next shows how tracing the strands of science serves it.
questions.rule: Education frees the mind through disciplined wonder.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: According to the authors, which are reasons for studying the history of science by tracing its strands? Choose three.
options: It removes the need for modern scientific textbooks
It shows reason working where it has had most success
It dispels some of the apparent unintelligibility of science
It is essential to education as the freeing of the mind
It trains readers to carry out research of their own
optionExplain: The lay reader's purpose differs from a student's; textbooks still serve current knowledge.
Right: the authors say this alone may justify the historical study of science.
Right: they say such study dispels, in some measure, science's apparent unintelligibility.
Right: they call this the most important reason of all.
The authors speak of understanding science, not of training researchers.
questions.explain: The authors give three reasons: reason at its most successful, making science less unintelligible, and education's aim of freeing the mind through wonder.
questions.rule: Three gains: see reason work, understand science, free the mind.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Tom knows that the Earth goes round the Sun but cannot say why anyone believes it. Which activity, in the authors' sense, would change this?
options: Learning the planets' orbits and distances more exactly than before
Tracing the observations and reasoning behind the conclusion
Accepting it, since today's experts agree on it
Reading a summary list of the main facts of astronomy
optionExplain: More precise facts are still facts without their reasons; Tom's gap is the link, not the detail.
Right: following how facts, assumptions and proofs connect is what makes a result intelligible.
Accepting on authority is the very thing that leaves science looking unintelligible.
A list of facts gives results without the strands joining them.
questions.explain: Tom has a result without its reasons. Tracing the strand from observations through assumptions to the conclusion turns a fact he was told into one he understands.
questions.rule: Understanding a result means following its reasons.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Suppose a reader traces only the facts of a science, collecting results but not the assumptions and proofs that join them. What does the authors' account suggest she misses?
options: Nothing important, since facts are the core of any science
How the results connect, which makes science intelligible
Only the mathematics, which a lay reader may skip anyway
The latest results, which the classics do not contain
optionExplain: Facts matter, but the strands are the relations among them; without those, science stays opaque.
Right: the authors define the activity as tracing how facts, assumptions, principles and proofs interrelate.
Proofs are not all mathematical, and the lost links include assumptions and principles.
Recency is not the issue here; the loss is the links among whatever results she has.
questions.explain: Change the condition by dropping the links, and the activity becomes fact-collecting. The authors' gains, such as dispelling unintelligibility, come from the connections.
questions.rule: The strands are the links, not the facts.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: A baker knows her bread recipe works but not why. She traces how yeast, sugar, warmth and time depend on one another. By analogy with tracing the strands of science, what does she gain beyond the recipe?
options: She can bake the same loaf faster than she did before
She learns that the recipe was wrong in several steps
She no longer needs a written recipe for any other kind of bread
She can see why the steps hold together, and adjust them
optionExplain: Understanding may help, but speed is not what tracing the links provides.
Tracing explains why steps work; it does not imply they were wrong.
Understanding the links helps her adapt recipes; it does not replace them all.
Right: knowing which step depends on which lets her adapt when conditions change, say a cold kitchen.
questions.explain: Tracing the links turns a working procedure into an understood one, so she can see what to change when one condition changes.
questions.rule: Knowing why lets you adjust how.
questions.teaches: By analogy, tracing why a practice works, not only that it works, lets a person adapt it when conditions change, because they can see which step depends on which.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: True or false: Tracing the historical strands of a science is the quickest way to get a result you need to act on today.
questions.explain: Tracing strands is slow work aimed at understanding. For a result to act on now, a reliable modern statement of it is quicker.
questions.rule: Tracing is for understanding, not for speed.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: According to the authors, what kind of research can a scientific book report?
options: Laboratory experiment or observation of nature
Only experiments done under laboratory control
Only reasoning from accepted mathematical axioms
Reflection on ordinary everyday experience
optionExplain: Right: the authors include research done experimentally and research done by observing nature in the raw.
The laboratory is one setting, but observation in the field counts too.
Reasoning from axioms describes mathematics, not the report of research findings.
Ordinary experience is what the authors elsewhere tie to philosophy, not to science.
questions.explain: Both experiment and observation count as research for the authors' definition. The card next gives the definition and the problem every scientific book faces.
questions.rule: Science reports experiment or observation.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: The authors say the scientific problem is to describe the phenomena as accurately as possible and to trace the ____ between different kinds of phenomena.
questions.explain: The scientific problem has two parts: accurate description, and tracing how different kinds of phenomena are interconnected.
questions.rule: Describe accurately, then connect.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: A geologist's book records the layers of a cliff in exact detail, then argues that the shell-rich layers formed when the area lay under the sea. Which part of the scientific problem does the second step address?
options: Describing the phenomena as accurately as possible
Stating the assumptions the author takes for granted
Tracing a connection between kinds of phenomena
Reporting a single case created by an experiment
optionExplain: Exact recording of the layers was the first step; the second goes beyond description.
Assumptions may lie behind the argument, but the step itself draws a connection.
Right: linking a kind of rock layer to a kind of past condition connects two kinds of phenomena.
The geologist observed a cliff; nothing in the step is an experiment.
questions.explain: Recording the layers describes; linking shell-rich layers to an ancient sea traces an interconnection between kinds of phenomena.
questions.rule: Linking kinds of events is the second job of science.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: Sort each book by whether it fits the authors' definition of a scientific book.

items.t: A report of field observations on how wolves hunt
An account of experiments on how plants turn toward light
A study of star positions measured over ten years
A guide telling parents how they ought to discipline children
A memoir of one climber's trip up a mountain
A treatise reasoning about justice from common experience

questions.explain: The first three report findings from observation or experiment. The guide argues what ought to be done, the memoir tells one particular story, and the treatise reasons from ordinary experience rather than research.
questions.rule: Scientific means a report of research findings.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: A shop report counts customers each hour with an electronic counter, then claims that visits rise on rainy days, using rainfall remembered by the manager. Judged by the two parts of the scientific problem, where is the weakness?
options: The visit counts are too exact to compare with rainfall
A shop is not a proper place to look for connections
The connection rests on a careless description of the rain
Tracing connections should come before any description
optionExplain: Exactness is a virtue; the problem is that the other side of the comparison lacks it.
By analogy, the two-part problem fits any careful study of events, wherever they occur.
Right: one phenomenon is described carefully and the other from memory, so the claimed link is only as good as the weaker description.
The authors put accurate description first; reversing the order would make things worse.
questions.explain: A connection joins two descriptions. When one of them is careless, the connection cannot be trusted, however precise the other side is.
questions.rule: A connection is no better than its weaker description.
questions.teaches: The two parts of the scientific problem depend on each other: a connection between kinds of phenomena can be no more trustworthy than the description of each, so careful description of one side does not rescue a careless description of the other.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: True or false: A book that uses many technical terms from physics counts as scientific in the authors' sense even if it reports no research at all.
questions.explain: The authors define a scientific book as a report of findings or conclusions from research. Borrowing the vocabulary of physics does not meet that definition.
questions.rule: Vocabulary does not make a book scientific.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the great works of science can contain bias even though they contain no propaganda.
questions.explain: They can have bias in the sense of initial presuppositions. The card next shows how to detect it.
questions.rule: No propaganda does not mean no presuppositions.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: According to the authors, how do you detect a scientific author's initial bias?
options: By separating what he assumes from what he proves
By checking whether he has a stake in the result
By looking for emotional language and appeals
By comparing his conclusions with later science
optionExplain: Right: the bias lies in presuppositions, so it shows up when you sort assumptions from conclusions.
Stakes matter in persuasion, but the bias the authors mean is a set of starting assumptions.
The authors say the great scientific works have no oratory, so emotional language is not where the bias lies.
Later science may correct a book, but that tests results; it does not reveal what the author took for granted.
questions.explain: The bias of a great scientific work is its set of initial presuppositions, which you find by telling what is assumed from what is argued for.
questions.rule: Find the bias in the assumptions.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: Each line describes how a claim appears in a book on animal nutrition. Sort the claims by whether the author assumes them or establishes them.

items.t: Stated at the outset without argument: the test rats are typical of their species
Asked of the reader at the start: weight gain measures how well food is used
Taken for granted throughout: the scales give accurate readings
Shown by feeding trials: rats fed polished rice lose weight
Concluded from repeated measurements: the added husk restores growth
Argued from three experiments: the loss is caused by the missing husk

questions.explain: Claims stated at the start, asked of the reader or taken for granted are presuppositions. Claims backed by trials, measurements or experiments are established through argument.
questions.rule: Granted at the start goes on one list; proved by evidence on the other.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: A reader finds that a physics classic assumes, without argument, that space is the same in every direction. She decides the book is biased and therefore worthless. Which statement corrects her reasoning?
options: She must prove the assumption false before she can fairly read on
Assumptions in physics are always proved later in the book
Bias matters only when an author uses oratory or propaganda
Having presuppositions does not make a scientific book worthless
optionExplain: Testing the assumption is fair later, but understanding the book does not wait on refuting it.
Some assumptions stay assumptions; the point of the sorting is that not everything is proved.
The authors say presuppositions are a real kind of bias, even without propaganda; they must be taken into account.
Right: every science starts from presuppositions; finding one tells her where conclusions depend, not that they fail.
questions.explain: The authors expect scientific works to have initial presuppositions. The reader's job is to spot them and allow for them, not to reject the book for having them.
questions.rule: An assumption marks a dependence, not a defeat.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: A town's forecast assumes the population will grow 2 percent a year and calculates the schools needed. A reader reruns it with 1 and 3 percent, and the number of schools changes by half. What does this show?
options: The forecast's arithmetic contains a hidden mistake
The conclusion depends heavily on that one assumption
The growth figure has now been established by argument
Growth assumptions do not matter for school planning
optionExplain: The arithmetic may be fine; the large swing comes from the changed starting point.
Right: when varying an assumption swings the result, the result hangs on it, so that is where scrutiny belongs.
Varying an assumption tests how much rides on it; it does not prove it.
The large swing shows the opposite: this assumption matters a great deal.
questions.explain: Varying an assumed figure and watching the conclusion move shows how much the argument rests on it. Here the assumption carries much of the weight.
questions.rule: Vary an assumption to see how much rides on it.
questions.teaches: Assumptions can be tested by changing them: if a conclusion barely moves when an assumption is varied, the assumption matters little; if it swings widely, the whole result hangs on it.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: True or false: If a scientific author does not say which starting points he is assuming, the reader may treat all of his claims as established.
questions.explain: Unstated assumptions are still assumptions. The reader then has to find them in the argument, by asking what each proof takes for granted.
questions.rule: Unstated assumptions still need finding.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: According to the authors, what does scientific objectivity consist in?
options: Having no presuppositions of any kind
Openly confessing one's initial bias
Keeping personal views out of the text
Agreeing with most experts in the field
optionExplain: This is the common picture the authors reject; some presuppositions are unavoidable.
Right: the authors say objectivity is attained by frank confession of bias.
Avoiding personal remarks is a style, but it can hide presuppositions rather than reveal them.
Consensus is a different matter; an author can agree with experts and still conceal his assumptions.
questions.explain: The authors locate objectivity in openness about presuppositions, not in having none. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Objectivity is candour about assumptions.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: Scientific objectivity, the authors say, is not the absence of initial bias but is attained by frank ____ of it.
questions.explain: The authors write that objectivity is attained by frank confession of initial bias.
questions.rule: Confess the bias; do not deny it.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: Which sentence from a research paper best shows objectivity in the authors' sense?
options: Our method rests on no presuppositions of any kind whatsoever
These results speak for themselves and need no further interpretation
As every competent researcher knows, the method is sound
We assume here that the samples were not contaminated in storage
optionExplain: Claiming to assume nothing is the false picture of objectivity the authors reject.
Saying results need no interpretation hides the assumptions behind reading them.
An appeal to common knowledge smuggles an assumption in instead of confessing it.
Right: it names an assumption outright and asks the reader to grant it.
questions.explain: Objectivity shows in an author stating plainly what he asks you to take for granted, as the first sentence does.
questions.rule: Look for named assumptions.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: A columnist opens with: I write as a lifelong cyclist, so weigh my view on bike lanes with that in mind. By analogy with the authors' view of objectivity, how should a reader take this?
options: As candour that helps her weigh the argument
As proof that the column is biased and worthless
As proof that the column is now free of bias
As irrelevant, since only evidence matters here
optionExplain: Right: like a confessed presupposition, the disclosure tells her where to look harder.
Declaring a standpoint does not make the argument worthless; it tells her what to check.
Disclosure reveals the standpoint; it does not remove it.
Evidence matters, but knowing the writer's standpoint helps her judge how he selects and reads it.
questions.explain: By analogy, stating one's standpoint makes a bias visible without removing it, and the reader can then weigh the argument with that in view.
questions.rule: Disclosure shows where to look; it does not settle the case.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a disclosure of interest, such as a declared funding source or personal stake, works like a confessed presupposition: the bias is still there, but the reader now knows where to look harder.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: True or false: Once an author frankly states an assumption, the reader should accept it, since confession is the mark of objectivity.
questions.explain: Confession makes the assumption visible, which is what objectivity requires. Whether to grant it is still the reader's judgment.
questions.rule: A confessed assumption is visible, not proved.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the main propositions of a scientific book are general statements, not tied to any particular time or place.
questions.explain: The authors say the main propositions of science are always general. The card next contrasts this with history.
questions.rule: Science states how things generally behave.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: Match each expression to its meaning in the authors' account of scientific books.
pairs: Tied to a particular time and place
Usually carried by a technical word
A general statement of how things behave
questions.explain: Science is not chronotopic; its leading terms show up as technical words and its main propositions are general, with particular observations serving as evidence.
questions.rule: Technical words, general propositions, particular evidence.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: A biology chapter contains these sentences. Which could be its main propositions, in the authors' sense? Choose two.
options: On 3 May the sample in jar B turned cloudy
The author first saw the effect while working in Lyon
The laboratory moved to a new building in 1950
Green plants release oxygen when exposed to light
Cells divide only after copying their genetic material
optionExplain: A dated observation in one jar is evidence, not a main proposition.
Where the author worked is a historical detail, tied to a time and place.
A fact about the laboratory's history is chronotopic, not a general claim about nature.
Right: it says how a kind of thing behaves, wherever and whenever.
Right: a general statement about cells, not about one cell at one time.
questions.explain: Main propositions in science are general. Dated observations and facts about the author's life are particular, so at most they serve as evidence or background.
questions.rule: If it names a date or place, it is not the main claim.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: A baking guide offers two sentences: In our test kitchen last June, the cake rose best at 180 degrees; and: Cakes rise best when the oven sets the crust soon after the batter expands. Which is closer to a scientific main proposition?
options: The first, since it reports a real and dated test
The first, since it gives an exact temperature
The second, since it states how cakes behave in general
Neither, since cooking cannot have general claims
optionExplain: A dated test is evidence, the kind of particular report a general claim rests on.
Exactness is not generality; the figure is tied to one kitchen on one occasion.
Right: remove the kitchen and the date and the second sentence still says something; it is general.
By analogy, any field can state general claims; the second sentence is one.
questions.explain: A quick test: strip out names, dates and places. The general sentence keeps its content; the particular report loses most of it.
questions.rule: Strip the time and place: what survives is general.
questions.teaches: Removing names, dates and places is a quick test of a sentence's kind: a general proposition survives unchanged, while a particular report loses most of its content.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: A reader lists every technical word in a chemistry classic and treats the list as a full statement of the author's terms. What has she missed?
options: Technical words are seldom the leading terms in scientific writing
Only words in the book's title can count as its terms
Each word's sense must still be learned from the author's use
Terms in science are carried by everyday words instead
optionExplain: The authors say the opposite: leading terms are usually expressed by technical words.
Titles help classify a book, but terms are found throughout it.
Right: a technical word points to a term, but the term is the meaning, which the author's use fixes.
Ordinary words can be technical, but the authors say science usually uses uncommon words for its terms.
questions.explain: Spotting the technical words is the easy part. Coming to terms means grasping the sense in which the author uses each one.
questions.rule: A word is a pointer; the term is its meaning.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: Suppose a book on cholera describes, step by step, how it spread through one city in 1854, and claims nothing about diseases in general. By the authors' account, what kind of propositions dominate it?
options: Particular ones, tied to a time and place, as in history
General ones, since its subject is a kind of disease, not a city
Technical ones, since it uses medical vocabulary
Inductive ones, since it reports many observations
optionExplain: Right: a step-by-step account of one outbreak is chronotopic, whatever its subject.
A scientific subject does not make the claims general; these are about one city and one year.
Technical words can appear in a history too; vocabulary does not decide whether claims are general.
Observations become an inductive argument only when used to establish a general claim, which this book does not make.
questions.explain: What matters is whether the propositions get away from time and place. An account of one outbreak, however medical, makes particular claims like a history.
questions.rule: Subject matter does not make a claim general.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: According to the authors, what are the two main difficulties in reading a scientific book?
options: Its old-fashioned language, and its length
Its many diagrams, and its foreign terms
Its errors, and its outdated conclusions
Following the arguments, and the mathematics
optionExplain: Old classics can be long and dated in style, but the authors locate the difficulty elsewhere.
Diagrams can trouble readers, and technical words appear, but the authors call technical terms relatively easy to spot.
Superseded content does not block a lay reader, who reads for the problems rather than current results.
Right: the authors name the arguments, with their evidence, and the mathematics.
questions.explain: The authors name two difficulties: the arguments and the mathematics. The card next takes up the first.
questions.rule: Two hurdles: the evidence and the mathematics.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the inductive argument, which rests on observable evidence, is the kind characteristic of science.
questions.explain: Science uses deductive arguments too, but the authors call it primarily inductive: its characteristic arguments establish general propositions from observable evidence.
questions.rule: Science is primarily inductive.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: Sort each argument by whether it is inductive or deductive in the authors' sense.

items.t: Ten thousand bird counts show the species is declining
One experiment shows the gas expands when heated
Readings from forty patients show the drug lowers fever
All metals conduct electricity; copper is a metal; so copper conducts
From two theorems already proved, a third follows about the orbit
Given the stated laws of motion, the path must be a certain curve

questions.explain: Inductive arguments rest on observed cases, whether one experiment or many observations. Deductive ones prove a proposition from propositions already established.
questions.rule: Cases point to induction; prior propositions to deduction.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: Sam reads that a scientist found a vaccine prevents a disease, and he accepts it. By the authors' standard, what must Sam do to understand the argument?
options: Check that most other scientists have accepted the result
Follow the trial the scientist reports as its basis
Learn the mathematics used in the paper first
Find the general law the result is deduced from
optionExplain: Agreement among scientists may be reassuring, but it is not the evidence for the claim.
Right: the conclusion is inductive, so understanding it means grasping the evidence it rests on.
Mathematics is a separate difficulty; the argument here rests on a trial.
This claim is established by evidence, not deduced from a law.
questions.explain: A claim that a vaccine works is a generalization from observed cases. Sam understands it only when he can follow the trial that supports it.
questions.rule: To understand induction, follow its evidence.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: A mattress maker cites a study in which 30 buyers rated their sleep as better after a month on the new mattress. Which question follows this evidence most closely?
options: How well known is the company that ran the study?
What were these buyers' nights compared against?
Which general law of sleep explains the result?
Were the buyers paid for taking part in the study?
optionExplain: Reputation is about the source, not the evidence the conclusion rests on.
Right: a claim that the mattress causes better sleep needs cases without it, such as a group on their old mattresses over the same month.
The claim is inductive; looking for a law to deduce it from leaves the evidence unexamined.
Payment might colour the ratings, but even unpaid buyers would leave the missing comparison.
questions.explain: Following inductive evidence means asking what was observed and how it bears on the claim. A claim about an effect needs a comparison, and the study as described has none.
questions.rule: Ask what the cases were compared with.
questions.teaches: Following the evidence includes asking what the observed cases were compared with: an inductive claim about an effect needs cases where the supposed cause was absent, not only cases where it was present.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: True or false: In a deductive passage of a scientific book, where a result is proved from propositions already established, following reported experiments is the reader's main task.
questions.explain: Where the argument is deductive, the reader follows the reasoning from the established propositions. Following reported evidence is the task for inductive arguments.
questions.rule: Deduction asks you to follow reasoning, not experiments.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: Which do the authors suggest when a scientific book alone fails to make its evidence clear? Choose three.
options: Handle apparatus like that described
Observe specimens or models in a museum
Accept the conclusion on the author's word
Turn to a modern summary of the results
Watch a laboratory demonstration
optionExplain: Right: handling similar apparatus makes descriptions of it concrete.
Right: specimens and models let you see what the author saw.
Taking the conclusion on trust is what the authors want the reader to avoid; the point is to grasp the evidence.
A summary reports results; it does not show the evidence the original describes.
Right: a demonstration supplies the special experience the text assumes.
questions.explain: All three ways give first-hand experience of what the author describes. The card next explains why that is the reader's one recourse.
questions.rule: When words fail, go and see.
