questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: The authors say there are classical ____ as well as classical books.
questions.explain: Crucial experiments belong to the history of science as much as its great texts do, and the authors want readers to know them by direct experience.
questions.rule: Know the classical experiments, not only the texts.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: Priya is reading an old anatomy book and cannot picture its descriptions of the heart's valves. What do the authors' suggestions point her toward?
options: Reading the passage aloud until it makes sense
Trusting the anatomist, since the book is a classic
Leaving anatomy to readers with medical training
Seeing a real or model heart, as in a museum
optionExplain: Rereading helps with hard prose, but no amount of it supplies a sight she has never had.
A classic still has to be understood; trusting it skips the evidence.
The authors want lay readers to read such classics and seek the experience they need.
Right: specimens and models give the special experience the description assumes.
questions.explain: Her trouble is not the words but the lack of the experience they assume. Seeing a heart or a good model supplies it.
questions.rule: Missing experience calls for experience, not rereading.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: A cookbook explains that a mayonnaise splits if the oil goes in too fast, and a reader cannot grasp what splitting means after three readings. By analogy with the authors' advice, what helps most?
options: Making a small batch and watching the change
Rereading until the description is memorized
Finding a longer description in a second cookbook
Accepting the rule and moving to the next recipe
optionExplain: Right: doing it gives the sight and feel of the change that the words could not.
Memorizing words does not supply an experience the reader has never had.
More words may help a little, but the gap is experience, not description.
Accepting the rule leaves the reader unable to recognize the problem when it happens.
questions.explain: Some things, such as how a sauce looks and feels as it changes, are hard to convey in words. Trying it at first hand supplies what rereading cannot.
questions.rule: Some evidence must be seen or felt.
questions.teaches: Experience of a procedure often supplies what words cannot, such as a feel for timing, texture or scale, which is why a first-hand trial can clear up a description that rereading does not.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: Suppose the next chapter describes its experiment with exact measurements, clear drawings and familiar materials, and Priya follows it easily. By the authors' account, what does she need now?
options: A museum visit anyway, since every classic requires one
A full repeat of the experiment before she reads further
No special trip, since the text has made the evidence clear
A modern textbook to confirm that the drawings are right
optionExplain: The authors make special experience a remedy for unclear evidence, not a rule for every page.
Repeating experiments can be rewarding, but it is not needed to follow evidence she already grasps.
Right: first-hand experience is the recourse when the book fails to enlighten; here it has not failed.
Her aim is to follow the author's evidence, which she has done; checking against modern texts is another task.
questions.explain: The authors' recourse is conditional: it applies if the book itself fails to enlighten the reader. When the text conveys the evidence, it is enough.
questions.rule: Seek experience where the text falls short.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, you cannot make a start on a scientific classic until you have gone through every step it describes for yourself.
questions.explain: The authors say plainly that you can make a start without going through all the steps, and they give Lavoisier's book as an example.
questions.rule: Start reading; seek experience where needed.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, you can take worthwhile impressions from a scientific classic without reading it through in detail.
questions.explain: The authors say some parts carry the main impression of a classic. The card next uses Lavoisier as the example.
questions.rule: A partial reading can still give the main impression.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: Match each element of a physical science, as Lavoisier describes it, to its role.
pairs: What represents the facts in the mind
What expresses and passes on the ideas
The language that must improve with the science
questions.explain: Lavoisier names facts, the ideas representing them and the words expressing them; since ideas live in words, improving a science and improving its nomenclature go together.
questions.rule: Better language, better science.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: Jonas has two evenings for a long scientific classic and wants its main impression. Following the authors' advice on Lavoisier, what should he do?
options: Read the first two chapters closely and stop there
Wait until he has time to read every chapter in detail
Read the parts that state its method and central ideas
Read a modern textbook on the subject instead
optionExplain: Opening chapters may be technical groundwork; the authors point to the most illuminating parts, wherever they are.
Waiting for a complete reading is the delay the authors' advice is meant to remove.
Right: parts such as a preface on method carry the main impression of the book.
A textbook gives current knowledge, not the impression of this classic that he wants.
questions.explain: The point of the Lavoisier example is that some parts of a classic give its main impression. Jonas should find and read those.
questions.rule: Find the parts that carry the book.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: A hospital replaces its single label minor incident with three precise categories and soon notices patterns in falls that it had missed. How does Lavoisier's view, as the authors report it, help explain this?
options: Improving a field's language can improve the field itself
More categories produce more accurate records, whatever the field
Precise labels matter only in the physical sciences
The patterns were found by experiment, not by naming
optionExplain: Right: sharper names let the hospital's ideas, and so its findings, become sharper.
More categories can also blur things if they are badly made; the gain came from precise ones.
Lavoisier spoke of physical science, but by analogy the link between words and ideas holds in any field.
No experiment was run; the new names let existing facts be seen differently.
questions.explain: Lavoisier held that ideas are kept and passed on by words, so better words make better science. By analogy, a sharper set of names let the hospital see patterns in facts it already had.
questions.rule: New names can reveal old facts.
questions.teaches: By extension, a change of names can be a discovery in itself: dividing a vague category into precise ones lets patterns appear that the old word hid.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: Suppose Jonas's aim changes: he now wants to judge whether one particular experiment in the classic supports its author's claim. What do the authors suggest?
options: The preface will be enough to settle the question
Reading the book's closing summary will settle it
He should skip it, since lay readers need not judge
He must read that experiment's evidence and steps
optionExplain: A preface gives the method and the main impression, not the details of one experiment.
A summary states conclusions; it cannot show whether the evidence supports them.
Judging is a fair aim for a lay reader once the argument has been understood.
Right: judging an argument needs its evidence and reasoning, not only the book's main impression.
questions.explain: Reading key parts suits the aim of getting a classic's main impression. When the aim becomes judging one argument, that argument must be read in full.
questions.rule: A new aim needs a fuller reading.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Suggestions for Reading Classical Scientific Books
questions.q: True or false: The authors recommend Lavoisier's Elements of Chemistry as a good textbook for a student preparing for a high school chemistry examination.
questions.explain: They say a student would be unwise to use it for that purpose. Its value for a lay reader lies in its revolutionary method and its conception of an element.
questions.rule: A classic is not a current textbook.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, words may be harder to follow than mathematical symbols, because the shifts in their meaning are less controlled.
questions.explain: The authors note that words shift too, more or less uncontrolled, while mathematical symbols shift in a controlled way. The card next shows how this bears on the fear of mathematics.
questions.rule: Symbols shift by rule; words do not.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Which explanations for the fear of mathematics do the authors mention? Choose two.
options: The emotional connotations of mathematical terms
A symbol blindness, as some psychologists suggest
The way mathematics has been taught
A lack of the inborn talent mathematics needs
The fact that mathematics is mainly a spoken skill
optionExplain: The authors say properly used mathematical terms have no emotional connotations.
Right: some psychologists propose symbol blindness, and the authors grant there may be something to it.
Right: others blame the teaching, and the authors welcome research on teaching it better.
Talent is a common explanation, but not one the authors put forward.
The authors say the opposite: mathematics is almost wholly a written language.
questions.explain: The authors mention symbol blindness and poor teaching, and add their own view that people are not told early enough that mathematics is a learnable language.
questions.rule: Symbol blindness and teaching are the explanations offered.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: True or false: If teaching methods for mathematics improved, the authors' account suggests some of the common fear of it could be reduced.
questions.explain: Those who blame the teaching would expect better teaching to help, and the authors are gratified by research on teaching mathematics better.
questions.rule: Better teaching could ease the fear.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Rosa wants to understand geometry but has not yet opened Euclid, because she is sure she cannot read mathematics. What would the authors advise first?
options: Accept the fear as a sign that she lacks the right mind
Try a few propositions, since fear is no proof of inability
Take a full course in algebra before opening Euclid
Read about geometry only in books without any symbols
optionExplain: This treats fear as evidence, the very conclusion the authors reject.
Right: the authors hold that the fear is common but does not show inability, and they suggest starting with Euclid.
Preparation can help, but Euclid's opening propositions need no algebra, and the authors suggest starting there.
Avoiding symbols keeps the fear untested and keeps her from the mathematics she wants.
questions.explain: Rosa's belief has never been tested. The authors' advice is to make an attempt, beginning with Euclid, rather than to treat the fear as a verdict.
questions.rule: Test the fear by trying.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Ben has avoided sheet music for years, sure he could not learn to read it. By analogy with the authors' advice on mathematics, which first step best tests his belief?
options: Waiting until the fear fades before trying
Learning to read one short tune, note by note
Opening an advanced score to see how it goes
Asking friends whether they find notation hard
optionExplain: Fear kept by avoidance rarely fades on its own, because nothing tests it.
Right: a small, low-stakes attempt gives him evidence about his ability that avoidance never can.
Starting with the hardest material is likely to confirm the fear rather than test it fairly.
Others' experience says nothing about whether he can learn it.
questions.explain: Avoidance leaves a fear untested. A small first attempt, like a few evenings with Euclid, lets the belief be checked against evidence.
questions.rule: A small attempt tests a large fear.
questions.teaches: Avoidance keeps a fear in place: someone who never tries a notation never gathers evidence that they can read it, so a small, low-stakes first attempt is the usual way to test the belief.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: True or false: The authors' answer to the fear of mathematics implies that advanced mathematical works can be read with no prior learning.
questions.explain: Their claim is that the elementary barrier is lower than fear suggests. Advanced works still build on earlier learning.
questions.rule: Less to fear is not nothing to learn.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Why do the authors say mathematics has to be learned only once, while our own language must be learned twice?
options: Its rules do not change once learned
It has far fewer symbols than English
It is learned after our own language
It is almost wholly a written language
optionExplain: Stable rules make mathematics reliable, but that is not why it is learned once.
The number of symbols is not the authors' point; the point is that mathematics is not first a spoken language.
Coming later does not halve the learning; what matters is that there is no spoken stage.
Right: we learn our own language once to speak and once to read; mathematics is learned in writing only.
questions.explain: Our own language is learned first as speech and then as writing. Mathematics is almost wholly written, so there is only one stage. The card next draws out what this means.
questions.rule: Mathematics is a written language.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Since mathematics is a language, the authors say it has its own vocabulary, grammar and ____.
questions.explain: Like any language, mathematics has vocabulary, grammar and syntax, which the beginning reader has to learn.
questions.rule: Learn the vocabulary, grammar and syntax.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Dev meets an unfamiliar symbol in a statistics book and stalls. Which response fits the authors' view of mathematics as a language?
options: Look up the symbol as he would an unknown word
Put the book aside, since symbols signal advanced work
Guess its meaning and press on without checking
Read faster so that its sense comes from the flow
optionExplain: Right: an unknown symbol is like an unknown word, an elementary problem solved by learning what it means.
A new symbol is a vocabulary problem, not proof that the book is beyond him.
Guessing may work with words in rich context, but symbols carry exact meanings that a wrong guess distorts.
Speed does not supply a meaning he has never learned.
questions.explain: The authors compare meeting a new symbol to meeting a word you must look up: reading at the elementary level, which even the best readers do now and then.
questions.rule: An unknown symbol is an unknown word.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Which task belongs to the elementary level of reading mathematics, in the authors' sense?
options: Judging whether a theorem's proof is sound
Seeing how a whole book's results fit together
Memorizing what each symbol stands for
Comparing two authors' treatments of a topic
optionExplain: Judging a proof is criticism, which comes after understanding at the higher levels.
Seeing the structure of a whole book is part of analytical reading, not elementary reading.
Right: recognizing symbols and memorizing their relations is the elementary task.
Comparing several authors belongs to syntopical reading.
questions.explain: Elementary reading is recognizing symbols and their relations. The other tasks belong to analytical or syntopical reading, which build on it.
questions.rule: Symbols first; structure and judgment later.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: A gardener finds fertilizer labels marked with N, P and K and numbers she has not learned. By analogy with the authors' view of mathematics, how should she approach them?
options: Avoid them, since chemistry needs years of formal training
Read the numbers as a quality score, higher meaning better
Learn what each symbol means, as a small vocabulary
Memorise the three numbers without asking what they stand for
optionExplain: Reading a label needs a few symbols, not a chemistry degree.
Guessing what numbers mean without the notation misreads them: they give each nutrient's share, not a grade.
Right: N, P and K are symbols for nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, and the numbers give their shares; a short vocabulary opens the label.
Numbers remembered without their meaning tell her nothing; a language is read by knowing what its symbols stand for.
questions.explain: Chemical notation, like mathematics, is a written language. A small vocabulary of symbols and what the numbers mean is enough to read the label.
questions.rule: Any notation is learned like a language.
questions.teaches: By analogy, other notations, such as musical scores, chemical formulas or programming code, are written languages too, and a newcomer reads them by the same elementary work of learning symbols and their relations before trying to follow what they say.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: True or false: Suppose a reader has memorized every symbol in a proof and how the symbols combine. She has then understood the proof.
questions.explain: Knowing the symbols lets her read the proof at the elementary level. Understanding why the steps follow belongs to the higher levels of reading.
questions.rule: Reading the symbols is not yet understanding the proof.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: According to the authors, what are the subjects of ordinary discourse mainly?
options: Emotional facts and relations
Physical objects and their motions
Logical arguments and their proofs
Historical events and their dates
optionExplain: Right: the authors say ordinary talk is mainly about emotional facts and relations.
People do talk about objects, but the authors characterize ordinary discourse differently.
Arguments and proofs are what logic and mathematics deal with, not ordinary talk.
Events come up in conversation, but they are not what the authors name.
questions.explain: The authors say ordinary discourse is mainly about emotional facts and relations, which no two people fully share. The card next contrasts mathematics.
questions.rule: Ordinary talk is mostly about feelings and relations.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, mathematical terms, propositions and equations, properly used, carry no emotional connotations.
questions.explain: This is the authors' claim, and they see it as an advantage: it lets mathematics avoid the misunderstandings that feelings bring.
questions.rule: Properly used, mathematics is free of connotations.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Sort each subject by whether two people could comprehend it as a third thing apart from both, or whether it is mainly a matter of emotional facts and relations.
groups: A third thing apart from both

items.t: The area of a rectangular field
The wiring diagram of a desk lamp
The rule for dividing one fraction by another
Whether a friend was hurt by a remark
How a family feels about selling the old house
Why a couple quarrelled at dinner

questions.explain: Areas, circuits and arithmetic rules are things outside both people, so both can grasp them alike. Hurt feelings and family attachments are emotional relations that no two people grasp in quite the same way.
questions.rule: Things outside us can be shared; feelings cannot fully be.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Two managers who dislike each other keep clashing over a project's delay. A colleague asks them first to agree on a chart of the tasks and their dates. By analogy with the authors' point, why might this help?
options: It proves which of the two managers caused the project's delay
It replaces their argument with a mathematical proof
It lets them avoid discussing the project at all
It gives them a third thing, free of feeling, to agree on
optionExplain: A chart may show where time went, but blame is a further, more emotional question.
A chart is not a proof; it is a shared description that both can check.
The chart puts the project at the centre; it does not take it off the table.
Right: a chart of tasks and dates is an object outside both, so they can agree on it before facing what divides them.
questions.explain: Agreement comes more easily on a thing apart from both people. Settling the shared facts first makes the remaining, emotional disagreement smaller and easier to see.
questions.rule: Agree on the third thing first.
questions.teaches: By analogy, moving a dispute onto a shared, emotionally neutral object, such as a chart, a measurement or a written definition, can make agreement possible on that part, leaving the emotional disagreement smaller and easier to see.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: A tax rate of 45 percent is quoted in a heated election debate. Compared with the same number in an arithmetic exercise, what has changed?
options: The number has become less exact than it was before
Feelings now attach to it, so readers may differ
The figure has turned into a syllogism about taxes
Nothing, since a number can carry no connotations
optionExplain: Forty-five percent is as exact as before; what changed is what people attach to it.
Right: the number is the same, but invested with emotional connotations it is no longer read as pure mathematics.
A figure is not an argument; it may be used in one, but it has not become one.
The authors' claim is about mathematics properly used; once feelings are attached, the trouble they describe returns.
questions.explain: The authors say trouble begins when we invest things with emotional connotations. Put into a debate, a plain figure gains them.
questions.rule: Context can load a neutral number.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: A student argues: since mathematics has no emotional connotations, the authors must think mathematics stirs no feeling in its readers. What is wrong with this?
options: The authors say mathematics does carry emotional connotations
The claim is about what the terms mean, not how readers feel
Feelings about mathematics are themselves mathematical objects
The authors say most readers find mathematics dull
optionExplain: They say the opposite of this, at least for mathematics properly used.
Right: the terms carry no connotations, yet the authors call mathematics beautiful and intellectually satisfying.
This confuses feelings about a subject with the subject itself.
The authors say people are not told how beautiful mathematics can be, which is not a claim that it is dull.
questions.explain: The absence of connotations concerns the meaning of mathematical terms. The authors themselves stress how beautiful and satisfying mathematics can be to read.
questions.rule: Neutral terms can still give real pleasure.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: What do the letters Q.E.D. at the end of a Euclidean proposition mark?
options: A construction: what was required to be done
A definition: what a term is taken to mean
A postulate: what is granted without proof
A theorem: what was required to be proved
optionExplain: A construction closes with a different mark, Q.E.F.
Definitions come before the propositions and carry no such closing mark.
Postulates are granted at the start; nothing is required to be shown for them.
Right: Q.E.D. stands for quod erat demonstrandum and closes a theorem.
questions.explain: Q.E.D. closes a theorem, which is proved. The card next shows the other kind of proposition and its own mark.
questions.rule: Q.E.D. means proved.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Match each item from Euclid to its description.
questions.explain: Constructions require something to be done and end with Q.E.F.; theorems require something to be proved and end with Q.E.D.
questions.rule: Done is Q.E.F.; proved is Q.E.D.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Sort these geometry propositions into construction problems and theorems.

items.t: To draw a square on a given straight line
To cut a given angle into two equal angles
To draw a perpendicular from a given point to a line
The three angles of any triangle together equal two right angles
The base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal
Two triangles with three equal sides have equal angles

questions.explain: Each construction asks you to make something with the allowed tools. Each theorem asserts a relation that must be proved true.
questions.rule: To make is a construction; to show is a theorem.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Suppose Proposition 3 were removed from Book I. By the authors' account, what would happen to Proposition 5?
options: Its proof would lose a step it depends on
Nothing, since theorems do not use constructions
It would turn into a construction problem itself
It would follow from Proposition 4 by itself
optionExplain: Right: Proposition 5 cuts a shorter line from a longer, which is what Proposition 3 provides.
The authors' point is the opposite: the constructions are needed in the proofs of theorems.
Removing a support does not change what Proposition 5 asserts; it still needs proving.
The authors trace Proposition 5 back through 3, 2 and 1; they do not say Proposition 4 would suffice.
questions.explain: Proposition 5's proof uses Proposition 3, which in turn needs 2 and 1. Take one away and the chain the theorem rests on breaks.
questions.rule: Remove a needed step and the proof fails.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: In a cookbook, the pie, the gravy and the soup all use the stock recipe from chapter one. The author changes the stock to cut its salt. By analogy with tracing Euclid's dependencies, what follows?
options: Only the stock recipe itself needs to be rechecked
The pie is unaffected, since it comes later in the book
Every recipe that uses the stock may need rechecking
Nothing, since each recipe stands on its own
optionExplain: The change does not stay in chapter one; every dish built on the stock inherits it.
Coming later is exactly what lets the pie depend on the stock.
Right: knowing what depends on the stock shows everything a change to it can reach.
These recipes do depend on one another; that is why the stock comes first.
questions.explain: Tracing dependence explains order, and it also shows what a change to an early item reaches. As Proposition 5 rests on Propositions 1 to 3, these dishes rest on the stock.
questions.rule: Change a foundation and recheck what rests on it.
questions.teaches: Tracing dependence also shows what breaks if an early item changes: alter a foundation and everything built on it may change too, which is why foundations are revised with care.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the reason the first three propositions are constructions can be seen from the first four propositions alone.
questions.explain: The authors say the dependence is not apparent in the first four propositions; it shows in the fifth, the first theorem that needs the constructions.
questions.rule: Dependence may show only further on.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: True or false: In Euclid, both postulates and construction propositions assert that some geometrical operation can be performed.
questions.explain: Both assert that an operation can be performed. The card next shows what separates them.
questions.rule: Postulates and constructions both concern what can be done.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: According to the authors, how does a construction proposition differ from a postulate?
options: It concerns figures, not lines or circles
It is stated before any of the definitions
Its possibility is proved, not assumed
Its proof makes no use of the postulates
optionExplain: Postulates do concern lines and circles, but the difference the authors draw is assumed versus proved.
Definitions come first; constructions are propositions that follow them.
Right: a postulate assumes an operation is possible; a construction proves it.
The authors say the opposite: the proof of a construction uses the postulates.
questions.explain: In a postulate the possibility is assumed; in a construction it is proved, using the postulates.
questions.rule: Postulate: assumed. Construction: proved.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: In a geometry text built like Euclid's, sort each statement by whether it would be assumed as a postulate or proved as a construction.

items.t: A straight line can be drawn between any two points
A circle can be drawn with any centre and radius
A finite straight line can be extended in a line
An equilateral triangle can be built on a given line
A given angle can be cut into two equal angles
A square can be drawn on a given straight line

questions.explain: Drawing lines and circles and extending lines are the basic operations Euclid grants. Triangles, bisected angles and squares are shown to be possible from them.
questions.rule: Basic operations are granted; the rest are built from them.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: A software library takes two basic operations as given, comparing two items and swapping them, and then supplies a sorting routine built only from those. By analogy with the authors' account, what does the sorting routine show?
options: That sorting is possible, given the two basic operations
That comparing and swapping need no assumptions
That sorting is itself a basic operation, like comparing two items
That the library's results hold on any machine at all
optionExplain: Right: like a construction, the routine proves a new operation possible from the ones granted.
Comparing and swapping are the granted operations; the routine relies on them rather than proving them.
Sorting is built from the basic operations, so it plays the part of a construction, not a postulate.
The routine's guarantee is conditional: it holds where the two basic operations work as assumed.
questions.explain: The basic operations play the role of postulates and the routine the role of a construction. Its result is conditional on the operations granted.
questions.rule: Built results rest on granted operations.
questions.teaches: By analogy, systems from software libraries to legal codes often take a few operations as given and build the rest from them; knowing which are given tells you where the system's guarantees ultimately rest.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: True or false: If a geometry book listed the drawing of an equilateral triangle among its postulates, that possibility would be assumed in that book rather than proved.
questions.explain: What makes something a postulate is that its possibility is granted, not shown. Moving the triangle into the postulates would turn a proved possibility into an assumed one.
questions.rule: Its place in the system decides whether a possibility is assumed.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Proposition 1 settles whether equilateral triangles really exist, quite apart from any assumptions.
questions.explain: Proposition 1 shows that equilateral triangles follow if straight lines and circles are granted. The authors leave aside the thorny question of whether mathematical objects exist at all.
questions.rule: A construction proves possibility relative to the postulates.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: When Euclid proves that the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal, what has he established?
options: That isosceles triangles really exist in the physical world
That every triangle whatever has two equal base angles
That the hypothesis of the theorem is itself true
That if a triangle is isosceles, its base angles are equal
optionExplain: The authors say it does not matter to Euclid whether there are such triangles; existence is not what is proved.
The theorem is about isosceles triangles only; others need not have equal base angles.
The hypothesis is supposed, not asserted; the proof shows what follows from it.
Right: the proof establishes the connection between hypothesis and conclusion.
questions.explain: A proved theorem establishes an if-then connection. The card next spells out what it does not assert.
questions.rule: A proof proves a connection.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: According to the authors, a proved proposition asserts an ____ relationship between its hypothesis and its conclusion.
questions.explain: The proposition asserts that if the hypothesis holds, and the definitions, postulates and earlier propositions are valid, the conclusion holds too.
questions.rule: Proved means: if this, then that.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: A carpenter measures a triangular frame and finds that its two sides differ by a centimetre. What does Euclid's Proposition 5 tell her about the frame's base angles?
options: That its base angles are equal, as the theorem proved
Nothing directly, since the frame fails the hypothesis
That its base angles must differ by a fixed amount
That the theorem has now been shown to be false
optionExplain: The proof covers isosceles triangles; applying it here ignores its hypothesis.
Right: the theorem speaks only of triangles with two equal sides; this frame is not one.
The theorem says nothing about how unequal sides affect the angles.
A case outside the hypothesis cannot refute a conditional; the theorem stands.
questions.explain: The theorem asserts a connection that applies only when its hypothesis is met. A frame with unequal sides lies outside it, so the theorem neither applies nor is refuted.
questions.rule: No hypothesis, no conclusion.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: A surveyor measures a triangle and finds its base angles are equal. Using Proposition 5's proved connection alone, what can she conclude about its sides?
options: That two of its sides must be equal, by Proposition 5
Nothing about its sides from Proposition 5 alone
That her measurement has now confirmed Proposition 5
That the triangle must be equilateral as well
optionExplain: This runs the connection backward; Proposition 5 does not say that equal angles bring equal sides.
Right: Proposition 5 runs from equal sides to equal angles; a figure with the conclusion need not have the hypothesis as far as this proof shows.
A proved connection is established by the proof, not by measurements, and her case does not even meet its hypothesis as far as she knows.
Nothing in the connection says anything about all three sides.
questions.explain: Proposition 5 asserts: if two sides are equal, the base angles are equal. Finding the conclusion true tells her nothing about the hypothesis. The reverse claim needs its own proof, which Euclid gives separately as Proposition 6.
questions.rule: A true conclusion does not prove the hypothesis.
questions.teaches: A proved if-then connection does not run in reverse: a figure that has the conclusion need not have the hypothesis, so a converse needs its own proof, which Euclid supplies as a separate proposition (Book I, Proposition 6).

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: An insurance policy says: if the insured car is stolen while locked, the insurer pays its value. Read as the authors read Euclid, what does this clause by itself establish?
options: That the car will in fact be stolen at some point in the future
That the car was locked when it was taken
That the insurer will pay for any lost car
Only that payment follows if the condition is met
optionExplain: The clause supposes a theft; it does not predict one.
Whether the car was locked is the hypothesis, which the clause does not assert.
The connection covers locked cars that are stolen, not every loss.
Right: like a theorem, the clause asserts a connection, not that its condition holds.
questions.explain: The clause asserts an if-then link. Whether the insurer pays depends on whether the hypothesis, a theft while locked, holds in the actual case.
questions.rule: A conditional clause promises a link, not a fact.
questions.teaches: By analogy, conditional clauses in contracts, warranties and policies assert only a link, so a dispute usually turns on whether the hypothesis, such as the car being locked, actually holds in the case.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: True or false: Before the proof of Proposition 5 is complete, the connection between its hypothesis and its conclusion is already seen to be true.
questions.explain: The authors say the connection is not seen to be true until the proposition is proved. The proof is what establishes it.
questions.rule: The proof is what makes the connection known.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a valid syllogism about animals and men needs its assumptions examined in a way that Euclid's theorem does not.
questions.explain: Its premises are about real things and may be false. The card next explains the contrast with Euclid.
questions.rule: Premises about real things need checking.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: According to the authors, why must the syllogism about animals and men have its assumptions examined?
options: It assumes something about real things that may be false
Its logical form is weaker than the form of Euclid's proofs
Syllogisms are never used in mathematical reasoning
Its conclusion does not follow from its two premises
optionExplain: Right: there really are animals and men, so the premises make claims about the world.
The authors say the conclusion follows with the same certainty as Euclid's; the form is not the problem.
The authors say the syllogism can be treated as a piece of mathematical reasoning.
The conclusion does follow; the question is whether the premises are true.
questions.explain: The form is as certain as Euclid's. What differs is that the premises are claims about real things, which may be true or false.
questions.rule: Valid form, but real premises.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Sort each argument by whether its premises need checking against the world or it holds as a pure if-then connection.
groups: Premises need checking against the world
Holds as a pure if-then connection

items.t: All the town's wells are safe; this is a town well; so it is safe
Every employee got the memo; Ana is an employee; so Ana got it
All swans on this lake are white; that bird is one; so it is white
If a figure is a square, its four angles are right angles
If two whole numbers are even, their sum is even
If a triangle is isosceles, its base angles are equal

questions.explain: The first three make claims about real wells, employees and swans, which could be false. The last three are mathematical connections that hold given their definitions, whatever exists.
questions.rule: Claims about real things must be checked; definitions-based connections need not.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: A colleague argues: all our suppliers passed the safety audit; this firm is one of our suppliers; so it passed. The logic is valid. By the authors' reasoning, what should you check?
options: Whether the argument's logical form is valid
Whether a mathematical proof could replace it
Whether the premises are true of the real suppliers
Whether the conclusion is phrased as a theorem
optionExplain: The form is already granted as valid; checking it again misses the real risk.
No proof about real firms can avoid premises about them; the issue is their truth.
Right: the argument is about real firms, so the premises must be examined.
Phrasing does not change whether the premises about suppliers are true.
questions.explain: A valid argument about real things is only as good as its premises. Did every supplier pass, and is this firm really one of them?
questions.rule: Valid is not the same as true.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: An engineer uses a proved formula for the strength of a beam, which holds if the beam is uniform throughout. Her real beam has a hidden crack. By the authors' contrast, what has gone wrong?
options: The formula's proof contains a logical mistake
Mathematics cannot be used for real objects at all
The real beam does not meet the formula's hypothesis
The crack shows the formula was never proved
optionExplain: The proof may be flawless; the problem is the fit between beam and hypothesis.
Mathematics is applied to real things constantly; the applier must check the fit.
Right: the formula's if-then connection stands; the real beam fails its if.
A beam outside the hypothesis says nothing against the proof.
questions.explain: The formula is certain as a connection. Applying it to a real beam adds a premise about the world, that this beam is uniform, which here is false.
questions.rule: Applying mathematics adds a premise about the world.
questions.teaches: By extension, mathematics applied to real objects takes on the syllogism's burden: the theorem is certain, but whether a real object satisfies its hypothesis is a factual question to be checked.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: True or false: If the syllogism were restated about imaginary creatures that exist only as defined in the argument, its premises would no longer need checking against the world.
questions.explain: The authors say that if we assume there are such things, the syllogism can be treated as mathematical reasoning. With nothing real claimed, there is nothing in the world to check.
questions.rule: No claim about the world, no check against it.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, when reading a scientific work that contains mathematics, skipping much of the mathematics is often the wiser course.
questions.explain: They call skipping the better part of valour in that case. The card next shows when the opposite holds.
questions.rule: In science books, skipping is often wise.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: According to the authors, which fit reading a mathematics book for itself? Choose two.
options: Reading only the statements and summaries
Avoiding the diagrams if they are troubling
Reading it from beginning to end
Writing in the margins and on scratch paper
Skipping the proofs on a first reading
optionExplain: Statements and summaries are the skimmer's route through a science classic, not through a mathematics book.
Passing over diagrams is advice for reading the Principia as science, not for studying mathematics.
Right: a mathematics book read for itself is read through.
Right: the authors say pencil work is more necessary here than with any other kind of book.
Skipping proofs suits a scientific work read for its science, not a mathematics book read for itself.
questions.explain: A mathematics book read for its own sake is read from beginning to end, with pencil work in the margins and on scratch paper.
questions.rule: Mathematics for itself: all of it, pencil in hand.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: Sort each reader by how the authors would have them handle the mathematics.

items.t: A student reading an algebra primer to learn algebra
A reader working through Euclid for its proofs
A learner using a statistics text to master its methods
A reader of the Principia seeking Newton's main problem
A lay reader following the story of a physics classic
A reader of a biology paper who wants its main finding

questions.explain: When the mathematics is what you are reading for, work through it. When it serves a scientific work you read for its science, much of it can be skipped.
questions.rule: Your aim decides: work it or skip it.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: Hana is reading a book on climate science with occasional equations. She wants to understand its argument, not do its calculations. What fits the authors' advice?
options: Skip most of the equations and follow the argument
Stop at each equation until she can derive it
Set the book aside until she has studied calculus
Read only the equations, which hold the real content
optionExplain: Right: she is reading a scientific work for its science, so skipping is the better part of valour.
That is the pencil-in-hand approach for a mathematics book read for itself.
The authors say you can usually understand something of the matter without going deeply into the mathematics.
The argument lives in the prose as well; equations alone would not give her what she wants.
questions.explain: Hana's object is the science. The authors' advice for such a reader is to skip freely through the mathematics.
questions.rule: For the science, skip the sums.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: A manager reads a report on remote work that ends with long statistical appendices. She wants its findings and the main reasons for them. By analogy with the authors' advice, how should she treat the appendices?
options: Work through every table before reading the report
Doubt the report, since appendices mean it is too technical
Read only the appendices, since the data are what count
Pass over them unless a key claim rests on them
optionExplain: That treats the appendices as her object, which they are not.
Technical support is no reason for distrust; it can be passed over or consulted as needed.
The data support the findings, but she wants the findings and reasons, which the report states.
Right: like mathematics in a science book, the appendices support points she can grasp without them, unless one matters to her.
questions.explain: Supporting apparatus can be read two ways. When it only supports points you can follow without it, pass over it; turn to it when a claim you care about depends on it.
questions.rule: Read support material when you need it.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any technical apparatus, such as statistical tables, code listings or legal citations, can be read in two ways: worked through when it is your object, passed over when it only supports a point you can grasp without it.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: Suppose Hana reaches a passage where the book's central claim, that warming will pass a certain threshold, rests on one calculation. What changes?
options: Nothing: she should skip it as she skipped the others
She should follow that calculation, as the claim rests on it
She should accept the claim, since it rests on mathematics, not opinion
She should skip the whole chapter it appears in
optionExplain: Skipping suits mathematics that supports what she can grasp otherwise; this calculation carries the claim.
Right: when a claim she cares about depends on the mathematics, the mathematics becomes part of her object.
Being mathematical does not make a claim true for her; she has to see how it is reached.
Skipping more would leave her unable to understand the book's central claim.
questions.explain: Skipping is advice tied to the reader's aim. When the central claim rests on a calculation, following that calculation serves the aim.
questions.rule: When the claim rests on the sum, do the sum.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: On a first reading of Newton's Principia, what do the authors suggest doing with the proof of each proposition?
options: Work it through on paper line by line
Glance down it to see how it is done
Skip it along with the proposition itself
Memorize it before going on to the next
optionExplain: Line-by-line work suits a mathematics book read for itself, not a first pass through a scientific classic.
Right: a glance gives an idea of how the proof works without working every step.
The statements are to be read; only the detailed working is passed over.
Memorizing proofs is far more than the authors ask of a lay reader.
questions.explain: The authors suggest reading the statement and glancing down the proof. The card next sets out the rest of the method.
questions.rule: Statement read, proof glanced at.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: The parts of the Principia that discuss how propositions relate to one another and to the work as a whole are called ____.
questions.explain: The scholiums are Newton's discussions of how the propositions relate to each other and to the whole; reading them shows how the system is built.
questions.rule: Scholiums tie the parts to the whole.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: Sort each part of the Principia by how the authors suggest a lay reader treat it on a first reading.

items.t: The statement of each proposition
The scholiums
The General Scholium at the close of Book III
The detailed working of each proof
The diagrams, if they trouble you
Much of the interstitial matter

questions.explain: Statements, scholiums and the main passages show what Newton claims and how the system fits together. Proof details, troublesome diagrams and interstitial matter can be glanced at.
questions.rule: Read the claims and the connections; glance at the working.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: Omar is reading a classic of mathematical astronomy and wants to see how its system fits together. By the authors' advice, which parts should he make sure not to skip?
options: The full working of each proof, step by step
The tables of numbers gathered in the appendices
The diagrams that accompany each of the theorems
Passages relating the propositions to the whole
optionExplain: Full working shows each step, but the authors suggest only glancing at proofs on a first reading.
Tables support particular results; they do not show how the system fits together.
The authors say diagrams may be avoided if they trouble the reader.
Right: such discussions, like Newton's scholiums, are where the parts are tied to the whole.
questions.explain: To see how a system is built, read the parts where the author relates propositions to each other and to the whole.
questions.rule: Find the passages that join the parts.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: A new programmer must understand a large codebase in a week. By analogy with the authors' Principia method, which approach fits?
options: Read each module's purpose, skim its code, and study the overview notes
Read every function line by line, starting from the first file
Read only the newest changes, since they show the current state
Run the program and skip the code, since what it does is what counts most
optionExplain: Right: module purposes play the part of statements, skimming the code of glancing at proofs, and overview notes of scholiums.
Line-by-line reading is the pencil approach, too slow to show the whole in a week.
Recent changes show details, not how the system is built.
Running it shows what it does, but not how its parts fit together.
questions.explain: By analogy, a first pass through any large system reads each part's statement and the commentary that ties parts together, leaving detailed working for later.
questions.rule: First read the architecture, then the working.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any large system, such as a codebase, a body of law or a long report, can be read first for its architecture by taking each part's statement and the connecting commentary, leaving detailed working for the parts one needs.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: True or false: A reader who has gone through the Principia by the authors' method has thereby checked that Newton's results are correct.
questions.explain: The method shows what Newton claims and how his system fits together. Checking a result means working its proof in full.
questions.rule: Seeing the structure is not checking the proofs.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Newton's Optics contains a great deal of mathematics, as its many diagrams suggest.
questions.explain: The diagrams make it look mathematical, but they illustrate experiments; there is very little mathematics in it. The card next shows how to read it.
questions.rule: Diagrams can illustrate experiments, not proofs.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: Besides the descriptions of experiments, which parts of the Optics do the authors suggest reading? Choose two.
options: The detailed geometry behind every diagram
Later commentaries correcting Newton's errors
Only the opening chapter of the first Book
The statements of the theorems or propositions
The discussions at the end of each of the Books
optionExplain: The diagrams are illustrations of experiments; there is little geometry to work through.
Later corrections serve a modern student; the authors point to Newton's own summaries.
The authors point to the end of each Book, especially Book III, not only the opening.
Right: the statements tell you what Newton claims.
Right: there Newton sums up his discoveries and suggests their consequences.
questions.explain: Along with the experiments, the authors recommend the statements of the propositions and Newton's summing-up discussions at the end of each Book.
questions.rule: Read the claims and the summaries.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: A reader of an old classic on electricity finds that one experiment needs only a glass rod, a silk cloth and scraps of paper. What do the authors' remarks on the Optics suggest?
options: Skip it, since experiments are for specialists
Read about it in a modern textbook instead
Repeat the experiment herself, since it is simple
Memorize its description and move on quickly
optionExplain: The authors want lay readers to see and do what the scientist describes where they can.
A textbook gives the modern account, not the experience of the experiment itself.
Right: simple experiments are worth repeating, and doing them makes the description vivid.
Memorizing words gives less than seeing the effect with her own eyes.
questions.explain: Where an experiment needs only everyday materials, repeating it is the authors' suggestion, as with Newton's prisms.
questions.rule: If it is simple, try it.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: A woodworking book is full of diagrams that look like engineering drawings, but each shows a joint a reader can cut with hand tools. By analogy with the Optics, what should a nervous reader do?
options: Avoid the book, since technical drawings need years of special training
Skip the diagrams and read only the surrounding prose
Check what the diagrams show before deciding they are too hard
Study drafting before attempting any of the joints
optionExplain: This judges the book by its look, as a reader might wrongly judge the Optics.
The diagrams here are the clearest guide to the joints; skipping them loses the most help.
Right: like Newton's diagrams, these illustrate things the reader can do, not hard theory.
The drawings illustrate cuts; they do not call for a drafting course.
questions.explain: A page's look can mislead about its kind. Asking what a figure is for comes before deciding it is beyond you.
questions.rule: Ask what a diagram is for before you fear it.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the look of a page can mislead about its kind: diagrams, tables or symbols may be illustrations of something you can do or see, so checking what a figure is for comes before deciding it is beyond you.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: Suppose a classic's key experiment needs a vacuum pump and glassware the reader does not have. What do the authors' suggestions point to now?
options: Seeing a demonstration, or relying on the description
Building the apparatus at home before reading on
Skipping the whole book as beyond a lay reader
Choosing a different classic whose experiments are simpler
optionExplain: Right: when repeating is out of reach, a demonstration or museum, or the text itself, must serve.
Repeating is advised where experiments are simple; this one is not.
One hard experiment does not close the book; other parts remain readable.
Switching books avoids the difficulty rather than meeting it; the authors offer demonstrations and museums for this case.
questions.explain: Repeating experiments is advice for simple ones. When the condition changes and the apparatus is out of reach, the other routes to first-hand experience, or the description, take over.
questions.rule: Repeat what is simple; seek demonstrations for the rest.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: True or false: The authors suggest repeating every experiment described in a scientific classic before reading further.
questions.explain: They say you can easily repeat some of Newton's experiments. The advice is to try some simple ones, not all of them first.
questions.rule: Some experiments, not all.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a scientific classic without mathematics can be harder to read than one that uses it.
questions.explain: The authors find this odd but true, and give Galileo's Two New Sciences as the case. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Less mathematics can mean more difficulty.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: The authors say scientific writers use mathematics mainly because of its preciseness, clarity and ____.
questions.explain: Mathematics is precise, clear and limited, which is why scientists use it and why its absence can leave a work harder to pin down.
questions.rule: Mathematics brings precision, clarity and limits.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: Reading a scientific dialogue, Lena finds three characters arguing back and forth about falling bodies. By the authors' account, what should be her main task?
options: Decide which character argues most vividly
Treat each character's view as the author's
Take the final speech as the book's answer
Work out what the author himself is claiming
optionExplain: Vividness is a dramatic quality; the author's claim may lie with a quieter voice.
Characters disagree; they cannot all speak for the author.
The last word in a dialogue need not be the author's conclusion.
Right: the difficulty of the form is discovering what is being said, and that is her task.
questions.explain: The authors say it is hard to discover what Galileo is saying in his dialogue. A reader's task is to pin down the author's claims from the exchange.
questions.rule: In a dialogue, find the author's claim.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: A podcast episode on nutrition is a loose conversation among three guests, with no summary. By analogy with the authors' point about Galileo, what makes it hard to learn from?
options: It has too many facts and figures for listeners to follow
Its claims are spread across speakers and must be pinned down
It is spoken rather than written, which makes it unreliable
Its guests are experts, so they speak only to other experts
optionExplain: The trouble with conversation is usually the opposite: claims are loose rather than packed with figures.
Right: as in a dialogue, what is asserted is scattered across voices and has to be reconstructed.
Speech can be reliable; the difficulty is the form, not the medium.
Expertise may play a part, but the conversation's shape is what scatters the claims.
questions.explain: Conversation spreads and qualifies claims across speakers. As with Galileo's dialogue, the listener must work to state what was asserted.
questions.rule: Conversation scatters claims; collect them.
questions.teaches: By analogy, conversational formats such as panels, interviews and podcasts share the dialogue's difficulty for conveying findings: claims are scattered and qualified across speakers, so the listener must reconstruct a statement of what was asserted.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: Which reader, by the authors' account, has met the primary obligation in reading Harvey on the circulation of the blood?
options: One who could now practise as a heart specialist
One who can state the problem Harvey set out to solve
One who has memorized all of Harvey's anatomical terms
One who has checked Harvey against modern data
optionExplain: Competence in the subject is what the authors say is not the reader's obligation.
Right: the primary obligation is to understand the problem.
Terms help, but memorizing them is not understanding the problem they serve.
Checking against modern data serves current knowledge, not the lay reader's aim.
questions.explain: The authors say the primary obligation is not to become competent in the subject matter but to understand the problem.
questions.rule: Understand the problem, not the whole subject.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.section: Handling the Mathematics in Scientific Books
questions.q: True or false: If Galileo had set out the same results mainly in mathematical form, the authors' account suggests what he says would be easier to pin down.
questions.explain: The authors value mathematics in science for its preciseness, clarity and limitedness, and trace the difficulty of Two New Sciences to its dialogue form.
questions.rule: Precise form makes claims easier to find.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Which do the authors say popularizations generally avoid? Choose two.
options: Technical words of every possible kind
Discussion of what the results mean
Detailed descriptions of experiments
Much mathematics, unless that is the subject
Any mention of the results of experiments
optionExplain: Some technical words appear; the authors name experiments and mathematics as what is skirted.
Explaining what results mean is much of what popularizations do.
Right: they report results instead of describing the experiments.
Right: they contain relatively little mathematics, except popular books on mathematics.
They do report results; it is the experiments behind them they leave out.
questions.explain: Popularizations skirt the two main difficulties of original scientific works: descriptions of experiments and mathematics. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Popularizations skip experiments and mathematics.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the general reader must fall back on scientific popularizations because he cannot become expert in every field.
questions.explain: Modern science assumes specialized training, and no one can be expert in all fields, so the general reader's route into current science is the popularization.
questions.rule: Specialization sends lay readers to popularizations.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: A popular book on the brain says a study found that sleep improves memory, with no account of how the study was done. Which of the two main difficulties has the book skirted?
options: The mathematics, since it uses no technical vocabulary at all
Neither, since the result has been stated in plain words
Stating the problem, since the book never names one
Following the evidence, since it reports the result only
optionExplain: Vocabulary and mathematics differ; the missing piece here is the study's description.
Plain words do not mean nothing was left out; the experiment was.
Stating the problem is the reader's task, not one of the two difficulties the authors name.
Right: by giving the result without the study, it spares the reader the evidence, the first difficulty.
questions.explain: Reporting a result without the study behind it skirts the first difficulty, following the evidence.
questions.rule: Results without method skirt the evidence.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: A cooking show presents a finished cake and says it used a new folding technique, without showing the technique. By analogy with popularizations, what does a viewer who wants to bake it lack?
options: The method, which she would need to reproduce the result
The ingredients list, since a show rarely gives exact amounts
Nothing, since knowing the outcome is all she needs
The judges' verdict on how the finished cake tasted
optionExplain: Right: a report of a result is enough to know about it, not to do it.
Amounts may be missing too, but what she most lacks to reproduce the cake is the technique itself.
Knowing a result is enough for some aims; to bake it she needs the method.
A verdict on taste helps her judge the cake, not bake it; the gap is the technique.
questions.explain: Like a popularization reporting results, the show gives the outcome without the procedure. That is fine for knowing, not for doing.
questions.rule: To reproduce a result, you need its method.
questions.teaches: Leaving out method makes a result easier to state but harder to reproduce: someone who wants to do what was done, not only know it, needs the original description.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Suppose a popular book's subject is mathematics itself, such as an introduction to what numbers are. By the authors' account, what changes?
options: Nothing: it will avoid mathematics like other popular books
It will describe many laboratory experiments instead
It will contain more mathematics, since that is its subject
It will be harder to read than any original classic
optionExplain: The authors exempt such books from the rule that popularizations contain little mathematics.
Mathematics is not an experimental subject; the change is in the amount of mathematics.
Right: the authors make an exception for popular books about mathematics itself.
More mathematics need not make it harder than an original classic.
questions.explain: Popularizations contain little mathematics unless they are about mathematics itself. Change the subject and that simplification no longer holds.
questions.rule: A popular book on mathematics will have mathematics.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Sort each feature by whether it is typical of a popularization or of an original scientific work.

items.t: Reports that a trial found a drug effective
Explains a finding in everyday words
Is written for a wide audience
Describes the apparatus and steps of the experiment
Sets out the mathematics behind the result
Gives the evidence in enough detail to check

questions.explain: Popularizations report and explain results for a wide audience. Original works describe the experiments and set out the mathematics, giving the evidence itself.
questions.rule: Popular works report; original works show.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, even the best-edited popular science magazines leave the reader dependent on reporters who filter the information.
questions.explain: However good the publication, the reader receives findings through someone else's report. The card next explains why this matters.
questions.rule: Popular science comes through a filter.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: According to the authors, what recourse does a lay reader have when a popular science reporter is not good?
options: Reading the original research paper instead
Writing to the magazine to demand corrections
Almost none, since the reader depends on the report
Checking the article against the same magazine
optionExplain: Original research is written by experts for experts, which is why the lay reader relies on reporters at all.
A letter may correct a later issue, but it does not give the reader the missing information now.
Right: the authors say that with a poor reporter we have almost no recourse.
The same publication shares the same filter, so it cannot check itself.
questions.explain: Because the original research is closed to the lay reader, a poor report leaves almost no way to find out what was actually found.
questions.rule: A poor filter leaves the lay reader stranded.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Which follow from depending on a reporter who filters scientific findings for you? Choose two.
options: The reader no longer needs to read actively
A good reporter leaves the reader well served
A poor report is hard for a lay reader to correct
The original research becomes easy to check
Every popular article misstates its sources
optionExplain: The authors say active reading matters more for popular science than almost anywhere else.
Right: the authors say that if the reporters are good, we are fortunate.
Right: with a poor reporter, the reader has almost no recourse.
Dependence on a filter means the source is not easily checked.
The authors praise some popular journals; dependence is not the same as constant error.
questions.explain: Dependence cuts both ways: a good filter serves you, a bad one leaves you with little recourse. It does not mean every article is wrong.
questions.rule: Your account is as good as your reporter.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: A busy executive learns about her company's problems only through summaries her staff prepare. By analogy with the authors' point, what is her position?
options: She depends on what her staff choose to keep or drop
She sees the problems more fully than her staff do
She can trust the summaries, since staff know the work
She has no need of summaries if she reads actively
optionExplain: Right: like a lay reader, she sees the facts only through others' choices, and cannot easily check what was left out.
Summaries give her breadth, but each passes through a filter, so she may see less than those closer in.
Knowing the work does not make a filter complete; good summaries serve her, poor ones mislead her.
Active reading helps her understand the summaries, but it cannot recover what they omit.
questions.explain: Anyone who learns through intermediaries shares the lay reader's dependence. One remedy is to keep more than one independent channel, so that what one drops another may keep.
questions.rule: Learning through intermediaries means trusting their filters.
questions.teaches: By analogy, anyone who learns through intermediaries faces the lay reader's dependence, and one remedy is to keep more than one independent filter, so that what one leaves out another may keep.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: True or false: The authors' point about filtering reporters means a reader should treat popular science articles as unreliable.
questions.explain: The authors praise good popular journals and say a good reporter is a stroke of fortune. The point is to remember the dependence, not to reject every report.
questions.rule: Remember the filter; do not reject every report.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a short popular science article with no diagrams or formulas can be read for understanding like a story, without much effort.
questions.explain: The authors say even a three-page article on DNA with none of those demands considerable effort. The card next explains what active reading involves here.
questions.rule: Popular science is not story reading.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Put these steps for reading a popular science work in the order the authors list them.
items: Identify the subject matter
Discover how the whole relates to its parts
Come to terms and find the propositions and arguments
Understand before criticizing or assessing significance
questions.explain: The steps follow the analytical rules: what the work is about and how it is built, then what it says, then judging it once understood.
questions.rule: Subject, structure, terms and arguments, then judgment.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Halfway through a popular book on black holes, Kim is writing objections in the margins, though she cannot yet say what the author's main argument is. Which rule has she skipped?
options: Identify the subject matter of the work
Read short articles mainly for information
Repeat the experiments the book describes
Understand the work before criticizing it
optionExplain: She knows the book is about black holes; the subject is not her problem.
That describes how much effort short pieces need; she is reading a book.
Black holes offer no simple home experiments, and the problem lies in her order of steps.
Right: she is judging before she understands the argument she is objecting to.
questions.explain: Objecting before she can state the main argument reverses the authors' order: understanding first, criticism after.
questions.rule: State it before you judge it.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Sort each piece by how much active thinking the authors would expect it to need.

items.t: A short news item on a newly found comet
A brief magazine note on a fossil find
A one-page report of a survey result
A compact popular book on relativity
A popular book on the environmental crisis
A popular book on the principles of mathematical reasoning

questions.explain: Short articles mainly inform, so following the account is often enough. Excellent popular books are compact and need constant attention and fuller analysis.
questions.rule: Short pieces inform; good popular books demand more.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: After a smooth, easy read of a popular article on economics, Ali feels he understood it, but he cannot say what its main argument was. By analogy with the authors' point, what happened?
options: He understood it, since the reading felt so easy to him
The easy read felt like understanding but was not
The article had no argument for him to find in it
Economics cannot be explained well to general readers
optionExplain: Ease is how it felt, not evidence of what he grasped.
Right: following smooth sentences can feel like understanding; being unable to state the argument shows it was not.
Most explanatory articles make an argument; his failure to state it is the clue.
Good popularizations exist in many fields; the problem was how he read.
questions.explain: Popular writing is never easy in the way a story seems to be. When an easy read leaves nothing he can state, the ease was misleading.
questions.rule: Feeling you understood is not understanding.
questions.teaches: Ease of reading can mislead: smooth prose without formulas may make a reader feel he understood when he only followed the sentences, so ease is not evidence of understanding.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: A reader who has been working through a compact popular book on black holes turns to a three-paragraph news item reporting that a comet will pass Earth next month. By the authors' account, what changes in how she should read?
options: She must outline its structure and arguments in full
She mainly needs to follow the account closely
She can read it without attention, as she would a story
She should criticize its claims first, then read it
optionExplain: Full analysis suits a compact popular book, not a short informational item.
Right: short articles are mainly informational and ask less active thinking.
