Less thinking is not none: she must still make the effort to follow the account.
The order stays the same: understand first, criticize after.
questions.explain: When the piece changes from a compact book to a short informational item, the demand drops to following the account carefully.
questions.rule: Match the effort to the piece.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a theoretical book that gives no rules of action can still have practical consequences for its reader.
questions.explain: The authors give Commoner's book on the environmental crisis as an example. The card next shows how the consequences arise.
questions.rule: Theory can bear on action.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: Match each popular book to the point the authors make about it.
pairs: A theory of environmental crisis with consequences for action
Barnett's The Universe and Dr. Einstein
A history of atomic research read amid fear of atomic war
Shows that the mathematician is no magician
questions.explain: Commoner's book implies action because the crisis is ours; Barnett's had practical weight when atomic war was feared; Whitehead's makes mathematics, a great modern mystery, less mysterious.
questions.rule: Each theoretical book mattered beyond theory.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: A popular book explains in theoretical terms how years of loud noise damage hearing, and gives no advice. By the authors' account, what would a careful reader do?
options: Treat it as theory with no bearing on her own life
Wait for the author to write a practical guide
Search the text for rules the author has hidden
Work out what it implies she should do about noise
optionExplain: The book is theoretical, but its conclusions bear on her situation, which is what the authors ask readers to notice.
The implication is there for a careful reader now; it need not wait for a guide.
The book stays theoretical; the step to action is her inference, not a hidden rule.
Right: if noise harms hearing and she is exposed, the theory implies she should act, say by protecting her ears.
questions.explain: As with Commoner's book, a theoretical account that bears on the reader's own situation carries a practical implication the careful reader draws for herself.
questions.rule: If the theory concerns you, ask what it asks of you.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: A theoretical book on how compound interest grows over decades contains no financial advice. Following the authors' reasoning about Commoner, what should a reader in her twenties consider?
options: What its conclusions imply for when she starts saving
Nothing, since the book offers no financial advice of its own
Whether the mathematics in the book is correct
How the author made his own investment choices
optionExplain: Right: growth over decades bears directly on someone with decades ahead, so the theory has a practical edge for her.
A lack of stated advice did not stop Commoner's book from having consequences; the same holds here.
Checking the mathematics may matter, but it is not the practical implication.
The author's choices are his own; the question is what the theory implies for her.
questions.explain: The implications of a theory depend on the reader's situation. For a young saver, growth over decades points to starting early; for someone near the end of a career it would point elsewhere.
questions.rule: Apply the theory to your own case.
questions.teaches: Whether a theoretical book bears on action depends on the reader as well as the book: the same account of compound growth implies one thing for a saver of twenty-five and another for one of seventy, so each reader must apply it to her own situation.

questions.unitTitle: How to Read Science and Mathematics
questions.q: True or false: By the authors' reasoning, every theoretical popular science book implies some action its readers should take.
questions.explain: Commoner's book implies action, but the value the authors find in Whitehead's is understanding: seeing what mathematics is and how a mathematician thinks.
questions.rule: Some theory calls for action; some for understanding.

questions.q: According to the authors, what mainly separates a child's questions from an adult's?
options: Their number: children ask far more questions daily
Their subject: children ask about animals and games
Their character: children ask why, adults ask whether
Their form: children use shorter, plainer words than adults do
optionExplain: Children may ask more often, but the authors say explicitly that number is not the difference.
Children's examples in the text include God and existence, so the subject is not what sets them apart.
Right: the authors say it is the character of the questions, not their number, that marks the child.
Plain wording is common to both; the authors locate the difference in what the question seeks.
questions.explain: Adults keep their curiosity, but it shifts to whether something is so; children ask why. The card next shows why this matters for reading philosophy.
questions.rule: The child asks why; the adult often asks only whether.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, adults keep their curiosity, but it narrows to whether something is so rather than why.
questions.explain: The authors say adults do not lose their curiosity; its quality deteriorates, so it turns to matters of fact and information.
questions.rule: Curiosity survives but narrows.

questions.q: Priya is reading a book about friendship and wants to find the question a philosopher would pursue. Which one is it?
options: Why do human beings need friends at all?
How many close friends does a typical adult have?
Did the author keep his own friendships for life?
Why have close friendships grown fewer in recent decades?
optionExplain: Right: it is a basic why-question about human nature that no survey or index could settle.
A survey can answer this; it asks whether and how many, the adult's information question.
This is a biographical fact about the author, not a question about friendship itself.
A why-question, but a factual one that surveys and history can answer; the philosopher's why is about friendship itself.
questions.explain: The child's kind of question asks why something is as it is, in a way no fact-finding could settle. Counts, biography and factual causes are information questions.
questions.rule: Look for the why beneath the facts.

questions.q: Sort these questions by whether they ask only for information or ask the child's kind of question.
groups: Asks the child's kind of question

items.t: In what year did the war end
How tall is the tallest tree on record
Which country has the most lakes
Is it ever right to break a promise
What makes a thing the same thing after it changes
Why is there anything at all rather than nothing

questions.explain: The first three can be looked up in a reference book. The last three ask why, or what something is, and no lookup could settle them.
questions.rule: If a reference book could settle it, it is an information question.

questions.q: A software firm gives new staff a long list of answers to common problems before they have used the product. By analogy with the authors' remark about questions and answers, what is the likely weakness?
options: Staff will reject the answers as too abstract to be useful
Long lists are harder to memorise than short ones, so staff forget
Staff will ask more questions than the firm can handle
Answers mean little to someone who has not felt the question
optionExplain: The answers here are concrete; the problem is not abstraction but the missing question.
Length may matter, but the authors' point concerns the order of question and answer.
The worry runs the other way: without felt questions, staff may not see what the answers are for.
Right: the authors say a mind not stirred by good questions cannot appreciate even the best answers.
questions.explain: The authors say it is easy to learn answers, but a mind not agitated by real questions cannot see their significance. By analogy, answers handed out before the problem is met tend to slide off.
questions.rule: The question gives the answer its value.
questions.teaches: According to the authors, a mind not stirred by real questions cannot appreciate even the best answers, so a question has to be felt before its answer can mean much.

questions.q: Dana argues that any question beginning with why is philosophical, so why her train is late belongs in a philosophy book. Where does her reasoning go wrong?
options: Philosophy asks whether things are so rather than why
A why-question with a factual answer is not that kind
Only questions about existence count as philosophical
Questions from daily life are too small for philosophy
optionExplain: This reverses the card: the adult's narrowed curiosity asks whether; philosophy keeps asking why.
Right: the train's delay can be found out from the timetable or the railway; the child's question is one no fact-finding settles.
Questions about good and evil are philosophical too, so existence is not the only subject.
Children's everyday questions, like what makes the cat tick, can be profound; daily life is not the problem.
questions.explain: The form why is not enough. The child's kind of question is one that no lookup or investigation could answer, and a late train has a findable cause.
questions.rule: Test a why-question by asking whether facts could settle it.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reader must think as children think in order to understand existence.
questions.explain: The authors say we need not think as children, who cannot understand existence; we must see, wonder and ask as they do. The card next explains the balance.
questions.rule: Ask like a child; do not reason like one.

questions.q: The authors say that to follow the great philosophers we must be childishly simple in our questions and maturely ____ in our replies.
questions.explain: The pairing puts simplicity in the question and wisdom in the reply.
questions.rule: Simple questions, wise replies.

questions.q: Which pairing fits the authors' ideal for philosophical inquiry?
options: A technical question and a carefully reasoned answer
A basic question and a carefully reasoned answer
A basic question and a quick, instinctive answer
A technical question and a quick, instinctive answer
optionExplain: Careful reasoning is right, but the authors want the question stripped of adult complexity, not made technical.
Right: the question is childishly simple, the reply maturely wise.
The basic question is right, but a quick answer is as childish as the question, the opposite of mature wisdom.
This gets both halves backwards: complexity in the question and haste in the answer.
questions.explain: The authors place the child's simplicity in the asking and adult wisdom in the answering. Each of the other pairings gets at least one half wrong.
questions.rule: Simplicity in asking, care in answering.

questions.q: A town council is lost in the details of a parking rule until one member asks what any rule of the road is for. What would the authors' ideal ask of the council next?
options: Adopt the first plain answer offered, since the question was plain
Set the question aside as too basic for a council of adults
Replace it with a narrower technical question about parking
Work out an answer that weighs the rules' purposes with care
optionExplain: A plain question does not call for a plain answer; the authors want wisdom in the reply.
The authors praise basic questions; calling them too basic is the adult habit they regret.
Going back to technicalities would bring back the complexity the simple question cleared away.
Right: a simple question has cleared away the clutter; now it needs a mature, carefully reasoned reply.
questions.explain: The member asked a childishly simple question. The authors' ideal now asks for a maturely wise answer, not a hasty one and not a retreat into detail.
questions.rule: After the simple question, take care over the reply.

questions.q: A consultant tells a firm its trouble is that it confuses urgent work with important work. The board replies that this is obvious and anyone could have seen it. In the light of the authors' remark about simple distinctions, what is the best response?
options: Its ease once stated does not show it was easy to find
If it is obvious, the board must already have acted on it
A distinction that sounds simple is unlikely to be true
Only a technical distinction could be worth paying for
optionExplain: Right: the authors say great distinctions are simple once stated and vastly difficult before.
This could be a fair challenge, but it does not answer the charge of obviousness; the real point is about hindsight.
The authors value simple distinctions; simplicity is no sign of falsehood.
The authors hold the reverse: clearing away complexity to a simple distinction is the achievement.
questions.explain: A good distinction looks easy after someone states it. The fair test is whether the board could have drawn it before hearing it.
questions.rule: Judge a distinction by how hard it was to see beforehand.
questions.teaches: Because a good distinction looks easy once stated, readers tend to underrate it; the fair test is whether they could have drawn it themselves before reading it.

questions.q: True or false: A reply that is as simple as the question it answers meets the authors' ideal for philosophical answers.
questions.explain: Simplicity belongs to the question. A reply as naive as the question is childish in the way the authors warn against; they ask for mature wisdom in replies.
questions.rule: A simple question does not license a simple answer.

questions.q: According to the authors, what is typical of philosophical questions about existence?
options: They are hard to state but easy once stated well
They are easy to state and easy to answer by thought
They are easy to state but enormously hard to answer
They are hard to state and answerable only by experts
optionExplain: It is a natural guess that difficulty lies in the wording, but the authors say the stating is easy.
Thinking is the method, but the authors say the answers are enormously difficult, not easy.
Right: the authors stress that these questions are simple to state and understand, yet very hard to answer.
The authors say the questions are easy to state, and they do not limit answers to experts.
questions.explain: Questions about being are simple to put and understand, but so hard to answer that some philosophers say they cannot be answered well. The card next lists them.
questions.rule: Easy to ask, hard to answer.

questions.q: Which of these are among the questions about being that the authors list?
options: How many stars does our galaxy contain?
Is there a universally valid line between good and evil?
Is the realm of the possible larger than the actual?
Can anything exist apart from material embodiment?
Do some things exist only in or for the mind?
optionExplain: This sounds large, but it is a factual question for astronomers, not a question about existence as such.
This is philosophical, but it belongs to the practical questions about good and evil, not to being.
Right: possible versus actual existence is one of the listed questions about being.
Right: whether everything exists physically is on the list.
Right: existence in the mind versus outside it is a question about modes of being.
questions.explain: The being questions ask what existing is, its modes, and whether things exist physically, necessarily or possibly. Star counts are factual; good and evil belong to another family.
questions.rule: Being questions ask what it is to exist and in what ways.

questions.q: A podcast debates whether numbers exist outside human minds or only in our thinking. What kind of question is it?
options: A question about good and evil
A question about kinds of change
A question about modes of being
A factual question for a survey
optionExplain: Nothing in the debate concerns what ought to be done; it asks how numbers exist.
The debate is not about numbers coming to be or altering; it is about their way of existing.
Right: whether some things exist only in or for the mind is one of the listed questions about being.
Polling mathematicians would report opinions, not settle how numbers exist.
questions.explain: Asking whether something exists only for the mind or apart from it is asking about modes of being.
questions.rule: Mind-dependent or not is a question about modes of being.

questions.q: True or false: Whether a newly reported deep-sea fish really exists is one of the philosopher's questions about being.
questions.explain: Whether one particular creature exists is settled by finding it. The philosopher's questions ask what existing is and in what ways things can exist.
questions.rule: Whether this thing exists is a fact; what existing is, is philosophy.

questions.q: Gamers pay real money for a sword that exists only as data in an online game. A designer asks in what sense the sword exists at all. What does this show?
options: A new kind of thing can revive an old question about being
Digital goods have made the old questions about being out of date
The question can be settled by checking the game's servers
Only physical objects raise any questions about existence
optionExplain: Right: the designer is asking the old question whether some things exist in a way other than physically.
The reverse: the new case makes the old question pressing again.
The servers show the data is stored; they do not say what kind of existence the sword has.
The listed questions include whether things can exist apart from matter, so non-physical cases are central.
questions.explain: Whether everything exists physically, and whether some things exist only for minds, are listed questions about being. A digital good puts them in a new setting.
questions.rule: Look for old questions about being behind new kinds of things.
questions.teaches: By analogy, new kinds of things, such as digital goods, revive the old questions about modes of being, so a modern topic can hide an ancient philosophical question.

questions.q: Suppose a reader ranks questions by how hard they are to state. Where would she likely put the question what all existing things have in common?
options: High, since it is among the hardest to state
Low, and rightly, since it has a quick and easy answer
High, since only experts can understand it
Low, though it is among the hardest to answer
optionExplain: The authors say such questions are not difficult to state, so this ranking misreads it.
Ranking it low would be her mistake; the authors say it is enormously hard to answer.
The authors say these questions are easy to understand, not reserved for experts.
Right: the question is easy to state, so her ranking would miss how hard it is to answer.
questions.explain: Stating difficulty is the wrong measure: questions about being are easy to put yet very hard to answer.
questions.rule: Do not judge a question's depth by its wording.

questions.q: True or false: The authors use learning as an example of a change in which the learner remains the same individual.
questions.explain: When you learn, you change in knowledge but stay the same person; otherwise you could not be said to have changed. The card next shows the questions this raises.
questions.rule: Change seems to need something that stays.

questions.q: Match each change to the kind of change it is.
pairs: An apple turning red as it ripens
A ball rolling across a field
questions.explain: The authors name coming to be and passing away, local motion, growth and alteration in quality as kinds of change we meet in experience.
questions.rule: Things come to be, move, grow and alter.

questions.q: Over many years every plank of a ship is replaced, yet the owners call it the same ship. Which question about change does this raise most directly?
options: How many different kinds of change exist
What, if anything, endures through the change
Whether the change made the ship better
Whether the ship exists only in the owners' minds
optionExplain: Kinds of change are another question; this case asks what persists.
Right: the puzzle is whether anything stays the same while every part alters.
Better or worse is a question of value, not of what change involves.
This touches modes of being, but the puzzle arises from replacement over time, a matter of change.
questions.explain: The ship case asks whether something endures unchanged while its parts alter, the first question the authors raise about any change.
questions.rule: Ask what stays when everything seems to change.

questions.q: Sort these questions into the authors' two theoretical families.

items.t: What is common to all things that exist
Can anything exist apart from matter
Is the possible larger than the actual
What endures when a thing changes
How many kinds of change are there
Do the same causes act in all change

questions.explain: Questions about existence, its modes and its range belong to being; questions about what change involves, its kinds and causes belong to becoming.
questions.rule: Being asks what is; becoming asks how things change.

questions.q: A court must decide whether a company is still bound by a contract after a merger changed its name, owners and staff. Which of the authors' questions about change is the court facing?
options: Whether causes of becoming equal causes of being
Whether something endures while other aspects alter
Whether the merger was good or bad for the company's workers
Whether the change was local motion or growth
optionExplain: This is a real question about change, but not the one the court needs settled.
Right: the court must decide whether the same party persists through the alterations.
That is a question of value; the court's question is about identity through change.
Naming the kind of change does not answer whether the same party survives it.
questions.explain: Like the learner who stays the same person, the court asks whether the company endures through change. Law meets the philosopher's question whenever it asks if the same party is still bound.
questions.rule: Identity through change is a question far beyond philosophy books.
questions.teaches: By analogy, law and business meet the philosopher's question of what endures through change whenever they must decide whether an altered party is still the same one.

questions.q: True or false: An engineer's study of why one steel beam cracked is asking the philosopher's question about the causes of change.
questions.explain: The engineer seeks the cause of one particular change by investigation. The philosopher asks what a cause of change is and whether there are different types.
questions.rule: A particular cause is found; the nature of causes is thought out.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the question whether the will is free belongs to the theoretical side of philosophy.
questions.explain: The authors list the freedom of the will among speculative questions, beside the powers of the mind and the extent of knowledge. The card next lists the rest.
questions.rule: Free will is a theoretical question.

questions.q: Which of these do the authors list among the further theoretical questions of philosophy?
options: Justice and rights in the economy
The nature and extent of human knowledge
Necessity and contingency
The powers of the human mind
Duties and obligations to others
optionExplain: The just economy is a question about how society ought to be, so it is practical, not theoretical.
Right: what we can know and how far knowledge reaches is on the theoretical list.
Right: whether things exist necessarily or might not have existed is a speculative question.
Right: the powers of the mind are listed among theoretical questions.
Duties are philosophical, but they concern what ought to be done, so they belong to the practical list.
questions.explain: Theoretical questions ask what is the case: about necessity, the mind, knowledge and freedom. Duties and the just economy ask what ought to be.
questions.rule: Theoretical lists ask what is; practical lists ask what ought to be.

questions.q: An article asks whether a computer could ever truly understand a sentence, or only process symbols. Where does its leading question belong?
options: Practical philosophy: how computers should be used
Practical philosophy: what duties we owe to machines
Engineering alone: a matter of better design
Theoretical philosophy: the powers of the mind
optionExplain: How to use computers is a practical matter, but the article asks what understanding is.
Duties toward machines would be practical, but the article asks what machines can do, not what we owe them.
Better design can make a program do more, but whether doing that counts as understanding is not a design question.
Right: what understanding is, and what kind of thing can have it, is a question about the powers of mind.
questions.explain: Asking whether something can truly understand is asking about the powers of mind, one of the listed theoretical questions.
questions.rule: What a mind can do is a theoretical question.

questions.q: Sort these questions by whether they ask what is the case or what ought to be done or sought.

items.t: Can anything exist without matter
How far can human knowledge reach
Is the human will free
What do we owe to strangers
Can a war ever be just
What goal should a human life aim at

questions.explain: The first three ask about how things are, including the mind and knowledge. The last three ask about duties, justice and life's goal, which concern what ought to be.
questions.rule: Sort by is versus ought, not by how human the topic sounds.

questions.q: Many legal systems excuse people who could not control their actions. How does this rule stand to the theoretical question whether the will is free?
options: The practical rule rests on a question it leaves open
The rule settles the free-will question for everyone it covers
The rule shows that free will is a practical question
The rule makes the theoretical question irrelevant
optionExplain: Right: the law acts as if people can usually control themselves, without proving what the will is.
A court decides cases; it does not settle what the will is, so the question stays open.
Bearing on conduct does not change the question's kind; it still asks what is the case.
The rule depends on some view of control, so the question still matters underneath it.
questions.explain: The legal rule is practical, but it presupposes an answer about human control. By analogy, many practical systems lean on theoretical questions they never settle.
questions.rule: Practical rules often stand on open theoretical questions.
questions.teaches: By analogy, practical systems such as law often rest their decisions on theoretical questions they do not settle, like whether a person could have acted otherwise.

questions.q: Jon classes a self-help book on habits as theoretical philosophy because one chapter mentions doubts about free will. The rest gives routines for change. What has Jon missed?
options: Free will belongs to practical, not theoretical, philosophy
Self-help books cannot raise any philosophical question
The book's main question is how to change habits
A book must discuss free will throughout to mention it
optionExplain: The authors list free will as theoretical, so Jon's mistake is elsewhere.
A practical book can raise a philosophical question in passing; that is not the issue.
Right: a book is classed by the question it mainly pursues, and this one pursues a practical aim.
Books may mention a topic briefly; the point is that a passing topic does not set the book's kind.
questions.explain: A passing theoretical question does not make a practical book theoretical. Classify by the leading question.
questions.rule: Classify by the leading question, not a passing topic.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the pair good and evil seems to refer to a different class of things from the pair right and wrong.
questions.explain: The authors say the pairs seem to refer to different classes of things: what is wrong is not always felt to be evil. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Good and evil is not right and wrong.

questions.q: Hamlet, echoing Montaigne, says there is nothing either good or bad but ____ makes it so.
questions.explain: The authors quote Hamlet's line as one possible answer to whether good and evil are universal: the view that they depend on how we think.
questions.rule: Hamlet's line states the view that good and bad are relative.

questions.q: An essay argues that cruelty to children for amusement is bad in every culture and every age. Which of the authors' questions is it answering?
options: Whether the many goods can be ranked in order of importance
Whether everything that exists might not have existed
Whether some things are bad whatever the circumstances
Whether a thing endures while its qualities change
optionExplain: Ranking goods is a related practical question, but the essay is about one thing being universally bad.
This is a question about being, not about good and evil.
Right: the essay claims a thing that is bad everywhere, which answers whether some things are always bad.
This is a question about change, unrelated to the essay's claim.
questions.explain: Claiming that something is bad in every time and place takes one side of the question whether there is a universally valid distinction between good and evil.
questions.rule: A claim of universal badness answers the universality question.

questions.q: The authors suggest that not everything wrong is evil. Which of these acts would most people call wrong without calling them evil?
options: Torturing a prisoner for amusement
Framing an innocent man for a crime
Poisoning a town's water for profit
Forgetting to return a borrowed book on time
Missing a promised phone call to a friend
optionExplain: This is both wrong and, for most people, evil, so it does not show the gap between the pairs.
Deliberately destroying an innocent person is a case most would call evil as well as wrong.
Harming a whole town for gain is a case most would call evil, not only wrong.
Right: a small breach of what you owe is wrong, but calling it evil would overstate it.
Right: breaking a minor promise is wrong without being evil.
questions.explain: Small breaches of obligation are wrong but hardly evil. Grave, deliberate harms are wrong and evil, so they do not show the difference between the pairs.
questions.rule: Look for wrongs too small to call evil.

questions.q: Criminal law separates minor offences, such as parking illegally, from grave crimes, such as murder. How does this bear on the authors' distinction?
options: It reflects the sense that not every wrong act is evil
It proves that good and evil are relative to the law
It shows that right and wrong are the same as good and evil
It settles that some acts are evil in every circumstance
optionExplain: Right: grading offences treats some wrongs as minor breaches, not as evil deeds.
Laws differ by place, but grading offences does not prove anything about whether good and evil are relative.
Grading wrongs by gravity points the other way: wrong and evil are being kept apart.
A legal grading records a society's judgment; it does not settle the philosophical question.
questions.explain: The law's grades echo the authors' remark that we do not feel every wrong to be evil. Practical systems often build in distinctions that philosophy tries to make precise.
questions.rule: Practical systems often encode distinctions philosophy examines.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the law's grading of offences from parking violations to murder mirrors the sense that not every wrong is evil, so practical systems often build in distinctions philosophy tries to make precise.

questions.q: A student writes that, according to the authors, good and evil are relative, since they quote Hamlet saying thinking makes things good or bad. What is wrong with this?
options: The authors reject Hamlet's view as both false and morally unwise
Hamlet's line concerns right and wrong, not good and evil
The authors say the view belongs to Montaigne, not Hamlet
The authors offer Hamlet's view as a question, not a verdict
optionExplain: The authors do not reject the view either; they leave the question open.
Hamlet's line speaks of good and bad, the pair the authors are discussing.
The authors say Hamlet was echoing Montaigne; who said it first is not the student's error.
Right: the authors ask whether Hamlet was right; they list the question without answering it.
questions.explain: The authors pose the question whether good and evil are universal or relative and quote Hamlet as one answer. They do not endorse either side here.
questions.rule: A quoted view is not the authors' verdict.

questions.q: The authors prefer to speak of many goods. Which question does that way of speaking open up?
options: Whether anything good can exist apart from matter
Whether the goods can be put in order of importance
Whether good things come to be and pass away
Whether good is another word for pleasure and nothing else
optionExplain: This is a question about being, not one opened by speaking of many goods.
Right: once there are many goods, one can ask how they rank, depend on each other and conflict.
Change applies to good things as to others, but it is not the question about goods the authors raise.
Defining good as pleasure would shrink the many goods to one; the authors' wording points the other way.
questions.explain: Speaking of many goods leads to questions about their order: which matter more, which depend on others, and when they conflict. The card next lists them.
questions.rule: Many goods raise the question of their order.

questions.q: Which questions about goods do the authors list?
options: Do some goods depend on others?
Can goods conflict so one is given up?
Can every good be measured in money?
Do goods exist only in the mind?
Can the goods be put in order?
optionExplain: Right: dependence of some goods on others is listed.
Right: conflicts that force choosing one good over another are listed.
Pricing goods is a common modern habit, but the authors do not raise it.
This resembles a question about being, not one of the listed questions about goods.
Right: ordering the goods is the first question listed.
questions.explain: The authors ask whether goods can be ordered, whether some are more important, whether some depend on others, and whether goods can conflict.
questions.rule: Order, importance, dependence, conflict.

questions.q: A memoir tells of a doctor who gave up evenings with her children to keep a clinic open. Which question about goods does her choice raise?
options: Whether whatever is wrong in her choice is also evil
Whether goods can conflict, so one is forgone
Whether everything good is also physical
Whether some goods exist necessarily
optionExplain: Nothing in her choice was wrong in the ordinary sense; the issue is two goods competing.
Right: family time and patient care are both goods, and she had to give up some of one for the other.
Whether goods are physical is a question about being, not about her choice.
Necessary existence is a metaphysical question unrelated to her dilemma.
questions.explain: Her case is a conflict of goods: choosing one meant forgoing part of another.
questions.rule: A hard choice between two goods is a conflict of goods.

questions.q: True or false: Comparing two phones to see which gives more features for the price is the philosophical question of ordering goods.
questions.explain: The phone comparison weighs means to an aim you already hold. Ordering goods asks how different goods, such as health and wealth, stand to one another.
questions.rule: Comparing means to one aim is not ranking goods.

questions.q: A family argues about whether to save more money or spend more time together. One member asks what the savings are for. What does that question help the family do?
options: Prove that money is not a good at all
Turn the question into one of fact
Show that the two goods cannot conflict at all
See whether one good depends on the other
optionExplain: Money can be a real good; the question asks how it stands to other goods, not whether it is one.
Purposes are not facts to look up; the question stays one about goods.
The goods can still conflict; the question helps decide how to weigh them when they do.
Right: if savings serve a good life together, their value depends on that good, which helps rank them.
questions.explain: Asking what a good is for reveals whether it serves another good. A good valued for what it makes possible depends on the goods it serves.
questions.rule: Ask what a good is for to see where it ranks.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a good valued for what it makes possible, as money is for what it buys, depends on the goods it serves, so asking what a good is for is one way to rank it.

questions.q: A reader decides to define the word good in a few minutes before starting a book on ethics. According to the authors, what is likely to happen?
options: She will find herself deep in philosophy before she knows it
She will find the everyday meaning settles the matter
She will find that the word has no meaning that can be stated
She will need a dictionary of technical terms to start
optionExplain: Right: the authors say trying to say what good means involves you very deeply in philosophy.
The word is everyday, but the authors warn that its meaning is far from settled by use.
The authors call it a heady exercise, not a hopeless one.
The difficulty is not technical jargon; good is a common word, which is why it seems easy.
questions.explain: Because good is both everyday and philosophical, a quick definition opens questions about the many goods and their order.
questions.rule: Defining good is a philosophical project.

questions.q: True or false: The authors count questions about war and peace among philosophy's practical questions.
questions.explain: War and peace close the authors' list of practical questions, with justice, the state and the good society. The card next gives the whole list.
questions.rule: War and peace is a practical question.

questions.q: Which of these belong to the authors' list of further practical questions?
options: The powers of the human mind
Virtues and vices
The state and the individual
Happiness and life's purpose
The freedom of the will
optionExplain: The mind's powers concern what is the case, so they are theoretical.
Right: virtues and vices are on the practical list.
Right: the state and the individual is a practical question about how society ought to be.
Right: happiness and life's goal concern what we ought to seek.
Free will bears on conduct, but the authors list it among theoretical questions.
questions.explain: Practical questions ask what ought to be done or sought: virtues, the state, happiness. Free will and the mind's powers ask what is.
questions.rule: Practical questions concern goals and standards of conduct.

questions.q: A pamphlet argues that employers owe workers at least one day off each week. What kind of question is its main one?
options: A theoretical question about the mind's powers
A theoretical question about kinds of change
A practical question about duties and justice
A factual question about current days off
optionExplain: Workers' minds are not the topic; the pamphlet asks what is owed.
Nothing in the pamphlet concerns what change involves.
Right: what employers owe workers is a question about obligations and justice in human relations.
Current practice could be surveyed, but the pamphlet argues about what ought to be, not what is.
questions.explain: Arguing about what one party owes another is a practical question about duties and justice.
questions.rule: What is owed is a practical question.

questions.q: Ana classes a military history of a famous battle as practical philosophy because it is about war. What has she missed?
options: War belongs to theoretical philosophy, not practical
Histories cannot be classified by their subject at all
Its question is what happened, not what ought to be
Only books about peace count as practical philosophy
optionExplain: The authors list war and peace among practical questions, so this is not her error.
Subject does help classify a book; the trouble is that she ignored the kind of question.
Right: a history asks what happened; only a question about what ought to be done makes it practical philosophy.
War and peace appear together on the practical list; war is not excluded.
questions.explain: The topic word war does not decide the kind of book. A battle history asks what happened; a work on whether a war can be just asks what ought to be.
questions.rule: Classify by the kind of question, not the topic word.

questions.q: Two parenting books both aim to raise good children. One lists rules children must keep; the other describes traits of character to cultivate. In terms of the authors' list, how do they differ?
options: One centres on duties, the other on virtues
One is practical, the other theoretical
One is about happiness, the other about the state
One is about good, the other about evil
optionExplain: Right: rules state what one must do; traits of character are virtues, what kind of person to become.
Both aim at how children ought to be raised, so both are practical.
Neither book is mainly about happiness or the state.
Both books aim at good; the difference is in how they frame it.
questions.explain: Duties and virtues are separate items on the authors' list. Questions about duties ask what one must do; questions about virtues ask what kind of person to be.
questions.rule: Duties ask what to do; virtues ask whom to become.
questions.teaches: Questions about duties ask what one must do, while questions about virtues ask what kind of person to become, so two practical books can share a goal yet frame it differently.

questions.q: True or false: A book that only reports which activities people say make them happiest is, for that reason, asking a practical philosophical question about happiness.
questions.explain: Reporting what people say is a factual matter. The practical question asks what happiness is and what a person ought to seek.
questions.rule: Reports of opinion are not answers to ought-questions.

questions.q: The authors say the practical division of philosophy is more accurately called by another name. Which name?
options: Applied
Ethical
Prudential
Normative
optionExplain: Applied suggests putting theory to use, but the authors' name stresses standards of what ought to be.
Ethics is one branch of this division, not its name; politics is the other branch.
Prudence suggests practical wisdom, but the authors' name for the division is normative, since it deals with what ought to be.
Right: the authors call it normative, since it deals with what ought to be done or sought.
questions.explain: The authors prefer normative for the division concerned with what ought to be done or sought. The card next shows how to tell it from theoretical philosophy.
questions.rule: Practical philosophy is better called normative.

questions.q: True or false: Questions about being and becoming belong to the theoretical, or speculative, division of philosophy.
questions.explain: Being and becoming concern what is or happens in the world, which is the business of theoretical or speculative philosophy.
questions.rule: Being and becoming are theoretical.

questions.q: Sort these philosophical works into the authors' two main divisions.

items.t: An essay on whether the past still exists in any sense
A treatise on what causes things to change
A study of whether we can know anything for certain
A tract on what a ruler owes his subjects
A dialogue on how one ought to face death
An essay on whether lying is ever permitted

questions.explain: Existence, change and knowledge concern what is. Duties, how to face death and whether lying is permitted concern what ought to be done.
questions.rule: Is goes to theoretical; ought goes to normative.

questions.q: A book argues that because human beings are social by nature, we ought to build communities that foster friendship. Where does it belong?
options: Theoretical, since it makes a claim about what human nature is
Normative, since its main question is what we ought to do
Both equally, since it has one claim of each kind
Neither, since it is a work of social science
optionExplain: The book does use a theoretical premise, but its leading question is about what ought to be built.
Right: the claim about human nature serves as a premise; the book's question is what we ought to do.
A book is placed by its leading question; a premise of the other kind does not split it in two.
Social science would study how communities work; this book argues for what we ought to build.
questions.explain: Normative works often rest on theoretical premises. The leading question, what we ought to build, decides the division.
questions.rule: A theoretical premise does not make a normative book theoretical.

questions.q: A city's building code requires buildings to withstand a certain earthquake. Engineers' studies measure how buildings behave in quakes. Which pairing matches the authors' division?
options: The code says what is; the studies say what ought to be done
The code says what ought to be done; the studies say what is
Both say what ought to be done, since both of them serve safety
Both say what is, since both rest on measurements
optionExplain: This reverses the roles: measurements describe, while a code prescribes.
Right: the code sets a standard to be met; the studies report how buildings in fact behave.
The studies serve safety but report facts; serving a goal does not make a report normative.
The code draws on measurements, but it states a requirement, which is a norm.
questions.explain: The authors' division is not limited to philosophy books. A standard states what ought to be, while research behind it states what is, and judging the standard needs both.
questions.rule: Ask of any document whether it states what is or what ought to be.
questions.teaches: By analogy, documents outside philosophy split the same way: a building code states what ought to be done, while the studies behind it state what is, so judging a code means asking for both its facts and its goals.

questions.q: True or false: If a book's leading question is about what ought to be, it belongs to normative philosophy even if many of its chapters describe how things are.
questions.explain: Descriptive chapters may supply premises, but the division follows the leading question. An ought-question puts the book in normative philosophy.
questions.rule: The leading question decides the division.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a cookbook can assume you want to cook well, without arguing that you ought to.
questions.explain: A cookbook can take your goal for granted and tell you how to reach it. The card next shows how normative philosophy differs.
questions.rule: How-to books assume their goal.

questions.q: According to the authors, what are books of normative philosophy primarily concerned with?
options: The steps for reaching a goal you hold
The facts about how people actually live
The causes of change in human affairs
The goals all people ought to seek
optionExplain: Steps toward a goal you already hold are the business of how-to books.
How people live is a factual matter; normative philosophy asks how they ought to live.
Causes of change belong to theoretical philosophy, not normative.
Right: goals such as a good life or a good society are their main concern.
questions.explain: Normative philosophy concerns the goals all ought to seek and argues for them, unlike books that assume a goal.
questions.rule: Normative philosophy argues for goals.

questions.q: Which of these books is closest to normative philosophy in the authors' sense?
options: A book arguing that a good life requires friendship
A guide to making friends after moving to a new city
A survey of how many friends adults report having
A manual of etiquette for hosting dinner parties
optionExplain: Right: it argues for a goal, friendship as part of a good life, that everyone ought to seek.
This assumes you want friends and gives steps, which is the how-to pattern.
A survey reports facts; it does not argue for any goal.
Etiquette manuals assume you want to host well and give particular rules.
questions.explain: Only the first argues that a goal ought to be sought. The others assume a goal or report facts.
questions.rule: Arguing for the goal marks normative philosophy.

questions.q: Which features mark a work of normative philosophy rather than a how-to book?
options: It assumes you already want the result
It sets out particular steps in order
It argues that a goal ought to be sought
It prescribes means only in universal terms
It concerns goals such as a good society
optionExplain: Assuming the reader wants the result is the how-to book's starting point.
Particular, ordered steps are what how-to books provide.
Right: normative philosophy cannot assume its goals, so it argues for them.
Right: it stops at means stated in the most universal terms.
Right: its goals are ones all ought to seek, such as a good life or a good society.
questions.explain: Normative philosophy argues for universal goals and prescribes means only generally. How-to books assume the goal and give particular steps.
questions.rule: Argue for ends and stay general, or assume ends and get specific.

questions.q: A constitution declares that the state shall protect each citizen's liberty, but says nothing of how a town should run its parking permits. In the light of the authors' contrast, what best explains the gap?
options: The constitution's drafters forgot to add the practical detail needed
Liberty is a theoretical question, not a practical one
Aims for all stay general; steps depend on local conditions
Liberty and parking are unrelated, so no gap needs explaining
optionExplain: Leaving detail out is part of the document's job, not an oversight.
Liberty concerns what ought to be secured, so it is a practical, normative matter.
Right: like normative philosophy, the constitution states aims and means universally and leaves particular steps to those who know the circumstances.
Parking rules can touch liberty; the gap reflects the level of generality at which the document works, not unrelated subjects.
questions.explain: Documents that set aims for everyone stay at universal means, because particular steps depend on circumstances that differ from place to place.
questions.rule: Universal aims leave particular steps to circumstance.
questions.teaches: By analogy, documents that set aims for everyone, such as constitutions, stop at universal means because particular steps depend on circumstances that vary, much as normative philosophy stops short of a how-to book's detail.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors' contrast, a cookbook that does not argue for the value of good cooking has failed at its job.
questions.explain: A how-to book may assume its goal; arguing for the goal is the job of normative philosophy, not of a cookbook.
questions.rule: Do not fault a how-to book for assuming its goal.

questions.q: Epistemology, the authors say, is another name for which of these?
options: Theory of being
Theory of change
Theory of knowledge
Theory of the good life
optionExplain: The study of being is metaphysics.
The study of change is the philosophy of nature.
Right: epistemology studies what knowing involves and the extent and limits of knowledge.
The good belongs to normative philosophy, not to a theoretical branch.
questions.explain: Epistemology is theory of knowledge. The card next sets it beside metaphysics and philosophy of nature.
questions.rule: Epistemology is theory of knowledge.

questions.q: Match each branch of theoretical philosophy to its main concern.
questions.explain: The three theoretical branches follow the three kinds of question: about being, about becoming and about knowing.
questions.rule: Being, change, knowledge.

questions.q: An essay asks whether anything we perceive could be a dream, and how far our certainty can reach. To which branch does it belong?
options: Epistemology
Metaphysics
Philosophy of nature
Normative philosophy
optionExplain: Right: its question concerns the certainty and limits of knowledge.
It touches on what exists, but its main concern is how far we can know.
Nothing in the essay asks what change is or what causes it.
It asks what we can know, not what we ought to do, so it is theoretical.
questions.explain: Doubt about perception and the reach of certainty are questions about knowledge, the concern of epistemology.
questions.rule: Certainty and its limits point to epistemology.

questions.q: True or false: A book reporting experiments on how fast different bodies fall belongs to the philosophy of nature in the authors' sense.
questions.explain: Measuring falling bodies is natural science, based on special experiment. Philosophy of nature asks what change is and what a cause of change is.
questions.rule: Philosophy of nature asks what change is, not how fast things move.

questions.q: A newsroom's guide asks when a source can be trusted and when a claim is certain enough to print. Which branch of philosophy do its underlying questions echo?
options: Metaphysics: what it is for something to exist
Philosophy of nature: what causes events to change
Ethics: how a person ought to live a good life
Epistemology: the grounds and limits of knowing
optionExplain: The guide does not ask what existing is; it asks how we know what happened.
Events change, but the guide's concern is how we come to know about them.
Reporters have ethical duties, but these questions are about knowing, not living well.
Right: trusting sources and judging certainty are questions about the grounds and limits of knowledge.
questions.explain: Practical fields that set standards of evidence lean on epistemology's questions, though they apply them rather than study them.
questions.rule: Standards of evidence rest on questions about knowledge.
questions.teaches: By analogy, fields that set standards of evidence, such as journalism or law, draw on epistemology's questions about the grounds and limits of knowledge, though they apply them rather than study them.

questions.q: A book opens by asking what change is, but most of its pages ask whether we can know that anything changes at all. How should you classify it?
options: As philosophy of nature, by its first question
As epistemology, by its main concern
As metaphysics, since both questions concern being
As unclassifiable, since it mixes two branches
optionExplain: The opening question matters, but the branch follows the main concern, which has shifted.
Right: the main concern has become what we can know, which places it in epistemology.
Neither question is mainly about being as such.
Books often mix branches; the main concern still decides the classification.
questions.explain: When a book's main concern shifts, its branch shifts with it. Here knowledge has become the main concern.
questions.rule: Classify by the main concern, not the opening line.

questions.q: True or false: In the authors' scheme, ethics and politics are both branches of normative philosophy.
questions.explain: Both ask what ought to be done or sought; they differ in whether the individual or the community is in view. The card next draws the line.
questions.rule: Ethics and politics are both normative.

questions.q: According to the authors, questions about the good society and the individual's conduct in relation to the community belong to ____.
questions.explain: The good society and the individual's relation to the community are the sphere of politics; the individual's good life is the sphere of ethics.
questions.rule: The good society is politics.

questions.q: Sort these questions into ethics and political philosophy.

items.t: Should I tell a dying friend a painful truth
Is courage needed for a good life
How should a person deal with envy
May a government censor the press in wartime
What makes a constitution good
Do citizens owe obedience to bad laws

questions.explain: The first three concern an individual's conduct and good life. The last three concern the community, including how an individual stands toward it.
questions.rule: One life is ethics; life in a community is politics.

questions.q: Lena classes an essay on whether a citizen must pay an unfair tax as ethics, because it concerns one person's choice. What has she missed?
options: Taxation is a theoretical subject, not a normative one
It concerns an individual's conduct toward the community
Any question involving money belongs to economics and not to ethics
Ethics deals with the good society, not with individuals
optionExplain: Whether one must pay is a question of what ought to be done, so it is normative.
Right: politics includes the individual's conduct in relation to the community, which is what a duty to pay tax is.
Money is involved, but the question is what a citizen owes, which is political philosophy.
This swaps the branches: ethics concerns the individual's good life, politics the good society.
questions.explain: A question can be about one person and still belong to politics, if it concerns that person's conduct toward the community.
questions.rule: One person's duty to the community is politics.

questions.q: A hospital board sets up a system that requires nurses to report colleagues who drink on duty. On what answer to an ethical question does this political-style arrangement rest?
options: That a hospital is a kind of state with its own constitution
That rules for a community settle nothing about individuals
That whether to report is a theoretical question about facts
That an individual nurse ought to report such a colleague
optionExplain: The analogy with politics does not make a hospital a state; the point is what the system assumes.
The case shows the reverse: the community's rule rests on a view of individual conduct.
Whether one ought to report is a normative question, not a factual one.
Right: the system for the whole presupposes that reporting is what each nurse ought to do.
questions.explain: By extension, questions about a community's arrangements often presuppose answers about individual conduct. Political questions can depend on ethical ones.
questions.rule: Ask what individual duty a rule for the whole assumes.
questions.teaches: By extension, questions about a community's arrangements often rest on answers about individual conduct, as a reporting system presupposes that each member ought to report, so political questions may depend on ethical ones.

questions.q: True or false: If an essay on the good life turned to how a community should arrange its laws so that people can live well, its question would move toward political philosophy.
questions.explain: Once the question is how the community should be arranged, the good society is in view, which is the sphere of politics.
questions.rule: When the community's arrangement is the question, it is politics.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: Which of these would the authors call a second-order question?
options: What do we mean by the word cause?
Does every event have a cause?
Ought we to keep every promise?
Is anything in the world unchanging?
optionExplain: Right: it asks about our language and thought, not directly about events in the world.
This asks about the world itself, so it is first-order.
This asks what we ought to do, a first-order normative question.
This asks about being, a first-order theoretical question.
questions.explain: A question about what a word means aims at our thought and language, which makes it second-order. The card next sets out the distinction.
questions.rule: Questions about our words and thoughts are second-order.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: True or false: In the authors' terms, a question about what people ought to do is a first-order question.
questions.explain: First-order questions include both what is and happens in the world and what people ought to do or seek.
questions.rule: Both is and ought questions are first-order.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: Sort these questions into first-order and second-order.

items.t: Is the soul immortal
Should the rich give to the poor
Does every change need a cause
What does the word ought mean in moral talk
How do statements about the past get their meaning
Is a sentence about God the kind that can be true or false

questions.explain: The first three aim at the world or at conduct. The last three aim at our words and statements about them.
questions.rule: World and conduct first; thought and language second.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: Two books share the title Justice. One asks what a fair society would require; the other analyses how the word justice works in arguments. Which description fits?
options: The first is second-order, the second first-order
Both are first-order, since both of them concern justice
The first is first-order, the second second-order
Both are second-order, since both use the word
optionExplain: This reverses them: analysing a word's use is the second-order task.
Sharing a topic does not make them the same order; their targets differ.
Right: the first aims at how society ought to be; the second aims at our language about it.
Every book uses words; only the one that studies the word's use is second-order.
questions.explain: Same topic, different targets. Asking what society requires is first-order; asking how the word functions is second-order.
questions.rule: Sort by target, not by topic.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: A court asks whether a builder broke his contract. A legal scholar asks what the word reasonable means across hundreds of contract cases. How do the two questions relate, by analogy with the authors' distinction?
options: The court asks about legal terms; the scholar, about the case
Both ask about the case, since both concern contracts
The court asks about the case; the scholar, about legal terms
Both ask about legal terms, since every court must interpret words
optionExplain: This reverses them: the scholar studies the term across cases, not this case.
The scholar is not deciding any contract; the question is about a word's meaning.
Right: one aims at what happened and what is owed; the other at the concepts and language used to decide such cases.
Courts read words, but the court's question is whether this builder broke this contract.
questions.explain: Fields outside philosophy have the same two levels: questions about their subject, and questions about their own concepts and language.
questions.rule: Every field has questions about its subject and about its own terms.
questions.teaches: By analogy, most fields have both levels: questions about their subject matter and questions about their own concepts and language, as law asks both whether a contract was broken and what its key words mean.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: Suppose a second-order study shows that the word good is used in two distinct senses. How might that bear on the first-order question whether pleasure is good?
options: It could show the question must be asked in each sense
It would answer the first-order question outright
It would show that the first-order question is meaningless
It would leave the first-order question untouched
optionExplain: Right: once two senses are found, the question splits, and each version may get a different answer.
Sorting senses clarifies the question but does not say whether pleasure is good.
Finding two senses refines the question; it does not empty it.
The orders are linked: clarifying the word changes how the question should be put.
questions.explain: Second-order work on words can sharpen first-order questions without answering them.
questions.rule: Clarifying words sharpens questions without settling them.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, most professional philosophers of their day no longer believed philosophers could answer first-order questions.
questions.explain: The authors say most had given up that belief and turned to second-order questions instead. The card next shows what this means for lay readers.
questions.rule: Modern professionals mostly gave up first-order questions.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: According to the authors, most professional philosophers now devote their attention to ____-order questions, often about language.
questions.explain: Modern professional philosophy, as the authors describe it, concentrates on second-order questions, very often about the language in which thought is expressed.
questions.rule: Modern philosophy is mostly second-order.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: A reader finds a recent philosophy paper unreadable: it analyses the logic of sentences using the word know, cites only specialists, and assumes their debates. What do the authors' remarks suggest?
options: She lacks the basic ability needed to read any philosophy
She should skim it quickly, then reread it slowly
The paper is badly written and should be ignored
It is a specialist second-order work, not a test of her
optionExplain: The authors say lay readers can read the classics; failing here says little about her ability.
Rereading helps with books written for her, but this paper assumes an expert's background.
It may be well written for its audience; the trouble is that she is not that audience.
Right: the authors say such work is written for experts and is as hard for outsiders as specialist science.
questions.explain: A second-order paper written for specialists is closed to lay readers in the way specialist science is. The authors offer no advice for reading it.
questions.rule: Specialist work is hard because of its audience, not your ability.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: True or false: By the authors' account, a recent philosophy book can be within a lay reader's reach if it asks first-order questions and is written for lay readers.
questions.explain: What closes modern philosophy to lay readers is second-order questions written for experts. A recent book without those features falls outside the complaint.
questions.rule: Judge by questions and audience, not by date.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: An economics journal devotes an issue to how economists should define and measure their own key terms. By the authors' reasoning about philosophy, why would a lay reader find it hard?
options: Economics is a theoretical subject closed to all outside readers
Questions about a field's own terms appeal mainly to insiders
Lay readers cannot follow any argument that uses numbers
Definitions in economics are kept secret from the public
optionExplain: Much economics is readable by outsiders; the difficulty here comes from the kind of question.
Right: like second-order philosophy, questions about a field's own concepts are of narrow appeal and written for experts.
Numbers are not the issue; the issue is that the questions concern the field's own tools.
The definitions are public; they are hard because the debate assumes expert background.
questions.explain: Questions about a field's own terms and methods interest mainly those inside it, so writing about them narrows to experts, as second-order philosophy did.
questions.rule: Method talk narrows the audience.
questions.teaches: By analogy, when any field turns to questions about its own terms and methods, its writing narrows to insiders, so method papers in economics or medicine are hard even for educated outsiders.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: Suppose a modern philosopher writes a book for ordinary readers asking whether life has a purpose. By the authors' account, how should a lay reader approach it?
options: As closed, since it was written well after about 1930
As readable: a first-order question for lay readers
As second-order, since a professional philosopher wrote it
As unreadable until she has first studied formal logic
optionExplain: The date is only a rough marker; the authors' reason concerns the questions and the audience.
Right: what closes modern philosophy to lay readers is second-order questions written for experts; this book has neither feature.
Who writes a book does not set the order of its question; its target does.
Logic training is needed for some second-order work, not for a first-order book written for lay readers.
questions.explain: The authors' complaint follows from the questions asked and the audience addressed. Change both, and the book becomes readable.
questions.rule: First-order questions for lay readers make a book readable.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: How do the authors view modern philosophers' attention to second-order questions?
options: As a waste of effort that ought to be stopped
As the only proper work left for philosophers today
As a passing fashion that has already ended
As good in itself, since criticism does no harm
optionExplain: The authors do not reject second-order work; their complaint lies elsewhere.
That is the view they attribute to the profession, not their own; they want first-order questions kept.
The authors describe it as the dominant practice of their day, not a past fashion.
Right: the authors call it all to the good, since being critical is never harmful.
questions.explain: The authors welcome critical work on thought and language; they regret only the abandonment of first-order questions. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Criticism is welcome.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: The authors say the trouble with modern philosophy is the wholesale giving up of ____-order questions.
questions.explain: The complaint is not that second-order questions are asked, but that first-order questions, the ones lay readers care about, have been dropped wholesale.
questions.rule: The loss is the first-order questions.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: A seminar on happiness spends every session on how the word happy is used and does not once ask what a happy life is. In the authors' terms, what has gone wrong?
options: Clarifying the word has replaced the first-order question
Studying how the word is used was a mistake from the start
Happiness cannot be discussed until the word is defined
The seminar should have studied first-order questions only
optionExplain: Right: the word study was useful, but it has crowded out the question it should serve.
The authors call critical work good; the mistake is letting it take over.
Clarifying helps, but waiting for a final definition keeps the main question from ever being asked.
The authors do not ask for first-order questions only; they welcome criticism too.
questions.explain: Second-order work is welcome; the failure is letting it replace the first-order question.
questions.rule: Let word study serve the question, not replace it.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: Which statements fit the authors' position on modern philosophy?
options: Giving up first-order questions wholesale is the trouble
Second-order work should be dropped as useless
Philosophy is properly read by experts alone
Criticism of thought and language does no harm
First-order questions most interest lay readers
optionExplain: Right: this is their complaint.
The authors call second-order work all to the good; they do not want it abandoned.
The authors want philosophy readable by ordinary people, and urge you to read the classics.
Right: the authors say this outright.
Right: the authors say first-order questions are most likely to interest lay readers.
questions.explain: The authors welcome criticism but regret the loss of first-order questions, which matter most to lay readers.
questions.rule: Keep criticism; keep the big questions.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: A software team spends months refining the terms and rules of its code-review process and ships nothing. Which reading of the authors' point fits this case best?
options: Refining tools is wasted effort and should be skipped
Shipping is all that matters, so process is not worth discussing
Refining tools is useful until it replaces the work they serve
The team should hire outside experts to settle its terms
optionExplain: The authors call critical work good; skipping it would lose its value.
The authors' balance keeps both; discussing method is fine so long as the main work goes on.
Right: like second-order philosophy, process work is good, but not when it crowds out the main task.
Bringing in experts does not address the problem, which is that the main task stopped.
questions.explain: By analogy, any practice can let the refinement of its tools crowd out the work those tools serve. The test of method work is whether it returns to the main task.
questions.rule: Method work should return to the main task.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any practice can let refinement of its tools crowd out the work the tools serve, so the test of method talk is whether it leads back to the main task.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a book devoted to the meaning of a single philosophical word is for that reason a sign of philosophy's decline.
questions.explain: The authors object to the wholesale abandonment of first-order questions, not to any particular study of words, which they call good.
questions.rule: One word study is not the wholesale loss.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the great philosophical classics from Plato onward were written for the general reader as well as for philosophers.
questions.explain: The authors say philosophers hoped to be read by their peers but also by ordinary, intelligent men and women. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: The classics were written for everyone.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: According to the authors, up to about the year ____, or a little later, philosophical books were written for the general reader.
questions.explain: The authors date the change to around 1930: before that, philosophers wrote for ordinary, intelligent readers as well as for each other.
questions.rule: Before about 1930, philosophy addressed everyone.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: Sam has no training in philosophy and wants to think about what makes a life go well. Following the authors, which should he pick?
options: A recent journal issue on the logic of moral terms
A survey of philosophers' current opinions
A classic that asks how one ought to live
An encyclopedia entry listing ethical theories
optionExplain: This is second-order work for specialists, the kind the authors say is closed to lay readers.
A survey reports opinions; the authors want him to meet the arguments themselves.
Right: a classic asks his first-order question and was written for readers like him.
A list of theories gives information about answers, not a book that works through the question.
questions.explain: The authors point lay readers to the classics: they ask first-order questions and were written for the general reader.
questions.rule: For a first-order question, go to a classic.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: True or false: When the authors call the classics accessible, they mean they can be read without much effort.
questions.explain: The authors say you can succeed if you wish to; the rest of the chapter is advice for the work involved. Accessible means within reach, not effortless.
questions.rule: Accessible means within reach, not effortless.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: By the authors' reasoning that books on questions of concern to everyone were written for everyone, which document would you expect an ordinary citizen to find most readable?
options: A bill of rights setting out what every citizen may claim
A tax code section written for corporate accountants
A regulation on testing aircraft engine components
A court rule on filing deadlines written for practising lawyers
optionExplain: Right: it addresses a matter that concerns every citizen, so it is written for every citizen.
Its matter concerns a narrow group, so it is written in their technical language.
Only engineers and inspectors need it, and it is written for them.
It concerns lawyers' procedure and assumes their training.
questions.explain: The breadth of a work's question tends to set its audience. Matters of concern to all are written for all, as the classic philosophers wrote for everyone.
questions.rule: Broad questions tend to bring broad audiences.
questions.teaches: By analogy, writing about matters that concern everyone tends to be addressed to everyone, so the breadth of a work's question is a clue to how readable it will be.

questions.section: Modern Philosophy and the Great Tradition
questions.q: Suppose a philosopher writes only for a handful of specialists. By the authors' account of who wrote for whom, which questions is he most likely pursuing?
options: First-order questions of concern to all
Practical questions about public life
Questions about being and about change in nature
Second-order questions of narrow appeal
optionExplain: First-order questions are the ones the authors say were written for everyone.
Public life concerns everyone, which by the authors' reasoning invites a wide audience.
Being and change are first-order questions, which the classics wrote about for lay readers.
Right: the authors link second-order questions with writing for experts.
questions.explain: The authors say it is no accident that first-order questions went with lay audiences; narrow, second-order questions go with expert audiences.
questions.rule: The audience follows the order of the question.

questions.q: According to the authors, how does a philosopher answer a question such as what change is?
options: By designing an experiment
By reflecting on the question
By searching old documents
By surveying the opinion of experts
optionExplain: Experiment suits scientific questions; no experiment shows what change is as such.
Right: the authors say there is nothing to do but think.
Documents serve historical questions; none can tell you what change is.
Gathering opinions reports what others think; it does not answer the question.
questions.explain: Philosophical questions cannot be settled by experiment, observation or documents; only reflection can answer them. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Philosophy's method is thinking.
