questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, no special phenomena can be observed that would show what change is or why things change.
questions.explain: The authors say there are no special kinds of phenomena to observe and no documents to read that would answer these questions; only reflection can.
questions.rule: No special observation answers a philosophical question.

questions.q: Sort these questions by how they would have to be answered.

items.t: Does this vaccine reduce infection
When was the city's first bridge built
Do heavier stones fall faster than lighter ones
What is it for something to exist
Does a promise bind when no one is watching
What do all changes have in common

questions.explain: Trials, records and experiments settle the first three. No experiment or document settles what existing is, whether promises bind, or what all change shares.
questions.rule: If research could settle it, it is not philosophy's question.

questions.q: A historian and a philosopher both study liberty. By the authors' test, which question belongs to the philosopher?
options: When the word liberty entered English
What liberty is, and whether it is a good
What a nation's founders meant by liberty
How many people today say they feel truly free
optionExplain: Dictionaries and old texts answer this; it is a historical question.
Right: no document or survey can settle what liberty is or whether it is good; only reflection can.
The founders' letters and speeches answer this; it is historical research.
A survey answers this; it reports opinions, not what liberty is.
questions.explain: Questions answerable from records or surveys belong to history or social research. What liberty is, and whether it is good, can only be thought through.
questions.rule: What a thing is, and whether it is good, is for reflection.

questions.q: A philosopher asks readers to imagine a machine that could give them any pleasant experience for life, and to ask whether they would plug in. Given the authors' account of method, what role does this imagined case play?
options: It is an experiment that gathers data on people's choices
It is a historical case drawn from documented events
It is a story added for colour, with no part in the argument
It tests an idea by reflection, in place of an experiment
optionExplain: No data are gathered; each reader consults his own judgment about an imagined case.
The machine does not exist; nothing documented is being examined.
The case carries the argument: if you would refuse, something besides pleasure matters to you.
Right: with no laboratory available, an imagined case lets the reader test an idea, here that pleasure is all we want, by thinking it through.
questions.explain: Because philosophy has nothing to do but think, it tests ideas by imagined cases worked through in the mind. Such thought experiments do the job that experiments do in science.
questions.rule: Thought experiments are philosophy's laboratory.
questions.teaches: By extension, thought experiments, imagined cases worked through in the mind, serve philosophy in place of a laboratory: they test an idea against cases without any apparatus.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a powerful enough new microscope could in principle show what all existing things have in common.
questions.explain: The authors say that if we could build a telescope or microscope to examine the properties of existence we should, but no such instrument is possible. Better instruments do not change the method.
questions.rule: No instrument examines existence as such.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, good philosophy is pure speculation, thinking divorced from experience.
questions.explain: The authors say good philosophy is not pure speculation; its answers face stringent tests based on common experience. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Philosophy is thinking, but not without experience.

questions.q: According to the authors, what are the tests of philosophical answers based on?
options: Common experience that every person has
Experiments that philosophers run themselves
The authority of earlier great thinkers
Logical form alone, apart from experience
optionExplain: Right: the tests rest on the experience you have as a human being, not as a philosopher.
Philosophers do no laboratory work; their tests use experience everyone already has.
Earlier thinkers are worth reading, but authority is not the test the authors name.
Reasoning matters, but the authors say philosophy divorced from experience is not good philosophy.
questions.explain: Philosophical answers are tested against common experience, which philosopher and reader share.
questions.rule: Common experience tests philosophy.

questions.q: A book claims that no one ever really chooses anything, since every act is forced. Using the authors' test, what should a reader do first?
options: Accept it, since philosophy need not match experience
Wait until a laboratory measures choices for her
Weigh it against her everyday experience of choosing
Reject it at once, since the claim is surprising
optionExplain: The authors say good philosophy is tested by experience, not free of it.
The test the authors name is common experience, which she already has.
Right: the claim must face the common experience of deliberating and choosing; the book then owes reasons for setting that experience aside.
Surprise is not refutation; she should test the claim and its reasons, not dismiss it.
questions.explain: Common experience is the test. A claim that clashes with it needs strong reasons, which the reader should look for and weigh.
questions.rule: Check the claim against what you meet every day.

questions.q: Which of these count as common experience in the authors' sense?
options: Viewing far galaxies through a telescope
Measuring brain activity in a scanner
Seeing things around you change
Choosing between things you want
Learning something you did not know
optionExplain: This needs special instruments, so it is special experience, the scientist's kind.
This needs special equipment and method, so it is special, not common, experience.
Right: everyone meets change daily, which is why the authors say you know it as well as any philosopher.
Right: choosing is part of every human life.
Right: the authors' own example of change is learning, which everyone has done.
questions.explain: Common experience is what you have by being human. Telescopes and scanners give special experience, which belongs to science.
questions.rule: Common experience needs no special equipment.

questions.q: An economic model concludes that people help strangers only when they gain by it. A reader recalls helping a stranger yesterday at a cost to herself. What does her memory do to the model's claim?
options: It proves the whole model is useless for every purpose
It counts for nothing, since it is not laboratory data
It gives one case that tests the sweeping claim
It confirms the model, since helping is a kind of gain
optionExplain: One counterexample tells against the universal claim, not against every use of the model.
Common experience is a real test; a clear case from it counts against a universal claim.
Right: a universal claim is tested by a single clear exception, and her own experience supplies one.
Redefining gain to cover every act would make the claim empty rather than confirmed.
questions.explain: Common experience tests claims outside philosophy too. A universal claim falls to one clear exception, so everyday counterexamples are a sharp test of sweeping conclusions.
questions.rule: One clear exception tests an all-or-nothing claim.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a single clear case from common experience can tell against a universal claim, so everyday counterexamples are a reader's sharpest test of sweeping conclusions in any field.

questions.q: True or false: If a philosophical answer fits common experience, that shows the answer is true.
questions.explain: Common experience tests answers: it can show that one fails. Several rival answers may all fit it, so fitting is not proof.
questions.rule: Fitting experience is passing a test, not proving a truth.

questions.q: According to the authors, what distinguishes the great philosophers from other people?
options: They thought more deeply about common experience
They had far more experience of life than other people
They ran investigations that others could not
They had access to rare and special documents
optionExplain: Right: the authors say they thought more profoundly about experience everyone has.
The authors say explicitly that it was not by having more experience than the rest of us.
The authors say it was not by investigation.
Documents are the historian's tools; the authors say philosophy has none to consult.
questions.explain: The greats share our experience; what sets them apart is the depth of their thinking about it. The card next shows what that means for a reader.
questions.rule: Greatness lies in the thinking, not the data.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a lay reader is as well placed as the greatest philosophers in the mere experience of change.
questions.explain: Everything around us manifests change, so in experience alone we are as well placed as the greatest philosophers to think about it.
questions.rule: Your experience is enough to follow them.

questions.q: Reading a classic on friendship, Omar notices it uses only everyday examples he knows himself. Following the authors, what should he attend to?
options: How many examples the author manages to give
How the author framed his questions
How the author built his answers step by step
Which special facts the author must have known
What private experiences the author drew on
optionExplain: The number of examples matters less than the questions asked and answers built from them.
Right: the great philosophers are marked by the penetrating questions they formulate.
Right: they are marked too by carefully worked-out answers, which a reader should trace.
The authors say philosophers rely on common experience, not special facts.
Philosophy uses experience everyone has, so the author's private experiences are not the key.
questions.explain: Since the examples are shared, the value lies in the questions the author asked and the answers he worked out.
questions.rule: Trace the question and the construction.

questions.q: A student says he cannot follow Kant because Kant must have had experiences the rest of us lack. What does the authors' account say?
options: The student is right that philosophy needs special experience
The student should first study Kant's life and travels
Kant's experiences were rare, so following him is hopeless
Kant's edge lay in his thinking, not in more experience
optionExplain: The authors say philosophy rests on common experience, not special experience.
Kant's life would not supply what the student lacks; the work is to follow his thinking.
The premise is wrong: the experience is common, so following him is possible.
Right: the authors say great philosophers think more profoundly about experience everyone has.
questions.explain: The student misplaces the difficulty. The experience is shared; the work lies in following how deeply Kant thought about it.
questions.rule: The difficulty is depth of thought, not missing experience.

questions.q: Two chess players look at the same position. The master finds a plan the novice misses, though both see every piece. What lesson from the authors' account of great philosophers does this case carry over?
options: Look for hidden information the master must have had
Study how the master reasons about what both can see
Accept that the master's insight cannot be followed
Collect more positions until the plan becomes visible
optionExplain: Both see the whole board; there is no hidden information.
Right: as with the great philosophers, the master's edge lies in what he does with shared material, so his reasoning is what to study.
The novice can follow the plan once it is laid out, as a reader can follow a philosopher's argument.
More positions do not help if the novice does not learn how the master thinks about them.
questions.explain: Where experts and learners share the same material, the gap is in reasoning. By analogy, a learner closes it by tracing how the expert reasons, not by hunting for hidden facts.
questions.rule: When the material is shared, study the reasoning.
questions.teaches: By analogy, in many fields mastery lies in what one does with shared material rather than in having more of it, so a learner gains most by tracing how the master reasons about what both can see.

questions.q: True or false: A modern reader who knows more science than Aristotle did is, for that reason, a better philosopher than he was.
questions.explain: Philosophical greatness lies in thinking profoundly about common experience. More scientific information does not supply that.
questions.rule: More information is not deeper thought.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, some questions great philosophers asked should have been left for later scientific investigation.
questions.explain: Some questions philosophers took up could later be answered by science, though they could not have known it. The card next shows how to spot them.
questions.rule: Not every philosopher's question is philosophical.

questions.q: Why did ancient philosophers conclude that heavenly bodies were made of a different matter from earthly ones?
options: They gave off their own light and heat
They seemed to change only in place
They were too far away ever to reach
Sacred texts called the heavens divine
optionExplain: Light is a natural guess, but the authors give the appearance of unchanging matter as the reason.
Right: unlike earthly things, they seemed only to move, never to come to be, grow or alter.
Distance made observation hard, but the argument rested on the kinds of change observed.
The authors present the conclusion as drawn from observation, not from scripture.
questions.explain: Celestial bodies appeared subject only to local motion, while earthly bodies change in other ways too, so the ancients inferred a different matter.
questions.rule: The ancient view rested on unaided observation.

questions.q: An old philosophical treatise argues at length about how the eye receives images of objects. What treatment do the authors' remarks suggest?
options: Treat it as the core of his philosophy
Reject the whole book as out of date
Accept it because a great author made it
Set it apart as a question for science
optionExplain: Optics is a question for research; mistaking it for his philosophy is the confusion the authors warn of.
Setting one question apart does not discredit his philosophical questions.
Greatness in philosophy does not make his science right; this question belongs to investigation.
Right: how the eye works can be settled by investigation, so it is not one of his philosophical questions.
questions.explain: Questions that investigation can settle should be set apart from a philosopher's truly philosophical questions, without throwing out the rest.
questions.rule: Separate the science from the philosophy.

questions.q: Put in order the steps by which, according to the authors, the question of heavenly matter passed to science.
items: The ancients conclude that heavenly matter differs from earthly matter
Galileo, using the telescope, discovers the moons of Jupiter
Kepler asserts that heavenly and earthly matter are the same
Newton applies one set of laws of motion to all bodies
questions.explain: Unaided observation led to the ancient view; Galileo's telescope opened the question; Kepler's assertion followed; and that laid the groundwork for Newton's universal mechanics.
questions.rule: Investigation settled the question step by step.
questions.teaches: Once investigation reopened the celestial question, each discovery built on the last, so a question handed to science may be settled by a chain of findings rather than one stroke.

questions.q: A modern book on ethics asserts, without data, that people make worse moral choices when tired, and builds its advice on that. Which part would the authors' test flag as a question for science?
options: The tiredness claim, which research could check
The question what makes a choice morally good
The question whether we ought to keep our promises
The question what a virtue of character is
optionExplain: Right: whether tiredness worsens choices is a factual question that studies can settle.
What makes a choice good is a normative question that only thinking can answer.
Whether we ought to keep promises is a philosophical question, not one for research.
What a virtue is calls for reflection, not experiment.
questions.explain: The test applies to new books as well as old ones. A factual claim about how people behave belongs to research, even inside a work of ethics.
questions.rule: Flag factual claims inside philosophy for investigation.
questions.teaches: By analogy, modern philosophers also raise questions that belong to empirical study, such as how people in fact behave, so the test applies to new books as well as to old ones.

questions.q: True or false: A philosopher's question about what change itself is should be set aside for science, since change is a natural phenomenon.
questions.explain: Mentioning nature does not make a question scientific. No experiment shows what change as such is, so the question remains philosophical.
questions.rule: A natural topic does not make a question scientific.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the scientific errors in classical philosophers' works are, on the whole, irrelevant to reading them as philosophy.
questions.explain: The authors say such errors are on the whole irrelevant, apart from the confusion they can cause. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Dated science seldom decides the philosophy.

questions.q: Why, according to the authors, is outdated science in a classical philosopher largely irrelevant?
options: His first readers knew the science was wrong
Science and philosophy have nothing in common
We read him for his philosophical questions
Later editors have corrected all the errors
optionExplain: His contemporaries mostly shared his science; their knowledge is not the authors' reason.
The two can touch, as the celestial example shows; the point is which questions we read him for.
Right: the authors say it is philosophical questions, not scientific ones, that we care about in a philosophical work.
Editors do not rewrite classics' science; the errors remain and the reader sets them aside.
questions.explain: In a philosophical work we are after the philosophical questions, which only thinking answers, so errors about scientific matters are mostly beside the point.
questions.rule: Read philosophers for their philosophy.

questions.q: A reader gives up on a classic of ethics because it states a mistaken theory of digestion. What do the authors' remarks suggest?
options: Give it up, since one error spoils a book
Fix the digestion theory before reading on
Judge its ethics on their own reasoning
Read it only for its history of medicine
optionExplain: One scientific error says little about the philosophy, which is what the book is read for.
Correcting the science is not needed to read the ethics, unless an argument depends on it.
Right: the ethics stands or falls by its own arguments; the digestion theory is dated science.
The history of medicine is a side interest; the book's value is its ethics.
questions.explain: Dated science is on the whole irrelevant to a philosophical work. The ethics must be judged on its own reasoning.
questions.rule: Do not drop the philosophy for the science.

questions.q: True or false: A classical philosopher's dated science does matter to judging his philosophy when one of his arguments rests on it.
questions.explain: The irrelevance holds on the whole, not always. If an argument depends on a scientific error, as the argument for a different heavenly matter did, the error weakens that argument.
questions.rule: Check whether the argument leans on the error.

questions.q: An old essay on courage illustrates its point with a battle whose details historians have since corrected. The argument does not depend on those details. How should a reader treat the error?
options: As a flawed illustration that leaves the argument standing
As a false premise that brings the whole argument down
As proof that the essayist was careless and so untrustworthy
As a reason to read only essays written in recent years
optionExplain: Right: an example can be wrong while the point it illustrates still stands.
It would be a premise only if the argument depended on the details, which it does not.
Writers of every age rely on the facts of their time; this says little about the argument.
Every essay may contain facts later corrected; date is not the test.
questions.explain: Ask what work a dated fact does. A wrong illustration leaves an argument intact; a wrong premise undermines it.
questions.rule: Ask whether a dated fact illustrates or supports.
questions.teaches: A wrong fact used only as an illustration leaves an argument standing, while a wrong fact used as a premise brings it down, so ask what work the dated fact does.

questions.q: A reader marks up an old philosophical work. Sort its contents into what to set aside as dated science and what to judge as philosophy.

items.t: The claim that the heavens are made of a fifth element
The claim that the heart is the seat of thought
The claim that four humours set a person's temper
The argument that understanding differs from sensing
The account of what any change involves
The argument that a good life needs friends

questions.explain: Claims that investigation can settle, about the heavens, the heart and the humours, are dated science. Arguments about understanding, change and the good life are the philosophy to judge.
questions.rule: Research questions go aside; thinking questions get judged.

questions.q: A scientist asks 1,000 people what kind of life they would like and treats the result as the answer to how one ought to live. How do the authors judge this?
options: As the best answer that can be had on the question
As a good start that needs more people
As sound if the sample is truly random
As irrelevant to the question he asked
optionExplain: The authors hold that thinking, not polling, is the only way to answer this question.
More respondents would give a better survey of wishes, but still no answer about what ought to be.
Good sampling improves the report of preferences, not its bearing on what one ought to do.
Right: the authors call it as irrelevant as Aristotle's speculations about heavenly matter.
questions.explain: How one ought to live is a normative question; polling reports wishes. The card next explains the mistake.
questions.rule: A poll does not answer an ought.

questions.q: The authors compare the polling scientist's answer to Aristotle's speculations about the matter of the ____ bodies.
questions.explain: Both are answers given by the wrong method: Aristotle used thought where research was needed, the scientist research where thought is needed.
questions.rule: Wrong method, irrelevant answer.

questions.q: A magazine announces the best way to live, chosen by its readers' votes. By the authors' reasoning, what does the vote show?
options: What the best way to live is for most people
What readers prefer, not what they ought to seek
Which way of life is right, given a large sample
What careful thinkers would conclude on reflection
optionExplain: This treats the most popular choice as the best, the very step the authors reject.
Right: a vote reports preferences; whether those preferences are worth having is a separate question.
Sample size improves the report of preferences, not its standing as an answer to an ought.
Votes record wishes; reflection on what ought to be sought is a different activity.
questions.explain: A vote answers a question of fact about wishes. How one ought to live calls for thought.
questions.rule: Preference is not prescription.

questions.q: How does the polling scientist's error mirror the ancients' error about heavenly matter?
options: He reasoned where research was needed; they polled where thought was
He polled where thought was needed; they reasoned where research was
Both of them applied research to questions only thought could answer
Both applied thought to questions only research could answer
optionExplain: This reverses both: the scientist polled, and the ancients reasoned without telescopes.
Right: the errors are mirror images, each applying the wrong method to its question.
The ancients did not do research on the heavens; they reasoned from unaided observation.
The scientist did not rely on thought; he ran a survey.
questions.explain: Each error matches method to question wrongly: thought for a scientific question, research for a normative one.
questions.rule: Match the method to the kind of question.

questions.q: A tech firm's tests show that a new feature keeps users scrolling longer, and the firm concludes it should ship the feature. What do the tests establish?
options: That the feature is good for its users
Little, since short tests miss long-term effects on users
That users ought to spend more time scrolling
The feature's effect, not that the effect is good
optionExplain: Treating longer use as good assumes the very goal in question.
Test length can matter, but even a long test would show only effects, not whether those effects are good.
No measurement shows what users ought to do; that is a normative claim.
Right: measurement shows what the feature does; whether longer scrolling is worth wanting needs a separate argument.
questions.explain: Like the poll, the test answers a question of fact. Calling the result a success assumes that more scrolling is good, a goal the data cannot justify.
questions.rule: A metric measures an effect, not its worth.
questions.teaches: By analogy, measurement can show what a design does but not whether that effect is worth wanting, so a metric such as engagement quietly assumes a goal that needs its own justification.

questions.q: True or false: By the authors' account, facts from research have no place at all in an argument about how one ought to live.
questions.explain: Facts can serve as premises, such as what people want or what a choice leads to. What research cannot supply by itself is the conclusion about what ought to be sought.
questions.rule: Facts can feed an ought; they cannot be it.

questions.q: How many styles of philosophical exposition do the authors identify in the Western tradition?
options: Five
Two
Three
Seven
optionExplain: Right: dialogue, treatise, meeting of objections, geometrical system and aphorism.
Two would match the theoretical and normative divisions, but those are kinds of question, not styles.
Three is a natural guess, but the authors list more.
The authors say they know of no important style beyond their list, which is shorter.
questions.explain: The authors name five styles, all serving one method. The card next lists them.
questions.rule: One method, five styles.

questions.q: Match each style of philosophical exposition to the philosopher the authors associate with it.
questions.explain: Plato wrote dialogues; Aristotle and Kant treatises; Aquinas perfected the meeting of objections; Descartes and Spinoza tried the geometrical style; Nietzsche wrote in aphorisms.
questions.rule: Know the five styles by their masters.

questions.q: A book takes each topic as a question, states a wrong answer with arguments for it, cites an authority against it, then gives the author's answer and replies to each argument. Which style is it?
options: The dialogue
The geometrical system of proofs
The meeting of objections
The aphoristic style
optionExplain: A dialogue presents a conversation among speakers, not a fixed article form.
The geometrical style uses propositions, proofs and corollaries.
Right: this is the article form Aquinas perfected.
Aphorisms are brief sayings with no stated arguments or replies.
questions.explain: Question, wrong answer, arguments, authority, the author's answer and replies: that is the meeting of objections.
questions.rule: Question, objections, answer, replies: Aquinas's form.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the five styles of exposition all serve a single philosophical method.
questions.explain: The authors say there is only one philosophical method, thinking, but several styles of presenting it.
questions.rule: Styles differ; the method does not.

questions.q: Two teachers explain the same proof: one through a back-and-forth conversation with students, the other as a numbered list of steps. Students assume the teachers taught different things. What is the best correction, in the light of the authors' account?
options: The conversation must have taught a different proof
The numbered list must be the more correct version
The form differs; compare what each one asserts
The two can be compared only by their difficulty
optionExplain: A conversation can reach the same proof by another route.
Neither form is more correct in itself; each has advantages and disadvantages.
Right: style is presentation; two forms can carry the same content, so the comparison belongs to the claims.
Difficulty depends partly on form; agreement is a matter of what is asserted.
questions.explain: Because style is presentation rather than method, works in different styles may agree in substance. Compare their claims, not their look.
questions.rule: Compare works by their claims, not their form.
questions.teaches: Because style is a matter of presentation, two works in different styles may agree in substance, so they should be compared by what they assert rather than by how they look.

questions.q: A philosopher wrote one book in geometrical form and another as a traditional treatise. A reader insists he must be assigned one style. What is the best reply?
options: Classify each work, since one author can use several styles
Assign him the style of his more famous work alone
Treat his writings as a sixth, mixed style of his own
Call it all treatise, since the treatise is the commonest style
optionExplain: Right: the authors note that a philosopher sometimes tries more than one style; Descartes did both.
Fame does not change the style of his other book.
The authors find no important sixth style; each work uses one of the five.
The treatise is the commonest style, but a geometrical work does not become a treatise by majority.
questions.explain: Styles belong to works, not to authors. One philosopher may use two of the five.
questions.rule: Classify styles work by work.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, several philosophers besides Plato have written dialogues as fine as his.
questions.explain: The authors say others, such as Cicero and Berkeley, tried with little success; there is no one like Plato. The card next explains the style.
questions.rule: Only Plato mastered the dialogue.

questions.q: What do the authors mean by calling Plato's dialogue style heuristic?
options: It states conclusions first and then sets out to defend them
It entertains readers rather than instructing them
It follows strict rules of formal logical proof
It leads readers to discover things for themselves
optionExplain: Stating conclusions first is closer to the treatise, the opposite of letting readers discover.
The drama entertains, but it serves discovery; the dialogue instructs by leading you to find things.
Formal proof belongs to the geometrical style, not to Plato's conversation.
Right: heuristic means it allows, indeed leads, the reader to discover things himself.
questions.explain: A heuristic style guides the reader to find things out himself, here through Socrates' questioning.
questions.rule: Heuristic: it leads you to discover.

questions.q: A reader finishes a Platonic dialogue that ends without agreeing what friendship is, and feels cheated of the answer. What do the authors' remarks suggest?
options: Look up Plato's real answer in a scholarly commentary instead
Value the questions and distinctions the talk uncovered
Take the last view stated as Plato's own doctrine
Conclude that the dialogue failed as philosophy
optionExplain: A commentary may offer a doctrine the dialogue does not; the authors stress discovering for yourself.
Right: Plato raised questions and led readers to discover; the unanswered question is part of what is gained.
Plato apparently had no fixed doctrine, so the last view stated need not be his answer.
Raising and sharpening questions is Plato's achievement, not a failure.
questions.explain: Plato's dialogues raise questions and lead readers to discover; an open ending fits that purpose.
questions.rule: From a dialogue, take away the questions and what you discovered.

questions.q: Which statements match the authors' account of Plato?
options: He set out a complete system in numbered steps
His dialogues were widely and successfully imitated
He raised most questions later philosophers took up
He apparently had no fixed philosophical system
His style is conversational, even colloquial
optionExplain: Numbered systems belong to the geometrical style of Descartes and Spinoza.
Imitators such as Cicero and Berkeley wrote flat, dull dialogues, the authors say.
Right: the authors say Plato and Socrates raised most of the important questions.
Right: the authors say he apparently had no system or doctrine, unless it was to keep talking.
Right: the authors call the style conversational, even colloquial.
questions.explain: Plato raised the lasting questions in conversational dialogues, apparently without a system, and no one has matched him.
questions.rule: Plato: questions, conversation, no system.

questions.q: A new teacher copies the Socratic method, asking question after question with no plan, and students leave confused. In the light of the authors' remarks on the dialogue, what does this suggest?
options: Students learn better from direct answers in every case
The form works only when a skilled guide directs it
The students were too young for this kind of teaching
Questioning fails as soon as students feel unsure
optionExplain: The failure here comes from unguided questioning, not from questioning as such.
Right: the authors say the dialogue is heuristic in the hands of a master; without that direction it flounders.
Age is not the cause the case points to; the plan was missing.
Some uncertainty is part of discovering; Socrates' partners fumble before the subject clears.
questions.explain: Heuristic forms depend on the guide's skill, which is one reason only Plato succeeded with the dialogue. Unguided questioning leaves learners confused.
questions.rule: Discovery needs a skilled guide.
questions.teaches: A heuristic form depends on its guide: questioning that wanders without a master's direction leaves learners confused rather than enlightened, which helps explain why the dialogue is so hard to do well.

questions.q: True or false: Because the dialogue is heuristic, a reader may skip the early fumbling exchanges and read only Socrates' closing remarks.
questions.explain: The discovery happens by following the questioning, including the fumbling. Like a play, a dialogue loses its sense when parts are skipped.
questions.rule: Do not skip in a dialogue.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, some of Aristotle's surviving treatises are mainly scientific rather than philosophical.
questions.explain: Some treatises are purely philosophical, some mix philosophy with early science, and some, like the biological works, are mainly science. The card next sorts them.
questions.rule: One philosopher, several kinds of work.

questions.q: Sort these works of Aristotle as the authors describe them.

items.t: Physics
Metaphysics
Ethics
Poetics
On the Soul
The biological treatises

questions.explain: The authors call the Physics, Metaphysics, Ethics, Politics and Poetics purely philosophical; On the Soul mixes theory and early science; the biological works are mainly science.
questions.rule: Know which works are philosophy and which are not.

questions.q: An author's collected writings include an essay on what makes a life good and a report on the breeding habits of bees. How should a reader approach them?
options: As philosophy, since a philosopher wrote both of them
As science, since both rest on observation
As one argument, since one author wrote them
As different kinds that need different reading
optionExplain: The author's name does not make a report on bees philosophical.
The essay draws on common experience, but its question is philosophical, not scientific.
One author can write several kinds of book; they need not form a single argument.
Right: the essay is philosophy, the bee report early science, and each is read and judged in its own way.
questions.explain: As with Aristotle, one author's works can belong to different kinds. Classify each before reading it.
questions.rule: Classify the work, not the author.

questions.q: Why do scholars suggest that Aristotle's surviving treatises may have been lecture notes?
options: They are hard to read, though he was lucid
They are written as dialogues with his students
They name the students who took them down
They were found together on papyrus in 1890
optionExplain: Right: the authors say their difficulty, from so clear a thinker, led scholars to that suggestion.
His dialogues survive only in fragments; the treatises are not dialogues.
The authors say we may never know whose notes they were, so no names settle it.
The 1890 papyrus held the constitution of Athens, not the treatises.
questions.explain: A clear thinker's surprisingly difficult texts suggest notes rather than finished books. That is also why Aristotle's principles are sometimes less lucid than one would like.
questions.rule: Unfinished form can explain difficulty.

questions.q: A famous physicist's collected writings include technical papers and essays on the meaning of life. How, by analogy with the authors' sorting of Aristotle, should a reader treat the essays?
options: Accept them, since the author's science earns him authority
Dismiss them, since a scientist cannot write philosophy
Read and judge them as philosophy, on their own arguments
Read them as part of his physics, since he wrote both
optionExplain: Authority earned in one kind of work does not carry over to another kind.
Anyone can write philosophy; the essays must be judged, not dismissed.
Right: the essays ask philosophical questions, so they are judged as philosophy, whoever wrote them.
The essays ask different questions from his papers and need a different kind of reading.
questions.explain: Like Aristotle's mixed output in reverse, a scientist's essays may be philosophy. Each work is classified by its questions and judged by the standards of its kind.
questions.rule: Judge each work by the standards of its kind.
questions.teaches: By analogy, authority an author earns in one kind of work does not carry over to another, so a famous scientist's essays on ethics must be read and judged as philosophy.

questions.q: True or false: In a mixed work such as On the Soul, a reader should classify passage by passage rather than treat the whole book as one kind.
questions.explain: A mixed work combines philosophical theory with early science, so its passages need sorting before they can be read and judged fairly.
questions.rule: Sort a mixed work passage by passage.

questions.q: Kant, the authors say, adopted the expository style of which philosopher?
options: Plato
Aquinas
Aristotle
Spinoza
optionExplain: Kant was more influenced by Plato philosophically, but he did not write dialogues.
Kant did not use Aquinas's article form.
Right: Kant wrote treatises in Aristotle's manner, though more influenced by Plato in philosophy.
Kant did not write in Spinoza's geometrical form.
questions.explain: Kant took Aristotle's style, the treatise, while owing more of his philosophy to Plato. The card next describes the treatise.
questions.rule: Kant wrote treatises like Aristotle.

questions.q: Put the parts of a Kantian treatise in the order the authors describe.
items: State the main problem
Go through the subject matter thoroughly
Treat special problems along the way or at the end
questions.explain: The treatise opens with the main problem, works through the subject in a business-like way, and handles special problems by the way or at the last.
questions.rule: Problem, treatment, special problems.

questions.q: A reader is lost in chapter five of a long treatise on knowledge. Following the authors' description, what should she look for first?
options: The main problem stated at the outset
The most dramatic clash between rival views
The special problems handled near the end
The author's biography and early influences
optionExplain: Right: the main problem comes first and organises the rest, so it tells her what chapter five is for.
The treatise lacks the dialogue's drama; its views are set out by straightforward exposition.
Special problems come by the way or last; they depend on the main treatment, not the reverse.
Biography does not show the treatise's order; its opening problem does.
questions.explain: A treatise's clarity lies in its order, which starts from the main problem. Finding it locates every later part.
questions.rule: When lost in a treatise, go back to its main problem.

questions.q: According to the authors, in what way is the treatise like the dialogue, and in what way unlike it?
options: Like it in having drama; unlike it in reporting no other views
Like it in being colloquial; unlike it in having a clear order
Like it in lacking any order; unlike it in being formal and dry
Like it in reporting others' views; unlike it in lacking drama
optionExplain: This reverses the account: the treatise has no drama, and it does report others' views.
The treatise is not colloquial; that is a feature of Plato's dialogue.
The treatise's strength is its order, so lacking order is not something it shares.
Right: Aristotle reports the views and objections of others, but develops his view by exposition, not dramatic conflict.
questions.explain: Both styles bring in other people's views, but the treatise develops a position by straightforward exposition rather than by a conflict of speakers.
questions.rule: Treatise: others' views without the drama.

questions.q: A consultant's report on a factory opens by stating that the problem is falling output. Its sections then cover machines, staffing and supply, and an appendix treats rare cases. How does the treatise model help a reader?
options: Read the appendix first, since special cases explain the rest
Read each section as part of the answer to falling output
Read the sections in any order, since each stands alone
Read only the opening, since the problem is the main point
optionExplain: In the treatise order, special cases come last and depend on the main treatment.
Right: once the opening problem is known, each section can be read as answering part of it.
The sections serve one stated problem; reading them as unrelated loses the thread.
The opening states the problem; the answer lies in the treatment that follows.
questions.explain: In an ordered exposition, the opening problem is a key: each later part answers some piece of it.
questions.rule: Read each part as an answer to the opening problem.
questions.teaches: In any ordered exposition, the opening statement of the problem is a key to the rest: once you know it, each section can be read as answering part of it.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Aristotle's treatises are finished works of art, as polished as Kant's.
questions.explain: The authors contrast them: Kant's are finished works of art, while Aristotle's, possibly lecture notes, are curiously difficult and state principles with less clarity.
questions.rule: Kant finished his treatises; Aristotle's may be notes.

questions.q: True or false: In an article of Aquinas's Summa, the first answer given to the question is the opposite of Aquinas's own view.
questions.explain: The article opens with the opposite, wrong answer and its arguments, so that they can be met. The card next lays out the whole form.
questions.rule: The first answer is the one to be refuted.

questions.q: In each article, Aquinas introduces his own solution with the words I ____ that.
questions.explain: I answer that marks the point where Aquinas stops reporting the opposing view and gives his own.
questions.rule: I answer that marks the author's view.

questions.q: These parts of an article on whether a ruler may break a treaty have been scrambled. Put them in the order Aquinas uses.
items: Whether a ruler may break a treaty
It seems that he may, since the people's safety comes first
Further, rulers are not bound as private persons are
On the contrary, Scripture commands that oaths be kept
I answer that a treaty binds a ruler as a promise binds anyone
Reply to the first: the people's safety is not served by bad faith
questions.explain: Question, wrong answer, a further argument for it, the authority against it, the author's own answer, then a reply to each argument.
questions.rule: Question, objections, authority, answer, replies.

questions.q: A student's essay quotes the first paragraph after an article's question as Aquinas's position. What has she quoted?
options: His reply to one of the objections
The wrong answer he sets out to refute
The authority he cites on his side
His main position, quoted correctly and in full
optionExplain: Replies come at the end of the article, after his own answer.
Right: the opening answer is the opposite view, given so that it can be met.
The authority comes after the objections, introduced as on the contrary.
His position comes after I answer that, not at the start.
questions.explain: Each article opens with the wrong answer and its arguments. Quoting it as Aquinas's view reverses his position.
questions.rule: Do not quote the objection as the author.

questions.q: A court judgment sets out each party's arguments, cites the governing law, states the court's holding and answers the losing side's points. By analogy with Aquinas's article, where is the court's own reasoning?
options: In the losing party's arguments at the start
In the quoted law, which decides the case by itself
In the replies alone, at the very end
In the holding, after the parties' arguments
optionExplain: Those are the views the court weighs and may reject, like the article's opening objections.
The law, like the article's authority, frames the matter, but the court still gives its own reasoning.
Replies apply the holding to each argument; the main reasoning is in the holding.
Right: as with I answer that, the court's own view comes after the arguments it must meet.
questions.explain: Formal judgments often share the article's shape. The same habit applies: find where the author's own answer begins.
questions.rule: Find where the author's own answer begins.
questions.teaches: By analogy, court judgments and formal reviews often share the article's shape, stating the opposing arguments before the ruling and answering each, so the habit of locating the author's own answer carries over.

questions.q: A reader treats the authoritative text cited in an article as Aquinas's whole argument for his position. What has she missed?
options: His own reasoning comes after I answer that
The authority is the view he goes on to refute
Aquinas does not quote authorities in articles
The authority takes the place of his replies
optionExplain: Right: the authority counters the objections; Aquinas's reasoning is given in his own answer.
The authority is cited against the wrong answer, so it is on his side.
Each article cites an authority, often Scripture, against the objections.
His replies to each argument still follow his answer.
questions.explain: The authority is one step; the author's argument comes in his own answer, followed by replies.
questions.rule: The authority counters; the answer argues.

questions.q: According to the authors, what is the most important feature of Aquinas's style?
options: Its neat and orderly division into many parts
Its frequent quotation of passages of Scripture
Its open facing of opposing views and objections
Its quotation of earlier philosophers as final authorities
optionExplain: The authors grant its neatness appeals to orderly minds, but say that is not the most important feature.
Scripture is often the authority cited, but the authors do not name it as the key feature.
Right: the authors single out his recognition of conflicts and his attempt to meet all objections.
Authorities are cited, but the authors single out his meeting of objections, not deference to others.
questions.explain: What matters most is the explicit facing of conflicts and objections. The card next explains why the authors prize it.
questions.rule: The heart of the style is meeting objections.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, in the Middle Ages a proposition was not accepted as true unless it could meet the test of open discussion.
questions.explain: Medieval philosophers defended their views in public disputes, and truth was thought to emerge from opposition.
questions.rule: Medieval truth had to survive debate.

questions.q: Two essays defend the same policy. Which one, by the authors' standard, gives a reader more to judge?
options: The one that presents its case without distraction from critics
The one that cites the greatest number of supporting experts
The one that states the strongest objections and answers them
The one that is shorter and so easier to hold in mind
optionExplain: Leaving critics out may read smoothly, but hides whether the view can stand up to them.
Supporting experts are not the same as answered objections.
Right: meeting objections lets the reader see whether the view survives opposition.
Length is not the authors' standard; facing opposition is.
questions.explain: A work that faces objections shows its view under test, which is what the authors value in Aquinas.
questions.rule: Prefer the work that meets its critics.

questions.q: Which conditions do the authors connect with the medieval spirit of debate?
options: Philosophers worked alone, avoiding opponents
Books were few and hard to come by
Philosophers defended views in public disputes
Civilization was essentially oral
Printing had made books cheap and plentiful
optionExplain: The authors say the philosopher was not a solitary thinker but faced his opponents.
Right: the authors say books were few, which kept the culture oral.
Right: public disputes, often attended by crowds of students, were expected.
Right: the authors call medieval civilization essentially oral.
Printing came later; scarcity of books is the condition the authors name.
questions.explain: Few books, an oral culture and public disputes made open discussion the test of truth.
questions.rule: An oral culture tested ideas in debate.

questions.q: Before approving a plan, a firm asks its team to imagine the plan has failed a year from now and to list the strongest reasons why. How does this practice relate to the authors' praise of Aquinas?
options: It meets the strongest objections before committing to a view
It replaces argument with an imagined story about the plan's future
It shows that every plan is bound to fail in the end
It hands the decision to the plan's harshest critics
optionExplain: Right: like an article, it states the strongest case against a position so that the position can be tested.
The story is a device for finding objections, which then must be argued with.
Imagining failure tests the plan; it does not predict failure.
The firm still decides; it has only made sure the objections were faced.
questions.explain: Imagining failure is a way of raising objections in advance. By analogy, it borrows the strength the authors find in Aquinas.
questions.rule: Raise the strongest objections before you commit.
questions.teaches: By analogy, practices such as a pre-mortem, imagining a plan has failed and asking why, borrow the objection-meeting style: they test whether a position survives its strongest opposition before it is adopted.

questions.q: True or false: A work that lists objections to its view has, by doing so, met them.
questions.explain: Listing objections is a start; meeting them means replying to them at their strongest. Weak replies or straw-man objections do not count.
questions.rule: Stating objections is not answering them.

questions.q: What inspired Descartes and Spinoza to give philosophy a new form?
options: The lasting success of Plato's dialogues
The public disputes of the Middle Ages
The wisdom books of the East
The promised success of mathematics
optionExplain: Plato's success inspired few imitators who succeeded; it was not their model.
Medieval disputation shaped Aquinas's style, not theirs.
Eastern wisdom books are linked by the authors to the aphoristic style.
Right: they hoped to organize philosophy as mathematics seemed set to organize knowledge of nature.
questions.explain: Mathematics' promise in organizing knowledge of nature led them to try a mathematical form for philosophy. The card next describes the result.
questions.rule: The geometrical style imitated mathematics.

questions.q: Which features mark the geometrical style, as the authors describe Spinoza's Ethics?
options: Scholiums
Speakers in conversation
Short enigmatic sayings
Propositions with proofs
Corollaries and lemmas
optionExplain: Right: scholiums, explanatory notes, are part of the form.
Conversation belongs to the dialogue style.
Brief, enigmatic sayings belong to the aphoristic style.
Right: propositions and proofs are the backbone of the form.
Right: corollaries and lemmas are among the mathematical devices listed.
questions.explain: Spinoza's Ethics uses the apparatus of geometry: propositions, proofs, corollaries, lemmas and scholiums.
questions.rule: Propositions, proofs, corollaries: the geometrical style.

questions.q: A modern book on ethics opens with numbered definitions and axioms, then derives Proposition 1 with a proof. How should a reader approach it?
options: Read for the drama between rival speakers
Trace each proof back to the items it relies on
Look for the words I answer that in each part
Supply the arguments the author has left out
optionExplain: Drama belongs to the dialogue; this book has none.
Right: in the geometrical style each proposition rests on earlier definitions, axioms and propositions.
I answer that marks Aquinas's article form, not the geometrical style.
Supplying missing arguments is what aphorisms demand; here the proofs are given.
questions.explain: The geometrical style sets out a chain of proofs. The reader follows each one back to what it uses.
questions.rule: In a geometrical work, follow the proofs back.

questions.q: True or false: Because Spinoza's Ethics is laid out like geometry, its conclusions about morals are as certain as geometric theorems.
questions.explain: The authors doubt that metaphysics and morals are satisfactorily handled in mathematical form. The layout imitates geometry's certainty without guaranteeing it.
questions.rule: A proof-like layout does not bring a theorem's certainty.

questions.q: A company handbook lists five axioms of good management and derives twenty numbered rules from them. Given the authors' view of the geometrical style, what should a careful reader do?
options: Accept the rules, since each one follows logically from the axioms
Test the axioms, since the layout lends rigor they may lack
Skip the axioms and read only the numbered rules
Dismiss it, since management cannot be reasoned about
optionExplain: Following from axioms makes the rules only as sound as the axioms, which need testing.
Right: a proof-like structure looks rigorous, but its conclusions are only as good as its starting points.
The rules depend on the axioms; skipping them leaves the rules unexamined.
Management can be reasoned about; the point is to test the reasoning's foundations.
questions.explain: By analogy, formal, proof-like layout outside mathematics can lend claims an air of rigor they have not earned. The starting points deserve the scrutiny.
questions.rule: Test the axioms, not the tidy layout.
questions.teaches: By analogy, casting non-mathematical claims in proof-like form, such as numbered principles in a policy, can lend them rigor they have not earned, so the reader should test the starting points rather than admire the structure.

questions.q: Despite their doubts about the geometrical style, what do the authors credit Descartes with?
options: Writing the most readable philosophical dialogues after Plato
Perfecting the article form of medieval disputation
Inventing the aphoristic style of modern philosophy
A partly justified demand for clarity and distinctness
optionExplain: The authors name Cicero and Berkeley as failed imitators of Plato; they do not praise Descartes for dialogues.
Aquinas perfected the article form.
The authors link the aphoristic style to Nietzsche and others, not to Descartes.
Right: the authors say his demand for clarity and distinctness was partly justified in the chaotic intellectual climate of his time.
questions.explain: The authors judge Descartes not wholly unsuccessful, and credit his demand for clarity and distinctness in a chaotic time.
questions.rule: Descartes: clarity and distinctness, partly justified.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reader can skip a great deal in Spinoza's Ethics.
questions.explain: The authors say you can skip a great deal in Spinoza, as in Newton, and take this as a sign that the form suits philosophy poorly. The card next explains where skipping fails.
questions.rule: Spinoza can be skipped in.

questions.q: Match each philosopher's works to what the authors say about skipping in them.
pairs: You can skip a great deal, as in Newton
Skip nothing: the line of reasoning is continuous
Skip nothing, any more than in a play or poem
questions.explain: Geometrical works allow skipping; treatises and dialogues do not, the first because the reasoning is continuous, the second because it works like drama.
questions.rule: Geometry allows skipping; treatise and dialogue do not.

questions.q: Pressed for time, a reader wants to skip parts of a philosophical book. By the authors' account, in which would skipping do least harm?
options: A work set out in propositions and proofs
A treatise with one continuous argument
A dialogue that unfolds like a play
A treatise that states its main problem first
optionExplain: Right: in a geometrical work propositions can be passed over and returned to when needed.
A continuous line of reasoning breaks when a part is skipped.
The authors compare skipping in Plato to skipping part of a play or poem.
Stating the problem first is a treatise's order; its reasoning still runs continuously.
questions.explain: Only the geometrical style allows skipping without losing the thread.
questions.rule: Skip only where the work is built from separable proofs.

questions.q: Why, according to the authors, can't you skip anything in Kant or Aristotle?
options: Their works are short enough to read whole
Their terms are defined only at the end
Their line of reasoning is continuous
Their books are written as dramatic poems
optionExplain: Kant's and Aristotle's works are long; length is not the reason.
The authors give no such reason; the issue is continuity of reasoning.
Right: each step builds on the one before, so a gap breaks the argument.
Drama is the reason for not skipping in Plato, not in Kant or Aristotle.
questions.explain: A treatise develops one continuous line of reasoning. Skipping part of it leaves later steps without their support.
questions.rule: Continuous reasoning cannot be skipped.

questions.q: Which of these documents could you most safely read selectively, going back to earlier parts only when they are cited?
options: A detective novel whose clues build steadily towards the ending
A legal argument that develops one line of reasoning
A building code whose clauses cite earlier clauses by number
A letter that tells a story from beginning to end
optionExplain: A novel's clues build continuously; skipping loses what the ending depends on.
One continuous line of reasoning is like a treatise; skipping breaks it.
Right: like a geometrical work, it is built from units that name exactly what they rely on.
A story told start to finish works like a play; skipping loses the thread.
questions.explain: A text allows skipping when its later parts cite earlier ones explicitly, so you can return for exactly what is needed. Texts that build silently on earlier parts do not.
questions.rule: Explicit cross-references make selective reading safe.
questions.teaches: A quick test of whether a text allows skipping is whether its later parts cite earlier ones explicitly, by number or name, so you can return for exactly what is needed, or build on them without saying so.

questions.q: True or false: When skipping propositions in a geometrical work, a reader need not even note what the skipped propositions state.
questions.explain: Later proofs may cite a skipped proposition. Noting what each one states lets the reader return to it when needed.
questions.rule: Skip the proof, keep the statement.

questions.q: Which pairing of subject and form do the authors doubt can produce a satisfactory work?
options: Philosophy in mathematical form
Philosophy in the form of a treatise
Theology in article form
Geometry in mathematical form
optionExplain: Right: they question whether philosophy can be written satisfactorily in mathematical form, as Spinoza tried.
The authors call the treatise the most common philosophical form and raise no such doubt.
Aquinas's article form is one the authors admire and regret seeing little used.
Mathematical form is the natural form for geometry; the doubt concerns philosophy.
questions.explain: The authors doubt that philosophy fits mathematical form, or science dialogue form. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Some forms fit some subjects poorly.

questions.q: True or false: The authors hold that strict, absolute rules of rhetoric settle which form each subject must take.
questions.explain: The authors say there are probably no absolute rules of rhetoric; their doubt about certain forms is a judgment, not a law.
questions.rule: No absolute rules, but real risks.

questions.q: A reader of a moral treatise set out as numbered propositions checks every proof for validity but does not ask whether its definitions fit her experience. What should she add?
options: Recheck each proof once more for validity
Give up the book because its form is wrong
Rewrite the whole book as a dialogue first
Test the definitions against her own experience
optionExplain: Validity is only half the matter; the form has distracted her from the premises.
A poor fit of form makes reading harder but does not make the content worthless.
Recasting a whole book is unnecessary; she needs to look past the form to its content.
Right: philosophy rests on common experience, so its starting points must be tested there, whatever the layout.
questions.explain: The mathematical form drew her toward checking deductions. Recovering the content means testing the definitions against common experience as well.
questions.rule: Look past the form to what the subject needs.

questions.q: Which statements fit the authors' view of form in philosophy and science?
options: Spinoza's mathematical form hindered his communication
Galileo's dialogue form hindered his communication
Every subject has exactly one form it must take
Form has no effect on what readers manage to grasp
There are probably no absolute rules of rhetoric
optionExplain: Right: the authors think the form was probably a major reason Spinoza partly failed to communicate.
Right: they say the same of Galileo's dialogue form.
The authors deny absolute rules, so no single required form follows.
Their whole point is that form can stand in the way of communication.
Right: the authors make this concession before stating their doubt.
questions.explain: No rule fixes the form, but a mismatched form can defeat communication, as with Spinoza and Galileo.
questions.rule: Form is not fixed by rule, but it matters.

questions.q: A hospital turns a nuanced ethics policy on end-of-life care into a rigid yes-or-no flowchart. Staff find it misleading in hard cases. What does the authors' point about form suggest?
options: Flowcharts are the best form for any hospital policy
A deductive form fits poorly where judgment is needed
The staff should follow the chart in every case
The policy's content must have been wrong from the start
optionExplain: Flowcharts suit some procedures, but the case shows they distort a nuanced ethical policy.
Right: like moral philosophy in mathematical dress, a rigid branching form strips out the qualification hard cases need.
Following a misleading chart in hard cases repeats the problem the form created.
The content may be sound; the trouble lies in the form chosen to convey it.
questions.explain: Forms built for strict step-by-step deduction suit subjects with fixed premises. Subjects that call for judgment and qualification fit them poorly.
questions.rule: Match the form to the kind of reasoning the subject needs.
questions.teaches: The fit of a form depends on the kind of reasoning a subject needs: forms built for strict deduction suit fixed premises, while subjects that call for judgment and qualification lose meaning when forced into them.

questions.q: True or false: The authors' view leaves room for a master to make an unlikely form work, as Plato did with the dialogue.
questions.explain: Because there are probably no absolute rules of rhetoric, a form that usually fails can succeed in a master's hands. Plato is the authors' own example.
questions.rule: A likely failure is not a certain one.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Pascal meant to leave his Pensées as a collection of short, enigmatic statements.
questions.explain: Pascal died before he could write the book out in essay form; its aphoristic shape was not his intention. The card next describes the style.
questions.rule: Pascal's aphorisms were unfinished, not chosen.

questions.q: According to the authors, what is the great advantage of the aphoristic style?
options: It defends each claim with a careful proof
It is heuristic: readers do much of the thinking
It sets out views in clear, continuous order
It reports and then answers all possible objections
optionExplain: Proofs belong to the geometrical style; aphorisms give none.
Right: readers make the connections and build the arguments themselves, so it feels as if more is said.
Continuous order belongs to the treatise; aphorisms jump from subject to subject.
Meeting objections is Aquinas's strength, not the aphorist's.
questions.explain: The aphorism leaves the thinking to the reader, which is both its charm and its weakness.
questions.rule: Aphorisms make the reader do the work.

questions.q: Reading a book of aphorisms, Maya finds herself agreeing with one saying. Which of these might she be supplying herself?
options: The subject the saying touches on
The connection to the saying before it
The argument that supports the saying
The exceptions the saying must allow
The words of the saying itself
optionExplain: The author names the subject; what he leaves out is the defence.
Right: aphorisms leave connections between statements to the reader.
Right: the reader constructs the arguments for positions, the authors say.
Right: an undefended saying states no limits, so the reader supplies them.
The author supplies the words; that is what the aphorism consists of.
questions.explain: The aphorist gives the saying and its subject; the reader supplies the links, the argument and the qualifications.
questions.rule: Mark which reasons are yours, not the author's.

questions.q: Why do the authors liken the aphoristic author to a hit-and-run driver?
options: He attacks other philosophers and then hides from them
He writes so fast that his errors go unnoticed by readers
He takes insights from others without giving them credit
He suggests an insight and moves on without defending it
optionExplain: The image concerns leaving claims undefended, not attacking others.
Speed of writing is not the point; the missing defence is.
The authors raise no charge of borrowing; the issue is undefended claims.
Right: he touches a subject, suggests a truth, and runs off to another without defending it.
questions.explain: The hit-and-run image captures the style's disadvantage: insights are left without the argument a serious reader wants to follow and criticize.
questions.rule: An aphorism touches and runs.

questions.q: A one-line post on social media is shared widely because it feels profound. Given the authors' account of aphorisms, what should a reader keep in mind?
options: Its force may come from reasons readers supply
Its wide sharing shows the claim is well supported
Its brevity proves the claim must be shallow
Its popularity means it is not worth thinking about
optionExplain: Right: like an aphorism, it feels deep because readers build the argument it never gave.
Sharing reflects appeal, not support; the post defends nothing.
Brief sayings can carry real insight; the issue is that it is undefended, not that it is shallow.
Popularity says nothing either way; the claim can still be thought through.
questions.explain: By analogy, slogans and short posts work like aphorisms: readers supply the argument, so felt force should not be mistaken for support.
questions.rule: Felt force is not support.
questions.teaches: By analogy, slogans and short social-media posts work like aphorisms: they feel profound because readers supply the argument, so their persuasive force should not be mistaken for support.

questions.q: True or false: Because an aphorism is undefended, the insight it states must be false.
questions.explain: An undefended claim may still be true. The aphorism's fault is that it gives the reader nothing to follow or criticize, not that its insight is wrong.
questions.rule: Undefended is not the same as false.

questions.q: Which style do the authors say is probably the most common form of philosophical writing?
options: The philosophical dialogue
The geometrical system
The treatise or essay
The aphoristic style
optionExplain: Dialogues are notoriously hard to write, so few have used them well.
The geometrical style is enormously difficult to write and read, and rare.
Right: the treatise or essay is the most common form, in the past and the present.
The authors call the aphoristic style probably less important than the other four.
questions.explain: The treatise or essay, from Kant's formal works to popular essays, is the commonest form. The card next gives the authors' verdicts on the rest.
questions.rule: Most philosophy comes as treatise or essay.

questions.q: Match each style to the authors' verdict on it.
pairs: Enormously difficult to write and to read
Little used today, which seems a shame
questions.explain: The authors rate each style: dialogues are hard to write, geometry hard to write and read, aphorisms philosophically unsatisfactory, and the Thomistic form a neglected one with real advantages.
questions.rule: Each style has its own difficulty.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Lucretius' On the Nature of Things, written in verse, represents a sixth philosophical style.
questions.explain: The authors say it is no exception: despite the verse, its style is that of a philosophical essay, and we usually read it in prose translation.
questions.rule: Verse alone does not make a new style.

questions.q: A book club picks Spinoza's Ethics as its first philosophy book, expecting a quick read. What do the authors' judgments suggest?
options: Expect drama and wit, as in the dialogues of Plato
Expect brief, undefended sayings, as in Nietzsche
Expect slow going, since the form is very hard to read
Expect the most common and most familiar form
optionExplain: Drama belongs to Plato's dialogues; Spinoza wrote in propositions and proofs.
Spinoza gives proofs for his propositions; undefended sayings are the aphorist's habit.
Right: the authors call the geometrical style enormously difficult both to write and to read.
The treatise is the common form; Spinoza's geometrical form is rare and demanding.
questions.explain: Spinoza's Ethics uses the geometrical style, which the authors call enormously difficult to read. The club should plan accordingly.
questions.rule: Set your pace by the style.

questions.q: A government website takes each common objection to a new law in turn and gives a reply beneath it. Which style does this resemble, and what test from the authors applies?
options: Meeting objections; check each reply meets the objection at its strongest
The dialogue; check whether it lets readers discover things for themselves
The geometrical style; check that each reply follows from stated axioms
The aphoristic style; check which arguments the reader is supplying
optionExplain: Right: objection followed by reply is the Thomistic pattern, and its value depends on whether the replies really meet the objections.
There is no conversation or drama here, only objections and replies.
No axioms or proofs are set out; the structure is objection and reply.
The site does give replies; the reader is not left to build them.
questions.explain: The objection-and-reply form the authors miss in modern philosophy survives in other guises, and the same standard applies: are the strongest objections met?
questions.rule: Judge objection-and-reply formats by the strength of the replies.
questions.teaches: The objection-and-reply form the authors find rare in modern philosophy survives in guises such as answer pages and debate formats, and readers can judge them by the same standard of meeting the strongest objections.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the Thomistic style's rarity today shows that it lacks real advantages.
questions.explain: The authors say its neglect seems a shame, considering all its advantages; perhaps modern readers would not accept it, but that is a matter of taste, not merit.
questions.rule: Rare is not the same as worse.

questions.q: According to the authors, what is the most important thing to discover in reading a philosophical work?
options: The author's life and times
The number of arguments it makes
The other books and sources that it cites
The questions it tries to answer
optionExplain: The authors later say a good theoretical work does not require knowing the author's background.
Counting arguments says nothing about what they are for; the questions do.
Sources can help, but the authors put the book's own questions first.
Right: the authors call the questions the most important thing to discover.
questions.explain: Philosophy is the asking and answering of basic questions, so the questions come first. The card next explains how to find them.
questions.rule: Find the questions first.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the questions a philosophical work tries to answer may be left partly implicit.
questions.explain: The questions may be stated explicitly or be implicit to a certain extent; either way, the reader must find out what they are.
questions.rule: Stated or not, find the questions.

questions.q: An essay on zoos describes animal-welfare research and visitor numbers at length. What should a reader look for first?
options: The most surprising statistic that it reports
The question all this material is meant to answer
The author's training and credentials in zoology
The section that runs to the greatest length
optionExplain: A striking figure catches the eye but does not show what the essay is for.
Right: perhaps whether keeping animals for display can be justified; once found, the research and numbers read as considerations toward it.
Credentials matter little to a philosophical question; the question itself comes first.
Length is not importance; the question shows how the parts fit.
questions.explain: The material serves a question, perhaps implicit. Finding it shows what each part of the essay is doing.
questions.rule: Ask what question the material serves.

questions.q: A reader tries to list a book's questions but some of her entries are only topics. Sort her entries.
groups: A topic, not yet a question
A question the book could answer

items.t: Friendship
War and its conduct
The soul
What do friends owe each other
Can a war ever be fought rightly
Does the soul outlive the body

questions.explain: A topic names a subject; a question asks something about it that an argument could answer. Titles and headings often give only topics.
questions.rule: Turn each topic into a question.

questions.q: A long meeting covers budgets, staffing and deadlines and ends without a decision. By analogy with the authors' advice on reading philosophy, which step would most help?
options: Cover more topics so that nothing is left out
State at the start the question the meeting must answer
Let each speaker talk for the same length of time, to be fair
Record every remark so it can be reviewed later
optionExplain: More topics without a question add to the drift.
Right: a stated question makes it possible to tell what each part of the discussion is for.
Equal time is fair but does not tell anyone what the talk should settle.
A record helps memory, but without a question it records drift.
questions.explain: A discussion without a stated question drifts, as a reading without one does. Stating it first lets each part be judged as relevant or not.
questions.rule: State the question to give the parts a purpose.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a discussion or report with no stated question drifts, so stating the question at the outset, as a reader does for a book, is how its parts are kept relevant.

questions.q: True or false: If a book's main conclusion answers none of the questions a reader has found, the likeliest explanation is that she has missed one of its questions.
questions.explain: Conclusions are answers to questions. A conclusion that answers nothing on her list is a sign that her list is incomplete.
questions.rule: An orphan conclusion points to a missing question.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a great philosopher's controlling principle may go unstated in every one of his works.
questions.explain: A philosopher may state his principles, treat them in another book, or let them pervade all his works without treating them explicitly. The card next shows how to find them.
questions.rule: Controlling principles can stay unstated.

questions.q: Socrates says in the Apology that the ____ life is not worth living, which the authors suggest may express Plato's controlling idea.
questions.explain: The remark is one of the few places where Plato's idea, that philosophical conversation matters supremely, comes close to being stated.
questions.rule: The unexamined life is not worth living.

questions.q: A political writer's speeches do not state a guiding principle, but in each one the heroes are those who compromise and the villains those who refuse. What does the authors' method suggest?
options: Nothing can be inferred that the speeches do not state
The speeches have no guiding principle of any kind
