Only a biography of the writer could reveal his principle
The recurring pattern points to an unstated principle
optionExplain: Plato's example shows that a controlling idea can be shown without being stated.
A consistent pattern of praise and blame is evidence of a principle at work.
The text itself shows the pattern; the authors look for principles in the works.
Right: as with Plato's scenes, what a work repeatedly shows can reveal a principle it never states.
questions.explain: Controlling principles can be shown rather than said. A pattern that recurs across a work is the evidence to look for.
questions.rule: Read the pattern, not only the statements.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, one scene in which a character walks away from a discussion is enough to establish an author's controlling principle.
questions.explain: Plato's idea shows up in many places, the Protagoras, the Republic and others. A controlling principle must recur and be defended from the text.
questions.rule: One scene is a clue; a pattern is evidence.

questions.q: A company's mission statement says customers come first, but its promotions consistently reward cutting costs, even at customers' expense. By analogy with the authors' method, what is the company's controlling principle more likely to be?
options: Cost-cutting, shown by what it repeatedly rewards
Customer care, since that is what it states
Nothing definite, since its words and deeds differ
Whatever its founders believed when they began
optionExplain: Right: like an unstated philosophical principle, the company's real priority shows in the pattern of what it does.
The statement says one thing, but the repeated practice is stronger evidence of what controls decisions.
A conflict between word and deed still leaves a pattern to read.
Founders' beliefs may have changed; the present pattern is what shows the principle now.
questions.explain: By analogy, an institution's controlling principle shows in what it repeatedly rewards. When this conflicts with its stated aims, the repeated practice is the better evidence.
questions.rule: What is repeatedly rewarded reveals what controls.
questions.teaches: By analogy, an organisation's controlling principle shows in what it repeatedly rewards, and where that conflicts with its stated aims, the repeated practice is the better evidence of what it values.

questions.q: Suppose Plato had stated his idea about philosophical conversation plainly in every dialogue. How would the authors' remark about it likely change?
options: It would stop being a controlling principle
It would become harder for readers to notice
It would probably be cited among Plato's ideas
It would show that Plato had a fixed system
optionExplain: Stating a principle does not stop it controlling the work; it only makes it visible.
Stating it would make it easier to notice, not harder.
Right: the authors say it is not usually cited as one of his ideas because it is seldom discussed explicitly.
One stated principle would not amount to the system the authors say he lacked.
questions.explain: The idea goes uncited because it is seldom stated. Stated plainly, it would be easy to list among his ideas, while controlling the work equally.
questions.rule: Unstated principles control as much as stated ones.

questions.q: According to the authors, which of Aristotle's works sets out the logical principles assumed in his Physics?
options: The Poetics
The Politics
The Organon
On the Soul
optionExplain: The Poetics treats poetry, not the principles of logic.
The Politics is a work of normative philosophy, not logic.
Right: the Organon expounds the basic principles of logic that the Physics assumes.
On the Soul mixes philosophy and early science; it is not the logical works.
questions.explain: Aristotle's Physics takes for granted the logic of the Organon. The card next explains why to look beyond the book in hand.
questions.rule: Aristotle's works lean on each other.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Kant assumes the limitation of the mind in the Critique of Judgment without stating it there.
questions.explain: It is stated explicitly in the Critique of Pure Reason and assumed, unstated, in the Critique of Judgment, where it still controls the argument.
questions.rule: Stated in one work, assumed in another.

questions.q: A reader of a philosopher's late book finds key terms used without definition. Following the authors, where should she look first?
options: In his earlier works, for principles assumed here
In a biography that describes the author's life and times
In a dictionary of the words' everyday meanings
In the most recent reviews of the late book
optionExplain: Right: the principles may be treated in another book and taken for granted in this one.
A biography tells of the life, not of the principles the late book assumes.
Philosophers use common words in special senses, so everyday meanings can mislead.
Reviews give someone else's reading; the author's own works state his principles.
questions.explain: An author may set out his principles in one book and assume them in later ones. His own earlier works are the place to look.
questions.rule: Look for missing principles in the author's other works.

questions.q: Kant contrasted his critical philosophy with ____, the presumption that pure thinking can reach the most important truths without knowing its own limits.
questions.explain: Kant charged earlier philosophers with dogmatism; his own first step was a critical survey of the mind's powers and limits.
questions.rule: Criticism versus dogmatism.

questions.q: A short regulation uses terms that are defined only in a separate parent act. By analogy with the authors' advice, what does a careful reader of the regulation need?
options: To read the terms in their everyday senses
To ask an official for a summary of its effect
To treat the undefined terms as meaningless
To find the parent act that defines its terms
optionExplain: Legal terms, like philosophical ones, often carry special senses the everyday meaning misses.
A summary gives someone else's account; the defining text gives the terms themselves.
The terms have meanings; they are set out in another text.
Right: like a book that assumes principles stated elsewhere, the regulation depends on the text that defines its terms.
questions.explain: Many texts depend on a parent text for their terms and principles. Finding that source is part of reading the dependent text.
questions.rule: Find the text a text depends on.
questions.teaches: By analogy, many texts depend on a parent text that fixes their terms, as a regulation does on its statute or a sequel on its predecessor, so locating that source is part of reading the dependent text.

questions.q: According to the authors, why should a reader of Aristotle's Physics keep his other works in mind?
options: The Physics was written as a commentary on the Poetics
The Physics assumes the logic set out in the Organon
The Physics borrows its key terms from the Politics
The Physics repeats the Ethics' argument about happiness
optionExplain: The Poetics treats poetry; the authors connect the Physics with the logical works instead.
Right: the authors say the basic principles of logic, expounded in the Organon, are assumed in the Physics.
The authors name no such borrowing; the link they give is to the Organon's logic.
Happiness is the Ethics' subject; the authors do not tie it to the Physics.
questions.explain: In reading any work of Aristotle, things said in his other works are relevant: the Physics takes for granted the logic of the Organon.
questions.rule: Aristotle's works assume one another.

questions.q: According to the authors, what is the controlling insight of Aristotle's Ethics?
options: Happiness is the highest of the goods
Happiness is the whole of the good
Happiness consists in self-perfection
Happiness is a lasting feeling of pleasure
optionExplain: This is the reading the authors reject: the highest good would be one good among others.
Right: the authors read happiness as the whole good, the quality of a whole life.
Self-perfection is the highest partial good, but on this reading not happiness itself.
Pleasure is one topic of the Ethics, not the controlling insight the authors name.
questions.explain: The authors find that happiness is the whole of the good, not the highest good. The card next shows why this controls the book.
questions.rule: Happiness: the whole good, not the highest.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say that if happiness were the highest good, it would be only one good among others.
questions.explain: A highest good is still one good in a ranking. Calling happiness the whole good puts every partial good inside it.
questions.rule: Highest means one among others; whole means all together.

questions.q: An athlete gives up friends, health and family to win titles. On the authors' reading of the Ethics, how would her happiness be judged?
options: As complete, since she pursues the highest excellence
As complete, so long as she feels pleased with her wins
As beyond judging, since happiness is a private feeling
As incomplete, since her life lacks parts of the good
optionExplain: Excellence may be among the highest partial goods, but the whole good includes the rest.
On this reading happiness is the quality of a whole life, not a feeling of pleasure.
The authors treat happiness as a quality of a whole life, which can be judged.
Right: if happiness is the whole of the good, a life missing friendship and health falls short of it.
questions.explain: Reading happiness as the whole good changes the verdict: one supreme achievement cannot make up for missing parts of the good.
questions.rule: A whole life needs all its parts.

questions.q: Which of these follow from the controlling insight as the authors state it?
options: Happiness is the single highest good
Happiness can be reached in one great moment
Self-perfection is not by itself happiness
Happiness is the quality of a whole life
Happiness involves every aspect of a life
optionExplain: This is the reading the authors reject.
A whole life is whole in time, so one moment cannot make it happy.
Right: self-improvement is the highest partial good, but the whole good includes more.
Right: the authors quote Aristotle that happiness is the quality of a whole life.
Right: whole means not only in time but in all the aspects from which a life can be viewed.
questions.explain: The insight shapes everything: no partial good, however high, is happiness, and happiness spans a whole life in every aspect.
questions.rule: One insight, many consequences.

questions.q: A school judges its success by test scores alone, though it also aims at character, health and curiosity. In terms of the authors' reading of Aristotle, what mistake might it be making?
options: Treating one partial good as if it were the whole
Ranking its goods instead of treating them as equal
Pursuing goods that cannot be measured at all
Aiming at too many goods to achieve any of them
optionExplain: Right: like taking the highest good for happiness, it takes one part of its aim for the whole.
Ranking goods can be sensible; the error is letting one stand for all.
Some goods are hard to measure, but the error is neglecting them, not pursuing them.
Many aims are compatible; the problem is counting only one.
questions.explain: By analogy, the whole good of a complex enterprise is not its most visible or highest single good. A one-number measure repeats the confusion the insight corrects.
questions.rule: Do not let one part stand for the whole good.
questions.teaches: By analogy, judging a complex enterprise by one measure, such as profit for a firm or test scores for a school, confuses a partial good with the whole, the same confusion the authors' reading of Aristotle corrects.

questions.q: True or false: The authors present their reading of Aristotle's controlling insight as beyond dispute among philosophers.
questions.explain: The authors say any example of a controlling principle they give would probably be disputed. A claimed insight is an interpretation to defend from the text.
questions.rule: A controlling insight is an interpretation to defend.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, discovering a philosopher's controlling principles can take years of reading and rereading.
questions.explain: The authors say it sometimes takes years and many rereadings. The card next explains why they still advise against the shortcut.
questions.rule: Controlling principles may take years to find.

questions.q: Why do the authors advise against reading books about philosophers' lives and opinions to find their principles?
options: Such books are usually inaccurate
Such books are too hard for lay readers
Your own discovery is worth much more
Such books leave the principles out
optionExplain: The authors do not claim such books are inaccurate; their point is the value of finding it yourself.
Difficulty is not the reason given; such books are often easier than the originals.
Right: the authors say the discovery you make on your own is much more valuable than someone else's ideas.
Such books may state the principles; borrowing them is what the authors discourage.
questions.explain: The objection is not to the books' quality but to what you lose by borrowing a discovery you could make yourself.
questions.rule: Make the discovery yourself.

questions.q: After one reading of a classic, Ravi cannot state its controlling principle. A friend offers a summary that names it. Following the authors, what should Ravi do?
options: Adopt the summary's statement and move on
Decide that the book has no controlling principle
Reread the classic to find the principle himself
Give up, since he has failed as a reader
optionExplain: This is the shortcut the authors advise against.
Every great philosopher has controlling principles; not seeing one yet does not mean it is absent.
Right: finding it may take several readings, and the discovery is worth more if it is his own.
The authors say it can take years; one reading without success is no failure.
questions.explain: Controlling principles often need rereading to find. Ravi should keep working at the text rather than borrow the answer.
questions.rule: Reread rather than borrow.

questions.q: Which kinds of help are consistent with the authors' advice on finding controlling principles?
options: Reading other great philosophers on the same problem
Taking a guide's statement of the principle on trust
Reading a biography in place of the work
Rereading the book several times
Reading the author's other works
optionExplain: Right: the authors urge listening in on the long conversation among philosophers.
This borrows someone else's discovery, the shortcut the authors reject.
Lives and opinions are what the authors advise against relying on.
Right: the authors say it may take many readings and rereadings.
Right: principles may be stated in another of the author's books.
questions.explain: The authors favour work on primary texts, the author's and other philosophers', over secondary accounts of lives and opinions.
questions.rule: Primary texts, not secondhand accounts.

questions.q: A maths student reads the worked solution to every problem before trying it herself. By analogy with the authors' advice, what is she losing?
options: The understanding that comes from finding it herself
The chance to check her answers against a key
The speed that comes from seeing many solutions
The habit of copying methods exactly as shown
optionExplain: Right: as with borrowed principles, a solution handed over is not understood as well as one found.
Checking against a key after trying is useful; reading it first is the problem.
Speed through solutions is not understanding of them.
Copying methods exactly is not a loss; it is closer to what she is doing already.
questions.explain: By analogy, in any learning an answer you work out is understood and kept better than one handed to you, so looking at the solution too early costs the discovery.
questions.rule: Try before you look.
questions.teaches: By analogy, in any learning an answer you work out yourself is understood and remembered better than one handed to you, so looking up a worked solution too early robs a learner of the discovery.

questions.q: True or false: By the authors' account, a reader who cannot state a classic's controlling principle after one reading has failed as a reader.
questions.explain: Finding controlling principles may take years and many rereadings; it is the ideal goal of thorough reading, not a first-reading test.
questions.rule: Not yet is not failed.

questions.q: According to the authors, how often do philosophers fail to keep to their own controlling principles?
options: Rarely, since the best are consistent
Only when writing for lay readers
Only in their early, immature works
Often, even the best of them
optionExplain: Greatness does not guarantee consistency, the authors say.
The authors tie inconsistency to no particular audience.
The authors do not limit the problem to early works.
Right: the authors say philosophers, even the best, often do not adhere to their principles.
questions.explain: Even the best philosophers often stray from their principles, so checking is part of reading them. The card next says what to do.
questions.rule: Check even great authors for consistency.

questions.q: If a philosopher is inconsistent, among which options do the authors say the reader must decide?
options: Both must be true despite the conflict
The conflict does not matter to his view
He really means his first principles
He really means his conclusions
Neither principles nor conclusions are valid
optionExplain: If they conflict, both cannot stand as stated; that is why a choice is needed.
The authors call inconsistency a serious problem.
Right: one possibility is that the stated principles are what he means.
Right: another is that he means the conclusions, which do not follow from the principles.
Right: the reader may also decide that neither is valid.
questions.explain: An inconsistency forces a choice: the principles, the conclusions, or neither.
questions.rule: Principles, conclusions, or neither.

questions.q: A political treatise begins with the principle that all people are equal in rights, then concludes that one family should rule by birth. Following the authors, what should the reader do?
options: Accept both, since a great author must be consistent overall
Decide if he means the principle, the conclusion or neither
Ignore the conflict, since consistency is for little minds
Accept the conclusion, since it comes at the end of the book
optionExplain: The authors say even the best philosophers are often inconsistent.
Right: the conclusion does not follow from the principle, so the reader must judge which the author really means.
The authors grant Emerson's remark but call inconsistency in a philosopher a serious problem.
Coming last does not make a conclusion the author's real view.
questions.explain: Where principle and conclusion conflict, the reader decides what the author really means, or rejects both.
questions.rule: Face the conflict and decide.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, Emerson's remark shows that inconsistency in a philosopher is not a serious problem.
questions.explain: The authors call the remark carefree and worth remembering, but say there is no doubt that inconsistency in a philosopher is a serious problem.
questions.rule: Inconsistency in a philosopher is serious.

questions.q: A contract's general clause lets either party end it on notice, but a later clause forbids ending it in the first year. By analogy with the authors' advice, what must a reader do?
options: Treat the whole contract as void because it conflicts
Decide which clause the parties really meant to govern
Follow whichever clause appears first in the text
Assume the two clauses mean exactly the same thing
optionExplain: One conflict does not empty the whole document; it calls for interpretation.
Right: as with a philosopher, an inconsistency calls for deciding which statement was really meant.
Order alone does not settle what was meant.
They plainly say different things about the first year, so they cannot mean the same.
questions.explain: Resolving an inconsistency means deciding which statement the author really meant. Law even has rules for it, such as letting the specific clause govern the general one.
questions.rule: An inconsistency calls for a judgment about what was meant.
questions.teaches: By analogy, legal drafting has rules for resolving conflicts, such as letting a specific clause govern a general one, which shows that resolving an inconsistency means deciding which statement was really meant.

questions.q: A reader finds a philosopher calling freedom both necessary and impossible and declares the book inconsistent. On checking, the author has defined freedom in two senses. What went wrong?
options: The author is inconsistent after all, whatever senses he defines
A philosopher should not use one word in two senses
The reader should have picked one sense at random
The apparent conflict came from a term used in two senses
optionExplain: Two defined senses remove the conflict; the claims are about different things.
Using a word in two defined senses is legitimate; the reader's job is to match each claim to its sense.
The senses are defined; the reader should match each claim to its sense.
Right: one sense may be necessary and the other impossible, so there is no contradiction.
questions.explain: Before charging inconsistency, check the terms. A word used in two senses can make consistent claims look contradictory.
questions.rule: Check the terms before charging inconsistency.

questions.q: According to the authors, what is the philosophical problem, as distinct from the scientific one?
options: To explain the nature of things
To describe how phenomena connect
To predict what will happen next
To measure things with precision
optionExplain: Right: philosophy seeks the ultimate causes and conditions underlying phenomena.
Describing connections of phenomena is what the authors assign to science.
Prediction is a scientific strength, not the philosophical problem the authors name.
Measurement is the scientist's tool; philosophy has no instruments.
questions.explain: Science describes; theoretical philosophy explains, seeking what underlies phenomena. The card next shows what to look for.
questions.rule: Philosophy explains; science describes.

questions.q: Philosophy, the authors say, seeks to penetrate to the ultimate ____ and conditions that underlie phenomena.
questions.explain: Theoretical philosophy goes past the connections between phenomena to the ultimate causes and conditions beneath them.
questions.rule: Ultimate causes and conditions.

questions.q: Sort these claims by whether they describe connections among phenomena or seek what underlies phenomena.

items.t: Water boils at a lower temperature at high altitude
Plants grow toward a source of light
Bluer stars are hotter than redder ones
What any change requires in order to be possible
Why there is any order in nature at all
What it is for a cause to produce an effect

questions.explain: The first three report how observed things are connected. The last three ask what underlies every case of change, order or causation.
questions.rule: Connections are described; foundations are explained.

questions.q: When, according to the authors, is a philosophical problem satisfactorily explored?
options: When its answers agree with the results of the latest experiments
When most philosophers have accepted its answers
When its answers rest on clear argument and analysis
When its answers are stated in technical terms
optionExplain: Experiments test descriptions; philosophical explanations stand on argument.
Agreement among philosophers is not the authors' standard; many problems stay disputed.
Right: the authors say such problems are satisfactorily explored only with clear arguments and analysis.
Technical wording is no substitute for argument.
questions.explain: Because philosophy explains rather than describes, its answers must be supported by argument and analysis.
questions.rule: Philosophical answers need argument and analysis.

questions.q: A historian describes how one empire declined after its trade routes shifted. A writer asks what makes any political order hold together at all. How do the two relate, by analogy with the authors' contrast?
options: Both describe connections between particular past events
Both seek ultimate causes, since both concern decline
One describes a link; the other seeks what underlies all cases
One is theoretical philosophy; the other is normative philosophy
optionExplain: The writer is not describing particular events; his question covers every case.
The historian traces one case's causes, not the ultimate conditions of all political order.
Right: the historian connects particular events; the writer asks what underlies every political order.
Neither asks what ought to be; the writer's question is about what holds orders together.
questions.explain: The contrast reaches beyond natural science. Describing how particular events connect differs from asking what underlies all events of a kind.
questions.rule: Particular connections versus underlying conditions.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the authors' contrast reaches beyond natural science: in history too, describing how particular events connect differs from asking what underlies all events of a kind, which is the philosophical question.

questions.q: True or false: An answer to a philosophical problem that sounds profound has met the authors' standard even without argument or analysis.
questions.explain: The authors say philosophical problems are satisfactorily explored only when answers are supported by clear argument and analysis. Sounding profound is not enough.
questions.rule: Depth without argument is not an answer.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, philosophers usually take their technical terms from common speech and use them in a special sense.
questions.explain: Unlike coined scientific terms, a philosopher's words usually come from everyday speech with a special meaning. The card next shows why that matters.
questions.rule: Philosophers borrow common words for special senses.

questions.q: According to the authors, where must a reader's major effort go in a theoretical philosophical work?
options: Into the terms and the initial propositions
Into the examples and the illustrations given
Into the final conclusions on their own
Into the author's historical setting
optionExplain: Right: the argument proceeds from these, so misreading them spoils everything after.
Examples help, but they serve the terms and propositions the argument rests on.
Conclusions make sense only through the terms and starting points that lead to them.
The authors later say a good theoretical work needs no study of the author's background.
questions.explain: Philosophical answers rest on argument from starting points, so the terms and initial propositions deserve the main effort.
questions.rule: Effort goes to terms and starting points.

questions.q: A reader finds the sentence nature does nothing in vain absurd, since nature is not a person with purposes. What should she do first?
options: Conclude that the author is talking nonsense
Read nature as the countryside and its wildlife
Skip the sentence as a mere figure of speech
Ask what the author means by nature in this book
optionExplain: The authors warn that reading familiar words in a familiar way makes nonsense of the book.
That is the everyday sense, the very reading that produces the absurdity.
A word bearing this much weight is likely a term; skipping it loses the claim.
Right: nature is a common word likely used in a special sense; finding it may turn absurdity into a definite claim.
questions.explain: Absurdity in a great author is a signal that a common word is being used in a special sense. Find that sense before judging.
questions.rule: When a sentence seems absurd, check the key word's sense.

questions.q: Which signs suggest that an ordinary word is serving as a philosopher's term?
options: It appears once, in a passing example
It recurs at key points in the argument
The author explains how he uses it
Its everyday sense makes a sentence absurd
It is a short, familiar, common word
optionExplain: A word used once in passing is unlikely to carry the argument.
Right: a word the argument keeps returning to is bearing weight.
Right: an author's explanation of his usage marks a special sense.
Right: absurdity under the everyday sense suggests another sense is meant.
Being short and familiar does not show a word is a term; most such words carry their usual sense.
questions.explain: Terms bear the argument's weight: they recur, they are explained, and their everyday sense often fails to fit.
questions.rule: Find the words that carry the weight.

questions.q: A novice baker reads the first step, cream the butter and sugar, as add cream to them, and every later step goes wrong. What does this show, by analogy with the authors' advice?
options: Recipes should avoid using everyday words altogether
A term misread at the start spoils all that builds on it
Later steps matter more than the opening instructions do
One small slip early on makes little difference later
optionExplain: Everyday words in special senses are common in crafts; the reader's job is to catch them.
Right: later steps depend on the first, so one misread term at the start ruins the whole.
The case shows the reverse: the opening step governs what follows.
The case shows the opposite: one early slip ruined every later step.
questions.explain: Because later steps build on earlier ones, a term misread at the start corrupts everything after. That is why the effort belongs at the beginning.
questions.rule: Get the starting terms right first.
questions.teaches: A misreading at the start spreads: because later propositions build on the initial ones, a term misread there turns every step that uses it into nonsense, which is why the effort belongs at the start.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, every ordinary word in a philosophical book should be read in a special technical sense.
questions.explain: Most words carry their usual sense. The care is for the words that bear the argument's weight, whose sense must be taken from the author's usage.
questions.rule: Special senses for the key words, not for every word.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, science as well as philosophy must use abstract terms.
questions.explain: No general knowledge can be expressed except in abstract terms, so science uses them as much as philosophy does. The card next explains what goes wrong with them.
questions.rule: All general knowledge is abstract.

questions.q: According to the authors, what you perceive through your senses is concrete and particular, while what you think with your mind is abstract and ____.
questions.explain: The senses give particulars; the mind grasps general aspects of them, which abstract words express.
questions.rule: Senses: particular. Mind: general.

questions.q: Trying to understand a philosopher's discussion of time, a reader keeps picturing a clock face. What do the authors' remarks suggest?
options: Find a better image, such as a river flowing to the sea
Stop picturing; grasp the general aspect the idea names
Give up, since abstract ideas cannot really be understood
Replace the word time with one concrete example of it
optionExplain: Any image is still a particular; swapping pictures does not reach the idea.
Right: an idea is understood, not imagined; the clock is one particular, not what time is.
The authors say abstractions are understood every day; the hopelessness comes from trying to picture them.
An example can point toward the idea but cannot replace the general term.
questions.explain: Trying to imagine what an idea refers to befuddles the reader. Understanding an abstract term means grasping the general aspect it names.
questions.rule: Understand ideas; do not picture them.

questions.q: Sort these by whether they are perceived by the senses or thought by the mind.

items.t: The red apple on this table
The bark of the neighbour's dog
This morning's cold wind
Redness as such
What all dogs have in common
Cause

questions.explain: Particular things and events reach us through the senses. General aspects, like redness or what all dogs share, are grasped by the mind and named by abstract words.
questions.rule: This one is perceived; what all share is thought.

questions.q: A news report mentions the average family with 2.4 children. A reader objects that no family has 0.4 of a child. What has gone wrong, by the authors' account?
options: The report has made an error in its arithmetic
Averages are meaningless because no one is average
The figure should be rounded to describe a real family
He is trying to picture what a general idea refers to
optionExplain: The arithmetic can be correct; the confusion lies in how he reads it.
Averages carry real information about many cases, though they picture none.
Rounding would make it describe one family, losing the general fact it states.
Right: the average names a general aspect of many families, not any family he could imagine.
questions.explain: By analogy, everyday statistical abstractions name a general aspect of many cases. Trying to imagine the thing they refer to produces nonsense.
questions.rule: Do not look for the picture behind an abstraction.
questions.teaches: By analogy, everyday statistical abstractions, such as the average family with 2.4 children, name a general aspect of many cases and describe no household you could picture, so trying to imagine one misleads.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, because abstract terms cannot be pictured, they must be vague.
questions.explain: Being unpicturable is what makes a term abstract, not what makes it vague. A well-defined abstract term can be precise.
questions.rule: Abstract is not vague.

questions.q: According to the authors, what should you do with an assumption a philosopher asks you to make?
options: Make it, to see what follows from it
Refuse it until he has proved it
Accept it as permanently settled
Ignore it and read the conclusions instead
optionExplain: Right: the authors say to make assumptions to see what follows, even contrary to your own.
Assumptions are by nature not proved; refusing them stops the reading.
Granting for argument's sake is not permanent acceptance.
The conclusions depend on the assumptions; ignoring them loses the argument.
questions.explain: Assumptions are no trouble: grant them and see where they lead. The card next adds a point about your own prejudgments.
questions.rule: Grant assumptions to follow the argument.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, it is a good mental exercise to pretend you believe something you do not.
questions.explain: Pretending to believe lets you follow an argument from assumptions you reject, which is what reading a philosopher fairly requires.
questions.rule: Pretending to believe is good exercise.

questions.q: A reader convinced that people are basically selfish opens a book that assumes people are basically cooperative. Following the authors, how should she read it?
options: Stop at the first page, since she rejects its starting point
Rewrite each argument from her own opposite assumption
Grant the assumption and follow the argument where it leads
Treat the assumption as proved once she has granted it
optionExplain: Contrary presuppositions are no reason to stop; the authors say to make the assumption anyway.
Substituting her own assumption means reading a different book.
Right: she can grant it for the argument's sake and judge it afterwards.
Granting for argument is not proof; she may challenge it later.
questions.explain: Contrary presuppositions are no bar to reading. Grant the author's assumption, see what follows, then judge.
questions.rule: Follow first, judge after.

questions.q: Match each kind of starting point to how the authors' advice treats it.
pairs: An assumption the author asks you to share
Make it, to see what follows
Your own prejudgment on the question
questions.explain: Assumptions are granted for the argument; self-evident claims are tested against the experience everyone shares; your own prejudgments are made explicit so they do not distort your judgment.
questions.rule: Grant, test, and know your own.

questions.q: In debate training, students are often assigned to argue the side they disagree with. How does this relate to the authors' advice?
options: It teaches students to change their real beliefs on demand
It shows that every position is equally well supported
It practises holding a view in mind without believing it
It trains students to hide their own real opinions
optionExplain: Students argue a side without adopting it; their beliefs need not change.
Arguing a side well does not make all sides equal; it lets them judge more fairly.
Right: like pretending to believe an author's assumption, it lets students see a view from inside before judging it.
The point is to understand the other side, not to conceal one's own.
questions.explain: By analogy, arguing the opposing side exercises the same capacity the authors recommend: entertaining a view without holding it, which sharpens judgment of it.
questions.rule: Entertain a view before judging it.
questions.teaches: By analogy, debaters who argue the side they oppose, or lawyers who prepare the other side's case, practise the same skill as granting an assumption: entertaining a view without holding it, which sharpens their judgment of it.

questions.q: Suppose a reader is unaware of her own prejudgment on the question a book addresses. By the authors' account, what is the risk?
options: She is more likely to misjudge the author's assumptions
She will read faster, free of any distraction
She will find it easier to agree with the author's claims
She will notice the author's assumptions sooner
optionExplain: Right: the authors say the clearer you are about your own prejudgments, the less likely you are to misjudge others'.
Speed is not the issue; an unnoticed prejudgment distorts judgment.
An unnoticed prejudgment is as likely to produce unfair disagreement as agreement.
Without awareness of her own, she is less well placed to see his with clarity.
questions.explain: Unnoticed prejudgments colour judgment of others' assumptions. Knowing your own guards against misjudging the author.
questions.rule: Know your own prejudgments to judge others fairly.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, you need laboratory evidence to test a philosopher's self-evident principles.
questions.explain: Self-evident principles come from common experience, so your own common sense and daily observation are the test. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Common experience tests self-evident claims.

questions.q: According to the authors, where do the self-evident propositions in philosophy come from?
options: From proofs built on other propositions
From special laboratory research
From definitions the author stipulates
Directly from common experience
optionExplain: Self-evident propositions are not proved from others; that is what makes them starting points.
Laboratory research gives special experience, the scientist's kind.
A proposition true by stipulated definition is a different thing from one drawn from experience.
Right: they are drawn directly from experience, the common experience of mankind.
questions.explain: Self-evident principles come straight from common experience, not from proof, research or definition.
questions.rule: Self-evident means drawn from common experience.

questions.q: A book claims it is self-evident that no one can be in two places at once. Which would be fair ways to test the claim, following the authors?
options: Accept it because the author is a famous thinker
Check whether the author proves it from other premises
Recall her own experience of moving between places
Ask whether anyone she knows has met a counterexample
Look for a laboratory experiment on human location
optionExplain: Fame is not a test; the claim must fit experience.
A self-evident claim is offered as a starting point, not as something proved.
Right: her own daily observation is the test the authors name.
Right: checking whether others' common experience agrees guards against her own prejudgment.
Special research is not needed; the claim appeals to common experience.
questions.explain: A self-evident claim is tested against common experience, hers and others'. Research, authority and proof are not the tests.
questions.rule: Test against daily experience, yours and others'.

questions.q: How does testing a philosopher's leading principles differ from testing a scientist's?
options: Philosophy's need special experience; science's need common
Philosophy's need common experience; science's need special
Both need special experience gained by methodical investigation
Neither can be tested against experience of any sort
optionExplain: This reverses the contrast the authors draw.
Right: the philosopher refers you to common sense and daily observation; the scientist to methodical investigation.
The authors say the philosopher's principles need no aid from methodical investigation.
Both are tested by experience; they differ in the kind of experience.
questions.explain: Philosophy's principles come from common experience and can be tested by it; science's rest on special experience from investigation.
questions.rule: Common experience for philosophy; special for science.

questions.q: A design book declares it self-evident that users prefer fewer clicks in every case. A reader recalls happily clicking through extra screens that made a hard task clear. What does her memory do?
options: It shows design books cannot state principles
It gives a counterexample from common experience
It counts for nothing without a formal study
It confirms the maxim, since she finished the task
optionExplain: Design books can state principles; this one has overstated its maxim.
Right: a maxim offered as self-evident is open to the same test, and her experience tells against it.
A maxim claimed as self-evident appeals to common experience, so common experience can rebut it.
Finishing the task with more clicks tells against the maxim, not for it.
questions.explain: By analogy, maxims in practical fields often present themselves as self-evident. Ordinary experience is a fair test of them, as of a philosopher's principles.
questions.rule: Test claimed obvious truths against ordinary experience.
questions.teaches: By analogy, maxims in practical fields often present themselves as self-evident, and ordinary experience can test them as it tests a philosopher's principles: one clear everyday case can rebut a maxim stated without exception.

questions.q: True or false: If a principle seems obvious to you, that settles that it is self-evident.
questions.explain: What seems obvious to one reader may reflect a personal prejudgment. Checking whether others' common experience agrees is part of the test.
questions.rule: Obvious to me is not yet self-evident.

questions.q: To which kind of book do the authors say the rules of analytical reading apply most directly?
options: History
Science
Imaginative literature
Philosophy
optionExplain: History allows outside aids such as documents and places; the fit is less direct.
Science may call for demonstrations and special experience beyond the text.
Imaginative literature needs rules of its own, different from those for expository books.
Right: reader and philosophical book face each other with no aid but the mind, the situation the rules were built for.
questions.explain: Philosophy leaves the reader alone with the book, which is the situation the analytical rules assume. The card next explains.
questions.rule: The analytical rules fit philosophy best.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the method of reading a philosophical book is very similar to the method by which it was written.
questions.explain: The philosopher can only think about his problem; the reader can only read, which means think about, his book.
questions.rule: Written by thinking, read by thinking.

questions.q: A reader stuck on a metaphysical argument looks for a laboratory demonstration or museum exhibit to help. What do the authors' remarks suggest?
options: No such aid exists; she must think the argument through
A demonstration will settle the argument for her
She should turn to a history of the subject instead of the text
She should wait for a scientific discovery to help
optionExplain: Right: there are no aids but the mind for a philosophical book.
No demonstration shows what metaphysics asks; it is answered by thinking.
A history may report what was argued, but she still has to think through the argument itself.
Philosophical questions are not settled by discoveries; waiting will not help.
questions.explain: Philosophical questions cannot be settled by research, so their books can only be read by thinking with them.
questions.rule: With philosophy, your mind is the only aid.

questions.q: Which of these could help with a history or science book but, by the authors' account, cannot do the work for a reader of a philosophical one?
options: Applying the rules of analytical reading
Watching a laboratory demonstration
Consulting archives and documents
Viewing specimens in a museum
Thinking about the argument
optionExplain: The authors say these rules apply most directly to philosophy.
Right: special experience can help with science, but philosophy rests on common experience.
Right: documents serve history; philosophy has none to settle its questions.
Right: specimens help with natural science, not with philosophical questions.
Thinking is what reading philosophy consists of.
questions.explain: Special experience and documents aid science and history. Philosophy leaves only thinking and the analytical rules.
questions.rule: Outside aids help other kinds; philosophy needs thought.

questions.q: A judge decides a case that no earlier ruling or statute covers, reasoning only from general principles. By analogy with the authors' account, how should a reader of her opinion approach it?
options: Check it against earlier rulings on the very same question
Accept it, since judges have the authority to decide
Follow and test the reasoning itself, as with philosophy
Look up the facts of the case in the court records
optionExplain: By hypothesis there are no earlier rulings on the question.
Authority settles the case, but the reader's question is whether the reasoning is sound.
Right: with no precedent to consult, the opinion stands or falls on its reasoning, which the reader must think through.
The facts may be recorded, but the opinion's worth lies in reasoning from principle.
questions.explain: Where a text proceeds by reasoning alone, the reader has no outside check and must think with it, as with philosophy.
questions.rule: Reasoning alone is read by reasoning.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a judge facing a question no precedent covers must reason from principles alone, so such opinions are read like philosophy: by following and testing the reasoning, not by checking outside records.

questions.q: True or false: Because a philosophical book is read with no aid but the mind, a reader should not read other philosophers on the same problem.
questions.explain: The authors urge listening in on the long conversation among philosophers before making up your mind. The point is that no special experience or research can replace thinking.
questions.rule: No outside aids, but other philosophers still help.

questions.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, you need not investigate the author's social and economic background to judge a good theoretical work of philosophy.
questions.explain: A good theoretical work is free from oratory and propaganda, so the author's personality and background need no investigation. The card next says what to read instead.
questions.rule: Theoretical philosophy does not need the author's background.

questions.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
questions.q: What do the authors say you should do before making up your mind about what any philosopher says?
options: Study the philosopher's life, background and times
Read a summary of current expert opinion
Listen in on the philosophers' long conversation
Wait until you have read every book on it
optionExplain: Life and times are not needed for a good theoretical work, the authors say.
A summary of opinion is not the same as hearing the philosophers argue.
Right: the authors say to listen in on the conversation philosophers have carried on through history.
The authors ask you to read others on the same problem, not every book before judging.
questions.explain: Other great philosophers on the same problem are the context that matters before judging any one of them.
questions.rule: Hear the conversation before judging.

questions.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
questions.q: Tom has read one classic argument that the mind is separate from the body and is ready to accept it. What would the authors advise him to do first?
options: Read other great philosophers on the same question
Research the author's family background and social class
Accept it, since it comes from a classic work
Reject it, since one book cannot be trusted
optionExplain: Right: the long conversation will show him where the argument is contested and how it holds up.
Background need not be investigated for a theoretical work.
A classic deserves serious reading, not acceptance before hearing the rest of the debate.
One book can be right; the point is to hear the conversation before deciding.
questions.explain: Before making up his mind, Tom should listen to the other voices in the conversation on the same problem.
questions.rule: Read the rivals before you decide.

questions.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
questions.q: Which does the authors' advice ask a reader of a theoretical philosophical work to attend to before judging?
options: The argument the author actually gives
The author's personality and his temperament
The author's income and social class
Others who dealt with the same problem
The long conversation in the history of thought
optionExplain: Right: the argument is what you judge, which is why background can be set aside.
The authors say you need not be concerned with the author's personality.
Social and economic background need not be investigated, the authors say.
Right: reading others on the same problem is what the authors recommend.
Right: the authors picture philosophy as a long conversation to listen in on.
questions.explain: Judge the argument in the light of the conversation it belongs to, not the author's personal or social circumstances.
questions.rule: Argument and conversation, not biography.

questions.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
questions.q: A new lawyer finds one old judgment persuasive on a question of law. By analogy with the authors' advice, what should she do before relying on it?
options: Look into the private life of the judge who wrote it
Rely on it, since an old judgment has stood the test of time
Set it aside, since older judgments are out of date
Read the other judgments that answered the same question
optionExplain: The judge's private life is beside the point; the reasoning and the other rulings matter.
Age alone does not show a judgment has stood up; later rulings may have answered it.
Age alone does not make a ruling wrong; it must be weighed against the others.
Right: like philosophy, case law is a long conversation, and one contribution is weighed against the others.
questions.explain: By analogy, any field with a long record of argument is read as a conversation: one contribution is judged against others on the same question.
questions.rule: Read one voice in the light of the others.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any field with a long record of argument, such as case law or a scientific controversy, is best read as a conversation: one contribution is judged against the others that answered the same question.

questions.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, listening in on the long conversation can take the place of making up your own mind.
questions.explain: The conversation prepares judgment; the authors insist that your responsibility is to make up your own mind.
questions.rule: Listening prepares judgment; it does not replace it.

questions.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
questions.q: How do the authors suggest a reader should regard persistent disagreement among philosophers?
options: As proof that philosophy is futile
As a sign of a deep unsolved problem
As a reason to side with the majority
As evidence that all views are equal
optionExplain: The authors draw the opposite lesson: it is good to know where the true mysteries are.
Right: persistent disagreement may point to a great unsolved, perhaps insoluble, problem.
Counting heads is not the authors' advice; each reader must judge for herself.
The authors ask you to judge what is true and false, so views are not all equal.
questions.explain: Lasting disagreement marks where the deep problems lie. The card next gives the authors' second reason.
questions.rule: Disagreement marks the mysteries.

questions.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
questions.q: Which reasons do the authors give for not being troubled by philosophers' disagreements?
options: Your own task is to make up your own mind
Philosophers secretly agree on most points
Disagreement shows that none of them is right
Experts will settle the matter in due course
It may point to a great unsolved problem
optionExplain: Right: others' disagreements matter less than your own judgment.
The authors make no such claim; the disagreements are real.
Disagreement leaves open which, if any, is right; it does not show all are wrong.
The authors say you cannot depend on experts for philosophical questions.
Right: it is good to know where the true mysteries are.
questions.explain: The two reasons are that disagreement marks deep problems and that your job is your own judgment, not others' agreement.
questions.rule: Mysteries are worth knowing; your judgment is your job.

questions.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
questions.q: A student says that because philosophers have argued about justice for centuries, studying it is pointless. Following the authors, how should she be answered?
options: She is right that the question is not worth further study
Lasting disagreement marks a deep problem worth knowing
She should adopt whichever view is most popular now
She should wait until philosophers reach agreement
optionExplain: The authors say the questions philosophers ask are more important than anyone else's.
Right: the authors see persistent disagreement as pointing to a great problem, and her task is still to judge it.
Popularity does not answer a philosophical question; she must decide for herself.
Agreement may never come; her responsibility is to make up her own mind now.
questions.explain: Centuries of disagreement show the depth of the question, not its pointlessness. Her job is to study it and judge.
questions.rule: A long dispute is a reason to study, not to stop.

questions.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
questions.q: Two writers seem to disagree about whether art imitates nature, but one means painting and the other music. What do the authors suggest?
options: Treat it as a deep mystery that cannot be solved
Side with the writer whose book appeared first
Conclude that one of the two writers must be mistaken
Check the terms; this may not be a real disagreement
optionExplain: Only persistent disagreement among serious thinkers on the same question marks a mystery.
Order of publication settles nothing about who is right.
They may both be right about different arts; a clash of terms is not yet a real disagreement.
Right: they may be talking about different things, so the dispute may come from terms, not from a real problem.
questions.explain: Before treating a disagreement as a mystery, check that the parties mean the same thing. A dispute over terms is no deep problem.
questions.rule: Confirm the disagreement is real before calling it a mystery.

questions.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
questions.q: In a long town dispute over a dam, both sides now accept the same cost figures, yet still disagree about whether the valley's beauty outweighs cheap power. What does this suggest?
options: The dispute now lies in values, which more data will not end
The cost figures must still be wrong, since the dispute goes on
One side is being dishonest, since the facts are agreed
The dispute will end once a larger study of costs is done
optionExplain: Right: once the facts are agreed, what remains is a disagreement about what matters more, which research cannot settle.
The disagreement survives agreement on the figures, so it is not about the figures.
Honest people who agree on facts can still weigh goods differently.
More cost data would answer a question no one is now disputing.
questions.explain: A disagreement that survives agreement on the facts lies in principles or values. That is the kind of persistent disagreement that marks a deep problem.
questions.rule: If the facts are agreed and the dispute remains, it is about values.
questions.teaches: By extension, a disagreement that survives agreement on the facts lies in principles or values, so more data will not end it; such disagreement is the kind that points to a deep problem.

questions.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
questions.q: True or false: Even if philosophers all agreed on an answer, the authors' advice would still leave each reader responsible for making up her own mind.
questions.explain: The authors say others' disagreements are relatively unimportant because your responsibility is your own judgment. Agreement would not change that responsibility.
questions.rule: Agreement or not, the judgment is yours.

questions.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, adopting the opinions of others on a philosophical question is a way of evading it.
questions.explain: The authors say taking others' opinions is not solving philosophical questions but evading them. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Borrowed answers evade the question.

questions.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
questions.q: The authors say the most distinctive mark of philosophical questions is that everyone must answer them for ____.
questions.explain: Philosophical questions are answered by each person's own thinking, grounded in argument.
questions.rule: Each must answer for himself.

questions.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
questions.q: Asked whether people have a duty to help strangers, Lee replies that a famous philosopher said yes, so that is his answer. What do the authors' remarks imply?
options: He has answered it well by citing a recognized expert
He should cite more philosophers to be on the safe side
He has evaded the question rather than answered it
He should answer only after a public survey is taken
optionExplain: Expert testimony may serve in science, but not for philosophical questions.
More borrowed opinions are still borrowed; the number does not help.
Right: taking another's opinion is evading the question; he needs his own grounded answer.
A survey reports opinions, which is no better than citing one philosopher.
questions.explain: Citing an authority is not answering a philosophical question. Lee needs reasons he can defend as his own.
questions.rule: An authority's answer is not yours.

questions.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
questions.q: Why may a reader reasonably rely on experts in science but not in philosophy?
options: Scientists are more trustworthy people than philosophers
Philosophical questions have no answers that anyone could ever give
Science may need special experience; philosophy needs thought
Scientific questions matter less than philosophical ones do
optionExplain: Trustworthiness is not the authors' point; the difference lies in the kind of question.
The authors ask for solidly grounded answers, so they think answers can be given.
Right: a reader cannot repeat special research, but she has the common experience and the mind philosophy needs.
Importance is part of why the authors care, but the reason experts cannot stand in is the method.
questions.explain: Scientific answers may rest on special experience a reader cannot have. Philosophical answers rest on thought about common experience, which every reader has.
questions.rule: Where you share the experience, you must do the thinking.

questions.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
questions.q: A student asks a career counsellor which path would make her life meaningful. By analogy with the authors' view, what can the counsellor properly supply?
options: Facts and arguments, but not the judgment itself
The answer, since counsellors are experts on careers
Nothing at all, since the question has no answer
A survey of which careers most people find meaningful
optionExplain: Right: information and reasons help, but what makes her life meaningful is a judgment she must make herself.
Expertise on job markets is not authority over what makes her life meaningful.
The question can be answered, by her, with reasons; help can still be given.
Others' preferences report opinions; they do not answer her question.
questions.explain: By analogy, questions about one's own values cannot be handed to experts. Advisers can supply facts and arguments; the judgment remains the person's own.
questions.rule: Advice can inform a value judgment, not make it.
questions.teaches: By analogy, decisions about one's own values, such as what would make a life worthwhile, cannot be delegated to experts: advisers can supply facts and arguments, but the judgment must be one's own.

questions.section: On Making Up Your Own Mind
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, answering philosophical questions for yourself means not reading what other philosophers have said.
questions.explain: The authors urge reading other philosophers on the same problem before judging. Answering for yourself means grounding your own answer in argument, not working in isolation.
questions.rule: Your own answer, informed by others.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, one kind of theology is a branch of philosophy.
questions.explain: Natural theology, reached by unaided reason, is a branch of philosophy, the last chapter of metaphysics. The card next sets it beside dogmatic theology.
questions.rule: Natural theology is philosophy.

questions.q: Match each term to its description in the authors' note on theology.
pairs: First principles reached by unaided reason
First principles held as articles of faith
Aristotle's name for an uncaused cause
What threatens if everything is caused
questions.explain: Natural theology reasons, as Aristotle did, from causation to an uncaused cause to avoid an infinite regress. Dogmatic theology begins from articles of faith.
questions.rule: Reason or faith decides the kind of theology.

questions.q: Which of these books is a work of natural theology in the authors' sense?
options: A commentary on a church's creed, written for its own members
A history of the councils that defined church doctrine
A guide to a religion's festivals and their meaning
An argument from the existence of change to a first cause
optionExplain: A creed is a set of articles of faith; commenting on it is dogmatic theology.
A history of councils is history, not theology reached by reason.
A guide to festivals describes practice; it does not reason from experience to God.
Right: it reaches its conclusion by the natural working of the mind, from experience anyone shares.
questions.explain: Natural theology argues from common experience by unaided reason. Works resting on a church's creed are dogmatic.
questions.rule: Unaided reason marks natural theology.

questions.q: According to the authors, what does every work of dogmatic theology depend on?
options: Proofs drawn from the common experience of all
Dogmas and the authority of a church
Historical documents and records
Experiments on religious feeling
optionExplain: Proof from common experience marks natural theology, which is philosophy.
Right: the authors say a work of dogmatic theology depends on dogmas and the church that proclaims them.
Documents serve history; dogmatic theology rests on articles of faith.
Experiments belong to science; dogmatic theology rests on faith.
questions.explain: Dogmatic theology's first principles are articles of faith, proclaimed by the authority of a church.
questions.rule: Dogma and church authority mark dogmatic theology.

questions.q: Two essays defend freedom of speech: one from reasons about human nature that any reader can weigh, the other from a nation's constitution taken as binding. Which could in principle persuade a reader in a country with a different constitution?
options: The second, since a constitution carries the force of law
The first, since its premises are open to any reader's reason
Both equally, since both defend the same freedom of speech
Neither, since arguments about rights persuade no outsider
optionExplain: That constitution binds only those who accept its authority; the foreign reader does not.
Right: like natural theology, an argument from reason addresses anyone who can follow it.
Sharing a conclusion does not mean sharing premises; the second depends on accepting one text.
Arguments from reason can persuade outsiders; that is their advantage.
questions.explain: As with natural and dogmatic theology, the starting point decides who an argument can reach: reason addresses anyone, an authority only those who accept it.
questions.rule: Reason reaches anyone; authority reaches its own.
questions.teaches: By extension, an argument from an accepted authority can persuade only those who accept that authority, while an argument from reason addresses anyone, so the choice of starting point decides whom an argument can reach.

questions.q: True or false: Once a book is classed as natural theology, its arguments can be taken as sound.
questions.explain: Classification says where the first principles come from. Whether the reasoning is sound still has to be judged, as with any philosophy.
questions.rule: Classifying is not judging.

questions.q: How do the authors suggest a reader outside a faith should treat the dogmas of a theological book?
options: As errors to be refuted before reading any further
As historical claims to be checked against records
As the author's private opinions, which the argument can do without
With the respect given to a mathematician's assumptions
optionExplain: Fighting the principles first keeps the reader from ever reading the book.
Dogmas are articles of faith, not historical claims to verify.
The argument rests on the dogmas as its first principles; they cannot be set aside.
Right: treat them as starting points, granted as a geometer's postulates are.
questions.explain: An outsider can read dogmatic theology well by granting its dogmas as a mathematician's assumptions are granted. The card next adds a caution.
questions.rule: Grant dogmas as starting points.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, for those who have faith, an article of faith is the most certain form of knowledge.
questions.explain: For the faithful, faith is the most certain form of knowledge, not a tentative opinion or an assumption.
questions.rule: For believers, faith is certainty.

questions.q: A non-believing student summarizing a theological treatise writes that the author assumes, for the sake of argument, that God exists. What is wrong with this?
options: For the author it is certain knowledge, not an assumption
The student should have stated the dogma in the author's own words
The student ought to have refuted the claim first
Works of dogmatic theology do not begin from principles
optionExplain: Right: the student may grant it as an assumption, but must not attribute that attitude to the author.
Exact wording is not the problem; the problem is calling the author's certainty an assumption.
Refuting the premise first is the mistake that stops a reader from attending to the book.
Its first principles are articles of faith; that is what makes it dogmatic.
questions.explain: The outsider's way of holding the dogma, as a granted starting point, is not the author's way, which is certainty. A fair summary keeps them apart.
questions.rule: Do not report the author's certainty as a supposition.

questions.q: Sort these descriptions of a dogma by whose standpoint they describe.
groups: How the outsider holds it while reading
What it is for the believer

items.t: A starting point granted for the argument
Treated like a geometer's postulate
Not binding on him once the book is closed
The most certain form of knowledge
Not a tentative opinion
Held with full certainty

questions.explain: The outsider grants the dogma as a working assumption. For the believer it is certain knowledge, not an assumption at all.
questions.rule: Granted by the outsider; certain for the believer.

questions.q: An anthropologist studies a community's beliefs about its ancestors. She does not share them. How, by analogy with the authors' advice, should she report them?
options: As hypotheses that the members are testing about their ancestors
As errors she should correct for the community's benefit
As the members hold them, as certainties, without sharing them
As her own beliefs, so she can understand them from inside
optionExplain: Calling them hypotheses misreports how the members hold them.
Her task is to understand and report, not to refute.
Right: like the non-believing reader, she can grant the beliefs a hearing while recording that the members hold them as certain.
She can understand them without adopting them, as the outsider grants dogmas without believing.
questions.explain: By analogy, a fair outside observer reports deep convictions as their holders hold them, as certainties, even while not sharing them.
questions.rule: Report convictions as held, without adopting them.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a fair outside observer of any community's deep convictions must report them as the members hold them, as certainties, even while not sharing them; describing them as hypotheses distorts them.

questions.q: True or false: The authors say a believing reader of a work essential to his faith faces difficulties different from a non-believer's.
questions.explain: The authors say the faithful reader of such a work has other difficulties to face, which are not confined to reading theology.
questions.rule: Believer and outsider face different problems.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the two mistakes the authors say readers make with dogmatic theology?
options: Reading it too slowly and with too much care
Paying too much attention to its arguments
Refusing its first principles even for a while
Reading other theologians on the very same question
optionExplain: The authors ask for all the care a good expository work deserves.
The arguments deserve close attention; treating them as beyond judgment is the other mistake.
Right: refusing even temporary acceptance keeps the reader struggling with the principles instead of reading the book.
Comparing theologians is not one of the mistakes the authors name.
questions.explain: One mistake is refusing to grant the first principles even temporarily. The card next gives the other.
questions.rule: Grant the principles to read the book.

questions.q: Which are the two mistakes the authors name?
options: Checking whether its reasoning is cogent
Refusing the first principles even for a time
Taking the arguments as dogmatic as the principles
Reading the book without belonging to its own church
Comparing it with the sacred books of other faiths
optionExplain: Checking the reasoning is what the authors recommend, not a mistake.
Right: this is the first mistake.
Right: this is the second mistake.
The authors say a non-believer can read such a book well.
The authors do not name comparison as a mistake.
questions.explain: The two mistakes are refusing the principles and treating the reasoning as dogma. Checking the reasoning is the remedy.
questions.rule: Do not fight the premises; do not exempt the reasoning.

questions.q: A sceptic spends her whole reading of a theological work disputing its premise that God exists, and afterwards cannot say what the book argues. Which mistake has she made?
options: Refusing to accept the first principles even temporarily
Treating the book's reasoning as if it were dogma
Reading too many other theologians on the topic
Accepting the book's conclusions far too quickly and easily
optionExplain: Right: by struggling with the first principle, she never attended to the book itself.
She did not exempt the reasoning; she never reached it.
Nothing suggests she read other theologians.
She accepted nothing; her trouble was refusing the premise.
questions.explain: Refusing to grant the premise even for the reading kept her from following the book at all.
questions.rule: Grant first, so you can read at all.

questions.q: A reader says that since a treatise's principles are dogmas, every argument in it is beyond criticism. What is wrong with this?
options: Dogmas are not the principles of dogmatic theology
Only believers have the right to criticize theology
Criticizing the arguments means rejecting the dogmas themselves
Reasoning from dogmas can still be valid or invalid
optionExplain: Articles of faith are exactly the first principles of dogmatic theology.
The authors say non-believers can read such books well, which includes judging the reasoning.
A reader can fault an inference while still granting its premises; that is the authors' point.
Right: defective reasoning leads to invalid conclusions even from the most acceptable principles.
questions.explain: Dogmatic principles do not make the reasoning dogmatic. Each argument can be checked for cogency.
questions.rule: Dogmatic premises, ordinary logic.

questions.q: A lawyer treats her country's constitution as binding, but finds a colleague's argument about what it requires to be weak. By analogy with the authors' advice, what should she do?
options: Accept the argument, since it starts from the constitution
Criticize the reasoning while accepting the constitution
Reject the constitution, since weak arguments come from it
Stay silent, since binding texts cannot be argued about
optionExplain: Starting from an accepted text does not make every argument from it sound.
Right: accepting a framework does not exempt reasoning within it from criticism.
A weak argument faults the reasoning, not the framework.
What a binding text requires is argued about all the time; the reasoning is open to judgment.
questions.explain: By analogy, reasoning inside any accepted framework can be judged sound or faulty, even when the framework itself is not in question.
questions.rule: Accept the framework; judge the reasoning.
questions.teaches: By analogy, reasoning inside any accepted framework, such as a constitution or a company's charter, can be judged sound or faulty even when the framework itself is not open to question.

questions.q: True or false: If a theological work's principles are accepted and its reasoning is cogent, its conclusions must be accepted, at least as far as the principles are.
questions.explain: Cogent reasoning carries acceptance from principles to conclusions. That is why the reasoning, not the dogma, is where a reader's critical care belongs.
questions.rule: Sound steps carry the premises' weight to the conclusion.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a book such as an army's infantry manual can be read canonically.
questions.explain: The authors extend canonical reading beyond scripture, to Marx, Freud and the U.S. Army's infantry manual. The card next gives its marks.
questions.rule: Canonical reading reaches beyond scripture.

questions.q: Which are the marks of an institution behind canonical reading, as the authors list them?
options: It is at least a century old
It is officially recognized by the state
It is a teaching institution
It has a body of doctrine to teach
It has a faithful and obedient membership
optionExplain: Age is not one of the marks; a new party or society can qualify.
State recognition is not one of the marks; a church, party or society may lack it.
Right: the institution teaches.
Right: it has a doctrine to teach.
Right: its members are faithful and obedient.
questions.explain: Teaching, doctrine and obedient members together produce reverential, canonical reading.
questions.rule: Teaching, doctrine, obedience.

questions.q: In a political movement, members study the founder's writings in classes, must accept its doctrine, and may not say the writings contain errors. How do they read those writings?
options: Critically, testing each of its claims for its truth
Canonically, as an authorized text beyond question
Inspectionally, skimming for the main points
As literature, for their style and imagery
optionExplain: Critical reading includes the freedom to find error, which these members lack.
Right: all three marks are present, so the members read reverentially and cannot question the authorized reading.
Skimming is a level of reading, not the reverential stance described.
Reading for style treats the writings as literature, not as authority.
questions.explain: A teaching institution with doctrine and obedient members makes its founding texts canonical for them.
questions.rule: The three marks make a reading canonical.

questions.q: Which of these ways of reading the Bible is not canonical in the authors' sense?
options: Reading it as the revealed Word of God
Reading it under a church's authorized interpretation
Reading it as a believer obliged to find it true
Reading it as literature, for its stories and style
optionExplain: This is the authors' prime example of canonical reading.
Accepting an authorized interpretation is a mark of canonical reading.
The obligation to find the text true is part of canonical reading.
Right: the authors say the Bible is canonical when read as the Word of God, not as literature.
questions.explain: Canonical is a way of reading. The same book read as literature is not read canonically.
questions.rule: The reading, not the book, is canonical.

questions.q: After a takeover, a firm's staff stop citing the old founder's handbook as beyond question, and the new owners train no one in it. What does this illustrate?
options: A text's canonical status depends on the institution behind it
The handbook must have contained errors all along
Canonical status belongs to a text whatever happens to its readers
Handbooks cannot be read canonically, unlike scriptures
optionExplain: Right: when the teaching institution and its obedient members change, the reading changes with them.
The change came from the institution, not from discovering errors.
The case shows the reverse: the status lapsed when the institution did.
The handbook was read canonically before; the authors' examples include an infantry manual.
