questions.explain: Canonical status rests on the institution. The authors note that orthodox Marxists read Stalin canonically depending on the political climate; status can come and go with circumstances.
questions.rule: Canonical status rises and falls with its institution.
questions.teaches: Canonical status depends on the institution and can change with it, as the authors note that orthodox Marxists read Stalin's works canonically depending on the political climate.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the faithful reader of a canonical book is debarred by his faith from finding error in the text.
questions.explain: The faithful do not, even cannot, question the authorized reading, and their faith bars them from finding error, let alone nonsense, in the text.
questions.rule: Faith bars finding error in the canon.

questions.q: The word orthodox, the authors note, comes from Greek roots meaning what?
options: Ancient teaching
Sacred book
Right opinion
Strict rule
optionExplain: Orthodox views are often old, but the roots mean right opinion.
Canonical books are often sacred, but the word orthodox does not mean that.
Right: orthodox means right opinion, which fits books with one right reading.
Orthodoxy can be strict, but the roots are about opinion, not rules.
questions.explain: Orthodox means right opinion: canonical books have one right reading. The card next sets out what that obliges.
questions.rule: Orthodox: right opinion.

questions.q: Put in order what the faithful reader of a canonical book is obliged to do when a passage puzzles him.
items: Try to make sense of it and find it true himself
If he cannot, go to someone who can
Accept the resolution that person offers
questions.explain: The reader first tries on his own to make sense of the text and find it true; failing that, he turns to the recognized authority and accepts the answer given.
questions.rule: Try, consult, accept.

questions.q: A party member finds a passage in the movement's founding text that seems to contradict another. As a faithful reader, what is she obliged to do?
options: Publish her finding that the founding text is in error here
Choose whichever passage she happens to prefer
Find a sense in which both are true, or ask an authority
Set the text aside as unreliable on this point
optionExplain: Finding error in the canonical text is what her faith debars.
Picking her own reading denies that there is one right reading.
Right: she must make sense of the text and find it true, and if she cannot, go to her superior and accept his resolution.
Treating the text as unreliable breaks the obligation to find it true.
questions.explain: The faithful reader may not conclude the text is wrong. She must reconcile the passages or accept the authorized reconciliation.
questions.rule: In canonical reading, apparent error calls for reconciliation.

questions.q: What do the authors say the faithful reader gains in return for reading without freedom?
options: A satisfaction possibly never found in other reading
Faster and more accurate reading of every text
Freedom to interpret the text in whatever way he likes
Proof that the text is true in every sense
optionExplain: Right: the authors say he gains a kind of satisfaction possibly never obtained from other books.
Nothing in the authors' account concerns speed or general accuracy.
This is the opposite: he reads essentially without freedom.
He must find the text true in one or another sense; no proof is gained.
questions.explain: Canonical reading trades freedom of judgment for a special satisfaction.
questions.rule: Freedom given up, satisfaction gained.

questions.q: A supreme court, bound to treat its constitution as authoritative, faces two clauses that seem to conflict. It reads one narrowly so that both can stand. How does this parallel the authors' account?
options: Like a critical reader, it declares one of the clauses mistaken
Like a free reader, it picks the clause it prefers
Like a skimmer, it sets the conflict aside unread
Like a faithful reader, it seeks a sense where both hold
optionExplain: The court does not declare a clause wrong; it reconciles them.
It does not choose freely; it searches for a reading consistent with both.
It engages the conflict directly; it does not ignore it.
Right: bound to the text, the court looks for a reading under which both clauses hold, as the faithful reader finds the text true in some sense.
questions.explain: Where a text cannot be called wrong, interpretation works by finding a sense in which it is true. Courts bound to a constitution often reason the same way.
questions.rule: Bound texts are reconciled, not corrected.
questions.teaches: Because the faithful reader must find the text true in some sense, interpretation in canonical traditions, and in courts bound to a constitution, works by finding senses in which apparent conflicts both hold rather than by admitting error.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the obligations of canonical reading are the right rules for reading any good book.
questions.explain: Canonical reading is reading without freedom, bound to an institution. With other books, the reader is free and indeed obliged to judge for himself.
questions.rule: Canonical rules are not general rules.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, almost all of us have come close to having to read canonically at some point.
questions.explain: Bar exams, professional tests and professors' required interpretations put most of us near canonical reading. The card next gives the examples.
questions.rule: Most of us have read canonically.

questions.q: Which example do the authors give of ordinary canonical reading?
options: A novelist reading the reviews of her latest book
A new lawyer studying for the bar exams
A tourist reading a guidebook abroad
A child reading a comic book for fun
optionExplain: A novelist may weigh reviews freely; no authorized reading binds her.
Right: to get a perfect score, the fledgling lawyer must read certain texts in a certain way.
A tourist uses a guidebook as she likes, with no authorized interpretation to match.
Reading for fun is free reading, the opposite of canonical.
questions.explain: The bar candidate must match an authorized reading to succeed, which puts him near canonical reading.
questions.rule: Exam reading can be canonical reading.

questions.q: A trainee pilot must learn the official procedures manual exactly as the airline interprets it in order to pass a check. How is she reading?
options: Critically, deciding for herself whether she agrees with it
Canonically, to match an authorized interpretation
Inspectionally, skimming for its main points
For pleasure, as one might read a good novel
optionExplain: She is not free to disagree with the manual during the check.
Right: her success depends on matching the airline's authorized reading, not on judging the manual.
She must learn it exactly, not skim it.
Pleasure reading is free; she is bound to the official interpretation.
questions.explain: Like the bar candidate, she reads to match an authorized interpretation, which is canonical reading.
questions.rule: Reading to match an authority is canonical.

questions.q: What do the authors say about reading Scripture as the Word of God?
options: In Europe the Bible has been the most carefully read book
It follows the same rules as any other expository book
The authors give detailed rules for doing it
It is the most difficult problem in reading
More books discuss it than all other reading together
optionExplain: Right: they say it has been the most widely and most carefully read book.
The authors treat it as a case apart, harder than any other.
The authors stop here; they give no rules for reading Scripture.
Right: the authors call it the most difficult problem in the whole field of reading.
Right: more has been written on reading Scripture than on all other aspects of reading together.
questions.explain: For believers Scripture is both the hardest and the most important reading, and the authors leave it there.
questions.rule: Scripture is the hardest reading.

questions.q: After years of exams that reward the official reading, an accountant finds she accepts every textbook claim without question, even in books nobody will grade her on. By the authors' account of canonical reading, what has she lost in that free reading?
options: Her speed in reading long technical texts
Her knowledge of the official interpretations
The accuracy of her reading of technical texts
The freedom to judge texts for herself
optionExplain: Speed is not what canonical reading costs; freedom of judgment is.
She knows the official readings well; the trouble is that she reads everything as if bound by them.
She may read accurately; what is missing is her own judgment of what she reads.
Right: canonical reading is reading without freedom, and she now reads that way where nothing requires it.
questions.explain: By extension, a habit of canonical reading formed where grading demands it can carry over into reading nobody grades, so the reader gives up freedom she still has.
questions.rule: Watch for canonical habits in free reading.
questions.teaches: By extension, the habit of canonical reading formed where grading demands it can carry over into reading nobody grades, so a reader may accept texts without question even when free to judge them.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, every professor fails students who disagree with the professor's interpretation.
questions.explain: The authors add that not all professors fail their students for disagreeing with them; required interpretation is one case, not the rule.
questions.rule: Not every classroom demands canonical reading.

questions.q: According to the authors, which part of a newspaper is most likely to limit itself to reporting facts?
options: A long analysis piece by a specialist reporter
A short who-what-when-where story on the front page
A signed column on the meaning of the week's events
A weekend feature on a new social trend
optionExplain: Specialist analysis is where interpretation is thickest, since its job is to explain the facts.
Right: the authors single out the shorthand front-page story as the kind that sticks to facts.
A column exists to comment, so it mixes facts with interpretation by design.
A trend feature explains why something is happening, which means interpretation.
questions.explain: The authors say modern journalism mostly enmeshes facts in interpretation, except for the brief front-page report. The card next shows where that interpretation comes from.
questions.rule: Most journalism interprets as well as reports.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, social science ideas reach readers through fiction as well as through non-fiction.
questions.explain: The authors describe social-science fiction: novels, plays, films and shows that build artificial models of society and so draw on and spread social science ideas.
questions.rule: Social science also travels in stories.

questions.q: Sort each sentence from a news story about a factory closing by whether it reports a fact or adds social science interpretation.

items.t: The plant closed on Friday after 40 years
About 600 workers lost their jobs
The company announced the closure in a press release
The closing will weaken the town's social cohesion
Job losses of this kind feed a cycle of family breakdown
The decision reflects a shift in the region's power structure

questions.explain: The first three could be checked by anyone on the scene or in the records. The last three explain the facts with social science concepts such as cohesion, family breakdown and power structure.
questions.rule: Ask what an eyewitness could confirm; the rest is interpretation.

questions.q: A novel imagines a city where a single credit score decides who may rent, marry or hold a job. How do the authors' remarks suggest a reader approach it?
options: As a prediction to be judged by whether it later comes true
As a history of a real city written in the form of a story
As entertainment that makes no claims about how society works
As a model of society that carries ideas from social science
optionExplain: Such fiction explores consequences; whether it comes true is not what makes it worth reading.
The city is invented, so the book is not history, even if it echoes real trends.
It is still fiction, but by building a model of society it does make points about how power and property work.
Right: the authors describe fiction that builds artificial models of society, drawing on and spreading social science.
questions.explain: Social-science fiction invents a society to explore how arrangements of power, property and wealth would play out. Reading it well means noticing the social ideas the model carries.
questions.rule: An invented society can carry a social science message.

questions.q: A news chart shows crime rates by neighbourhood, with the neighbourhoods grouped by poverty level. Extending the authors' point about journalism, what should a careful reader notice?
options: The grouping already suggests an explanation, linking crime to poverty
A chart is only numbers, so it cannot carry any interpretation
The chart is interpretation only if a reporter's opinion sits beside it
The grouping matters only if some numbers in the chart are wrong
optionExplain: Right: choosing poverty as the grouping points the reader toward one social science explanation before a word of comment is written.
Numbers can be accurate while the way they are grouped still steers the reader to a cause.
Comment is one way interpretation enters; the choice of categories is another.
Accurate numbers can still be grouped in a way that favours one explanation over others.
questions.explain: The reporter could have grouped neighbourhoods by age, policing or housing density. Picking poverty frames the facts with one theory of crime.
questions.rule: The categories chosen for facts can already interpret them.
questions.teaches: By analogy, interpretation can enter a news piece before any commentary is written: the categories chosen to group facts, as in a chart, already suggest which social science explanation to reach for.

questions.q: True or false: If an editor cut a long news analysis down to a short who-what-when-where report, the authors' view suggests that most of its social science interpretation would survive the cut.
questions.explain: The authors contrast the shorthand factual story with the commentary and analysis where social science concepts do their work. Cut the analysis and mostly the facts remain.
questions.rule: Less analysis, less borrowed theory.

questions.q: A reader says: This article uses the term status, so it is biased propaganda and I can ignore it. What is wrong with the reasoning?
options: Status is not a social science term, so the article borrows nothing
Borrowing a concept shows where the ideas come from, not that they are wrong
Articles that use social science terms are more reliable than others
The reader should ignore only articles that use several such terms
optionExplain: Status is one of the social science terms the authors list as part of everyday talk.
Right: spotting a borrowed concept tells you to read the interpretation carefully, not to dismiss it.
This swaps one shortcut for another; the term proves nothing either way about reliability.
Counting terms is still judging by vocabulary instead of by the argument.
questions.explain: Noticing the social science behind an interpretation tells you what kind of claim you are reading. Whether it is sound still has to be judged on its evidence and reasoning.
questions.rule: A borrowed term marks the claim; it does not refute it.

questions.q: Which of these fields do the authors place in the central core of social science? Select all that apply.
options: Economics
Public administration
Sociology
Psychology
Anthropology
History
optionExplain: Right: economics is one of the four core fields.
Much writing in public administration counts, but it sits in the fringe, not the core.
Right: sociology is one of the four core fields.
Much psychology counts, but its place is disputed, so it is fringe rather than core.
Right: anthropology is one of the four core fields.
History supplies data, but the authors do not count it as a social science.
questions.explain: The core is anthropology, economics, politics and sociology. The card next shows which fields sit around it.
questions.rule: Four fields form the core.

questions.q: According to the authors, schools of law, business and education are usually kept apart from social science divisions because their main purpose is to train for ____ work outside the university.
questions.explain: The core departments aim at systematic knowledge of society; the schools aim at preparing people for professions outside the university.
questions.rule: Knowledge of society versus training for practice.

questions.q: Sort each work by whether it falls in the core of social science or in the fringe the authors describe.

items.t: An economist's study of how tariffs change prices
A sociologist's survey of friendship networks in cities
An anthropologist's account of kinship among herders
A study of how school funding rules shape class sizes
A legal scholar's study of how sentencing laws affect prison numbers
A psychologist's study of how crowds sway individual choices

questions.explain: Economics, sociology and anthropology are core fields. Education, law and psychology supply much social science writing, but they sit in the fringe.
questions.rule: Core fields first; law, education and psychology in the fringe.

questions.q: Priya finds two books from a business school. One analyses how global firms change local labour markets; the other is a guide to running sales meetings. By the authors' purpose test, how should she classify them?
options: Both are social science, since a business school produced both
Neither is social science, since business schools train professionals
The labour-market study is social science; the guide is training
The guide is social science, since it describes how people behave
optionExplain: The school's name does not decide it; the authors say only some business writing falls inside.
The authors count some business writing as social science, so a blanket exclusion goes too far.
Right: the study seeks knowledge of how society works, while the guide prepares people for a job.
Describing behaviour in passing is not the aim of a how-to guide; its aim is practice.
questions.explain: The authors separate seeking systematic knowledge of society from training for professional work. Applied to single books, that test splits Priya's pair.
questions.rule: Classify the work by its aim, not its school.

questions.q: True or false: If a law school study stopped describing how sentencing works and began advising lawyers how to win appeals, the authors' purpose test would move it toward professional training.
questions.explain: Advice on winning cases serves professional practice. Describing how an institution works serves systematic knowledge of society.
questions.rule: Change the aim and the classification changes.

questions.q: A city publishes a report that blends polling, population statistics and economics to forecast school enrolments. Given the authors' warning about interdisciplinary work, what should a reader do first?
options: Accept the forecast, since several specialties agree in one report
Reject the forecast, since mixed methods cannot produce knowledge
Check only the economics, since economics is a core social science
Work out which specialty supplies each main finding in the report
optionExplain: Putting specialties in one report does not mean each one's evidence is sound or that they agree.
The authors warn that such reports are hard to judge, not that they are worthless.
The polling and population figures could carry the forecast; checking one strand leaves the rest untested.
Right: the authors say sophistication is needed even to discern the strands, so naming them comes before judging.
questions.explain: The authors warn that seeing the separate strands of an interdisciplinary report is hard before any judging starts. Listing which specialty backs each finding turns that warning into a first step.
questions.rule: Untangle the specialties before you judge the findings.
questions.teaches: A practical first step with an interdisciplinary report is to list which specialty supplies each main finding, because a reader cannot weigh a finding until she knows what kind of evidence stands behind it.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, history counts as a social science because social scientists draw on it for data.
questions.explain: Social science does draw on history, but the authors hold that history, as an account of particular events, does not of itself yield laws of behavior. The card next explains the edge cases.
questions.rule: Supplying data does not make a field a social science.

questions.q: Match each edge case with how the authors describe it.
pairs: Leave it out: it studies individual traits
Count it: the individual cannot be cut off from society
Accounts of particular events and persons
questions.explain: Psychology splits on whether the individual can be studied apart from society. Behavioral science stresses measurement. History tells of particulars rather than finding laws.
questions.rule: Each edge case turns on a different question.

questions.q: Which of these studies would even the looser social scientists hand over to the biological sciences?
options: A study of how hormone levels change heart rate under stress
A study of how job loss affects quarrels within families
A study of how rumours spread among office workers
A study of how immigrants adjust to a new language
optionExplain: Right: this is physiological psychology, which even the looser view places under biology.
Family life under economic strain puts the person in a social setting, so the looser view counts it.
Rumours spread through social ties, so this is about people in groups.
Adjusting to a new language and country concerns the person in a social environment.
questions.explain: The looser view counts psychology because the individual is bound up with his surroundings, but it still gives physiological psychology to biology.
questions.rule: Bodily mechanisms go to biology even on the looser view.

questions.q: Tom reads a history of one city's bread riots in the 1930s, then a study comparing food riots in thirty cities to find the conditions that usually come before them. By the authors' distinction, which is closer to social science?
options: The single-city history, because it gives the richest detail
Both equally, because both are about the same kind of event
The thirty-city study, because it looks for a general pattern
Neither, because both rely on records of past events
optionExplain: Detail serves an account of particulars, which is what the authors call history.
Sharing a subject does not make two works the same kind; what they seek differs.
Right: seeking a pattern that holds across cases is what history alone does not do.
Social science draws data from the past too; what matters is whether it seeks patterns.
questions.explain: The authors separate accounts of particular events from systematic knowledge of patterns or laws. The comparison seeks a pattern; the single history tells what happened.
questions.rule: Particulars point to history; patterns point to social science.

questions.q: True or false: On the looser view, if a psychology study moved from measuring nerve responses to studying how a classroom shapes a child's confidence, it would move toward social science.
questions.explain: Nerve responses belong to physiological psychology, which goes to biology. A child's confidence in a classroom concerns the individual in his social environment.
questions.rule: The social setting pulls psychology toward social science.

questions.q: A shop's report counts exactly how many customers used the self-checkout each day last March. Using the authors' remarks on behavioral science and history, what does the report give?
options: A law of shopper behavior, since the behavior was measured
Measured data about one place and time, not yet a general pattern
Nothing of value, since only experiments can study behavior
A history in the authors' sense, since it tells a story of March
optionExplain: Measurement is necessary for behavioral science, but counting one month in one shop does not find a law.
Right: the counts are observable and measurable, but they describe particulars until used to find or test a pattern.
The authors praise observable, measurable behavior as a basis for verifiable findings; experiments are not the only route.
A table of counts is not a narrative account of events and persons.
questions.explain: Behavioral science values observable, measurable behavior, but a law is a pattern that holds beyond one case. Counts from one shop in one month stay particular until compared or tested more widely.
questions.rule: Measured is not the same as general.
questions.teaches: Measuring behavior is not the same as finding a law: a count of observable behavior can stay a record of one time and place, like history's particulars, until it is used to find or test a general pattern.

questions.section: The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
questions.q: Which feature do the authors say makes social science seem easy to read?
options: Its use of mathematics most readers learned at school
Its short books, written for busy general readers
Its avoidance of technical terms of every kind
Its data, drawn from experiences readers know
optionExplain: The authors say social science has typically not been mathematical, and mathematics would make it seem harder, not easier.
The authors say nothing about length; the ease comes from what the books contain.
Social science is full of jargon; the trouble is that the jargon has become familiar.
Right: the data often come from experiences familiar to the reader, as in poetry or philosophy.
questions.explain: Familiar data and a narrative style make social science look easy. The card next shows why that look deceives.
questions.rule: Familiar material feels easy.

questions.section: The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
questions.q: Which features do the authors list as making social science seem easy to read? Select all that apply.
options: Data drawn from familiar experience
A mainly mathematical form of argument
A narrative style known from fiction and history
Jargon that readers already use daily
An absence of strong feeling in the writing
optionExplain: Right: readers already know the experiences the data come from.
Mathematics would make reading harder, and the authors say social science has typically not been mathematical.
Right: the narrative style is familiar from fiction and history.
Right: terms like status and consensus turn up in everyday talk.
The authors say the opposite: deep feeling often imbues the writing and adds to the deceptive ease.
questions.explain: Familiar data, a narrative style, everyday jargon and strong feeling all make the pages go down smoothly.
questions.rule: Familiar data, style, words and feelings smooth the way.

questions.section: The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
questions.q: Which reaction best shows the deceptive ease the authors warn about?
options: Reading slowly because the topic and its terms are new
Finishing a chapter fast but unable to define its key term
Skipping a chapter's tables because they look hard
Disliking the style while restating the argument well
optionExplain: Slow reading of unfamiliar material is honest difficulty, not deceptive ease.
Right: the reading felt easy, yet the key term was never grasped.
Skipping hard parts is a different problem; nothing here felt deceptively easy.
Restating the argument well shows understanding, whatever the reader thinks of the style.
questions.explain: Deceptive ease means feeling you understood because the material was familiar, while the author's terms and argument escaped you.
questions.rule: Fast and agreeable is not the same as understood.

questions.section: The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
questions.q: Sam reads a magazine piece on why young people change jobs often. It is full of stories like his friends'. What self-test fits the authors' warning before Sam says he understands it?
options: Count how many of the stories match his friends' lives
Check whether the piece left him feeling strongly about it
State the author's key terms and main claim in his own words
Compare how fast he read it with harder articles he knows
optionExplain: Matching his experience is what made the piece feel easy; it does not test his grasp of the argument.
Strong feeling is one of the things the authors say makes the reading deceptively easy.
Right: restating terms and claims tests understanding rather than familiarity.
Speed measures familiarity, which is exactly the feeling that can deceive.
questions.explain: The ease comes from familiar stories and feelings. Only stating what the author means and claims shows whether Sam grasped the piece.
questions.rule: Test understanding by restating, not by recognising.

questions.section: The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
questions.q: A wellness podcast tells three vivid stories of people who slept better after giving up screens at night, then says screens ruin sleep. Extending the authors' warning about familiar data, what should a listener notice?
options: Familiar, vivid cases feel like proof, but three stories show no pattern
Personal stories are unreliable, so the claim about screens must be false
The stories match common experience, so the claim is well supported
The claim is a matter of taste, so evidence has no bearing on it
optionExplain: Right: recognising the cases makes the general claim feel shown, though a few cases cannot establish it.
Weak support does not make a claim false; it leaves it unproven.
Matching common experience is the familiarity that deceives; it is not a test of the general claim.
Whether screens affect sleep is a question of fact that evidence can address.
questions.explain: Familiar examples can do more than make reading easy: they can make a general claim feel proven. Three cases, however vivid, cannot show what usually happens.
questions.rule: A recognised case is not a proven pattern.
questions.teaches: By analogy, familiar examples can do more than make reading easy: a vivid case you recognize can feel like evidence for a general claim, though a few cases cannot show a pattern.

questions.section: The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
questions.q: True or false: If an essay on a familiar topic reads smoothly and you can restate its key terms and argument accurately, the authors' warning gives no reason to doubt your understanding.
questions.explain: The warning is about mistaking familiarity for understanding. Once you can state the terms and argument, the ease was real, not deceptive.
questions.rule: Ease that survives the restating test is real.

questions.section: The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a word we use often in everyday talk is usually a word we understand well when it appears in social science writing.
questions.explain: The authors warn that familiar jargon gives a false sense of understanding. The card next shows how slippery words like society and social are.
questions.rule: Familiar is not the same as understood.

questions.section: The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
questions.q: The authors call society a ____-like word, because so many adjectives can be placed in front of it while it keeps only a broad meaning.
questions.explain: Like a chameleon taking the colour of its background, society takes on whatever adjective is attached, while keeping only the broad notion of people living together.
questions.rule: Society changes colour with its adjective.

questions.section: The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
questions.q: A news analysis blames a city's decline on political, economic and social problems. Following the authors' advice, which question should a reader press hardest?
options: Which political party governed the city during the decline?
How many problems the writer counts in each of the three groups
Whether the decline was faster than in neighbouring cities
What social adds here that political and economic do not
optionExplain: Party control is a factual detail; it does not test whether the writer's key phrase means anything definite.
Counting problems assumes the groups are clear, which is exactly what is in doubt for social.
A useful comparison, but it leaves the vague term in place.
Right: the authors pick out social problems as the phrase readers and writers use without being able to say what it means.
questions.explain: Most readers can say what political and economic problems are. The third word is the one that often carries no definite meaning, so it is the one to pin down.
questions.rule: Ask what the vague word adds to its neighbours.

questions.section: The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
questions.q: A student sums up an article as: The author argues that society is to blame for rising crime. A tutor calls the summary incomplete. By the authors' standard, what is the most likely gap?
options: It does not say which sense of society the author meant
It leaves out the particular crimes the author discussed
It does not give the student's own view of the claim
It states the conclusion without listing the evidence
optionExplain: Right: society can mean the government, the economy, neighbours, families or culture; until the sense is fixed, the claim says little.
Details of the crimes matter less than what is being blamed for them.
A summary reports the author's view first; the student's own view comes later.
Evidence matters, but the claim itself is unclear until society is pinned down.
questions.explain: Society keeps only the broad sense of people living together. Blaming it for crime could mean many different claims, each needing different evidence.
questions.rule: A claim built on a chameleon word needs its sense fixed.

questions.section: The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
questions.q: A company memo says the new open-plan office will improve our culture. Extending the authors' advice on chameleon words, which test best pins down culture here?
options: Look up culture in a dictionary and apply its first sense
Try narrower words, such as how often teams talk, in its place
Accept the word, since everyone at the company uses it daily
Ask colleagues whether they like the company's culture now
optionExplain: A dictionary gives general senses; it cannot tell you which one the memo's writer had in mind.
Right: if a narrower phrase fits, it shows what the memo means; if none fits, the promise may be too vague to check.
Daily use is exactly what makes the word feel clear when it may not be.
Liking the culture is a separate question; it does not fix what the memo claims will improve.
questions.explain: Substituting narrower words forces a choice of meaning. The phrase that keeps the sentence sensible shows what the claim really is, and what evidence would test it.
questions.rule: Swap in narrower words to find the meaning.
questions.teaches: One way to pin down a chameleon word is substitution: try narrower words in its place and see which keeps the sentence true; the one that fits shows the meaning, and if none fits, the claim may be too vague to test.

questions.section: The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
questions.q: True or false: If an author opens by defining status as rank in a workplace hierarchy and keeps to that sense, a reader of that book still needs to treat status as an unpinned chameleon word.
questions.explain: The danger is a familiar word used without a fixed sense. Once the author fixes and keeps a sense, the reader's job is to hold him to it.
questions.rule: A defined term is pinned; hold the author to it.

questions.section: The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
questions.q: Compared with philosophy, what do the authors say readers bring to social science?
options: Stronger opinions on the matters the books discuss
Less background knowledge of the subject matter
More patience with long and difficult arguments
Greater trust in the expertise of the authors
optionExplain: Right: on social science matters readers are likely to have strong opinions, unlike most philosophical questions.
If anything, readers feel they know the subject well, since they hear about it almost daily.
The authors say nothing about patience; the difference they stress is commitment.
Trust in authors is not the contrast the authors draw.
questions.explain: Readers are seldom committed on philosophical questions but usually are on social ones. The card next shows how that makes the reading feel easier than it is.
questions.rule: Social science meets readers with their minds made up.

questions.section: The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
questions.q: True or false: The authors say philosophy, unlike social science, deals with matters remote from the world as we commonly know it.
questions.explain: Both deal with the common world. The difference the authors draw is that readers are seldom committed on philosophical questions but often are on social ones.
questions.rule: Same world, different commitment.

questions.section: The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
questions.q: Sort each question by whether readers are likely to come to it already committed, in the authors' sense.

items.t: Do minimum wage laws cost jobs?
How should police handle street protests?
Should schools group pupils by ability?
Does time exist apart from change?
Are numbers real things?
What makes a thing the same thing over time?

questions.explain: Wages, policing and schooling touch readers' interests and loyalties, so most arrive with settled views. Questions about time, numbers and identity matter, but few people feel committed on them.
questions.rule: Interests and loyalties mark the committed questions.

questions.section: The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
questions.q: Ana, a passionate opponent of school uniforms, finishes a study of them in half her usual time and feels she understood it fully. In the light of the authors' remarks, which explanation should she check first?
options: The study was badly written, which made it unusually quick to read
She reads social science faster than she reads other subjects
Her strong feelings made a familiar subject seem easier than it was
The study agreed with her, so it held nothing new for her to learn
optionExplain: Bad writing usually slows a reader down; nothing suggests it here.
General speed would not explain feeling she understood this study fully.
Right: the authors say readers' firm attitudes on social matters make the reading deceptively easy.
She has not shown what the study said, so she cannot yet know whether it agreed with her.
questions.explain: Ana came to the subject committed, and the authors count such commitment among the sources of deceptive ease. Her quick, confident reading is the pattern to check by stating the study's argument.
questions.rule: Strong feeling can make a hard text feel easy.

questions.section: The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
questions.q: A lifelong fan of a football club reads two match reports: one praises the club's tactics, the other criticises them. Extending the authors' point about commitment, which risk is the fan least likely to notice?
options: Dismissing the critical report before reading it through
Treating both reports as equally ignorant of football
Mistaking the reports' match facts for interpretation
Accepting weak arguments in the praising report
optionExplain: This is a real risk, but a fan tends to notice his own hostility to criticism.
A fan's commitment is to the club, not against football writers in general.
Commitment bends judgments about the club, not the reading of the score or the scorers.
Right: agreement feels like good judgment, so weak arguments for his side slip past without notice.
questions.explain: Commitment works on both reports. Resistance to the critical one is easy to feel; easy acceptance of the friendly one feels like seeing clearly, so it hides.
questions.rule: Commitment flatters the arguments on your side.
questions.teaches: A strong commitment distorts in both directions: it makes arguments against your view look weak, and it also makes weak arguments for your view look sound, which is the harder distortion to notice.

questions.section: The Apparent Ease of Reading Social Science
questions.q: True or false: If the same reader turned from a book on crime policy to one on whether colours exist outside the mind, the authors' contrast suggests her prior commitments would weigh less on her reading.
questions.explain: Crime policy is a social science matter on which readers usually hold firm views. The nature of colour is a philosophical question on which most readers are not committed, so less of the deceptive ease comes from prior opinion.
questions.rule: Less commitment, less pull on the reading.

questions.q: According to the authors, at which point must a reader of social science set aside his own opinions?
options: Only after deciding whether the book is true
While working out what the book says
Only when the author holds the opposite view
At no point, since good reading starts from conviction
optionExplain: Deciding truth comes last; opinions must be set aside before that, while understanding.
Right: outlining and interpreting require hearing the book without your verdict getting in the way.
Agreement distorts reading too, so the rule is not only for opposing authors.
Conviction has its place in judging, but it blocks hearing the book first.
questions.explain: The authors tie the setting aside to the first two questions of analytical reading. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Understand first, with your opinions parked.

questions.q: The authors say that to answer the first two questions of analytical reading you must, as it were, check your ____ at the door.
questions.explain: Like a coat left at a cloakroom, your opinions wait outside while you work out what the book says.
questions.rule: Opinions wait outside while you outline and interpret.

questions.q: Which of these readers have checked their opinions at the door in the authors' sense? Select all that apply.
options: A reader who outlines a book she dislikes as its author would
A reader who stops at each claim to note why it is wrong
A reader who restates an opponent's argument before replying
A reader who skips the chapters that clash with his politics
A reader who marks a claim she rejects and reads on for its support
optionExplain: Right: she lets the book's structure, not her dislike, shape the outline.
Rebutting each claim as it comes means judging before the book has been heard.
Right: restating first shows he has heard the argument he is about to answer.
Skipping clashing chapters refuses to hear the parts that matter most to a fair reading.
Right: noting her disagreement without acting on it lets her hear the author's support.
questions.explain: Checking opinions at the door does not mean having none. It means not letting them shape the outline or cut the hearing short.
questions.rule: Hear the whole case before you answer it.

questions.q: Leo, a union member, reads a book arguing that unions slow wage growth. Halfway through, his notes are a list of rebuttals. What would the authors say he has missed?
options: He should have chosen a book that matches his own views
He has read too slowly to see the book's overall plan
His rebuttals belong in a separate notebook, not the margins
He has started criticising before hearing the book's case
optionExplain: Reading only agreeable books avoids the problem without solving it, and leaves him unable to judge the other side.
Speed is not his trouble; his notes show he is arguing rather than outlining.
Where the notes go does not matter; what they contain shows he is judging too early.
Right: he is answering the book before he can state what it says.
questions.explain: Leo's notes should first capture the author's claims and reasons. Rebuttals made before that answer a book he has not yet heard.
questions.rule: Notes first record the case, then answer it.

questions.q: True or false: If Leo were reading a book that agreed with his views, the authors' rule about checking opinions at the door would no longer apply to him.
questions.explain: The rule serves understanding, and agreement can block hearing as surely as hostility, by letting a reader see only what he expected. The opinions still wait outside while he outlines and interprets.
questions.rule: Agreement, too, must wait at the door.

questions.q: A reader concludes: To read social science analytically, I must give up my convictions on the subject for good. What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing; the authors ask readers to drop their convictions
The setting aside serves understanding, not a ban on judging
Convictions need setting aside only for books that agree with you
The authors want convictions voiced at every page instead
optionExplain: The authors ask readers to check opinions at the door, which implies collecting them again, not discarding them.
Right: the rule covers outlining and interpreting; judging comes after the book has been heard.
The rule covers any book, agreeing or not, while you work out what it says.
Voicing convictions at every page is the very habit that keeps a reader from hearing the book.
questions.explain: The authors tie the stance to the first two questions. Convictions return for the later questions about truth and significance.
questions.rule: Park your views; do not abandon them.

questions.q: A juror must hear both sides before deciding, but keeps having strong reactions during the testimony. By analogy with the authors' rule, which way of taking notes fits best?
options: Two columns kept apart: what each witness said, and her reactions
One running list of her reactions, to save time when deciding
No notes at all, so her reactions cannot shape her memory
Notes only on the testimony she finds convincing as she hears it
optionExplain: Right: the account of the testimony stays clean, and her reactions are saved for the time to judge.
A list of reactions records her verdicts, not what was said, so the hearing is lost.
Dropping notes does not stop reactions; it only loses the record of what was said.
Noting only what convinces her lets her reactions decide what gets recorded.
questions.explain: Checking opinions at the door does not require having none. Keeping what the source says apart from what you think lets you hear the case fully and still bring your views back when it is time to judge.
questions.rule: Record the case and your reactions separately.
questions.teaches: One practical way to check opinions at the door without losing them is to keep two separate records, what the source says and what you think of it, so reactions are saved for later without shaping the account.

questions.q: What do some social scientists object to in popular journalism, according to the authors?
options: Reporting economic figures without naming a source
Avoiding technical terms readers would need to learn
Using technical terms far beyond their limited sense
Giving too much space to social scientists' views
optionExplain: Sourcing matters, but it is not the complaint the authors report.
The complaint runs the other way: technical terms are used too much, not too little.
Right: the example is GNP, made to do too much work by writers who do not fully understand it.
The authors report no complaint about coverage of social scientists.
questions.explain: The complaint is about popular writers stretching technical concepts. The card next shows what that does to readers.
questions.rule: Popular use can stretch technical terms.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, if the writer you are reading is confused about a key term, you as reader will be confused too.
questions.explain: A reader comes to terms with the writer, so a writer's muddled term passes straight into the reader's understanding.
questions.rule: The writer's confusion becomes yours.

questions.q: Sort each sentence by whether it keeps GNP to its limited sense or stretches it.

items.t: GNP grew last year, so the nation produced more in value
GNP fell during the recession as output declined
GNP per person rose more slowly than total GNP
GNP rose, so the nation's quality of life has improved
Rising GNP proves that people are happier than before
Falling GNP shows that the nation's values are in decline

questions.explain: GNP measures the value of what a nation produces, in total or per person. Claims about quality of life, happiness or values load it with meaning it does not carry.
questions.rule: Keep a technical term to the work it can do.

questions.q: A blog post says a country's rising GNP shows that its schools are improving. Following the authors' warning, what should a reader check first?
options: Whether GNP's careful sense says anything about schools
Whether the GNP figure is the most recent one available
Whether other blogs report the same rise in GNP
Whether the blogger has trained as an economist
optionExplain: Right: the claim rests on GNP meaning something about schools, which its limited sense does not.
A current figure still cannot carry a claim the term does not support.
Agreement on the figure does not test whether the term is being stretched.
Training may help, but the use of the term can be checked directly.
questions.explain: The figure may be accurate. The fault, if any, lies in what the writer makes the term mean.
questions.rule: Test the term's use before the figure.

questions.q: A TV segment quotes a newspaper, which quoted a columnist who stretched the term GNP. Extending the authors' point about confused writers, what should a viewer do?
options: Trust the segment, since several outlets repeated the claim
Ignore the term, since popular uses of GNP are always wrong
Find which outlet first reported the claim, then accept it
Trace the term back to a careful source for its limited sense
optionExplain: Repetition spreads a stretched sense; it does not correct it.
Some popular uses are careful; the task is to check, not to dismiss.
The first outlet may be the very columnist who stretched the term.
Right: the careful sense shows whether the claim survives once the term is used properly.
questions.explain: Each writer who repeats a stretched term passes on the confusion, and repetition makes it look settled. Going back to careful usage breaks the chain.
questions.rule: Trace a borrowed term to its careful source.
questions.teaches: Confusion passes down a chain of sources: each writer who repeats a stretched term spreads the stretch, and repetition makes it look settled, so trace a key term back to the most careful source you can find.

questions.q: True or false: If a writer explains that he is using GNP in a wider, stated sense and keeps to it throughout, the authors' worry about confused terms still applies in full.
questions.explain: The worry is a writer confused about his term. A stated and steady sense lets the reader come to terms with him, even if the sense is wider than usual.
questions.rule: A stated, steady sense is not confusion.

questions.q: In the authors' comparison, what does a game of poker share with a hard science book?
options: Both reward the reader who spots a hidden trick
Both get easier the more often you repeat them
Both have rules you accept rather than dispute
Both are learned best by watching experts at work
optionExplain: Neither depends on a trick; the comparison is about agreed starting rules.
Practice helps with many things, but that is not the point of the comparison.
Right: as a poker player accepts that three of a kind beats two pairs, a reader accepts a scientist's stipulated terms.
Watching experts is a way to learn, but the comparison concerns rules laid down at the start.
questions.explain: The authors say the hard sciences have a game structure: their terms are stipulated like rules. The card next explains what that means for the reader.
questions.rule: Stipulations work like a game's rules.

questions.q: Match each phrase with its meaning in the authors' account.
pairs: Telling the reader which terms matter and how they are used
Stipulated usage working like a game's rules
The usual form stipulations take at a book's start
questions.explain: A hard scientist stipulates his usage, usually in opening definitions, postulates and axioms, which gives his field its game structure.
questions.rule: Stipulation sets the rules at the start.

questions.q: A chemistry textbook says at the start that mole will mean a fixed number of particles. A student keeps objecting that a mole is a small animal. What would the authors advise?
options: Use the everyday sense wherever the definition is not repeated
Read the book with both senses in mind at every step
Accept the stated usage and follow the argument from there
Look up mole in a general dictionary before going further
optionExplain: A stipulation holds for the whole book, not only where it is restated; switching senses invites confusion.
Holding the everyday sense alongside the stipulated one only invites confusion.
Right: the stipulation is a rule of the game, to be accepted for the reading.
A general dictionary gives everyday senses; the book has told you its own.
questions.explain: The author has stipulated his usage. Within the book, mole means what he says it means, as three of a kind beats two pairs within poker.
questions.rule: Read a stipulated term in its stipulated sense.

questions.q: A reader of a geometry book writes: The author defines a point as having no size, but every point I draw has some size, so the book starts from a falsehood. What is the reader's mistake?
options: Drawing points too large to match the author's figures
Treating a stipulated rule of the game as a claim to dispute
Reading the definitions before the book's main theorems
Reading the theorems in a different order from the author's
optionExplain: Drawing smaller points would not help; any drawn point has some size.
Right: the definition sets how the term is used in the book; it is to be accepted, not argued with.
Definitions come first because the theorems depend on them.
Order of reading is not his trouble; he would make the same mistake in any order, because he is disputing a stipulation.
questions.explain: The definition of a point is a stipulation, like a rule of a game. A reader accepts it and goes on, rather than refuting it with drawings.
questions.rule: Do not argue with the rules of the game.

questions.q: A sociologist states at the outset: in this book, a household is poor if its income is below half the national median. Applying the authors' advice on stipulation, how should a reader take the book's conclusions about poverty?
options: As true of poverty in every sense of the word
As worthless, since social terms cannot be defined
As holding for poverty in the defined sense
As settled once the reader likes the definition
optionExplain: The conclusions rest on the stated definition; other senses of poor, such as lacking food, are not covered automatically.
The authors say defining social terms is hard, not impossible, and this author has done it.
Right: the reader accepts the stipulation for the reading, and the conclusions hold for poverty as defined.
Liking a definition does not settle whether the conclusions follow or apply elsewhere.
questions.explain: A stipulation is accepted for the reading, so the conclusions follow within it. Whether they hold for other senses of poverty is a further question.
questions.rule: A conclusion holds in the sense its terms were given.
questions.teaches: When a social scientist does stipulate a term, such as a poverty line, the reader accepts it for the reading, but the book's conclusions then hold for that defined sense, not automatically for every everyday use of the word.

questions.q: True or false: If a physics book stated no definitions or postulates at the start, the authors' account suggests the reader's work of coming to terms would be no harder than before.
questions.explain: The stipulations at the start do much of the work of coming to terms for the reader. Without them, the reader would have to dig the terms out himself.
questions.rule: Stated rules save the reader work.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, defining a term like economic depression is about as easy as defining a circle.
questions.explain: The authors use exactly this contrast: a circle can be defined cleanly, an economic depression cannot. The card next shows what that means for readers.
questions.rule: Social terms resist clean definition.

questions.q: Which reasons do the authors give for stipulated usage being less common in social science? Select all that apply.
options: The social sciences were typically not mathematical
Social scientists are less careful thinkers than physicists
Terms like mental health are harder to define than a triangle
Social science books are written mainly for other specialists
Readers tend to question a social scientist's definitions
optionExplain: Right: the authors name the lack of mathematics as one reason.
The authors blame the subject matter, not the thinkers.
Right: depression and mental health resist the clean definitions geometry allows.
Audience is not among the reasons the authors give.
Right: even when a social scientist defines a term, readers are inclined to dispute it.
questions.explain: The authors point to the lack of mathematics, the difficulty of defining social terms, and readers' readiness to question definitions when they are offered.
questions.rule: Hard subjects, no mathematics, doubting readers.

questions.q: Sort each term by whether it is easy or hard to stipulate, in the sense of the authors' contrast.

items.t: Circle
Isosceles triangle
Square
Economic depression
Mental health
Social class

questions.explain: Geometric figures can be defined exactly and nobody disputes the definition. Terms for social conditions have fuzzy edges and readers dispute any definition offered, as with social class by analogy.
questions.rule: Figures define cleanly; social conditions do not.

questions.q: Nadia reads a study of urban poverty in which community seems to mean a neighbourhood in one chapter and a network of friends in another. Following the authors, what should she do?
options: Look up community in a dictionary and use that sense throughout
Note each use and read each chapter's claims in its own sense
Pick the sense she prefers and apply it to every chapter
Assume the second sense, since later chapters correct earlier ones
optionExplain: A dictionary gives general senses; it cannot tell her which one the author meant in each chapter.
Right: tracking each use lets her come to terms with the author as his usage shifts.
Imposing her own sense replaces the author's meaning with hers.
A later sense need not be a correction; it may be a different use for a different point.
questions.explain: Because the author cannot fix his terms once and for all, the reader tracks them. Reading each claim in the sense it was made keeps her understanding honest.
questions.rule: Track the term; read each claim in its own sense.

questions.q: A government survey counts as unemployed only people without work who looked for a job in the past four weeks. Extending the authors' point about stipulation, what has the survey done?
options: Used the everyday sense of the word, which leaves nobody out
Avoided defining the term, so its figures cannot be read
Fixed a countable sense that leaves out some jobless people
Made the term vaguer, at the cost of precise figures
optionExplain: Everyday usage would include people who have given up looking; the survey's sense is narrower.
The survey has defined the term very precisely, by how it is counted.
Right: the counting rule stipulates a precise sense, but someone who has stopped looking falls outside it.
The rule makes the term more exact, not vaguer.
questions.explain: Defining a term by how it is counted is a way of stipulating it. It gains precision, but it may cover less than the everyday word, so readers should check what it leaves out.
questions.rule: A counting rule is a definition; check what it leaves out.
questions.teaches: A measurement rule is a form of stipulation: defining a term by how it is counted, as with unemployment, buys precision but can cover less than the everyday word, so a reader should check what the count leaves out.

questions.q: True or false: If a social scientist states an exact definition of his key term and keeps to it, a reader should read that book by the definition, even though social science usually lacks such stipulation.
questions.explain: The struggle the authors describe comes from missing or unstable usage. Where usage is stipulated, the reader treats it as in a hard science.
questions.rule: Where usage is stipulated, read by it.

questions.q: What do the authors call the most important source of difficulty in reading social science?
options: Its heavy use of mathematics and statistics
Its lack of any classic or famous books
Its authors' habit of hiding their opinions
Its mixture of several kinds of writing
optionExplain: The authors say social science has typically not been mathematical; mathematics is the hard sciences' obstacle.
The authors do note few classics, but that explains why we read several books, not the main difficulty.
The authors do not charge social scientists with hiding opinions.
Right: social science is a mixed kind of expository writing, and the mixture shifts.
questions.explain: The authors single out the mixture of science, philosophy, history and some fiction. The card next shows why it is hard to handle.
questions.rule: The mixture is the main difficulty.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, history keeps one familiar mixture of kinds, while the mixture in social science shifts from book to book.
questions.explain: History always mixes fiction and science, so readers have grown used to it. Social science mixes different strands in different proportions, even within one book.
questions.rule: A shifting mixture is harder than a fixed one.

questions.q: Match each passage from a book on housing with the strand it belongs to.
pairs: City records show rents doubled between 1990 and 2010
Across 200 cities, each new zoning rule raised rents about 2 percent
A society owes every family a decent home
Imagine Maria, a nurse, priced out of the street she grew up on
questions.explain: An account of what happened in one city is history; a measured pattern across many cities is science; a claim about what society owes is philosophy; an invented person is fiction.
questions.rule: Each strand has its own signature.

questions.q: Ravi is reading a book on crime that moves from prison statistics to a long argument about what punishment ought to achieve. By the authors' account, what should he notice?
options: The author has lost the thread, so the book is badly built
The book has shifted strands, from science toward philosophy
The argument must be judged by the same statistics as before
The book has stopped being social science at that point
optionExplain: The authors expect strands to change within a single book; a shift is not a sign of poor construction.
Right: measured findings give way to an argument about ends, a different strand.
Statistics cannot settle what punishment ought to achieve; that part asks for a different kind of support.
Social science is itself the mixture, so the philosophical strand is part of it.
questions.explain: The strands can change within one book. Noticing the shift tells Ravi that the next part is a different kind of writing.
questions.rule: Notice when the strand changes.

questions.q: A podcast episode on diet mixes a listener's story, a summary of clinical trials, and the host's view that eating meat is wrong. Extending the authors' idea of strands, how should a listener weigh these parts?
options: By the clinical trials, since they are the strongest evidence
By the kind of support each part's strand calls for
By the listener's story, since it is the most vivid part
As one whole, since all the parts share a single topic
optionExplain: Trials can test what diets do, but not whether eating meat is wrong.
Right: the trials answer to data, the moral view to reasons, and the story stands as an illustration.
A vivid story illustrates; it cannot carry a general claim.
A shared topic does not make the parts the same kind of claim.
questions.explain: Each strand asks for its own kind of support. Asking a moral view for trial data, or a story for proof, judges it by the wrong test.
questions.rule: Judge each strand by its own kind of support.
questions.teaches: Each strand carries its own kind of support: a measured finding answers to data, an account of the past to records, an argument about values to reasons, and an imagined case to plausibility, so misnaming a strand leads you to ask for the wrong support.

questions.q: True or false: If a social science paper reports a single measured finding with little else, identifying its strands matters as much as in a book that blends story, records and argument.
questions.explain: The difficulty comes from a shifting mixture. A narrow paper that stays in one strand poses little of it, so sorting strands matters less.
questions.rule: Less mixture, less need to sort strands.

questions.q: For a social science book, which step of analytical reading do the authors call both the first and the most important?
options: Outlining the major parts of the book
Finding the author's leading propositions
Deciding what kind of book it is
Judging whether the book is true
optionExplain: Outlining comes early, but the authors say it poses no special problem here.
Propositions pose no special problem in a good book, the authors say.
Right: classifying is the first task and, for social science, the most important.
Judging comes last in analytical reading, after understanding.
questions.explain: The question of what kind of book it is comes first and, here, matters most. The card next rates the other steps.
questions.rule: Classify first; it matters most.

questions.q: Sort each step of analytical reading by how the authors rate it for social science.

items.t: Outlining the book's parts
Finding propositions and arguments in a good book
Saying what kind of book it is
Coming to terms with the author
Asking what of it

questions.explain: Outlining and, in a good book, propositions and arguments go as usual. Classifying and coming to terms are hard, and what of it calls for restraint.
questions.rule: Classifying and terms are the hard steps.

questions.q: Why do the authors find classifying a social science book harder than classifying a history?
options: History mixes no kinds of writing, while social science mixes many
Social science books are longer and harder to inspect quickly
History is always one mix, while social science's mix shifts
Social science books seldom name their field on the cover
optionExplain: History is itself a mixture of fiction and science, so this gets history wrong.
Length is not the authors' reason; the trouble is the changing blend of strands.
Right: readers know history's fixed mix, but social science weaves its strands differently from book to book.
Covers are not the authors' point; even a book labelled sociology may weave in history, philosophy and fiction.
questions.explain: Both are mixed, but history's mixture is familiar and stable. Social science's mixture changes, so the reader cannot rely on knowing what he holds.
questions.rule: A changing mixture makes classifying hard.

questions.q: Mei outlined a long report on housing policy in an hour but cannot tell what the author means by affordable. By the authors' account, what does this pattern suggest?
options: Her outline must be wrong, since outlining is the hard step
She has reached the step the authors expect to be hard
The report is badly written, since terms should come easily
She should judge the report now and settle terms later
optionExplain: The authors say outlining poses no special problem, so a quick outline is no warning sign.
Right: coming to terms is the hard step in social science, because usage is seldom stipulated.
Even good social science struggles with terms; difficulty here is expected, not a sign of bad writing.
Judging before coming to terms reverses the order of analytical reading.
questions.explain: Quick outlining and hard terms is the pattern the authors predict. Mei should work toward a common understanding of affordable before going further.
questions.rule: Expect terms, not outlines, to slow you down.

questions.q: A reader starts a book on migration and labels it mostly history, but by chapter 5 it is fitting statistical models to data. Extending the authors' advice, what should she do with her first label?
options: Keep it, since a first classification governs the whole book
Stop until she can classify the whole book at once
Revise it to name the new strand, then keep reading
Label it a mixed book and stop tracking its strands
optionExplain: Strands can change within a single book, so the first label may no longer fit.
Classifying is hard; waiting for a complete answer before reading would stall her.
Right: a provisional label, revised as strands appear, keeps classifying useful without stalling the reading.
Calling it mixed names the difficulty without doing the work; the authors want the strands identified.
questions.explain: Because classifying social science is hard and strands shift, a first label can be a working guess. Updating it as the book moves on keeps the most important step alive.
questions.rule: Classify provisionally and revise as you go.
questions.teaches: Because classifying social science is so hard, a first classification can be provisional: start with your best label and revise it as the strands show themselves, rather than stalling until the whole book can be named.

questions.q: True or false: If a social science book were badly written, the authors' remark that its propositions and arguments pose no special problem might not hold.
questions.explain: The authors attach a condition: no special problem if the book is a good one. A badly built book can hide its propositions and tangle its arguments.
questions.rule: The easy steps assume a good book.

questions.q: A reader says of a social science book: I cannot fault its conclusions, but I still disagree. How do the authors explain this?
options: The reader's prejudgments about the subject are at work
The author has hidden a flaw too subtle for most readers
Social science conclusions cannot be judged by argument
The reader has misread the book's key terms throughout
optionExplain: Right: the authors trace this response to the reader's prejudgments about the author's approach and conclusions.
A hidden flaw is possible in a given case, but it is not the authors' explanation of this common response.
The authors treat social science as open to argument; the problem lies with the reader's commitments.
Misreading could cause disagreement, but this reader claims to understand and finds no fault.
questions.explain: The authors say this response comes from the reader's prejudgments. The card next shows what restraint asks of him.
questions.rule: Disagreement without a flaw points to prejudgment.

questions.q: According to the authors, the last question, what of it, requires considerable ____ on the part of a reader of social science.
questions.explain: Because readers come committed, the question of significance is where their prejudgments most easily take over.
questions.rule: What of it calls for restraint.

questions.q: Sort each reader's response by whether it criticises the book or shows prejudgment.

items.t: The survey covered one city, yet the author generalises to the nation
Chapter 4's conclusion does not follow from the data in chapter 3
The argument trades on two senses of the word community
I cannot find a flaw, but this conclusion cannot be right
Authors from that school of thought get everything wrong
The conclusion would hurt causes I care about, so I reject it

questions.explain: Each criticism points to a defect in the sample, the reasoning or the terms. The other responses reject the conclusion without showing anything wrong in how it was reached.
questions.rule: A criticism names a defect; a prejudgment does not.

questions.q: Omar finds a study of minimum wages sound in its data and reasoning, but its conclusion clashes with his politics. By the authors' account, what does restraint call for?
options: Writing a review that rejects the study on political grounds
Looking for a study whose conclusion fits his politics
Declaring the question a matter of opinion beyond argument
Recognising his prejudgment and holding back his verdict
optionExplain: Rejecting on political grounds is the prejudgment acting, not a criticism of the study.
Shopping for agreeable conclusions lets the commitment choose the evidence.
Wages and jobs are questions evidence can address; calling it opinion dodges the study.
Right: he can find no flaw, so the disagreement is his prior view; restraint means not passing it off as a criticism.
questions.explain: Omar can point to no defect. The authors' diagnosis fits: his prior view is doing the disagreeing, and restraint means seeing that before he acts on it.
questions.rule: No flaw found means no verdict yet.

questions.q: A manager rejects a well-supported proposal that would shrink her department, though she cannot name a flaw in it. Extending the authors' point, which self-test would best expose her prejudgment?
options: Ask if she would accept the same argument were it in her favour
Count how many colleagues share her doubts about the proposal
Check whether the proposal's author has her department's trust
Wait a week and see whether her doubts about it fade
optionExplain: Right: if she would accept identical reasoning for a welcome conclusion, her objection is to the conclusion, not the argument.
Shared doubts may share the same interest; counting them does not test the argument.
Trust in the author is about the person, not the reasoning.
Fading doubts show only that feelings change; they do not test the argument.
questions.explain: Reversing the conclusion while keeping the evidence and reasoning fixed isolates the argument. If she would accept it reversed, her disagreement comes from where the conclusion lands.
questions.rule: Reverse the conclusion to test your objection.
questions.teaches: A useful test for prejudgment is reversal: ask whether you would accept the same evidence and reasoning if they led to a conclusion you favoured; if you would, the disagreement comes from the conclusion, not the argument.

questions.q: True or false: If, on rereading, a reader who felt a disagreement finds that the author's data leave out a key group, her disagreement now rests on a defect she can point to, not only on prejudgment.
questions.explain: The felt disagreement led her to a real flaw in the evidence. Once she can name it, she is criticising the book, not only reacting to its conclusion.
questions.rule: A felt doubt becomes a criticism when it finds a flaw.

questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a social science reader usually does best by finding the one authoritative book on a subject and reading it thoroughly.
questions.explain: The authors say there is typically no single authoritative work on a social science subject, so several must be read. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Social science is read as a literature.

questions.q: Which reasons do the authors give for reading several social science works rather than one? Select all that apply.
options: The field is young and has few classic texts
Each social science book is too short to cover its subject
Readers usually focus on a problem rather than an author
Reading many books is quicker than reading one book well
There is typically no single authoritative work on a subject
optionExplain: Right: the authors call social science a relatively new field with few classics.
Length is not the issue; the authors point to the lack of an authoritative work.
Right: interest centres on a matter such as taxation, not on one author.
Several works are needed, and each still has to be read well; speed is not the reason.
Right: no one work settles subjects like education or local government.
questions.explain: Few classics, a focus on problems, and no single authority on most subjects all push the reader toward several works.
questions.rule: Few classics, problem focus, no single authority.

questions.q: According to the authors, how does the need to read several works in social science compare with philosophy and history?
options: It is more urgent, since one authoritative work is rarer
It is the same in all three, since no field has classics
It is less urgent, since social science books are revised
It arises only in social science; the others need one book
optionExplain: Right: philosophy and history are likelier to have one major work, so the need is most pressing in social science.
Philosophy and history do have major works; that is the difference the authors draw.
Frequent revision is a sign that no work settles a subject, which makes the need greater.
The authors say a similar situation holds, to some extent, in philosophy and history.
questions.explain: The authors find the same need in philosophy and history to some extent, but there a single major work is more likely, so in social science reading several is much more urgent.
questions.rule: Most urgent where authorities are rarest.

questions.q: Jon wants to understand why crime fell in his city. He owns a well-known 1985 book on crime. By the authors' advice, what should he do?
options: Read the 1985 book closely, since a famous work settles it
Wait until one authoritative work on his city's crime appears
Read only the newest article, since it replaces all older work
Gather several recent works on the problem and read them together
optionExplain: The authors say there is typically no single authoritative work, and older social science is quickly superseded.
Such a work is unlikely ever to appear; the authors' answer is to read several.
Newer work supersedes older, but one article is still one work, not a literature.
Right: a problem focus, several works and current editions match the authors' account.
questions.explain: No one book settles a social problem, and older works are soon superseded. Jon's best course is several current works, read with his problem in view.
questions.rule: Several current works, one problem.

questions.q: A nurse wants to understand why patients from poor neighbourhoods miss appointments. Following the authors' problem-centred approach, how should she build her reading list?
options: Read everything by the best-known author on health care
Collect works on the problem from whatever fields address it
Stay within nursing journals, since the problem arises in nursing
Read one classic of sociology, then apply it to her ward
