optionExplain: Following one author is the book-centred reading the authors set aside for social science.
Right: starting from the problem, she gathers economics on costs, sociology on neighbourhoods and more.
The problem has causes outside nursing, such as transport, income and work hours.
One classic is one book; the authors say social science problems need several.
questions.explain: When the problem, not the author or the field, chooses the books, the list draws on every discipline that addresses it.
questions.rule: Let the problem choose the books.
questions.teaches: Choosing a problem first also decides what to collect: a problem-centred reading list cuts across disciplines, drawing on economics, sociology, psychology or law wherever they address the problem, rather than staying in one field or with one author.

questions.q: True or false: The reasoning behind the authors' advice suggests that someone needing one narrow figure, such as last year's national birth rate, gains less from reading several works than someone studying a broad problem like crime.
questions.explain: The advice rests on there being no single authoritative work on broad social problems. A narrow figure often has one reliable source, so the case for several works is weaker.
questions.rule: The broader the problem, the more works it needs.

questions.q: According to the authors, why does the chapter on social science come last in Part Three?
options: Social science is the hardest kind of book to classify
Social science is the newest of the fields discussed
Social science draws on all the earlier kinds of book
Social science needs to be read syntopically
optionExplain: Classifying is hard here, but the authors give a different reason for the order.
The field is young, but youth is not why it comes last.
It does mix kinds, but the authors tie its place to how it must be read.
Right: its need to be read across several works leads straight into Part Four.
questions.explain: Social science comes last because it must be read syntopically, which makes it the bridge to the fourth level. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Social science leads into syntopical reading.

questions.q: Put these kinds of reading in the order the authors look back on them at the end of Part Three.
items: Practical books
Fiction and poetry
Science and mathematics
Philosophy
Social science
questions.explain: Practical books come first because of their call to action, then imaginative literature, then three kinds of theoretical writing ending with social science.
questions.rule: Practical, imaginative, then theoretical, ending with social science.

questions.q: Kim has read three books on school funding analytically, one at a time. By the authors' account, what does she still need?
options: Rules for relating the books to one another on the subject
A fourth analytical reading of the strongest book alone
Nothing more, since analytical rules cover any number of books
A summary written by someone who has read all three books
optionExplain: Right: the analytical rules serve each book; relating them calls for the new rules of syntopical reading.
Another reading of one book still leaves the three unrelated.
The authors say the analytical rules are not in themselves applicable to several works on one subject.
Someone else's summary replaces her own work of relating the books.
questions.explain: Each book has been read well, but how they bear on one another is a different task with its own rules.
questions.rule: Reading each well is not yet relating them.

questions.q: A patient weighing a treatment reads three studies with different results. Extending the authors' point, what further task faces her after reading each study well?
options: Picking the study with the most patients and ignoring the rest
Averaging the three results into one overall number
Trusting the newest study, since newer work supersedes older
Working out how the studies bear on one shared question
optionExplain: Size matters, but discarding the rest skips the work of relating them.
An average assumes the studies measured the same thing in the same way, which has to be checked first.
Newer is not always better; the studies may answer different questions.
Right: the studies may differ because they studied different patients or measured different outcomes, which only relating them to one question reveals.
questions.explain: Reading each study well is the analytical step. Relating them to her question shows whether they truly conflict or answered different questions about different patients.
questions.rule: Check whether conflicting sources asked the same question.
questions.teaches: Sources that seem to conflict may not: different results often come from studying different groups or measuring different outcomes, so before treating studies as disagreeing, check whether they asked the same question of the same people.

questions.q: True or false: If a reader skipped the analytical reading of each work and went straight to comparing them, the authors' account suggests the comparison would lose nothing.
questions.explain: The authors say the analytical rules still apply to each work read. A comparison of works not understood compares guesses.
questions.rule: Syntopical reading builds on analytical reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the hardest part of starting to read several books on one question is finding out that more than one book on it exists.
questions.explain: The authors call that the first and easier requirement; knowing which books should be read is much harder. The card next sets out both requirements.
questions.rule: Knowing books exist is the easy part.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: According to the authors, knowing that more than one book is relevant to a particular question is the ____ requirement in any project of syntopical reading.
questions.explain: The first requirement is knowing that several books are relevant; the second, knowing which to read, is much harder.
questions.rule: First: several books are relevant. Second: which ones.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A home baker researching how sourdough fermentation works finds forty books that mention sourdough. In the authors' terms, where does he stand?
options: He has met both requirements, since forty titles already make a ready reading list
He has met neither requirement, since he has not yet read any of the forty books
He has met the first requirement; he still has to judge which titles bear on his question
He has met the second requirement; he still has to confirm that more books exist
optionExplain: A list feels like a plan, but forty titles that mention sourdough have not been sorted for his question about fermentation.
Reading is not needed to know that relevant books exist; finding them meets the first requirement.
Right: he knows several books are relevant, but not yet which of them should be read for his question.
This reverses the two: confirming that books exist is the first requirement, and he has done that.
questions.explain: Finding the forty books shows that the subject has a literature. Choosing which of them really address fermentation is the second, harder requirement.
questions.rule: A found list meets the first requirement only.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, saying which books share one subject is somewhat clearer when the subject is a single historical event than when it is an idea such as love.
questions.explain: The authors grant that the same subject may be clear enough for a single historical period or event, but say there is little clarity in almost any other sphere.
questions.rule: A single event marks out its subject better than an idea does.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A city planner learns that thousands of reports discuss traffic congestion. How does the size of this literature bear on her two requirements?
options: It makes the first easy and raises the stakes of the second
It meets the second, since a large literature covers every angle
It makes the first hard, since so many reports must be confirmed
It lets her skip both and read the best-known report in depth
optionExplain: Right: a vast literature proves several works are relevant, and makes choosing among them matter more.
Covering every angle is not the same as telling her which reports bear on her question.
Confirming relevance does not need every report checked; one look shows many exist.
Fame does not show that a report addresses her question, and one report is not a syntopical reading.
questions.explain: The authors note that a vast literature makes a bibliography easy to create. By extension, the larger it is, the more the hard second requirement, choosing what to read, decides the outcome.
questions.rule: The bigger the literature, the more choosing matters.
questions.teaches: By extension, meeting the first requirement easily can make the second harder: the larger the literature you find, the more depends on choosing well within it.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A student writes: I confirmed that four books discuss my question, so my reading list is settled: those four. Where is the error in her reasoning?
options: She should have confirmed that at least ten books exist
She should have read one of them analytically before listing
Four books is too few to count as syntopical reading at all
Four relevant books do not show which books should be read
optionExplain: No number is set; the first requirement is that more than one book is relevant.
Reading one book deeply first is not one of the two requirements, and the chapter later warns against it.
Syntopical reading is defined as reading two or more books on one subject, so four is enough in number.
Right: she has met the first requirement and treated it as the second; other books may matter more, and some of the four may not fit.
questions.explain: Knowing that some books are relevant does not answer which books should be read. She has collapsed the second requirement into the first.
questions.rule: Relevant is not the same as the right list.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Two books both have the word freedom in their titles. What does this tell a reader who plans to compare them?
options: That they share a subject, since the key word is the same
That they may share a subject, which still has to be checked
That they disagree, since authors seldom repeat each other
That they belong together only if written in the same period
optionExplain: Matching words feel decisive, but the same word can name quite different subjects.
Right: a shared word is a lead, but each book may use it for a different matter.
Whether they disagree can only be known after the subject is settled and both are read.
Date has nothing to do with it; books from one period can still be on different subjects.
questions.explain: A shared word is a reason to look, not a conclusion. The card next shows why the same subject is harder to pin down than it seems.
questions.rule: A shared title word is a lead, not proof.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: The authors say Gone With the Wind and War and Peace, though both novels about a great war, resemble each other in little else.
questions.explain: Both are novels about a great war, and there, for the most part, the resemblance stops. The shared war does not make a shared subject.
questions.rule: A shared war is not a shared subject.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A reader is studying the question What makes sleep restorative? Sort each item by whether it addresses her question or only shares the label.

items.t: A laboratory study of memory after deep sleep
A review of how sleep stages repair the body
A survey of how shift work disrupts recovery in sleep
A thriller titled Sleep No More about a missing heiress
A history of the mattress industry
A poetry collection titled Lullabies

questions.explain: The first three ask why or how sleep restores. The others carry the word or the setting of sleep but put their attention elsewhere: a plot, a trade, poems.
questions.rule: Sort by the question addressed, not by the word used.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Which pair of works is most likely to be on the same subject in the authors' sense?
options: Two novels set in the same city during the same plague year
Two differently titled essays arguing whether punishment should deter
Two books titled Power, one on electricity and one on politics
Two biographies of people who were born in the same small town
optionExplain: A shared time and place is a setting; the two stories may be about entirely different things.
Right: different titles, but both address one question, so they share a subject.
A shared title word can name unrelated subjects, as here.
A shared birthplace is a coincidence of background, not a shared question.
questions.explain: What makes a shared subject is a shared question. The essays meet that test despite their titles; the other pairs share only a word or a setting.
questions.rule: Same question, same subject, whatever the titles.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A podcast host wants episodes for a series on how habits form. Her archive tag productivity returns 120 episodes. How should she treat the tag results?
options: As the series list, since producers assigned the tags with care
As useless, choosing episodes from memory instead of the tag
As the list once she keeps only those with productivity in the title
As candidates, checking what each episode actually addresses
optionExplain: Careful tagging records a label, but the label productivity is wider than her question about habits.
The tag is a fair lead; throwing it away loses relevant episodes along with the irrelevant.
A title word is a label too, so filtering by it repeats the same mistake.
Right: a tag groups by label, so each episode still has to be checked against her question.
questions.explain: The authors' warning about books sharing a word carries over to any system that groups items by label. The tag finds candidates; her question decides which stay.
questions.rule: Tags and keywords find candidates; your question chooses.
questions.teaches: By extension, the same check applies to any system that groups items by label, such as search results, tags or library subject headings, not only to book titles.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: By the authors' reasoning, a shared key word is of no use to a reader building a list of books on one subject.
questions.explain: A shared word is a useful lead for finding books; what it cannot do is prove that a book treats your subject. The check comes when deciding what stays on the list.
questions.rule: Use the word to find books, the question to keep them.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a novel set during a great war is, for that reason, a good book to read if your main aim is to study war.
questions.explain: War may be the novel's setting, but the novelist fixes attention on the story. The card next explains the difference between backdrop and subject.
questions.rule: A war setting does not make a book about war.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: The authors say that in War and Peace war provides the context or ____ of the story, while attention is fixed on the story itself.
questions.explain: War is the context or background of both Tolstoy's and Stendhal's stories; the stories are what the authors rivet attention on.
questions.rule: Context is not concern.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A student researching the economics of whaling has a novel about a whaling voyage and a study of whale oil prices in the 1800s. By the authors' test, how should she treat the novel?
options: As background that may give incidental details, not a main source
As a main source, since it describes whaling work at great length
As irrelevant, since a novel can teach nothing true about whaling
As the best source, since a story shows the human side of trade
optionExplain: Right: the voyage is the novel's setting; its attention is on the story, though she may pick up a few details.
Length of description does not change where the novel fixes attention; it is not studying prices.
Tolstoy learned about battles from Stendhal, so a novel's backdrop can teach some true things.
The human side may be vivid, but her question is economic, and the novel does not address it.
questions.explain: The novel's concern is its story, so whaling economics is at most its background. The price study addresses her question directly.
questions.rule: Study a subject from books whose concern it is.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the gap between a book's setting and its subject is found only in fiction.
questions.explain: The authors say the situation could be expected in fiction, but that it obtains in expository works as well, as their example of love goes on to show.
questions.rule: Expository books can have backdrops too.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A nurse studying the 1918 influenza watches a drama series set in a 1918 army camp and notes several accurate details about treatment. How is she best advised to use them?
options: As a complete account, since the details she noted were accurate
As worthless, since a drama cannot get any medical detail right
As leads to check, since the show includes only what its plot needs
As proof that the series is about the epidemic as its subject
optionExplain: Accurate details do not make a complete account; the show covers only what the drama calls for.
She has already found accurate details, so the backdrop can teach something.
Right: what a story shows of its backdrop depends on what the plot needs, so the details are real but patchy.
Accurate background is still background; the series fixes attention on its characters.
questions.explain: Like Tolstoy learning from Stendhal, she can learn from a backdrop. But what a story shows of its setting is chosen to serve the plot, so it cannot cover her subject.
questions.rule: Backdrop facts are real but selected by the story.
questions.teaches: Incidental learning from a backdrop is real but unsystematic: what you pick up depends on what the story happens to need, so it cannot cover your subject.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Suppose a novelist sets a story in a war and has the characters debate, page after page, whether a war can ever be justified. What changes for a reader studying the ethics of war?
options: Nothing changes, since a novel cannot bear on a question of this kind
The novel turns into a treatise, and she can read it as one
The debate may bear on her question, though the story stays the focus
The war setting itself now becomes the subject of the novel
optionExplain: The authors deny that novels are the place to study a subject, not that a passage can ever touch it.
Talk inside a story does not turn the story into an expository argument.
Right: the passages touch her question, but the novel's concern is still its story.
The debate is about justice in war; the setting is still the story's backdrop.
questions.explain: A passage can touch your question even when the book's attention is elsewhere. The book as a whole remains a story with a war as its context.
questions.rule: A relevant passage does not change a book's concern.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Three people say I love cheese, I love football and I love mankind. What should a reader studying love ask first?
options: Whether the word has any common sense across the three uses
Which of the three uses is the correct one for the study
Which of the three speakers feels the strongest love
How often each use appears in the books about love
optionExplain: Right: before comparing, you need to know whether the three uses name one thing.
Picking a correct use assumes the others are mistakes, which has not been shown.
Strength of feeling does not tell you whether the word means the same thing each time.
Frequency shows which use is common, not whether the uses share a meaning.
questions.explain: Cheese is eaten, football played, and neither act fits mankind, yet all three use one word. The card next shows why this matters.
questions.rule: Ask whether one word names one thing.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: The authors report that, across the literature, love has been attributed to almost everything in the universe.
questions.explain: Everything that exists has been said by someone to love or be loved, from stones and iron filings to heavenly bodies and God.
questions.rule: Love has an enormous range of reference.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A reader studying health finds the word used for bodies, economies, forests and marriages. What is her best next move before comparing books?
options: Compare all the books at once, since they share the word
Keep only medical books, since doctors own the word
Treat the most frequent use as the subject of the study
Ask whether these uses share any common meaning
optionExplain: A shared word does not guarantee a shared subject, so comparing now may set unlike things side by side.
Narrowing may come later, but choosing by who uses the word most skips the question of meaning.
Frequency is not meaning; the rarer uses may share or lack the common sense she needs.
Right: she has met a wide range of reference and must ask whether there is one subject behind it.
questions.explain: Like love, health is applied very widely. Until she knows whether the uses share a meaning, she does not know what her subject is.
questions.rule: A wide range of reference calls for the common-meaning question.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, because the cheese, football and mankind statements differ so much, the three uses of love can have nothing in common.
questions.explain: The authors ask whether there may be some deep reason, not apparent on the surface, for the shared word. They leave the question open rather than deny a common meaning.
questions.rule: Different on the surface is not proof of nothing in common.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: In one company, sales, product and support teams each report a number called engagement: clicks, minutes of use and survey scores. An analyst wants one study of engagement. What is her first task?
options: Average the three numbers into one combined score
Find what, if anything, the three measures have in common
Adopt the definition used by the largest of the teams
Study each team apart and drop the shared name for good
optionExplain: Averaging assumes the three measure one thing, which is the point in doubt.
Right: the answer to that question, if there is one, tells her what engagement means for her study.
Size of team is no reason to think its measure captures what the others mean.
Dropping the name before asking skips the possibility that a common meaning exists.
questions.explain: The shared name raises the same question as love: is there one subject here? Answering it is not a preliminary chore; it becomes the definition of what she studies.
questions.rule: The common meaning, if found, defines the subject.
questions.teaches: Asking what different uses of a word have in common is itself part of the inquiry: the answer, if one is found, becomes the working definition of your subject.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Put these moves in order for a reader facing a word with a vast range of reference.
items: Collect works that use the word
Survey the range of things the word is applied to
Ask whether the uses share a common meaning
Decide what the subject of the study is
questions.explain: You cannot see the range until you have the works, and you cannot settle the subject until you have asked whether the uses share a meaning.
questions.rule: Range first, common meaning next, subject last.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A reader studying love decides to consider only love between human beings. What is she most likely to find?
options: A single agreed definition of love shared by the writers in the field
A workable field that still holds sharply different conceptions of love
That few writers have anything at all to say about human love
That the field is every bit as chaotic as it was before narrowing
optionExplain: Narrowing feels as if it should produce agreement, but the writers on human love still conceive it differently.
Right: the oddest uses are gone, but writers still disagree about what love is.
Human love has a vast literature; narrowing to it leaves plenty to read.
Narrowing does remove stones, magnets and beefsteaks, so the field is more manageable than before.
questions.explain: Limiting the enquiry makes it workable without ending the disagreement inside it. The card next shows the conceptions that remain.
questions.rule: Narrowing removes odd uses, not rival views.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Match each term to its meaning in the authors' discussion of human love.
pairs: Wanting a good for someone else
Love as an act of the intellect
Confining the study to love between human beings
questions.explain: The three conceptions that survive narrowing are acquisitive desire, benevolence and the cognitive view; narrowing to human love is what brought them into view.
questions.rule: Three rival conceptions survive the narrowing.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A student narrows a project on courage to courage in battle. Which finding fits the authors' account best?
options: All the writers now agree, since the field has become narrow
No books remain, since battle is a setting and not a subject
The narrowed subject turns out identical to the original one
Writers still disagree over what courage in battle consists in
optionExplain: A narrower field is easier to manage, but narrowness does not produce agreement.
Battle can be a setting in novels, but expository works on courage in battle treat it as their subject.
Narrowing changes the field; it removes courage in other settings from the study.
Right: as with human love, a narrower field still holds competing conceptions.
questions.explain: The authors' example shows that narrowing makes a field workable while leaving rival conceptions within it.
questions.rule: Expect rival conceptions inside a narrowed field.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, writers who hold the cognitive view of love deny that desire plays any part in love.
questions.explain: These writers do not deny that desire enters into the picture; they deny that desire should be called love. Knowing comes first, desire follows.
questions.rule: The cognitive view demotes desire; it does not deny it.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A team studying customer satisfaction limits itself to studies available free online, because those are easiest to get. By extension of the authors' reasoning, what is the risk?
options: The line follows convenience, not the question, and may drop key works
There is none, since any narrowing makes a project more workable
The field will still be far too wide to read in a single year
Free studies will all share one conception of satisfaction
optionExplain: Right: narrowing to human love followed the question; narrowing by ease of access follows something unrelated to it.
Workable is not enough if the works cut out are the ones that bear on the question.
Size may still be a problem, but the main risk is what the arbitrary line removes.
Where a study is published says nothing about which conception of satisfaction it holds.
questions.explain: The authors narrowed love by a line drawn from the subject itself. A line drawn by convenience can make a field small while cutting away what matters.
questions.rule: Narrow by your question, not by what is easy to reach.
questions.teaches: By extension, the line you narrow by should come from your own question; narrowing for convenience, such as what is easy to obtain, can cut off the works that matter most.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A reader writes: I limited my study to human love, so I now know exactly what my subject is. What is wrong with her claim?
options: She should have limited the study to sexual love from the start
Human love is not part of the literature on love that matters
Narrowing removed the odd uses but left rival conceptions unresolved
She should never narrow a subject before reading every book on it
optionExplain: Choosing one conception in advance would assume an answer to the very question still open.
Human love is the part the authors themselves suggest focusing on.
Right: acquisitive desire, benevolence and the cognitive view still compete; she does not yet know which conception, if any, unites them.
The authors present narrowing as a reasonable move when faced with chaos; the error is thinking it settles the subject.
questions.explain: Narrowing made her field workable, not settled. What human love is remains in dispute among the writers she will read.
questions.rule: A narrowed subject is not yet a defined one.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: Wanting a good for oneself and wanting a good for someone else can be shown to share something in common.
questions.explain: Opposed as they look, both are forms of tending toward something, a desire in a very abstract sense. The card next shows how such a shared note helps.
questions.rule: Opposites can share an abstract note.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Which of these questions do the authors raise about how love shows itself among human beings? Select all that apply.
options: Is love between nations the same as love between persons?
Was romantic love invented in a particular century?
Is courting love the same as love in marriage?
Can two men of different ages be friends?
Can we love someone we have never met, like a movie star?
optionExplain: This sounds like their questions, but their list stays with persons; love between nations is not on it.
A fair historical question, but the authors' list asks about relationships, not about when ideas of love arose.
Right: the authors ask whether love changes between courtship and marriage, and between youth and old age.
Right: they ask whether friends can differ in age, wealth or intelligence.
Right: they ask whether we can love someone we have never met, such as a movie star or the President.
questions.explain: The authors' questions vary the relationship: courting or married, young or old, parent or friend, met or never met. Each variation raises a new question about love's forms.
questions.rule: Each relationship raises its own question about love.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Some writers describe ambition as a craving for fame; others describe it as a drive to do excellent work. Following the authors, what should a reader of both look for first?
options: Which of the two descriptions is the true one
A third writer who has already reconciled the two
A note both share, such as striving toward some goal
Evidence that the writers mean unrelated things
optionExplain: Judging which is true comes later; first she needs to know whether they are about one thing.
Another writer's reconciliation would be one more view, not her own finding of the common note.
Right: as acquisitive desire and benevolence share tendency, these two may share striving.
Unrelated meanings are possible, but the authors' approach is to look for a common note before concluding that.
questions.explain: The authors find a common note even between apparently opposed conceptions. That is the first thing to look for before deciding the conceptions are unrelated.
questions.rule: Seek the shared note before declaring a split.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A legal researcher has found a common meaning across medical, contractual and personal consent. Which plan, modelled on the authors' questions about love, best opens up the forms of consent?
options: Vary one factor, such as age or relationship, and ask if consent changes
Collect one definition of consent from each field and stop the study there
Pick the field where consent is clearest and set the other fields aside
Ask experts in each field which form of consent is the real one
optionExplain: Right: the authors' list works this way, changing age, relationship, sex or distance and asking whether love stays the same.
Definitions give the common meaning she already has; they do not explore how consent varies.
Setting fields aside discards the forms she wants to explore.
Asking for the real form assumes one form is genuine and the rest are not.
questions.explain: The authors generate their questions by changing one feature of the relationship at a time. The same method opens up the forms of any subject once its common meaning is in hand.
questions.rule: Vary one factor at a time to map a subject's forms.
questions.teaches: The forms of a subject can be explored by varying one factor at a time, such as age, relationship or distance, which is how the authors' list of questions about love is built.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: In the authors' account, once a common meaning of human love is found, the reader's problems about the subject are solved.
questions.explain: The authors say that even with a common meaning, not all problems are solved: the many forms love takes between people raise further questions.
questions.rule: A common meaning opens questions; it does not close them.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A reader argues: love and friendship are different words, so they must name different emotions. How would the authors treat this reasoning?
options: It is sound, since each word in a language names exactly one emotion
It is wrong, since love and friendship are known to be the same thing
It is wrong, since neither word names any kind of emotion at all
Different words do not settle whether the things differ; that is a question
optionExplain: Languages often use different words for one thing and one word for different things.
The authors do not assert that they are the same; they leave it as a question.
The authors raise doubt about whether emotions are what the words name, but do not assert that they are not.
Right: the authors ask whether the different words mean the emotions differ, and even whether emotions are what they name.
questions.explain: The authors turn this inference into a question: does the difference in words mean the things differ? A difference in words is a reason to ask, not an answer.
questions.rule: Different words are a question, not a conclusion.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: In a project of reading many books on one subject, when is the subject fully identified, according to the authors?
options: Before any reading, since the books are chosen by the subject
In a sense, only after much of the reading has been done
Once the first book on the list has been read analytically
When a teacher or adviser assigns the subject to the reader
optionExplain: The definition suggests this, which is exactly why the authors call the situation a paradox.
Right: the authors call this a paradox: the subject must in a sense follow the reading.
One book gives one author's view of the subject, not the subject the whole literature shares.
An assigned topic is a starting label; what the subject really is still has to be discovered.
questions.explain: You choose books by a subject, yet only reading tells you what the subject is. The card next explains this paradox.
questions.rule: The subject is settled by the reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: The authors call it a curious ____: syntopical reading is defined by a subject named in advance, yet the subject must in a sense be identified after the reading.
questions.explain: The definition implies that the subject is identified before reading begins, while in practice it can only be settled by reading.
questions.rule: Name a subject to start; discover it by reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A graduate student must state her thesis subject exactly before she has read anything. How does the authors' paradox bear on her statement?
options: It fixes the subject, so her reading cannot change it
It can only be a working guess to be refined by her reading
She should name no subject until she has read everything
She should pick a subject that no book has treated yet
optionExplain: Fixing it ignores the authors' point that the subject is discovered through the reading.
Right: a starting subject is needed to choose books, but the reading will refine it.
Without any starting idea she cannot choose anything to read, so total refusal stalls her.
Syntopical reading needs several books on the subject; an untreated subject has none.
questions.explain: The paradox does not forbid a starting statement; it makes that statement provisional. She should expect her reading to reshape it.
questions.rule: State the subject provisionally, then let reading reshape it.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: What is most likely to happen if a reader fixes her subject firmly at the start and refuses to revise it as she reads?
options: She will save time, since no rethinking of the subject is needed
She will find the authors agree, since her subject is clear
Nothing changes, since the subject has no effect on the reading
She may keep off-subject books and miss what unites the field
optionExplain: Time saved on rethinking is lost on books that do not belong and on a subject misjudged.
Her clarity of definition does not make the authors agree with one another.
The subject decides which books and passages count as relevant, so it shapes the whole reading.
Right: without revising, she cannot discover which conception unites the field, or drop works that turn out to be off it.
questions.explain: The authors expect the reading to show what the subject is and which works belong. A subject frozen at the start blocks both discoveries.
questions.rule: A frozen subject keeps the wrong books in.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A product team interviews users about a problem it calls slow onboarding. After thirty interviews it sees that the real issue is users not trusting the app with their data. How does this fit the authors' paradox?
options: As with the syntopical subject, the problem was identified by the inquiry
It shows the team chose the wrong problem and wasted the interviews
It shows a problem should be settled before any interviews begin
It does not fit, since the paradox applies only to reading books
optionExplain: Right: the team started with a working label, and the investigation revealed what the problem really was.
The interviews were how they found the real problem, so they were not wasted.
Settling it in advance would have locked in the wrong label, the risk the paradox warns of.
By extension, the same structure appears in any inquiry where investigating defines the problem.
questions.explain: The authors' paradox is about books, but the structure is general: you need a starting statement to begin, and the investigation tells you what you were really looking at.
questions.rule: In real inquiry, the problem is clarified by investigating it.
questions.teaches: By extension, the paradox fits any inquiry in which the problem is defined by investigating it, such as gathering user requirements: the working statement is revised by what the investigation finds.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: The authors' paradox means a syntopical reader should start reading with no idea of the subject at all.
questions.explain: The paradox says the subject is identified, in a sense, after the reading; a working idea is still needed to choose what to read. Like this chapter's love example, the reader begins with a subject and refines it.
questions.rule: Start with a guess, not with nothing.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A reader has read forty books chosen as being on her subject. Once the subject is clear, how many might turn out to be off it, by the authors' estimate?
options: None, if the list was made with care
Only one or two at the very most
As many as half of them
Roughly one in ten, as a rule
optionExplain: Care helps, but a list made before the subject is clear cannot avoid guesswork.
The authors' estimate is far higher than this.
Right: the authors say you might conclude that half the works were not on the subject at all.
The authors give no such rule; their figure is much larger.
questions.explain: A list made before the subject is clear rests on guesses, so a large share may prove irrelevant. The card next says what to do about it.
questions.rule: Expect many early picks to fall away.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: The authors suggest that, after much reading, you might conclude that half the works you read were not on the subject at all.
questions.explain: This follows from the paradox: until the reading has settled the subject, which works belong to it cannot be known.
questions.rule: Half may be off the subject.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Having settled that her subject is fairness in distributing goods, a reader finds that several books she read deal with fair trials. What does the authors' account suggest she do?
options: Widen the subject so the books still fit
Keep them so the reading time is not wasted
Set them aside as off this subject
Start again with a wholly new list of books
optionExplain: Stretching the subject to fit the books reverses the order: the subject decides the books.
Time already spent does not make a book relevant to her question.
Right: fair trials share the word but not her settled subject.
Most of her list may still be sound; dropping the misfits is enough.
questions.explain: Once the subject is clear, it decides what belongs. Works that only share the word are set aside, not absorbed.
questions.rule: The subject decides the books, not the reverse.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Sort each consideration by whether it is a reason to set a book aside from your syntopical project.
groups: Not a reason to set it aside

items.t: It addresses a different question from the one you settled on
It uses the key word in a sense outside your subject
Your subject turns out to be only its backdrop
Its argument is hard to follow
You disagree with its conclusion
It took you a long time to read

questions.explain: Relevance depends on whether a book addresses your subject. Difficulty, disagreement and time spent say nothing about that, and a book you disagree with may be central to the discussion.
questions.rule: Drop for irrelevance only, not for difficulty or disagreement.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: An auditor collects 200 documents before knowing which transactions are suspect. After defining the suspect pattern, she finds 90 documents irrelevant. By analogy with the authors, how should she read that number?
options: As expected, since the set was gathered before the problem was clear
As proof that her first search was badly carried out
As a sign that the suspect pattern has been defined wrongly
As a reason to keep all 200 in case some of them matter
optionExplain: Right: a collection made before the problem is defined has to be made by guesses, so a high discard rate is normal.
The search could only use guesses at that stage, so many misses do not show carelessness.
Discarding documents follows from defining the pattern; it does not show the pattern is wrong.
Keeping irrelevant items clutters the work; they can be set aside and recovered if the problem shifts.
questions.explain: The authors expect up to half the works to fall away once the subject is clear. By analogy, a large discard rate is the normal price of collecting before the problem was defined.
questions.rule: A high discard rate is normal when you gathered before defining.
questions.teaches: By extension, the share of items found irrelevant reflects how unclear the subject was when the list was made, so a high rate early in a project is expected rather than alarming.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: What follows, by the same reasoning, if the reader's subject shifts again later in the project?
options: Nothing, since works once dropped stay dropped
Every work must be reread from the very beginning
The new subject must be rejected to protect the list
Some works set aside may become relevant once more
optionExplain: Dropping a work was a judgment about one subject, not about the work for all time.
Only works whose relevance changes need another look, not the whole list.
Protecting a list over a better subject reverses the order: the subject decides the list.
Right: relevance depends on the subject, so a new subject can bring back works that did not fit the old one.
questions.explain: Relevance is always relevance to a subject. Since the subject can shift as the paradox implies, the judgments about which works belong can shift with it.
questions.rule: Relevance moves with the subject.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Which level of reading do the authors say comes into its own as a major tool in syntopical reading?
options: Elementary reading
Inspectional reading
Analytical reading
None: it needs wholly new skills
optionExplain: Elementary reading is assumed at every level, but it is not singled out here.
Right: with a long list of books, inspection becomes a major instrument.
Analytical skill is still used, but the authors give inspection the starring role at this level.
Syntopical reading has its own steps, but it builds on the lower levels rather than replacing them.
questions.explain: Because syntopical reading starts from many books, the fast survey of inspection becomes its major tool. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Inspection is the major tool of syntopical reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Match each kind of reading to what it prepares for, in the authors' account.
pairs: Coming to terms and following arguments
questions.explain: Each lower step anticipates a higher one: inspection's two steps prepare for analytical reading, and both lower levels prepare for syntopical reading, where inspection handles the large list.
questions.rule: Lower levels prepare for higher ones.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: An engineer starting a review has eighty research papers on batteries. According to the authors, what should occupy most of her first weeks?
options: Reading the most cited paper analytically first
Inspecting all eighty to see what each one is about
Reading every paper analytically in date order
Waiting for a review article to sum up the field
optionExplain: Citations show fame, not whether the paper is central to her question, and deep reading comes later.
Right: with a large list, inspection is the tool for the first stage.
Reading eighty papers analytically would take far too long, the very problem inspection solves.
Someone else's summary gives their view of the field, not her own survey of the papers.
questions.explain: Scale decides the tool. Eighty papers call for a fast survey before any deep reading.
questions.rule: Many works: inspect first.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: Because inspection is the major tool of syntopical reading, the authors treat analytical skill as unnecessary at this level.
questions.explain: The authors say you still read each relevant work with the skills learned in analytical reading. Inspection leads; it does not replace understanding.
questions.rule: Inspection leads, analysis still serves.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A lawyer receives 3,000 documents a month before trial. Which approach matches the authors' view of inspection as a tool?
options: Read each document closely in the order in which they arrived
Read only the documents the other side has highlighted
Read a random sample closely and assume the rest are similar
Survey all quickly to learn what each holds, then study the key ones
optionExplain: Close reading of 3,000 documents in a month is not possible, and order of arrival is not importance.
The other side chose those for its own purposes; relying on them hands over her survey.
A sample can miss the one document that decides the case; inspection covers everything lightly.
Right: a fast survey fits the job of covering many items; close study fits the few that matter.
questions.explain: A tool is judged by its fit to the job. Surveying many documents is the job inspection fits; understanding a key document is the job analytical reading fits.
questions.rule: Match the kind of reading to the job.
questions.teaches: Calling inspection a tool means judging it by its fit to a job: a fast reading is good when the job is surveying many items, and poor when the job is understanding one.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: By the authors' reasoning about scale, what would change if a reader's bibliography held only two short books?
options: Inspection would matter less, since both could soon be read analytically
Inspection would matter more, since so few books need deeper checking
Syntopical reading would become impossible with only two books
Analytical reading would no longer be needed for either book
optionExplain: Right: inspection's special role comes from the size of the list; with two short books, that pressure is gone.
Fewer books reduce the need for a fast survey rather than increase it.
Syntopical reading is defined as reading two or more books on one subject, so two is enough.
A short list makes analytical reading more practical, not less needed.
questions.explain: Inspection comes into its own because of the number of books. Shrink the list and the case for leaning on inspection shrinks with it.
questions.rule: Inspection's importance grows with the list.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a serious reader could read a hundred books on one subject analytically in a few months of spare time.
questions.explain: The authors estimate it might take ten years, and many months even working full time. The card next shows what follows from that.
questions.rule: A hundred analytical readings take years.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: The authors say that to read a hundred books analytically might well take you ____ years.
questions.explain: Ten years, or many months even full time: far too long, so a short cut is needed.
questions.rule: Ten years for a hundred books read analytically.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A doctoral student finds 150 papers on her topic. What does the authors' reasoning suggest she do?
options: Read all 150 thoroughly, since nothing less would be honest work
Choose twenty at random and read those thoroughly instead
Use a fast first pass to find the papers that deserve thorough reading
Read only the abstracts and treat them as if they were the papers
optionExplain: Thoroughness everywhere sounds rigorous, but it would take years and delay the papers that matter.
Random choice saves time but ignores which papers bear on her question.
Right: the short cut is a faster first pass that directs where thorough reading goes.
Abstracts can help a first pass, but taking them for the papers drops thorough reading altogether.
questions.explain: The cost of thorough reading forces a choice; a fast first pass makes the choice informed rather than random.
questions.rule: Survey fast, then read deep where it counts.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A reader says: since a short cut is needed, I will read every book on my list quickly and stop there. What has he misunderstood?
options: He should read every book slowly, since speed always loses understanding
He should cut his list to a single book, so no short cut is needed
The short cut is a first pass; the works that matter still need thorough reading
He should skip the books and rely on published summaries of them
optionExplain: Slow reading of everything is the cost problem that made a short cut necessary.
One book cannot make a syntopical reading, which needs two or more on a subject.
Right: the faster reading decides where thorough reading goes; it does not replace it.
Summaries give someone else's reading, and he still has no thorough reading of the key works.
questions.explain: The short cut saves time on the survey so that thorough reading can go where it pays. Stopping after the fast pass drops half the plan.
questions.rule: The short cut leads to deep reading; it does not end the reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A manager has 400 job applications and time for 15 interviews, so she screens quickly first. When unsure about an applicant in the screen, which choice better protects the short cut?
options: Keep the doubtful applicant for a second look
Reject the applicant to keep the pile small
Interview the applicant at once to settle it
Ask the applicant to rate their own fit
optionExplain: Right: wrongly dropping a strong candidate costs more than briefly keeping a weak one.
A small pile is the aim, but rejecting on doubt risks losing the best candidate for good.
Interviewing every doubtful case spends the scarce interviews the screen was meant to save.
Self-ratings shift the judgment to the applicant and do not resolve her doubt.
questions.explain: A fast pass saves time only if it does not throw away what matters. By extension, when in doubt the screen should keep, since a second look is cheap and a lost key item is not.
questions.rule: When the fast pass is unsure, keep for a second look.
questions.teaches: By extension, a short cut is safe only if the first pass leans toward keeping doubtful items, because wrongly dropping a key item costs more than briefly keeping a weak one.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: By the authors' cost argument, a reader with only three short books on her subject needs a short cut as much as one with a hundred books.
questions.explain: The short cut is needed because of the time a long list would take. Three short books could be read analytically in reasonable time.
questions.rule: The need for a short cut grows with the list.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: You have assembled a list of 25 books on your subject. What do the authors advise doing first?
options: Read the most famous of them analytically first
Read them analytically in the order you found them
Read the newest first, since it sums up the others
Inspect all 25 before reading any of them analytically
optionExplain: Fame does not show that a book is central to your subject, and you have not yet surveyed the rest.
The order of finding is accidental and says nothing about which books matter.
A recent book may review others, but it is still one author's view, and the rest stay unsurveyed.
Right: survey the whole list before committing deep effort to any book.
questions.explain: Deep reading before surveying risks spending weeks on a book that turns out to be marginal. The card next gives the authors' rule.
questions.rule: Survey the whole list first.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: The authors say you should not read any book on your list analytically before inspecting all of them.
questions.explain: Inspection of every book comes first; analytical reading of some of them comes after.
questions.rule: Inspect all before analysing any.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A teacher with twelve books on climate history is excited by the first one and wants to read it closely right away. What would the authors advise?
options: Read it closely now, since her enthusiasm will help understanding
Inspect the other eleven first, then decide what to read closely
Read it closely, then inspect the rest if time allows
Drop it, since the first book found is seldom central
optionExplain: Enthusiasm is welcome, but it does not show the book is central to her subject.
Right: only after surveying all twelve can she tell whether this one is central.
This puts deep reading before the survey, the order the authors reject.
Nothing marks the first book as unimportant; it has not yet been compared with the rest.
questions.explain: The rule is about order, not about this book's merits. The survey of all twelve tells her where close reading should go.
questions.rule: Excitement about one book can wait for the survey.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, inspecting all the books on your list will acquaint you with all the intricacies of the subject.
questions.explain: The authors say inspection will not give you all the intricacies or all the insights. It gives a survey, which is what the first stage needs.
questions.rule: Inspection surveys; it does not exhaust.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A couple has twelve house listings. They spend a whole weekend studying the first house in detail before looking at any others. By extension, what risk does the authors' rule help them avoid?
options: Missing the chance to make a quick offer on the first house
Judging every other house against the first one studied deeply
Seeing too many houses to remember any one of them well
Spending too little time studying the very first house
optionExplain: Speed of offer is a separate concern; the rule is about the order of looking.
Right: whatever is examined in depth first tends to become the yardstick for the rest.
A quick look at each is what inspection recommends; it is not the risk here.
They have spent more time on the first house, not less.
questions.explain: Surveying all options before going deep keeps any one option from setting the standard by accident. That is one reason, by extension, for the authors' order.
questions.rule: Survey all before one becomes your yardstick.
questions.teaches: By extension, surveying all options before committing guards against anchoring: the first option examined in depth tends to become the standard the others are judged by.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Put these actions in the order the authors advise for the start of a syntopical project.
items: Assemble the bibliography
Inspect every book on it
Choose which books to read analytically
Read the chosen books analytically
questions.explain: The list comes first, then inspection of all of it, and only then analytical reading of the books the inspection picks out.
questions.rule: List, inspect all, choose, then read deeply.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: What can a quick inspection of every book on your list do for you? Select all that apply.
options: Give you every insight the authors offer
Give you a clearer idea of the subject
Let you shorten the list
Tell you which author is right
Replace the need for thorough reading
optionExplain: Inspection gives a survey, not all the insights a full reading would yield.
Right: seeing what each book covers sharpens your idea of the subject.
Right: books found off the subject can be dropped.
Judging who is right needs understanding first; inspection only surveys.
Inspection directs thorough reading to the books that deserve it; it does not replace it.
questions.explain: Inspection clarifies the subject and trims the list. The card next shows how the two functions work together.
questions.rule: Inspection clarifies and trims.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: According to the authors, inspecting the books lets you cut your bibliography down to a more ____ size.
questions.explain: Cutting the list is the second function; the first is getting a clear enough idea of the subject.
questions.rule: Inspection makes the list manageable.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: After inspecting thirty books, a podcaster sees that her interest is coffee as a trade, and she drops the cookbooks. Which use of inspection is she relying on?
options: Judging which of the authors is right about coffee's history
Gaining every insight the cookbooks have to offer
Outlining the full structure of each cookbook
Cutting the list, guided by a clearer idea of the subject
optionExplain: She has not judged anyone right or wrong; she has judged relevance.
Inspection does not exhaust a book's insights, and she dropped the cookbooks.
Outlining a book fully belongs to analytical reading, not to this survey.
Right: the clearer subject told her which books to drop, the two functions working together.
questions.explain: She used the first function, a clearer subject, to perform the second, a shorter list.
questions.rule: A clearer subject guides the cuts.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: What would happen if a reader inspected her list but did not sharpen her idea of the subject while doing so?
options: Her cuts would rest on guesses, since a clear subject guides what to drop
Her cuts would be more accurate, being free of any bias about the subject
Nothing would change, since the two functions are unrelated to each other
She would have to read every one of the books analytically instead
optionExplain: Right: without a clearer subject she has no good basis for deciding which books are off it.
Without a subject to judge by, the cuts are not unbiased but unguided.
The functions feed each other; losing one weakens the other.
She could still inspect and cut, only less wisely; the result is poorer cuts, not a return to reading everything.
questions.explain: Cutting needs a standard, and the standard is the subject. If the subject stays vague, the cuts become guesses.
questions.rule: No clear subject, no sound cuts.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A curator is inspecting 200 objects for an exhibition on the theme of work. After looking at the first twenty, she wants to cut half the remaining list. What does the link between the two functions suggest?
options: Cut boldly, since early cuts save the most inspection time
Cut nothing until every object is studied in depth
Cut cautiously, since her idea of the theme is still forming
Let the first twenty objects fix the theme for good
optionExplain: Early cuts do save time, but they are made with the least clear standard.
Deep study of all 200 is the cost that inspection is meant to avoid.
Right: cuts depend on a clear theme, and after twenty objects her theme is still taking shape.
Fixing the theme from a tenth of the list ignores what the other objects may show.
questions.explain: Because cutting depends on the subject and the subject sharpens as inspection goes on, the earliest cuts are made on the weakest basis.
questions.rule: Cut lightly early, firmly later.
questions.teaches: Because the two functions depend on each other, early cuts should be cautious: the subject is least clear at the start of an inspection, so the first judgments of relevance are the weakest.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, inspection gives you a final and complete understanding of your subject.
questions.explain: Inspection gives a clear enough idea of the subject to make later analytical reading productive. The subject goes on sharpening as you read.
questions.rule: Clear enough, not final.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: According to the authors, what makes the research reading of many capable graduate students wasteful?
options: They cannot read actively or analytically at all
They read too few books on their subjects to judge
They spend the same time and effort on every book
They take far too many notes while they are reading
optionExplain: The authors grant that some of these students can read actively and analytically.
The problem they name is how time is spread, not how many books are read.
Right: reading everything at one rate shortchanges the best books and overspends on the rest.
Note-taking is not the waste the authors point to.
questions.explain: The authors' complaint is about uniform effort, not lack of skill. The card next explains why that is wasteful.
questions.rule: Uniform effort is the waste.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: The authors say such students do not read the books that deserve a really good reading as well as those books deserve.
questions.explain: Spreading effort evenly means the best books are underread, while weaker works take more time than they merit.
questions.rule: Even effort underreads the best books.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A research assistant gives each of forty articles a careful three-hour reading. Which change would the authors recommend?
options: Inspect all forty, then give the central ones far more time
Give every article four hours instead of three, to be safe
Read only the ten shortest articles, but read them with care
Read every article at the fastest pace he can manage
optionExplain: Right: a survey first, then time weighted by what each article deserves.
More time for all keeps the uniform rate, the very fault the authors name.
Length is not worth; the central articles may be long.
A faster uniform rate is still uniform, and now the central articles are rushed.
questions.explain: The fix is not a different single speed but different speeds for different works, decided after inspection.
questions.rule: Weight time by worth, not by a fixed rate.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: What happens to the most important book on a list when a reader gives every book equal time?
options: It gets more attention than it deserves
It gets the attention it needs, no more
It gets skipped, since short books win
It gets less attention than it deserves
optionExplain: Equal time gives extra attention to weak books, not to the strongest.
Only if every book needed the same time; the most important one needs more.
Equal time per book does not favour short books or skip any.
Right: the book that deserves a really good reading gets only the same share as the rest.
questions.explain: The authors say the books that deserve a really good reading do not get it under a uniform rate.
questions.rule: Equal shares shortchange the best book.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: An editor gives each of sixty submitted manuscripts exactly one hour, to be fair to all the authors. What does the authors' point reveal about this policy?
options: It is the fairest policy, since no manuscript is favoured over another
Equal time is itself a judgment, giving weak and strong work one share
It is wasteful only if the editor happens to be a slow reader
It fails mainly because sixty manuscripts are too many to read
optionExplain: Equal treatment looks neutral, but it shortchanges the strong manuscripts that need more time.
Right: a fixed rate treats every manuscript as equally deserving, which is a decision about importance.
Reading speed is beside the point; the issue is how time is spread.
Sixty is manageable with a survey first; the fault is uniform effort, not number.
questions.explain: Giving every item the same time looks like having no policy, but it amounts to judging them all equal. By extension of the authors' point, that judgment is usually wrong.
questions.rule: A fixed rate per item is a hidden ranking.
questions.teaches: By extension, uniform effort is a hidden decision: a fixed rate per item treats weak and strong items as equally deserving, which is itself a judgment about importance.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Sort each reading plan by whether it varies time according to what each work deserves.
groups: Varies time by what each deserves
Does not vary time by worth

items.t: A quick look at all, then days on the three central works
Skim the marginal works and study the key ones closely
Extra time for the books that bear most on the question
One hour per book, whatever the book
Every article read twice with full notes
Time set by page count alone

questions.explain: The first three weight effort by importance to the question. The others use one rule for all, or a rule, like page count, that ignores worth.
questions.rule: Vary effort by importance to your question.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: A quick inspection can tell you whether a book says something important about your subject, even before you know what that something is.
questions.explain: The authors say a skilful inspection reveals whether a book matters for your subject, while what it says may wait for another reading. The card next explains the verdict.
questions.rule: Whether before what.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: The authors say a skilful inspection shows whether a book is one to which the reader must ____ for light, or one that need not be read again.
questions.explain: Inspection sorts books into those you must return to for light and those that contain no enlightenment on your subject.
questions.rule: Return for light, or set aside.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Inspecting a lively travel memoir for a study of how cities grow, a planner finds colourful facts but no account of why cities grow. What should she record?
options: To be read analytically, since it is so well written
Not to be reread for this study, enjoyable as it is
To be reread, since it is informative about cities
To be quoted as evidence of how cities come to grow
optionExplain: Good writing does not make a book bear on her subject.
Right: it throws no light on her question, however enjoyable it is.
Informative is not the test; light on her question is.
It offers no account of growth, so it cannot serve as evidence for one.
questions.explain: The authors' test is whether a book holds enlightenment on your subject. Enjoyment and information do not pass that test by themselves.
questions.rule: Informative is not the same as illuminating.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: When inspection marks a book as one to return to, the reader already knows what the book's important point is.
questions.explain: The authors say the reader may not yet know precisely what the important thing is; that discovery will probably wait for another reading.
questions.rule: Marked important is not yet understood.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A genealogist inspects forty archive boxes in a day and marks twelve as worth returning to. What should she expect when she returns to the twelve?
options: All twelve will prove central, since the inspection was done with skill
None will need a closer look, since the inspection has done the work
She must first study the other twenty-eight boxes in full detail
Some will prove less useful than they seemed, and need sifting again
optionExplain: Skill makes the verdicts good, not infallible; a day for forty boxes leaves room for error.
The verdict says a box matters, not what it holds; finding that out is the return visit's job.
Re-examining the rejected boxes in depth would undo the point of the survey.
