Right: a quick verdict can err, so the return visit sifts the twelve further.
questions.explain: An inspection verdict is made quickly and says only that an item is worth a return. By extension, the return visit is where the verdict itself gets tested.
questions.rule: A must-return pile is sifted again on return.
questions.teaches: Because the inspection verdict is quick, it can be wrong, so the pile marked for return will itself be sifted again in the later, closer readings.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: What happens to the verdict on a book when the same book is inspected for a different study?
options: It may change, since the verdict depends on the subject
It stays the same, since it is about the book's quality
It waits until the book has been read analytically
It must match, or else the first inspection was poor
optionExplain: Right: the verdict asks whether the book throws light on this subject, so a new subject can change it.
The verdict is not about quality; an excellent book can hold no light for a given subject.
The point of the verdict is that it can be made during inspection, before any analytical reading.
Different subjects call for different verdicts; disagreement does not show either inspection was poor.
questions.explain: The question inspection answers is relative to a subject. Change the subject and the same book may move from set aside to must return.
questions.rule: The verdict is relative to the subject.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: The authors believe a very skilful reader can inspect all the books on a list and read them analytically at the same time.
questions.explain: The authors say they do not believe any reader, however skilful, can do this. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: Survey and deep reading are separate passes.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: The authors say that, trying to collapse inspection and analytical reading into one, younger researchers end up reading everything at the same ____.
questions.explain: One rate for everything is too fast for some works and too slow for others, and so wrong for most of them.
questions.rule: Merged passes produce one wrong rate.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A researcher reads each book carefully as she finds it, judging its relevance as she goes. Ten books in, she has lavished time on marginal books and hurried a central one. What went wrong?
options: She should have read each of the ten books even more carefully than she did
She should have read the books in order of their dates of publication
She judged relevance while reading deeply, so her speed could not match worth
She should have read only one book a month to give each its full due
optionExplain: More care for every book keeps the single rate, which is the fault.
Date order is no better a guide to importance than the order she found them in.
Right: without a prior survey she could not know which books deserved more time, so her rate fit none of them.
A slower uniform pace is still uniform, and the project would take years.
questions.explain: This is the collapse the authors warn against. Relevance has to be judged across the whole list before effort can be matched to each book.
questions.rule: Judge relevance first, across the whole list.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: The authors grant that within a single analytical reading, a skilled reader can do at once steps that a beginner must take separately.
questions.explain: That is the analogy that tempts researchers. It holds inside one analytical reading, but the authors say it does not extend to inspecting a whole list while reading its books analytically.
questions.rule: Steps merge within a reading, not across the list.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A reviewer must assess 30 pull requests, a few of them critical. She plans to review each in full detail as it comes up, judging its priority along the way. What does the authors' warning predict?
options: She will finish sooner than if she triaged first
Full review will make her priority calls sharper
Her pace will not match each request's importance
Only the critical requests will get full detail
optionExplain: Detailed review of every request is slower than a quick triage followed by focused review.
Detail on one request does not tell her how it ranks against the rest she has not seen.
Right: a survey asks whether something matters, detailed review asks what it does, and mixing the two per item leaves her rate wrong for most requests.
She cannot know which are critical until she has looked at all of them.
questions.explain: A survey and a deep treatment answer different questions. By extension of the authors' warning, switching between them item by item spoils both.
questions.rule: Triage the whole set, then go deep.
questions.teaches: By extension, a survey and a deep treatment ask different questions, whether an item matters and what it says, and switching between them item by item spoils both.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: What would the authors say if the reader were the most skilful reader in her field?
options: The advice still holds: inspect the whole list before reading analytically
She can merge the two steps, since great skill allows steps to combine
She can read the first half analytically and then inspect the rest
She can rely on analytical reading alone and skip inspection entirely
optionExplain: Right: the authors say no reader, however skilful, can inspect and read analytically at once.
Skill lets steps merge within one analytical reading, but not across this pair.
A half-and-half plan still reads some books deeply before the whole list is surveyed.
Skipping inspection means reading everything analytically, the cost the short cut avoids.
questions.explain: The authors' denial is explicit about skill: no reader, no matter how skilful, can collapse these two steps.
questions.rule: Skill does not merge inspection with analysis.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Once inspection has identified the relevant books, how do the authors say you proceed?
options: Read each analytically in turn
Summarise each in a paragraph
Read the best and skim the rest
Read them syntopically
optionExplain: This is what most readers expect, which is why the authors stress that they did not say it.
Summaries may help later, but they are not how the authors describe the next stage.
Picking one best book returns to single-book reading, not reading several on a subject.
Right: the authors note they said syntopically, not analytically, because the aim is different.
questions.explain: The authors make a point of the word syntopically. The card next explains the difference in aim.
questions.rule: Next comes syntopical, not analytical, reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: The authors say the art of analytical reading applies to reading a single book when understanding that book is the aim.
questions.explain: Analytical reading is aimed at understanding one book. Syntopical reading uses its skills but aims elsewhere.
questions.rule: Analytical: one book, understood.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A lawyer reads five court opinions on privacy, using close-reading skills on each. By the authors' distinction, what is her aim?
options: Mastering each opinion as a whole, one after another
Building an answer to a question that spans the opinions
Finding which of the judges wrote the best opinion
Memorising the facts of each case for later use
optionExplain: That would be five analytical readings, each aimed at one opinion for its own sake.
Right: her aim is a problem across the opinions, how courts weigh privacy against security.
Ranking opinions is a judgment about authors, not the aim the authors set out.
Facts may help, but memorising them is not the aim of reading across the opinions.
questions.explain: She uses analytical skills, but her aim is the shared problem. That is what makes the reading syntopical.
questions.rule: Skills from analytical reading, aim from your problem.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Sort each aim by whether it belongs to analytical reading or to syntopical reading.

items.t: Understand this book as a whole
Outline this book's structure
State this author's main argument
Learn what several books say on my problem
Find how these authors bear on one question
Use passages to build my own account

questions.explain: Analytical aims centre on one book and its author. Syntopical aims centre on a problem and use many books to address it.
questions.rule: One book's understanding versus one problem's light.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A baker once read a bread cookbook analytically. Now she consults it again, with four others, to settle how long to proof dough. How has her reading of that book changed?
options: Nothing has changed, since the content of the book is still the same
Same book, but now read for her problem, not for the book as a whole
She must reread it analytically before she can use it a second time
She should leave it out, since she has already read the book once
optionExplain: The content is the same, but what she reads it for has changed, and that changes the reading.
Right: the level of reading depends on her aim, which is now a question that spans five books.
Her earlier analytical reading already gives her the understanding she needs to use it now.
Having read it is an advantage for syntopical use, not a reason to leave it out.
questions.explain: By extension, the level of reading is set by the aim, not by the book. One book can be read analytically on one occasion and syntopically on another.
questions.rule: The aim, not the book, sets the level.
questions.teaches: By extension, the same book can be read analytically on one occasion and syntopically on another; the reader's aim, not the book, decides the level of reading.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Role of Inspection in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: Because syntopical reading has a different aim, a syntopical reader need not understand the passages she uses.
questions.explain: The authors say you read each work with the skills of analytical reading. The aim shifts to the problem, but using a passage still requires understanding it.
questions.rule: A new aim does not excuse misunderstanding.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Which of these is the first step of syntopical reading proper, according to the authors?
options: Defining the issues between authors
Analyzing the discussion as a whole
Getting the questions clear
Finding the relevant passages
optionExplain: Issues come fourth; they need terms and questions first.
Analyzing the discussion is the last step, built on the other four.
Questions come third, after the passages are found and the terms set.
Right: before anything else you locate the passages that bear on your problem.
questions.explain: You cannot set terms or frame questions until you have the passages in hand. The card next lists all five steps.
questions.rule: Passages first.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Put the five steps of syntopical reading in the order the authors give them.
items: Find the relevant passages
Bring the authors to terms
Get the questions clear
Define the issues
Analyze the discussion
questions.explain: Passages supply the material, terms give a common language, questions turn it into neutral propositions, issues come from differing answers, and the analysis orders the whole.
questions.rule: Passages, terms, questions, issues, discussion.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A student framing her questions finds she must revise the neutral terms she set earlier. By the authors' account, is she doing it wrong?
options: No: the order is rough, and the steps depend on one another
Yes: each step must be finished before the next one begins
Yes: she should have defined the issues before any terms
No: the steps can be taken in any order the reader likes
optionExplain: Right: the authors say all the steps must take place for any of them to, so revising earlier work is expected.
The authors present the order as rough, not as a sequence of sealed stages.
Issues depend on questions, which depend on terms, so issues cannot come first.
The order is rough but real; the authors still present the steps in a sequence.
questions.explain: Looping back is a sign the steps are working together, as the authors describe, not a sign of failure.
questions.rule: Looping back is part of the method.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: The authors call the five steps rules, because syntopical reading is impossible without each one.
questions.explain: The authors say they will not call them rules, although they might, since leaving out a step makes syntopical reading much more difficult, perhaps impossible.
questions.rule: Steps, not rules, but none is optional in practice.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A team writing a market study has five stages, each needing results from the others. Echoing the authors' remark that all the steps must happen for any to, which plan fits best?
options: Perfect the first stage completely before starting on the second
Do the stages in reverse order, so the result can be checked first
Do a rough pass through all stages, then refine each in later passes
Give each stage to a separate team that works without conferring
optionExplain: Perfecting stage one first is impossible when it depends on what later stages reveal.
Reversing the order does not remove the dependence; the last stage still needs the first.
Right: when stages depend on each other, a rough version of all of them lets each inform the others.
Separate teams cut the links between stages that the work depends on.
questions.explain: Interdependent steps cannot each be finished in isolation. By extension, they are best run in passes, each pass improving all of them.
questions.rule: Interdependent steps: work in passes.
questions.teaches: By extension, when steps depend on one another they are best run in passes: a rough version of every step first, then refinement, rather than perfecting each step in turn.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: According to the authors, what happens to a syntopical project if the reader skips bringing the authors to terms?
options: Nothing much, since the steps are only loose suggestions
The reading turns into a series of analytical readings
Syntopical reading becomes much harder, perhaps impossible
The issues will emerge by themselves without the terms
optionExplain: They declined the word rules but not the importance of each step.
Skipping a step does not change the level; it leaves the syntopical reading crippled.
Right: the authors say leaving out any step makes syntopical reading much more difficult, perhaps impossible.
Issues depend on clear questions, which depend on shared terms; they do not appear unaided.
questions.explain: Each step supplies what the next needs. Without shared terms, questions cannot be put to all the authors, and the issues cannot be defined.
questions.rule: Skip a step and the rest falter.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: In syntopical reading, once a book is judged relevant, you usually need to read the whole of it thoroughly.
questions.explain: Usually only some passages of a relevant book bear on your problem, and the first step is to find them. The card next explains this step.
questions.rule: Relevant books, relevant passages.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: The first step of syntopical reading proper is to find the relevant ____ in the books already identified as relevant.
questions.explain: The step is a second inspection of the relevant books, aimed at the passages most germane to your needs.
questions.rule: Step 1: find the passages.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A historian of public health in Victorian cities finds that, in a biography of an engineer, two chapters on sewers bear on her question. What does step one ask of her?
options: Mark those two chapters as the passages that bear on her question
Read the whole biography thoroughly, since it was judged relevant
Drop the biography, since most of it is off her subject
Read only the preface and conclusion for the author's view
optionExplain: Right: step one is to locate the passages most germane to her needs.
The book is relevant only in part; reading all of it thoroughly puts the book ahead of her problem.
Being mostly off her subject does not cancel the two chapters that are on it.
The preface and conclusion state the author's purpose, which is not her problem.
questions.explain: A book can be relevant through a small part of it. Step one finds that part.
questions.rule: Take the part that bears on your problem.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: The inspection in step one asks the same question as the earlier inspection of the whole list: is this book relevant?
questions.explain: The earlier inspection asked which books were relevant and helped clarify the subject. Step one asks which passages within the relevant books are most germane.
questions.rule: First which books, then which passages.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A policy analyst needs what ten long government reports say about rural broadband. Which use of each report's index and contents best serves step one?
options: Read the contents page to classify each report by its general kind
Use the index to count how often each report mentions broadband
Skip the index, since it reflects the author's purpose, not hers
Look up broadband topics to find the pages that bear on her problem
optionExplain: Classifying the report was the business of earlier inspection; step one wants passages.
Counting mentions shows frequency, not which pages actually address her question.
An index is organised by the author's topics, but it can still point her to passages on her own.
Right: here the index and contents work as search tools pointing to passages on her problem.
questions.explain: In ordinary inspection the index and contents tell you what a book is about. By extension, in step one they serve a different job: locating the passages on your problem.
questions.rule: In step one, the index is a passage finder.
questions.teaches: By extension, a book's index and table of contents, tools of inspection, become search tools in step one: they point to passages on your problem rather than describing the book as a whole.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: According to the authors, what should you do if, unusually, a whole book is on your subject?
options: Read it analytically, since all of it is relevant
Read it quickly, keeping your own problem in view
Treat it as the authority over the other books
Set it aside, since step one is about passages
optionExplain: Being wholly relevant does not change the aim; you still read for your problem, not for the book.
Right: even then, the authors say to read it quickly, for the light it throws on your problem.
Full relevance does not make one author the judge of the others.
A wholly relevant book is the richest source of passages, not one to set aside.
questions.explain: The authors say that even a book wholly on your subject should be read quickly, so you do not lose sight of the purpose you read it for.
questions.rule: Even a wholly relevant book is read for your purpose.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: According to the authors, what is primarily to be served in syntopical reading?
options: The books and their authors
You and your concerns
The traditions of the field
The plans of your teachers
optionExplain: That is the priority of analytical reading, where you work to understand the book itself.
Right: the books serve you, not the other way around.
A field's traditions may shape your list, but they are not what the reading serves.
Teachers may set topics, but the authors put the reader's own concerns first.
questions.explain: The authors reverse the usual order: your problem first, the books second. The card next shows what that changes.
questions.rule: The books serve you.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: The authors say that in syntopical reading you read each book for an ____ purpose: the light it may throw on your own problem.
questions.explain: An ulterior purpose lies beyond the book itself; here it is your problem.
questions.rule: Read for a purpose beyond the book.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A teacher studying how persuasion works in advertising opens a classic on rhetoric with long sections on ancient law courts. What should she do with those sections?
options: Read them closely, since the book is a recognised classic
Read them first, to grasp the author's own purpose fully
Drop the whole book, since parts of it are off her topic
Pass over them unless they bear on persuasion in advertising
optionExplain: A classic's standing does not make every part of it serve her problem.
The author's purpose is the analytical reader's concern; hers is her own problem.
Off-topic parts do not cancel the parts on rhetoric that may bear on her question.
Right: she reads for her problem, taking what bears on it and leaving the rest.
questions.explain: With her problem first, the question for each section is whether it throws light on persuasion in advertising.
questions.rule: Ask of each section: does it serve my problem?

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A reader writes: this book is squarely on my problem, so I will read it slowly and follow its argument wherever it goes. What has the reader missed, according to the authors?
options: Even a book on the subject is read quickly, for the reader's purpose
A book on the problem should be read twice rather than only once
Books squarely on the problem should be skipped as too partial
Following any argument is analytical work and is banned here
optionExplain: Right: the authors say read even such a book quickly, so the ulterior purpose stays in view.
Rereading may come later, but it does not fix following the book wherever it leads.
A book on the problem is a prime source, not one to avoid.
Analytical skills are still used; the error is letting the book's path replace the reader's problem.
questions.explain: Following a book wherever it goes puts the book first. The authors keep the reader's problem in charge even when a book is wholly relevant.
questions.rule: Do not let the book's path replace your problem.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A product designer reads hundreds of reviews of a rival app to learn why users abandon its onboarding. Most reviews dwell on pricing. How should she treat that emphasis?
options: As proof that pricing is the reason users abandon the onboarding
As a sign she should change her question to one about pricing
As the reviewers' focus, not a guide to what matters for her question
As a reason to read only the reviews that discuss pricing
optionExplain: Talking most about pricing does not show pricing causes abandonment.
Her problem comes first; the sources' interests do not set it.
Right: reading for her own problem, she cannot let the sources' emphasis decide what is important.
Following the sources' emphasis would hand her problem over to them.
questions.explain: When you read for an ulterior purpose, what a source spends most space on is its own concern. By extension, it need not be what matters most for your question.
questions.rule: A source's emphasis is not your priority.
questions.teaches: Reading for an ulterior purpose makes a source's emphasis an unreliable guide: what the author spends most space on need not be what matters most for your problem.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: Putting your problem first entitles you to read an author as saying whatever would best suit your problem.
questions.explain: Your problem decides what you look for, not what the author said. Passages must still be read accurately; the chapter later demands quotations so others can check your reading.
questions.rule: Your problem picks the passages; it does not rewrite them.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Early in a project, a reader marks relevant passages in each book while still deciding which books belong. What risk do the authors see?
options: None, since doing both at once is a pure saving of time
Reading too few books to cover the whole subject
Mistaken passages that must be corrected later, at a cost
Becoming too attached to the first author she reads
optionExplain: It saves time only if the problem is already clear; early on it often is not.
Combining steps does not shrink the list; the risk is in the passages chosen.
Right: the authors warn of serious mistakes in identifying passages, with time and effort wasted correcting them.
Attachment may be a danger, but it is not the one the authors name here.
questions.explain: Before the problem is clear, you do not know what a relevant passage looks like. The card next explains when the two steps may merge.
questions.rule: Unclear problem, unreliable passages.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: The authors say that with books read late in a project, once the problem is clear, judging relevance and finding passages can coalesce.
questions.explain: With later books you probably have a fairly clear idea of the problem, so the two steps can be done together.
questions.rule: Late books: the steps may merge.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A researcher marked passages on solitude in her first three books, then found her subject was social isolation in old age, and had to redo most marks. What should she have done with those first books?
options: Judged their relevance first, and marked passages once the problem was clearer
Marked even more passages, to be safe, so nothing could be missed later
Read the first three books analytically before marking anything at all
Dropped the first three books and begun again with a fresh list
optionExplain: Right: with early books the authors advise keeping the two steps rigorously separate.
More marks made on an unclear problem are more marks to redo.
Analytical reading of early books is the costly route the short cut avoids.
The books may still be relevant; the error was in timing, not in the books.
questions.explain: Her marks were made before the problem was clear, which is why they went wrong. Separating the steps would have postponed passage-hunting until the subject was settled.
questions.rule: Mark passages after the problem is clear.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Sort each situation by whether the authors' advice is to keep the two steps separate or to let them coalesce.

items.t: The first books of a new project
Your problem is still taking shape
You are new to the subject
Books reached after reading many others
You already understand the problem well
You are very skilful and know the field

questions.explain: The deciding factor is how clear the problem is. Early in a project, or for a newcomer, it is not; later, or for a skilled and familiar reader, it may be.
questions.rule: Clarity of the problem decides whether the steps merge.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A journalist starts tagging quotes from her first interviews under themes, before she knows what her story is about. By extension of the authors' warning, what is the best practice?
options: Tag every quote in full detail from the very first interview
Stop interviewing until the themes are fixed in advance
Use the first interviewee's themes for the whole story
Keep early tags light and provisional, expecting to redo them
optionExplain: Detailed tags made early are the costly marks most likely to be redone.
The themes come from the interviews, so they cannot be fixed before them.
One interviewee's themes are one view, chosen before the story is clear.
Right: categories set before the subject is clear will shift, so early labels should be cheap to change.
questions.explain: The authors' warning is that early passage-marking is redone at a cost. By extension, any early labelling should be light until the categories settle.
questions.rule: Label lightly until the categories settle.
questions.teaches: By extension, labels applied before the categories are settled will have to be redone, so early labelling should be light and provisional.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: By the authors' account, what changes if a reader is already quite familiar with her subject at the start of a project?
options: She must keep them apart until the very last book
She may merge the steps sooner, as the authors allow
She can skip the search for passages altogether
She must inspect every book twice as often as others
optionExplain: The separation is advised for when the problem is unclear; familiarity changes that.
Right: the authors say unless you are very skilful or already familiar with the subject, keep the steps separate, so familiarity relaxes the rule.
Familiarity speeds the search; it does not remove the need for passages.
Familiarity reduces the work rather than doubling it.
questions.explain: The rule exists because the problem is unclear early on. A reader who already knows the subject has that clarity sooner.
questions.rule: Familiarity lets the steps merge sooner.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: A book written for one purpose can help solve a problem its author did not have in mind.
questions.explain: The authors say an author can help you solve your problem without having intended to. The card next explains how to use this.
questions.rule: Help can be unintended.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: The authors say an author can help you solve your own problem without having ____ to.
questions.explain: The author's purpose and your use of the book can be far apart, and at this stage that does not matter.
questions.rule: Your use need not match the author's aim.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A planner studying how people find their way in unfamiliar places finds a medieval pilgrim's diary full of notes on landmarks and getting lost. Should she use it?
options: No: it was written for a religious purpose, not for hers
Yes: its notes bear on her question, whatever the diary's aim
Only after reading it analytically as a pilgrimage text
Only if the pilgrim treated wayfinding as his main topic
optionExplain: A different purpose is exactly what the authors say need not stop you.
Right: the passages throw light on her problem, and the author's different purpose does not matter here.
Understanding the whole diary as a pilgrimage is not her task in this step.
Requiring the author to share her topic would discard most useful sources.
questions.explain: The authors' test at this stage is usefulness to your problem, not agreement with the author's aim.
questions.rule: Judge passages by what they show about your problem.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: In her report the planner writes: the pilgrim meant his diary as a study of how travellers navigate. What is wrong with this sentence?
options: She should not have drawn on the diary in her study at all
She should have quoted the diary at far greater length
She should have used a modern travel guide instead
It turns her use of the passages into a claim about his purpose
optionExplain: Drawing on the diary was legitimate; the error is in how she describes his aim.
Length of quotation does not fix a false statement about his purpose.
The diary is a fair source; swapping it out does not address the misstatement.
Right: she may use his notes for her problem, but his purpose was a religious record, and she must report it fairly.
questions.explain: Using a book for an unintended purpose is fine; attributing that purpose to the author is not. The two must be kept apart.
questions.rule: Use freely, attribute accurately.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: An engineer designing quieter fans reads zoology papers on how owls fly silently. The zoologists were studying how owls hunt. What does the authors' point suggest about such sources?
options: Distant fields can light a problem from a side its own field misses
They are risky, since their authors never set out to address fans
They count only after an engineer has repeated their findings
They are beside the point, since owls are not machines
optionExplain: Right: written without her problem in mind, they show it from an angle her own field may not have tried.
The authors say an author's different purpose does not matter at this stage.
Checking findings may be wise later, but it is not a condition of their usefulness.
What matters is whether the passage throws light on her problem; the owls' wing structure does.
questions.explain: An author can help without intending to. By extension, sources from distant fields are valuable because they were not written from inside your problem.
questions.rule: Distant sources can show your problem anew.
questions.teaches: By extension, sources from distant fields are often useful for exactly this reason: written without your problem in mind, they can show it from an unexpected side.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a passage can be relevant to your problem only if its author meant to address that problem.
questions.explain: The authors say a book may be useful in a connection very far from the author's own purpose. Relevance depends on your problem, not on his intention.
questions.rule: Relevance is set by your problem, not his intention.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Which level of reading do the authors call the most active reading you can do?
options: Analytical reading
Inspectional reading
Syntopical reading
Elementary reading
optionExplain: Analytical reading is active, but the reader there follows the author as disciple.
Inspection is active and quick, but it surveys rather than directs an inquiry.
Right: because the books serve the reader's problem, the reader directs everything.
Elementary reading is the basic skill of reading the words.
questions.explain: The authors call syntopical reading the most active because the reader is in charge. The card next explains the change in role.
questions.rule: Syntopical reading is the most active.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Match each item to its description in the authors' account.
pairs: Reader as master of the situation
questions.explain: In analytical reading the book leads and the reader learns from it; in syntopical reading the reader's problem leads and the books are called on to serve it.
questions.rule: Analytical: follow. Syntopical: direct.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A manager reads four books on negotiation. Which of these marks her reading as syntopical rather than analytical?
options: She follows each author's framework through to its very end in turn
She picks the most expert author and adopts his view as her own
She sets the question and calls on each author where he speaks to it
She reads all four books one after another, cover to cover
optionExplain: Following each framework is the disciple's stance of analytical reading, repeated four times.
Adopting one author's view makes her his disciple, not master of the situation.
Right: she directs the inquiry and uses the authors where they help.
Reading every book whole puts the books ahead of her problem.
questions.explain: The mark of syntopical reading is who sets the agenda. Here she does, and the authors answer to her question.
questions.rule: Whoever sets the question is master.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: Being master of the situation in syntopical reading means knowing more about the subject than the authors you read.
questions.explain: Mastery here is about directing the inquiry: setting the problem and deciding how each author bears on it. A reader can do that while knowing much less than the authors.
questions.rule: Master of the inquiry, not of the subject.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A committee chair hears five experts on flood defence; under the hearing's rules, each may only answer the questions she sets. The final report misses a key risk because no question raised it. By analogy with the authors' master role, whose fault is the gap?
options: The chair's, since she set the questions that framed the inquiry
The experts', since they ought to have raised it without being asked
No one's, since some risks cannot be foreseen by anyone at all
Shared equally, since chair and experts built the report together
optionExplain: Right: whoever directs an inquiry answers for its shape, including what it never asked.
The experts could answer only the questions put to them; the framing was the chair's.
The risk was foreseeable enough to count as key; the gap came from the questions.
The experts supplied answers, but only to her questions; direction, and so the gaps, lay with the chair.
questions.explain: The disciple can blame the master for what the book leaves out. By analogy, the master of an inquiry cannot: the questions are the reader's own.
questions.rule: Whoever frames the inquiry owns its gaps.
questions.teaches: Directing an inquiry carries a duty the disciple does not have: if the questions are badly set or incomplete, the fault lies with the reader who set them, not with the authors.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: What would happen if a syntopical reader took the disciple's stance toward each author in turn?
options: She would understand her problem better through her careful deference
Nothing would change, since stance has no effect on the result
She would finish faster, since disciples read with more speed
Each author's framing would take over, and her own problem would drift
optionExplain: Deference helps in understanding one book, but here it hands the agenda to each author in turn.
Stance decides who sets the agenda, which shapes the whole result.
Following each author's full line of thought is slower, not faster.
Right: each book would set its own agenda, and no single problem would hold the reading together.
questions.explain: The disciple follows the master's agenda. With many masters in turn, the reader would have many agendas and no inquiry of her own.
questions.rule: Many masters, no inquiry.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: When reading several authors on one subject, whose terms should you work in, according to the authors?
options: The terms of the most famous author
Terms you establish yourself
Each author's own terms, in turn
The terms of the earliest author
optionExplain: Fame does not make one author's vocabulary fit the others.
Right: you set the terms and bring every author to them.
Switching vocabularies author by author leaves no common language for comparing them.
The earliest author's words may not suit later writers or your problem.
questions.explain: With many authors using different words, someone must supply a common language, and in syntopical reading that is you. The card next explains this step.
questions.rule: You set the terms.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: In syntopical reading, the authors say you must bring your authors to your terms rather than come to theirs.
questions.explain: Since the authors will not share one vocabulary, it is you who must establish the terms and bring them to it.
questions.rule: Bring the authors to your terms.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Comparing books on happiness, a reader finds the words flourishing, contentment and pleasure. What does step two ask of her?
options: Adopt flourishing, since it is the richest of the three
State each author's view in terms she sets herself
Read each author in his own words and compare the words
Drop the authors whose words differ from the majority
optionExplain: Taking one author's word as the framework favours his view and may distort the others.
Right: her own terms give one language in which all three views can be set side by side.
Comparing words compares vocabularies, not views; different words may mean the same thing.
Different words do not mean an author is off the subject.
questions.explain: The three words may or may not name different things. Only by stating each view in common terms can she tell.
questions.rule: Translate every author into one set of terms.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Match each item to its description.
pairs: Discover how one author uses his key words
State many authors' views in terms you set
A word an author uses in a special sense
One set of terms applied to every author
questions.explain: Analytical reading adopts one author's usage to understand him; syntopical reading imposes the reader's terms on all the authors so they can be compared.
questions.rule: Analytical adopts; syntopical imposes.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A researcher merges patient records from three hospitals that label the same conditions differently. Which practice best mirrors the authors' step two?
options: Adopt the labels of the largest hospital for all of the merged records
Keep each hospital's labels and compare the records side by side
Drop the records whose labels do not match those of the others
Set her own labels and keep a table linking each hospital's labels to hers
optionExplain: The largest hospital's labels may not fit the others' categories, as one author's terms may not fit the rest.
Side-by-side labels leave no common language, so like may not be matched with like.
Different labels do not make records irrelevant; they need translating, not discarding.
Right: her labels give a common language, and the table records how each source's words were translated.
questions.explain: Imposing common terms is step two. By extension, recording how each source's words map to those terms lets anyone check the translation.
questions.rule: Keep a record of how each source maps to your terms.
questions.teaches: By extension, a shared terminology works best with a mapping: a record, for each author, of which of his words corresponds to which of your terms, so the translation can be checked.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: Because the syntopical reader sets the terms, she need not first understand how each author uses his own words.
questions.explain: You cannot translate an author into your terms without knowing what his words meant. The analytical skill of coming to terms is still needed; it now serves translation.
questions.rule: Understand his words before translating them.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: When comparing several authors on one subject, the safest course is to adopt the terminology of the greatest author among them.
questions.explain: The authors warn that adopting any one author's terms helps you understand him but leaves the others obscure. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: No author's vocabulary is the framework.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: The authors call bringing the authors to terms probably the most ____ step in syntopical reading.
questions.explain: It forces each author into your language, against every habit of deferring to an author's own terms.
questions.rule: Step two is the hardest.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A student comparing economists on inequality adopts one famous author's vocabulary. Now two other writers look confused. What is the remedy?
options: Set neutral terms in which all three authors' views can be stated
Read the other two through the famous author's terms anyway
Drop the two writers who do not share his vocabulary
Adopt instead the vocabulary of the most recent of the three
optionExplain: Right: the trouble came from one author's terms; terms of her own let all three be read fairly.
Persisting forces the two into a scheme that makes them look confused.
Looking confused in his terms does not make them irrelevant to the subject.
Switching to another author's vocabulary repeats the same mistake with a different author.
questions.explain: As the authors predict, adopting one author's terms made his book clear and the others obscure. Only a terminology belonging to no single author can serve all three.
questions.rule: One author's terms make the others look wrong.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, our normal reading habits support forcing an author to use our language.
questions.explain: The authors say all our normal reading habits are opposed to it, because we treat the author as our better and accept his terms.
questions.rule: Habit pulls toward the author's terms.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A mediator in a dispute between landlords and tenants keeps describing the issue as rent recovery, the landlords' phrase. What problem does the authors' warning point to?
options: None, since the landlords' phrase describes the issue accurately
The mediator should switch to using the tenants' phrase instead
Using one side's terms frames the issue its way and obscures the other
The mediator should avoid naming the issue at all in talks
optionExplain: Accuracy from one side's point of view is the problem: the phrase builds in that point of view.
Swapping sides repeats the error with the other party's framing.
Right: one side's vocabulary carries its view of the matter, so the other side's case is hard to state in it.
An issue that cannot be named cannot be discussed; neutral terms are the answer.
questions.explain: Adopting one author's terms makes the others hard to understand. By extension, in a dispute it also makes the person using them look partial.
questions.rule: One side's words carry one side's view.
questions.teaches: By extension, adopting one party's vocabulary in a dispute frames the issue that party's way, so neutral terms are needed both to understand every side and to be seen as fair.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: What follows if a reader adopts one author's organization of the subject, though not his actual words?
options: No trouble, since only words, not schemes, cause confusion
It helps, since organization matters less than terminology
Similar trouble: the other authors are forced into his scheme
It is required, since some author's scheme must be chosen
optionExplain: An author's way of dividing the subject can distort other authors as much as his words.
The authors name organization alongside terms as what we wrongly tend to accept.
Right: the authors warn against accepting an author's terms and his organization of the subject alike.
The reader builds her own organization; she need not borrow any author's.
questions.explain: The habit the authors warn against covers both an author's terms and his organization of the subject. Either one, adopted as the framework, bends the other authors to fit.
questions.rule: Do not borrow one author's scheme either.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: When an author uses the exact term you planned to use, that is a good reason to adopt more of his vocabulary.
questions.explain: The authors say such a coincidence is accidental and often inconvenient, because one borrowed term invites the rest. The card next explains the danger.
questions.rule: A matching term is not an invitation.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: The authors say any coincidence of terminology between you and one of your authors should be considered ____.
questions.explain: A match between your term and an author's is accidental, and it may be inconvenient if it tempts you to borrow more of his terms.
questions.rule: Matches are accidents.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A reader adopted one author's term intrinsic drive and now finds his other words creeping into her notes. What should she do?
options: Check what the term carries from him, and stop his other words creeping in
Adopt his whole vocabulary, since his terms hang together so well
Abandon the study, since her terminology is now compromised for good
Ask the author which of his other terms she ought to use as well
optionExplain: Right: this is the inconvenience the authors warn of; she must keep her own terminology in charge.
Terms that hang together are exactly how one borrowed word pulls in a whole framework.
The drift can be corrected by restating the authors in her own terms; nothing is lost for good.
Taking more terms from him deepens the problem rather than solving it.
questions.explain: One borrowed term has started to pull in others, as the authors predict. She needs to restate her terms as her own and keep his framework out.
questions.rule: Stop the drift into one author's vocabulary.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A reader reasons: my key term matches Author A's, so Author A must share my view of the subject. What is the flaw?
options: Author A must disagree, since terms do not match by chance
The reader ought to change her term to avoid any match
A matching term shows A is the most important author
A matching word is accidental and shows nothing about agreement
optionExplain: Matches can happen by chance; the authors call them accidental.
Changing the term may not be needed; the error is in the inference, not the word.
A shared word gives Author A no special standing among the authors.
Right: the same word can carry different meanings, so a match settles nothing about views.
questions.explain: The authors treat coincidence of terms as accidental. A word in common is not a view in common.
questions.rule: A shared word is not a shared view.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A team designing a booking system borrows the term session from a popular software library, then finds itself also using the library's words token, scope and expiry. What best explains the drift?
options: The library's words are better than any the team could ever invent
A term's meaning leans on its neighbours, so borrowing one draws in the rest
The team lacked the skill to coin any terms of its own for the design
Borrowed terms are easier to remember than terms the team invents
optionExplain: Quality is not the cause; even good terms bring their framework with them.
Right: session is defined against token, scope and expiry, so using it pulls the whole set along.
Skill is not the issue; the pull comes from how the borrowed term is defined.
Memory may play a part, but it does not explain why these particular words arrived together.
questions.explain: The authors warn that one borrowed term tempts you to take others. By extension, this happens because terms get their meaning partly from the other terms in the same scheme.
questions.rule: Terms come in families.
questions.teaches: Words come in families: a term gets its meaning partly from the terms around it in an author's scheme, which is why one borrowed word tends to drag its neighbours in.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: By the authors' account, you may keep an author's word when it truly fits, provided you check its meaning and do not drift into his other terms.
questions.explain: The warning is against unexamined borrowing, not against every shared word. A word you have tested and kept under your own control can stay.
questions.rule: Keep a borrowed word only under your own control.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: The authors describe syntopical reading as, to a large extent, an exercise in what?
options: Memorising
Translation
Summarising
Debating
optionExplain: Remembering what each author said is not the core of the work.
Right: each author's terms are translated into a common terminology the reader imposes.
Summaries come into it, but the authors' word for the core task is translation.
Debate is what the authors carry on among themselves; the reader's task is different.
questions.explain: You carry each author's meaning into one shared terminology. The card next says what that terminology must do.
questions.rule: Syntopical reading translates.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: What must the syntopical reader's set of terms do, according to the authors? Select all that apply.
options: Match the words of the greatest author
Avoid every word any author has used
Copy the standard terms of the field
Help you understand all of your authors
Help you solve your problem
optionExplain: Matching one author's words is the trap the authors warn against.
Coincidence with an author's word is accidental, not forbidden.
A field's standard terms were not made for your problem and may suit only some authors.
Right: the terms must work for all the authors, not only one or a few.
Right: they must also serve the problem you set out to solve.
questions.explain: The terms have a double job: fit every author and advance your problem.
questions.rule: Fit all the authors; serve the problem.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Comparing writers on humours, miasma and germs, a historian builds terms such as cause located in the body and cause carried from outside. Why are these good choices?
options: They are the terms that most of the writers actually used themselves
They are modern terms, so they correct the older writers' mistakes
They let her avoid the topic of contagion, which is in dispute
Every writer's view can be stated in them, and they fit her question
optionExplain: None of the writers used these phrases; the reader built them.
The aim is to state the writers' views, not to correct them in the translation.
Contagion is her question; the terms help her address it, not avoid it.
Right: they meet both demands, fit with all the authors and use for her problem.
questions.explain: Good syntopical terms belong to no author, yet let every author's view be stated, and they are shaped by the reader's problem.
questions.rule: Good terms belong to no author and fit every author.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A reader's terms fit all her authors neatly, but they are so broad that every author's view comes out the same. Which demand has failed?
options: Usefulness: the terms no longer help with her problem
Fit: the terms fail to cover all of the authors
Neither: identical views show the terms are working
Both: the terms fit none of the authors at all
optionExplain: Right: terms that erase real differences cannot shed light on the problem.
The terms cover every author; that part has succeeded.
Identical results from different authors suggest the terms are blurring differences.
The terms do fit the authors, too loosely; fit has not failed.
questions.explain: The two demands pull against each other: terms broad enough to fit everyone may be too broad to separate real differences.
questions.rule: Terms must fit and still distinguish.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A consultant states the views of four department heads in one shared set of terms for a board report. Which check best tests her translation?
options: Whether the board finds the summary easy and quick to read
Whether the terms came from the most senior of the four heads
Whether each head would recognise the summary as their own view
Whether all four views come out sounding much the same
optionExplain: Readability matters, but an easy summary can still misstate a view.
Taking the senior head's terms is the one-author trap, applied to an office.
Right: a faithful translation is one the original speaker would accept as saying what they meant.
Sameness may mean the terms are blurring real differences.
questions.explain: Translation is good when nothing essential is lost. By extension, the test is whether each author would recognise your statement of his view.
questions.rule: Would the author recognise your version?
questions.teaches: By extension, a practical test of a common terminology is whether each author, reading your statement of his view, would recognise it as his own.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, your authors may lack the ideal terminology for your problem because they may not have been concerned with that problem.
questions.explain: The authors say the writers may not have been specifically concerned with the problem you are trying to solve, and so may not have created the ideal terminology for it.
questions.rule: Authors' terms were made for their problems, not yours.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: How do the authors suggest a syntopical reader establish neutral propositions?
options: Quote one key sentence from each author
Adopt the propositions of the main author
Frame questions that each author answers
List each author's conclusions in turn
optionExplain: Key sentences are in each author's own terms, so they are not neutral.
Adopting one author's propositions makes his view the frame for all.
Right: each author's answer to your question becomes his proposition in neutral form.
A list of conclusions in the authors' words gives nothing common to compare them on.
questions.explain: Questions give every author the same thing to answer. The card next explains this step.
questions.rule: Neutral propositions come from questions.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: The authors say the best way to establish neutral propositions is to frame a set of ____ to which each of your authors gives answers.
questions.explain: Questions that shed light on your problem, answered by each author, turn scattered statements into comparable propositions.
questions.rule: Frame the questions.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A reader frames the question of whether punishment should aim mainly at deterring future crime. Three authors' discussions now become yes, no, and yes with reform. What has the question done?
options: Turned each author's discussion into a comparable answer in her terms
Shown which of the three authors is right about punishment
Removed any need to read what the three authors wrote
Made all three authors agree with one another on deterrence
optionExplain: Right: the authors' differently written discussions now line up as answers to one question.
Comparable answers are not yet a verdict; judging comes much later, if at all.
She could only record their answers by reading them.
The answers differ; the question exposes the disagreement rather than ending it.
questions.explain: A shared question makes unlike texts comparable. That is the work of step three.
questions.rule: A shared question makes unlike texts comparable.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: In step three, the propositions compared are the authors' own key sentences, quoted as written.
questions.explain: The propositions are neutral: each author's answer to the reader's question, stated in the reader's terms. Quotations come in later as support, not as the propositions themselves.
questions.rule: Neutral propositions are answers in your terms.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A buyer compares five insurance policies, each written in its own style and order. Following the authors' step three, what is her best method?
options: Read each policy in full and form an overall impression of each
Adopt the structure of the first policy and fit the others to it
Compare the policies' key sentences with each other word for word
Put the same questions to every policy and record each one's answer
optionExplain: Overall impressions are hard to compare and easy to sway.
The first policy's structure is one author's organization imposed on the rest.
Different wording may hide the same terms, and similar wording different ones.
Right: fixed questions, such as what is covered and what is excluded, turn unlike documents into comparable answers.
questions.explain: By extension, a comparison checklist is step three in everyday form: the same questions put to every document.
questions.rule: Compare documents through a fixed set of questions.
questions.teaches: By extension, any comparison of differently written documents works the same way: a fixed list of questions put to each one, like a comparison checklist, turns unlike texts into comparable answers.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A reader frames a question asking how economic growth causes the moral decline of a society. Why may this fail as a step-three question?
options: It is too short to capture the whole of the subject under study
It assumes an answer some authors deny, so they cannot answer it fairly
It uses the word moral, which some of the authors do not use
It mentions economics, which belongs to a separate field of study
optionExplain: Length is not the issue; one clear question can be short.
Right: authors who deny that growth causes decline have no fair way to answer a question that presumes it.
The reader sets the terms; authors need not use her words to answer.
A question can cross fields; what matters is whether the authors can answer it.
questions.explain: Questions must be framed so all or most authors can be read as answering. A question that builds in a disputed answer shuts out those who dispute it.
questions.rule: Do not build a disputed answer into the question.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: An author can be read as answering a question that he did not think of as a question.
questions.explain: The authors say the questions you want answered may not have been seen as questions by your authors, yet they can often be interpreted as answering them. The card next explains how.
questions.rule: Authors can answer questions they never asked.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: According to the authors, what must your step-three questions do? Select all that apply.
options: Be answerable by all or most authors
Use the wording each author used himself
Be questions each author asked explicitly
Be settled by agreement among the authors
Help you solve the problem you started with
optionExplain: Right: all or most authors must be interpretable as answering them.
Using each author's wording would undo the neutral terms of step two.
The authors often did not see your questions as questions at all.
If the authors agreed, there would be no problem; disagreement is expected.
Right: the questions are stated and ordered to serve your problem.
questions.explain: The two demands are serving your problem and fitting most authors. Neither requires the authors to have asked your questions.
questions.rule: Serve the problem; fit most authors.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A designer asks whether city streets should favour walkers over drivers. Writers from the 1800s wrote about carriages, trade and health. How can she use them?
options: Leave them out, since none of them ever posed her question
Read their views on streets as answers to her question
Change her question to one about carriages and trade
Treat their silence on cars as agreement with her view
optionExplain: An author need not have posed a question to be read as answering it.
Right: their views on what streets are for can be interpreted as answers to her question.
Her question must serve her problem; swapping it for theirs drops the first demand.
Silence is not agreement; and they could not be silent on cars they never knew.
questions.explain: The authors' view of the subject differs from hers, so the answers come by interpretation, not by quotation of a direct reply.
questions.rule: Find answers by interpretation when authors saw the subject differently.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: For a study of whether schools should teach character, which question best meets both demands?
options: Is the character program now used in one city's schools effective?
What is the best way to run a school in every respect?
Why do modern schools neglect the teaching of character?
Should schooling aim to form character as well as to give knowledge?
optionExplain: Few authors on education can be read as answering a question about one current program.
So broad a question does little to advance the specific problem.
It assumes schools neglect character, an answer some authors would deny.
Right: it bears on the problem, and most writers on education can be read as answering it.
questions.explain: A good question is central to the problem and wide enough that most authors have something to say on it, without presuming an answer.
questions.rule: Central to your problem, open to most authors.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A researcher asks how old legal codes treated data privacy, though none of them knew of data. Following the authors, what is her best approach?
options: Read their rules on private letters and homes as answers to her question
Conclude that the codes can say nothing about the question she is asking
Rephrase her question so that it asks only about letters and homes
Treat each code's silence about data as consent to collecting it
optionExplain: Right: the codes addressed parts of her question they did know, and those parts can be assembled into an answer.
Not knowing of data does not mean having no view on privacy.
Narrowing to letters and homes drops her actual problem.
Silence on something unknown cannot be read as consent.
questions.explain: When sources predate a question, they can still answer parts of it. By extension, the reader builds an answer from what they said about the pieces they knew.
questions.rule: Assemble answers from the parts of the question a source knew.
questions.teaches: By extension, when sources predate your question, look for what they said about the parts of it they did know, and assemble their answer from those parts.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: A question that serves your problem perfectly but that none of your authors can be read as answering meets the authors' standard for step three.
questions.explain: The questions must be framed so that all or most authors can be interpreted as answering them. A question no author answers fails that demand, however well it serves the problem.
questions.rule: A question no author answers fails step three.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: An author's book says nothing that bears on one of your questions. What should you record?
options: That he agrees with the majority view
That he would answer no to the question
That he is silent on that question
That his whole book is off your subject
optionExplain: Silence is not agreement; nothing he wrote places him with the majority.
Saying nothing is not the same as saying no.
Right: record the gap honestly rather than filling it.
He may answer your other questions; one silence does not make him irrelevant.
questions.explain: An answer must come from the author's text. Where there is none, the record says so. The card next explains.
questions.rule: No answer in the text, no answer in the record.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: When an author gives no answer to one of your questions, the authors say you must record him as silent or ____ on it.
questions.explain: Silent or indeterminate: the record shows that this author does not give an answer to the question.
questions.rule: Silent or indeterminate.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A philosopher discusses cruelty to animals but does not address whether animals have rights. What is the honest entry for him on the rights question?
options: Yes, since anyone opposed to cruelty must support rights
No, since he did not argue that animals have rights
Silent on rights, with his views on cruelty noted elsewhere
Off the subject, so he should be dropped from the study
optionExplain: Opposing cruelty does not commit one to rights; the inference puts words in his mouth.
Not arguing for rights is not arguing against them.
Right: his text does not answer the rights question, though his views on cruelty may matter for other questions.
His views on cruelty bear on the subject, so he stays in the study.
questions.explain: An author can be relevant to a subject while silent on one question within it. The record should show both facts.
questions.rule: Relevant to the subject, silent on the question.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: Recording an author as silent on a question means he has nothing to contribute to your study.
questions.explain: Silence is recorded question by question. The same author may answer other questions fully, and his silence itself shows where his view of the subject differs from yours.
questions.rule: Silence is per question, not per author.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A pollster codes survey replies. Some people skipped a question; others answered that it cannot be known. How should the two groups be coded?
options: Separately: skipping is silence, while cannot be known is an answer
Together, since neither group gave a plain yes or a plain no
Both as no, since neither group supported the claim in question
Both dropped, since neither group adds anything to the results
optionExplain: Right: saying the question cannot be settled is a position; saying nothing is not.
Lumping them together erases a real difference between a view and no view.
Neither group said no; coding them so invents answers.
The second group gave a definite answer, and the first group's silence is itself a finding.
questions.explain: By extension of the authors' advice, silence must be kept apart from a middle position. One who says the answer cannot be known has answered; one who said nothing has not.
questions.rule: Silence is not a middle answer.
questions.teaches: By extension, silence must be kept distinct from a middle position: an author who says nothing on a question differs from one who answers that it cannot be settled.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: What would happen to a study's map of positions if every silence were filled with the reader's best guess?
options: It would be more complete and so more accurate
Nothing, since guesses and silences count the same
The authors' stated answers would be lost from it
It would show positions some authors never took
optionExplain: Complete is not accurate when the added entries are guesses.
A guess asserts a position; a silence asserts none.
The stated answers remain; the harm is in the false entries added beside them.
Right: the map would mix the authors' views with the reader's inventions.
questions.explain: Filling silences with guesses puts words into authors' mouths, which the authors warn against.
questions.rule: Guesses in the record misstate the authors.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: A careful reader may sometimes attribute to an author an answer to a question the author did not discuss.
questions.explain: The authors say you can sometimes find an implicit answer, one the author would have given had he considered the question. The card next sets the limits.
questions.rule: Implicit answers are allowed, with care.
