questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: The authors say restraint is necessary: we cannot put thoughts into our authors' minds or words into their ____.
questions.explain: An implicit answer must come from the author's text, not from what the reader would like him to say.
questions.rule: No words in their mouths.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: An author does not discuss remote work but argues that trust between colleagues grows only through daily face-to-face contact. Which entry for him is fair?
options: Strongly opposed to remote work and to video calls in particular
Implicitly doubtful of remote work, citing his argument on daily contact
Silent, since he never once mentions remote work anywhere in the book
In favour of remote work, since he places such value on trust
optionExplain: Strong opposition and views on video calls go beyond what his text supports.
Right: his stated view points plainly to an answer, and the entry cites the passage it rests on.
Silence would be right if nothing pointed to an answer, but his argument on contact does.
Valuing trust, as he describes it, points the other way.
questions.explain: An implicit answer is fair when the text points plainly to it, and it should go no further than the text goes.
questions.rule: Infer only as far as the text points.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A reader writes: Author B defends free markets, so he would oppose minimum wage laws; I record him as opposed, though he does not discuss wages. What is wrong?
options: She should have recorded him as in favour of the laws instead
She infers from a label, not from passages in his own text
Free-market authors do not discuss wages, so he must be silent
She should have waited for another reader to confirm her view
optionExplain: Swapping the answer repeats the error; neither entry rests on his text.
Right: an implicit answer must rest on what his book argues, not on what people of his school are assumed to think.
Whether such authors discuss wages is beside the point; what matters is what this book supports.
Another reader's agreement cannot replace grounding in the text.
questions.explain: Restraint means an implicit answer must be found in the book. Inferring from a school or label puts words in the author's mouth.
questions.rule: Implicit answers come from his text, not his label.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A lease says nothing about who repairs a broken boiler, but it makes the landlord responsible for all heating and hot water. By analogy with the authors' balance, what may be concluded?
options: The lease is silent, so nothing at all can be said about the boiler
Either party may be given the job, since the text omits boilers
The tenant must repair it, since the lease does not name boilers
The written terms point plainly to the landlord, so that may be implied
optionExplain: Refusing every inference ignores what the lease does say about heating.
The text is not neutral between the parties; its terms on heating point one way.
Not naming boilers is no reason to place the duty on the tenant.
Right: the stated terms point plainly to an answer, in the way an author's stated views can imply one.
questions.explain: By analogy, an unstated answer may be implied when the stated terms point plainly to it, and only then. Interpreting a silent contract calls for the same restraint.
questions.rule: Imply only what the stated terms plainly point to.
questions.teaches: By analogy, interpreting a contract that is silent on a point calls for the same balance: an answer is implied when the written terms point plainly to it, not merely because it would be convenient.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: When an author's stated views do not point plainly to any answer, the authors advise recording him as silent rather than inferring one.
questions.explain: Restraint is the deciding factor. If the text does not point plainly, any answer would be the reader's invention, so silence is the honest record.
questions.rule: Unclear pointer, record silence.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Which kind of question do the authors say usually comes first in a syntopical reading?
options: Whether the thing exists, or what its character is
What follows from the authors' various answers
How the thing is known, or how it shows itself
Which of the authors is the most reliable one
optionExplain: Right: questions about existence or character come first.
Consequences come last, since they follow from earlier answers.
How a thing is known can only be asked once it is said to exist.
Ranking authors is not one of the questions about the subject.
questions.explain: You cannot ask how a thing is known, or what follows from it, until you know whether it exists and what it is. The card next gives the full pattern.
questions.rule: Existence and character first.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Put these kinds of question in the general order the authors suggest.
items: Does it exist, and what is its character?
How is it known, or how does it show itself?
What follows from these answers?
questions.explain: Each kind presupposes the one before: how something is known assumes it exists, and consequences follow from the earlier answers.
questions.rule: Exists, known, consequences.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A reader studying luck drafts four questions. Which should come first?
options: How do people come to know that they are lucky?
What follows from luck for how we judge success?
Is there such a thing as luck, and what is it?
How does luck show itself in games of chance?
optionExplain: How luck is known assumes there is such a thing.
Consequences come last in the authors' pattern.
Right: existence and character come before everything else.
How luck shows itself also assumes it exists.
questions.explain: The other three questions all presuppose an answer to the first.
questions.rule: Ask whether it exists before asking how it works.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, further questions may be asked of an author's book once he says the phenomenon exists or has a certain character.
questions.explain: The authors make the later questions conditional: if an author says the phenomenon exists, you may then ask how it is known or how it shows itself.
questions.rule: Later questions follow from earlier answers.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: An engineer receives a report of an intermittent software fault. Following the authors' order of questions, what should she establish first?
options: What damage the fault would do to the customers
How the fault shows itself on different devices
Whether the fault really exists and what exactly it is
Which member of the team introduced the fault
optionExplain: Consequences come last; they depend on what the fault is.
How it shows itself presupposes that it exists.
Right: confirming the fault is real, and what it is, comes before anything else.
Blame is not part of understanding the fault, and it presupposes the fault is real.
questions.explain: By extension, the authors' order suits any investigation, because each stage presupposes the one before it.
questions.rule: Confirm the thing is real before studying its effects.
questions.teaches: By extension, the same order suits any investigation, from a reported fault to a rumour: settle that the thing is real and what it is, then how it shows itself, then what follows, since each stage presupposes the one before.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A reader opens with a question about the effects of progress on happiness. Some of her authors deny that progress occurs at all. What is wrong with her order?
options: It asks about consequences before settling whether the thing exists
It should begin instead with how progress comes to be known
It uses the word happiness, which no card has yet defined
Nothing, since consequences are the most important question
optionExplain: Right: authors who deny progress cannot answer a question about its effects, so existence must come first.
How progress is known also presupposes that it exists.
Wording is not the problem; the reader can set her terms.
Importance and order differ; the question about effects depends on the earlier one.
questions.explain: A question about consequences presupposes an answer to the question of existence. Putting it first shuts out the authors who deny the thing exists.
questions.rule: Consequences after existence.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: What happens to the later questions for an author who denies that the phenomenon exists?
options: He must still answer them, since every author answers every question
His denial should be recorded as silence on the first question
He should be removed from the study as off the subject
They may not apply to him, since they presuppose the thing exists
optionExplain: Questions that presuppose existence cannot fairly be put to someone who denies it.
A denial is an answer to the first question, not silence.
Denying the phenomenon is a position on the subject, so he stays in the study.
Right: how a thing is known or what follows from it are questions for those who say it exists.
questions.explain: The authors make later questions conditional on earlier answers. An author who denies existence has answered the first question and may have no answer to the rest.
questions.rule: A denial answers the first question and may close the rest.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, if all your authors answered your questions in the same way, your problem would already be solved.
questions.explain: The authors say it would have been solved by consensus, leaving no problem. The card next shows what the expected disagreement is for.
questions.rule: Unanimity would leave no problem.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: If all the authors answered alike, the authors say, the problem would have been solved by ____.
questions.explain: Because the problem is open, the authors will differ, and their differences lead to the next step.
questions.rule: Differences are expected.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A reader asks whether homework improves learning and gets yes, no, and only for older pupils. How should she treat this spread of answers?
options: As a sign that her question was badly framed after all
As the material for defining the issues in the next step
As noise to be averaged into a single combined view
As proof that the subject cannot be studied usefully
optionExplain: Disagreement is what a good question on an open problem should reveal.
Right: differing answers to a clear question are what issues are made of.
Averaging erases the differences the analysis needs to show.
Disagreement is the normal condition of such subjects, not a bar to studying them.
questions.explain: The authors expect differences and use them: they lead straight to defining the issues.
questions.rule: Differing answers feed the next step.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: On one question every author gives the same answer. What do the authors advise the reader to check?
options: Nothing, since a unanimous answer ends the whole inquiry
Whether the question is too vague to bring out real differences
Whether she has misread every single one of the authors
Whether to drop the question from the study for good
optionExplain: Agreement on one question does not settle the whole problem.
Right: agreement may be real, but a vague question can hide differences.
Misreading all of them is possible but far less likely than a vague question.
If the agreement is real, the question stays as a point of agreement.
questions.explain: Unanimity is possible, so the card does not deny it. It asks the reader to rule out a question too loose to show where authors differ.
questions.rule: Test unanimity before trusting it.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A patient wonders whether to seek several opinions on a routine, well-settled treatment. Following the authors' reasoning, what is the case for many opinions?
options: Strong: each extra opinion adds information, whatever the question
Strong: agreement among experts tends to hide their private doubts
Weak: medical opinions cannot be compared with one another at all
Weak: where experts agree, one reliable opinion settles the matter
optionExplain: Extra opinions on a settled question repeat the same answer and add little.
Agreement can be real; assuming hidden doubt has no basis here.
Opinions can be compared; the point is that on this question they would agree.
Right: consulting many sources pays where they are expected to differ; on a settled question they would not.
questions.explain: The authors say agreement would mean no problem to solve. By extension, a question is worth taking to many sources when you expect them to differ.
questions.rule: Consult many sources where they differ.
questions.teaches: By extension, a question is worth taking to many sources only when you expect them to differ; where they would all agree, one reliable source settles it.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: Expecting authors to differ entitles the reader to describe them as disagreeing on a question where they in fact agree.
questions.explain: Expecting difference is a reason to look for it, not to invent it. Where authors agree, the report must say so.
questions.rule: Expect difference; do not manufacture it.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: According to the authors, when has an issue been defined?
options: When a clear question gets different answers from different authors
When one author states a strong opinion on the subject at hand
When the reader finds she disagrees with one of the authors
When two authors use the same key word in different senses
optionExplain: Right: a clear question plus opposing answers defines an issue between the two groups of authors.
A strong opinion from one author is a position, not yet an issue between authors.
The issue lies between the authors, not between the reader and an author.
Different senses of a word are a matter for terms, and may hide that there is no shared question.
questions.explain: An issue needs two things: a clear question and authors answering it differently. The card next explains how issues are set out.
questions.rule: Clear question plus opposing answers equals an issue.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, when only two answers are given by all the authors examined, the issue is relatively simple.
questions.explain: Two answers make a simple issue. With more than two, the answers must be ordered in relation to one another.
questions.rule: Two answers, simple issue.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: On whether punishment should aim mainly at deterrence, a reader finds three answers. What does step four ask her to do?
options: Pick the answer most authors give and set the remaining answers aside
Treat the middle answer as a compromise that settles the issue
Order the three answers relative to one another, authors under each
Reduce the answers to two by merging the closest pair of them
optionExplain: Majority does not settle an issue, and setting answers aside loses part of the discussion.
A middle position is one more side of the issue, not its resolution.
Right: with more than two answers, the authors say to order them and classify the authors by their views.
Merging distinct answers hides a real difference among the authors.
questions.explain: Several answers make a more complex issue, but the task is the same: lay out the sides and who stands on each.
questions.rule: Several answers: order them, group the authors.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Sort each case by whether an issue has been defined.

items.t: Clear question; some authors say yes, others no
Clear question; three authors give three different answers
Clear question; one group says yes, another says it cannot be known
Clear question; every author answers yes
Vague question that the authors seem to answer differently
Authors discuss the topic but answer no shared question

questions.explain: An issue needs both a clear question and differing answers. Unanimity gives no issue; a vague question or no shared question gives no issue yet.
questions.rule: No clear question or no difference, no issue.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A council receives 300 responses on a parking plan, falling into five distinct positions. Following step four, which presentation is most useful?
options: List all 300 responses in the order the council received them
Report only the most common of the five positions and its backers
Order the five positions relative to one another and list who holds each
Count responses for and against the plan, ignoring the rest
optionExplain: Order of arrival says nothing about how the positions relate.
The other four positions are part of the discussion and would be lost.
Right: ordering the positions shows which are neighbours and which are opposites, with supporters under each.
Forcing five positions into two hides the middle ground and the differences within each side.
questions.explain: By extension, arranging several answers along a line shows how they relate, which a plain list or a yes-no count hides.
questions.rule: Arrange positions to show neighbours and opposites.
questions.teaches: By extension, ordering several answers in relation to one another, from one extreme to the other, shows which positions are neighbours and which are opposites, something a plain list hides.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: If authors seem to answer differently but the question itself is unclear, an issue has already been defined.
questions.explain: The authors require a clear question. Apparent differences on an unclear question may come from authors reading the question differently.
questions.rule: Clarify the question before declaring an issue.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Two authors give opposite answers to a question that sounds the same in both books. What must hold for them to be truly disagreeing?
options: They understand the question in the same way
They wrote in the same century and language
They both argue at length for their answers
They are experts in the same field of study
optionExplain: Right: only a shared understanding of the question makes opposite answers a real disagreement.
Authors from different centuries can disagree genuinely, and contemporaries can talk past each other.
Length of argument does not show they are answering the same question.
Shared expertise does not guarantee a shared conception of the question.
questions.explain: Opposite answers to differently understood questions are not opposed at all. The card next gives the authors' test.
questions.rule: Same question understood the same way, or no real clash.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: The authors say an issue is truly ____ when two authors who understand a question in the same way answer it in contrary or contradictory ways.
questions.explain: A joined issue is a real disagreement: the same question, understood alike, answered in opposing ways.
questions.rule: Joined: same question, opposing answers.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: One writer says markets are free, meaning no government sets prices; another says they are not, meaning poor buyers have no real choice. What should the reader conclude?
options: They disagree sharply, since one says yes and the other says no
They agree, since both writers care about buyers and sellers
One of them must have misread the evidence about markets
The issue is not yet joined; they understand the question differently
optionExplain: Yes and no look opposed, but they answer different conceptions of the question.
Shared concern is not agreement; their answers address different matters.
Both may read the evidence correctly; they are asking different things of it.
Right: they are answering two different questions under one form of words.
questions.explain: The difference in answers comes from a difference in the question. Until the question is understood the same way, the issue is not joined.
questions.rule: Check the question before recording opposition.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: According to the authors, how often are differences in answers due to different conceptions of the question?
options: Rarely, since authors usually share their questions
As often as to different views of the subject
Never, once the reader has set the terms
Only in fiction, not in expository works
optionExplain: The authors say a truly joined issue happens less often than one might wish.
Right: the authors say differences in answers must be ascribed to different conceptions of the question as often as to different views.
Setting terms helps, but authors may still conceive the question differently.
The point is made about the expository authors of a syntopical project.
questions.explain: Because differing conceptions of the question are so common, the reader must check every apparent disagreement.
questions.rule: Suspect a different question as often as a different view.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Two managers argue over whether a project is on schedule: one says yes, the other no. Which step best tests whether their issue is joined?
options: Ask a third manager to cast a deciding vote on it
Ask each what would make the other's answer correct
Ask which manager has more experience with projects
Ask both to restate their reasons more forcefully
optionExplain: A vote picks a side without checking whether there are really two sides of one question.
Right: if each describes a different situation, such as the original plan versus the revised one, they are answering different questions.
Experience does not show whether they understand the question alike.
Force adds heat but does not reveal what each means by on schedule.
questions.explain: By extension, asking what would make the other side right exposes each side's conception of the question. Matching conceptions mean a joined issue; different ones mean two questions.
questions.rule: Ask what would make the other side right.
questions.teaches: A quick test of whether an issue is joined is to ask each side what would make the other's answer correct; if the replies describe different situations, they are answering different questions.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: If two authors give the same answer to a question but understand the question differently, they truly agree.
questions.explain: The same logic that applies to disagreement applies to agreement: matching answers to differently understood questions are not a real agreement.
questions.rule: Matching words can hide different questions.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a syntopical reader may need to frame a question in a way that no author explicitly uses.
questions.explain: To make sure issues are joined as well as may be, the reader sometimes has to frame questions no author posed. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: The reader may frame the joining question.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: The authors say defining joined issues sometimes forces the reader to frame the question in a way that is not explicitly employed by any ____.
questions.explain: The reader's question can be new, as long as each author's view, translated, answers it.
questions.rule: The joining question may be new.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: One writer says zoos educate the public; another says captive animals suffer. A reader asks whether the benefits of keeping wild animals outweigh the harms to them. What has her question achieved?
options: It shows that the two writers really agree about zoos after all
It replaces both writers' views with the reader's own opinion
It proves that the second writer has misunderstood what zoos do
It makes both writers' views answers to one question, joining the issue
optionExplain: They still differ; the question shows how their views oppose each other.
The question records their views; it does not substitute hers.
Framing a question proves nothing about who is right.
Right: each writer spoke to one side of the balance, and the question brings them face to face.
questions.explain: The writers talked past each other. A question no one posed turns their separate claims into opposing answers.
questions.rule: A well-framed question brings authors face to face.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A reader frames a question asking whether zoos should be abolished at once, and lists the education writer as answering no, though he says only that zoos teach visitors. What is the risk?
options: The question goes beyond his view, giving him a position he never took
He should have been listed as answering yes to the question instead
Constructed questions are forbidden by the authors' rules for step four
The question ought to have used the education writer's exact words
optionExplain: Right: saying zoos teach is not saying they should not be abolished; the fit has been forced.
Yes would be equally forced; his text answers neither way.
The authors allow, even require, constructed questions; the problem is this one's fit.
The reader sets the terms; the problem is the question's reach, not its wording.
questions.explain: A constructed question must fit each author's actual view. When it outruns what an author said, the debate it shows is partly fabricated.
questions.rule: A constructed question must fit what each author said.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: In a policy dispute, the finance team writes only about the cost of a new safety rule, and the safety team only about the lives it would save. Following the authors, which question best joins the issue?
options: How much will the new safety rule cost?
How many lives might the new rule save?
Do the lives saved justify the rule's cost?
Which team understands the rule better?
optionExplain: Only the finance team speaks to this; the safety team has no answer to give.
Only the safety team speaks to this; the finance team has no answer to give.
Right: it names the trade-off, so both teams' claims become answers to one question.
This asks about the teams, not the rule, and joins no issue about it.
questions.explain: Each side spoke to one half of a trade-off. By extension, the joining question often has to name the trade-off itself.
questions.rule: Join the issue by naming the trade-off.
questions.teaches: By extension, a joining question often has to name the trade-off both sides care about, such as cost against safety, because each side has spoken only to its own half.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: However skilfully the reader frames a question, some authors may still turn out to be answering different questions.
questions.explain: The authors ask for issues joined as well as may be, which admits that perfect joining is not always possible.
questions.rule: Joined as well as may be, not always perfectly.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: In the authors' vocabulary, what is a controversy?
options: A single disagreement between two named authors
A dispute about which books belong on the list
A group of issues around closely connected questions
A public quarrel carried on between authors in print
optionExplain: A single disagreement on one question is an issue, not a controversy.
Choosing books is part of the preparation, not what the authors call a controversy.
Right: connected issues around a closely connected set of questions form a controversy.
The authors' sense is structural: connected issues, whether or not authors ever addressed each other.
questions.explain: A controversy is a level above the issue: a cluster of linked issues. The card next shows how to arrange them.
questions.rule: Controversy: a cluster of linked issues.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: The authors say the syntopical reader must arrange a controversy in an orderly fashion even if no author has managed to do that.
questions.explain: Sorting and arranging controversies is the reader's task, whether or not any author has done it.
questions.rule: The reader orders what no author ordered.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A reader on privacy finds issues about what privacy is, whether it is a right, and whether it covers personal data. Which arrangement fits the authors' advice?
options: A controversy on the nature of privacy and another on its scope
One long list of every issue in the order she came across it
A separate controversy for each author's book on privacy
A single issue: privacy, for it or against it, in general
optionExplain: Right: the issues group by connected questions, nature and scope, each laid out in order.
Order of discovery hides how the issues connect.
Controversies group questions, not books; each author may join several.
Collapsing everything into one issue loses the separate questions.
questions.explain: Grouping follows the connections between questions. Nature and scope are two connected sets, so they make two controversies.
questions.rule: Group issues by connected questions.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Match each part of a syntopical analysis to its description.
pairs: A word fixed by the reader for all the authors
What each author can be read as answering
Opposing answers to one clear question
Connected issues around closely related questions
questions.explain: Terms make neutral questions possible, questions produce issues when answers differ, and issues cluster into controversies.
questions.rule: Terms, questions, issues, controversies.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A product team has twenty open disagreements about a new feature. A lead groups them into three clusters of connected questions. What does the grouping reveal that a flat list hides?
options: Which team member raised each of the points
Which of the disagreements is the oldest
Which points can be left out of the plan
Which disagreements stand or fall together
optionExplain: Authorship can be tracked in a list; grouping is about how questions connect.
Age is a property of each item, visible without grouping.
Grouping does not decide what to drop; it shows how the questions connect.
Right: issues on connected questions depend on each other, so settling one may shift the rest of its cluster.
questions.explain: By extension, a controversy shows dependence: issues built on connected questions move together.
questions.rule: Clusters show which issues move together.
questions.teaches: By extension, grouping issues into controversies shows which disagreements stand or fall together, so settling one issue in a group may shift the others.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, every issue must belong to some larger controversy.
questions.explain: Issues are likely to fall into groups, but the grouping follows real connections. An issue with no close neighbours can stand alone.
questions.rule: Group where connections are real.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Steps one to four of syntopical reading correspond to which part of analytical reading?
options: The third group of rules: whether the book is true
The first two groups of rules: what it says, and how
Only the very first rule: classifying the book by kind
None, since syntopical reading follows its own logic
optionExplain: Truth and significance belong to the fifth step's parallel, not the first four.
Right: like those rules, the first four steps tell you what is said and how.
Classifying a book is one rule; the four steps parallel two whole groups.
The authors draw the parallel explicitly.
questions.explain: The first four steps describe the discussion; the fifth turns to judging it. The card next sets out the parallel.
questions.rule: Steps 1 to 4: what and how.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Match each part of reading to the questions it answers, in the authors' parallel.
pairs: First two groups of analytical rules
What a book says and how it says it
Whether a book is true and what of it
What the discussion says and how it is arranged
Is the discussion true, and what of it
questions.explain: The syntopical steps repeat the pattern of analytical reading at the level of a whole discussion: first describe, then judge.
questions.rule: Describe, then judge, at both levels.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A reader has mapped what eight economists say about minimum wages and how their positions divide. What is she now ready to do?
options: Begin finding the passages on minimum wages in each book
Ask how far the discussion is true and what follows from it
Set the neutral terms she will use for the eight economists
Classify each economist's book by the kind of book it is
optionExplain: Finding passages is step one, which her map shows is done.
Right: with what and how established, the fifth step's questions come next.
Terms are step two, already behind her.
Classifying books belongs to analytical reading of a single work.
questions.explain: Her map answers what the discussion says and how. The remaining questions are about truth and significance.
questions.rule: After the map comes the judgment.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A reader starts deciding which economist is right before she has framed the questions or defined the issues. By the authors' parallel, what is wrong?
options: She should judge each economist's prose style first instead
She should not judge any economist at any stage of the work
She should have judged them earlier, while inspecting the books
She is judging before establishing what the discussion says
optionExplain: Style is not the first concern, and judging it first still skips the steps.
The fifth step does take up questions like Is it true?, so judgment has its place.
Inspection decides relevance, not who is right.
Right: steps one to four establish what is said; judgment belongs after them.
questions.explain: As in analytical reading, judging comes after understanding. Here the thing to understand is the whole discussion.
questions.rule: Map the discussion before judging it.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A journalist maps a debate on phones in schools: who holds which position and why. She has no time to judge it. By extension of the authors' parallel, what has she produced?
options: A real result: what the debate says and how it divides
Nothing usable, since judging is the only goal that counts
A judgment in disguise, since every map takes a side
A summary of one author's view, not of the whole debate
optionExplain: Right: answering what and how about a debate is already a substantial result.
In analytical reading too, knowing what a book says is worth having before any verdict.
A careful map can be fair; the chapter goes on to describe how.
She mapped many positions, so it is a map of the debate.
questions.explain: By extension, the first four steps yield something of value on their own: a clear account of what a debate says and how its positions divide.
questions.rule: A fair map of a debate is a result in itself.
questions.teaches: By extension, a map of a debate is valuable even if no judgment follows: knowing what is said and how the positions divide is more than most participants in the debate have.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: In the parallel, step five asks whether one chosen author's propositions are true, as criticism does for a single book.
questions.explain: Step five asks its questions of the discussion as a whole. The object judged is the whole discussion, not one author.
questions.rule: Step five judges the discussion, not one author.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: On a problem thoughtful people have argued over for centuries, where do the authors say the truth is to be found, if at all?
options: In the answer of the greatest author
In whatever most authors agree on
In the conflict of opposing answers
In the most recent author's answer
optionExplain: Greatness does not put the whole truth of a perennial problem in one author's hands.
On a perennial problem, a majority still faces strong opposing reasons.
Right: the authors look for it in how the well-supported answers conflict.
Recency does not settle a problem that has stayed open for centuries.
questions.explain: The authors think it presumptuous to expect the whole truth in one set of answers. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Look in the conflict, not in one answer.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: On a perennial problem, the authors say, the truth is to be found, if at all, in the ____ of opposing answers.
questions.explain: Many opposing answers may have persuasive evidence and convincing reasons, so the truth is sought in their conflict.
questions.rule: Truth in the conflict.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: On whether people are selfish by nature, a reader finds strong evidence and arguments on several sides. Which approach fits the authors' view?
options: Choose the answer that has the most famous defenders behind it
Average all the answers into a single moderate view of the matter
Study how the well-supported answers conflict and what each explains
Set the question aside as one that no reader can ever answer
optionExplain: Fame of defenders is not evidence that one answer holds the whole truth.
Averaging blurs the answers instead of studying how they bear on each other.
Right: on a perennial problem, the conflict of strong answers is where the truth is sought.
The authors say if at all, but they do not tell the reader to give up.
questions.explain: With strong reasons on several sides, the conflict itself is the object of study, not a contest to be decided by reputation.
questions.rule: Study the conflict; do not crown a winner by reputation.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: To which question does the authors' view of truth in conflict apply least?
options: What the boiling point of water is at sea level
Whether people are by nature mostly selfish
Whether history shows real moral progress
What makes a government's power legitimate
optionExplain: Right: a settled factual question is not a perennial problem with strong opposing answers.
A classic perennial question with strong arguments on several sides.
A long-disputed question, as the authors' own progress study shows.
A question political thinkers have disputed for centuries.
questions.explain: The authors' view is framed for perennial problems on which good people disagree. A settled question has a known answer.
questions.rule: Truth in conflict is for perennial problems.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A health agency reviews studies on whether a diet prevents heart disease and finds strong, careful studies on both sides. By extension of the authors' view, what does that pattern tell it?
options: That one side must have made errors it has not yet discovered
That the question is meaningless and should be dropped at once
That the larger group of studies must be the one that is right
That the problem is hard, not that one side's studies are careless
optionExplain: Errors are possible, but strong work on both sides is the mark of a hard problem, not proof of a hidden error.
A hard question is not a meaningless one.
Size of camp is not strength of evidence.
Right: strong evidence on several sides marks a genuinely difficult problem.
questions.explain: The authors expect persuasive reasons on several sides of a perennial problem. By extension, that pattern is information about the problem itself.
questions.rule: Strong evidence on all sides marks a hard problem.
questions.teaches: By extension, strong evidence on several sides is itself a finding: it tells you the problem is genuinely hard, not that one side's authors are careless.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors' view, every answer to a perennial problem is equally good.
questions.explain: The authors say many, not all, opposing answers may have persuasive evidence. Looking for the truth in their conflict is not saying all answers are equal.
questions.rule: Truth in conflict is not that all answers are equal.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Which of these must a syntopical reader do before claiming to have analyzed a discussion? Select all that apply.
options: Quote every author in full on every question
Ask the questions in an order she can defend
Show how answers differ and try to say why
Point to texts supporting each classification
Declare which answer to each question is true
optionExplain: Supporting passages are needed, not complete quotations of every author.
Right: the order of questions must be defensible.
Right: differences must be shown, and the reader must try to explain them.
Right: each classification of an author must rest on texts she can point to.
Declaring the truth is not one of the demands, as the next section stresses.
questions.explain: The analysis is complete when its order, its account of differences and its classifications can all be defended. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Order, explain, document.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: According to the authors, the truth, insofar as it can be found, consists in the ordered ____ itself rather than in any set of propositions about it.
questions.explain: That is why the analysis presents the discussion in order instead of a list of the reader's own conclusions.
questions.rule: The truth lies in the ordered discussion.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A reader has framed her questions and listed every author's answers, but cannot say why she put the questions in that order. What is missing?
options: A verdict on which of the answers are true
A defence of the order, one of the three demands
A longer list of authors and their answers
Nothing, since a list of answers is enough
optionExplain: A verdict is not required, and would not supply the missing defence.
Right: the questions must be asked in an order she can defend.
More authors do not fix an order she cannot justify.
The authors say more than asking and answering is needed.
questions.explain: An undefended order may be arbitrary, and an arbitrary order can hide how the questions depend on one another.
questions.rule: Be able to defend the order.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A report says Author C holds the third position on an issue but gives no page or passage for it. Which demand has the report failed?
options: Ordering the questions so the order can be defended
Pointing to the texts that support the classification
Showing how answers differ and trying to say why
Setting neutral terms that fit all of the authors
optionExplain: The order of questions is a separate demand; this is about one placement.
Right: each placement of an author must be backed by texts the reader can point to.
Showing differences is separate; the gap here is the missing support.
Terms belong to step two; this gap is in the documentation.
questions.explain: Without a cited passage, no one can check whether Author C really belongs in the third position.
questions.rule: Every placement needs its text.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A policy analyst finds experts split on whether a tax is fair. Trying to say why, she sees the split follows their definitions of fairness: equal rates versus equal burden. What has this step revealed?
options: That one group of experts has made an error in its arithmetic
That the question of fairness can never be usefully discussed
That she should adopt whichever definition is more popular
That the dispute turns on an earlier disagreement about definitions
optionExplain: Nothing suggests an arithmetic error; both sides may calculate correctly.
Finding the source of a split makes discussion more useful, not impossible.
Popularity does not settle a dispute about definitions.
Right: explaining the difference located where the discussion really turns.
questions.explain: By extension, trying to say why answers differ often uncovers a prior disagreement, which shows where the discussion actually turns.
questions.rule: Explaining a split can uncover the disagreement beneath it.
questions.teaches: By extension, trying to say why answers differ often reveals that a disagreement rests on an earlier one, such as a different definition, which shows where the discussion really turns.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: A reader who has answered every question herself, with good arguments, has thereby analyzed the discussion in the authors' sense.
questions.explain: The authors say the task is not only to answer the questions oneself. Analysis means ordering the questions, explaining the different answers and citing the texts.
questions.rule: Answering is not analyzing.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a careful map of a disagreement can help someone else make a breakthrough on the problem.
questions.explain: The authors say a thorough analysis can prepare the way for an original thinker's breakthrough. The card next explains how.
questions.rule: A map of a debate can enable a breakthrough.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: The authors say a thorough analysis can clear away the ____ and prepare the way for an original thinker to make a breakthrough.
questions.explain: Clearing away what is settled or confused lets others see the dimensions of the problem.
questions.rule: Clear the deadwood.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A review maps forty years of conflicting research on sleep and memory, showing which questions are settled and which split the field. How does it help a young scientist?
options: It shows the problem's dimensions, so she sees where an experiment could decide
It tells her which account is true, so no further experiment is needed
It saves her from ever reading any of the studies the review covers
It hands her a ready-made conclusion she can publish as her own
optionExplain: Right: by making the problem's dimensions visible, the review points to where new work can count.
A map of the discussion does not declare a winner; the open questions remain open.
She will still need the studies that bear on her experiment; the review shows which.
The review prepares the ground; the breakthrough would be her own work.
questions.explain: The value for others lies in seeing the shape of the problem: what is settled, what is open, and where the open questions turn.
questions.rule: A good map shows where new work can decide.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: In the authors' view, the analysis of a discussion is itself the breakthrough on the problem.
questions.explain: The analysis prepares the way for an original thinker's breakthrough; it is groundwork, not the breakthrough itself.
questions.rule: Groundwork, not breakthrough.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Maintainers of a software project write a document mapping ten years of proposals for a feature, marking which disputes were only about naming and which are still open. Whom does this most help, and how?
options: The original proposers, who can now claim credit for their ideas
Users, who learn they no longer need the feature in question
Newcomers, who can put their effort into the disputes still open
Managers, who can now pick a winner without reading anything
optionExplain: Credit may follow, but the map's main use is to guide further work.
Mapping the debate does not change what users need.
Right: clearing away settled and verbal disputes lets new contributors work where the problem is open.
The map informs judgment; it does not replace reading the open proposals.
questions.explain: By extension, clearing away deadwood means marking what is settled or only verbal, so others spend effort only where the problem is still open.
questions.rule: Mark what is settled so others work where it is open.
questions.teaches: By extension, clearing away deadwood includes showing which disputes are only verbal or already settled, so newcomers spend effort only where the problem is still open.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Five Steps in Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Which feature would make an analysis least useful as groundwork for others?
options: Covering a large number of authors on the problem
Ordering the questions from general to more specific
Leaning toward one side, so others cannot trust its map
Citing the texts that support each classification
optionExplain: Wide coverage helps others see the full discussion.
A clear order helps others follow how the questions connect.
Right: a slanted map shows the problem as one side sees it, so others cannot build on it safely.
Citations let others check the map, which makes it more useful.
questions.explain: Others can build on an analysis only if they can trust it to show every side. That demand for fairness is the subject of the next section.
questions.rule: A slanted map is poor groundwork.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, on most issues in a discussion each opposing view is held by a single author.
questions.explain: The authors say that on most issues each side is shared by several authors, often by many; a solitary exponent is rare. The card next explains what to report.
questions.rule: Sides usually have many members.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: The authors say an adequate analysis identifies and reports the major issues, or basic intellectual ____, in a discussion.
questions.explain: The major issues are the basic oppositions; the report also shows the agreement within each side.
questions.rule: Report the basic oppositions.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A report on a debate lists five issues, naming one author on each side of each. What would the authors want added?
options: The other authors who share each side
A verdict on which side of each is right
A short biography of each named author
The number of pages each author wrote
optionExplain: Right: agreement accompanies disagreement, so each side's other members belong in the report.
A verdict would make the report dogmatic, as the next ideas explain.
Biography does not show how the discussion is arranged.
Page counts measure output, not who shares which view.
questions.explain: Naming one author per side makes each view look like a lone voice. The report should show the camps.
questions.rule: Show who stands with whom.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: Authors who stand together on one issue must agree on every other issue as well.
questions.explain: Camps are formed issue by issue. Allies on one question may take opposite sides on the next.
questions.rule: Camps are issue by issue.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: An analyst charts how twenty legislators voted on six related bills. The same eight vote together on every bill; the rest shift from bill to bill. What does charting the camps reveal?
options: That the eight have copied one another's speeches word for word
That the shifting legislators hold no settled views at all
That the six bills are in fact one and the same bill
A stable bloc, and issues that divide the others independently
optionExplain: Voting together shows shared positions, not copying.
Shifting may reflect considered views that differ bill by bill.
Different bills can draw the same bloc without being identical.
Right: a group that stays together across issues forms a bloc, while shifting groups show issues that cut separately.
questions.explain: By extension, mapping camps across several issues shows which groupings are stable and which issues divide people in different ways.
questions.rule: Camps across issues reveal blocs and independent issues.
questions.teaches: By extension, showing camps across several issues reveals coalitions: authors grouped together on issue after issue form a school, while shifting groups show the issues are independent.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: What would a reader of an analysis that names only one author per side be likely to conclude?
options: That the discussion holds no real disagreement at all
That each view is a lone voice, misjudging its support
That every author agrees on all the major issues
Nothing different, since support makes no difference
optionExplain: The oppositions are still shown; what is missing is the agreement within them.
Right: hiding the camps makes widely shared views look solitary.
Opposing sides are named, so total agreement would not be the impression.
How widely a view is shared bears on how it should be weighed, as the next idea shows.
questions.explain: The authors stress that a solitary exponent is rare. A report that shows only one author per side misrepresents how views are held.
questions.rule: Hidden camps distort the picture.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: When many authors in a field agree on an opinion, what does that establish, according to the authors?
options: Proof that the opinion is in fact true
Some presumption that the opinion is true
Nothing whatever about its truth
A presumption that the opinion is false
optionExplain: A presumption falls short of proof; agreed opinions can still be false.
Right: agreement gives some presumption of truth, a starting assumption rather than proof.
The authors say agreement does count for something.
Agreement points toward truth, not falsity.
questions.explain: Agreement weighs in favour of truth without settling it. The card next adds what disagreement suggests.
questions.rule: Agreement presumes truth, without proving it.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Match each item to its meaning in the authors' account.
pairs: A counter-presumption that no side is wholly true
A reasonable starting assumption, not a proof
questions.explain: Agreement and disagreement each create a presumption, pointing in different directions, and neither is a proof.
questions.rule: Two presumptions, neither a proof.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Historians nearly all agree on the year of a famine but disagree sharply about its causes. What do the two patterns suggest?
options: Both the date and the causes are now proven beyond any reasonable doubt
Neither the date nor any account of the causes can be trusted at all
The causes are settled, since so many historians have written on them
The date is presumed true; no one account of the causes may be wholly right
optionExplain: Presumptions are not proofs, and the causes are in dispute.
Agreement on the date counts for something; distrusting everything ignores it.
Many writers disagreeing is the opposite of settled.
Right: agreement on the date gives a presumption of truth; disagreement on causes gives the counter-presumption.
questions.explain: The two patterns create different presumptions about the two claims.
questions.rule: Read agreement and disagreement claim by claim.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, an opinion on which all seem to agree cannot be false.
questions.explain: The authors say it is possible for the opinion on which all seem to agree to be false. Agreement creates a presumption, not a guarantee.
questions.rule: Even consensus can be wrong.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Thirty news sites report the same figure for a company's losses, all citing a single anonymous post. How much presumption of truth does their agreement carry?
options: Little, since they repeat one source instead of agreeing independently
A great deal, since thirty separate sources agree on the same figure
None, since figures in the news must first be checked by auditors
Full proof, since not one of the sites disputes the reported figure
optionExplain: Right: thirty echoes of one post amount to one source, not thirty agreeing judgments.
The thirty are not separate in the way that matters; they share one origin.
Agreement can carry weight before an audit; the problem here is the shared source.
Lack of dispute is not proof, and agreement is at most a presumption.
questions.explain: By extension, agreement counts as a presumption of truth only when the agreeing sources reached their view independently.
questions.rule: Agreement counts only when it is independent.
questions.teaches: By extension, agreement creates a presumption of truth only if the agreeing sources are independent; many authors repeating one source add little.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: By the authors' account, when opinions conflict, the opinion held by the larger group must be wholly true.
questions.explain: Disagreement creates the counter-presumption that none of the conflicting opinions, shared or not, may be wholly true. A larger camp does not escape it.
questions.rule: A bigger camp is not exempt from the counter-presumption.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Two authors' opinions on a disputed question conflict. Which of these are possible, according to the authors? Select all that apply.
options: Both are wholly true in every respect
Their conflict proves the question has no answer
One is wholly true and the other false
Each holds some portion of the truth
Both are false, and an unstated view is nearer
optionExplain: Conflicting opinions cannot both be wholly true in every respect.
Conflict is a counter-presumption about the opinions, not proof that there is no answer.
Right: the authors allow that one may be wholly true and the rest false.
Right: each may express some portion of the whole truth.
Right: all may be false, and some opinion not yet expressed may be nearer the truth.
questions.explain: The authors list several possibilities and rule none out in advance. The card next sets them out.
questions.rule: Keep several possibilities open.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: The authors say each of several conflicting opinions may express some ____ of the whole truth.
questions.explain: Besides one being wholly true, each may hold part of the truth, all may be false, or an unexpressed opinion may be nearer.
questions.rule: Each may hold a portion.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: In a report on the debate over teaching reading by phonics or by whole-language methods, which sentence best reflects the authors' stance?
options: Phonics is right, and the whole-language methods are plainly wrong
Since experts disagree, nothing at all can be known about teaching
The evidence leaves open that each method captures part of what works
Whichever method is newer is likely to be the closer to the truth
optionExplain: Declaring one side wholly right closes the other possibilities and takes a side.
Disagreement is a counter-presumption, not proof that nothing can be known.
Right: it keeps open that each side holds a portion of the truth, without declaring a winner.
Newness has no bearing on which possibility holds.
questions.explain: The report keeps the possibilities open instead of asserting one.
questions.rule: Report possibilities, not verdicts.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A reader concludes: the two camps conflict, so one must be right and the other wrong. What has she overlooked?
options: That both camps are certainly right in everything they say
That their conflict proves neither teaching method works
That each may hold part of the truth, or both may be wrong
That teaching methods cannot be studied by any reader
optionExplain: Conflicting views cannot both be wholly right.
Conflict among opinions about methods does not show the methods fail.
Right: one wholly right and one wholly wrong is only one of the authors' possibilities.
The methods can be studied; the error is in narrowing the possible outcomes.
questions.explain: The authors allow several outcomes besides one wholly right side. Assuming a single winner closes them off too early.
questions.rule: Conflict does not mean one winner.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A team torn between two website designs finds that both test poorly with users. Following the authors' possibilities, what is a sensible next step?
options: Consider that an option not yet proposed may be better, and look for it
Pick whichever design tested slightly less badly, and ship it now
Merge both designs, since each must hold half of the right answer
Abandon the project, since the conflict shows no design can work
optionExplain: Right: when both options fail, the possibility of an unexpressed better one is a reason to keep searching.
The least bad option may still be far from good when both fail.
Each may hold part of the answer, but it is not given that merging them works.
Two failures do not show that every design must fail.
questions.explain: By extension, when every proposed option has serious flaws, the possibility of an unexpressed opinion nearer the truth becomes practical advice.
questions.rule: When all options fail, look for one not yet proposed.
questions.teaches: By extension, when every proposed option has serious flaws, the possibility that an unexpressed option is better is a reason to keep searching rather than to settle for the least bad.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, if two opinions flatly contradict each other, both may still be false.
questions.explain: The authors exempt flat contradictions from the possibility that all conflicting opinions are false: of two contradictories, one must be true. Such cases, they add, are rare in these discussions.
questions.rule: Flat contradictories cannot both be false.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A report on a debate ends by arguing that one side is right. In the authors' terms, what has the report become?
options: Dialectical, since it reaches a conclusion
Syntopical, since it covers many authors
Analytical, since it judges an argument
Dogmatic: one more voice in the debate
optionExplain: Reaching a verdict is what the authors call dogmatic, the opposite of dialectical.
Covering many authors is not enough; taking a side makes it cease to be syntopical.
Judging one book's argument is analytical criticism; this report has taken a side in a whole debate.
Right: asserting the truth of a view makes the report dogmatic and one more voice.
questions.explain: A report that takes sides joins the debate instead of mapping it. The card next explains the authors' ideal.
questions.rule: Taking a side ends detachment.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: The authors sum up the special quality a syntopical analysis tries to achieve in two words: dialectical ____.
questions.explain: Dialectical objectivity: a detached, objective presentation of the discussion that takes no side.
questions.rule: Dialectical objectivity.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A scholar is writing the final chapter of an analysis of the nuclear power debate. Which ending keeps her book syntopical?
options: One that argues nuclear power is the best answer
One that lays out every side fairly and argues for none
One that argues nuclear power is far too dangerous
One that endorses a middle view between the sides
optionExplain: Arguing for nuclear power makes the book one more voice in the debate.
Right: presenting the sides without asserting any keeps the analysis dialectical.
Arguing against it is equally a side.
A middle view is still a view; endorsing it takes a position.
questions.explain: Any endorsement, including a compromise, makes the book a participant. The syntopical ending maps the debate and stops.
questions.rule: A compromise is still a side.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, one more voice in a discussion of important issues carries no weight.
questions.explain: The authors say the point is not that one more voice carries no weight, but that a different kind of contribution can and should be made.
questions.rule: Voices matter; the syntopical report contributes differently.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Before a vote, a parliament's research office writes a briefing on a contested bill that sets out every side's arguments without recommending any. Why might both parties value it?
options: It quietly supports whichever party commissioned the briefing
Taking no side, it can be trusted by each to show the other's case
It saves members from forming any view of their own on the bill
It ensures the bill will pass by removing every disagreement
optionExplain: If it favoured one party, the other would have reason to distrust it.
Right: a map that takes no side is one each side can rely on, including to understand its opponents.
Members still decide; the briefing informs their views rather than replacing them.
A fair map does not remove disagreement; it clarifies it.
questions.explain: By extension, the detachment the authors demand is what makes the analysis useful to people on every side.
questions.rule: Neutral maps serve all sides.
questions.teaches: By extension, a detached analysis is valuable precisely to people who disagree: because it takes no side, each side can trust it and use it to understand the other.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: According to the authors, what happens to a syntopical analysis that tries to prove one view on an important issue?
options: It becomes more useful, since readers want clear answers
Nothing changes, provided its proof is a sound one
It turns into an analytical reading of a single author
It ceases to be syntopical and loses its detached character
optionExplain: Readers may want answers, but the analysis then gives up its distinct contribution.
Even a sound proof makes the report dogmatic rather than dialectical.
It still covers many authors; what changes is that it now takes a side.
Right: it becomes one more voice in the discussion, losing its detached and objective character.
questions.explain: The authors are explicit: asserting or trying to prove any view would make the analysis cease to be syntopical.
questions.rule: Proving a side ends the syntopical analysis.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Which is easier for a syntopical reader, according to the authors?
options: Taking no sides
Looking at all sides
Both are equally easy
Both are impossible
optionExplain: Right: he may succeed in taking no sides, but he will fail to look at all sides.
All sides of an issue cannot be listed exhaustively, so this is the harder half.
The authors rank them: taking no sides is easier.
The authors say he may succeed in taking no sides, so not both are impossible.
questions.explain: The authors say taking no sides is easier than looking at all sides. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: No sides is easier than all sides.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: The authors say that taking no sides is ____ than looking at all sides.
questions.explain: Impartiality toward the sides you know is achievable; finding every possible side is not.
questions.rule: Taking no sides is the easier half.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: An analyst fairly reported two camps in the rent control debate, then learned of a third position rejecting both camps' framing. What does this show?
options: She was partial to the two camps she happened to find
Her analysis is worthless and should be withdrawn
She took no side, but had not yet seen all the sides
The third position must be the correct one after all
optionExplain: Missing a side is not favouring one; she treated the two she found fairly.
Every analysis falls short of all sides; she should add the third and continue.
Right: she met the easier half of the ideal and fell short on the harder one, as the authors expect.
Discovering a position says nothing about its truth.
questions.explain: The authors expect this kind of failure in looking at all sides. The response is to keep trying, not to give up.
questions.rule: Add missed sides and keep looking.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A reader says: I treated both camps with perfect fairness, so my analysis is objective. What has she overlooked?
options: Whether one camp deserves more of her sympathy
Whether fairness requires her to take one side
Whether there are sides beyond the two she found
Whether the two camps are equal in their size
optionExplain: Sympathy for a camp would undo the half she has achieved.
Taking a side is what objectivity forbids.
Right: impartiality between known sides is only half the ideal; she must also look for others.
Size of camps is not the issue; completeness of sides is.
questions.explain: Taking no sides is the easier half. Her claim ignores the harder half, looking at all sides.
questions.rule: Fair to two sides is not yet objective.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A news programme covers a policy debate by inviting one guest for the policy and one against it. By extension of the authors' warning, what may it miss?
options: Positions that reject the framing both guests share
The need to give each of the guests equal time
The views of the programme's own presenters
The need to name a winner at the end of the show
optionExplain: Right: a duel between two sides can hide positions that accept neither side's terms.
Equal time addresses taking no sides, which the format may already manage.
Presenters' views would add a side-taker, not a missing side.
Naming a winner is the opposite of the detachment the authors ask for.
questions.explain: By extension, presenting two sides as if they were all the sides is a distortion of its own, even when each side is treated fairly.
questions.rule: Two sides are seldom all the sides.
questions.teaches: By extension, presenting two sides as if they were all the sides is itself a distortion: a debate framed as a duel can hide positions that reject both.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: Because all sides of an issue cannot be listed, the authors excuse the syntopical reader from trying to find them.
questions.explain: The authors say he will fail to list all sides, and nevertheless he must try.
questions.rule: Certain failure is no excuse for not trying.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: A report that does not state which side is right can still be biased.
questions.explain: Bias can enter through summaries, emphasis, tone and order even without any explicit verdict. The card next lists the ways.
questions.rule: No verdict does not mean no bias.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Through which of these can partiality intrude into a report, according to the authors? Select all that apply.
options: The order in which answers appear
Quoting authors in their own words
Citing pages for each classification
How arguments are summarized
Shades of emphasis and neglect
optionExplain: Right: the order in which answers are presented can favour one.
Quoting is the authors' remedy for distortion, not a source of it.
Citing texts lets readers check the report; it guards against bias.
Right: the manner of summarizing is one of the authors' subtle routes for bias.
Right: what is stressed and what is passed over can tilt a report.
questions.explain: The authors name summary, emphasis and neglect, tone and passing remarks, and order. Quotation and citation are safeguards.
questions.rule: Summary, emphasis, tone, order.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A report on a vaccine debate gives one side two pages and the other a paragraph, and describes them in unequal language. Which change best addresses its partiality?
options: Add a final verdict, so that its leaning is at least explicit
Remove all mention of the side that is less popular
Cut both sides down to a single sentence each
Even out the space, wording and treatment given to each side
optionExplain: An explicit verdict makes the report dogmatic instead of fixing it.
Dropping a side is the extreme of neglect.
