Equal brevity removes the bias by removing the content the analysis needs.
Right: the bias lives in emphasis and wording, so those are what must be corrected.
questions.explain: The report's partiality is in its emphasis and tone. Fairness is restored by treating each side's case with comparable care.
questions.rule: Fix bias where it lives: emphasis and tone.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A writer introduces one camp's view as what research confirms and the other's as what some people argue. Which route for partiality is this?
options: The order in which the answers are presented
The colour of the wording and passing remarks
Neglect of one side's argument altogether
An explicit verdict on which side is true
optionExplain: Order is a different route; here both views appear, framed unequally.
Right: the framing words colour each view before it is stated.
Both views are mentioned, so this is not neglect.
No verdict is stated; the bias is in the framing words.
questions.explain: The words used to introduce a view can tilt the reader without any explicit judgment.
questions.rule: Framing words can carry a verdict.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A comparison of three phone plans consistently presents the writer's favourite plan last. Why might this matter, by extension of the authors' list?
options: The first option is the one readers remember best, so the favourite loses
The last option tends to read as the conclusion, tilting readers toward it
Order makes no difference if every plan is described accurately
Presenting it last hides it, so most readers will overlook it
optionExplain: First options can be memorable, but the last tends to read as the verdict.
Right: the final position reads like the outcome of the comparison.
The authors name order of presentation as a route for partiality even with accurate content.
The last place is prominent, not hidden; that is why it tilts.
questions.explain: The authors list order as a source of partiality. By extension, the final position often reads as the conclusion, so its use should be justified or rotated.
questions.rule: The last word reads as the verdict.
questions.teaches: By extension, order effects are strong: the position presented last often reads as the conclusion, so justifying or varying the order guards against bias.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: Giving one side more space can be fair when its argument is genuinely longer and more complex.
questions.explain: The concern is emphasis and neglect that distort, not every difference in length. The test is whether each side would accept its treatment as fair.
questions.rule: Fair is not the same as identical.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: In presenting a syntopical analysis, what do the authors say should accompany your summary of an author's view?
options: Your judgment of whether the author is right
A summary in the author's own terminology
A biography placing the author in history
A quotation in the author's own words
optionExplain: A judgment of truth would make the analysis dogmatic.
Summaries stay in your neutral terms; the author's language enters through quotation.
Background may interest readers, but it does not let them check your interpretation.
Right: the quotation lets readers judge whether your interpretation is correct.
questions.explain: The authors pair a neutral summary with the author's own words. The card next explains why there is no contradiction.
questions.rule: Summary plus quotation.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: The authors say the author's own words, carefully quoted so as not to wrench them out of ____, must accompany the summary.
questions.explain: A faithful quotation lets readers judge the interpretation; one torn from context defeats that purpose.
questions.rule: Quote in context.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A report summarises a philosopher's view of liberty in its neutral terms. What else should it include, according to the authors?
options: A short, fair quotation from his own text
His own terms in place of the summary
An argument for or against his view
His critics' views in place of his
optionExplain: Right: the quotation lets readers check that the neutral summary is fair to him.
The summary must stay in neutral terms; his words accompany it, not replace it.
Arguing for or against him would end the report's detachment.
His critics belong on their own sides of the issue, not as substitutes for him.
questions.explain: The neutral summary makes authors comparable; the quotation makes the summary checkable.
questions.rule: Neutral summary, checkable by quotation.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A report quotes half of an author's sentence on war and leaves off the qualification that followed it. What has gone wrong?
options: The quotation should have been put in neutral terms
Quoting at all is a departure from neutrality
The quotation is wrenched from context and misleads
The report should have quoted his critics instead
optionExplain: Quotations are in the author's language by definition; the summary is the neutral part.
The authors recommend quoting as a safeguard of objectivity.
Right: cutting the qualification changes what the author said, defeating the purpose of quoting.
His critics cannot show what he himself held.
questions.explain: The authors require quotations to be careful not to wrench words out of context. A truncated quotation becomes a source of distortion.
questions.rule: A torn quotation distorts.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A user researcher summarises interviews in neutral terms and adds one quotation per participant. Which quotation should she choose for each?
options: The most vivid line, even if the participant said it only once
The line that best supports the researcher's own conclusion
The passage most representative of what that participant said
The shortest line, to keep the report brief and readable
optionExplain: A vivid but untypical line can misrepresent the participant.
Choosing quotations to support a conclusion turns quoting into a tool of bias.
Right: a representative passage lets readers check the summary honestly.
Brevity is a minor gain if the line does not represent the view.
questions.explain: By extension, which passage is quoted is itself a choice that can slant a report. The test is representativeness, not vividness.
questions.rule: Quote the representative, not the striking.
questions.teaches: By extension, choosing which passage to quote is itself a judgment that can slant a report, so pick the most representative passage, not the most striking one.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, quoting an author's own words contradicts the requirement to present summaries in neutral terms.
questions.explain: The authors say it may appear to, but it does not: the summary is in neutral terms, and the quotation accompanies it so readers can judge the interpretation.
questions.rule: Neutral summary and quotation work together.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: According to the authors, who alone can know whether a syntopical report has met the demands of objectivity?
options: The syntopical reader who wrote it
Any careful reader of the report
The authors whose views it covers
An editor who checks the report
optionExplain: Right: only the writer can know whether he satisfied the requirements.
Readers can judge the report's effectiveness, but not fully whether the writer met these demands.
The authors covered can check their own treatment, but not the whole effort of balance.
An editor sees the text, not the writer's intentions and choices.
questions.explain: Much of objectivity lies in choices only the writer sees. The card next explains.
questions.rule: The writer answers for objectivity.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Which efforts does the ideal of dialectical objectivity demand, according to the authors? Select all that apply.
options: Give every author the same word count
End with a balanced verdict on the truth
Balance question against question
Forgo any prejudicial comment
Check over- or underemphasis
optionExplain: Balance is fair treatment, not identical length.
Any verdict, balanced or not, makes the report dogmatic.
Right: questions must be balanced against each other.
Right: any comment that might be prejudicial is to be forgone.
Right: tendencies toward overemphasis or underemphasis must be checked.
questions.explain: The authors name three deliberate efforts: balancing questions, forgoing prejudicial comment, and checking emphasis.
questions.rule: Balance, forgo, check.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Revising a report on school testing, an analyst evens out the probing questions she put to each camp and cuts a witty aside about one camp's author. What does this illustrate?
options: The need to hand every report to an editor for a check on its fairness
That witty asides are the only form of bias worth any attention
That one camp deserved more probing questions than the other
The firm intention to avoid partiality, applied by the writer herself
optionExplain: An editor may help, but the authors say only the writer's intention can prevent these departures.
She also balanced the questions; asides are one route among several.
She evened the questions out, the opposite of favouring one camp.
Right: she balanced questions and forwent a prejudicial comment, by her own effort.
questions.explain: Both fixes are the deliberate efforts the authors describe, made by the only person who could see the need for them.
questions.rule: Objectivity is a deliberate effort by the writer.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, quoting the authors is enough on its own to prevent every departure from objectivity.
questions.explain: Quoting helps avoid some dangers. The authors say other departures can be prevented only by the writer's firm intention to avoid them.
questions.rule: Quoting helps; intention does the rest.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A grant reviewer summarises two competing proposals and wants to check her own fairness, since no one else can see her intentions. Which self-check fits the authors' point best?
options: Count the words given to each proposal and make the two counts equal
Reread it as a supporter of each proposal in turn, noting what feels unfair
Ask the stronger applicant whether the summary seems fair to them
Add a note to the summary saying she has no conflicts of interest
optionExplain: Equal counts can hide unequal tone and emphasis, and fair treatment need not be equal length.
Right: reading from each side's position brings slanted emphasis and remarks to light.
One applicant can speak only for their own side.
A declaration of no conflict does not check the text itself.
questions.explain: Since only the writer can know whether she met the requirements, she needs ways to see her own text as the sides would see it. By extension, rereading from each side's position is one.
questions.rule: Reread as each side would.
questions.teaches: By extension, because only the writer can fully know, practical self-checks help, such as rereading the report as a supporter of each side in turn and noting what feels unfair.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a report's readers, not its writer, are the final judges of whether the writer met the requirements of objectivity.
questions.explain: Readers may judge the report's effectiveness, but the authors say only the writer can know whether he satisfied the requirements.
questions.rule: Readers judge effect; the writer knows the effort.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: Roughly how large did the authors' final bibliography on the idea of progress become?
options: About 45 items
More than 450 items
About 4,500 items
Exactly 100 items
optionExplain: Far too small; the list was ten times this.
Right: the bibliography finally ran to more than 450 items.
This is closer to the number inspected than to the final list, which was over 450.
A hundred is the authors' example size for the love bibliography, not the progress list.
questions.explain: The list ran past 450 items, drawn from several times as many works inspected. The card next explains how it was built.
questions.rule: Over 450 items, from many more inspected.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: The authors say many items finally judged relevant to progress were found more or less by accident, or with the help of educated ____.
questions.explain: Relevant works do not announce themselves; many turned up by chance or by informed guesswork.
questions.rule: Accident and educated guesses find many works.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: A reader studying resilience searches catalogues for the word and finds only recent books. Why might her search miss important works?
options: Catalogues list only books published in recent years
Resilience is not a subject that books discuss
Keyword searches find too many works to read
Older works treat the subject without using the word
optionExplain: Catalogues include older books; the problem is that those books use other words.
Recent books show it is discussed; older ones discuss it under other names.
Her problem is missing works, not finding too many.
Right: as with progress, older relevant works may never use the modern term.
questions.explain: The authors found that most older books on progress do not use the word. Any subject with a recent name has the same trap.
questions.rule: Search beyond the subject's modern name.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: True or false: The authors say most of the older books relevant to progress do not even use the word progress.
questions.explain: Recent books often have progress in their titles, but most of the older relevant books do not even employ the term.
questions.rule: Older works may lack the word.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: A lawyer researching a legal doctrine finds that recent cases name it, but older cases discuss the same idea in other words. Which method best reaches the older cases?
options: Follow the citations in recent cases back to the older ones
Search again using only the doctrine's modern name
Assume no older cases exist on the doctrine at all
Read every case in the archive in order of date
optionExplain: Right: citations link works by subject, not by word, so they lead to older discussions under other names.
The modern name is exactly what the older cases lack.
The older cases exist; they use different words.
Reading everything is the cost the short cut of inspection exists to avoid.
questions.explain: The authors found many relevant works by accident or educated guesses. By extension, following the references in early finds is a systematic way to reach works that never use your keyword.
questions.rule: Follow references back to works without your keyword.
questions.teaches: By extension, following references backward, from your early finds to the works they cite, reaches older works that never use your keyword, because citations link works by subject rather than by word.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: How many works did the authors inspect to reach their final list of more than 450?
options: Exactly the 450 that ended on the list
About half as many as the final list
Several times as many as the final list
Only those with progress in the title
optionExplain: Inspection is how the list was cut down, so more were inspected than kept.
The list cannot hold more works than were inspected to make it.
Right: the list came from inspectional readings of several times that many pieces.
Many relevant works lacked the word, so a title search alone could not have built the list.
questions.explain: Inspection does two jobs here: it finds and it filters. That means inspecting far more works than end up on the list.
questions.rule: Inspect many to keep some.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: Why is it hard to place a novel on one side of an issue in a syntopical study?
options: Novels are read for pleasure, so their ideas do not count
Novelists write too briefly to state any positions
A character's speech may not be the author's own view
Novels are too old to bear on any current issue
optionExplain: Reading for pleasure does not cancel a novel's ideas; the problem is attributing them.
Many novels are long; length is not the obstacle.
Right: the author may be ironic, or showing the folly of a view his character holds.
Novels of every period exist; age is not the issue.
questions.explain: A novel speaks through characters, and the author's own position may differ from any of theirs. The card next gives the authors' reasons.
questions.rule: A character is not the author.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: Which reasons do the authors give for the difficulty of including fiction in a syntopical project? Select all that apply.
options: Readers enjoy fiction too much to analyse it
A story's backbone is its plot, not positions
Characters seldom take clear positions
A character's speech may not be the author's view
Fiction is less truthful than exposition
optionExplain: Enjoyment is not among the reasons given.
Right: the essence of a story is its plot.
Right: characters mostly talk about other matters, chiefly emotional relations.
Right: the author may be ironic or showing a view's foolishness.
The authors do not call fiction less truthful; their point is about positions on issues.
questions.explain: The authors give three reasons: plot is the backbone, characters rarely take clear positions, and a speech may not be the author's view.
questions.rule: Plot, unclear positions, uncertain voice.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: A novel's hero praises machines in a rousing speech, then is ruined by his invention. A reader studying whether technology improves life wants to place the novel. What should she do?
options: Leave it out, since its position cannot be placed with confidence
Record the author as praising machines, on the strength of the speech
Record the author as opposing machines, on the strength of the ending
Give it extra weight, since a story moves readers more than an essay
optionExplain: Right: speech and ending pull in different directions, and the author's view is uncertain.
The speech may be the target of the author's irony.
The ending is suggestive, but reading it as a thesis needs the intensive interpretation the authors find dubious.
Emotional force is not a position on the issue.
questions.explain: The authors advise abstaining when placing a fiction would need great interpretive effort with dubious results.
questions.rule: When the author's stance is uncertain, abstain.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, no novel or poem may be read at all in a syntopical project.
questions.explain: A few fictional and poetical works were read in the progress study. The advice is to concentrate on expository works and usually abstain from placing fiction on an issue.
questions.rule: Concentrate on exposition; fiction is not banned.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: A researcher studying views on immigration wants to cite a comedian's sketch in which a character rants against newcomers. Following the authors' caution, how should she treat it?
options: As the comedian's own view, since he wrote the rant himself
As the opposite of his view, since comedy is always ironic
As a strong source, since comedy reaches so many people
As unplaceable, since the rant may be the target of the satire
optionExplain: Writing a character's words does not make them the writer's view.
Irony is possible, not certain; reversing the rant is as unsafe as accepting it.
Reach does not tell her what position the comedian holds.
Right: a performed character, like a fictional one, may voice what the creator mocks.
questions.explain: By extension, the authors' caution about fiction applies to any form where a persona speaks: satire, parody, staged debate.
questions.rule: A persona's words are not the creator's position.
questions.teaches: By extension, the same caution applies to any form in which a persona speaks, such as satire, parody or a staged debate: the persona's words are not the creator's position.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: Suppose a novelist also wrote an essay stating his view on progress plainly. What changes for a syntopical reader?
options: The novel can now be placed without any further interpretation
The essay can be placed on the issue as an expository work
Both works must be left out, since the fiction taints the essay
The essay must be ignored, since its author is a novelist
optionExplain: The essay does not settle what the novel's characters stand for; that would still need interpretation.
Right: an expository statement of his view raises none of the problems that fiction does.
Writing fiction does not disqualify an author's expository work.
Who wrote it matters less than what kind of work it is.
questions.explain: The difficulty lies in the form of fiction, not in the author. His expository work can be read like any other.
questions.rule: The form, not the author, is the problem.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: Most authors use a key word to mean change for the better; a few use it for change that is not an improvement. What should a syntopical reader do?
options: Use the word for both senses and let context decide
Keep the word for the majority sense and rename the other
Drop the minority authors from the study entirely
Use the minority's sense, since it is more exact
optionExplain: Context is unreliable when the two senses contradict each other at their core.
Right: one word cannot serve two incompatible ideas, so one sense gets a new name.
The minority's view is part of the discussion and must be reported.
Exactness is not the criterion; the authors kept the word for the majority.
questions.explain: The authors faced exactly this with progress. The card next shows their solution.
questions.rule: One word, one idea.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: The authors referred to the minority as authors who assert non-meliorative ____ in history.
questions.explain: Non-meliorative advance means movement forward without betterment, the minority's conception, which could not be called progress.
questions.rule: Non-meliorative advance: forward, not better.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: Most economists in a study mean rising wellbeing by growth; a few mean any rise in output, even if people end up worse off. What naming fits the authors' practice?
options: Use growth for both senses and explain the difference in a footnote
Call both views growth and treat them as a single position
Rename the majority view, since the minority's sense is narrower
Keep growth for rising wellbeing and give the other sense a new name
optionExplain: A footnote leaves one word standing for two ideas in the body of the analysis.
Treating them as one position hides a basic difference.
The authors kept the word for the majority, not for the narrower sense.
Right: the majority keeps the word; the incompatible minority sense gets its own neutral name.
questions.explain: Like progress, growth here carries two incompatible ideas. One of them needs a different name.
questions.rule: Give the incompatible sense its own name.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: Which situation calls for a new neutral name, by the authors' practice?
options: Authors use one word for ideas incompatible in their essence
Authors use one word with slightly different shades of meaning
Authors use different words for what is the same idea
Authors use one word in exactly the same way throughout
optionExplain: Right: when betterment is essential to one sense and absent from the other, one word cannot cover both.
Shades of meaning can be handled in the analysis without renaming.
Different words for one idea are brought together under the reader's common term, not split apart.
Uniform usage raises no naming problem.
questions.explain: The authors handled shades of meaning within the analysis and renamed only where the conceptions were incompatible.
questions.rule: Rename for incompatibility, not for shades.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: On a team, most people say a task is done when it reaches customers, but some say done when the code is merged. A lead keeps done for the first sense and calls the second merged. What does this guard against?
options: Arguments over who should do the work that remains
Delays caused by customers rejecting new features
Reports that seem to agree while meaning different things
Confusion over which team owns which part of the code
optionExplain: Who does the work is a separate question from what done means.
Customer reactions are not affected by internal naming.
Right: without separate names, two people saying done would appear to agree when they do not.
Code ownership is unrelated to the meaning of done.
questions.explain: By extension, a separate name for each sense protects the analysis from false agreement, as well as from false disagreement.
questions.rule: Separate names prevent false agreement.
questions.teaches: By extension, renaming one sense protects against false agreement: when two sides use the same word, readers would otherwise assume they mean the same thing.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, keeping a word for the majority sense shows that the majority's view is the correct one.
questions.explain: The authors chose the majority sense for the word because most authors used it that way and betterment was essential to it. That is a naming decision, not a verdict on truth.
questions.rule: Naming is not judging.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: What did the authors find was the primary question in their study of progress?
options: Who first used the word progress?
Is progress good for human beings?
Does progress occur in history?
How fast does progress take place?
optionExplain: The history of the word is not a question about progress itself.
For most authors betterment is part of what progress means, so this question is not the primary one.
Right: whether the course of history moves toward improvement is the question all authors can be read as answering.
Speed presupposes that progress occurs, so it cannot come first.
questions.explain: The primary question is about existence, as the general pattern of ordering suggests. The card next gives the answers found.
questions.rule: First: does it occur?

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: What were the basic answers to the primary question about progress? Select all that apply.
options: Only in the arts
Only before 1800
Yes
No
We cannot know
optionExplain: Areas of progress belong to later, subordinate issues among progress authors, and the arts are the area where no one genuinely asserts it.
No answer of this kind is among the three basic ones.
Right: some authors say progress occurs.
Right: some deny it.
Right: some say we cannot know whether it occurs.
questions.explain: Three basic answers: yes, no, and we cannot know, each given in several different ways.
questions.rule: Yes, no, cannot know.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: A reader asks whether economic growth makes people's lives better overall. Which plan follows the authors' example?
options: Sort writers into yes, no and cannot tell, then note the variety within each
Count only the writers who answer yes, since they form the majority
Ask first which areas of life growth improves the most, then the rest
Decide herself whether growth helps before reading any of the writers
optionExplain: Right: sort by the primary question's main answers, then record the different ways each is given.
Leaving out the no and cannot-tell camps distorts the discussion.
Which areas improve is a later question for those who say growth helps at all.
Deciding first replaces the authors' answers with her own.
questions.explain: The progress study models the method: a primary question, its main answers, and the variety within each camp.
questions.rule: Main answers first, then their varieties.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, all those who answer yes to the primary question say yes in the same way.
questions.explain: The authors found a number of different ways of saying yes, several of saying no, and at least three of saying we cannot know.
questions.rule: Each camp has internal variety.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: Reviewing studies on whether remote work raises productivity, an analyst finds some say the data are too poor to tell, and others say productivity cannot be measured at all. How should she record them?
options: As giving no answer, since neither says yes or no
As the no camp, since neither supports the claim
As a single view, since both groups are sceptical
As one cannot-know camp, with two different reasons noted
optionExplain: Saying we cannot know is an answer, not silence.
Doubt about whether it can be known is not denial.
Grouping them is right, but the different reasons are part of the variety within the camp.
Right: both answer that we cannot know, for different reasons, which the record should show.
questions.explain: The authors found at least three ways of saying we cannot know. By extension, the sceptical camp has its own internal divisions, usually over why the question cannot be settled.
questions.rule: Record the sceptics' different reasons.
questions.teaches: By extension, a cannot-know answer deserves its own camp with its own varieties: some sceptics say the evidence is lacking, others that the question cannot be settled even in principle.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: What would happen if a reader of the progress literature began instead with a question about the areas in which progress occurs?
options: Every author could answer it equally well from the start
Authors who deny progress would have no way to answer it
It would sort the authors better than the primary question does
It would make the primary question unnecessary to ask
optionExplain: Only authors who say progress occurs can say where it occurs.
Right: the question presupposes that progress occurs, which some authors deny.
It would leave the deniers and doubters unsorted.
The areas question depends on the primary question's answer.
questions.explain: The primary question comes first because later questions presuppose a yes to it.
questions.rule: Questions that presuppose an answer come later.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: True or false: In a syntopical study, some issues may be joined only by authors who share a basic answer to the primary question.
questions.explain: Issues about the nature of something can only be joined by those who say it exists. The card next shows how the authors handled this with progress.
questions.rule: Some issues belong to one camp.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: Match each term to its meaning in the authors' study of progress.
pairs: Issues every author with something significant to say takes sides on
Issues joined only by authors who assert progress
Authors who assert that progress occurs
One issue of the special controversy
questions.explain: The general controversy grows from the primary question; the special controversy concerns the nature of progress and is joined only by those who assert it.
questions.rule: General for all; special for progress authors.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: In a study of whether cities improve their residents' lives, which issue belongs to a special controversy?
options: Whether cities improve residents' lives at all
Whether improvement is inevitable as cities grow
Whether we can know if cities improve lives
Whether cities make residents' lives worse
optionExplain: This is the primary question, the ground of the general controversy.
Right: only those who say cities do improve lives can argue over whether it is inevitable.
The cannot-know answer belongs to the general controversy.
A no answer to the primary question is part of the general controversy.
questions.explain: Questions about the nature of the improvement presuppose that it happens, so only the yes camp joins them.
questions.rule: Questions about its nature presuppose that it occurs.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: Which are issues of the special controversy about progress? Select all that apply.
options: Can we know whether progress occurs?
Is progress necessary or contingent?
Will progress continue indefinitely?
Is there progress in human nature itself?
Does progress occur in history at all?
optionExplain: This is the cannot-know answer to the primary question, part of the general controversy.
Right: necessity versus contingency is one of the three special issues.
Right: whether progress goes on indefinitely or plateaus is another.
Right: progress in human nature versus only in institutions is the third.
This is the primary question, which every author answers in the general controversy.
questions.explain: The special issues concern the properties of progress, so they presuppose that it occurs. The other two belong to the general controversy.
questions.rule: Special issues concern what progress is like.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: Two doctors both hold that a therapy works but disagree about whether its benefits last. A journalist reports that the doctors disagree about the therapy. What has the journalist done, by the authors' scheme?
options: Reported the general controversy accurately and fairly
Correctly shown that one doctor denies the therapy works
Left out the special controversy from the report altogether
Treated a special issue as if it were the general question
optionExplain: On the general question, whether it works, the doctors agree.
Neither doctor denies it works.
The report is about the special issue; the problem is that it is presented as the basic one.
Right: they agree on the basic answer; their dispute is a special issue among those who say it works.
questions.explain: By extension, disagreements among people who share a basic answer form a special controversy. Presenting them as disagreement over the basic answer exaggerates the split.
questions.rule: Do not inflate a special dispute into a general one.
questions.teaches: By extension, when people share a basic answer, their further disagreements form a special controversy, and reporting these as disagreement over the basic answer exaggerates the split.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: True or false: An author who denies that progress occurs takes part in the special controversy about whether progress will continue indefinitely.
questions.explain: The special controversy is joined only by progress authors. Someone who denies progress has no stake in how long it lasts.
questions.rule: Deniers do not join the special controversy.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: In which of these areas did the authors find that no author genuinely asserts that progress occurs?
options: Fine arts
Technology
Knowledge
Economics
optionExplain: Right: in the authors' opinion no one genuinely asserts aesthetic progress, though some deny it.
Technological progress is one of the areas where some authors assert progress.
Progress in knowledge is asserted by some authors.
Economic progress is asserted by some authors.
questions.explain: The fine arts are the odd one out among the six areas. The card next sets out all six.
questions.rule: No one genuinely asserts progress in the arts.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: Which were among the six areas of the subordinate issues about progress? Select all that apply.
options: Progress in the fine arts
Progress in religion
Progress in family life
Moral progress
Political progress
optionExplain: Right: the fine arts are the sixth area, with their special problem.
Religion is not among the six areas the authors list.
Family life is not among the six areas.
Right: moral progress is one of the six.
Right: political progress is one of the six.
questions.explain: The six are knowledge, technology, economics, politics, morals and the fine arts.
questions.rule: Six areas of progress.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: An author says medicine has improved overall but denies improvement in end-of-life care. How should the map record him?
options: As denying any medical improvement in general
As silent on whether medicine has improved
As denying improvement in end-of-life care only
As agreeing with every other writer who sees improvement
optionExplain: He affirms improvement overall; his denial is limited to one area.
He answers the general question plainly, with yes.
Right: he affirms the general claim and denies it in one area, which is what subordinate issues record.
Writers who see improvement may differ area by area, as he does.
questions.explain: Subordinate issues let the map show where an author who asserts improvement draws the line.
questions.rule: Record affirmations and denials area by area.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: True or false: An author who asserts progress could deny that progress occurs in all six areas.
questions.explain: Progress authors may deny progress in one or more areas, but not in all, since by definition they assert some kind of progress.
questions.rule: A progress author affirms progress somewhere.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: Reviewing assessments of a reorganisation, an analyst finds that in five areas some reviewers report improvement and others deny it, but on morale every reviewer who addresses it denies improvement. How should she report morale?
options: As a joined issue, adding an opposing side to keep the map balanced
As the most hotly disputed of the six areas in the whole review
As an area of agreement among those who address it, not a joined issue
As silence, since no reviewer reports any improvement in morale
optionExplain: Inventing an opposing side fabricates a debate.
Everyone who speaks to it agrees, so it is the least disputed.
Right: like the fine arts for progress, a one-sided area is reported as it is found.
Reviewers do address morale; they deny improvement, which is an answer, not silence.
questions.explain: The authors report the fine arts as an area where some deny progress and none genuinely assert it. By extension, a one-sided area is a finding about the discussion, reported as agreement.
questions.rule: Report a one-sided area as agreement, not as a debate.
questions.teaches: By extension, an area in which every author who speaks denies the phenomenon and none affirms it is a finding about the discussion: report it as a point of agreement rather than as an issue.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: An Example of an Exercise in Syntopical Reading: The Idea of Progress
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a syntopical reader needs to define the issues and analyze the discussion only if he plans to write a book about his research.
questions.explain: The authors say something like their structure must always be done by a syntopical reader, although he does not always have to write a long book reporting it.
questions.rule: Steps four and five are always done; the book is optional.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: According to the authors, which part of syntopical reading may take longer than all the other steps combined?
options: Finding the relevant books and passages
Bringing the authors to common terms
Defining the issues among the authors
Analyzing the discussion as a whole
optionExplain: Right: the authors say finding them may exceed the time for all the other steps together.
Bringing authors to terms is the hardest step intellectually, but not the one named as taking the most time.
Defining issues is demanding, but the time problem lies in finding the material.
Analysis comes last and depends on material already found.
questions.explain: This is the fundamental problem: knowing where to start. The card next explains it and the trouble with advisers.
questions.rule: Finding the material is the big time cost.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: The authors state the paradox: unless you know what books to read, you cannot read syntopically, but unless you can read syntopically, you do not know what to ____.
questions.explain: The circle is the paradox; its practical form is the fundamental problem of where to start.
questions.rule: Knowing what to read and reading syntopically depend on each other.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: A student asks a professor who wrote a book on civil disobedience where to read about it. He lists passages and explains what each really means. What risk does she face?
options: Missing passages that the professor happened to forget to list
Spending too long reading the professor's own book on the subject
Disagreeing with the professor before she understands him
Reading the passages through his interpretation before forming her own
optionExplain: Gaps in the list are possible, but the authors' warning is about interpretation.
His book may be on her list; the problem is his commentary shaping her reading.
Premature disagreement is a different danger from the one the authors name here.
Right: an adviser who has researched the subject finds it hard to say where to read without saying how.
questions.explain: The authors say a researching adviser's guidance may hinder almost as much as it helps, because it brings his reading of the passages with it.
questions.rule: Take the where, not the how.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: An adviser who has not researched the subject offers a reading list. What do the authors warn about?
options: He will tell you exactly how to read each passage he lists
He may know little more than you, though it seems otherwise
His list will be far too long for you to use in practice
He will recommend only works that he himself has written
optionExplain: That is the risk with an adviser who has done special research.
Right: without special research he may know little more than you, though it may seem otherwise to both of you.
Length is not the authors' concern here.
The authors do not raise self-promotion.
questions.explain: The authors describe two kinds of adviser and a different risk for each. The one who has not researched the subject may not know where to look.
questions.rule: Two advisers, two risks.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: A new analyst wants to learn the history of a contested company decision from a senior colleague who argued for it. Which approach best uses his knowledge while limiting the risk the authors describe?
options: Ask him to explain the decision fully before she reads any records at all
Ask him only where the records are, and read them before hearing his view
Avoid him, since a person involved in the decision cannot help in any way
Read only the documents that he says are the important ones to read
optionExplain: Hearing his account first is exactly how an adviser's interpretation shapes the reading.
Right: she takes his knowledge of where to look and forms her own reading first.
He knows where the records are; refusing that help is a needless loss.
His choice of documents may carry his view of the decision.
questions.explain: By extension, the expert's knowledge of where things are can be separated from his interpretation by asking only where, and by reading before listening.
questions.rule: Ask where; read before you hear how.
questions.teaches: By extension, you can use an expert's knowledge while limiting his influence: ask only where to look, and read the sources before hearing his interpretation.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reader who already knows where every idea is discussed in the literature needs no help with the fundamental problem.
questions.explain: The authors call this the theoretical resolution: such a reader needs no help from anybody. The rest of us need a starting point.
questions.rule: Total knowledge of the literature solves the problem, in theory.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: What kind of reference work do the authors say is needed for the fundamental problem?
options: One that summarizes each author's view on every listed topic
One that ranks the best books on each subject from first to last
One that gives an expert's interpretation of each listed passage
One that shows where passages are, without saying how to read them
optionExplain: Summaries interpret, which brings back the adviser's problem.
Rankings judge books before you have read them.
An expert's interpretation is the hindrance the authors warn about.
Right: it locates passages without prejudging their meaning or significance.
questions.explain: The ideal finding aid solves the where without imposing the how. The card next describes the authors' example.
questions.rule: Point, don't interpret.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: Which statements about the Syntopicon are true, according to the authors? Select all that apply.
options: It lists some 3,000 topics
It explains what each passage means
It covers every important book
It was produced in the 1990s
It indexes one set of great books
optionExplain: Right: it lists references under some 3,000 topics.
It points to passages without prejudging their meaning.
Its major defect is that it covers only one set of books.
It was produced in the 1940s.
Right: it is a topical index to Great Books of the Western World.
questions.explain: The Syntopicon is a topical index to one large set of books, listing page references under some 3,000 topics.
questions.rule: One set, about 3,000 topics, no interpretation.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: A reader on courage gets references from a topical index to a collection of classics. Why should she extend her search beyond it?
options: It covers only one set of books, so other relevant works lie outside it
Its references are unreliable and must each be rechecked by hand
It tells her how to read each passage, which would bias her reading
It lists too few topics to include a subject such as courage
optionExplain: Right: this is the defect the authors name: one set of books, with only rough hints about others.
Nothing suggests the references are unreliable.
The index points without interpreting; that is its strength.
With thousands of topics, a subject like courage is the kind it covers.
questions.explain: The index is a starting point, not the whole literature. Modern psychology on courage, for instance, lies outside it.
questions.rule: Start in the index; do not stop there.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the Syntopicon tells the reader what each listed passage means.
questions.explain: Its value is that it tells you where to find passages without saying how to read them.
questions.rule: The index locates; you interpret.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: A researcher can start with a topic index of a large archive that lists pages without comment, or a guide that lists fewer sources but explains what each one shows. By the authors' standard, which is the better starting point?
options: The guide, since its explanations will save the researcher time
The guide, since fewer sources are easier to read and compare
The topic index, since it points to passages without prejudging them
Neither, since any finding tool will bias the research process
optionExplain: Saved time comes at the cost of reading through someone else's interpretation.
Fewer sources narrow the field before she has surveyed it.
Right: it meets the authors' test of pointing without interpreting, and it covers more.
The authors hold that a non-interpreting index avoids that bias.
questions.explain: By extension, a finding aid can be judged by two tests the authors' account implies: does it point without interpreting, and how much of the literature does it cover?
questions.rule: Judge a finding aid by neutrality and coverage.
questions.teaches: By extension, any finding aid can be judged by two tests drawn from the authors' account: whether it points without interpreting, and how much of the relevant literature it covers.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: What would happen if a reader treated a topical index of one set of books as covering the whole literature on her subject?
options: She would read every relevant work on the subject
She would fall into the expert adviser's bias
She would miss relevant works outside the indexed set
She would have no place at all to start from
optionExplain: Only works in the set are indexed, so coverage would be incomplete.
The index does not interpret, so the adviser's bias is not the risk here.
Right: the index covers one set; the rest of the literature would go unread.
The index is exactly a place to start; the problem is stopping there.
questions.explain: The authors call the single-set coverage the index's major defect. Treating the index as complete turns that defect into a gap in the study.
questions.rule: A starting point is not the whole field.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, reading programs that require whole great books, from easier to harder, seldom achieve the desired result.
questions.explain: The authors say it is a matter of general experience that such programs seldom work. The card next describes their alternative.
questions.rule: Whole-book programs often stall.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: The authors say the Syntopicon helps us read in the great books before we have read ____ them.
questions.explain: Reading in means short passages on a chosen subject; reading through means whole books. The first can lead to the second.
questions.rule: Read in before reading through.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: A nurse reads short classic passages on what makes a death good, then reads most of one book and starts on grief. Which of the authors' uses does her experience show?
options: Starting from her interest, then being led further
Learning each author's whole system from summaries
Replacing whole books with short passages for good
Getting an expert's interpretation of each passage
optionExplain: Right: the initiative use got her started; the suggestive use drew her into context and a new topic.
She read passages, not summaries, and was drawn into a whole book.
She ended up reading most of a book, the opposite of replacing books.
The index gives references, not interpretations.
questions.explain: Her interest got her in, and the passages pulled her further: the initiative and suggestive effects together.
questions.rule: Interest starts the reading; context extends it.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the Syntopicon is more useful to the mature scholar than to the beginner.
questions.explain: The authors say it is useful to the scholar but much more useful to the beginner, in three ways.
questions.rule: Most useful to beginners.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: Someone who finds classical music forbidding is advised to work through the symphonies in order, from easiest to hardest. Following the authors' reasoning, what alternative is more likely to work?
options: Begin with the longest symphonies, to get the hardest done first
Read composers' biographies before listening to any of the music
Listen to every symphony once, quickly, without stopping to think
Start with short pieces on a theme she already cares about
optionExplain: Starting with the hardest makes the forbidding feeling worse.
Biographies may help later, but they postpone the music itself.
A rapid pass through everything still lacks a starting interest.
Right: an existing interest gives a way in that a prescribed sequence lacks.
questions.explain: The authors' point about the classics carries over: a prescribed sequence of whole works often fails, while starting from your own question gives you a reason to go on.
questions.rule: Enter a hard field through a question you care about.
questions.teaches: By extension, starting from a question you already care about is a general way into a difficult body of work: interest supplies the motive that a prescribed sequence lacks.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: What does the suggestive effect predict for a reader who starts on one listed passage?
options: She will read only the listed passage and then stop
She may go on to read its context, and much of the book
She will lose interest once the passage comes to an end
She will need an adviser before she can go any further
optionExplain: The authors expect the opposite: the passage draws the reader into its surroundings.
Right: once started on an author, it is hard not to explore the context, the authors say.
The suggestive effect is that interest grows, not that it fades.
Following the context needs no adviser; the book itself leads on.
questions.explain: The authors say that before you know it, you have read a good portion of the book.
questions.rule: One passage tends to lead to the book.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: A topical index lists a passage under the topic justice. What does that tell you about the passage?
options: Exactly what the passage says about justice
That it bears on justice in some way you must work out
That it is the author's main statement on justice
That it agrees with the other passages listed there
optionExplain: The index does not say what the passage means; that is the reader's job.
Right: the topic gives direction, but a passage may bear on it in several ways.
Listing does not mark a passage as the author's main or only statement.
Passages on one topic often conflict; listing implies no agreement.
questions.explain: The topic points the reader in a direction without settling the meaning. The card next shows how this trains interpretation.
questions.rule: The topic directs; you interpret.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: Match each of the three instructive ways to what it involves.
pairs: Discover how a passage bears on its topic
Read passages on one topic against each other
Interpret one passage under several topics
questions.explain: Relevance to a topic, comparison across passages, and multiple interpretation of a single passage are the three ways.
questions.rule: Relevance, comparison, multiple readings.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: A reader interprets one classic passage on friendship as about loyalty, about what friends owe each other, and about the good life, under three different topics. Which instructive effect is she experiencing?
options: Discovering which one topic the passage really belongs to
Learning the author's entire system from a single passage
Finding that the index has misfiled the passage twice
Seeing the passage's amplitude of meaning under several topics
optionExplain: The point is that it belongs to several topics, not to one.
One passage cannot give a whole system; it gives several strains of meaning.
Being listed under several topics is normal for a rich passage, not an error.
Right: this is the third way, multiple interpretation of a passage cited under several topics.
questions.explain: A rich passage bears on several topics. Reading it for each brings out different strains of its meaning.
questions.rule: One rich passage, several readings.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: Two passages from different authors on the same topic contrast sharply. According to the authors, what can reading them together do?
options: Accentuate the meaning of each by contrast
Show which of the two authors is correct
Cancel them out, leaving neither meaningful
Prove that the topic was badly chosen
optionExplain: Right: the meaning of contrasting passages is accentuated when they are read against one another.
Contrast sharpens understanding; it does not settle truth.
Contrast makes each clearer, not emptier.
Conflict on a topic is expected; it does not show the topic was poor.
questions.explain: This is the second instructive way: reading passages against each other sharpens the interpretation of each.
questions.rule: Contrast sharpens meaning.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: A reader says: since this passage is listed under three topics, it can mean whatever each topic needs. What has she missed?
options: A passage can belong to only one topic at a time
Listed passages should not be interpreted at all
Each reading must still fit the text of the passage
The last topic listed is the passage's true one
optionExplain: Rich passages do belong to several topics; that is the third way's premise.
Interpretation is exactly the skill the topics train.
Right: multiple interpretation finds strains of meaning in the text; it does not invent them.
The order of listing does not rank the topics.
questions.explain: The authors speak of interpreting a passage somewhat differently for different topics, drawing on its amplitude of meaning. The readings come from the passage, not from the topic alone.
questions.rule: Many readings, all grounded in the text.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: A student reads five historians on one event. Her reading of one makes him contradict the other four on a basic fact that none of them disputes elsewhere. What does the second instructive way suggest she do?
options: Conclude he is wrong on the fact, since four historians outweigh one
Ignore the other four historians and trust her first reading of him
Recheck her reading of him, since comparison can expose a misreading
Drop that historian from her study, since he does not fit the rest
optionExplain: Majority may matter for truth, but the first question is whether she read him correctly.
Ignoring the others throws away the check that comparison provides.
Right: reading passages against each other sharpens interpretation, and an odd clash may mean she misread.
Dropping him avoids the question instead of answering it.
questions.explain: By extension, comparing passages on one topic is a check as well as a sharpener: a reading that makes one source clash oddly with all the rest deserves a second look.
questions.rule: Use other passages to test your reading of one.
questions.teaches: By extension, comparing several sources on one question checks your interpretation of each: a reading that makes one passage clash oddly with all the others deserves a second look.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: True or false: The authors say multiple interpretation tends to make the mind habitually alert to the many strains of meaning that a rich passage can contain.
questions.explain: Besides being a basic exercise in reading, multiple interpretation builds a habit of alertness to layered meaning.
questions.rule: Multiple readings build alertness.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, syntopical reading can be done only with the help of the Syntopicon.
questions.explain: The authors distinguish the general level of reading, which applies widely, from reading the great books with the Syntopicon. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Syntopical reading is wider than the index.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: What does Syntopical reading with a capital S mean, according to the authors?
options: Reading the great books with the help of the Syntopicon
Any reading of two or more books on a single subject
Reading one great book analytically from start to end
Reading the Syntopicon itself from cover to cover
optionExplain: Right: capital S names this particular use of the index.
That is the small-s, general sense.
Analytical reading of one book is a different level.
The index is consulted, not read straight through.
questions.explain: Capital S is the narrow sense tied to the index; small s is the general level of reading.
questions.rule: Capital S: great books with the Syntopicon.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: A team studying trust in online marketplaces starts with classic passages found through the index, then reads mostly economics papers. How do the two senses apply to their project?
options: The whole project is capital-S, since it began in the index
Neither applies, since most of what they read is modern
Only the economics papers count as syntopical reading
The index start is capital-S; the project as a whole is small-s
optionExplain: Beginning in the index does not make the whole project capital-S.
Small-s syntopical reading covers modern works too.
The classic passages are part of the project, read syntopically as well.
Right: the capital-S part forms one piece of a wider small-s project.
questions.explain: The authors say capital-S reading can be part of any small-s project. Here it is the opening part.
questions.rule: Capital S can open a small-s project.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: Sort each activity by whether it is capital-S Syntopical reading or syntopical reading in the general sense only.

items.t: Reading great-books passages on justice found through the index
Following the index to classic passages on love
Using the index to find what Aristotle says on friendship
Comparing recent journal articles on sleep
Reading housing policy reports side by side
Comparing modern marketing textbooks on one question

questions.explain: Capital S requires the great books and the index. Comparing other works on one subject is syntopical reading in the wider sense.
questions.rule: Index plus great books is capital S; the rest is small s.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: A company calls all its customer interviews by the name of the app it first used to record them. A new hire assumes interviews must be done in that app. What confusion, parallel to the authors' distinction, has she made?
options: Taking the app for a better tool than any other on offer
Taking a general practice for the one tool that named it
Taking interviews for a less useful method than surveys
Taking the company's name for the name of the app
optionExplain: Whether the app is better is a separate question.
Right: as with small-s and capital-S, the practice is wider than the tool that lent its name.
Her confusion is about the name, not the value of interviews.
The confusion is between practice and tool, not company and app.
questions.explain: By extension, when a tool lends its name to a practice, the practice can outgrow it. Confusing the two makes the method seem to depend on one resource.
questions.rule: A practice can outgrow the tool that named it.
questions.teaches: By extension, a named tool can lend its name to a general practice, but the practice outruns the tool; confusing the two makes the method seem to depend on one resource.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: The Syntopicon and How to Use It
questions.q: True or false: The authors suggest it may be wise, in any syntopical project, to begin with Syntopical reading of the great books.
questions.explain: The authors say perhaps it would always be wise to start there, while stressing that small-s syntopical reading reaches much further.
questions.rule: Perhaps start with the great books.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: On the Principles That Underlie Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Critics say syntopical reading distorts authors by translating their terms into the reader's. How do the authors reply?
options: Authors' terms are sacrosanct, so the critics are right
Translation is difficult, but the difficult is not the impossible
Translation is easy for any careful and patient reader
Terminology does not matter at all, only conclusions do
optionExplain: The authors reject the claim that an author's terms are sacrosanct.
Right: the authors grant the difficulty and deny the impossibility.
The authors call it difficult, not easy.
Terms matter a great deal; that is why step two is so demanding.
questions.explain: The authors agree translation between terminologies is hard and insist it can be done. The card next sets out all three objections.
questions.rule: Difficult, not impossible.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: On the Principles That Underlie Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Match each objection to the authors' reply.
pairs: The difficult is not the impossible
Books can talk through an interpreter
questions.explain: Translation is possible though hard; the reader interprets between books as an interpreter between people; and what is said can be understood apart from how.
questions.rule: Translate, interpret, attend to content.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: On the Principles That Underlie Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A colleague tells a reader that an ancient physician and a modern epidemiologist cannot be compared at all, since they belong to different worlds. Which reply follows the authors?
options: The colleague is right, so she should study only modern writers
The two share a language, so no interpreting is needed at all
Different worlds can be compared only by counting shared words
With care, the reader can act as interpreter so the two books talk
optionExplain: The authors reject the separate-universes objection.
They do need interpreting; the point is that interpreting is possible.
Counting words compares vocabularies, not views.
Right: as with Aristotle and an interpreter, books can talk through the syntopical reader.
questions.explain: The authors' reply to the separate-universes objection is that the reader serves as interpreter, knowing both books as well as she can.
questions.rule: The reader is the interpreter between books.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: On the Principles That Underlie Syntopical Reading
questions.q: What point do the authors make with the example of being told to follow Corridor B to the exit?
options: What is said can be understood and tested, whatever the tone
Tone of voice carries all of the meaning in human speech
Directions are given in a neutral tone, unlike arguments
People react to tone far more strongly than to content
optionExplain: Right: whatever the tone, you can follow Corridor B and find out whether the speaker was right.
The example is meant to show the opposite.
The tone could be anything; the point is that it does not decide the content.
Reactions to tone are real, but the example shows content is understood too.
questions.explain: The example answers the style objection: human communication has a rational content that can be understood apart from manner.
questions.rule: Content survives any tone.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: On the Principles That Underlie Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A reader writes: since translating terms is possible, I can put each author into my terms without knowing his book well. What has she missed?
options: Translation between terms is impossible after all
She ought to use one author's terms for all of them
The interpreter must know both books as well as he can
She ought to avoid quoting the authors in her report
optionExplain: The authors defend the possibility; her error lies elsewhere.
Adopting one author's terms is the trap of step two.
Right: the authors say care is required and the reader should know both languages, both books, as well as possible.
Quoting is the safeguard the authors recommend.
questions.explain: Possible does not mean easy. The authors' reply comes with a condition: the interpreter must know both books well.
questions.rule: Possible, with care and knowledge.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: On the Principles That Underlie Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A critic says a modern reader cannot put a medieval writer in conversation with a modern one, because each lives in his own universe. What is the strongest reply, extending the authors' argument?
options: The critic is right about medieval writers but wrong about the modern ones
Medieval and modern writers use the same words, so no real gap exists
If that held, a modern reader could not understand the medieval writer even alone
Only trained historians can read medieval writers in the first place
optionExplain: The critic's claim is about the gap between them, which this does not answer.
Their words often differ; the reply does not depend on shared words.
Right: reading any author from another age already bridges the gap the critic calls impassable.
Training helps, but the objection would forbid understanding altogether.
questions.explain: By extension, the objection proves too much: if each author were a closed universe, no one could read an author from another age at all.
questions.rule: An objection that forbids all understanding proves too much.
questions.teaches: By extension, the separate-universes objection proves too much: if it held, no reader could understand an author from another age even alone, since reading him is already interpretation across time.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.section: On the Principles That Underlie Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: If someone gave you directions to the exit in an angry tone instead of a calm one, the authors' reply implies you could still test what he said by following the directions.
questions.explain: In the authors' Corridor B example, the directions are right or wrong whatever the tone, and you find out by following them. Tone matters, especially where emotional relations are the content, but there is a rational content too.
questions.rule: Tone matters, but it is not everything.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: What are the two main stages of syntopical reading in the authors' summary?
options: Surveying the field, then syntopical reading proper
Analytical reading, then inspectional reading
Reading the books, then writing up the report
Finding the issues, then deciding the truth
optionExplain: Right: a preparatory survey, then the five steps of syntopical reading proper.
This reverses the levels and leaves out the syntopical steps.
A report may come at the end, but the two stages the authors name are survey and reading.
Deciding the truth is not a stage; the analysis stays dialectical.
questions.explain: Preparation surveys the field; syntopical reading proper takes the five steps. The card next details the preparation.
questions.rule: Survey, then read syntopically.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Which sources do the authors name for creating a tentative bibliography? Select all that apply.
options: Newspaper book reviews
Library catalogues
Advisers
Bibliographies in books
Bestseller lists
optionExplain: Reviews are not among the sources the authors list.
Right: catalogues are one of the three sources named.
Right: advisers are named, with the cautions given in the Syntopicon section.
Right: the bibliographies in good books on the subject are the third source.
Popularity is not among the sources the authors name.
questions.explain: Catalogues, advisers and the bibliographies in books are the three sources the summary names.
questions.rule: Catalogues, advisers, bibliographies.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
