questions.q: While inspecting her list on civic trust, a reader adds three works on local associations and drops five on trust in banks. What does this show?
options: A mistake in the original list she should have avoided
The beginning of syntopical reading proper
That her bibliography is now complete and final
The second preparatory step modifying the first
optionExplain: A tentative list is expected to change; that is not a mistake.
She is still preparing: judging which books are germane.
The list remains tentative; more changes may come.
Right: the authors note that inspection, in particular, serves to modify the bibliography.
questions.explain: The preparatory steps interact: inspecting reveals what the subject is, which reshapes the list.
questions.rule: Inspection reshapes the list.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the two preparatory steps are strictly separate in time, with the first finished before the second begins.
questions.explain: The summary notes that the two steps are not strictly chronologically distinct; they affect each other, with inspection modifying the bibliography.
questions.rule: The preparatory steps interact.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A buyer lists ten suppliers from a directory, then inspects each and learns that her real need is fast delivery, not low price. What should she do with the list?
options: Keep it fixed and rank the ten suppliers by delivery speed alone
Revise it, adding fast suppliers the directory missed and dropping others
Order at once from the cheapest supplier on the original list
Discard what she learned and inspect the same list once again
optionExplain: Ranking the original ten ignores suppliers the directory missed.
Right: what inspection taught her about her need should change the list itself, not only its ranking.
She has learned price is not her main need.
Throwing away what she learned wastes the inspection.
questions.explain: By extension, any search that starts with a guessed list improves when examining the candidates is allowed to reshape the list, as inspection reshapes a bibliography.
questions.rule: Let examination reshape the list, not only rank it.
questions.teaches: By extension, any search that starts from a guessed list, of suppliers, candidates or sources, improves when examining the candidates is allowed to change the list itself, not only to rank it.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: Put these steps in the order the authors' summary gives them.
items: Create a tentative bibliography
Inspect all the books on it
Find the most relevant passages
Bring the authors to terms
Define the issues
Analyze the discussion
questions.explain: Two preparatory steps come first, then the steps of syntopical reading proper, from passages and terms through issues to the analysis.
questions.rule: Prepare, then passages, terms, issues, analysis.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: In the authors' summary, which issues should come first when the discussion is analyzed?
options: The most hotly disputed issues
The more general issues
The issues with the most authors
The most recently raised issues
optionExplain: Heat of dispute is not the ordering principle.
Right: more general issues precede less general ones.
Number of authors does not set the order.
Recency does not decide the order.
questions.explain: The summary orders issues by generality. The card next sets out what else the summary adds.
questions.rule: General issues first.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: The summary says one way to keep dialectical detachment is to accompany each interpretation of an author's views with an actual ____ from his text.
questions.explain: A quotation lets readers check that the interpretation is fair.
questions.rule: Pair interpretation with quotation.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A report on immigration puts the issue of whether nations may restrict entry at all before the issue of how many to admit. Why is that the right order?
options: It is the issue that the largest number of authors write about
It is the issue that arose most recently in the long debate
It is the issue the reader herself thinks matters the most
It is more general, and the narrower issue depends on its answer
optionExplain: Numbers of authors do not set the order.
Recency is not the principle.
The reader's own view of importance would bring in partiality.
Right: how many to admit arises only for those who say entry may be restricted, so the general issue comes first.
questions.explain: General before less general lets each narrower issue appear with the answer that gives rise to it.
questions.rule: Order by generality and dependence.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: True or false: According to the summary, neutral terms must be words that every author actually used.
questions.explain: The summary says the authors can be interpreted as employing the terms whether they actually employ the words or not.
questions.rule: Neutral terms need not be the authors' words.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: A report on a city budget debate lists six issues separately. On inspection, four of them stem from one disagreement over whether to raise taxes. What would showing the relations among the issues achieve?
options: It would reveal one underlying dispute behind four apparent ones
It would show that the four issues are trivial and can be dropped
It would prove that the tax side is right on all four issues
It would lengthen the report without adding any information
optionExplain: Right: linking the issues shows that four entries are faces of one disagreement.
Being linked does not make them trivial; they matter as parts of one dispute.
Showing relations takes no side.
The relations are information the separate list lacked.
questions.explain: By extension, one disagreement can surface as several issues. Showing how issues relate prevents a report from counting one dispute as many.
questions.rule: Link issues to avoid counting one dispute as many.
questions.teaches: By extension, showing the relations among issues prevents double counting: one underlying disagreement can surface as several issues, and linking them shows it is one dispute, not many.

questions.unitTitle: The Fourth Level of Reading: Syntopical Reading
questions.q: One author out of thirty cannot be read in the reader's neutral terms. Does the terminology fail the summary's standard?
options: Yes: every single author must fit the terms exactly
Yes: the terms must now become that author's own
Not necessarily: all or the great majority must fit
No: fit with the authors does not matter at all
optionExplain: The summary's standard is all or the great majority, not every one.
Switching to one author's terms is the trap of step two.
Right: the summary asks that all, or the great majority, can be interpreted in the terms.
Fit matters; the terms must work for nearly all the authors.
questions.explain: The summary's wording allows for a few authors who do not fit, though the reader should check whether the terms need refining.
questions.rule: All or the great majority.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, once you have learned the rules of reading, it matters little which books you practise them on.
questions.explain: The authors say the method needs fit materials: books that call for it. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: The rules need books worth applying them to.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: The authors give the word means two senses: the rules of reading, and the ____ you read.
questions.explain: Means can be the method, the rules, or the materials, the books you apply the rules to. Each is useless without the other.
questions.rule: Means are both method and materials.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: Priya has studied the rules of analytical reading and wants to keep improving. For a year she applies them only to light thrillers and short how-to articles. What do the authors' remarks predict?
options: Steady gains, since practising the rules on anything builds skill
Faster gains, since easy texts let her practise more rules an hour
Gains in speed only, since easy books train the eye, not the mind
Little improvement, since these texts do not call for the method
optionExplain: Practice does build skill, but only on material that demands it; the authors say books well within your capacity do not improve you.
More repetitions sound useful, but rules applied where they are not needed are not really exercised.
Speed is not the authors' point here; they say such reading leaves your skill, of any kind, essentially where it was.
Right: the method needs materials that call for it, and amusing or fact-giving texts do not.
questions.explain: Method without fit materials is as useless as materials without method. Thrillers and how-to snippets amuse or inform, but they leave a reader's skill where it was.
questions.rule: Easy materials leave the method unexercised.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, since the rules apply to any kind of book, every book you read deserves the full analytical treatment.
questions.explain: The rules fit any kind of book, but many books do not call for the full analytical method. Fitting every kind is not the same as being needed for every book.
questions.rule: Fitting every kind of book is not needing every book.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: A cooking school teaches superb knife and sauce technique, but its students practise only on toast and instant noodles. Reasoning from the authors' point about means, what second ability should the school also teach?
options: Choosing dishes that put the techniques to real use
Cooking faster, so more dishes fit into each lesson
Memorizing more recipes, so students know more dishes
Relying on ingredients, since good food cooks itself
optionExplain: Right: technique grows only on material that demands it, so picking that material is a skill of its own.
Speed adds repetitions of the same easy task, and easy tasks do not exercise the technique.
More recipes is more information, a change in quantity rather than in skill.
This swaps method for materials, the opposite mistake: materials without method are as useless as method without materials.
questions.explain: If the materials never demand the technique, the technique does not grow. So the school must teach students to pick dishes worth their skill, as a reader must pick books worth the rules.
questions.rule: Choosing material is part of growing a skill.
questions.teaches: The authors draw the consequence that a reader needs two abilities: to read well, and to recognize which books make the demands that improvement requires.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: Suppose a reader picks only the most demanding books she can find but reads them passively, without using the rules. By the authors' account, what follows?
options: She improves fast, since hard books force the method on her
She gains a lot of wisdom but no reading skill at all
She gains little, as materials without method are as useless
She gains as much as an active reader, only more slowly
optionExplain: Hard books invite the method, but they cannot apply it for her; passive reading leaves them unread in the authors' sense.
Wisdom from a good book comes through reading it well, so passive reading does not deliver it either.
Right: the authors say materials with no method are as useless as a method with no materials.
The authors tie gains to active, effortful reading; passivity is not a slower version of it.
questions.explain: The rule cuts both ways. Fit books without the method waste the books, as surely as the method without fit books wastes the method.
questions.rule: Good books need an active method too.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: According to the authors, which books will do most to improve your reading skill?
options: Books on subjects you already know well, so you can follow them
Books that seem beyond your present capacity
Short books, so that you can finish many more of them
Books written for beginners in the field you are learning
optionExplain: Familiar subjects feel productive, but a book you can follow easily does not make you stretch.
Right: only books that seem over your head make you stretch, and stretching is how you learn.
Finishing many books adds to the count, but count is not skill.
Beginner books are within your reach by design, so they make few new demands.
questions.explain: The authors say improvement comes from books that seem beyond you. The card next explains why, and why they need not frighten you.
questions.rule: Books over your head make you stretch.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: True or false: The authors promise that applying the rules will let you master any hard book at the first attempt.
questions.explain: They say no book is wholly out of your grasp if you apply the rules, but also that the rules work no immediate miracles. Some books keep extending even the best readers.
questions.rule: Within reach is not within reach at once.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: Leo wants his next two books to sharpen his analytical reading. Which choices fit the authors' advice? Choose two.
options: A popular history he can read in two evenings without pausing
The third novel by a favourite author whose style he knows well
A philosophy classic he expects to struggle with in places
A dense treatise on a subject he has never studied
A short summary of a hard classic, to get its ideas without strain
A hobby magazine on a topic he already knows inside out
optionExplain: An easy read is pleasant, but it uses only the skills he has.
Familiar style means few new demands; comfort is not stretch.
Right: a book he expects to struggle with is one that seems beyond him.
Right: unfamiliar and dense, it will make him reach.
A summary removes the very struggle that would stretch him.
Knowing a topic inside out means the magazine asks nothing new of him.
questions.explain: The authors' test is whether a book seems beyond you. The classic and the treatise both do; the others are well within Leo's capacity.
questions.rule: Choose books you expect to struggle with.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: A friend says that because a treatise seemed beyond him after one chapter, it is too hard for him, and he will wait until he is a better reader before trying it. By the authors' account, where does his reasoning go wrong?
options: Seeming beyond him is the mark of a book worth practising on
One chapter is too small a sample to judge any book's difficulty
He should read a summary first, then come back to the treatise
Treatises are meant for experts, so he was right to put it down
optionExplain: Right: the authors say the books to practise on are the ones that seem beyond you, and that the rules can bring them within reach.
Sample size matters, but even a whole book that seemed beyond him would be a reason to read it, not to wait.
A summary can help later, but it sidesteps the struggle that would make him a better reader.
The authors hold that no book is wholly out of a reader's grasp with the rules; expertise is not the gate.
questions.explain: He treats the feeling that a book is beyond him as a reason to stop. On the authors' account it is the reason to start: he becomes a better reader by working on such books, not by waiting.
questions.rule: Feeling outmatched is a reason to read on.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: A new runner finds that her faster training runs leave her winded, while easy jogs feel fine. She wonders whether the strain means she is doing something wrong. Reasoning by analogy with the authors' advice on books, how should she read the strain?
options: As a sign to go back to easy jogs until hard runs feel easy
As the stretching itself, the part of training that builds her
As proof that her form is wrong and needs fixing by a coach
As wasted effort, since only comfortable training can last
optionExplain: Waiting until hard runs feel easy is the friend's mistake with the treatise: the hard runs are what make them easier.
Right: as with a book over your head, the reach is where growth happens.
Form may need work, but strain on its own does not show that; it is what a demanding task feels like.
Comfort can be kept up, but comfortable work is the jog that leaves her where she is.
questions.explain: By analogy, the discomfort of reaching is not a sign of failure but the experience of stretching. Easy jogs, like easy books, use the capacity she already has.
questions.rule: Strain is what stretching feels like.
questions.teaches: By analogy with physical training, the strain of reading a book over your head is the stretching itself, not a sign that you are failing at it.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: Suppose that, after years of practice, a reader finds every book on his shelves now easy. On the authors' account, what should he do next?
options: Stop practising, since he has learned all that reading can teach
Reread his old books faster, to keep his skills from fading
Turn to lighter books, since hard ones have no more to teach him
Seek out books that still extend him, which the authors say exist
optionExplain: The authors say some books keep extending a reader however good he becomes, so there is always more to learn.
Speed on easy books keeps him where he is; it does not make him stretch.
This reverses the advice: the books that still extend him are the ones that can teach him.
Right: the books that keep extending even a skilled reader are, the authors say, the very ones to seek out.
questions.explain: Change the condition from struggling beginner to skilled reader and the advice keeps its shape: find the books that are still beyond you. The authors say such books exist for every reader.
questions.rule: As you improve, move to books still beyond you.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: According to the authors, which kind of great book is likely, in the long run, to be the most demanding to read?
options: Great works of mathematics, because of their symbols
Great works of science, because of their technical terms
Great works of history, because of their sheer length
Great poetical works, such as epics and plays
optionExplain: Symbols look forbidding, but mathematical authors state their terms and steps with great care.
Many readers think so, but scientific authors help you come to terms, which makes their books easier in the long run.
Length adds time, not the kind of difficulty the authors mean.
Right: poetical works lack the helps scientific authors give, so they tend to demand the most.
questions.explain: The authors expect poetical works to be the hardest in the long run. The card next gives their reason.
questions.rule: The hardest books may be poems.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: Which helps do the authors say great scientific authors give their readers? Choose three.
options: Care in making their terms clear
Pointing out their key propositions
Setting out their main arguments
Vivid characters to hold the reader
A summary of rival views per chapter
optionExplain: Right: scientific authors help you come to terms.
Right: they help you identify the key propositions.
Right: they state their main arguments.
Characters belong to imaginative works, and the authors do not list them as a scientific help.
Some textbooks do this, but it is not among the helps the authors name.
questions.explain: The three helps match the steps of analytical reading: terms, propositions and arguments. Poetical works leave all three to the reader.
questions.rule: Science helps with terms, propositions and arguments.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: True or false: By the authors' reasoning, a scientific book whose author neither made his terms clear nor stated his arguments would lose much of the advantage that makes science easier than poetry.
questions.explain: The advantage the authors credit to scientific books is the help their authors give with terms, propositions and arguments. Remove those helps and that advantage goes with them.
questions.rule: The ease of science comes from its authors' helps.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: A book club has spent two years on scientific and philosophical classics and wants its next project to be the most demanding yet. Following the authors, what might it choose?
options: Another physics classic, since science is the hardest field
A great epic poem, since it offers none of science's helps
A logic textbook, since formal reasoning is hardest to follow
A long modern biography, since length is the real difficulty
optionExplain: This is the very mistake the authors name: assuming the endless challenge lies only in science.
Right: without help with terms, propositions and arguments, a great poem leaves all the work to the reader.
Formal reasoning is demanding, but a textbook states its terms and steps, the kind of help that eases reading.
Length takes time, but it is not the difficulty the authors have in mind.
questions.explain: The authors think great poetical works are likely the hardest in the long run, because their authors give none of the helps scientific authors do.
questions.rule: For the hardest reading, look to great imaginative works.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: Using the authors' reasoning, why can a short lyric poem take longer to understand than a long instruction manual for a dishwasher?
options: The poem uses rarer words, and vocabulary is the main barrier
The manual states its terms and steps; the poem leaves them to you
The manual covers fewer ideas, though it fills far more pages
A poem is meant only to be felt, so no one fully understands it
optionExplain: Rare words can slow you, but many great poems use plain words and remain hard.
Right: the difficulty lies in how much of the work of finding terms, claims and structure the text leaves to the reader.
The manual may have fewer ideas, but the authors' point is about help given, not the count of ideas.
The authors treat poems as works to be read well, not as beyond understanding.
questions.explain: The manual, like a scientific book, names its parts and states each step. The poem gives no such guidance, so the reader must find everything for himself, which takes longer however short the text.
questions.rule: Difficulty tracks how much a text leaves to the reader.
questions.teaches: By extension, a text's difficulty depends less on its length or vocabulary than on how much of the work of locating terms, claims and structure it leaves to the reader.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: A student reads a great epic and a great scientific treatise for the first time and finds the epic easier and more rewarding. By the authors' account, what is the best conclusion?
options: The epic is the easier book, so she can set it aside for good
She misread the treatise, since science is easier at first
Her impression fits; the epic may still prove harder over time
She should reread the treatise until it feels as easy
optionExplain: A first impression of ease does not show a book is exhausted; the authors expect great poetry to demand more over time.
The authors allow that you may get more from Homer than Newton the first time, so her reaction is no sign of misreading.
Right: the authors say you may get more from Homer at first, yet Homer is in many ways harder to read than Newton.
Making the treatise feel easy is not the goal, and it does not bear on which book is harder in the long run.
questions.explain: The authors' claim stops short of the first reading: a poem can be easier and richer at first and still be the harder book in the long run.
questions.rule: Easier at first can still mean harder in the long run.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, if a book is hard to read, its difficulty shows that it is worth the effort.
questions.explain: Bad books are hard to read too, for a different reason. The card next shows how the two kinds of difficulty differ.
questions.rule: Difficulty alone does not show worth.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: According to the authors, a good book ____ you for trying to read it, and the best books do so most of all.
questions.explain: A good book pays back the effort of reading it; a bad one gives nothing for the struggle because there is nothing in it to pin down.
questions.rule: Good books reward the effort.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: Tom spends three evenings on a management book. Each time he tries to restate a chapter's point, it turns into a slogan he cannot tie to any claim or argument. What do the authors' remarks suggest?
options: The book must be over his head, so he should keep at it longer
The book may be bad, and more struggle is unlikely to repay him
He should find a commentary that explains the book to him
He should memorize the slogans, since they are its main point
optionExplain: Persisting is right with a good hard book, but his repeated honest attempts find nothing to grasp, which is the sign of a bad one.
Right: a book that slips away every time he pins it down may have nothing to pin down.
A commentary cannot supply content the book lacks, and the authors advise doing your own work first.
Memorizing slogans is not understanding; there is no claim behind them to learn.
questions.explain: The mark of a bad book is that effort yields nothing: no terms, no propositions, no argument. After honest tries, the authors say such a struggle is not worth it.
questions.rule: If effort finds nothing to grasp, the book may be empty.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: Sort each experience by what it suggests about a hard book.
groups: Sign of a good difficult book

items.t: Rereading a hard passage brings its claim into focus
Each attempt to state the point slips away
Key words settle into one definite sense as you work
Restated plainly, its sentences say almost nothing
The struggle leaves you understanding more than before
Repeated effort yields no terms, propositions or argument

questions.explain: Both kinds of book resist. The difference shows in what the effort produces: understanding from a good book, nothing from a bad one.
questions.rule: Judge a hard book by what the effort yields.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: A council member's speech is full of long words and hard to follow. A listener transcribes it and tries to state each sentence as a plain claim. By the authors' reasoning, what can this test reveal?
options: Whether the speaker is honest, since jargon is a sign of deceit
Whether the listener has the schooling to follow such a speech
Whether the difficulty hides real content or covers its absence
Whether the speech will be popular, since plain words win votes
optionExplain: Jargon may be a habit rather than a lie; the test shows whether there is content, not what the speaker intends.
Restating tests the listener too, but here it is also a test of the text: empty sentences cannot be restated as claims.
Right: rich difficulty survives being put in plain words, while empty difficulty disappears.
Popularity is a separate question from whether the speech says anything.
questions.explain: A good difficult text has something to pin down, so plain restatement brings it out. An empty one has nothing, so plain restatement shows how little was said.
questions.rule: Plain restatement separates rich from empty difficulty.
questions.teaches: By extension, restating a difficult text in plain words tests the text as well as the reader: rich difficulty survives restatement, while empty difficulty disappears in it.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: After one chapter of a demanding philosophy classic, Mia says that since she could not pin anything down, it must be a bad book and not worth the effort. By the authors' account, what is wrong with her conclusion?
options: Philosophy classics are good by definition, so it cannot be bad
Bad books are easy to read, so this difficulty proves it is good
She should read a summary of it before judging the classic
A good book also resists at first; she has not yet done the work
optionExplain: A book's reputation does not settle its worth; the point is that she has not tested it yet.
The authors say bad books are hard too, so difficulty proves nothing either way.
A summary would replace her own reading rather than test the book.
Right: resistance at first is common to good and bad books; only honest work with the rules tells them apart.
questions.explain: She judged the book empty before doing the work that would show whether anything is there. Early resistance does not separate a good book from a bad one.
questions.rule: Judge a book empty only after honest work.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: True or false: By the authors' account, if Mia then works through the whole book with the rules and still finds no terms, propositions or argument to grasp, she may fairly stop struggling with it.
questions.explain: Change the condition from one chapter to an honest, complete effort and the verdict changes. A book that yields nothing to full effort fits the authors' description of a bad book, which is not worth the struggle.
questions.rule: After full honest effort, emptiness is the book's fault.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: According to the authors, what is the more important reward, in the long run, of reading a good difficult book?
options: Learning more about the world and yourself
Greater skill in reading other hard books
A larger store of facts about its subject
A faster reading speed on later books
optionExplain: Right: the authors rank learning about life above the gain in skill.
Better skill is a real reward, the first of the two, but the authors call the second more important.
Facts make you more knowledgeable, which the authors distinguish from what the best books give.
Speed is not one of the rewards the authors name here.
questions.explain: The authors name two rewards and rank one above the other. The card next sets them out.
questions.rule: Good books teach about life as well as reading.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: Match each term with its meaning in the authors' account.
pairs: The first reward of tackling a good, difficult book
A deeper awareness of the enduring truths of human life
What books of information alone can give
questions.explain: Skill is the first reward and wisdom the second, more important one. Knowledge is what informative books give, and the authors keep it distinct from wisdom.
questions.rule: Skill, wisdom and knowledge are three different gains.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: Which reader has become wiser, in the authors' sense, rather than only more knowledgeable?
options: Raj, who can now list the date of every battle in a long war
Omar, who has learned the chemical makeup of a dozen minerals
Lena, who now sees better why loyalty and justice can clash
Bea, who can recite the plots of twenty well-known novels
optionExplain: Dates are facts; knowing more of them makes Raj more knowledgeable, not wiser.
Chemical facts add to Omar's knowledge without deepening his grasp of human life.
Right: a deeper grasp of a lasting human conflict is the awareness the authors call wisdom.
Plots remembered are information about books, not insight drawn from them.
questions.explain: Wisdom, for the authors, concerns the great and enduring truths of human life. Facts, however many, add to knowledge.
questions.rule: Wisdom deepens; information accumulates.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: A colleague says he reads hard classics only to become a better reader, and that once his skill is good enough he will stop. Suppose he does reach that point. What do the authors suggest he would be giving up?
options: Nothing, since skill is the only lasting gain from hard books
The second, larger reward: what good books teach about life
Speed, which he can keep only by reading classics every day
Facts, which classics supply better than any other books
optionExplain: This is his assumption, but the authors name a second reward they think matters more.
Right: even with skill to spare, good books go on teaching about the world and oneself.
Speed is not a reward the authors discuss here.
Facts are what informative books give; the authors do not rank classics by their facts.
questions.explain: Even when the first reward, skill, has been earned, the second remains. On the authors' account the wisdom is the more important reason to keep reading.
questions.rule: Skill is not the end of reading.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: A young doctor spends a year working beside a wise older physician. She leaves a sharper diagnostician, and also with a changed sense of how to sit with dying patients. By analogy with the authors' two rewards, which gain matches the one they rank higher?
options: The sharper skill at reaching a diagnosis
The many new facts about rare diseases
The large number of cases she has seen
The changed sense of how to be with the dying
optionExplain: Skill matches the first reward, the one the authors rank lower.
New facts make her more knowledgeable, not wiser.
A count of cases is experience in quantity, not the deeper awareness the authors mean.
Right: a deeper grasp of a lasting human situation is the analogue of the wisdom good books give.
questions.explain: The year gave her both kinds of gain. The skill matches the first reward; the deeper sense of how to meet death matches the second, which the authors value more.
questions.rule: Look for both gains in any demanding encounter.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the two rewards are not special to books: any demanding encounter with a better mind can yield both a sharper skill and a deeper grasp of human life.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: True or false: By the authors' account, a reader who finishes a good book much better informed about its subject is, for that reason, wiser.
questions.explain: Being better informed makes you more knowledgeable, which even books of fact alone can do. The authors reserve wiser for a deeper awareness of enduring truths of human life.
questions.rule: Better informed does not mean wiser.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the greatest books are valuable mainly because they give final answers to life's hardest questions.
questions.explain: The authors say some of these questions have no final answer at all. The card next shows what the greatest books offer instead.
questions.rule: Great books help you think; they do not close the question.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: Which matters do the authors name as ones on which no one can have the last word? Choose three.
options: The relation between parents and children
Nature and its laws
The relation between men and women
The rules for moving pieces in chess
The spelling of common English words
optionExplain: Right: the authors list it among everyday matters with no last word.
Right: final understanding of nature and its laws, they say, has not been and will not be reached.
Right: another of the everyday relations they name.
Chess rules are fixed by agreement; a question about them has a settled answer.
Spelling can be looked up; it is a settled matter, not an enduring problem.
questions.explain: The authors' list runs from science and philosophy to everyday relations. What these share is that no one can have the final word on them.
questions.rule: Some questions, great and everyday, have no final answer.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: Nadia is torn over whether to care for her ageing mother at home. A friend gives her a great novel about duty within families. On the authors' view, what can she reasonably expect from it?
options: Help in thinking about the question more deeply, not a verdict
A clear answer, since great authors settled such questions
Little of use, since novels deal only with invented people
Practical facts about care homes, their costs and services
optionExplain: Right: the greatest books help readers think better about questions that have no final answer.
The authors say no one has the last word on such relations, great authors included.
The authors count great imaginative works among the books that teach about life.
Facts may help her decision, but they are not what a great novel offers.
questions.explain: Her question is one of the everyday relations on which no one has the last word. A great book can deepen her thinking about it, because its author thought about it better than most.
questions.rule: Expect deeper thinking, not a verdict.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: Which question best fits the authors' account of matters on which no one can have the last word?
options: How many bones there are in an adult human hand
Which train reaches the city first tomorrow morning
How to change the oil in a car engine safely
What a good relation between friends asks of each
optionExplain: This has a settled answer that a reference book gives.
A timetable settles this; it is a question of fact.
This is a matter of technique that a manual can settle.
Right: a relation among human beings, like those the authors list, has no final answer.
questions.explain: The authors' examples are relations among people, or between people and the world, about which thinking can always go further. Facts and techniques can be settled.
questions.rule: Relations among people resist a final answer.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: A discussion group debates each month whether it is ever right to lie, and no meeting ends in agreement. A new member decides the meetings are a waste because nothing gets settled. Following the authors' reasoning, what does he miss?
options: The group should vote, so that every meeting reaches a verdict
On such questions, thinking better is the gain, even unsettled
Experts have settled such questions, so the group should ask them
Questions with no final answer are not worth discussing at all
optionExplain: A vote ends a meeting, not a question; it would hide the problem rather than think it through.
Right: where no one can have the last word, the progress lies in thinking better about the question.
The authors say no one has the last word on such matters, experts included.
The authors say the opposite: these are questions you cannot think about too much.
questions.explain: On a question with no last word, progress cannot mean reaching a final answer. It means thinking better: finer distinctions, stronger reasons, a deeper view of what is at stake.
questions.rule: Measure progress on open questions by better thinking.
questions.teaches: By extension, progress on an unsettled question is measured by the quality of one's thinking, such as finer distinctions and better reasons, rather than by arriving at a final answer.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: What Good Books Can Do for Us
questions.q: True or false: A woman torn over how to care for her ageing mother is given a great novel about duty in families. If her question were instead a settled one, such as which care home is nearest, the authors' reason for turning to a great book would no longer apply.
questions.explain: The authors' reason is that great books help you think better about questions with no last word. A question of fact has an answer a map or directory can give, so that reason drops away.
questions.rule: Great books help most where answers run out.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: Roughly what share of the books in the Western tradition do the authors say cannot make enough demands on you to improve your reading?
options: About half of them
About three quarters
About nine in ten
More than 99 per cent
optionExplain: Half sounds like a cautious guess, but the authors put the figure far higher.
Three quarters is closer, but the authors' estimate leaves only a tiny fraction.
Nine in ten is still too low; the authors say fewer than one in a hundred is a good book.
Right: the authors estimate more than 99 per cent.
questions.explain: The authors' figure is more than 99 per cent, and they admit it may seem an overestimate. The card next shows the whole pyramid.
questions.rule: Nearly all books sit at the base.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: Put the authors' classes of books in order from the largest to the smallest.
items: Books for amusement or information only
Good books worth one analytical reading
Inexhaustible books that grow with you
questions.explain: The base holds more than 99 per cent of books; the good books number a few thousand; the inexhaustible ones fewer than a hundred.
questions.rule: Base, good books, great books: each far smaller than the last.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: Ken picks up a breezy bestseller of productivity tips. On the authors' scheme, how should he read it if he wants the tips?
options: Skim it for the tips, since analytical reading would be wasted
Read it analytically, since every book deserves full effort
Read it twice, first fast and then slowly with notes
Avoid it, since books at the base are not worth any reading
optionExplain: Right: books at the base serve amusement or information, and skimming will do.
Full effort on every book spends analytical reading where it cannot repay.
Two readings, one careful, is more than a book of tips can repay.
The authors say such books can be read for amusement or information; they need only a skim.
questions.explain: A tip book sits at the base: it can inform, but it cannot stretch a reader. Skimming gets what it offers.
questions.rule: At the base, skimming will do.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, books at the base of the pyramid are not worth reading in any way.
questions.explain: The authors say they can be read for amusement or information, which may be interesting in many ways. What they cannot do is improve your reading, so they need no analytical reading.
questions.rule: Base books are for skimming, not for nothing.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: A commuter follows dozens of podcasts. Applying the pyramid by analogy, how might she spend her listening time?
options: Give every episode full attention, so that nothing is missed
Play every episode at double speed to fit all of them in
Skim most for news or fun; give full attention to the rare few
Keep only one show, since no other can be worth her time
optionExplain: Equal attention to everything spends her best effort where it cannot repay.
Speed treats all episodes alike; the pyramid sorts them by what they can give.
Right: most material repays a quick pass, and a small share repays full attention.
The pyramid's top is small but not a single item, and the base still has uses.
questions.explain: If only a tiny share of a large stream can repay full attention, the sensible budget is a quick pass for most and real effort for the few that make her think hardest.
questions.rule: Budget attention by what the material can give.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the pyramid's proportions suggest a budget for any large stream of material: since only a tiny share repays full attention, a reader's time is best spent finding that share rather than giving equal time to everything.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: Suppose a reader insists on reading every book he meets analytically, cover to cover. By the authors' scheme, what is the likely result?
options: He becomes the best reader, since practice on anything helps
Most of his effort goes to books that cannot repay it
He finds that most books reward analysis after all
He reads too few base books to stay well informed
optionExplain: Practice helps only on books that demand it; most books do not.
Right: more than 99 per cent of books cannot repay analytical reading, so most of his effort is spent where it yields little.
The authors' estimate says the opposite: only a tiny fraction does.
Reading slowly does cut his range, but the main loss the authors' scheme points to is wasted effort.
questions.explain: Analytical reading is costly. Spent on the base of the pyramid it buys little, and it leaves less time for the few books that deserve it.
questions.rule: Spend analytical effort where it can repay.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, most good books must be read analytically several times before you have got everything out of them.
questions.explain: The authors say a skilful reader can get everything from a good book in one good reading. The card next shows what that means for your shelf.
questions.rule: One good reading can empty a good book.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: According to the authors, the good books in the second class are worth reading analytically ____.
questions.explain: A skilful reader gets everything such a book can give in one good reading, then shelves it.
questions.rule: Good books: one analytical reading.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: Three years after reading a good book on negotiation analytically, Jo needs to recall its point about opening offers for a meeting. What would the authors suggest?
options: Reread the whole book carefully, since her memory has faded
Read a newer book on the subject in place of the old one
Use her margin notes to find and check the passage
Trust her memory, since a good reading lasts for good
optionExplain: A full rereading is more than she needs; the book has already given what it had.
A newer book may help, but she wants this book's point, which her notes can find.
Right: returning to check a point is what notes in a good book are especially valuable for.
Memory fades; the authors expect readers to return to such books to refresh it.
questions.explain: The authors allow returns to check points or refresh memory, and say notes made in the book make those returns easy.
questions.rule: Return through your notes, not a full rereading.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: A teacher read a good book on statistics thoroughly years ago and must now teach a course from it. By the authors' scheme, is going back to it a breach of the read-once advice?
options: No; going back for a new, specific purpose fits their advice
Yes; once shelved, a good book should stay on the shelf
Yes; she should use another book to avoid repeating herself
No; good books always need to be reread in full in the end
optionExplain: Right: the authors expect returns to check points and refresh memory; a new purpose such as teaching is that kind of return.
Read once means no further growth to be had from the book, not a ban on opening it.
Using the book she knows well is no fault; the point is not novelty.
The authors say a good book does not have to be read again; returns are for checking, not rereading in full.
questions.explain: Read once means the book will not change you further. Going back to use it for a new task, checking and refreshing points, fits the returns the authors allow.
questions.rule: Read once is about growth, not about never opening it.
questions.teaches: By extension, the read-once advice concerns needing the book again for growth; going back for a new practical purpose, such as teaching from it, fits the authors' allowance for returns to check points and refresh memory.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: Ravi read a good book quickly last month, skipping its hard chapters, and has shelved it as done. By the authors' account, what is the problem?
options: Good books must be read at least twice in full
He should have skimmed it, since it is a good book
His reading was not complete, so it got less than all
Nothing; shelving after one reading is their advice
optionExplain: The authors say one reading suffices, so the number is not the issue.
Skimming is for the base of the pyramid; good books deserve analytical reading.
Right: the authors' once assumes a skilful reading that gets everything; skipping the hard parts is not that.
The advice is to shelve after one good reading, and his was not one.
questions.explain: One reading is enough only when it is a skilful, complete analytical reading. A quick pass that skips the hard chapters leaves much of the book ungotten.
questions.rule: Once means one good reading, not one pass.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: True or false: The authors' remarks suggest that a reader who made no notes during her one analytical reading of a good book will find later returns to check points harder.
questions.explain: The authors say notes made in such books are especially valuable for returning to check points or refresh memory. Without them, she must search the book again to find what she needs.
questions.rule: Notes make later returns quick.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: According to the authors, how do you know that you will not need to read a good book again?
options: By counting how many notes you made in it
By your own mental reaction to reading it
By checking what critics have said about it
By testing whether you can recite its points
optionExplain: Notes help later returns, but their number does not tell you whether the book has more to give.
Right: the authors say you know it by your own mental reaction to the experience.
Critics may help you judge a book, but the authors place this knowledge in the reader's own reaction.
Reciting points tests memory, not whether the book could still change you.
questions.explain: The authors place the signal inside the reader, in a reaction they call somewhat mysterious. The card next describes the two reactions.
questions.rule: Your own reaction tells you if a book is finished.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, if you know exactly what you missed in a book, you should go back to it right away to find it.
questions.explain: Your obligation as an analytical reader would take you back at once. The sneaking suspicion is different because you cannot say what you missed.
questions.rule: A known gap sends you straight back.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: Sort each reaction after a careful reading by what it suggests.

items.t: You sense it will not change you any further
You keep thinking about it long afterward
You feel grateful but know it has no more to give
You suspect you got less than it holds
You cannot forget it and in the end return
You feel you have grasped it in its entirety

questions.explain: A book milked dry leaves you grateful and finished with it. A book with more in it leaves a suspicion and keeps working on you until you return.
questions.rule: Finished books rest; inexhaustible ones nag.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: Ella read a philosophical dialogue carefully a year ago. She cannot say what she missed, yet it keeps coming back in her thoughts and conversations. What do the authors' remarks suggest?
options: Leave it, since a careful reading gets everything from a book
Read a commentary to learn exactly what she missed first
Ignore the pull, since a feeling is no ground for rereading
Return to it, since this pull is how such books call you back
optionExplain: That holds for most good books, but the authors describe a few that even the best reading cannot exhaust.
A commentary might help later, but the authors describe the reader returning to the book itself.
The authors treat this very feeling as the sign that leads a reader back.
Right: a book you cannot forget, with more you cannot name, is the kind the authors say you return to.
questions.explain: Ella's experience matches the authors' description: a suspicion of more, an inability to forget the book, and finally a return.
questions.rule: A book you cannot forget deserves a return.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: A pianist has learned many pieces thoroughly and set them aside. One sonata, which she played well, keeps sounding in her head years later. By analogy with the authors' account, what does this suggest?
options: The sonata may hold more than she has yet heard in it
She played it badly and must relearn all of its notes
She is bored with the pieces she is working on now
The sonata is simpler than the rest, so easier to recall
optionExplain: Right: like a book you cannot forget, a work that keeps working on you after a good performance may have more in it.
She played it well; the pull is not a sign of a poor first effort.
Boredom elsewhere might explain a passing thought, not a work that keeps returning for years.
Simple pieces are easy to recall but tend to leave, not linger; the pull suggests depth.
questions.explain: The authors' sign is not how hard a work felt but whether it keeps working on you after you did your best with it. The same sign can work in music.
questions.rule: A work that keeps working on you may hold more.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the sign works in any art and does not depend on how hard the work felt: even a piece you performed well can keep working on you if there is more in it than you have grasped.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the sneaking suspicion that a book holds more proves that it belongs to the highest class.
questions.explain: The authors call it a suspicion because that may be all it is at this stage. Only the return shows whether the book really has more to give.
questions.rule: The suspicion is a lead, not a proof.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: According to the authors, why does a good but not great book often seem to hold less when you return to it years later?
options: Its ideas have gone out of date in the meantime
Your memory made it seem better than it was
You read it less carefully the second time
You have grown since you first read it
optionExplain: Dating can happen, but the authors' explanation lies in the reader, not the book.
Memory can flatter, but the authors say the book seems smaller because you are larger.
Carelessness could explain it, but it is not the authors' account.
Right: the book has not changed; your mind is fuller and your understanding greater.
questions.explain: The authors locate the change in the reader. The card next contrasts this with a book that seems to grow.
questions.rule: A smaller book on return means a larger reader.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, when a great book seems to have grown with you, your earlier sound understanding of it turns out to have been false.
questions.explain: The earlier understanding is as true as ever, in the same ways; the book is now true in other ways too.
questions.rule: New readings add to sound old ones.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: Sam rereads a well-made book on habits that impressed him at twenty-five, and at forty finds it thin and obvious. What do the authors' remarks suggest?
options: He has grown, partly through books like it; it gave what it had
He misread it at twenty-five, since a sound reading lasts
It is a great book whose depths he missed this time round
Books on habits lose their value as the research moves on
optionExplain: Right: a good book of the second class seems smaller on return because the reader has grown.
His first reading could have been sound; the change is in him, not in its accuracy.
A great book would seem larger on return, not thinner.
Research may move on, but the authors explain the effect by the reader's growth.
questions.explain: The disappointment of a return is the authors' sign of a book from the middle of the pyramid. Sam has outgrown it.
questions.rule: Disappointment on return marks a book you outgrew.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: Which observations on a return visit point to a book of the highest class? Choose two.
options: You see whole sets of new things in it
It seems smaller than you remembered it
Your old reading holds, and new truths appear
It confirms exactly what you took from it
You finish it faster and with less interest
optionExplain: Right: the authors say you see whole sets of new things.
This is the sign of a good book you have outgrown.
Right: the earlier understanding stays true, and the book is true in still other ways.
Pure confirmation means the book has nothing new for you, the mark of a book milked dry.
Less interest fits a book you have outgrown, not one that grows with you.
questions.explain: A great book seems to grow with you: new things appear while a sound first reading still stands.
questions.rule: A great book adds without cancelling.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: A child learns the rules of chess in an afternoon; twenty years later, as a strong player, she still finds new depth in the game. By analogy with the authors' account of great books, what explains this?
options: The rules have quietly changed over the twenty years
She misunderstood the rules when she first learned them
Strong players imagine depth that is not in the game
The game is open at many levels and stays above her
optionExplain: Chess, like a published book, has not changed; she has.
Her early grasp of the rules was sound and still holds; she now sees more.
The depth she finds is real, as the new things in a great book are.
Right: like a great book, the game is accessible at different levels, so it remains above even a strong player.
questions.explain: The game has not changed, and her first understanding was not wrong. It was so far above her at the start that it still is, which is the authors' explanation for great books.
questions.rule: What is open at many levels keeps lifting you.
questions.teaches: By analogy, anything accessible at different levels, a game, a craft or a field of study, can be entered by a beginner and still exceed an expert, which is why it can keep teaching for a lifetime.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: Suppose Ana had read the great play carelessly at twenty and got its plot wrong. On a return at forty, what would the authors' account lead her to expect?
options: Her old reading would stand, since great books hold every reading
The play would seem smaller, since she has grown since then
Her old reading would need correcting, not only adding to
The play would seem the same, since books do not change
optionExplain: The authors' claim that the earlier reading still stands assumes it was a good reading.
A great book seems larger on return, whatever happened the first time.
Right: only a sound first reading survives; a careless one must be fixed as well as built on.
The book is unchanged, but she is not, so it will not seem the same.
questions.explain: The authors add a condition: assuming you read it well the first time. Change that condition and the old reading no longer stands as it was.
questions.rule: Only a sound first reading survives the return.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the same small set of books will prove inexhaustible for every serious reader.
questions.explain: The authors say readers differ in taste as well as in power of mind, so each reader's set is different and smaller. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Each reader's great books differ.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: According to the authors, why might Newton not be one of your great books? Choose two.
options: You may read him so well that you never need to return
Mathematical systems of the world may not appeal to you
Scientific books cannot rank among the great books
Later physics has made his work no longer worth reading
He wrote only for specialists, not for lay readers
optionExplain: Right: if one reading exhausts what Newton can give you, he is not inexhaustible for you.
Right: taste differs, and his subject may not appeal to you.
The authors suggest Newton may be one of the great books for a reader like Darwin.
The authors do not dismiss Newton on these grounds; their reasons concern the reader.
The great scientific classics were written for lay readers as well.
questions.explain: Both reasons lie in the reader, not in Newton: one reading may exhaust him for you, or his subject may not appeal to you.
questions.rule: A great book must be great for you.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: Mei finds a published list of a hundred great books. On the authors' view, how should she use it?
options: As a syllabus to finish in order before reading anything else
As candidates to try, finding which ones grow with her
As a final verdict on which books she must find great
As a list to avoid, since lists cannot suit one person's taste
optionExplain: A fixed syllabus ignores the authors' point that the great books differ for each reader.
Right: the authors offer their own list as books that have had this value for many, and leave each reader to find her own few.
The authors decline to say any book must be great for a given reader.
The authors do give such a list, as a place to look rather than a verdict.
questions.explain: A list records what has proved great for many readers. Which of its books will keep lifting Mei, only her own reading and returning can show.
questions.rule: Use lists as places to look.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: True or false: On the authors' view, a book a reader rereads every year for comfort, finding nothing new in it, counts for her as one of the inexhaustible books.
questions.explain: The mark of the highest class is that the book seems to grow with you and lifts you again. A comfortable reread that shows nothing new does not meet that test, however much she likes it.
questions.rule: Liking a book is not the test; growing with it is.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: A critic publishes a list of the ten greatest albums. A listener who has bought all ten wants to know which will be his own great albums. By analogy with the authors' view, how can he find out?
options: Trust the critic's ranking, since experts know best
Pick the ones he enjoyed most on the first play
Ask other fans which albums they return to most
Return to them over months and see which keep giving more
optionExplain: A ranking records what lasted for the critic and others; it cannot tell which will last for him.
A first hearing shows only a first hearing; a work may please at once and give nothing more later, or the reverse.
Other fans' returns show what grows for them; taste differs, as Newton differs for different readers.
Right: only returning shows whether a work keeps revealing more for him, so his list builds up over time.
questions.explain: Reputation and first impressions come before the test can be run. Whether a work keeps growing for him shows only when he comes back to it, again and again.
questions.rule: Returning, not reputation, is the test.
questions.teaches: By analogy, neither reputation nor a first impression can pick out your own great works in advance: only returning to a work over time shows whether it keeps revealing more, so a personal short list is built slowly, by rereading.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.q: Suppose a reader reads Newton so well that one reading gives him everything Newton can give. By the authors' account, what follows for that reader?
options: Newton turns out not to be a good book after all
For him, Newton sits with the books read once
He misread Newton, since great books never run dry
He should reread Newton until new things appear
optionExplain: A book read once can still be a good book; it is not inexhaustible for him.
Right: the authors give this very case as one reason Newton may not be one of a reader's great books.
The authors allow that a skilled reader may exhaust Newton.
Forcing new things misses the test; if none appear on return, the book has given what it had for him.
questions.explain: The authors say you may read Newton so well that you do not have to read him again. For that reader, Newton belongs to the second class, though he may be great for others.
questions.rule: A book's class can depend on its reader.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
questions.q: According to the authors, what is the most instructive result of choosing ten books to take to a desert island?
options: A reading list to follow over the coming year
A ranking of the great books from best to worst
What you learn about yourself and your resources
Which books would best survive the island's damp
optionExplain: A list is one product, but the authors call it of minor importance.
Ranking books is not the point; the choice is meant to reveal the chooser.
Right: the authors say what you learn about yourself matters more than the list.
Practical worries about the books miss the point of a thought experiment about the mind.
questions.explain: The authors value the test less for the list than for what it shows about you. The card next explains why.
questions.rule: The island test is about you, not the list.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
questions.q: According to the authors, we all face the challenge of finding the ____ within ourselves to live a good human life.
questions.explain: On the island, or in ordinary life, the challenge is the same: inner resources rather than outside stimulation.
questions.rule: A good life needs resources within.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
questions.q: Asked for her desert-island ten, Rosa lists ten books she has already read once and fully grasped. By the authors' reasoning, what might the exercise show her?
options: She would soon have little left to occupy her mind
She has chosen well, since she knows these books well
She should take the longest books, for the most pages
She should take reference books, for the most facts
optionExplain: Right: books already milked dry have nothing more to give, a poor stock for a lifetime alone.
Familiarity is comfort, but books she has exhausted cannot keep her mind growing.
Length adds pages, not the power to keep lifting her.
Facts run out like amusement; the island needs books that keep giving understanding.
questions.explain: For a long time alone she needs books that can keep teaching her, the inexhaustible kind. Thinking it through shows her what her mind would need.
questions.rule: Choose for the island books that keep giving.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the main value of the desert-island test is the list of books it produces.
questions.explain: The authors call the list probably of minor importance compared with what you learn about yourself when you imagine life without the usual sources of amusement, information and understanding.
questions.rule: The list is a by-product.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
questions.q: A scientist will spend a winter at a remote polar station with no internet. By analogy with the desert-island test, what is planning for that winter most likely to reveal?
options: Which gadgets she most depends on in her work
How well her body copes with cold and darkness
How far she can keep her mind busy unaided
Which colleagues she will get along with best
optionExplain: Gadgets matter to the work, but the analogy is about what feeds her mind.
Physical hardship is real, but the island test concerns mental resources.
Right: like the island, the station strips away outside stimulation and shows what she can supply herself.
Company matters, but the test is what she brings within herself.
questions.explain: Cut off from the usual stream of news and entertainment, the scientist must rely on what her own mind can supply, which is what the island test probes.
questions.rule: Isolation shows what comes from within.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any stretch cut off from ordinary stimulation, a long illness, a remote posting or a lockdown, works like the desert island: it shows how much of a person's mental life comes from within.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
questions.q: Suppose the island had radio and television after all. By the authors' reasoning, how would the test change?
options: It would reveal less, since broadcasts could hide a lack within
It would be harder, since broadcasts would distract from books
It would be no different, since the ten books are the whole point
It would be easier, since broadcasts add understanding to books
optionExplain: Right: the test works by removing outside sources, so adding them back would mask what a person lacks within.
Distraction is a fair worry, but the larger loss is that the test would no longer show what you can supply yourself.
The authors stress the absence of radio and television; it is part of the test, not a detail.
Ease is not the aim; the test is meant to expose what you can do without such sources.
questions.explain: The authors stress that the island has no radio, television or library. That absence is what makes the test reveal a person's inner resources.
questions.rule: The test works by taking outside stimulation away.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the mind, like the body, reaches its peak around the age of thirty and then declines.
questions.explain: The authors draw a sharp contrast: the body peaks around thirty, but the mind can keep growing much longer. The card next explains the contrast and its danger.
questions.rule: The mind can outgrow the body's limits.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
questions.q: The authors warn that the mind can ____, like the muscles, if it is not used.
questions.explain: Atrophy of the mind is the penalty for not taking mental exercise, and the authors call it a terrible one.
questions.rule: An unused mind atrophies.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
questions.q: Four people retire in the same year. Which one do the authors' remarks suggest is most at risk?
options: Beth, who read and studied hard books alongside her work
Carl, who changed careers twice and kept learning each time
Ali, whose demanding job was his only mental exercise
Dina, whose work was light but who read actively each evening
optionExplain: Beth's mind had its own source of activity, which retirement does not remove.
Carl's learning came from changing work, but his habit of learning goes with him.
Right: Ali's mind was kept active from outside, so when the job ends, the demands end too.
Dina's activity never depended on her job, so retirement takes little from it.
questions.explain: The danger the authors describe falls on people whose minds were propped up by their work and who have no resources of their own when it stops.
questions.rule: Minds kept busy only by work are at risk when work ends.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
questions.q: A columnist argues that since busy people who retire tend to die sooner, the secret of a long life is to keep working for as long as possible. By the authors' own reasoning, what is wrong with this?
options: The authors say retirees outlive people who keep working
Their point is inner resources; a job is an outside prop
The authors say mental activity has no effect on health
Their point is the body, which declines after thirty
optionExplain: The authors make no such claim; they describe busy people dying soon after retirement.
Right: the authors say work propped these minds up from outside; the remedy is mental activity of one's own, not endless work.
The authors suggest the reverse, that atrophy of the mind may be a mortal disease.
The body's peak is part of their contrast, but the danger they describe is in the mind.
questions.explain: The columnist keeps the prop and misses the cure. On the authors' account, the people at risk had no inner resources; work only hid the lack until it ended.
questions.rule: The cure is inner activity, not more outside demand.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
questions.q: An airline pilot who flies mostly on autopilot notices that her hand-flying skills are fading. By analogy with the authors' warning about the mind, what is happening?
options: Her skill had a built-in age limit that she has now reached
Autopilot teaches by example, so her skill has improved
A skill left to an outside system weakens from disuse
Skills once learned stay intact whatever happens later
optionExplain: The authors say the mind's growth has no fixed age limit short of senescence; disuse is the likelier cause.
Watching a machine do the work is not exercising the skill yourself.
Right: like an unused mind, a skill handed over to something outside atrophies.
The authors' muscle comparison says the opposite: what is not used wastes away.
questions.explain: The autopilot does the work her skill used to do, so the skill goes unexercised and weakens, as the authors say a mind does when its activity comes only from outside.
questions.rule: Hand a capacity's work away and it fades.
questions.teaches: By analogy, atrophy threatens any capacity whose work is handed over to something outside, a machine or a routine, so the capacity must be exercised on purpose to be kept.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
questions.q: True or false: By the authors' account, a person whose job made few mental demands but who read actively every day would have less to fear from retirement than one whose job was her only mental exercise.
questions.explain: Change where the mind's activity comes from and the risk changes. The daily active reader has resources within herself that retirement does not take away.
questions.rule: Inner resources survive the end of work.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
questions.q: According to the authors, why do sources such as television and radio fail to keep the mind growing?
options: They make us react to outside stimuli in place of our own activity
They give false or slanted information too often to be trusted
They are too difficult for most people to follow closely
They take time that should go to sleep and to exercise
optionExplain: Right: they only seem to make the mind active, because we react to them; the activity is not our own.
Accuracy is a fair concern, but the authors' complaint is about how they work on the mind.
The trouble is the reverse: they ask little of us.
Time spent is a cost, but the authors' point is that their effect on the mind fades.
questions.explain: The authors call such sources artificial props. The card next explains what they mean and what they offer instead.
questions.rule: Reacting to stimuli is not thinking.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
questions.q: Match each phrase with its meaning in the authors' account.
pairs: An outside source that makes the mind seem active
Needed in ever larger doses, with less and less effect
Reading actively, which keeps the mind alive and growing
questions.explain: Props work from outside and wear off like drugs. Active reading supplies activity from within.
