questions.rule: Props wear off; active reading builds.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
questions.q: Lina feels her mind is busy all day because she listens to talk radio and follows the news constantly. On the authors' view, what should she ask herself?
options: Whether the stations she hears are accurate enough to trust
Whether she is following enough different sources at once
Whether any of the activity is her own, or only reaction
Whether she could listen faster and so cover more ground
optionExplain: Accuracy matters for information, but it does not tell her whether her mind is growing.
More sources means more stimuli, the drug-like pattern the authors warn about.
Right: a mind busy reacting to outside stimuli can feel active without doing its own work.
Speed adds stimuli; it does not supply activity of her own.
questions.explain: Feeling busy is the impression props give. The authors' test is whether the activity comes from within her.
questions.rule: Ask where the mind's activity comes from.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the trouble with television and radio is that they contain nothing worth knowing.
questions.explain: The authors treat them as sources of amusement and information. Their objection is that relying on them gives only the impression of an active mind, and their effect wears off.
questions.rule: The trouble is reliance, not content.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
questions.q: A teenager finds that a phone game that thrilled him in March barely holds him by June, though he plays it more. By analogy with the authors' account, what is happening?
options: He has mastered the game, so it now stretches his mind
Like a drug, the stimulus fades as he grows used to it
The game has become worse through its recent updates
He is outgrowing games as his body grows and matures
optionExplain: Mastery would make the game easier, not more stretching; and more play with less effect is the drug pattern.
Right: he needs more of it for less effect, the pattern the authors describe.
Updates could change it, but the pattern of rising use and falling effect points elsewhere.
Bodily growth is not the authors' account of why outside stimuli lose their power.
questions.explain: He plays more and feels less, which is the drug-like pattern the authors ascribe to outside sources of stimulation.
questions.rule: Rising use with falling effect is a warning sign.
questions.teaches: By analogy, any source of stimulation that works by holding attention from outside, such as a game or a feed, tends to show tolerance: the same dose does less, so use rises while the effect falls.

questions.unitTitle: Reading and the Growth of the Mind
questions.section: The Life and Growth of the Mind
questions.q: Suppose someone reads many books, but passively, letting them wash over him as a television programme might. By the authors' reasoning, would this reading keep his mind growing?
options: Yes, since books are better than broadcasts in any manner
Yes, provided he reads enough books every single year
No, since books harm the mind when read for pleasure
Not much, since they credit active reading, not reading as such
optionExplain: The medium is not what the authors credit; they say reading well means reading actively.
Quantity without activity is the widely read but not well read reader.
The authors do not condemn reading for pleasure; they say it does not improve skill.
Right: it is active reading, with the activity coming from the reader, that keeps the mind alive.
questions.explain: The authors define reading well as reading actively. Change the manner to passive and the book becomes one more outside stimulus.
questions.rule: Only active reading keeps the mind growing.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: You want to understand a subject, such as why prices rise, that many books treat in different ways. According to the authors, which level of reading fits that aim best?
options: Inspectional reading of the best-known book
Analytical reading of the most recent book
Syntopical reading of several books on it
Elementary reading done with extra care
optionExplain: Inspection shows what one book covers in a short time; it does not build an understanding of a subject across books.
Analytical reading aims at understanding one book; a subject that runs through many books calls for more.
Right: syntopical reading relates many books to a subject they share and builds an analysis of it.
Elementary reading settles what sentences say; care at that level does not relate books to a subject.
questions.explain: A subject treated by many books calls for syntopical reading, the level that relates them to one another and to the subject. The card next shows how goal and object together pick the level.
questions.rule: A subject across many books calls for syntopical reading.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, analytical reading is hardly ever necessary when your goal is information or entertainment.
questions.explain: The authors say analytical reading is preeminently for the sake of understanding, and hardly ever necessary if your goal is information or entertainment.
questions.rule: Analytical reading serves understanding.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each reading situation to the level it calls for.
pairs: Deciding in fifteen minutes whether a report deserves careful study
Working through a hard essay whose argument you do not yet follow
Building your own account of remote work from six books
Making out the words of a notice in a language you barely know
questions.explain: Sizing up in a set time is inspection; understanding one hard work is analysis; an account of a subject across books is syntopical; trouble with the words themselves is elementary.
questions.rule: Goal and object together pick the level.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Four readers each handle several texts. Which one is reading syntopically in the authors' sense?
options: Ana reads three reviews of a kettle to decide which model to buy
Cleo maps where five sleep books agree and clash, then writes her own view
Ben sets two summaries of one book side by side to see which is fuller
Dev rereads one long book on sleep slowly, checking every single claim
optionExplain: Several texts, but the aim is one fact for a purchase; that is reading for information, not an analysis of a subject.
Right: she relates the books to one another and to their shared subject, and builds an account none of them gives.
Setting summaries side by side is comparison; the authors say mere comparison of texts is not enough.
Careful work on one book is analytical reading; syntopical reading needs many books related to a subject.
questions.explain: Syntopical reading relates many works to a subject and builds an analysis that may be in none of them. The number of texts alone, or comparison alone, does not make it.
questions.rule: Syntopical means relating works to build an account of a subject.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A manager skims a book on negotiation for tips. Halfway through she finds its argument about trust challenges how she leads her team, and she wants to understand it. On the authors' scheme, what should happen to her reading?
options: It should rise to analytical reading, since her goal is now understanding
It should stay a skim, since the level is fixed when a book is first opened
It should jump to syntopical reading, since trust is a subject many books treat
It should stay a skim but slow down, since care is what understanding needs
optionExplain: Right: the level follows the goal, and understanding one book's argument calls for analytical reading.
Nothing fixes the level at the first opening; the authors say the reader's goal decides how he reads.
She may later read other books on trust, but first she must understand this one; syntopical reading rests on that.
A slower skim is still a skim; understanding needs the organised questions of analytical reading, not care alone.
questions.explain: The goal decides the level, so a change of goal changes the reading. Wanting to understand one book's argument calls for analytical reading.
questions.rule: When the goal changes, the level changes.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A student reasons: this report was hard, and I read every line of it with great care, so I read it analytically. What is wrong with his conclusion?
options: Care alone does not make it analytical; organised questioning does
Hard texts cannot be read analytically until they are made easier
Reports are not books, so analytical reading does not apply to them
Analytical reading needs two full readings, so one pass cannot count
optionExplain: Right: the authors mark analytical reading by many, organised questions asked until the work is one's own, not by care alone.
Difficulty is where analytical reading pays most; hard texts are its proper object.
The authors say the four questions apply to anything worth reading, articles and reports included.
The authors allow a practised reader to do all the stages at once; the number of passes is not the test.
questions.explain: Analytical reading is marked by organised questioning aimed at understanding, not by care over each line. A careful reading that asks no such questions may be no more than careful reading for information.
questions.rule: The level is in the questions asked, not in the care taken.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A cook reads four books on Thai cooking, notes where they agree and clash on technique, and drafts her own account of the cuisine's principles. The books are practical and easy. Which level is she using?
options: Inspectional, because practical books need only a quick survey
Analytical, because she studies each book's advice closely
Elementary, because easy books pose no real reading problem
Syntopical, because she builds an account across the books
optionExplain: Practical books often deserve more than a survey, and her work goes beyond what inspection gives.
She does read closely, but her aim is an account of the cuisine across the books, not of one book.
Ease of language says nothing about the level; relating the books is hard work even when each is easy.
Right: relating several works to a shared subject and building one's own analysis is syntopical reading.
questions.explain: What makes a reading syntopical is the aim and the work: relating several works to one subject and building an analysis. The authors stress that it is demanding even when the materials are easy.
questions.rule: The aim, not the kind of book, makes a reading syntopical.
questions.teaches: By extension, syntopical reading is not reserved for theoretical subjects: practical books on one subject, such as cookbooks on one cuisine, can be read syntopically when the aim is an account of the subject across them.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, the typical question at the inspectional level is: what does the sentence say?
questions.explain: That is the elementary question. Inspection asks what the book is about, what kind it is and what its parts are. The card next matches each level's question to its kind of difficulty.
questions.rule: Each level has its own question.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each level of reading to its typical question.
pairs: What is the book about, and what kind is it?
What is said in detail, is it true, and what of it?
How do many works bear on one subject?
questions.explain: The authors give the sentence question to the first level and the what-is-it-about question to the second; the analytical reader asks organised questions of one book, and the syntopical reader relates many books to a subject.
questions.rule: Know each level by its question.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A reader follows every sentence of a philosophy essay but, at the end, cannot say what the author argued or why. At which level does her difficulty lie?
options: Elementary: she needs a dictionary for the hard words
Inspectional: she should have read it faster first
Analytical: she must find the terms, claims and arguments
Syntopical: she must read other essays on the subject first
optionExplain: She follows every sentence, so the words are not her obstacle; a dictionary answers a question she has already answered.
A fast first reading helps, but her trouble is grasping the argument, which is analytical work.
Right: following sentences without grasping the case calls for the interpretive work on terms, propositions and arguments.
Other essays may help later, but she must first understand this one; syntopical reading builds on that.
questions.explain: Her sentences are clear but the argument is not, so the elementary question is answered and the analytical one is not. The remedy lies at that level.
questions.rule: Clear sentences but no grasp of the case: work at the analytical level.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Sort each complaint by the level where the difficulty lies.

items.t: I keep stopping to puzzle out what a sentence says
The grammar of these long sentences defeats me
I cannot tell what kind of book this is
Halfway in, I have no idea where the book is going
I cannot make out the words on this foreign sign
I cannot say what the book's main parts are

questions.explain: Sentence-level trouble is elementary. Not knowing a book's kind, subject or plan is a lack of the surface knowledge that inspection supplies.
questions.rule: Words and sentences are elementary; kind, subject and plan are inspectional.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: If a reader who cannot make out a book's sentences turns to drawing up a careful outline of it instead, the authors' scheme suggests her basic difficulty will be solved.
questions.explain: Levels are cumulative: outlining rests on being able to read the sentences. Work at a higher level cannot remove an obstacle at a lower one.
questions.rule: A higher level cannot fix a lower-level obstacle.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A tutor hears a student say only: I don't get this book. Carrying over the idea of placing a difficulty at its level, what should the tutor do first?
options: Explain the whole book to the student from the beginning
Recommend a good summary or commentary on the book
Tell the student to read the book again more slowly
Ask which level's question the student cannot yet answer
optionExplain: Explaining everything spends effort on parts the student may already grasp, and does the student's work for him.
A summary may help, but the authors advise aids only after one's own best effort, and only for what remains unclear.
Slower reading helps some difficulties; if the trouble is structure or argument, pace is not the cause.
Right: each level's question points to a different kind of help, so locating the difficulty comes first.
questions.explain: Different levels fail for different reasons, so the first step is to find which question the student cannot answer: what the sentences say, what the book is about, what it argues, or how it bears on other works.
questions.rule: Locate the difficulty before choosing the help.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a helper who hears only that a text is hard should first ask which question the reader cannot answer, sentence, subject, argument or relation to other works, because each calls for a different kind of help.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: You have thirty minutes with a long, important book you will discuss tomorrow. Which use of the time do the authors' definitions favour?
options: Reading the first chapter as carefully as possible
Skimming the whole, then reading straight through fast
Reading the publisher's blurb and stopping there
Reading the last chapter closely for the conclusion
optionExplain: Close reading of one chapter leaves the whole book unknown; in limited time the authors favour inspection.
Right: inspection is the best and most complete reading possible in a limited time.
The blurb is one part of a skim, but stopping there wastes most of the time inspection could use.
The ending is worth a look in a skim, but close work on one chapter is not the most complete use of short time.
questions.explain: Inspectional reading is, by the authors' definition, the best reading possible in a limited time. The card next shows how to treat what it yields.
questions.rule: Short time calls for a full inspection.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: According to the authors, analytical reading is the best and most complete reading possible given ____ time.
questions.explain: Inspection is the best reading in a limited time; analytical reading is the best given unlimited time.
questions.rule: Limited time: inspect. Unlimited time: analyze.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: After a twenty-minute inspection of a book on diet, Omar feels sure its central claim is false. On the authors' view, how should he hold that judgment?
options: As settled, since inspection is the best reading in limited time
As worthless, since only analytical reading may form views
As provisional, a hunch to test in a later careful reading
As a reason to drop the book, since doubt ends the reading
optionExplain: Best in limited time is not best possible: inspection answers the first two questions more accurately than the last two.
Inspection helps with all four questions; its hunches are useful if held loosely.
Right: answers about truth that come from inspection are hunches to check, not verdicts.
A doubt may be the very reason to read closely; deciding a book is false needs understanding first.
questions.explain: The authors say inspection answers the first two questions more accurately than the last two. A verdict on truth after twenty minutes is a hunch, to be tested.
questions.rule: Inspectional verdicts are provisional.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which of these can a full inspection of a work reasonably supply? Select all that apply.
options: What kind of work it is
What it is about as a whole
A first idea of how its parts are arranged
A final verdict on whether its arguments hold
A full account of every term and argument
optionExplain: Right: the authors expect an inspection to tell you what kind of book it is.
Right: what the book is about is the typical inspectional question.
Right: structure and parts are surface questions that inspection answers.
Inspection gives hunches about truth; a final verdict needs analytical reading.
Terms and arguments are interpretive work at the analytical level.
questions.explain: Inspection answers the surface questions of kind, subject and structure. Interpretation and verdicts belong to analytical reading.
questions.rule: Inspection gives kind, subject and plan.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Suppose Priya's forty minutes become a free afternoon, and the report turns out to be only twelve pages long. On the authors' scheme, what changes?
options: She can now read it analytically, since time no longer limits her
Nothing; reports should only be inspected, whatever the time
She should inspect it several times over instead of reading closely
She should skip the skim, since a short text needs no surface survey
optionExplain: Right: with time to finish, the best reading of a work she must understand is analytical, begun with a quick skim.
Nothing restricts reports to inspection; the authors apply the rules to anything worth reading.
Repeated inspection stays on the surface; with ample time the deeper level is open to her.
Skimming is always a good idea, the authors say, even for a work you mean to read carefully; here it is brief.
questions.explain: The time limit was what made inspection the best choice. Remove it, and a work she must understand calls for analytical reading, still begun with a skim.
questions.rule: Remove the time limit and the deeper level opens.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A student has half an hour to inspect a long classic poem that scholars spend whole careers on, and feels it is pointless to try. What do the authors say about such a short inspection?
options: It is presumptuous, since great works must be read fully or not at all
It is superficial but not vain: one can learn a lot in half an hour
It is useful only for books of no great importance
It replaces a full reading if the inspection is done well
optionExplain: The authors reject that view: of half an hour on Dante's poem they say it is not presumptuous or vain.
Right: they admit thirty minutes is superficial but say one can learn a lot about the poem in that time.
The authors' own example is one of the greatest poems, so inspection is not only for slight books.
Inspection prepares for a full reading; it does not stand in for it.
questions.explain: In their exercises the authors give half an hour to Dante's Divine Comedy, which scholars have studied for thirty years, admit this is superficial, and still say one can learn a lot about the poem in that time.
questions.rule: A short inspection of a great work is worth doing.
questions.teaches: The authors hold that a short inspection of even a great work is not presumptuous: half an hour on a poem scholars spend decades on is superficial, yet it is not vain and can teach a lot.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, many more books should only be inspected than are worth reading well.
questions.explain: The authors say there are many books worth reading well and a much larger number that should only be inspected. The card next shows how each level decides on the next.
questions.rule: Most books earn only inspection.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Put these rungs in the order a reader climbs them with a book that keeps proving its worth.
items: Skim it systematically
Read it straight through without stopping
Read it analytically
Relate it to other works on its subject
questions.explain: The two inspectional steps come first, then analytical reading of the one book, and only then relating it to other works on its subject, which is syntopical reading.
questions.rule: Skim, read through, analyze, relate.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: After a skim, Sam knows a gardening book's main advice and that it is a practical guide for beginners, which is all he needed. What is the authors' view of stopping there?
options: Stopping is a failure, since every book deserves a full reading
Stopping is fine only if he repeats the skim a second time
Stopping is a failure unless he has judged the book true or false
Stopping is fine, since the skim gave what the book is worth to him
optionExplain: The authors say most books should only be inspected; reading by merit means not every book gets a full reading.
Repeating the skim adds nothing; what matters is whether it gave him what he needed.
Judging truth belongs to analytical reading; a skim that ends the matter need not reach a verdict.
Right: a skim that tells him the book's kind and main advice, all he needs, has done its job.
questions.explain: Reading each book according to its merits includes stopping when a book has given what it can give you. The skim did its job.
questions.rule: Stopping after a skim can be the right call.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A reader opens a 600-page history at page one and plans to read it analytically, slowly, start to finish, without having looked at its contents. Which move do the authors warn against?
options: Reading a history analytically, since history needs only inspection
Committing to full analytical reading without first inspecting it
Reading too slowly, since a history should be read at one fixed speed
Starting at page one, since histories should be read from the end
optionExplain: Histories can deserve analytical reading; the problem is committing before inspecting.
Right: he skips the gate that would tell him whether, and how, the book deserves a full reading.
The authors reject any single right speed; pace is not the error here.
Nothing requires reading from the end; the error is skipping the survey of the whole.
questions.explain: Committing to the slowest, fullest reading of an uninspected book skips the gate that decides whether it deserves that reading, and leaves him learning its layout and its meaning at once.
questions.rule: Inspect before committing to analysis.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: On the authors' view, a book Sam set aside after a skim last year could deserve an analytical reading now that his needs have changed.
questions.explain: A stop is tied to present purposes. When the goal changes, a gate that stayed closed can open.
questions.rule: A stop is not a permanent verdict.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A reader who knows nothing of a long classic poem has ten minutes and only its table of contents to hand. According to the authors' exercises, what can that do for her?
options: Nothing useful, since a contents page is not the work itself
Tell her the poem's truth, since contents state the author's thesis
Serve as a first text to inspect, which may lead her on to the whole
Replace reading the poem, since the contents hold its whole plan
optionExplain: The authors treat a contents page as a text worth inspecting in its own right.
A contents page shows plan and subject, not whether the work is true.
Right: the authors say a careful inspection of a table of contents may lead a reader to inspect the whole work, or even read it analytically.
The contents give a plan to inspect; they do not stand in for the poem.
questions.explain: In their exercises the authors treat the table of contents of the Divine Comedy as though it were a book in itself, and say inspecting it may induce a reader to inspect the whole work, or even read it analytically.
questions.rule: Even a contents page can be the first rung.
questions.teaches: The authors treat a table of contents as a text that can be inspected in its own right: inspecting it alone can be the first rung, leading a reader on to inspect the whole work or even read it analytically.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: The rules of analytical reading fall into three stages, yet the authors ask four basic questions. How do the two fit together?
options: The first stage answers two questions at once
The fourth question has no rules of its own at all
The third stage serves both of the last two questions
The second stage is split between two of the questions
optionExplain: The first stage answers only the first question, what the book is about as a whole.
The fourth question is served by the critical rules, together with the third.
Right: the seven critical rules help answer both is it true and what of it.
The second stage answers one question: what is said in detail, and how.
questions.explain: The authors say the last seven rules help answer the third and fourth questions together. The card next lays out the whole map.
questions.rule: Stage 3 serves questions 3 and 4.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each group of rules to the basic question it helps answer.
pairs: What is the book about as a whole?
What is being said in detail, and how?
Is it true, and what of it?
questions.explain: The structural rules answer the first question, the interpretive rules the second, and the critical rules the last two.
questions.rule: Structure, interpretation, criticism: questions 1, 2, then 3 and 4.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A reader is working on a book about city transport. Sort each of her activities into the stage it belongs to.
groups: Stage 1: what the book is about

items.t: Stating the book's unity in two sentences
Listing the questions the author set out to answer
Naming the kind of book it is
Working out what the author means by congestion
Putting a key claim into her own words
Finding the steps of the main argument

questions.explain: Kind, unity and the author's problems belong to the structural stage. Terms, propositions and arguments belong to interpretation.
questions.rule: Whole and parts first; terms, claims and arguments second.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which of these belongs to the third stage rather than the second?
options: Deciding which of the author's problems he solved
Showing where the author's account is incomplete
Finding the author's arguments in sequences of sentences
Interpreting the author's key words in their context
optionExplain: This is Rule 8, the last step of interpretation: noting what he solved, not yet judging the work.
Right: Rule 15, showing wherein an account is incomplete, is a criterion of criticism.
Finding the arguments is Rule 7, part of interpretation.
Coming to terms is Rule 5, the first rule of interpretation.
questions.explain: Rule 8 records which problems the author solved; Rule 15 judges whether his account falls short. The first is interpretation, the second criticism.
questions.rule: Noting what was solved is interpretation; judging completeness is criticism.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: Because the rules are numbered 1 to 15, the authors expect a practised reader to finish all of Rules 1 to 4 before touching Rule 5.
questions.explain: The numbering shows the logical order. The authors say the practised reader carries out the stages together, though criticism still waits for understanding.
questions.rule: The numbering is logical order, not a schedule.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A study guide sums up: Rules 1 to 4 tell you what the book says in detail, and Rules 5 to 8 tell you whether it is true. What is wrong with this summary?
options: Rules 1 to 4 find the whole, and 5 to 8 interpret rather than judge
Nothing; it matches the authors' account of the first two stages
Rules 1 to 4 judge truth and Rules 5 to 8 find the book's structure
Rules 1 to 4 and 5 to 8 both judge, differing only in strictness
optionExplain: Right: the first stage finds what the book is about as a whole, the second what it says in detail; judging comes only in the third.
The guide shifts each stage one question forward: it skips the whole and gives judging to interpretation.
Neither group judges truth; that is the work of Rules 9 to 15.
Judging belongs only to the third stage; the first two are about understanding.
questions.explain: The guide moves each stage one question forward. Structure answers what the book is about as a whole, interpretation what it says, and only the critical rules judge.
questions.rule: Neither of the first two stages judges.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A listener wants to review a podcast episode that argues for a four-day working week, following the authors' map. Which plan follows it?
options: Decide whether she agrees, then note the parts that support her view, then summarise them
List every fact the host cites, check each one, and stop once the facts have been checked
Note its subject and parts, restate its terms and reasons, then judge it and weigh what follows
Weigh what a four-day week would mean for her, then work out what the host actually claimed
optionExplain: Deciding first reverses the order; the maxims ask for understanding before agreement or disagreement.
Checking facts is one ground of criticism, but it skips structure and interpretation and ignores significance.
Right: it takes the questions in order: the whole, the detail, then truth and significance.
Weighing significance first puts the fourth question before the second; what of it depends on what was said.
questions.explain: The four questions, and the rules that serve them, fit any argued work: first its whole, then its detail, then whether it is true and what follows.
questions.rule: Whole, detail, truth, significance: in that order.
questions.teaches: By extension, the map serves spoken argument as well as print: a talk or podcast episode can be taken through the same four questions, though a listener usually has to note its structure and key terms while hearing it, since speech has no contents page.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: In the authors' order of rules, which of these does a reader need before she can state an author's propositions?
options: A verdict on whether the book is true
The author's key terms and their meanings
A list of the problems the author left unsolved
A comparison with other books on the subject
optionExplain: A verdict comes last, in the third stage; it cannot come before the propositions it judges.
Right: terms are the building blocks of propositions, so coming to terms comes first.
Noting unsolved problems is Rule 8, which follows the propositions and arguments.
Comparing books is extrinsic or syntopical work, not a step before propositions in reading one book.
questions.explain: Propositions are made of terms, so Rule 5 comes before Rule 6. The card next traces what each step hands to the next.
questions.rule: Terms before propositions.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Put these results in the order in which each one feeds the next.
items: The author's key terms
His leading propositions
His arguments
Which of his problems he solved
Whether his account is complete
questions.explain: Terms build propositions, propositions build arguments, the arguments show which problems were solved, and criticism then judges whether the account is complete.
questions.rule: Each result is material for the next.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Mara's criticism of a book on markets keeps attacking claims the author did not make. Looking back along the chain, where is the fault most likely to lie?
options: In her verdict, which needs to be stated more forcefully
In the book's classification, which no later step can affect
In the third stage alone, since criticism has its own rules
In her interpretation of the author's terms and propositions
optionExplain: Force does not help a criticism aimed at the wrong target; the target came from her interpretation.
Classification matters, but the symptom, attacking claims he did not make, points to how she read his terms and propositions.
The critical rules work on the results of interpretation; Rule 9 makes them depend on it.
Right: criticism aims at what interpretation says the author claims, so misfiring criticism points back to stage 2.
questions.explain: Criticism takes its targets from interpretation. If it keeps hitting claims the author did not make, the misreading lies in the terms or propositions she attributed to him.
questions.rule: Misfiring criticism points back to interpretation.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which of these show a later step using an earlier step's result? Select all that apply.
options: Rule 8 checks off the problems that Rule 4 listed
Arguments are built from the author's propositions
Rule 15 measures completeness against the stated problems
Coming to terms depends on first judging the book true
Classifying the book depends on first finding its arguments
optionExplain: Right: the problems found in outlining are what interpretation checks as solved or not.
Right: propositions serve as the premises and conclusions of arguments.
Right: completeness looks back to how the problems were stated and how far they were solved.
Judging comes last; terms are found before any verdict.
Classification comes first and tells you what kind of arguments to expect, not the reverse.
questions.explain: Problems, propositions and stated aims are handed forward to later steps. Verdicts and arguments do not come before terms and classification.
questions.rule: Later steps use earlier results.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: On the authors' view, if a reader has rechecked every earlier step and a book's parts still will not hang together, the fault may lie in the book rather than in her reading.
questions.explain: Rechecking the chain removes the reader's own errors, but a book with no real unity cannot be repaired by the reader. The authors hold that a badly made book can be judged as such.
questions.rule: After rechecking, the fault may be the author's.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Ines states the unity of a gardening book as a guide to growing roses. As she outlines it, chapters on soil, water, pests and planning a whole garden keep refusing to fit under that statement. Which earlier result should she revisit first?
options: Her statement of the book's unity, which looks too narrow
Her list of key terms, which must have been misread
Her verdict on the book, which she should now soften
Her decision to outline, since some books have no parts
optionExplain: Right: parts that will not fit the whole point to a unity stated too narrowly; the outline is correcting it.
Terms come later in the chain; the misfit is between the parts and the whole.
No verdict should exist yet, and softening one would not make the parts fit.
A book worth outlining has parts; the trouble is how she framed the whole.
questions.explain: The outline uses the statement of unity, and parts that will not fit it are evidence against it. Here the later step corrects the earlier one: the book is about gardening as a whole, not only roses.
questions.rule: Parts that will not fit point back to the unity.
questions.teaches: When parts keep refusing to fit an outline, the statement of unity is the first suspect: the outline is meant to show how the parts make up the whole, so a misfit is evidence that the unity was framed too narrowly.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, it is generally best to read a scholar's introduction to a classic before reading the classic itself.
questions.explain: The authors advise reading someone else's commentary, scholarly introductions included, only after the book. The card next places aids in the whole sequence.
questions.rule: Others' commentary comes after the book.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Put these steps for reading one hard book in the order the authors give.
items: Skim it for kind and structure
Read it through without stopping at hard places
Outline and interpret it closely
Consult aids for what still resists you
State and support your verdict
questions.explain: Inspection comes first in its two steps, then analytical reading, then outside help for what remains unclear, and the verdict last.
questions.rule: Inspect, read through, analyze, seek help, judge.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Halfway through a first straight-through reading of a book on climate economics, Tom meets a page of equations he cannot follow. What does the sequence advise?
options: Stop and look up every unfamiliar symbol before going on
Read on past it and come back to it in the closer reading
Find a commentary at once that explains the equations
Abandon the book, since it is beyond his present level
optionExplain: Stopping to look things up on the first reading is what the authors warn against; it costs the sense of the whole.
Right: on the first reading, pass over what you do not understand; the closer reading will return to it.
Aids come after your own best effort, and a first reading is not yet that effort.
A book that is at first beyond you is the kind that can raise your understanding; difficulty is no reason to stop.
questions.explain: The first reading passes over what it cannot yet grasp, so that the whole is seen. Hard passages wait for the closer reading, and aids wait until after that.
questions.rule: On the first pass, read on.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which of these should come before reading the book itself?
options: The author's own preface to the book
A critic's essay on the book's main argument
A teacher's notes explaining the argument
A review that sums up the book's thesis
optionExplain: Right: the author's own preface belongs to the book and is read first; others' commentary comes after.
A critic's essay is commentary; read first, it tends to make you see only the critic's points.
A teacher's explanation is outside help; the authors advise doing your own best work first.
A review summing up the thesis is commentary, best read after your own reading.
questions.explain: The author's preface is part of the book. Other people's essays, notes and reviews are extrinsic aids that come after your own reading.
questions.rule: The author's preface first; others' commentary after.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, a reader who consistently does all she can with a book before seeking help will find she needs less and less outside help.
questions.explain: The authors say that if you act consistently on the principle of doing all you can by yourself first, you will need less and less outside help.
questions.rule: Self-reliance shrinks the need for aids.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A pianist learning a hard sonata wants to follow the spirit of the reading sequence. Which plan fits it best?
options: Listen to three famous recordings first, then imitate the one she likes
Perfect each bar in order from the first, not moving on until it is right
Decide her interpretation first, then practise only the passages that fit it
Play it through, work the hard bars, then ask about what still eludes her
optionExplain: Starting from others' versions is like reading commentary first: it tends to fix her on their choices.
Refusing to move on until each bar is right is the stop-at-every-difficulty habit the first reading avoids.
Deciding the interpretation first puts the verdict before understanding the work.
Right: a whole first pass, focused work, then outside help for what remains follows the sequence.
questions.explain: The sequence carries over: take in the whole, work at the difficulties yourself, seek help for what still resists, and form a view last.
questions.rule: Whole first, own work next, help after, verdict last.
questions.teaches: By analogy, the sequence fits learning any complex work, such as a piece of music: a rough pass for the whole, then focused work on the hard parts, then a teacher's help for what still resists, with the interpretation settled last.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: According to the authors, do the fifteen rules of analytical reading apply unchanged to novels, plays and poems?
options: Yes, since every book has terms, propositions and arguments
No, a parallel set built on the same four questions applies
No, imaginative works are read for pleasure with no rules at all
Yes, though only the critical rules are needed for a story
optionExplain: Stories do not proceed by terms, propositions and arguments; their content is not logical.
Right: the authors give parallel rules for imaginative literature, developed from the same four questions.
The authors reject that view: imaginative literature has its own rules, which also enrich the pleasure.
Criticism of stories rests on different premises, and the parallel rules cover structure and interpretation too.
questions.explain: The authors say the fifteen rules do not apply to fiction and poetry, but a parallel set, developed from the same four questions, does. The card next shows how classifying selects the rules.
questions.rule: Stories take parallel rules.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which of these are adaptations or parallels the authors' point names? Select all that apply.
options: Practical book: find what he wants you to do
Story: find the unity of its plot
Story: appreciate before you criticize
Practical book: skip outlining its parts
History: disregard its subject and its limits
Story: hunt for its key propositions
optionExplain: Right: the adapted Rule 4 for practical books asks what the author wants you to do.
Right: the parallel structural rule for fiction asks for the unity of the plot.
Right: the parallel critical maxim asks you to appreciate before you criticize.
A practical book is still expository, so its structure must still be outlined.
The card has you note a history's subject and limits, not disregard them.
Stories do not proceed by propositions; the parallel rules look to characters and incidents instead.
questions.explain: The practical adaptation sharpens Rules 4 and 8; the parallel rules for stories look to plot, characters and appreciation. Nothing on the card drops outlining or a history's limits.
questions.rule: Adapt for practical books; use parallels for stories.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A reader treats a short lyric poem like an essay, hunting for its thesis and its arguments. On the authors' view, what has she missed?
options: A lyric conveys a single emotional experience, not an argument
A lyric must be judged true or false like an expository claim
A lyric needs no reading rules, so any approach serves equally
A lyric keeps its arguments in its title, not in its lines
optionExplain: Right: a lyric tells its story mainly through a single emotional experience; it does not proceed by propositions and arguments.
Poetical truth is of another kind; a poem is not judged like a claim in a treatise.
The authors give parallel rules for imaginative works; it is not that anything goes.
A title can be a clue to a poem, but the poem does not hold arguments to extract.
questions.explain: Classifying the poem as a lyric would have switched her to the parallel rules, which look for its emotional experience and its unity, not a thesis.
questions.rule: A lyric is read for its experience, not an argument.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Sort each reading move by the kind of work it suits.

items.t: Find the author's key terms
Follow the unfolding of the plot
Get to know the characters
Construct the arguments from sequences of sentences
Appreciate what the author tried to make you feel before criticizing
Show wherein the author is misinformed

questions.explain: Terms, arguments and the criteria of criticism belong to expository works. Plot, characters and appreciation belong to the parallel rules for imaginative works.
questions.rule: Terms and arguments for exposition; plot and characters for stories.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A novel turns, in its last chapters, into an extended argument about how cities should be governed. What do the authors suggest?
options: Keep reading it strictly as a story, since Rule 1 is settled once
Reset the switch for those chapters and weigh the argument as such
Stop classifying, since a mixed work cannot be read by any rules
Treat the whole novel as a treatise, since it ends in an argument
optionExplain: A classification is a first guess; when the work shifts, the authors' advice on mixed books is to notice how it proceeds at that point.
Right: by extension of the authors' advice on mixed books, the reading shifts when the work does.
Mixed works still repay classifying, with more care; giving up is not the advice.
An argumentative ending does not turn the whole story into a treatise; the earlier chapters remain a story.
questions.explain: By extension of the authors' advice on mixed books, notice how the work is proceeding at each point. Where it argues, read the argument as argument; where it tells a story, read the story.
questions.rule: When the work shifts kind, shift the reading.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A reader picks up a collection of essays expecting a novel, looks for characters and a plot, and decides the book has no unity. Carrying over the idea of the switch, what is the better conclusion?
options: The book is badly made, since good books have a plot
The reader should look harder for the hidden characters
The rules failing is a sign to go back and reclassify
The essays should be judged as a weak kind of fiction
optionExplain: Expository books have unity without a plot; the missing plot says nothing about quality.
Looking harder with the wrong rules will not find what the book does not contain.
Right: when the rules being applied keep finding nothing, the classification is the first thing to recheck.
Judging essays as fiction carries the misclassification into criticism.
questions.explain: When the later rules find nothing to grip, the likely fault is the first decision. Essays read by the rules for stories seem shapeless because their unity lies in a thesis, not a plot.
questions.rule: Rules that find nothing point back to Rule 1.
questions.teaches: By extension, a misclassification usually shows itself later: when the rules you are applying keep finding nothing to work on, such as a plot in a book of essays or arguments in a lyric, go back and recheck Rule 1.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: According to the authors, which of the four questions changes most when you read a practical book rather than a theoretical one?
options: What is the book about as a whole?
What is being said in detail, and how?
Is the book true, in whole or part?
What of it?
optionExplain: The authors say the first question does not change very much; the book must still be outlined.
The second question changes little; you still find terms, propositions and arguments.
The third changes somewhat more, to whether the ends and means are right, but not the most.
Right: agreeing with a practical book implies action, so what of it changes most of all.
questions.explain: For a practical book the authors say the first two questions change little, the third somewhat more, and the fourth most, because agreement implies action. The card next shows where other kinds put the weight.
questions.rule: For practical books, what of it changes most.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each kind of book to the one of the four questions that, according to the authors, needs special care for that kind.
pairs: What of it: agreement commits you to act
What it is about: its exact subject and limits
What kind of book: which strands it mixes
What is said in detail: following the inductive arguments needs the reported evidence
questions.explain: Each kind keeps all four questions but loads one of them: action for practical books, scope for histories, classification for social science, and, for science, following the evidence behind its inductive arguments.
questions.rule: Each kind loads a different question.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A reader finishes a history of the Spanish Civil War and complains that it barely mentions Spanish painting of the period. What should she check before treating this as a fault?
options: Whether the author set out to cover the arts at all
Whether other histories mention painting more often
Whether the author's prose style is pleasant to read
Whether the book's index lists painters by name
optionExplain: Right: a history is judged by what it set out to do, so its subject and limits come first.
Other histories may have other subjects; their coverage does not set this book's task.
Style is beside the point; the question is the book's chosen scope.
The index may show what is covered, but the fair test is the scope the author chose.
questions.explain: With a history, the first question carries extra weight: what it covers and what it does not. The authors say an author cannot be blamed for not doing what he did not try to do.
questions.rule: Know a history's limits before criticizing its omissions.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which statements match the authors' account of where the weight falls for each kind of book? Select all that apply.
options: Social science: classifying is hardest and most important
Science book: terms are usually easy to spot
Practical book: the fourth question changes most
Story: the fourth question demands a plan of action
History: scope need not be noted before criticism
optionExplain: Right: the authors call naming a social science book's strands the reader's first and most important task.
Right: scientific authors usually make their terms and propositions easy to find.
Right: agreement with a practical book implies action, so the fourth question changes most.
For a story the fourth question, strictly speaking, asks nothing of the reader.
A history's scope is exactly what must be known before criticizing it.
questions.explain: Classification weighs most in social science, terms are easiest in science, and what of it changes most for practical books. Stories ask no action, and histories need their scope noted first.
questions.rule: Know which question each kind loads.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A reader is fully convinced by a practical book on saving energy at home: its ends seem right and its means likely to work. On the authors' view, what follows?
options: Nothing more, since agreement is only a change of mind
He should act as the book recommends, as agreement implies
He should find a second book before changing anything
He should judge its style, since its truth is now settled
optionExplain: That holds for theoretical books, where mental adjustment is enough; practical agreement goes further.
Right: the authors find it hard to see how one can accept both ends and means and refuse to act.
Other books can help judge, but he has already accepted ends and means; delay is not what agreement implies.
Style is beside the point; accepting ends and means points to action.
questions.explain: Agreeing with both the ends and the means of a practical book commits the reader to act. That is why the fourth question changes most for this kind.
questions.rule: Practical agreement implies action.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A reader reasons: practical books barely change the first question, so I can skip outlining this manual and go straight to its instructions. What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: Practical books need only their theory read, not their instructions
Manuals should be read as stories, so outlining does not apply
Nothing; outlining matters only for theoretical books
Changing little is not vanishing: the book still needs outlining
optionExplain: The instructions are what a practical book is for; skipping them would miss what it wants you to do.
A manual is expository, not a story; the parallel rules for fiction do not apply.
The authors say a practical book is expository, so it is still necessary to outline its structure.
Right: the first question changes little because the outline is still required, not because it is dropped.
questions.explain: The weights are emphases, not exemptions. The authors say a practical book is expository, so answering the first question still means outlining its structure.
questions.rule: Emphasis is not exemption.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A traveller holds a guidebook to Rome and a history of ancient Rome. Carrying over the authors' view of how each kind of book shifts the weight of the four questions, where should each reading put its weight?
options: On scope for both, since they share the subject of Rome
On action for both, since travel is a practical matter
On action for the guidebook and on scope for the history
On beauty for both, since Rome is mainly an artistic subject
optionExplain: A shared subject does not make a shared kind; the guidebook is practical and the history theoretical.
The history is not practical because the reader is travelling; it reports what happened.
Right: the guidebook is pressed on what it wants you to do; the history first on what it covers.
Neither book is imaginative literature; beauty is the measure for stories and poems, not these.
questions.explain: The kind of book, not its subject, sets the weight. A guidebook is practical, so its weight falls on what it wants you to do; a history's falls first on its exact scope.
questions.rule: Kind, not subject, sets the weight.
questions.teaches: By extension, two books on one subject can call for different weights: the subject does not fix the kind, so a guidebook and a history of the same city are pressed on different questions.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: According to the authors, an analytical reading is not satisfactorily accomplished until you have some idea of the book's truth and its significance.
questions.explain: The authors say an analytical reading has not been accomplished satisfactorily until you can answer the last two questions, if only in your own scheme of things. The card next lists what a finished reading holds.
questions.rule: Finished means all four questions answered.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Sort each item of a finished record by the part of the reading that produces it.

items.t: An outline of the major parts
The leading propositions in your own words
Which problems the author solved
Where the author is misinformed
Whether you agree, disagree or suspend judgment
Where the account is incomplete

questions.explain: Outline, propositions and solved problems record understanding. Points of criticism and the verdict record judgment.
questions.rule: The record has an understanding part and a judging part.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Zara says she has finished a book on urban design: she agrees with it wholeheartedly, but when asked she cannot say what its main argument is. What do the authors say?
options: Her reading is finished, since agreement shows understanding
Her reading is finished, since only disagreement needs reasons
Her reading is unfinished only if she later changes her mind
Her reading is unfinished: agreement needs a restatable message
optionExplain: Agreeing with what you cannot state is the empty agreement the authors found in many students; it does not show understanding.
Rule 11 asks for good reasons for any critical judgment, agreement included.
Changing her mind later is not the test; being able to state the argument now is.
Right: a verdict, even agreement, is premature until she can restate the book's message in her own words.
questions.explain: Rule 9 applies to agreement as much as to disagreement: say I understand before you agree. If she cannot restate the argument, the second stage is unfinished and the verdict premature.
questions.rule: No verdict, not even agreement, before you can restate.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Two readers finish a hard book. Ravi agrees, disagrees and suspends judgment on different parts, giving reasons for each. Sue agrees with the whole because she likes the author. Which reading do the authors count as finished?
options: Ravi's, since a reasoned, part-by-part verdict is what is asked
Sue's, since a single overall verdict is clearer than a mixed one
Both, since any verdict at all completes the third stage
Neither, since a finished reading must reach one final verdict
optionExplain: Right: verdicts may differ part by part, as long as each rests on reasons.
Liking the author is not a reason about the book; a clear verdict without grounds is opinion, not criticism.
Rule 11 asks for good reasons; a verdict from liking does not meet it.
The authors allow agreement in part and suspended judgment; one overall verdict is not required.
questions.explain: The verdict of a finished reading can be mixed, and must be reasoned. Agreement grounded in liking the author shows personal opinion, not judgment.
questions.rule: A finished verdict is reasoned, and may be mixed.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: On the authors' view, a reader who suspends judgment on a book's main conclusion, and gives her reasons, can still count the reading as finished.
questions.explain: Suspending judgment is one of the three positions a critic can take. With reasons given, it is a proper result of the third stage, not a gap in it.
questions.rule: A reasoned suspension is a finished verdict.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A journal editor asks a reviewer for a report on a research paper. Carrying over the authors' point, which report has the shape of a finished reading?
options: A list of every flaw found, ranked from worst to least serious
A verdict of accept or reject, with the reviewer's overall feel
A fair summary, reasoned criticism, then what the paper adds
A rewrite of the paper's argument the way the reviewer would make it
optionExplain: Flaws without a fair statement of what the paper says risk attacking claims it never made.
A verdict without restatement or reasons skips both understanding and the grounds for judgment.
Right: it restates the paper fairly, judges it with reasons, and says what it adds.
Rewriting the argument replaces the author's case with the reviewer's, so the paper itself is never judged.
questions.explain: A finished reading moves from fair restatement to reasoned judgment to significance. A report built the same way judges the paper actually written.
questions.rule: Restate, judge with reasons, then weigh.
questions.teaches: By analogy, a good referee's report on a paper has the shape of a finished reading: a summary of what the paper sets out to do and argues, fair enough for its authors to recognise, then reasoned criticism, then an assessment of what it adds.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: According to the authors, what is the aim of a project of syntopical reading?
options: Final answers to the questions the project raises
An objective analysis of the discussion itself
A ranking of the books from most to least reliable
A summary of each book read, set side by side
optionExplain: The authors say outright that final answers are not the aim of a syntopical project.
Right: the aim is a detached, dialectically objective analysis of the discussion.
Ranking books takes sides; the syntopical reader tries to look at all sides and take none.
Summaries side by side are comparison; the authors ask for an analysis of the discussion.
questions.explain: The authors say the aim is not final answers but an objective analysis of the discussion. The card next sets out the finish line at each level.
questions.rule: Syntopical reading ends in an objective analysis, not answers.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each level to the notes that record a finished reading at that level.
pairs: Structural notes on the contents or title page
Conceptual notes on the author's ideas and your own
Dialectical notes on the shape of the discussion
questions.explain: The authors tie the kind of note to the level: structure for inspection, concepts for analysis, the shape of the discussion for syntopical reading.
questions.rule: Structural, conceptual, dialectical.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: After twenty minutes with a book on negotiation, Lina can say it is a practical guide, that it argues for knowing your walk-away point, and that it has three parts. She decides it deserves no more. Is her inspection finished?
options: No, she has not yet judged whether its advice is true
No, an inspection is finished only when the book is read
Yes, she has its kind, subject, order and a decision
Yes, but only once she also writes a conceptual note
optionExplain: Judging truth belongs to the analytical finish line, not the inspectional one.
Inspection is limited by time; it can be finished without reading every page.
Right: kind, subject, structure and a decision about going further complete an inspection.
Conceptual notes belong to analytical reading; an inspection's record is structural.
questions.explain: An inspection's finish line is the surface answers and a decision. Her decision to stop is itself a proper result.
questions.rule: Inspection ends with kind, subject, order and a decision.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Sort each result by the level whose finished reading it marks.

items.t: A reasoned verdict on one book's truth
What one book means for your own view
One author's terms and arguments restated
The questions on a subject set in a defensible order
Several authors' answers grouped into issues, with texts cited
A report that takes no side on the disputed issues

questions.explain: An analytical reading ends with one book understood and judged. A syntopical reading ends with an ordered, objective map of a discussion across many books.
questions.rule: One book judged, or a discussion mapped.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: If a syntopical report on a disputed question ended by arguing that one side is right, the authors would say it had stopped being syntopical.
questions.explain: The authors say such a report would be dogmatic, not dialectical: it would become one more voice in the discussion and lose its detached, objective character.
questions.rule: Taking a side ends the syntopical stance.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A journalist has spent a week reading many works on a long-disputed question, and is discouraged that her map of the debate keeps changing. On the authors' account, what should she expect?
options: A settled map within a week, or else her method is wrong
A fixed map from the start, since the books set the questions
No map at all, since disputed questions cannot be analyzed
Many false starts, since such work can take months or years
optionExplain: The authors say such understanding is not attained in a day; a week is no measure of method.
The syntopical reader frames the questions herself; the books do not hand them over ready-made.
The authors hold that disputed discussions can be analyzed; that is what syntopical reading does.
Right: the authors say it often takes months or years, with many false starts and tentative analyses.
questions.explain: In their appendix the authors say syntopical understanding often takes months or years to reach, with many false starts and tentative organizations of the discussion along the way.
questions.rule: Syntopical maps are revised many times.
questions.teaches: The authors say a syntopical understanding of an important question is not reached in a day: it often takes months or years, with many false starts and tentative organizations of the discussion before light is thrown on it.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: When the authors apply Rule 1 to How to Read a Book itself, how do they classify it?
options: As a theoretical book about how the mind learns
As a work of social science on literacy
As a practical book
As a history of education and of reading
optionExplain: The book teaches a skill to be practised, not knowledge of how minds work for its own sake.
It draws on education, but its aim is to help you read better, which makes it practical.
Right: they say they have not concealed that it is a practical book, so Rule 1 is easy to apply.
It touches on the history of reading instruction, but that is not its main business.
questions.explain: The authors say they have not concealed that this is a practical book, so applying the first rule to it is easy. The card next follows their hints through the other rules.
questions.rule: How to Read a Book is a practical book.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which of these do the authors' own hints say about their book? Select all that apply.
options: It is a practical book
Its account of syntopical reading is incomplete
Its problem is not teaching reading in general
Its terms are listed for you in the appendix
It solves every reading problem readers face
optionExplain: Right: they classify it as practical and call Rule 1 easy here.
Right: they say they did not say all that could be said about syntopical reading.
Right: they warn that the problem is not teaching people to read in general.
They decline to list their terms, propositions or arguments; that work is left to the reader.
They deny solving every problem; many involve individual differences no general book can meet.
questions.explain: The hints classify the book, admit incompleteness on syntopical reading, and narrow its problem. They refuse to list terms and deny solving every problem.
questions.rule: The authors give hints, not answers.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A reader writes, for Rule 4: the book's problem is how to teach people to read. On the authors' hints, what is wrong with this statement?
options: Too narrow: its problem is really how to live a whole good life
Nothing: teaching people to read in general is exactly its problem
Rule 4 does not apply to practical books such as this one
Too broad: its problem is reading in a certain way, for certain goals
optionExplain: The book touches on the growth of the mind, but its problem is about reading, not living in general.
The authors reject this: nothing in the book would be of much help to a first- or second-grade teacher.
Rule 4 applies to every expository book; for practical books it becomes even more important.
Right: they say the problem is reading in a certain way, with certain goals, to be described precisely.
questions.explain: The authors warn that their problem is not teaching people to read in general. It concerns reading in a certain way and with certain goals, which a good Rule 4 statement must describe.
questions.rule: State the problem precisely, not generally.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A reviewer complains that How to Read a Book is incomplete because it gives first-grade teachers little help with teaching children to decode words. What is the flaw in this criticism?
options: It judges the book by a task it never set
It is a fair charge the authors failed to foresee
It confuses incompleteness with being misinformed
It should have been made before reading the book
optionExplain: Right: incompleteness is measured against the book's chosen task, and teaching beginners was not it.
The authors foresaw it: they say the book would not be of much help to a first- or second-grade teacher.
Misinformed means asserting what is false; the complaint is about scope, not a false claim.
Criticism comes after understanding, not before; timing is not the flaw here.
questions.explain: A charge of incompleteness must name what the author's own task required and he left out. The authors say outright that helping first-grade teachers was not their task.
questions.rule: Judge completeness against the task the book set.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: Following the authors' hints, a reader who largely agrees with How to Read a Book can still fairly judge its account incomplete in places.
questions.explain: The authors themselves name gaps, on elementary and syntopical reading. Failing the first three criteria you must agree at least in part, but the fourth lets you judge the account incomplete.
questions.rule: Agreement and a charge of incompleteness can go together.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A student asks her teacher for model answers to the four questions about a set text before she has tried them herself. Carrying over the authors' stance in their appendix, what should she be told?
options: Model answers are best read first, then checked against the text
The answers lie in the book, and finding them is her own work
The four questions have no answers for a set text, only opinions
Only a teacher can say whether her answers are right or wrong
optionExplain: Reading answers first is like reading commentary first: it tends to fix her on someone else's reading.

questions.explain: The authors refuse to supply answers to the four questions about their own book: the answers are in the book, and analytical reading is work the reader must do alone.
questions.rule: The answers are in the book; the work is yours.
questions.teaches: The authors give no answers to the four questions about their own book: the answers are in the book itself, and analytical reading is lonely work, in which the reader has no resource but his own thought.
